National Football League Game Officials Self-Rating of Knowledge in Neuro-Ophthalmic Principles and Practice: A Pilot Program to Improve Precision and Accuracy of Game Official Calls. J Neuroophthalmol. 2024;00:1-6. doi:10.1097/WNO.0000000000002129
abstract: PDF extraction note: the source filename names an NFL Dynamic Kickoff injury-incidence paper, but the readable PDF content is a Journal of Neuro-Ophthalmology article on NFL game officials' neuro-ophthalmic education. The study tested whether a structured curriculum on neuro-ophthalmic principles improved NFL officials' self-rated knowledge and likelihood of using terms relevant to play-calling. At the 2023 NFL Official Training Camp, 142 officials, replay officials, and officiating staff completed pre- and postlecture feedback. Self-rated understanding of saccades, pursuit, vestibulo-ocular reflex, selective attention deficit, dynamic visual acuity, and visual field improved significantly, and officials rated the curriculum and game-video examples as highly relevant.
tldr: The PDF appears mislabeled; the extracted study supports structured perceptual-decision training for NFL officials, not a Dynamic Kickoff injury analysis.
methods: A formal neuro-ophthalmic principles curriculum was delivered in person to 121 NFL game officials, 17 replay officials, and 4 officiating staff at NFL Official Training Camp in Irving, Texas on September 8-9, 2023. Participants completed anonymous hard-copy Likert feedback forms before and after the lecture/videos. Paired two-tailed t tests compared pre- and postintervention self-rated knowledge and likelihood of using neuro-ophthalmic terms.
findings: All 142 participants completed the main survey items. Understanding of saccade, pursuit, and vestibulo-ocular reflex rose from roughly 2.6-2.7 to 7.9-8.0 on a 10-point scale. Understanding of selective attention deficit, dynamic visual acuity, and visual field rose to 7.7, and likelihood of using oculomotor terms rose from 2.9 to 7.5. Curriculum and video relevance were rated about 8.8/10, with strong interest in more content.
limitations: This was a self-rating education study, not an objective test of officiating accuracy, injury outcomes, or player safety. The available NFL official cohort was small, some participants may have completed a prior pilot curriculum, anonymous surveys prevented removing those individuals, and one back-page question had lower response.
practicalImplications: For Baylor football staff, the transferable point is that shared vocabulary and video-based perceptual training may improve real-time decision quality. Similar concepts could be applied to sideline spotting, practice safety observation, return-to-play monitoring, and staff communication around line of sight, visual field, attention, and movement constraints.
athleteDev: No player-development outcomes were studied. Indirectly, better staff and official decision training can support safer environments by improving detection, communication, and positioning decisions during chaotic football actions.
rtp: No RTP data or player injury management protocol was provided in the extracted PDF content.

citation: Sirisena D, Walter J, Probert J. National Football League concussion lawsuit: what it means for other sports and observations from Singapore Rugby. Br J Sports Med. 2017;51:696-697. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2016-096565
abstract: This editorial uses the NFL concussion lawsuit and Singapore Rugby experience to discuss medicolegal and practical risks for sports that do not detect, communicate, and manage concussion adequately. The authors note the NFL settlement may set precedent for other sports, while media scrutiny increases pressure on sideline clinicians. They contrast regulated approaches such as World Rugby's Head Injury Assessment and pitchside medical training with challenges in global soccer and multilingual settings, including Head Injury Assessment translation problems in Singapore. They call for legislation, stakeholder education, clinical guidance, and evidence-based best practice across sports.
tldr: Concussion management is a governance, education, communication, and legal-risk issue; standardized protocols and stakeholder education protect athletes and staff.
methods: This was an editorial commentary rather than an empirical study. The authors synthesized legal context from the NFL concussion settlement, published concussion-incidence comparisons across youth sports, World Rugby policy experience, FIFA implementation challenges, and local observations from Singapore Rugby.
findings: The NFL lawsuit highlighted the risk of inadequate concussion warning, recognition, and management. Rugby has adopted more explicit head injury substitution, HIA tools, and medical training, while soccer faces implementation challenges across levels and countries. Singapore Rugby experience showed that language and translation can weaken assessment quality and communication of seriousness.
limitations: The article is opinion/commentary and does not provide new outcome data, effect sizes, or validated intervention testing. Its observations may not generalize across all sports systems, and it predates later consensus updates and protocol changes.
practicalImplications: For Baylor football, the message is to keep concussion education current and documented for athletes, coaches, families, and staff; use standardized sideline pathways; and remove ambiguity from who can evaluate, who can clear, and how symptoms are communicated. Translation, health-literacy, and cultural barriers should be planned for before the season.
athleteDev: Athlete development should include repeated concussion literacy: symptom reporting, teammate reporting, why removal is protective, and why hiding symptoms threatens long-term availability. Coaches and performance staff need the same language so competitive pressure does not dilute clinical decisions.
rtp: No detailed RTP protocol is tested. The editorial supports cautious removal and qualified medical management after suspected concussion, with return decisions handled by clinicians using current evidence-based guidelines rather than game context or media pressure.

citation: Ellenbogen RG, Batjer H, Cardenas J, Berger M, Bailes J, Pieroth E, et al. National Football League Head, Neck and Spine Committee's Concussion Diagnosis and Management Protocol: 2017-18 season. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52:894-902. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2018-099203
abstract: This consensus statement describes the NFL Head, Neck and Spine Committee's 2017-18 concussion diagnosis and management protocol and its clinical rationale. The protocol synthesizes contemporary concussion science, including the Berlin consensus, and adapts it to NFL practice and game-day realities. It details preseason education and baseline assessment, sideline and locker-room evaluation, roles for team physicians, unaffiliated neurotrauma consultants, athletic trainer spotters, medical timeouts, serial follow-up, documentation, quality assurance, and graduated return to participation with independent neurological consultant confirmation before full return.
tldr: The NFL protocol emphasizes immediate recognition, removal when indicated, independent consultation, serial assessment, documented checklists, and a staged no-symptom progression before full football clearance.
methods: This was a consensus/protocol article, not a trial. The NFL Head, Neck and Spine Committee synthesized available evidence and international consensus guidance, then described the operational protocol used at the end of the 2017-18 NFL season, including game-day roles, checklist requirements, and return-to-participation steps.
findings: Key components include preseason education and baseline data, sideline screening for observed or reported signs, no-go criteria requiring removal to the locker room, UNC involvement as an independent co-pilot, ATC spotters with video review and medical-timeout authority, full locker-room concussion assessment, Madden Rule protections after diagnosis, next-day reassessment, mandatory game-day checklist documentation, and quality review of possible violations.
limitations: Concussion remains a clinical diagnosis; the article notes no validated real-time biomarker, imaging tool, or biomechanical technology can unequivocally diagnose sport-related concussion. Brief exams can be limited by practice effects and may appear normal despite concussion, so clinician familiarity with the athlete and serial assessment remain essential. Authors also had NFL roles or reimbursements, and the protocol requires yearly revision as evidence evolves.
practicalImplications: For Baylor football, this is a strong operational template: define roles before the season, rehearse communication between medical staff and spotters, document each step, empower medical timeouts/removal, repeat evaluation before athletes leave the venue, and separate medical decisions from coaching decisions.
athleteDev: Education should normalize symptom reporting by players, teammates, and coaches. Baseline cognitive, vestibular, ocular, and symptom profiles help staff recognize subtle changes, while culture-building is needed so players do not treat reporting as weakness.
rtp: The protocol uses individualized progression with no fixed timeline. Step 1 is relative physical and cognitive rest until symptoms and neurologic exam return to baseline. Step 2 is light aerobic exercise. Step 3 increases aerobic work and introduces strength training. Step 4 adds noncontact football-specific activity. Step 5 allows full football practice/contact after symptom-free noncontact work and baseline neurocognitive testing. Step 6 requires independent neurological consultant review and face-to-face confirmation before game clearance.

citation: Haralson W, Garlapaty A, Baumann J, Jackson G, Cook JL, DeFroda SF. National Football League Players Have Higher Rates of Knee Extensor Mechanism Tears During Short and Normal Rest Weeks versus Long Rest Weeks. J Knee Surg. 2025. doi:10.1055/a-2585-5099
abstract: This retrospective observational study examined whether NFL quadriceps tendon and patellar tendon tears were associated with short, normal, or long rest weeks between games. Public sources including NFL injury reports, ESPN, and Pro-Football-Reference were used to identify regular-season extensor mechanism tears from 2009-2023, excluding preseason, postseason, practice, and week 1 injuries. Fifty-eight players met criteria. Injury rates did not differ between short and normal weeks, but players were more likely to sustain extensor mechanism tears during normal weeks and short weeks than during long weeks. Artificial turf was also associated with more overall extensor mechanism tears than natural grass.
tldr: Longer-than-normal rest appeared protective for NFL knee extensor mechanism tears; short weeks were not worse than normal weeks, but both carried higher rates than long weeks.
methods: The authors searched public NFL injury reports, ESPN, Pro-Football-Reference, NFL.com, and team sources for quadriceps or patellar tendon tears in NFL regular-season games from 2009-2023. Injuries after week 1 were classified by days since the player's previous game: short (<7 days), normal (7 days), or long (>7 days). Age, position, BMI, and playing surface were collected. Fisher's exact or chi-square tests, one-way ANOVA, and descriptive statistics were performed in Python.
findings: There were 58 extensor mechanism tears: 20 quadriceps tendon and 38 patellar tendon. Eight occurred in short weeks, 47 in normal weeks, and 3 in long weeks. Rates were 0.011 for short weeks, 0.015 for normal weeks, and 0.003 for long weeks. Normal weeks had 4.7 times higher risk than long weeks, and short weeks had 3.7 times higher risk than long weeks. Short and normal weeks did not differ. Artificial turf was associated with higher overall extensor mechanism tear occurrence.
limitations: The dataset came from publicly accessible reports, which can omit details or contain reporting errors. Days between games may not reflect each player's true recovery, practice load, rehabilitation exposure, travel, or readiness. The sample was small because extensor mechanism tears are rare and the inclusion criteria focused on regular-season game injuries.
practicalImplications: For Baylor football, treat extra recovery days as meaningful protection for severe knee tendon injury risk, especially around congested game stretches. Build additional tendon-load management, eccentric/isometric quadriceps capacity, monitoring, and recovery emphasis into short and normal weeks, and be attentive to surface exposure when planning practices and return progressions.
athleteDev: Linemen and other high-load athletes may need year-round quadriceps and patellar tendon capacity work, landing/deceleration quality, body-composition support, and individualized recovery plans. The surface finding supports tracking artificial-turf exposure as part of athlete workload history.
rtp: The study does not provide RTP criteria. It emphasizes that quadriceps and patellar tendon ruptures often require season-ending surgery, so RTP should be surgical-team led and based on tendon healing, strength symmetry, progressive football-specific loading, position demands, and tolerance across repeated high-force practices.

citation: LaPlaca DA, McCullick BA. National Football League Scouting Combine Test Results of Elite-Level National Football League Players. Research Quarterly for Exercise and Sport. Published online February 7, 2025. doi:10.1080/02701367.2024.2448827
abstract: This secondary analysis used NFL Scouting Combine and early-career NFL participation data to identify position-specific combine test results associated with elite-level NFL game participation. The authors analyzed all offensive and defensive players who attended the combine from 2006-2016 (N=3,438) and grouped athletes by whether they averaged at least 10 NFL games played per active season from 2006-2018. Combine measures included 40-yard dash, vertical jump, bench press, broad jump, three-cone drill, shuttle run, height, and weight across 15 position groups. Every position group had at least one combine measure that significantly differentiated players averaging at least 10 games per season from those below that threshold. The study provides normative and position-specific benchmarks intended to help teams identify the physical tests most relevant to durable early-career NFL participation.
tldr: Combine testing is not one-size-fits-all. Across 15 NFL position groups, at least one physical test separated players who became regular game participants from those who did not. For Baylor football staff, the main value is not treating the 40-yard dash or any single drill as universally predictive, but building position-specific profiles where the most relevant movement qualities differ by role.
methods: Secondary data analysis of publicly available Pro Football Reference combine records. The sample included offensive and defensive players attending the NFL Scouting Combine from 2006-2016 across QB, FB, RB, WR, TE, OT, G, C, CB, FS, SS, OLB, ILB, DE, and DT. NFL participation was tracked from 2006-2018, allowing at least three professional seasons after draft eligibility. Players were grouped by average active-roster games played per season: at least 10 games versus fewer than 10 games. Descriptive statistics and independent-samples t-tests compared combine measures by position group.
findings: For each of the 15 position groups, at least one combine metric significantly differed between players who averaged at least 10 games per season and those who did not. The relevant metric varied by position, reinforcing that physical testing must be interpreted through role demands. The paper reports position-specific averages and ranges for successful versus less successful early-career players, giving scouts and performance staff concrete benchmark values rather than only correlations.
limitations: The study uses retrospective public data and games played as the main success marker, which does not separate injury, roster context, coaching decisions, scheme fit, draft capital, or true performance quality. Combine participation and missing tests may bias results. The analysis is observational, so test results should be treated as screening information rather than causal determinants of NFL success. The 2006-2016 cohort may not perfectly reflect current player development, tactics, or testing preparation.
practicalImplications: Use combine-style testing as a position-specific profiling tool, not a universal ranking system. For Baylor football, benchmarks can help identify whether an athlete has physical traits aligned with his projected role, but decisions should combine testing with film, practice load tolerance, medical history, and position skill. Staff can also use these norms to set development targets for athletes seeking professional evaluation.
athleteDev: Long-term development plans should map physical qualities to role demands. Skill players, linemen, linebackers, and specialists need different combinations of acceleration, power, agility, size, and strength endurance. The paper supports building position-specific testing dashboards and avoiding overemphasis on a single marquee combine number when guiding athletes toward NFL readiness.
rtp: The paper is not an injury return-to-play study, but its position-specific benchmarks can provide late-stage performance targets after injury. A returning athlete should be compared with relevant positional norms and his own baseline, especially for the qualities most tied to participation at his position, before unrestricted football exposure.

citation: Vincent LM, Blissmer BJ, Hatfield DL. National Scouting Combine scores as performance predictors in the National Football League. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2018;XX(X):000-000.
abstract: This study examined whether National Scouting Combine measures predict early NFL on-field performance by position. Combine participants from 2005-2010 who subsequently played in the NFL were analyzed at quarterback (n=44), running back (n=82), wide receiver (n=116), linebacker (n=139), defensive end (n=59), and defensive tackle (n=72). Raw combine scores included 40-yard dash, countermovement vertical jump, standing long jump, and 20-yard shuttle; calculated horizontal and vertical power variables were also tested. At least one combine measure correlated with on-field performance at every position, but predictive strength varied widely. Regression models explained 4%-62% of selected performance outcomes, with stronger relationships for quarterback rushing, running back production, and defensive end tackling than for wide receiver and defensive tackle outcomes. The authors recommend adding power calculations and more position-specific tests to the combine battery.
tldr: Combine tests can predict some NFL outcomes, but only modestly and differently by position. Speed and broad jump mattered for running backs, power measures were useful for quarterbacks and defensive ends, and the standard shuttle had limited broad value. For Baylor staff, the lesson is to convert raw testing into role-specific performance questions rather than assume a better test number automatically means better football output.
methods: Retrospective observational study of NFL combine attendees from 2005-2010 who recorded position-specific NFL statistics over their first four seasons for quarterbacks and first three seasons for all other positions. Positions analyzed were QB, RB, WR, LB, DE, and DT. Combine variables were 40-yard dash time, countermovement vertical jump, standing long jump, 20-yard shuttle, and calculated horizontal/vertical power measures. Pearson correlations assessed associations with on-field statistics, and hierarchical linear regression tested how much variance combine variables explained within each position.
findings: At quarterback, power variables helped explain rushing attempts and rushing yards, with grouped power and non-power variables accounting for up to 62.2% of variance in rushing yards. At running back, 40-yard dash and standing long jump predicted rushing yards, attempts, and yards per game, while horizontal power plus 40-yard time related to touchdowns. Wide receiver relationships were minimal. At linebacker, sacks related to multiple combine measures and total variance explained was modest. At defensive end, horizontal and vertical power predicted tackling outcomes and vertical jump/standing long jump related to sacks. Defensive tackle prediction was limited, with standing long jump explaining a small portion of sack variance.
limitations: The study is retrospective and limited to players who both attended the combine and later accumulated NFL statistics, which may exclude important selection effects. Performance statistics are position-dependent and influenced by scheme, opportunity, health, depth chart, and teammate quality. Some combine events had missing data by position. The analysis covers a 2005-2010 cohort and may not reflect current training preparation, tactical trends, or athlete profiles.
practicalImplications: Testing batteries should include power interpretation, not just raw times and jump heights. For Baylor football, horizontal and vertical power estimates may add value when evaluating players whose roles require explosive displacement from static or constrained positions. Staff should also prioritize position-specific agility and skill tests, because the traditional 20-yard shuttle showed limited predictive value outside linebacker sacks.
athleteDev: Development goals should be tied to the football actions that matter for a position. Running backs benefit from speed and explosive horizontal displacement, defensive ends from power out of stance and contact-ready acceleration, and mobile quarterbacks from power qualities that translate to rushing. This supports individualized physical preparation rather than generic combine chasing.
rtp: This is not an RTP study, but the findings can shape late-stage performance testing. Returning athletes should demonstrate restoration of the position-relevant qualities linked to production, such as RB sprint/broad-jump capacity, DE horizontal and vertical power, or QB lower-body power for designed or reactive rushing demands.

citation: Wang H, Martone M, Owens ME, Lemoine NP Jr, Marucci J, Calvert D, Mullenix S, Church TS, Rood J, Harrell B, Irving BA, Spielmann G, Johannsen NM. NCAA Division I American football players with sickle cell trait have altered hematological responses and hydration status. Scientific Reports. 2021;11:1844. doi:10.1038/s41598-021-81473-4
abstract: This longitudinal field study examined hematological responses and hydration status in NCAA Division I American football players with sickle cell trait (SCT). Across two years, 10 SCT players and 10 position-matched controls from a southeastern U.S. university were assessed at pre-camp, post-camp/preseason, and post-season. Blood testing included hemoglobin electrophoresis, complete blood counts, and chemistry panels; hydration assessment during preseason camp included body-weight change, urine specific gravity, urine electrolytes, and sweat electrolytes. SCT players had confirmed HbS values averaging 37.9%, higher red cell distribution width, higher serum uric acid, and higher pre-camp creatine kinase than controls. During camp, SCT players showed lower urine specific gravity and urine electrolytes but higher sweat sodium. The authors conclude that altered kidney and muscle-damage markers may help inform SCT surveillance and that hydration education remains critical.
tldr: SCT players in Division I football showed measurable hematological and hydration differences across a season, including higher RDW, uric acid, and pre-camp CK, plus different urine and sweat electrolyte patterns. For Baylor staff, SCT status should trigger deliberate heat, hydration, acclimatization, and biomarker surveillance rather than a generic participation restriction.
methods: Longitudinal observational study over two football seasons. Participants were 10 NCAA Division I football players with SCT and 10 position-matched controls with similar anthropometrics and football exposure. Blood was collected pre-camp, about 48 hours post-camp/preseason, and about 48 hours after the final competition. Measures included hemoglobin variants, complete blood counts, chemistry panel, estimated glomerular filtration rate, body-mass change, urine specific gravity, urine electrolytes, sweat electrolytes, and wet-bulb globe temperature during camp.
findings: SCT players averaged 37.9% HbS and had greater red cell distribution width than controls across visits. Serum uric acid was higher in SCT players (7.3 +/- 1.0 mg/dL vs 6.1 +/- 0.6 mg/dL; p=0.001). Pre-camp creatine kinase was higher in SCT players (1617.0 +/- 1034.8 IU/L vs 1037.4 +/- 602.8 IU/L; p=0.03). SCT players had lower pre- and post-practice urine specific gravity and urine electrolytes during camp, but higher sweat sodium concentrations (55.4 +/- 13.6 mmol/L vs 45.5 +/- 10.6 mmol/L; p<0.001).
limitations: Small sample size from one Division I program limits generalizability. Three SCT players were enrolled in both years, which may reduce independence and obscure true variability. Fluid intake during camp practices was not measured, so the cause of lower urine electrolytes and urine specific gravity cannot be determined. The field-based observational design improves applied relevance but limits control over confounding variables and exact assessment timing.
practicalImplications: SCT athletes should receive repeated education on hydration, heat stress, symptom reporting, and pacing during high-intensity conditioning. Baylor staff can consider preseason and in-season biomarker surveillance for SCT athletes, especially uric acid, CK, renal markers, hydration status, and sweat/urine electrolyte patterns. Slow acclimatization, rest breaks, and clear emergency action plans remain essential.
athleteDev: For athlete development, SCT should be integrated into individualized conditioning plans. Progressions should avoid abrupt high-volume or high-intensity spikes, especially in heat and humidity, and should include gradual acclimatization. Education should be delivered repeatedly to athletes, coaches, strength staff, and athletic trainers so SCT management is operational rather than only a preseason screening item.
rtp: For SCT athletes returning from illness, exertional symptoms, heat illness, or high-load layoffs, RTP should be conservative and staged. Clearance should include hydration status, symptom resolution, renal and muscle-damage markers when indicated, heat-acclimatization status, and tolerance of progressively intense football conditioning with adequate rest intervals.

citation: Gardner CH, Kotlier JL, Fathi A, Castonguay J, Thompson AA, Bolia IK, Petrigliano FA, Liu JN, Weber AE, Gamradt SC. NCAA football players are at higher risk of upper extremity injury after first-time concussion. The Physician and Sportsmedicine. Published online March 5, 2024. doi:10.1080/00913847.2024.2327275
abstract: This retrospective cohort study tested whether NCAA Division I football players are at increased risk of upper-extremity musculoskeletal injury after a first diagnosed concussion. De-identified injury data from a single Division I conference database were queried for football players diagnosed with their first concussion from 2017-2021. After exclusions, 160 players were reviewed for upper-extremity injuries in the year before concussion and in the year beginning 90 days after concussion. The odds of upper-extremity injury were 2.36 times higher after first concussion than before it (95% CI 1.13-4.95, p=0.02). Shoulder injuries accounted for 57.7% of post-concussion upper-extremity injuries, followed by hand, elbow, and forearm injuries. The authors suggest concussion rehabilitation should account for longer-term musculoskeletal injury risk beyond symptom resolution.
tldr: After a first diagnosed concussion, NCAA football players had more than double the odds of a later upper-extremity injury, with the shoulder most commonly involved. For Baylor football, concussion RTP should not stop at symptom and cognitive clearance; it should include upper-extremity coordination, contact readiness, shoulder control, and football-specific dual-task work.
methods: Retrospective review of the Pac-12 Sports Injury Research Archive for NCAA Division I football players with first diagnosed concussion from 2017-2021. Each included athlete served as his own pre/post comparison. Upper-extremity injuries were counted during the year before concussion and during the year beginning 90 days after concussion. Odds ratios, 95% confidence intervals, and p values were calculated for pre- versus post-concussion injury risk.
findings: A total of 160 football players met inclusion criteria. Upper-extremity injury odds were 2.36 times higher in the year after first diagnosed concussion than in the year before concussion (95% CI 1.13-4.95, p=0.02). Shoulder was the most common injury site after concussion (57.7%), followed by hand (19.2%), elbow (15.4%), forearm (7.7%), and wrist (0%). The finding extends the known post-concussion musculoskeletal injury concern beyond lower-extremity injuries.
limitations: The database did not include concussion history before NCAA participation, playing time, position, age, starter status, or enough demographic detail to build reliable non-concussed matched controls. The authors could not determine specific pathology or mechanisms for upper-extremity injuries. Career progression may naturally increase injury exposure, so the design may overestimate the concussion-specific contribution to later upper-extremity injury.
practicalImplications: Sports medicine and performance staff should monitor shoulder and upper-extremity injury risk after concussion clearance. Baylor concussion RTP protocols should include upper-extremity neuromuscular control, postural control, catching/blocking/contact progressions, and cognitive-motor dual-task challenges. A player who is symptom-free may still need targeted work to reduce subsequent musculoskeletal injury risk.
athleteDev: Athletes with concussion history may need additional development around visual-motor integration, bracing mechanics, tackling/blocking posture, and shoulder girdle control. Incorporating these elements into routine post-concussion return progressions could reduce downstream shoulder and arm injuries during a season.
rtp: RTP after concussion should include progressive exertion plus football-specific upper-extremity demands, not just symptom resolution and neurocognitive testing. Late-stage progression should include catching, ball security, blocking, tackling technique, reactive bracing, and dual-task drills before full contact exposure.

citation: Cole WR, Brett BL, Lempke LB, Mannix R, DeFreese JD, Echemendia RJ, McCrea M, Guskiewicz KM, Meehan WP III. Neither American Football Playing Position Nor Total Years Playing Football Are Associated with Neurobehavioral Health Outcomes: An NFL-LONG Study. Current Sports Medicine Reports. 2025;24(11):372-379.
abstract: This cross-sectional NFL-LONG study examined whether primary football position or total years playing football were associated with concussion history and neurobehavioral health outcomes in former NFL players. The final sample included 1,544 former NFL players who completed online or paper questionnaires. Outcomes were PROMIS Cognitive, Depression, and Anxiety T-scores and Neuro-QOL Emotional-Behavioral Dyscontrol T-scores. Positions were grouped as offensive/defensive linemen, running back/linebacker/tight end, quarterback/wide receiver/defensive back, and special teams. Years played did not differ meaningfully across position groups, and after adjusting for concussion history and health covariates, position group, total years played, and their interaction were not statistically or clinically associated with worse neurobehavioral outcomes. Linemen and RB/LB/TE groups reported higher rates of 10 or more concussions, but position and years played were poor standalone proxies for long-term neurobehavioral status.
tldr: In a large sample of former NFL players, position group and total years playing football did not meaningfully predict cognitive, depression, anxiety, or emotional-behavioral dyscontrol scores once concussion history and health factors were considered. For Baylor staff, this argues against using position or career length alone as a head-impact risk story; direct concussion history, symptoms, sleep, pain, and mental health screening matter more.
methods: Cross-sectional analysis within the NFL-LONG study. Recruitment occurred from January 1, 2019 to June 1, 2023 through retired player networks and NFL-related partners. From 1,983 former NFL players with at least one NFL season, 1,544 had complete primary-position data and were included. Questionnaires captured demographics, football history, concussion history, health covariates, and PROMIS/Neuro-QOL outcomes. Analysis of variance tested years played across position groups, and multivariable regressions tested associations among position, years played, their interaction, and neurobehavioral outcomes while adjusting for covariates.
findings: Participants averaged 50.27 +/- 16.4 years old and 17.68 +/- 4.32 total years playing football. Position distribution was 36.2% OL/DL, 30.5% RB/LB/TE, 28.6% QB/WR/DB, and 4.7% special teams. A history of at least one concussion was reported by 72.9%, and 12.6% reported 10 or more concussions. OL/DL and RB/LB/TE groups had higher rates of 10 or more concussions, but position group, years played, and their interaction were not meaningfully associated with PROMIS cognitive, depression, anxiety, or Neuro-QOL emotional-behavioral dyscontrol outcomes after adjustment.
limitations: The study relied on self-reported concussion history, football exposure, and symptoms, creating recall and attribution bias. Concussions from earlier playing eras may have been underrecognized or inconsistently documented. The cross-sectional design cannot determine causality or symptom trajectories. Position and total years played are broad exposure proxies and do not capture actual head-impact counts, severity, practice exposure, style of play, or individual medical history.
practicalImplications: Do not infer long-term neurobehavioral risk from position group or years played alone. Baylor staff should prioritize direct concussion assessment, symptom tracking, sleep screening, pain interference, mental health monitoring, and individualized clinical history. Exposure proxies can support context, but they should not replace direct measures in player health decisions.
athleteDev: Development systems should teach athletes and coaches that concussion reporting and symptom care are more informative than assumptions based on position. Even if certain roles have higher reported concussion counts, individual monitoring should drive education, risk management, and referral decisions.
rtp: The study does not provide acute RTP criteria, but it supports careful concussion history collection and ongoing neurobehavioral monitoring after athletes return. Position and years played should not be used as shortcuts for RTP risk; individualized symptoms, objective testing, sleep, pain, mental health, and clinical exam should guide decisions.

citation: Schaffert J, Didehbani N, LoBue C, Hart J Jr, Motes M, Rossetti H, Wilmoth K, Goette W, Lacritz L, Cullum CM. Neurocognitive outcomes of older National Football League retirees. Brain Injury. Published online November 27, 2022. doi:10.1080/02699052.2022.2143567
abstract: This study examined whether head-injury exposure was associated with later-life cognition in retired NFL players age 50 and older. NFL retirees with neuropsychological data were classified as cognitively normal (n=26) or cognitively impaired with mild cognitive impairment or dementia (n=27). Cognitively normal retirees were age- and education-matched to healthy controls, while cognitively impaired retirees were matched to a clinical sample by age, sex, education, and diagnosis. Twenty-nine retirees returned for longitudinal follow-up 13-59 months later. Cognitively normal retirees had slightly lower baseline memory scores than healthy controls, but still performed in the average range. No other group differences were observed, and self-reported concussions, concussions with loss of consciousness, and NFL games played did not predict baseline cognition or cognitive change over time.
tldr: In this older retired NFL sample, concussion count, concussion with loss of consciousness, and games played did not predict later-life neuropsychological performance or change over time. For Baylor football staff, the applied message is to avoid simplistic dose-response assumptions from career exposure alone and to prioritize individualized neurocognitive, mental health, sleep, and medical follow-up.
methods: Prospective longitudinal cohort analysis of retired NFL players age 50 or older from a contact-sport aging study. Retirees completed clinical interview, neuropsychological testing, neuroimaging, neurologic exam, concussion-history interview, and football exposure history. Cognitive status was determined by actuarial MCI criteria and clinical consensus. ANOVAs compared cognitive composites for executive function/attention/speed, language, and memory against matched control groups. Change scores were analyzed in follow-up participants. Linear regressions tested whether number of concussions, concussions with loss of consciousness, and NFL games played predicted baseline scores or change over time.
findings: At baseline, cognitively normal NFL retirees had lower memory scores than healthy controls (mean T-score 50.69 vs 57.08; p=0.005), but the retiree mean remained solidly average and the authors questioned the clinical significance. Cognitively impaired retirees did not differ meaningfully from the clinical comparison group. No significant group differences appeared for executive/attention/speed or language composites. Head-injury exposure variables did not significantly predict baseline cognitive performance or longitudinal change, and position grouping as speed versus non-speed did not alter the main pattern.
limitations: The sample was small, especially for longitudinal follow-up and position subgroup analyses. Concussion history relied on self- or informant report and may be vulnerable to recall bias. Games played is only a rough proxy for subconcussive head impact exposure and does not capture practice exposure, helmet-impact metrics, style of play, or medical management. The clinical comparison sample was retrospective and not recruited alongside the NFL cohort. Healthy controls had above-average memory scores, which may have exaggerated the baseline memory difference.
practicalImplications: For football medicine and performance staff, this paper supports careful individual monitoring rather than assuming that more games or more recalled concussions automatically means measurable late-life decline. Retired and active athletes with cognitive concerns still warrant comprehensive evaluation, but exposure proxies should be interpreted alongside mood, sleep, pain, vascular risk, substance use, family history, and objective neuropsychological data.
athleteDev: Long-term athlete development should include concussion education, honest symptom reporting, medical documentation, and transition planning beyond football. The findings argue for building durable health records and individualized follow-up pathways rather than relying on position or career length as a stand-alone risk profile.
rtp: This is not an acute return-to-play study. Its RTP relevance is indirect: concussion clearance and long-term monitoring should be individualized, documented, and based on clinical recovery rather than assumptions that simple exposure counts can predict future cognitive status.

citation: Grandhisiri T. NFL Draft Modelling: Loss Functional Analysis. arXiv:2504.07291. Published April 11, 2025.
abstract: This arXiv preprint proposes a norm-based framework for evaluating NFL draft pick trade fairness and value distribution. Draft pick values were modeled using an exponential Massey-Thaler style curve, with Weibull-like decay parameters fitted from NFL draft pick trades from 2006-2023. The author compared Mean Absolute Error/L1 and Mean Squared Error/L2 optimization, using L-BFGS-B and bootstrap resampling for 95% confidence intervals. L2/MSE produced a steeper curve that heavily favored early picks and resembled top-heavy trade charts, while L1/MAE produced a flatter curve that assigned more value to later picks. The paper frames these curves as different roster-building philosophies: star-seeking versus depth-oriented.
tldr: The same trade data can imply very different draft values depending on the loss function. MSE makes premium picks look much more valuable; MAE spreads value deeper into the draft. For Baylor staff, the useful lens is decision discipline: draft capital models should match the team's development philosophy and should not be treated as objective truth without considering player outcomes and roster needs.
methods: The paper used a public draft trade dataset filtered to 2006-2023. Pick numbers were parsed into upward and downward trade components, while future picks, players, and cash were excluded to simplify immediate pick-for-pick valuation. A two-parameter exponential value curve was fitted under L1/MAE and L2/MSE loss functions with L-BFGS-B optimization. Bootstrap resampling generated empirical parameter distributions and 95% confidence intervals. Fitted curves were compared with each other and with the Jimmy Johnson draft value chart.
findings: MSE/L2 optimization sharply discounted later picks and emphasized early picks, reflecting a top-heavy strategy. MAE/L1 optimization declined more gradually and assigned substantially more value to mid- and late-round selections, aligning with depth and long-term development logic. Parameter estimates differed by loss function, and confidence intervals showed greater uncertainty for later picks. The L2 curve more closely resembled the traditional Jimmy Johnson chart, while the L1 curve likely overstated late-round pick value relative to observed player impact probabilities.
limitations: The analysis excludes future picks, players, cash, and other trade assets that are common in real NFL transactions. It models pick value rather than actual player performance, salary-cap value, roster fit, injury risk, or development outcomes. The data and framework are useful for trade structure but do not establish which curve produces better football decisions. The paper is an arXiv preprint and not presented as peer-reviewed in the local PDF.
practicalImplications: For football operations and sport science, draft value should be connected to a development model. If a program believes it can identify, develop, and retain later-round traits, a flatter valuation logic may fit. If a decision-maker prioritizes rare elite traits, a steeper curve may fit. Either way, staff should audit whether trade models are aligned with scouting confidence, positional scarcity, injury history, and the organization's ability to develop players.
athleteDev: The paper reinforces that player development changes the practical value of draft capital. A team with strong developmental infrastructure may rationally value more selections and depth, while a team seeking immediate high-end traits may accept top-heavy costs. For Baylor, this supports tracking how physical traits, coachability, durability, and role fit convert into multi-year value.
rtp: This is not an injury or RTP study. Its indirect RTP relevance is roster planning: pick valuation models should account for medical risk and availability when teams compare one premium prospect with multiple developmental options.

citation: Yurko R, Nguyen Q, Pelechrinis K. NFL Ghosts: A framework for evaluating defender positioning with conditional density estimation. arXiv:2406.17220. Published June 25, 2024.
abstract: This preprint introduces a public framework for evaluating NFL defender positioning and trajectory against a distribution of hypothetical baseline 'ghost' defenders. Using NFL Big Data Bowl 2021 tracking data from the 2018 season, the authors focused on nearest defender positioning at the moment of catch on completed passes outside the end zone. Random forests for conditional density estimation modeled both the receiver yards-after-catch distribution and the two-dimensional location distribution of ghost defenders. The framework converts observed versus ghost positioning into expected play value changes. In an example play, Jaire Alexander's observed location was worth about -0.93 expected points relative to the ghost baseline. Across 10,363 plays, player and team metrics showed meaningful relationships with YAC allowed and pass-defense EPA.
tldr: This paper turns tracking data into an interpretable defender-positioning score by asking: how much better or worse was the real defender than a plausible ghost defender? For Baylor football staff, the approach points toward evaluating coverage and pursuit with context, not just outcomes like completion, YAC, or tackles.
methods: The authors used 2018 NFL Big Data Bowl tracking data recorded at 10 Hz. After filtering to completed passes outside the end zone with complete features, 10,363 plays were analyzed. Features included adjusted x/y locations, speed, movement direction, orientation, distance to receiver, first-down distance, and relative offensive and defensive positions at catch or pass release. Random forests for conditional density estimation with 500 trees estimated receiver YAC distributions and ghost defender location distributions. Expected play value at catch was calculated by integrating modeled YAC outcomes through an expected-points utility function, then comparing observed defender value with the ghost baseline.
findings: The example play showed that the observed nearest defender was positioned in a highly favorable defensive location, producing a change of about -0.93 expected points compared with the ghost baseline. Across the season, the top accumulated defender values included mostly cornerbacks, with Adoree' Jackson leading at -7.23 total expected points across 56 plays. Average change in expected play value correlated moderately with average YAC allowed (overall r=0.65), and team-level ghost metrics correlated with pass-defense EPA on total and average scales. The framework separated process quality from raw outcomes, such as identifying defenders who were positioned well but still allowed YAC.
limitations: The model evaluates only the nearest defender at the moment of catch, which may not always be the true coverage responsibility. It simplifies football by moving one defender while holding teammates fixed, so team scheme and coordinated coverage are not fully represented. The analysis considers completed passes and YAC after the catch, not target prevention, incompletions, interceptions, route leverage before the catch, or full continuous-time coverage. Position and coverage type were not fully conditioned in the main ghost model.
practicalImplications: For Baylor staff, this framework suggests a way to grade defensive backs and linebackers on spatial process quality rather than only results. Practice and game review could use similar logic to identify whether defenders are arriving at high-value locations, whether poor outcomes are tackling failures versus positioning failures, and whether coverage calls consistently place athletes in favorable leverage.
athleteDev: Athlete development can use ghost-style evaluation to teach leverage, angle, speed control, and pursuit positioning. Instead of telling a defender only that he allowed YAC, coaches can show whether his body position, distance, and trajectory at the catch were better or worse than a context-aware baseline. This supports individualized technical feedback for coverage, tackling setup, and spatial awareness.
rtp: This is not an RTP study, but the framework could support return-to-performance decisions for defensive players. A returning DB or LB could be compared with his pre-injury positioning, speed, and trajectory benchmarks in coverage drills before full game exposure.

citation: Evans BA, Adams C, Pitts JD, Lingerfelt D. NFL Quarterback Development—The Role of Competing Quarterbacks, Rookie Playing Time, and Team Quality. The American Economist. 2024;0(0):1-16. doi:10.1177/05694345241292611
abstract: This sports economics study examined how competing quarterback quality, rookie playing time, and drafting team quality relate to NFL quarterback development. Using Pro-Football-Reference data for quarterbacks drafted from 1994-2017, the authors analyzed 277 quarterbacks after excluding expansion-team cases and players drafted as quarterbacks but expected to play another position. Outcomes included games started, passing yards, and approximate value during the rookie year, seasons two through five, and after season five. The analysis found that quarterbacks playing alongside a Pro Bowl quarterback early in their career had worse mid- and late-career outcomes, quarterbacks drafted by worse teams tended to have better later-career trajectories, and rookie playing time showed evidence of reducing later-career outcomes.
tldr: QB development appears strongly shaped by context outside the player's control. Early rookie starts were not clearly beneficial long term, Pro Bowl incumbent competition was associated with worse future outcomes, and being drafted by a bad team predicted better later opportunity and production. For Baylor staff, developmental timing and environment matter as much as raw talent.
methods: Cross-sectional econometric analysis of quarterbacks drafted from 1994-2017 using Pro-Football-Reference data. The sample included 277 drafted quarterbacks after exclusions. Dependent variables included rookie games started, games started in seasons two through five, games started after season five, passing yards over the same windows, and approximate value. Independent variables included draft pick, age, incumbent quarterback Pro Bowl measures before/during/after the rookie season, incumbent age, drafting-team wins before and during the rookie year, and prior playing-time variables. Models included team and draft-year fixed effects.
findings: Earlier draft picks were more likely to start as rookies, and teams with worse prior records created more rookie opportunity. After season five, each additional prior-year team win was associated with fewer later starts, passing yards, and approximate value. Playing alongside a Pro Bowl quarterback as a rookie was associated with about 9.2 fewer starts after season five and lower later passing output. More games started in seasons two through five predicted later starts, but rookie starts had a negative coefficient for later starts and approximate value, giving modest support to the idea that too much rookie playing time can hurt long-term development.
limitations: The study is observational and cannot prove causality. Quarterback outcomes are influenced by coaching quality, injuries, offensive line, scheme, roster turnover, salary-cap decisions, and unobserved talent evaluation. Approximate value and passing yards are useful but imperfect measures of quarterback quality. The sample ends with the 2017 draft to allow at least five seasons, so newer developmental models and rule environments may not be fully captured.
practicalImplications: For Baylor football, the paper supports deliberate quarterback development plans that manage timing, confidence, game exposure, and support quality. Simply playing a young quarterback early is not automatically development. Staff should separate practice readiness, game-plan protection, offensive line quality, opponent load, and psychological readiness when deciding how quickly to expand a QB's live role.
athleteDev: Quarterback development should be staged. Young QBs need reps, but their early exposure should be structured so they build decision speed and leadership without being overloaded by poor protection, low-support rosters, or unstable role definition. Competition can be useful, but sitting behind a high-status incumbent may reduce meaningful reps and delay relationship-building with starters.
rtp: This is not an injury RTP study. Its RTP relevance is developmental: after injury or time away, quarterback reintegration should consider depth-chart context, practice reps with starters, offensive support, and staged exposure rather than relying only on medical clearance.

citation: Quinn M, Painter DF, Ahn BJ, Byrne RA, Testa EJ, Albright A, Tabaddor RR, DeFroda SF. NFL Quarterbacks with Ulnar Collateral Ligament Injuries Have High Return to Play Rates, but Older Players Have Inferior Post-Injury Performance. Arthroscopy, Sports Medicine, and Rehabilitation. 2024. doi:10.1016/j.asmr.2024.100954
abstract: This Level IV therapeutic case series characterized NFL quarterback ulnar collateral ligament injuries from 1991-2023. Using the Pro Sports Transactions Archive, team and league reports, Associated Press-affiliated media reports, and Pro Football Reference, the authors identified 21 UCL injuries in 20 quarterbacks. They recorded injury mechanism, age, treatment strategy, return-to-play time, and performance from the season before injury through two seasons after injury. Sixteen players returned to play, with mean RTP around 163-166 days overall. UCL repair or reconstruction required substantially longer RTP than nonoperative management (about 359 days vs 98 days; p=0.014). Injuries after 2006 were associated with better post-injury performance, while older age at injury was associated with worse post-injury performance.
tldr: NFL QBs usually returned after UCL injury, but surgery took much longer and older quarterbacks had worse post-injury performance. For Baylor football, elbow UCL RTP should separate medical return from performance restoration, especially for older or high-mileage throwers.
methods: Retrospective case series of NFL quarterbacks with UCL injuries from January 1, 1991 to February 1, 2023. Injuries were identified from the Pro Sports Transactions Archive and verified with team reports, NFL.com, Associated Press-affiliated reports, prior literature, and Pro Football Reference. Variables included contact versus non-contact mechanism, operative versus nonoperative management, days to RTP, age, body size, and performance statistics. Principal component analysis compressed games played, quarterback rating, completion percentage, touchdowns, and interceptions into an overall performance metric. Statistical comparisons assessed management strategy, injury era, age, and mechanism.
findings: The authors identified 21 injuries in 20 quarterbacks, with 10 contact and 11 non-contact injuries. Thirteen injuries were managed nonoperatively and eight underwent UCL repair or reconstruction. Sixteen players returned for at least one more NFL season; nine played at least two more post-injury seasons. Mean RTP was about 163 days overall, but operative cases averaged 359 days compared with 98.25 days for nonoperative cases (p=0.014). Performance did not differ significantly by management strategy, but injuries from 2006 onward showed better post-injury performance (p=0.041). Increasing age at injury correlated with worse post-injury performance (p=0.048).
limitations: The study is retrospective and depends on public injury reporting, which limits injury grading, rehab details, PRP or biologic use, surgical technique, and exact medical decision-making. The sample is small because NFL quarterback UCL injuries are rare, reducing power for subgroup analyses. Findings may not generalize to college quarterbacks, non-quarterbacks, or other throwing sports. Post-injury performance was not able to fully account for team context, coaching changes, offensive line quality, role changes, or personal factors.
practicalImplications: For Baylor sports medicine, quarterback elbow UCL cases should be managed with a clear distinction between RTP and return to prior performance. Nonoperative cases may return faster when injury severity permits, while repair/reconstruction timelines are closer to a full-season planning problem. Older throwers may need more conservative workload progression, objective throwing-quality monitoring, and realistic performance expectations.
athleteDev: Quarterbacks need long-term elbow capacity development, not just symptom management. Throwing volume, recovery, mechanics, shoulder and trunk contribution, forearm strength, and workload spikes should be monitored across the year. Younger quarterbacks may have better performance resilience after injury, but all throwers benefit from proactive arm-care systems and staged exposure.
rtp: RTP after QB UCL injury should be staged by tissue status, symptoms, throwing mechanics, velocity/accuracy tolerance, workload accumulation, and competitive performance. Nonoperative management in this cohort averaged about 98 days to RTP, while UCL repair/reconstruction averaged about 359 days. Clearance should include progressive throwing, practice integration, contact-risk planning, and performance monitoring after return.

citation: Baker HP, Kahn AJ, Rosenberg S, Qin C, Portney D, Athiviraham A. NFL total quarter back rating (QBR) is not decreased following sport related concussion injury. Sport Sciences for Health. 2021. doi:10.1007/s11332-020-00705-8
abstract: This retrospective case-control study tested whether NFL quarterback performance, measured by total quarterback rating (QBR), declined after return to play from sport-related concussion. The authors identified 42 regular-season quarterback concussion cases from 2006 to 2019 using public NFL injury reports and matched them 1:1 by age to quarterbacks with other musculoskeletal injuries. Quarterbacks with concussion missed 2.83 weeks on average versus 2.33 weeks in controls. The concussion group had lower career QBR than controls, but the key return-to-play comparison showed no statistically significant difference between season QBR and weekly QBR in the first 6 weeks after return when concussion cases were compared with controls. The authors concluded that QBR did not decrease in the weeks after quarterbacks returned from concussion.
tldr: In NFL quarterbacks who returned from reported concussions, QBR did not fall below season expectation more than it did in age-matched injured controls, but QBR is a blunt public-facing performance metric and should not be treated as proof of neurologic recovery.
methods: Retrospective Level III case-control study of NFL quarterbacks listed with concussion from 2006-2019; preseason injuries and players who did not return during the regular season were excluded; public injury reports and transaction sources were cross-checked; 42 concussion cases were age-matched to 42 quarterbacks with non-concussion injuries using MEDCALC; outcomes included age, years in NFL, weeks missed, career QBR, season QBR, and weekly QBR for the first 6 weeks after return; independent samples t tests were run in SPSS with p<0.05.
findings: The concussion and control groups did not differ significantly in age, NFL experience, or weeks missed. Quarterbacks with concussion averaged 27.2 years old, 5.9 NFL seasons, and 2.8 missed weeks. Career QBR was lower in the concussion group than controls (81.2 vs 89.1; p=0.01), but weekly QBR changes versus season QBR were not significantly different between groups at weeks 1-6 after return (p values 0.79, 0.11, 0.87, 0.28, 0.18, and 0.51). The study did not support the hypothesis that post-concussion quarterback performance is detectably worse after clearance.
limitations: Public injury reporting may miss or underclassify concussions; concussion severity, symptom course, neurocognitive testing, and physiologic recovery were unavailable; QBR may not be sensitive to subtle decision-making, vision, processing speed, or risk tolerance changes; small quarterback sample limits power; concomitant injuries were not modeled; a quarterback with an apparent severe concussion and no return-season QBR was excluded.
practicalImplications: For Baylor football, the main operational message is not that concussion is harmless to performance, but that box-score outcomes can look normal after RTP. Staff should keep concussion management anchored to symptom evaluation, graded exertion, vestibular/ocular findings, cognitive load, sleep, and medical clearance rather than relying on practice or game productivity as evidence of full recovery.
athleteDev: Quarterbacks need protected development of decision-making under fatigue and contact exposure, but concussion education and honest reporting remain central. Building a culture where QBs can report symptoms without fear of losing status is more actionable than trying to infer brain recovery from passing efficiency after return.
rtp: The paper addresses post-concussion RTP outcomes but does not validate RTP criteria. It supports a cautious interpretation: once NFL quarterbacks were medically cleared and returned, QBR was not detectably reduced, yet RTP should remain individualized and criteria-based because performance metrics cannot rule out persisting symptoms, physiologic vulnerability, or reinjury risk.

citation: Burgess CJ, Singh V, Lygrisse KA, Choy K, Cohn RM, Bitterman A. National Football League wide receivers and running backs have decreased production following ACL reconstruction: An evaluation of fantasy football performance as an outcome measure. Arthroscopy, Sports Medicine, and Rehabilitation. 2021. doi:10.1016/j.asmr.2021.09.021
abstract: This retrospective study used fantasy football scoring and position-specific statistics to evaluate NFL offensive skill player production before and after isolated unilateral ACL reconstruction from 1988 to 2017. The final sample included 13 quarterbacks, 30 running backs, and 29 wide receivers who played at least three regular-season games before and after injury; tight ends were excluded because of small numbers. Matched controls with similar demographics were used for post-index comparisons. Quarterbacks showed no statistically significant decline in fantasy points or performance after ACL reconstruction. Running backs had markedly lower career fantasy points after ACL reconstruction than controls (129.6 vs 553.6; p<0.0001) and lower points per game (4.4 vs 11.2; p<0.0001). Wide receivers also had lower career fantasy points (145.3 vs 460.9; p=0.002) and lower points per game (5.0 vs 7.7; p=0.042).
tldr: ACL reconstruction did not meaningfully reduce NFL quarterback production, but running backs and wide receivers had large post-surgery drops in fantasy output, games played, and position-specific production compared with controls.
methods: Retrospective review of public NFL injury and performance data for QBs, RBs, WRs, and TEs with isolated unilateral ACL injury from 1988-2017; included players had at least three regular-season games before and after injury; prior ACL injury, concomitant ipsilateral knee ligament/meniscus injury, and other concurrent injuries were excluded; TEs were excluded for low sample size; matched controls were selected; position statistics and fantasy points were compared before versus after ACL reconstruction and against post-index controls using independent two-sided t tests in SPSS.
findings: Thirteen QBs, 30 RBs, and 29 WRs met criteria. QBs did not differ significantly from controls in post-ACL fantasy points or most performance variables. RBs showed significant post-ACL declines in games played, rushing volume, rushing yards, receiving production, touchdowns, points per game, points per season, and total fantasy points. WRs showed significant declines in games played, targets, receptions, receiving yards, touchdowns, and fantasy scoring compared with controls. The authors emphasized that combine-style physical measures may return, but game production for RBs and WRs may remain lower.
limitations: Retrospective public-data design; small position-specific samples; fantasy football points are not a validated medical outcome; talent, role, depth chart opportunity, team context, coaching, and contract status are difficult to control; surgical technique, graft choice, rehab quality, and complications were unavailable; players naturally had fewer career years remaining after injury, which may partly explain lower cumulative output.
practicalImplications: For Baylor football, ACLR expectations should be position-specific. RBs and WRs depend heavily on cutting, deceleration, route separation, contact balance, and explosive reacceleration, so medical clearance and strong testing numbers may not equal restored football production. Return plans should include progressive open-field speed, route/cut density, reactive change of direction, contact tolerance, and workload restoration before assuming full role readiness.
athleteDev: Skill players should develop durable knee capacity before injury: eccentric quad and hamstring strength, hip/trunk control, deceleration mechanics, single-leg stiffness, landing quality, and repeated sprint/cut exposure. Development plans for RBs and WRs after ACLR should also target confidence, proprioception, and repeatability of high-speed football actions, not only peak strength.
rtp: Highly relevant to RTP. The study suggests QBs may return to statistical production more reliably than RBs and WRs, while RB/WR clearance should be framed as return to performance over months, not just return to participation. RTP criteria should combine strength symmetry, hop/change-of-direction testing, GPS workload, position-specific drills, contact progression, psychological readiness, and staged snap-count management.

citation: NFL-PFATS. Sports Science Research Update: April 2023. 2023.
abstract: The April 2023 NFL-PFATS Sports Science Research Update is a 23-page practitioner digest summarizing recent papers on subjective monitoring, hamstring mechanics, hamstring injury classification and RTP, eccentric prevention programs, compression garments, recovery protocols, nutrition/ergogenic aids, hydration bioavailability, nonoperative NFL hip/core injuries, and training-load metrics. A major theme is hamstring injury management: the update highlights high-speed running EMG differences across hamstring muscles, the London hamstring consensus series on classification, operative management, rehabilitation/running/RTP, evidence that reduced match exposure before injury may signal hamstring risk, and medical-officer views that communication, high-speed exposure, and load management are key modifiable risk factors. It also includes an NFL-specific study showing all players returned after nonoperative hip/core injury, but defensive players had fewer games and lower performance ratings after hip/core injuries than controls.
tldr: April 2023 is a hamstring-heavy digest: classify injuries better, do not use imaging alone to clear RTP, build high-speed exposure, coordinate medical and coaching decisions, and monitor recovery with more than one metric.
methods: Monthly evidence digest compiled from recent peer-reviewed sport science and sports medicine papers. The PDF provides article titles, citations, abstracts or structured summaries, and key-point excerpts rather than a new original study. Topics were synthesized here for football sport science application, with emphasis on papers most transferable to American football: hamstring injury prevention/RTP, high-speed running, recovery, hip/core injury, athlete monitoring, and training-load measurement.
findings: Key applied findings include: world-class athletes' honesty in subjective monitoring is shaped by trust, perceived compassion, and how staff use the data; hamstring activation during high-speed running is heterogeneous across biceps femoris, semitendinosus, and semimembranosus; eccentric hamstring programs can reduce lower-extremity injury risk, but implementation details matter; the London consensus recommends MRI for diagnosis/prognosis but not as the sole rehab or RTS decision tool; hamstring rehabilitation should integrate running progression and sport demands; reduced recent match exposure was associated with hamstring injury in professional soccer; European club CMOs rated poor medical-coaching communication and lack of regular high-speed exposure as important hamstring risk factors; nonoperative NFL hip/core injuries allowed RTP, but defensive players showed reduced post-injury games and performance.
limitations: This is a curated digest, not a systematic review or primary dataset. Included studies vary widely in design, sport, population, and quality. Many papers are soccer-based and require translation to American football demands. The update provides brief summaries rather than full methods, effect sizes, and risk-of-bias appraisal for every article.
practicalImplications: For Baylor football, this update supports a shared hamstring operating model between sports medicine, S&C, sport science, and position coaches. The practical stack is: regular high-speed exposure, objective strength and sprint progression, clear communication on practice content, subjective monitoring delivered with trust, and caution against using MRI resolution alone as a green light. Hip/core injuries in defensive players deserve close workload and performance follow-up after return.
athleteDev: Development programming should expose athletes year-round to sprinting, acceleration, deceleration, trunk/hip control, and eccentric hamstring strength in doses that fit the weekly plan. Monitoring should include both athlete-reported readiness and objective field/weight-room data, with staff behavior encouraging truthful reporting instead of compliance theater.
rtp: The April update is strongly RTP relevant. The London hamstring consensus emphasizes classification, criteria-based rehabilitation, running progression, and sport-specific return rather than imaging-only decisions. The hip/core NFL summary also reinforces that RTP can occur while performance remains affected, so return-to-performance tracking should continue after medical clearance.

citation: NFL-PFATS. Sports Science Research Update: August 2023. 2023.
abstract: The August 2023 NFL-PFATS Sports Science Research Update is a 21-page digest covering football brain health, tackling technique, sodium bicarbonate, CBD, commotio cordis, the Amsterdam 2022 concussion consensus, hamstring fatigue and fiber typology, creatine and brain health, neurodiversity, plant-based diets, high-speed sprint exposure programming, psychological readiness for RTP, and sleep-wake disorders after concussion. Football-specific highlights include a 1000-tackle NCAA Division I video study showing head-up, at-or-above-waist, inside-shoulder tackles had the highest success rates; the Amsterdam concussion statement with updated CRT6, SCAT6, and SCOAT6 tools and support for early aerobic exercise and cervicovestibular rehab; a review emphasizing AED access and rapid response for commotio cordis; and a worldwide practitioner survey showing broad agreement that high-speed and sprint exposure matter but inconsistent definitions and monitoring methods.
tldr: August 2023 centers on football safety and return-to-performance: teach safer and more effective tackling, update concussion workflows to Amsterdam tools, treat sleep and psychological readiness as RTP variables, and standardize high-speed running exposure.
methods: Monthly practitioner digest of recently published sport science and sports medicine literature. The PDF summarizes selected peer-reviewed studies, consensus statements, reviews, and editorials with abstracts and key points. This record synthesizes the digest for American football application, prioritizing tackling, concussion, emergency action planning, high-speed exposure, hamstring fatigue, nutrition/supplements, psychological readiness, and sleep.
findings: Head-up tackles were successful in 76.2% of attempts versus 55.1% for head-down tackles, and inside-shoulder tackles had the highest success rate at 93.2% in the NCAA video study. Oral sodium bicarbonate improved repeated sprint time and Yo-Yo IR2 performance in recreational team-sport athletes, while topical bicarbonate improved repeated sprint time but not blood acid-base measures. The Amsterdam concussion consensus introduced updated recognition, acute assessment, and office assessment tools, discouraged using computerized neurocognitive testing alone, and supported early physical activity plus cervicovestibular rehab when indicated. Sleep-wake disturbances after SRC were described as independent risk factors for prolonged recovery. Practitioners agreed high-speed and sprint exposure is important, but definitions, thresholds, and scheduling vary widely.
limitations: The digest is not a formal systematic review and does not rate evidence quality across all included papers. Several studies are non-football, small-sample, review-based, or focused on soccer/team-sport settings rather than NCAA football. Supplement findings may not generalize to elite collision-sport athletes, and some topics such as CBD and creatine-brain health remain emerging.
practicalImplications: For Baylor football, the strongest takeaways are operational: reinforce head-up/inside-shoulder tackling as both safer and more effective; keep AED access, rehearsal, and commotio cordis response visible in emergency action planning; update concussion processes around CRT6/SCAT6/SCOAT6 concepts; screen sleep after concussion; and align staff definitions for high-speed and sprint exposure so weekly plans are consistent across position groups.
athleteDev: Development should connect skill safety with performance. Tackling technique work should reward head-up leverage and inside-shoulder mechanics, not only collision outcome. Sprint exposure should be planned for starters and developmental players, with nonstarters receiving enough high-speed work to maintain readiness. Nutrition and supplement conversations should be evidence-led and compliance-aware.
rtp: RTP themes are prominent: concussion management should include updated assessment tools, early controlled activity, targeted cervicovestibular rehab, sleep management, and monitoring for symptoms beyond 4 weeks. Orthopedic RTP should include psychological readiness and fear-of-reinjury screening, while high-speed exposure programming helps bridge rehab completion to game-speed availability.

citation: NFL-PFATS. Sports Science Research Update: February 2023. 2023.
abstract: The February 2023 NFL-PFATS Sports Science Research Update is a 26-page digest summarizing research on ankle ligament repair, CBD after exercise, air quality and NFL/MLB errors, acceleration/deceleration event definitions, cold-water immersion, NFL crowd effects on penalties, hamstring injury trends, elevated NFL injury rates after the COVID-19 disruption, head acceleration measurement standards, hamstring architecture after injury, microcycle rest planning, post-game hamstring strength recovery, football age of first exposure, CMJ metric selection, supplement risk, sleep after concussion, concussion knowledge in British American football, heat and decision-making, fixture congestion, and repeated high-intensity efforts. Football-relevant highlights include an NFL injury-report study showing 2021 injury incidence remained elevated versus 2018-2019 and 2020, a UEFA hamstring study showing hamstrings rose to 24% of all injuries with many recurrences within 2 months of return, and CHAMP guidance on better head acceleration measurement practices.
tldr: February 2023 is a broad load-management and injury-risk digest: hamstring burden is rising, NFL injuries stayed elevated after the COVID-era disruption, recovery/rest timing matters, and metric definitions can change what staff think they are measuring.
methods: Monthly evidence digest summarizing recent peer-reviewed articles and reviews. The PDF provides citations, abstracts, structured summaries, and practical points rather than original data collection. This record synthesizes the update for Baylor football staff, emphasizing American football injury surveillance, hamstring recurrence, recovery modalities, microcycle planning, monitoring metrics, concussion/sleep, environmental stress, and supplement risk.
findings: Early lateral ankle ligament repair in 147 elite athletes produced 100% return to preinjury sport level with median RTS of 69 days, while associated deltoid, syndesmosis, or osteochondral injuries delayed return. CBD did not reduce inflammation, fatigue, or performance loss after eccentric muscle damage in trained female athletes. Air quality predicted MLB errors and NFL quarterback mistakes in one environmental study. Changing acceleration/deceleration minimum-duration criteria changed which player actions were detected. Cold-water immersion outperformed several common recovery methods for soreness but was not clearly superior for all performance outcomes. UEFA hamstring injuries doubled as a share of injuries over 21 seasons, reaching 24% of all injuries and 20% of absence days in 2021/22, with about 18% recurrences and many within 2 months. NFL 2021 injury incidence was higher than pre-COVID seasons and increased after week 4. AFE to football had weak associations with self-reported outcomes and was not associated with medical diagnoses in former NFL players.
limitations: This is a curated monthly update, not a systematic review. Studies span different sports, levels, countries, and methods. Several findings come from soccer or AFL and need careful American football translation. Public NFL injury-report studies undercount practice and less severe injuries. The digest format limits full appraisal of bias, confounding, and measurement reliability.
practicalImplications: For Baylor football, the update argues for precision in monitoring and recovery decisions. Staff should standardize acceleration/deceleration definitions, interpret GPS events by actual football actions, maintain hamstring prevention through the first 2 months after RTP, plan off-feet recovery strategically after games, and avoid overpromising CBD or any supplement without evidence and compliance review. Mid-to-late season injury surveillance deserves special attention.
athleteDev: Athlete development should build resilience to repeated high-intensity efforts, sprinting, deceleration, heat, and congested weeks. CMJ and GPS metrics should be selected for a purpose: performance profiling, fatigue monitoring, or rehab testing. Hamstring history should trigger individualized post-game strength monitoring and sustained eccentric/high-speed exposure rather than a short rehab-only emphasis.
rtp: RTP relevance is high across ankle, hamstring, concussion, and monitoring topics. The digest supports criteria-based ankle RTS with attention to associated injuries, extended hamstring surveillance for at least 2 months after return, sleep screening after sport-related concussion, and using CMJ/GPS metrics that match the specific RTP question rather than collecting default numbers.
