findings: Cannabis use varied with age, sex, race, sexual orientation, competition level, and country. Available studies did not support athletic-performance benefit and reported impaired objective performance and potential adverse cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, cognitive, psychiatric, and dependence-related outcomes.
limitations: This was a clinical narrative review rather than a pooled systematic analysis. Much prevalence evidence was self-reported, athlete-specific causal evidence was limited, and cannabis products, THC and CBD content, dosing, routes, and regulatory environments were heterogeneous.
practicalImplications: Ask about cannabis without stigma, distinguish THC from CBD and prescribed medication, and discuss health, cognition, driving, eligibility, and product-contamination risks. Do not endorse cannabis as a performance or recovery intervention from current evidence.
athleteDev: Build pain, sleep, stress, and recovery support around evidence-based training, medical, nutrition, and mental-health care. Young athletes need clear education about brain development, dependence risk, and team or anti-doping rules.
rtp: Acute intoxication, withdrawal, mental-health symptoms, or cardiovascular effects can compromise safe participation. Return decisions require clinical assessment and functional readiness, not simply elapsed time since reported use.

citation: Castro-Sepulveda M, Cancino J, Fernández-Verdejo R, et al. Basal serum cortisol and testosterone/cortisol ratio are related to rate of Na+ lost during exercise in elite soccer players. International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism. 2019;29(6):658-663.
abstract: This cross-sectional study examined whether basal testosterone, cortisol, or their ratio was related to sweat sodium-loss rate during one training session in 22 elite male soccer players.
tldr: Higher basal cortisol was associated with greater sodium-loss rate and a higher testosterone-to-cortisol ratio with lower loss, independent of sweat rate. These modest correlations do not establish causality, the proposed transport mechanism, or a hormone-based sodium prescription.
methods: Basal serum testosterone and cortisol were measured before exercise. Sweat samples and sweat rate were collected during training, sodium-loss rate was calculated, and associations were examined while accounting for sweating rate.
findings: Sodium-loss rate correlated positively with cortisol at r=.43 and negatively with the testosterone-to-cortisol ratio at r=-.46. The study proposed possible regulation through the cystic-fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator but did not test that pathway.
limitations: The sample included only 22 elite men and one training exposure. Cross-sectional correlations are sensitive to hormonal, dietary, environmental, acclimation, and measurement variation and cannot define individual replacement needs or prove a biological mechanism.
practicalImplications: When sodium replacement precision matters, measure individual sweat rate and sweat sodium under representative conditions. Do not substitute basal hormone testing for direct sweat assessment.
athleteDev: Teach athletes to individualize fluid and sodium plans for duration, climate, acclimation, and known sweat losses. Reassess across materially different environments rather than relying on a permanent label.
rtp: Hormone values from this study do not determine readiness. During heat, illness, or heavy training, use symptoms, hydration status, environmental exposure, medical context, and a progressive return plan.

citation: Bishop C, Clarke R, Freitas TT, et al. Change-of-direction deficit vs. deceleration deficit: A comparison of limb dominance and inter-limb asymmetry between forwards and backs in elite male rugby union players. Journal of Sports Sciences. 2021;39(10):1088-1095.
abstract: This cross-sectional study compared change-of-direction and deceleration deficits, limb dominance, asymmetry, jumping, and speed in 25 elite male rugby-union players at the end of preseason.
tldr: Change-of-direction and deceleration tests produced only moderate agreement on limb dominance, and asymmetry direction varied across tasks. Deficit and asymmetry scores also related weakly to general jump and speed performance, so these measures are not interchangeable athlete traits.
methods: Players completed bilateral jump, linear-speed, 505 change-of-direction, and deceleration tests. Left- and right-side deficits, asymmetry, limb-dominance agreement, correlations, and forward-versus-back differences were calculated.
findings: Dominance agreement between change-of-direction and deceleration deficits was moderate. Jump and linear or change-of-direction speed relationships were moderate to large, but deficit and asymmetry relationships were small. Backs were faster over 15 m and performed better in most jump tests than forwards.
limitations: The sample was small, male, elite, rugby-specific, and assessed at one time point. Test-specific calculations, no prospective injury or performance outcomes, and no intervention or between-session reliability analysis prevent stable labeling or causal interpretation.
practicalImplications: Choose a test that matches the decision and preserve its exact setup. Interpret change-of-direction, stopping, and limb outputs separately and confirm unexpected findings across repeated representative tasks.
athleteDev: Develop acceleration, braking, reacceleration, and directional skill while accounting for position demands. Avoid building a program around a favored limb that changes with the task.
rtp: Track repeatable performance in the exact change-of-direction and deceleration tasks relevant to reintegration. Clearance should include symptoms, absolute capacity, movement quality, directional variety, fatigue, and rugby exposure.

citation: Nobari H, Praça GM, Clemente FM, et al. Comparisons of new body load and metabolic power average workload indices between starters and non-starters: A full-season study in professional soccer players. Proceedings of the Institution of Mechanical Engineers, Part P: Journal of Sports Engineering and Technology. 2021;235(2):105-113.
abstract: This full-season observational study compared body-load- and metabolic-power-derived weekly training monotony and strain between starters and nonstarters in 21 professional Iranian Premier League soccer players.
tldr: Starters showed very large higher derived monotony and strain values than nonstarters in early, mid, and end-season periods, largely reflecting match exposure. The one-team data identify workload divergence but do not validate the indices as readiness or injury-risk measures.
methods: Players wore GPS devices throughout the season and were classified weekly according to match and training participation. New body load and average metabolic power were used to calculate weekly monotony and strain across preseason and three in-season periods.
findings: Starters had very large higher values across all four indices in early, mid, and end season, with standardized differences generally above 2.4 and reaching 3.58. The groups did not show the same clear pattern during preseason.
limitations: The study involved one small team, weekly changing group membership, repeated observations, and proprietary derived variables. It did not test injury, recovery, performance, or whether manipulating the reported indices improves outcomes.
practicalImplications: Use match participation to anticipate divergent exposure and compare starters and nonstarters across the actual underlying load measures. Avoid red-light decisions or injury claims from derived monotony and strain values alone.
athleteDev: Provide nonstarters with planned exposure that preserves relevant running and mechanical qualities while managing the greater match-driven load of starters. Individual response should determine the adjustment.
rtp: Use the athlete's accumulating training and match exposure to plan reintegration, but do not equate a target monotony or strain score with readiness. Pair load with symptoms, function, and recovery response.

citation: Dauty M, Menu P, Fouasson-Chailloux A. Cutoffs of isokinetic strength ratio and hamstring strain prediction in professional soccer players. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2018;28(1):276-281.
abstract: This prospective cohort analysis tested whether preseason bilateral, conventional, or functional isokinetic knee-strength-ratio cutoffs predicted moderate hamstring strain in 194 professional soccer players observed across 15 seasons.
tldr: Thirty-six players sustained hamstring strain, but neither common published cutoffs nor cohort-specific 10th-percentile cutoffs predicted injury. Isokinetic testing can describe strength capacity; converting ratios into binary injury-risk labels was not supported.
methods: Bilateral concentric and eccentric hamstring ratios, conventional hamstring-to-quadriceps ratios, and mixed functional ratios were calculated at preseason. Multiple published cutoffs and cohort-derived cutoffs were tested with odds ratios against subsequent injury.
findings: No bilateral, conventional, or functional cutoff predicted hamstring strain in univariate analysis. Very few injured players fell below some commonly used thresholds, and population-specific thresholds were not more successful.
limitations: Only 36 injuries occurred, data spanned 15 seasons, and strength ratios depend on testing velocity, contraction mode, equipment, and protocol. Injury is multifactorial, and failure of cutoffs does not mean absolute hamstring strength or repeated testing lacks clinical value.
practicalImplications: Stop using one preseason isokinetic ratio as a hamstring-injury prediction test. Review absolute knee-flexor capacity, exposure, prior injury, sprint preparation, symptoms, and change over time together.
athleteDev: Train hamstring strength across relevant lengths, velocities, and functions and maintain high-speed-running exposure. Aim to improve capacity rather than merely cross an unvalidated ratio threshold.
rtp: Ratios may supplement side-specific capacity assessment after injury, but clearance should not depend on a cutoff. Include absolute strength, symptoms, sprint progression, fatigue tolerance, and football-specific exposure.

citation: Jorge A, Lichtenstein E, Faude O, Roth R. Muscle activity and kinematics during three hamstring strengthening exercises compared to sprinting: A cross-sectional study. International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy. 2024;19(5):569-580.
abstract: This laboratory study compared hamstring and posterior-chain surface electromyography and lower-limb kinematics during three hip-dominant exercises, Nordic hamstring exercise, and treadmill running in eight healthy male athletes.
tldr: Explosive rocker and fast-perpetuum-mobile variants generated the greatest hamstring activity, but every exercise reached peak activity at shorter hamstring lengths than high-speed running. High activation can complement sprint preparation but does not reproduce sprint mechanics or prove injury prevention.
methods: Surface electromyography measured biceps femoris, semitendinosus, gluteus maximus, and medial gastrocnemius activity, normalized to maximal sprinting. Three-dimensional motion capture compared joint angles during exercises and treadmill running at 75% of maximal sprint velocity.
findings: Hamstring activity ranged from 63.9% of normalized sprint values for the rocker to 32.1% for the slow perpetuum-mobile exercise. Biceps femoris activity exceeded semitendinosus across exercises, while all exercise peaks occurred with less hamstring elongation stress than running.
limitations: Only eight healthy men participated. Surface electromyography is not direct muscle force, treadmill running at 75% differs from maximal field sprinting, and the cross-sectional study did not measure adaptation, injury, soreness, or program effectiveness.
practicalImplications: Select exercises by the joint, speed, muscle-length, and activation stimulus required. Combine strength work with progressive sprint exposure rather than choosing exercises solely because an electromyographic value is high.
athleteDev: Use multiple hamstring strategies across hip- and knee-dominant patterns, tempos, and lengths, then integrate high-speed running. Progress load based on technique and tolerance.
rtp: Exercise activity data can guide early and middle rehabilitation loading, but sprint-specific length and speed demands must be restored separately before unrestricted return.

citation: McCall A, Wolfberg A, Ivarsson A, et al. A qualitative study of 11 world-class team-sport athletes' experiences answering subjective questionnaires: A key ingredient for visible health and performance monitoring? Sports Medicine. 2023;53(5):1085-1100.
abstract: This phenomenological qualitative study explored why 11 world-class team-sport athletes were or were not honest when answering subjective health and performance questionnaires.
tldr: Athlete disclosure was shaped by pursuit of an ideal self, personal barriers, social facilitators, and perceived compassion from staff. Subjective-monitoring quality is partly a relationship and system-design problem, not simply athlete compliance.
methods: Five women and six men were interviewed about monitoring experiences. Researchers extracted significant statements, formulated meanings, coded categories, developed themes, and created a blended thematic story across athlete accounts.
findings: Four themes emerged: pursuit of the ideal self, individual barriers to engagement, social facilitators, and feeling compassion from performance staff. Athlete emotions and the behavior of staff asking the questions influenced willingness to disclose honestly.
limitations: The small purposive elite sample and qualitative interpretation cannot estimate how common a behavior is, validate a questionnaire, or prove that a specific staff intervention changes response accuracy. Findings are context dependent.
practicalImplications: Explain why data are collected, respond consistently and compassionately, protect appropriate confidentiality, and demonstrate that honest answers lead to useful support rather than punishment. Review the workflow when responses appear unreliable.
athleteDev: Build athlete agency and communication skills alongside self-awareness. Monitoring should create a safe conversation and shared decision surface, not a surveillance exercise.
rtp: Subjective readiness is valuable when trust permits honest disclosure, but it should be combined with clinical findings, functional testing, load tolerance, and the athlete's informed voice.

citation: Sartori S, Whiteley R. Pectoralis major ruptures during rugby league tackling: Case series with implications for tackling technique instruction. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2019;22(12):1298-1303.
abstract: This retrospective case series described three complete pectoralis-major ruptures sustained while tackling by players from one 36-man professional rugby-league squad during the same season.
tldr: All three injuries occurred with the shoulder in outer-range abduction and horizontal abduction during contact after a defensive approach change. Each player underwent acute repair and returned at the same level, but three clustered cases cannot prove that the technique change caused the injuries.
methods: The authors reviewed the injury mechanisms, squad incidence, treatment, and outcomes of three professional players and compared the cluster with available literature. Tackle position and organizational context were reconstructed for each case.
findings: The three players appeared to tear the pectoralis major while attempting the tackle from a similar vulnerable shoulder position. Acute surgical management was used in all cases, and each returned to play at the prior level.
limitations: This uncontrolled three-case series from one squad and season cannot estimate causal risk or separate technique, exposure, strength, fatigue, individual anatomy, and chance. The mechanism assessment was observational and retrospective.
practicalImplications: When changing tackle technique, introduce it progressively, monitor unintended exposures, and coordinate coaching, medical, and performance feedback. Prepare shoulder and pectoral capacity for the positions the new technique creates.
athleteDev: Develop contact skill and shoulder-girdle capacity together, particularly for outer-range force acceptance. Technical changes require rehearsal and progressive collision exposure rather than verbal instruction alone.
rtp: The cases returned after surgical repair, but the series does not define a timeline or clearance test. Restore healing, strength through range, contact mechanics, confidence, and progressive tackle exposure.

citation: Ross S, Ripley NJ, Comfort P. Practices and perceptions in hamstring training for injury prevention and enhancement of athletic performance: A qualitative analysis. International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching. 2025:17479541251374792.
abstract: This qualitative study interviewed 12 strength-and-conditioning and physiotherapy practitioners to understand how hamstring-injury-prevention and performance research is translated into applied programs.
tldr: Limited athlete contact, fixture congestion, and multidisciplinary planning constrained practice; microdosing and isometrics were common adaptations. Some low-volume Nordic and minimum-effective-dose findings were not consistently translated, highlighting an implementation and communication gap rather than proof of one best method.
methods: Semi-structured interviews covered practitioner role, job constraints, resistance training, high-speed running, testing and monitoring, and views of research. Thematic analysis identified shared challenges, strategies, and evidence-to-practice gaps.
findings: Practitioners described time, schedules, and multidisciplinary coordination as major constraints. They used microdosed resistance work and isometrics during congestion, while calling for better education, team planning, and research on minimum effective strength doses.
limitations: The purposive sample was small and mixed across sports and roles. Self-reported perceptions do not establish intervention efficacy, prevalence, adherence, or athlete outcomes, and qualitative themes depend partly on researcher interpretation.
practicalImplications: Plan hamstring exposure across the multidisciplinary team, protect a minimum effective stimulus during congestion, and document what is actually delivered. Distinguish evidence, local constraints, and practitioner preference.
athleteDev: Maintain year-round hamstring strength and sprint exposure with doses that fit the calendar. Education and athlete buy-in help preserve consistency when full sessions are not possible.
rtp: Rehabilitation and team training should share a clear progression for strength, running speed, volume, and role demands. Practitioner consensus alone should not determine clearance.

citation: Minniti MC, Statkevich AP, Kelly RL, et al. The safety of blood flow restriction training as a therapeutic intervention for patients with musculoskeletal disorders: A systematic review. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2020;48(7):1773-1785.
abstract: This systematic review summarized adverse-event reporting from 19 blood-flow-restriction-training studies involving 322 people with musculoskeletal disorders.
tldr: Fourteen adverse events were reported: 10 among 168 blood-flow-restriction participants and four among 154 controls. Three rare events in blood-flow-restriction groups included deep-vein thrombosis and rhabdomyolysis; the evidence was mostly knee related and safety reporting was incomplete, so the intervention appears feasible but not risk free.
methods: MEDLINE, CINAHL, and Embase were searched for human musculoskeletal studies using blood-flow restriction that addressed adverse events. Diagnoses, protocols, common and rare events, and randomized comparisons were synthesized.
findings: Nine studies reported no adverse events. Randomized trials did not show a higher overall event likelihood than exercise alone, while three rare events and several episodes of acute pain or fatigue were documented. Many otherwise eligible studies were excluded because safety was not reported.
limitations: Samples were small, diagnoses and protocols varied, adverse-event definitions were inconsistent, and evidence concentrated on knee disorders. Nonreporting can hide events, and the review could not establish safety for every diagnosis, vascular-risk profile, cuff, or occlusion pressure.
practicalImplications: Use medical screening, individualized arterial-occlusion pressure, appropriate cuffs and loads, supervision, symptom education, and explicit adverse-event documentation. Stop and assess concerning pain, neurologic, vascular, or systemic symptoms.
athleteDev: Blood-flow restriction can provide a lower-load strength stimulus when heavier loading is not tolerated, but it should transition into broader capacity development as appropriate rather than replace conventional training indefinitely.
rtp: Use blood-flow restriction as one rehabilitation tool under qualified supervision, not as a clearance test. Progress tissue loading, absolute strength, function, and sport exposure while accounting for contraindications and adverse response.

citation: Cormier P, Freitas TT, Seaman K. A systematic review of resistance training methodologies for the development of lower body concentric mean power, peak power, and mean propulsive power in team-sport athletes. Sports Biomechanics. 2024;23(10):1229-1262.
abstract: This systematic review evaluated 19 studies of resistance-training methods intended to improve lower-body concentric mean, peak, or mean-propulsive power in team-sport athletes and considered their seasonal implementation.
tldr: Traditional strength and combination methods had the strongest evidence, with support for optimal-load and velocity-based training when monitoring was available. Flywheel, eccentric-overload, and weightlifting methods were also favorable but backed by fewer studies; no single method was universally superior.
methods: The authors extracted baseline-to-post percentage change, effect sizes, and evidence level for power outcomes. Methods included traditional, complex, contrast, optimal-load, velocity-based, flywheel, eccentric-overload, and weightlifting approaches.
findings: Traditional and combination training were supported by higher-level evidence. Optimal-load and velocity-based approaches were practical when movement velocity and power could be monitored, while several specialized methods showed promise with lower evidence certainty.
limitations: The 19 studies varied in athlete level, sport, training history, power metric, device, duration, and reporting of concurrent sport load. Some methods had few studies, and the review did not identify one optimal method or annual plan for all team sports.
practicalImplications: Choose the simplest method that targets the athlete's power limitation and fits the calendar, coaching expertise, and available measurement. Track actual load, velocity, and adaptation rather than following a method label.
athleteDev: Build a strength foundation, then expose athletes to force- and velocity-oriented power work across the year. Adjust volume during congested technical and competition periods while preserving enough stimulus to maintain power.
rtp: Power training can support late-stage rehabilitation after sufficient tissue and strength preparation. Progress force, velocity, landing, and sport-specific expression; do not use a program category as a clearance criterion.

citation: Jebabli A, Delleli S, Mahdi N, Ben Maaoui K, Del Coso J, Chtourou H, Ardigò LP, Ouergui I. Effect of a 90-Minute Nap at Different Times of the Day on Physical Performance, Psycho-Cognitive Responses, and Perceived Recovery in Trained Youth Male Athletes. Sports. 2025;13:395.
abstract: This randomized crossover study tested whether the timing of a 90-minute nap changes afternoon physical performance, psycho-cognitive responses, and perceived recovery in trained youth male athletes.
tldr: In 14 trained young men, a 90-minute nap beginning at 13:00 improved selected shuttle-run and attention outcomes compared with later or no-nap conditions. Effects were not consistent across fatigue, feeling, sleep, and recovery measures, so the study supports a promising timing option rather than a universal nap prescription.
methods: Fourteen trained male athletes aged 18 plus or minus 1 year completed four randomized crossover conditions: no nap with testing at 13:00 or 15:00 and a 90-minute nap beginning at 13:00 or 15:00. Outcomes included repeated 5-m shuttle-run best and total distance, fatigue index, RPE, soreness, perceived recovery, digit cancelation, feeling, sleepiness, sleep quality, and Hooper questionnaire scores.
findings: Total shuttle-run distance was higher after the 13:00 nap than after the 15:00 nap and 15:00 no-nap condition. Best distance was higher after the 13:00 nap than after either no-nap condition, and digit-cancelation performance also improved. RPE was higher in the 13:00 nap condition, while fatigue index, feeling state, and Hooper scores did not differ significantly.
limitations: The study used a small sample of trained young men, one nap duration, and one intermittent running protocol. It did not personalize timing by chronotype or sleep need, and standardized post-nap light and television exposure may have influenced responses.
practicalImplications: When schedules permit and prior sleep is controlled, trialing an early-afternoon 90-minute nap may help selected athletes preparing for later training or competition. Evaluate the athlete's sleep inertia, logistics, and repeated individual response before routine use.
athleteDev: Teach sleep planning as an individualized performance skill. Track bedtime, wake time, nap timing, post-nap alertness, and training response so athletes learn whether napping supports their schedule rather than treating it as mandatory.
rtp: A nap may support perceived readiness during return-to-training days, but it does not replace medical clearance, progressive exposure, or objective task tolerance. Avoid interpreting temporary alertness as restored tissue or systemic capacity.

citation: Jagim AR, Wright GA, Camic CL, Kisiolek JN, Luedke J, Oliver JM, Fischer KM, Jones MT. Relationship between training load and recovery in collegiate American football players during pre-season training. Science and Medicine in Football. 2021;5(4):330-338.
abstract: This 14-day collegiate American football cohort study examined how internal and external practice-load measures related to next-day neuromuscular performance and perceived recovery during preseason.
tldr: Session RPE load and mechanical load related to different next-day recovery signals in 17 collegiate football players. The study supports a low-cost multimethod monitoring approach, but its small one-team sample does not justify universal thresholds or single-score readiness decisions.
methods: Seventeen players, including six linemen and 11 non-linemen, wore accelerometer and heart-rate sensors during preseason practice and reported session RPE immediately afterward. Before the next practice they completed a drop-jump reactive strength index test and rated perceived recovery; loaded countermovement-jump performance was assessed before and after preseason.
findings: Each unit increase in session-RPE load was associated with a 0.03-unit decline in next-day reactive strength index, while each unit increase in mechanical load was associated with a 0.01-unit reduction in perceived recovery. Non-linemen accumulated greater mechanical load, and load and recovery variables were generally lower in week 2 than week 1.
limitations: Only 17 athletes from one team completed analysis after seven monitored players were excluded because of injury. Position subgroups were very small, observation lasted 14 days, and the relationships may change across season phases, programs, or monitoring systems.
practicalImplications: Pair a simple internal-load measure such as session RPE with an external mechanical-load measure and at least one next-day recovery check. Review trends by athlete and position rather than collapsing all players into one team threshold.
athleteDev: Use monitoring conversations to help players connect perceived intensity, contact and movement exposure, sleep, soreness, and next-day output. The goal is better self-regulation and communication, not punishment for reporting fatigue.
rtp: Returning players may need individualized comparison with their own recent workload and recovery pattern. A normal subjective score or jump result alone should not override clinical status, exposure progression, or sport-specific function.

citation: Hides JA, Brown DA, Anning LN, Blanch PD, Leung FT. Decreased isometric neck strength is a risk factor for head, neck and face injuries in professional rugby league players. Journal of Sports Sciences. 2024. Published online ahead of print.
abstract: This exploratory prospective study tested whether preseason cervical strength, endurance, and proprioception measures were associated with head, neck, and face injuries causing missed games in professional rugby league players.
tldr: In one 32-player professional rugby league squad, lower neck-extensor strength and lateral-flexor asymmetry were associated with greater odds of head, neck, or face injury. The findings justify further testing and targeted assessment, not universal cut points or a claim that neck strengthening prevents injury.
methods: Thirty-two adult male players from one professional Queensland rugby league squad completed preseason measures of cervical flexor, extensor, and lateral-flexor isometric strength, flexor endurance, and joint-position error. Preseason and playing-season injuries leading to missed games were recorded, and unadjusted odds ratios were estimated from cross-tabulations.
findings: Players below the study's extensor-strength cut points of 36.4 kg or 3.4 N/kg had an unadjusted injury odds ratio of 8.0, and those with a left-to-right lateral-flexor strength ratio below 0.91 had an odds ratio of 12.6. Confidence intervals were wide and the asymmetry association was a novel finding.
limitations: This was a convenience sample from one team with few injuries, wide confidence intervals, and insufficient power for some variables. Analyses were unadjusted, multiple comparisons were not corrected, and exposure, collision frequency, position, and prior-injury confounding were not fully modeled.
practicalImplications: Cervical strength and side-to-side capacity can be included in contact-sport profiling when staff can test reliably and connect findings to progressive training. Treat the published cut points as local exploratory references and validate changes against the athlete's own function and exposure.
athleteDev: Build neck capacity progressively alongside tackle technique, trunk control, and contact preparation. Explain that strength is one modifiable factor within a broader injury-risk system rather than a guarantee of protection.
rtp: After head, neck, or face injury, cervical testing may complement symptom, neurological, range-of-motion, strength-endurance, and contact-tolerance criteria. Do not use these preseason cut points as stand-alone clearance tests.

citation: Oliva-Lozano JM, Gómez-Carmona CD, Rojas-Valverde D, Fortes V, Pino-Ortega J. Effect of training day, match, and length of the microcycle on the worst-case scenarios in professional soccer players. Research in Sports Medicine. 2021. Published online ahead of print.
abstract: This professional soccer cohort study described rolling worst-case locomotor demands across training days and matches and examined whether training-day peaks differed with microcycle length.
tldr: Across 23 professional soccer players, 43 training sessions, and 13 matches, match peak demands exceeded training across all tested durations. Training peaks varied by day and microcycle length, supporting locally calibrated rolling peak-demand planning rather than fixed generic drill targets.
methods: Twenty-three Spanish second-division outfield players were monitored across four competitive mesocycles comprising 43 training sessions and 13 matches. Rolling 1-, 3-, 5-, and 10-minute worst-case windows were calculated for total distance, high-speed-running distance, and sprinting distance and compared by day relative to match and microcycle length.
findings: Matches produced the highest worst-case values at every intensity and duration. Among training days, the largest distance, high-speed, and sprint peaks generally occurred four or three days before the match and one day after; training-day peaks differed across shorter, regular, and longer microcycles, while match peaks did not.
limitations: Data came from one team and four mesocycles, excluded goalkeepers and incomplete sessions, and depended on GPS accuracy. The observational analysis did not determine whether reproducing match peaks in training improves adaptation, performance, or injury outcomes.
practicalImplications: Calculate rolling peak demands from the team's own match data, then design selected drills and weekly exposures around relevant time windows. Adjust targets by position, schedule length, recent match minutes, and the intended purpose of each day.
athleteDev: Expose athletes progressively to the intensity and duration combinations their roles require while preserving technical quality. Use peak-demand data to explain preparation goals and avoid turning a single maximal value into the target for every session.
rtp: Compare a returning player's rolling high-intensity exposures with role-specific training and match references as one part of reconditioning. Peak running exposure does not replace clinical criteria, movement quality, contact readiness, or accumulated-load tolerance.

citation: Gołaś A, Pietraszewski P, Roczniok R, Terbalyan A, Maszczyk A, Opaliński R, Zając A. Effects of an 8-week pre-season targeted training on sprinting performance, agility and lower limb muscular asymmetries in elite soccer players. Biology of Sport. 2024;41(4):69-76.
abstract: This randomized preseason study tested whether adding a targeted unilateral movement-pattern program improved sprinting, change-of-direction performance, and lower-limb muscle-activation asymmetry in elite soccer players.
tldr: An eight-week bundled program of unilateral bodyweight exercises performed four days per week improved selected sprint and change-of-direction outcomes in 32 elite soccer players. The study does not show which component mattered or that changing EMG asymmetry prevents injury.
methods: Thirty-two elite soccer players were randomized to 16-player control and experimental groups. Both were tested before and after an eight-week preseason for 5- and 30-m sprint, randomized ZigZag change of direction, and bilateral quadriceps, hamstring, and gluteal EMG; the experimental group added six unilateral bodyweight exercises four times weekly with progressive volume.
findings: The experimental program produced statistically significant improvement in 5-m and 30-m sprint performance and change of direction, with the largest gains in the change-of-direction test and a reduced change-of-direction deficit. The authors also reported altered activation patterns and partial reductions in muscular asymmetry.
limitations: The small sample, single preseason, and bundled intervention limit attribution to any one exercise. Surface EMG measured activation rather than muscle force or adaptation, and no prospective injury outcome was collected despite proposed injury-risk implications.
practicalImplications: A short, frequent unilateral movement-pattern circuit may be one component of preseason preparation when it complements sprint, change-of-direction, and resistance work. Track performance and tolerance directly instead of assuming EMG normalization is the mechanism.
athleteDev: Progress movement quality, unilateral control, acceleration, and change-of-direction skill together. Individualize volume and exercise difficulty so added accessory work supports rather than displaces high-value field and strength exposures.
rtp: The circuit may provide low-equipment supplemental work during late reconditioning, but return decisions require progressive high-speed running, braking, cutting, and sport-specific exposure rather than asymmetry or EMG results alone.

citation: Niederer D, Engeroff T, Wilke J, Vogt L, Banzer W. Return to play, performance, and career duration after anterior cruciate ligament rupture: A case-control study in the five biggest football nations in Europe. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2018.
abstract: This five-year media-based case-control study compared return, competitive level, match performance, and career survival after ACL rupture with matched controls in elite male European soccer.
tldr: Nearly all 125 injured professional players returned after ACL rupture, but only 59.4% returned at the same level and career survival and match performance were lower than in matched controls. Binary return rate therefore overstates recovery of competitive function.
methods: The authors identified 132 ACL ruptures in 125 male players from the first two leagues of England, Spain, Italy, Germany, and France during 2010/11 and 2011/12. Each injured player was matched to two controls by age, position, country and league, and market value; validated public databases supplied five-year participation, injury, performance, and career data.
findings: The overall return-to-play rate was 98.2%, but return at the same level was 59.4%. Five years after return, 69.9% remained in football and 40.9% at the same level; career duration differed from controls, and scoring points, passing measures, and minutes played were lower in the return and post-return seasons.
limitations: Media sources did not provide clinical confirmation, injury side, surgical technique, rehabilitation detail, symptoms, or non-time-loss history. Although database validation and matching strengthen the design, residual confounding and incomplete injury characterization remain.
practicalImplications: Report return as a multidimensional outcome: availability, same-level participation, minutes, role, performance, subsequent injury, and career continuity. Prepare stakeholders for a high chance of playing again without promising immediate or complete competitive restoration.
athleteDev: Maintain long-horizon physical, technical, and psychological development after the first match back. Continued exposure progression and role support matter because the return date is the start of performance restoration, not its endpoint.
rtp: Clearance should distinguish return to training, return to competition, return to the prior level, and sustainable performance. Monitor match minutes, high-intensity actions, confidence, knee response, and subsequent injuries beyond initial return.

citation: Collings TJ, Bourne MN, Barrett RS, Meinders E, Gonçalves B, Shield A, Diamond LE. Reconsidering Exercise Selection with EMG: Poor Agreement between Ranking Hip Exercises with Gluteal EMG and Muscle Force. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2025. Published ahead of print.
abstract: This laboratory study compared rankings of hip-focused exercises based on gluteal surface EMG with rankings based on muscle-force estimates from neuromusculoskeletal modeling.
tldr: Eight hip exercises ranked differently when judged by peak gluteal EMG versus estimated gluteal muscle force in 14 female footballers. EMG may help with within-person comparisons of similar tasks, but peak activation alone is a weak basis for choosing among biomechanically different exercises.
methods: Fourteen healthy female footballers aged 18-30 performed eight hip-focused exercises using body weight and 12-repetition-maximum loads. Full-body kinematics, ground-reaction forces, and EMG from 12 lower-limb muscles were inputs to a neuromusculoskeletal model; normalized exercise rankings and EMG-force relationships were compared.
findings: Rank correlations between EMG and estimated force were weak, with Spearman rho values of 0.29-0.51. Peak EMG alone explained 5% of gluteus-maximus and 19% of gluteus-medius peak-force variation across exercises, although models accounting for participant and exercise effects explained 80-85% within that structured context.
limitations: The sample was small and female, only eight exercises were studied, and force estimates were not directly validated against in-vivo muscle force. Muscle-tendon parameters were not fully personalized, and neither proxy measured chronic adaptation or clinical outcome.
practicalImplications: Choose exercises from the athlete's goal, joint mechanics, external load, range, tolerance, and progression options. Use EMG to answer narrow within-athlete questions among comparable tasks, not to create universal best-exercise rankings.
athleteDev: Teach athletes that feeling or seeing high activation does not automatically mean greater force or better adaptation. Progress exercise challenge through load, range, intent, control, and transfer to the required task.
rtp: During rehabilitation, do not advance or reject an exercise from EMG amplitude alone. Combine symptoms, movement quality, strength capacity, loading tolerance, and task-specific progression with any instrumented information.

citation: Mattocks KT, Jessee MB, Mouser JG, Dankel SJ, Buckner SL, Bell ZW, Owens JG, Abe T, Loenneke JP. The Application of Blood Flow Restriction: Lessons From the Laboratory. Current Sports Medicine Reports. 2018;17(4):129-134.
abstract: This narrative review translated laboratory evidence on blood-flow restriction into practical guidance for exercise and rehabilitation, emphasizing how cuff and individual characteristics determine the applied restriction.
tldr: Blood-flow restriction can produce muscular adaptation with low loads and may help when heavy loading is not appropriate, but pressure is not interchangeable across cuffs or athletes. Individualized arterial-occlusion-based dosing and trained oversight are central safety requirements.
methods: The authors narratively reviewed laboratory and clinical evidence on blood-flow restriction alone and with low-load resistance or aerobic exercise. They discussed cuff width and material, limb size, arterial occlusion, common repetition structures, practical wrapping, rehabilitation applications, and safety considerations.
findings: Low-load blood-flow-restriction training can increase muscle size and strength and may support rehabilitation or disuse periods. Wider cuffs require less absolute pressure, larger limbs generally require more pressure, and the same absolute pressure can create very different restriction across individuals; the review recommends relative individualized pressure.
limitations: This was not a systematic review or a new comparative trial. Protocols and populations varied, adverse-event evidence was incomplete, and practical elastic wrapping had limited validation outside young resistance-trained men and uncertain vascular effects.
practicalImplications: Use blood-flow restriction only within an established clinical or performance protocol that includes contraindication screening, appropriate equipment, individualized pressure, staff competency, symptom monitoring, and documented progression.
athleteDev: Position blood-flow restriction as a temporary loading tool rather than a shortcut. Preserve technical development and progressively restore conventional strength, power, and sport exposure as capacity permits.
rtp: Blood-flow restriction may help maintain or rebuild muscle when high external loads are temporarily limited. It does not establish tissue readiness or sport clearance and should remain subordinate to diagnosis-specific healing, strength, function, and exposure criteria.

citation: Pippas C, Dagloukiaris N, Antypas A, Touloupis E, Gioftsos G. The effect of the Copenhagen Adduction and Nordic Hamstring exercises on muscle strength and athletic performance: a quasi-experimental study. Journal of Orthopaedic Reports. 2024;100524.
abstract: This quasi-experimental preseason study examined strength and performance changes after adolescent male soccer players combined Nordic hamstring and Copenhagen adduction exercises for four weeks.
tldr: The twice-weekly four-week program increased hamstring and hip-adduction strength in 38 adolescent male soccer players, but did not produce clear jump or sprint improvement. The uncontrolled design cannot separate the program from normal preseason change.
methods: Thirty-eight male players from one Greek soccer club completed a progressive four-week preseason program combining Nordic hamstring and Copenhagen adduction exercises twice weekly. Hand-held dynamometry assessed isometric hamstring and eccentric adduction strength; jump, sprint, and perceived-exertion outcomes were also recorded.
findings: Isometric hamstring strength increased about 11% and eccentric hip-adduction strength about 17%. Jump performance declined 5-7%, sprint performance changed about 2-3% with inconsistent statistical significance, and perceived exertion did not differ meaningfully between the exercises.
limitations: The study lacked randomization and a control group, experienced substantial loss to follow-up because testing occurred on separate occasions, and ran alongside normal preseason training. These limitations weaken causal attribution and may contribute to imprecise performance findings.
practicalImplications: Nordic hamstring and Copenhagen adduction exercises can be paired as a concise targeted-strength block, but staff should manage preseason dose and evaluate sprint and jump response separately rather than assuming automatic performance transfer.
athleteDev: Build eccentric hamstring and hip-adduction capacity progressively with sound technique and tolerable soreness. Integrate the work with sprinting, jumping, and soccer practice so targeted strength supports broader development.
rtp: These exercises may contribute to criterion-based hamstring or groin rehabilitation after appropriate progression. Strength improvement alone does not establish sprinting, cutting, kicking, or competition readiness.

citation: Lemes IR, Smaira FI, Ribeiro WJD, Favero NK, Matos LDNJ, Pinto ALS, Dolan E, Gualano B, Coalition SPORT-COVID-19. Acute and post-acute COVID-19 presentations in athletes: a systematic review and meta-analysis. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2022.
abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis characterized acute symptoms, persistent symptoms, and cardiac findings after COVID-19 in professional, amateur, collegiate, and university athletes.
tldr: Across 43 studies and 11,518 athletes, most infections were mild or asymptomatic and severe illness was uncommon, while a minority reported persistent symptoms. Cardiac abnormalities varied with testing and controlled studies did not confirm that COVID-19 caused myocardial involvement.
methods: MEDLINE, EMBASE, Scopus, and SPORTDiscus were searched for observational athlete studies published from 2019 through January 6, 2022. Forty-three studies with 11,518 athletes met criteria; Joanna Briggs Institute tools assessed risk of bias and random-effects models pooled acute, post-acute, and cardiac event rates.
findings: The pooled asymptomatic estimate was 25.5% and severe acute disease 1.3%, indicating about 94% experienced mild or no acute symptoms. Persistent symptoms were estimated at 8.3%. Myocardial involvement was 5.0% among athletes receiving any cardiac testing and 2.5% with MRI, but controlled studies did not establish causality.
limitations: Studies varied substantially in athlete selection, testing indication, timing, symptom and cardiac definitions, follow-up, and risk of bias. Serial assessments were uncommon, confidence intervals were wide for persistent symptoms, and imaging findings were not consistently linked with symptoms or clinical consequences.
practicalImplications: Most athletes can follow a symptom-guided graded return after appropriate medical review, but persistent cardiopulmonary, systemic, or exercise-intolerance symptoms warrant individualized assessment. Avoid indiscriminate imaging or reassurance based solely on population averages.
athleteDev: Support honest symptom reporting and a gradual rebuild of aerobic, strength, and sport-specific work after illness. Normalize short-term modification so athletes do not hide symptoms to accelerate return.
rtp: Return timing should reflect illness severity, current symptoms, exercise response, and relevant medical findings. Persistent chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, syncope, or disproportionate fatigue requires clinical evaluation; incidental imaging findings need expert interpretation.

citation: Jukic I, García-Ramos A, Helms ER, McGuigan MR, Tufano JJ. Acute Effects of Cluster and Rest Redistribution Set Structures on Mechanical, Metabolic, and Perceptual Fatigue During and After Resistance Training: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Sports Medicine. 2020.
abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis compared traditional resistance-training sets with cluster and rest-redistribution structures for acute mechanical, metabolic, and perceptual responses.
tldr: Across 32 studies, distributing rest within or between sets generally preserved velocity and power and reduced lactate and perceived exertion. Cluster sets often showed larger effects partly because they added more total rest, and the review did not establish superior long-term adaptation.
methods: Five databases were searched through June 2019 under PRISMA guidance for healthy-adult studies comparing traditional, cluster, or rest-redistribution sets. Thirty-two studies were included, with random-effects meta-analysis, subgroup analysis, and meta-regression used where data allowed.
findings: Alternative structures improved absolute mean and peak velocity and power and more strongly reduced the decline in velocity and power during and after training. They also reduced lactate accumulation and perceived exertion; cluster sets generally produced larger fatigue-mitigation effects than rest redistribution.
limitations: Exercises, loads, repetitions, failure proximity, total rest, training status, and outcomes varied. Cluster protocols often increased total rest relative to traditional sets, subgroup samples were small, and the evidence primarily concerned acute responses rather than chronic strength, hypertrophy, or power development.
practicalImplications: Use clusters or redistributed rest when the session priority is preserving repetition speed, power, or technical quality or constraining acute fatigue. Match total rest when evaluating whether the set structure itself adds value, and preserve traditional sets when metabolic stress is intentional.
athleteDev: Teach athletes to align set structure with the day's objective. Repeated high-quality efforts may benefit from planned micro-rest, while work-capacity or hypertrophy goals may deliberately accept more fatigue.
rtp: Alternative set structures can help reintroduce resistance work while limiting velocity loss and perceived strain. They do not replace diagnosis-specific load limits, symptom response, or progression to continuous sets and sport demands.

citation: Cecilia-Gallego P, Odriozola A, Beltran-Garrido JV, Álvarez-Herms J. Acute effects of overspeed stimuli with towing system on athletic sprint performance: A systematic review with meta-analysis. Journal of Sports Sciences. 2022.
abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated acute sprint-speed, spatiotemporal, force, and electromyographic responses when athletes sprinted with towing-assisted overspeed systems.
tldr: Towing assistance acutely increased maximum running speed and stride length and reduced contact time across 16 studies. The evidence could not determine whether these changes reflected athlete neuromuscular behavior or direct device assistance, and it did not establish retained unassisted speed gains.
methods: PubMed, SPORTDiscus, and Google Scholar were searched using PRISMA methods. Sixteen studies involving 240 men and 56 women aged 14-31 years were included, and acute assisted-sprint outcomes were pooled where appropriate.
findings: Overspeed towing produced a large acute increase in maximum running speed, a moderate increase in stride length, a small increase in flight time, a trivial increase in stride rate, and a small decrease in contact time. Ground-reaction-force and EMG evidence was too inconsistent to explain the mechanism.
limitations: Towing systems, assistance loads, sprint protocols, athlete levels, and biomechanical measures varied, with limited elite-sprinter evidence. Most outcomes were immediate responses under assistance, force and EMG data were sparse, and long-term unassisted transfer was not established.
practicalImplications: If overspeed towing is used, quantify and individualize assistance, preserve upright mechanics, and stop when athletes lose control. Evaluate subsequent unassisted sprint performance over time rather than counting the assisted speed itself as adaptation.
athleteDev: Introduce supramaximal exposure only after athletes demonstrate robust unassisted sprint mechanics and adequate tissue capacity. Keep assisted work as a small, monitored complement to acceleration, maximum-velocity, strength, and technical training.
rtp: Overspeed towing is generally a late-stage performance tool, not an early return intervention. Require symptom-free high-speed running and progressive unassisted exposure before considering assisted velocities.

citation: Philipp NM, Crawford DA, Cabarkapa D, Fry AC. Strength and Power Thresholds to Identify High and Low Linear Sprint Speed Performers in Collegiate American Football Players. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2024;38(1):74-79.
abstract: This cross-sectional classification study evaluated strength and power thresholds associated with faster and slower 40-yard-dash performance in collegiate American football players grouped by body mass.
tldr: Vertical and broad jumps best distinguished faster from slower 40-yard-dash performers in 294 collegiate football players, while relative hang clean and squat added group-specific information. The cut points are roster-specific classification references, not universal speed prescriptions.
methods: Researchers analyzed 294 NCAA football players and divided them into high-body-mass and low-body-mass groups of 147 athletes each. Players completed a hand-timed 40-yard dash, vertical and broad jumps, and relative 3-repetition-maximum strength and power tests. Median splits defined faster and slower groups, and receiver-operating-characteristic and logistic-regression analyses quantified discrimination and thresholds.
findings: Areas under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve ranged from 0.695 to 0.903. In the high-body-mass group, vertical jump had an AUC of 0.903, broad jump 0.883, and relative hang clean 0.848. In the low-body-mass group, vertical jump had an AUC of 0.779, broad jump 0.753, and relative squat 0.740. Threshold values varied by body-mass group and test.
limitations: The study was cross-sectional and used a median split, hand timing, jump-mat measures, and 3-repetition-maximum lifts. Nutrition and hydration were not controlled, and the male collegiate-football thresholds were not tested prospectively or in an external roster.
practicalImplications: Use jump and relative-strength results as supporting context when profiling speed qualities within comparable position and body-mass groups. Build local reference distributions and validate any cut points against the program's own timing and testing methods before using them in decisions.
athleteDev: Show athletes how relative force and power qualities relate to sprint profiles without turning one threshold into a label. Pair test results with technical sprint observation, training history, position demands, and repeat testing.
rtp: These thresholds were derived from healthy players and are not return-to-sport criteria. During reconditioning, compare the athlete with preinjury and position-relevant trends while restoring sprint exposure and task tolerance progressively.

citation: Mah CD, Mah KE, Kezirian EJ, Dement WC. The Effects of Sleep Extension on the Athletic Performance of Collegiate Basketball Players. Sleep. 2011;34(7):943-950.
abstract: This uncontrolled pre-post study examined whether extending sleep opportunity affected sport performance, vigilance, sleepiness, and mood in men's collegiate basketball players.
tldr: Eleven collegiate basketball players slept about 111 minutes longer and improved sprint, shooting, vigilance, sleepiness, and mood measures during a sleep-extension phase. Because the study lacked a control group, it supports correcting sleep insufficiency but cannot isolate sleep as the cause of every change.
methods: Eleven healthy Stanford men's varsity basketball players completed a 2- to 4-week habitual-sleep baseline and then 5 to 7 weeks of sleep extension with a goal of at least 10 hours in bed each night. Wrist actigraphy, sleep logs, a timed sprint, free throws, three-point shots, psychomotor vigilance, Epworth Sleepiness Scale, and mood measures were collected repeatedly.
findings: Objective sleep duration increased by 110.9 plus or minus 79.7 minutes. Mean sprint time improved from 16.2 to 15.5 seconds, free-throw accuracy increased by 9 percentage points, and three-point accuracy increased by 9.2 percentage points. Psychomotor vigilance, daytime sleepiness, and mood also improved during the extension phase.
limitations: The sample was small, male, and drawn from one team, with no randomization, crossover, or concurrent control. Season progression, practice exposure, expectancy, and repayment of accumulated sleep debt could have influenced the outcomes.
practicalImplications: When an athlete is habitually undersleeping, create more sleep opportunity and monitor actual sleep, alertness, mood, and performance over several weeks. Set schedules around individual sleep need rather than treating 10 hours in bed as a mandatory universal dose.
athleteDev: Teach athletes to recognize chronic sleep restriction and to plan bedtime, wake time, travel, study, and recovery routines. Use repeated data to connect sleep opportunity with how the athlete feels and performs.
rtp: Adequate sleep supports recovery and learning during rehabilitation, but improved alertness does not equal restored tissue capacity. Integrate sleep support with medical criteria, progressive loading, and task-specific reconditioning.

citation: Draper G, Atkinson G, Chesterton P, Portas M, Wright M. Elite North American Soccer Performance in Thermally Challenging Environments: An Explorative Approach to Tracking Outcomes. Journal of Sports Sciences. 2023;41(11):1107-1114.
abstract: This longitudinal observational study explored associations between environmental heat measures, match-running output, and differential perceived exertion in elite North American soccer.
tldr: Across four seasons, hotter conditions had mostly trivial-to-small associations with elite soccer running outputs, including small reductions in high-speed running and a small increase in breathlessness RPE. Environmental heat is useful context, not a stand-alone predictor of match demand.
methods: Thirty-seven elite male soccer players contributed between 3 and 98 match observations across four North American seasons. GPS-derived total and high-speed distance and differential ratings of perceived exertion were paired with kickoff temperature, weekly temperature change, and heat index. Within-player general linear models and repeated-measures correlations estimated associations.
findings: Associations between thermal variables and total distance were trivial to small. Higher temperature and heat index were associated with small reductions in high-speed running, with correlations of approximately -0.17 to -0.14 for most thermal measures. Heat index also had a small positive relationship with breathlessness RPE, while other perceptual associations were limited.
limitations: Players contributed unequal numbers of matches, and wet-bulb globe temperature was unavailable. The models could not fully account for fixture congestion, substitutions, tactics, travel, hydration, cooling, or individual acclimatization.
practicalImplications: Add heat and heat index to match-context dashboards and compare each athlete's output and perceptual response with similar exposures. Use the signal alongside role, minutes, tactics, travel, and recovery status when planning hydration, cooling, substitutions, and subsequent training.
athleteDev: Help athletes develop individualized heat plans through practice exposures, hydration and cooling routines, and postmatch review. Emphasize that perceived breathing strain and external output may respond differently.
rtp: During return to competition in hot conditions, progress environmental and match demands together. A small group-average temperature effect does not replace symptom monitoring, medical judgment, or individual heat-tolerance assessment.

citation: Daly E, Pearce AJ, Esser P, Ryan L. Evaluating the Relationship Between Neurological Function, Neuromuscular Fatigue, and Subjective Performance Measures in Professional Rugby Union Players. Frontiers in Sports and Active Living. 2022;4:1058326.
abstract: This professional rugby case series evaluated relationships among neurological, autonomic, neuromuscular, mood, and injury-status measures collected repeatedly during the competitive season.
tldr: Neurological, neuromuscular, autonomic, and subjective readiness measures in 11 professional rugby players were largely nonredundant; reactive strength had only a weak association with direct-current potential. The results favor a multi-signal review over one proprietary readiness score.
methods: Eleven male senior professional rugby union players were tested three times per week for six weeks during midseason. Measures included Omegawave direct-current potential and heart-rate-variability outputs, countermovement-jump reactive strength index modified, Profile of Mood States, and injury status. Repeated observations were examined for relationships among measures.
findings: Reactive strength index modified and direct-current potential had a weak negative correlation of r = -0.17. The broader neurological, autonomic, neuromuscular, and subjective measures showed limited convergence, suggesting that they reflected different aspects of player status rather than one interchangeable readiness construct.
limitations: The case series involved 11 male players in one professional environment over six weeks and had no control group. A proprietary system generated neurological values, and the study did not establish prospective injury prediction, decision thresholds, or long-term validity.
practicalImplications: Review readiness signals together and investigate meaningful within-athlete deviations rather than expecting one metric to summarize the athlete. Document the decision rule, repeatability, context, and action linked to each measure before it enters daily practice.
athleteDev: Use monitoring conversations to build athlete self-awareness and reporting trust. Explain what each measure can and cannot indicate so athletes do not interpret a single low score as proof of fatigue or injury.
rtp: A multi-domain dashboard can support reconditioning review, but none of these measures is a clearance test. Return decisions still require clinical status, progressive exposure, function, and sport-specific tolerance.

citation: Bramah C, Tawiah-Dodoo J, Rhodes S, Elliott JD, Dos'Santos T. The Sprint Mechanics Assessment Score: A Qualitative Screening Tool for the In-field Assessment of Sprint Running Mechanics. American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2024;52(6):1608-1616.
abstract: This methodological study developed and tested the rater reliability of a 12-item field-based qualitative score for maximum-velocity sprint mechanics in elite soccer players.
tldr: The 12-item Sprint Mechanics Assessment Score showed good within- and between-rater reliability on elite soccer sprint video, with a 1-point standard error. It can structure observation, but reliability does not establish injury prediction or coaching effectiveness.
methods: Maximum 35-m sprint videos from 136 elite soccer players were scored using the 12-item Sprint Mechanics Assessment Score. A balanced subgroup of 36 players, 18 men and 18 women, was rescored to assess intrarater and interrater reliability with intraclass correlations, standard error of measurement, and item-level agreement.
findings: Intrarater reliability was good with an ICC of 0.828 and interrater reliability was good with an ICC of 0.799; both had a standard error of measurement of 1 point. Item agreement ranged from 75.0% to 88.8% within raters and 66.6% to 88.8% between raters. Overall scores did not differ by sex.
limitations: The study established reliability only. It used a single sprint trial and assessors familiar with the method, and it did not test prospective injury risk, sensitivity to intervention, novice-rater performance, or transfer beyond elite soccer.
practicalImplications: Use the score as a repeatable vocabulary for reviewing sprint video and prioritizing a deeper technical assessment. Account for the 1-point measurement error and avoid acting on isolated item changes without repeat observation and performance context.
athleteDev: Pair video and the score with athlete-friendly technical feedback, one or two trainable priorities, and repeat trials. Preserve individual solutions instead of treating every flagged item as a fault that must be standardized.
rtp: The score may help document sprint-mechanics progression after injury, but it is not a validated injury-risk or clearance tool. Combine it with symptoms, capacity, exposure, speed, and sport-task tolerance.

citation: Miller RM, Chambers TL, Burns SP. Validating InBody 570 Multi-frequency Bioelectrical Impedance Analyzer Versus DXA for Body Fat Percentage Analysis. Journal of Exercise Physiology Online. 2016;19(5):71-78.
abstract: This validation study compared body-fat percentage from the InBody 570 multifrequency bioelectrical impedance analyzer with dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry in recreationally active university adults.
tldr: InBody 570 and DXA body-fat percentages were strongly correlated in 110 young adults, but InBody averaged 4.62 percentage points lower. The devices should not be treated as interchangeable for absolute body-fat values.
methods: Seventy-two men and 38 women aged 18 to 25 years completed InBody 570 and DXA assessment during the same visit after instructions to fast for 12 hours, avoid exercise for 12 hours, and avoid alcohol for 24 hours. Correlations, shared variance, and mean differences were calculated for the full sample and sex subgroups.
findings: InBody and DXA body-fat percentages correlated at r = 0.94, representing 88% shared variance. Mean body-fat percentage was 25.61% by DXA and 20.99% by InBody, and the overall and subgroup method differences were statistically significant at P less than .0001.
limitations: Correlation measures association rather than agreement, and the report did not provide a Bland-Altman analysis. The sample was young and recreationally active, preparation compliance was self-reported, hydration was not objectively verified, and results are specific to the tested device and algorithm.
practicalImplications: For longitudinal monitoring, standardize preparation, time of day, device, and operator and interpret change against normal device error. Do not compare an athlete's InBody percentage directly with a DXA percentage as though they share the same scale.
athleteDev: Frame body-composition data as one imperfect monitoring input, protect athlete privacy, and avoid value judgments around a single percentage. Focus feedback on health, fueling, training, and meaningful trends.
rtp: Body-fat percentage is not a general return-to-sport criterion. If composition monitoring is medically relevant, use consistent methods and integrate the result with clinical, nutrition, and functional information.

citation: Liu M, Yu Y. Adverse Effects of Anabolic Androgenic Steroid Abuse in Athletes and Physically Active Individuals: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Substance Use and Misuse. 2025;60(6):873-887.
abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis quantified cardiovascular, hepatic, lipid, and endocrine differences associated with anabolic-androgenic steroid abuse in athletes and physically active individuals.
tldr: Anabolic-androgenic steroid abuse was associated with meaningfully higher blood pressure, LDL cholesterol, and liver enzymes and lower testosterone. Heterogeneous observational exposure evidence supports medical concern but cannot predict an individual athlete's exact effect.
methods: The authors systematically identified studies comparing athletes or physically active anabolic-androgenic steroid users with nonusers and pooled continuous cardiometabolic, hepatic, and endocrine outcomes. Random-effects analyses generated weighted mean differences and 95% confidence intervals, with study quality and publication-bias considerations reported.
findings: Steroid abuse was associated with systolic blood pressure 12.43 mmHg higher, 95% CI 9.59 to 15.26; diastolic pressure 8.09 mmHg higher, 95% CI 5.62 to 10.57; LDL cholesterol 9.12 mg/dL higher; AST 14.47 U/L higher; ALT 12.16 U/L higher; and testosterone 141.57 ng/dL lower than comparison groups.
limitations: Studies varied in quality, steroid type, dose, duration, co-use, and outcome assessment and were vulnerable to selection and publication bias. Most exposure evidence was observational, and unmeasured polysubstance use and comorbidities limit causal and individual-level interpretation.
practicalImplications: Provide confidential, nonpunitive screening and education about cardiovascular, hepatic, endocrine, and mental-health risks. Abnormal history, symptoms, blood pressure, or laboratory findings should trigger appropriate medical assessment rather than performance-staff diagnosis.
athleteDev: Build supplement and drug literacy, explain that appearance and short-term performance do not indicate safety, and make help-seeking pathways clear. Avoid stigma that discourages honest disclosure.
rtp: Athletes with suspected adverse effects need clinician-led evaluation and individualized activity decisions. Normalization of one marker does not by itself establish recovery or readiness for unrestricted training.

citation: da Silva CA, Helal L, da Silva RP, Belli KC, Umpierre D, Stein R. Association of Lower Limb Compression Garments During High-Intensity Exercise With Performance and Physiological Responses: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Sports Medicine. 2018;48(8):1859-1873.
abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated whether lower-limb compression garments worn during high-intensity exercise improve performance or physiological and perceptual responses.
tldr: Across 23 randomized trials, lower-limb compression garments worn during intense exercise did not meaningfully improve running, jumping, oxygen uptake, lactate, or perceived exertion. Comfort or recovery preferences should be separated from acute performance claims.
methods: The review included 23 randomized controlled trials in athletes and physically active adults. Meta-analyses compared compression garments with control conditions for running performance across distances, vertical jump, maximal and submaximal oxygen uptake, blood lactate, and rating of perceived exertion.
findings: No meaningful benefit was found for the pooled performance or physiological outcomes. The weighted mean difference for 50- to 400-m running was 0.06 seconds, 95% CI -1.99 to 2.11, and the pooled RPE difference was -0.20 units, 95% CI -0.48 to 0.08. Heterogeneity was generally low.
limitations: Several trials incompletely reported randomization and allocation. Garment pressure, exercise protocols, and running distances varied; some analyses shared control groups, and the evidence focused on garments worn during exercise rather than every possible postexercise recovery use.
practicalImplications: Do not allocate training or competition resources on the assumption that lower-limb compression garments reliably enhance acute high-intensity performance. If athletes prefer them, assess comfort, fit, cost, and the separate evidence for the intended recovery use.
athleteDev: Teach athletes to distinguish plausible mechanisms and marketing claims from demonstrated performance effects. An individual preference can be respected without presenting it as a proven ergogenic aid.
rtp: Compression garments are not a substitute for progressive loading, symptom monitoring, or objective function. Any use during rehabilitation should be tied to a specific comfort or clinical purpose rather than presumed performance restoration.

citation: Vasireddi N, Hahamyan HA, Gould HP, Gregory AJM, Gausden EB, Dodson CC, Voos JE, Calcei JG. Athlete Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators Abuse: A Systematic Review. American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2025;53(4):999-1009.
abstract: This systematic review synthesized athlete SARM use, potential performance effects, adverse outcomes, and the reliability of products marketed as selective androgen receptor modulators.
tldr: The SARM literature suggests low but uncertain athlete use, possible lean-mass effects, serious hepatic and other safety concerns, and frequent mismatch between product labels and contents. No SARM is approved for athlete performance use.
methods: The review included 72 articles published from 2003 through 2022, spanning prevalence surveys, clinical and preclinical studies, product analyses, and case reports. Thirteen case reports described 15 men, including eight athletes, with a median age of 32 years and a mean reported oral exposure of eight weeks.
findings: Available athlete surveys estimated SARM use at approximately 1% to 3%. The literature described possible lean-mass and performance-related effects alongside hepatic, cardiovascular, endocrine, and tendon concerns. Online products were often contaminated, mislabeled, or supplied at doses above those studied clinically.
limitations: Study designs and outcomes were too heterogeneous for meta-analysis. Only four SARMs were emphasized, case reports and co-supplementation prevent causal attribution, abstracts were excluded, and the prevalence evidence was limited and vulnerable to underreporting.
practicalImplications: Ask explicitly about SARMs and internet-purchased supplements during health and nutrition reviews. Treat the product label as unreliable, reinforce anti-doping implications, and direct symptoms or use disclosures to qualified medical care.
athleteDev: Teach athletes that selective marketing does not mean tissue-selective safety and that an unapproved product can contain undeclared drugs. Make confidential disclosure and help-seeking easier than concealment.
rtp: Potential hepatic, cardiovascular, endocrine, or tendon effects require clinician-led evaluation. Stopping use or feeling better is not by itself sufficient evidence for unrestricted return.

citation: Singh U, Leicht AS, Connor JD, Brice SM, Alves A, Doma K. Biomechanical Determinants of Change of Direction Performance: A Systematic Review. Sports Medicine. 2025;55(9):2207-2224.
abstract: This systematic review synthesized biomechanical variables associated with faster preplanned change-of-direction performance across different cutting angles.
tldr: Faster change of direction was associated with shorter contact, greater approach and exit speed, stronger braking and propulsion, lower center of mass, and task-specific trunk and joint mechanics. These correlates vary by angle and do not establish one universal causal technique.
methods: Thirteen studies involving 374 participants were reviewed, with methodological quality scores ranging from 73% to 96%. Studies examined preplanned 45- to 180-degree change-of-direction tasks and related completion time or velocity to ground-contact, force, center-of-mass, trunk, joint-moment, power, and kinematic variables.
findings: Faster performance was commonly associated with shorter ground-contact time, higher approach and exit velocity, greater braking and propulsive forces, greater trunk inclination, a lower center of mass, and larger task-specific lower-limb moments and power. The relevant strategy changed with cut angle and task constraints.
limitations: The evidence was correlational, tasks and timing methods were heterogeneous, and 79.4% of participants were male. No included study examined unplanned or reactive change of direction, and sex-, sport-, and training-status moderation were poorly resolved.
practicalImplications: Profile change-of-direction tasks by angle, approach speed, braking demand, exit objective, and decision component. Coach the athlete's limiting strategy and retest the same task rather than applying one technical cue across every cut.
athleteDev: Develop braking capacity, reacceleration, trunk control, and perception-action skill progressively. Use video and force information to help athletes understand tradeoffs between speed, control, and joint loading.
rtp: Progress from planned to increasingly reactive and sport-specific cuts while monitoring symptoms, speed, braking exposure, and movement strategy. Cross-sectional biomechanical correlates are not clearance thresholds.

citation: Barber-Westin S, Noyes FR. Blood Flow-Restricted Training for Lower Extremity Muscle Weakness Due to Knee Pathology: A Systematic Review. Sports Health. 2019;11(1):69-83.
abstract: This systematic review evaluated blood-flow-restricted training for lower-extremity weakness in patients with ACL reconstruction, knee arthroscopy, osteoarthritis, or patellofemoral pain.
tldr: Blood-flow-restricted exercise improved strength in six of seven controlled knee-rehabilitation studies, but protocols were heterogeneous and evidence for hypertrophy, hamstrings, and safety was less complete. Use it as a supervised load-management option, not a universal replacement for heavy resistance training.
methods: Nine controlled studies, eight level 1 and one level 2, included 165 patients and 170 control participants with ACL reconstruction, knee arthroscopy, knee osteoarthritis, or patellofemoral pain. The review compared blood-flow-restricted protocols with conventional rehabilitation for strength, muscle size, function, and reported complications.
findings: Six of seven studies that measured strength reported significant benefit from blood-flow-restricted training. Some studies reported quadriceps cross-sectional-area gains, while only two addressed hamstring outcomes. No training complications were reported in the included studies.
limitations: Studies were small and differed in knee pathology, cuff system, pressure, load, duration, and comparator. Most evidence concerned quadriceps strength, significance was not consistently linked to minimal clinically important change, and zero reported complications cannot establish safety across broader populations.
