practicalImplications: Consider blood-flow-restricted exercise when pain, healing status, or joint tolerance limits heavy loading. Screen contraindications, use individualized occlusion pressure and trained supervision, and progress toward conventional resistance and functional loading as tolerance allows.
athleteDev: Explain the purpose, expected discomfort, safety checks, and progression criteria before use. The method should expand the athlete's loading options while preserving confidence in the longer rehabilitation plan.
rtp: Improved strength under blood-flow restriction is one rehabilitation input, not proof of sport readiness. Restore unrestricted strength, rate of force, movement, running, and sport exposure before clearance.

citation: Diaz-Lara J, Nieto-Acevedo R, Abian-Vicen J, Del Coso J. Can Caffeine Change the Game? Effects of Acute Caffeine Intake on Specific Performance in Intermittent Sports During Competition: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2024;19(11):1180-1196.
abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated acute caffeine effects on competition-specific actions and external-load outcomes in intermittent team, racket, and combat sports.
tldr: Across 24 double-blind crossover studies, acute caffeine produced small-to-moderate increases in several intermittent-sport actions, including sprints, accelerations, decelerations, impacts, offensive efforts, and successful actions. Individual response and sleep or side-effect costs still require trialing.
methods: Twenty-four double-blind randomized crossover studies included 399 participants, 264 male and 135 female, from team, racket, and combat sports. Caffeine doses were generally about 3 to 6.4 mg/kg, and meta-analyses pooled competition or competition-like counts of sprints, impacts, accelerations, decelerations, offensive actions, and successful sport-specific efforts.
findings: Caffeine increased sprints with an SMD of 0.48, impacts 0.28, accelerations 0.35, decelerations 0.63, offensive efforts 0.36, and successful actions 0.44. Effects were not uniform across every sport or outcome and represent acute group-average responses.
limitations: Sports, caffeine forms, timing, doses, and outcome definitions varied. Only two studies checked blinding, while habitual caffeine use, expectancy, adverse effects, sex-specific response, and the effect of late-day intake on sleep were inconsistently assessed.
practicalImplications: Trial caffeine in training with the exact competition timing, food, hydration, and sleep context. Start near the lower end of effective dosing, record benefit and adverse response, and avoid assuming more caffeine produces more performance.
athleteDev: Teach dose literacy, product verification, and the tradeoff between an acute stimulus and later sleep. Athletes should have a rehearsed plan and a clear option not to use caffeine.
rtp: Caffeine may alter alertness and output but does not restore tissue capacity or substitute for graded exposure. During return to sport, avoid using stimulation to mask symptoms or exceed the planned workload.

citation: Metoyer CJ, Lever JR, McGinty M, Landow L, Hunt R, Hauenstein JD, Huebner A, Stone MH, Wagle JP. The Impact of Localized Muscle Mass on Sprint Mechanics During the Swing and Stance Phases of Division I Collegiate American Football Players. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2025;39(9):959-963.
abstract: This cross-sectional study examined how MRI-measured lower-extremity muscle volumes related to sprint swing and stance times across three position groups of Division I football players.
tldr: Localized muscle-volume relationships with sprint phase times differed among Skills, Mids, and Bigs. The findings support position-specific profiling questions, but they do not show that selectively increasing or limiting one muscle will improve speed.
methods: One hundred eight male Division I football players were classified as Skills, Mids, or Bigs. Lower-extremity muscle volumes were quantified with MRI, maximal-sprint stance and swing times were captured with inertial sensors, and stepwise multiple regressions were conducted separately within each position group.
findings: Different muscle volumes were associated with shorter or longer swing and stance times in each position group. For example, greater vastus intermedius and sartorius volume related to shorter swing time in Skills, while other quadriceps, hamstring, hip, and lower-leg associations varied across Mids and Bigs. No single muscle profile generalized across positions.
limitations: The cross-sectional regressions cannot establish training causality and may overfit correlated muscle measures. Testing occurred across multiple sites, involved one male collegiate program, and did not test longitudinal adaptation, change of direction, injury, or whether isolated muscle targeting improves performance.
practicalImplications: Use body-composition and sprint-mechanics information to form position-specific hypotheses and select broader training priorities. Validate any proposed relationship through repeat sprint testing and training response rather than acting directly on one regression coefficient.
athleteDev: Help athletes understand that useful mass depends on role, distribution, force expression, and movement skill. Avoid labeling one muscle as good or bad from a cross-sectional association.
rtp: These healthy-athlete associations are not clearance criteria. During reconditioning, prioritize restored capacity, sprint exposure, phase mechanics, symptoms, and position-specific task tolerance.

citation: Oldham JR, Lanois CJ, Caccese JB, Crenshaw JR, Knight CA, Berkstresser B, Wang F, Howell DR, Meehan WP III, Buckley TA. Association Between Collision Sport Career Duration and Gait Performance in Male Collegiate Student-Athletes. American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2022;50(9):2526-2533.
abstract: This cross-sectional study tested whether longer collision-sport career duration was associated with poorer single- or dual-task gait in male collegiate athletes.
tldr: Among 168 male collegiate collision-sport athletes, career duration was not associated with gait, cognitive accuracy, or dual-task cost. The null findings apply to healthy young men and do not establish that cumulative head impacts are harmless or predict later-life outcomes.
methods: Male football, lacrosse, ice hockey, and wrestling athletes completed preseason instrumented single- and dual-task walking. Gait speed, stride length, working-memory accuracy, and dual-task costs were related to self-reported collision-sport career duration using linear regression.
findings: Career duration was not significantly associated with single-task gait speed, beta -0.004, P=.35, or dual-task gait speed, beta -0.003, P=.57. Stride length, cognitive accuracy, and motor or cognitive dual-task costs were also not significantly associated with career duration.
limitations: Exposure duration and continuity were self-reported, actual head-impact dose and sport rule differences were unavailable, and the study included only healthy college-aged men. Cross-sectional clinical gait testing may miss subtle or later-emerging effects.
practicalImplications: Do not use years played alone or a normal gait test as a cumulative-brain-health verdict. Maintain exposure reduction, symptom reporting, concussion care, and longitudinal multimodal assessment.
athleteDev: Explain that a null group result is reassuring only for the measured tasks and age range. Encourage honest symptom reporting and long-term brain-health habits without using career duration to frighten or falsely reassure athletes.
rtp: Instrumented gait can contribute to concussion assessment, but this study does not validate it as a stand-alone clearance test or cumulative-exposure screen.

citation: Nosek P, Brownlee TE, Drust B, Andrew M. Feedback of GPS Training Data Within Professional English Soccer: A Comparison of Decision Making and Perceptions Between Coaches, Players and Performance Staff. Science and Medicine in Football. 2021;5(1):35-47.
abstract: This survey study compared how professional-soccer coaches, players, and performance staff perceived GPS training feedback, decision value, barriers, and preferred delivery.
tldr: Professional-soccer stakeholders valued GPS feedback but wanted different information and delivery. Too much data, poor communication, and no shared purpose reduced usefulness, making report design and conversation as important as metric collection.
methods: An online convenience survey was completed by 176 coaches, players, and performance staff working in professional soccer. Questions covered the importance of data to reflection and decision making, desired variables, barriers to use, behavior-change perceptions, and player delivery preferences.
findings: All groups rated training data as at least somewhat important. Coaches most wanted high-intensity actions and work-rate information; players preferred total distance, high-speed running, and sprint distance and commonly favored messages or changing-room displays. Information volume, communication, and lack of a common goal emerged as barriers.
limitations: The convenience sample was small relative to professional soccer, could include clustered responses from the same clubs, and measured perceptions rather than observed decisions or performance. The findings concerned GPS and do not automatically transfer to other monitoring systems.
practicalImplications: Define the decision and audience before sending data. Use a small metric set, shared language, appropriate timing, and a clear action or reflection prompt; evaluate whether feedback changes understanding and behavior.
athleteDev: Give athletes concise, role-relevant feedback and invite interpretation rather than sending unexplained numbers. Athlete input on timing, format, and usefulness should be part of the monitoring process.
rtp: Return-to-sport dashboards should communicate the current question, comparison, uncertainty, and next action. More GPS variables do not make a clearance decision stronger without clinical and functional context.

citation: Askling C, Karlsson J, Thorstensson A. Hamstring Injury Occurrence in Elite Soccer Players After Preseason Strength Training With Eccentric Overload. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine and Science in Sports. 2003;13(4):244-250.
abstract: This randomized trial evaluated whether additional preseason flywheel hamstring training affected hamstring injury occurrence, strength, and sprint speed in elite male soccer players.
tldr: Ten weeks of additional concentric-eccentric flywheel hamstring training was followed by fewer injured players, 3 of 15 versus 10 of 15, plus strength and sprint gains. The small trial and unusually high control injury rate limit the precision and portability of the effect.
methods: Thirty elite male players from two Swedish teams were randomized to ordinary training or 16 additional hamstring sessions over 10 weeks. The intervention used bilateral knee flexion on a flywheel device with eccentric overload. Isokinetic strength and maximal running speed were tested, and hamstring injuries were recorded over 10 months.
findings: Hamstring injuries occurred in 3 of 15 training-group players and 10 of 15 controls. The intervention group significantly improved concentric and eccentric hamstring strength and maximal running speed, but performance changes were not clearly coupled to individual injury occurrence.
limitations: The sample was small and unblinded, detailed football exposure was not recorded, team personnel registered injuries, and control-group injury occurrence was unusually high. The combined flywheel protocol does not isolate an exercise, dose, or mechanism.
practicalImplications: Include progressive eccentric-overload hamstring work during preseason, but treat it as one component of preparation. Monitor tolerance and combine it with sprint exposure, total loading, availability, and ongoing injury surveillance.
athleteDev: Teach athletes why hamstring capacity and high-speed exposure are developed progressively. Build technique and adherence without implying that completing one exercise eliminates injury risk.
rtp: Eccentric hamstring work can support reconditioning, but return requires restored strength, sprint exposure, symptoms, confidence, and sport-specific tolerance rather than completion of a flywheel protocol alone.

citation: Guerrero-Calderón B, Klemp M, Morcillo JA, Memmert D. How Does the Workload Applied During the Training Week and the Contextual Factors Affect the Physical Responses of Professional Soccer Players in the Match? International Journal of Sports Science and Coaching. 2021;16(4):994-1003.
abstract: This season-long observational study modeled how weekly GPS training load and contextual factors related to subsequent match-running output in two professional soccer teams.
tldr: Weekly training and match context explained substantial variation in professional-soccer running output. Higher weekly high-intensity distance related positively and total distance negatively to match output, but the observational models are local planning evidence rather than a causal microcycle formula.
methods: GPS training and match records from Spanish first- and second-division teams were analyzed across a season using linear mixed models. Weekly total, high-intensity, and sprint distance were related to match outputs while accounting for player, position, season period, division, opposition quality, and formation.
findings: Conditional R-squared values were 0.51 for match total distance, 0.58 for high-intensity running, and 0.60 for sprint distance. Weekly total distance had a negative relationship with match output, high-intensity distance had a positive relationship, and position, season period, division, and opposition quality contributed context.
limitations: The two-team observational design cannot establish that changing weekly load causes the predicted match response. Results depend on GPS thresholds and model choices and did not fully represent tactical, technical, internal-load, wellness, or availability factors.
practicalImplications: Build team-specific models and review high-intensity exposure alongside total volume and match context. Use estimates to support, not dictate, microcycle decisions and monitor whether changes improve availability and match preparation.
athleteDev: Explain why similar weekly totals can contain different intensity and recovery demands. Use individual trends and role requirements to help athletes understand the purpose of each exposure.
rtp: A returning player's weekly load should be progressed against individual tolerance and planned match demands. Group associations do not provide clearance thresholds or justify rapid high-intensity escalation.

citation: Docter S, Khan M, Gohal C, Ravi B, Bhandari M, Gandhi R, Leroux T. Cannabis Use and Sport: A Systematic Review. Sports Health. 2020;12(2):189-199.
abstract: This systematic review synthesized athlete cannabis-use prevalence, evidence on performance and recovery, and sport-policy variation.
tldr: About 23.4% of respondents across 11 athlete studies reported past-year cannabis use, but performance evidence was sparse and inconsistent and no direct recovery evidence was found. Cannabis, THC, and CBD should not be presented as interchangeable or proven recovery tools.
methods: PubMed, MEDLINE, and Embase were searched through November 2018, supplemented by sport policies and official documents. Thirty-seven studies were included; 11 prevalence studies represented 46,202 respondents, and most research was cross-sectional in elite or university athletes.
findings: Approximately 23.4% of athletes reported cannabis use in the prior 12 months. Two studies reported negative performance effects and two reported no effect. No eligible study directly assessed athletic recovery, and sport organizations varied widely in urine THC thresholds and sanctions at the time of review.
limitations: Evidence was primarily level-4, self-reported, and heterogeneous in athlete population, product, cannabinoid, dose, timing, and outcome. Recovery evidence was absent, and regulations summarized in 2020 may no longer be current.
practicalImplications: Use confidential, nonjudgmental screening and distinguish THC, CBD, route, dose, timing, product quality, and current anti-doping policy. Do not recommend cannabis for recovery based on this evidence.
athleteDev: Build substance and product literacy, including impairment, contamination, legal, and anti-doping risks. Make help-seeking easier than concealment and avoid assuming use means misuse.
rtp: Cannabis should not be used to mask pain, sleep difficulty, or anxiety during return to sport. Symptoms and use disclosures may require medical assessment, but use history alone is not a clearance decision.

citation: McHugh C, Hind K, Davey D, Wilson F. Cardiovascular Health of Retired Field-Based Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2019;7(8):2325967119862750.
abstract: This systematic review evaluated cardiovascular risk factors and subclinical disease in retired male football and soccer athletes.
tldr: Retired football and soccer athletes had a mixed cardiovascular profile rather than durable protection from prior sport. Higher body mass and lineman history identified greater concern, supporting structured health transition and long-term screening.
methods: Thirteen studies included 4,350 retired male field-sport athletes aged approximately 42 to 66 years, and eight studies included controls. Cardiovascular risk factors, coronary calcium, carotid plaque, and position-related findings were reviewed with methodological-quality assessment and random-effects analysis where possible.
findings: Four of six studies reported higher systolic blood pressure in retired athletes, about half reported higher HDL, about 80% lower triglycerides, and all reporting LDL comparisons found higher LDL. Coronary calcium and carotid plaque were similar to controls, while retired linemen had roughly twice the cardiometabolic-syndrome prevalence of nonlinemen.
limitations: Definitions and reporting were inconsistent, observational studies were vulnerable to selection, survivor, body-mass, and lifestyle confounding, and only male football and soccer athletes were represented. The evidence did not support one pooled retired-athlete risk estimate.
practicalImplications: Create a transition pathway that preserves activity and follows blood pressure, lipids, body composition, symptoms, sleep, and primary care after sport. Give added attention to athletes leaving high-body-mass roles.
athleteDev: Prepare athletes for health after eligibility or retirement, including sustainable training, nutrition, medical follow-up, identity transition, and social support. Prior fitness is not permanent protection.
rtp: This review concerns long-term health rather than injury clearance. Cardiovascular symptoms or abnormal screening during return to activity require clinician-led evaluation and individualized exercise decisions.

citation: van der Vlist AC, Breda SJ, Oei EHG, Verhaar JAN, de Vos RJ. Clinical Risk Factors for Achilles Tendinopathy: A Systematic Review. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2019;53(21):1352-1361.
abstract: This systematic review evaluated longitudinal clinical factors associated with the development of Achilles tendinopathy.
tldr: Ten high-risk-of-bias cohort studies provided only limited evidence for nine possible Achilles-tendinopathy risk factors, while 26 commonly proposed factors were not associated. The review does not support a universal screening score.
methods: Five databases were searched through February 2018 for human cohort studies of clinical risk factors. Ten cohorts were retained from 5,111 records. Imaging-only factors were excluded, risk of bias was assessed, and heterogeneity prevented quantitative pooling.
findings: Limited evidence implicated prior lower-limb tendinopathy or fracture, ofloxacin exposure, cold-weather training, reduced plantar-flexor strength, selected gait features, moderate alcohol use, and renal or transplant-related factors. Overweight, static foot posture, physical activity level, and 23 other proposed factors were not associated.
limitations: Every included study had high risk of bias, definitions and populations were heterogeneous, only English-language publications were selected, and several signals arose from nonathlete medical populations. No causal effect or validated multivariable prediction rule was established.
practicalImplications: Prioritize history, symptoms, recent exposure, plantar-flexor capacity, medication, and medical context. Avoid using static posture, body mass, or an isolated screening measure as proof of future tendinopathy.
athleteDev: Teach progressive calf and tendon loading, recovery, and early symptom reporting. Frame risk as modifiable context and capacity rather than a fixed label.
rtp: Return decisions should follow symptoms, tendon loading tolerance, calf capacity, running and jumping exposure, and sport demands. The reviewed risk factors are not clearance thresholds.

citation: Henderson MJ, Grandou C, Chrismas BCR, Coutts AJ, Impellizzeri FM, Taylor L. Core Body Temperatures in Intermittent Sports: A Systematic Review. Sports Medicine. 2023;53(11):2147-2170.
abstract: This systematic review characterized peak competition core temperatures reported in healthy adult intermittent-sport athletes.
tldr: Most intermittent-sport studies observed competition hyperthermia: 24 of 34 reported peaks between 38.5 and 39.5 degrees Celsius and six reported at least 39.5 degrees. Heterogeneity prevents a universal threshold or one proven intervention.
methods: Web of Science, MEDLINE, and SPORTDiscus were searched through April 2023. Thirty-four studies with at least 386 participants were included if core temperature was measured during competition without an intervention intended to alter heat strain. Methodological characteristics were evaluated and findings synthesized descriptively.
findings: Four studies found no hyperthermia, 24 found modest hyperthermia with peak core temperature from 38.5 to 39.5 degrees Celsius, and six found marked hyperthermia at or above 39.5 degrees. Twenty-seven studies were observational, with the remainder experimental or quasi-experimental.
limitations: Sports, competition duration, environment, athlete level, measurement method, and sampling schedule were too heterogeneous for meta-analysis. Peak-temperature categories do not define individual illness, and intervention effectiveness was not evaluated.
practicalImplications: Prepare heat-acclimation, cooling, hydration, substitution, monitoring, and emergency plans for intermittent competition. Interpret temperature with symptoms, environment, workload, medical risk, and individual response.
athleteDev: Rehearse heat strategies and teach early symptom reporting. Athletes should understand that high strain can occur even when the sport includes breaks and that tolerance is not permission to ignore warning signs.
rtp: Progress environmental exposure alongside sport load after illness, injury, or heat intolerance. Core temperature alone is not a return criterion; medical history and symptom response remain central.

citation: Delgadillo BE, Montz F, Ward B Jr, Herson AB, Toldi JP. Current Evidence for the Use of Jugular Vein Compression Collars in Sport: A Systematic Review. Current Sports Medicine Reports. 2025;24(1):18-27.
abstract: This systematic review evaluated whether external jugular-vein compression collars reduce concussion or head-impact-related brain changes in high-impact sports and tactical activity.
tldr: Fifteen collar studies reported favorable selected imaging, neurocognitive, vascular, and pulse-pressure signals, but concussion incidence did not differ. Visible devices, team-level randomization, adolescent samples, and substantial manufacturer-linked evidence prevent a prevention claim.
methods: A multiple-database search through June 2024 identified 15 studies of jugular compression collars, including randomized trials and prospective analyses in sport and tactical settings. Outcomes included white-matter imaging, neurocognitive testing, vascular measures, pulse pressure, head impacts, and concussion incidence.
findings: Collar groups showed less alteration in selected white-matter measures, favorable short-term neurocognitive findings, larger internal jugular and smaller internal carotid cross-sectional area, and moderated peak pulse pressure. No significant concussion-incidence difference was established.
limitations: Most evidence involved adolescents, randomization was commonly by team, participants and observers could see collar assignment, and off-season impacts were not controlled. The Q-Collar inventor advised the company that funded most included studies, creating a material conflict-of-interest concern.
practicalImplications: Do not substitute a collar for established concussion prevention, exposure management, recognition, removal, and clinical care. Treat surrogate imaging and short-term findings as preliminary until independent trials demonstrate meaningful clinical benefit.
athleteDev: Explain the difference between a biomarker change and proven protection. Equipment should never encourage riskier contact behavior or reduced symptom reporting.
rtp: Jugular compression collars do not prevent the need for concussion assessment or alter return-to-sport progression. They are not clearance or treatment devices based on current evidence.

citation: Wittbrodt MT, Millard-Stafford M. Dehydration Impairs Cognitive Performance: A Meta-analysis. Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise. 2018;50(11):2360-2368.
abstract: This meta-analysis quantified how dehydration magnitude related to cognitive performance across different tasks and experimental protocols.
tldr: Dehydration produced a small overall cognitive decrement, with larger effects for attention, motor coordination, and executive function and above 2% body-mass loss. The 2% comparison is a group pattern, not a universal athlete threshold.
methods: Thirty-three studies provided 280 effect estimates from 413 participants with 1% to 6% body-mass loss. Standardized mean differences were pooled with multivariate meta-analysis, and cognitive domain, outcome type, dehydration magnitude, and study-design moderators were examined.
findings: The overall effect was -0.21, 95% CI -0.31 to -0.11. Attention was -0.52, motor coordination -0.40, and executive function -0.24. Effects were larger above 2% body-mass loss, -0.28, than at or below 2%, -0.14, while reaction-time-specific tasks were not significantly impaired.
limitations: Dehydration methods, heat and exercise exposure, cognitive tests, outcome definitions, and samples varied with significant heterogeneity. Mood, thirst, and effort may contribute, and many samples were small and convenient; subgroup results do not establish an individual cutoff.
practicalImplications: Protect hydration before decision-heavy practice and competition, especially in heat, and monitor individual fluid loss and response. Use body-mass change as context rather than a rigid cognitive-performance threshold.
athleteDev: Teach athletes to start hydrated, use rehearsed fluid plans, and recognize concentration, mood, coordination, and heat symptoms. Avoid both underdrinking and forced overdrinking.
rtp: Correct dehydration during illness or reconditioning, but do not interpret rehydration alone as restored readiness. Symptoms, medical status, and progressive task tolerance still govern return.

citation: O'Bryan KR, Doering TM, Morton RW, Coffey VG, Phillips SM, Cox GR. Do Multi-ingredient Protein Supplements Augment Resistance Training-induced Gains in Skeletal Muscle Mass and Strength? A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of 35 Trials. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2020;54(10):573-581.
abstract: This meta-analysis compared multi-ingredient protein supplementation with placebo, other non-multi-ingredient conditions, and protein-only supplementation during at least six weeks of resistance training.
tldr: Multi-ingredient protein products improved pooled fat-free mass and strength versus all non-multi-ingredient conditions, but they were not superior to protein alone. Training, adequate protein, safety, and cost remain the first decisions.
methods: Thirty-five randomized resistance-training trials lasting at least six weeks included 1,387 participants. Random-effects analyses pooled fat-free mass, fat mass, and upper- and lower-body one-repetition maximum strength, with subgroup analyses by training status and age.
findings: Versus all non-multi-ingredient conditions, multi-ingredient supplementation favored fat-free mass by 0.80 kg, lower-body one-repetition maximum by 4.22 kg, and upper-body one-repetition maximum by 2.56 kg. Benefits appeared larger in untrained and older groups, but direct comparisons showed no superiority to protein-only supplementation.
limitations: Only retrievable English-language trials were included, ingredients and comparators varied, and moderate heterogeneity remained. Pooling placebo and active controls can magnify the apparent blend effect, and product-specific results do not generalize to every formulation.
practicalImplications: First ensure sufficient energy, total protein, meal distribution, and progressive resistance training. If a multi-ingredient product is considered, compare it with a simpler protein option and verify dose, safety, third-party testing, cost, and athlete need.
athleteDev: Teach athletes to evaluate the full ingredient list and evidence rather than assuming more ingredients means more adaptation. Supplements should fill a defined need within a sound nutrition plan.
rtp: Protein supplementation may help meet rehabilitation nutrition targets, but a blend does not replace progressive loading or demonstrate readiness. Coordinate use with nutrition and medical staff.

citation: Watkins RA, Sugimoto D, Hunt D, Oldham J, Cacolice PA, Stracciolini A. Association of Social Media Use on Sleep Quality and Performance Among Collegiate Athletes. Clinical Journal of Sport Medicine. 2022;32(5):486-492.
abstract: This cross-sectional study examined associations among objectively recorded social-media time, sleep disturbance, and competition results in NCAA Division III track-and-field and swimming athletes.
tldr: Athletes using social media more than five hours per day reported worse sleep than those at two hours or less. Facebook time had a small association with competition outcomes, but total social-media time did not independently predict performance and the study cannot establish causation.
methods: Eighty-seven athletes from two Division III colleges provided seven days of iPhone screen-time data and completed lifestyle and PROMIS sleep-disturbance measures. Athletes were grouped as no more than 2, more than 2 to 5, or more than 5 hours of daily social-media use; season or personal-best competition results were classified from public records and analyzed with adjustment for candidate confounders.
findings: Mean social-media use was 4.6 ± 3.4 hours per day. The greater-than-5-hour group had worse sleep than the no-more-than-2-hour group (p=0.033). Greater Facebook time had a small adjusted association with not improving a season or personal best (adjusted OR 0.990, 95% CI 0.981-0.999), while total social-media time was not independently associated with the performance outcome.
limitations: The cross-sectional design cannot establish causation. The sample came from two colleges and two sport settings, platform tracking was limited to iPhone use and selected applications, the performance outcome was coarse, and residual confounding and multiple comparisons make the Facebook finding uncertain.
practicalImplications: Include digital habits in sleep and readiness conversations, especially when late or prolonged use coincides with poor sleep. Favor individualized routines, notification control, and protected wind-down time over a universal social-media ban.
athleteDev: Teach athletes to review their own screen-time and sleep pattern, test a realistic pre-sleep routine, and evaluate whether the change improves sleep and next-day function rather than treating one platform as inherently performance-limiting.
rtp: Social-media exposure is not a return-to-sport criterion. During rehabilitation, use sleep and digital routine as modifiable context alongside symptoms, training tolerance, and clinical progression.

citation: Cobian DG, Knurr KA, Joachim MR, Bednarek AL, Broderick AM, Heiderscheit BC. Does It Matter? Isometric or Isokinetic Assessment of Quadriceps Strength Symmetry 9 Months After ACLR in Collegiate Athletes. Sports Health. 2025;17(2):365-373.
abstract: This cross-sectional study compared isometric and isokinetic quadriceps limb-symmetry indices and their relationships with functional kinetics and self-reported knee function in collegiate athletes approximately nine months after ACL reconstruction.
tldr: Isometric and isokinetic symmetry agreed at the group level, but individual differences were wide enough that the modes should not be switched casually. Either can support testing when used consistently and interpreted with functional kinetics and athlete-reported status.
methods: Thirty-five NCAA Division I athletes at 8.9 ± 2.5 months after ACL reconstruction completed isometric and isokinetic knee-extension testing on an isokinetic dynamometer, countermovement jumps, treadmill running, and the IKDC subjective knee form. Bland-Altman analysis assessed agreement, and correlations and regressions assessed relationships with knee kinetics and IKDC scores.
findings: The mean difference between isokinetic and isometric strength symmetry was 1.0%, but 95% limits of agreement ranged from -25.1% to 23.0%. Isometric symmetry correlated moderately to strongly with running and jump kinetics (r=0.64-0.80), while isokinetic symmetry correlations were moderate (r=0.41-0.58). Both had weaker relationships with IKDC scores.
limitations: The sample was small, narrow, and mostly bone-patellar tendon-bone autografts from one Division I setting. All testing used an isokinetic dynamometer, fatigue may have affected a long testing battery, and sex, sport, graft type, and concomitant procedures could not be fully examined.
practicalImplications: Select the contraction mode that fits available equipment and the program's testing history, then keep it consistent across serial assessments. Interpret strength symmetry with absolute torque, movement kinetics, symptoms, confidence, and progressive sport exposure.
athleteDev: Explain that an apparently similar group average does not make the two tests identical for one athlete. Show the athlete trends from the same protocol and connect those trends to functional tasks.
rtp: Either isometric or isokinetic symmetry can contribute to an ACL return-to-sport battery, but neither is a stand-alone clearance test. Avoid comparing a current score with a prior score collected in the other mode.

citation: Pareja-Blanco F, Pereira LA, Reis VP, Fernandes V, Arruda AFS, Guerriero A, Alcaraz PE, Freitas TT, Loturco I. Impact of Sled Loads on Performance and Kinematics of Elite Sprinters and Rugby Players. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2022;17(3):465-473.
abstract: This acute experimental study compared sprint velocity and lower-limb kinematics when elite sprinters and rugby-union players towed sleds loaded at fixed percentages of body mass.
tldr: The same 20% and 60% body-mass sled loads did not create the same velocity or technical response in elite sprinters and rugby players. Sled prescription should be individualized by observed velocity decrement and mechanics, not body-mass percentage alone.
methods: Eight elite male sprinters and ten male rugby-union players performed 20-m sprints with 0%, 20%, and 60% of body mass on their sport-specific surfaces. Timing splits were recorded over 0-5, 5-10, and 10-20 m, and an eight-sensor motion-analysis system measured stride length and hip, knee, and ankle angles.
findings: Sprinters were faster unloaded and at 20% body mass, but group speed differences were no longer significant at 60%. Sprinters showed less velocity decrement than rugby players at 20% but more at 60%. Stride length did not differ consistently, while hip flexion and plantar-flexion responses differed by group and load.
limitations: The acute cross-sectional comparison included only 18 elite men and tested 20 m. Sport-specific surface and footwear differed between groups, and the study did not establish longitudinal training effects, longer-distance transfer, or injury implications.
practicalImplications: Choose a target velocity decrement and inspect sprint technique under load. Recalibrate sled mass when athlete, surface, footwear, or training phase changes rather than assuming the same body-mass percentage creates the same stimulus.
athleteDev: Teach athletes that heavier is not automatically better and that the goal is a specific acceleration stimulus with acceptable mechanics. Use timing feedback to make the intended overload visible.
rtp: For reconditioning, progress sled work by symptoms, velocity decrement, mechanics, and exposure tolerance. These healthy-athlete acute data do not define return-to-sprint or clearance thresholds.

citation: Thornton HR, Delaney JA, Duthie GM, Dascombe BJ. Importance of Various Training-Load Measures in Injury Incidence of Professional Rugby League Athletes. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2017;12(6):819-824.
abstract: This three-season cohort study examined how internal and external training-load features related to injury status across positions and individual professional rugby-league players.
tldr: The load variables most associated with injury differed by position and athlete. The study supports individualized monitoring but does not provide universal workload thresholds or prove that a machine-learning alert prevents injury.
methods: Daily training-load and injury-status data were collected from 25 National Rugby League players across the 2013-2015 seasons. Inputs included session-RPE load, total distance, high-speed-running distance, and high-metabolic-power distance across rolling windows and ratios. Generalized estimating equations and random forests were applied by position and athlete.
findings: For adjustables, 7-day total distance and high-metabolic-power distance ranked highly; for hit-up forwards, session-RPE ratio and 14-day total distance were prominent; outside backs emphasized longer session-RPE windows, and wide-running forwards emphasized the session-RPE ratio. Individual models showed substantial variation in feature importance.
limitations: The observational study involved one club and 25 players. Feature importance may be specific to that team's exposures, availability definition, and monitoring workflow; flexible individual models can overfit repeated data, and association with injury status cannot establish causal thresholds or prospective decision benefit.
practicalImplications: Build monitoring around the athlete's role, history, and current capacity. Use load features to structure questions and multidisciplinary review, and prospectively test whether local alerts improve decisions before treating them as risk rules.
athleteDev: Frame workload feedback as a shared planning tool rather than a prediction that an athlete will be injured. Pair the data with the athlete's symptoms, context, and training goals.
rtp: Do not apply the paper's positional variables as return-to-sport cutoffs. During reconditioning, compare current exposures with the athlete's own staged plan, clinical status, and position demands.

citation: Miguens N, Brocherie F, Moulié L, Milhet P, Bon M, Lassus P, Toussaint JF, Sedeaud A. Individual In-Situ GPS-Derived Acceleration-Speed Profiling: Toward Automatization and Refinement in Male Professional Rugby Union Players. Sports Medicine - Open. 2024;10(1):6.
abstract: This methodological study automated acceleration-speed profiling from routine GPS data and quantified profile reliability, measurement error, positional differences, and session-type differences in professional rugby union.
tldr: Routine GPS data produced reliable-looking individual acceleration-speed profiles with automated outlier handling and explicit measurement error. The outputs are theoretical, data-quality dependent, and not validated as injury or return-to-sport decision rules.
methods: Data from 49 male professional rugby-union players included 61.5 million GPS positions across 51 training sessions and 11 matches. Acceleration was derived from speed, density-based clustering removed atypical points, and linear profiles produced theoretical maximal acceleration, theoretical maximal speed, and slope. Two two-week phases were compared for reliability.
findings: Every individual relationship was linear with R-squared above 0.81. Two-week ICCs ranged from 0.72 to 0.92 and SEM from 4.2% to 8.6%. Profiles differed by position and session type; matches tended to expose the highest theoretical acceleration while speed sessions exposed the highest theoretical speed.
limitations: Results depend on GPS quality and acceleration derived from changes in speed rather than the embedded accelerometer. The intercepts are modeled rather than directly achieved maxima, the sample was one male professional setting, and no performance, injury, or return-to-sport outcome validation was performed.
practicalImplications: Use routine data to supplement formal speed testing and to identify whether training and competition expose the athlete's profile. Display uncertainty and require changes to exceed measurement error before acting.
athleteDev: Show athletes how different sessions expose acceleration and speed qualities, while explaining that the profile is an estimate shaped by the data captured rather than a fixed label of ability.
rtp: A profile may help document exposure progression, but its theoretical values are not clearance criteria. Combine them with direct sprint testing, symptoms, tissue capacity, mechanics, and sport-specific task tolerance.

citation: Suarez-Arrones L, Núñez FJ, Lara-Lopez P, Di Salvo V, Méndez-Villanueva A. Inertial Flywheel Knee- and Hip-Dominant Hamstring Strength Exercises in Professional Soccer Players: Muscle Use and Velocity-Based Mechanical Eccentric Overload. PLOS ONE. 2020;15(10):e0239977.
abstract: This acute experimental study compared mechanical output and regional hamstring MRI responses to flywheel leg curl and conic-pulley hip extension in elite male professional soccer players.
tldr: Flywheel leg curl and hip extension created different regional hamstring-use patterns, and eccentric overload depended on the metric and exercise. The acute MRI response can guide exercise emphasis but does not prove injury prevention or long-term adaptation.
methods: Nineteen elite male professional soccer players were enrolled and 18 analyzed after assignment to flywheel leg curl (n=10) or conic-pulley hip extension (n=8). Athletes completed four sets of eight repetitions. Encoder measures quantified concentric and eccentric power, velocity, and time, while pre/post 3-T functional MRI T2 shifts assessed regional hamstring response.
findings: Leg curl produced broader use of all four hamstring bellies and greater emphasis on semitendinosus and short-head biceps femoris. Hip extension emphasized proximal and medial long-head biceps femoris. Eccentric overload was observed for peak power in hip extension but was not consistently present across mean power, velocity, and exercise comparisons.
limitations: The sample was small and unfamiliar with inertial devices, the study measured one acute session, and MRI T2 change is a metabolic proxy affected by tendon and elastic work. No longitudinal strength, hypertrophy, sprint, injury, or reinjury outcome was measured.
practicalImplications: Select knee- and hip-dominant flywheel exercises according to the desired regional emphasis and movement role, provide familiarization, and monitor technique and output. Use a broader hamstring program rather than assuming one device supplies complete eccentric overload.
athleteDev: Explain why two hamstring exercises may feel and load differently even when both are described as eccentric. Use objective output and tolerance to progress the exercise rather than chasing soreness.
rtp: Regional emphasis may help exercise selection after hamstring injury, but the study does not establish reinjury protection or a lesion-specific protocol. Progress by healing status, symptoms, strength, sprint exposure, and sport function.

citation: O'Riordan SF, Bishop DJ, Halson SL, Broatch JR. Do Sports Compression Garments Alter Measures of Peripheral Blood Flow? A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis. Sports Medicine. 2023;53(2):481-501.
abstract: This systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis evaluated whether sports compression garments change peripheral arterial or venous blood-flow measures at rest, during, immediately after, and in recovery from physiological challenges.
tldr: Compression garments produced small changes in peripheral blood-flow measures, especially venous flow, but effects varied by timing and vessel type. A blood-flow surrogate should not be interpreted as proof of improved recovery or performance.
methods: Twenty-two studies of healthy, active participants were included from 899 identified records. Twenty-three blood-flow measures were synthesized with random-effects models, and standardized mean differences were calculated by vessel type and timing relative to exercise or another physiological challenge.
findings: Overall peripheral flow improved modestly (SMD 0.32, 95% CI 0.13-0.51), as did venous (0.37) and arterial (0.30) flow. During a challenge the pooled effect was 0.44; immediately afterward there was no overall change. In recovery, overall flow was not significant, although the venous subgroup improved while arterial flow did not.
limitations: Studies varied across garments, applied pressure, timing, challenges, and 23 measurement methods. Participant and researcher blinding and pressure verification were often weak. The review team reported a research grant from 2XU, while stating that the manufacturer had no role in analysis or publication.
practicalImplications: Compression garments may be offered as an optional, low-complexity strategy when fit, pressure, comfort, and timing are controlled. Judge usefulness by the athlete's target outcome and response, not by the proposed blood-flow mechanism alone.
athleteDev: Set expectations that compression is an adjunct rather than a recovery substitute. Athletes should prioritize sleep, nutrition, hydration, and load management before relying on garments.
rtp: Blood-flow changes in healthy participants are not return-to-sport criteria. Use garments only as a tolerated adjunct within the clinical and loading plan, not as evidence that tissue readiness has been restored.

citation: Ward C, Ó Catháin C, Ní Chéilleachair N, Grassick S, Kelly DT. Does Resisted Sprint Training Improve the Sprint Performance of Field-Based Invasion Team Sport Players? A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Sports Medicine. 2024;54(3):659-672.
abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis compared resisted and unresisted sprint training and examined how load and prescription method influenced sprint outcomes in field-based invasion-sport players.
tldr: Resisted and unresisted sprinting improved sprint performance similarly. Resisted work was most useful for early acceleration, while no maximum-velocity improvement was detected, so it should complement rather than replace free sprinting.
methods: Twenty-one studies were included after PRISMA-guided searches. Between-group analyses compared resisted with unresisted sprinting; within-group analyses estimated change in early acceleration, late acceleration, and maximum velocity. Subgroups examined external load and prescription by percentage velocity decrement.
findings: Between-group analyses found no difference between resisted and unresisted sprint training across sprint phases. Resisted groups improved early acceleration (SMD -0.80) and late acceleration (-0.28) but not maximum velocity. Light and very heavy loads both improved early acceleration, and velocity-decrement prescription showed larger benefits than coarser load labels.
limitations: Loading methods, sports, concurrent team training, interventions, and risk of bias varied. Favorable phase estimates often came from within-group change, while the direct comparison showed equivalence, and the evidence does not identify one universally optimal load.
practicalImplications: Use resisted sprinting when the goal is acceleration-specific overload and retain adequate unresisted and maximum-velocity sprint exposure. Prescribe and monitor the actual velocity decrement rather than body-mass percentage or a light/heavy label alone.
athleteDev: Help athletes connect sled load with the intended acceleration quality and technical response. Stop adding load when velocity loss or mechanics no longer match the session goal.
rtp: Resisted sprinting can be one graded reconditioning tool, but these training studies do not define injury-specific progression or clearance. Advance alongside free sprinting, symptoms, mechanics, and exposure tolerance.

citation: Silva LM, Neiva HP, Marques MC, Izquierdo M, Marinho DA. Effects of Warm-Up, Post-Warm-Up, and Re-Warm-Up Strategies on Explosive Efforts in Team Sports: A Systematic Review. Sports Medicine. 2018;48(10):2285-2299.
abstract: This systematic review examined warm-up content and strategies for preserving or restoring explosive performance during the delay before play and at halftime in team sports.
tldr: Short, progressive, sport-specific warm-ups with explosive tasks generally supported sprint, jump, and agility performance. When athletes must wait, heat retention and brief re-warm-ups may preserve readiness, but protocol heterogeneity prevents one universal formula.
methods: Thirty articles published from 1981 through August 2017 met inclusion criteria after searches of four databases. The authors assessed risk of bias and recalculated Cohen's d for warm-up, post-warm-up, and re-warm-up strategies affecting explosive team-sport efforts.
findings: Examples included improved sprint performance after eight 60-m efforts and improved sprint, jump, and agility after dynamic activity following jogging. Heated garments outperformed passive rest in some transitions, while brief explosive re-warm-ups were most useful when delays exceeded 15 minutes and at halftime. The authors proposed a generally shorter 10-15 minute progressive warm-up.
limitations: Protocols, intensities, durations, recovery periods, control groups, sports, and outcomes varied widely. Several recommendations came from single studies, and the heterogeneity prevented meta-analysis or a definitive optimal protocol across populations.
practicalImplications: Design the warm-up backward from the first competitive demands and the expected delay before play. Preserve temperature during unavoidable inactivity and use a brief explosive re-warm-up when rules, space, and athlete readiness allow.
athleteDev: Give athletes a simple personal warm-up and re-warm-up menu that they can execute reliably under travel, bench, and halftime constraints, while retaining the team's common structure.
rtp: Reintegrate warm-up and re-warm-up demands progressively during return to sport. The review does not provide injury-specific readiness thresholds, so pair explosive preparation with clinical and exposure criteria.

citation: Davies TB, Kuang K, Orr R, Halaki M, Hackett D. Effect of Movement Velocity During Resistance Training on Dynamic Muscular Strength: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Sports Medicine. 2017;47(8):1603-1617.
abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis compared fast or explosive with moderate-slow resistance-training repetitions when prescribed intensity and volume were matched.
tldr: Fast and moderate-slow repetitions produced similar dynamic-strength gains overall. Faster movement at moderate loads showed only a small nonsignificant trend, so velocity should be selected for the exercise and adaptation goal rather than treated as universally superior.
methods: Fifteen comparative studies involving 509 participants aged 19-73 years met the criteria. Programs lasted at least four weeks, compared fast with moderate-slow isotonic training under matched prescribed intensity and volume, and measured dynamic strength. Subgroups examined intensity, age, and training status.
findings: Strength gains were similar when all intensities were pooled. At moderate intensities of 60-79% 1RM, faster training showed a small favorable trend (effect size 0.31, p=0.06). Age and training status did not explain a clear difference between velocities.
limitations: Loading, actual velocity, age, training status, exercise selection, and intervention duration varied substantially. More than half the interventions lasted only six to eight weeks, athlete-specific evidence was limited, and the moderate-load result did not reach conventional significance.
practicalImplications: Program repetition intent and speed alongside load, range of motion, fatigue, and technical quality. Use fast intent where power and rapid force expression matter, while recognizing that controlled slower work can still build strength.
athleteDev: Teach athletes that repetition speed is a programming variable, not a contest. The correct speed is the one that matches the load, exercise, and session goal while maintaining control.
rtp: Select movement velocity according to healing, symptoms, load tolerance, and the next functional demand. The review does not support a single velocity threshold for return-to-sport progression.

citation: Gong M, Sun M, Sun Y, Jin L, Li S. Effects of Acute Sleep Deprivation on Sporting Performance in Athletes: A Comprehensive Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Nature and Science of Sleep. 2024;16:935-948.
abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis quantified the effects of acute whole-night and partial sleep deprivation on multiple categories and times of athletic performance.
tldr: Acute sleep deprivation impaired athletic performance overall, with larger pooled effects for high-intensity intermittent work and skill control. Heterogeneous and sparse subgroups mean the exact effect size and time-of-day pattern should not be treated as a universal rule.
methods: Twenty-seven studies contributing 75 performance indicators were synthesized using Stata. Analyses estimated overall performance effects, compared whole-night and partial deprivation timing, grouped outcomes by athletic ability, and compared morning with afternoon performance after acute sleep deprivation.
findings: The overall effect was -0.56. Reported effects were -1.57 for high-intensity intermittent exercise, -1.06 for skill control, -0.67 for speed, -0.54 for aerobic endurance, and -0.39 for explosive power. Late-night or early-morning sleep loss and afternoon testing produced larger estimates in selected subgroup analyses.
limitations: Underlying studies varied in quality, deprivation protocol, athlete population, and outcome. Some subgroups contained very few indicators, outcome classification was debatable, and multiple indicators from studies may create more apparent precision than the independent evidence supports.
practicalImplications: Protect sleep before high-intensity, speed, skill, and decision-critical sessions. When acute loss is unavoidable, consider lowering complexity or dose, increasing monitoring, and rescheduling the most consequential work when feasible.
athleteDev: Build a practical sleep-loss plan before travel or schedule disruption: report the loss honestly, avoid compensating with reckless training or stimulant use, and coordinate adjustments with staff.
rtp: Acute sleep loss can reduce the quality of rehabilitation and testing. If readiness is clearly impaired, interpret performance tests cautiously and adjust the session rather than mistaking fatigue for tissue or skill capacity.

citation: Moran J, Ramirez-Campillo R, Liew B, Chaabene H, Behm DG, García-Hermoso A, Izquierdo M, Granacher U. Effects of Bilateral and Unilateral Resistance Training on Horizontally Orientated Movement Performance: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Sports Medicine. 2021;51(2):225-242.
abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis compared bilateral and unilateral resistance-training effects on sprinting and other horizontally oriented movement outcomes.
tldr: Both bilateral and unilateral training improved horizontal movement performance, and neither was superior overall. Programming can use both according to loading capacity, stability, symptoms, and movement goals.
methods: Eleven studies met inclusion criteria. Random-effects meta-analyses calculated standardized mean differences for short sprint and related horizontal movement outcomes, comparing bilateral with unilateral programs and exploring training type, duration, frequency, experience, and other moderators.
findings: Bilateral training improved performance with an SMD of 0.60 and unilateral training with an SMD of 0.57. The direct difference was nonsignificant (SMD 0.17, 95% CI -0.15 to 0.50), with moderate heterogeneity. Combined strength-plus-plyometric approaches tended to produce larger effects than strength-only programs.
limitations: Programs and outcomes varied, between-study heterogeneity was moderate, and moderator analyses split continuous variables and tested factors independently. Those choices limit power and cannot account for interactions among load, exercise, experience, and program design.
practicalImplications: Use a multidimensional program that includes bilateral and unilateral work. Let absolute-load needs, stability, equipment, movement direction, athlete preference, and response determine the balance rather than assuming specificity makes unilateral work superior.
athleteDev: Explain that bilateral and unilateral exercises solve different programming problems and both can transfer to movement. Progress quality and loading instead of treating one category as more athletic.
rtp: Unilateral work may help grade side-specific loading and bilateral work may restore higher absolute force, but neither mode is a clearance test. Select and progress both according to symptoms, capacity, mechanics, and sport demands.

citation: Kowal I, Donohue B, Barchard KA, Kraus SW, Allen DN. Examination of the Impact of Substance Use on Sport Training and Competition in Collegiate Athletes. Sport Social Work Journal. 2025;Advance online publication.
abstract: This methodological study developed and evaluated a four-item self-report measure of perceived alcohol- and illicit-drug interference with collegiate sport training and competition.
tldr: The four-item measure showed good one-week stability and expected relationships with substance use and psychiatric symptoms. It may support confidential screening conversations, but it is not a diagnosis or an objective measure of performance loss.
methods: A total of 285 NCAA, club, and intramural collegiate athletes completed the four interference items, validated psychiatric-symptom and substance-frequency measures, and demographic items. Reliability and construct relationships were evaluated; a selected subsample of 74 substance-using athletes interested in intervention also completed a structured diagnostic interview.
findings: One-week test-retest reliability was good. Interference scores related positively to psychiatric symptoms, substance-use frequency, and age, and males scored higher. NCAA athletes reported significantly less interference than club and intramural athletes (F(2,277)=8.11, p<.001), although the abstract states that athlete type had no effect. In the 74-athlete subsample, higher scores among those with a current substance-use disorder were only a nonsignificant trend (p=0.08).
limitations: The measure is self-reported and may be affected by stigma or perceived consequences. The diagnostic comparison used a small, selected intervention-interested subsample, and the study did not validate the score against objective training, competition, safety, or longitudinal outcomes.
practicalImplications: If used, embed the four questions in a confidential, supportive workflow with clear referral options and limits on data access. A positive response should prompt conversation and clinical assessment rather than automatic action.
athleteDev: Normalize early, confidential help-seeking and explain how substance use can interact with sleep, mood, recovery, safety, and performance. Preserve athlete trust by separating care from discipline whenever policy permits.
rtp: The score is not a clearance tool. Substance-related readiness decisions require clinical assessment of health, cognition, withdrawal or intoxication risk, treatment progress, and the demands and safety requirements of participation.

citation: Losak JM, Posmanick BJ, Sauer RD. On the Value of a Premium College Football Player: Evaluating the Literature. Journal of Sports Economics. 2024;25(4):472-506.
abstract: This sports-economics article reviewed and updated methods for estimating the marginal revenue product of premium college football players in a changing compensation environment.
tldr: Top college football players appear to generate substantially more institutional value than historical cost-of-attendance compensation, but the exact gap is highly model-dependent. This is athlete-welfare context, not health or training evidence.
methods: The authors reviewed foundational and contemporary marginal-revenue-product approaches and updated estimates using modern college-football revenue, draft-pick, team-performance, and institutional data. Alternative specifications included player-value measures and school and year fixed effects.
findings: Across historical and updated approaches, premium players generated values materially above cost-of-attendance compensation. Conservative fixed-effect estimates still supported a substantial gap, while estimated magnitude changed with how player quality, team success, revenue, institutional stability, and endogeneity were handled.
limitations: Marginal revenue product is sensitive to model specification, revenue-sharing and accounting choices, selection of premium-player proxies, and unmeasured program context. Fixed effects can absorb stable talent differences, causality remains uncertain, and the compensation and legal landscape continues to evolve.
practicalImplications: Use the work to understand the institutional and welfare context surrounding collegiate athletes and resource conversations. Current compensation policy or individual valuation requires current legal, financial, and governance expertise beyond this paper.
athleteDev: Recognize that financial treatment, role expectations, and perceived fairness can shape athlete trust and wellbeing. Keep those conversations distinct from judgments about commitment, health status, or training behavior.
rtp: The paper provides no rehabilitation or clearance evidence. Financial or roster context should not alter clinical standards, privacy, informed consent, or an athlete-centered return-to-participation process.

citation: D'Onofrio R, Laterza F, Sannicandro I, Masucci M, Bovenzi A, Manzi V. Injury Prevention in Professional Soccer Players: Can Re-warmup Training Be Organized in the Post-warmup and Half-time During a Soccer Game in a Short Time? Journal of Sports Medicine and Physical Fitness. 2024;64(9):950-957.
abstract: This narrative review synthesized brief re-warm-up strategies that could fit the post-warm-up delay and halftime of professional soccer competition.
tldr: Brief high-intensity activity can help preserve temperature and explosive readiness after passive match delays. The highlighted one-minute protocol is a practical template, not proof of injury prevention or a universal prescription.
methods: The authors searched PubMed, Web of Science, PEDro, SPORTDiscus, and Google Scholar without a date limit and narratively synthesized 26 papers relevant to professional-soccer post-warm-up or halftime reactivation. The review emphasized strategies lasting less than approximately 90 seconds.
findings: The review found that re-warm-up activity can mitigate decrements after passive rest. It highlighted one minute of high-intensity exercise near 90% VO2max that preserved sprint performance, muscle strength, and temperature and increased muscle activation without additional measured physiological or psychological fatigue.
limitations: The review did not systematically grade certainty, and its concise one-minute recommendation rests on limited and heterogeneous evidence. Most outcomes were performance, temperature, or activation rather than match injury incidence, and feasibility depends on competition rules and space.
practicalImplications: Build a rehearsed post-warm-up and halftime menu that preserves temperature and briefly restores explosive activity without creating fatigue. Test exact timing, modality, footwear, surface, staff roles, and substitute-specific options in the team's environment.
athleteDev: Teach athletes why passive waiting can reduce readiness and give them a short, repeatable reactivation routine they can execute under bench and halftime constraints.
rtp: Re-warm-up exposure can be progressed during reconditioning, but tolerance of one brief protocol is not clearance. Combine it with symptoms, capacity, football-specific exposure, and medical and performance criteria.

citation: Pietraszewski P, Gołaś A, Matusiński A, Mrzygłód S, Mostowik A, Maszczyk A. Muscle Activity Asymmetry of the Lower Limbs During Sprinting in Elite Soccer Players. Journal of Human Kinetics. 2020;75:239-245.
abstract: This laboratory study examined bilateral quadriceps, hamstring, and gluteal EMG activity and side-to-side asymmetry during maximal sprinting in elite male soccer players.
tldr: Hamstring and gluteal activation asymmetry related to 5-m and 30-m sprint time in a small elite-soccer sample. The measurements are descriptive and do not prove injury risk or that targeted activation work improves outcomes.
methods: Sixteen elite male soccer players completed two maximal 30-m sprints separated by five minutes. Textile electrodes recorded bilateral quadriceps, hamstring, and gluteal muscle-group activity, and regression analyses examined relationships between side-to-side average activation asymmetry and 5-m and 30-m sprint times.
findings: Hamstring asymmetry had significant regression relationships with 5-m (p=0.044) and 30-m (p=0.045) times, and gluteal asymmetry with 5-m (p=0.044) and 30-m (p=0.043) times. The largest descriptive imbalance occurred in the gluteal group and the smallest in the quadriceps.
limitations: Only 16 athletes were assessed in one session. Textile EMG samples broad muscle regions, external sprint mechanics and gastrocnemius and tibialis activity were not measured, and cross-sectional associations do not establish causation, injury risk, or a response to training.
practicalImplications: When bilateral activation data are available, interpret them alongside sprint splits, technique, strength, symptoms, history, and repeated measurements. Program hamstring and gluteal work for demonstrated performance needs rather than an isolated percentage.
athleteDev: Explain that some side-to-side difference is expected and task-dependent. Focus on producing effective sprint shapes and force while building both limbs, instead of chasing perfect EMG symmetry.
rtp: A single EMG asymmetry result is not a reinjury or clearance marker. Use repeated sprint exposure, symptoms, strength and power, mechanics, and sport tolerance to judge progression.

citation: Mitchell A, Greig M. Peak Instantaneous PlayerLoad Metrics Highlight Movement Strategy Deficits in Professional Male Soccer Players. Research in Sports Medicine. 2024;32(1):61-71.
abstract: This cross-sectional study tested whether mid-calf accelerometry adds movement-strategy information to multidirectional single-leg hop distance in professional male soccer players with and without previous injury.
tldr: Previously injured players hopped less far and their affected limb reached peak mediolateral loading later, despite no consistent reduction in peak load. Accelerometry may add context to performance scores, but it is not an injury or readiness threshold.
methods: Twenty-five professional male players from one English Championship club completed three anterior, medial, and lateral hops per limb in one familiarized session. Twelve were classified as not previously injured and 13 as previously injured; hop distance and planar peak instantaneous PlayerLoad magnitude and timing were analyzed by task, injury status, and limb dominance.
findings: Task and previous injury affected hop distance (p<0.001), dominance did not, and no overall bilateral asymmetry was detected (p=0.668). Previously injured players did not consistently show lower peak loading, but time to peak mediolateral loading was longer in the affected limb (p=0.001), especially when the injury involved the nondominant limb.
limitations: The small one-club sample combined different previous injuries and relied on retrospective history. Accelerometer PlayerLoad is a surrogate measured during one session, and no prospective injury, rehabilitation response, or return-to-sport outcome was tested.
practicalImplications: Assess performance outcome and movement strategy together and inspect both limbs. If time-to-peak or planar loading differs, use the result to guide further clinical and biomechanical assessment rather than applying an automatic decision rule.
athleteDev: Show athletes that achieving hop distance can mask a changed landing strategy. Use the data to explain targeted landing and loading work without framing every difference as pathology.
rtp: Accelerometry can complement a return-to-sport battery, particularly when both limbs and multiple directions are assessed. It cannot replace symptoms, force and capacity measures, running and change-of-direction exposure, or sport-specific progression.

citation: Hedlund DP. Performance of Future Elite Players at the National Football League Scouting Combine. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2018;32(11):3112-3118.
abstract: This retrospective cohort analysis compared NFL Scouting Combine characteristics across position groups and later Pro Bowl and All-Pro recognition.
tldr: Combine characteristics differed between later award groups, but the patterns were position-specific and sometimes counterintuitive. The data provide descriptive context rather than a validated individual prediction model.
methods: Secondary combine and NFL career data were compiled for 5,506 athletes who attended the combine and were drafted between 2002 and 2016. Height, mass, 40-yard dash, vertical jump, bench press, shuttle, and three-cone results were compared within eight position groups by later Pro Bowl and All-Pro status.
findings: Awarded players differed from nonawarded players on selected physical measures, with the relevant direction and combination varying by position. Faster 40-yard performance was common across several elite groups, while body size, jumping, bench repetitions, shuttle, and three-cone patterns were not uniformly favorable across positions.
limitations: The analysis excluded undrafted attendees and nonattendees, contained missing test data, and included active careers. Pro Bowl and All-Pro recognition depends on voting, opportunity, team and role; many comparisons were made, and no out-of-sample individual prediction model was validated.
practicalImplications: Use positional distributions to frame preparation and identify a prospect's development priorities while preserving football skill and health. Evaluate the whole player and the uncertainty around every test.
athleteDev: Help prospects treat combine tests as trainable expressions within a larger football profile. Avoid unsafe mass change or overfitting preparation to a benchmark that does not guarantee a career outcome.
rtp: Combine norms are not rehabilitation standards. A recovering athlete must first demonstrate tissue capacity, football-specific exposure, and safe test readiness before maximal showcase preparation.

citation: Warneke K, Freundorfer P, Plöschberger G, Behm DG, Konrad A, Schmidt T. Effects of Chronic Static Stretching Interventions on Jumping and Sprinting Performance: A Systematic Review with Multilevel Meta-analysis. Frontiers in Physiology. 2024;15:1372689.
abstract: This systematic review with multilevel meta-analysis evaluated whether chronic static-stretching programs improve jumping and sprinting performance.
tldr: Chronic static stretching produced only a trivial pooled jump improvement and no significant sprint effect. It may serve mobility goals but should not displace sprint, plyometric, or resistance training for performance development.
methods: Fourteen studies identified through PubMed, Web of Science, and Google Scholar contributed 29 effect sizes: 20 jump and nine sprint outcomes. Multilevel models pooled dependent effects, and jump subgroups were analyzed by stretch-shortening-cycle characteristics.
findings: Six of 20 jump tests and six of nine sprint tests were individually positive, while two studies reported negative adaptations. The pooled jump effect was positive but trivial (effect size 0.16, p=0.04), jump subgroup effects were nonsignificant (p=0.09-0.44), and the sprint effect was nonsignificant (p=0.08).
limitations: The evidence base was small and heterogeneous in population, stretching intensity, weekly volume, duration, comparator, and outcome. Positive individual tests did not create consistent subgroup effects, and the review could not identify a performance-enhancing dose.
practicalImplications: Program static stretching for a demonstrated range-of-motion need, tolerance, or preference. If sprint and jump development is the priority, retain direct high-velocity, plyometric, and strength stimuli and monitor whether stretching volume competes with them.
athleteDev: Set the expectation that flexibility work can improve motion without automatically making an athlete faster or more explosive. Match the tool to the goal and track the outcome that matters.
rtp: Static stretching may support graded range of motion, but it is not evidence of restored tissue capacity or explosive readiness. Progress loading and sport exposure independently.

citation: Hamad MJ, Alcaraz PE, Sáez de Villarreal E. Effects of Combined Uphill-Downhill Sprinting Versus Resisted Sprinting Methods on Sprint Performance: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Sports Medicine. 2024;54(1):185-202.
abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis compared combined uphill-downhill and resisted-sprint interventions with traditional sprint training.
tldr: Combined uphill-downhill training had a small pooled advantage over traditional sprinting, while resisted sprinting did not. The hill evidence was sparse and did not test early acceleration, so superiority remains uncertain.
methods: Twenty-two studies yielded 24 eligible groups completing at least four weeks of training with a traditional-sprint control: six combined uphill-downhill and 18 resisted-sprint groups. Random-effects standardized mean differences compared pre-post sprint performance changes between intervention and control groups.
findings: Combined uphill-downhill training modestly outperformed traditional sprinting (SMD -0.41, 95% CI -0.79 to -0.03; p=0.03). Resisted sprinting did not significantly outperform traditional sprinting (SMD -0.14, 95% CI -0.36 to 0.07; p=0.19), although both approaches improved from baseline.
limitations: Only six uphill-downhill groups were included, five involved nonprofessional participants, and none tested sprint distances below 35 m. Slopes, resistance loads, populations, and tests varied, and sparse data limited subgroup and meta-regression confidence.
practicalImplications: Combined hill sprinting can be considered when a safe, consistent surface is available and the goal includes later acceleration or maximum-speed exposure. Compare it with simpler sprint options using actual athlete splits and technical response.
athleteDev: Teach how uphill and downhill segments change force and velocity demands. Introduce downhill exposure gradually and prioritize control and surface safety over chasing overspeed.
rtp: Hill and resisted sprinting are loading tools, not clearance tests. Progress slope, speed, resistance, and total distance only after appropriate running capacity and symptom response are established.

citation: Ahokas EK, Hennessy RS, Hanstock HG, Kyröläinen H, Ihalainen JK. Effects of Post-Exercise Heat Exposure on Acute Recovery and Training-Induced Performance Adaptations: A Systematic Review. Sports Medicine - Open. 2025;11:106.
abstract: This systematic review examined the acute recovery and longer-term performance effects of whole-body heat exposure applied after exercise in healthy adults.
tldr: Post-exercise sauna or hot-water immersion produced mixed acute recovery findings and limited, mode-specific chronic benefits. Heat is an additional stressor and should be prescribed for a defined goal with hydration and safety controls.
methods: Fourteen randomized or crossover studies with 194 participants compared whole-body post-exercise heat of at least 36°C with passive or placebo recovery. Nine assessed acute performance recovery and five repeated exposure alongside training; risk of bias was evaluated, but design heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis.
findings: Among acute studies, four found no performance effect, four a benefit, and one an adverse effect. Repeated heating may have improved running performance, particularly in hot conditions, but did not improve cycling performance or VO2max. Overall evidence quality was low to moderate.
limitations: Samples were small and heat modality, temperature, duration, exercise, outcome, recovery interval, and training status varied markedly. Too few comparable studies were available for pooling, so no definitive recovery or adaptation effect can be estimated.
practicalImplications: State the purpose before adding heat: recovery, heat acclimation, or a training stimulus require different protocols. Screen medical risk, control hydration and supervision, and monitor the athlete's next-session performance and perceived recovery.
athleteDev: Explain that feeling relaxed after heat does not prove physiological recovery. Athletes should report dizziness, excessive fatigue, illness, or hydration problems and should not use heat to compensate for poor sleep or nutrition.
rtp: Heat may increase cardiovascular and hydration strain during rehabilitation. Introduce it only when clinically appropriate and never interpret tolerance of a sauna or hot bath as evidence of tissue or sport readiness.

citation: Xu K, Jukic I, Cross MR, Hicks DS, Yin M, Zhong Y, Tang W, Li Y, Liang Z, Wang R, Morin JB, Girard O. Effects of Resisted-Sprint Training on Sprint Performance and Mechanics: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis Focusing on Load Magnitude.
