Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2025;35:e70182.
abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined resisted-sprint load magnitude, sprint performance, and macroscopic sprint mechanics across direct and network comparisons.
tldr: Resisted sprinting modestly outperformed unresisted sprinting overall, mainly for early acceleration, with selected advantages at moderate and very heavy loads. High bias and uneven evidence make the reported load threshold a hypothesis, not a universal prescription.
methods: Forty-nine longitudinal studies involving 1,281 participants were analyzed with single-arm exploratory, direct two-arm, multilevel, and Bayesian network models. Loads were classified by body-mass percentage or velocity decrement, moderators were explored, and certainty was graded.
findings: Resisted sprinting outperformed unresisted sprinting by Hedges' g -0.30 with moderate certainty. Moderate and very heavy categories, but not light or heavy categories, showed advantages; very heavy loads outperformed light loads in selected models and improved theoretical force and power metrics. Benefits were largely driven by 0-5-m acceleration.
limitations: Randomized studies were rated high risk of bias and many nonrandomized studies serious risk. Load categories, training volumes, and mechanical outcomes were uneven, female representation was low, and the 20.7% body-mass meta-regression threshold is not a prospectively validated cutoff.
practicalImplications: Prescribe sled resistance from the targeted sprint phase and measured velocity decrement, then verify posture, contact strategy, distance, and adaptation. Heavier work can be useful for trained athletes, but maintain unresisted acceleration and maximum-speed exposure.
athleteDev: Connect sled load to a clear purpose rather than a heavier-is-better mindset. Athletes should understand the acceptable velocity loss and technical standard for each rep.
rtp: Resisted sprinting can grade horizontal force demand, but load categories are not injury-specific progression criteria. Advance resistance, speed, and free sprinting according to symptoms, mechanics, tissue capacity, and total exposure.

citation: Kong Y, Yu B, Guan G, Wang Y, He H. Effects of Sleep Deprivation on Sports Performance and Perceived Exertion in Athletes and Non-athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Frontiers in Physiology. 2025;16:1544286.
abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesized randomized and crossover evidence on sleep deprivation, performance, and perceived exertion in athletes and healthy nonathletes.
tldr: Sleep deprivation impaired multiple athlete performance domains and increased perceived exertion. The direction is actionable, but heterogeneous protocols and sparse subgroups do not provide a precise decrement for an individual athlete.
methods: Forty-five randomized controlled or randomized-crossover studies identified through five databases to September 2024 were synthesized. Outcomes included aerobic and anaerobic endurance, explosive power, maximum force, speed, skill control, and perceived exertion, with subgroup analyses by population, deprivation type, and test time.
findings: Athlete performance declined for aerobic endurance (SMD -0.66), explosive power (-0.63), maximum force (-0.35), speed (-0.52), and skill control (-0.87), while perceived exertion increased (0.39). Healthy nonathletes also had lower aerobic endurance, and several early- or late-partial-deprivation and afternoon subgroups were adverse.
limitations: Studies varied in sleep manipulation, baseline sleep control, population, outcome, and bias. Some subgroups were small, female participation was insufficient for sex analysis, and multiple subgroup tests make exact timing and deprivation-type estimates less certain than the overall direction.
practicalImplications: Protect sleep before demanding aerobic, strength, speed, skill, and decision-heavy work. After verified loss, consider reducing complexity or dose, increasing monitoring, and rescheduling high-consequence assessment where feasible.
athleteDev: Build a travel and disruption plan that emphasizes honest reporting, consistent sleep opportunity, and coordinated training adjustments. Discourage reckless stimulant use or extra training intended to compensate for fatigue.
rtp: Sleep loss can depress rehabilitation and testing performance without reflecting tissue capacity. Interpret a poor session cautiously, address safety and cognition, and repeat high-stakes testing under representative recovery when possible.

citation: Murphy MC, Travers MJ, Chivers P, Debenham JR, Docking SI, Rio EK, Gibson W. Efficacy of Heavy Eccentric Calf Training for Treating Mid-portion Achilles Tendinopathy: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2019;53(17):1070-1077.
abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis compared heavy eccentric calf training with natural history, traditional physiotherapy, and other exercise for chronic mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy.
tldr: Heavy eccentric calf training was better than passive or traditional-physiotherapy comparisons in low-certainty evidence but was not better than other progressive exercise. It is one loading option, not a mandatory gold-standard protocol.
methods: Seven randomized trials with 241 adults who had mid-portion Achilles symptoms for more than three months were included. Pain and function were measured with VISA-A, risk of bias and evidence quality were assessed, and pooled comparisons were made against natural history, traditional physiotherapy, and other exercise.
findings: VISA-A favored heavy eccentric training over natural history by 20.6 points (one study) and traditional physiotherapy by 17.70 points (two studies). Against other exercise, the pooled difference was nonsignificant; after removing one high-risk study, other exercise was favored by 5.65 points, a difference judged unlikely to be clinically important.
limitations: All studies were small and evidence was low or very low quality. Participants were generally middle-aged with longstanding symptoms, exercise protocols and adherence varied, and there were too few studies to assess publication bias or confidently generalize to younger competitive athletes.
practicalImplications: Select eccentric, heavy-slow, or other progressive calf loading according to athlete tolerance, access, adherence, and the force-speed demands being restored. Monitor symptoms and function and integrate running, plyometrics, and sport exposure rather than relying on one exercise recipe.
athleteDev: Explain that tendon rehabilitation requires progressive loading and patience, but one famous protocol is not the only route. Choose a sustainable program and track meaningful function rather than soreness alone.
rtp: VISA-A improvement and calf loading are components of rehabilitation, not clearance by themselves. Progress return to running and sport using symptoms, plantar-flexor capacity, elastic tasks, repeated exposure, and sport-specific demands.

citation: Skripnikov A. Partially Constrained Group Variable Selection to Adjust for Complementary Unit Performance in American College Football. Journal of Applied Statistics. 2024;51(3):606-620.
abstract: This methodological application developed offense and defense ratings that adjust college-football team performance for schedule, home field, and complementary-unit effects.
tldr: Complementary-unit adjustment identified plausible team interactions but did not clearly improve game prediction beyond schedule and home field. Reverse causality remains central, so the method is an analytics template rather than a causal performance model.
methods: Game-level Football Bowl Subdivision data from 2009-2019 were modeled with natural cubic splines, grouped penalties, and partially constrained optimization. Models fully adjusted strength of schedule and home field, selected efficiency-based complementary features, and compared ranking and game-outcome prediction approaches.
findings: Non-scoring defensive turnovers were the most consistent positive complement to offensive scoring. Defensive yards allowed per play had a nonlinear relationship with complementary offensive yardage. Schedule-plus-home-field and efficiency-complement models had similar test performance, while including any complementary total performed worse because of reverse causality.
limitations: Score state and play calling make within-game variables endogenous. Efficiency measures did not eliminate reverse causality, play-by-play sequencing was unavailable, and the similar prediction errors do not establish incremental decision value.
practicalImplications: When building team ratings, separate schedule, venue, unit interaction, and game-state effects and test whether added complexity improves out-of-sample decisions. Preserve transparent base models as comparators.
athleteDev: Use team analytics to improve tactical understanding and unit coordination, not to assign individual blame from aggregate ratings.
rtp: The model contains no individual health or rehabilitation evidence and should not influence return-to-sport clearance or medical workload decisions.

citation: Donahue PT, Moore J, Peel SA, Oglesby L. Positional Comparison of Countermovement Jump Performance in American Collegiate Football Athletes. International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching. 2026;OnlineFirst.
abstract: This cross-sectional force-platform study compared countermovement-jump performance and strategy among lineman, midskill, and skill groups in Division I football.
tldr: Skill players jumped higher and faster, while linemen produced the greatest absolute momentum with longer movement phases. Position and mass change the meaning of CMJ metrics, so group values are context rather than universal standards.
methods: Eighty-five Division I male players were grouped as linemen (32), midskill (29), or skill (24). Each completed three hands-restricted countermovement jumps on a 1000-Hz force platform, and force-time, phase-duration, jump-height, reactive-strength, and momentum outcomes were compared by one-way ANOVA.
findings: Jump height and modified reactive-strength index were highest in skill and lowest in linemen. Linemen had the greatest body mass, takeoff momentum, peak and mean propulsive force and power, and longer braking, propulsive, and time-to-takeoff durations; countermovement depth did not differ.
limitations: The single-program cross-sectional male sample used broad position groups. No longitudinal sensitivity to fatigue, adaptation, football performance, injury, or talent outcomes was tested.
practicalImplications: Select CMJ variables that match the position and question: relative explosiveness, absolute momentum, and phase strategy provide different information. Monitor each athlete against a stable protocol and personal baseline.
athleteDev: Explain why a lineman and skill player can express high performance through different jump profiles. Set role-relevant goals instead of rewarding jump height alone.
rtp: Position norms can contextualize recovery, but they are not clearance values. Compare the athlete with preinjury data and combine force-time measures with symptoms, capacity, running, contact, and football exposure.

citation: Farley T, Barry E, Sylvester R, De Medici A, Wilson MG. Poor Isometric Neck Extension Strength as a Risk Factor for Concussion in Male Professional Rugby Union Players. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2022;56(11):616-621.
abstract: This prospective-season cohort study examined associations between multidirectional isometric neck strength and clinically diagnosed concussion in professional male rugby.
tldr: Higher neck extension strength was associated with a lower concussion rate, but no other direction was significant and the study did not test whether strengthening prevents concussion. Treat neck work as one part of a wider prevention system.
methods: A cohort of 225 professional male rugby players underwent isometric neck-strength testing preseason, with 179 retested midseason and 74 at season end. Clinically diagnosed concussions and match exposure were recorded, and adjusted incidence-rate models evaluated strength directions and composite scores.
findings: Thirty concussions occurred in 29 players, or 13.7 per 1000 player-hours. A 10% increase in extension strength was associated with a 13% lower concussion rate (adjusted IRR 0.87, 95% CI 0.78-0.98). Other directions and composite scores were not significant, and average strength increased after preseason.
limitations: The association is observational and based on 30 events. Attrition and injury or international-duty absences may bias repeated testing, residual confounding is possible, and male professional-rugby findings may not generalize.
practicalImplications: Include technically sound, progressive neck extension within whole-body collision preparation while preserving tackle technique, exposure management, rule enforcement, and concussion recognition and management.
athleteDev: Frame neck strength as a modifiable capacity that may help control the head during contact, not armor against concussion or permission to take unsafe contact.
rtp: Neck strength can be measured after concussion or cervical injury but is not a stand-alone return-to-contact criterion. Follow the clinical concussion pathway and graded sport-specific progression.

citation: Vázquez-Villarreal LG, Carvajal-Veitía W, Guevara-Balcázar G, Maceroni C, López-Sánchez P, Castillo-Hernández MDC. Position-Specific Kinanthropometric Traits of Professional American Football Players: A Study of Mexican LFA Players. Journal of Functional Morphology and Kinesiology. 2026;11(1):109.
abstract: This cross-sectional study described ISAK-standard position-specific anthropometry, body composition, somatotype, and proportionality in Mexican professional American football players.
tldr: Mexican LFA players showed expected position-related morphology, especially greater size and tissue mass in linemen, but anthropometry classified position only moderately well. The profiles are descriptive, not body targets or performance determinants.
methods: During the 2019-2020 seasons, 189 players across seven positions completed 26 ISAK-standard measurements. Five-way body-composition fractionation, somatotype, and proportionality were compared by position, and exploratory stepwise discriminant analysis assessed classification.
findings: Offensive and defensive linemen had the greatest size and adipose, muscle, and bone mass, while wide receivers and defensive backs had lower endomorphy. Arm relaxed girth, biiliocristal breadth, and sitting height formed the exploratory discriminant model, which classified 57.7% correctly without cross-validation.
limitations: The sample was league- and era-specific, excluded kickers, used anthropometric fractionation rather than imaging, and measured no performance outcome. Cross-sectional patterns and an unvalidated exploratory classifier cannot establish selection utility or causation.
practicalImplications: Use the profiles as contextual references for an underrepresented league and assess health, function, speed, power, skill, and role alongside morphology. Avoid forcing athletes toward a positional body template.
athleteDev: Discuss body composition in terms of health, function, and sustainable role demands. Protect athletes from unnecessary weight gain or loss driven by group averages.
rtp: Morphology is not a readiness marker. Monitor clinically meaningful composition change during rehabilitation without substituting it for tissue capacity, conditioning, and football exposure.

citation: Hart LM, Cohen DD, Patterson SD, Springham M, Reynolds J, Read P. Previous Injury Is Associated with Heightened Countermovement Jump Force-Time Asymmetries in Professional Soccer Players. Translational Sports Medicine. 2019;2(5):250-256.
abstract: This cross-sectional study compared dual-force-platform countermovement-jump asymmetry in professional male soccer players with and without previous severe lower-extremity injury.
tldr: Previously injured players produced equal bilateral jump outcomes while retaining larger phase-specific force asymmetries. Outcome alone can hide strategy, but asymmetry was not tested as a prospective reinjury predictor.
methods: Thirty-four professional male soccer players, 17 previously severely injured and 17 uninjured, completed three hands-on-hips countermovement jumps on synchronized force platforms. Concentric and eccentric limb contributions and bilateral performance outcomes were compared between groups.
findings: Previously injured players had greater asymmetry in concentric variables with strong effects and in most eccentric variables with medium-to-large effects; eccentric deceleration impulse was the exception. Bilateral jump-performance measures did not differ between groups.
limitations: The design lacked preinjury values and cannot establish direction or prospective risk. Different injuries were pooled in a small sample, mechanisms underlying force differences were not measured, and results may be soccer-specific.
practicalImplications: Evaluate bilateral outcome and how each limb produces it, using phase- and variable-specific repeated measures. Investigate persistent differences rather than assuming equal jump height means equal recovery.
athleteDev: Show athletes that compensation can preserve performance. Use the information to target capacity and coordination while avoiding alarm over a single asymmetry number.
rtp: CMJ force-time asymmetry can complement the battery, but no universal cutoff is supported. Combine it with symptoms, strength, elastic and change-of-direction work, and progressively representative soccer exposure.

citation: Liston M, Fuller C, Dahly D, Falla D, McLoughlin R, Yeomans C, van Dyk N, Falvey E. Profile of Cervical Endurance and Peak Isometric Strength in Elite Professional Male Rugby Players. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2024;54(3):201-208.
abstract: This cross-sectional study established position-specific cervical peak-strength and endurance profiles in elite professional male rugby players.
tldr: Cervical strength and endurance differed by position, age, mass, and individual, with front-row forwards strongest. These are contextual norms, not concussion-protection or return-to-contact thresholds.
methods: One hundred thirty-six players, grouped as front row, other forwards, or backs, completed multidirectional peak isometric tests followed by loaded flexion and extension endurance tests. Strength was normalized to body mass and regression examined demographic and position relationships.
findings: Front-row forwards were strongest and backs weakest. Extension produced 429 ± 104 N and flexion 275 ± 65 N overall; flexion and extension endurance averaged 52.9 ± 20.1 and 55.7 ± 17.1 seconds. Peak flexion strength related to flexion endurance, while other forwards had lower extension endurance.
limitations: Testing occurred once in preseason with varied prior training. The male professional sample may not generalize, criterion validity was unestablished, the best of three trials ignored variability, test order was fixed, and endurance termination used visual judgment.
practicalImplications: Standardize cervical testing and interpret results by position, body mass, age, technique, and the athlete's repeat history. Use strength and endurance as different capacities rather than interchangeable scores.
athleteDev: Build neck capacity progressively and explain why positional contact demands differ. Avoid presenting a population average as a pass-fail target.
rtp: Use cervical testing as one component after head or neck injury. Clinical status, symptom-free exertion, neurologic and musculoskeletal findings, contact progression, and sport demands remain essential.

citation: Thompson C, Schabrun S, Romero R, Bialocerkowski A, van Dieen J, Marshall P. Factors Contributing to Chronic Ankle Instability: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Systematic Reviews. Sports Medicine. 2018;48(1):189-205.
abstract: This overview of systematic reviews reanalyzed primary evidence on balance, reaction time, strength, proprioception, and other factors associated with chronic or nonspecific ankle instability.
tldr: Dynamic balance, peroneal reaction time, and eversion strength were supported for nonspecific ankle instability, but most studies did not define chronic ankle instability properly. Apply a multidomain assessment without claiming one causal deficit.
methods: Twelve systematic reviews were quality-rated with modified R-AMSTAR. Comparable primary studies were reanalyzed by outcome, evidence strength was synthesized, and participant criteria were checked against International Ankle Consortium recommendations.
findings: Strong evidence supported dynamic-balance, peroneal-reaction-time, and eversion-strength deficits and moderate evidence proprioception and static-balance deficits in nonspecific instability. Only 17% of primary studies measured a clearly defined CAI population, substantially limiting CAI-specific inference.
limitations: Definitions, inclusion criteria, outcomes, and primary studies overlapped and were heterogeneous, with wide prediction intervals. Most evidence preceded consensus criteria, and later research was not included.
practicalImplications: Assess history, symptoms, recurrent giving way, dynamic and static balance, strength, reaction, range, and functional demands. Treat the pattern of deficits rather than one proposed mechanism.
athleteDev: Explain that chronic ankle instability is multifactorial and trainable. Progress balance, strength, reaction, and sport tasks based on the athlete's demonstrated needs.
rtp: No single balance or strength test is a clearance criterion. Confirm symptom control, multidirectional capacity, reactive tasks, confidence, and full sport exposure.

citation: Konrad A, Nakamura M, Tilp M, Donti O, Behm DG. Foam Rolling Training Effects on Range of Motion: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Sports Medicine. 2022;52(10):2523-2535.
abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated chronic foam-rolling effects on joint range of motion in healthy participants.
tldr: Repeated foam rolling moderately improved range of motion on average, particularly beyond four weeks, but response differed by joint and muscle and did not establish a performance or injury benefit.
methods: Eleven randomized or controlled studies with 290 participants and 46 effects were pooled in random-effects models. Subgroups compared intervention duration, muscle group, and study design.
findings: Foam rolling favored control with an effect size of 0.823 (95% CI 0.325-1.322; p=0.001; I2=72.76%). Interventions longer than four weeks produced larger gains, and hamstring and quadriceps rolling improved ROM while triceps-surae rolling did not improve dorsiflexion.
limitations: Heterogeneity was substantial and one study had an extreme effect. Dose, pressure, frequency, population, and outcome varied; only three moderators were tested, and participants were mostly young healthy adults.
practicalImplications: Use repeated foam rolling when a specific ROM outcome, tolerance, and available time justify it. Measure the target joint and stop if the intervention adds burden without useful change.
athleteDev: Foam rolling is an option rather than a requirement. Athletes can choose it when it helps motion or preparation while keeping strength, skill, and recovery priorities intact.
rtp: ROM improvement does not demonstrate tissue capacity or sport readiness. Combine any foam-rolling response with progressive loading and functional exposure.

citation: Wynne JL, Wilson PB. Got Beer? A Systematic Review of Beer and Exercise. International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism. 2021;31(5):438-450.
abstract: This systematic review evaluated acute and chronic beer ingestion in relation to hydration, recovery, performance, adaptation, and health outcomes around exercise.
tldr: Lower-alcohol beer retained fluid better than stronger beer under controlled conditions, but evidence was small, male-dominant, and artificial. Alcoholic beer should not be recommended as recovery, and nonalcoholic-beer findings are distinct.
methods: Two reviewers searched three databases and included 16 randomized or nonrandomized human experiments, 12 acute and four chronic. Outcomes included hydration, performance, soreness, muscle protein synthesis, body composition, strength, and respiratory illness; mean PEDro quality was 5.1.
findings: Lower-alcohol beer generally produced less diuresis than stronger beer, and added sodium sometimes improved retention with palatability tradeoffs. One nonalcoholic polyphenol-rich beer study suggested fewer postmarathon respiratory infections. Moderate beer intake showed no clear chronic body-composition or strength effect.
limitations: Samples were small and mostly male, blinding was difficult, protocols and doses varied, most hydration studies fixed drink volume and withheld food, and chronic studies lasted only four to ten weeks.
practicalImplications: For recovery, prioritize nonalcoholic fluids, sodium when indicated, carbohydrate, protein, and food. If an adult athlete elects alcohol, discuss dose, fluid losses, sleep, medication, safety, policy, and timing without presenting beer as therapeutic.
athleteDev: Make alcohol conversations factual and nonjudgmental. Separate social choice from recovery need and help athletes plan transport, hydration, nutrition, and next-day demands.
rtp: Alcohol can impair judgment, sleep, hydration, and medication safety. It has no role as a readiness test or rehabilitation treatment and may warrant modification or avoidance during recovery.

citation: Stevens CJ, Borg D, Brade C, Carter S, Filingeri D, Lee J, Lim L, Mündel T, Taylor L, Tyler CJ. Head, Face, and Neck Cooling for Performance: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2025;20(6):743-763.
abstract: This systematic review and multilevel meta-analysis evaluated head, face, and neck cooling for physical and cognitive performance, physiology, perception, and adverse events.
tldr: Local cooling reliably improved thermal comfort but produced inconclusive performance effects and negligible core-temperature change. It can be tested as an adjunct, never as a substitute for heat-safety controls.
methods: Sixty-three controlled studies with 618 participants tested 75 strategies including water-perfused devices, collars, headwear, cold air, packs, towels, menthol, and water spraying. Multilevel models pooled physical, physiological, and perceptual outcomes; cognitive outcomes were too heterogeneous to pool.
findings: Self-paced and fixed-intensity performance intervals ranged from no effect to medium benefit and excluded meaningful harm. Cooling improved target-site temperature, thermal sensation, and comfort, while heart rate, core temperature, and mean skin temperature changed negligibly. Adverse events were rare and no modality was superior.
limitations: Sixty-one studies had some risk-of-bias concern and two high risk. The sample was 86.6% male, cognitive evidence was sparse, and modality, dose, environment, and task varied.
practicalImplications: Trial accessible, rule-compatible cooling during representative heat exposure and assess comfort and performance. Maintain acclimation, hydration, environmental monitoring, work-rest modification, and emergency action plans.
athleteDev: Teach athletes that feeling cooler does not necessarily mean core temperature is lower. They must continue to report heat symptoms and follow safety plans.
rtp: Cooling may improve tolerance during graded heat re-exposure, but it must not mask symptoms or accelerate return. Medical risk, environment, workload, and acclimation remain decisive.

citation: López-Torres O, Rodríguez-Longobardo C, Escribano-Tabernero R, Fernández-Elías VE. Hydration, Hyperthermia, Glycogen, and Recovery: Crucial Factors in Exercise Performance—A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Nutrients. 2023;15(20):4442.
abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined interactions among hydration, exercise heat strain, muscle glycogen use, and postexercise glycogen restoration.
tldr: Hyperthermia showed a clearer adverse association with muscle glycogen than hydration status alone, while hydration estimates were highly heterogeneous. Manage heat, fluid, and carbohydrate together without assuming one universal recovery formula.
methods: Eighteen studies with 158 participants were reviewed and 13 entered meta-analysis. Ten hydration comparisons and four temperature comparisons assessed muscle glycogen during exercise or recovery; PEDro ratings were fair or poor.
findings: Hydration versus remaining dehydrated had a nonsignificant pooled glycogen effect (estimate 0.79, 95% CI -0.54 to 2.12; p=0.24; I2=91.88%). Higher temperature was associated with lower postexercise glycogen across four studies (estimate -1.52, 95% CI -2.52 to -0.53; p=0.003; I2=66.81%).
limitations: The small, often old studies used varied heat, dehydration, exercise, biopsy, and recovery protocols and had low quality scores. Heat and dehydration were difficult to separate, and glycogen measures are mechanistic rather than direct performance outcomes.
practicalImplications: Plan fluid, sodium, carbohydrate, cooling, and recovery time from environmental load, sweat losses, gastrointestinal tolerance, and the next performance demand. Verify hydration and fueling rather than relying on thirst or a fixed recipe alone.
athleteDev: Teach athletes to start demanding heat sessions prepared, replace realistic losses, and pair postexercise fluid with carbohydrate and food when rapid turnaround matters.
rtp: During reconditioning, heat and dehydration can amplify session strain. Progress environmental exposure deliberately and monitor symptoms, fluid balance, fueling tolerance, and next-session recovery.

citation: Conde-Pipó J, Mora-Fernandez A, Martinez-Bebia M, Gimenez-Blasi N, Lopez-Moro A, Latorre JA, Almendros-Ruiz A, Requena B, Mariscal-Arcas M. Intermittent Fasting: Does It Affect Sports Performance? A Systematic Review. Nutrients. 2024;16(1):168.
abstract: This systematic review summarized effects of intermittent fasting and time-restricted eating on athlete performance, physical capacities, and body composition.
tldr: Performance was often maintained and fat mass sometimes decreased, but fasting format, calorie intake, training, sleep, hydration, and Ramadan context were too heterogeneous to claim a performance benefit.
methods: Twenty-five adult-athlete or exercising-population studies published since 2013 were selected from PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus. The review summarized aerobic and anaerobic capacity, strength, power, lean and fat mass, and risk of bias without meta-analysis.
findings: Most time-restricted or intermittent-fasting studies reported maintained strength and sport performance with possible fat-mass reduction and lean-mass preservation. Selected Ramadan-fasting studies showed lower aerobic test performance, reflecting combined changes in food, fluid, sleep, and activity timing.
limitations: Interventions, fasting hours, calorie control, populations, tests, and outcomes varied markedly. Some studies did not measure energy intake, many were short, and caloric deficit and Ramadan-specific sleep and hydration changes confounded conclusions.
practicalImplications: Use intermittent fasting only when it fits the athlete's goals, health, preference, schedule, and ability to meet energy, protein, carbohydrate, micronutrient, and fluid needs. Coordinate training and feeding with a sports dietitian.
athleteDev: Avoid presenting fasting as a shortcut. Protect energy availability, sleep, recovery, and relationship with food, while respectfully planning around religious practice when applicable.
rtp: Fasting should not compromise rehabilitation energy, protein distribution, hydration, medication, or session quality. Modify timing with the clinical and nutrition team when recovery demands are high.

citation: Wittels SH, Renaghan E, Wishon MJ, Wittels HL, Chong S, Wittels ED, et al. Recovery of the Autonomic Nervous System Following Football Training Among Division I Collegiate Football Athletes: The Influence of Intensity and Time. Heliyon. 2023;9(7):e18125.
abstract: This prospective observational study examined how the duration and intensity of football training related to autonomic recovery and function 24 hours later in male Division I athletes.
tldr: More time at the highest heart-rate thresholds was associated with poorer next-day cardiac recovery in one college football team. Use the signal to support individualized planning, not as a universal cutoff or causal rule.
methods: Fifty male Division I football athletes wore ECG-capable armband monitors during 128 training sessions over 135 days of a 25-week season, yielding 2,735 observations. Regression models related time within heart-rate thresholds to next-day resting heart rate and heart-rate recovery.
findings: Longer duration at 150 and 160 bpm thresholds showed stronger associations with higher next-day resting heart rate and slower heart-rate recovery than lower-intensity exposure. The authors interpreted the highest-intensity bouts as requiring more than 24 hours for autonomic restoration.
limitations: The study assessed only the 24-hour time point, included one male football program, and did not control sleep, nutrition, hydration, or recovery treatment. Observational associations cannot establish an individual causal threshold, and several authors had financial relationships with the device company.
practicalImplications: Track high-intensity duration alongside the athlete's next-day response and broader workload. When recovery markers and context agree, shorten strenuous bouts, extend between-session recovery, or modify the next exposure, then verify the response.
athleteDev: Teach athletes that recovery needs depend on intensity, duration, sleep, fueling, hydration, and accumulated work. Encourage honest reporting rather than presenting a device threshold as a pass-fail grade.
rtp: During reconditioning, use cardiac response only as an adjunct to symptoms, tissue status, strength, movement, conditioning, and graded football exposure. One heart-rate pattern does not determine readiness.

citation: McDuff D, Stull T, Castaldelli-Maia JM, Hitchcock ME, Hainline B, Reardon CL. Recreational and Ergogenic Substance Use and Substance Use Disorders in Elite Athletes: A Narrative Review. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2019;53(12):754-760.
abstract: This narrative review summarized prevalence, patterns, risk factors, performance effects, and interventions for recreational and performance-enhancing substance use among elite athletes.
tldr: Substance patterns vary substantially by sport and population, and diagnosed disorder prevalence in elite athletes was unknown. Build confidential support and referral systems without stereotyping or diagnosing from one behavior.
methods: The authors conducted a broad literature search for studies comparing athlete and non-athlete substance use or describing demographic, sport, risk, motive, performance, and intervention patterns across major recreational and performance-enhancing substance classes.
findings: Alcohol, cannabis, tobacco, prescribed opioids, and stimulants were commonly reported and often lower than in non-athletes, while binge alcohol, oral tobacco, non-prescription opioids, and anabolic-androgenic steroid use were higher in some athlete groups, particularly power and collision sports. Use varied by country, sport, sex, ethnicity, and competitive level.
limitations: No included evidence established the prevalence of diagnosed substance-use disorders in elite male or female athletes, and few studies used direct comparison groups. Definitions, self-report, testing, populations, and substances were heterogeneous, and a narrative review cannot provide pooled certainty.
practicalImplications: Create confidential education, screening, clinical assessment, and referral pathways that distinguish occasional use, misuse, and disorder. Review pain, sleep, stress, mental health, medication, supplements, team culture, and current antidoping rules together.
athleteDev: Use nonjudgmental conversations that protect trust and make help-seeking safe. Explain performance, health, legal, and antidoping risks while avoiding assumptions based on sport, position, or identity.
rtp: Substance use can interact with symptoms, medication, sleep, judgment, hydration, and adherence. Return decisions require clinical assessment and a support plan when use creates safety or functional concerns.

citation: Daly E, Blackett AD, Pearce AJ, Ryan L. Protect the Player, Protect the Game: Reflections from Ex-Professional Rugby Union Players on Law Changes, Protective Equipment, and Duty of Care in the Professional Game. Journal of Functional Morphology and Kinesiology. 2022;7(4):91.
abstract: This qualitative study interviewed retired professional male rugby-union players about concussion management, protective equipment, law changes, workload, return to play, and duty of care.
tldr: Former players described pressure and test manipulation and wanted medically independent, more conservative return decisions. Their accounts support stronger safeguards but do not estimate how common these practices are today.
methods: Twenty-three retired professional male rugby-union players, 61% with international test experience, completed interviews that were analyzed for themes concerning duty of care, concussion return to play, protective equipment, and law or workload changes.
findings: Participants reported pressure from coaches or clubs to play with symptoms and described manipulating concussion tests. They favored independent medical decisions, longer return processes, ongoing care after retirement, and reduced match or contact-training exposure; they did not believe current protective equipment or law changes eliminated concussion risk.
limitations: The small retrospective male sample retired within the prior decade and may be affected by selection, recall, and social-desirability bias. Policies, laws, workloads, and clinical practice may have changed, and qualitative reports are not prevalence estimates.
practicalImplications: Separate medical clearance authority from performance pressure, protect symptom disclosure, prohibit coaching influence over testing, audit return-to-play processes, and manage contact volume. Extend referral and follow-up support beyond roster status when feasible.
athleteDev: Make clear that symptom reporting protects the athlete and teammates and will not be treated as a character failure. Teach why trying to beat a concussion test can increase long-term risk.
rtp: Concussion return should remain clinician-led, symptom-responsive, and progressively exposed to cognitive, physical, and contact demands. Equipment use never replaces recognition, removal, assessment, and conservative progression.

citation: Modric T, Jelicic M, Sekulic D. Relative Training Load and Match Outcome: Are Professional Soccer Players Actually Undertrained During the In-Season? Sports. 2021;9(10):139.
abstract: This observational study examined associations between training-to-match running-load ratios within the weekly microcycle and subsequent match outcome in professional soccer.
tldr: One team won more often after a week with high-intensity work in midweek, greater earlier volume, and lower final-two-day volume. The pattern is a periodization hypothesis, not proof that manipulating a ratio causes wins.
methods: Twenty-one professional players were monitored by GPS during 67 training sessions and 14 official matches. Training-to-match ratios were calculated by day for total, low-, running-, and high-intensity distance plus acceleration and deceleration variables, then correlated with win, draw, or loss.
findings: Better match outcome correlated with more high-intensity-running load three days before the match, more total and low-intensity distance and acceleration-deceleration volume five days before it, and lower volume in those variables one and two days before the match.
limitations: Only one team and 14 matches were observed, and eligible players completed full training and the following match. Correlation cannot isolate effects from opponent, tactics, selection, schedule, score state, or other confounding, and internal load was unavailable.
practicalImplications: Consider early-week volume, a purposeful midweek high-speed exposure, and reduced final-two-day volume, but calibrate the pattern to the athlete and schedule. Evaluate it locally with readiness, availability, and performance rather than match result alone.
athleteDev: Explain how the week builds, exposes, and tapers different qualities so athletes understand why hard and easy days are sequenced. Use feedback to individualize without promising that one loading pattern determines outcome.
rtp: Returning players should not inherit the team ratio automatically. Progress their high-speed, acceleration, deceleration, and soccer volume from individual capacity toward role-specific training and match demands.

citation: Read PJ, Davies WT, Bishop C, McAuliffe S, Wilson MG, Turner AN. Residual Deficits in Reactive Strength After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction in Soccer Players. Journal of Athletic Training. 2023;58(5):423-429.
abstract: This cross-sectional study evaluated a repeated single-leg vertical hop as a measure of residual function after ACL reconstruction in soccer players completing rehabilitation.
tldr: Soccer players completing ACL rehabilitation still showed lower repeated-hop performance and greater asymmetry than controls. Vertical rebound testing adds sensitivity but cannot clear an athlete by itself.
methods: Seventy-three soccer players with ACL reconstruction and 195 matched controls completed a 10-second single-leg vertical hop measuring jump height, reactive-strength index, and asymmetry. Drop-jump performance, isokinetic knee-extension torque, and self-reported knee function were examined as predictors.
findings: Between-limb differences were present only in the ACLR group, whose asymmetry exceeded controls. Single-leg drop-jump reactive strength and knee-extension torque predicted portions of repeated-hop height and reactive-strength performance, suggesting residual strength and stretch-shortening-cycle deficits.
limitations: Cross-sectional comparisons lacked preinjury baselines and cannot show prospective reinjury risk or successful return. Control matching does not define an individual's target, and the predictor models left substantial performance variance unexplained.
practicalImplications: Include repeatable vertical rebound tasks when they add information beyond horizontal hop distance. Inspect height, contact time, reactive strength, asymmetry, symptoms, and strategy across serial tests rather than using a single score.
athleteDev: Explain that completing rehabilitation or restoring horizontal distance may not fully restore rapid elastic function. Use test results to target quadriceps strength and reactive loading without framing asymmetry as failure.
rtp: Combine vertical rebound testing with symptoms, knee examination, strength, power, movement quality, confidence, conditioning, change of direction, and progressive soccer exposure. No single limb-symmetry threshold is sufficient.

citation: Riboli A, Esposito F, Coratella G. The Distribution of Match Activities Relative to the Maximal Intensities in Elite Soccer Players: Implications for Practice. Research in Sports Medicine. 2022;30(5):463-474.
abstract: This match-monitoring study characterized how average, above-average, and one-minute peak locomotor demands were distributed in elite Italian soccer.
tldr: Whole-match averages substantially diluted short high-intensity demands, and positions differed in distance accumulated above average. Prescribe from multiple references because a match peak is still not an athlete's maximum capacity.
methods: One hundred forty-eight Serie A players contributed 680 samples across 46 official matches. Total distance, high- and very-high-speed running, sprinting, acceleration, and deceleration were expressed relative to each player's one-minute match peak, with time and distance above the 90-minute average also calculated.
findings: The 90-minute average was 59.6% of one-minute peak for total distance but only 26.2% for high-speed running, 16.0% for very-high-speed running, 9.3% for sprinting, 19.2% for acceleration, and 15.4% for deceleration. Distance above average differed by position.
limitations: A match peak can remain below individual maximal capacity. Internal load, high-intensity action counts, directional change, venue, opponent, congestion, and seasonal timing were not included, and locomotor data do not capture all technical or tactical demand.
practicalImplications: Build drills from a demand envelope that includes average, above-average duration, peak, position, and individual capacity. Combine soccer-specific play with supplemental running or neuromuscular work when drills do not reach the intended exposure.
athleteDev: Show athletes why average match output is not the ceiling and why role-specific peak preparation matters. Pair external-load targets with perceived and physiological response.
rtp: Progress from controlled individual intensity to position-specific peak and repeated-demand exposure, then team practice and competition. Match-derived targets must be scaled to current capacity and tissue tolerance.

citation: Novak JI, Novak AR. Is Additive Manufacturing Improving Performance in Sports? A Systematic Review. Proceedings of the Institution of Mechanical Engineers, Part P: Journal of Sports Engineering and Technology. 2021;235(3):163-175.
abstract: This systematic review evaluated empirical evidence for additively manufactured sporting equipment, protection, and comfort products across multiple sports.
tldr: Some 3D-printed sports products performed better than conventional comparators, but most applications were isolated and weakly replicated. Validate fit, safety, durability, rules, and field performance before adoption.
methods: Four databases were searched from 1984 through May 2019 under a PRISMA-based protocol. Twenty-six articles across 12 sports were analyzed for application, performance comparison, manufacturing process, software, scanning, and reported opportunities or constraints.
findings: Ten articles reported improved product performance, eight similar performance, and five lower performance than conventional products. Running or walking dominated, half used powder-bed fusion, 42% used 3D scanning, and many failed to identify the printer or design software.
limitations: The small, heterogeneous evidence base could not be pooled and was dominated by single studies. Sample size, laboratory transfer, long-term durability, material interfaces, postprocessing, regulation, and incomplete technical reporting constrain confidence and replication.
practicalImplications: Treat additive manufacturing as a prototyping and customization pathway. Before athlete use, define the problem and comparator, verify material and fit, test safety and durability under representative load, confirm rules, and monitor failures and athlete response.
athleteDev: Invite athlete input on fit and function without implying that customized or novel means superior. Record comfort, performance, skin or pressure issues, and durability over time.
rtp: A customized brace, orthosis, guard, or equipment component needs clinical and engineering validation for the intended task. Do not let novelty accelerate exposure or replace established protection and capacity criteria.

citation: Drummond FR, Drummond LR, Campos HO, Fernandes JGRP, Monteiro MC, Lara HFG, et al. Is Melatonin as an Ergogenic Hormone a Myth? A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Endocrine. 2024;83(2):302-321.
abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated melatonin supplementation for exercise performance and recovery and examined exercise-related melatonin secretion.
tldr: Melatonin did not improve pooled aerobic or strength performance. Evidence for recovery was narrow and should not be generalized into a performance supplement recommendation.
methods: Twenty-one studies met systematic-review criteria and 19 entered meta-analysis. Models examined time-trial and oxygen-uptake performance, strength, postexercise recovery biomarkers, and endogenous melatonin immediately and 60 minutes after exercise.
findings: Supplementation did not improve time-trial, oxygen-uptake, or strength performance. Glutathione peroxidase increased, while other pooled recovery outcomes did not establish a broad ergogenic effect; exercise did not consistently change immediate or 60-minute melatonin secretion.
limitations: Few studies were available, and some individuals contributed multiple outcomes or trials. Dose, timing, task, population, and recovery measures varied, and evidence for a general recovery benefit rested on limited biomarkers rather than consistent performance restoration.
practicalImplications: Do not use melatonin to enhance strength or endurance. If sleep or travel is the target, first address schedule, light, behavior, and sleep opportunity, then involve qualified medical or nutrition staff for product, dose, timing, interaction, and side-effect review.
athleteDev: Separate sleep support from performance enhancement and discourage self-escalation. Ask athletes to report next-day drowsiness, unusual dreams, headaches, medication use, and product source.
rtp: Melatonin is not a readiness marker or tissue-recovery treatment. Any use during rehabilitation should support an identified sleep plan and avoid side effects that impair training, driving, or clinical monitoring.

citation: Clarkson MJ, May AK, Warmington SA. Is There Rationale for the Cuff Pressures Prescribed for Blood Flow Restriction Exercise? A Systematic Review. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2020;30(8):1318-1336.
abstract: This systematic review examined how blood-flow-restriction studies selected individualized cuff pressure and whether the selected percentage of occlusion pressure was justified.
tldr: Even individualized BFR studies used 30% to 100% occlusion pressure, rarely with clear rationale. Measure with the actual setup, screen risk, and avoid a universal pressure prescription.
methods: Fifty-one acute or chronic BFR-exercise studies that measured limb or arterial occlusion pressure were identified and assessed with a bespoke 13-point quality tool. Pressure, population, cuff, exercise, methodology, and stated rationale were extracted.
findings: Prescribed pressure ranged from 30% to 100% of measured occlusion pressure, and only seven study applications justified the selected percentage. Individualization addressed some equipment and participant variability but did not create consistent prescription or reporting.
limitations: The review did not compare adaptation or adverse outcomes across pressures. Heterogeneity in population, exercise, cuff width and material, device regulation, body position, and reporting prevents identification of an ideal pressure.
practicalImplications: Screen contraindications, measure occlusion in the exercise-specific body position with the actual cuff, prescribe the lowest justified individualized pressure, monitor symptoms and response, and document equipment and method for repeatability.
athleteDev: Explain that more pressure is not automatically more effective. Athletes should immediately report numbness, unusual pain, discoloration, dizziness, or symptoms beyond expected exertion.
rtp: BFR can supplement low-load rehabilitation when clinically appropriate, but it does not replace progressive tissue loading. Pressure and exercise must be individualized and supervised within the medical plan.

citation: Oranchuk DJ, Storey AG, Nelson AR, Cronin JB. Isometric Training and Long-Term Adaptations: Effects of Muscle Length, Intensity, and Intent: A Systematic Review. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2019;29(4):484-503.
abstract: This systematic review examined how muscle length, contraction intensity, and intent influence medium- to long-term morphological, neural, tendon, and performance adaptations to isometric training.
tldr: Longer muscle lengths favored hypertrophy and transfer, ballistic intent favored rapid force, and higher intensity appeared important for tendon adaptation. Prescribe to the target rather than using one generic isometric protocol.
methods: Four databases were searched for human studies lasting at least three weeks. Twenty-three research outputs were quality-evaluated and synthesized by joint angle or muscle length, contraction intensity, intent, volume, and morphological, neural, tendon, or performance outcome.
findings: Long-muscle-length training generally produced greater hypertrophy and dynamic transfer than shorter-length work. Ballistic intent improved activation and rapid force production, contractions at or above 70% MVC appeared necessary for tendon structure and function, and hypertrophy and maximal force improved across intensities.
limitations: The number of direct comparisons was limited and interventions, muscle groups, doses, and outcomes varied. Closed-chain and dynamic transfer, fatigue, rehabilitation populations, contraction subtypes, free-weight use, and sequencing with later dynamic training need more research.
practicalImplications: Start with the adaptation required: use tolerable longer-muscle-length positions for morphology and transfer, fast intent for early force, and sufficiently high force for tendon goals when clinically appropriate. Progress volume, angle, intensity, and intent separately.
athleteDev: Teach athletes that an isometric can target pain-tolerant loading, position-specific strength, tendon force, or rapid recruitment depending on execution. Quality and intent matter even when no movement is visible.
rtp: Use isometrics to bridge capacity at controlled joint angles, then demonstrate transfer through dynamic, elastic, multidirectional, and sport-specific tasks. Isometric improvement alone does not establish return readiness.

citation: Zhao Z, Liu Y, Xu K. Optimizing Agility Training in Team Sport Players—The Role of Perception-Action Coupling: A Systematic Review with Multi-Level Meta-Analysis. Journal of Sports Science and Medicine. 2026;25:84-111.
abstract: This systematic review and multilevel meta-analysis evaluated agility training that coupled perception with action in team-sport athletes and explored moderators and dose-response patterns.
tldr: Perception-action training improved reactive agility, but the apparent seven-to-eight-week dose was not a proven optimum. Use representative stimuli and monitor total load while accounting for limited female and non-soccer evidence.
methods: Twenty-eight studies met the review criteria, and 26 contributed 53 effect sizes after influential-study exclusions. Three-level models pooled reactive-agility, preplanned-agility, and reaction outcomes; subgroup and meta-regression analyses explored population and training dose.
findings: Reactive-agility performance improved with a large effect (0.65), preplanned agility with a moderate effect (0.55), and reaction outcomes with a nonsignificant moderate estimate (0.52). Favorable effects clustered around seven to eight weeks, more than three weekly sessions, and 20 to 25 minutes per session.
limitations: Certainty was moderate for reactive agility and low or very low for secondary outcomes. Heterogeneity, possible publication or outcome-reporting bias, soccer and basketball dominance, female underrepresentation, inconsistent training-load reporting, and sparse retention data limit dose claims.
practicalImplications: Use decision-rich drills with representative visual or human stimuli and retain separate change-of-direction capacity work where needed. Progress complexity and exposure from athlete response rather than copying the pooled frequency as a formula.
athleteDev: Develop scanning, anticipation, decision speed, and movement execution together. Give athletes feedback on the decision and solution, not only completion time.
rtp: Reintroduce agility from predictable movement to increasingly representative perception-action tasks, then uncontrolled team play. Account for physical, cognitive, and total-session load throughout the progression.

citation: Finnern LS, Wilke J, Willwacher S, Pasanen K, Hollander K, Dalos D, et al. Qualitative and Quantitative Situational Characteristics of Muscle Strains in Sports: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2026;60(3):211-226.
abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesized video-recorded situational and kinematic characteristics of indirect and non-contact muscle injuries across sports and muscle groups.
tldr: Most recorded strains were non-contact and many were running-related, but patterns differed by muscle and sport. Prepare athletes for representative high-force length changes without claiming one video position caused the injury.
methods: Twenty-one video-analysis studies reported 728 indirect or non-contact muscle injuries. Contact mechanism, activity, movement direction, joint position, timing, and muscle-specific patterns were synthesized qualitatively and, when possible, quantitatively.
findings: Seventy-four percent of injuries were non-contact and nearly half were running-related. Many occurred during active rapid muscle-tendon length change, with recurring but distinct patterns for hamstring, adductor, rectus-femoris, and calf injuries and additional sport-specific kicking, reaching, deceleration, or perturbation situations.
limitations: Football and hamstring evidence dominated, female athletes and several muscles were underrepresented, terminology and methods varied, and study quality ranged from low to high. Video angle, quality, rater expertise, and missing clinical or imaging context limit causal inference.
practicalImplications: Prepare the relevant muscle for its sport-specific high-force, long-length, sprinting, kicking, acceleration, deceleration, reaching, and perturbation demands. Confirm proposed prevention elements prospectively rather than assuming mechanism resemblance guarantees efficacy.
athleteDev: Teach athletes to build exposure to the situations the sport requires instead of fearing a single movement. Progress speed, range, force, fatigue, and uncertainty while maintaining technical options.
rtp: Rehabilitation should recreate the injured muscle's likely demand profile and the athlete's position and sport situations. Video patterns can guide exposure selection but cannot replace clinical diagnosis, tissue criteria, confidence, or full practice progression.

citation: Sanders GJ, Boos B, Shipley F, Scheadler CM, Peacock CA. An Accelerometer-Based Training Load Analysis to Assess Volleyball Performance. Journal of Exercise and Nutrition. 2021;1(1). doi:10.53520/jen2018.1034.
abstract: This prospective single-athlete observational study tracked one Division I female outside hitter across a competitive volleyball season. Practice and match activity were recorded with a Catapult microsensor, weekly approach-jump power was used as a neuromuscular-performance measure, and match statistics were compared with practice-load variables. Forward regression related selected acceleration, deceleration, and jump counts to weekly jump power, while high-intensity practice jumps and hitting percentage were compared between wins and losses.
tldr: A season-long case study found strong within-sample associations among selected wearable-load variables, weekly approach-jump power, and match outcomes in one collegiate volleyball athlete. The analysis demonstrates a possible monitoring workflow, but the single athlete, many candidate predictors, and observational design make the estimates unsuitable as population thresholds or causal dose recommendations.
methods: One 20.5-year-old Division I female outside hitter who remained in matches was monitored through practices and games. A Catapult microsensor quantified accelerations, decelerations, and jumps at multiple intensity bands. The athlete completed a weekly approach-jump test, match statistics were recorded, and forward linear regression selected load variables associated with weekly relative jump power. Practice loads and match statistics were also compared between subsequent wins and losses.
findings: Selected acceleration, deceleration, and jump variables jointly explained 91.7% of the observed within-sample variation in weekly relative approach-jump power. High-intensity practice jumps were lower before wins than losses (49.6 ± 26.7 versus 69.2 ± 39.8), and hitting percentage was higher in wins (.266 ± .190 versus .130 ± .129). These associations occurred in one athlete and do not establish that changing jump volume would cause better performance.
limitations: The study followed one athlete for one season, so it cannot establish population norms, universal alert thresholds, or effects across roles and competition levels. Forward selection from many candidate predictors creates substantial overfitting risk, and the reported 91.7% explained variation was not tested out of sample. Win-loss results are also influenced by teammates, opponents, tactics, schedule, and other unmeasured factors. The observational analysis cannot establish causation.
practicalImplications: Use the paper as a model for individualized longitudinal monitoring rather than as a prescription to cap high-intensity jumps at a fixed value. Predefine a small set of meaningful load and performance variables, visualize their time order, interpret changes in the athlete's role and technical context, and require prospective or out-of-sample confirmation before treating an association as decision guidance.
athleteDev: For volleyball performance monitoring, pair position-specific jump exposure with a repeatable approach-jump measure and contextual match information. Evaluate whether within-athlete trends are stable enough to inform training conversations, while avoiding direct transfer of this athlete's counts or regression coefficients to other athletes.
rtp: The study did not evaluate injury rehabilitation or return to sport. Its single-athlete monitoring structure could inform how jump exposure and performance tests are displayed during reconditioning, but it supplies no clearance criterion, reinjury threshold, or validated return-to-volleyball progression.

citation: Collings TJ, Diamond LE, Barrett RS, Saxby DJ, Lloyd DG, Whiteley R, Patterson BE, Crossley KM, Bourne MN. An Evidence-Based and Mechanistic Approach to Reducing the Risk of Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury: An Exercise and Sport Science Australia Position Statement. Sports Medicine. 2026. doi:10.1007/s40279-026-02450-3.
abstract: This Exercise and Sport Science Australia position statement combined two systematic searches with mechanistic evidence to evaluate exercise-based ACL injury-risk reduction and propose a tiered prescription framework. Tier 1 comprises population-level multicomponent neuromuscular or structured warm-up programs. Tier 2 comprises targeted movement, strength, feedback, and neurocognitive strategies whose mechanistic rationale currently exceeds their direct injury-incidence evidence.
tldr: Multicomponent neuromuscular and structured warm-up programs have the strongest evidence for reducing ACL injury incidence, particularly in adolescent female soccer, basketball, and handball. Individualized biomechanical or neurocognitive strategies may be useful adjuncts, but they have not yet demonstrated reduced ACL injury incidence.
methods: The authors searched Scopus, Embase, and PubMed. One search identified controlled and cohort studies evaluating exercise interventions against ACL injury incidence; a second identified prospective intrinsic risk-factor studies. They integrated those findings with video, in vivo, in vitro, and in silico biomechanical evidence to develop a two-tier exercise framework.
findings: Meta-analyses summarized by the statement estimate an approximately 60% reduction in ACL injury risk from multicomponent programs in female soccer, basketball, or handball players aged 14–18 years. Effective programs commonly included plyometric, bodyweight-strength, balance or proprioception, mobility, and agility elements for 10–30 minutes, two to three times weekly. Higher adherence was associated with greater effectiveness. Direct injury-incidence evidence for targeted Tier 2 strategies remains limited.
limitations: The strongest intervention evidence is concentrated in adolescent female cutting and landing sports. Evidence in males, elite athletes, American football, and several other sports is limited. The statement combines multiple evidence types with different inferential strength, and modifiable biomechanical associations do not by themselves establish causal injury mechanisms or prevention effects.
practicalImplications: Prioritize a sustainable multicomponent Tier 1 program, monitor delivery and adherence, and adapt implementation to the sport and training environment. Add targeted Tier 2 work only for a clearly defined athlete need and describe it as an adjunct with mechanistic support rather than as a proven way to reduce ACL injuries.
athleteDev: Build landing, deceleration, strength, balance, and agility exposure progressively within normal training. Preserve individual coaching and movement assessment, but do not convert a screening score or movement pattern into a deterministic injury label.
rtp: This statement addresses primary injury-risk reduction rather than return-to-play clearance. Its exercise categories may inform late-stage reconditioning after ACL injury, but it provides no validated clearance threshold, reinjury prediction rule, or sport-specific return progression.

citation: Akkus C, Pakoz B, Gultekinler BD, Turgut E. Mapping the evidence on dual-task training in musculoskeletal injury rehabilitation: a systematic review. Research in Sports Medicine. 2026:1–36. doi:10.1080/15438627.2026.2673035.
abstract: This preregistered systematic review mapped randomized evidence for repeated motor-cognitive or motor-motor dual-task training in adult musculoskeletal rehabilitation. Eight trials involving 224 adults covered ankle instability, ACL reconstruction, knee ligament-dominance deficit, and elbow fracture. Heterogeneity prevented quantitative pooling, so the authors used a best-evidence synthesis.
tldr: Dual-task rehabilitation can improve selected outcomes, but the clearest ACL-reconstruction evidence indicates results comparable to single-task training rather than superior. The small, heterogeneous evidence base does not establish better return-to-sport or reinjury outcomes.
methods: The review included peer-reviewed English or Turkish randomized trials in adults aged 18–65 years that compared repeated dual-task rehabilitation with single-task training, usual care, or no intervention. The authors assessed risk of bias and graded condition-specific consistency using a best-evidence framework because injuries, interventions, comparators, and outcomes were too heterogeneous for meta-analysis.
findings: Eight trials included 224 adults, and four trials were rated high risk of bias. Strong evidence indicated comparable postural-control and patient-reported improvements from dual- and single-task training after ACL reconstruction. Moderate evidence indicated dual-task training was comparable to single-task training and superior to no intervention for selected ankle-instability outcomes. Evidence for several proprioceptive, neuromuscular, and kinematic outcomes was conflicting or limited.
limitations: Only eight small trials were included, half were high risk of bias, and outcome measurement was a recurring concern. Evidence was concentrated in lower-extremity conditions, interventions lasted 4–12 weeks, and long-term retention, reinjury, and return-to-sport outcomes were not established. Database and language restrictions may have omitted relevant studies.
practicalImplications: Use dual-task progressions when the secondary demand matches a meaningful rehabilitation objective and the athlete can maintain movement quality. Do not assume that adding cognitive load is inherently superior; compare it with a clear single-task baseline and monitor task-specific response.
athleteDev: Progress from stable single-task execution to controlled secondary demands that reflect the athlete's sport and decision environment. Preserve technical quality and expose complexity deliberately rather than using dual-task difficulty as a generic marker of readiness.
rtp: The review does not validate a dual-task clearance test or show reduced reinjury. Dual-task performance may contribute contextual information during late-stage rehabilitation, but it should sit alongside tissue recovery, strength, power, movement, exposure, symptoms, and sport-specific progression.

citation: Vitale J, McCall A, Athlete Travel & Sleep Interest Group (ATSIG), et al. From GPT-4 to Expert-Endorsed Athlete Guidance: A Delphi Consensus on Sleep and Jet Lag. Sports Medicine. 2026. doi:10.1007/s40279-026-02484-7.
abstract: This modified Delphi study asked an international panel of 17 sleep, travel, sport-science, clinical, and elite-athlete-support experts to review and revise 20 GPT-4-derived guidance items on athlete sleep and jet lag. The process converted preliminary model output into expert-endorsed material while retaining two topics that did not reach consensus.
tldr: Expert review produced consensus on 18 of 20 athlete sleep and jet-lag guidance items, while injury-risk wording and sleep-aid or melatonin guidance remained unresolved. The study supports AI as a drafting aid under expert governance, not as an independent authority.
methods: Seventeen purposively selected experts completed two modified Delphi rounds. Experts rated the appropriateness of draft answers, provided revisions, and re-rated steering-committee-adapted items. Consensus was evaluated with rating distributions, interquartile ranges, and round-to-round comparisons.
findings: Consensus increased from 15 of 20 items in round one to 18 of 20 in round two. Injury-risk guidance remained near-threshold non-consensus, and sleep-aid or melatonin guidance remained non-consensus in both rounds. Expert revision repeatedly identified insufficient athlete specificity, misalignment with evidence, formatting problems, and imprecise or misleading draft content.
limitations: The panel was small, purposively selected, and drawn from experts already involved in the earlier language-model evaluation. Delphi consensus represents agreement within that panel, not clinical effectiveness or universal guidance. The study did not test whether the recommendations improved sleep, travel adaptation, health, or performance outcomes.
practicalImplications: Use the expert-endorsed content as a structured starting point for individualized sleep and travel planning. Treat injury-risk claims, melatonin, and other sleep-aid decisions as unresolved or clinically governed topics, and preserve human review for any AI-generated athlete guidance.
athleteDev: Teach athletes repeatable sleep, light-exposure, caffeine, and travel-planning behaviors while adapting timing to destination, schedule, individual response, and medical context. Avoid presenting a generic AI answer as a personalized prescription.
rtp: The study did not evaluate rehabilitation or return to sport. Sleep and travel management may support readiness during recovery, but the consensus items provide no clearance criterion, reinjury estimate, or condition-specific return-to-play protocol.

citation: Dillon MR, Mastroianni MA, Frappa N, Evoniuk C, Curtis W, Trofa DP, Jobin CM, Ablove R, Levine WN, Ahmad CS. Return to Play, Performance, and Career Longevity After Shoulder Labral Repair in the National Football League: A Matched Cohort Analysis. Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2026;14(7):23259671261454331. doi:10.1177/23259671261454331.
abstract: This retrospective matched-cohort study used public injury reporting and NFL participation and performance data to examine return to play, workload, PFF grade, and career longevity after reported isolated shoulder labral repair. Cases were matched with controls by season, position, age, and preindex snap rate.
tldr: Most identified NFL players returned after reported shoulder labral repair, and first-season participation workload was broadly similar to matched controls. Defensive-player performance grades declined more than controls, but public-record limitations and selection of established returners prevent clinical or causal interpretation.
methods: The authors identified procedures through injury transactions, team or NFL communications, and corroborating media reports. Return was the first regular-season snap after the reported surgery date. Cases and controls were matched by season and position, then age and preindex snap rate. Outcomes included games, snaps, snaps per game, season-level PFF grades, and postreturn career duration.
findings: Ninety-six of 111 identified episodes returned to NFL play, an 86.5% rate, at a median 265 days; 73.9% returned within one year and 84.7% within two years. First-season changes in games and snap workload did not differ significantly from controls. Defensive cases had larger PFF-grade declines than controls, while offensive-grade differences and career-duration comparisons were not statistically significant.
limitations: Public reporting could not confirm diagnosis, tear characteristics, bone loss, operative details, rehabilitation, recurrence, or clinical milestones. Requiring at least 100 snaps before and after return selected healthier, established returners for performance analysis. PFF grades are influenced by scheme, coaching, role, utilization, concurrent injury, and other unmeasured factors. The observational design cannot establish that surgery caused any outcome.
practicalImplications: Separate participation, workload tolerance, role-specific performance, and career continuity when discussing return after shoulder labral repair. Use the reported timeline as descriptive NFL context, not as an individual prognosis or clearance target.
athleteDev: Rebuild contact tolerance, position-specific shoulder demands, football workload, and technical performance progressively. Evaluate the athlete's actual role and preinjury baseline rather than treating a return to snaps as full performance restoration.
rtp: This study provides descriptive return timing and postreturn outcomes but no clinical clearance criteria. Individual decisions still require tissue and symptom status, strength and function, contact exposure, position demands, recurrence risk, athlete preference, and interdisciplinary judgment.

citation: Pickler MC, Funderburk LK, Lee KM, Bolden LK, Chapman-Lopez TJ, Heileson JL, Gallucci AR. Observation of Altered Iron Status Development During Noncompetitive Season Training in NCAA Division I Female Acrobatics and Tumbling Athletes. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2026. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000005584.
abstract: This longitudinal observational study followed 29 NCAA Division I female acrobatics and tumbling athletes during a noncompetitive training period. Pre-post blood biomarkers and body composition were used to describe iron-status development in an understudied collegiate female sport.
tldr: Serum ferritin declined across the training period while group hemoglobin and red-cell indices did not significantly change. The trend supports clinically governed surveillance in this population but does not identify a cause, establish anemia, or define a universal treatment threshold.
methods: Blood biomarkers were assessed from October 1 to December 15, with DXA body-composition assessments in August and December. Serum ferritin, hemoglobin, red blood cell count and distribution width, total protein, estradiol, and progesterone were measured. Paired changes were tested with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, and ferritin status was categorized using four previously published thresholds.
findings: Serum ferritin decreased significantly, while red blood cell count, hemoglobin, and red-cell distribution width did not significantly change. Thirteen athletes, or 44%, were below 35 ng/mL before training compared with 79% after training. At the post-training assessment, one athlete exceeded 51 ng/mL and 96% were at or below 50 ng/mL.
limitations: The study followed one team without a control group and did not measure dietary iron intake, detailed training exposure, menstrual history, supplementation adherence, inflammation, or other plausible contributors. Threshold classifications vary across clinical and sport contexts. Biomarker changes do not identify their cause, establish symptoms, or demonstrate that a specific intervention is required.
practicalImplications: Use repeated iron-status assessment within an interdisciplinary clinical process for female collegiate athletes, especially when training exposure, symptoms, nutrition, or menstrual factors create concern. Interpret ferritin alongside hematology, symptoms, inflammation, diet, supplementation, and medical history rather than applying a single cutoff in isolation.
athleteDev: Integrate nutrition education, recovery behaviors, symptom reporting, and clinically governed biomarker follow-up into the development environment. Avoid labeling an athlete's readiness or potential from ferritin alone.
rtp: The study did not evaluate injury rehabilitation or return to sport. Iron-status findings may inform broader medical and readiness management, but they provide no clearance criterion or sport-participation restriction by themselves.

citation: Myszka S., Yearby T., Davids K. Being Water : how key ideas from the practice of Bruce Lee align with contemporary theorizing in movement skill acquisition. Sport, Education and Society. 2024;29(4):451-467. doi:10.1080/13573322.2022.2160701.
abstract: This paper addresses the following question: How do Bruce Lee’s documented coaching ideas align—or conflict—with contemporary ecological-dynamics concepts? Conceptual insight paper, not a participant study. Uses historical accounts, Lee’s writings, and selected empirical and theoretical examples. Narrative conceptual analysis. The authors map themes from Jeet Kune Do to ecological dynamics.
tldr: The authors frame skill as adaptable problem solving shaped by performer–environment interaction rather than reproduction of one ideal technique. They propose deceptive actions and opponent-responsive movement problems as relevant design features for field and court sports. Use the paper to audit whether a drill preserves the information and decisions athletes need in competition.
methods: Narrative conceptual analysis. The authors map themes from Jeet Kune Do to ecological dynamics. Claims are interpretive and are not a systematic evidence review.
findings: The authors frame skill as adaptable problem solving shaped by performer–environment interaction rather than reproduction of one ideal technique.
