They propose deceptive actions and opponent-responsive movement problems as relevant design features for field and court sports. They explicitly reject uncritical adoption of Lee’s ideas when those ideas conflict with variability and representative design. Decontextualized drills are presented as possible supplementary work, with overreliance risking low fidelity to competition.
limitations: Historical anecdotes and philosophical alignment cannot establish comparative training effectiveness. Martial-arts examples require careful transfer to football constraints and contact rules. “Representative” practice still needs appropriate task difficulty, safety, and progression. The paper offers design principles, not a validated prescription.
practicalImplications: Use the paper to audit whether a drill preserves the information and decisions athletes need in competition. Retain isolated work when it serves a clear capacity or coordination purpose, then reconnect it to live problems.
athleteDev: For athlete development, use the paper to audit whether a drill preserves the information and decisions athletes need in competition. Retain isolated work when it serves a clear capacity or coordination purpose, then reconnect it to live problems. Apply the finding within the population and setting described in the source rather than treating it as a universal threshold.
rtp: The paper did not validate a rehabilitation or return-to-sport decision rule. Its findings may inform supporting training or monitoring during reconditioning, but it provides no standalone clearance threshold or progression criterion.

citation: Webster K.E., Ristanis S., Feller J.A. A longitudinal investigation of landing biomechanics following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction. Physical Therapy in Sport. 2021;50:36-41. doi:10.1016/j.ptsp.2021.03.012.
abstract: This paper addresses the following question: Do between-limb landing asymmetries diminish from the first postoperative year to three years after ACL reconstruction and return to sport? Participants: Fourteen patients after ACL reconstruction. Sport and level: Athletes who intended to return to high-impact sport and had returned by the three-year assessment. Design: Prospective longitudinal study. Exposure or intervention: Time and return to sporting activity; no assigned training intervention.
tldr: Most biomechanical variables changed little; the operated-knee external adduction moment increased with an effect size of 0.5 but remained below the contralateral side. Reduced knee-flexion angles persisted relative to the uninvolved limb, with effect sizes from 0.76 to 0.90. Do not treat return to sport as proof that landing mechanics have normalized.
methods: Design: Prospective longitudinal study. Exposure or intervention: Time and return to sporting activity; no assigned training intervention. Comparator: Operated versus contralateral limb and change across the two assessments. Measurements and outcomes: Three-dimensional single-limb landing kinematics and kinetics. Analysis: Across-time and across-limb ANOVA models.
findings: Most biomechanical variables changed little; the operated-knee external adduction moment increased with an effect size of 0.5 but remained below the contralateral side. Reduced knee-flexion angles persisted relative to the uninvolved limb, with effect sizes from 0.76 to 0.90. Reduced knee-flexion moments persisted, with effect sizes from 0.56 to 0.90, alongside larger hip-flexion moments with effect sizes from 0.60 to 0.75.
limitations: The sample contained only 14 patients, and the observational design cannot determine whether the identified strategy causes reinjury or later joint problems. The authors state that the long-term implications of controlling landing through a larger hip moment remain unknown.
practicalImplications: Do not treat return to sport as proof that landing mechanics have normalized. When relevant to the athlete's sport and history, compare limb strategy over time and examine how force is distributed across knee and hip rather than relying on a single performance outcome. The study supports surveillance and targeted training, not a universal symmetry cutoff.
athleteDev: For athlete development, do not treat return to sport as proof that landing mechanics have normalized. When relevant to the athlete's sport and history, compare limb strategy over time and examine how force is distributed across knee and hip rather than relying on a single performance outcome. The study supports surveillance and targeted training, not a universal symmetry cutoff. Apply the finding within the population and setting described in the source rather than treating it as a universal threshold.
rtp: For rehabilitation and return-to-sport decisions, do not treat return to sport as proof that landing mechanics have normalized. When relevant to the athlete's sport and history, compare limb strategy over time and examine how force is distributed across knee and hip rather than relying on a single performance outcome. The study supports surveillance and targeted training, not a universal symmetry cutoff. Use the paper as one input to interdisciplinary judgment, not as a standalone clearance criterion or reinjury prediction rule.

citation: Davidson R., Gordon S., Hussain A., Schneider S. An Analysis of the Association Between National Football League Players Association (NFLPA) Ratings and Player Injuries. Cureus. 2026. doi:10.7759/cureus.110909.
abstract: This paper addresses the following question: At the NFL-team level, are NFLPA rankings of training staffs or strength coaches correlated with the number of players missing games or total player-weeks missed because of injury? Participants: No individual participant cohort was analyzed; the unit was all 32 NFL teams, using aggregated public data. Sport and level: Professional American football, 2024–2025 NFL regular season. Design: Cross-sectional ecological correlation study with team-level aggregation (n=32). Exposure or intervention: NFLPA anonymous player-survey rankings for “Training Staff” and “Strength coaches”; lower rank indicated a better rating.
tldr: Across the season, 1,149 players missed a game and 5,811 player-weeks were missed; team means were 36.097 players and 183.645 player-weeks. Pearson correlations were not statistically significant for training-staff rank versus players missing games (r=-.0300, p=.435), strength-staff rank versus players missing games (r=-.2675, p=.063), training-staff rank versus weeks missed (r=-.0310, p=.433), or strength-staff rank versus weeks missed (r=-.2378, p=.089). NFLPA ratings may describe player experience and workplace environment, but these data do not validate them as performance indicators for medical or strength-and-conditioning staffs.
methods: Design: Cross-sectional ecological correlation study with team-level aggregation (n=32). Exposure or intervention: NFLPA anonymous player-survey rankings for “Training Staff” and “Strength coaches”; lower rank indicated a better rating. Comparator: Each staff ranking against (1) players missing at least one game and (2) total player-weeks missed. Measurements and outcomes: Public NFLPA rankings and Pro-Football-Reference injury reports; outcomes were unadjusted team counts and player-weeks, not unique injury events or individual risk. Analysis: Pearson product-moment and Spearman rank correlations, significance threshold p=.05.
findings: Across the season, 1,149 players missed a game and 5,811 player-weeks were missed; team means were 36.097 players and 183.645 player-weeks. Pearson correlations were not statistically significant for training-staff rank versus players missing games (r=-.0300, p=.435), strength-staff rank versus players missing games (r=-.2675, p=.063), training-staff rank versus weeks missed (r=-.0310, p=.433), or strength-staff rank versus weeks missed (r=-.2378, p=.089). Spearman correlations were likewise nonsignificant: ρ=.0344 (p=.574), -.2014 (p=.130), -.0374 (p=.420), and -.2274 (p=.099), respectively. Linear fits explained little variance: R²=.001 for both training-staff comparisons, .072 for strength-coach rank versus players missing games, and .057 for strength-coach rank versus weeks missed.
limitations: Authors emphasized ecological fallacy, uncontrolled confounding (age, experience, playing style, facilities, surfaces, environment), possible illness/suspension miscoding, likability bias, ambiguous “Training Staff” wording, and retrospective selection/recall bias. Additional transfer limitation — interpretation: NFLPA satisfaction ranks and raw NFL team injury counts are not equivalent to objective evaluations of staff practice, program quality, or individual injury risk. Additional causal limitation — interpretation: Null team-level correlations neither show that staff quality has no effect nor identify causes of injury burden.
practicalImplications: NFLPA ratings may describe player experience and workplace environment, but these data do not validate them as performance indicators for medical or strength-and-conditioning staffs. Staff evaluation should use objective process and outcome measures with appropriate exposure adjustment and individual-level longitudinal data; this ecological null result should not drive personnel judgments.
athleteDev: For athlete development, nFLPA ratings may describe player experience and workplace environment, but these data do not validate them as performance indicators for medical or strength-and-conditioning staffs. Staff evaluation should use objective process and outcome measures with appropriate exposure adjustment and individual-level longitudinal data; this ecological null result should not drive personnel judgments. Apply the finding within the population and setting described in the source rather than treating it as a universal threshold.
rtp: For rehabilitation and return-to-sport decisions, nFLPA ratings may describe player experience and workplace environment, but these data do not validate them as performance indicators for medical or strength-and-conditioning staffs. Staff evaluation should use objective process and outcome measures with appropriate exposure adjustment and individual-level longitudinal data; this ecological null result should not drive personnel judgments. Use the paper as one input to interdisciplinary judgment, not as a standalone clearance criterion or reinjury prediction rule.

citation: Thomas C., Jones P.A., Rothwell J., Chiang C.Y., Comfort P. An Investigation Into the Relationship Between Maximum Isometric Strength and Vertical Jump Performance. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2015;29(8):2176-2185. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000000866.
abstract: This paper addresses the following question: How are maximal isometric strength variables associated with squat-jump and countermovement-jump force, power, velocity, and height, and do relatively stronger collegiate athletes outperform weaker peers? Participants: 22 male collegiate athletes, age 21.3±2.9 years, height 175.63±8.23 cm, mass 78.06±10.77 kg. Sport and level: Collegiate cricket, judo, rugby, and soccer. Design: Cross-sectional correlational study with a secondary median-split comparison. Exposure or intervention: IMTP peak force, maximum rate of force development, impulses at 100/200/300 ms, and total impulse.
tldr: Absolute IMTP impulses at 100–300 ms correlated with CMJ peak force (r=.63–.64, p≤.01), SJ peak force (r=.56–.58, p≤.01), CMJ peak power (r=.49–.51, p≤.05), and SJ peak power (r=.59–.60, p≤.01); correlations with jump height were near zero and nonsignificant. Stronger and weaker groups differed in relative IMTP peak force (38.72±2.08 vs 30.40±4.01 N/kg, p=.01, d=2.60) and relative maximum RFD (172.59±37.64 vs 103.12±35.95 N/kg/s, p=.01, d=1.89). IMTP impulse and absolute force can complement jump peak-force and peak-power profiling, but they should not be treated as substitutes for jump height or dynamic performance.
methods: Design: Cross-sectional correlational study with a secondary median-split comparison. Exposure or intervention: IMTP peak force, maximum rate of force development, impulses at 100/200/300 ms, and total impulse. Comparator: IMTP variables versus squat-jump and countermovement-jump variables; strongest n=11 versus weakest n=11 by relative peak force. Measurements and outcomes: Force-platform peak velocity, peak force, peak power, and flight-time jump height. Analysis: Pearson correlations; independent t tests and Cohen's d for group comparisons; significance p≤.05.
findings: Absolute IMTP impulses at 100–300 ms correlated with CMJ peak force (r=.63–.64, p≤.01), SJ peak force (r=.56–.58, p≤.01), CMJ peak power (r=.49–.51, p≤.05), and SJ peak power (r=.59–.60, p≤.01); correlations with jump height were near zero and nonsignificant. Stronger and weaker groups differed in relative IMTP peak force (38.72±2.08 vs 30.40±4.01 N/kg, p=.01, d=2.60) and relative maximum RFD (172.59±37.64 vs 103.12±35.95 N/kg/s, p=.01, d=1.89). They did not differ significantly in CMJ height (0.33±0.05 vs 0.36±0.05 m, p=.19) or SJ height (0.29±0.06 vs 0.33±0.05 m, p=.14). Relative IMTP impulse measures were not significantly associated with vertical-jump performance measures in this sample.
limitations: The small, homogeneous, mixed-sport male sample limits precision and sport-specific transfer. Jump height derived from flight time can be influenced by takeoff and landing body configuration. Maximum RFD showed high variability (%CV=15.1), and findings depended on the sampling/scaling method. Additional causal limitation — interpretation: Correlations do not show that increasing IMTP impulse will cause improved jump performance.
practicalImplications: IMTP impulse and absolute force can complement jump peak-force and peak-power profiling, but they should not be treated as substitutes for jump height or dynamic performance. In collegiate American football, the study is best used to reinforce construct specificity and the need for stable within-athlete methods, not as a source of sport-specific cut points.

In collegiate American football, the study is best used to reinforce construct specificity and the need for stable within-athlete methods, not as a source of sport-specific cut points. Apply the finding within the population and setting described in the source rather than treating it as a universal threshold.

citation: Della Villa F., Ghibellini A., Buckthorpe M., Bononi L., Gabbrielli M., Grassi A., et al. abstract: This paper addresses the following question: Can unsupervised machine learning identify distinct 90° change-of-direction biomechanical phenotypes in a large cohort of healthy young soccer players? Participants: 1,002 competitive soccer players, age 16.3±2.8 years, including 264 females, free from severe musculoskeletal injury. Sport and level: Amateur and professional youth/young-adult soccer, age range 14–21 years. Design: Secondary cross-sectional analysis of the prospective CUTtheACL cohort. Exposure or intervention: Laboratory 90° cuts on artificial turf after warm-up/familiarization.
tldr: Four clusters emerged with silhouette=.43. Cluster sizes were low-force/low-control n=289, low-force/high-control n=242, high-force/low-control n=229, and high-force/high-control n=242. Multivariable clustering can be a useful descriptive layer for organizing complex cutting profiles, but these labels should not trigger ACL-risk classification or individualized “prevention” prescriptions without reliability and prospective-outcome validation.
methods: Design: Secondary cross-sectional analysis of the prospective CUTtheACL cohort. Exposure or intervention: Laboratory 90° cuts on artificial turf after warm-up/familiarization. Comparator: Four data-derived clusters rather than prespecified clinical groups. Measurements and outcomes: Three high-speed cameras, force platform, 2D kinematics, ground-reaction forces, speed/time variables, and Movement Analysis Test scores; 42 normalized biomechanical features entered clustering. Analysis: t-SNE dimensionality reduction, Ward agglomerative clustering, silhouette optimization, ARI stability/consensus analyses, random-forest threefold classification, and between-cluster tests.
findings: Four clusters emerged with silhouette=.43. Cluster sizes were low-force/low-control n=289, low-force/high-control n=242, high-force/low-control n=229, and high-force/high-control n=242. Stability across high perplexities was ARI=.701, stability across random seeds was ARI=.717, and consensus with K-means was ARI=.658. Random-forest cross-validation predicted the cluster labels with precision .91–.95, recall .90–.94, and F1 .91–.94. Peak posterior GRF differed across clusters (1.0±0.3, 0.9±0.2, 1.3±0.3, and 1.5±0.4 N/BW; ηp²=.40, p<.001), illustrating the force dimension used to interpret phenotypes.
limitations: Preplanned 90° cutting may not represent unplanned or varied in-game tasks; no strength or EMG data were collected. The 14–21-year soccer cohort limits transfer to adult professionals or American football. Dimensionality reduction can oversimplify individual strategies; each player was tested once, so phenotype test–retest reliability was unknown. Most importantly, no injury outcome was included; the clusters are descriptive movement phenotypes, not validated ACL-risk categories.
practicalImplications: Multivariable clustering can be a useful descriptive layer for organizing complex cutting profiles, but these labels should not trigger ACL-risk classification or individualized “prevention” prescriptions without reliability and prospective-outcome validation. For collegiate American football, both task and population differ substantially, so any analogous workflow requires sport-specific data and external validation.

citation: King R. Blended Intelligence: A Framework for How Professionally Diverse Multi-disciplinary Teams Solve Problems in Elite Sport. Lancashire Online Knowledge - University of Lancashire. 2026. doi:10.17030/UCLAN.THESIS.00058103.
abstract: This paper addresses the following question: How do individual practitioners, multidisciplinary teams, and high-performance leaders conceptualize and execute problem solving? tldr: The thesis proposes “blended intelligence” as combining deep specialist expertise with collaborative problem-solving capability. Practice implications emphasize structured collaboration, cognitive flexibility, shared language, and leadership conditions that allow expertise to integrate. methods: Pragmatic mixed qualitative design. Used Likert surveys, heat-map visualization, focus groups, and semistructured interviews. Reflexive thematic analysis supported an inductive, researcher-involved interpretation.
findings: The thesis proposes “blended intelligence” as combining deep specialist expertise with collaborative problem-solving capability. citation: Vecchiato M., Palermi S., Zamodics M., Babity M., Eftekhari M., Ryali R., et al. Cardiovascular Implications of the Enhanced Games: Performance Enhancing Drugs in Competition and Recreation. Sports Medicine - Open. 2026;12(1):48. doi:10.1186/s40798-026-01026-9.
abstract: This paper addresses the following question: What ergogenic and cardiovascular evidence exists for PED classes relevant to pharmacologically enhanced sport, and what screening and monitoring framework is justified? Participants: No new cohort; the review synthesizes studies of PED-exposed athletes and nonathletes. Sport and level: Enhanced Games, elite/recreational strength athletes, and the broader recreational-use context. Design: Narrative clinical review, not a systematic review or meta-analysis. Exposure or intervention: AAS, growth hormone/IGF-1, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, stimulants, β2-agonists, diuretics, metabolic modulators, and incretin-based weight-management therapies.
tldr: Across drug classes, ergogenic evidence was inconsistent; the review judged AAS and erythropoiesis-stimulating agents to have the clearest performance signals alongside associations with myocardial remodeling, arrhythmia, and thrombotic events. Much existing evidence consisted of case reports, small series, scarce registries, nonathlete data, and cohorts confounded by comorbidity and polypharmacy/“stacking.” When PED exposure is disclosed, use a nonjudgmental harm-reduction pathway with sports-medicine/cardiology oversight, exact exposure history, baseline evaluation, and longitudinal follow-up.
methods: Design: Narrative clinical review, not a systematic review or meta-analysis. Exposure or intervention: AAS, growth hormone/IGF-1, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, stimulants, β2-agonists, diuretics, metabolic modulators, and incretin-based weight-management therapies. Comparator: PED-exposed versus nonexposed evidence where available; otherwise mechanistic, case, small-cohort, or clinical-population evidence. Measurements and outcomes: Ergogenic effects, cardiac structure/function, blood pressure, rhythm, thrombotic events, metabolic effects, and screening markers. Analysis: Narrative synthesis with proposed risk-adapted preparticipation and longitudinal monitoring; no pooled quantitative analysis.
findings: Across drug classes, ergogenic evidence was inconsistent; the review judged AAS and erythropoiesis-stimulating agents to have the clearest performance signals alongside associations with myocardial remodeling, arrhythmia, and thrombotic events. Much existing evidence consisted of case reports, small series, scarce registries, nonathlete data, and cohorts confounded by comorbidity and polypharmacy/“stacking.” Exposure characterization was often inadequate for compound, cumulative dose, duration, and use pattern, so much evidence supports association rather than causation and cannot precisely quantify cardiovascular risk. The authors propose individualized baseline cardiovascular screening plus serial reassessment and, when indicated, advanced imaging and rhythm monitoring; they state no dedicated evidence-based eligibility thresholds exist for enhanced athletes.
limitations: This narrative review did not report a reproducible systematic search, risk-of-bias assessment, or pooled effects. Evidence underrepresented women, non-White athletes, elite competitors, and well-characterized doses; selection and publication bias were plausible. Medical oversight in an observational enhanced-sport setting cannot remove confounding or establish safety, and the authors explicitly reject treating the Enhanced Games as proof of safe enhancement. Additional transfer limitation — interpretation: This review supports referral and surveillance, not institutional approval of PED use or a dosing protocol.
practicalImplications: When PED exposure is disclosed, use a nonjudgmental harm-reduction pathway with sports-medicine/cardiology oversight, exact exposure history, baseline evaluation, and longitudinal follow-up. Do not imply that medical supervision makes supraphysiologic use safe; the evidence is heterogeneous, causal dose–response data are sparse, and standard athlete-heart findings may overlap with early toxicity.

citation: Lahti J., Huuhka T., Romero V., Bezodis I., Morin J.B., Häkkinen K. Changes in sprint performance and sagittal plane kinematics after heavy resisted sprint training in professional soccer players. PeerJ. 2020;8:e10507. doi:10.7717/peerj.10507.
abstract: This paper addresses the following question: Do nine weeks of heavy sled sprinting at 50% or 60% velocity decrement improve sprint performance and mechanics compared with normal training in professional soccer players? Participants: 32 male Finnish Premier League players, age 24.1±5.1 years, height 180±10 cm, mass 76.7±7.7 kg. Sport and level: Professional male soccer; goalkeepers excluded. Design: Nonrandomized pre/post, three-group team-based experiment. Exposure or intervention: Fifteen training opportunities over nine weeks, with individually loaded sleds producing 50% or 60% maximal-velocity decrement, followed by a two-week taper.
tldr: HS50% improved 10 m by 3.37% (2.14±0.06 to 2.07±0.06 s, p<.001, d=-1.25), 20 m by 3.07% (p<.001, d=-1.15), and 30 m by 2.89% (p<.001, d=-1.18). HS60% improved 10 m by 3.05% (p=.001, d=-.96), 20 m by 2.45% (p=.008, d=-.77), and 30 m by 2.04% (p=.021, d=-.62). Individually loaded heavy sled sprinting can be a pragmatic acceleration stimulus, with the 50% decrement showing the clearest 10-m advantage here.
methods: Design: Nonrandomized pre/post, three-group team-based experiment. Exposure or intervention: Fifteen training opportunities over nine weeks, with individually loaded sleds producing 50% or 60% maximal-velocity decrement, followed by a two-week taper. Comparator: Control team continued normal training without systematic acceleration or resisted-sprint work. Measurements and outcomes: 5-, 10-, 20-, and 30-m splits; radar-derived sprint force–velocity profile; manually digitized 2D sagittal kinematics and spatiotemporal variables. Analysis: Baseline-adjusted within/between-group tests, effect sizes, and comparison with between-session minimal detectable change.
findings: HS50% improved 10 m by 3.37% (2.14±0.06 to 2.07±0.06 s, p<.001, d=-1.25), 20 m by 3.07% (p<.001, d=-1.15), and 30 m by 2.89% (p<.001, d=-1.18). HS60% improved 10 m by 3.05% (p=.001, d=-.96), 20 m by 2.45% (p=.008, d=-.77), and 30 m by 2.04% (p=.021, d=-.62). Only the 10-m change showed a group×time interaction (F(2,24)=4.031, p=.031); HS50% improved more than control (p=.03, d=1.03). Both sled groups improved F0, 10-m mean force ratio, and Pmax, but F0 changes (7.83% and 9.23%) remained below the 9.53% between-session MDC. Observed technique fluctuations remained below the minimal detectable change and did not support longitudinal technical breakdown.
limitations: Intervention and control were different teams with different training/recovery cultures; no randomized unloaded-acceleration control. Small groups may have been underpowered; 2D kinematics used only two instants and lower-resolution video, with wide ICC confidence intervals. Professional soccer transfer to NCAA American football is limited by sport demands, calendar, and exposure. Additional causal limitation — interpretation: Team allocation and concurrent training prevent clean attribution of all changes to sled loading.
practicalImplications: Individually loaded heavy sled sprinting can be a pragmatic acceleration stimulus, with the 50% decrement showing the clearest 10-m advantage here. Treat the 50% versus 60% contrast as provisional, monitor actual split-time change against test error, and do not infer that unchanged 2D snapshots prove technique is unaffected in every athlete or task.

abstract: This paper addresses the following question: Which intrinsic and extrinsic contextual factors should shape load planning when the control-chaos continuum is used during return to sport in elite football? tldr: The continuum progresses from high control to high chaos while constraints are manipulated toward the demands of the injury case and competitive football. A central objective is to rebuild preinjury chronic running load while progressively restoring movement, football-skill, and cognitive demands. methods: Design: Narrative applied review and framework refinement. Exposure or intervention: Progression from high-control general work toward high-chaos football-specific activity. findings: The continuum progresses from high control to high chaos while constraints are manipulated toward the demands of the injury case and competitive football. citation: Xu R., Song Z., Hou T., Yang H., An Z., Yao Y., et al. Current challenges and future directions in Achilles tendon rupture repair: A biomechanical perspective. Journal of Biomechanics. 2026;204:113347. doi:10.1016/j.jbiomech.2026.113347.
abstract: This paper addresses the following question: How do macro-, micro-, and nanoscale Achilles tendon structures support mechanical function, what limits current rupture-repair strategies, and what design priorities should guide tissue-engineered scaffolds? Participants: No new human cohort; narrative synthesis of human, animal, mechanical, and tissue-engineering research. Sport and level: Achilles rupture across clinical and sports contexts; not restricted to athletes or a competition level. Design: Interdisciplinary narrative review. Exposure or intervention: Conservative/surgical repair and tissue-engineered scaffold strategies.
tldr: The review describes native Achilles tendon as a multiscale system of twisting tripartite subtendons, hierarchical collagen fibers, and quarter-staggered/cross-linked collagen that supports nonlinear and negative-Poisson-ratio behavior. Cited estimates indicate Achilles loading of 2.70–3.95 times body weight during walking and >12 times body weight during running. Use this paper to understand the biological/mechanical reasons that tendon length, stiffness, and functional capacity may remain altered after rupture.
methods: Design: Interdisciplinary narrative review. Exposure or intervention: Conservative/surgical repair and tissue-engineered scaffold strategies. citation: Phrathep D., Colon D., Schoch B.S., Pagan-Rosado R.D. Distal Biceps Tendon Injuries in Athletes: Management Strategies, Return-to-Sport Predictors, and Performance Outcomes. Current Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation Reports. 2026;14(1):21. doi:10.1007/s40141-026-00546-5.
abstract: This paper addresses the following question: What does the current literature indicate about diagnosis, management, rehabilitation, return-to-sport predictors, and performance outcomes after distal biceps tendon injury in athletes? Participants: No new cohort; evidence summarized from injured patients and athletes. Sport and level: General active populations, strength athletes, and professional American-football players. Design: Current narrative review. Exposure or intervention: Operative and nonoperative management, surgical approaches, and rehabilitation strategies.
tldr: In a cited meta-analysis of 2,481 cases, operative treatment was associated with higher flexion strength and endurance, higher supination strength and endurance, and better MEPS and DASH scores than nonoperative treatment; these are pooled clinical associations, not randomized causal estimates. Across the reviewed athletic literature, reported return-to-sport rates after repair ranged from 91.5% to 97.5%; 65.6% returned at the same or higher intensity, while another synthesis reported 93.4% returning at any level. For a high-demand athlete with a suspected complete rupture, the review supports prompt specialist assessment and a shared medical decision that weighs sport demands, injury features, and athlete preferences.
methods: Design: Current narrative review. Exposure or intervention: Operative and nonoperative management, surgical approaches, and rehabilitation strategies. Comparator: Treatment and technique comparisons reported in underlying reviews and cohorts. Measurements and outcomes: Strength, endurance, patient-reported function, complications, return-to-sport rate and timing, and post-return performance. Analysis: Narrative synthesis of underlying meta-analyses, systematic reviews, and observational cohorts; no new quantitative pooling or formal risk-of-bias appraisal was reported.
findings: In a cited meta-analysis of 2,481 cases, operative treatment was associated with higher flexion strength and endurance, higher supination strength and endurance, and better MEPS and DASH scores than nonoperative treatment; these are pooled clinical associations, not randomized causal estimates. Across the reviewed athletic literature, reported return-to-sport rates after repair ranged from 91.5% to 97.5%; 65.6% returned at the same or higher intensity, while another synthesis reported 93.4% returning at any level. In an NFL cohort, 94% returned to play at a mean of 351 days; most career and performance outcomes were comparable with matched controls, although offensive linemen played fewer games per season after return. Mean return-to-sport timing across broader cohorts was approximately 6.0 to 6.3 months. Earlier return was associated with injury, surgical, and rehabilitation characteristics, but these observational associations do not establish that changing any single factor will accelerate safe return. The review advocates criteria-based rehabilitation using objective function and patient-reported outcomes rather than relying only on elapsed time.
limitations: As a narrative review without reported systematic methods or formal risk-of-bias appraisal, it is vulnerable to selection and interpretation bias. The underlying studies vary in injury severity, surgical technique, sport, competitive level, rehabilitation exposure, outcome definitions, and follow-up; this is an additional transfer limitation based on the review's diverse evidence base. Operative versus nonoperative comparisons are subject to treatment-selection confounding; the reported differences should not be read as randomized causal effects. Professional-football results may inform American-football expectations but should not be directly generalized to collegiate players, other positions, or other sports. Return-to-sport percentage and time do not by themselves demonstrate restored readiness, durability, or reinjury risk.
practicalImplications: For a high-demand athlete with a suspected complete rupture, the review supports prompt specialist assessment and a shared medical decision that weighs sport demands, injury features, and athlete preferences. Rehabilitation and clearance should use serial range-of-motion, strength, task-specific loading, functional testing, symptoms, and patient-reported status; a six-month average is a planning reference, not a clearance rule. Surgical technique and progression decisions remain the responsibility of the treating medical team.

Use the paper as one input to interdisciplinary judgment, not as a standalone clearance criterion or reinjury prediction rule.

citation: Winchester S., Chang H.C.H. Does online negativity influence performance? Investigating the impact of social media on male professional soccer players. Online Social Networks and Media. 2026;54:100353. doi:10.1016/j.osnem.2026.100353.
abstract: This paper addresses the following question: Do sentiment and content features in fan comments posted before matches predict immediate match performance among English Premier League defenders? Participants: 156 male Premier League defenders contributing 2,814 player-match observations; 82 players had recoverable non-zero Instagram sentiment/content data. Sport and level: Men's professional soccer in the English Premier League. Design: Prospective observational panel study. Exposure or intervention: Aggregated pre-match Instagram-comment sentiment and content scores generated with VADER, LDA, and BART-based classification.
tldr: The performance dataset contained 2,814 player-match observations from 156 defenders; after comment processing and match-level aggregation, 1,063 performances were paired with sentiment and content scores derived from 270,007 English-language comments. Across OLS models, sentiment and content scores had limited predictive power, with R² values from 0.012 for normalized yellow cards to 0.028 for passing-completion percentage. Staff should not treat online sentiment as a validated readiness or match-performance signal.
methods: Design: Prospective observational panel study. Exposure or intervention: Aggregated pre-match Instagram-comment sentiment and content scores generated with VADER, LDA, and BART-based classification. Comparator: Within- and between-player differences in comment features; no randomized intervention. Measurements and outcomes: Errors, normalized yellow cards, second yellow cards, passing-completion percentage, and red cards from FBref. Analysis: OLS models, CatBoost regression with controls and lagged performance, SHAP feature attribution, and player fixed-effects models.
findings: The performance dataset contained 2,814 player-match observations from 156 defenders; after comment processing and match-level aggregation, 1,063 performances were paired with sentiment and content scores derived from 270,007 English-language comments. Across OLS models, sentiment and content scores had limited predictive power, with R² values from 0.012 for normalized yellow cards to 0.028 for passing-completion percentage. CatBoost models did not explain errors, yellow cards, second yellow cards, or red cards beyond R² values of 0.00 to 0.02; the passing-completion model reached R² = 0.34, but sentiment/content features accounted for only approximately 13.53% of its explained variation. In player fixed-effects analysis, the apparent passing-completion associations disappeared: within-player R² fell to 0.008, and Mental Health Spread and Sentiment Volume were no longer significant. Five of 14 OLS-significant coefficients survived fixed-effects estimation, all for disciplinary outcomes; this is prospective within-player covariation and does not establish that comment content caused cards.
limitations: Excluding non-English comments reduced the comment dataset by nearly 80%, limiting representation of the multilingual commentary received by Premier League players. The study could not determine whether players saw or read the analyzed comments, so measured comment content is an uncertain proxy for exposure. Repeated player-match observations were not independent; fixed effects addressed stable player characteristics but not unmeasured time-varying confounding. Restriction to Premier League defenders and a narrow performance-outcome set limits transfer to other positions, competitions, sports, wellbeing outcomes, and longer time horizons. The authors lacked data on social-media consumption, mental health, and pre-match psychological state, so mechanisms could not be tested.
practicalImplications: Staff should not treat online sentiment as a validated readiness or match-performance signal. The broad null and low-predictive-power findings argue against adding scraped fan commentary to athlete monitoring for performance prediction. Social-media abuse can still matter for wellbeing even when immediate performance effects are not detected; support should therefore be athlete-centered and confidential, not inferred from card or passing outcomes. Any monitoring initiative would also require explicit ethical, privacy, platform-policy, and athlete-consent review.

citation: Marques Dias N., Martins T.B., Raulino Silva May E., De Menezes F.S., Beppler Martins T., Okubo R. Epidemiology of musculoskeletal injuries in Brazilian American football: associations with pre-activity routines, sleep, and mood. Research in Sports Medicine. 2026;:1-16. doi:10.1080/15438627.2026.2673042.
abstract: This paper addresses the following question: What is the self-reported musculoskeletal-injury profile of Brazilian American-football players, and are injury histories associated with individual characteristics, training and game habits, pre-activity routines, sleep, or mood? Participants: 60 adult male athletes, mean age 30.3 ± 6.9 years, from a convenience sample recruited in Brazil. Sport and level: Active Brazilian American-football players spanning positions and amateur or semi-professional contexts. Design: Retrospective, cross-sectional observational epidemiology study conducted August–October 2025. Exposure or intervention: Self-reported training/game volume, pre-activity routines, sleep symptoms, mood, and other athlete characteristics; no intervention.
tldr: Thirty-three of 60 athletes reported at least one injury in 2024–2025, giving a self-reported prevalence of 55.0%; 93 total injuries were reported, with a median of 2.0 injuries per injured athlete. Estimated incidence was 7.26 injuries per 1,000 hours overall, 18.59 per 1,000 game-hours, and 1.36 per 1,000 training-hours; these rates use retrospectively estimated exposure rather than prospective attendance records. The strongest use of this paper is to inform what a prospective surveillance system should measure: verified exposure, injury context, anatomical region, mechanism, severity/time loss, recurrence, preparation routines, sleep, and mood.
methods: Design: Retrospective, cross-sectional observational epidemiology study conducted August–October 2025. Exposure or intervention: Self-reported training/game volume, pre-activity routines, sleep symptoms, mood, and other athlete characteristics; no intervention. Comparator: Injured versus non-injured respondents. Measurements and outcomes: Author-developed online questionnaire; injuries broadly defined as sport-related musculoskeletal complaints causing pain, functional limitation, or time loss; BRUMS mood scale and adapted Mini Sleep Questionnaire. Analysis: Descriptive statistics, estimated injuries per 1,000 exposure-hours, t tests, chi-square or Fisher tests, and a post hoc power calculation.
findings: Thirty-three of 60 athletes reported at least one injury in 2024–2025, giving a self-reported prevalence of 55.0%; 93 total injuries were reported, with a median of 2.0 injuries per injured athlete. Estimated incidence was 7.26 injuries per 1,000 hours overall, 18.59 per 1,000 game-hours, and 1.36 per 1,000 training-hours; these rates use retrospectively estimated exposure rather than prospective attendance records. The most frequently affected regions among injured athletes were ankle/foot (42.4%), knee (39.4%), shoulder/clavicle/arm (33.3%), thigh (30.3%), and wrist/hand/fingers (30.3%). Strains were reported by 54.5% and sprains by 42.4% of injured athletes; multiple responses were allowed, so these percentages are not proportions of all 93 injury events. Injured athletes were taller than non-injured athletes (180.8 ± 6.3 versus 176.0 ± 6.8 cm, p = 0.007), while age, body mass, playing experience, and weekly training/game volume did not differ significantly. No tested categorical variable—including position, unit, training level, additional activity, or pre-training/pre-game routine count—was significantly associated with injury occurrence.
limitations: Cross-sectional retrospective self-report introduces recall bias and may overrepresent severe injuries while missing minor or transient conditions. Injuries were not necessarily clinically confirmed, and the broad complaint-based definition differs from standardized prospective surveillance definitions. Exposure was calculated from self-reported average training/game time rather than verified athlete-exposures or participation minutes. The convenience sample was small, heterogeneous by position and competitive level, and may have been underpowered for smaller associations. Sleep and mood symptoms were described, but the reported inferential table did not establish them as injury predictors; athlete beliefs about sleep or warm-up are perceptions, not causal evidence. Brazilian amateur/semi-professional infrastructure, age distribution, and exposure differ materially from NCAA American football, so absolute rates should not be imported into Baylor benchmarks.
practicalImplications: The strongest use of this paper is to inform what a prospective surveillance system should measure: verified exposure, injury context, anatomical region, mechanism, severity/time loss, recurrence, preparation routines, sleep, and mood. It does not justify screening athletes by height or claiming that warm-up, sleep, or mood caused the observed injuries. For collegiate practice, local prospective data with standardized definitions and medical verification should remain the decision source.

citation: Carrier B., Melvin A.C., Outwin J.R., Wasserman M.G., Audet A.P., Soldes K.C., et al. Evaluation of Exertional Sweat Loss Estimates in Wearable Technology. Sports Health: A Multidisciplinary Approach. 2026;18(3):507-520. doi:10.1177/19417381251388642.
abstract: This paper addresses the following question: How accurately do the Samsung Galaxy Watch5 and Garmin Forerunner 945 estimate sweat loss during running compared with change in nude body mass? Participants: 111 physically active adults, age 40 ± 14 years, body mass 70.8 ± 14.7 kg, and VO₂max 46.8 ± 8.7 mL/kg/min. Sport and level: Recreationally active runners rather than a sport-team or elite-athlete sample. Design: Cross-sectional concurrent-validity study within a repeated testing protocol. Exposure or intervention: Up to three sweat-loss running trials per participant using fixed device/software versions.
tldr: Across 293 completed running trials, the devices produced 291 paired estimates; criterion sweat loss averaged 658.57 mL and ranged from 80 to 3,300 mL. Samsung had MAE 151.05 mL, MAPE 25.38%, and CCC 0.90; Garmin had MAE 217.58 mL, MAPE 33.21%, and CCC 0.77. The tested smartwatch sweat-loss values should not be used as stand-alone prescriptions for individualized fluid replacement.
methods: Design: Cross-sectional concurrent-validity study within a repeated testing protocol. Exposure or intervention: Up to three sweat-loss running trials per participant using fixed device/software versions. Comparator: Criterion sweat loss from pre/post nude body mass with fluid intake and urine output restricted around trials. Measurements and outcomes: Smartwatch-estimated sweat loss, mean absolute error, mean absolute percentage error, concordance and Pearson correlations, Deming regression, equivalence testing, and Bland–Altman agreement. Analysis: Overall and stratified validation by distance, environment, sex, body mass, and fitness; combined validity required MAPE 0.7, and supported equivalence.
findings: Across 293 completed running trials, the devices produced 291 paired estimates; criterion sweat loss averaged 658.57 mL and ranged from 80 to 3,300 mL. Samsung had MAE 151.05 mL, MAPE 25.38%, and CCC 0.90; Garmin had MAE 217.58 mL, MAPE 33.21%, and CCC 0.77. Equivalence was not supported for either device, and Bland–Altman limits of agreement were −428.61 to 490.62 mL for Samsung and −464.01 to 726.73 mL for Garmin. No distance, environment, sex, body-mass, or fitness-level stratification met the authors' combined validity criteria. Distance, environment, and their interaction did not significantly change device error in MANOVA, but this null result does not establish equivalence across all environmental conditions.
limitations: Proprietary algorithms are not public and may change with hardware or software updates, so these device/version-specific estimates can drift. Participants were not fully randomized to the variable-distance condition, and temperature and humidity were not included in the analysis. Wrist placement was standardized rather than randomized. Validation covered running to 20 km, criterion losses up to 3,300 mL, and body-mass losses up to about 2.7%; accuracy outside those conditions is unknown. The sample's mean age, body mass, fitness, activity, and running context differ from collegiate American-football athletes wearing protective equipment in hot practice environments. Acceptable CCC values reflect covariation, not individual-level agreement; the large percentage errors and limits of agreement are the decision-relevant validation results.
practicalImplications: The tested smartwatch sweat-loss values should not be used as stand-alone prescriptions for individualized fluid replacement. When accuracy matters, staff should retain standardized pre/post body-mass procedures with recorded fluid intake and output. A watch estimate may be treated as a coarse exploratory trend only after local validation on the exact device, firmware, athlete population, activity, and environment—and even then should not override symptoms, clinical judgment, or established heat-safety procedures.

citation: Carter B., James N., Parmar N. Identification & interpretation of playing styles in the National Football League (NFL). International Journal of Performance Analysis in Sport. 2026;:1-20. doi:10.1080/24748668.2026.2682075.
abstract: This paper addresses the following question: Can offensive and defensive playing styles be empirically identified from NFL technical performance variables, and how strongly are the resulting latent styles related? Participants: No human participants; 1,311 NFL regular-season games yielding 2,622 team-game observations. Sport and level: Professional American football. Design: Retrospective observational performance-analysis study. Exposure or intervention: Aggregated team-game technical and situational variables; no intervention.
tldr: Optimal coordinates retained eight components explaining 57% of variance across 2,622 team-game observations; parallel analysis suggested 10 components but the two additional features added only about 2% variance. The eight components were interpreted as passing efficacy, deep passing, scrambling, rushing, passing efficiency under pressure, coverage, defensive disruption, and tackling. The eight-component structure is best treated as a candidate feature map for film, self-scout, and opponent-analysis workflows.
methods: Design: Retrospective observational performance-analysis study. Exposure or intervention: Aggregated team-game technical and situational variables; no intervention. Comparator: Covariation among 46 candidate variables and correlations among extracted components. Measurements and outcomes: Public play-by-play indicators spanning passing, rushing, scrambling, coverage, disruption, and tackling. Analysis: Correlation-based principal component analysis, KMO and Bartlett suitability tests, parallel analysis and optimal coordinates for retention, and direct-oblimin rotation; loadings below |0.32| were excluded from interpretation.
findings: Optimal coordinates retained eight components explaining 57% of variance across 2,622 team-game observations; parallel analysis suggested 10 components but the two additional features added only about 2% variance. The eight components were interpreted as passing efficacy, deep passing, scrambling, rushing, passing efficiency under pressure, coverage, defensive disruption, and tackling. Passing efficacy and deep passing accounted for 12% and 9% of total variance, respectively; scrambling and rushing each accounted for 8%. The defensive-disruption component loaded most strongly on sacks (0.61), tackles for loss (0.51), and interceptions (0.47), while the tackling component was marked by rushing broken tackles (0.60) and defensive missed tackles (0.58). Only one component correlation was described as meaningful: passing efficacy and deep passing correlated at 0.35; the remaining styles were largely uncorrelated.
limitations: Public play-by-play data emphasize actions by or toward the ball carrier and omit important off-ball, blocking, spacing, and interaction information. The input set was uneven: passing components represented 48% of proportional explained variance, rushing/scrambling 29%, and defensive features 23%. Component selection and naming depend on retained variables, rotation, loading thresholds, and analyst interpretation; some factors may be areas of performance rather than stable “styles.” The study did not validate component stability out of sample, link styles to winning or future behavior, or test decision utility. NFL patterns from 2018–2022 require explicit replication before transfer to current NFL seasons or collegiate American football. Team-game aggregation can obscure opponent, score, down-distance, personnel, and game-state effects.
practicalImplications: The eight-component structure is best treated as a candidate feature map for film, self-scout, and opponent-analysis workflows. Before operational use, a collegiate program should rebuild the inputs from its own definitions, stratify by game situation and personnel, test year-to-year and opponent-adjusted stability, and validate whether the scores improve a concrete decision. Component labels should support analyst conversation, not be mistaken for causal mechanisms or forecasts.

citation: McMahon J., Lake J., Comfort P. Identifying and reporting position-specific countermovement jump outcome and phase characteristics within rugby league. PLOS ONE. 2022;17:e0265999. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0265999.
abstract: This paper addresses the following question: Which countermovement-jump force-time and outcome variables differ between rugby-league forwards and backs, and how should individual results be presented alongside position norms? Participants: Fifty-four senior men's English Rugby League Championship players: 27 forwards and 27 backs. Sport and level: Senior professional-level rugby league. Design: Cross-sectional observational comparison. Exposure or intervention: Three countermovement jumps on a force platform.
tldr: No countermovement or propulsion phase variable differed significantly by position; effects were small or less, with P values at least 0.09 and effect sizes no larger than 0.46. Backs jumped higher and had greater take-off velocity, with P = 0.03 and an effect size of 0.60. Select CMJ variables from the decision they are intended to support.
methods: Design: Cross-sectional observational comparison. Exposure or intervention: Three countermovement jumps on a force platform. Comparator: Global forwards versus backs. Measurements and outcomes: Countermovement and propulsion phase variables, jump height, take-off velocity, take-off momentum, and body mass. Analysis: Between-position significance tests, effect sizes, and individual-data visualization.
findings: No countermovement or propulsion phase variable differed significantly by position; effects were small or less, with P values at least 0.09 and effect sizes no larger than 0.46. Backs jumped higher and had greater take-off velocity, with P = 0.03 and an effect size of 0.60. Forwards produced greater take-off momentum, with P < 0.01 and an effect size of 1.01, but individual outcomes overlapped considerably between positions.
limitations: The cross-sectional study cannot show how the selected variables respond to training, fatigue, injury, or changes within an athlete. Global forward/back categories may conceal meaningful role and body-size differences; the observed individual overlap limits deterministic position classification.
practicalImplications: Select CMJ variables from the decision they are intended to support. Jump height and momentum describe different performance expressions, and body mass strongly shapes their positional meaning. Use position distributions as context, then prioritize within-athlete longitudinal change and uncertainty rather than labeling a player from the position mean alone.

citation: Bergmann J., Schmidt M., Jaitner T. Kinematic and electromyographic effects of different execution modalities during the Nordic Hamstring Exercise. Sports Biomechanics. 2026;:1-20. doi:10.1080/14763141.2026.2657898.
abstract: This paper addresses the following question: How do partner fixation, rigid heel fixation, and a specialized training-device setup affect Nordic Hamstring Exercise break-point angle, segment orientation, and biceps femoris/semitendinosus activation? Participants: 42 healthy recreationally active adults, age 26.4 ± 4.0 years; 24 men and 18 women. Sport and level: Mixed recreational activity rather than elite or team-sport athletes. Design: Preregistered cross-sectional randomized-order within-subject comparison. Exposure or intervention: Three Nordic modalities: partner-held heels on a mat, rigid heel fixation on a mat, and a device combining rigid fixation, elevated/controlled kneeling height, and unrestricted patellar glide.
tldr: Mean break-point angles were 74.8° ± 9.4° with partner fixation, 74.3° ± 11.1° with rigid heel fixation, and 56.0° ± 13.8° with the training device; the device differed from both alternatives, while partner and rigid fixation did not differ. All participants reached their most extended break-point knee angle in the training-device condition. Nordic execution should be documented and standardized rather than treated as one interchangeable exercise.
methods: Design: Preregistered cross-sectional randomized-order within-subject comparison. Exposure or intervention: Three Nordic modalities: partner-held heels on a mat, rigid heel fixation on a mat, and a device combining rigid fixation, elevated/controlled kneeling height, and unrestricted patellar glide. Comparator: Each participant performed all three modalities. Measurements and outcomes: Knee break-point angle, thigh and shank orientation, and surface-EMG RMS and integrated EMG for biceps femoris and semitendinosus. Analysis: Friedman tests with Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon post hoc comparisons, repeated-measures correlation, effect sizes, confidence intervals, and reliability assessment.
findings: Mean break-point angles were 74.8° ± 9.4° with partner fixation, 74.3° ± 11.1° with rigid heel fixation, and 56.0° ± 13.8° with the training device; the device differed from both alternatives, while partner and rigid fixation did not differ. All participants reached their most extended break-point knee angle in the training-device condition. Shank orientation was associated with break-point knee angle within participants (rrm = 0.38, 95% CI 0.18–0.55, p < 0.001), indicating that setup-dependent segment configuration contributed to the angle difference. RMS activation was higher with the device than with partner or rigid fixation for both biceps femoris and semitendinosus, while the two traditional setups did not differ. Integrated EMG was highest on average with the device, but its difference from rigid heel fixation was not statistically significant; the device exceeded partner fixation.
limitations: This was an acute cross-sectional comparison, so it cannot establish long-term strength, fascicle, sprint, injury, or performance adaptations. Recreationally active adults may differ from elite athletes and collegiate American-football players in strength, familiarity, and hamstring-injury risk. Few participants reached the most injury-relevant extended knee angles, limiting competitive-sport transfer. Hamstring force was not measured directly; eccentric demand was inferred from break-point geometry and EMG. Surface EMG reflects electrical activation, not force or injury protection, and is sensitive to measurement and normalization choices. Results apply to the tested device configuration as a package; they do not isolate which feature—heel rigidity, kneeling height, knee pad, or patellar glide—produced each effect.
practicalImplications: Nordic execution should be documented and standardized rather than treated as one interchangeable exercise. Stable heel resistance, controlled kneeling height, shank position, and unimpeded patellar movement can change the acute stimulus. Staff can use these factors to improve repeatability and progression, but should not claim that the specialized device prevents hamstring injury or is superior for longitudinal adaptation until those outcomes are tested directly.

citation: Sanhueza Tapia H.G., Giakoni-Ramírez F., De Souza-Lima J., Diaz Suarez A. Machine Learning and Non-Invasive Monitoring Technologies for Training Load Management in Women’s Volleyball: A Scoping Review. Sports. 2026;14(2):74. doi:10.3390/sports14020074.
abstract: This paper addresses the following question: What non-invasive monitoring and AI/ML approaches have been used for load, fatigue, performance, and injury-related outcomes in women’s volleyball? Female volleyball players at any level, plus mixed-sex studies with at least 35% female participants. Evidence published from January 2020 through September 2025. JBI-guided scoping review reported with PRISMA-ScR. Searched Scopus, Web of Science, and PubMed.
tldr: Fifty-three sources were included: 48 primary studies and five secondary syntheses. IMUs, force plates, heart-rate/HRV measures, wellness questionnaires, and positioning systems were common; ML applications were less frequent. Use the review to choose candidate signals, then validate them locally.
methods: JBI-guided scoping review reported with PRISMA-ScR. Searched Scopus, Web of Science, and PubMed. Narrative/thematic evidence mapping without formal risk-of-bias appraisal.
findings: Fifty-three sources were included: 48 primary studies and five secondary syntheses. IMUs, force plates, heart-rate/HRV measures, wellness questionnaires, and positioning systems were common; ML applications were less frequent. External-load intensity indicators were reported more often as fatigue-sensitive than accumulated volume, but heterogeneous definitions prevent a universal metric hierarchy. Female biological moderators, including menstrual-cycle context, were rarely addressed.
limitations: No formal quality appraisal was performed, so this is an evidence map rather than an effectiveness ranking. Language and full-text restrictions may have excluded studies. Methods, technologies, metrics, and outcomes were highly heterogeneous. Volleyball findings do not automatically transfer to football movement or contact demands.
practicalImplications: Use the review to choose candidate signals, then validate them locally. Favor interpretable measures tied to a decision and resist deploying ML until labels, missingness, external validation, and female-specific context are explicit.

citation: Lau E.N., Brown C.L., Saggar R., Mullen J., Olawin A., Lunn K., et al. Managing Shoulder Instability in the Contact and Collision Athlete. Current Reviews in Musculoskeletal Medicine. 2026;19(1):34. doi:10.1007/s12178-026-10011-4.
abstract: This paper addresses the following question: How should anterior and posterior shoulder instability be assessed and managed in contact and collision athletes to restore stability, function, and safe sport participation? Participants: No new cohort; the review summarizes clinical studies of patients and athletes with shoulder instability. Sport and level: Contact and collision sports, with mechanisms and decisions applicable to rugby and American football. Design: Current narrative review. Exposure or intervention: Nonoperative rehabilitation and bracing; arthroscopic Bankart repair, remplissage, Latarjet, posterior capsulolabral repair, and other stabilization procedures.
tldr: The review cites randomized trials reporting recurrent anterior instability near 10% after operative intervention versus 70% after nonoperative treatment in high-risk populations; these estimates come from underlying studies and are not a pooled effect calculated by this review. Arthroscopic Bankart repair recurrence rates were reported between 4% and 19%, with failure risk associated with multiple dislocations, hyperlaxity, glenoid bone loss, off-/near-track lesions, and longer delay to surgery. A contact athlete with instability needs prompt sports-medicine assessment that distinguishes direction, recurrence, apprehension, bone loss, track status, position demands, season timing, and future goals.
methods: Design: Current narrative review. Exposure or intervention: Nonoperative rehabilitation and bracing; arthroscopic Bankart repair, remplissage, Latarjet, posterior capsulolabral repair, and other stabilization procedures. Comparator: Treatment and procedure comparisons reported in underlying trials, cohorts, and reviews. Measurements and outcomes: Recurrent instability, bone loss, complications, patient-reported outcomes, return to sport, residual deficits, and revision. Analysis: Narrative synthesis rather than new quantitative pooling.
findings: The review cites randomized trials reporting recurrent anterior instability near 10% after operative intervention versus 70% after nonoperative treatment in high-risk populations; these estimates come from underlying studies and are not a pooled effect calculated by this review. Arthroscopic Bankart repair recurrence rates were reported between 4% and 19%, with failure risk associated with multiple dislocations, hyperlaxity, glenoid bone loss, off-/near-track lesions, and longer delay to surgery. For contact/collision athletes with on- or near-track lesions and subcritical bone loss, the reviewed evidence associated Bankart repair plus remplissage with recurrence as low as 5% and outcomes similar to Latarjet in selected cases. Latarjet recurrence was reported as low as 0.8% in recurrent instability with critical bone loss, but complication rates were reported as high as 30%. After arthroscopic Bankart repair, a cited cohort found residual strength or functional deficits in 38 of 43 athletes at six months, supporting criteria-based rather than time-only clearance.
limitations: The review does not report systematic methods or formal certainty/risk-of-bias grading, so evidence selection and weighting may be subjective. Underlying estimates mix first-time and recurrent instability, anterior and posterior pathology, bone-loss severity, surgical techniques, sports, ages, and competitive levels. High same-season return after nonoperative care is not equivalent to low recurrence; the review emphasizes that many athletes experience another instability event. Procedure comparisons are vulnerable to treatment-selection confounding because anatomy and risk often determine the operation. Reported thresholds for “critical” glenoid bone loss vary, and procedure choice cannot be reduced to one percentage. Return at 4–6 months is a broad clinical timeline, not evidence that every athlete is functionally ready.
practicalImplications: A contact athlete with instability needs prompt sports-medicine assessment that distinguishes direction, recurrence, apprehension, bone loss, track status, position demands, season timing, and future goals. In-season return decisions should explicitly discuss recurrent instability and progressive tissue/bone damage. After treatment, clearance should combine pain-free motion, strength, stability/apprehension, task-specific exposure, functional testing, and psychological readiness. Procedure and rehabilitation decisions belong to the treating surgical and rehabilitation team.

citation: Sharma S., Whiteley R., Rani B., Sartori S., Sharma H., Gabbett T.J. Mapping the Existing Return-to-Sport Criteria After Pectoralis Major Tendon Injury in Different Sports: A Scoping Review for Getting Back to the Game. Sports Health: A Multidisciplinary Approach. 2026;18(3):685-696. doi:10.1177/19417381251408058.
abstract: This paper addresses the following question: Which criteria have been used to clear adult athletes for return to sport after surgical or nonsurgical management of complete or incomplete pectoralis major tendon injury? Participants: 1,129 injured athletes across 39 studies; only one participant was female and the reported mean age was 30.1 years. Sport and level: Elite and recreational contact and noncontact sport, including NFL football, rugby, wrestling, weightlifting, and bench press. Design: OSF-registered PRISMA-ScR scoping review. Exposure or intervention: Surgical and conservative management with any rehabilitation approach.
tldr: Thirty-nine studies were included: 33 case reports/series, five cohort/longitudinal studies, and one epidemiological study. The evidence represented 1,129 athletes but only one female; 841 athletes returned to sport among studies reporting the outcome, while 216 were reported to return fully to preinjury performance. There is no evidence-supported single test or timeline for pectoralis-major clearance.
methods: Design: OSF-registered PRISMA-ScR scoping review. Exposure or intervention: Surgical and conservative management with any rehabilitation approach. Comparator: No required comparator; designs included case reports/series, cohorts, and epidemiology. Measurements and outcomes: Rehabilitation protocol, strength, range of motion, pain, functional outcomes, return time/rate, return to preinjury performance, and reinjury. Analysis: Multi-database and grey-literature search, blinded independent screening, consensus resolution, and descriptive evidence mapping.
findings: Thirty-nine studies were included: 33 case reports/series, five cohort/longitudinal studies, and one epidemiological study. The evidence represented 1,129 athletes but only one female; 841 athletes returned to sport among studies reporting the outcome, while 216 were reported to return fully to preinjury performance. Surgery was the primary management in 38 of 39 studies, and no included study reported a specific standardized rehabilitation protocol. Mean reported return-to-sport time was 7.5 months across 30 studies, with substantial variation from three months to four years. No included study reported specific, objective, validated clearance criteria; commonly measured domains were strength, range of motion, pain, and functional scales. Return to sport/participation was reported in 34 of 39 studies, but return to preinjury performance was reported in only 20 of 39.
limitations: The evidence base was dominated by case reports and series, limiting causal and prognostic inference. Almost all participants were male, so applicability to female athletes is unknown. The review mapped criteria but did not test their predictive validity for successful or durable return. Management approaches, injury location/severity, sports, athlete levels, rehabilitation, and outcome definitions were heterogeneous. The review could not determine how treatment choice affected return-to-sport or return-to-performance success across sports. A mean return time is descriptive, not a clearance criterion, and should not be interpreted as a safe universal threshold.
practicalImplications: There is no evidence-supported single test or timeline for pectoralis-major clearance. A multidisciplinary decision should document tissue healing and symptoms, active range of motion, bilateral adduction/flexion/rotation strength and endurance, kinetic-chain function, psychological readiness, progressive contact and sport-specific loading, and the athlete's positional demands and risk tolerance. Returning to participation, returning to sport, and returning to prior performance should be tracked separately.

citation: Moore S.R., Bruinvels G., Smith-Ryan A.E. Menstrual Cycle Phase–Based Strength & Conditioning Training for Elite Team Sport Female Athletes. Strength & Conditioning Journal. 2024. doi:10.1519/SSC.0000000000000879.
abstract: This paper addresses the following question: How might practitioners organize menstrual-cycle-informed strength and conditioning for eumenorrheic elite team-sport athletes while accounting for physiology, individual variation, privacy, and total stress? Participants: No intervention cohort; the proposed model targets eumenorrheic elite female team-sport athletes. Sport and level: Collegiate and professional team sport. Design: Evidence- and experience-based applied narrative. Exposure or intervention: Proposed adjustment of training stress across menstrual-cycle phases.
tldr: The authors state that performance changes across the menstrual cycle appear highly individual, so their model is not based on a universal acute-performance response. The proposed periodization model targets a theorized capacity for adaptation while balancing training stress and recovery, rather than using symptoms or cycle phase alone. Begin with voluntary education, informed consent, secure data handling, and athlete-specific observations.
methods: Design: Evidence- and experience-based applied narrative. Exposure or intervention: Proposed adjustment of training stress across menstrual-cycle phases. Comparator: None. Measurements and outcomes: Theoretical adaptive capacity, symptoms, performance, recovery, health, and athlete experience. Analysis: Physiological rationale, practical model construction, privacy considerations, and future research directions.
findings: The authors state that performance changes across the menstrual cycle appear highly individual, so their model is not based on a universal acute-performance response. The proposed periodization model targets a theorized capacity for adaptation while balancing training stress and recovery, rather than using symptoms or cycle phase alone. The authors identify the absence of an evidence-based team-sport resource for cycle-based strength-and-conditioning periodization as the gap their applied model seeks to address.
limitations: This is a proposed applied model, not evidence that phase-based programming improves performance, health, or injury outcomes. The authors explicitly acknowledge individual performance variation and emphasize privacy considerations. citation: Pellegrini A., Della Villa F., Zago M. Methodological approaches in video analysis studies of hamstring injuries in football: a systematic review. Science and Medicine in Football. 2026;:1-22. doi:10.1080/24733938.2026.2691453.
abstract: This paper addresses the following question: What methodological approaches have been used in video-analysis studies of hamstring injuries in football, and how consistent and methodologically robust are those approaches? The review included 11 studies published from 2021 to 2024 involving professional association-football (soccer) players. Individual studies analyzed between 8 and 61 injury videos, and only one included female players. This was a systematic review. Two reviewers independently selected studies and extracted data, with a third reviewer available to resolve disagreements.
tldr: Eleven studies met inclusion criteria; they focused on professional soccer, included 8–61 injury videos per study, and only one study included female players. Only two studies assessed inter- or intra-rater reliability. Video review can support structured description and hypothesis generation after a hamstring injury, but it should not be treated as a stand-alone causal test.
methods: This was a systematic review. Two reviewers independently selected studies and extracted data, with a third reviewer available to resolve disagreements. Extraction focused on injury mechanism, inciting activity, biomechanics, and injury circumstances. Risk of bias and reporting quality were assessed using Joanna Briggs Institute tools and the QA-SIVAS instrument. Because of substantial methodological heterogeneity, the authors used descriptive narrative synthesis rather than meta-analysis.
findings: Eleven studies met inclusion criteria; they focused on professional soccer, included 8–61 injury videos per study, and only one study included female players. Only two studies assessed inter- or intra-rater reliability. Injury diagnosis was confirmed by MRI in three studies and clinical examination in one, while other studies relied on medical records or media information. QA-SIVAS scores ranged from 9 to 14 out of 18; no study satisfied every video-quality requirement, only one included a noninjured control group, and none of the three quantitative biomechanical studies used a validated measurement method. Video-based identification can miss injuries that occur off camera, are obscured, or do not have a visually detectable event, creating selection and ascertainment limits. None of the included studies satisfied the QA-SIVAS requirement for validated parallax correction or motion quantification, and the general absence of control observations prevents causal conclusions about the observed movements. The literature showed substantial methodological, taxonomic, and operational heterogeneity; the review's proposed synthesis is descriptive and has not yet been validated as a guideline, checklist, or standardized framework.
limitations: The review was limited to English-language studies, had restricted gray-literature coverage, and was dominated by male professional soccer. The authors caution that results may not transfer to youth, female, or nonprofessional populations; the search was last updated on 12 December 2024. The included studies were heterogeneous and frequently lacked validated kinematic methods, controls, diagnostic confirmation, and reliability assessment. Applicability to collegiate American football is indirect because the sport, movement demands, contact environment, and injury-documentation systems differ.
practicalImplications: Video review can support structured description and hypothesis generation after a hamstring injury, but it should not be treated as a stand-alone causal test. Programs should clinically verify the diagnosis, define the injury frame and allowable timing uncertainty, use multiple blinded raters where possible, report camera views and frame rate, and distinguish visible observations from biomechanical estimates. The paper supports improving review procedures in soccer; it does not validate a specific screening or prevention rule for American football.

citation: Aychman M.M., Vinson K., Tasnim N., Perez J., Hodes G.E., Basso J.C. abstract: This paper addresses the following question: How do salivary biomarkers, countermovement-jump measures, workload, sleep, and soreness change across a season, and do associations differ by team role? Thirty-nine male NCAA Division I football athletes, ages 18–25. One program across a 15-week competitive season. Longitudinal observational monitoring. Pre-, mid-, and postseason saliva assessed cortisol, testosterone, IL-6, and TNF-α.
tldr: Among starters, higher testosterone-to-cortisol ratios were associated with lower soreness and better sleep; IL-6/cortisol was associated with RSImod. Nonstarters showed different associations, including poorer recovery alongside higher IL-6/cortisol despite lower external load. Separate starter and developmental-player exposure histories when reviewing fatigue signals.
methods: Longitudinal observational monitoring. Pre-, mid-, and postseason saliva assessed cortisol, testosterone, IL-6, and TNF-α. CMJ, PlayerLoad, sleep quality, and soreness were tracked and analyzed through associations.
findings: Among starters, higher testosterone-to-cortisol ratios were associated with lower soreness and better sleep; IL-6/cortisol was associated with RSImod. Nonstarters showed different associations, including poorer recovery alongside higher IL-6/cortisol despite lower external load. The authors interpreted IL-6/cortisol as a potentially informative multimodal signal, not a standalone diagnosis. Role-specific patterns were exploratory and did not establish that measured athletes had clinically confirmed NFOR.
limitations: Small convenience sample from one team and one season. Subgroup models may be underpowered and overfit. Associations cannot establish causal pathways or individual diagnostic cutoffs. Biomarker timing and analytic reliability matter before applied use.
practicalImplications: Separate starter and developmental-player exposure histories when reviewing fatigue signals. Use biomarkers only alongside workload, CMJ strategy, sleep, soreness, illness, and performance—never as a single clearance or NFOR threshold.
