citation: Pipping-Gamón J., Gebauer M., Lee V., Watts K., Wyner A.J. Opponent-Adjusted Evaluation of NFL Pass Blocking and Pass Rushing Performance. Source publication. 2026. doi:10.48550/arXiv.2604.01491.
abstract: This paper addresses the following question: Can ridge-regularized Bradley–Terry models produce useful opponent-adjusted NFL pass-block and pass-rush ratings for binary wins and outcome severity? The analysis used 2021 NFL regular-season Hudl tracking data. After filtering, the dataset contained 153,138 blocker–rusher interactions from 33,283 pass plays in 266 games, involving 620 rushers and 348 blockers; 42.7% of interactions were labeled as double teams. The authors constructed a binary rusher win outcome based on becoming closer to the quarterback than the blocker within 2.5 seconds, plus a four-class outcome ordered as loss, win, hit, and sack. Two ridge-regularized Bradley–Terry models included blocker effects, rusher effects, and a double-team indicator.
tldr: The win model improved holdout log loss by 0.0068 over the global baseline and 0.0014 over the stronger matchup baseline; both bootstrap intervals were positive. The severity model improved log loss by 0.0077 over the global baseline and 0.0015 over the matchup baseline, but the severity-versus-matchup interval included zero, making that comparison directional rather than decisive. The framework is best used as an opponent-adjusted analytic layer beside film and contextual grading.
methods: The authors constructed a binary rusher win outcome based on becoming closer to the quarterback than the blocker within 2.5 seconds, plus a four-class outcome ordered as loss, win, hit, and sack. Two ridge-regularized Bradley–Terry models included blocker effects, rusher effects, and a double-team indicator. Models were evaluated on an ordered 80/20 holdout with log loss, compared against global and player-history matchup baselines, and assessed with game-level bootstrap resampling. AP All-Pro alignment was used as face validation, not as a gold-standard outcome.
findings: The win model improved holdout log loss by 0.0068 over the global baseline and 0.0014 over the stronger matchup baseline; both bootstrap intervals were positive. The severity model improved log loss by 0.0077 over the global baseline and 0.0015 over the matchup baseline, but the severity-versus-matchup interval included zero, making that comparison directional rather than decisive. The severity model produced higher All-Pro rank AUC than its raw baseline in three of four role/accolade comparisons; enrichment gains were non-negative in all comparisons. Ratings measure efficiency within observed blocker–rusher engagements, not all-snap overall player value, and scores should not be compared across the win and severity models. Weekly trajectories were explicitly descriptive rather than predictive, with wider uncertainty early in the season when exposure was sparse.
limitations: This is a preprint and had not completed peer review at the time of this record. The work is a 2026 preprint analyzing one NFL season. Its distance-based win label may not represent functional pressure quality, the severity mapping is only one possible value calibration, and a binary double-team flag incompletely represents chips, slides, and other help. Quarterback time-to-throw, play design, teammate effects, role specialization, and position hierarchy remain incompletely modeled. All-Pro comparison is face validation with few positives, not proof of personnel-value accuracy. Transfer to collegiate football requires validation against college tracking, schemes, rosters, and labeling practices.
practicalImplications: The framework is best used as an opponent-adjusted analytic layer beside film and contextual grading. Small but consistent holdout gains support further validation; they do not justify treating the resulting leaderboard as ground truth. Staff should retain uncertainty intervals, minimum-exposure rules, and labels for protection structure, quarterback behavior, rush lane, play design, and role. A college implementation should be recalibrated and prospectively checked within its own data environment before informing high-stakes personnel decisions.

citation: Mann J.B., Bird M., Signorile J.F., Brechue W.F., Mayhew J.L. Prediction of Anaerobic Power From Standing Long Jump in NCAA Division IA Football Players. Journal of Strength & Conditioning Research. 2021;35(6):1542-1546. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000004043.
abstract: This paper addresses the following question: Can standing long jump distance and anthropometric measurements estimate force-plate-derived peak and average horizontal power in NCAA Division I football players? Fifty-eight adult players from one NCAA Division IA American-football program were tested after a 10-week winter conditioning program. Standing long jump was already part of their routine evaluation, so the athletes were familiar with the task. This was a single-cohort, cross-sectional prediction study. After warm-up and familiarization, players completed two maximal standing long jumps from a three-dimensional force plate sampled at 1,000 Hz.
tldr: Standing-long-jump distance and peak power were highly reliable between trials, with ICCs of 0.944 and 0.926, respectively. The peak-power equation was: power in watts = 32.49 × jump distance in centimeters + 39.69 × body mass in kilograms − 7,608; model R was 0.86, standard error of estimate was 488 W, and CV was 9.3%. The equation can provide a practical estimate when body mass and a standardized standing long jump are available, but the raw jump distance remains the directly observed measurement and may be more stable for longitudinal monitoring.
methods: This was a single-cohort, cross-sectional prediction study. After warm-up and familiarization, players completed two maximal standing long jumps from a three-dimensional force plate sampled at 1,000 Hz. Jump distance, body mass, height, and leg segment lengths were evaluated as predictors. Stepwise regression selected predictors, and random 70%/30% subsamples were used for internal cross-validation.
findings: Standing-long-jump distance and peak power were highly reliable between trials, with ICCs of 0.944 and 0.926, respectively. The peak-power equation was: power in watts = 32.49 × jump distance in centimeters + 39.69 × body mass in kilograms − 7,608; model R was 0.86, standard error of estimate was 488 W, and CV was 9.3%. Jump distance contributed 56.8% and body mass 43.2% of the explained peak-power variance; leg lengths and ratios did not add significantly. Internal split-sample correlations between predicted and measured peak power were 0.83 in the 70% subset and 0.70 in the 30% subset. The estimated smallest worthwhile changes were 10.4 cm for jump distance and 632 W for peak power, emphasizing that small observed changes may be measurement noise.
limitations: The equation was derived from 58 experienced adult male athletes in one Division I program at one time point. The 70%/30% procedure was internal split-sample checking, not external validation in a new team, season, testing surface, or device. Stepwise selection can be sample-sensitive, and the peak-power standard error of 488 W is material for individual interpretation. The equation estimates the specific force-plate power outcome used here; it does not establish anaerobic capacity, sprint ability, game performance, or training causality.
practicalImplications: The equation can provide a practical estimate when body mass and a standardized standing long jump are available, but the raw jump distance remains the directly observed measurement and may be more stable for longitudinal monitoring. Keep technique, warm-up, surface, footwear, and landing rules consistent. Interpret predicted power alongside the 488-W error and the study's change thresholds. Before using the equation for selection, return-to-play, or position norms, locally compare estimates against force-plate data and assess bias across position and body-mass groups.

citation: Norris D., Joyce D., Siegler J., Clock J., Lovell R. Recovery of Force–Time Characteristics After Australian Rules Football Matches: Examining the Utility of the Isometric Midthigh Pull. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2019;14(6):765-770. doi:10.1123/ijspp.2018-0349.
abstract: This paper addresses the following question: Do IMTP peak force and rate-of-force-development metrics show different recovery patterns and between-match variability after elite Australian rules football competition? Eight elite national-competition Australian rules football players from several positions were observed after three in-season matches. Sixty of 72 planned IMTP samples were collected, and average game time was 106 minutes. This was a repeated-measures observational study. Two rested baseline sessions preceded postmatch testing at 48, 72, and 96 hours.
tldr: RFD from 0–50 ms was reduced relative to baseline at 48, 72, and 96 hours by 25.8%, 17.8%, and 16.9%, respectively. RFD from 100–200 ms was reduced at 48 and 72 hours by 15.7% and 11.7%, while its 96-hour change was classified as trivial. Peak force alone may miss postcompetition changes visible in force-development rate, but early RFD is sensitive to contraction-onset detection and has substantial measurement noise.
methods: This was a repeated-measures observational study. Two rested baseline sessions preceded postmatch testing at 48, 72, and 96 hours. Players performed standardized IMTP trials on dual force plates sampled at 1,000 Hz. Outcomes were peak force, RFD from 0–50 ms, and RFD from 100–200 ms. Mixed-effects models accounted for repeated player and match observations, and changes were classified against study-defined smallest worthwhile changes.
findings: RFD from 0–50 ms was reduced relative to baseline at 48, 72, and 96 hours by 25.8%, 17.8%, and 16.9%, respectively. RFD from 100–200 ms was reduced at 48 and 72 hours by 15.7% and 11.7%, while its 96-hour change was classified as trivial. Peak-force changes were classified as trivial at all three postmatch time points. Baseline coefficient of variation was 16.4% for 0–50-ms RFD, 12.2% for 100–200-ms RFD, and 4.8% for peak force, showing that the more responsive metrics were also noisier. Between-match variability was higher for 0–50-ms RFD than for 100–200-ms RFD or peak force at each reported postmatch time point.
limitations: Only eight players and three matches contributed data, 17% of planned observations were missing, and no immediate or 24-hour assessments were collected. The classification used magnitude-based inference with 90% intervals and study-specific smallest-worthwhile-change rules, so the labels should not be treated as conventional hypothesis-test results. Australian rules football differs from collegiate American football in match structure, collision distribution, running demands, and weekly schedule. The study demonstrates metric behavior, not that IMTP-guided decisions improve performance or reduce injury.
practicalImplications: Peak force alone may miss postcompetition changes visible in force-development rate, but early RFD is sensitive to contraction-onset detection and has substantial measurement noise. If IMTP is used operationally, standardize posture, pretension, instruction, onset processing, testing time, and athlete readiness. Favor within-athlete baselines and confidence bands over single cut points, and interpret RFD alongside exposure, soreness, wellness, and performance. The 100–200-ms window may offer a better sensitivity–reliability compromise in this dataset, but it requires local reliability testing before adoption.

citation: Latreche A., Kelaiaia R., Chemori A., Kerboua A. Reliability and validity analysis of MediaPipe-based measurement system for some human rehabilitation motions. Measurement. 2023;214:112826. doi:10.1016/j.measurement.2023.112826.
abstract: This paper addresses the following question: How reliable are MediaPipe-derived shoulder range-of-motion measurements, and how closely do they agree with a universal goniometer and digital angle ruler? Fifty healthy volunteers aged 21–42, mostly tested at the University of Skikda, performed active shoulder abduction, adduction, flexion, and extension. A physical therapist instructed participants and collected the reference-device measurements. Each healthy volunteer completed three MediaPipe measurements for reliability and one measurement with a clinical goniometer and digital angle ruler. MediaPipe BlazePose estimated 33 landmarks from RGB video, and joint angles were calculated geometrically.
tldr: MediaPipe ICCs were 0.968 for abduction, 0.990 for adduction, 0.990 for extension, and 0.992 for flexion. Reported minimal detectable changes ranged from 1.046° for abduction to 1.864° for flexion. MediaPipe may be adequate for low-cost, constrained active shoulder ROM tracking when the environment, camera position, lighting, movement plane, and instructions match the validation setup.
methods: Each healthy volunteer completed three MediaPipe measurements for reliability and one measurement with a clinical goniometer and digital angle ruler. MediaPipe BlazePose estimated 33 landmarks from RGB video, and joint angles were calculated geometrically. Reliability was summarized with ICC, SEM, and minimal detectable change; agreement was assessed with Bland–Altman mean bias and 95% limits of agreement.
findings: MediaPipe ICCs were 0.968 for abduction, 0.990 for adduction, 0.990 for extension, and 0.992 for flexion. Reported minimal detectable changes ranged from 1.046° for abduction to 1.864° for flexion. Mean bias versus the universal goniometer ranged from −0.55° for abduction to −0.01° for extension. The widest reported 95% limits of agreement versus the goniometer were approximately −2.94° to 1.83° for abduction. The patient example showed serial knee-motion recordings, but it was an uncontrolled descriptive case and does not establish that the technology or rehabilitation caused improvement.

The paper reports only one reference-device measurement per participant, which prevents estimating reference-rater repeatability. Camera position and lighting affected detection; the system handled only one person per frame and was not tested for complex movements or arbitrary orientations. The article states that no indication of ethics approval was given, although participant consent is described. These findings do not validate sport-specific high-speed movement, lower-extremity kinetics, occlusion, multiple athletes, or clinical decision thresholds.
practicalImplications: MediaPipe may be adequate for low-cost, constrained active shoulder ROM tracking when the environment, camera position, lighting, movement plane, and instructions match the validation setup. Treat the reported minimal detectable changes as study-specific, not universal. Before clinical or athlete use, verify device/version behavior, local repeatability, camera geometry, clothing and occlusion effects, and agreement against the program's reference method. The system should augment clinician review rather than independently diagnose progress or readiness.

citation: Petrakos G., Morin J.B., Egan B. Resisted Sled Sprint Training to Improve Sprint Performance: A Systematic Review. Sports Medicine. 2016;46(3):381-400. doi:10.1007/s40279-015-0422-8.
abstract: This paper addresses the following question: How effective is resisted sled sprint training compared with unresisted sprint training, and how do sled loads influence acceleration and maximal-velocity outcomes? Participants: Athletes from 11 eligible longitudinal training studies. Sport and level: Sprint-trained, strength-trained, and team-sport participants. Design: Systematic review. Exposure or intervention: Resisted sled sprint training prescribed by percentage body mass, velocity decrement, or absolute load.
tldr: Eleven studies met the eligibility criteria, with load prescribed inconsistently as body-mass percentage, velocity decrement, or absolute kilograms. Light loading below 10% body mass or 10% velocity decrement ranged from a 1.5% decrement in acceleration (effect size 0.50) to a 2.4% improvement in maximal velocity (effect size 0.80) in sprint-trained participants. Program sled work from the target adaptation rather than a universal percent-body-mass rule.
methods: Design: Systematic review. Exposure or intervention: Resisted sled sprint training prescribed by percentage body mass, velocity decrement, or absolute load. Comparator: Unresisted sprint training and different sled-load categories. Measurements and outcomes: Acceleration and maximal sprint velocity, summarized with percentage changes and Cohen's d. Analysis: PubMed and SPORTDiscus search with eligibility filtering and effect-size comparison.
findings: Eleven studies met the eligibility criteria, with load prescribed inconsistently as body-mass percentage, velocity decrement, or absolute kilograms. Light loading below 10% body mass or 10% velocity decrement ranged from a 1.5% decrement in acceleration (effect size 0.50) to a 2.4% improvement in maximal velocity (effect size 0.80) in sprint-trained participants. Loads from moderate to very heavy produced acceleration changes from 0.5% to 9.1% with effect sizes from 0.14 to 4.00, but superiority over unresisted sprinting remained equivocal.
limitations: Between-study comparison was limited by differences in participant training status, training phase, and load prescription. The review could not define an optimal sled load or volume for each sprint outcome.
practicalImplications: Program sled work from the target adaptation rather than a universal percent-body-mass rule. Record velocity decrement so the actual resistance stimulus is visible, retain unresisted sprint exposure, and monitor whether the intended part of the sprint improves. The evidence supports sleds as a potentially useful option, not an automatically superior one.

citation: Cawley W.C., Hwang P., Mittal R., Zochowski Y., Darwish I., O’Keefe R., et al. Rethinking the Lisfranc injury: Rationale for and development of a new classification system for Lisfranc injuries. Injury. 2026;57(8):113422. doi:10.1016/j.injury.2026.113422.
abstract: This paper addresses the following question: Does the newly developed Suthersan classification produce better inter- and intra-rater agreement than the Myerson–Hardcastle classification for indirect Lisfranc injuries? The cohort comprised 176 patients older than 16 years with indirect Lisfranc injuries and accessible three-dimensional imaging, treated by one surgeon at an Australian tertiary trauma hospital from 2018 to 2024. Mean age was 41.6 years and 45.5% were female. This was a retrospective analysis of prospectively collected surgical-database data. The proposed system classifies indirect injuries by the entry and propagation of force, distinguishing lesser-arc from greater-arc patterns.
tldr: Combined inter-rater kappa was 0.95 for the Suthersan classification and 0.65 for Myerson–Hardcastle. Suthersan intra-rater agreement was 96.6%, 96.6%, and 100% across the three raters, compared with 74.1%, 96.6%, and 92.9% for Myerson–Hardcastle. The classification can structure specialist discussion of indirect Lisfranc morphology and prompt review of the wider midfoot on CT.
methods: This was a retrospective analysis of prospectively collected surgical-database data. The proposed system classifies indirect injuries by the entry and propagation of force, distinguishing lesser-arc from greater-arc patterns. Two fellowship-trained foot-and-ankle surgeons and one hand surgeon independently classified blinded imaging with both systems. A subset was reclassified after six months; Cohen's kappa summarized agreement.
findings: Combined inter-rater kappa was 0.95 for the Suthersan classification and 0.65 for Myerson–Hardcastle. Suthersan intra-rater agreement was 96.6%, 96.6%, and 100% across the three raters, compared with 74.1%, 96.6%, and 92.9% for Myerson–Hardcastle. Nineteen of 176 CT scans, or 10.8%, were not classifiable with the Myerson system. About 14% of injuries involved the navicular, talus, naviculocuneiform joint, or talonavicular joint, supporting broader midfoot assessment in this series. In the small outcome subset, median AOFAS score did not significantly differ between grade 1 and grades 2–4.
limitations: The system was developed by one surgeon and tested on that surgeon's single-center case series, creating incorporation and preference risks. Approximately 20% of identified indirect injuries lacked accessible imaging, only three surgeons rated scans, and race, ethnicity, and sex/gender subgroup analyses were unavailable. Crush injuries were excluded, image quality may have affected classification, and clinical outcome correlation was outside the main study scope. High agreement does not establish diagnostic accuracy, prognostic value, treatment effectiveness, or return-to-sport guidance.
practicalImplications: The classification can structure specialist discussion of indirect Lisfranc morphology and prompt review of the wider midfoot on CT. It should not yet drive fixation strategy, prognosis, or return-to-play by grade alone. In athlete care, use it alongside mechanism, weight-bearing imaging when appropriate, symptoms, instability, specialist examination, and functional progression. Prospective, multi-center studies with broader raters and patient outcomes are needed before treating its categories as management algorithms.

citation: Creighton D.W., Shrier I., Shultz R., Meeuwisse W.H., Matheson G.O. Return-to-Play in Sport: A Decision-based Model. Clinical Journal of Sport Medicine. 2010;20(5):379-385. doi:10.1097/JSM.0b013e3181f3c0fe.
abstract: This paper addresses the following question: Can return-to-play decision making be organized into a clinically useful sequence that makes the inputs and judgment thresholds explicit? Participants: No participant sample; this is a conceptual review and model-development paper. Sport and level: Sport broadly, with examples across injuries, illnesses, positions, and levels of participation. Design: Narrative review and conceptual model development. Exposure or intervention: Not applicable.
tldr: The model separates the decision into health status, participation risk, and decision modifiers rather than treating clearance as a single test result. Participation risk is informed by current health plus sport-risk modifiers such as position and the ability to protect the injury. Use the model as a structured decision record: document health evidence first, then sport-specific exposure risk, then external or contextual modifiers.
methods: Design: Narrative review and conceptual model development. Exposure or intervention: Not applicable. Comparator: Not applicable. Measurements and outcomes: Organization of factors used in return-to-play decisions. Analysis: Synthesis of the literature into a three-step decision model.
findings: The model separates the decision into health status, participation risk, and decision modifiers rather than treating clearance as a single test result. Participation risk is informed by current health plus sport-risk modifiers such as position and the ability to protect the injury. The acceptable-risk threshold can differ between decision makers and change with context, making the value judgment important to document.
limitations: This is a conceptual model, not a validated prediction rule, and it supplies neither quantitative criteria nor weights for its components. Interpretation: The framework can improve transparency, but it cannot determine whether a particular athlete is medically ready or estimate reinjury probability.
practicalImplications: Use the model as a structured decision record: document health evidence first, then sport-specific exposure risk, then external or contextual modifiers. Do not let schedule pressure or stakeholder preference masquerade as biological recovery. The framework is most useful for clarifying who owns each judgment and why reasonable professionals may reach different thresholds.

citation: Gordji-Nejad A., Matusch A., Kleedörfer S., Jayeshkumar Patel H., Drzezga A., Elmenhorst D., et al. Single dose creatine improves cognitive performance and induces changes in cerebral high energy phosphates during sleep deprivation. Scientific Reports. 2024;14(1):4937. doi:10.1038/s41598-024-54249-9.
abstract: This paper addresses the following question: Does one high dose of creatine monohydrate alter cerebral energy metabolites, subjective fatigue, and cognitive performance during overnight sleep deprivation? Fifteen healthy adults, including eight women, aged 20–28 completed two supervised overnight laboratory sessions. Participants had no reported sleep, neurologic, psychiatric, substance-use, smoking, or medication issues and standardized sleep timing before sessions. This was a double-blind, randomized, balanced crossover trial. Each participant received creatine monohydrate at 0.35 g/kg on one night and corn-starch placebo on another, separated by at least five days.
tldr: Compared with placebo, creatine reduced the pooled subjective fatigue score at 2 a.m. and 4 a.m. by 8%. Pooled across three postdose time points, word-memory accuracy improved by 10.3%, and processing time improved for word memory, language, logic, and numeric tasks. The study supports further research on creatine as an acute countermeasure to sleep-loss-related cognitive decline.
methods: This was a double-blind, randomized, balanced crossover trial. Each participant received creatine monohydrate at 0.35 g/kg on one night and corn-starch placebo on another, separated by at least five days. During approximately 21 hours of wakefulness, cognition, fatigue, and cerebral metabolites were repeatedly assessed using a test battery, 31P-MRS, and 1H-MRS.
findings: Compared with placebo, creatine reduced the pooled subjective fatigue score at 2 a.m. and 4 a.m. by 8%. Pooled across three postdose time points, word-memory accuracy improved by 10.3%, and processing time improved for word memory, language, logic, and numeric tasks. Creatine altered cerebral phosphate measures, including regional increases in PCr/31P and reductions in Pi/31P, and prevented the sleep-deprivation-associated fall in pH in measured regions. Cognitive and metabolic effects were observed from about 3.5 hours after ingestion and persisted through the final measurement ending about nine hours after dosing. Correlations between regional metabolite changes and cognitive changes were exploratory associations and do not prove that the measured metabolite shifts mediated performance.
limitations: The sample was only 15 healthy young adults in a tightly controlled laboratory crossover, not athletes performing physical work, travel, or competition. The dose of 0.35 g/kg is substantially higher than common single maintenance doses, and the article does not establish an optimal or routine dose. Many cognitive tasks, time points, voxels, and metabolites were analyzed; although Bonferroni thresholds were used for parts of the analysis, multiplicity and regional-selection complexity remain important. Voxel coverage was limited, circadian effects could have contributed to ATP changes, and proposed uptake mechanisms are inferential. Safety and effectiveness with repeated use, dehydration, heat, renal risk, or other supplements were not established.
practicalImplications: The study supports further research on creatine as an acute countermeasure to sleep-loss-related cognitive decline. It does not justify using 0.35 g/kg as a team protocol or as a substitute for sleep. Any applied consideration should go through sports medicine and sports nutrition, with attention to medical history, product quality, gastrointestinal tolerance, hydration context, and governing-body policy. For operations, prioritize sleep opportunity, travel planning, and fatigue-aware decision design; treat supplementation as a secondary, clinically governed option.

citation: Maestroni L., Read P., Bishop C., Turner A. Strength and Power Training in Rehabilitation: Underpinning Principles and Practical Strategies to Return Athletes to High Performance. Sports Medicine. 2020;50(2):239-252. doi:10.1007/s40279-019-01195-6.
abstract: This paper addresses the following question: Which residual neuromuscular deficits commonly remain after musculoskeletal injury, and which strength and power strategies can be used to address them during rehabilitation? Participants: No single cohort; the article reviews evidence from athletic and rehabilitation populations. Sport and level: Athletic populations across sports. Design: Narrative evidence review with practical programming examples. Exposure or intervention: Maximal-strength, ballistic-power, rate-of-force-development, and reactive-strength training.
tldr: Residual deficits in maximal strength, rate of force development, and reactive strength are documented after musculoskeletal injury. Rehabilitation should prepare athletes for loads and velocities across the force-velocity spectrum rather than restoring high force at low velocity alone. Build late rehabilitation as physical preparation, not merely symptom resolution.
methods: Design: Narrative evidence review with practical programming examples. Exposure or intervention: Maximal-strength, ballistic-power, rate-of-force-development, and reactive-strength training. Comparator: Varies across the cited literature. Measurements and outcomes: Strength, power, rate of force development, reactive strength, sprinting, and jumping. Analysis: Applied synthesis of mechanisms, documented deficits, and training strategies.
findings: Residual deficits in maximal strength, rate of force development, and reactive strength are documented after musculoskeletal injury. Rehabilitation should prepare athletes for loads and velocities across the force-velocity spectrum rather than restoring high force at low velocity alone. The review cites evidence suggesting maximal-strength training should remain dominant in relatively weak athletes below approximately 1.6 times body mass in the back squat, while stressing the broader individual context.
limitations: The paper integrates heterogeneous injuries and supporting studies, so its programming examples are principles rather than validated universal return-to-play criteria. Interpretation: Strength ratios and loading benchmarks must be adjusted for the athlete, injury, exercise technique, sport demands, and stage of tissue recovery.
practicalImplications: Build late rehabilitation as physical preparation, not merely symptom resolution. Profile which qualities remain constrained, select exercises by the force and velocity demands they expose, and progress from force capacity toward fast and reactive expression. Treat any strength benchmark as context for programming, not as a stand-alone clearance threshold.

citation: Harries S.K., Lubans D.R., Callister R. Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Linear and Undulating Periodized Resistance Training Programs on Muscular Strength. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2015;29(4):1113-1125. doi:10.1519/jsc.0000000000000712.
abstract: This paper addresses the following question: Do linear and undulating periodized resistance-training programs differ in their effects on upper- and lower-body muscular strength? Participants: 510 participants across 17 included studies. Sport and level: Mixed training backgrounds; few studies specifically examined adolescent or athletic populations. Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis. Exposure or intervention: Linear periodization versus daily or weekly undulating periodization.
tldr: Seventeen studies with 510 total participants met the inclusion criteria. Sixteen studies reported significant strength increases with both approaches, while only five reported significant between-group differences. Choose linear or undulating organization from schedule, athlete response, exercise exposure, and the need to manage fatigue—not ideology.
methods: Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis. Exposure or intervention: Linear periodization versus daily or weekly undulating periodization. Comparator: Direct between-model comparisons. Measurements and outcomes: Upper- and lower-body muscular-strength changes. Analysis: MEDLINE, SCOPUS, and SPORTDiscus search followed by quantitative comparison.
findings: Seventeen studies with 510 total participants met the inclusion criteria. Sixteen studies reported significant strength increases with both approaches, while only five reported significant between-group differences. Meta-analysis found no difference between linear and undulating periodization for either upper- or lower-body strength.
limitations: Short study durations and participants' prior training histories were important confounders. Few studies involved adolescent or athletic populations, limiting direct transfer to long-term high-performance planning. The comparison does not show that periodization itself is irrelevant; it shows that these two broad labels did not produce reliably different strength outcomes in the included evidence.
practicalImplications: Choose linear or undulating organization from schedule, athlete response, exercise exposure, and the need to manage fatigue—not ideology. Preserve progressive overload and sufficient novelty, then judge the program by longitudinal athlete outcomes. The broad periodization label is less informative than what loading, volume, specificity, and recovery were actually delivered.

citation: Lazarev A., Pujalte G.G., Philibert C., Meek S.E., Broderick G.A., Zapp D.G., et al. Testosterone-Optimizing Strategies in Athletes. Sports Health: A Multidisciplinary Approach. 2026;18(3):477-488. doi:10.1177/19417381251411933.
abstract: This paper addresses the following question: What lifestyle, training, nutritional, environmental, medication-related, and supplemental strategies have been proposed to influence testosterone in athletes, and what evidence and practical cautions accompany them? The review concerns healthy adults and athletes, but the underlying literature is heterogeneous and includes nonathletes, men more often than women, and some animal or in-vitro studies. Its relevance is greatest for athlete-health assessment and counseling, not for predicting performance gains from a particular testosterone value. This was a narrative review classified by the authors as Level 5 evidence with Strength of Recommendation B. The authors searched PubMed for English-language peer-reviewed literature and selected studies by their judgment of relevance and scientific impact; they did not report a systematic-review protocol, exhaustive search strategy, formal risk-of-bias assessment, or quantitative synthesis.
tldr: Low energy availability and relative energy deficiency in sport can suppress reproductive hormones; restoring adequate intake and adjusting training load are presented as foundational responses when under-fueling is present. Evidence for commercial “testosterone boosters” and their constituent compounds is generally weak, inconsistent, or context dependent, while products may carry risks of contamination, undeclared prohibited substances, and adverse events. Use symptoms, training context, nutrition history, sleep, recovery, medications, and repeated standardized laboratory assessment—not a single value or an acute postexercise spike—to decide whether sports-medicine evaluation is warranted.
methods: This was a narrative review classified by the authors as Level 5 evidence with Strength of Recommendation B. The authors searched PubMed for English-language peer-reviewed literature and selected studies by their judgment of relevance and scientific impact; they did not report a systematic-review protocol, exhaustive search strategy, formal risk-of-bias assessment, or quantitative synthesis.
findings: Low energy availability and relative energy deficiency in sport can suppress reproductive hormones; restoring adequate intake and adjusting training load are presented as foundational responses when under-fueling is present. Evidence for commercial “testosterone boosters” and their constituent compounds is generally weak, inconsistent, or context dependent, while products may carry risks of contamination, undeclared prohibited substances, and adverse events. Sleep loss and sleep-disordered breathing may contribute to impaired testosterone regulation; the review highlights sleep assessment, including possible obstructive sleep apnea in contact-sport athletes, while noting that evidence for sleep extension or melatonin as testosterone-enhancing interventions is not established. Moderate-to-high-intensity exercise and large-muscle resistance exercise can produce transient postexercise testosterone increases, but the review does not establish that chasing acute hormonal spikes causes superior long-term adaptation or performance. Evidence concerning environmental exposures, radiofrequency electromagnetic radiation, common analgesics, seasonal variation, sexual activity, and recovery modalities is mixed and often indirect, so these factors do not support firm athlete-facing prescriptions. Female-specific evidence is limited; hormonal contraception can affect measured testosterone, and dehydroepiandrosterone is prohibited in sport, but testosterone-focused manipulation should not substitute for individualized clinical assessment.
limitations: The narrative, author-selected search makes evidence omission and selection bias possible. The review combines heterogeneous populations, study designs, exposures, and outcomes without formal quality grading, and some claims depend on animal, in-vitro, observational, or surrogate hormone data. Male evidence predominates, female-athlete applicability is limited, and transient serum testosterone changes should not be treated as proof of meaningful adaptation, health benefit, or performance improvement. Some cited areas are internally uncertain or appear vulnerable to citation-quality problems, further favoring conservative interpretation. Applicability to collegiate American football is therefore indirect: the health-screening themes are relevant, but the paper does not test a football-specific intervention or demonstrate performance benefit.
practicalImplications: Use symptoms, training context, nutrition history, sleep, recovery, medications, and repeated standardized laboratory assessment—not a single value or an acute postexercise spike—to decide whether sports-medicine evaluation is warranted. First investigate reversible health issues such as low energy availability, sleep deficiency or apnea, illness, and medication effects. Do not recommend “testosterone boosters” as a routine performance strategy; any supplement consideration should involve qualified medical and sports-dietetic oversight, third-party testing, and a current anti-doping check. The paper is best used to structure questions for clinical review, not as a menu of optimization tactics.

citation: Griffin A., Kenny I.C., Comyns T.M., Lyons M. The Association Between the Acute:Chronic Workload Ratio and Injury and its Application in Team Sports: A Systematic Review. Sports Medicine. 2020;50(3):561-580. doi:10.1007/s40279-019-01218-2.
abstract: This paper addresses the following question: What evidence links the acute:chronic workload ratio to injury in team sports, and which calculation method is most defensible for application? Participants: Athletes represented in 22 included articles. Sport and level: Team-sport cohorts across the included literature. Design: Systematic review. Exposure or intervention: Acute and chronic workload summarized through rolling-average or exponentially weighted models.
tldr: Twenty-two articles met the inclusion criteria; median Newcastle-Ottawa Scale quality was 8, with a range of 5 to 9. The review reported associations between ACWR and non-contact injury but recommended its use only within a broader multifactorial monitoring system. ACWR may describe recent loading in relation to prior loading, but it should not be used as a traffic-light injury oracle.
methods: Design: Systematic review. Exposure or intervention: Acute and chronic workload summarized through rolling-average or exponentially weighted models. Comparator: Different workload ratios, time windows, variables, and injury outcomes across studies. Measurements and outcomes: Non-contact injury and study-specific internal or external workload measures. Analysis: Six-database search, data extraction, and Newcastle-Ottawa Scale assessment of cohort-study quality.
findings: Twenty-two articles met the inclusion criteria; median Newcastle-Ottawa Scale quality was 8, with a range of 5 to 9. The review reported associations between ACWR and non-contact injury but recommended its use only within a broader multifactorial monitoring system. Both calculation models had support; the authors favored the exponentially weighted approach for sensitivity while noting that suitable windows and variables depend on the sport.
limitations: The evidence base was observational and heterogeneous, so association should not be interpreted as proof that manipulating ACWR reduces injury. The authors called for work across more sports, time frames, both sexes, and combinations with other risk factors. Later methodological criticism should be read alongside this review before operational thresholds are adopted.
practicalImplications: ACWR may describe recent loading in relation to prior loading, but it should not be used as a traffic-light injury oracle. Preserve the underlying daily load data, make calculation choices explicit, inspect context and uncertainty, and use the ratio as one descriptive signal among exposure, availability, symptoms, capacity, and schedule constraints.

citation: Kozinc Ž., Žitnik J., Smajla D., Šarabon N. The difference between squat jump and countermovement jump in 770 male and female participants from different sports. European Journal of Sport Science. 2022;22(7):985-993. doi:10.1080/17461391.2021.1936654.
abstract: This paper addresses the following question: Do athlete groups with better squat-jump and countermovement-jump performance also show a larger relative difference between those jumps, and how do sport and sex relate to the three outcomes? The convenience sample included 712 competitive athletes and 58 physically active physical-education students across basketball, dance, karate, long-distance running, soccer, speed skating, tennis, short-distance running, and volleyball. Mean subgroup ages ranged from 15.7 to 36.3 years; soccer and volleyball included only males, and subgroup sizes were highly unequal. This was a cross-sectional, single-session study. After a standardized warm-up and familiarization, participants completed randomized squat-jump and countermovement-jump conditions with three recorded trials each, hands on hips, and approximately 90 degrees of knee flexion.
tldr: Sport and sex were associated with squat-jump and countermovement-jump height, with short-distance runners producing the highest mean heights and long-distance runners generally the lowest; these group comparisons describe this sample rather than causal sport effects. Only 48.4% of participants had a countermovement jump clearly higher than their squat jump; 17.5% jumped higher in the squat jump, and 34.0% had a between-jump difference smaller than the cited typical inter-repetition error of 1.51 cm. Do not label a large countermovement-jump versus squat-jump difference as automatically “good,” or prescribe training from that difference alone.
methods: This was a cross-sectional, single-session study. After a standardized warm-up and familiarization, participants completed randomized squat-jump and countermovement-jump conditions with three recorded trials each, hands on hips, and approximately 90 degrees of knee flexion. Jump height was derived from force-platform impulse and takeoff velocity; the best trial was retained, and the relative difference was calculated as (CMJ minus SJ) divided by SJ times 100. Two-way ANOVA examined sport and sex effects, with correlations used for secondary associations.
findings: Sport and sex were associated with squat-jump and countermovement-jump height, with short-distance runners producing the highest mean heights and long-distance runners generally the lowest; these group comparisons describe this sample rather than causal sport effects. Only 48.4% of participants had a countermovement jump clearly higher than their squat jump; 17.5% jumped higher in the squat jump, and 34.0% had a between-jump difference smaller than the cited typical inter-repetition error of 1.51 cm. Physical-education students showed the largest relative jump difference despite not being the highest-performing jump group, whereas most athlete groups had broadly similar values. The relative difference was moderately associated with countermovement-jump height across the full sample (r = 0.41) but was not associated with squat-jump height (r = 0.03); this association does not identify the mechanism producing the difference. Sport-group patterns differed depending on whether the outcome was jump height, peak power, or push-off time, undermining a single universal interpretation of the countermovement-jump versus squat-jump difference. The authors concluded that a larger difference is not necessarily better and may reflect several factors, including muscle-tendon slack, rate-of-force-development capability, technique, or task familiarity rather than only superior stretch-shortening-cycle use.
limitations: The cross-sectional design cannot establish why groups differed or how training changes the metric. Recruitment was by convenience; subgroup ages, sizes, sex representation, and training backgrounds were unbalanced, with very small speed-skating and sprint subgroups and no women in soccer or volleyball. Within-group variability was substantial, the best trial rather than an average was analyzed, and the composite difference inherits error from both jump tests. No collegiate American football players were studied, so direct norm transfer is inappropriate. The broad measurement lesson is applicable, but football-specific reference values and longitudinal sensitivity require local validation.
practicalImplications: Do not label a large countermovement-jump versus squat-jump difference as automatically “good,” or prescribe training from that difference alone. Examine the two component jumps, their force-time characteristics, technique quality, reliability, and change relative to the athlete’s own typical error. In collegiate American football, use position- and athlete-specific longitudinal baselines and pair any difference score with direct measures relevant to the question, such as jump height, impulse, strategy, or force-velocity characteristics. This paper supports cautious interpretation; it does not validate a diagnostic cutoff or a training algorithm.

Examine the two component jumps, their force-time characteristics, technique quality, reliability, and change relative to the athlete’s own typical error. In collegiate American football, use position- and athlete-specific longitudinal baselines and pair any difference score with direct measures relevant to the question, such as jump height, impulse, strategy, or force-velocity characteristics. This paper supports cautious interpretation; it does not validate a diagnostic cutoff or a training algorithm. Apply the finding within the population and setting described in the source rather than treating it as a universal threshold.

citation: Liu Y., Li Q., Yang C., Wan X. The effect of fatigue on peak strain of hamstring muscles in dominant and non-dominant sides during sprinting: a pre-post intervention study. BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders. 2026;27(1):305. doi:10.1186/s12891-026-09699-9.
abstract: This paper addresses the following question: Does an acute intermittent-running fatigue protocol alter modeled optimal length, peak length, and peak strain of the biarticular hamstrings during sprinting, and do those changes differ between dominant and non-dominant limbs? Nineteen male, high-national-level track-and-field athletes aged 18 to 25 years participated; mean age was 19.2 years, and all had 100-m personal bests of 11.74 seconds or faster. None reported a hamstring strain in the prior two years or a significant lower-limb or foot injury in the prior six months. This was a single-group pre-post laboratory intervention. Participants completed maximal 40-m sprint trials, isokinetic knee-flexion testing, and a modified Loughborough Intermittent Shuttle Test individualized from VO2max, followed by repeated testing.
tldr: Maximal hamstring strength decreased after the fatigue protocol in both limbs, supporting that the protocol induced an acute loss of force-generating capacity. Modeled optimal length shortened after fatigue for all three biarticular hamstrings in the non-dominant limb, with large within-limb effects, whereas changes in the dominant limb were not statistically significant. Treat the results as a reason to preserve sprint quality and account for fatigue exposure, not as evidence that the non-dominant limb is categorically at greater injury risk.
methods: This was a single-group pre-post laboratory intervention. Participants completed maximal 40-m sprint trials, isokinetic knee-flexion testing, and a modified Loughborough Intermittent Shuttle Test individualized from VO2max, followed by repeated testing. Three-dimensional motion capture, force platforms, and a musculoskeletal model estimated optimal muscle length, sprint-phase peak muscle length, and strain for biceps femoris long head, semimembranosus, and semitendinosus. Strain was calculated relative to the modeled optimal length; paired tests and repeated-measures ANCOVA examined time and limb effects.
findings: Maximal hamstring strength decreased after the fatigue protocol in both limbs, supporting that the protocol induced an acute loss of force-generating capacity. Modeled optimal length shortened after fatigue for all three biarticular hamstrings in the non-dominant limb, with large within-limb effects, whereas changes in the dominant limb were not statistically significant. Peak absolute hamstring length and maximal hip-knee angle during sprinting did not change significantly after fatigue in either limb. Peak modeled strain increased in the non-dominant biceps femoris long head and semimembranosus, but not significantly in the dominant limb or non-dominant semitendinosus. Despite the within-limb findings, changes in peak strain did not differ significantly between limbs, and adjustment for baseline strength removed the apparent between-limb contrast. Peak strain continued to occur in late swing, approximately 85% to 95% of the gait cycle, and fatigue did not significantly change its timing.
limitations: The sample was small, male-only, and limited to trained track athletes; estimated post-hoc power was no greater than 0.64 for subtle effects. There was no non-fatigued control condition, so time, repeated maximal sprints, modeling, or order-related influences cannot be fully separated from the intervention. The fatigue protocol may not reproduce American football practice or game fatigue, dominance was defined by ball striking in sprinters, and muscle behavior was modeled from surface-marker kinematics and isokinetic testing rather than measured at fascicle level. Neuromuscular activation was not recorded. The study measured acute biomechanical surrogates, not hamstring injuries, so it cannot establish that the observed strain changes cause injury or justify a screening threshold.
practicalImplications: Treat the results as a reason to preserve sprint quality and account for fatigue exposure, not as evidence that the non-dominant limb is categorically at greater injury risk. In collegiate American football, monitor within-athlete sprint mechanics, strength capacity, exposure, and symptoms across realistic practice demands; do not infer injury probability from modeled strain or a single asymmetry. Where a meaningful and repeatable limb difference is present, investigate whether unequal strength or relative loading contributes, but keep decisions within a multifactorial hamstring-risk framework.

citation: Myslinski T., Kiely J., Gabbett T., Park G. The Indirect Contact ACL Injury Cascade: Why Current Prevention Falls Short. Sports Health: A Multidisciplinary Approach. 2026;:19417381261457125. doi:10.1177/19417381261457125.
abstract: This paper addresses the following question: Why might prevention and rehabilitation programs built primarily around predictable, preplanned movement tasks fail to address the externally triggered, rapidly unfolding cascade proposed for indirect-contact ACL injuries? This is an editorial synthesis, not an original participant study. Its scope is competitive field sports, with examples and cited evidence from association football, the National Football League, change-of-direction tasks, and jump landings. The article is labeled a guest editorial and presents a narrative, mechanistic argument supported by 12 cited sources. It does not describe a systematic search, participant recruitment, intervention, comparator, statistical analysis, or prospective outcome assessment.
tldr: The authors cite evidence estimating that indirect-contact mechanisms account for approximately 25% to 33% of ACL injuries in competitive field sports; this is a literature-derived estimate, not a new prevalence analysis performed in the editorial. Indirect contact is defined as an external interaction away from the knee—such as a bump, push, pull, hand-off, or mid-air collision—that unexpectedly destabilizes control and may be misclassified as noncontact. Preserve interventions with established value—strength, landing and deceleration capacity, movement skill, and existing multicomponent ACL-prevention work—because the editorial does not show that these should be replaced.
methods: The article is labeled a guest editorial and presents a narrative, mechanistic argument supported by 12 cited sources. It does not describe a systematic search, participant recruitment, intervention, comparator, statistical analysis, or prospective outcome assessment. The authors distinguish direct contact, indirect contact, and noncontact mechanisms; propose a temporal cascade linking unexpected perturbation, disrupted postural control, trunk and center-of-mass displacement, knee loading, and ACL failure; and derive three research and practice priorities from that model.
findings: The authors cite evidence estimating that indirect-contact mechanisms account for approximately 25% to 33% of ACL injuries in competitive field sports; this is a literature-derived estimate, not a new prevalence analysis performed in the editorial. Indirect contact is defined as an external interaction away from the knee—such as a bump, push, pull, hand-off, or mid-air collision—that unexpectedly destabilizes control and may be misclassified as noncontact. The proposed cascade begins with an unanticipated perturbation that disrupts coordinated trunk, pelvis, and limb control; lateral trunk motion and center-of-mass displacement may then increase rotational and valgus loading at a relatively extended knee. The authors propose that the cascade can unfold in roughly 30 to 50 milliseconds, which may outpace voluntary corrective activation and some reflex responses; these timings are drawn from cited sources rather than measured in a new experiment. Elevated decision-making and attentional demands are proposed to further constrain responsiveness to an unexpected mechanical perturbation, linking biomechanical robustness with neurocognitive responsiveness in the conceptual model. Established programs such as FIFA 11+ and PEP reduce ACL injuries overall, but the editorial argues that predictable tasks do not specifically reproduce externally imposed indirect-contact perturbations. The authors state that no validated prevention protocol specifically targets indirect-contact ACL mechanisms and call for standardized surveillance, progressive research on externally triggered challenges, and inclusion of neurological and psychophysiological factors. Female athletes are reported to sustain ACL injuries at two to eight times the rate of male athletes while representing fewer than half of participants in the referenced rehabilitation literature; the editorial identifies this evidence gap as a constraint on generalizability and equity.
limitations: The article is a three-page editorial and does not provide original epidemiological, biomechanical, rehabilitation, or injury-prevention outcomes. Its cascade is a synthesis of cited studies and theory, so the sequence should be treated as a testable model rather than a directly validated causal pathway. The 25% to 33% estimate depends on how surveillance studies identify and classify indirect contact, precisely the classification problem the authors describe. The authors acknowledge that no validated indirect-contact-specific protocol exists and that complete prevention is unlikely. Consequently, the paper does not establish that adding external perturbation, reactive drills, monitoring technologies, or neurocognitive tasks reduces ACL incidence. For NCAA American football, the mechanism may be relevant, but sport-, position-, sex-, exposure-, and return-to-play-specific effectiveness and safety remain untested.
practicalImplications: Preserve interventions with established value—strength, landing and deceleration capacity, movement skill, and existing multicomponent ACL-prevention work—because the editorial does not show that these should be replaced. Use the indirect-contact framework to improve video classification and to ask whether later-stage training and rehabilitation ever expose a prepared athlete to representative perception, decision, opponent, and off-axis perturbation demands. Any external perturbation should be progressive, controlled, and matched to current tissue, strength, movement, and contact-readiness capacity. Do not infer individual injury risk from performance on a reactive drill, and do not present “chaos” exposure as proven ACL prevention. For American football, staff could first audit actual injury video and exposure patterns by position before designing mechanism-specific progressions.

citation: Dhaliwal R., Pope H.G. The wild west of bodybuilding supplements: Three examples of unregulated compounds widely marketed online. Performance Enhancement & Health. 2026;14(3):100424. doi:10.1016/j.peh.2026.100424.
abstract: This paper addresses the following question: How large is online interest in three representative bodybuilding compounds, how much human and safety research exists, how familiar are sports-medicine authors with them, and how accurately do selected turkesterone products match their labels? The study did not enroll athletes as an intervention cohort. It analyzed worldwide internet activity and product listings, reviewed PubMed literature, surveyed corresponding authors of papers indexed under “sports medicine,” and chemically analyzed ten turkesterone products bought online. The authors combined Google Trends data from 2022 through 2024, accessible Bodybuilding.com and Reddit discussions, YouTube videos, online seller listings, and Amazon review or purchase proxies. PubMed searches counted human, anabolic-effect, and safety papers.
tldr: Relative Google search interest for turkesterone, ibutamoren, and ostarine was 2.39, 1.42, and 1.96 times the interest in nandrolone, respectively, within the authors’ specified comparison. Online forums, videos, and sellers showed extensive discussion and ready availability, including content apparently aimed at or used by teenagers; these engagement metrics indicate visibility, not verified prevalence or safe use. Ask nonjudgmentally and specifically about SARMs, “research chemicals,” growth-hormone secretagogues, ecdysteroids, stacks, and products promoted by influencers—not only conventional vitamins or anabolic steroids.
methods: The authors combined Google Trends data from 2022 through 2024, accessible Bodybuilding.com and Reddit discussions, YouTube videos, online seller listings, and Amazon review or purchase proxies. PubMed searches counted human, anabolic-effect, and safety papers. An anonymous familiarity survey was sent to 6,885 email addresses scraped from sports-medicine publications, and ten products advertised as turkesterone underwent liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry.
findings: Relative Google search interest for turkesterone, ibutamoren, and ostarine was 2.39, 1.42, and 1.96 times the interest in nandrolone, respectively, within the authors’ specified comparison. Online forums, videos, and sellers showed extensive discussion and ready availability, including content apparently aimed at or used by teenagers; these engagement metrics indicate visibility, not verified prevalence or safe use. The PubMed review found only two human turkesterone studies and no systematic human safety study; results on anabolic effects were conflicting. Ibutamoren evidence was concentrated in older or growth-hormone-deficient populations, included adverse effects, and did not establish performance benefits in healthy athletes; growth-hormone secretagogues are prohibited in sport. Ostarine had limited human research and case reports of serious adverse events; as a SARM, it is prohibited in sport and is not an approved dietary supplement. None of ten products advertised as turkesterone contained more than 0.5% of the labeled amount, and other unlabeled ecdysteroids were detected; the analysis did not comprehensively identify all possible adulterants. Only 375 of roughly 6,500 delivered professional surveys were returned, and respondents showed very low familiarity with the three target compounds.
limitations: Digital-search, post, view, upvote, review, and purchase-proxy metrics cannot identify unique users, confirm ingestion, establish demographics, or produce prevalence estimates. Search-term choices and inaccessible posts can undercount or bias comparisons, while publicity can inflate interest. The professional survey had a response rate below 6%, a heterogeneous sampling frame, and substantial selection-bias risk. The PubMed analysis was bibliometric rather than a formal systematic review with risk-of-bias grading. Only ten turkesterone products were chemically tested, so the results do not estimate the entire market or prove the contents of any other product. Applicability to collegiate American football is practical rather than population-specific: athletes may encounter these products online, but the study did not measure football-player use or outcomes.
practicalImplications: Ask nonjudgmentally and specifically about SARMs, “research chemicals,” growth-hormone secretagogues, ecdysteroids, stacks, and products promoted by influencers—not only conventional vitamins or anabolic steroids. Treat ostarine and ibutamoren as prohibited/high-risk athlete-health and anti-doping concerns, and do not infer safety from “natural,” “research use only,” or dietary-supplement labeling. A third-party certification lowers but does not eliminate risk; products from unregulated online sources should not be used. When exposure is disclosed, involve sports medicine, sports dietetics, and compliance, document the exact product and lot if available, and consult the current governing-body and WADA rules.

citation: Impellizzeri F.M., Ward P., Coutts A.J., Bornn L., McCall A. Training Load and Injury Part 2: Questionable Research Practices Hijack the Truth and Mislead Well-Intentioned Clinicians. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2020;50(10):577-584. doi:10.2519/jospt.2020.9211.
abstract: This paper addresses the following question: Is the methodological rigor of training-load and injury studies sufficient to support clinical decisions about modifying training for injury reduction? Participants: No new participant sample; this is a clinical and methodological commentary. Sport and level: Training-load and injury research across sport. Design: Clinical commentary and methodological critique. Exposure or intervention: Not applicable.
tldr: The authors argue that absent conceptual and causal frameworks plus unreliable methods create conditions for selective reporting and confirmation bias. They conclude that evidence-based practical load-injury applications cannot currently be identified with confidence from the available research. Keep monitoring load because exposure matters operationally, but separate description, prediction, and causation.
methods: Design: Clinical commentary and methodological critique. Exposure or intervention: Not applicable. Comparator: Not applicable. Measurements and outcomes: Conceptual clarity, causal structure, researcher degrees of freedom, selective reporting, and clinical claims. Analysis: Examples and reasoning about bias, P hacking, hypothesizing after results, and confirmation bias.
findings: The authors argue that absent conceptual and causal frameworks plus unreliable methods create conditions for selective reporting and confirmation bias. They conclude that evidence-based practical load-injury applications cannot currently be identified with confidence from the available research. Their strongest practical statement is the generic principle not to do too much too soon, explicitly presented as accepted training practice rather than a finding confirmed by the reviewed studies.
limitations: This is an expert critique, not an empirical estimate of the size of bias or a test of a replacement monitoring model. Interpretation: The paper challenges unsupported causal and prescriptive claims; it does not argue that training load is irrelevant or should not be monitored.
practicalImplications: Keep monitoring load because exposure matters operationally, but separate description, prediction, and causation. Predefine questions where possible, retain continuous data, avoid post-hoc threshold shopping, show uncertainty, and resist converting associations into injury-prevention guarantees. Contextual coaching judgment remains necessary, but should be labeled as judgment.

citation: Cosio P.L., Pinal‐Fernandez I., Moreno‐Simonet L., Cadefau J.A., Mammen A.L., Rodas G., et al. Transcriptomic Profiling of the Biceps Femoris Long Head 72 h Following a Football Match and Associations With Recovery Biomarkers. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2026;36(7):e70339. doi:10.1111/sms.70339.
abstract: This paper addresses the following question: What gene-expression and pathway-level changes remain in the biceps femoris long head three days after a high-load soccer match, and how are those changes associated with creatine kinase, hamstring rate of torque development, and sprint performance? Ten male outfield players from a regional first-division soccer competition participated; mean age was 20.6 years. One biopsy yielded insufficient RNA, leaving nine players for transcriptomic analyses. This was a secondary integrative analysis of a previously studied cohort with no non-match control group. Dominant-leg biceps femoris long-head biopsies were collected seven days before and 72 hours after a standardized FIFA-rules match.
tldr: MYH1, which encodes type IIx myosin, was the only listed top gene that remained statistically significant after false-discovery-rate correction, with downregulation at 72 hours. Pathway analysis showed coordinated positive enrichment in stress response, immune and cytokine signaling, protein turnover, mitochondrial quality control, translation, and structural remodeling, while muscle-contraction pathways were negatively enriched. Use the study as evidence that a fixed 72-hour calendar rule may miss ongoing hamstring recovery in some athletes, especially after high-speed exposure.
methods: This was a secondary integrative analysis of a previously studied cohort with no non-match control group. Dominant-leg biceps femoris long-head biopsies were collected seven days before and 72 hours after a standardized FIFA-rules match. All players exceeded predefined match-load thresholds, then completed only low-volume recovery assessments for three days. Bulk RNA sequencing used paired linear modeling and false-discovery-rate correction; clinical measures included creatine kinase, hamstring rate of torque development to 100 milliseconds, and 40-m sprint performance before and at 24, 48, and 72 hours after the match.
findings: MYH1, which encodes type IIx myosin, was the only listed top gene that remained statistically significant after false-discovery-rate correction, with downregulation at 72 hours. Pathway analysis showed coordinated positive enrichment in stress response, immune and cytokine signaling, protein turnover, mitochondrial quality control, translation, and structural remodeling, while muscle-contraction pathways were negatively enriched. Creatine kinase remained elevated, early hamstring rate of torque development remained reduced, and sprint time remained slower than pre-match at 24, 48, and 72 hours in the nine-player subgroup. Transcriptomic pathways related to stress, apoptosis, immune response, protein metabolism, and remodeling were associated with changes in creatine kinase and rate of torque development. Reduced MYH1 expression was associated with larger decrements in hamstring rate of torque development, but these small-sample correlations are associative and exploratory. The combined molecular and clinical pattern indicates ongoing remodeling at 72 hours in this cohort; it does not define when every player is fully recovered.
limitations: The final sample comprised only nine young male regional-level soccer players, with no control group and only two biopsy time points. The pre-match biopsy followed three days of rest, which may still have contained residual effects from earlier soccer exposure. Biopsy location, tissue heterogeneity, RNA processing, and sampling different sites can add technical and biological variation. Only one gene survived gene-level multiple-comparison correction, making pathway-level interpretations more prominent but not equivalent to direct protein or functional recovery. The standardized soccer match involved more than 10 km of running and substantial high-speed exposure, so direct transfer to collegiate American football is limited by sport, position, collision load, substitution patterns, and training schedule. Molecular remodeling also does not itself establish injury risk or contraindicate training.
practicalImplications: Use the study as evidence that a fixed 72-hour calendar rule may miss ongoing hamstring recovery in some athletes, especially after high-speed exposure. For collegiate American football, integrate individual exposure, symptoms, prior injury, sprint readiness, force or rate-of-force-development measures, and schedule demands. Do not biopsy athletes or use creatine kinase alone to clear or restrict participation. A pragmatic application is to preserve individualized recovery options and avoid assuming that normal-looking wellness or time elapsed means complete tissue recovery.

citation: Berberet D., Petway A., Bell K., Gillen Z., Mundy P., Barrera H., et al. Unlocking Basketball Athletic Performance: Countermovement Jump Rebound (CMJ-RE) Normative Reference Values Derived from Force Plate Data Across Seven NCAA Division-I Power Five Men’s College Basketball Teams. International Journal of Strength and Conditioning. 2025;5(1). doi:10.47206/ijsc.v5i1.555.
abstract: This paper addresses the following question: Can a countermovement-jump rebound test provide reliable reactive-strength information and position-specific reference values? Ninety-six NCAA Division I men’s basketball players from seven teams. Eighty-seven passed quality filters: 53 guards, 31 forwards, and three centers. Cross-sectional normative study using bilateral force plates. Examined 38 metrics, position differences, reliability, effort filters, and percentile bands.
tldr: Position differences appeared in 37% of reported metrics; rebound jump height favored guards, while other significant metrics favored forwards. Mean ground-contact times exceeded 250 ms, so the test should not be treated as equivalent to a short-contact drop jump. Use the authors’ effort filters before interpreting CMJ-rebound data.
methods: Cross-sectional normative study using bilateral force plates. Examined 38 metrics, position differences, reliability, effort filters, and percentile bands. Center comparisons were restricted by the very small subgroup.
findings: Position differences appeared in 37% of reported metrics; rebound jump height favored guards, while other significant metrics favored forwards. Mean ground-contact times exceeded 250 ms, so the test should not be treated as equivalent to a short-contact drop jump. Eight metrics had coefficients of variation above 10%, making small changes difficult to interpret. Day-of-week effects appeared for modified RSI, while AM versus PM effects did not.
limitations: Cross-sectional percentiles describe this sample and do not establish optimal values. Only one session was collected and familiarization remains a concern. Multiple comparisons and position imbalance increase false-positive risk. Basketball norms should not be used as football thresholds.
practicalImplications: Use the authors’ effort filters before interpreting CMJ-rebound data. Prefer within-athlete trends and metric reliability over traffic-light norms, particularly when return-to-play decisions are involved.

citation: Hanson N.J., Scheadler C.M., Katsavelis D., Miller M.G. Validity of the Wattbike 3-Minute Aerobic Test: Measurement and Estimation of V̇o2max. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2022;36(2):400-404. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000003440.
abstract: This paper addresses the following question: Does the Wattbike three-minute aerobic test elicit a measured V̇O2max comparable with a self-paced maximal test, and does the Wattbike software estimate agree with the measured criterion? Thirteen low-risk adults with recent cycling experience completed the study: ten men and three women, mean age 29.2 years, with widely varying cycling histories. Participants were recruited from a university and local cycling clubs and averaged approximately 107 km of cycling per week. This was a repeated-measures validation study across two visits. Participants first completed a 10-minute self-paced maximal oxygen-uptake test, then 48 hours to one week later completed the Wattbike three-minute aerobic test after a standardized 20-minute warm-up.
tldr: Mean estimated V̇O2max from the Wattbike, measured V̇O2max during the three-minute test, and measured V̇O2max during the self-paced criterion test did not differ statistically. The correlation between measured V̇O2max in the self-paced and three-minute tests was high at ICC 0.96, and the association between the self-paced measure and Wattbike estimate was also high at ICC 0.91. The Wattbike three-minute test can be a pragmatic estimate when cycle testing is appropriate, athletes complete the full warm-up, and the same protocol is standardized over time.
methods: This was a repeated-measures validation study across two visits. Participants first completed a 10-minute self-paced maximal oxygen-uptake test, then 48 hours to one week later completed the Wattbike three-minute aerobic test after a standardized 20-minute warm-up. A metabolic cart measured respiratory variables in both sessions, and the Wattbike supplied its proprietary estimate. Repeated-measures comparisons, intraclass correlations, and Bland-Altman agreement analyses were used.
findings: Mean estimated V̇O2max from the Wattbike, measured V̇O2max during the three-minute test, and measured V̇O2max during the self-paced criterion test did not differ statistically. The correlation between measured V̇O2max in the self-paced and three-minute tests was high at ICC 0.96, and the association between the self-paced measure and Wattbike estimate was also high at ICC 0.91. Mean bias between the Wattbike estimate and self-paced measured V̇O2max was only 0.29 mL per kg per minute, but individual 95% limits of agreement were wide, approximately minus 10.77 to plus 11.34 mL per kg per minute. The three-minute test produced higher carbon-dioxide output and respiratory exchange ratio and a slightly lower peak heart rate than the self-paced test, indicating that the protocols were physiologically similar in V̇O2max but not interchangeable in all responses. Eight participants used a conservative or even-paced strategy and five used an aggressive declining-power strategy; both patterns reached similar maximal oxygen uptake in this small sample. The standardized 20-minute warm-up likely contributed to successful V̇O2max attainment and is part of the tested protocol rather than an optional detail.
limitations: The validation sample was only 13 cyclists, included just three women, and spanned broad age and training experience. Test order was fixed rather than randomized, the self-paced test was treated as the criterion rather than compared against a conventional graded test in the same study, and the proprietary estimation equation was not recalibrated or externally cross-validated. High correlation and similar group means do not guarantee close individual agreement, as shown by limits spanning roughly 22 mL per kg per minute. The study assessed concurrent validity, not test-retest reliability or sensitivity to training change. Direct applicability to collegiate American football is limited because cyclists were tested in a cycling-specific modality and V̇O2max is not a complete measure of football conditioning.
practicalImplications: The Wattbike three-minute test can be a pragmatic estimate when cycle testing is appropriate, athletes complete the full warm-up, and the same protocol is standardized over time. Use the result for broad profiling or within-athlete trends, not as a precise laboratory-equivalent number for an individual. Before adopting it with collegiate American football players, establish familiarization, repeatability, positional tolerability, and local comparison with the program’s reference conditioning measures. Account for the test’s high anaerobic demand and avoid testing when fatigue or lower-limb status makes a maximal three-minute effort inappropriate.
