methods: Physical and technical measures from 32 competitive matches were classified by whether players completed a 15-20-minute morning routine involving mobility, core and lower-body resistance, and reactive agility work. Analyses considered match context.
findings: Primed matches had higher total running distance (d=0.34), moderate-intensity distance (d=0.52), and high-intensity distance (d=0.30); frequency of duels was also higher (d=0.26). Technical measures were generally similar across conditions.
limitations: The comparison was nonrandomized within one club, primed and unprimed observations were unequal, and residual match, selection, or player-state confounding may explain part of the association.
practicalImplications: A brief low-burden morning routine can be evaluated as a local match-preparation option. Track athlete response, session cost, and match context before adopting a standard protocol.
athleteDev: Explain the purpose of an optional priming session and gather player feedback; avoid promising a match-performance gain from this single observational study.
rtp: A match-day priming routine is not a return-to-play test and should be adjusted or omitted according to individual rehabilitation and exposure plans.

citation: West SW, Williams S, Cazzola D, Kemp S, Cross MJ, Stokes KA. Training Load and Injury Risk in Elite Rugby Union: The Largest Investigation to Date. International Journal of Sports Medicine. Published online December 8, 2020.
abstract: A two-season multicenter professional-rugby analysis compared how different acute:chronic workload-ratio calculations related to subsequent injury.
tldr: ACWR-injury associations changed with the calculation method, and no method consistently identified a risk sweet spot. A single ratio is not a validated injury decision rule.
methods: Investigators analyzed session-RPE load and injury records from 696 players at 13 professional rugby clubs over two seasons, including 1,718 injuries of all types and a soft-tissue subset. They compared multiple ratio windows, averaging methods, and coupling choices.
findings: Across 192 comparisons for each injury grouping, 40% of all-injury and 31% of soft-tissue analyses were significant. The apparent relationships were inconsistent across calculation methods.
limitations: Observational associations cannot establish causation or injury prevention. Session-RPE was the single load measure, and results depend on injury definitions, model choices, rugby context, and covariate control.
practicalImplications: Use load trends as context for a discussion of progression, symptoms, and planned exposure. Do not operationalize an ACWR cutoff or sweet spot as a stand-alone red/green rule.
athleteDev: Explain why one workload number cannot diagnose readiness or predict an individual's injury. Encourage honest symptom and exposure reporting.
rtp: Return progression should integrate clinical status, functional milestones, and graded sport exposure; a workload ratio alone cannot clear an athlete.

citation: Martins F, Marques A, França C, Sarmento H, Henriques R, Ihle A, et al. Weekly External Load Performance Effects on Sports Injuries of Male Professional Football Players. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. 2023;20(2):1121.
abstract: A one-season prospective observational study compared GPS-derived external-load blocks before injury, after return, and with each player's season average in professional soccer.
tldr: Pre-injury four-week blocks had higher measured loads than post-return blocks and season averages in one team. The comparison does not establish a causal injury threshold.
methods: Thirty-three male professional soccer players wore 10-Hz GPS units during one season. Total distance, high-speed running, accelerations, and decelerations were compared across four weeks before injury, four weeks after return, and season averages.
findings: Fifteen players sustained 24 recorded injuries. Total distance, high-speed running, accelerations, and decelerations were significantly higher in the pre-injury block than in post-return and average comparisons.
limitations: The study involved one team and season, few injuries, and pandemic conditions. A post-injury comparison is affected by return management; match context and injury severity were not fully modeled, so predictive or causal interpretations are unsafe.
practicalImplications: Review sustained load changes in context with availability, symptoms, prior exposure, and training plan. Local prospective monitoring is needed before using any athlete-specific threshold.
athleteDev: Use GPS trends to open a conversation about workload and recovery, not to assign blame for an injury or claim an individual injury forecast.
rtp: Post-return load is deliberately managed; do not treat the lower post-return values here as a universal return target or clearance criterion.

citation: Gómez-Piqueras P, Martínez-Serrano A, Freitas TT, Gómez Díaz A, Loturco I, Giménez E, et al. Weekly Programming of Hamstring-Related Training Contents in European Professional Soccer. Sports. 2024;12(3):73.
abstract: A cross-sectional survey described how professional European soccer strength and conditioning coaches schedule hamstring-demanding exercises and running tasks during a match week.
tldr: Coaches reported concentrating demanding hamstring work earlier in the match week and reducing it near games. These are practice patterns, not proof of an optimal injury-prevention schedule.
methods: An international fixed-response questionnaire asked professional soccer strength and conditioning coaches about 26 training activities and their frequency and placement from postmatch days to the days before the next match.
findings: Respondents commonly placed high-demand acceleration and deceleration or force tasks around match day minus four, with more high-speed exposure around match day minus three; heavy hamstring-demanding tasks were uncommon on the two days immediately before games.
limitations: Self-report and uneven league participation limit representativeness; England and Germany were absent. The study did not collect team injury or performance outcomes and cannot show that these schedules prevent hamstring injury.
practicalImplications: Use the survey as a reference for discussing microcycle options, then adapt exercise dose and timing to schedule, athlete capacity, and local outcomes rather than copying a fixed template.
athleteDev: Help players understand why high-speed and strength exposures are placed at particular points in the week and invite feedback on fatigue and readiness.
rtp: A team microcycle survey does not define an injured player's reintroduction schedule; progression still depends on individual criteria and graded high-speed exposure.

citation: Eccles DW, Twedell H, DeCouto BS. What does mental rest mean to professional athletes? A study of National Football League players. Psychology of Sport & Exercise. 2026;82:103029.
abstract: Sixteen NFL players were interviewed about mental rest, and a thematic analysis tested whether an existing model of mental rest from college athletes applies to professional athletes. The model generalized well, with sleep and several wakeful resting experiences found, but public recognition and job pressures created departures from the model. Mental rest was linked by players to concentration, recovery and health.
tldr: NFL players described mental rest in ways that largely match a model built on college athletes, including a break from thinking about football and a sense of control over one's time. Public recognition and job insecurity made it harder for them to switch off, so rest planning should account for these pressures.
methods: Qualitative description design with semi-structured interviews of 16 NFL players recruited through personal contacts and one franchise's clinical psychologist. Interviews lasted 13 to 45 minutes. A medium-Q thematic analysis was conducted by one researcher, with a critical friend, using codes from the Eccles-Kazmier model plus inductive codes.
findings: Players described sleep and wakeful resting, and six of the seven wakeful resting experiences in the model were found, including a break from thinking about sport and from effortful thinking, control over one's life, and a break from routines and training demands. Constant thinking about football was linked to job precarity and family income pressure. Players reported that public recognition often blocked escape, so they stayed home or avoided public places. The academic work experience in the model was not found.
limitations: Each player was interviewed once in a short session, and the sample was convenience-based and mostly African American, which differs from the college sample in the model. The findings describe experiences and do not estimate how common they are, and they may not extend to less recognizable professional athletes.
practicalImplications: The authors suggest helping players choose in-season rest activities that give several breaks at once (from football, from effortful thinking, from routine) and fitting them into the easiest points of a busy week. For recognizable players, consider identifying rest locations with few football cues, since players reported that public places often brought unwanted football conversations.
athleteDev: Players linked poor mental rest to weaker concentration, more mental errors and lower physical output in their own words. Use this to support in-season routines that include low-demand, non-football activities and time with family, and plan rest locations with few football cues.
rtp: Limited use. The study examined mental rest in active NFL players and did not assess injury, rehabilitation or return to play, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions or set criteria for them.

citation: Meng CR, Walts CT, Ryan LJ, Stearne DJ, Clark KP. Spatiotemporal kinematics during top speed sprinting in male intercollegiate track and field and team sport athletes. Sports Biomechanics. 2024.
abstract: Ninety-eight male intercollegiate track and field and team sport athletes completed 40 m sprints filmed for analysis between 30 and 40 m. Contact time, step rate, step length, flight length and duty factor were meaningfully correlated with top speed. At matched top speeds, team sport athletes used a more ground-based pattern, with longer contact times and shorter flight times, than slower track athletes, so track-based technical models may need modification for team sport athletes.
tldr: Across 98 male college athletes, the sprint measures that tracked top speed were contact time, step rate, step length, flight length and duty factor. Team sport athletes reached the same top speed as slower track athletes but with more ground contact, so track-based sprint models may not fit team sport athletes directly.
methods: Cross-sectional study with 98 male varsity athletes (28 track and field, 70 team sport) tested in one session. Two 40 m sprints per athlete were filmed at 240 frames per second, and the faster 30 to 40 m split was analysed with Kinovea using five-frame stride digitizing. Pearson or Spearman correlations were used across the sample, and independent t tests compared matched slow track (n = 14) and fast team sport (n = 22) subgroups with a Bonferroni-adjusted alpha of 0.007.
findings: Across all athletes, contact time, step rate, step length, flight length and duty factor were meaningfully correlated with top speed (0.51 to 0.78), and flight time and contact length were weakly correlated (0.27 to 0.34). In matched subgroups at about 9.3 m/s, team sport athletes had longer contact time (0.114 vs 0.104 s), shorter flight time (0.109 vs 0.124 s), longer contact length (1.06 vs 0.97 m), shorter flight length (1.02 vs 1.16 m) and higher duty factor (0.255 vs 0.228), while step rate and step length did not differ significantly.
limitations: Only male athletes were studied, track athletes ran in sneakers rather than spikes, and the analysis used a single sagittal video view, one stride, one rater (intra-rater differences of about 0.2% to 1.6%) and a 30 to 40 m field of view. The subgroup comparison used small samples, and Fast team sport athletes were about 7 kg heavier than Slow track athletes. Force, energy cost and joint angles were not measured, so the paper cannot show whether the team sport pattern is more efficient or safer.
practicalImplications: Use contact time, step rate, step length, flight length and duty factor as descriptive measures of top speed sprinting, but do not assume that a track-style pattern is the target for team sport athletes. Team sport athletes who reach the same top speed may do so with longer ground contact and a higher duty factor, so coaches should be cautious about applying track-based technical models and normative metrics to them.
athleteDev: Profile sprint mechanics in team sport athletes without assuming a track-only reference. Faster team sport athletes here reached similar top speed with longer contact time and a higher duty factor, but the authors also note that training toward a track model might raise top speed, so neither pattern was shown to be the better target.
rtp: Not applicable. Athletes were injury-free and the study did not assess injury, rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.

citation: Carmona G, Moreno-Simonet L, Cosio PL, Astrella A, Fernández D, Padullés X, et al. Acute changes in hamstring injury risk factors after a session of high-volume maximal sprinting speed efforts in soccer players. Sports Health. 2024.
abstract: Fifteen healthy male amateur soccer players completed 10 maximal 40 m sprints, and sprint performance, posterior chain strength, range of motion, dynamic pelvic tilt and muscle damage markers were measured for 72 hours afterward. Top speed and posterior chain strength declined for 48 to 72 hours and creatine kinase and soreness rose, while the pelvic tilt change was not significant. The authors suggest that sprint dosage could be individualized by risk factor profile, which was not tested.
tldr: In healthy amateur soccer players, a session of 10 maximal 40 m sprints reduced top speed and posterior chain strength for 48 to 72 hours and raised muscle damage markers. Individual responses varied widely, so sprint planning should consider recovery time and individual monitoring.
methods: Prospective observational case series with a single group of 15 healthy male amateur soccer players. Players performed 10 maximal 40 m sprints with 3 minutes of rest. Measures at baseline and 24, 48 and 72 hours included 10 m and 30 m sprint times, theoretical maximal force and velocity from a field force-velocity method, 90:20 isometric posterior chain strength, hip flexor and hamstring range of motion, dynamic pelvic tilt from an inertial sensor, serum creatine kinase and perceived soreness. Analysis used bootstrap effect sizes against baseline.
findings: Theoretical maximal velocity was reduced through 48 hours (9.05 to 8.65 m/s, ES -0.71), and 30 m time was slower at 48 and 72 hours. Posterior chain strength was reduced through 48 hours in the non-dominant leg (192 to 166 N, ES -0.60) and through 72 hours in the dominant leg (213 to 194 N, ES -0.40). Creatine kinase peaked at 24 hours (840 U/L, ES 1.28) and soreness peaked at 48 hours. Dynamic pelvic tilt rose non-significantly (P = 0.06), and range of motion showed no significant change.
limitations: The study had one group, no control condition and only 15 players, and the authors describe it as a pilot. Individual responses varied widely, so group means may hide player-level patterns, and the study did not include lower-limb kinematics, injury outcomes or players by position. The Discussion gives a different Sdec value (3.62%) from the Results (3.67%).
practicalImplications: After a high-volume maximal sprint session like this one, expect top speed and posterior chain strength to stay reduced for up to 48 to 72 hours in amateur players; some deficits were still present at 72 hours, the last time point measured. Check individual responses before scheduling further maximal sprint volume, since responses varied widely; the authors suggest but did not test individualizing sprint dosage by risk factor profile.
athleteDev: Use this to inform sprint dosage in healthy amateur players: a single session of 10 maximal 40 m sprints reduced top speed and strength for 48 to 72 hours. The study did not test when the next high-speed exposure is safe, and responses varied widely, so monitor individuals rather than applying the group average.
rtp: Limited. The players were healthy and no injured players were tested, so the findings describe recovery after sprinting in healthy players and cannot set return-to-play criteria or show when strength or sprint capacity is safe after a hamstring injury.

citation: Nuuttila O-P, Seipäjärvi S, Kyröläinen H, Nummela A. Reliability and sensitivity of nocturnal heart rate and heart-rate variability in monitoring individual responses to training load. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2022. (Ahead of print.)
abstract: Recreational runners recorded nocturnal heart rate and heart rate variability after two identical low-intensity sessions (n = 15) and before and after a 3000 m test (n = 23). Night-to-night reliability was very high for all indices and segments. After the 3000 m test, heart rate rose and heart rate variability fell in the 4-hour and full-night segments, but not in the morning value.
tldr: Wearable nocturnal heart rate and HRV were highly reliable from night to night in recreational runners. After a hard 3000 m test, the 4-hour and full-night values showed clear changes, but the morning value did not.
methods: Recreational male and female runners wore a Firstbeat Bodyguard 2 device overnight. Average heart rate, LnRMSSD and LnHF were calculated for a full night, a 4-hour segment starting 30 minutes after sleep onset, and a morning value. Reliability was tested with ICC and CV after two identical low-intensity sessions (n = 15); sensitivity was tested with repeated-measures models after a rest day versus the night after a 3000 m test (n = 23).
findings: After the two low-intensity sessions, nights were similar, with ICC of 0.97 to 0.98 for heart rate, 0.92 to 0.97 for LnRMSSD and 0.91 to 0.96 for LnHF, and between-night CV of 2.1% to 3.8%. After the 3000 m test, the 4-hour segment showed heart rate rising from 51.2 to 55.0 bpm and LnRMSSD falling from 4.19 to 4.02 ms. The full-night segment showed similar changes, while the morning value did not change.
limitations: The reliability sample (n = 15) and sensitivity sample (n = 23) were small, and many possible participants were excluded for lack of full-night data. Sexes were not analyzed separately, and readiness to train was the only external reference for recovery. Bedtime was later after the 3000 m test, which may have affected the nocturnal values.
practicalImplications: Nocturnal recordings can be used for resting heart rate and HRV monitoring in recreational runners, because the day-to-day variation is low. Use the same segment consistently; after a hard test, the 4-hour and full-night values showed clear changes while the morning value did not, so the choice of segment affects the interpretation.
athleteDev: Use nocturnal heart rate and HRV in endurance athletes to track responses to hard sessions, and keep one analysis segment for each athlete. The sensitivity results come from recreational runners, so confirm the response to maximal efforts in the athletes being monitored.
rtp: Not applicable. The study used recreational runners without injury and did not assess injury, rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.

citation: Kristiansen J, Eddy C, Magnusson SP. Reliability and validity of the end range hamstring strength test with handheld dynamometry. International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy. 2024;19(3):268-274.
abstract: Twenty healthy active participants were tested for hamstring strength in a lengthened position with a handheld dynamometer and an isokinetic Biodex on two days. Handheld dynamometer scores correlated strongly with the Biodex, and intra-rater reliability was excellent while inter-rater reliability was moderate to good. The authors conclude that the test is a reliable and valid, low-cost option for measuring hamstring strength at long muscle lengths.
tldr: A handheld dynamometer test of hamstring strength in a lengthened position agreed well with an isokinetic machine and was reliable when the same tester repeated it. Inter-rater reliability was weaker, especially for the left leg.
methods: Twenty healthy active participants were tested with the Biodex and a handheld dynamometer on test day 1, and the handheld test was repeated 7 to 10 days later by two testers. Pearson correlations, Bland-Altman plots, paired t tests and ICC (two-way random, single measure, consistency) with SEM and minimal detectable difference were calculated.
findings: Handheld dynamometer and Biodex scores correlated strongly (r = 0.87 right, r = 0.911 left), and Bland-Altman mean differences were 12 N (left) and 22 N (right) with all points inside the limits of agreement. There was no systematic bias between test days or testers. Intra-rater ICC was 0.91 right and 0.93 left (SEM 8.5% and 8.2%, minimal detectable differences 26.3% and 24.2%), and inter-rater ICC was 0.83 right and 0.71 left (SEM 11.2% and 16.1%, minimal detectable differences 34.9% and 47.7%).
limitations: The sample was 20 healthy active participants recruited by convenience, including hospital employees and local club athletes, and sex was not reported in the text. Two testers of different sex, handedness and experience were used, the left-leg inter-rater ICC had a wide 95% CI (0.39 to 0.87), the first test day was not blinded, and Bland-Altman plots suggested larger differences at higher force. The abstract gives r = 0.87 for both legs and the Discussion gives SEM ranges that differ from Table 2; the Results and Table 2 values are reported here.
practicalImplications: Use the handheld dynamometer end-range hamstring test with the same tester for repeat measures. Only changes larger than about 24% to 26% for same-tester testing, and much larger changes between testers, should be treated as real. The test has not been validated for injured athletes, so it cannot set return-to-play thresholds.
athleteDev: Use this low-cost test to profile hamstring strength at long muscle lengths in athletes, with the same tester for repeat tests. Do not read small changes as real because the measurement error is large.
rtp: Limited use. The authors suggest the test may help monitor rehabilitation and detect deficits before and after return to play, but the sample was healthy participants, so it does not establish injury-specific cutoffs or return-to-play criteria.

citation: Parry GN, Herrington LC, Horsley IG. The test-retest reliability of force plate-derived parameters of the countermovement push-up as a power assessment tool. Journal of Sport Rehabilitation. 2020;29(3):381-383.
abstract: This test-retest study measured force plate variables from the countermovement push-up in 10 male college athletes on two occasions 7 days apart. No differences were found between sessions. Intraclass correlation coefficients were 0.88 to 0.98 across parameters, with peak force and mean force reliable and rate of force development the least reliable.
tldr: Peak force, mean force, flight time and impulse from a force plate countermovement push-up were reliable across two sessions in 10 male college athletes, while rate of force development was not. Whether the test detects training change was not studied.
methods: Single-group repeated-measures test-retest design. Ten male college athletes, each performing three maximal-effort countermovement push-ups on two force plates on two occasions 7 days apart. Flight time, peak force, mean force, rate of force development and impulse were taken from the force-time curve and analyzed with paired t tests, ICC, CV, SEM and SDD.
findings: No significant differences were found between the two test occasions for any measure (P greater than .05). Flight time, peak force, mean force and impulse had ICC of 0.96 to 0.98 and CV of 1.7% to 6.9%, while rate of force development fell outside acceptable reliability (CV 14.1%, ICC 0.878). The smallest detectable differences were 7.5% for peak force, 8.6% for mean force and 11.2% for rate of force development, and impulse had an SDD of 26.1% in Table 1.
limitations: The sample was 10 male college athletes, so estimates are imprecise and may not apply to other groups, and responsiveness to training was not tested. The abstract reports CV of 5.5% to 14.1% while Table 1 shows 1.7% to 14.1%, the Discussion gives the RFD CV as 14.9%, and some Table 1 values do not reconcile with the stated formulas (mean force SEM 1.7 N with SDD 50.3 N); the Results and Table values are reported here.
practicalImplications: In similar trained college athletes, peak force and mean force from the countermovement push-up can be tracked, treating only changes larger than about 7.5% for peak force and 8.6% for mean force as beyond measurement error (the authors suggest 8% to 9%). Avoid relying on rate of force development, and expect impulse to need a change of about 26% before it exceeds measurement error.
athleteDev: Use peak and mean force from the force plate countermovement push-up to monitor upper-body power in similar college athletes, using the reported smallest detectable differences to judge real change. Do not use rate of force development as a tracking measure until its reliability is shown.
rtp: Not applicable. The study tested reliability in active college athletes and did not assess injury, rehabilitation or return-to-sport readiness, so it cannot be used to judge readiness after injury.

citation: Lauersen JB, Andersen TE, Andersen LB. Strength training as superior, dose-dependent and safe prevention of acute and overuse sports injuries: a systematic review, qualitative analysis and meta-analysis. Br J Sports Med 2018;0:1-8.
abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis pooled six randomised controlled trials of strength training for sports injury prevention in 7738 participants aged 12-40 years. The cluster-adjusted intention-to-treat relative risk was 0.338 (95% CI 0.238 to 0.480), and the authors report a dose-dependent relationship between strength training volume and intensity and injury reduction.
tldr: Across six randomised trials, mostly in soccer players, strength training reduced sports injuries by about two-thirds overall. Larger weekly training volume and higher intensity were associated with bigger reductions.
methods: PRISMA systematic review (PROSPERO CRD42015006970) of randomised trials of strength training for primary sports injury prevention, searched to July 2017. Two reviewers screened studies and rated risk of bias, and the authors pooled cluster-adjusted relative risks, rated GRADE certainty, tested heterogeneity and publication bias, and ran a post hoc meta-regression of volume, intensity and duration.
findings: Six trials (7738 participants, 177 injuries) gave a pooled relative risk of 0.338 with no heterogeneity (I2 = 0%), rated high certainty by GRADE, and no publication bias was detected. In the post hoc meta-regression, a 10% increase in weekly repetitions was associated with the pooled relative risk falling from 0.338 to 0.295 (4.3 percentage points, 13% relative), and higher intensity was also associated with lower risk, while duration was not significant. Four trials reported no adverse events among 3991 participants.
limitations: Trial populations, programmes and injury definitions differed, and one trial was excluded from the meta-regression for insufficient data. The dose-response result comes from a post hoc analysis across trials, so it does not show that individuals who train at a higher dose will be protected to the same degree. Compliance was high in research settings, and the authors note club adherence remains a challenge.
practicalImplications: Strength training programmes with adequate weekly volume and intensity can be used for sports injury prevention, with a familiarisation or technique phase before progressive loading, as the authors recommend. The review does not show equal benefit in every sport or setting, and the evidence covers intensities of about 6.9-9.3 RM.
athleteDev: Strength training can be built into pre-season or in-season injury prevention plans, with weekly volume and intensity planned within the range studied. The review supports it as a prevention tool; it does not show a direct performance benefit.
rtp: This review covers injury prevention in injury-free athletes, not rehabilitation after injury, so it cannot guide return-to-sport loading or readiness after an injury.

citation: Li X, Fan D, Feng J, Lei Y, Cheng C, Li X. Systematic review of motion capture in virtual reality: enhancing the precision of sports training. Journal of Ambient Intelligence and Smart Environments 2025;17(1):5-27.
abstract: This systematic review examines the use of motion capture within virtual reality for sports training, covering 54 studies published 2018-2023. The authors describe applications in physical conditioning, cognitive training, sport-specific training, team collaboration and rehabilitation, and identify real-time feedback as the main benefit alongside hardware, data processing and interface limitations.
tldr: This review of 54 studies describes how motion capture combined with virtual reality is being used in sports training, mainly to give real-time feedback. Many of the examples are small pilot or user studies, so the review maps possibilities rather than proving performance gains.
methods: Literature review following PRISMA guidance across Scopus, Web of Science, PsycINFO, ScienceDirect, IEEE Xplore, Embase and PubMed, limited to English articles published 2018-2023. Of 987 records, 756 remained after duplicate and title screening, 214 full texts were assessed, and 54 were included. Studies were summarized qualitatively by application theme and in tables of design, participants, VR setup and outcome measures.
findings: The authors report that motion capture in VR offers real-time feedback, immersive training and tailored regimes across the reviewed applications. Examples include a basketball shooting algorithm that the authors say raised shooting percentages by up to 14% when combined with resistance training, and a randomized trial in which Kinect-based VR plus physical therapy improved upper extremity motor function in chronic stroke compared with physical therapy alone.
limitations: The review reports no pooled effects and no per-study risk of bias ratings, although it describes using the Cochrane tool, and the synthesis is narrative. Many included studies are small pilot studies, and the authors' claims about AI, mixed reality and societal implications are forward-looking rather than drawn from the included studies.
practicalImplications: Motion capture in VR may be worth piloting for technique feedback and decision-making practice, especially where real-time feedback is hard to give in the field. Before adoption, staff should check cybersickness, sensor comfort and whether skills transfer to the real sport, because the review does not establish transfer.
athleteDev: Use VR with motion capture as a supplementary way to practise technique and decision-making, and check transfer with field performance measures before relying on it. The evidence base is mostly small pilot work, so it supports trialling the approach rather than adopting it as a performance standard.
rtp: The review includes rehabilitation studies in stroke, neck pain and pediatric brain injury, but no return-to-sport criteria for athletes. It cannot be used to decide when an injured athlete is ready to return to sport.

citation: Johnston K, Wattie N, Schorer J, Baker J. Talent identification in sport: a systematic review. Sports Med 2017.
abstract: This PRISMA systematic review of 20 longitudinal and retrospective studies from 1990 to 2015 compared performance variables between highly skilled and less-skilled elite athletes. The authors found a high degree of variability in which factors discriminated skill levels, with physical profiles, male samples and athletes aged 10-20 years overrepresented.
tldr: Across 20 longitudinal or retrospective studies, no set of performance measures consistently predicted later success in elite sport. Coaches should treat talent selection based on current test results as uncertain.
methods: PRISMA systematic review of English-language, peer-reviewed longitudinal or retrospective studies from January 1990 to July 2015, drawn from Web of Science and SPORTDiscus, reference lists and an expert panel. Studies had to compare at least two skill groups of elite or expert athletes over at least 12 months. Of 1695 unique records, 399 went to full-text review and 20 were included.
findings: Sixteen studies were longitudinal, two retrospective and two mixed; 60% examined physical profiles, 65% included only males, and 60% examined athletes aged 10-20. Sprint ability discriminated skill levels in eight studies, agility drills did so in several sports, and none of the body composition measures distinguished skill levels. Results were inconsistent overall, and the authors report that all four mixed-measurement studies (physical, psychological and sport-specific variables) found some predictive utility.
limitations: Only 20 studies met the criteria, and the review excluded grey-area topics such as relative age, birthplace and deliberate practice. Skill-level labels (elite, professional, selected, drafted) varied so much that comparisons are difficult, and only English peer-reviewed articles were included.
practicalImplications: Do not rely on a single physical test or an early selection result for talent decisions; use several measures and track athletes over time. The authors argue that selecting athletes before age 10 lacks support, and that evidence for female athletes is especially thin.
athleteDev: For talent decisions, combine physical, psychological and sport-specific measures and review athletes repeatedly rather than treating one test as predictive. The evidence base is thin for female athletes and for children under 10.
rtp: This review covers talent selection in youth and elite athletes, not injury rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions.

citation: Jeckell AS, Fontana RS, Gonzalez R. Review of media representation of sport concussion and implications for youth sports. Clin Sports Med 2023.
abstract: This narrative review examined 20 Google News articles on sport-related concussion published 2012-2022, counting terms such as concussion, CTE, retirement and dementia, and summarized research on how athletes, parents and coaches understand and report concussion. The authors conclude that media coverage can misrepresent concussion and that clinicians should correct misconceptions among patients and athletes.
tldr: Media coverage of concussion often uses misleading terms and emphasizes CTE and retirement, which can encourage fear about youth sport. Clinicians should ask where patients get concussion information and correct misunderstandings about risk and recovery.
methods: Narrative review combining a random sample of 20 Google News articles (from 25 selected from the first 100 search results, after excluding those behind subscriptions or cookie walls) published 2012-2022, with counts of key terms per article, and a summary of the literature on concussion epidemiology, youth sport participation, and athlete and parent knowledge.
findings: All 20 articles mentioned concussion, 13 mentioned CTE, 10 mentioned dementia, 9 mentioned retirement, and 'mild' or 'minor' described concussion in 7. The authors cite prior studies reporting that 15% to 45% of collegiate athletes choose not to report suspected concussion, and that accurate knowledge does not reliably lead to reporting. They also report that 96% of parents believed there are long-term effects of concussion, as cited from a prior survey.
limitations: The media sample was a random selection of 20 articles from one search engine's news results rather than a systematic search, and the literature summary is narrative with no quality grading. The authors do not measure how media changes athletes' or parents' behavior. The Discussion reports retirement in 50% of articles, while the Results and Table 1 give 9 of 20 (45%).
practicalImplications: Ask patients and athletes where they get concussion information, and correct common misconceptions about CTE, long-term risk and phrases such as 'ding' or 'bell rung'. Stress full recovery and return to baseline before full return to sport, and note the authors' view that complete removal from all sport is rarely necessary.
athleteDev: Staff should expect athletes and parents to arrive with fears from media coverage, which can affect participation and symptom reporting. Encourage prompt symptom reporting, since the review notes athletes often hide symptoms to avoid losing playing time.
rtp: The review supports a full recovery and return to baseline before full return to sport, but it does not set return-to-play criteria or timelines. Use it to frame education and symptom-reporting expectations, not as a clinical return-to-play protocol.

citation: Obana KK, Mueller JD, Zhong JR, et al. Targeting rule implementation decreases neck injuries in high school football: a national injury surveillance study. The Physician and Sportsmedicine 2021.
abstract: This retrospective NEISS analysis of high school football players aged 14-18 compared emergency department neck injuries before (2009-2013) and after (2015-2019) the 2014 NFHS targeting rule. Average yearly overall neck injuries fell from 5,278 to 3,481 and helmet-to-helmet injuries from 851 to 508; injuries with an unspecified mechanism also fell significantly, while the other named mechanisms did not change significantly.
tldr: Emergency department neck injuries among high school football players fell after the 2014 targeting rule, especially helmet-to-helmet injuries. The study cannot prove the rule caused the drop, but it supports continued enforcement of rules against targeting.
methods: Retrospective analysis of NEISS data for football-related neck injuries (product codes 1211 and 89) in players aged 14-18, January 2009 to December 2019. Narratives were reviewed to exclude non-organized or non-football injuries and to code mechanism, setting, loss of consciousness and injury type. Poisson regression and t-tests compared pre- and post-rule periods, with 2014 removed.
findings: Post-rule years had fewer neck injuries than pre-rule years (average 3,481 vs 5,278 per year, P=0.004), helmet-to-helmet injuries fell (508 vs 851, P=0.04), and unspecified-mechanism injuries fell (2,265 vs 3,546, P=0.002). Neck injuries were already declining across 2009-2019 (Poisson coefficient -0.0121 per year, P=0.0003), and the post-rule period remained significantly lower than the pre-rule reference (coefficient -0.3454, P<0.0001), with a rise again in 2019. Strains made up 59.8% of injuries, and 52.0% of injuries with a known setting occurred in competition vs 48.0% in practice.
limitations: Only emergency department visits are captured, so milder injuries managed by athletic trainers or clinics are missed, and 67% of injuries lacked mechanism detail. The before-and-after design cannot establish causation, and the Discussion's pre-rule average (5,287) differs slightly from the Results (5,278).
practicalImplications: Support enforcement of the targeting rule and limit helmet-to-helmet contact in practice as well as games, since neck injuries with a known setting occurred about equally in both. Treat the rule change as associated with fewer ED-treated neck injuries rather than proven to cause the drop.
athleteDev: The study does not measure performance or tackling technique. Its use for coaching staff is limited to supporting rules and practice plans that reduce helmet-to-helmet contact, where nearly half of these injuries occurred.
rtp: The study counts emergency department diagnoses and does not address return-to-play decisions after a neck injury, so it cannot guide clearance. Injuries handled only by athletic trainers or clinics are not captured.

citation: Cicchella A, He J. A systematic review of effects on ACL injury of soccer shoe outsoles, soccer playing field surfaces, and outsole-surface interface. Encyclopedia 2024;4:888-899.
abstract: This PRISMA systematic review of 58 papers examines how soccer shoe outsoles, playing surfaces and the outsole-surface interface relate to ACL injury. The authors identify outsole design, shear and rotational forces, artificial turf characteristics, surface aging and weather as the main biomechanical factors.
tldr: Boot stud design and playing surface both change traction, and traction is linked to forces on the knee, but the evidence does not show which combination lowers ACL injury risk. Staff should treat boots and pitch condition as exposures to monitor, not as proven fixes.
methods: PRISMA systematic review of PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and SPORTDiscus, with reference-list searching and an external expert check. Studies had to address soccer outsoles or playing surfaces and ACL injury mechanics, be peer-reviewed English articles in SCI-indexed journals, and not be narrative reviews. From 252 search results, 84 full texts were assessed and 58 papers were included.
findings: Outsole type made little difference to translational or rotational traction except for soft-ground and turf designs, and soft-ground boots gave the highest rotational traction on natural grass. Artificial turf produced greater rotational traction than natural grass in several experiments, and drier soil and higher air temperatures on natural grass were associated with higher traction. Cited epidemiology is mixed: several studies found similar overall injury rates on artificial and natural turf, one reported 30-50% higher lower-extremity injury rates on artificial turf, and none isolated ACL effects.
limitations: Epidemiological data cannot separate surface effects from weather, grass conditions and playing time, and many experiments are old, laboratory-based or cadaveric. The authors describe AXIS quality appraisal but report no quality results, found no comparative studies of hybrid surfaces, and note there is no universal index of cleat performance for ACL risk. The abstract's statement that ACL injuries 'dramatically increase' on artificial surfaces is not supported by the reviewed epidemiology.
practicalImplications: Consider boot stud type and pitch condition together, since outsole type, surface type, moisture and temperature all change traction. Field condition can drift with wear, and the authors note worn fields may not match FIFA standards, so checking pitch condition across a season is reasonable. The review does not identify any boot or surface that reduces ACL injury.
athleteDev: Track boot type and pitch condition (wear, moisture, temperature) as part of the injury-risk picture, since traction changes with each. The review does not show which combination lowers ACL risk, so use it to flag exposures rather than to prescribe equipment.
rtp: The review concerns ACL injury mechanisms and prevention, not return to play after an ACL injury, so it cannot guide clearance or return-to-play decisions.

citation: McClure M, Cooke B, Elphingstone J, et al. Orthopaedic consequences of modern gladiators: a systematic review of lower extremity musculoskeletal issues in retired NFL players. The Physician and Sportsmedicine 2022.
abstract: This PRISMA systematic review of nine studies with 16,593 retired NFL players examines lower extremity musculoskeletal outcomes after retirement. The authors report arthritis prevalence more than twice that of US males, osteoarthritis in about 37% of players, and higher hip and knee replacement rates than the general population, especially under age 50.
tldr: Retired NFL players have more arthritis and joint replacement than the general population, and these rates rise with repeated lower-extremity injuries. The evidence is mostly survey-based, so the size of the risk is approximate.
methods: PRISMA systematic review of CENTRAL, Scopus, Medline, PubMed, Embase and Google Scholar searched to February 2021. Two reviewers screened studies of retired NFL players with lower extremity injury, osteoarthritis or arthroplasty outcomes, and risk of bias was rated with the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Nine studies were included, and pooled prevalence and chi-square and relative risk comparisons were made against general-population data.
findings: Lower extremity injury prevalence ranged from 44% to 79% across studies, and pooled osteoarthritis prevalence (body-wide, not joint-specific) was about 37%. In one survey, arthritis, defined broadly to include rheumatoid arthritis and fibromyalgia, was 2.2 times as prevalent as in US males (95% CI 2.1-2.3), and players under 50 had 16.1 and 13.8 times higher TKA and THA risk, respectively, per the text. Osteoarthritis prevalence rose with lower-extremity injuries, for example from 26% with none to 44% with two or more in one study.
limitations: The authors note the included studies are level III-IV evidence with some lacking standardized protocols or adequate sample sizes, heterogeneous outcomes, that most osteoarthritis data are body-wide rather than lower-extremity specific, and that statistical pooling was only possible for arthroplasty and limited arthritis data. Only professional football was studied, and the authors suggest including high school, college and other contact sports.
practicalImplications: The authors suggest standardized musculoskeletal evaluation as players leave the league, weight management after retirement, and attention to knee ligament and ankle injury prevention. These recommendations follow from the link between repeated injuries, obesity and later osteoarthritis, but the review did not test any of these interventions directly.
athleteDev: For athletes with a long career ahead, the review suggests joint health is affected by repeated lower-extremity injuries, so reconditioning and injury prevention matter for life after sport. It does not give training prescriptions or performance measures.
rtp: The review covers long-term musculoskeletal outcomes after retirement, not return to play after an injury, so it cannot guide return-to-play decisions. It supports longer-term follow-up of joint health after athletes leave the sport.

citation: Kenneally-Dabrowski C, Brown NAT, Serpell BG, Perriman D, Spratford W, Sutherland A, et al. Hamstring musculotendon mechanics of prospectively injured elite rugby athletes. Research in Sports Medicine. 2023.
abstract: Two elite rugby union players had hamstring musculotendon mechanics estimated during pre-season high-speed running, before each later sustained a hamstring injury in competition. Measurements used motion capture, force plates, hamstring MRI and musculoskeletal modelling. The biceps femoris long head had the greatest strain of the hamstring muscles during late swing, and its force relative to muscle capacity was highest in one athlete and similar to semimembranosus in the other.
tldr: In two elite rugby players who later injured a hamstring, the biceps femoris long head showed the highest modelled strain during late swing sprinting. This is a hypothesis-generating case series, not proof of an injury mechanism.
methods: Two elite male rugby union players completed three maximal 50 m sprints during pre-season on a 20-camera motion capture system with force plates, and hamstring MRI was taken within 48 hours. Muscle volumes gave physiological cross-sectional area, and an OpenSim model with computed muscle control estimated musculotendon strain, force and power during late swing.
findings: Peak strain was greatest in the biceps femoris long head in both athletes (7.07% and 9.31%). Peak force relative to body mass was greatest in semimembranosus. Relative to muscle capacity, biceps femoris long head force was highest in Athlete A (120.8 N/PCSA) and similar to semimembranosus in Athlete B. Injuries occurred 139 and 192 days after testing, and Athlete A's injury was in the right biceps femoris long head.
limitations: Two athletes only, with no control group, and the model used generic rather than subject-specific muscle inputs. Athlete A had three prior left hamstring injuries, and Athlete B's injury was not assessed by MRI. The abstract says biceps femoris long head had the greatest force relative to capacity, but Table 1 shows semimembranosus slightly higher in Athlete B (110.89 vs 109.38 N/PCSA).
practicalImplications: Staff can treat high late-swing biceps femoris long head load and strain as a plausible hypothesis to test in larger samples. The paper does not support using this modelling to screen individual athletes, since it requires MRI and laboratory equipment and was not tested as a predictor of injury.
athleteDev: The findings describe how hamstring loads may be distributed during fast running in two athletes. They do not show that any sprint training change reduces hamstring injury risk, so they should not be used to set training targets.
rtp: This study cannot guide return to sport decisions. It reports pre-injury measurements in two athletes and does not test rehabilitation, running load progression or readiness after injury.

citation: Kelly S, Polglass G, Giakoumis M, Pollock N, Shaw JW. Calf muscle injury in elite athletics: an 8-season prospective cohort study. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2025.
abstract: Indirect calf muscle injury was recorded prospectively over eight seasons in 201 elite track and field athletes (616 athlete-seasons). There were 85 injuries, a third of them severe, with the soleus most often affected. The raw incidence was 0.14 medical-attention injuries per athlete-season, and older age and previous lower-limb injury were associated with higher incidence, while sex was not.
tldr: About one in nine elite track and field athletes had a calf muscle injury each season, and soleus injuries carried the largest time-loss burden and recurrence. Older athletes and those with previous lower-limb injury had higher rates, though these are associations from an observational study.
methods: Prospective observational study of British Athletics World Class Programme athletes from December 2011 to November 2019, with injuries diagnosed clinically and recorded in an athlete management system. Injuries were classified by time loss, severity, muscle and onset. Poisson regression models examined age, sex and event group, and the results also report the count of previous lower-limb injuries.
findings: There were 85 calf injuries, 77 of them time-loss, and 52 involved the soleus (61%). The incidence was 0.14 medical-attention injuries per athlete-season (95% CI 0.11 to 0.17), with male and female rates not significantly different. Each additional year of age was associated with 1.09 times the medical-attention incidence (p = .0025) and 1.11 times the time-loss incidence (p = .005). Each previous lower-limb injury was associated with 1.21 times the medical-attention incidence (p = .025), but not time-loss incidence. Mean time loss was 29 days, 33% of injuries were severe, and 14 injuries were recurrences.
limitations: Exposure was measured per athlete-season, not per hour, and injuries were not graded with BAMIC or re-examined by imaging for all cases. Power was low for sex (about 18%), and the previous-injury effect was not significant for time-loss, although the abstract describes a significant effect for previous lower-limb injury without this distinction. Only 85 injuries were recorded, which limits between-event comparisons.
practicalImplications: Staff working with elite track and field athletes can expect calf injury to be common, with soleus injuries the most frequent and most disruptive. Injury counts peaked in April, ahead of the summer season, and the authors suggest increasing prevention efforts before that period, although no prevention strategy was tested. Older athletes and those with previous lower-limb injury may merit closer attention, but the study does not show that monitoring reduces injury.
athleteDev: Calf injuries in this cohort were often severe, with a mean time loss of 29 days, and counts peaked in April before the summer competition season. The study describes injury patterns by event group, not the effect of any training change, so it does not show which programme changes would lower calf injury risk.
rtp: The study can inform expected severity and recurrence, with recurrences occurring a mean of 364 days after the index injury and a median of 214 days. It does not test rehabilitation or return-to-training criteria, so these timings should not be used as a fixed return-to-sport timeline.

citation: Bramah C, Rhodes S, Clarke-Cornwell A, Dos'Santos T. Sprint running mechanics are associated with hamstring strain injury: a 6-month prospective cohort study of 126 elite male footballers. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2025.
abstract: This prospective cohort study scored sprint running mechanics in 126 professional male footballers with the Sprint Mechanics Assessment Score (S-MAS), a video-based screen, and followed them for six months. Higher S-MAS scores were found in players with previous sprint-related hamstring injury and in players who later sustained one. After adjusting for age and previous injury, each one-point increase in S-MAS was associated with a 33% higher rate of new sprint-related hamstring injury.
tldr: Players with poorer sprint mechanics on a video-based screen had a higher rate of later sprint-related hamstring injury. The screen is quick to use, but its accuracy for predicting injury is modest, so it should be one part of a wider screening process.
methods: Players from eight English Football League clubs were filmed during two maximal 35 m sprints at 240 fps, in pre-season or in-season. A single blinded biomechanist scored each sprint with the 12-item S-MAS. Clubs reported new hamstring injuries monthly for six months, confirmed by MRI. Poisson regression estimated incidence rate ratios, adjusted for age and previous hamstring injury, and ROC analysis chose the cut-off.
findings: In the retrospective analysis of 118 players, those with a previous sprint-related hamstring injury had higher S-MAS scores (median 6 vs 5, p = 0.007). In the prospective analysis of 92 players, 14 had a sprint-related injury, with median S-MAS 6 vs 4 (p = 0.006). The unadjusted IRR was 1.38 per point (95% CI 1.06 to 1.79), and the adjusted IRR was 1.33 (95% CI 1.01 to 1.76, p = 0.044). A cut-off of 5.5 gave sensitivity 78.6%, specificity 65.4% and AUC 0.732. The categorical IRR was 2.8 (95% CI 0.94 to 8.35, p = 0.065), which was not significant.
limitations: The S-MAS was not validated against 3D motion capture and was scored by one experienced rater. Training and match load were not monitored, and players with other severe non-hamstring time loss were removed from the uninjured group. The power calculation used the same data as the analysis, and seven players were lost to follow-up. Only male players were studied, and players were followed for different parts of the season.
practicalImplications: Practitioners can use the S-MAS from routine sprint video to flag players whose sprint mechanics may be suboptimal, particularly those with a previous hamstring injury. Because sensitivity and specificity are modest, a flagged score should prompt a wider review of strength, load and injury history rather than a decision on its own.
athleteDev: The S-MAS is a video-based sprint technique screen that could be used alongside performance testing to track running mechanics across a season. The study does not show that changing sprint technique reduces hamstring injury, so it should not be used as a stand-alone target for training changes.
rtp: The study does not test return to sport. It suggests that sprint mechanics may be neglected in rehabilitation after a previous sprint-related hamstring injury, but it does not show that retraining mechanics restores readiness or lowers reinjury risk.

citation: Vermeulen R, Whiteley R, van der Made AD, van Dyk N, Almusa E, Geertsema C, et al. Early versus delayed lengthening exercises for acute hamstring injury in male athletes: a randomised controlled clinical trial. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2022.
abstract: Ninety male athletes with an MRI-confirmed acute hamstring injury were randomised to add lengthening (eccentric) exercises either on day 1 of a standard rehabilitation programme or after they could run at 70% of maximal speed. Time to return to sport did not differ between the groups (adjusted HR 0.95, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.60), and neither did reinjury rates over 12 months. Early introduction did not shorten return to sport or lower reinjury risk, though the median difference of 8 days favoured the early group.
tldr: Starting lengthening exercises on day 1 rather than after about 70% running speed did not change return-to-sport time or reinjury rates in male athletes with acute hamstring injuries. The median return was about 8 days sooner in the early group, but this was not statistically significant.
methods: Single-centre, parallel-group, randomised superiority trial at the Aspetar sports medicine hospital in Qatar, with blinded assessors and a blinded statistician. Both groups followed the same six-stage criteria-based programme, differing only in when Askling lengthening exercises began. Primary outcome was days to full training or match play, analysed by Cox regression (intention to treat). Reinjury was followed by telephone at 2, 6 and 12 months.
findings: Median return to sport was 23 days (IQR 16 to 35) in the early group and 33 days (IQR 23 to 40) in the delayed group. The unadjusted HR was 1.15 (95% CI 0.72 to 1.84, p=0.57), and the adjusted HR was 0.95 (95% CI 0.56 to 1.60, p=0.84). Reinjury within 2 months was 8.8% early and 8.3% delayed, with no significant differences at 2 to 6 or 6 to 12 months. Eccentric strength at 60 degrees per second was higher in the early group at return to sport (198 Nm vs 182 Nm, p=0.029), but no other outcome differed.
limitations: Loss to follow-up was 19% against a planned 10%, handled by a consensus-based return-to-sport date that was not in the protocol, and reinjury data were missing for 20% to 28% of participants. The trial was sized for a 6.6-day difference and the authors note it is potentially underpowered, and treating clinicians could not be blinded to group. The Results text gives the 2-month reinjury percentages in reverse compared with Table 3 (Table 3: early 8.8%, delayed 8.3%).
practicalImplications: Starting lengthening exercises on day 1 of rehabilitation after a grade I or II hamstring strain in men produced similar reinjury rates to a delayed start, but reinjuries were few and the confidence intervals were wide (2-month OR 0.94, 95% CI 0.18 to 5.0). The trial did not show a significant reduction in time to return, although the 8-day median difference and possible underpowering mean a benefit cannot be ruled out, so timing can rest on the individual clinical picture.
athleteDev: Performance staff may note that the early group had higher eccentric knee flexor strength at return to sport, but this was a secondary outcome in a small trial and was not the focus of the study. It does not show that early lengthening improves sprint or running performance.
rtp: This trial directly informs return-to-sport planning for male athletes with MRI-confirmed grade I or II acute hamstring injury. Starting lengthening exercises early did not significantly change time to return or reinjury rate, so it should not be used to predict a specific return date. It does not apply to women, grade III injuries or injuries without MRI confirmation.

citation: Webster KE, Hewett TE. What is the evidence for and validity of return-to-sport testing after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction surgery? A systematic review and meta-analysis. Sports Medicine. 2019;49:917-929.
abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) return-to-sport (RTS) test batteries. Across 18 studies, only 23% of patients passed the batteries before returning to sport. Passing was linked to lower graft rupture risk and higher contralateral ACL injury risk, while the overall ACL re-injury risk was not significantly different. The authors conclude the evidence on the validity of current batteries is equivocal.
tldr: Only about one in four patients pass ACL return-to-sport test batteries, and passing was not associated with a clear reduction in overall ACL re-injury risk. Passing was associated with lower graft rupture risk but higher contralateral ACL injury risk, so the batteries cannot yet be relied on as a safety clearance.
methods: Five databases (PubMed, MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL and SPORTDiscus) were searched to May 2018, following PRISMA. Studies of ACLR patients that reported how many passed a full RTS battery were included. Pooled pass rates used random-effects proportion meta-analysis, and subsequent injury was analysed with risk ratio meta-analysis. Overlapping patient groups were excluded from the same pooled analysis.
findings: Before return to sport, 23% of patients passed RTS batteries (95% CI 8% to 43%, I2 97.5%, eight studies, 876 patients). After return to strenuous sport, the pass rate was also 23% (95% CI 18% to 29%, three studies). For any knee injury, RR was 0.28 (95% CI 0.04 to 0.94, p = 0.09, two studies). For any ACL injury, RR was 0.80 (95% CI 0.27 to 2.3, p = 0.7, five studies). Graft rupture RR was 0.40 (95% CI 0.23 to 0.69, p < 0.001), and contralateral ACL injury RR was 3.35 (95% CI 1.52 to 7.37, p = 0.003). One study found that patients who passed at 6 months were more likely to have returned to sport at 12 months (81% vs 44%).
limitations: Only one included study assessed return to sport and only five reported subsequent injury, with small samples and broad inclusion criteria (age limits typically 14 to 50 years, mixed graft types and sports) and no control of confounders or exposure. RTS definitions and follow-up varied, and overlapping patient groups were handled by excluding some studies from the same pooled analysis. For any knee injury the Results report RR 0.28 (95% CI 0.04 to 0.94, p = 0.09), but the Discussion describes the interval as a 93% reduction to a 21% increase, so the printed CI is inconsistent with the non-significant result.
practicalImplications: Staff should not present a passed test battery as proof that ACL re-injury risk has fallen, because the pooled evidence does not show a reduction in overall ACL injury. Because only 23% of patients pass batteries, most reconstructed athletes will fail some criteria, and staff should decide on return using the wider clinical picture. Monitoring both knees is advisable, given the signal of higher contralateral ACL injury among those who passed.
athleteDev: Performance staff may use test results to track rehabilitation progress, but a pass on a battery does not confirm that an athlete is ready for high performance demands. The one study that linked passing to later return to sport is a single observational report, so it should not be used to set performance targets.
rtp: This review is directly relevant to return-to-sport decisions after ACL reconstruction, but it shows that test batteries have uncertain validity for deciding safe return. Passing a battery was not associated with a lower overall ACL injury risk and was associated with a higher contralateral injury risk, so it should not by itself clear an athlete to return. The review does not define a validated pass rule or cut-off, so it cannot say which battery or threshold makes return safe.

citation: Lapica HE, Burgmeier RJ, Ravich JW, Schurhoff MR, Vargas LA. Return to Play After Rotator Cuff Tear in National Football League Athletes. JSES International. 2023.
abstract: Publicly available data were used to identify 29 NFL players (mean age 27.4 years) who sustained a rotator cuff tear between 2000 and 2019. Return to play (RTP) was defined as being on an active roster for at least one regular-season game after treatment. Twenty-three of 29 players (79%) returned, after an average of 198 days. Players who returned were younger and had shorter pre-injury careers, and return rates did not differ between operative and nonoperative treatment.
tldr: About 8 in 10 NFL players in this small series returned to play after a rotator cuff tear. Players who did not return were older (mean 30.3 vs 26.7 years) and had longer careers, and return rates did not differ between surgery and nonoperative care in this cohort of 29.
methods: Retrospective case series using publicly available NFL injury reports, play-by-play documents, and player statistics. A position-specific performance score was normalized per game and compared before and after injury, with each player serving as his own control. Groups were compared with Mann-Whitney U tests and binomial proportions with 95% confidence limits.
findings: Twenty-three of 29 players (79%; 95% CI 59.2% to 89.4%) returned to play, after an average of 198.4 days, and returners had a mean performance score ratio of 1.0. Non-returners were older (30.3 vs 26.7 years, p=0.02), 4 of the 6 were over 30, and they had longer pre-injury careers (7.5 vs 4.0 years, p=0.01). Return rates did not differ between operative (19/24) and nonoperative (4/5) players (p=0.95), and time to return was 259.5 days after surgery compared with immediate return in the nonoperative group (p=0.001).
limitations: Data came from third-party public sources, not medical records, so diagnosis, tear size and pattern, and surgical details are unknown. The authors state the sample is likely underpowered, and the reasons for not returning could not be determined. The performance score excludes offensive linemen. Table IV lists a career length of 23.0 years for players at other positions, which conflicts with the text (about 3 years) and is likely a reporting error. The operative vs nonoperative return-rate P value is .95 in the Results text but .97 in Table II.
practicalImplications: For NFL players with a rotator cuff tear, this series supports counseling around a return rate of about 8 in 10. Older, veteran players returned less often, so the authors advise counseling players over 30 about that risk. Treatment type did not separate outcomes here, but the sample is too small to choose between surgery and nonoperative care.
athleteDev: This study describes career outcomes after injury rather than training or testing. It is useful for roster and career-stage planning for veteran players, since older players returned less often, but it does not inform training prescription.
rtp: Use this study to counsel NFL players after a rotator cuff tear: about 79% returned in this series, and those who did not return were older on average, with 4 of 6 over 30. It cannot be used to choose between surgery and nonoperative care, predict an individual player's recovery, or estimate outcomes in non-NFL athletes.

citation: Okoroha KR, Taylor KA, Marshall NE, Keller RA, Fidai M, Mahan MC, et al. Return to play after shoulder instability in National Football League athletes. J Shoulder Elbow Surg. 2018;27:17-22.
abstract: Eighty-three NFL players who sustained an in-season shoulder instability event between 2006 and 2014 were compared with matched control players who had no such injury. Return to play (RTP), time to RTP, recurrent instability, games played and treatment type were recorded. Overall, 92.8% of players returned to regular-season play. Players who had surgical repair had fewer recurrent instability events and a longer interval before any recurrence, and RTP games per season fell after injury.
tldr: Most NFL players with an in-season shoulder instability event returned to play. Players who had surgery had fewer repeat episodes, but they missed much more time before returning.
methods: Retrospective cohort study using publicly available internet injury reports verified against NFL.com. Players were included if they had been drafted and had played at least one NFL game before the instability event. Injured players were compared with age-, size-, position- and experience-matched NFL controls. Categorical variables were compared with chi-square or Fisher exact tests and continuous variables with t tests or Wilcoxon rank sum tests.
findings: Of 83 players, 77 (92.8%) returned to regular-season play, and 36 of these 77 (46%) had a recurrent instability event. Among those who returned, the surgical group had a lower recurrence rate (26% vs 55%, P=.021) and a longer median recurrence-free interval (14.7 vs 2.5 weeks, P=.050). Median time to RTP was 39.3 weeks operatively and 2.3 weeks nonoperatively (P<.001), and nonoperative subluxations returned faster than dislocations (0.0 vs 3.0 weeks, P=.029) but recurred sooner (1.5 vs 5.0 weeks, P=.044). Returners played about 1.5 fewer games per season than before injury (P=.014), but games, seasons and Pro Bowls after return did not differ from matched controls.
limitations: The data came from third-party internet sources, which may contain inaccuracies and may miss some players. Treatment was not randomized, and players were more likely to have surgery if injured later in the season or on the right arm; instability direction and surgical procedure were not recorded. The abstract and conclusion say subluxations are more likely to recur, but the Results report no difference in recurrence incidence between dislocations and subluxations, only a shorter time to recurrence. The abstract reports 92% and 47%, while the Results give 92.8% and 46%; the Results figures are used here.
practicalImplications: For NFL players with an in-season shoulder instability event, the study supports counseling that most will return, with a high chance of repeat instability. Surgery was associated with fewer repeat episodes and longer intervals, but it also meant a much longer time to return. The drop in games per season after return did not differ from matched controls, so it should not be presented as an injury-specific loss.
athleteDev: The study tracks games played per season before and after instability, but post-return games and seasons did not differ from matched controls. Its career and game-count findings are descriptive and do not provide training or performance prescriptions.
rtp: Use this study to set return expectations for NFL players after a shoulder instability event: most returned, but nearly half of returners had a recurrence. It cannot establish that surgery prevents recurrence in an individual athlete, and it does not provide clearance criteria or return timelines for non-NFL athletes.

citation: Manoharan A, Barton D, Khwaja A, Latt LD. Return to Play Rates in NFL Wide Receivers and Running Backs After ACL Reconstruction: An Updated Analysis. Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2021;9(1):2325967120974743.
abstract: Publicly available NFL injury reports from the 2009-2010 to 2015-2016 seasons were used to identify running backs (RBs) and wide receivers (WRs) who underwent ACL reconstruction. Return to play (RTP) was defined as playing at least one NFL game after reconstruction. Overall, 61.8% of players returned, at a mean of 13.6 months. The RTP group had more career games before injury, and WRs who returned had decreased performance after reconstruction compared with matched uninjured controls.
tldr: Fewer than two-thirds of NFL running backs and wide receivers returned to a game after ACL reconstruction in this 2009 to 2016 window. Wide receivers who returned produced less after injury than matched uninjured controls.
methods: Retrospective descriptive study using publicly available injury reports, team rosters, and statistics sites. RTP was defined as playing at least one NFL game after reconstruction. Pre- and postinjury position-specific statistics were compared with paired t tests, and returners were compared with matched controls (same position, same team where possible, with 4 healthy seasons) using unpaired t tests.
findings: Of 76 players, 47 (61.8%) returned to play (64.5% of RBs and 60% of WRs), at a mean of 13.6 months (median 12 months for RBs, whose mean was inflated by one 47-month return). RTP players had more career games before injury (72.2 vs 40.1, P=.0128). In the performance analysis (36 returners), WR receptions per game fell from 2.86 to 1.95 (P=.0013), yards per reception from 12.71 to 9.92 (P=.0143) and receiving touchdowns per season from 3.71 to 2.12 (P=.0011), and all three were lower than controls after injury. RB yards per rush fell from 4.45 to 3.42 (P=.0044), but no RB measure differed from controls after injury.
limitations: The study is retrospective and based on public sources, so concomitant meniscal or cartilage injuries, surgical technique and rehabilitation protocols are unknown. The control group was designed to match opportunity, not to represent a true intervention. The Results and Discussion describe RB performance as a non-significant drop, but Table 2 reports a significant fall in yards per rush (P=.0044), so the table values are used here. Reasons for not returning are not known, and results apply only to RBs and WRs with successful return.
practicalImplications: Counseling for RBs and WRs after ACL reconstruction should allow for a return rate near 6 in 10 and a recovery period of about 12 to 14 months. Wide receivers who return may have lower production, so expectations for their post-injury output should be realistic. The RB decline in yards per rush is a measured finding, but the lack of change in rushes per game limits what can be concluded about overall role.
athleteDev: Performance staff can use the before-and-after statistics to set realistic expectations for production in the season after an ACL reconstruction, especially for wide receivers. The study measures game statistics, not physical capacity, so it does not guide training or testing.
rtp: Use this study to counsel NFL running backs and wide receivers about return rates (about 62%) and typical timelines (12 to 14 months) after ACL reconstruction. Timelines partly reflect the season calendar rather than readiness alone, and the study cannot predict an individual player's return, define clearance criteria, or be applied to other positions or leagues.

citation: Kruse RC, Volfson E. Platelet-Poor Plasma for the Treatment of Acute Hamstring Muscle Injuries in Collegiate Football Athletes: A Cohort Study. Clinical Journal of Sport Medicine. 2024.
abstract: Twenty consecutive collegiate football players with an acute hamstring injury treated with platelet-poor plasma (PPP) injection from 2021 to 2022 were reviewed. Players returned to full unrestricted sport after an average of 29.4 days, pain improved significantly by 2 weeks after injection, and no recurrent injuries were seen within 12 months. The authors conclude that PPP may be a safe and effective treatment that could expedite return to play.
tldr: In 20 collegiate football players with grade 3b hamstring strains, a platelet-poor plasma injection was followed by return to sport in about a month and no recurrences in a year. Without a comparison group, this is an early, uncontrolled signal rather than proof of benefit.
methods: Retrospective cohort study of 20 consecutive male Division I or III football players with an acute hamstring injury confirmed by ultrasound and graded with a modified BAMIC system. Each player received an ultrasound-guided PPP injection and a standard rehabilitation progression. Outcomes were days to full unrestricted sport, VAS pain, duration of postinjection pain, and recurrence within 12 months, analyzed with descriptive statistics and a Wilcoxon signed-rank test.
findings: All 20 patients had grade 3b injuries, most often of the semitendinosus (65%). Players returned to full unrestricted sport after a mean of 29.4 days (SD 7.2) following injection, or 34.6 days after the original injury. VAS pain fell from 4.8 before injection to 0.7 at 2 weeks (change 4.1, P<.001) and to 0.0 at 6 weeks. No recurrent injuries were recorded within 12 months, and there were no complications beyond soreness.
limitations: The study is a small, uncontrolled, single-physician series with only grade 3b injuries, male football players and no comparison group. The abstract reports the 29.4-day return as days postinjury, but the Discussion clarifies that 29.4 days is measured from the injection and 34.6 days from the original injury. The article type is labeled Case Report while the design is a retrospective cohort. The authors state that the small sample may not reflect the true recurrence risk. The single treating physician reports a consulting relationship with Lipogems.
practicalImplications: This series alone does not justify adopting PPP injections for grade 3b hamstring strains, because it has no comparison group and cannot separate the injection from rehabilitation and natural healing. The return times and absence of recurrence can be cited as an early, uncontrolled signal in clinical discussions, alongside the authors' call for comparative trials. Findings do not extend to lower-grade injuries, women or non-football athletes.
athleteDev: This study concerns injury treatment rather than training or performance. It does not provide training prescriptions or performance benchmarks, but it may help performance and medical staff discuss expected time away from sport after a grade 3b hamstring strain.
rtp: Use this study to discuss expected return timelines for male collegiate football players with a grade 3b hamstring strain treated with PPP, which were about 29 days after injection in this series. It cannot establish that PPP shortens return to play compared with standard care, and it should not be applied to lower-grade injuries, female athletes or other sports.

citation: Harada GK, Rugg CM, Arshi A, Vail J, Hame SL. Multiple Concussions Increase Odds and Rate of Lower Extremity Injury in National Collegiate Athletic Association Athletes After Return to Play. American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2019.
abstract: From 2001 to 2016, 48 NCAA Division I athletes with multiple concussions were matched by sex, sport, position and games played to athletes with a single concussion and to athletes with no concussion history. Lower extremity injury after return to play was more frequent in the multiple-concussion group (75% vs 52% and 56%), and multiple-concussion athletes had higher odds of injury (OR 3.00 vs single concussion; OR 1.66 vs no concussion) and a shorter time to injury. No difference was found between the single-concussion and no-concussion groups.
tldr: Among male collegiate athletes, those with repeated concussions were more likely to be injured in the lower extremity after return to play, and sooner, than matched athletes with one or no concussions. Whether this reflects neuromuscular deficits or player behavior is unresolved.
methods: Retrospective matched cohort study using sports injury records from one NCAA Division I institution.
