practicalImplications: Sports dietitians can check that athletes are not chronically low in energy availability, which the review identifies as a major bone injury risk, and can plan calorie cycling around competition. During an injury, the review supports keeping protein high and avoiding large energy cuts, with supplements such as vitamin D used when a deficiency is confirmed and tested for contamination.
athleteDev: Relevant to performance staff who plan training and competition fuelling. The review links low energy availability and nutrient gaps to bone injury risk, but it does not show that any nutrition strategy improves sprint, jump or throw performance.
rtp: Partly relevant to return to sport. The review offers guidance on protein, energy and micronutrient intake during recovery from muscle, bone, tendon and ligament injury, but the authors state that the evidence for speeding recovery is indirect and cannot set a return-to-sport timeline or clearance criteria.

citation: Owen JA, Fortes MB, Ur Rahman S, Jibani M, Walsh NP, Oliver SJ. Hydration marker diagnostic accuracy to identify mild intracellular and extracellular dehydration. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2019;29(6):604-611.
abstract: In 15 young healthy men, the diagnostic accuracy of 15 hydration markers was tested after euhydration, mild intracellular dehydration from exercise and fluid restriction, and mild extracellular dehydration from diuretic use. Thirst on a 0-9 scale and urine osmolality identified both dehydration types, and a thirst score of 4 or more was the only threshold that worked for both.
tldr: A simple 0-9 thirst rating, with a cut-off of 4 or more, detected about 2% body mass loss in young men with reasonable accuracy in both exercise-type and diuretic-type dehydration. It is a practical screen, but it needs testing in women, older adults and other conditions before wider use.
methods: Fifteen healthy men completed three randomised 48-hour trials: euhydration, intracellular dehydration (exercise and water restriction to 2 ml per kg per day), and extracellular dehydration (furosemide with a 4-hour diuresis). Fifteen hydration markers were measured, including thirst, urine, saliva, heart rate variability, postural changes and plasma osmolality. Accuracy was assessed with ROC-AUC and Youden-derived thresholds, with body mass change as the reference.
findings: Body mass fell by 1.9% after intracellular dehydration and 2.0% after extracellular dehydration. Thirst 0-9 had ROC-AUC 0.97 for intracellular and 0.78 for extracellular dehydration, and urine osmolality had 0.99 and 0.81 (Table 3), with a thirst threshold of 4 or more giving sensitivity 99% and specificity 87% for intracellular, and 71% and 87% for extracellular dehydration (Table 4). Tear osmolality, supine blood pressure and supine heart rate did not discriminate either type.
limitations: The abstract reports sensitivity of 100% for the thirst threshold, but Table 4 shows 99% for intracellular dehydration. The sample was 15 young men only, dehydration was induced in a controlled laboratory, and thresholds were not tested on separate participants. The extracellular dehydration accuracy for thirst (ROC-AUC 0.78, lower confidence bound 0.59) is moderate, and the authors note that thirst may differ in women, older adults and people taking medications.
practicalImplications: Practitioners working with young men in similar conditions can ask for a 0-9 thirst rating, with 4 or more suggesting mild dehydration needing fluid intake, as the authors recommend thirst as the initial screen. Urine osmolality also discriminated both types, but its thresholds differed by dehydration type (above 595 mOsm/kg for intracellular, above 341 mOsm/kg for extracellular), and urine specific gravity and colour identified only intracellular dehydration. Do not apply the thirst threshold to women, older athletes or heat exposure without further validation.
athleteDev: Relevant to performance staff because the paper frames mild dehydration as the level at which performance is affected, and it offers a low-cost fluid check. The study did not measure any performance outcome, so it cannot show that correcting the thirst-flagged deficit improves performance.
rtp: Cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. The participants were healthy men without injury, and the study did not assess rehabilitation, injury or recovery outcomes.

citation: Margolis LM, Allen JT, Hatch-McChesney A, Pasiakos SM. Coingestion of carbohydrate and protein on muscle glycogen synthesis after exercise: a meta-analysis. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2021;53(2):384-393.
abstract: This meta-analysis of 20 crossover studies compared carbohydrate-plus-protein with carbohydrate alone for muscle glycogen replenishment after exercise. Overall, the combined drink did not significantly increase glycogen synthesis, but it did when it provided more total energy than carbohydrate alone.
tldr: Adding protein to a carbohydrate recovery drink improved muscle glycogen replenishment only when it added energy on top of the carbohydrate. When total energy was matched, protein did not add a measurable benefit to glycogen synthesis.
methods: Crossover trials comparing carbohydrate-plus-protein with carbohydrate alone for post-exercise glycogen synthesis were identified from PubMed and the Cochrane Library, with a PRISMA-based search. Twenty studies with 23 intervention groups were pooled using Hedges' g and random effects. Subgroup analyses split studies by isocaloric versus non-isocaloric designs and by high versus low relative carbohydrate intake (median 0.8 g per kg per hour).
findings: The overall effect was 0.13 (95% CI -0.04 to 0.29), not significant. Non-isocaloric comparisons showed a positive effect of 0.26 (95% CI 0.04 to 0.49), while isocaloric comparisons showed -0.05 (95% CI -0.23 to 0.13). In the isocaloric studies, carbohydrate-plus-protein gave similar glycogen synthesis to carbohydrate alone despite about 30% less carbohydrate (mean 0.63 vs 0.86 g per kg per hour, plus 0.22 g per kg per hour of protein, Table 3).
limitations: The overall heterogeneity was substantial (I2 = 71%), and publication bias was detected (P = 0.03), driven by positive studies in the non-isocaloric group. The sample was 158 men and 18 women in laboratory studies, and a correlation of 0.80 was imputed for all studies. The abstract reports the high-carbohydrate subgroup CI as -0.11 to 0.22, but the Results text gives -0.11 to 0.25.
practicalImplications: Adding protein on top of a fixed carbohydrate dose increased glycogen synthesis in the pooled non-isocaloric studies, while replacing part of the carbohydrate with protein at equal energy gave similar glycogen synthesis to carbohydrate alone. The authors suggest about 0.9 g per kg per hour of carbohydrate plus 0.3 g per kg per hour of protein as an energy-matched alternative to 1.2 g per kg per hour of carbohydrate, which also supports muscle protein synthesis, but this specific split was not tested as a subgroup.
athleteDev: Relevant to performance staff who plan fuelling between sessions, especially for athletes with two sessions a day. The study measures glycogen synthesis, not performance, and the authors note that one study reported a performance increase while systematic reviews found no overall performance benefit.
rtp: Cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. The studies used healthy trained or untrained adults in laboratory exercise, not injured athletes, and did not assess rehabilitation, tissue healing or return-to-play outcomes.

citation: Tam R, Beck KL, Manore MM, Gifford J, Flood VM, O'Connor H. Effectiveness of education interventions designed to improve nutrition knowledge in athletes: a systematic review. Sports Med. 2019.
abstract: This systematic review of 32 studies tested nutrition education interventions aimed at improving nutrition knowledge in athletes. Most interventions reported significant knowledge gains, but the wide range of knowledge tools and the predominance of face-to-face delivery prevented identification of the most effective method or dose.
tldr: Nutrition education programmes for athletes usually raise nutrition knowledge scores, but the included studies are short and mostly used tools with limited validation. The review cannot say which teaching method or how much contact time works best.
methods: Six databases were searched up to June 2019, with hand searching of reference lists, for original human research in athletes of any level that used a scored knowledge test before and after an education intervention. Study quality was rated with a modified Downs and Black checklist, and Hedges' g effect sizes were calculated. A meta-analysis was not conducted because of variation in tools and interventions.
findings: Thirteen RCTs (weighted mean change +19.2% for intervention groups, ES 2.9, versus +2.2% for controls) and 19 single-arm studies (+12.7%, ES 0.88) reported knowledge change, with 30 of 35 interventions (85.7%) showing significant gains. Average quality was 17 of 28 for RCTs and 11.7 of 22 for single-arm studies. Most interventions were face-to-face and under 5 hours of total contact time.
limitations: The authors state that only 15.6% of studies used well-validated knowledge tools, and most were author-designed or modified. Only two studies assessed knowledge retention, no meta-analysis was performed, and individual effect sizes varied widely (one RCT reported 17.1), so the 1.72 average is a descriptive figure rather than a pooled estimate. Searching and screening were done by one author, and no RCT blinded participants, facilitators or outcome assessment.
practicalImplications: Short group education programmes can produce measurable knowledge gains in athletes. The authors recommend establishing the validity and reliability of the knowledge test before running a programme, and handouts alone produced smaller gains than presentations or cooking classes in the two studies that compared them. Technology-based delivery had lower attrition in the four studies that used it, so it may be worth piloting, but it is not yet shown to be superior.
athleteDev: Relevant to performance staff who run nutrition education as part of athlete development. The review shows knowledge gains, but it does not measure dietary behaviour, body composition or performance, so it cannot show that education improves performance.
rtp: Cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. The review did not examine injured athletes or rehabilitation outcomes.

citation: Elosegui S, López-Seoane J, Martínez-Ferrán M, Pareja-Galeano H. Interaction between caffeine and creatine when used as concurrent ergogenic supplements: a systematic review. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2022. Ahead of print.
abstract: This systematic review of 10 placebo-controlled trials examined whether caffeine and creatine interact when taken together to enhance exercise performance, and what doses allow their combined use. Acute caffeine after creatine loading did not impair the benefit, while chronic combined use gave mixed results across studies.
tldr: Taking caffeine on the day of a session after a creatine loading phase did not appear to reduce creatine's benefits. Daily caffeine during creatine loading gave conflicting results, and the review suggests it could interfere.
methods: A systematic search of PubMed, Web of Science, MEDLINE, CINAHL and SPORTDiscus up to November 2021 followed PRISMA. Included studies were randomised, placebo-controlled trials in healthy adults that gave creatine and caffeine together and measured performance. Risk of bias was rated with the Cochrane tool.
findings: Three studies found that creatine loading before an acute caffeine dose did not interfere with caffeine's effect. For chronic use, one study reported synergy, two reported that caffeine interfered with creatine's effect on muscle relaxation time or torque, and three showed no interaction. The authors suggest that creatine loading does not seem to affect acute caffeine effects, but chronic caffeine during creatine loading could interfere with creatine's benefit.
limitations: The authors describe small sample sizes, few randomised and blinded trials, heterogeneous supplementation protocols and exercise tests, and gastrointestinal discomfort reported in some trials. The included trials were mostly male, aged 18 to 25, and conducted in laboratories.
practicalImplications: In the three trials that gave 5 to 6 mg per kg of caffeine about an hour before exercise after a creatine loading phase, caffeine's ergogenic effects were preserved. Daily caffeine during creatine loading is the scenario with conflicting results, including blunted dynamic torque and relaxation-time benefits, so staff may prefer to avoid it until better evidence is available. Gastrointestinal tolerance should be monitored when both are used.
athleteDev: Relevant to performance staff who advise athletes on combined supplements. The review reports performance outcomes such as time to exhaustion, sprint power and torque, but the evidence is small and mixed, so it cannot promise a performance gain from combining the two.
rtp: Cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. The review excluded injured or ill participants and did not assess rehabilitation, tissue healing or return-to-play outcomes.

citation: Möller GB, Goulart MJVC, Nicoletto BB, Alves FD, Schneider CD. Supplementation of Probiotics and Its Effects on Physically Active Individuals and Athletes: Systematic Review. International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism. 2019;29(5):481-492.
abstract: This systematic review pooled findings from 24 controlled trials of probiotic supplementation in healthy adults who exercise, including athletes and physically active people. The trials included 1,680 participants, 67.5% of them male, with a mean age of 30.9 years. Five databases were searched, and study quality was rated with GRADE.
tldr: Probiotics reduced respiratory and gastrointestinal symptoms in some trials of physically active people, but results were inconsistent. The review found weak evidence that probiotics improve exercise performance.
methods: A PRISMA-based systematic review (registered as CRD42017070151) searched MEDLINE, Embase, SciELO, Scopus and Lilacs. Two reviewers screened studies and extracted data independently, and GRADE was used to rate evidence quality. Eligible studies were controlled trials of probiotics in healthy adults who exercised, with no pooled statistical analysis.
findings: The authors report that five trials showed fewer respiratory symptoms or shorter or milder illness with probiotics (their list cites six), and two more reported fewer respiratory episodes, while three found no respiratory effect. Most trials found no effect on immune markers, and inflammatory and gut permeability results were mixed. Performance was assessed in seven studies, and the authors judged that evidence weak and inconclusive.
limitations: The trials were small and varied in strain, dose, duration, outcomes and population, which makes the results hard to compare. No meta-analysis was done, and two studies were excluded because their authors could not be contacted. The abstract and discussion state that probiotics improved immunologic markers, but the results report that most studies found no immune effect; the results are used here.
practicalImplications: Probiotics may help reduce some respiratory or gastrointestinal symptoms in physically active people, but the benefit was not consistent across trials. Any product should match the strain and dose that were tested. This review does not support claims of better performance or immune protection for all athletes.
athleteDev: This review does not support using probiotics as a performance aid, because the performance evidence was weak and mixed. Any use should be framed as an illness-prevention option to discuss with the medical staff.
rtp: This review cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It includes no injured athletes and no return-to-play outcomes.

citation: Doma K, Ramachandran AK, Boullosa D, Connor J. The Paradoxical Effect of Creatine Monohydrate on Muscle Damage Markers: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Sports Medicine. 2022.
abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis pooled 23 placebo-controlled trials of creatine monohydrate (CrM) in healthy adults exposed to muscle-damaging exercise. Outcomes were indirect damage markers, inflammation, oxidative stress, muscle soreness and muscle force at 24-36 h and 48-90 h, and the trials were split into single-bout (acute) and multi-week training (chronic) responses.
tldr: Creatine was linked to lower muscle damage markers 2 to 4 days after a single hard session, but after several weeks of training the same markers were higher with creatine at 24 h. Creatine did not clearly improve recovery of muscle force or soreness.
methods: A PRISMA systematic review (PROSPERO CRD42020207421) searched PubMed, Scopus, SPORTDiscus, CINAHL and Web of Science in August 2021. Two reviewers screened studies, one author rated quality with a modified PEDro scale, and random-effects meta-analyses of standardised mean differences were run with Egger's test where at least ten studies were available.
findings: After a single bout, damage markers were lower with CrM at 48-90 h (SMD -1.09, p = 0.03) but not at 24-36 h, and oxidative stress was lower at 24-36 h (SMD -1.37, p < 0.001); inflammation showed large but non-significant reductions. After training, damage markers were higher with CrM at 24 h (SMD 0.95, p = 0.04), and the 48 h difference was large but not significant (p = 0.06). Muscle force and soreness differences were not significant.
limitations: Training status ranged from sedentary and older adults to trained athletes, and only about 10% of participants were female. Protocols, doses, damage markers and follow-up times varied with high heterogeneity, and over 70% of studies did not assess creatine bioavailability. The abstract states that oxidative stress differences were not significant, but the results report a significant difference at 24-36 h (p < 0.001); the results values are used here.
practicalImplications: Creatine around a single strenuous session was linked to lower damage markers 2 to 4 days later, but not at 24 h and not on every marker. Staff should not expect creatine to speed recovery of muscle force or soreness on this evidence. During long creatine-supported training blocks, damage markers may read higher at 24 h, so interpret creatine kinase values with supplement use in mind.
athleteDev: The review does not show that creatine improves performance or muscle force recovery, so it should not be promoted as a recovery aid on this evidence. Any change in training load because of creatine should be guided by monitored soreness and damage, not assumed benefit.
rtp: This review cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It studied healthy adults after exercise-induced muscle damage, with no injured athletes and no return-to-play outcomes.

citation: Shannon OM, Allen JD, Bescos R, Burke L, Clifford T, Easton C, et al. Dietary Inorganic Nitrate as an Ergogenic Aid: An Expert Consensus Derived via the Modified Delphi Technique. Sports Medicine. 2022.
abstract: A 12-member expert panel used a modified Delphi technique over three rounds to vote on 222 statements about dietary inorganic nitrate as an ergogenic aid. Statements covered activity type, population, supplementation strategy, physiological effects, safety and toxicity, quality of evidence, and the ethos of Olympic sport. Consensus required more than 80% agreement.
tldr: An expert panel agreed on some practical points for dietary nitrate, including doses, timing before exercise, and benefit mainly at low to moderate aerobic fitness. Most questions were judged to have insufficient evidence.
methods: Twelve experts (PhD-qualified, with publications or applied experience) completed three voting rounds on 222 statements: two anonymous questionnaire rounds and one videoconference discussion. Consensus was defined a priori as more than 80% agreement, and statements with more than 80% insufficient-evidence votes were removed from further voting.
findings: Thirty-nine statements (17.6%) reached consensus: 20 yes and 19 no. Acute doses of 8-16 mmol and chronic doses of 4-16 mmol/day were judged ergogenic, taken 2-4 h before exercise, with beetroot juice and nitrate salts supported as forms. Benefit was agreed for low aerobic fitness (VO2peak below 45 ml/kg/min) and for chronic use at moderate fitness (below 60 ml/kg/min), and acute doses up to about 16 mmol were judged safe. The panel agreed the 3.7 mg/kg/day ADI is not appropriate, and no consensus was reached on sex or age effects.
limitations: Expert opinion from 12 panelists is subjective and may not represent all researchers. The panel had less experience with clinical populations, and the clinical statements were broad. Sex, age and sport-specific effects were largely left as insufficient evidence. Nine of the 16 listed authors reported receiving discounted or free beetroot juice for research, one received free nitrate gels, and several reported industry-linked funding or consultancy.
practicalImplications: For athletes with low to moderate aerobic fitness, the consensus supports considering nitrate at 8-16 mmol before a single session or 4-16 mmol/day over several days, with the dose taken 2-4 h before exercise. The panel agreed beetroot juice and nitrate salts are ergogenic, but the authors advise vegetable-derived sources such as beetroot juice for safety. The authors judge effects diminished above about 60 ml/kg/min VO2peak, and most other questions, including specific sports, sex and age, remain unsettled.
athleteDev: Dietary nitrate is most likely to help athletes with low to moderate aerobic fitness. The panel reached no consensus that it helps highly trained athletes, and the authors conclude effects appear diminished above about 60 ml/kg/min VO2peak. Performance changes should be checked against an individual baseline, since the panel found insufficient evidence for most sport-specific effects.
rtp: This consensus cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. Its statements about clinical populations were largely judged insufficient or without consensus, and it does not address injured athletes.

citation: Nilsson KJ, Flint HG, Gao Y, Kendrick L, Cutchin S, Pentecost R, et al. Repetitive Head Impacts in Youth Football: Description and Relationship to White Matter Structure. Sports Health. 2019.
abstract: This prospective cohort study compared diffusion tensor imaging fractional anisotropy (FA) before and after a season in 8-12 year old males in youth tackle football (35) and age-matched swimmers (12). Head impacts were recorded with helmet-mounted accelerometers in the football group, and the study tested whether impact number, magnitude or location correlated with FA change.
tldr: In this small pilot study, one season of youth tackle football did not change white matter FA compared with swimmers. Higher total lateral head-impact magnitude was linked to increased left cingulate FA, but its meaning is unclear.
methods: Males aged 8-12 in tackle football (35) and swimming (12) had 3T brain MRI with DTI before and after the season. Football players wore Shockbox accelerometers that recorded 1,905 impacts over the season, and FA was measured in manually placed regions of interest. A mixed-model repeated-measures MANOVA compared groups, and correlation and regression linked impact measures to FA change.
findings: There was no group-by-time interaction for FA, and no pre-to-post change within the football group. Impacts were 17.9% in games and 82.1% in practices, with 301 impacts of 80 g or more. Total magnitude of lateral impacts correlated with increased left cingulate FA (r = 0.40, p = 0.03; regression beta 0.028).
limitations: The study was a pilot with no sample-size estimate, so non-significant results are uninformative. The accelerometers did not record impacts below 30 g or rotational acceleration, and parents reported some data. The text gives 35 football players in one place and 34 in the hit data, and five MRI scans were excluded.
practicalImplications: Practices produced most recorded head impacts because there were far more practices than games (31 vs 7), while the impact rate per session was similar (1.5 per game and per practice). Accelerometer counts of high-magnitude impacts should be interpreted cautiously, since this cohort's share of impacts of 80 g or more was far higher than in prior youth studies. Do not use the cingulate FA correlation to judge an individual athlete's brain health or injury risk, since the study does not show whether it is harmful.
athleteDev: This study has no performance outcomes. For performance staff, its only use is to show how head-impact exposure accumulated across practices and games in one youth season. It should not be used to judge cognition, readiness or athlete development.
rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It has no return-to-play, symptom or recovery outcomes, and its imaging findings should not be used to clear or hold an athlete.

citation: Brilliant AN, Meehan WP III, Howell DR. Static and Dynamic Cognitive Performance in Youth and Collegiate Athletes With Concussion. Clinical Journal of Sport Medicine. 2019.
abstract: This cross-sectional study compared cognitive task performance while standing still and while walking in youth and collegiate athletes with concussion and uninjured controls. Concussed athletes were tested within 10 days of injury, and the primary outcomes were accuracy and the number of task items completed.
tldr: Athletes with a recent concussion answered fewer cognitive items while standing and walking, and were less accurate on two tasks only while walking. Dual-task testing may help show post-concussion deficits, but it has not been validated as a diagnostic test.
methods: Ninety-four athletes with concussion (tested a mean of 5.1 days after injury while still symptomatic) and 97 uninjured controls, aged 8-21, completed three cognitive tasks (backward spelling, serial subtraction and reverse months) in a 30-second standing condition and while walking 8 m. Accuracy and completion rate were compared with ANCOVA adjusted for sex, height and concussion history, and gait speed and symptoms were also measured.
findings: Concussed athletes completed fewer responses while standing (37.3 vs 45.1, p = 0.03) and while walking (22.7 vs 33.6, p < 0.001). Overall accuracy did not differ while standing (p = 0.11) or walking (p = 0.15), but while walking they were less accurate on backward spelling (81.2% vs 89.8%, p = 0.049) and reverse months (95.8% vs 98.2%, p = 0.031). Concussed athletes also walked more slowly in both single-task and dual-task conditions and reported more symptoms.
limitations: This was a single cross-sectional test, with no recovery follow-up and no test of diagnostic accuracy, and recruitment came from one clinic and one university. The standing task was always done before the walking task in a fixed order, and the per-task accuracy differences were borderline with several comparisons. The abstract gives p = 0.034 for reverse months while Table 3 gives p = 0.031; the table value is used here. Concussed athletes had more prior concussions (64% vs 27%) and were shorter, which was handled with covariates, but residual confounding is possible.
practicalImplications: Within about 10 days of a concussion, a brief walking-plus-cognitive task may show slower responses and some accuracy loss, so it can be a useful adjunct to the full evaluation. Record the number of responses as well as accuracy, since the response count showed the most consistent group difference. Do not use these scores alone to clear an athlete or to rule a concussion in or out.
athleteDev: This study has no performance or development outcomes. Its relevance for performance staff is limited to the idea that cognitive performance under movement may be a useful adjunct measure after concussion, not a training or readiness metric for healthy athletes.
rtp: This study cannot establish when an athlete is ready to return to sport. It tested athletes while still symptomatic within 10 days of injury and did not follow recovery; the authors suggest the method may help assess readiness, but that was not tested.

citation: Murray NG, Fenner M, Szekely B, Quigley KG, Islas A, Cipriani D, et al. Smooth Pursuit Velocity After a Season of Repetitive Head Impacts in American Football Players. JAMA Ophthalmology. 2025.
abstract: This single-center cohort study measured smooth pursuit eye movement velocity with a Landolt-C eye-tracking task at preseason, midseason and postseason in 25 male Division I football players and 10 noncontact controls. Football players were grouped as high-dose or low-dose by instrumented mouthguard head-impact totals, and the study tested whether impacts were associated with smooth pursuit velocity across one season.
tldr: Smooth pursuit eye velocity did not fall over one football season, and it was not linked to head-impact totals. Players later classed as high-dose were already slower than controls before the season, which the authors suggest may reflect prior contact history.
methods: Players wore instrumented mouthguards that recorded impacts of 5 g or more, with a random sample of sessions video-verified, and completed eye tracking before contact practice, at midseason and within 2 weeks after the season. Players were split after the season into high-dose (above the 50th percentile on total impacts, peak linear and peak angular acceleration) and low-dose groups. Eye tracking used a Landolt-C target moving horizontally at 30 and 90 deg/s, and a mixed-model repeated-measures ANOVA with Bonferroni-corrected follow-ups and Pearson correlations were used.
findings: Smooth pursuit velocity had a main effect of group but no time effect and no group-by-time interaction. Before the season, high-dose players were slower than controls (10.01 vs 15.60 deg/s), and at midseason both high-dose and low-dose players were slower than controls. No impact metric correlated with smooth pursuit velocity at any time point.
limitations: The study was exploratory, from one team, with 25 players and 10 controls. Mouthguard data were missing for about 5 percent of impacts, controls were not matched for sex or sport and were tested over shorter intervals during their own terms, and only horizontal movements were measured. The text gives conflicting values for the preseason difference (4.28 in the abstract, 6.34 and 5.59 elsewhere) and gives 27 rather than 25 players in one place.
practicalImplications: Eye-tracking values recorded before contact practices may already differ between high-exposure players and controls, so record a pre-season baseline if this measure is used. This study does not show that smooth pursuit tracks head-impact exposure during a season, so it should not be used alone to assess brain health or injury risk. Its finding of no seasonal decline supports only short-term stability in this small sample.
athleteDev: Smooth pursuit velocity showed no seasonal decline and no link to head-impact totals in this study, so it is not a training or performance metric here. Its only practical value for performance staff is as a possible baseline measure, not as a readiness or development indicator.
rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. Players were medically cleared at baseline, and the study has no concussion, symptom or return-to-play outcomes, so smooth pursuit values should not be used to clear or hold an athlete.

citation: Jo J, Wong G, Williams KL, Davis PJ, Rigney GH, Zuckerman SL, et al. Age of First Exposure to Contact Sports Is Not Associated With Worse Later-In-Life Brain Health in a Cohort of Community-Dwelling Older Men. Clin J Sport Med. 2024:1-8.
abstract: This cross-sectional survey of 69 community-dwelling older men with contact sport histories compared those who first played before age 12 (n=24) with those who started at 12 or older (n=45). Early exposure was not associated with depression, anxiety, general health problems, motor symptoms or functional status. After adjusting for age, prior concussions and total years of contact sport, early exposure was linked to lower cognitive complaint and neurobehavioral symptom scores.
tldr: In this small survey of older men, starting contact sport before age 12 was not linked to worse later-life brain health. The study cannot show that early play is beneficial, and the lower symptom scores in the early group should be read cautiously.
methods: Men in a memory research registry completed an online or paper survey on age of first exposure to contact sport, sport history, concussion history, depression (PHQ-9), anxiety (GAD-7), cognitive complaints (BC-CCI), neurobehavioral symptoms (NSI), general health, motor symptoms and functional status. Groups were compared with t tests and chi-square tests, and multivariable linear and logistic regressions adjusted for age, prior concussions and total contact sport years.
findings: Early exposure (before 12) was not associated with depression or anxiety scores in adjusted models. In adjusted models the early-exposure group had lower BC-CCI and NSI scores (standardized beta 0.29 for both, P=0.03), but the unadjusted differences for these two measures were not significant (P=0.065 and P=0.072), and the early group reported more total years of contact sport (10.8 vs 5.6, P=0.016).
limitations: The sample is small (69 men, 24 in the early group), relies on self-report and recall, and was not verified with clinical or neuropsychological testing. The authors' clinical relevance statement that early benefits may outweigh head-impact risks goes beyond what a cross-sectional survey can show.
practicalImplications: Based on this study alone, early contact sport participation should not be assumed to cause worse brain health in older men. Long-term benefit cannot be concluded from these data, and decisions about youth participation need evidence from prospective studies.
athleteDev: This study does not measure athletic performance, skill development or training outcomes, so it cannot guide talent identification, sport selection or training decisions.
rtp: Not applicable to return to sport. The study surveyed older men years after their playing careers and did not assess concussed athletes, symptom recovery or return-to-play timing.

citation: Uchiyama K, Peeling P, Halson SL, Reid M, Wallman K, Walsh J, et al. Sleep Architecture Immediately After a Sport-Related Concussion Sustained During a Professional Rugby Union Match: A Retrospective Case Study. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2025 (ahead of print).
abstract: This retrospective case study describes sleep architecture and overnight physiology in one professional rugby union player across four nights: before injury, the night of a concussion, the second night after injury with westward travel, and after recovery. On the night of injury, deep (N3) and REM sleep were reduced and total sleep was under 6 hours. The second night showed partial recovery of sleep stages but persistent fragmentation, lower oxygen saturation, higher heart rate, lower heart rate variability and more respiratory events.
tldr: A single case showed that sleep became shorter and more fragmented, with less deep and REM sleep, on the night of a rugby concussion and remained disrupted the next night. Because this is one player with no repeated baselines, the findings suggest a pattern to test in larger studies rather than a settled effect.
methods: Home-based polysomnography (Somfit) recorded sleep on one pre-injury night, the night of injury, the second night after injury and a night 24 days later. Sleep stages were manually scored in 30-second epochs, and heart rate, oxygen saturation, heart rate variability and respiratory events were extracted and analyzed descriptively against clinically meaningful thresholds.
findings: On the night of injury, total sleep was 332 minutes (vs 261 pre-injury), with lower N3 (19%) and REM (18%) percentages than on all other nights. On the second night, sleep onset was 23 minutes, wake after sleep onset was 69 minutes, and sleep efficiency was below 85%. Mean heart rate was higher and heart rate variability was lower (65.1 and 66.9 ms vs 74.2 and 74.0 ms) on the injury and second nights than before and after injury, and respiratory events were higher (69 and 104 vs 14 pre-injury).
limitations: The study is one player with a single pre-injury baseline night, so the apparent increase in sleep duration on the injury night probably reflects short sleep before injury rather than a concussion effect. Caffeine, alcohol and medication use were not recorded, and travel fatigue was not separated from concussion effects. The abstract says respiratory events were greater on the injury and second nights, but the results also report more events on the recovered night (46 vs 14).
practicalImplications: In a concussed athlete, sleep quality may be poor for the first one to two nights, so staff could ask about sleep and monitor it in that window. Travel on the night after injury may add to sleep disruption, which is a reason to consider travel timing in the early phase. Routine sleep-apnea screening for collision athletes is a reasonable question to raise, but this case alone does not establish that it improves recovery.
athleteDev: This study does not assess performance, training adaptation or skill, so it cannot guide training load or performance targets.
rtp: The study can suggest that sleep should be checked in the first 72 hours after a concussion, but it cannot set return-to-play criteria or show that sleep disruption delays return to sport. It was one player with no symptom data reported, so it should not be used to time clearance.

citation: Inclan PM, Kuhn AW, Chang PS, Mack C, Solomon GS, Sills AK, et al. Validity of Research Based on Publicly Obtained Data in Sports Medicine: A Quantitative Assessment of Concussions in the National Football League. Sports Health. 2023.
abstract: This systematic review identified 20 NFL concussion studies that relied on publicly obtained internet data and compared the studies' counts with the NFL injury database for 2015 to 2019 where possible. The public-data studies captured about 70% of concussions on average, with a range of 20% to 90%. They over-represented running backs and quarterbacks and under-represented offensive linemen, defensive backs and linebackers, and misclassified special teams injuries.
tldr: Concussion counts drawn from public internet sources captured on average about 70% of NFL concussions, with wide variation between studies. Public-data concussion research in the NFL should be read with caution, and curated league data are preferable.
methods: A PRISMA-guided systematic search of medical and gray literature for NFL concussion studies that used publicly obtained data was completed in November 2020, and two reviewers independently screened and extracted data. Studies were compared with the NFL injury database (2015 to 2019) for capture rate, game phase distribution and position representation, using a relative representation ratio.
findings: Of 20 included studies, 12 could be compared with NFL data, and they captured on average 70.0% (SD 25.0%) of concussions, with a range of 20.1% to 90.2%. Public-data studies reported 55% of concussions on offense, 45% on defense and under 1% on special teams, versus 44%, 37% and 18% in the NFL data. Running backs (ratio 1.46) and quarterbacks (1.42) were over-represented, and defensive backs (0.88), linebackers (0.82) and offensive linemen (0.93) were under-represented.
limitations: The review depends on the NFL database as the reference standard, which the authors note still relies on clinical reporting across 32 teams, and several authors are NFL employees or consultants. Capture rates divide each study's annual count by NFL annual averages from 2015 to 2019, even though most included studies covered earlier seasons. None of the included studies described how concussions were diagnosed, and return-to-play outcomes were not analyzed.
practicalImplications: Concussion counts or position-specific risks taken from public internet sources should not be used alone to estimate NFL injury risk, since they miss many injuries and over-represent high-profile positions. Staff who need reliable concussion data should prefer curated, clinically reported surveillance data where it can be obtained.
athleteDev: This review addresses injury data quality and not performance measurement, so it cannot guide training or talent decisions. Performance statistics from public sources were not validated in this review.
rtp: None of the included public-data studies described how concussions were diagnosed, and the review does not report return-to-play findings. It cannot be used to set or judge return-to-play timing for individual players.

citation: Stokes KA, Locke D, Roberts S, Henderson L, Tucker R, Ryan D, et al. Does reducing the height of the tackle through law change in elite men's rugby union (The Championship, England) reduce the incidence of concussion? A controlled study in 126 games. Br J Sports Med. 2019:1-6.
abstract: This observational cohort study compared two competitions in English elite men's rugby during 2018/19, one played under standard tackle laws and one with the maximum tackle height lowered to the armpit line. The lowered tackle height reduced upright tackles and head and neck contact by ball carriers. Concussion incidence did not differ between the two settings, but tacklers were concussed more often under the lowered tackle height.
tldr: Lowering the maximum tackle height in English elite rugby changed how players tackled, but it did not reduce overall concussion rates and tacklers were concussed more often. Law changes like this should be tested with larger, better-controlled studies before they are used to reduce concussion.
methods: Video analysts coded 52 game and tackle variables for 126 matches, and injury and concussion data were collected by club medical staff using the standard head injury assessment protocol. Tackle behaviour and concussion incidence per 1000 hours and per 1000 tackles were compared between the standard-law Championship (90 matches) and the lowered-height Championship Cup (36 matches) using rate ratios.
findings: Under the lowered height, tacklers made head and neck contact with ball carriers about 30% less often (RR 0.70), and tacklers were upright less often and fully bent more often. Overall concussion incidence was 16.9 per 1000 hours under standard laws and 22.2 under lowered height (RR 1.31, 95% CI 0.85 to 2.01, not significant). Tacklers had higher concussion incidence (6.9 vs 13.2 per 1000 hours, RR 1.90, 95% CI 1.05 to 3.45).
limitations: The two periods were different competitions, so differences in squad selection, match importance and season timing may explain the results. Concussion rates were 20% higher in the post-law period under standard laws, which may reflect better reporting because of the study, and two rounds with unusually high or low counts influenced the comparison. Data were available for 86% of players, and the study was not powered for concussion outcomes.
practicalImplications: Lowering the tackle height changed tackle technique but did not reduce concussion in this study, and tacklers had a higher concussion incidence and propensity under the lowered height. Medical and coaching staff should not assume that a tackle-height law change will reduce concussion without monitoring outcomes in their own competition.
athleteDev: This study addresses tackle behaviour and injury risk rather than performance, so it cannot guide performance targets. Under the lowered height, tacklers entered contact fully bent more often and made more passive shoulder and arm tackles, which describes how technique shifted but not whether it is safer to coach.
rtp: The study does not address return to play, symptom recovery or clearance after concussion, so it cannot be used to set return-to-play timing. Its concussion counts describe incidence only.

citation: Knowles P, Schneider K, Bugwadia AK, Sorcar P, Pea RD, Daneshvar DH, et al. The importance of language in describing concussions: A qualitative analysis. PM&R. 2024:1-8.
abstract: This secondary qualitative analysis of 94 phone interviews with high school sports stakeholders examined whether people who rated concussion as more severe were more likely to describe it using the word brain. The association was significant overall and among coaches, but not among athletes, parents, educators or the athletic director. The authors conclude that precise medical language may support concussion education and reporting.
tldr: People who saw concussion as more severe were more likely to describe it as a brain injury, and this was clearest among high school coaches. Concussion education for coaches may benefit from clear brain-injury language, although this study did not measure reporting.
methods: Semistructured telephone interviews were conducted in July 2017 with 94 participants from a larger set of 316, selected because one interviewer asked the same questions and the interviews were recorded. Two coders assigned each participant to a minimum, moderate or maximum severity category based on how they ranked concussion among common injuries, and recorded whether they used brain language. Chi-square tests, Fisher's exact tests and odds ratios were used for the analysis.
findings: Brain language was used by 1 of 19 minimum-severity participants (5%), 10 of 43 moderate (23%) and 18 of 32 maximum (56%), P<.001 overall. With maximum severity as the reference, the odds of using brain terms were lower in the minimum (OR 0.05, 95% CI 0.00 to 0.30) and moderate (OR 0.24, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.65) groups. The association held for coaches (P=.002; OR 0.06 and 0.14 versus maximum) but not for parents, athletes or educators (all P>.05).
limitations: The sample came from convenience recruitment, mostly through cold emails and LinkedIn, and some participants were known to the interviewer, which may have influenced responses. Severity was coded from open-ended answers that could mean pain, time out or long-term effect. The subgroup analyses were small, and the authors note that the non-coach results may reflect low power rather than no relationship.
practicalImplications: Concussion education for coaches could describe concussion explicitly as a brain injury, which is consistent with the link between brain language and perceived severity seen here. The study shows an association only and did not measure reporting, so staff should not expect that changing wording alone will change how often athletes report concussions.
athleteDev: This study is about how people describe and rate concussion severity and does not address performance, training or skill development, so it cannot guide performance decisions.
rtp: The study records attitudes about whether an athlete would return to the game after a concussion, but it did not measure return-to-play decisions or outcomes. It should not be used to set return-to-play criteria or timing.

citation: Poysophon P, Rao AL. Neurocognitive Deficits Associated With ADHD in Athletes: A Systematic Review. Sports Health. 2018.
abstract: This systematic review of 17 studies examined whether athletes with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) have more neurocognitive deficits, concussion risk, symptom reporting and slower recovery. Athletes with ADHD generally scored lower on neurocognitive testing, reported more symptoms, and in several studies had higher concussion risk. Evidence that stimulant medication changes these risks was sparse.
tldr: Athletes with ADHD in these studies tended to score lower on neurocognitive testing and report more concussion-like symptoms, and several studies found higher concussion rates. Many differences were small and the stimulant evidence is limited, so ADHD history should be used as context rather than as a diagnostic or return-to-play decision.
methods: PubMed, CINAHL, PsychInfo and Cochrane were searched for studies of athletes aged 15 to 19 with ADHD that used neuropsychological testing, with 17 studies meeting criteria from the 2013 to 2017 literature. Findings were grouped by study type, sample size and effect size and synthesized qualitatively, because the data were too variable for quantitative analysis.
findings: Athletes with ADHD had lower ImPACT composite scores in several studies, with differences of 0.01 to 6 points that the authors describe as small and within the normative range for adolescents. Six mostly cross-sectional studies found more frequent prior concussion in athletes with ADHD (for example, 1 or more prior concussions in 50.4% vs 14.4% in one study), while two found no difference. Stimulant-treated athletes had worse verbal and visual memory and higher symptom scores than controls in one study, and the evidence on stimulants was limited and conflicting.
limitations: The authors note that ADHD diagnoses were self-reported or from charts without clinical confirmation, stimulant use was self-reported, only two studies were prospective, and confounders were inconsistently controlled. The abstract states that there was no evidence that stimulant treatment changed these risks, but the text reports one study (Iverson et al) where stimulant use was associated with a higher concussion risk. The abstract gives a prevalence range of 4.2% to 8.1%, while the discussion gives 4% to 14.3%.
practicalImplications: Athletes with a known ADHD history may have lower baseline test scores and higher self-reported symptoms, so staff should interpret baseline and post-concussion testing with that history in mind and not treat it as a diagnosis. This review does not support a conclusion on whether stimulant medication is safe or effective in athletes, so medication decisions should involve the treating clinician and not be based on this review alone.
athleteDev: This review does not address performance or training outcomes, so it cannot guide talent identification or training decisions.
rtp: The review reports ImPACT scores and symptoms relevant to concussion, but it does not establish return-to-play criteria. Its finding of longer recovery is based on one small study that was not statistically significant, so it should not be used to set return-to-play timing for athletes with ADHD.

citation: McCrea M, Meier T, Huber D, Ptito A, Bigler E, Debert CT, et al. Role of advanced neuroimaging, fluid biomarkers and genetic testing in the assessment of sport-related concussion: a systematic review. Br J Sports Med. 2017 (published online April 28, 2017).
abstract: This systematic review of 98 studies assessed advanced neuroimaging, fluid biomarkers and genetic testing in sport-related concussion. Neuroimaging, biomarker and genetic studies all showed concussion-related effects, but the authors rated the evidence for clinical use as low in each area. They conclude that these methods are promising research tools that need further validation before clinical use.
tldr: Advanced brain imaging, blood biomarkers and genetic tests showed concussion-related changes in research studies, but none is ready for routine clinical use. These methods should be treated as research tools and not as diagnostic or return-to-play measures.
methods: Three separate systematic searches of Medline, PubMed, CINAHL, PsycINFO, Scopus and Cochrane covered neuroimaging, biomarkers and genetics in sport-related concussion, from January 2000 to December 2016. Two reviewers screened articles, risk of bias was rated with a modified QUADAS-2 tool, and the level of evidence was graded with a modified GRADE approach. Findings were summarized in tables and narrative synthesis.
findings: Across 76 neuroimaging and electrophysiology studies (DTI 18, task fMRI 15, EEG/qEEG 16, MRS 13, resting-state fMRI 8, and fewer using other methods), each modality showed significant concussion-related effects, although directions varied between studies and some reported null results. Eleven of 16 fluid biomarker studies found significant changes in blood markers such as S100B, total tau and AMPAR, while markers including NSE, VILIP-1 and salivary cortisol did not distinguish concussed athletes. The six genetic studies were small and provided proof of concept only, for example a GRIN2A variant associated with recovery times over 60 days.
limitations: The review notes high or moderate risk of bias in most studies, driven by limited generalizability (male-only, collegiate, or single-sport samples), small samples, lack of preinjury baselines, inconsistent definitions of concussion, and publication bias. The authors also note that the review was broad by design and included few studies per marker, so the evidence for individual markers is thin.
practicalImplications: Advanced neuroimaging, blood biomarkers and genetic testing should not be used for routine concussion diagnosis or management based on this review. Staff interested in these tools should look for studies with preinjury baselines, standardized protocols and clinically relevant outcomes before considering their use.
athleteDev: This review concerns concussion assessment and biology and does not address performance measurement or training, so it cannot guide performance decisions.
rtp: The authors state that these markers are not validated for clinical decisions, including when an athlete is fit to return to activity. The review cannot be used to set return-to-play criteria or timing, though it suggests future studies may link biomarkers to recovery.

citation: Cosh SM, McNeil DG, Jeffreys A, Clark L, Tully PJ. Athlete mental health help-seeking: A systematic review and meta-analysis of rates, barriers and facilitators. Psychology of Sport & Exercise. 2024.
abstract: Systematic review and meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD42022341981) of 22 studies of current elite athletes that pooled formal mental health help-seeking rates and synthesised barriers and facilitators. Eleven studies (N=3,415) gave a pooled help-seeking rate of 22.4% (95% CI 16.2 to 30.2), barriers were reported in 13 studies, and facilitators in six.
tldr: About one in five elite athletes in these studies had sought professional mental health help. Stigma linked to athlete identity, team culture, and doubts about confidentiality were the main barriers, while normalising help-seeking through role models and encouragement from coaches and staff were the main facilitators.
methods: Searched PubMed, PsycINFO and SportDiscus from inception to January 2023, and contacted authors for unpublished studies. Two raters screened records, one author extracted data with verification, and JBI checklists were used for quality appraisal. Help-seeking proportions were pooled with random-effects models, and barriers and facilitators were meta-synthesised.
findings: The pooled formal help-seeking proportion was 22.4% across 11 cross-sectional studies (I2=95.7%), and trim and fill gave 24.4%. Age and the proportion of female participants did not explain heterogeneity, and subgroup differences (for example, team-sport-only samples) had overlapping confidence intervals. The most commonly reported barriers were stigma (12 studies), poor mental health literacy (7 studies), and concerns about confidentiality and trust in sport services.
limitations: Help-seeking was self-reported and symptom profiles were inconsistently measured, so the rate cannot be matched to athletes who need help. Heterogeneity was very high, quality varied, and only six studies reported facilitators. The review was limited to English-language studies, with few para-athletes and few racial or ethnic minority samples.
practicalImplications: The review cannot say how many athletes who needed help went without it, but its barrier findings suggest that screening and referral alone may not lead to service uptake. Staff can target the barriers the review identified: clear confidentiality terms, stigma reduction that addresses athlete identity, athlete role models who talk openly about mental health, and coaches or staff who arrange or prompt appointments.
athleteDev: Team culture is part of mental health support: coaches and sport staff can normalise conversations about mental health and make referrals easier to act on, with confidentiality made explicit. The review does not evaluate any programme, so it shows which barriers exist but not which interventions increase service use.
rtp: This review cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It concerns help-seeking in current athletes, and only one included qualitative study (Gaelic footballers after injury) touches on injury.

citation: Romdhani M, Bentouati E, Abid R, Moussa-Chamari I, Chamari K, Ben Saad H, et al. Reciprocal relationships between sleep quality, mental health and the quality of life in elite athletes: A pilot study. Biol Sport. 2026;43:267-279.
abstract: Cross-sectional survey of 118 highly trained athletes (39 female, 50 world class) in Tunisia, measuring sleep quality (PSQI), insomnia (ISI), daytime sleepiness (ESS), depression, anxiety and stress (DASS-21), and quality of life (WHOQOL-BREF). Sleep quality was low in 62% of athletes, and higher negative emotions and insomnia severity were associated with poorer sleep and lower quality of life.
tldr: Most elite athletes in this survey slept poorly, with 62% reporting low or very low sleep quality. Poorer sleep went with more insomnia, more negative emotions and lower quality of life, so sleep belongs in athlete wellbeing checks.
methods: Arabic online survey completed by athletes on phones or computers during sleep-hygiene awareness sessions in small groups in September 2022. Measures were PSQI, ISI, ESS, WHOQOL-BREF, DASS-21 and self-reported sleep-hygiene items. Analyses used independent t-tests with Cohen's d, stepwise multiple regression and mediation analysis.
findings: Sixty-two percent had a PSQI score of 5 or more, and 51% reported excessive or severe daytime sleepiness (ESS 11 or more). Female athletes had higher PSQI, ESS and DASS scores than males, athletes aged 25 or under had higher PSQI and DASS scores, and individual-sport athletes had higher ESS and lower quality of life than team-sport athletes. Higher DASS scores were associated with higher PSQI (beta 0.3) and ISI (beta 0.36) scores, and higher PSQI scores with lower WHOQOL scores (beta -0.41).
limitations: The single cross-sectional design means the reciprocal links cannot be tested as cause and effect. All measures were self-reported, the sample was small and entirely Tunisian, and 49 of the 76 individual-sport athletes were combat athletes. The survey was taken in September, when some athletes were in post-season and others in pre-season, and the authors suggest August heat may have affected the month of sleep being recalled.
practicalImplications: Sleep questions can sit alongside mental health and quality-of-life checks, because poor sleep clustered with negative emotions and lower quality of life in this sample. The subgroup findings (female, younger and individual-sport athletes, all small to moderate effects) suggest where sleep support may be needed first. Education can cover habits the regression models linked to poorer sleep or more insomnia, such as soda intake, later bedtimes and longer daily screen time, and sport-related issues such as early training.
athleteDev: Sleep should be tracked as part of performance and wellbeing monitoring, since this sample showed high daytime sleepiness and insomnia alongside lower quality of life. The authors suggest extra night sleep or daytime napping, but this survey did not test either approach, so it cannot show that they improve performance or mood.
rtp: This study does not inform return-to-sport decisions. Athletes with a major injury in the previous month were excluded, and it measured sleep, mood and quality of life only, so it should not guide return-to-play.

citation: Lundqvist C, Camps J, Vertommen T, Barker-Ruchti N, Kolbeinsson Ö. Toxic leadership in high-performance sports and its consequences for mental health and performance: a scoping review. International Review of Sport and Exercise Psychology. 2025.
abstract: Scoping review (PRISMA-ScR) of 26 empirical studies of toxic leadership in high-performance sport, published 2004 to 2023 and mostly from North America and Europe. Studies used inconsistent definitions, but the empirical literature linked toxic leadership with negative effects on athletes' mental health, injuries and motivation to remain in high-performance sport.
tldr: Toxic and abusive leadership is reported across elite sport, and the most often reported consequence is harm to athlete mental health, with fewer studies linking it to dropout or early retirement and one to injury. The research is at an early stage, with varied definitions and methods, and no study showed that toxic leadership improves performance.
methods: Searched Scopus, PsycINFO, PubMed, Web of Science and Google Scholar, with a final search on 20 August 2023 and reference-list screening. One author screened titles and abstracts, two authors reviewed full texts, and two authors coded aims and findings with a predetermined template. Eligible studies were empirical, peer-reviewed and in English, and focused on toxic or dark leadership in youth to senior elite sport.
findings: Of 26 studies, 14 used interviews and 6 used questionnaires. The most common consequence was a negative effect on athlete mental health, with links to injury, dropout and early retirement, and one survey of 995 Canadian national team athletes found that 75% had experienced some form of maltreatment. Antecedents included dark personality traits, performance-focused culture, power imbalances and weak reporting systems. Six studies suggested that dark-side behaviours might help performance, but none showed an empirical performance gain.
limitations: As a scoping review, the paper does not pool results or appraise study quality. Definitions and methods were inconsistent, and most studies are retrospective interviews or cross-sectional surveys. The included studies are mostly North American and European, and the search was limited to English-language, peer-reviewed articles.
practicalImplications: Staff should treat toxic or abusive leadership as a real risk in their own programmes: one survey of 995 Canadian national team athletes found 75% reported some form of maltreatment, with coaches the most common perpetrators of most types. Included studies suggest clear reporting routes with independent oversight, coach education on non-abusive development methods, and attention to athlete wellbeing alongside performance, although the review found few empirically evaluated solutions. There is no empirical support in this review for harsh or intimidating coaching as a performance strategy.
athleteDev: Performance programmes should not assume that intimidating or abusive leadership improves results, because the review found no empirical performance gain and found links with mental health problems and dropout. Staff can review reporting systems, coach education and power imbalances between leaders and athletes, and track athlete wellbeing alongside performance outcomes.
rtp: This review does not inform return-to-sport decisions. Its only injury finding is a single link between toxic leadership and physical injury (Smits et al.), which the text does not explain in detail, so it cannot guide return-to-play.

citation: Myall K, Montero-Marin J, Gorczynski P, Kajee N, Syed Sheriff R, Bernard R, et al. Effect of mindfulness-based programmes on elite athlete mental health: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Br J Sports Med. 2022;0:1-12 (published online ahead of print).
abstract: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 12 randomised controlled trials (613 current or former elite athletes; 313 mindfulness-based programmes and 300 controls) of mental health outcomes. Programmes reduced anxiety and stress and improved psychological well-being, with an overall mental health effect of g=-0.75, but the certainty of evidence was moderate and heterogeneity was high.
tldr: Mindfulness-based programmes produced moderate to large improvements in anxiety, stress and well-being in elite athletes compared with controls. The evidence is promising but provisional, because the trials were small and heterogeneous and the depression result was not significant.
methods: Searched eight databases, including Embase, PsycINFO, SPORTDiscus, MEDLINE, Scopus, CENTRAL and Google Scholar, plus forward and backward reference searching, following PRISMA and a PROSPERO-registered protocol (CRD42020176654). Two authors screened records, the JBI checklist for RCTs assessed risk of bias, and GRADE assessed certainty. Random-effects meta-analysis used Hedges' g, with subgroup, meta-regression and trim-and-fill analyses.
findings: Mindfulness-based programmes improved anxiety (g=-0.87, 6 studies, 409 athletes, p=0.017), stress (g=-0.91, 5 studies, p=0.012) and psychological well-being (g=0.96, 5 studies, p=0.039), with smaller effects on psychological distress (g=-0.40, 4 studies) and mindfulness (g=0.62, 10 studies). The overall mental health effect was g=-0.75 across 9 studies. The depression effect was large but not significant (g=-0.90, 3 studies, p=0.13), and trim-and-fill reduced it to g=-0.02. Dropout was lower in the programme groups (relative risk 0.48).
limitations: The review pooled only 12 trials, mostly with small samples and 75% male athletes, with 3% para-athletes, so results may not generalise. Heterogeneity was high (I2 up to 90%), and publication bias was suspected for depression, distress and mindfulness. The abstract reports 614 athletes (314 programme), but the results report 613 (313 programme); the results figures are used here. The well-being effect was non-significant (g=0.49) after removing one outlier, and subgroup and meta-regression findings are exploratory.
practicalImplications: Mindfulness-based programmes are an option for elite athletes' anxiety and stress, and attrition was lower in programme groups (4%) than in control groups (9%). The authors recommend keeping the core elements of MBSR or MBCT, adapting them to the sport, using a qualified mindfulness teacher, and seeking coach endorsement. The depression evidence is inconclusive (3 trials, not significant), so these programmes should not be relied on as a depression treatment.
athleteDev: Mindfulness programmes may be framed as performance support, which the authors suggest could reduce stigma and improve engagement, and the trials reported reductions in competition anxiety. Performance was not a pooled outcome: the authors excluded performance and injury outcomes from their analysis, so the review cannot show a performance gain.
rtp: This review does not inform return-to-sport decisions. Two included trials looked at injury or concussion recovery, but the authors did not analyse injury outcomes, so the review cannot guide return-to-play.

citation: Gill VS, Sullivan G, Stearns H, Tummala SV, Haglin JM, Economopoulos KJ, et al. Mental Health in Elite Athletes: A Systematic Review of Suicidal Behaviour as Compared to the General Population. Sports Medicine. 2024.
abstract: Systematic review (PROSPERO CRD42023395990) of 22 cross-sectional studies of suicidal ideation, attempt or completion in elite athletes, searched from 1990 to January 2023. Ten studies compared athletes with non-athletes or the general population; most found lower suicide-related risk in athletes, and one found higher suicide mortality among former Swedish power-sport athletes.
tldr: Across 22 cross-sectional studies, elite athletes generally had lower rates of suicidal thoughts, attempts and deaths than non-athletes. The authors name male sex, non-white race, older age and depression as risk factors, but study results for sex, race and age were mixed and the evidence is heterogeneous.
methods: Searched MEDLINE, EMBASE, Scopus and Web of Science from 1990 to January 2023 for English, peer-reviewed studies of suicidal ideation, attempt or completion in varsity, professional, national or Olympic athletes. Two reviewers screened records, one author extracted data and a second checked it, and quality was rated with the JBI cross-sectional checklist. Rates were summarised as sample-weighted averages, without a meta-analysis.
findings: Suicidal ideation averaged 14.5% in professional or international athletes (6.9% to 18% across four studies) and 4.8% in collegiate athletes (3.7% to 6.5% across three studies). Of ten comparison studies, six found athletes at significantly lower risk, three found no significant difference, and one found suicide mortality 2 to 4 times higher in former Swedish power-sport athletes. Depression predicted ideation in both studies that tested it, while sex, race and age findings were mixed (for example, two collegiate studies found higher risk in non-white athletes and three studies found no race difference), and position and sport showed little consistent effect.
limitations: All studies were cross-sectional and most measured lifetime rather than recent suicidal behaviour, so causal or time-specific conclusions are not possible. Definitions and populations varied, and one study of 774 athletes shapes the professional ideation rate. The race and sex findings rest on few collegiate studies, and the abstract's emphasis on higher athletic level is based on a single study that the body text describes only as a trend. The search excluded high-school, Paralympic and non-English work.
practicalImplications: Staff should not assume elite athletes are protected from suicide, because some top-level samples reported ideation rates up to 18%. Depression was a risk factor in both studies that tested it; the authors also flag male sex, non-white race and higher competitive level, but each of these rests on few or conflicting studies. The included studies did not link injury or retirement with higher risk, but only one to two studies tested them and the authors call for these periods to be studied, so staff should not treat them as low risk.
athleteDev: The review is about suicide risk rather than performance, and it does not examine performance outcomes. The one study that tested training load found no link with suicidal ideation, so the review gives no basis for changing training to reduce risk. The higher-level finding comes from a single study of Chinese national athletes, so it is not a sound basis for targeting checks by competitive level.
rtp: This review does not inform return-to-sport decisions. Two included studies found no link between sports injury or pain and suicidal ideation, but the authors call for research on injury and retirement periods, so the review cannot be used to judge risk during rehabilitation or return to play.

citation: Ivarsson A, Johnson U, Andersen MB, Tranaeus U, Stenling A, Lindwall M. Psychosocial Factors and Sport Injuries: Meta-analyses for Prediction and Prevention. Sports Medicine. 2016.
abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis tested the psychosocial variables proposed in the model of stress and athletic injury as predictors of injury, and the effects of psychologically based interventions on injury occurrence. The review included 48 studies with 161 effect sizes for prediction and 7 intervention studies. Stress responses and history of stressors had the strongest associations with injury, and all seven intervention studies reported fewer injuries in intervention groups.
tldr: Psychosocial stress is linked to injury risk, but the associations are small. Psychologically based programmes were associated with fewer injuries in the seven included prevention studies, although the evidence base is small.
methods: The authors searched four databases and several sport psychology journals, and included prospective or experimental studies that measured injury frequency and used traumatic injury definitions. Correlations were pooled with a meta-analytic approach that corrected for measurement error, and a meta-analytic path analysis tested the stress-injury model. Moderator analyses were run where heterogeneity reached 50%.
findings: Stress responses (r = 0.27, k = 4) and history of stressors (r = 0.13, k = 72) had the strongest associations with injury rate, while coping (r = -0.07) and personality (r = 0.01) were weak. The path model fit acceptably (CFI 0.93, RMSEA 0.06) and explained 7.3% of injury variance. The seven prevention studies gave a pooled d of -0.63 (80% CI -0.88 to -0.38), with larger effects in at-risk samples (d = -0.88) than in normal samples (d = -0.45). Note: the Results text gives the stress-response upper CI as 0.37, while Table 3 gives 0.33; this review uses Table 3.
limitations: Stress response was based on only four effect sizes, the path between interventions and stress response could not be tested, and the path model borrowed estimates from a meta-analysis outside sport for cells with no sport data. Most predictors were measured once with self-report, and none of the intervention studies measured mechanisms. Prevention moderator groups were very small (k = 3 at-risk, k = 4 normal).
practicalImplications: Psychological stress and recent life stressors are worth screening for alongside physical risk factors. Psychologically based programmes can be considered as part of injury prevention, and the review did not compare them directly with physical programmes.
athleteDev: Stress management and mindfulness-type programmes may be worth piloting with athletes who report high stress, with injury tracking in place to judge their effect. The review does not show that these programmes improve performance.
rtp: This review can inform awareness of psychological stress as an injury risk factor, but it does not provide evidence on how to manage the psychological recovery of athletes returning from injury.

citation: Currie A, McDuff D, Johnston A, Hopley P, Hitchcock ME, Reardon CL, et al. Management of mental health emergencies in elite athletes: a narrative review. Br J Sports Med. 2019;0:1-7.
abstract: Mental health emergencies need a rapid, effective response, and sports teams should anticipate which emergencies are likely. The authors searched the literature and found five papers, none on elite athletes, so they relied on general non-sporting guidelines. The review covers how common emergencies such as delirium, substance misuse, suicidality, anxiety and personality disorders may present in athletes, and how to assess and manage them.
tldr: Elite athletes can present with the full range of mental health emergencies, but there is almost no sport-specific evidence to guide care. Clinicians should use standard emergency mental health procedures and have a written, rehearsed action plan in place before an emergency happens.
methods: Narrative review. Key databases (PubMed, SPORTDiscus, PsycINFO, Scopus, Cochrane) were searched for English-language papers by one author, yielding 96 articles that were reduced to 5 relevant papers. All authors then used these to find supplementary material, and the non-sporting literature on diagnosis, prevalence and treatment of mental health emergencies was reviewed.
findings: The review found very limited data on the nature and frequency of mental health emergencies in elite athletes. At London 2012, the Olympic psychiatry service received 12 referrals (11 athletes, 1 administrator), of which 4 were mental health emergencies (2 adjustment disorder, 1 panic disorder, 1 PTSD). The authors recommend a written, rehearsed emergency action plan, structured assessment, verbal de-escalation before oral and then parenteral medication, and state that no sport-specific treatments exist.
limitations: There is no systematic synthesis of sport-specific evidence, and the search was limited to English-language papers by a single author. The review relies on expert opinion and extrapolation from non-sporting populations, and the London 2012 figures are unpublished service data.
practicalImplications: Sports organisations should write and rehearse a mental health emergency action plan that covers suicidal or homicidal ideation, acute intoxication, delirium, psychosis and sexual assault. Staff should know local procedures for involuntary retention and when to contact emergency services. Reviewing each emergency afterwards is advised.
athleteDev: For performance staff, the paper supports planning for mental health emergencies during travel and major events, including who will respond and where care will be given. It gives no evidence on how emergencies affect performance outcomes.
rtp: The paper notes that time away from sport for injury or illness can raise distress and the risk of emotional decompensation, and that exclusion from training should be planned with mental health support. It does not provide a return-to-sport protocol and cannot be used to set return-to-sport criteria.

citation: Purcell R, Frost J, Pilkington V. Mental Health of Elite Sport Coaches and Entourage. Clin Sports Med. 2023.
abstract: The mental health of elite coaches and entourage staff has been understudied compared with that of elite athletes. These staff face similar sport-related stressors, and the available evidence, though scarce, shows depression, anxiety and psychological distress at levels similar to elite athlete samples. The authors propose that mental health screening, literacy, psychological safety and pathways to support should be extended to coaches and entourage in high-performance environments.
tldr: Elite coaches and support staff face many of the same stressors as athletes, and the limited data suggest similar rates of mental health symptoms. Screening and support designed for athletes should be extended to these staff, although the evidence base is still small.
methods: Narrative review of published studies on mental health, burnout and wellbeing in elite coaches, with a summary of the authors' 2022 survey of Australian high-performance coaches and support staff (coaches n = 78; entourage n = 174), conducted March to May 2020. Outcomes were probable caseness (GHQ-28), psychological distress (K-10), sleep disturbance (ASSQ) and risky alcohol use (AUDIT-C).
findings: Reported anxiety and depression prevalence in elite coach samples ranged widely (e.g., 14.1% to 39.5% for distress or symptom thresholds in different studies). In the 2022 survey, probable caseness was 43.6% for coaches and 40.1% for entourage, high to very high psychological distress 10.3% and 15.5%, moderate to severe sleep disturbance 23.4% and 15.1%, and risky drinking 48.1% and 39.0%. No significant group differences were found, and satisfaction with life balance and social support were the strongest correlates. The authors note that age was the only demographic correlate of distress, with younger staff reporting more distress.
limitations: Most included studies had predominantly male samples, used different measures and cut-offs, and were small. The key survey was cross-sectional, collected during COVID-19 lockdowns, and relied on self-report. The review is narrative, so its selection of studies is not systematic.
practicalImplications: Coaches and support staff can be included in mental health screening, literacy training and clear referral pathways alongside athletes. Organisations can check life balance, social support and psychological safety as practical correlates to monitor.
