Concussed patients showed higher heart rates, lower RR intervals and higher perceived exertion at similar workloads, and exercise-based treatment studies reported symptom reduction in persistent post-concussion cohorts, while most symptom-monitored acute exertion studies showed a decrease or no change.
limitations: The authors note that exercise protocols differed widely, cohorts were predominantly male and under 30, and fitness ranged from sedentary to elite. Section 4 gives 40 to 50% and 60 to 70% of HRmax for untrained and well-trained patients, while the conclusions give 40% and 60%; the conclusions are reported here. The paper itself says the value of starting by day three is likely prudent but warrants investigation.
practicalImplications: The review supports a conservative start with low-intensity aerobic exercise in the subacute phase, after a short rest, with heart rate or RPE monitored closely. Suggested doses are about 10 to 15 minutes at 40% of HRmax for untrained or deconditioned patients, or 15 to 20 minutes at 60% of HRmax for well-trained patients, on a treadmill where possible.
athleteDev: Coaches and performance staff can use the review's view that low-intensity exercise is tolerable to plan light aerobic work for an athlete with a recent concussion, under clinical supervision. The paper does not address training load, sport-specific conditioning or when an athlete can progress beyond low-intensity work.
rtp: The review places low-intensity aerobic exercise within a graded return-to-play protocol, but it does not set return-to-play or clearance criteria. Where lower-extremity injury or severe vestibular dysfunction prevents treadmill use, the authors suggest a stationary bike or upper-body ergometer.

citation: Schallmo MS, Singh SK, Barth KA, Freshman RD, Mai HT, Hsu WK. A cross-sport comparison of performance-based outcomes of professional athletes following primary microfracture of the knee. The Knee. 2018.
abstract: Professional athletes in four North American leagues who had knee microfracture were tracked against their own pre-surgery season. Most returned to play, and basketball and baseball players had lower performance one season after surgery, with baseball recovering by seasons two to three and basketball not.
tldr: Most professional athletes returned to a major league game after knee microfracture, but how well they performed afterwards depended on the sport. Basketball players stayed below their pre-surgery level in later seasons, and NFL players returned less often but did not show a performance drop.
methods: The authors identified 131 men who had primary unilateral knee microfracture while on an active roster, using news archives and team reports cross-checked against two sources. Return to play meant at least one regular-season game in a major league after surgery. Performance scores (OPS, WHIP, PER and sport-specific scores) were compared with the season before surgery, using paired t-tests, adjusted for each sport's season and career length.
findings: A total of 103 of 131 athletes (78.6%) returned, with 100% of MLB players returning versus 75% of all other sports combined (p = 0.013), and 71.1% of NFL players versus 89.0% of others (p = 0.017). Games started as a share of games played before surgery predicted return (p = 0.002). Basketball and baseball players had lower performance one season after surgery (-14.8%, p = 0.029; -12.9%, p = 0.002), and basketball players remained lower in seasons two to three (-9.7%, p = 0.024).
limitations: The text says differences in change in performance (career before vs career after surgery) between individual sports were not significant, which conflicts with the abstract and conclusion that performance varied significantly by sport; the sport findings are each sport compared with its own baseline or with all other sports combined. Performance scores were available for only 82 of the 103 returners (offensive linemen, rookies and the 3 NHL players were excluded), with 40 having two or more years of follow-up. Cases came from public sources, so concomitant procedures, lesion details and rehabilitation were unknown, and only men were studied.
practicalImplications: When counselling an athlete with a knee chondral injury, staff should use the sport, position and pre-surgery level of play, as the authors suggest, rather than a single return-to-play rate. Basketball and baseball players may need longer performance expectations, but the study does not show that these differences are larger than those in other sports.
athleteDev: Baseball players dropped in performance in the first season after microfracture but recovered by seasons two to three, NFL players who returned showed no performance drop, and basketball players stayed below baseline in seasons two to three. Staff should not assume the same performance trajectory across sports.
rtp: The study is directly about return to professional play after knee microfracture, and found that 78.6% of players returned. It does not capture rehabilitation progress, readiness criteria or complications, so it cannot be used to set a return-to-play clearance standard.

citation: Yung KK, Ardern CL, Serpiello FR, Robertson S. A framework for clinicians to improve the decision-making process in return to sport. Sports Medicine - Open. 2022;8:52.
abstract: This narrative review applies a decision analysis model to return-to-sport decisions, covering test methodology, decision-making theories and the perspectives of athletes and staff. It proposes a three-step framework for clinicians to improve decision quality in return to sport.
tldr: Return-to-sport decisions can be improved by making the basis for each decision explicit: choose and interpret tests carefully, check the reasoning for predictable biases, and reach a shared decision with the athlete and staff. The framework is conceptual and has not been tested against return-to-sport or re-injury outcomes.
methods: This is a narrative review rather than a systematic review. The authors adapt a decision analysis model to structure the decision basis (alternatives, information, decision models and preferences) and discuss test validity, normative and descriptive decision theories, and shared decision-making. A hypothetical anterior cruciate ligament case and two worked tables using arbitrary units illustrate the criteria and rule-based approaches.
findings: The review reports that the 90% limb symmetry index threshold has little evidence behind it, and that passing a test does not show a satisfactory return outcome, since a recent study found no association between functional test cut-offs and new ACL injury. It notes that some tests normalise at different times, and that a 12.96% change is the smallest meaningful change for the 6-m timed hop test. It also describes how heuristics and biases can shape clinicians' return-to-sport judgements, and reports that the decision-making literature in sports medicine is sparse.
limitations: As a narrative review, the search and selection of evidence are not reproducible, and the authors say that empirical knowledge of how sports decisions are made is limited. The worked ACL examples are hypothetical, with equal importance in Table 1 and clinician-chosen weights in arbitrary units in Table 2, so they show how the rules could be applied rather than what good decisions look like.
practicalImplications: Clinicians can use the three steps (choose and interpret tests, check for predictable biases in the reasoning, and involve the athlete and coach in a shared decision) to make the basis for a return-to-sport decision explicit and open to challenge. Staff should not treat a single passing test score, such as a 90% limb symmetry index, as proof that an athlete is ready to return to play.
athleteDev: The review gives staff a way to talk through return-to-sport decisions with coaches and athletes, including the competition calendar and the athlete's own priorities. It does not provide performance outcomes or a validated performance measure.
rtp: The review is directly about return to sport and recommends a shared, transparent decision process. It does not provide validated clearance criteria, so it cannot be used as a clearance standard on its own.

citation: Mendiguchia J, Brughelli M. A return-to-sport algorithm for acute hamstring injuries. Physical Therapy in Sport. 2010:1-13 (in press).
abstract: Clinical commentary proposing a step-by-step return-to-sport model after acute hamstring injury. The model uses objective clinical and functional tests, with a treatment protocol at each step. The authors argue that current programmes rely on pain, time and isokinetic criteria, and they present the model as a foundation for future research.
tldr: Pain-free movement and time-based criteria may miss strength, flexibility and asymmetry deficits that may drive re-injury. The authors propose objective tests to pass at each phase, but the algorithm itself is unvalidated.
methods: Clinical commentary (Masterclass) with no original data. It summarises seven published hamstring management programmes in tables and builds a three-phase algorithm from the cited literature on muscle injury, strength, flexibility, neural tension, hip and trunk function, and imaging. No systematic search method or quality appraisal is described.
findings: The authors note that most of the seven prior programmes progress athletes on pain, time or range of motion, and only three use an objective isokinetic asymmetry criterion. They propose criteria including no problems 5 days after injury before the sub-acute phase and a hamstring strength asymmetry below 10% in prone isometric testing at 15 degrees of knee flexion (citing Warren et al., 2008), and they cite 45.9% leg asymmetry in horizontal running force in previously injured Australian rules football players (Brughelli et al., 2009). They also state that imaging alone cannot establish a safe return to play.
limitations: The algorithm is stated to be unvalidated, and its criteria come largely from small, retrospective or experimental studies that the authors cite but do not appraise. The full step-by-step algorithm is in Figure 1, which is not in the extracted text; the body text gives some pass thresholds (5-day check, under 10% strength asymmetry, ASLR without anterior pelvic tilt) but not numeric pass values for every functional-phase test. The authors note that prospective, retrospective and training studies are needed.
practicalImplications: Do not clear an athlete after acute hamstring injury on pain-free movement alone; the authors recommend adding objective strength, flexibility and symmetry tests. Test hamstring strength at long muscle lengths, such as prone isometric at 15 degrees of knee flexion, and treat the proposed asymmetry threshold of under 10% as a hypothesis to test. Use imaging alongside functional tests rather than alone.
athleteDev: The paper addresses injury rehabilitation rather than performance. It suggests horizontal force and eccentric hamstring training to reduce leg asymmetries, but it reports no performance outcomes.
rtp: The paper proposes return-to-sport criteria, including a 10% hamstring strength asymmetry threshold, but states the algorithm is not validated. It should not be used as a return-to-play clearance standard until prospective validation exists, and several functional-phase tests lack pass values in the text.

citation: Kerin F, O'Flanagan S, Coyle J, Curley D, Farrell G, McCarthy Persson U, et al. Are all hamstring injuries equal? A retrospective analysis of time to return to full training following BAMIC type 'c' and T-junction injuries in professional men's rugby union. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2024;34:e14586.
abstract: Retrospective review of 91 hamstring muscle injuries in 46 professional men's rugby union players over five seasons. Injuries with intramuscular tendon involvement took longer to return to full training, while neither intramuscular tendon nor T-junction involvement was associated with a higher rate of subsequent injury.
tldr: In this professional rugby cohort, hamstring injuries with intramuscular tendon involvement took much longer to return to full training, about three times longer by the authors' account. These injuries did not show a higher rate of subsequent injury in the same limb.
methods: Retrospective cohort review of electronic medical records at one professional club, July 2015 to June 2021. A blinded musculoskeletal radiologist classified MRI-confirmed injuries using the BAMIC framework and T-junction status. Time to full training and subsequent injury within 12 months were compared with Kaplan-Meier, log-rank, Fisher exact and odds ratio analyses.
findings: Of 143 registered injuries, 91 in 46 players were analysed; 26 (29%) were intramuscular tendon injuries (BAMIC 'c'). Median time to full training was 81 days (IQR 38 to 112) with intramuscular tendon involvement against 18 days (IQR 14 to 24) without (p < 0.0001; hazard ratio 2.99, 95% CI 1.98 to 4.51). For biceps femoris injuries, median time to full training was 18 days without and 24 days with T-junction involvement (hazard ratio 1.08, 0.59 to 1.94). Subsequent hamstring injury to either leg within 12 months followed 42 of 91 injuries (46%); odds ratios for re-injury/subsequent injury were 0.96 (0.37 to 2.64) for intramuscular tendon and 1.03 (0.30 to 3.99) for T-junction involvement, neither significant.
limitations: The study was retrospective, players and clinicians were not blinded to MRI results, and only MRI-confirmed injuries with more than 7 days absence from one male club were included, with small numbers in some categories. The abstract disagrees with the results: it gives 78 versus 24 days for intramuscular tendon injuries and 29 versus 27 days for T-junction injuries, while the results give medians of 81 versus 18 days and 24 versus 18 days; the T-junction result is printed as p < 0.0001 yet called not significant (its hazard ratio CI of 0.59 to 1.94 is consistent with no difference). The Discussion also gives 24% intramuscular tendon injuries against 29% in the results; the record uses the results values.
practicalImplications: Medical staff should tell an injured player and coaches that a hamstring injury with intramuscular tendon involvement is likely to need a much longer time to full training, though part of the gap may reflect more cautious management by unblinded clinicians. T-junction involvement in biceps femoris injuries did not significantly change time to full training in this cohort of 18 such injuries.
athleteDev: Performance and conditioning staff should expect a longer reconditioning and staged loading period for hamstring injuries with intramuscular tendon involvement, because full training took much longer in this cohort. Subsequent injury rates did not differ significantly by tendon involvement, but the wide confidence intervals cannot rule out a difference.
rtp: The study measures time to full training, not time to match play, and it does not test rehabilitation methods, so it can set an expected timeline but not clearance criteria.

citation: Hong CC, Calder J. Ability to return to sports after early lateral ligament repair of the ankle in 147 elite athletes. Knee Surgery, Sports Traumatology, Arthroscopy. 2022.
abstract: Retrospective review of 147 elite athletes treated with a modified Broström repair for acute grade III lateral ligament injury (2015 to 2019, minimum 2-year follow-up). All returned to pre-injury level with a median return time of 69 days, and associated deltoid, syndesmosis and osteochondral lesions predicted longer return times. Re-injury occurred in 2% of athletes.
tldr: Elite athletes who had early surgical repair for an acute grade III ankle ligament tear returned to their pre-injury sport in about 10 weeks in this series, with re-injury in 2%. Associated deltoid, syndesmosis or talar cartilage injury added time to recovery.
methods: Single-surgeon retrospective review of prospectively collected records of elite athletes (national or international level, or paid) who had a modified Broström repair within 3 weeks of an MRI-confirmed grade III injury. Time to return was taken from club medical staff. Groups were compared with chi-square, Fisher exact and Mann-Whitney tests, and multiple linear regression adjusted for age, sex and associated injuries.
findings: All 147 athletes returned to pre-injury level, with a median of 69 days (range 58 to 132). Isolated lateral ligament injuries returned in a mean of 68.6 days against 82.8 days with associated injuries (p = 0.004). Regression estimates for longer return were deltoid injury +7.5 days (95% CI 2.9 to 12.3), syndesmosis injury +6.7 days (0.5 to 12.8) and osteochondral lesion +30.3 days (25.1 to 35.5). Three athletes (2%) re-injured the same ankle, and four (2.7%) had superficial wound infection; age, sex and sport type were not associated with return time.
limitations: The study is retrospective with no control group, no patient-reported outcome measures, a single surgeon, and return times reported by club staff; athletes with associated OLT or deltoid injuries followed slower rehabilitation protocols, which may explain part of their delay. The results state '101 patients (89.1%) were males', but 101 of 147 is 68.7%, so the sex split is uncertain; the abstract gives 66.0% soccer players where the results give 65.9% (97 of 147). Associated-injury subgroups are small (9 deltoid, 5 syndesmosis, 7 OLT, 4 combined).
practicalImplications: For elite athletes with an acute grade III ankle ligament injury treated by early repair, plan for about 10 weeks to return to pre-injury sport. Expect about a week longer with a deltoid or syndesmosis injury and about a month longer with an osteochondral lesion, partly because those athletes followed slower rehabilitation protocols.
athleteDev: Performance staff can set return-to-sport expectations for elite athletes after early repair: a median of 69 days when isolated, and longer when the imaging shows a deltoid, syndesmosis or talar lesion.
rtp: This study supports a return-to-sport timeline for elite athletes after early Broström repair of an acute grade III injury. It does not test return criteria or strength and function measures, and it should not be applied to non-elite athletes or chronic instability.

citation: Chen P, Wang L, Dong S, Ding Y, Zuo H, Jia S, et al. Abnormal Lower Limb Biomechanics During a Bilateral Vertical Jump Despite the Symmetry in Single-Leg Vertical Hop Height in Athletes After ACL Reconstruction. Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2024;12(2):23259671241230989.
abstract: Athletes after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) who reached a limb symmetry index above 90% on the single-leg vertical hop still showed between-limb differences in joint moments and vertical ground-reaction force during a bilateral vertical jump. The study compared 46 athletes after ACLR (mean 15.8 months post surgery), grouped by vertical hop symmetry, with 24 noninjured athletes using motion capture and force plates. The authors conclude that symmetric vertical hop height did not represent normal lower-limb biomechanics in this sample.
tldr: After ACL reconstruction, athletes who reached 90% or better limb symmetry on the single-leg vertical hop still showed altered operated-side mechanics during a bilateral vertical jump. A symmetric single-leg vertical hop should not be taken as proof of normal jump mechanics or return-to-sport readiness.
methods: Controlled laboratory case-control study. Athletes after ACLR (autograft bone-patellar tendon-bone or hamstring), all cleared by surgeon and rehabilitation specialist to return to high-level activity, with a horizontal hop limb symmetry index above 90% and preinjury Tegner of 7 or more, were split by single-leg vertical hop limb symmetry index into below 90% and above 90% groups and compared with 24 noninjured athletes. Nine-camera motion capture (200 Hz) and four force plates (1000 Hz) gave joint angles and body-weight-normalized joint moments during a bilateral vertical jump; within-group paired t tests and between-group one-way ANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc tests were used.
findings: In the above 90% group, the operated side showed a lower knee extension moment during propulsion than the nonoperated side (P=.001), and at peak vertical ground-reaction force a higher hip extension moment (P=.002), lower knee extension moment (P<.001), lower ankle plantarflexion moment (P<.001) and lower vertical ground-reaction force (P=.023). Compared with controls, both the operated (P=.016) and nonoperated (P=.040) sides of this group had a lower knee internal rotation moment at peak vertical ground-reaction force. Athletes below 90% (vertical hop limb symmetry index 78.8%) showed larger and more widespread deficits, including higher hip flexion angles than controls on both sides at initial contact and peak vertical ground-reaction force.
limitations: Graft types were not uniform, quadriceps strength and hip, knee and ankle range of motion were not measured, and sports were not separated. Men and women were not analyzed separately because of sample size. The study compares groups at one time point and does not test whether these patterns predict reinjury. The explanations offered in the Discussion, such as fear of reinjury, are not tested by the study.
practicalImplications: Passing a 90% vertical hop limb symmetry index does not confirm normal bilateral landing and jump mechanics after ACL reconstruction. Where motion analysis or video is available, a bilateral vertical jump can add a check of operated-side knee extension moment and vertical ground-reaction force to return-to-sport testing. These are group findings from 46 athletes and should not be applied as individual cut-offs.
athleteDev: A symmetric single-leg vertical hop did not mean the operated limb shared load evenly in a bilateral jump in this sample. Performance staff with force plates can look at between-limb force and loading in bilateral jumps rather than relying on hop symmetry alone, though the study did not test any training intervention.
rtp: The study can inform the choice of return-to-sport tests, because a 90% or higher vertical hop symmetry did not guarantee normal bilateral jump mechanics. It cannot be used to set a return-to-sport cut-off or to show that an athlete is safe to return, since it did not measure reinjury or sport outcomes.

citation: Brauner T, Pourcelot P, Crevier-Denoix N, Horstmann T, Wearing SC. Achilles Tendon Load is Progressively Increased with Reductions in Walking Speed. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2017;49(10):2001-2008.
abstract: Ultrasound velocity was measured in the Achilles tendon of 33 healthy adults walking on a treadmill at slow, preferred and fast speeds. Velocity fell as speed increased, despite higher vertical ground reaction forces and greater ankle plantarflexion. The authors interpret this as lower tendon load at faster speeds, which questions the common practice of starting tendon rehabilitation with slow walking.
tldr: In healthy adults, an ultrasound measure of Achilles tendon velocity fell as walking speed increased, even though ground reaction force rose. This challenges the common assumption that slow walking gives the lowest tendon load, but the findings come from healthy adults on a treadmill.
methods: Repeated-measures laboratory study. Thirty-three healthy adults (mean age 29 years, mean weight 71.4 kg) walked barefoot on an instrumented treadmill at slow, preferred and fast speeds, with 6 minutes of steady-state walking and 60 seconds of data at each speed. Transmission-mode ultrasound (1 MHz probe over the right Achilles tendon) measured tendon transmission velocity, alongside ankle goniometry and vertical ground reaction force; speed effects were tested with repeated-measures ANOVA.
findings: Faster walking produced higher vertical ground reaction force peaks (first peak 1.08, 1.11 and 1.17 body weight), roughly double the loading rate from slow to fast, and shorter stance. Tendon transmission velocity during stance fell with each increase in speed, with the first minimum falling by 16 m/s from slow to preferred and 23 m/s from preferred to fast (P=0.002) and the first peak falling from 2255 to 2232 to 2212 m/s (P=0.007), while swing-phase values did not change. The authors interpret the decline as a speed-dependent reduction in tensile load and call it likely clinically significant, but the total change from slow to fast is about 2% of the slow-speed value (2017 to 1978 m/s).
limitations: Participants were healthy, recreationally active adults walking barefoot on a treadmill over a narrow speed range, so the results may not transfer to people with Achilles tendon disorders, to running, or to shod or overground walking. Tendon load is inferred from ultrasound transmission velocity, and no electromyography or direct force was measured, so tendon load cannot be separated from muscle activity or passive structures. The text has minor inconsistencies with its tables: the Results say faster walking had a longer stride duration where Table 1 shows it shorter (1.27 to 1.01 s), and the first plantarflexion peak described as increasing gets smaller in Table 3 (-5.6 to -5.2 degrees).
practicalImplications: Do not reverse walking-speed progressions in Achilles tendon rehabilitation on the basis of this study alone. The findings are a hypothesis to test in people with Achilles tendon disorders, not a loading prescription.
athleteDev: This study concerns walking speed and an indirect tendon load measure in healthy adults, not training or performance. It should not be used to set running or jumping loads.
rtp: The authors argue that the usual order of slow walking first may be wrong, but that conclusion comes from healthy adults and an indirect measure. The study cannot set return-to-sport loading or show that faster walking is safe or useful for injured athletes.

citation: Howell DR, Seehusen CN, Carry PM, Walker GA, Reinking SE, Wilson JC. An 8-Week Neuromuscular Training Program After Concussion Reduces 1-Year Subsequent Injury Risk: A Randomized Clinical Trial. Am J Sports Med. 2022.
abstract: This pilot randomized trial tested an 8-week neuromuscular training program started after return-to-play clearance in 27 youth athletes with a recent concussion. Athletes in the training group had fewer sports-related time-loss injuries over the following year than the standard-of-care group, with an age- and sex-adjusted hazard ratio of 3.56. The authors describe the result as preliminary.
tldr: In a small pilot trial, an 8-week neuromuscular training block after return-to-play clearance was associated with fewer time-loss injuries over the next year in youth athletes after concussion. The trial is too small to confirm an injury-prevention effect.
methods: Block-stratified randomized trial (1:1) in which 27 athletes aged 12 to 18 years were randomized after return-to-play clearance to 8 weeks of supervised neuromuscular training (two sessions per week, about 18 minutes each) or no added program. Monthly online logs tracked time-loss injuries and competition exposure for 12 months. The primary analysis was per-protocol, with a Cox model and negative binomial models adjusted for age and sex.
findings: Injury was reported by 75% (12/16) of the standard-of-care group and 36% (4/11) of the training group. The age- and sex-adjusted hazard ratio for any subsequent injury was 3.56 (95% CI, 1.11-11.49; P = .0334). The incidence rate ratio for all injuries was 2.96 (95% CI, 0.89-9.85; P = .076), and the lower-extremity injury rate ratio was 2.55 (95% CI, 0.54-12.16; P = .2394), which was not significant. Reported sports participation did not differ between groups.
limitations: The trial is a small, single-site pilot with a per-protocol primary analysis (two randomized intervention athletes who declined the program were analyzed as standard of care), and the enrollment target of 40 was not reached; the authors report the intention-to-treat results as consistent. Injuries were self-reported, contact and noncontact injuries were not separated, the training group had more prior physical activity and more history of multiple concussions at baseline, and COVID-19 restrictions in 2020 may have affected exposure and reporting. The text also leaves an unfilled editorial placeholder where the significance test for the unadjusted lower-extremity incidence comparison should be, so that result has no reported test.
practicalImplications: An 8-week, twice-weekly program of guided strength and landing exercises can be added after return-to-play clearance for youth athletes with a recent concussion, with low time demand and high adherence in this sample. Staff should treat the injury-reduction signal as a reason to study the approach further, not as established protection. The study did not test the program against an active control or assess injury risk in adult or elite athletes.
athleteDev: The program is a feasible, low-time-cost block (about 40 minutes per week for 8 weeks) that uses strength and landing work, and 91% of athletes completed at least 75% of the sessions. Its effect on later performance was not measured. Staff should not expect a performance benefit from this study.
rtp: The program was started after return-to-play clearance and during the early return to sport, so this study can support adding a neuromuscular training block at that stage for youth athletes with a recent concussion. It cannot establish that clearance criteria should change, and it does not show that the program reduces injury risk in adults or elite athletes.

citation: Liu JN, Gowd AK, Garcia GH, Manderle BJ, Beletsky A, Nicholson GP, et al. An Analysis of Return to Sport and Weight Training After Repair of the Pectoralis Major Tendon. Am J Sports Med. 2019;47(9):2151-2157.
abstract: This retrospective case series reviewed 44 men who had pectoralis major tendon repair and were followed up for a mean of 51 months. Clinical scores improved significantly, and 97.7% returned to sport at some level, but only 50% returned at the same or better intensity. Reported weight-lifting strength was lower after surgery, and 38.6% had apprehension about lifting.
tldr: After pectoralis major tendon repair, most patients returned to sport at some level, but only half returned at their previous intensity. Strength for bench pressing and push-ups was reported lower on average, and many had apprehension about lifting.
methods: Retrospective review of a prospectively maintained database of patients who underwent pectoralis major repair between January 2010 and August 2016. Patients were contacted by telephone and completed a standardized questionnaire on pre- and postinjury sport, competition level, self-reported one-repetition and five-repetition maximums, push-up counts, ASES and SANE scores. Pre- and postinjury values were compared with Student t tests, and a stepwise logistic regression looked at factors linked to return to sport at the same or better intensity.
findings: Return to sport at any level was 43 of 44 (97.7%), and 22 of 44 (50.0%) returned at the same or better intensity. Mean self-reported declines were 23.3% for 1RM barbell bench press, 14.7% for 5RM barbell bench press, 24.3% for 1RM dumbbell bench press, 35.7% for 1RM dumbbell fly and 15.6% for push-up count. ASES and SANE scores improved significantly (P < .001). In the multivariable model, injury during sport was associated with return at the same or better intensity (OR 2.231; 95% CI, 1.234-4.031), and contralateral shoulder surgery was associated with a lower likelihood (OR 0.600; 95% CI, 0.389-0.925). Three patients (6.8%) needed return to the operating room.
limitations: This is a single-center, uncontrolled series of men only, with 16 of 60 patients lost to follow-up, and strength values were self-reported and recalled from the 3 years before injury rather than measured. The stepwise regression used many variables in 44 patients, and its reporting is inconsistent: Table 3 gives acute repair an OR of 0.745 with a 95% CI of 0.608-1.060 (P = .053) while the text gives 0.559-0.993, the text lists contralateral surgery as both increasing and decreasing the likelihood of return, acute repair is defined as under 6 months in the Methods but under 6 weeks in the regression, and the Discussion says sport injury was the only associated variable. The clavicular head row (OR 1.536, 95% CI 1.144-4.221, P = .237) is also internally inconsistent, so the regression results should be treated as unreliable.
practicalImplications: Counsel patients that nearly all return to some sport, but about half return at their previous intensity, and that self-reported pressing and push-up numbers were lower on average. Injury during sport and prior contralateral shoulder surgery were the associated factors with consistent reporting, but the regression is too small and inconsistently reported to guide individual expectations. Plan for apprehension with lifting, which 38.6% reported, and do not treat the strength decline figures as precise, given their wide spread.
athleteDev: Expect lower pressing and push-up output after pectoralis major repair, with an average self-reported 1RM bench press decline of about 23% and wide variation between patients. Build the return-to-lifting progression around these changes, and monitor apprehension as well as load, since it affected 38.6% of patients.
rtp: The series can inform return-to-sport expectations: 97.7% returned to sport at some level, 50.0% at the same or better intensity, and full-duty sport at a mean of 7.7 months (SD 3.3), with three patients taking 36 to 50 months. It cannot set clearance criteria, because it did not test strength or readiness against return outcomes and the outcome measures were self-reported.

citation: Berckmans K, Castelein B, Borms D, Palmans T, Parlevliet T, Cools A. Analysis of Scapular Kinematics and Muscle Activity by Use of Fine-Wire Electrodes During Shoulder Exercises. Am J Sports Med. 2020.
abstract: This descriptive laboratory study measured 3D scapular kinematics with surface and fine-wire EMG during four common early shoulder rehabilitation exercises in 23 healthy men. Scapular position and deep muscle activity differed between exercises, with the lawnmower showing less pectoralis minor activity than the low row. The authors conclude that the lawnmower gave a favorable scapular position, and that three of the exercises should not be used in early rehabilitation because of moderate infraspinatus activity.
tldr: In healthy men, the lawnmower and robbery produced more rhomboid activity and less pectoralis minor activity than the inferior glide and low row, and the low row produced the least infraspinatus activity. Muscle activity and scapular position in healthy people do not show how these exercises perform in injured patients.
methods: Twenty-three healthy men performed four exercises, each five times. Three-dimensional scapular position was measured with motion capture, and EMG was recorded from upper, middle and lower trapezius and serratus anterior with surface electrodes, and from levator scapulae, rhomboid major, pectoralis minor and infraspinatus with fine-wire electrodes. EMG was normalized to % MVIC, and the isometric end-hold of each exercise was analyzed with a linear mixed model with Bonferroni correction.
findings: The inferior glide and low row had scapular internal rotation of about 31 and 42 degrees, compared with about 13 to 15 degrees for the lawnmower and robbery, and only the lawnmower produced posterior tilt. Middle trapezius activity was 36% and 39% MVIC for the lawnmower and robbery, significantly higher than the inferior glide (18%) but not the low row (26%) in the pairwise tests, although the abstract reports both. Rhomboid major activity was 59% and 66% for the lawnmower and robbery against about 27% to 28% for the other two, and pectoralis minor activity was 9.5% and 12% against 34% to 44%. Infraspinatus activity was 13% MVIC for the low row and 24% to 37% for the other exercises.
limitations: Only healthy, young men without a stated sport background (no more than 4 hours a week of overhead activity) were tested, and the authors note some discomfort may have been present with fine-wire placement. The exercises could not be fully standardized, and only the infraspinatus of the rotator cuff was measured. The abstract states that middle trapezius activity was higher for the lawnmower and robbery than for both the inferior glide and low row, but the Table 4 pairwise tests show significance only against the inferior glide.
practicalImplications: Use the study as a comparison of scapular position and deep muscle activity across these four exercises, not as a set of rules for injured patients. The authors suggest the lawnmower when posterior tilt is needed and pectoralis minor activity should be kept low, and the low row when infraspinatus activity should be kept low, but these suggestions were not tested in patients. Confirm any exercise choice against the patient's own symptoms and presentation.
athleteDev: This study does not address strength, power or performance outcomes. It is relevant only to the choice of scapular exercise in rehabilitation, where the authors compare muscle activity levels in healthy men.
rtp: The study describes muscle activity during four early shoulder rehabilitation exercises in healthy men and cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. The authors' suggestions on which exercises to avoid in early rehabilitation were drawn from healthy-participant data, not from injured athletes, so they should not be used as return-to-sport criteria.

citation: Dekker TJ, Goldenberg B, Lacheta L, Horan MP, Millett PJ. Anterior Shoulder Instability in the Professional Athlete: Return to Competition, Time to Return, and Career Length. Orthop J Sports Med. 2020;8(11):2325967120959728.
abstract: Retrospective case series of 23 professional athletes who had surgery for anterior shoulder instability. Return to the previous competition level occurred in 96% at a mean of 4.5 months, with similar return times for contact and noncontact athletes and for Bankart repair and Latarjet procedures.
tldr: Most professional athletes in this single-surgeon series returned to their previous competition level after anterior shoulder stabilization, at about 4.5 months. Return times did not differ by contact status or by procedure, and the apparent difference in career length was not statistically significant.
methods: Retrospective case series of professional athletes (full-time at the highest level and paid) treated by one surgeon between 2007 and 2018, identified from a prospective patient registry, medical records and public sources such as team and search websites. Outcomes were return to competition at the same level, time to return, recurrence and career length after surgery. Groups compared were contact vs noncontact athletes and Bankart repair vs open Latarjet; the authors note that patients with more bone loss and prior surgery were selected for Latarjet.
findings: 22 of 23 athletes (96%) returned to the same level, at a mean of 4.5 months (range 3-8); the one non-returner, a baseball player, had recurrent instability after Bankart repair, was revised to Latarjet and then tore his ACL. Return time was 4.6 months after Bankart repair and 4.2 months after Latarjet, and 4.1 vs 4.4 months for contact vs noncontact athletes, with no significant differences. Twelve athletes were still competing at a mean of 4.3 years after surgery, and 11 had retired at a mean of 4.8 years. Play after surgery was 3.8 years for contact and 5.8 years for noncontact athletes (P>.05).
limitations: Small retrospective single-surgeon series with no comparison group, so instability after the follow-up period may have gone unrecorded. Procedure groups were not matched, the return-to-competition criteria were partly set by the senior author's rehabilitation protocol, and results may not generalize to recreational athletes. The abstract conclusion and Discussion state that contact athletes had shorter careers, but the reported comparison was not significant (P>.05).
practicalImplications: Sports medicine teams can tell professional athletes that most returned to their previous level at about 4.5 months after stabilization in this series. Procedure choice here followed bone loss and prior surgery, so the results do not support choosing one procedure for faster return. Early mobilization and close surveillance are the features the authors link to quick return, but this series cannot separate their effect from athlete selection.
athleteDev: Performance staff can use the 4.5-month mean (range 3-8) as a planning reference for elite athletes after this surgery, with the caveat that it comes from one surgeon's series. The shorter career for contact athletes was not statistically significant, so it should not be used alone to change load or career planning.
rtp: The outcome is return to competition, with clearance by the treating surgeon for full unrestricted activity. The series supports that most professional athletes returned to their prior level at about 4.5 months. It does not test return-to-sport criteria, strength or function measures, or instability recurrence in athletes who were not followed.

citation: Smeets A, Vanrenterghem J, Staes F, Vandenneucker H, Claes S, Verschueren S. Are Anterior Cruciate Ligament-reconstructed Athletes More Vulnerable to Fatigue than Uninjured Athletes? Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2020;52(2):345-353.
abstract: Twenty-one athletes after ACL reconstruction and 21 uninjured controls performed unilateral landing tasks before and after a match-simulation protocol, with kinematics, kinetics and muscle activation recorded. The groups responded similarly to fatigue overall, with only two group-by-fatigue interactions, both in the injured leg.
tldr: Athletes after ACL reconstruction and uninjured controls responded similarly to a match-simulation fatigue protocol during landing tasks. Two task-specific differences appeared in the injured leg, so fatigue testing may reveal deficits in some tasks but this study does not establish a clinical threshold.
methods: Twenty-one athletes who had ACL reconstruction with a semitendinosus autograft, and 21 matched uninjured controls, performed five unilateral landing tasks before and after a 5-minute match-simulation protocol (SAFT5). Three-dimensional kinematics, kinetics and EMG from seven muscles were analysed with a mixed-model two-way ANOVA (group and fatigue) and one-dimensional statistical parametric mapping over the first 500 ms after initial contact.
findings: Fatigue increased RPE-L and RPE-B in both groups (ACL group RPE-L 10.3 to 15.6, RPE-B 9.4 to 16.7) and reduced single-leg hop distance (ACL 1.87 to 1.79 m; control 1.87 to 1.77 m), with no group or interaction effects for RPE or jump performance. Both groups showed smaller hip, knee and ankle flexion angles after fatigue in several tasks. Only two interactions were significant in the injured leg vs controls: knee abduction moment in the lateral hop (interaction P = 0.044; post hoc increase in the ACLR leg only, 30-51 ms, P = 0.0069, ES 0.57) and thorax flexion angle in the vertical hop with 90 degrees medial rotation (interaction P < 0.001; post hoc ACLR leg vs controls 72-106 ms, P = 0.012, ES 0.55).
limitations: Only two interactions were found among many comparisons, each in one task, so these may be fragile findings. The fixed-demand protocol produced different fatigue levels between athletes, some reported very low RPE scores, and the authors note false negatives are more likely. The ACLR group was older than controls (23.8 vs 21.5 years, P = 0.028), the 5-minute protocol is shorter than real match play, and jump performance fell after fatigue without correction; the text and Table 3 give slightly different time windows (43-53 vs 43-54 ms) and P values (0.0023 vs 0.023) for some effects.
practicalImplications: The authors advise adding frontal-plane tasks, such as the lateral hop, to return-to-sport test batteries alongside forward and vertical tasks, because the knee abduction difference appeared only in that task. Staff should not conclude from this study that fatigue testing identifies athletes at risk of re-injury, since no injury outcomes were measured.
athleteDev: Both groups landed in a more extended pattern when fatigued, which the authors link to higher injury risk in both ACLR and uninjured athletes. The ACLR group also showed higher hamstring activation than controls, but the study did not test any training intervention, so it cannot guide performance programming beyond showing that fatigue responses were broadly similar between groups.
rtp: The authors advise including frontal-plane tasks such as the lateral hop in return-to-sport test batteries, because the knee abduction difference showed up only in that task. The study cannot show whether fatigued testing predicts re-injury or sets a clearance threshold, and it tested athletes about 8.5 months (258.6 +/- 54 days) after surgery.

citation: Beattie CE, Barnett RJ, Williams J, Sim J, Pullinger SA. Are return-to-play times longer in lower-limb muscle injuries involving the intramuscular tendon? A systematic review. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2023.
abstract: Nine studies of elite athletes were synthesised to compare return-to-play times for lower-limb muscle injuries with and without intramuscular tendon involvement. Best-evidence synthesis found no strong overall difference, and a pooled BAMIC 'b' vs 'c' analysis favoured the musculotendinous junction injuries (Hedges g 0.67), but the evidence rests mainly on high-risk-of-bias studies.
tldr: Lower-limb muscle injuries that involve the intramuscular tendon do not clearly take longer to return to play overall. A larger tendon disruption, MRI waviness or loss of tendon tension is associated with longer return times, but the evidence is weak because most studies had high risk of bias.
methods: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD42022343009) of English-language studies from six databases searched to 31 July 2023. Nine studies of elite athletes that compared time to return to play for lower-limb muscle injuries with and without IMT involvement were included, and risk of bias was rated with a modified QUIPS tool. The BAMIC 'b' vs 'c' estimates were pooled as Hedges g, and a best-evidence synthesis was applied to the other prognostic factors.
findings: The nine studies included 441 injuries in 319 athletes (57 women): seven hamstring and two quadriceps studies. Best-evidence synthesis found conflicting evidence for grade-by-grade differences, moderate evidence that hamstring and quadriceps IMT involvement were associated with longer return times, moderate evidence linking larger percentage cross-sectional tendon disruption, MRI waviness and loss of tendon tension to longer return times, and moderate evidence of no association for craniocaudal length. The pooled BAMIC 'b' vs 'c' estimate (11 estimates from seven studies, 160 injuries) was Hedges g 0.67 (95% CI 0.20 to 1.15; P = 0.002), a mean difference of 8.93 days (95% CI 1.63 to 16.22) favouring 'b', with I2 of 36.6%; the 3b vs 3c subgroup was imprecise (g 0.64, 95% CI -0.13 to 1.40).
limitations: Eight of nine studies were at high risk of bias, mainly from attrition and inconsistent prognostic-factor measurement, and only two reported that rehabilitation clinicians were blinded to MRI findings, so protective rehabilitation of IMT injuries may have lengthened return times. Return-to-play definitions varied, two studies included recurrences, several medians were converted to means, and the prediction interval (-0.39 to 1.73) includes zero. Table 4 counts Tears et al. as showing a CSA association although Table 2 reports a non-significant correlation for that study (r = 0.02, P = 0.91).
practicalImplications: The authors state that prognosis for muscle injuries with IMT involvement is still hard to pin down, but moderate evidence favours a better prognosis for BAMIC 'b' than 'c' injuries. Clinicians should be cautious with injuries that have a large percentage of cross-sectional tendon disruption, MRI waviness or loss of tendon tension, since these were associated with longer return times. The review found no strong evidence that longitudinal tendon length changes the prognosis.
athleteDev: The review addresses return-to-play timing, not performance, so it gives no direct guidance on training prescription. Its relevance to performance staff is in planning expected time lost after a BAMIC 'c' injury or one with large tendon disruption, waviness or loss of tendon tension, with the caveat that the evidence is mostly high risk of bias.
rtp: The study is directly about return-to-play prognosis. It supports expecting longer return times for BAMIC 'c' injuries and for injuries with larger tendon disruption, waviness or loss of tendon tension, but the prediction interval includes zero, so it does not support a precise date for an individual athlete. It also does not measure clearance criteria or re-injury risk.

citation: Tenan MS, Rezai AR, Vigotsky AD. A Causal and Replication Analysis of Claims that Jet Lag Affects Team Sport Performance. American Journal of Epidemiology. 2025.
abstract: Using the potential outcomes framework, the authors tested whether jet lag, conditional on game time, causes collegiate football teams to under- or over-perform the Las Vegas spread across 6,245 games from nine seasons. A generalized additive model with independence weights was used, and randomization inference gave P=0.133, compatible with no effect. Exact replications of two NFL analyses on the collegiate data were also compatible with the null hypothesis.
tldr: Across 6,245 collegiate football games, hours gained or lost in travel showed no discernible effect on beating the Vegas spread, and two NFL analyses did not replicate in this dataset. Because jet lag was measured only through a travel proxy, the result argues against assuming a large effect rather than proving that none exists.
methods: Observational analysis of NCAA football games from 2013 to 2022 (excluding 2020), with stadium time zones matched to Pro Football Focus game data and the consensus Las Vegas spread from the day before each game. Hours gained or lost in travel, conditional on kickoff time, was the exposure, with energy-balancing independence weights and a generalized additive model with penalized splines. Significance came from randomization inference, comparing the observed F-statistic with 5,000 simulated noise datasets, and the authors also replicated the analyses of Smith et al. and Roy and Forest on the collegiate data.
findings: The conditional effect of travel-related hours gained or lost on beating the spread was compatible with no effect (randomization inference P=0.133), and the lowest P value among 98 point predictions was 0.10. Replicating Smith et al. gave β=-0.081 (±1.327, P=0.952), and evening games gave β=-1.111 (±2.204, P=0.617). The Roy and Forest linear probability model gave β=-0.023 (P=0.056, R2=0.001) in the collegiate data, against β=5.5 (P=0.049) in the original NFL analysis.
limitations: Hours gained or lost in travel is a proxy for jet lag, with no measures of sleep, circadian phase or individual exposure. Weather was randomly sampled for indoor games, the positivity assumption is structurally violated, and eastward travel with late kickoffs is sparse (Figure 3B). The outcome is beating the Vegas spread, which the authors acknowledge cannot capture all in-game factors, and this is a submitted manuscript rather than the final published version.
practicalImplications: The study does not show that travel across time zones lowers team performance in college football, so travel decisions should not rest on an assumed large jet lag effect. The authors state that it is unclear whether interventions for teams crossing fewer than three time zones are warranted to optimize winning, and the study does not settle that question for other sports or for individual players.
athleteDev: Performance staff should not assume that time-zone travel lowers team results on the basis of this study. Its outcome was the betting-spread result of games rather than athlete performance measures, and it does not test any travel, sleep or circadian intervention.
rtp: Not applicable to return to sport. The study concerns collegiate team game results and does not assess injured or rehabilitating athletes.

citation: Hatia M, Loureiro N, Ribeiro J, Moeda F, Melo M, Tocha J, et al. A Narrative Review of the Impact of Sleep on Athletes: Sleep Restriction Causes and Consequences, Monitoring, and Interventions. Cureus. 2024;16(12):e76635.
abstract: Narrative review of evidence on how sleep affects athletic performance, the prevalence and causes of sleep disturbance, and monitoring and intervention strategies, drawing on PubMed, Cochrane Library and Google Scholar searches up to July 2024. The review reports that inadequate sleep can impair strength, endurance, cognition, injury risk and mental health, and it describes sleep tracking, sleep extension, sleep hygiene and, when necessary, pharmacological approaches. The authors conclude that tailored sleep strategies are needed to optimize athletic performance and recovery.
tldr: Short or poor sleep is common in athletes, and the review links it to lower endurance, strength and power, higher injury and concussion risk, and slower recovery. It supports sleep extension through naps or longer nights, sleep hygiene and sleep monitoring, but the long-term effects of these interventions are not established.
methods: Narrative review of case studies, observational studies, randomized controlled trials, systematic reviews and meta-analyses found in PubMed, the Cochrane Library and Google Scholar up to July 2024. The paper does not describe search terms, inclusion criteria or quality appraisal, and it organizes the evidence by prevalence, causes, consequences, monitoring and interventions.
findings: Charest and Grandner are cited for average actigraphy sleep of about 6.5 hours in elite athletes, 39.1% self-reporting less than seven hours of sleep, and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index scores above 5 in 19.8% to 50% of athletes. The review cites an adolescent study in which athletes sleeping under eight hours were 1.7 times more likely to be injured, and a study in students, footballers and judo athletes in which a single night of 4-hour sleep restriction reduced Wingate power output. For interventions, the review cites a systematic review (Cunha et al.) reporting that naps of 20 to 90 minutes or extra nighttime sleep improve physical and cognitive function, and Bonnar et al. reporting that acute sleep hygiene measures did not significantly change subsequent performance or recovery.
limitations: The review notes variable methods, sample sizes, demographics and sleep measures, heavy reliance on self-reported data, and little research on long-term intervention effects. Several citations do not match their claims: the 8.1-hour injury finding is attributed to reference 4 (Charest and Grandner), the melatonin and sedative-hypnotic statements cite a systematic review of benzodiazepines (Holgado et al.), and the O'Sullivan and Johnston injury finding is cited to what appears to be a 2021 conference abstract (IOC supplement).
practicalImplications: Where athletes are short on sleep, the review suggests delaying morning training by 30 minutes, encouraging earlier bedtimes, or taking a nap at least two hours after training. Limiting weekend lie-ins to within one hour of the usual wake time and reducing screen use before bed are described as low-cost measures, and the review suggests consistent practice for one to three months before expecting improvements.
athleteDev: Performance staff can use questionnaires such as the Hooper index or actigraphy to track sleep and spot declines in performance. The review links sleep restriction to lower endurance, strength and power and faster exhaustion, but the studies it cites are mostly small or self-reported, so the findings guide monitoring and education more than specific prescriptions.
rtp: Return to sport is not a main focus of the review. It notes that sleep disturbance can impair recovery after injury and that persistent sleep disturbance after concussion is associated with a longer recovery period, but it does not set a return-to-sport standard and should not be used as a clearance criterion.

citation: Reiner MM, Glashüttner C, Bernsteiner D, Tilp M, Guilhem G, Morales-Artacho A, et al. A comparison of foam rolling and vibration foam rolling on the quadriceps muscle function and mechanical properties. European Journal of Applied Physiology. 2021.
abstract: In 21 physically active men, a 3-minute bout of vibration or non-vibration foam rolling of the quadriceps was followed by changes in hip extension range, passive resistive torque, maximal isometric strength and muscle shear modulus. Hip extension range increased only after vibration rolling, while strength rose after both and rectus femoris stiffness fell after both.
tldr: A single 3-minute session of vibration foam rolling increased hip extension range by about 3 degrees, which non-vibration rolling did not. Both rollers produced similar strength gains and similar drops in rectus femoris stiffness, so the advantage of vibration is limited to range of motion in this study.
methods: Twenty-one physically active men completed two sessions, 2 to 7 days apart, in random order: 1 minute each of vastus lateralis, vastus medialis and rectus femoris rolling with a vibrating roller (32 Hz) or the same roller switched off. Before and after each session the authors measured isometric knee extensor torque, passive resistive torque on an isokinetic dynamometer, hip extension range by 3D motion capture, and shear modulus of three quadriceps muscles by shear wave elastography. Comparisons used two-way repeated-measures ANOVA or Friedman tests with post hoc tests.
findings: Hip extension range increased by 3.3 degrees after vibration rolling (d = 0.85), with a significant time x group interaction (P < 0.01), but not after non-vibration rolling (P = 0.51). Knee extensor MVIC rose by 14.2 Nm after vibration and 8.6 Nm after non-vibration rolling, with no significant difference between the changes (P = 0.28). Rectus femoris shear modulus fell in both conditions (P < 0.01), while vastus lateralis and vastus medialis were unchanged, and passive resistive torque showed only an overall time effect (P = 0.04) with no change within either condition.
limitations: The abstract says participants were randomly assigned to one of two groups, but the methods show that all 21 men completed both conditions in random order, so the abstract is inconsistent with the design. The abstract and discussion give rectus femoris shear modulus changes of -7.2 and -4.7 kPa, but Table 1 means show 10.4 to 8.0 kPa (vibration) and 9.5 to 8.0 kPa (non-vibration), which match the reported percentage drops (-23.2% and -16.4%) rather than the kPa values. The authors compared overall thigh stiffness only within each condition and inferred from effect sizes that vibration lowers it more, and MVIC was not normalised to antagonist activity.
practicalImplications: In a warm-up for a sport with flexibility demands, vibration rolling may add a short-term hip extension gain of about 3 degrees, but this study does not show that the gain carries into training or competition. Staff should not expect either roller to change passive resistive torque or vastus lateralis and vastus medialis stiffness after one short session, since only rectus femoris shear modulus fell.
athleteDev: Vibration rolling may be worth trialling in warm-ups where extra hip extension range matters. The study does not show that either roller improves maximal strength more than the other, because the strength gains did not differ significantly.
rtp: The study tested healthy, physically active men and did not assess injured athletes or return to sport. It cannot be used to decide whether vibration rolling helps regain range of motion or strength after injury.

citation: Lehmann L, Saidi O, Giacomoni M, Del Sordo G, Maso F, Margaritis I, et al. A delayed evening meal enhances sleep quality in young rugby players. International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism. 2022 (ahead of print).
abstract: Twelve adolescent rugby players spent five days with a 19:00 dinner and five days with a 21:00 dinner, and sleep was measured by polysomnography. The later dinner was followed by longer total sleep time, higher sleep efficiency and less fragmented sleep.
tldr: Moving dinner from about 3.5 hours to about 1.5 hours before bed increased total sleep time by about 24 minutes and reduced wake and awakenings in young rugby players. The study is small and short, so the change should be tried and checked in the athletes concerned rather than applied as a fixed rule.
methods: Twelve male rugby players (aged 14.9 to 16.6 years) completed two five-day blocks in random order, with a two-week washout, eating either a routine dinner at 19:00 or a late dinner at 21:00 in a boarding school, with bedtime fixed at 22:30 and the same food, energy intake and training in both conditions. Sleep was measured by polysomnography on days 0 and 3 of each block, with activity by accelerometry and sleep diaries. Paired t tests or Wilcoxon tests compared the two conditions, with Cohen's d for effect size.
findings: On day 3, total sleep time was 455.4 vs 431.2 minutes (+24 min, p = .001, d = 1.24) and sleep efficiency 89.3% vs 84.5% (p = .001) with the late dinner. Wake after sleep onset fell by 25 minutes (p = .014), microarousals by 0.3 per hour (p = .049) and awakenings of 90 seconds or more by 0.4 per hour (p < .01). N3 latency was 6.9 minutes shorter (p = .026), while sleep onset latency was 9 minutes shorter but not significant (p = .065).
limitations: The baseline (day 0) REM latency differed between conditions (118 vs 141 min, p = .035), which the authors do not discuss, and the abstract refers to first and last nights while the methods use day 0 (Monday) and day 3 (Thursday). The conclusion that dinner timing improves sleep quality rests on one comparison night per condition in a 12-person crossover, and the proposed mechanisms (hunger, satiety, digestion) were not measured.
practicalImplications: For adolescent athletes who eat dinner about 3.5 hours before a fixed bedtime, moving dinner to about 1.5 hours before bed may lengthen and consolidate sleep over a few days, while keeping total energy intake the same. Staff should check the effect in individual athletes, since the study tested 12 boys and excluded athletes with obstructive sleep apnea.
athleteDev: The study measured sleep only and did not test any performance outcome, so it does not show that a later dinner improves performance. Its value to performance staff is as a low-cost sleep intervention for adolescent players.
rtp: The study tested healthy adolescents with no injury at the time of the study and does not address return to sport. It cannot be used to guide sleep or dinner timing after injury.

citation: Bender AM, Lambing KA. A practical guide to improve sleep and performance in athletes. International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching. 2023:1-12.
abstract: Narrative review of sleep in athletes, covering the prevalence of sleep problems, sport-specific and non-sport barriers to sleep, and strategies to improve sleep. The authors propose 10 practical recommendations, including sleep education, validated sleep screening, banking sleep, planned napping, evening light management, pre-sleep routines, a cool, dark and quiet bedroom, chronotype-based training times, jet lag strategies, and careful use of caffeine and supplements.
tldr: Sleep is a practical lever for athletes, but the 10 recommendations are a narrative synthesis rather than a set of proven athlete protocols. Screen for clinically relevant sleep problems, plan naps of 20 to 90 minutes between 1 and 4 p.m., and manage evening light and jet lag.
methods: Narrative review with practical recommendations, drawing on athlete studies and general-population research. No systematic search, inclusion criteria or quality appraisal are described. The text states that the article is based on a presentation to an expert panel.
findings: The authors report that many elite athletes have daytime sleepiness, poor sleep quality or sleep-disordered breathing risk, and that about 25% of athletes screened with the Athlete Sleep Screening Questionnaire required intervention. In cited studies, sleep extension increased total sleep time, and some athletes showed gains in sprint, reaction time or accuracy measures. Nap benefits were not found in every study, and caffeine improved exercise performance in some athletes while worsening sleep.
limitations: No systematic search or quality appraisal is described, so the selection of evidence is not reproducible. Many cited athlete studies are small, short-term or observational, and the authors state that more rigorous athlete studies are needed, especially for jet lag, supplements and long-term sleep change.
practicalImplications: Screen athletes for clinically relevant sleep problems with a validated tool such as the ASSQ, ideally outside the competitive season, and refer those flagged to a sleep specialist. Where scheduling allows, plan naps of 20 to 90 minutes between 1 and 4 p.m. with at least 30 minutes before activity, and limit bright and blue light within 2 hours of bedtime. Treat caffeine timing as an individual decision given its effects on subsequent sleep.
athleteDev: Consider banking sleep before key competitions and travel, and align training times with chronotype where the schedule allows. The cited studies link more sleep to faster sprints, reaction time and accuracy in some athletes, but the review gives no sport-specific effect sizes, so treat performance gains as indicative.
rtp: This review does not address return to sport, injury rehabilitation or clearance decisions. Its sleep screening and referral advice applies to sleep problems and must not be used as a return-to-play judgment.

citation: Caldwell LK, Kraemer WJ, Post EM, Volek JS, Focht BC, Newton RU, et al. Acute Floatation-REST Improves Perceived Recovery After a High-Intensity Resistance Exercise Stress in Trained Men. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2022;54(8):1371-1381.
abstract: Eleven resistance-trained men completed two crossover testing blocks, each with six sets of ten back squats at 80% 1RM. One block was followed by 1 h of floatation-REST and the other by a seated sensory-stimulating control, with blood markers, jumps and perceptions tracked for 48 h.
tldr: A 1 h floatation session after heavy squatting reduced perceived soreness, fatigue and negative mood in trained men compared with a seated control. Muscle damage, inflammation and jump performance did not differ between conditions.
methods: Within-subject crossover with two testing blocks separated by a 2-week washout, with measures before, immediately after, after 1 h of recovery, and at 24 and 48 h. Outcomes included lactate, catecholamines, cortisol, testosterone, creatine kinase, myoglobin, IL-6, TNF-alpha, squat and countermovement jumps, visual analogue soreness, PANAS and POMS, analysed with repeated-measures ANOVA and effect sizes.
findings: Soreness was lower with floatation across recovery (P = 0.035), most of all immediately after the intervention (36% lower than control, P = 0.002, ES 1.3), with no treatment difference in pain intensity. Norepinephrine returned to baseline after floatation but stayed elevated after control, and testosterone declined less at the post-treatment point after floatation (P = 0.028). Negative affect, total mood disturbance and experienced fatigue improved more after floatation than control over the hour (P = 0.008 to 0.029), while structural damage and inflammation markers rose after exercise in both conditions with no treatment difference.
limitations: Eleven participants limit detectable effects, as the authors acknowledge. Order was counterbalanced by enrolment rather than randomised, the control was a passive TV session, and negative affect was already higher after exercise in the floatation block, which may inflate the change-score benefit. The abstract reports P = 0.001 for fatigue while the results report P = 0.008, and the abstract's performance-readiness claim goes beyond the data because no performance outcome improved.
practicalImplications: A single 1 h floatation session after high-volume squatting reduced soreness and fatigue and improved mood compared with a seated control, without changing damage or inflammation markers. The authors observed no adverse effects, but the study shows no effect on strength, jump or sprint performance.
athleteDev: Floatation could be considered as a recovery option to improve perceived readiness after heavy resistance sessions. Jump performance did not improve, so it should not be presented as a performance enhancer.
rtp: The study used healthy trained men after one session, not injured athletes, so it cannot guide return-to-sport decisions or show faster healing; the authors found no difference in structural damage markers.

citation: Di Lorenzo L, Forte AM, Agosti V, Forte F, Lanciano T, Pirraglia N, et al. Advances in Non-Pharmacological Strategies for DOMS: A Scoping and Critical Review of Recent Evidence. J Funct Morphol Kinesiol. 2025;10:452.
abstract: This scoping review maps non-pharmacological interventions for delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS) in athletes, using studies published from 2020 to 2025. Interventions covered include physical and mechanical therapies, thermal therapies, neurophysiological techniques, nutrition and imaging. The authors report that cryosauna, vibration therapy, percussive massage and polyphenol supplementation reduced DOMS symptoms in the studies they reviewed, and they recommend multimodal, personalised approaches.
tldr: Several non-drug options for DOMS, including delayed whole-body cryotherapy, percussive massage, vibration and polyphenols, showed benefit in small studies. The evidence is limited and inconsistent, and the review found no pooled effect.
methods: Scoping review of PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science searches for English-language human studies on non-pharmacological DOMS interventions in athletes, following the Arksey and O'Malley framework and PRISMA-ScR reporting. Quality was rated with PEDro, AMSTAR 2 and ROBIS, but no protocol was registered and no pooled analysis was performed. The flow table reports 461 records identified and 23 studies included.
findings: The review reports that delayed whole-body cryosauna (48 to 72 h after exercise) reduced muscle stiffness, leukocytes and creatine kinase in one randomised trial, and that percussive massage of 40 minutes improved pain and jump performance in another. Polyphenol and BCAA results were described as promising but drawn from small or preliminary studies. Electrical stimulation showed no significant effect versus placebo, and aqua cycling gave no added benefit over passive recovery.
limitations: The review states an inclusion window of 2020 to 2025, but its evidence table includes studies from 2016 to 2019, the abstract says 25 studies were included while the results and flow table say 23, and the evidence table lists 22 unique studies (one is entered twice) while key trials discussed in the text, such as the percussive massage trial, are not in it. Its discussion attributes a conclusion on stretching to Wiecha et al. (2024), but that reference is a published protocol with no results. The abstract describes polyphenols as showing significant benefit, while the body calls the polyphenol evidence small-scale and preliminary.
practicalImplications: Staff can consider delayed cryotherapy, massage, vibration or compression as options for DOMS, because several small trials report benefit. The review itself calls for larger randomised trials before a fixed protocol is adopted, so these should be tested against the athlete's own response rather than applied as a standard. Electrical stimulation and aqua cycling should not be relied on as primary recovery tools based on the reported trials.
athleteDev: Performance Application: Post-training recovery options such as delayed cryotherapy, percussive massage or vibration may help reduce soreness and maintain function before the next session. The evidence comes from small trials, and the review does not show that these options improve performance outcomes.
rtp: This review does not inform return-to-sport decisions. DOMS is a transient, self-limiting response to exercise, not an injury, and the review notes that few studies address return-to-performance timelines.

citation: Weber Rawlins ML, Valovich McLeod TC. A mixed methods investigation into athletic trainer and dietitian's nutrition practices for sport-related concussion patients. J Concussion 2023;7:1-12.
abstract: This mixed-methods survey described how athletic trainers and dietitians use nutrition, through food and supplements, to prevent concussion and to manage patients after concussion, and the barriers reported by those who do not. Most athletic trainers did not use nutrition for prevention, while dietitians used nutrition practices more often than not. Lack of clinician knowledge and athlete compliance were commonly reported barriers.
tldr: Few athletic trainers (2.7%) use nutrition to prevent concussion, though about half offer at least some nutrition advice after one; dietitians report these practices more often. Lack of clinician knowledge was the most common barrier for athletic trainers. The study describes practice and cannot show whether any nutrient helps concussion outcomes.
methods: Convergent parallel mixed-methods design. An online survey was distributed through the NATA Research Survey Service, the CPSDA discussion board and social media. Open-ended responses were coded with consensual qualitative research methods and checked by an external auditor, multiple-choice items were summarised with descriptive statistics, and the new survey had expert face and content validity review but no reliability analysis.
findings: Among athletic trainers who accessed the survey (n = 1,465), 2.7% (39) reported using nutrition to prevent concussion, 28.5% (418) offered post-concussion nutrition recommendations, and 4.8% (70) changed nutrition for patients after concussion. Among dietitians (n = 51), the matching figures were 33.3% (17), 56.9% (29) and 29.4% (15). Respondents most often named clinician knowledge (49.4% of athletic trainers, 9.8% of dietitians) and athlete compliance (26.3%, 9.8%) as reasons for not implementing prevention nutrition.
limitations: The design is cross-sectional and descriptive, the response rate was low (7.3% of athletic trainers contacted and 3.6% of dietitians accessed the survey), and only 25 dietitians completed it. The Discussion says most dietitians were Division I, but Table 1 shows 25.5% (13) in Division I with 51% not responding. No validated survey existed, so the team built one reviewed only for face and content validity, and the authors call for longitudinal intervention studies.
practicalImplications: The authors note that the current literature does not support nutrition for concussion prevention or post-injury care, so staff should not present it as a proven treatment. Because hydration status can change concussion symptoms, the authors advise relying on other assessments or delaying return-to-activity decisions until the athlete is euhydrated if dehydration is suspected. Interprofessional collaboration emerged as a theme, and the authors suggest athletic trainers and dietitians work together on any concussion nutrition plan.
athleteDev: The authors suggest that, until more is known about nutrition and concussion, nutrition efforts may be better focused on athletic performance and injury recovery in general. The survey did not measure performance outcomes.
rtp: The study does not test any return-to-play intervention. The authors cite the FDA position that there is no scientific evidence nutrition changes allow athletes to return to activity sooner, so nutrition should not be presented as a way to speed return to play.

citation: Ryan T, Nagle S, Daly E, Pearce AJ, Ryan L. A potential role exists for nutritional interventions in the chronic phase of mild traumatic brain injury, concussion and sports-related concussion: a systematic review. Nutrients 2023;15:3726.
abstract: This systematic review, registered on PROSPERO and conducted to PRISMA guidance, searched five databases for nutrition or dietary interventions in adults with chronic symptoms (at least one month) after mild traumatic brain injury, concussion or sport-related concussion. Nine studies met the criteria, covering omega-3 fatty acids, melatonin, Enzogenol, MLC901, a ketogenic diet and phytocannabinoids. Findings were narrative because of heterogeneity, and the authors conclude that higher-quality human trials are needed.
tldr: Few human trials have tested nutrition for symptoms that persist after mild brain injury, and the nine studies identified were small and varied. Several interventions were safe and some symptoms improved, but the review cannot establish whether any nutrient speeds recovery.
methods: Systematic review registered on PROSPERO (CRD42021277780) and conducted following PRISMA 2020. Five databases were searched (PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, SPORTDiscus, CINAHL and Cochrane), with the search first run in 2020 and updated in 2023, identifying 6,164 records. Screening was done by two researchers with a third reviewer for disagreements, study quality was rated with a modified Black and Downs tool (maximum 28 points), and heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis.
findings: The nine studies covered omega-3 fatty acids, melatonin, Enzogenol, MLC901, a ketogenic diet and phytocannabinoids. Trials reported some benefits, including lower self-reported anxiety with melatonin (p = 0.006 in Grima et al.), better executive functioning and complex attention with MLC901 (36 participants randomised to it), and possible benefit to visual memory and symptoms with a ketogenic diet in 11 completers of a feasibility study. The two omega-3 studies were multi-component programmes without a randomised control, so effects cannot be attributed to omega-3; one melatonin trial (Kemp et al.) found no sleep improvement; and the average quality score was 18.6 of 28.
limitations: Samples were small: the Kemp et al. melatonin crossover study had seven participants and no power calculation, and the ketogenic study was a feasibility study with 11 completers. Only one study ran a sensitivity analysis, four studies did not adjust adequately for confounding, and all studies reported positive effects, which the authors flag as possible publication bias. The review was limited to adults in the chronic phase, so the findings do not apply to children, to acute injury or to moderate and severe TBI, and several trials mixed in moderate and severe TBI cases.
practicalImplications: Because the evidence is limited, staff should not present any of these nutrients as an established treatment for persistent concussion symptoms.
