The interventions were feasible and well tolerated in these studies, but doses varied widely and the ketogenic diet needed ongoing dietitian input, so any use should be coordinated with a dietitian and monitored. Staff should also note the side effects reported in the trials, including headache and sleep disturbance with Enzogenol and headache and itchiness with MLC901.
athleteDev: The review reports no performance outcomes. Its trial in college athletes with a history of concussion (Walter et al.) tested Enzogenol for residual symptoms and reported improved sleep disturbance and mental fatigue, but it did not measure performance.
rtp: The review measured symptoms, cognition, sleep and mood rather than return to play, and it does not identify an intervention that shortens recovery. Nutrition should therefore not be used to accelerate return to activity or to inform return-to-play timing.

citation: Pallangyo P, Bhalia SV, Komba M, Mkojera ZS, Manji ES, Millinga J, et al. Acute myocardial infarction following "dry scooping" of a pre-workout supplement in a healthy young man of African origin: a case report. SAGE Open Medical Case Reports. 2024;12:1-6.
abstract: A previously healthy 25-year-old man presented with chest pain after a gym session, having used a pre-workout supplement for 8 months and dry-scooped it for 3 days. He had an anterolateral STEMI from a thrombotic proximal LAD occlusion, treated with a drug-eluting stent, and the authors use the case to raise awareness of pre-workout misuse.
tldr: Dry scooping a pre-workout powder preceded an acute heart attack in a healthy young gym user, whose coronary blockage was treated with a stent. The cause is uncertain, so the case supports warning against dry scooping but does not prove a mechanism.
methods: Clinical case description covering history, ECG, echocardiography, coronary angiography, laboratory tests, treatment and follow-up at 4 weeks. Written consent for publication was obtained, and the institution did not require ethics approval for an individual case report.
findings: Peak troponin I was 5.14 ng/mL and CK-MB 78.1 ng/mL. Angiography showed a thrombotic total occlusion of the proximal LAD with TIMI 0 flow and no atherosclerosis, restored to TIMI 3 flow by stenting, and coagulation and lipid tests were unremarkable. At 4 weeks he reported normal functional capacity with a normal ECG, and echocardiography showed preserved EF with limited residual anterior hypokinesia; the authors suggest pre-workout-induced coronary spasm as a possible but unproven cause.
limitations: This is one patient, with no testing of the supplement content and no test for coronary spasm. The authors acknowledge that the cause of the thrombus remains uncertain, so the spasm explanation is speculative.
practicalImplications: The case supports advising gym users and athletes not to dry scoop pre-workout powder, and asking about supplement use when a young person presents with chest pain. It does not establish how often dry scooping causes harm or the risk for any specific product.
athleteDev: For performance staff, the case is a reason to ask athletes about pre-workout and stimulant use, especially dry scooping and high-caffeine products. It cannot be used to estimate how common the risk is.
rtp: The case does not give return-to-sport criteria. It reports normal functional capacity, a normal ECG and limited residual anterior wall hypokinesia at 4 weeks after stenting, but this is one patient and no return-to-exercise decision is described.

citation: Puscasiu D, Flangea C, Vlad D, Popescu R, Vlad CS, Barac S, et al. Adulteration of Sports Supplements with Anabolic Steroids-From Innocent Athlete to Vicious Cheater. Nutrients. 2025;17:3146.
abstract: This narrative review covers two situations: an athlete who tests positive after unknowingly taking a supplement adulterated with anabolic steroids, and an athlete who uses steroids and masks them. It describes testosterone synthesis and metabolism, the WADA steroid profile markers, isotope ratio mass spectrometry, and masking agents such as finasteride, probenecid, diuretics and azole antifungals.
tldr: Protein and other supplements can contain undeclared anabolic steroids, so an athlete can test positive without intending to dope. This review explains the steroid profile markers and masking agents that anti-doping labs use, and it says medical staff should recommend only contamination-free supplements.
methods: Narrative review drawing on PubMed, Google Scholar and ScienceDirect, including review articles, original research, case reports, meta-analyses and current WADA documents. Conference abstracts, letters, editorials and comments without peer review were excluded. No systematic search protocol or formal quality assessment is described.
findings: The review reports that earlier studies identified 54, 67 and 93 steroid substances in protein supplements, that 52.2% of supplements in one study were contaminated with anabolic steroids, and that 25 of 66 supplements in another contained prohibited substances. It sets out WADA screening thresholds, including urinary testosterone above 200 ng/mL in men, a testosterone to epitestosterone ratio above 4, and an isotope ratio difference above 3 per mil as indicating exogenous steroid use. It also describes masking agents that change the steroid profile, for example finasteride combined with 19-norandrostenedione lowering urinary norandrosterone by up to 84%, ketoconazole reducing urinary testosterone, androsterone, etiocholanolone and the testosterone to epitestosterone ratio, and miconazole reducing androsterone and etiocholanolone.
limitations: This is a narrative review without a systematic search or appraisal of study quality, so the selection of evidence may be biased. Many cited mechanistic and masking data come from small studies, including animal work, and the review does not report new human data. The adulteration figures are from earlier product testing and may not reflect current supplements.
practicalImplications: Staff should treat supplements, especially protein products, as a possible source of undeclared steroids; the authors say medical staff should recommend only contamination-free supplements and athletes should use supplements under sports medicine supervision. Medical staff should coordinate prescribed medications such as anxiolytics and antidepressants with anti-doping rules. Athletes are judged on the test result regardless of intent, so they should be told this.
athleteDev: Supplements that promise rapid strength or muscle gains deserve extra scrutiny, because the review describes undeclared steroids being added to protein products to drive sales, and a positive test can end a career. The review supports using only controlled supplements recommended by medical staff; it does not test or rank specific products.
rtp: This review does not inform return-to-sport decisions. It does not study injury, rehabilitation or return-to-play clearance, and its doping and supplement content should not be used to judge an athlete's readiness to play.

citation: Tranaeus U, Gledhill A, Johnson U, Podlog L, Wadey R, Wiese Bjornstal DM, et al. 50 Years of Research on the Psychology of Sport Injury: A Consensus Statement. Sports Medicine. 2024.
abstract: Consensus statement by seven experts in the psychology of sport injury, summarising research on injury risk, rehabilitation and return to sport. The panel drew on literature from the 1980s to the present, rated evidence quality with a modified GRADE approach, and produced practitioner recommendations. The statement reports stress responses as the strongest psychological risk factor for acute injury, stress management and mindfulness interventions that reduced injuries in the studies reviewed, and competence, autonomy and relatedness as needs of returning athletes.
tldr: Psychological factors matter across the injury pathway, and this consensus statement gives practitioners evidence-rated recommendations on injury risk, rehabilitation and return to sport. The strongest support is for stress management and mindfulness approaches to reduce injury risk, while the return-to-sport evidence is mostly cross-sectional, retrospective or qualitative.
methods: Expert panel of seven researchers, each with at least 10 years of applied experience and 20 publications on sport injury psychology. The panel met digitally from May 2022 to July 2023 and in person in Stockholm in December 2022, with pairs drafting the risk, rehabilitation and return-to-sport sections. Literature was searched in five databases without an exhaustive protocol, evidence was rated with a modified GRADE approach, and three sports medicine practitioners reviewed the draft.
findings: Among psychological factors, stress responses had the strongest relationship with acute injury risk in a systematic review cited by the panel, with evidence rated moderate for study design and consistency. Stress management and mindfulness interventions were reported to reduce injuries in all 12 intervention studies in Table 2 (samples of 20 to 401 athletes), and the panel rated this evidence moderate to high quality with high consistency. For return to sport, the panel rated the evidence on psychological factors as low to moderate quality, and identified competence, autonomy and relatedness as psychological needs that returning athletes commonly experience.
limitations: The authors state the statement is not a systematic review and covers only English-language literature, with no Southern Hemisphere authors. The seven-person panel was selected by the lead author, and the statement excludes concussion and parasport. The intervention studies in Table 2 are small and report injury counts without pooled effect sizes, so the description of the reduction as clinically meaningful is the panel's judgment.
practicalImplications: Screen athletes regularly for psychosocial stress, sleep quality and perceived recovery, and use mindfulness, acceptance-based or stress management approaches to reduce acute injury risk. In rehabilitation, allow time for social support and use cognitive-behavioural or acceptance-based coping programs. During return to sport, support competence, autonomy and relatedness, and keep clear lines of communication between athletes, coaches and medical staff.
athleteDev: Performance staff can use the recommendation to screen for psychosocial stress, sleep and perceived recovery, and to build stress management and mindfulness practice into athlete routines. The statement does not report performance outcomes, and its support for these approaches comes from a small set of intervention studies.
rtp: The return-to-sport recommendations are to build competence, autonomy and relatedness, to simulate the competitive environment progressively (for example, coaches simulating matches against lower-calibre opponents), and to keep communication clear across athletes, coaches and medical staff. The evidence for these is largely cross-sectional, retrospective or qualitative, so it should guide communication and readiness practice rather than set clearance criteria.

citation: Kim SK, Roche MD, Fredericson M, Dragoo JL, Horton BH, Avins AL, et al. A genome-wide association study for concussion risk. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2020 (published ahead of print).
abstract: A genome-wide scan of 4,064 concussion cases and 291,472 controls from two health-record biobanks identified two genetic variants, in SPATA5 and PLXNA4, associated with concussion. Previously proposed candidate genes, including ApoE4, were not associated with concussion in this larger dataset.
tldr: Two rare genetic variants were linked to recorded concussion in large general-population biobanks, but candidate genes such as ApoE4 did not replicate. The findings are unreplicated and not athlete-specific, so they do not support genetic screening of athletes.
methods: Concussion cases were identified from ICD-9/ICD-10 codes in Kaiser Permanente Northern California records (3,170 cases, 80,244 controls) and from primary care Read codes in UK Biobank (894 cases, 211,228 controls), restricted to European ancestry. Each cohort was analysed by logistic regression on imputed SNPs, adjusted for sex, height, weight and 10 principal components (plus age in UK Biobank), and the two cohorts were combined by fixed-effects meta-analysis with a genome-wide threshold of p < 7.7x10-9. Previously reported candidate gene variants were also tested.
findings: rs144663795 in SPATA5 (OR 2.91 per allele copy, p = 9.7x10-11) and rs117985931 in PLXNA4 (OR 3.59, p = 3.97x10-9) were associated with concussion, with risk allele frequencies of 1.4% and 0.13% in UK Biobank; the authors caution that the PLXNA4 signal is close to the threshold. ApoE4 (p = 0.19), rs405509 (p = 0.31) and variants in BDNF, DRD4, SLC17A7 and NGF were not associated (p > 0.05), and ApoE2 was borderline (p = .067). Concussion was recorded in 3.8% of the Kaiser cohort but only 0.42% of UK Biobank.
limitations: Concussion was defined from diagnosis codes, likely under-recorded, with no information on mechanism, prior concussions or symptom severity, and sport-related concussions could not be separated from other causes. The analysis was limited to European ancestry, the associations have not been validated in an independent cohort, and the lead author leads a sports-injury genetic testing company. The discussion of sex, height and weight effects names the same cohort (described as RPGEH and as KPRB) for opposite results, so that passage cannot be interpreted reliably.
practicalImplications: The study does not support using these markers to screen athletes, restrict sport choice or change concussion management, because the cohorts were not athletes and the results are unreplicated. It does suggest that single candidate-gene findings, such as ApoE4, should not be used to judge an athlete's concussion risk.
athleteDev: The study measured concussion diagnoses only and has no performance outcomes, so it cannot inform training or performance decisions.
rtp: The study did not examine recovery or return to play, and the authors list recovery time as future work. It cannot be used to guide concussion clearance or return-to-play timing.

citation: Iverson GL, Kissinger-Knox A, Huebschmann NA, Castellani RJ, Gardner AJ. A narrative review of psychiatric features of traumatic encephalopathy syndrome as conceptualized in the 20th century. Front Neurol 2023;14:1214814.
abstract: This narrative review re-examined case descriptions of 155 boxers from 21 articles published between 1928 and 1999. It tested whether psychiatric problems were described as clinical features of 20th-century chronic traumatic encephalopathy. Psychiatric problems were recorded in 34.8% of cases, but only 6.5% were described as primarily psychiatric. The authors conclude that depression, suicidality and anxiety were not clinical features of the condition, which supports the 2021 consensus criteria dropping them.
tldr: Psychiatric problems were noted in about a third of 20th-century boxers, but usually alongside neurological signs and rarely as the main problem. The authors argue that depression, suicidality and anxiety should not be treated as features of traumatic encephalopathy syndrome.
methods: Narrative review of clinical descriptions in 21 articles from 1928 to 1999, drawn from three earlier reviews. Two authors reviewed each article, extracted quotes and coded cases for psychiatric features. Duplicate and non-boxer cases were excluded, leaving 155 boxers, and results are reported as frequencies and percentages.
findings: Of 155 boxers, 34.8% had a psychiatric, neuropsychiatric or neurobehavioural problem recorded, and 6.5% were described as primarily psychiatric. Documented rates were 11.0% for depression, 0.6% (one case) for suicidality, 3.9% for anxiety, 20.0% for anger control problems and 25.2% for personality change. The authors also cite a separate 2021 study of 336 brain donors, which found no association between these psychiatric features and CTE neuropathologic change.
limitations: Case descriptions record a feature only when authors mention it, so 44.5% to 87.7% of cases are coded as unknown or not mentioned for each feature. The text gives anger control problems as 19.0%, but Table 5 gives 20.0% (31 cases); this summary uses the table value. The claim that psychiatric features are not associated with CTE neuropathology rests on the separate 2021 brain-donor study, not on this review's data.
practicalImplications: Depression, anxiety or suicidal thoughts in a former contact-sport athlete should be assessed for the usual causes seen in the general population, since the authors argue these features do not point to traumatic encephalopathy syndrome. Staff should not treat mood or behaviour change as evidence of the neurological condition without the clinical signs the historical cases describe, such as dysarthria, gait disturbance and cognitive decline.
athleteDev: The review has no direct performance application. Because it concerns former boxers with established neurological damage, its findings should not be used to read mood or behaviour changes in current athletes as signs of traumatic encephalopathy syndrome.
rtp: The review cannot inform return-to-sport decisions, since it studies historical case descriptions and does not examine return to play or its criteria. The authors argue that psychiatric features should not raise the level of certainty of underlying pathology in the consensus criteria, so they should not be used alone to support a diagnosis that bears on an athlete's future participation.

citation: Mavroudis I, Chatzikonstantinou S, Petridis F, Balmus IM, Ciobica A. A review of the personality traits in post-concussion syndrome. Acta Neurologica Belgica. 2024.
abstract: Narrative review of 16 studies on whether personality traits predict post-concussion syndrome after mild traumatic brain injury. The authors report that emotional reserve, cognitive resilience and lower somatic trait anxiety were linked to better outcomes, while anxiety sensitivity, pain catastrophizing, helplessness and sports-concussion symptom load were linked to worse outcomes. Parental anxiety was not linked to persistent symptoms in children, and the authors call for further research on samples that include healthy comparison groups.
tldr: Traits such as resilience, somatic trait anxiety and anxiety sensitivity appear to relate to whether concussion symptoms persist. The evidence is mostly from non-athlete samples, so use it to flag possible risk rather than to set athlete screening thresholds.
methods: Review with narrative synthesis of 16 studies identified by searching PubMed, Embase and PsycINFO to April 2023, plus reference lists. Two authors screened titles, abstracts and full texts, and study quality was rated with the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, with no quality concerns reported. Studies were grouped by personality trait because designs and outcome measures varied, and no pooled analysis was done.
findings: In a 1-year mTBI cohort of 122 patients, lower psychological resilience, higher somatic trait anxiety, embitterment and mistrust were linked to persistent symptoms, and in 61 mTBI patients anxiety sensitivity and alexithymia were correlated with more post-concussion symptoms. In 332 adolescents and young adults with sport-related concussion, lower resilience was linked to more symptoms and delayed recovery. In 98 children with concussion, parental anxiety was not associated with persistent symptoms at 1 month, although parents of persistently symptomatic children remained more anxious; these are observational associations, not tested predictive models.
limitations: Most included samples are general mTBI populations such as falls, road traffic and trauma patients, three samples are healthy volunteers, and sport-related samples are a small subset. The authors note small samples and reliance on self-report, and designs and measures vary. Reporting is inconsistent: the abstract lists four databases while the methods list three, the abstract mentions polygenic risk score analyses and a publication-bias analysis that are not presented, Table 1 cites reference 13 for two different studies, and its row for the 329-athlete meta-analysis repeats results reported for another study.
practicalImplications: The authors suggest that psychological resilience, somatic trait anxiety, embitterment and mistrust be considered when assessing risk of persistent symptoms after concussion, and that anxiety sensitivity and alexithymia may be worth identifying early. Treat these as risk markers from mostly non-athlete studies rather than validated screening tools or cut-offs. One included study suggests that children whose symptoms last at least 1 month may benefit from neuropsychological care alongside usual concussion management.
athleteDev: The review is about symptom persistence after concussion, not performance. Its one performance-adjacent finding is that lower resilience was linked to more symptom aggravation during physical or cognitive activity in young people with sport-related concussion, which is not a performance measure.
rtp: The review does not set return-to-play criteria. Its personality findings may help flag athletes at higher risk of persistent symptoms, but they cannot be used as a clearance tool or to decide when an athlete can return to sport.

citation: Gibson LP, Giordano GR, Bidwell LC, Hutchison KE, Bryan AD. Acute Effects of Ad Libitum Use of Commercially Available Cannabis Products on the Subjective Experience of Aerobic Exercise: A Crossover Study. Sports Medicine. 2023.
abstract: Regular cannabis users ran for 30 minutes on a treadmill once after ad libitum use of a THC-dominant or CBD-dominant cannabis flower product and once without cannabis. Cannabis runs were rated more positively, with more enjoyment, positive affect and runner's high symptoms, but also with more perceived exertion. The size of some effects differed by product, and the authors urge caution in interpreting these differences given the small groups.
tldr: In regular cannabis users running on a treadmill, cannabis before exercise increased enjoyment, positive mood and runner's high symptoms, but also perceived exertion, with the exertion increase seen mainly after the THC-dominant product. The study had no placebo arm, a small CBD group and no performance outcome.
methods: Laboratory crossover study. Forty-two regular cannabis users (28 men, 12 women, 2 non-binary; about 383 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous exercise per week) who had used cannabis while running completed a baseline Talk Test to set a treadmill speed and incline near the ventilatory threshold, then two 30-minute runs at least 48 hours apart in randomized order: one without cannabis and one about 33 minutes after ad libitum home use of an assigned flower product (THC-dominant, 24% THC and 1% CBD, or CBD-dominant, 1% THC and 20% CBD). Products were allocated by a die roll that participants could decline, and exertion, pain, affect, arousal, enjoyment and runner's high were rated during or after each run and analysed with mixed-effects models.
findings: Cannabis runs were rated higher for affective valence, enjoyment and runner's high symptoms (all P<0.001). Exertion was higher on cannabis runs overall (B=0.32, P=0.04), with the difference present in the THC group (P<0.001) and not the CBD group (P=0.93). The enjoyment and affect differences were larger in the CBD group (interaction P=0.02 and P=0.003), and resting heart rate was higher before cannabis exercise in the THC group only (P<0.001). Pain was very low on both runs (about 1 out of 10), and %HRmax did not differ overall (P=0.15).
limitations: Participants knew their product, and the groups were unbalanced (31 THC, 11 CBD) after several CBD-assigned participants switched to THC and CBD attrition was slightly higher, so the product comparisons are underpowered. There was no placebo and participants held favourable beliefs about cannabis with exercise (90.5% said it increased enjoyment), so expectancy and prior experience cannot be separated from drug effects; heart rate was available for only 31 participants and pain scores were at a floor. The text has internal inconsistencies: mean plasma THC in the THC group is 114 ng/mL in Table 2 but 148 ng/mL in the Discussion, and the Figure 3 note gives a 1 to 6 range for affective valence although the Feeling Scale runs from -5 to +5; table values were used.
practicalImplications: Staff who discuss cannabis use around training with athletes can note that, in this sample, cannabis before a run changed how the run felt, with more enjoyment and some extra effort. The study measured no performance benefit, so it does not support cannabis for improving training or competition, and its safety for athletes was not tested.
athleteDev: In this sample, cannabis before running changed how the run felt, with more enjoyment and some extra effort after the THC-dominant product, but no performance outcome was measured. The study does not show a training benefit.
rtp: The study cannot inform return to sport. It excluded people with musculoskeletal problems or injuries that limit exercise, and it studied neither injured athletes nor recovery, so its low pain findings should not be used to support cannabis for pain after injury.

citation: Hecksteden A, Pitsch W, Julian R, Pfeiffer M, Kellmann M, Ferrauti A, et al. A new method to individualize monitoring of muscle recovery in athletes. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2016 (accepted manuscript).
abstract: The paper tests whether individualized Bayesian reference ranges for creatine kinase (CK) and urea classify recovered and non-recovered states more accurately than group-based cut-offs. Priors came from routine data of 883 squad athletes (1758 measurements), and classification was tested in 14 junior elite triathletes and swimmers over five weekly microcycles. For CK, individualized cut-offs gave significantly lower error rates than group cut-offs; for urea, the difference was not significant.
tldr: A Bayesian method that personalizes CK reference ranges reduced misclassification of recovered and non-recovered states in 14 junior elite athletes. Urea moved in the same direction without a significant gain, and the evidence is small and single-sample.
methods: Log-transformed, sex-specific priors and repeated-measures SDs for CK and urea were estimated by leave-multiple-records-out jackknife from routine data. Individual posterior ranges were updated stepwise, and cut-offs were placed at equal distance from the recovered and non-recovered posterior means. Classification used Monday (recovered) and Friday (non-recovered) blood samples over five weeks and was compared with group-based cut-offs from the same data using exact binomial tests, with Monte Carlo intervals for the error rates.
findings: For CK, test-pass error fell from 0.333 (group) to 0.180 (individualized, p=0.008), and test-fail error fell from 0.317 to 0.074 (p<0.001). For urea, error rates were numerically lower (test-pass 0.286 vs 0.304; test-fail 0.250 vs 0.279) but not significant (p=0.637 and p=0.601). Non-recovered CK and urea means were higher than recovered means, as expected.
limitations: The 14-athlete sample is small and its sex split (nine male, four female) sums to 13, so the count needs checking. The group comparator came from the same data, and the criterion classification relied on schedules, questionnaires and logs rather than an objective gold standard. The results text reverses the CK p-values relative to Table 3 and the abstract, and gives the Monte Carlo lower limit as 0.087 where Table 4 gives 0.081; table values are reported here.
practicalImplications: Individualized CK ranges may improve classification accuracy for staff tracking recovery in elite athletes, but the method needs confirmation in a larger group. Plotting repeated values against the developing ranges gives a plausibility check that staff can review with athletes. Urea showed no significant gain with this method.
athleteDev: Individualized CK ranges let coaches judge an athlete's recovery against that athlete's own baseline rather than a squad average. The method needs several repeated measurements per athlete before the ranges are useful, and the paper does not show that it improves training decisions.
rtp: The study did not examine injured athletes or return-to-play decisions, so its cut-offs should not be used for that purpose.

citation: Dallman J, Herda A, Cleary CJ, Morey T, Diederich A, Vopat BG, et al. A brief review of the literature for published dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry protocols for athletes. Sports Health. 2023.
abstract: This brief review looks at what published studies say about dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DXA) protocols and body composition tracking in athletes. Of 14 articles, most recommend phantom quality-assurance scans and standardized prescan conditions, but only one reports a full athlete protocol and only one gives reporting guidance. The authors recommend using the Nana et al (2015) protocol for scanning and the Hind et al (2018) guidance for reporting until athlete-specific data exist.
tldr: DXA can track athlete body composition, but published protocols are sparse and rely on standardized prescan conditions. Until athlete-specific reference values exist, staff should follow one published scan protocol and report precision error and least significant change.
methods: Brief literature review of PubMed and Google Scholar articles from 2012 to 2022 on DXA protocols in athletic and active populations, with one researcher searching and extracting data. Articles that were duplicated, non-English, lacked DXA analysis, or did not concern sport or body composition were excluded, leaving 14 included articles.
findings: Phantom calibration quality-assurance scans and athlete prescreening standardization were routinely recommended, with 12 of 14 studies using or recommending them. Only one study (Nana et al, 2015) reported a specific athlete DXA protocol, and only one (Hind et al, 2018) described how to report results, while the authors note that detecting small changes is difficult. The authors conclude there is a lack of athlete reference values and that DXA is suitable for most athletes, with validation in athletes still in progress.
limitations: The authors state that participant demographics were limited in most included studies, and several cohort samples were resistance-trained or physically active adults rather than competitive athletes, with one cohort of non-athletes. The review is brief, with a single researcher searching and extracting data from the first 50 hits per database, and it does not grade the strength of the protocol evidence.
practicalImplications: A program that uses DXA should follow one published protocol, such as the Nana et al (2015) athlete protocol: minimal clothing, fasted with no fluid that morning, no exercise that morning, hydration checked by urine specific gravity, a voided bladder, standardized positioning, and one technician. Reports should include the scanner model, software, reference population and precision error, with a least significant change for each outcome, which Hind et al give as 2.77 times precision error (printed as 277 in the table).
athleteDev: Performance staff can use DXA to follow body composition over time only if scans are standardized, since the included studies found that food, fluid and daily activity shift estimates and that real changes in trained athletes are often small. The review gives no reference values for specific athletic populations, so comparing an athlete with norms is not supported.
rtp: The review does not address return to sport. It mentions that DXA could compare contralateral limbs to evaluate recovery from injury, but it reports no outcome data for that use.

citation: Cross MR, Samozino P, Brown SR, Morin JB. A comparison between the force-velocity relationships of unloaded and sled-resisted sprinting: single vs. multiple trial methods. European Journal of Applied Physiology. 2018.
abstract: In 27 male athletes, force-velocity relationships from a single unloaded sprint were compared with those built from several sled-resisted sprints. The two methods agreed closely for theoretical maximal velocity and optimal velocity, but agreed less well for maximal power, maximal force and optimal load.
tldr: A single unloaded sprint gives a force-velocity profile that closely matches the one from multiple sled sprints, especially for maximal velocity. Power and force estimates from the two methods differ enough that the single-sprint approach should not be treated as interchangeable for those measures.
methods: Twenty-seven male athletes performed 6 or 7 maximal sprints, one unloaded (45 m) and the rest towing a sled at 20-120% body mass, with velocity measured by radar. Force-velocity and power-velocity relationships were built two ways: from acceleration in the unloaded sprint (single trial method) and from peak velocity in each resisted sprint (multiple trial method). Results were compared using regression, absolute bias with 90% confidence intervals, Pearson correlation and typical error of the estimate.
findings: Theoretical maximal velocity was almost identical between methods (v0 9.27 vs 9.13 m/s; r = 0.99; bias -0.14 m/s). Maximal power was lower with the multiple trial method (1370 vs 1286 W; r = 0.84; bias -84.75 W, 90% CI -132.37 to -37.14; typical error 147.9 W, large). Theoretical maximal force (r = 0.71) and optimal load (Lopt, r = 0.71, about 3.1 kg lower with multiple trials) also differed with large error, and optimal velocity agreed closely (vopt 4.60 vs 4.58 m/s; r = 0.99).
limitations: The authors state that the resisted loading was incremental and not randomised, so fatigue may have affected later sprints. The abstract gives the velocity bias as -0.04 to 0.00 m/s, but Table 1 gives -0.14 m/s (-0.18 to -0.09) for v0 and -0.02 m/s (-0.04 to 0.00) for vopt, so the abstract appears to mix the two. The paper gives no volume, issue or page numbers in the extracted text, and the year is taken from the 2018 copyright line.
practicalImplications: A staff member can estimate an individual's maximal velocity and optimal velocity from one unloaded sprint, but should not assume the same single-sprint estimate of power or maximal force matches a multi-load profile. Any sled-load prescription should be checked against the surface and sled friction, since the authors say these change the load that is actually applied.
athleteDev: The single-sprint method may be a practical screen for maximal velocity and optimal velocity in these athletes, which could help set sprint speed targets. It is not validated as a way to set sled loads for training power or force, because the power and force estimates differed by large margins.
rtp: The study tested healthy athletes only and does not address return to sport. It cannot be used to judge sprint capacity or load tolerance after injury.

citation: Riem L, DuCharme O, Coggins A, Kenney A, Cousins M, Feng X, et al. A deep learning algorithm for automatic 3D segmentation and quantification of hamstrings musculotendon injury from MRI. Scientific Reports. 2025;15:33497.
abstract: Two deep learning models were trained to segment hamstring muscles, tendons and edema on MRI, and were checked against manual segmentation in 28 scans from 18 collegiate football players. Edema volume correlated strongly with manual measurements (R = 0.97), and edema measures rose with clinical BAMIC grade.
tldr: An AI tool can automatically outline hamstring muscles, tendons and edema on MRI, with strong agreement for muscles and edema volume. It tends to under-measure edema and some tendon regions, so it should support rather than replace expert reading.
methods: Manual 3D segmentations of T1 (muscles and tendons) and T2 (edema) MRI from 360 and 198 training datasets trained two 3D U-Net models. Validation used 28 scans from 18 athletes with 22 injuries, mostly from two sites held out of training plus three subjects from training sites, with a radiologist assigning BAMIC grades. AI outputs were compared with ground truth using correlation, mean difference, coefficient of variation and Bland-Altman analysis, and BAMIC groups were compared with unpaired t-tests.
findings: For edema, the AI's total volume correlated with ground truth at R = 0.97, but the mean difference was 17.37 mL (CV 55.2%) and the AI volumes were significantly lower on average. Hamstring muscle volumes correlated at R >= 0.92 with DSC of 0.96 or above, while the biceps femoris-semitendinosus joint tendon had R = 0.42. Edema volume was higher in BAMIC grades 2/3 than 0/1 at myotendinous and myofascial sites (p = 0.01), but the percentage of muscle impacted was not significant there (p = 0.07), and only the maximum muscle impact differed between tendinous grades 2 and 3 (p = 0.02).
limitations: The abstract and discussion say edema volume and the percentage of muscle impacted both rose significantly with BAMIC grade, but the results show the muscle-impact measure was not significant at myotendinous and myofascial sites (p = 0.07) and tendinous total edema volume was not significant (p = 0.12). The edema volume mean difference was 17.37 mL (CV 55.2%) with significant proportional bias, which the abstract's summary of strong agreement does not reflect; the abstract also gives muscle R >= 0.99 where the results give R > 0.92, and processing time is given as under 10 minutes per scan in the methods but under 1 minute in the discussion. The validation set includes only male football players, three validation subjects came from training sites, and no return-to-sport outcome was tested.
practicalImplications: A clinician could use the automated edema volume and muscle-involvement measures to compare the extent of injuries on the same scanner protocol, but should check the segmentation on the images because the AI under-segmented small edema. Edema volume should not be used alone to predict time to return, since the study tested only its association with the BAMIC grade.
athleteDev: The study does not address performance outcomes. Its relevance to performance staff is limited to the tool's ability to quantify hamstring injury extent.
rtp: The study measured injuries at time of injury and return to sport, but did not test whether AI-measured edema predicts time to return or re-injury. It can support the injury grading step, but it cannot set return-to-sport criteria, which the authors list as future work.

citation: Ferre A, Delvaux F, Schwartz C, Croisier JL. A new field-test for assessing the medial and lateral hamstring strength at long-muscle length. J Bodyw Mov Ther 2025;41:78-84.
abstract: This cross-sectional laboratory study examined how tibial rotation affects hamstring activity and knee flexion strength at three knee angles in 36 healthy amateur male athletes. It also tested the reliability of a hand-held dynamometer test, the Knee-Rotation test. Medial to lateral strength ratios were about 0.93 to 0.94 at all three angles. The authors propose the test for separating the two hamstring groups and identifying which one to strengthen.
tldr: In healthy amateur male athletes, medial and lateral tibial rotation changed hamstring strength and activation, so the authors propose a field test that assesses the two hamstring groups separately. Strength reliability was high, but muscle activation reliability was low to moderate, and the test was not studied in injured athletes.
methods: Cross-sectional laboratory study of 36 healthy male volunteers active 3 to 8 hours per week in soccer and rugby. Knee flexion strength was measured with a fixed hand-held dynamometer at 30, 60 and 90 degrees of knee flexion in medial, neutral and lateral tibial rotation, with surface EMG of biceps femoris long head and semitendinosus recorded at the same time. Reliability was assessed with intraclass correlation between two test sessions on the same day 30 minutes apart, and repeated-measures ANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc tests examined the effect of tibial position.
findings: Peak strength was 9.1 N.m higher in neutral than in medial rotation (p = 0.023, Cohen's d = 0.26), with no significant difference between neutral and lateral rotation. Biceps femoris activity rose 19.2% in lateral rotation and fell 23.0% in medial rotation compared with neutral, while semitendinosus activity fell 20.7% in lateral rotation compared with neutral and medial rotation. Strength reliability was high (ICC 0.87 to 0.97), but EMG reliability was low to moderate (ICC 0.22 to 0.73).
limitations: All participants were healthy male volunteers with no recent injury, and reliability was tested only within one day, so the results do not show how the test performs in injured athletes or across days. The abstract's figures of 33.6% (biceps femoris, lateral vs medial) and 22.6% (semitendinosus, medial vs lateral) are not reported in the results, which give the values above, and the abstract's ICC above 0.87 applies to strength only. The Discussion also states the medial-neutral strength difference as 9.1% in one place and about 12% in another.
practicalImplications: The study supports assessing the medial and lateral hamstring groups separately, because tibial position changed both strength and activation in healthy athletes. Since EMG reliability was low to moderate, staff should give more weight to the strength ratio than to activation differences when choosing a strengthening target. The test has not yet been shown to detect injury, post-injury weakness or re-injury risk.
athleteDev: The study shows that knee flexion strength depends on tibial position, with neutral rotation giving the highest peak strength in these healthy players. The authors suggest the test can identify the main hamstring group to strengthen, but the study did not test whether strengthening it improves performance.
rtp: The authors suggest the medial to lateral strength ratio could help detect deficits in athletes with previous injury before return to sport, but the study included no injured group. The ratio should not be used alone for return-to-sport decisions until it is validated in people recovering from hamstring injury or ACL reconstruction, which the authors name as the next step.

citation: Lahti J, Mendiguchia J, Edouard P, Morin JB. A novel multifactorial hamstring screening protocol: association with hamstring muscle injuries in professional football (soccer) - a prospective cohort study. Biol Sport 2022;39(4):1021-1031.
abstract: This pilot prospective cohort study tested whether an 11-test multifactorial hamstring screening protocol, covering posterior chain strength, sprint mechanical output, lumbopelvic control and range of motion, was associated with hamstring muscle injury in professional male footballers over one season. Of 161 recruited players, 95 were analysed after pre-season testing and 69 also completed mid-season testing. No single test was associated with injury across the season, but maximal horizontal force during sprinting was associated with injuries between the two screening sessions.
tldr: No single test in this hamstring screening protocol predicted hamstring injury over a whole season. Maximal horizontal force during sprinting was associated with injuries in the first half of the season, but this was a small pilot and the authors call for replication before it is used to manage risk.
methods: Single-season prospective cohort pilot. The 11 tests were completed at pre-season and mid-season, about 90 days apart, by one experienced practitioner, with two trials averaged per test. Hamstring injuries, including cramp or spasm without a structural lesion, were recorded by team physiotherapists and confirmed clinically, by ultrasound or by MRI. Univariable Cox regression assessed each test against injury across the season and against injury between the two screens, and paired t-tests compared the two screening sessions.
findings: Across the season, no screening test was associated with the 17 new hamstring injuries, and every confidence interval includes 1. Between the pre-season and mid-season screens, maximal theoretical horizontal force (F0) was associated with 14 injuries (HR 4.02, 95% CI 1.08 to 15.0, p = 0.04), and hip extensor strength showed a non-significant trend (HR 2.32, 95% CI 1.00 to 5.37, p = 0.05). Knee flexor strength, F0 and ASLR asymmetry changed significantly between the two sessions, and the authors caution that these changes may reflect measurement error or fatigue.
limitations: The sample is small (95 players, 17 injuries over the season and 14 in the pre-to-mid window), and no correction for the 11 tests is reported, so the confidence intervals are wide. The F0 hazard ratio is above 1 while the Discussion describes low F0 as the risk, and the Methods describe adjusted Cox models while Table 4 is labelled univariable, so the direction and adjustment of the association are unclear. Injuries included cramp or spasm without a structural lesion.
practicalImplications: Staff should not use any single test from this protocol to identify players at risk of hamstring injury, because none was associated with injury across the season. In this cohort, 70% of injuries occurred during sprinting and the match incidence (8.50 per 1000 hours) was about 18 times the training incidence (0.47 per 1000 hours), but the study did not test any exposure or prevention intervention. Scores changed between the two screens, so a single pre-season result should not be treated as the player's current status.
athleteDev: The study reports that maximal horizontal force during sprinting, a performance measure, was associated with hamstring injury in the first half of the season, and the authors suggest this could justify more frequent F0 monitoring. F0 and knee flexor strength rose from pre-season to mid-season in this group, but the study did not test whether improving F0 reduces injury.
rtp: The study is not a return-to-play study, and players with ongoing rehabilitation were excluded. It does not show whether a player with a low screening score is ready or not ready to return, and the authors state that the findings need replication in larger cohorts before any clinical use.

citation: Secomb JL. A practitioner's guide to isometric hip adduction and abduction test selection: Maximal force, asymmetry, and muscle activity comparisons between assessment positions. Journal of Sports Sciences. 2024 (published online 24 Nov 2024).
abstract: Compares maximal hip adduction and abduction force, adduction-to-abduction ratio, inter-limb asymmetry and muscle activity across five isometric hip strength positions in male ice hockey athletes. Seated and supine 45-degree hip flexion positions produced the highest relative force and torque, while the unilateral ankle position showed the greatest adduction asymmetry. Muscle activity varied by position and muscle, which the author argues should guide the choice of test position for each goal.
tldr: The hip strength test position changes the result: seated and 45-degree supine positions gave the highest force, while the unilateral ankle position showed the most asymmetry. Match the position to the outcome you need, and do not assume values transfer between positions.
methods: Twenty male national-level ice hockey athletes completed five isometric hip adduction and abduction positions in randomised order in one pre-season session, using a rigid frame with four load cells (ForceFrame). Surface EMG recorded five hip and abdominal muscles, normalised to the highest value each athlete reached across the five positions (or a resisted adduction sit-up for rectus abdominis), and asymmetry was calculated with the symmetry angle. Linear mixed models with Bonferroni post hoc tests and Cohen's d effect sizes were used.
findings: Seated and supine 45-degree hip flexion positions gave significantly higher relative peak force and torque for adduction and abduction than the bilateral and unilateral ankle positions (effect sizes 1.03 to 1.91). The unilateral ankle position had the largest adduction and adduction-to-abduction asymmetry, and the 45-degree position gave the highest adductor longus and gracilis activity during adduction (about 86% and 91% of maximal EMG). Within-session reliability was high (ICC 0.95 to 0.99; CV 2.0 to 5.5%).
limitations: Only male ice hockey athletes from one team were tested, so the results may not transfer to other sports, women or other populations. The study does not link any position to injury risk or rehabilitation outcomes. Table 2 flags the supine knee 0-degree adduction-to-abduction ratio as different only from the 45-degree and bilateral ankle positions, while the text and abstract also report a difference from the seated position, and Table 2 does not flag the unilateral ankle versus 45-degree difference in adduction-to-abduction asymmetry that the text describes.
practicalImplications: Choose the hip adduction and abduction test position to match the measure of interest: seated or supine 45-degree hip flexion for maximal force, and the unilateral ankle position for side-to-side asymmetry. Because the positions gave different values, compare repeated results within the same position. The author proposes the bilateral ankle position for monitoring adductor or core rehabilitation, which these healthy athletes did not test.
athleteDev: Select the position by the outcome that matters: seated or 45-degree supine for maximal force, and the unilateral ankle position for asymmetry screening. These results come from male ice hockey players and do not link any position to sport performance.
rtp: The study tested healthy male athletes and did not examine injured athletes, so it cannot set return-to-sport criteria or clearance thresholds. The author's suggestion to use the bilateral ankle position for monitoring after adductor or core injury is untested in injured athletes.

citation: de Ruiter CJ, Baak LM, Westerling Y, Wilmes E. A simple on-field fast knee-flexion test to assess acute knee flexor fatigue. European Journal of Applied Physiology. 2025.
abstract: Introduces a simple field test of knee flexor contractile function, using maximal fast knee flexions measured with an inertial sensor on the shin, to assess fatigue quickly after exercise. In 14 amateur football players the test was reliable within the session, peak angular acceleration fell after a series of 40 m sprints, and it rose again after 5 minutes of rest. The authors report that the fall in acceleration was related to the rise in sprint time, and they call for larger studies to confirm this.
tldr: A 5-kick prone test with a shin sensor can be run on the field within seconds of a hard effort and showed good reliability in amateur players. Its link to sprint fatigue comes from 14 players in one session, so treat it as an exploratory fatigue check, not a validated injury tool.
methods: Fourteen amateur football players (13 male, 1 female) performed five maximal fast knee flexions in the prone position with an inertial sensor on the shin, before, 20 s after, and 5 minutes after fourteen maximal 40 m sprints, with a 15th sprint after 6 minutes. Peak angular acceleration was taken as the mean of the three best attempts at each time point. Repeated-measures ANOVA was used for sprint times and peak acceleration, with ICC and CV for reliability, Pearson correlation for the relations, and Friedman tests for perceived exertion.
findings: Peak knee angular acceleration fell from 107.1 to 94.1 rad/s² after the sprints (about 12%), and sprint time rose from 5.96 to 6.55 s (n = 13 for sprint times). After rest, acceleration rose to 103.1 rad/s², not significantly different from baseline (p = 0.08), while the recovery sprint (6.15 s) was still slower than the first. The percentage fall in acceleration was related to the percentage rise in sprint time (r² = 0.48, p = 0.01; r² = 0.41, p = 0.02 without the female player), but the relation between pre-sprint acceleration and first sprint time (r² = 0.33, p = 0.03) was not significant without her (p = 0.08).
limitations: The sample is small and includes one woman, and the link between unfatigued acceleration and sprint speed is not robust without her. Reliability was tested within one session, and whether the test tracks fatigue across days is unknown. Pacing, motivation and the end-spurt may also affect the sprint measure, and without EMG the knee-flexor origin of the signal is inferred. No injury outcomes were measured.
practicalImplications: A prone fast knee flexion check with a shin sensor can be run within seconds of a hard sprint block to see whether knee flexor acceleration has dropped. Use the same protocol with the same players to track change, since between-day reliability and validity are not yet established. Combine it with other fatigue and load information rather than making load decisions from this test alone.
athleteDev: Within one session, a larger fall in knee flexor acceleration went with a larger slowdown across repeated 40 m sprints. Use the test to track fatigue rather than to predict sprint speed, because the link to unfatigued sprint speed was not robust.
rtp: The study tested healthy amateur players and measured no injury or recovery outcomes, so it cannot judge readiness to return after a hamstring injury. The authors' suggestion that the test could guide training load around hamstring risk is untested for return-to-play decisions.

citation: Pimenta R, Antunes H, Nakamura FY. Acceleration and Deceleration Profiles: Comparison Between the 5-0-5 Test and Seasonal Peak Player Performance. Sports. 2026;14:9.
abstract: Nineteen national-level under-23 football players completed the 5-0-5 change-of-direction test with a 10 Hz GPS unit. Normalized acceleration and deceleration variables from the test showed good within-session repeatability, and the starting acceleration correlated moderately with each player's season peak acceleration. The study shows that the test values sit close to season peaks for some variables, but it does not establish the test as a validated benchmark for maximal capacity.
tldr: Within-session repeatability of the 5-0-5 test is good when GPS acceleration values are expressed as a percentage of each player's season peak, but absolute deceleration and re-acceleration values were not repeatable in this sample. Preseason starting acceleration is moderately related to season peak acceleration, though it was lower on average than that peak.
methods: Methodological study using retrospective data from one team's preseason testing. Players performed the 5-0-5 test on artificial turf, with the test-day best and average of two valid repetitions recorded by a 10 Hz GPS unit (Catapult Vector S7, Accel Set 2 algorithm). Within-session repeatability was assessed with ICC(3,1), coefficient of variation and standard error of measurement, and each value was compared with the mean of each player's three highest season values using paired t tests and Pearson correlations, with Bonferroni adjustment.
findings: Normalized variables were repeatable (ICC 0.81 for starting acceleration, 0.76 for deceleration before the turn and 0.85 for re-acceleration after the turn, all as a percentage of season maximum), while absolute deceleration (ICC -0.49) and absolute re-acceleration (ICC 0.29) were poor. Average and best starting accelerations were lower than the season's average peak acceleration (4.75 and 4.88 vs 5.36 m/s2; P=0.004), with moderate correlations to that peak (r=0.48, P=0.040; r=0.50, P=0.028). The average re-acceleration after the turn was also lower than season peak (4.78 vs 5.36 m/s2; P=0.016), whereas the best repetition was not (5.04 m/s2; P=0.208), and deceleration before the turn did not differ from season peak deceleration for either the average or the best repetition.
limitations: The sample was one team, 19 players after goalkeepers were excluded, tested once in preseason, and the authors state results should not be generalized to females or other competitive levels. Repeatability was intra-session only, GPS acceleration is less accurate in sharp-turn movement, and the normalized variables are divided by season peaks that are only known after the season. Several values conflict across the text, so the Results tables were used: the Abstract gives the average deceleration (-6.47 m/s2) as the best-repetition value (Table 5 gives -6.69 m/s2), the Conclusions describe best-repetition values as comparable to season peaks although the best starting acceleration differed significantly (P=0.004), and some ICCs in the Results text differ slightly from Table 1.
practicalImplications: Absolute deceleration and re-acceleration values from two 5-0-5 repetitions were not repeatable, so single-test absolute values for those phases should not be used to judge an individual player. The authors suggest using preseason best values as an individual reference for monitoring, but the repeatable normalized values required season-long peaks, and the study did not test whether test values predict match performance or injury.
athleteDev: Starting acceleration from the 5-0-5 was moderately related to season peak acceleration but sat below it, so the test may underestimate a player's top acceleration. Deceleration in the test was numerically at or above season peak deceleration (102.8% average, 106.5% best; not significant), which suggests in-season GPS peaks may not capture maximal braking capacity, though absolute test deceleration was not repeatable between trials.
rtp: The study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions, since it included no injured players and no rehabilitation or return-to-play data. Its values should not be used as return-to-play criteria.

citation: Feigenbaum L, Gaunaurd I, Kim KJ, Raya M, Ruiz JT, Rapicavoli J, et al. Accuracy of the Region of Limb Stability in Predicting Risk for Lower Limb Injury. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2020. Published ahead of print.
abstract: The authors tested whether an inertial-sensor measure of knee stability during single-leg stance, the Region of Limb Stability (ROLS), could predict lower limb injury requiring surgery in Division I collegiate football players. Players who were injured in season had a lower between-limb symmetry index before the season than uninjured players. The symmetry index had good discrimination (AUC 0.80), and the authors describe the injury classification as having good sensitivity and specificity.
tldr: A pre-season single-leg stance measure of knee stability, expressed as a between-limb symmetry index, was lower in football players who later needed surgery for a lower limb injury. The thresholds were not tested in a separate group of players, so the accuracy figures are in-sample.
methods: Cohort study of 104 Division I collegiate football players tested within a month before each of three seasons. Each player stood on one leg for 30 seconds on each limb while wearing knee sleeves with four inertial sensors, and the ROLS (cm2) and ROLS symmetry index were calculated. Players who needed surgery for a lower limb injury during the season were compared with those who did not, using t tests, ROC curve analysis, and a confusion matrix with cut-offs of ROLS above 10 cm2 and symmetry index below 80%.
findings: The injured limb of the injured group had a higher ROLS value than the right limb of the non-injured group (11.40 vs 6.94 cm2; P=0.003). The ROLS symmetry index was lower in the injured group (65.58% vs 82.86%; P<0.001 in Table 3), with an AUC of 0.80 (95% CI 0.71 to 0.88) compared with 0.72 (95% CI 0.62 to 0.83) for the injured-limb ROLS value alone. Using the stated cut-offs, the authors report accuracy 0.92, sensitivity 0.94 and specificity 0.91, with 31 true positives and 6 false positives.
limitations: Only collegiate football players from one institution were studied, the authors note that other sports, sexes and populations are unknown, and two authors stand to gain commercially from the device. Injury history was not documented at baseline even though the group definitions refer to no previous lower limb injury, and the injury list includes a lumbar discectomy that is not a lower limb injury. The text conflicts on counts and values: the Abstract and Table 3 give the injured mean as 65.58% but the Results text gives 66.41%, the injured group is 34 in the text but 33 in the confusion matrix, which totals 103 rather than 104, the false positive and false negative rules use 'and/or' while the classification rule uses 'and', and no formal test compares the two AUCs, so the claim that the symmetry index is more accurate than the limb value is not tested.
practicalImplications: A low between-limb symmetry index on this single-leg stance test may flag players for closer review before the season, but it is not a decision tool on its own. The predictions apply only to injuries that needed surgery, and the study did not show that acting on a flag reduces injury. The authors suggest repeat testing before and after the season, which was not tested here.
athleteDev: The between-limb symmetry index from this single-leg stance test can prompt closer review of lower limb stability for players with a low score. The study does not show that changing the score through training reduces injury risk.
rtp: The authors suggest repeated measures during rehabilitation could help set return-to-play criteria, but this was not tested. The study cannot be used for return-to-play clearance, since it did not follow injured players through rehabilitation or measure their return to sport.

citation: Ruas CV, Pinto RS, Haff GG, Lima CD, Pinto MD, Brown LE. Alternative Methods of Determining Hamstrings-to-Quadriceps Ratios: a Comprehensive Review. Sports Med Open. 2019;5:11.
abstract: This comprehensive review examines alternative methods of calculating the hamstrings-to-quadriceps ratio beyond peak torque, including angle-specific torque, rate of torque development, muscle size, fatigue index and muscle activation. The authors conclude that these methods may give useful insight into knee neuromuscular mechanisms, but that there is insufficient evidence to recommend any of them as sensitive clinical tools for predicting injury risk or monitoring knee integrity. They recommend future longitudinal studies with injury incidence data.
tldr: Hamstrings-to-quadriceps ratios based on peak torque miss angle, speed, size, fatigue and muscle activation. Alternative versions of the ratio may add information about the knee's strength balance, but they are not yet validated as injury-prediction or monitoring tools.
methods: Comprehensive narrative review of 27 studies published between 1998 and 2018, identified through PubMed, Web of Science and SPORTDiscuss using predefined search terms, with 44 additional articles used for background. Eligible studies calculated an H:Q ratio using isokinetic dynamometry, MRI, ultrasound or EMG. Studies are summarised by topic in a table, with the measurement methods and calculations listed separately. No formal risk-of-bias assessment or pooled analysis is reported.
findings: Angle-specific ratios changed with knee angle and velocity. One study found the ratio lower near full knee extension in women than men, and another found lower ratios near full knee flexion and higher ratios near full extension after hamstring-graft ACL reconstruction. In one study of 35 elite soccer players, the fatigue index ratio was 1.25 to 1.38 and only weakly correlated with the conventional ratio. Rate-of-torque-development ratios from 0 to 50 ms were lower than isometric ratios in soccer players, and the reliability of this measure was reported as high. Angle-specific ratios showed poor reliability compared with peak torque ratios in one study of 50 recreational athletes (ICC 0.1 to 0.6 vs 0.3 to 0.7). Muscle size ratios were related to strength ratios in one study of 31 men but not in another of 9 soccer players, and a case-control study of 100 ACL tears reported a vastus medialis to semimembranosus ratio about 23% higher than in controls.
limitations: The review is not systematic and gives no risk-of-bias assessment, and most primary studies are small (for example 9, 16, 17 and 26 participants) and cross-sectional or laboratory based. Reliability has been studied for only two alternative ratios, and the review describes the angle-specific reliability study as 'intra session' in one place and 'inter session' in the conclusions. The two female players with 37 to 48% lower rate-of-torque-development ratios who later had ACL injuries are anecdotal, and cited injury-risk figures (4 to 5 times risk in 687 soccer players, 17 times in sprinters) refer to conventional strength imbalances and are reported as published, not verified here.
practicalImplications: Staff may use angle-specific or rate-of-torque-development ratios as supplementary descriptions of knee strength balance alongside peak torque ratios, since they can show angle-specific or early-phase differences that peak torque misses. They should not be used to classify injury risk or set return-to-play thresholds until reliability, normative values and prospective injury data are available. If angle-specific ratios are used, the cited reliability study recommends extra familiarisation with the isokinetic test to reduce torque variability at extreme angles.
athleteDev: Performance Application: Alternative ratios such as angle-specific torque, rate of torque development or fatigue index may show strength imbalances that peak torque misses, which may help target hamstring training. The review does not establish that changing these ratios improves performance or reduces injury.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: The review does not validate any alternative H:Q ratio for return-to-play decisions. It reports that alternative ratios lack reliability data and normative values, so they should not be used as criteria to clear an athlete, and any such use is outside the evidence reviewed.

citation: Kavanagh R, McDaid K, Rhodes D, McDonnell J, Oliveira R, Morgans R. An Analysis of Positional Generic and Individualized Speed Thresholds Within the Most Demanding Phases of Match Play in the English Premier League. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2023 (ahead of print, first published online December 21, 2023).
abstract: This retrospective study analyzed match tracking data from 17 male professional outfield players across two English Premier League seasons. The authors compared generic and individualized speed measures over the most demanding 1-, 3-, 5- and 10-minute periods by position. Central defenders had the lowest outputs on most measures, and the individualized metrics were presented as a more comparable measure across the other positions.
tldr: In one Premier League squad, central defenders produced lower output than other positions in the most demanding match periods, whichever speed measure was used. Individualized maximal aerobic speed distances were more similar across the non-central-defender positions than high-speed running distances.
methods: Retrospective analysis of Second Spectrum optical tracking data from 76 official league matches in 2019-20 and 2020-21. The most demanding periods were found with rolling 1-, 3-, 5- and 10-minute windows. Generic high-speed running (above 5.5 m/s) and individualized maximal aerobic speed (from a 1200-m shuttle test, mean 4.65 m/s) distances were compared across five positions with linear mixed models that included a random intercept for each player.
findings: Central defenders covered less distance in the most demanding periods than the other positions (the text reports effect sizes of 0.6 to 2.2), and had lower high-speed running and maximal aerobic speed distances in most windows. For the 1-minute window under the maximum high-speed running criterion, forwards had higher maximal aerobic speed distance than central defenders (82.9 vs 67.5 m/min, as tabled). Under the maximum high-speed running criterion, the largest effect size difference among central midfielders, wide midfielders and fullbacks was 0.49 for high-speed running and 0.315 for maximal aerobic speed distance in the 10-minute window, and smaller in shorter windows.
limitations: The sample is 17 players from one club, and the match tracking system has no published reliability or validity data. Maximal aerobic speed came from a preseason shuttle test (repeated once in January), not from each match, and the sprint speed used in the anaerobic speed reserve metric was taken from match data. Acceleration, team formation, match location and score were not analyzed. The paper does not test whether individualized metrics are more precise than generic ones.
practicalImplications: The authors suggest setting short high-intensity training targets for non-central-defender positions using distance above maximal aerobic speed as well as generic high-speed running; this was not tested as an intervention. Central defenders had lower outputs in these periods on most measures, so their targets should be set separately. The authors also note that position differences depend on the metric and window, so more than one measure should be monitored.
athleteDev: Distance above maximal aerobic speed may help staff compare positional demands in short high-intensity periods for non-central-defender positions in this squad. Training prescriptions should still be checked against the player's own data, because the study does not show that these thresholds improve performance.
rtp: This study describes match demands in a single Premier League squad and cannot inform return-to-play decisions. It does not test injury risk, readiness, or thresholds for returning players.

citation: Wang C, Trejo Vargas J, Stokes T, Steele R, Shrier I. Analyzing Activity and Injury: Lessons Learned from the Acute:Chronic Workload Ratio. Sports Med. 2020.
abstract: This review argues that the acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR), recommended by an IOC consensus for monitoring injury risk, has conceptual and analytical limits that should discourage its use. The authors discuss the coupled and uncoupled forms, the initial-load problem of exponentially weighted averages, discretization, sparse data, bias in injured athletes, confounding and subsequent injuries. They propose causal-inference strategies for future analyses.
tldr: The acute:chronic workload ratio is a proportion rather than a true measure of change, and the injury-risk bands built from it rest on sparse and biased data. Staff should not use those bands to set training load, and should record planned training schedules.
methods: Narrative review with worked illustrations. The authors discuss the mathematical properties of the coupled and uncoupled ACWR and the exponentially weighted moving average, using a 28-day worked example and an example drawn from a published training profile. They then review how the ACWR has been implemented, and propose causal strategies including instrumental variables, nested case-control and case-crossover designs, and g-methods. No search or selection method is described.
findings: The coupled ACWR has a theoretical maximum of 4 regardless of the size of the acute load, and the uncoupled form avoids that bound. With an exponentially weighted moving average, the day-0 load can outweigh the most recent load, and the two ACWR estimates converged only after about 50 days in the authors' example (3.65 vs 1.00 on day 1). The established injury-risk model that defines a 0.8 to 1.3 sweet spot and a danger zone above 1.5 is based on three studies with 28, 53 and an unreported number of athletes, and the increase in risk appears to be driven by points at an ACWR of 2.0. Weekly calendar blocks can produce a spurious rise in risk at low ratios, because athletes injured early in the week have lower acute loads.
limitations: The paper is a critique rather than a test of data, and the authors say its causal alternatives need appropriate study designs and data, such as recording training schedules. They do not estimate how often each problem changes a real conclusion. The review does not describe how the sources were selected.
practicalImplications: Do not use the ACWR bands from the established model as load limits, since the review argues that they rest on sparse, discretized and biased data. The uncoupled ratio avoids the coupled ratio's ceiling of 4, but the authors still prefer modeling acute and chronic loads as separate continuous variables, and exponentially weighted averages needed about 50 days to converge in their example. Record the planned training schedule alongside actual load, interpret weekly ratios with caution when athletes are injured early in the week, and expect the ACWR to be a poor guide during tapering before competition.
athleteDev: The review argues against using ACWR sweet-spot ranges to plan weekly load increases. It recommends recording planned training schedules and using continuous load measures, and it notes that the ACWR is poorly suited to tapering before competition.
rtp: This review does not give return-to-play criteria or load targets for injured athletes. It notes that athletes may be at higher risk of subsequent injury if they are not fully rehabilitated, and that standard ACWR models do not account for this, so the paper cannot be used to set return-to-play loads.

citation: Thevis M, Kuuranne T, Geyer H. Annual Banned-Substance Review 17th Edition: Analytical Approaches in Human Sports Drug Testing 2023/2024. Drug Test Anal. 2025;17:1417-1442.
abstract: Seventeenth annual review of literature published from October 2023 to September 2024 on analytical approaches in human sports drug testing. New detection methods, metabolism and elimination studies are organized by WADA Prohibited List class, with emphasis on anabolic agents, peptide hormones and gene doping detection.
tldr: An annual update for anti-doping and sports medicine staff on new detection methods and on which substances are hard to detect or slow to clear. The main new work covers anabolic agents, peptide hormones and gene doping detection, and some substances have detection windows of days to many months.
methods: Annual narrative review of literature published October 2023 to September 2024. The text reports no search protocol or inclusion criteria. Studies are grouped by WADA Prohibited List class and by analytical approach (GC-MS, LC-MS, IRMS and complementary methods) in Table 2.
findings: Anabolic agents were the most frequently detected class in 2022 doping controls, with 42% of adverse analytical findings, of which more than 86% were anabolic androgenic steroids. Some newly described methyltestosterone metabolites were detectable for up to 14 days with conventional methods. Roxadustat was detected in 6 of 7 patients 184 to 540 days after stopping, at 2 to 50 pg/mL. For erythropoietin, recombinant EPO was detectable for at least 168 h after an epoetin alfa dose in urine, venous serum and capillary serum, and dried blood spots were more sensitive than urine after an epoetin theta microdose. Gene doping work (transgene and CRISPR-based detection) is reported in mouse models and whole blood, and these are presented as proof-of-concept studies.
limitations: This is an analytical-chemistry review with no stated search method, so study selection cannot be reproduced. Many results come from small volunteer groups (for example 10 men and 10 women) or from in vitro and animal work, and the review does not assess effects on athletes.
practicalImplications: Anti-doping and medical staff should account for long detection windows when interpreting a finding, since the review reports detection for months after stopping some substances. Case management of an adverse finding should weigh the contamination and exposure scenarios the review describes, such as SARMs and chlortalidone. Do not assume a test exists for every listed substance, because several new methods are still at proof-of-concept stage.
athleteDev: Performance staff should treat this as anti-doping background rather than training evidence, since the review does not assess performance effects. Where athletes use supplements, consider the contamination cases described here, such as SARM and chlortalidone findings.
rtp: The review addresses detection in doping control, not injury recovery or return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It may matter when a medication an athlete needs contains a prohibited ingredient, because the detection windows reported here affect what a later test can show.

citation: Serafini S, Charrier D, Izzicupo P, Esparza-Ros F, Vaquero-Cristobal R, Petri C, et al. Anthropometric-based predictive equations developed with multi-component models for estimating body composition in athletes. Eur J Appl Physiol. 2024.
abstract: Systematic (scoping) review of anthropometric-based predictive equations for body mass components, developed in athletes with multicomponent models. From 29 studies, 40 equations were identified, most for fat mass and most applicable to males, with 13 for mixed athletes and the rest for specific sports.
tldr: Practitioners who estimate body composition from skinfolds or girths should choose an equation developed in athletes of the same sport and sex, with the same reference method. The review lists 40 such equations and notes that equations for female and youth athletes are scarce.
methods: Scoping review following PRISMA-ScR, although the abstract calls it systematic. Two reviewers searched PubMed and Scopus on 1 October 2024 for multicomponent body composition models with anthropometric prediction in athletes, screened records and extracted equations, populations, reference methods and validation statistics. Excluded were non-athletic samples, validation-only studies, body density equations and studies without a recognized reference method.
findings: The review identified 40 equations across 29 studies with 2,194 participants. Of these, 36 applied to males and 17 to females, and 26 estimated fat mass. Most were developed against DXA, and one used a four-compartment model (Evans et al. 2005). The authors state that no study considered biological maturity in youth athletes and that female athletes are underrepresented.
limitations: Intrinsic to the scoping design, so no quality assessment of included studies was made. Some equations lack validation, DXA manufacturers disagree with each other, geographic origin was not discussed, and maturation was not considered.
practicalImplications: Choose an equation developed in athletes whose sport, sex and, where reported, playing position match the athlete, and use the same reference method and measurement protocol as the equation. Where no suitable equation exists, track raw measures such as the sum of skinfolds or girths alongside the estimated values, as the authors recommend.
athleteDev: Performance staff who track body composition should check the equation's sport, sex and reference method before use, and track raw skinfold sums or girths over time as a backup. Equations for female and youth athletes are scarce.
rtp: The review concerns estimating body composition and does not examine injury, rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.
