Only one trial per condition was run, running technique was not controlled, the multidirectional trial lasted longer (1428 vs 1382 s), and GPS repeatability for acceleration and deceleration counts is less certain than for distance. The ratio results are non-significant differences, not evidence of equivalence, and no metric was compared against a criterion measure.
practicalImplications: When monitoring multidirectional sessions, do not rely on high-speed distance alone, since it was much lower in the multidirectional trial even though heart rate and blood lactate were higher. Time at high metabolic power can be used alongside high-speed distance, with the caution that this study gives only a small, single-session comparison.
athleteDev: Use time at high metabolic power, together with heart rate or blood lactate where available, to judge the internal demand of multidirectional drills and games, rather than high-speed distance alone. Treat the threshold choice as a practical convention, since the study did not test whether the 20 W/kg cut-off predicts individual responses better than other settings.
rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It recruited university athletes and did not test injured athletes or return-to-play decisions. The authors suggest the metric might help when moving from linear to multidirectional work after injury, but this was not tested.

citation: Sugisaki N, Tsuchie H, Takai Y, Kobayashi K, Yoshimoto T, Kanehisa H. Causes of Different Force-Velocity Relationships in Sprint Running Depending on Horizontal Loads and Profiling Methods. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2025;57(5):1032-1042.
abstract: This study clarified how the horizontal force-velocity relationship in overground sprint running differs with horizontal resistance loads and with profiling methods (multiple-trial and single-trial). Twelve males sprinted unresisted and with five resistance loads while ground reaction forces were recorded on a 50-m force plate system. Force-velocity plots overlapped during acceleration but deviated to lower forces near maximal velocity, the single-trial linear parameters depended on load, and the multiple-trial linear relationship was biased toward lower forces with less negative slopes. Curvilinear models fitted the pooled data better, while the unresisted linear relationship was almost linear.
tldr: Using a 50-m force plate, the sprint force-velocity profile changed with resistance load and with profiling method. The authors recommend the single-trial method with a linear fit to unresisted sprinting over the multiple-trial method for over-ground sprint profiling.
methods: Twelve males each completed six sprints: one unresisted and five resisted at 4, 6, 8, 10 and 12 kg, pulled by a motorized loading device, in ascending load order with at least 5 minutes of rest between trials. Horizontal and vertical ground reaction forces were sampled at 1000 Hz, and step-averaged force-velocity profiles were built with single-trial and multiple-trial methods and fitted with linear, Hill's equation and second-order polynomial models.
findings: Force-velocity plots overlapped across loads during acceleration, but horizontal force dropped near maximal velocity. With the single-trial method, F0 rose and the slope became more negative with heavier loads (unresisted F0 7.26 N/kg, 12 kg 8.67 N/kg), while Pmax did not differ significantly. The multiple-trial method gave lower F0 (6.08 N/kg), lower Pmax and a less negative slope (-0.60 vs -0.71 N/kg per m/s) than the unresisted single-trial method, and curvilinear models fitted the pooled data better (adjusted R2 0.986 to 0.987) than a linear fit to the pooled data (0.977) or the unresisted linear profile (0.964).
limitations: This study used 12 men (nine sprinters and three soccer players) and a fixed ascending load order, and the authors could not measure fatigue, so they cannot exclude a fatigue effect on the force drop near maximal velocity. Only step-averaged values were analysed, and intra-step and stance-averaged analyses were not done. The curvilinear models have more parameters, so part of their better fit reflects extra degrees of freedom, and some participants had very high F0 values (up to 12.3 N/kg).
practicalImplications: For over-ground sprint profiling with force plates, follow the authors' recommendation to use the unresisted single-trial method with a linear fit, rather than fitting loaded trials at maximal velocity. Force-velocity values from different profiling methods are not interchangeable, so F0 and slope values should not be compared across studies that used different methods. Loaded sprints should not be assumed to reproduce the profile of unresisted sprints, particularly at very low velocities.
athleteDev: The authors suggest the unresisted single-trial linear profile is the more practical choice for profiling sprint force-velocity, because its fit is close to the curvilinear fits. The paper does not measure performance, and its performance links (v0 and Pmax, not F0) come from earlier studies it cites.
rtp: This study does not address injury or return to sport, and its participants were male sprinters and soccer players. It cannot be used to judge rehabilitation or return-to-play readiness from loaded sprint force data.

citation: Ellens S, Carey D, Gastin P, Varley MC. Changing the criteria applied to acceleration and deceleration efforts changes the types of player actions detected. Science and Medicine in Football. 2022.
abstract: Acceleration and deceleration efforts of 22 elite Australian football players across two matches were labeled with the player action at the time, using synchronized video and 10-Hz GNSS data. Linear movement and jumps were most common in high accelerations, and stops and tackles in high decelerations. The authors report that higher commencing speed was linked to longer durations above the deceleration threshold.
tldr: In elite Australian football, high accelerations were mostly linear running and high decelerations mostly stops and contact actions, and the actions captured shift with the minimum duration above threshold. The authors suggest a dwell time of at least 0.5 s if the goal is to count linear accelerations.
methods: Efforts above plus or minus 3 m/s2 were detected from filtered 10-Hz GNSS data for 22 players, and each effort was labeled with one of 15 player actions by manual video coding in Hudl Sportscode. Linear mixed models with player and game random effects tested commencing speed by action and commencing speed against effort duration.
findings: High accelerations were mostly linear movement (about 5 per player per match) and jumps, and high decelerations were mostly stops (about 10 per player per match), being tackled (6) and tackling (4). Commencing speed differed by action only for decelerations, with jumps (+14%, P=.022) and tackles (+17%, P=.003) starting faster than stops, and each 1 m/s higher commencing speed added 0.14 s above the deceleration threshold (95% CI 0.12 to 0.16). Most high accelerations exceeded the threshold for 0.3 s or less (228 of 268 by the reported counts), while about half of decelerations did.
limitations: Two matches from one elite team, a single absolute 3 m/s2 threshold, and device validity taken from manufacturer testing only. Reported numbers do not fully reconcile: 46 efforts per player per match across 22 players and two matches does not match the 1,178 total, the duration counts sum to 1,172, and the Discussion states that most deceleration efforts lasted 0.3 s or less although the counts put about half there. The 0.5 s recommendation for linear movement is read from a histogram, not tested, and only about 30 acceleration efforts lasted 0.5 s or more.
practicalImplications: Choose the minimum duration above threshold to match the actions of interest, because the mix of detected actions changes with it. The authors also recommend training accelerations and decelerations across a range of commencing speeds; this follows from the speed spread observed but was not tested as a training intervention.
athleteDev: If the aim is to count linear accelerations, a longer minimum duration (the authors suggest 0.5 s) helps exclude jumps and other actions. Set the minimum duration to match the action of interest rather than accepting the software default.
rtp: Not applicable: this is match profiling in healthy elite players with no injury or return-to-play outcome. The link between high decelerations and muscle damage that the authors cite comes from other work and was not tested here.

citation: Geneau MC, Gastin PB, Robertson S, James LP. Classification of lower body strength qualities: A data-driven approach. Int J Sports Sci Coach. 2025:1-24.
abstract: This systematic review grouped lower-body extensor strength metrics from multi-joint, weight-bearing tests by how much variance they share. The authors propose five domains of lower-body strength: reactive dynamic, unloaded dynamic, loaded dynamic, early isometric and maximal isometric. They call for more empirical work to test these domains before they are used in practice.
tldr: Lower-body strength metrics appear to fall into five groups that measure different things, which may help choose a smaller test battery. Treat the grouping as a proposal: the relationships depend on how each metric is calculated, and no single study has tested the full classification.
methods: Systematic search (September 2024) of Google Scholar, MEDLINE, SportDiscus, Cochrane and CINAHL, English language, no date limit, with reference-list checks. Included studies assessed multi-joint, vertical, dynamic or isometric lower-body tests in athletes or resistance-trained people and compared metrics statistically. Metrics were classified by muscle action, external load and time constraint, then compared within and across categories, with 49% or more shared variance (r of 0.70 or more) treated as similar. No meta-analysis was performed.
findings: Within most task categories, metrics shared more than 50% of variance, except timing and outcome metrics in unloaded ballistic tasks, which shared about 1 to 10%. Drop and rebound jump metrics shared only about 50% of variance with other dynamic and isometric tests, and drop-jump RSI correlated with 1 to 3RM at r = 0.07 to 0.33 in absolute and r = 0.52 to 0.69 in relative values. CMJ height and peak power shared R2 from 0.07 to 0.94 across studies depending on calculation method, and the authors propose five domains while grouping unloaded ballistic timing and outcome metrics into one domain because evidence for separating them was insufficient.
limitations: The authors state that variable methods and populations limit consolidation, the 49% threshold is a simplification, most studies were cross-sectional, and highly correlated metrics can reflect different physiology. The authors say it is unclear where loaded ballistic tasks belong, yet loaded dynamic is listed as a domain, and the five domains need direct testing. The acknowledgements state the work is part of a PhD project partially funded by VALD Performance, while the funding statement reports no financial support.
practicalImplications: The authors recommend a parsimonious test battery, so choosing one test per proposed domain is a reasonable starting point to test. For drop-jump tasks, check that contact time stays under 0.25 s, and confirm how each metric is calculated before comparing values across tools or studies.
athleteDev: The domains can help decide which strength qualities a test battery covers, so that staff do not run several tests that measure the same quality. Because the domains are a proposal, confirm them with each sport's athletes before using them to set training priorities.
rtp: The review does not study injured athletes or return-to-sport criteria, so it cannot set return-to-play thresholds. It can only help choose lower-body strength tests, and the reactive and maximal isometric domains would need checking in injured groups before use in return-to-sport testing.

citation: Rial-Vázquez J, Mayo X, Tufano JJ, Fariñas J, Rúa-Alonso M, Iglesias-Soler E. Cluster vs. traditional training programmes: changes in the force-velocity relationship. Sports Biomech. 2022;21(1):85-103.
abstract: A 5-week randomised trial compared traditional and cluster set structures, matched for load, volume and rest, on the force-velocity (F-V) profile of bench press and squat. Cluster training shifted the squat F-V profile toward velocity, while the two set structures changed the bench press profile in similar ways.
tldr: With load, volume and rest matched, cluster sets moved the squat force-velocity profile toward higher velocity and kept velocity loss lower than traditional sets. Bench press profiles changed similarly under both set structures, so the benefit may be specific to lower-body work.
methods: Participants were randomised to traditional (4 x 8 reps, 5 min rest), cluster (16 x 2 reps, 1 min intra-set rest) or control groups, all at 10RM load for 10 sessions over 5 weeks. F-V profiles were derived from a linear velocity transducer during a progressive 1RM test before and after training, and velocity loss, lactate and accumulated work were tracked across sessions. Group x time ANOVAs were used for the outcome measures.
findings: In the squat, cluster training produced a less steep slope, a higher velocity intercept (V0) and a higher F1RM/F0 ratio, while traditional training raised only the force intercept (F0); squat mean propulsive power at the best load rose only after cluster training. Bench press F0, V0 and Pmax rose in both training groups with no change in slope. 1RM rose in both training groups but not in control, and cluster sets produced lower peak lactate, less within-session velocity loss and a higher average training velocity in the squat (P = 0.049).
limitations: Small sample of mixed-sex students with about 3 months of resistance training experience, and a 5-week, 10-session intervention. Table 1 reports a significant time x group 1RM interaction for bench press (P = 0.001) and squat (P < 0.001), but the paper reports no traditional vs cluster 1RM contrast, so the Discussion's 'similar gains' is untested. Smith machine load limits (21.4 kg minimum) restricted data at high velocities, especially for women, and 4.52% of F-V fits had R-squared below 0.800.
practicalImplications: For squat work aimed at velocity, cluster sets at 10RM (2 reps with 1 minute intra-set rest) kept velocity higher across a session than 4 x 8 with 5 minutes of rest, with equal total rest. Both set structures raised 1RM over 5 weeks, and the authors describe the gains as similar, so set structure can be chosen around the velocity or force emphasis wanted. These results come from students with limited lifting experience and should not be assumed for advanced athletes.
athleteDev: Cluster sets may help a squat program shift the force-velocity profile toward velocity with less velocity loss per session. Bench press changes did not differ between set structures, so set configuration may matter more for lower-body than upper-body work. The findings come from 5 weeks of training in students, not from athletes in a competitive season.
rtp: Not a return-to-sport study. Participants were injury-free, and no injury or rehabilitation outcome was measured, so the paper does not support cluster sets as a rehabilitation or return-to-sport loading strategy.

citation: Brink MS, Frencken WGP, Jordet G, Lemmink KAPM. Coaches' and Players' Perceptions of Training Dose: Not a Perfect Match. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2014;9:497-502.
abstract: Across a full competitive season, session RPE and duration reported by 33 elite youth soccer players were compared with the intensity and duration coaches had planned for each session. Players rated training as harder than intended, and the coach-player correlations were weak.
tldr: Young elite soccer players rated their sessions as harder than coaches intended, and their ratings agreed only weakly with the coach's plan over a whole season. Planned easy and intermediate sessions felt harder to players, while planned hard sessions felt easier.
methods: Before each session, coaches recorded intended exertion (session RIE, 6 to 20 scale) and planned duration for every player. About 30 minutes after each session, players rated session RPE and duration, and load was calculated as RPE x duration. Sessions were grouped as easy, intermediate or hard by intended exertion and compared using two-way ANOVA with Pearson correlations.
findings: Players rated intensity (14.0 vs 13.6) and training load (944 vs 923 AU) higher than coaches intended (P < .0001), with no duration difference, and the coach-player correlations were weak (r = .24 to .49). For sessions coaches intended as easy, players rated intensity (13.3 vs 11.3) and load (884 vs 743 AU) higher, and intermediate sessions followed the same pattern, while intended hard sessions were rated lower for intensity (14.4 vs 15.3), duration and load (1004 vs 1091 AU). First-year U-17 players rated intensity higher than the coach intended (13.7 vs 13.3), and second-year players did not differ.
limitations: Observational design with no injury, illness or performance outcomes, so the stated risk of overtraining and injury is not tested here. Players' accuracy with session RPE may vary, and the authors note that individual validity of RPE in young players ranges widely. Two squads with one coach each limit generalisation to other settings.
practicalImplications: Compare the coach's intended exertion with each player's session RPE across the week, so that a mismatch on an easy or hard day is spotted early. The authors suggest heart rate feedback can help young players calibrate their RPE, and that players should be taught why easy days should not feel hard. Check training dose at age-group transitions, since first-year U-17 players rated their sessions harder than intended.
athleteDev: For performance staff, the gap between planned and felt sessions is a check on whether hard days are hard enough and easy days stay easy. The authors argue that players who train harder than planned on easy days may not recover and adapt, so comparing planned and felt load is a practical way to spot that pattern.
rtp: Not a return-to-sport paper. It studies training dose perception in academy players and measured no injury, recovery or clearance outcome, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.

citation: Martín-San Agustín R, Castillo-Ballesta L, Llobat Sancho J, Esbri-Navarro R, Sánchez-Barbadora M. Comparison of Electromyographic Activity During Hip Extension Exercises Under Gravitational or Inertial Loading Conditions. Sports Health. 2021.
abstract: Electromyography study of 15 resistance-trained men performing unilateral straight knee bridge, 45-degree hip extension and stiff-leg deadlift under gravitational and inertial loading, with biceps femoris, semitendinosus, gluteus maximus and gracilis recorded. Inertial loading produced greater concentric hamstring activation, and the knee bridge and hip extension produced greater biceps femoris and semitendinosus activation than the stiff-leg deadlift.
tldr: In 15 resistance-trained men, inertial loading produced higher concentric hamstring and gluteus maximus activation than gravitational loading, and the knee bridge and hip extension produced more biceps femoris activity than the stiff-leg deadlift. This is a single-session EMG study in healthy men, so it describes activation patterns rather than injury or strength outcomes.
methods: Within-subject, repeated-measures EMG study (the paper's header labels it cross-sectional) in which each participant completed three sessions a week apart: familiarization, determination of the load giving maximum concentric power with a linear encoder, and EMG recording at that load in randomized, counterbalanced order. Surface EMG from the biceps femoris, semitendinosus, gluteus maximus and gracilis was normalized to MVIC, averaged over five repetitions, and analysed with two-way repeated-measures ANOVA and Bonferroni post hoc tests.
findings: In the concentric phase, inertial loading exceeded gravitational loading for biceps femoris (15%, P = 0.003), semitendinosus (9.9%, P = 0.007) and gluteus maximus (21.5%, P = 0.001). In the eccentric phase, only gluteus maximus differed between loading types (18.1% higher with inertial loading, P = 0.003), and a modality by exercise interaction showed this for the knee bridge and stiff-leg deadlift. Knee bridge and hip extension produced higher biceps femoris activity than stiff-leg deadlift in both phases, and the biceps femoris to semitendinosus ratio was higher for hip extension than stiff-leg deadlift in both phases (concentric 1.50 vs 1.24, P = 0.002; eccentric 1.41 vs 1.05, P = 0.001).
limitations: The study included only 15 healthy men with no recent injury, so the patterns may not apply to women or to athletes with a strain history, and only three exercises were tested. Concentric power was used to set the load, which may influence the eccentric comparison. The abstract attributes the eccentric semitendinosus difference to hip extension, but the Results and Table 2 attribute it to the knee bridge (P = 0.008), the Results report the eccentric ratio for inertial stiff-leg deadlift as a percentage (1.17% vs 0.93), and the conclusion's claim of high biceps femoris specificity for the knee bridge is not supported by a significant ratio difference.
practicalImplications: When hamstring work is programmed, this study suggests that the knee bridge and 45-degree hip extension produce more hamstring activation than the stiff-leg deadlift, and that hip extension is more biceps femoris selective than the stiff-leg deadlift. The concentric advantage of inertial loading does not extend to the eccentric hamstring phase in this study, so the paper does not show that inertial loading is superior for eccentric hamstring work.
athleteDev: The study measures muscle activation, not strength or power gains. Inertial loading produced higher concentric hamstring and gluteal activation, which the authors use as a rationale for inertial hip-extension exercise, but no training outcome was measured.
rtp: All participants were healthy and injury-free, so the study does not show which exercises are safe or effective for athletes returning from hamstring strain. The authors suggest hip extension may suit biceps femoris-related rehabilitation, but the paper does not test rehabilitation or re-injury outcomes, so that suggestion rests only on activation ratios.

citation: Banyard HG, Tufano JJ, Delgado J, Thompson SW, Nosaka K. Comparison of the Effects of Velocity-Based Training Methods and Traditional 1RM-Percent-Based Training Prescription on Acute Kinetic and Kinematic Variables. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2019; ahead of print.
abstract: Fifteen resistance-trained men completed four randomized back squat sessions at 80% 1RM: percent-based training, a load-velocity profile session, and two velocity-loss-threshold sessions (fixed sets and variable sets, each with a 20% velocity loss threshold). Load-velocity and fixed-set sessions produced faster mean and peak velocities than percent-based training, and both involved less time under tension. Force, power and total work were similar across sessions.
tldr: In a single session of back squats at 80% 1RM, two velocity-based methods (load adjusted to a velocity target, and fixed sets stopped at a 20% velocity loss) let trained men move the bar faster with less time under tension, while force and power stayed similar. These are acute results and do not show which method builds more strength.
methods: Randomized crossover design in 15 resistance-trained men who completed four sessions 96 h apart: 5 x 5 at 80% 1RM (PBT); 5 x 5 with the load changed by 5% 1RM between sets whenever set mean velocity was more than 0.06 m/s away from the target taken from each person's load-velocity profile (LVP); 5 sets at 80% 1RM ended at a 20% velocity loss (FSVL20); and 25 total repetitions at 80% 1RM split into as many sets as needed to stay within a 20% velocity loss (VSVL20). Velocity was measured with four linear position transducers and force and power with a force plate during the concentric phase.
findings: Mean velocity was 0.60 m/s in LVP and 0.58 m/s in FSVL20 versus 0.53 m/s in PBT (effect sizes 1.05 and 0.81), and peak velocity was also faster in both (effect sizes 1.12 and 0.98). LVP used a mean load of 120.5 kg versus 122.4 kg for PBT (not significantly different), mean repetition time under tension (total and concentric) was lower in LVP, and session totals were lower in FSVL20, but not in VSVL20. FSVL20 completed 23.6 repetitions versus 25 in the other sessions, and VSVL20 took 9:02 versus 10:36 min for PBT with no significant difference in velocity, force, power, work or load.
limitations: Only 15 men were tested in one acute session, and chronic outcomes were not measured. Participants were told to stop sets or had loads changed when velocity targets were missed, so they could tell whether their previous set was above or below threshold, and two VSVL20 participants needed six sets. The velocity-loss threshold was set from the single warm-up repetition at 80% 1RM.
practicalImplications: Coaches with velocity-monitoring equipment can use a velocity target or a 20% velocity loss threshold to limit repetitions and keep bar speed higher within a session. The study does not show that this improves strength or power over a season, so the choice should follow the training goal.
athleteDev: For a strength-focused block in healthy, resistance-trained men, the LVP and fixed-set sets kept bar speed higher and reduced time under tension compared with percent-based sets, with similar force and power output. Whether this leads to more strength or power over weeks is not shown here.
rtp: This study tested healthy men without musculoskeletal injury and cannot inform return to sport. It should not be used to set rehabilitation loads or to judge the safety of velocity-based training after injury.

citation: Nuzzo JL, Pinto MD, Nosaka K. Connective Adaptive Resistance Exercise (CARE) Machines for Accentuated Eccentric and Eccentric-Only Exercise: Introduction to an Emerging Concept. Sports Medicine. 2023.
abstract: This concept paper introduces connected adaptive resistance exercise (CARE) machines, which adjust load in real time to allow accentuated eccentric and eccentric-only training. The authors review existing eccentric equipment and present preliminary machine data from laboratory and non-laboratory use.
tldr: CARE machines adjust resistance within and between repetitions, which lets users perform eccentric overload and eccentric-only sets without spotters or releasers. The authors present the concept and preliminary load data, but the paper does not show effects on strength, muscle size, injury or rehabilitation.
methods: Narrative review of resistance equipment and practitioner survey data, with a description of one CARE machine (Vitruvian Trainer+). Preliminary data came from one individual performing one 25-repetition maximal biceps curl set in each of two modes in the laboratory, and from machine-recorded loads of a random sample of 100 male users (2,124 accentuated sets) and 26 of those men (135 eccentric-only sets) in non-laboratory settings.
findings: In the non-laboratory sample, average eccentric loads exceeded concentric loads (eccentric:concentric ratio 1.42 across 18,174 accentuated repetitions; 4.99 across 900 eccentric-only repetitions from 26 men), with sets done at varied, unrecorded intensities. In the single-person laboratory example, the machine's delivered load fell 61.4% (eccentric) and 85.5% (concentric) from repetition 2 to 24 in the accentuated set, and 37.9% (eccentric) in the eccentric-only set. The authors also cite two earlier experiments reporting strong correlations (r >= 0.94) between machine concentric strength and a dumbbell 1RM test.
limitations: The paper is a concept piece with uncontrolled, machine-generated load data and no outcome measures; the laboratory data come from one individual and the field data from machine users of unstated training status. Reliability, validity and effectiveness of CARE machines are described as limited, and two authors previously worked for the company that makes the machine described. The authors' statement that home machines 'appear to provide a stimulus sufficient for neuromuscular adaptation' rests on load data only, and they note longer-term training studies are required.
practicalImplications: Where eccentric overload or eccentric-only work is planned but spotters or releasers are not available, a CARE machine may be a practical option to evaluate. Its load outputs do not show training benefit, so any program change should be assessed against local outcome measures. Practitioners should weigh the company link when reading the machine's validation data.
athleteDev: CARE machines may allow eccentric overload, eccentric-only sets and automatic drop sets without spotters or releasers, which could widen the options for strength programs. The paper does not show that these methods improve strength, power or sport performance.
rtp: This paper cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It mentions rehabilitation as a possible use, but it reports no clinical outcomes, injury data or rehabilitation trials.

citation: Wirth K, Hartmann H, Mickel C, Szilvas E, Keiner M, Sander A. Core Stability in Athletes: A Critical Analysis of Current Guidelines. Sports Med. 2016.
abstract: Core stability exercise guidelines for athletes were adapted from back pain rehabilitation, and most exercise specifications have not been tested for effectiveness or compared with strength-training loads. The authors critically analyze concepts including the global and local muscle classification, selective activation, trunk-rotation exercises and training on unstable surfaces. They recommend classical strength-training exercises because these provide the stimuli needed for adaptation.
tldr: Core stability guidelines borrowed from back pain rehabilitation have little evidence in athletes. The authors recommend classical strength training over selective core exercises and unstable-surface training.
methods: Narrative critical analysis of the literature on core stability, trunk muscle EMG, and unstable-surface training. No systematic search strategy is described. The authors examine back pain guidelines, EMG studies of transversus abdominis and multifidus activation, and studies comparing stable and unstable squat training.
findings: The authors state that the corset-like, feed-forward stabilizing role claimed for transversus abdominis rests on unilateral EMG recordings and that selective activation deficits or selective atrophy of deep trunk muscles have not been shown. They report that loads in unstable conditions are about 40 percent lower than in stable conditions, citing McBride et al. and Saeterbakken and Fimland, and that no longitudinal study has shown superiority of unstable-surface training. Citing Lederman and others, they conclude that the global and local muscle classification is inappropriate because trunk muscles act together in task-specific patterns.
limitations: The conclusions depend heavily on the absence of evidence, and the authors do not describe a search, so the literature they critique cannot be reproduced. The authors note the limits of surface EMG, including crosstalk, subcutaneous fat and normalization to MVC.
practicalImplications: Exercises labelled core stability, functional or specific should not be assumed to strengthen deep trunk muscles or to outperform conventional strength training. Programs for athletes can prioritize loaded classical strength exercises, and unstable-surface training should be treated as unproven. Selective activation drills should not be justified by an assumed deficit in deep trunk muscles, since the authors found no evidence of one in strength-trained athletes.
athleteDev: For athletes, the paper supports building trunk strength through loaded classical exercises rather than unstable-surface or selective core drills, which the authors say lack evidence of superiority. The authors also question trunk-rotation exercises because of the shear forces they place on intervertebral discs.
rtp: The paper cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It does not study injured athletes or return-to-play criteria, and its discussion of back pain concerns rehabilitation guidelines that the authors judge unsuitable for athletes.

citation: Gabbett TJ. Debunking the myths about training load, injury and performance: empirical evidence, hot topics and recommendations for practitioners. Br J Sports Med 2018;0:1-9.
abstract: This education review addresses five common myths about training load, injury and performance: that load explains all injuries, that a 10% weekly limit is a rule, that spikes and troughs must be avoided, that an acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR) of 1.5 is a threshold, and that the ratio is all that matters. It draws on recent team sport and athlete studies and argues that load should be judged against chronic load and individual moderators such as age, fitness and injury history.
tldr: Training load matters for injury, but no single rule, such as a 10% weekly limit or an ACWR of 1.5, explains injury risk on its own. Judge each change in load against the athlete's chronic load and individual risk factors.
methods: A narrative education review by a single author, organised around five myths and drawing on recent team sport and athlete studies. No systematic search or appraisal method is described; the PubMed count in Figure 1 shows publication growth only.
findings: Across 38 studies in 11 sports over five years, rapid increases in workload were associated with greater injury risk (as the author reports). In team sport, weekly load increases of 15% or more were linked to about 21% injury likelihood, against 7.5% at 10% or less, and in cricket fast bowlers, players with greater chronic workloads had a fivefold lower injury risk than those with low chronic workloads.
limitations: This single-author narrative has no described search or appraisal, so the evidence chosen cannot be verified, and the author declares consulting work for high-performance organisations. Injury prediction using training load data was only slightly better than chance (AUC 0.64 to 0.76), as the review reports, and most cited work is observational in single teams of senior elite athletes.
practicalImplications: Judge each week's load change against the athlete's chronic load rather than a fixed 10% rule: the author's model suggests smaller increases when chronic load is extremely low or extremely high, and that larger increases may be tolerated with moderate to high chronic load and may be needed to speed rehabilitation. Avoid large week-to-week spikes but do not assume troughs are safe, since undertraining can also raise risk. Read load data alongside fitness, injury history, age and well-being rather than the ACWR alone.
athleteDev: The review treats training load as a driver of both performance and injury, with higher chronic load linked to better performance and lower injury risk when built gradually. It notes that athletes who cut load most during a taper tended to improve most and that a 13-day shock block improved soccer players' performance, though most such studies in elite athletes lacked a control group.
rtp: The review covers return from injury: early staged loading can shorten time to return to play, and in one study starting rehabilitation 2 days after injury rather than 9 days shortened return by 3 weeks. It also notes that building high chronic workloads may delay return to play, but it does not set return-to-play criteria.

citation: Mandorino M, Lacome M. Defining Worst-Case-Scenario Thresholds in Soccer: Intensity Versus Volume. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2024 (ahead of print).
abstract: This brief report describes worst-case scenario (WCS) values and the time spent above 80% and 90% of WCS for total distance (TD) and high-speed running (HSR) in professional soccer matches. Data from 31 players were compared by playing level (first team vs U19) and position. The U19 team had higher HSR WCS, and the first team spent more time above 80% and 90% of TD WCS.
tldr: Peak match demands (WCS) do not show the whole picture. Time spent above 80% and 90% of WCS adds information about how often players work near their peak, and it varies by level and position.
methods: Ten-hertz microtechnology (WIMU PRO) recorded 31 players across full matches in the 2022-23 season. WCS was the maximum 1-minute rolling average of TD and HSR, and time above 80% and 90% of the mean WCS was computed. Linear mixed models with player as a random effect compared level and position.
findings: U19 players had higher HSR WCS than the first team (63.6 vs 56.3 m/min, P < .01, ES 0.88), and TD WCS did not differ by level. The first team spent more time above 80% (6.4 vs 5.6 min, P < .05, ES 0.27) and 90% (1.5 vs 1.2 min, P < .01, ES 0.29) of TD WCS. Midfielders had the highest TD WCS (about 208 m/min) and spent more time above 80% of TD WCS, forwards had the highest HSR WCS (about 71 m/min) and spent more time above 80% of HSR WCS, and no position differences were found above 90% of TD WCS.
limitations: Single club and season, with unequal groups (18 first team, 13 U19), position groups of 6 to 10 players, and only full-match appearances included. Only a 1-minute window was tested, and the study has no measures of internal load or fatigue, so the authors' suggestion that more time near WCS probably means higher internal load is untested. Sex is not stated in the text.
practicalImplications: When prescribing training for different playing roles, consider the volume of work close to WCS (time above 80% and 90%) as well as the peak WCS value. Staff can use this to compare how often first-team and U19 players work near their peak demands.
athleteDev: Use time above 80% and 90% of WCS, alongside peak WCS, to compare how much work players do near their peak match demands by level and position. Training prescriptions can then match playing roles.
rtp: Not applicable. This study describes match demands in squad players and does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to play. It cannot be used to set return-to-play loads.

citation: Næss TC. Determining the optimal blood flow restriction protocol for maximising muscle hypertrophy and strength, pressure and cuff width: A mini-review. Journal of Human Sport & Exercise. 2021;16(4):752-759.
abstract: This mini-review summarises research on blood flow restriction (BFR) training protocols, focusing on limb occlusion pressure and cuff width. It finds no uniform protocol that maximises hypertrophy and strength across studies. The author argues that occlusion pressure is best set relative to arterial occlusion pressure, and that cuff width's effect on long-term adaptation is unclear.
tldr: BFR training produces gains across many protocols, but this review finds no single optimal occlusion pressure or cuff width. Setting pressure as a percentage of arterial occlusion pressure gives a more controlled stimulus, and the long-term effect of cuff width is still uncertain.
methods: Mini-review of the BFR literature. The author searched PubMed, Google Scholar and Web of Science for BFR and Kaatsu terms up to June 2019, limited to English-language human studies, and checked reference lists. Protocol details (cuff width, pressure, load and volume) are tabulated for 26 study entries.
findings: Absolute pressures across studies ranged from 40 to 200 mmHg, and relative pressures from 40 to 90% of arterial occlusion pressure. In Lixandrao et al. (2015), 80% vs 40% of occlusion pressure at 20% of 1RM gave a 2.44% larger muscle mass, with no meaningful difference at 40% of 1RM. Counts et al. (2016) found no significant difference in hypertrophy or strength between 40% and 90% of occlusion pressure. Narrow cuffs needed more absolute pressure to occlude flow (Jessee et al., 2016; Loenneke et al., 2012). At equal relative pressure, 100 mm and 120 mm cuffs gave similar blood flow (Mouser et al., 2018). Laurentino et al. (2016) found similar strength and size gains with 50 mm and 100 mm cuffs at 80% of occlusion pressure.
limitations: Narrative mini-review with no formal quality appraisal or pooled analysis. Searches were limited to English-language articles up to June 2019. Protocols differ widely, and several Table 1 entries list cuff width as unknown, which hampers direct comparison. Evidence on cuff width and long-term adaptation is described as sparse.
practicalImplications: Report occlusion pressure and cuff width in full, since these vary widely across studies and change the stimulus. Where possible, set pressure as a percentage of arterial occlusion pressure, which the author describes as more controlled than a fixed mmHg value. The author advises a lower relative pressure as the more conservative choice, and notes that higher pressures showed benefit mainly with low loads (about 20% of 1RM).
athleteDev: Blood flow restriction training can add to low-load strength and size work, but the review does not identify one best pressure or cuff width. Use a relative pressure setting, record the cuff width used, and keep the protocol consistent so that changes can be read.
rtp: The review mentions BFR use in rehabilitation, citing single studies on Achilles tendon rupture and extremity injury, but gives no return-to-sport protocol, criteria or injury outcomes. It cannot be used to set BFR loads or to clear an athlete to return after injury.

citation: Drury B, Peacock D, Moran J, Cone C, Ramirez Campillo R. Different Interset Rest Intervals During the Nordic Hamstrings Exercise in Young Male Athletes. J Athl Train. 2021;56(9):952-959.
abstract: This crossover study compared 1-minute and 3-minute interset rest intervals during the Nordic hamstring exercise in 10 well-trained young male team-sport athletes. Force indices and interlimb asymmetry did not differ between rest conditions or sets. Peak force declined within sets from about the fourth repetition.
tldr: A 1-minute rest between Nordic hamstring sets kept force and asymmetry similar to a 3-minute rest in 10 well-trained athletes. Peak force still fell within each set, so staff should expect drop-off from about repetition 4.
methods: Randomized repeated-measures crossover laboratory study. Ten uninjured male athletes who met baseline criteria (eccentric peak force of at least 337 N, asymmetry under 15%, weekly NHE exposure and no lower-limb injury in the prior 6 months) completed 2 sets of 6 repetitions on the NordBord with either a 1-minute or 3-minute interset rest. Peak force, average force, percentage maintenance and interlimb asymmetry were analyzed with 2-way repeated-measures ANOVA.
findings: No main effects or interactions for rest condition were found for any force index or asymmetry (P > .05). Peak force was lower than repetition 1 from repetition 4 onward in set 1 for both limbs, and from repetition 5 onward in set 2 for the dominant limb. Interlimb asymmetry was about 8% to 9% in both conditions and did not change between sets. Percentage maintenance was above 93% across sets.
limitations: Ten participants, one session per condition and a single set pair limit power, so null results do not show the two rest intervals are equivalent; the power analysis used an effect size from a different NHE training study. Inclusion criteria selected injury-free, stronger athletes, so results may not apply to injured or less trained players. Standardized between-condition differences slightly favored the 3-minute rest (small magnitude), and the Key Points mention modest benefits of 3 minutes, but no difference was significant.
practicalImplications: For uninjured athletes already familiar with the NHE, a 1-minute rest between sets did not reduce force or change asymmetry in this study. Because peak force still fell from repetition 4 onward, use fewer repetitions per set or add a brief rest after each repetition. Interpret asymmetry individually, as the authors recommend.
athleteDev: In an eccentric hamstring block for well-trained athletes, a 1-minute interset rest did not cost force. Set structure matters more: plan fewer repetitions or a rest between repetitions, because peak force fell from repetition 4 onward.
rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport or rehabilitation rest prescription. It tested uninjured athletes only and excluded anyone with a lower-limb injury in the prior 6 months.

citation: Carroll KM, Bernards JR, Bazyler CD, Taber CB, Stuart CA, DeWeese BH, et al. Divergent Performance Outcomes Following Resistance Training Using Repetition Maximums or Relative Intensity. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2018 (accepted manuscript).
abstract: Fifteen well-trained men completed 10 weeks of resistance training in a repetition maximum (RM, n = 8) or relative intensity by sets and repetitions (RISR, n = 7) group. The RISR group showed moderate between-group effect sizes favoring it for squat and countermovement jump height, and training strain was statistically greater in the RM group, which also showed decreases in early rate of force development.
tldr: Over 10 weeks with similar volume load, relative intensity training with heavy and light days improved jump height and early rate of force development more than repetition maximum training to failure in well-trained men. Both groups gained maximal isometric strength by a similar amount, and with 7 or 8 men per group the findings are preliminary.
methods: Fifteen well-trained men (age 26.9 years) were ranked and paired on baseline allometric isometric peak force, then randomly assigned to repetition maximum zone (RM, n = 8) or relative intensity by sets and repetitions (RISR, n = 7) training for 10 weeks, 3 days per week, plus a common sprint program on two other days. Squat and countermovement jumps (unweighted and 20 kg) and isometric mid-thigh pull peak force and rate of force development were tested at five time points. Mixed-design ANOVAs and Hedges g with 90% confidence intervals (within-group from pre and post values, between-group from change scores) were used.
findings: Volume load displacement did not differ between groups at post hoc testing, but training strain was greater in RM in weeks 3 to 10 (p < 0.05). RISR increased unweighted squat jump height pre to post (p = 0.009) while RM did not, and between-group effects favoured RISR for all jump heights (g = 0.76 to 1.07) and for early RFD (g = 0.89 to 1.25). Isometric peak force rose significantly only in RISR (p < 0.001), although RM showed moderate within-group gains (g = 0.83 to 0.98) and the between-group effect was trivial to small (g = 0.18 to 0.20); RM significantly decreased RFD at 0 to 50 ms (p = 0.018) and 0 to 100 ms (p = 0.014).
limitations: The sample is small (15 men in two groups) with no non-training control and many outcomes; between-group 90% confidence intervals are about plus or minus 0.83, so the CMJ 20 kg jump height (g = 0.76) and all peak force effects include zero. RFD reliability was poor (CV 21 to 24% for 0 to 50 and 0 to 100 ms), and baseline RFD was higher in RM than RISR (for example 5,534 vs 3,646 N/s at 0 to 50 ms), which may contribute to the divergent changes (Inference). The abstract places the taper in weeks 8 to 10, whereas the Methods describe the final two weeks as the taper; this record follows the Methods.
practicalImplications: In well-trained men, varying intensity across the week (heavy and light days, with loads set from set and repetition maxima) gave larger jump and early RFD gains than repeatedly training to failure at similar volume load, which the authors link to lower training strain. Both approaches raised maximal strength, so the choice matters most when jump and rapid force are the goal. Both groups improved after the two-week taper, but there was no no-taper comparison, so the taper's own effect is not isolated.
athleteDev: For jump height and rapid force goals in trained men, the study supports varying loads across the week over repeated sets to failure. For maximal strength alone the two methods gave similar gains. Effects come from 7 to 8 men per group over 10 weeks, so treat the principle as a hypothesis to test with your own athletes.
rtp: Not applicable. The sample was well-trained men without injury, and no rehabilitation or return-to-sport outcome was measured, so the study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.

citation: Svantesson E, Hamrin Senorski E, Webster KE, Karlsson J, Diermeier T, Rothrauff BB, et al. Clinical Outcomes After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury: Panther Symposium ACL Injury Clinical Outcomes Consensus Group. The Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2020;8(7):2325967120934751.
abstract: A multidisciplinary international panel of ACL experts used a modified Delphi process at the 2019 Panther Symposium to agree on how clinical outcome after ACL treatment should be measured and reported. The consensus covers study planning, clinical assessment, osteoarthritis, laxity and patient-reported outcomes (PROs).
tldr: Report ACL outcomes in four categories: early adverse events, PROs, graft failure or reinjury, and clinical knee function and structure. Aim for at least 2 years of follow-up with about 80% retention, describe pretreatment status, and use the IKDC-SKF as the preferred knee-specific PRO.
methods: A 25-member working group discussed 13 draft statements, which were pre-voted through an online survey and then debated at an in-person meeting in June 2019. Statements needed 80% agreement; nine reached consensus, and four were excluded or merged into others. The liaisons completed a MEDLINE literature review for each final statement.
findings: Consensus was reached on: an a priori power calculation (25 of 25); a pretreatment description including demographics, a knee PRO, HRQoL and preinjury sport level (statement 2 was merged, so no agreement percentage is reported); a follow-up length set by the outcome being assessed, optimally including 80% of the cohort (25 of 25); a minimum 2-year assessment covering adverse events, knee function and structure, PROs, activity level and reinjury (25 of 25); osteoarthritis assessment at 5 years; AP and rotatory laxity testing; a PRO set of one knee-specific tool, one activity scale and one HRQoL measure; the PASS; and the IKDC-SKF as the recommended knee-related measure (24 of 25).
limitations: This is expert opinion built on voting and literature review, with no formal evidence grading. The symposium was industry-sponsored and many authors report industry ties. The paper itself notes gaps in the tools it recommends, including the lack of structural validity evidence for the IKDC-SKF and limited responsiveness of the KOOS after ACL injury.
practicalImplications: For ACL outcome tracking, record the pretreatment knee PRO, preinjury sport or activity level (Marx scale) and HRQoL, and report knee laxity alongside PROs. Read PRO change against the MDC and MCID, and use the PASS to see whether the patient reaches an acceptable knee state.
athleteDev: The paper concerns outcome reporting after ACL treatment, not training. For performance staff, it supports recording preinjury sport level and the exact knee-specific tool used, so that return-to-sport and rehab outcomes can be compared across athletes and time points.
rtp: Supports a 2-year outcome battery for ACL reconstruction (clinical knee exam with laxity, IKDC-SKF, activity scale, HRQoL and reinjury history) as a reporting standard. It does not set return-to-sport criteria or timing; the paper refers readers to a separate Panther Symposium consensus on return to sport.

citation: Peng T, Trollinger Derry L, Yogeswaran V, Goldschlager NF. Commotio cordis in 2023. Sports Med. 2023.
abstract: A narrative review of commotio cordis, sudden cardiac arrest caused by blunt trauma over the heart, prompted by the 2023 collapse of an NFL player. It summarises epidemiology, registry data, mechanisms, diagnosis, management and return to play, and calls for better reporting, defibrillator access and medical cover at sports events.
tldr: Commotio cordis is a rare but important cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes, and survival depends on fast CPR and defibrillation. Staff should recognise it early, have AEDs and trained responders at training and games, and support better case reporting.
methods: A narrative review drawing on registry reports, case series, animal models and guidelines, organised around epidemiology, pathophysiology, diagnosis, presentation, management and future directions. The authors state only that they performed an initial literature search; no search protocol or inclusion criteria are given.
findings: The review describes commotio cordis as the third most common cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes, with more than 75% of cases occurring in sport and baseball the most common sport. In the US National Commotio Cordis Registry, survival rose from 10 to 15% in early reports to 58% in a 2013 update, with 40% survival when resuscitation began within 3 minutes and 5% when it was delayed beyond 3 minutes. In swine models, ventricular fibrillation followed impacts only within a narrow window of the T wave, and AED shocks given at 1-minute intervals gave 100% survival compared with 46% at 4 minutes.
limitations: A narrative review with no described search or evidence grading. Registry case counts are dated (216 as of 2012) and reporting is not standardised, so true incidence is unknown, as the authors note. The timing and projectile findings come from animal models, and several return-to-play and equipment points rest on expert opinion or on case reports.
practicalImplications: Ensure AEDs are accessible within 5 minutes at organised sport events, and train coaches, staff and players in CPR and AED use. A collapse after a chest blow should prompt immediate CPR and defibrillation, and the case should be reported to a registry. Chest protectors have not been shown to prevent this in registry or swine data, so they should not be relied on, and age-appropriate safety baseballs are recommended for children up to 13 years old.
athleteDev: For performance staff, the review's relevance is emergency readiness rather than training. Survival depends on CPR and AED use within minutes, so defibrillator access and staff training should cover practices as well as games.
rtp: The review states that return to play after commotio cordis is decided case by case, and that implantable defibrillators have not been recommended for survivors, since no data show later sudden death risk in them. It gives no return-to-play criteria, and it notes that recurrence is extremely rare, with one reported suspected case.

citation: Salzillo C, Marzullo A. Commotio Cordis in Sudden Cardiac Death in the Young: A State-of-the-Art Review. Rev. Cardiovasc. Med. 2025;26(9):43357.
abstract: Narrative review of commotio cordis, a rare but often fatal cause of sudden cardiac death in young people, particularly athletes exposed to non-penetrating chest impact. The authors summarize pathophysiology, epidemiology, postmortem diagnosis, medicolegal issues and prevention, including AED access, CPR training and chest protectors.
tldr: Commotio cordis is a rare, often fatal arrhythmia caused by a chest blow in a young person without structural heart disease, and survival depends on immediate CPR and defibrillation. The evidence that chest protectors prevent it is debated, so the review's practical emphasis is AED access, CPR training and emergency planning.
methods: Narrative review. The paper does not describe a search strategy, selection criteria or appraisal method, and reports no original data. It draws on autopsy series, national registries, a systematic review of 334 documented cases, and experimental and biomechanical studies.
findings: The authors report approximately 15-25 US cases per year and state that the true incidence is likely underestimated. They report that 36% of 334 documented cases occurred outside sport, with higher mortality in non-sport events (88% vs 66%), attributed to lower bystander CPR (27% vs 97%) and defibrillation (17% vs 81%) rates. They state that defibrillation within three minutes can raise survival above 70%, and cite a study showing that not all commercially available chest protectors offer sufficient protection.
limitations: The review has no stated search method, so the choice of sources cannot be checked. Post-mortem diagnosis depends on autopsy protocols that often omit genetic testing, which the authors note makes case counts difficult. The section on delayed-onset arrhythmias and the efficacy ratings in Table 2 are not tied to a described method or to clinical outcome data in the text.
practicalImplications: Staff responsible for contact-sport athletes should confirm AED availability and CPR-trained personnel at training and competition venues, since the authors identify these as the most effective measures for survival. Any collapse after a chest blow should prompt immediate CPR and defibrillation. If chest protectors are used, the review points to certified standards such as ND200, but it does not establish that protectors prevent commotio cordis.
athleteDev: The review has no performance-training content. Its relevant point is emergency preparedness in contact and collision sport, specifically AED access, CPR-trained staff and emergency action plans.
rtp: The review does not address return to sport and gives no return-to-play criteria. It notes that subacute post-traumatic arrhythmias may need prolonged ECG surveillance, cardiac imaging and genetic testing even without symptoms, but it does not say when an athlete may return after a chest-trauma event.

citation: Moiroux-Sahraoui A, Mazeas J, Bener E, Bouzekraoui Alaoui I, Douryang M, Forelli F. Comparative Electromyographic Activity of Hamstrings During Sprinting Versus Strengthening Exercises: Implications for Injury Prevention. Cureus. 2024;16(8):e66370.
abstract: Pilot study comparing hamstring EMG activity in 15 sprint-exposed field athletes during maximal 30-m sprints, Nordic hamstring exercise (NHE) and high-speed isokinetic knee flexion at 300 deg/s. Sprinting produced the highest mean hamstring activity, followed by NHE and then isokinetic exercise, and the authors suggest that sprinting be combined with NHE in prevention and rehabilitation.
tldr: In 15 sprint-exposed athletes, 30-m sprinting produced higher hamstring EMG than Nordic hamstring exercise, which in turn exceeded fast isokinetic knee flexion. This is a small pilot that measured muscle activation only, not injury or strength outcomes, so it supports exercise selection as a starting point rather than proof of prevention.
methods: Single-group pilot with all exercises performed by each participant in randomized order. Surface EMG from the semitendinosus and biceps femoris was normalized to a prone isometric MVIC and compared with two-tailed Student's t-tests, with a one-sided Wilcoxon test also reported for one comparison.
findings: Mean hamstring EMG was 0.48 ± 0.19 during sprinting, 0.32 ± 0.09 during NHE and 0.25 ± 0.07 during isokinetic flexion. Sprinting exceeded NHE for the biceps femoris (p < 0.01) and the two-muscle mean (p = 0.02), but not the semitendinosus (NS). NHE exceeded isokinetic flexion for the semitendinosus (p = 0.03) and the mean (p = 0.02), but not the biceps femoris (NS). Sprinting exceeded isokinetic flexion for all muscle measures (p < 0.01).
limitations: The text gives n = 15 in the methods, abstract and Table 1 but n = 10 in the limitations, and states that only males were studied while Table 1 reports 13 male participants out of 15. The conclusions say the single-muscle differences were not significant, which conflicts with Tables 2-4 (for example ST p = 0.03 and BF p < 0.01). The reported BMI (13.85 ± 8.28 kg/m2) is implausibly low for adult athletes, set and repetition counts differ between the abstract and methods, the MVIC is introduced as a quadriceps test but described as a prone hamstring test, and EMG is described as normalized to MVIC yet reported in microvolts. The sample size calculation called for 381 participants, the authors acknowledge a 25% margin of error, and fatigue and electrode variability were not controlled.
practicalImplications: When the goal is high hamstring muscle activity, this pilot suggests sprinting and NHE load the hamstrings more than fast isokinetic knee flexion, so isokinetic work should not be the main choice for that purpose. Because the study measured EMG amplitude only, it supports including sprint exposure alongside NHE, but it does not show that either exercise lowers injury rates.
athleteDev: In this pilot, high-speed sprinting produced more hamstring EMG than NHE or fast isokinetic flexion, which suggests sprint work as a high-intensity hamstring stimulus. The study did not measure force, speed or sprint performance, so it cannot rank these exercises for performance gain.
rtp: All participants were healthy athletes with no hamstring injury in the previous six months, so the study cannot show which exercises are safe or effective for an injured athlete returning to sport. It may serve as a reference for muscle activation during rehabilitation planning, but it does not provide evidence about recovery, re-injury risk or return-to-play readiness.

citation: de Castro Fernandes JV, Pedrinelli A, Rubio-Arias JÁ. Comparative analysis of treatment strategies for groin injuries in athletes: Effects on successful recovery and recurrence of sports conditions - A systematic review. Apunts Sports Medicine. 2025;60:100481.
abstract: Systematic review of 30 studies (1,931 athletes) comparing surgical and conservative treatments for groin and adductor pain in athletes, with return to sport and recurrence as the main outcomes. The authors propose a stepped strategy that starts with shockwave therapy, manual therapy or exercise, with surgery considered if there is no improvement after 3 to 6 months.
tldr: Across 30 studies with 1,931 athletes, surgical procedures such as adductor tenotomy and selective partial adductor release were reported to return most athletes to sport, and shockwave and manual therapy were linked to faster return in single studies. The authors propose 3 to 6 months of conservative care before surgery, but the included studies are heterogeneous and 12 of 30 were rated low quality.
methods: Systematic review following PRISMA and pre-registered in PROSPERO (CRD42023430694), with AMSTAR used for methodological quality. Searches of PubMed-MEDLINE, Web of Science and Cochrane Library ran from inception to 30 April 2023, identifying 1,296 records, 86 full texts and 30 included studies. Included studies were case-control studies or case series with n of at least 10, published from 2005 in English, Spanish or Portuguese, and were rated with the Downs and Black scale by two reviewers.
findings: The authors summarize surgical return-to-sport success at around 75-80%. Individual studies reported about 75% return to previous level after adductor and/or rectus abdominis tenotomy, 42 of 43 athletes returning after selective partial release of the long adductor (mean 9.21 weeks), and 80% good or excellent results after adductor tenotomy with or without hernioplasty in a 155-athlete study. Shockwave therapy was associated with earlier return to football (p = 0.048), and manual therapy with a shorter time to return than exercise therapy (12.8 vs 17.3 weeks, p = 0.043). Eighteen studies were rated high quality and 12 low quality (mean score 16.6, SD 5.6).
limitations: The review has no pooled analysis and mixes injury sites, treatments and follow-up periods, and 13 studies did not specify the type of pubalgia. Recurrence, named in the title, is reported for only a few studies. The abstract describes a qualitative analysis while the results describe a statistical analysis, the text sets high quality as above 16 points while Table 2 rates scores of 16 as high, the roughly 75% tenotomy return rate comes from two studies the review rated low quality, and a randomized trial is included although inclusion was limited to case-control studies or case series. The authors also note possible publication bias, which they do not quantify.
practicalImplications: For athletes with persistent groin pain, the review supports starting with conservative care such as shockwave therapy, manual therapy or exercise, and considering surgery if there is no improvement after 3 to 6 months, as the authors propose. The authors stress that the choice between surgical approaches should follow an individual assessment of injury severity and response to conservative treatment.
athleteDev: The review does not address training load or performance enhancement. It reports return-to-play rates, pain and functional scores after treatment rather than measured sport-performance outcomes.
rtp: Return to sport is the review's main focus. The reported return rates (about 75% to 98% in individual surgical studies) and times to return (about 9 to 17 weeks in individual studies) can inform expectations, but they come from heterogeneous, mostly uncontrolled series. The stepped algorithm is the authors' proposal and has not been validated.

citation: Wright BS, Dykowski S, Bretzin AC, et al. Comparing Time to Recovery Between Initial and Repeat Concussion in Athletes. Clin J Sport Med. 2024;00:1-7.
abstract: Retrospective review of 50 athletes treated at an interdisciplinary concussion clinic, comparing time to return-to-sport clearance after first versus second (primary) and first versus last (secondary) concussions. Time to recovery did not differ between initial and repeat concussions, and the authors conclude that recovery was not longer after repeat injury in these athletes.
tldr: In 50 athletes treated at one concussion clinic, time to return-to-sport clearance did not differ between a first and a repeat concussion once initial symptom severity and time to first visit were accounted for. Earlier clinic presentation and lower initial SCAT symptom scores were associated with faster recovery.
methods: Retrospective review of electronic medical records for athletes with more than one concussion who first attended a sports neurology clinic within 30 days of injury (2016 to 2020). Time to recovery was compared between first and second concussions (primary) and first and last concussions (secondary) using Cox regression, adjusted for time to initial visit and SCAT symptom severity, with sensitivity analyses by visit timing and interval between injuries.
findings: Median days to recovery were 42 after first, 34 after second and 34 after last concussion, and the difference was not statistically significant. Multivariable HRs were 1.02 (95% CI 0.65-1.62, P = 0.92) for second vs first and 1.01 (95% CI 0.64-1.62, P = 0.91) for last vs first. Longer time to initial clinic visit and higher SCAT symptom number and severity were each associated with slower recovery, while age, sex, concussion history and loss of consciousness were not.
limitations: The observational, retrospective design cannot establish causality, and the data reflect routine clinical documentation across several providers and years, with recovery dates tied to clinic visit timing. The sample is small, 19 of 105 injuries occurred outside sport, and only 7 patients had three or more concussions. The text reports a univariate injury-number result of HR 1.39, P = 0.008 while stating injury number was not associated with recovery, and Table 3 lists HR 1.39 (P = 0.24) for male sex; the text also gives HR 1.02, P = 0.92 for the multivariable first vs last model where Table 4 and the abstract give HR 1.01, P = 0.91. This record uses the Table 4 values.
practicalImplications: A repeat concussion should not be assumed to lengthen recovery on injury number alone in this clinic's experience. At the first visit, prompt assessment and SCAT symptom scoring matter, since earlier presentation and lower initial symptom severity were associated with faster recovery.
athleteDev: The study does not address training or performance outcomes. Its only performance-adjacent content is time to return-to-sport clearance after concussion.
rtp: Time to return-to-sport clearance is the main outcome. Once initial symptom burden and time to first visit are considered, the study does not support a longer recovery after a repeat concussion. It cannot set return-to-play criteria, because clearance dates were set by treating physicians in one clinic.

citation: Prock M, O'Sullivan DM, Tiernan S. Comparing return to play protocols after sports related concussion among international sporting organisations. The Physician and Sportsmedicine. 2024.
abstract: Comparison of return-to-play protocols and medical rules of 12 international sporting organisations in combat, contact and collision sports, accessed through official websites. Six organisations published their own protocol, step counts were similar, initial rest and minimum time to return varied widely, and none reflected the 2023 CISG consensus statement at the time of the review.
tldr: Of 12 international sporting organisations in combat, contact and collision sports, only six published their own return-to-play protocol, and minimum times to return ranged from 5 to 180 days. None of the accessible protocols had been updated to the 2023 CISG consensus statement when the documents were reviewed.
methods: Structured document review (the authors call it a commentary) of concussion guidelines and medical rules from 12 of 14 eligible organisations, retrieved from official websites and Google searches on 9 September 2023 using defined keywords, and screened for concussion terms. Content was extracted into a spreadsheet under seven categories: initial rest, number of steps, sport-specific training, resistance training, medical clearance, minimum time to return, and accelerated pathways. No outcome data were analysed.
findings: Six organisations published an RTP protocol, three (FIH, WL, WT) uploaded only the SCAT5, and three (IJF, WAKO, WKF) provided only medical-rule recommendations such as suspension periods. Table 2 shows six steps for eight organisations and five for FIBA, and initial rest was 24-48 hours in most; World Rugby required one week of relative rest for adults and two weeks for children (each including 24 hours of complete rest), and boxing required a 30-day suspension before step 2. Minimum time to return after a single concussion ranged from 5 days (FIBA) to 180 days (WAKO, loss of consciousness over one minute), resistance training began at step 3 or step 4, and FIFA, IIHF and World Rugby allowed accelerated pathways.
limitations: The review depends on publicly available documents from one date, and the authors note that no organisation answered requests for supplementary material. The narrative text says eight organisations require six steps but names seven (Table 2 lists eight, including IFAF), and the discussion says IFAF and WR lacked a 24-48 hour rest period while FIBA's is listed as 24 hours. The paper uses the CISG statement as its benchmark without assessing how any protocol performs in practice, and it describes itself as a commentary.
practicalImplications: Staff working with athletes in combat, contact or collision sports should identify which return-to-play protocol their governing body uses, since minimum return times and resting requirements vary widely. Where a sport has no published protocol, the paper recommends the 2023 CISG framework, which includes starting the first step within 24 hours, health-care clearance before collision-risk activity, and cognitive assessment alongside symptoms.
athleteDev: The paper addresses return to play rather than training design. Its performance-relevant point is that sport-specific drills and intensities should be specified at each RTP step, which the authors find in detail only in the FIFA protocol, with FIBA and IBA giving brief examples.
rtp: This is the paper's full subject. It shows which steps, resting periods and clearance points each organisation requires, but it does not establish a safe return date for any athlete. The authors argue that minimum return times should follow current evidence and that accelerated pathways, such as those in FIFA, IIHF and World Rugby, rest on symptom reports the paper describes as low in reliability.

citation: Oleksak P, Nepovimova E, Valko M, Alwasel S, Alomar S, Kuca K. Comprehensive Analysis of Prohibited Substances and Methods in Sports: Unveiling Trends, Pharmacokinetics, and WADA Evolution. Environmental Toxicology and Pharmacology. 2024. Journal pre-proof.
abstract: This narrative review covers the substances and methods on the 2023 WADA Prohibited List, organised by list section, with pharmacokinetic and metabolite notes and a summary of adverse analytical findings reported from 2003 to 2021. Anabolic agents were the most common class of findings, followed by stimulants and diuretics and masking agents. The authors also outline the history of anti-doping testing and the role of WADA.
tldr: This review maps the 2023 WADA Prohibited List by section and summarises which substances were most often reported in doping tests from 2003 to 2021. It is useful for orientation, but it does not measure health or performance effects in athletes.
methods: Narrative review of the 2023 WADA Prohibited List, with sections on each list category, pharmacokinetic and metabolic notes, and tables and charts of adverse analytical and atypical findings from WADA annual reports (2003 to 2021). The text does not describe a systematic literature search.
findings: Anabolic agents (S1) made up 49.5% of reported findings from 2003 to 2021, with testosterone (40.6%), stanozolol (11.0%) and nandrolone and 19-norsteroids (10.0%) the most common S1 compounds. Stimulants (12.1%) and diuretics and masking agents (8.7%) were the second and third most common sections, and no non-approved substance (S0) finding was reported. The authors state that the implementation of the Steroidal Module of the Athlete Biological Passport in 2014 'significantly affected' laboratory reports, seen as a marked fall in testosterone findings.
limitations: The review does not describe how the literature was searched or selected, so coverage of individual substances is not reproducible. Counts of findings depend on testing volume, detection methods, list revisions (for example clenbuterol moving from S3 to S1 in 2006) and the COVID-19 pandemic, which the authors say affected 2020 and 2021. The authors note eight-finding discrepancies between WADA summary tables and resolved them by using the tables of identified substances.
practicalImplications: Staff can use the section structure of the Prohibited List and the review's description of therapeutic use exemptions as orientation when a medication or supplement may contain a prohibited substance. The list is updated every year, so decisions should be checked against the current list rather than this 2023 summary, and the finding counts do not show how often athletes use each substance.
athleteDev: The review helps staff understand which substance classes are prohibited and how they are classified, which supports education on clean-sport rules. It does not assess training methods or performance outcomes.
rtp: This review cannot inform return to sport. It describes prohibited substances and anti-doping testing, not injury treatment, rehabilitation or the timing of return to play.

citation: Lumba-Brown A, Teramoto M, Bloom OJ, Brody D, Chesnutt J, Clugston JR, et al. Concussion Guidelines Step 2: Evidence for Subtype Classification. Neurosurgery. 2019;0:1-12.
abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis pools prevalence of five concussion subtypes (cognitive, ocular-motor, headache/migraine, vestibular and anxiety/mood) and sleep disturbance within 3 days of injury, and compares concussed patients with controls. Headache/migraine and cognitive subtypes were the most prevalent in children and adults respectively, and adults were more likely than controls to show cognitive, vestibular and anxiety/mood subtypes. Cognitive symptoms were worse than in controls in both age groups, and cervical strain could not be analysed.
tldr: Pooled acute data show that headache, vestibular, cognitive and mood features are common within 3 days of concussion, and that cognitive symptoms are worse than in controls. The authors recommend subtype assessment at the first clinical contact, but the evidence is mostly symptom reports from a small number of studies.
methods: Systematic review and meta-analysis following PRISMA and MOOSE guidance, searching MEDLINE, SCOPUS, Cochrane registers, PsycINFO and SPORTDiscus for English-language studies published 1990 to 2017. Studies of concussed patients with clinical evaluation within 3 months were included, and the acute analyses used assessments within 0 to 3 days, pooling proportions, prevalence ratios against uninjured or baseline controls, and standardized mean differences with random-effects models, Egger tests and trim-and-fill adjustment.
findings: Ten studies gave prevalence data and 15 gave symptom or test data. Headache/migraine (0.52, 95% CI 0.37 to 0.67) and vestibular (0.50, 0.40 to 0.60) were the most prevalent subtypes in children, and cognitive (0.40, 0.25 to 0.55) was most prevalent in adults. Adults with concussion were 4.4, 2.9 and 1.7 times as likely as controls to show the cognitive, vestibular and anxiety/mood subtypes, and cognitive symptoms were higher than in controls in children (SMD 0.66) and adults (SMD 0.24), with vestibular symptoms higher in both groups (SMD 0.18 and 0.36).
limitations: Several analyses rest on very few studies, for example 2 studies for the pediatric sleep disturbance SMD, and no cervical strain study met inclusion criteria. Publication bias was suspected for some pooled estimates, the sample is mainly North American sport concussion, and the search end date is November 2017 in the abstract but July 2017 in the methods. The text also conflicts internally: the Discussion calls headache/migraine the most common subtype in adults although Table 3 shows cognitive (0.40) above headache/migraine (0.38), and the ocular-motor SMD of 0.72 is assigned to adults in the abstract and Table 5 but to pediatric patients in the Results text.
practicalImplications: Clinicians can screen for cognitive, vestibular, headache, mood and sleep symptoms at the first encounter after concussion, since these features were common within 3 days of injury. The authors recommend assessing all five subtypes and sleep disturbance early, but the paper does not show that subtype-specific management improves outcomes.
athleteDev: For performance staff, the paper is a reminder that cognitive, vestibular and mood symptoms can be present early after a head impact and should be flagged to medical staff. It does not evaluate training or performance outcomes.
rtp: The paper does not study return to play. Its subtype assessment within 3 days of injury may inform the first evaluation, but it reports no recovery trajectories and cannot set return-to-play timing, which the authors say will be reported in a later step.
