citation: Donahue CC, Resch JE. Concussion and the Sleeping Brain. Sports Medicine - Open. 2024;10:68.
abstract: This review proposes that the concussion neurometabolic cascade and neuroinflammation alter sleep-wake physiology through noradrenaline, glymphatic clearance and extracellular ion changes. Sleep disturbance is common after concussion and is associated with longer symptom resolution and recovery in adolescents and adults. The authors conclude that sleep should be assessed across baseline, acute and later recovery, although no evidence-based sleep management guidance yet exists.
tldr: Sleep changes after concussion are common and are linked to slower symptom resolution, and this review proposes a physiological model for why. The model is theoretical, so it should guide questions about sleep assessment rather than treatment decisions.
methods: Narrative review with a theoretical model, drawing on the sleep and concussion literature. The paper does not describe a systematic search, study selection or quality appraisal.
findings: The authors report that up to 70% of concussed people endorse sleep changes, and that sleep disturbance is associated with more symptoms and longer symptom resolution. In one study of adolescents aged 11 to 18, reporting sleep symptoms was linked to up to a fourfold increase in recovery time, and in high school and collegiate athletes less than seven hours of sleep before computerized neurocognitive testing was associated with more reported symptoms and with slower reaction times and lower ImPACT memory scores.
limitations: The review does not describe how sources were selected, and its mechanistic model is an interpretation that has not been tested. The cited studies differ widely in timing after injury (from the first 48 h to years later), sample and sleep measure, and the authors state that research on sleep and concussion is still in its infancy.
practicalImplications: Staff can ask about sleep at baseline and after injury, because sleep changes are common and linked to slower recovery. The review gives no validated sleep assessment or management protocol: the authors note that no validated concussion-specific sleep guidelines exist and that the SCOAT sleep questions come from a questionnaire not yet validated in concussed people.
athleteDev: For performance staff, the practical message is to protect sleep before baseline neurocognitive testing, since poor sleep can lower test scores. The review does not evaluate training or performance interventions.
rtp: The review links persistent sleep symptoms to longer recovery and suggests adding clinical sleep measures to the concussion management protocol, but it gives no criteria or timing for return to play. It should inform the sleep questions asked in a concussion protocol, not decide clearance alone.

citation: Jadischke R, Viano DC, McCarthy J, King AI. Concussion with primary impact to the chest and the potential role of neck tension. BMJ Open Sport & Exercise Medicine. 2018;4:e000362.
abstract: This laboratory study tested chest impacts on a helmeted and unhelmeted crash-test dummy and reconstructed two NFL collisions that caused concussion. Helmeted impacts produced higher neck tension and head flexion, and the authors estimated upper cord and brainstem strain in the two cases.
tldr: Helmet mass in chest-primary football impacts increased neck tension in a crash-test dummy. In two concussive NFL collisions, the authors estimated high cord and brainstem strain from combined neck tension and flexion, which is a proposed mechanism that needs further study.
methods: A Hybrid III dummy was struck in the chest with and without a helmet at 5-10 m/s (test series 1). Two NFL game collisions were reconstructed on the same dummy, and a finite element head and neck model estimated cervical strain.
findings: The helmeted dummy had 40% +/- 10% higher upper neck tensile force (t=9.84, p<0.001) and 8% +/- 3% higher head flexion angle (t=7.267, p<0.001) than unhelmeted impacts of equal severity, with about 18% less head displacement and rotational velocity. In the two reconstructions, neck tension was 2646 N (case A) and 1342 N (case B), and estimated cord and brainstem strain was 13.0%-18.6% and 8.7%-12.2% from combined tension and flexion.
limitations: Two cases is a very small sample, and the dummy is not human, so tissue strain was estimated rather than measured. The model was not validated for brainstem or spinal cord tissue, the 0.65 coupling ratio rests on limited data, and in case A the facemask also appears to have contacted the other player's helmet. The abstract gives 10%-20% strain and states that strain 'is a factor in concussion', while the body reports 13.0%-18.6% and 8.7%-12.2% (Table 3 simple sums are 14.4%-20.5% and 10.1%-14.1%) and frames neck tension as a possible mechanism needing further research.
practicalImplications: Helmet mass added to the head can raise neck tension in chest-primary impacts, so chest-to-chest impacts should be considered alongside head-to-head impacts when evaluating helmets. Neck tension should be treated as a candidate mechanism, not an established concussion measure.
athleteDev: This study does not address training or performance. Its relevance is to equipment design, since helmet mass increased neck tension in dummy chest impacts.
rtp: This study cannot be used for return-to-play decisions for an individual athlete. It offers no clinical test, threshold or clearance criterion, and its two case reconstructions do not establish a diagnostic or prognostic standard.

citation: Patricios JS, Schneider KJ, Dvorak J, Ahmed OH, Blauwet C, Cantu RC, et al. Consensus statement on concussion in sport: the 6th International Conference on Concussion in Sport-Amsterdam, October 2022. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2023;57:695-711.
abstract: This consensus statement from the 6th International Conference on Concussion in Sport summarises evidence and expert recommendations on concussion prevention, assessment, management, return to learn and sport, and long-term effects. It introduces updated sideline and office assessment tools.
tldr: After a suspected concussion, remove the athlete and do not return them that day unless an experienced clinician has evaluated them. Use a multimodal assessment of at least 10-15 minutes, relative rest for up to 48 hours, then a graded return to learning and sport with written clearance.
methods: Expert panel of 31 members voted anonymously on recommendations at the October 2022 conference and follow-up meeting, using an 80% majority as consensus. Recommendations were informed by 10 systematic reviews, and the statement reports dissent alongside the votes.
findings: Mouthguard use was associated with a 28% lower concussion rate in ice hockey, and a policy disallowing body checking in child and adolescent ice hockey reduced game concussions by 58%. Limiting contact practice in American football was associated with a 64% reduction in practice-related concussions. Prescribed subsymptom-threshold aerobic exercise within 2-10 days was reported as effective for reducing persisting symptoms, and unrestricted return to sport typically occurs within 1 month (pooled mean 19.8 days, 95% CI 18.8 to 20.7, 57 studies, I-squared 99.3%).
limitations: The authors state that the statement reflects evidence available at the conference, will need updating, and is not a prescriptive standard. Evidence is limited for para athletes, females, preadolescents and children aged 5-12, and the SCAT6 and SCOAT6 still require validation. The definition of concussion did not reach 80% agreement, and the expert panel had limited demographic and geographic diversity. Several authors disclose paid or unpaid roles with leagues and sport bodies.
practicalImplications: Remove any athlete with suspected concussion and do not return them to play that day unless an experienced clinician has evaluated them. Allow at least 10-15 minutes for a multimodal off-field assessment, and do not rely on neurocognitive scores alone for management or clearance.
athleteDev: Performance and sport science staff should not use baseline or neurocognitive scores in isolation to clear an athlete for training. The statement supports mouthguards in child and adolescent ice hockey and neuromuscular warm-ups in rugby, but it gives no performance training prescription.
rtp: Return to sport follows six steps: symptom-limited activity, aerobic exercise, individual sport-specific exercise, non-contact drills, full-contact practice, then full game play. Each step typically takes at least 24 hours, and athletes should not begin any at-risk activity until symptoms and clinical findings have resolved. Unrestricted return requires written readiness from a healthcare professional under local rules, and the statement gives no fixed day count.

citation: Bolling C, van Mechelen W, Pasman HR, Verhagen E. Context Matters: Revisiting the First Step of the 'Sequence of Prevention' of Sports Injuries. Sports Medicine. 2018;48:2227-2234.
abstract: This review argues that sports injury prevention should describe the injury problem in its context, using the socioecological model. The authors propose qualitative research methods as a way to explore injury context before preventive measures are designed.
tldr: Injury prevention work often describes the injury problem without context, which can produce interventions that work in controlled settings but not in practice. The authors propose exploring the athlete's context with qualitative methods before designing an intervention.
methods: Conceptual review. The authors revisit the four-step sequence of prevention, draw on the socioecological model, and cite prior reviews, a RE-AIM review and a survey of teams. No systematic search or formal appraisal of sources is described.
findings: The authors argue that the first step, describing the injury problem, has mostly been done without considering context, which may help explain the limited real-world effect of efficacious interventions. They cite a systematic review of 52 injury prevention trials using the RE-AIM framework, which identified major gaps in the adoption and maintenance of interventions. They also cite the Nordic Hamstring Survey, in which teams did not adopt an exercise programme with well-documented effects on injury and re-injury risk and kept using exercises with little supporting evidence.
limitations: This is a conceptual argument, and the proposed qualitative approach is not tested for its effect on injury outcomes. Its claims rest on selected literature and analogy, and no search method is reported.
practicalImplications: Staff planning an injury prevention program should describe the injury problem in context, including the athlete, sport, setting and coach or organizational factors, before choosing an intervention. The authors suggest qualitative work with athletes, coaches and health providers as a way to do this, but present it as a research approach rather than a tested staff procedure.
athleteDev: The paper addresses injury prevention rather than performance. Its relevance to performance is the authors' point that an exercise program with good efficacy may not be adopted by teams, so staff should consider how athletes and coaches will use a program in their own setting.
rtp: This paper does not address rehabilitation or return to sport. It concerns injury prevention and should not be used to guide return-to-play decisions.

citation: Forlizzi JM, Ward MB, Whalen J, Wuerz TH, Gill TJ IV. Core Muscle Injury: Evaluation and Treatment in the Athlete. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2022:1-9.
abstract: Narrative review of core muscle injury in athletes, covering pathoanatomy, history and examination, imaging, nonoperative rehabilitation, and operative treatment and return to play. It draws on a literature search and the senior author's experience with professional, collegiate and elite athletes.
tldr: Core muscle injury is a clinical diagnosis to consider in any athlete with inguinal pain, and adductor or hip pathology often coexists. Structured rehabilitation is the first step, and surgery with mesh and a relaxing myotomy is considered after persistent symptoms despite 12 weeks of nonoperative care.
methods: Narrative and literature review. The authors state that a comprehensive literature search identified studies on diagnosis, treatment and rehabilitation, and that the senior author's experience was compared with established treatment algorithms. No databases, dates or inclusion criteria are reported.
findings: The authors state that pain proximal to the inguinal ligament, with tenderness at the rectus abdominis insertion, is highly suggestive of core muscle injury, that adductor longus tendinopathy is not uncommon, and that MRI may underestimate the extent of injury. Cited rehabilitation evidence includes a single-blinded randomized trial in which active rehabilitation produced more pain-free return to play than conventional therapy (13/20 vs 3/20). Cited surgical outcomes include 90% return to sport at 3 months after surgery versus 27% with physical therapy in a randomized trial, and an 89% return-to-play rate in 27 hips treated for combined hip and core pathology.
limitations: The review states that evidence in this field is lacking and that large comparative studies of operative techniques have not been done. Many outcomes come from small or heterogeneous series, and several recommendations reflect the senior author's practice.
practicalImplications: Staff should consider core muscle injury in any athlete with groin pain above the inguinal ligament, and check the adductor longus for coexisting injury. Nonoperative rehabilitation of about 2 to 3 months, progressing to sport-specific work, is the first step, and the authors advise surgical referral after 12 weeks of persistent symptoms.
athleteDev: The review does not measure performance. It notes that persistent groin pain can limit athletic performance, and that core strengthening and postural balance are central to nonoperative care.
rtp: The review gives return-to-play timelines of about 4 weeks for isolated sports hernia repair and about 12 weeks when an adductor release is added. The authors' return criteria are healed wounds, full painless hip range, painless adductor activity and resolved preoperative groin pain, but these timelines reflect their protocol and small series, so they are reference points rather than validated criteria.

citation: Bulut Y, Rasmussen JJ, Brandt-Jacobsen N, Frystyk J, Thevis M, Schou M, et al. Coronary Microvascular Dysfunction Years After Cessation of Anabolic Androgenic Steroid Use. JAMA Network Open. 2024;7(12):e2451013.
abstract: In 90 men in recreational strength training, impaired myocardial flow reserve measured by rubidium-82 PET/CT was more frequent in men with current or former anabolic androgenic steroid use than in controls. Among former users, longer accumulated duration of use was associated with higher odds of reduced flow reserve. The authors conclude that impaired coronary microcirculation may persist after AAS use ends.
tldr: Men who used anabolic steroids had more impaired coronary microvascular function on PET imaging than men who had never used them, including former users years after stopping. Longer cumulative use was linked to worse flow reserve among former users, although the sample was small.
methods: Cross-sectional study following STROBE reporting. Men aged 18 years or older in recreational strength training were grouped as current AAS users, former users (at least 4 weeks of use and stopped at least 3 months earlier), or controls with no AAS use. Use was checked with urine testing, and myocardial flow reserve was measured with rest and adenosine stress rubidium-82 PET/CT.
findings: Impaired MFR below 2.0 occurred in 6 of 32 current users (18.8%) and 1 of 31 former users (3.2%), and in none of 27 controls (overall P = .02); the adjusted pairwise comparison of current users vs controls was not significant (P = .08). MFR below 2.5 occurred in 9 current users (28.1%), 8 former users (25.8%) and 1 control (3.7%) (overall P = .02), with nonsignificant pairwise comparisons (current vs control P = .05; former vs control P = .09). Mean MFR did not differ significantly between groups (P = .15). Among former users, each doubling of accumulated AAS duration was associated with MFR below 2.5 (odds ratio 2.1, 95% CI, 1.03-4.35; P = .04), and time since cessation was not.
limitations: The primary outcome, mean MFR, did not differ significantly between groups, and post hoc pairwise comparisons were not significant; the authors say the sample was not large enough for prevalence comparisons with multiple-comparison adjustment. Group allocation relied on self-report, and urine testing detected AAS in 3 participants (10%) classed as former users. Selection bias cannot be excluded, the design cannot show causation, and the groups differed in blood pressure, LDL cholesterol, body fat and illicit drug use, which the authors treat as potential confounders.
practicalImplications: When an athlete or trainee reports past or current AAS use, staff could treat coronary microvascular health as a possible concern that may persist after stopping and refer for cardiology assessment. The paper cannot quantify an individual's risk or define a screening protocol.
athleteDev: The study does not test training outcomes. Its relevance to performance is indirect: it suggests that supraphysiologic AAS use in strength-trained men may carry cardiovascular risk that persists after cessation, which matters for athletes who use these drugs.
rtp: Not applicable to return-to-sport decisions. The study enrolled men without established cardiovascular disease and did not study injured athletes, so it cannot clear anyone for return to sport or judge cardiac fitness after AAS use.

citation: Racinais S, Dablainville V, Rousse Y, Ihsan M, Grant ME, Schobersberger W, et al. Cryotherapy for treating soft tissue injuries in sport medicine: a critical review. Br J Sports Med. 2024.
abstract: The authors found no human evidence that cryotherapy limits secondary injury or improves tissue regeneration, and they rely largely on animal studies. Cryotherapy may be recommended in the first 6 hours after injury to reduce pain and possibly haematoma, but it should be used with caution beyond 12 hours because animal studies suggest it may interfere with healing. More human research is needed.
tldr: Human evidence supports cryotherapy only for short-term pain relief, with no proven healing benefit. Animal studies suggest icing may delay muscle regeneration after large injuries, though it may help limited injuries, so the authors advise caution with continued use beyond the first hours.
methods: Critical review with a structured search of Medline and Web of Science without automatic filters, using combined terms for cryotherapy, soft tissue and injury. Records were screened by two reviewers against criteria covering acute muscle, tendon or ligament injury, cryotherapy compared with a control, application only after injury, original research and English language. Of 452 records screened, one human and 26 animal studies were eligible, and the authors synthesized them with clinical literature.
findings: The single human study, a pilot trial in gastrocnemius tears, did not show a difference between cryotherapy and control in pain, functional recovery or convalescence time; the authors note that an RCT able to detect a 10 percent difference in full recovery would need 396 participants. Among 25 animal muscle studies, cryotherapy reduced early swelling, microvascular permeability and some inflammatory markers, but several studies reported delayed necrotic fibre removal, smaller regenerating fibres and slower regeneration after large injuries, while repeated icing of a limited injury in rats facilitated recovery. The only tendon study reported 46 percent and 51 percent reductions in prostaglandin E2 in patellar and Achilles tendons within 3.5 hours.
limitations: The human evidence base is one pilot study, and the sample was too small to detect differences. Animal injury models, cooling methods and outcome measures varied widely, and the authors note that cooling temperatures reached in animals may not be achievable in humans. The authors declare no competing interests.
practicalImplications: Cryotherapy may be used for pain relief in the first hours after an injury, but staff should not present it as healing treatment. The authors advise caution with continued cryotherapy beyond the early hours, since animal studies suggest it may interfere with regeneration. Staff should set expectations that the evidence for protocols on timing, duration and temperature is not yet available.
athleteDev: The review does not address performance. The authors do note that a reduction in pain could in theory allow earlier and more aggressive rehabilitation, but they state that no evidence currently supports this.
rtp: The review concerns acute soft tissue injury management and does not study return to sport. Its advice to limit cryotherapy beyond the first hours is a caution about tissue healing and cannot be used to set return-to-play timing.

citation: Point M, Guilhem G, Hug F, Nordez A, Frey A, Lacourpaille L. Cryotherapy induces an increase in muscle stiffness. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2017;1-7.
abstract: Ten healthy volunteers underwent four 4-minute sets of air-pulsed cryotherapy (-30°C) over the gastrocnemius medialis, with 1-minute recovery between sets. Muscle temperature fell, and shear modulus measured by ultrasound elastography rose: +11.5% after the second set, +34.7% at 30 minutes and +25.4% at the end of a 40-minute follow-up. Ankle passive torque and EMG amplitude did not change, and the authors attribute the stiffness increase to a temperature-driven change in the tissue rather than to muscle activation.
tldr: Cold air applied to the calf made the muscle measurably stiffer on ultrasound elastography, and the change lasted at least 40 minutes after treatment. Passive ankle torque did not change, and no injury or performance outcome was measured.
methods: Ten healthy volunteers lay prone with the right ankle at 0°. Air-pulsed cryotherapy (-30°C) was applied to the gastrocnemius medialis in four 4-minute sets, and shear modulus, muscle temperature, passive torque and EMG were recorded at baseline, during treatment and for 40 minutes afterward. Two participants' EMG and torque data were lost, and repeated-measures ANOVA was used.
findings: Muscle temperature fell by 6.1 ±1.8°C at the end of treatment and reached its lowest point 9 minutes after treatment (-7.1 ±1.0°C). Shear modulus rose by +11.5% after the second set (P=.011), +34.7% at 30 minutes (P<.001) and +25.4% at the end of follow-up (P<.001). Passive torque (P=.878) and EMG amplitude (P=.871) showed no significant change.
limitations: The design was single-group with no control condition or washout, so reversibility could not be tested. The sample was ten healthy volunteers. The temperature probe was not guided by ultrasound, so temperature and stiffness were not measured from exactly the same tissue.
practicalImplications: Cold air applied to the calf may leave the muscle stiffer for at least 40 minutes. For return to play immediately or within 40 minutes of cryotherapy, the authors advise avoiding it on strain-prone muscles and locations or following it with a progressive, specific warm-up. These are the authors' recommendations drawn from a single-group stiffness study, not outcome-tested guidance.
athleteDev: Cryotherapy before performance work may leave the calf muscle stiffer for about 40 minutes, but passive torque did not change. No sprint, jump, strength or other performance measure was taken, so this paper does not show a performance effect.
rtp: After cryotherapy, the authors suggest a progressive, specific warm-up before return to activities that load muscle, and avoiding cryotherapy in strain-prone muscles. The study measured stiffness only, in healthy volunteers, and cannot show that these steps reduce strain or reinjury.

citation: Alvacite Cardenas D, Preston N. Does strengthening the cervical spine musculature enhance neck strength and reduce sports-related concussions in rugby and football players? A systematic literature review. J Bodyw Mov Ther. 2025;45:332-358.
abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis searched seven databases from January 2002 to September 2022 for neck strengthening studies in rugby and football players, with 10 studies and 3,453 players included. Two male rugby trials (3,125 players) showed fewer concussions with programmes that included neck strengthening (risk ratio 0.55, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.92). No study showed a concussion benefit in football or female rugby players, and neck strength gains were seen mainly in rugby neck extension.
tldr: In two trials of male rugby players, injury-prevention programmes that included neck strengthening were linked to roughly half the concussion rate, but no included study showed this in football or female players. Do not assume the rugby result transfers to other groups or reflects neck work alone.
methods: PRISMA-guided systematic review registered with PROSPERO, searching seven databases (2002 to September 2022) and trial registries for RCTs and cohort or pre-post studies of cervical strengthening in rugby and football players. Risk of bias was assessed by the primary author with CASP and, for RCTs, RoB 2; seven RCTs were pooled in RevMan with random-effects models, and GRADE was used for certainty.
findings: Two rugby RCTs (3,125 players) gave a pooled concussion risk ratio of 0.55 (95% CI 0.33 to 0.92), about 14 fewer concussions per 1,000 players than the 30 per 1,000 control rate. Across five RCTs (191 players), no pooled neck strength plane differed significantly; in subgroups, rugby neck extension favoured strengthening (SMD 0.63, 95% CI 0.03 to 1.24, P = 0.04), while football neck flexion (SMD -0.73) and extension (SMD -0.55) favoured the control group. Total neck strength (SMD 1.3, 95% CI -0.05 to 2.65, P = 0.06) did not reach significance.
limitations: Only two male rugby trials inform the concussion result; both used multicomponent movement-control programmes and are rated at high risk of detection bias, yet GRADE certainty is rated High, and Table 3 gives Hislop et al. a concussion RR of 0.72 (90% CI 0.51 to 1.0, P = 0.11). The discussion calls the non-significant total neck strength result significant, the abstract counts eight neck-strength studies while the results pool five, the stated age range differs (12 to 26 in results, 7 to 26 in discussion), and the PROSPERO number differs between abstract (CRD4202236054) and methods (CRD42022360574). The 'football' subgroup includes female Australian football players.
practicalImplications: For male rugby players, the review supports including neck strengthening within an injury-prevention or strength programme, which can be done in the field, since two trials of such programmes were linked to fewer concussions. For football and female players, the evidence shows no concussion benefit and no consistent strength gain, so programmes should not be presented as concussion prevention. The authors suggest neck strength and imbalance screening to identify higher-risk athletes, but this was not tested.
athleteDev: Neck strength gains were seen mainly in rugby neck extension, in trials running about 5 to 14 weeks, which may matter for contact positions. The review did not measure sport performance, and its total neck strength result did not reach statistical significance.
rtp: The review does not study return to play or rehabilitation after concussion or neck injury. Its suggestion that neck strength could guide return-to-play decisions comes from the authors' citation of earlier work and was not tested here.

citation: McBurnie AJ, Harper DJ, Jones PA, Dos'Santos T. Deceleration Training in Team Sports: Another Potential 'Vaccine' for Sports-Related Injury? Sports Medicine. 2021.
abstract: This Current Opinion article reviews the biomechanical and physiological features of horizontal deceleration in team sports. It links these features to injury mechanisms and offers considerations for assessing, training and monitoring deceleration. The authors propose that deceleration be treated as a key performance indicator alongside sprinting.
tldr: Horizontal decelerations are frequent in team sports and load the body in a distinct way. The authors argue they should be assessed, trained and monitored like sprinting, but the injury benefit of training them is not yet shown.
methods: Narrative review. No search strategy is described. The authors synthesise biomechanical, physiological and injury literature and summarise proposed mechanisms in a table.
findings: The authors report that high-intensity decelerations occur more often than equally intense accelerations in several team sports, and produce high impact peak forces, loading rates and eccentric demands. They cite Jaspers et al. finding that higher cumulative deceleration loading over 2 to 4 weeks led to increased overuse injury risk. They report that two field-based 6-week multidirectional speed interventions, with deceleration drills in the early weeks, reduced surrogates of ACL injury risk and improved change-of-direction performance.
limitations: This is a narrative review without a described search or quality appraisal. The authors state that the link between decelerations and injury is not clearly established, and the long-term injury effect of deceleration training is unknown. Several mechanistic points come from laboratory and animal studies.
practicalImplications: Consider adding a deceleration capacity test to athlete testing batteries, alongside linear speed and jump tests. Track high-intensity decelerations alongside sprinting and high-speed running, and periodise their exposure. These are the authors' recommendations and are not yet tested for injury outcomes.
athleteDev: The authors recommend that field testing of deceleration capacity and technique be included in testing batteries in the same way as linear speed and jump testing, and that deceleration ability and deceleration-focused resistance training be developed progressively within multidirectional speed programmes. These are untested recommendations, not trial results.
rtp: The paper gives no return-to-sport criteria or data from injured athletes. It can inform the idea of progressive deceleration exposure, but it cannot be used to set a return-to-play threshold or clearance.

citation: Baize D, Mériaux-Scoffier S, Massamba A, Hureau T, Reneaud N, Garcia-Gimenez Y, et al. Development of a preliminary multivariable model predicting hamstring strain injuries during preseason screening in soccer players: a multidisciplinary approach. Annals of Medicine. 2025;57(1):2494683.
abstract: This prospective cohort study built a preliminary logistic regression model to predict hamstring strain injuries from preseason screening in French soccer players. The model combined personal, psychological, sprint and knee-flexor fatigability measures. It identified 79% of players who were later injured in this sample, but it has not been externally validated.
tldr: A short preseason screen combining personal, psychological and sprint-fatigue measures identified most players who later had a hamstring strain in this sample. The model is preliminary and untested in a separate group, so it should not yet be used to decide who is at risk.
methods: Prospective cohort during the 2022 preseason. The text reports 122 participants from five French clubs, with 2 excluded for knee pain and 120 analysed. Players completed psychological, nutrition, sleep and burnout questionnaires, had isometric knee flexor and extensor torque measured, and performed ten 30-m sprints with photocells, radar and video, with knee-flexor torque retested after the sprints. Injuries were self-reported monthly and cross-checked with club staff, and variables were screened by univariate tests and entered into Wald backward stepwise logistic regression, with 200 bootstrap resamples for internal validation.
findings: Twenty-nine players (24%) sustained at least one HSI. The final eight-variable model included sex, age, HSI history, best sprint time, post-sprint knee-flexor torque change, maximal theoretical velocity (V0), squared perceived vulnerability and subjective norms, with an AUC of .815 (95% CI .719 to .912), sensitivity 79.3% and specificity 75.6%. Injured players had a larger post-sprint knee-flexor torque loss than uninjured players (-11.7% vs -4.8%), and this was the only significant modifiable predictor (OR .48, 95% CI .27 to .84); female sex was also significant (OR 9.61, 95% CI 1.15 to 80.74), while HSI history (OR 2.81), age (OR 1.43), best sprint time, V0 and the psychological variables were not significant at p < .05.
limitations: The authors state the model needs external validation and that event-per-predictor recommendations were not reached, so overfitting is possible. Imputation was 14.2% for force-velocity variables, including V0, and 9.0% for running kinematics. Sample counts conflict in the source: the text reports 22 female and 100 male participants before 2 exclusions, while Table 3 lists 22 female and 98 male among the 120 analysed; the abstract also describes the sample as regional and national players although Table 2 lists 6 international players. The authors describe the female subgroup as small and the model as most applicable to young male players.
practicalImplications: The model uses two psychological questionnaires and one repeated-sprint test with knee-flexor torque before and after, which the authors describe as a short preseason screen. Because the model is preliminary and untested externally, use it as a research prompt alongside clinical judgement rather than to exclude players from training. The authors propose testing whether targeted prevention for flagged players reduces injuries.
athleteDev: In this sample, injured players lost more knee-flexor torque after repeated sprints, and players with faster best sprint times tended to have higher odds (OR .44, not significant), while the V0 association was also not significant. Post-sprint hamstring torque loss is a candidate monitoring marker, but the evidence comes from one preliminary, unvalidated model.
rtp: The study predicts a first hamstring strain in players screened without a current injury or hamstring pain. It does not address recovery, return to play or re-injury, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions or post-injury loading.

citation: Mechó S, Iriarte I, Lisbona R, Pérez-Andrés R, Pruna R, Rodríguez-Baeza A. Different anatomic patterns of the indirect tendon of the rectus femoris. Surg Radiol Anat. 2024.
abstract: This cadaver study dissected 48 hemipelves to describe anatomical variants of the indirect tendon of the rectus femoris proximal tendinous complex. Superior and inferior aponeurotic expansions and an unusual myotendinous junction origin were common, and four indirect tendon patterns were defined, three of them complex. The authors suggest complex patterns may stiffen the tendon and act as non-modifiable risk factors for rectus femoris injury.
tldr: About 60% of 48 cadaver specimens had variants of the rectus femoris indirect tendon, and the authors classify four patterns. Any link to injury risk in athletes is a hypothesis, not a finding.
methods: Standardized anterior-to-posterior dissection of 48 embalmed hemipelves with thigh from donors aged 54 to 98 years. Variants were recorded as frequencies and percentages, and associations with sex and side were tested with Pearson chi-square (P < .05).
findings: Variants were found in 29 of 48 specimens (60.4%): inferior aponeurotic expansion in 23 (47.9%), superior expansion in 21 (43.7%; more than one in 6 of these) and an unusual myotendinous junction origin in the free portion of the indirect tendon in 19 (39.6%). Based on the expansions, patterns were standard in 19 (39.6%), superior and inferior complex in 15 (31.2%), inferior complex in 8 (16.7%) and superior complex in 6 (12.5%). No variant was associated with sex or side (P = .25 to .85).
limitations: Specimens came from elderly donors, not athletes, and only one hemipelvis per donor was studied without the full lower limb. Stiffness and injury risk were not measured, and the authors state they speculate on the biomechanics and propose MRI or ultrasound studies to confirm the link.
practicalImplications: Clinicians reading proximal rectus femoris imaging can expect superior or inferior expansions of the indirect tendon in many people, as described here. The authors' suggestion to screen athletes for complex patterns and target them with prevention programs is untested.
athleteDev: This study cannot guide training or performance decisions. It describes tendon anatomy in elderly cadavers and did not test athletes or prevention programs.
rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It did not study injured athletes, healing or re-injury, and the proposed role of complex tendon patterns in rectus femoris injury is unconfirmed.

citation: Kjær M, Petersen J, Dünweber MR, Andersen JL, Engebretsen L, Magnusson SP. Dilemma in the Treatment of Sports Injuries in Athletes: Tendon Overuse, Muscle Strain, and Tendon Rupture. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2025;35:e70026.
abstract: This special issue article reviews current treatments for tendon overuse injury, acute muscle strain and tendon rupture in athletes. Although evidence-based prevention and treatment exist, incidence remains high and single treatments give only partial recovery. The authors highlight unresolved dilemmas in each injury type.
tldr: Strength training with reduced sport load is the best-supported treatment for tendinopathy. Muscle strain and Achilles rupture still leave athletes with incomplete recovery, and the best timing, type of rehabilitation and return-to-sport criteria remain unresolved.
methods: Narrative review of published trials, meta-analyses and clinical studies on tendinopathy, acute hamstring and calf strain, and Achilles tendon rupture. The authors do not describe a systematic search or inclusion criteria.
findings: For tendinopathy, loading therapies outperform non-loading care, benefit was kept when strength training intensity was cut from 80 to 90% to 55% 1RM, and limiting sport to a self-monitored pain level of 2 to 5 out of 10 did not limit improvement. For acute hamstring strains, progressive eccentric strengthening with graded running gave the fastest return to play and the lowest re-injury rate in a cited review, and one study found that each extra day before return lowered re-injury risk by about 1.5%. After Achilles tendon rupture, both surgery and nonoperative care lead to tendon elongation (longer with nonoperative care), and greater elongation is linked to poorer function.
limitations: The review does not describe how sources were selected, and many of its specific estimates come from single studies or small trials. Several key questions, such as how much sport-specific training to allow and when to return elite athletes to sport, are listed as unresolved rather than answered.
practicalImplications: For tendinopathy, use progressive strength training with a reduction in sport load rather than rest alone, and do not expect PRP, oral NSAIDs or injected IGF-I to add benefit to strength training. For acute hamstring strain, use progressive eccentric and running rehabilitation; the clinical tests and MRI features linked to re-injury in one study are risk markers, since the authors state that how to judge tissue readiness remains unknown. For Achilles rupture, the authors suggest elite athletes may benefit more from surgery because of tendon elongation, while noting that the optimal treatment is unresolved.
athleteDev: In elite athletes, adding strength training on top of full training without reducing sport load had no benefit in one cited trial, while pain-monitored sport at 2 to 5 out of 10 did not slow recovery. How much sport-specific training to keep during heavy loading is unresolved, so set it case by case.
rtp: For hamstring-type strains, the review supports graded eccentric and running rehabilitation, and reports that a longer return-to-play period lowers re-injury risk, based on one study. For Achilles rupture, it shows that functional deficits persist after surgery or nonoperative care, and it does not give a validated return-to-sport standard for elite athletes.

citation: Nagamoto H, Kimura R, Hata E, Kumai T. Disabled throwing shoulder/elbow players have high rates of impaired foot function. Research in Sports Medicine. 2022.
abstract: In 91 baseball players with a disabled throwing shoulder or elbow, impaired foot function was found in 83 (91%) and floating toes in 74 (81%). Of the players with impaired foot function, 73 (88%) also had floating toes, and of those with floating toes, 73 (99%) had impaired foot function; both associations were statistically significant (P < 0.001).
tldr: Among 91 young baseball players with a disabled throwing shoulder or elbow, most had impaired foot function (91%) and floating toes (81%), and the two findings usually occurred together. The study cannot show whether foot dysfunction contributes to the injury.
methods: Retrospective observational study of 91 male baseball players aged 12 to 17 years diagnosed at one outpatient clinic with a disabled throwing shoulder or elbow. Foot function was tested with a rock-paper-scissors toe movement test, and floating toes were recorded when no toe touched the mat in standing. Associations were tested with chi-square tests.
findings: Impaired foot function was found in 83 of 91 players (91%) and floating toes in 74 (81%). Of the 83 with impaired foot function, 73 (88%) had floating toes, compared with 12% of those without impaired function (P < 0.001). Of the 74 with floating toes, 73 (99%) had impaired foot function, compared with 59% of those without floating toes (P < 0.001).
limitations: There was no control group, the design is retrospective, and the study is from one clinic, so causation and generalisation cannot be shown. The Methods state that 167 players diagnosed at the clinic were included, while the Results report 91 who met the inclusion criteria; the exclusion criteria (foot function not evaluable, history of foot injury) are listed but the number excluded for each is not reported. Floating toes were not analysed by toe or by throwing side, footwear was not recorded, and one examiner did all assessments, which removes inter-rater error but leaves examiner bias unaddressed (Inference).
practicalImplications: A simple foot check (the rock-paper-scissors toe test and a standing check for floating toes) can be added to the assessment of a thrower with shoulder or elbow pain, since most players in this sample showed both findings. The paper does not show that the findings cause injury, so they should be recorded as observations, not treated as the cause. Staff should note that the authors call for controlled studies before foot training is assumed to reduce injury.
athleteDev: No performance outcome was measured. Staff working with young baseball players may use the two foot tests as part of a movement screen, but the paper does not show that the tests predict throwing performance or change after training.
rtp: The study assessed players once, at the clinic visit, and did not follow them through rehabilitation or back to throwing, so it cannot show whether restoring foot function changes return-to-throw outcomes. The authors state that future studies are needed to test whether improving foot function affects injury occurrence.

citation: Di Paolo S, Bragonzoni L, Della Villa F, Grassi A, Zaffagnini S. Do healthy athletes exhibit at-risk biomechanics for anterior cruciate ligament injury during pivoting movements? Sports Biomechanics. 2022.
abstract: Thirty-four healthy competitive pivoting-sport athletes performed a frontal deceleration and a 90 degree change of direction, measured with wearable inertial sensors. An at-risk trial, defined as at least five of nine ACL risk factors present at once, occurred in 9% to 12% of trials; 24 athletes (71%) showed the profile in at least one trial. Higher approach speed (OR 4.3) and female sex (OR 4.8) were significantly associated with the profile.
tldr: A multi-joint pattern similar to the ACL injury mechanism was common in healthy pivoting-sport athletes during cutting and deceleration, and was linked to higher approach speed and female sex. The study has no injury outcome, so it shows occurrence of the pattern, not injury risk.
methods: Cross-sectional study of 34 healthy competitive athletes (18 men, 16 women; mean age 22.8 years) in soccer, rugby and basketball, performing three valid trials per leg of a frontal deceleration and a 90 degree change of direction. Full-body kinematics came from 15 wearable inertial sensors at 60 Hz, and nine risk factors were assessed at initial contact and maximum knee flexion. Logistic regression tested sex, limb dominance, age and approach speed, and SPM1D compared knee moment waveforms.
findings: Of 398 valid trials, the at-risk profile occurred in 9.0% at maximum knee flexion and 12.1% at initial contact, with no significant difference by task or frame. Twenty-four athletes (71%) showed the profile in at least one movement and 5 (15%) in at least three. In the change-of-direction model at maximum knee flexion, approach speed (OR 4.3, 95% CI 1.6 to 11.7) and female sex (OR 4.8, 1.2 to 19.8) were associated with the profile, and at-risk trials showed greater knee abduction, flexion and rotation moments over parts of stance.
limitations: The 5-of-9 threshold is arbitrary, as the authors acknowledge, and the frontal and transverse cut-offs came from this cohort's quartiles, so the rate is partly sample-specific. Four regression models were built but only the change-of-direction model at maximum knee flexion fit significantly, trials from the same athlete were pooled, and there was no injured or ACL-reconstructed comparison group or injury outcome. Only two pre-planned tasks were studied, and kinematics came from wearable sensors rather than marker-based capture.
practicalImplications: A multi-joint screen of this kind can show how often an athlete moves in patterns resembling the ACL injury mechanism, and the authors recommend testing at game-like speeds because faster approaches were linked to the profile. Results support awareness and screening, not labelling athletes as high ACL risk, because the cut-offs are not validated against injury.
athleteDev: Faster approach speed was associated with the at-risk profile and with the authors' description of a performance and injury-risk conflict in cutting. The paper does not test any technique intervention, so it cannot show whether changing these patterns lowers injury rates or affects cutting performance.
rtp: The study did not include injured or ACL-reconstructed athletes, and the authors state that the profile's sensitivity in reconstructed athletes is unknown. It cannot inform return-to-sport decisions, although the authors suggest future studies in reconstructed athletes.

citation: Verschueren J, Tassignon B, De Pauw K, Proost M, Teugels A, Van Cutsem J, et al. Does Acute Fatigue Negatively Affect Intrinsic Risk Factors of the Lower Extremity Injury Risk Profile? A Systematic and Critical Review. Sports Medicine. 2019.
abstract: Systematic review of whether acute fatigue changes prospectively identified modifiable intrinsic risk factors for lower extremity injury in healthy athletes or physically active people; 43 studies reported relevant fatigue effects and 8 matched all extraction criteria. The authors report that acute fatigue can decrease single-leg postural control, ankle joint position sense and isokinetic hamstring and quadriceps strength and can affect hamstring to quadriceps ratios, and conclude that it alters lateral ankle sprain, patellofemoral pain and hamstring injury risk profiles.
tldr: Acute fatigue lowers some tests linked to patellofemoral pain and hamstring injury risk, such as isokinetic quadriceps and hamstring strength, and broader evidence suggests it worsens single-leg balance. The evidence comes from few, small, mostly male studies with no injury outcomes, so it supports testing athletes in a fatigued state, not predicting injury from one test.
methods: Systematic review registered with PROSPERO and reported to PRISMA-P, searching PubMed, Web of Science, PEDro and the Cochrane Library to 29 May 2019, plus reference lists. Eligible studies used an acute fatigue protocol in healthy athletes or physically active people and measured an outcome identified as a significant prospective injury risk factor, excluding children, older adults, pregnant women and injured populations. Two authors screened records independently, and the Cochrane risk of bias tool was applied to included studies.
findings: Of 68 full texts assessed, 43 studies reported acute fatigue effects on modifiable risk factors, and 8 matched all extraction criteria. Quadriceps concentric peak torque at 60 degrees/s decreased in all three studies that measured it (significant in two), and hamstring concentric (one study) and eccentric normalized (one study) strength decreased; hamstring to quadriceps ratios fell in one of four studies at 60 degrees/s and one of three at 180 degrees/s. Ankle joint position sense decreased in one study (n = 72) but not another (n = 19), and no included study used the original postural control measures, although the wider set of 29 studies predominantly showed decreased single-leg postural control.
limitations: Only eight studies met the criteria, with high risk of bias and mainly male soccer players, and no meta-analysis was possible. Only 4 of the 8 studies reported the time from fatigue to testing. Table 3 lists the Cohen et al. eccentric hamstring test at 60 degrees/s while Table 4 lists 120 degrees/s, and the text says seven women were included in one study while Table 4 gives six.
practicalImplications: The authors advise that functional testing and injury risk profiling should include a fatigued condition, since single tests give only a snapshot. They suggest tracking each athlete's fatigue response (for example percentage decline or absolute test decrement) over a season rather than relying on group averages. Record the fatigue protocol and the time from fatigue to testing, which only 4 of the 8 included studies reported.
athleteDev: The review suggests fatigue reduces balance, stability and strength measures that matter in sport, so performance staff may track these tests late in sessions or matches. The authors cite a higher injury rate late in matches and training, which they link to fatigue, but they do not test that link.
rtp: The review excludes injured populations and does not assess rehabilitation or return-to-sport decisions, so it cannot inform them. The authors say fatigue-based profiling could be applied to rehabilitation and return to sport, but that has not been tested.

citation: Huygaerts S, Cos F, Cohen DD, Calleja-González J, Pruna R, Alcaraz PE, Blazevich AJ. Does Muscle-Tendon Unit Structure Predispose to Hamstring Strain Injury During Running? A Critical Review. Sports Med. 2020.
abstract: A critical review of how biceps femoris long head muscle-tendon architecture, fibre type and innervation may predispose the muscle to strain injury during running. The authors conclude that the evidence is insufficient to confirm any single mechanism and that prospective and imaging studies are needed.
tldr: Hamstring strain injury most often involves the biceps femoris long head, and differences in its architecture may explain some of the individual risk. The proposed mechanisms are not yet confirmed, so they should not be used alone to identify at-risk athletes.
methods: Critical narrative review of anatomical, architectural, fibre-type and innervation evidence for the biceps femoris long head and its relation to hamstring strain injury during sprint running. No systematic search method is described.
findings: Isolated injury to the biceps femoris long head is the most common acute hamstring strain in intermittent running sports, most often during sprinting (51% of cases). The authors report that fascicles are longer and pennation greater in the proximal and middle sections, which may increase strain. They cite Timmins et al. as finding that professional soccer players with fascicles shorter than 10.6 cm had about fourfold higher injury risk. Evidence on fibre type and innervation is inconsistent, and no single mechanism is confirmed.
limitations: The authors note that current evidence is largely from imaging, modelling, cadaveric and small cohort studies. Ultrasound fascicle length estimates required large (over 60%) extrapolation and can be altered by light pressure on relaxed muscle, and no prospective study has tested whether these structural features cause injury.
practicalImplications: Staff who assess hamstring risk may record biceps femoris long head structure where measurement is available, but should treat it as one risk factor within a wider profile. Prospective data are needed before structure-based screening or targeted training decisions are made.
athleteDev: Performance Application: this review does not support a training prescription. It suggests that eccentric and strength-endurance hamstring work is a plausible way to reduce risk, with the mechanisms still unconfirmed. Monitoring fascicle length or architecture is a research-stage option rather than a validated screen.
rtp: This review does not give return-to-sport criteria. It addresses injury predisposition in healthy running athletes and does not test whether fascicle length, pennation or fibre type should guide the timing of return after a hamstring strain.

citation: Davoren AK, Rulison K, Milroy J, Grist P, Fedoruk M, Lewis L, et al. Doping Prevalence among U.S. Elite Athletes Subject to Drug Testing under the World Anti-Doping Code. Sports Med Open. 2024;10:57.
abstract: An anonymous survey of U.S. elite athletes in the USADA testing pool (n = 1,398 analysed) estimated that 6.5 to 9.2% had used a prohibited substance or method without a TUE in the past 12 months. Category-level use ranged from 0.1% to 4.2%, with in-competition cannabinoids the most common.
tldr: About 7 to 9 in 100 U.S. elite athletes in this anonymous survey reported using a banned substance or method in the past year, with cannabinoids the most common. The figure is self-reported and depends on how inconsistent answers are handled.
methods: Cross-sectional anonymous web survey of athletes in the USADA Olympic and Paralympic testing pool, administered through Qualtrics by an independent research team (April to June 2020). Direct questions covered each WADA Prohibited List category without a TUE over the past 12 months, with validation and consistency items. Two prevalence calculations were made. Of 2,616 athletes in the sampling frame, 1,398 were analysed after exclusions.
findings: Overall prevalence was 9.2% (n = 128) by the first method and 6.5% by the second. Category prevalence ranged from 0.1% (diuretics or masking agents; stem cell or gene editing) to 4.2% (in-competition cannabinoids), and 1% reported asthma inhalers beyond the allowable dose. Of those who reported doping, 84.4% reported one category. Athletes who reported doping were younger (mean 26.4 vs 28.1 years, p = 0.008); prevalence did not differ by sex, competition level or sport risk category.
limitations: Self-reported and anonymous, so under-reporting and social desirability bias are possible. Some respondents gave inconsistent answers, and 31 were excluded for failing validation items, although the authors state that the prevalence rates were identical when these athletes were included. Non-response may bias the estimate, and the survey was taken at the start of COVID-19 competition stoppages. Sport was not asked directly, and only 53.4% of the targeted population (1,398 of 2,616) gave usable responses.
practicalImplications: Anti-doping education and detection may need to focus on specific categories, especially in-competition cannabinoids and asthma inhalers used beyond the allowable dose, rather than on doping in general. Staff can use these category-level results when discussing medication use, TUEs and in-competition rules with athletes, but the figures should not be read as a measure of an individual team or sport.
athleteDev: Performance Application: staff working with athletes in competitive environments may use these findings to raise awareness of cannabinoid and inhaler rules during in-competition periods. The results are population estimates and cannot identify doping in any named athlete.
rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It surveyed elite athletes about past doping behaviour and did not assess injury, medical treatment or clearance.

citation: Gleaves J, Petróczi A, Folkerts D, de Hon O, Macedo E, Saugy M, et al. Doping Prevalence in Competitive Sport: Evidence Synthesis with "Best Practice" Recommendations and Reporting Guidelines from the WADA Working Group on Doping Prevalence. Sports Med. 2021.
abstract: A systematic review of 105 studies (102,515 surveyed athletes) found doping prevalence in competitive sport ranging from 0 to 73%, with most estimates under 5%. The authors rated the quality of the evidence as mostly moderate or low and published best-practice reporting recommendations.
tldr: Doping prevalence estimates in competitive sport come from weak and inconsistent studies, and the reported figures range widely. The authors recommend standard survey wording, defined timeframes and clear reporting of athlete level and sport.
methods: PRISMA-guided systematic review and evidence synthesis with no time restriction. Studies with prevalence data (survey or sample analysis) from competitive athletes were included. Two quality tools were developed (QUAD-SRP for self-report surveys and QUAD-SAP for sample analysis), and studies were graded high, moderate or low. Results were synthesised descriptively, because data were too inconsistent for meta-analysis.
findings: Of 105 studies, 89 used self-reported surveys and 17 used sample analysis (one used both). Prevalence ranged from 0 to 73%, with most under 5%. Quality ratings were 20 high, 60 moderate and 25 low. Among the 17 sample-analysis studies, only 3 were rated high. Ten studies used randomized response technique surveys. Ten of the 20 high-rated studies reported 0 to 5%, while the single highest-scoring randomized response study reported 43.6 to 57.1%. The authors say that higher figures should not be assumed to be closer to the truth without considering method and population.
limitations: Heterogeneous studies that differed in substances, timeframes, populations and reporting, so meta-analysis was not possible. The U.S. (26 studies) and a few sports (for example weightlifting and cycling) dominate the evidence, and many countries and sports have none. Quality criteria were developed for this review. Counts are internally inconsistent: the abstract gives 17 sample-analysis studies and 35 countries with 12 international studies, while the Results text gives 34 countries with 15 international studies and the Discussion refers to 10 and to nine sample-analysis studies.
practicalImplications: When reading doping prevalence figures, check the substance list, timeframe, population and whether therapeutic use exemptions and inadvertent positives were handled. Treat the 0 to 73% range as evidence of wide methodological variation, not as a sport or team estimate. The authors' recommendations on defining doping, asking about behaviour in a defined period, and reporting athlete level and sport are a reasonable checklist for staff reviewing anti-doping survey work.
athleteDev: Performance Application: this review does not give a doping estimate for a specific sport, position or level, so it cannot inform team-level planning. It is most useful for judging how strong a doping prevalence claim is before it is used in an anti-doping or education discussion.
rtp: This review cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It covers doping prevalence in competitive athletes and does not address injury, rehabilitation or medical clearance.

citation: Kocak UZ, Stiffler-Joachim MR, Heiderscheit BC. Comparison of eccentric hamstring strength and asymmetry at return-to-sport after hamstring strain injury among those who did and did not re-injure. Physical Therapy in Sport. 2023;59:25-29.
abstract: Study of 60 NCAA Division I athletes with an index hamstring strain injury, comparing eccentric hamstring strength and between-limb asymmetry at return to sport between athletes who did and did not re-injure within 1 and 3 months. The authors found no differences in strength or asymmetry between groups and conclude that these measures at return to sport do not distinguish athletes who re-injure.
tldr: In 60 collegiate athletes returning from a hamstring strain, eccentric strength and between-limb asymmetry at return to sport did not differ between those who re-injured within three months and those who did not. Only 11 athletes re-injured, so the results argue against using a single return-to-sport strength value alone to predict re-injury.
methods: Analysis of routinely collected Division I health and performance records (July 2017 to March 2020), with injuries captured in a larger prospective observational study, for athletes with an index hamstring strain who were tested on a NordBord at return to sport. Peak eccentric force for each limb, total force and between-limb asymmetry were compared with Mann-Whitney U tests between athletes who did and did not re-injure the same limb within 1 and 3 months, with injury severity grouped by days to return.
findings: Eight athletes (13%) re-injured within 1 month and 11 (18%) within 3 months, and none of the 11 women re-injured. Peak eccentric force (injured limb, uninjured limb and total) and asymmetry did not differ between groups at either time point (asymmetry median 8.2% vs 7.8% at 1 month and 8.3% vs 7.1% at 3 months). Re-injuries occurred in moderate-severity injuries (8 of 38 within 1 month and 10 of 38 within 3 months) and in one severe injury within 3 months, and no mild-injury athlete was re-injured.
limitations: The study uses routinely collected data, with strength testing timed inconsistently after return (mean 6.8 days, typically within 7 days) and no complete injury history, and re-injury counts are small (8 and 11). Results and tables disagree: the text gives p = 0.49 and 0.48 for the moderate-severity comparisons while Table 3 gives 0.89 and 0.79, and the text gives asymmetry p values of 0.43 or above while the abstract and Table 2 give 0.91 and 0.96. The paper labels itself cross-sectional, although it follows athletes forward for re-injury, which is a cohort design.
practicalImplications: A single eccentric strength or asymmetry value at return to sport should not be used on its own to decide that an athlete is at lower or higher re-injury risk, since this study found no difference between athletes who did and did not re-injure. The authors suggest eccentric strength can still be used to track strength development after injury, which is a monitoring use rather than a risk-screening use.
athleteDev: The study does not measure performance outcomes. Its only performance-relevant content is the authors' suggestion that eccentric strength can monitor strength development in injured athletes.
rtp: This is the study's setting. Eccentric strength and between-limb asymmetry measured at return to sport did not separate athletes who re-injured from those who did not within one or three months, so these values should not be used alone to judge re-injury risk at return. Re-injury occurred in the moderate-severity group (21% within 1 month, 26% within 3 months) and in one severe injury at 3 months, and the comparison within the moderate group was not significant.

citation: Power LC, Kenny IC, Zynda AJ, Mulvihill JJE, Collins MW, Kontos AP, et al. Concussion recovery time, return-to-play protocols, and mandated sit-out periods among adult amateur contact field sports: A systematic review. Irish Journal of Medical Science. 2026; online.
abstract: This systematic review compared sport-related concussion recovery times, return-to-play protocols and mandated sit-out periods across adult amateur contact field sports. Nineteen studies with 58 datasets were included, and the authors found wide variation between and within sports. The most common protocol was 7 days and the most common sit-out rule was no same-day return, and the authors conclude that recovery time should be read in light of sport type and local policy.
tldr: Recovery times after concussion in adult amateur contact sports vary widely, and the authors suggest the sport's return-to-play and sit-out rules may shape the reported figures. Staff should not quote one sport's recovery time as a typical return date for their athletes.
methods: Systematic review following PRISMA and PERSiST guidance. MEDLINE, CINAHL Complete, SPORTDiscus, APA PsycInfo and APA PsycArticles were searched on 13 May 2024 for English-language, peer-reviewed studies from 2015 to 2024 of adults in amateur field-based contact sports with recovery time data. One reviewer screened titles and abstracts, two did full-text review, one extracted data, and one rated risk of bias (NIH tool) and certainty (SORT).
findings: Nineteen of 6,085 records (under 1%) met criteria, covering 58 datasets. Median recovery ranged from 6.5 days (male soccer, n = 4) to 37 days (female field hockey, n = 3, which the authors flag as a possible outlier), and rugby was consistently longer than American football (18.5 to 34 vs 7 to 16 days). Protocol duration was most often 7 days (31 of 58 datasets) and the most common sit-out was no same-day return (25 of 58); only rugby and ladies Gaelic football had extended sit-out periods (11 to 21 days), with rugby union longest at 21 days.
limitations: The authors note limited study quality (six studies at level 3 evidence and eight rated fair), very small samples in some codes, only one study each for ladies Gaelic football and sprint football, and that protocol and sit-out rules had to be interpreted by the first author. The abstract and results disagree: the abstract gives 34 days as the longest field hockey recovery while Table 3 gives a 37-day median, and the abstract gives 10/19 American football and 9/19 lacrosse studies while the results give 11/19 and 9/15.
practicalImplications: When setting expectations for amateur adult players after concussion, staff should check which return-to-play protocol and sit-out rule applies to that sport and league. Recovery times reported from another sport or policy should not be transferred directly.
athleteDev: For performance and strength staff, the paper suggests that return times in adult amateur sport may depend on the rules and medical support in place, so training reintroduction should follow the medical clearance process in that setting. The paper does not assess training or performance outcomes.
rtp: This paper is directly about return to play: median return times ranged from 6.5 to 37 days by dataset, with protocols of 5 to 21 days and sit-out periods from no same-day return to 21 days. The authors caution that policies vary, were often interpreted by the reviewer, and that compliance and medical access were rarely reported, so the figures describe published policy and outcomes, not a rule to apply to an individual athlete.

citation: Hickey JT, Timmins RG, Maniar N, Williams MD, Opar DA. Criteria for Progressing Rehabilitation and Determining Return-to-Play Clearance Following Hamstring Strain Injury: A Systematic Review. Sports Med. 2017;47:1375-1387.
abstract: Nine studies with 601 athletes who had acute hamstring strain injury were reviewed. Rehabilitation progression was largely guided by pain, and clinical assessments and performance tests were the most common return-to-play criteria. Isokinetic dynamometry was linked to shorter mean return-to-play times, and the Askling H-test to lower re-injury rates. The authors call for more objective and practical criteria.
tldr: Hamstring rehabilitation progression is mostly guided by pain, and return-to-play decisions usually rely on subjective clinical tests. Isokinetic testing was linked to shorter return-to-play times, and the Askling H-test to fewer re-injuries, but both findings need confirmation.
methods: Systematic review following PRISMA, searching six databases from inception to July 2015. Studies were included if they reported acute hamstring strain injury diagnosed within 10 days, described rehabilitation progression and return-to-play criteria, and reported return-to-play time and re-injury rates with at least 6 months of follow-up. Methodological quality was rated with a modified Downs and Black checklist.
findings: Nine studies with 601 participants were included, mostly male (80.6 percent) and drawn from professional, collegiate and recreational sport. Rehabilitation was kept within pain-free limits in six studies. The most common return-to-play categories were clinical assessments (eight studies) and performance tests (seven studies), while isokinetic dynamometry was used in three studies and the Askling H-test in two. Mean return-to-play times were 12 to 25 days with isokinetic dynamometry and 36 to 63 days with the H-test. Re-injury rates were 1.3 to 3.6 percent with the H-test and 6.25 to 13.9 percent with isokinetic dynamometry, and 9.1 to 63.3 percent in the clinical and performance test studies.
limitations: The review pooled return-to-play times and re-injury rates regardless of injury type, severity and rehabilitation approach. Definitions of return-to-play and follow-up periods varied. The authors state that the categories were chosen by them, and that the search was limited to English-language articles.
practicalImplications: Return-to-play decisions for hamstring strain should not rely only on manual strength tests and pain-free status. The authors suggest more objective strength measures, such as isokinetic or hand-held dynamometry, while noting that isokinetic testing has limited ability to predict individual re-injury risk and that the H-test may lower re-injury but lengthens time to return. Staff should weigh return-to-play time against re-injury risk for each athlete.
athleteDev: The paper addresses return-to-play criteria, not training. It notes that the performance tests used to clear athletes show readiness for sport but do not directly measure the known risk factors for re-injury, such as eccentric hamstring strength.
rtp: This review directly addresses return to play after acute hamstring strain. It supports pain-free progression as the common practice but finds that most clearance criteria are subjective, and that isokinetic dynamometry and the Askling H-test are associated with different trade-offs between time to return and re-injury. The authors call for more objective and practical criteria rather than naming a validated one.

citation: Rambaud AJM, Ardern CL, Thoreux P, Regnaux JP, Edouard P. Criteria for return to running after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: a scoping review. Br J Sports Med. 2018.
abstract: This scoping review of 201 studies found that time was the most frequently reported criterion for returning to running after primary anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction. The median time was 12 postoperative weeks. Fewer than one in five studies reported clinical, strength or performance-based criteria, and the authors recommend combining performance-based and time-based criteria.
tldr: Most ACL reconstruction protocols clear athletes to run based on time alone, with a median of 12 weeks. Only a minority of studies used clinical, strength or performance criteria, and the authors suggest adding those to time-based decisions.
methods: Scoping review following the Arksey and O'Malley and Joanna Briggs Institute frameworks. Six electronic databases were searched in November 2016, with reference list screening and forward citation tracking. Two reviewers screened and extracted data independently. Included studies were skeletally mature patients with primary autograft ACL reconstruction, and the review included all study designs. Time criteria were summarized as median and IQR, and trends over time were examined with local regression.
findings: Of 201 included studies, 198 reported a time criterion, and the median time to permit running was 12 postoperative weeks (IQR 3.3). Open surgery with protective rehabilitation had a median of 29 weeks and arthroscopic surgery with protective rehabilitation 21 weeks, while under contemporary rehabilitation the medians were 10 and 12 weeks. Thirty-six studies (18 percent) used specific clinical, strength or performance criteria: 20 used clinical criteria, 30 strength criteria and 13 performance-based criteria. The most common objective strength criteria were isometric quadriceps limb symmetry index above 80 percent and isokinetic quadriceps and hamstring limb symmetry index above 70 percent.
limitations: Time criteria are general milestones reported by study authors and do not show when each patient actually started running, and definitions of running differed across studies. Included sources ranged from trials to rehabilitation protocols and clinical commentaries, were not appraised for risk of bias, and the review did not assess whether running at 12 weeks was safe. Some counts differ between the results and discussion (strength criteria 30 vs 31 studies; performance-based criteria 13 vs 17 articles).
practicalImplications: Running after ACL reconstruction should not be cleared on time alone. Staff could combine a time milestone with set criteria such as full knee extension, pain below 2 out of 10, no effusion, and knee flexion range near the uninjured side, plus strength and hop-test limb symmetry where available. The authors suggest that criteria be individualized rather than applied as a fixed timeline.
athleteDev: Performance-based criteria such as single-leg squats, step-ups, and balance tests can show movement quality before running, and the authors note these tests can double as rehabilitation exercises. The review gives no evidence that any specific threshold improves later performance.
rtp: This review directly addresses the transition to running, which is an early step of return to sport after ACL reconstruction. It does not establish that a given criterion or time point is safe, so it should not be used alone to clear an athlete to run; the authors recommend combining time with clinical, strength and performance criteria.

citation: Tassignon B, Verschueren J, Delahunt E, Smith M, Vicenzino B, Verhagen E, et al. Criteria-Based Return to Sport Decision-Making Following Lateral Ankle Sprain Injury: a Systematic Review and Narrative Synthesis. Sports Med. 2019;49:601-619.
abstract: No prospective studies were found that applied a criteria-based return-to-sport decision process after lateral ankle sprain, so no pooled analysis was possible. The authors provide a narrative synthesis of questionnaires and clinical and functional tests used in ankle sprain research. They propose that complex systems theory and the return-to-sport continuum could guide development of a criteria-based decision paradigm, and they advise against time-based decisions.
tldr: No published study has used criteria to clear patients with ankle sprains to return to sport. The authors suggest a multifactorial framework combining clinical, functional, sport-specific and psychosocial measures, but its criteria are untested.
methods: Systematic review with a protocol registered with PROSPERO and developed in line with PRISMA-P. Seven databases were searched from inception to 23 November 2018, with reference list screening, and two reviewers screened titles, abstracts and full texts. Eligible studies prospectively applied a criteria-based return-to-sport process in adults with lateral ankle sprain. Because none qualified, the authors built an inventory of questionnaires and tests from the screened literature and wrote a narrative synthesis.
findings: Of 948 articles identified, 33 were assessed in full and none met the eligibility criteria. The authors extracted 47 questionnaires, 45 clinical and functional tests, and four criteria from the wider ankle sprain literature. Only one study applied criteria, a limb symmetry index of at least 80 percent on triple hop tests, but it was excluded because it judged return after the athletes had already returned to sport. The authors report that return-to-sport decisions after ankle sprain are generally time-based.
limitations: The review found no direct evidence on criteria-based decisions, so the proposed variables are a theoretical synthesis linked to tests used in ankle rehabilitation. The authors state that these variables must be applied to actual return-to-sport decisions in prospective studies, and only articles published in peer-reviewed journals were considered.
practicalImplications: Staff should not assume a validated criteria-based return-to-sport standard exists for ankle sprains. In the meantime, the authors suggest that clinicians consider a combination of clinical measures (ankle laxity, pain and swelling), functional and sport-specific tests, load monitoring, and psychological readiness, rather than time alone. Staff should treat the framework as a discussion aid, not a clearance protocol.
athleteDev: The authors suggest that sport-specific performance profiles, movement quality, fatigue, and acute to chronic workload ratios could inform progression toward full performance. These are proposals from the synthesis, not tested training outcomes.
rtp: This review directly addresses return to sport after lateral ankle sprain. It does not supply validated criteria, so it cannot be used to clear an athlete. Its main value is in highlighting that time-based decisions are common and that criteria-based decisions remain untested.

citation: Ivanova VS, Tong KPS, Neagu C, King CM. Current Concepts in Achilles Tendon Ruptures. Clin Podiatr Med Surg. 2024;41:153-168.
abstract: Acute Achilles tendon ruptures can be treated without surgery or with surgery, and both pathways use functional rehabilitation with early range of motion. Surgical options include percutaneous, minimally invasive and open repair, and recent literature reports low complication rates and similar functional outcomes. The review also covers tendon anatomy and blood supply, gap-distance measurement, a phased rehabilitation protocol and chronic rupture repair.
tldr: Acute Achilles ruptures can be managed with or without surgery, and both routes use early functional rehabilitation with weight-bearing. Recent comparisons show similar re-rupture rates, so the choice depends on the patient, the rupture and the surgeon.
methods: This narrative review summarises the anatomy, diagnosis, conservative and surgical treatment of Achilles tendon ruptures, and presents the authors' Kaiser Permanente early functional rehabilitation protocol (Table 1). No systematic search method is described.
