findings: Recent studies cited show similar re-rupture rates for surgical and nonsurgical care when early range of motion and weight-bearing are used. Minimally invasive repair had lower wound and infection rates than open repair in the pooled data cited (deep infection 2.20% vs 5.11%), but a higher risk of sural nerve injury. In one cohort of 82 patients, a plantarflexion gap over 5 mm predicted lower patient-reported outcomes, whereas a case series of 56 found no such link when the gap was measured in neutral.
limitations: This is a narrative review with no described search, so selection and weighting of studies cannot be verified. Several cited figures come from older trials or from populations that are not athlete-specific, and the review does not grade the strength of the evidence.
practicalImplications: The review supports early functional rehabilitation with weight-bearing whether or not surgery is performed, and stresses early diagnosis. The authors state that open repair is well accepted for chronic ruptures and for acute ruptures in young, healthy, athletic patients, while the choice of procedure otherwise depends on the surgeon and patient.
athleteDev: The review touches on performance only briefly. It notes that soleus atrophy and loss of end-range plantar flexion torque are common after rupture and can limit return to activity. It gives no training or performance guidance.
rtp: The return-to-sport content comes from the authors' clinic protocol (Table 1): 90% limb symmetry on single-leg heel raise and single-leg hop for distance before running, and a 90% drop countermovement jump symmetry plus a declined heel raise before unrestricted sport in the 6-month phase. The protocol is presented as clinical practice and its criteria are not tested against outcomes. In a cited WNBA cohort, 23.5% of players did not return to the sport after the injury.

citation: Fournier-Farley C, Lamontagne M, Gendron P, Gagnon DH. Determinants of Return to Play After the Nonoperative Management of Hamstring Injuries in Athletes: A Systematic Review. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2016;44(8):2166-2172.
abstract: This systematic review summarises the factors that influence return to play after nonoperative management of hamstring injuries in athletes. Clinical, MRI and ultrasound prognostic factors and rehabilitation approaches were reviewed. Several factors were linked to longer recovery, and two rehabilitation approaches were linked to shorter rehabilitation.
tldr: Stretching-type injuries, structural injury on imaging, greater range-of-motion deficit and delayed first consultation were linked to longer return to play. The evidence is mostly low-level, so these factors guide prognosis rather than fixed timelines.
methods: Systematic review following PRISMA guidance. Four databases (CINAHL, MEDLINE, Embase, EBM Reviews) were searched in June 2014, with reference-list checks. Two reviewers screened titles and abstracts, and 24 studies were included. Study quality was rated with Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine levels.
findings: Clinical factors linked to longer recovery included stretching-type injury, recreational-level sport, structural rather than functional injury, a larger range-of-motion deficit, first consultation more than 1 week after injury, higher pain scores and more than 1 day to walk pain free. On MRI, positive findings, higher injury grade, more than 75% muscle involvement and proximal tendon involvement were among factors linked to longer recovery. In one level 2 study, hamstring loading during extensive lengthening (L-protocol) shortened rehabilitation compared with conventional exercise, and in another, four daily static stretching sessions shortened rehabilitation compared with one; the authors note conflicting results between studies for several factors.
limitations: Only 4 of the 24 studies were randomised trials, and most were level 4 evidence. Diagnosis criteria, outcome measures and populations varied widely, and only English and French articles were included. The authors note that these factors need stronger evidence before they can be used to improve clinical decisions.
practicalImplications: Record the injury type (stretching or sprinting), pain score, time to first consultation and time to walk pain free after an acute hamstring injury, since these were linked to longer recovery. Treat these as prognostic signals that flag athletes who may need a longer timeline, not as fixed return dates. The rehabilitation findings support considering loaded lengthening, but rest on a small number of studies.
athleteDev: This review cannot inform performance programming. Its rehabilitation findings on loaded lengthening exercise come from injured athletes, and the review measures no performance outcomes.
rtp: Use the prognostic factors (stretching-type injury, structural injury on MRI or ultrasound, range-of-motion deficit, pain, delayed first consultation) to flag athletes who may need a longer timeline. The review gives no return-to-play criteria or validated thresholds, and most factors come from single studies with inconsistent results, so it cannot be used to clear an athlete to return.

citation: Behm DG, Wilke J. Do Self-Myofascial Release Devices Release Myofascia? Rolling Mechanisms: A Narrative Review. Sports Medicine. 2019;49:1173-1181.
abstract: This narrative review argues that the term 'self-myofascial release' is misleading for foam rollers and similar devices. The authors find insufficient evidence that releasing myofascial restrictions is the primary mechanism behind range of motion and pain changes, and describe neural, pain-modulatory, circulatory and local thixotropic alternatives.
tldr: Foam rolling and roller massage increase short-term range of motion and reduce pain sensitivity, but the authors argue that breaking up adhesions is unlikely to be the main reason. Neural and pain-modulation mechanisms fit the evidence better, so the term self-myofascial release should be used with caution.
methods: Narrative review of the literature on foam rollers, roller massagers and balls, covering trigger point evidence, tissue stiffness and blood flow studies, non-local (contralateral) rolling effects, and the mechanical plausibility of tissue release. The authors cite PubMed title and abstract hit counts for 'self-myofascial release' (25 since 2005) and 'foam roller' or 'roller massage' (48, 2005 to 2019) to show how common the term is. No systematic search strategy or quality appraisal is reported.
findings: In one study, four 45 s rolling bouts reduced anterior thigh stiffness by 15% to 24%, and another found a 13% reduction in iliotibial band stiffness at 30 minutes in experienced users only. Rolling the untreated leg reduced pain sensitivity in three studies, which the authors read as a global pain-modulatory response. The authors also cite estimates that the force needed to break up adhesions would exceed what most people can apply with a roller.
limitations: The review is narrative, reports no systematic search or appraisal, and its main conclusion rests on the authors' interpretation of mostly small studies. One range of motion study had 13 participants per group and no significant between-group difference. Most trials included healthy active participants, which the authors note may not reflect people with pain.
practicalImplications: Foam rolling can be used for short-term gains in range of motion and reduced pain sensitivity, since these effects are reported more consistently than tissue release. Because the review points to neural and global mechanisms, staff should not explain rolling to athletes as a way to break up adhesions. One cited study found that 60, 90 and 120 s of rolling between sets of knee extensions all reduced repetitions (by 8 to 14%), so rolling between working sets may cost performance.
athleteDev: The review cites studies in which rolling did not typically impair subsequent strength, jump height, sprint time or endurance, so rolling before training is a reasonable choice when a range-of-motion gain is wanted. Some studies report improvements in strength, power or sprint speed, but the review also cites a meta-analysis describing performance and recovery effects as generally small to negligible.
rtp: The review covers mechanisms in mostly healthy participants and does not assess rehabilitation outcomes or return-to-sport decisions. It cannot show that rolling restores tissue or supports return to sport. The authors call for trials in patients and athletes with pain syndromes.

citation: McLagan B, Silvey K, Roberts T, Erceg D, Sum JC, Schroeder ET. Consensus on the Use of Therapeutic Interventions in Pain Management, Recovery, and Athletic Performance: A Delphi Study. International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy. 2025;20(3):420-428.
abstract: A four-round Delphi survey of physical therapists and athletic trainers asked when they would consider using percussive, vibration, infrared, heat and cryotherapy. Several local heat, cryotherapy, vibration and percussive uses reached the 70% consideration threshold, but the paper reports no outcome data.
tldr: Clinicians in this survey would consider local heat, vibration or percussive therapy before activity and local cryotherapy for acute joint or soft tissue pain, along with several chronic-pain uses. These are opinions about when to consider a modality, not evidence that it improves recovery or pain.
methods: Delphi survey in four rounds, with experts helping write items and screening criteria requiring licensure, at least 1,000 hours with athletic populations and recent use of one modality. Consensus was set at more than 70% agreement, and 'consideration' meant selecting 'in some instances' or 'in most instances'.
findings: In round 4 (n=32), consideration reached the 70% threshold for local heat (96.9%), local vibration (75.0%) and percussive therapy (75.0%) before activity; local cryotherapy in recovery (93.8%); local cryotherapy for acute joint pain (100%) and acute soft tissue pain (96.9%); local heat (100%) and local cryotherapy (87.5%) for chronic joint pain; and local vibration (84.4%), percussive therapy (78.1%), local heat (100%) and local cryotherapy (87.5%) for chronic soft tissue pain. Local infrared therapy did not reach the threshold in any circumstance, and 81.3% agreed percussive therapy applied directly to the joint should rarely be used for acute joint pain.
limitations: Only 32 of 74 round-1 respondents completed round 4, and the round-4 sample was mostly white and male (29 of 32 men). The authors report that no single response category reached 70% agreement, so they pooled 'In Some Instances' and 'In Most Instances' into a broad 'consideration' measure that cannot rank priorities; Table 1 also omits the consensus asterisk on the 96.9% cryotherapy cell for acute soft tissue pain. The conclusion lists percussive and vibration therapy for recovery, but Table 1 shows 68.8% for both, below the threshold.
practicalImplications: In the listed circumstances, clinicians in this survey would consider local heat before activity, local cryotherapy for acute pain, and heat or cryotherapy for chronic joint pain. Use should still depend on patient presentation, contraindications and available equipment, since the paper finds the choice relies on those factors. Staff should not read these figures as proof that a modality improves outcomes.
athleteDev: Performance staff can use these results to see which modalities clinicians would consider before activity, such as local heat or percussive and vibration devices. The data reflect clinician opinion and do not show a performance benefit.
rtp: This paper cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It gives no outcomes, timing or clearance criteria, so its consideration percentages should not be used to set return-to-play decisions.

citation: Mawhinney C, Heinonen I, Low DA, Han C, Jones H, Kalliokoski KK, et al. Cool-Water Immersion Reduces Postexercise Quadriceps Femoris Muscle Perfusion More Than Cold-Water Immersion. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2022;54(7):1085-1094.
abstract: Healthy men cycled to a core temperature of 38°C and then received 10 minutes of 8°C or 22°C water immersion, or seated rest. Oxygen-15 labeled water PET measured quadriceps muscle perfusion, with cutaneous blood flow and temperature also assessed.
tldr: Ten minutes of 22°C water after cycling reduced global quadriceps blood flow beyond a clinically relevant threshold, while 8°C water did not. Blood flow was measured only for 10 minutes after immersion, so the study does not show a recovery benefit.
methods: Randomized, parallel-group laboratory trial. Thirty recreationally active healthy men were allocated by covariate adaptive randomization (10 per group) and cycled at 70% VO2peak to a core temperature of 38°C, then received 10 minutes of 8°C or 22°C water immersion or seated rest. Quadriceps perfusion was measured by PET with oxygen-15 labeled water, with the post-immersion scan starting 10 minutes after immersion, with skin blood flow by laser Doppler and muscle temperature by needle thermistor.
findings: Global quadriceps perfusion fell by 2.5 mL per 100 g per minute (95% CI -3.9 to -1.1) in 22°C water versus control, above the predefined threshold of 0.75; the 8°C effect on global perfusion was not clinically relevant. Within the quadriceps, 8°C water reduced rectus femoris and vastus lateralis perfusion versus control, and 22°C water reduced vastus lateralis perfusion, while vastus intermedius and vastus medialis were not clinically affected. Thigh skin blood flow fell by 69.3% after 8°C and 52.1% after 22°C, each versus control, and 8°C also reduced calf skin blood flow.
limitations: Ten men per group, with a between-group design and measurements taken only 10 minutes after immersion, so later effects are unknown. Despite matching, the control group had lower VO2peak (41.9 vs 51.1 and 49.7 mL/kg/min) and higher body fat than the cooling groups, no multiplicity adjustment was made, and deep muscle shivering was not measured. Participants were recreationally active men rather than trained athletes, and no women were included.
practicalImplications: When cold-water immersion is used after exercise, staff should know that water temperature changed quadriceps blood flow and muscle temperature in different ways. In this study 22°C water reduced quadriceps blood flow beyond the threshold, while 8°C did not, but the authors do not show a recovery benefit, so this finding alone should not set the water temperature for recovery.
athleteDev: The study measured blood flow and temperature, not performance. It does not show that either water temperature improves or impairs later performance, so it should not inform performance decisions on its own.
rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It used healthy men after a standardized cycling bout, with no injured muscle, rehabilitation or return-to-play outcome.

citation: Knufinke M, Nieuwenhuys A, Geurts SAE, Møst EIS, Moen MH, Maase K, et al. Dim light, sleep tight, and wake up bright: Sleep optimization in athletes by means of light regulation. Eur J Sport Sci. 2021;21(1):7-15.
abstract: This crossover study tested whether morning bright light and evening blue-light restriction, combined with fixed sleep-wake times, improve sleep in recreational athletes. Self-reported sleep onset latency improved, with larger effects in athletes who kept strict schedules, but actigraphy showed no differences. Adherence to the fixed sleep-wake schedule was low, and the light-emitting goggles were rated rather uncomfortable.
tldr: Morning bright light and evening amber glasses shortened self-reported sleep onset in recreational athletes by 8 to 17 minutes, depending on schedule adherence. Objective sleep did not change, and the goggles were uncomfortable, so less obtrusive methods are needed.
methods: Within-subject crossover with counterbalanced order. Athletes completed a light-regulation week and a control week, with a standardized bed and rise time (maximum deviation 30 minutes) and guidance on caffeine and alcohol. Sleep was measured with diaries and wrist actigraphy, and effects were analyzed with repeated-measures ANOVA in two datasets: 8 athletes with strict schedules and 25 with more variable schedules.
findings: Self-reported sleep onset latency was 17 minutes shorter with light regulation in the strict dataset (F(1,7) = 14.64, p = .006) and 8 minutes shorter in the 25-athlete dataset (p = .023). Subjective sleep quality improved in the strict dataset (by 0.42 on a 10-point scale, p = .011) but not in the larger dataset. No actigraphy-based sleep measure differed significantly between conditions, and lights-off time in the larger dataset was about 27 minutes later with light regulation.
limitations: Only 8 athletes met the strict schedule criteria, and the two datasets were built after low schedule adherence was found. Athletes who adhered may have believed in the intervention, and sleep ratings were taken on waking, when sleep inertia may affect them. Morning and evening components were combined, so their separate effects cannot be judged, and the authors note light exposure was not consistently timed.
practicalImplications: Morning bright light with evening blue-light restriction may shorten self-reported sleep onset in recreational athletes who keep fairly regular schedules. The light-emitting goggles were rated rather uncomfortable and athletes had difficulty wearing the evening glasses for the full three hours, so plan for practical barriers. The stronger effects came from athletes who kept fixed bed and rise times, so schedule regularity should come first.
athleteDev: For sleep as part of recovery planning, light regulation may help athletes who keep regular bed and rise times, with self-reported onset up to 17 minutes faster. The authors suggest combining it with other sleep hygiene measures rather than using it alone, and objective sleep did not change.
rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It tested recreational athletes without severe sleep complaints and did not assess injured athletes, recovery from injury or readiness to return to competition.

citation: Dergaa I, Ghram A, Romdhani M, Souissi A, Ammar A, Farahat RA, et al. Does wet-cupping therapy improve repeated sprint ability, perceived wellness, and rating of perceived exertion in young active males? Sports Med Health Sci. 2023.
abstract: In 49 active men, repeated sprint performance, wellness and perceived exertion were compared between a control session and a session 24 hours after wet-cupping therapy. Sprint power was higher, and perceived sleep, stress and exertion were lower, after cupping.
tldr: Wet-cupping 24 hours before testing was followed by higher sprint power and lower perceived exertion and stress in this single-group study. Because there was no sham comparator, the results should be treated as preliminary.
methods: Single-group experimental design with a control session and a post-cupping session two weeks apart, in counterbalanced order, in 49 active adult men. Wet-cupping (250-300 mmHg, superficial scarification) was applied 24 hours before testing. Outcomes were a six-sprint running test (maximum, mean and minimum power), the Hooper wellness questionnaire and Foster CR-10 RPE. Paired t-tests and effect sizes were used.
findings: In Table 1, maximum, mean and minimum sprint power were higher after cupping than in the control session (mean differences 68.64 W, 43.32 W and 30.76 W; all p = 0.001; effect sizes 0.6, 0.6 and 0.5). Perceived sleep (mean difference 0.97, effect size 0.9), perceived stress (0.46, effect size 0.6) and RPE (0.71, effect size 1.1) were better after cupping. Perceived fatigue and muscle soreness did not differ (p = 0.26 and 0.79).
limitations: Single-arm design without a sham or blinded comparison, and a single post-treatment session. Participants were police officers rather than athletes and were not in a fatiguing training block, so the fatigue and soreness results may not generalize. Nitric oxide, lactate and other mechanistic markers were not measured. The abstract gives p < 0.05 (maximum power) and p < 0.01 (mean and minimum power), mean power ES 0.5, minimum power ES 0.6 and sleep ES 0.85, while Table 1 gives p = 0.001 for all three, mean power ES 0.6, minimum power ES 0.5 and sleep ES 0.9.
practicalImplications: Cupping is not established as a performance aid by this study. Staff should not add it to sprint preparation on the strength of these results, and any use should follow safety and hygiene standards, because the authors note risks of scarring, bruising and infection.
athleteDev: Performance Application: this study does not support using wet-cupping to improve sprint performance or reduce exertion. The reported gains come from a single-group design with no sham comparator and need to be replicated in controlled trials before any performance recommendation.
rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It tested healthy men without injury, and it did not assess muscle damage, soreness or readiness after injury or illness.

citation: Leota J, Presby DM, Le F, Czeisler ME, Mascaro L, Capodilupo ER, et al. Dose-response relationship between evening exercise and sleep. Nature Communications. 2025;16:3297.
abstract: In 14,689 physically active adults wearing a wrist biometric device for one year (4,084,354 person-nights), later exercise timing and higher exercise strain were associated with delayed sleep onset, shorter sleep, lower sleep quality, higher nocturnal resting heart rate and lower nocturnal heart rate variability. Exercise ending at least 4 hours before sleep onset was not associated with changes in sleep, regardless of strain.
tldr: In physically active adults, hard exercise late in the evening was linked to later sleep onset, shorter sleep, and higher overnight resting heart rate with lower HRV. The authors suggest finishing exercise at least 4 hours before sleep onset, or choosing lighter sessions if evening training cannot move earlier.
methods: Retrospective cohort using WHOOP wearable data from September 2021 to August 2022, including adults with at least 350 days of wear and at least 50 logged exercises in the analysis window. Exercise timing was measured relative to each participant's habitual sleep onset and to actual sleep onset that night, and strain was the summated heart rate zone score grouped into light, moderate, high and maximal. Generalized additive mixed models with a random intercept for participant were used, with contrasts at 2-hour intervals and p < 0.005.
findings: Maximal rather than light strain ending 2 hours before habitual sleep onset was associated with 36.0 minutes later sleep onset, 22.2 minutes less sleep, 0.87 percentage points lower sleep quality, 3.9 bpm higher nocturnal RHR and 8.3 RMSSD units (14.1%) lower. Ending 2 hours after habitual sleep onset produced larger differences (80.0 minutes later onset, 42.6 minutes less sleep, 5.6 percentage points lower quality, 9.4 bpm higher RHR and 14.6 RMSSD units (32.6%) lower). When light or moderate strain ended more than about 2 hours before habitual sleep onset, sleep onset and sleep quality were similar to non-exercise nights.
limitations: The design is observational, so the associations cannot show that exercise caused the changes, and light exposure, caffeine, alcohol and diet were not controlled. Sleep onset was detected by the device rather than by sleep attempt, and the strain score (SHRZS) may underestimate strength training. The sample was physically active adults rather than athletes, 73.8% men, and two authors are WHOOP employees whose employer provided salaries.
practicalImplications: For physically active adults, finishing hard or long sessions at least 4 hours before habitual sleep onset is the timing the data support for protecting sleep. If evening training cannot move earlier, lighter sessions in that window were associated with smaller sleep and heart rate changes than maximal sessions.
athleteDev: Use the timing rule to place the last high-strain session of the day, since later and harder sessions were linked to delayed and shorter sleep. The authors' comment on evening elite competitions is discussion, not a measured result, because the sample was not athletes and sport performance was not measured.
rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions because it included no injured athletes and did not link sleep or heart rate measures to injury, symptoms or clearance.

citation: Kviatkovsky SA, Hickner RC, Ormsbee MJ. Collagen peptide supplementation for pain and function: is it effective? Curr Opin Clin Nutr Metab Care. 2022;25(6):401-406.
abstract: This narrative review summarises recent work on collagen peptide supplementation and connective tissue turnover, pain, function, strength and body composition. It focuses on hydroxyproline-containing bioactive peptides as a possible mechanism, and concludes that the benefits may depend on those peptides.
tldr: Collagen peptides may reduce pain and support strength and lean mass gains when combined with resistance training, but the human evidence is limited and mixed. The mechanism, including the role of bioactive peptides, is not yet established.
methods: A narrative review of the recent literature, covering 12 to 18 months, on collagen turnover, strength and body composition, pain and function, and bioactive peptides. The review draws on mechanistic, animal and human studies, and no systematic search method is described.
findings: The authors report improved pain or function in some trials, including KOOS physical function at 10 g/day over 6 months in older adults, while a 12-week trial at 10 g/day found no difference in knee pain. In resistance training trials, collagen increased lean mass or tendon size in several studies, but strength gains were often similar to placebo, and whey protein produced greater muscle thickness gains than collagen in one 10-week trial. The authors argue that Hyp-containing bioactive peptides are the likely drivers, but this rests on animal, cell and digest studies.
limitations: Narrative review with no search method. The authors' own pain and function trial is cited only from conference proceedings, and their collagen research is funded by PB Leiner, maker of the supplement used, although no conflicts are declared. The review states that the literature does not support muscle hypertrophy while also citing lean mass gains with collagen, and it notes that bioactive peptide content varies widely between products.
practicalImplications: Collagen peptides are best considered as an add-on to a loading or rehabilitation program, not a replacement for it, because the reported benefits appeared alongside training. Set expectations with care: the human pain evidence is limited and mixed, and strength gains were often similar to placebo. Product composition matters, so the bioactive peptide content of a specific product should be checked before it is recommended.
athleteDev: Several trials reported lean mass gains with collagen plus resistance training compared with placebo, but strength gains were often similar to placebo. Performance staff should not expect collagen to add strength beyond training alone, and whey protein gave greater muscle thickness gains in one trial.
rtp: Supports collagen peptides as a possible adjunct to rehabilitation for connective tissue injury or pain, with human evidence described as limited and mixed. The review does not address return-to-sport timing, tendon loading or clearance criteria.

citation: Antonio J, Evans C, Ferrando AA, Stout JR, Antonio B, Cinteo H, et al. Common questions and misconceptions about protein supplementation: what does the scientific evidence really show? Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition. 2024;21(1):2341903.
abstract: A narrative review of 11 common questions about protein supplementation, covering kidney and bone safety, body fat, plant protein, meat, post-exercise timing, per-meal intake and endurance athletes. The authors conclude that protein is well tolerated by healthy exercise-trained people at intakes several times the RDA, and that supplements are optional rather than required.
tldr: For healthy, exercise-trained people, the review finds no evidence that higher protein intakes harm the kidneys or bones, or that they add body fat on their own. Protein powder is not required, but it is a convenient way to reach daily targets.
methods: The review answers 11 questions in turn, summarising selected human trials, meta-analyses, reviews and position statements. No systematic search, inclusion criteria or quality rating is described; the only search detail is a PubMed remark in the abstract.
findings: The authors report intakes of 3.2 to 4.4 g/kg/day as well tolerated, and a one-year study at about 2.5 to 3.3 g/kg/day found no change in kidney markers in resistance-trained men. In one trial, 4.4 g/kg/day raised energy intake without changing body composition, and a higher-protein group had greater fat loss than a lower-protein group in another. They also state that 1.4 to 2.0 g/kg/day with adequate leucine and essential amino acids supports training in vegans and vegetarians, and that protein timing within an hour of training is not essential, with total daily intake more important.
limitations: The narrative format with no described search or evidence grading means study selection cannot be checked, and many cited safety and body composition trials come from the lead author's own group. Several key claims rest on short or small trials and case reports, such as a two-year series of case reports in male bodybuilders cited for kidney and liver safety, and the plant protein advice is internally inconsistent (53% to 75% more plant protein in the text vs about 20% to 40% in the section summary). The lead author is CEO of the ISSN, which receives grants from protein product companies, and other authors report supplement industry funding, consulting or EAA patents.
practicalImplications: For healthy, exercise-trained adults, the review treats protein intakes of up to about 4 to 5 times the RDA as tolerated, so targets can be set around training goals rather than kidney concerns. For active people, the review's 1.4 to 2.0 g/kg/day range is the working target, with plant-based athletes planning for more total protein to match leucine and essential amino acids. Protein powder is optional, but it is a practical way to reach a target without large calorie loads.
athleteDev: The review supports 1.4 to 2.0 g/kg/day for athletes, with total daily protein the main driver of body composition. It suggests 20 to 30 g per meal for most people while noting that some data show larger single doses give a higher and longer anabolic response.
rtp: Not an injury or return-to-sport paper. It mentions muscle damage markers after marathons and strength recovery after soccer matches, but it does not address rehabilitation or return-to-play decisions.

citation: Peeling P, Sim M, McKay AKA. Considerations for the Consumption of Vitamin and Mineral Supplements in Athlete Populations. Sports Medicine. 2023.
abstract: This review argues that athletes have higher micronutrient demands and that supplementation should follow a structured assessment of energy intake, diet, biochemistry, clinical status and environment. It summarises key vitamins and minerals and gives special considerations for female athletes.
tldr: Assess energy intake, diet, blood markers and clinical status before adding a vitamin or mineral supplement, since food-first is the main goal. Iron, vitamin D, calcium and B vitamins have the most athlete-specific relevance, and female athletes have distinct needs.
methods: Narrative review with no described literature search. It draws on prior meta-analyses, trials, position statements and consensus documents on iron, B vitamins, bone health, immune function and female athlete nutrition.
findings: The review cites a meta-analysis showing unchanged performance with iron supplementation in iron-deficient non-anaemic athletes, although iron supplementation improved haemoglobin and ferritin and reduced exercise fatigue in iron-deficient non-anaemic individuals. In meta-analyses of athletes and military personnel, low 25(OH)D (<30 ng/mL) was associated with greater stress fracture risk (7 studies, 3,625 participants), and vitamin D supplementation above sufficiency (>75 nmol/L) appeared to give no ergogenic benefit. Zinc (75 mg/day started within 24 hours of symptoms) reduced upper respiratory infection duration by about 33%, and vitamin C attenuated the oxidative stress and inflammatory response to a single exercise bout in 18 trials (n=313).
limitations: The review has no described search method, so its evidence selection cannot be checked. Several claims are mechanistic or based on small or observational data, such as the oestrogen and iron absorption link, for which no study has directly measured iron absorption across the menstrual cycle in female athletes. A cited audit found no study that classified menstrual status to best-practice standards and only 13% of participants were female athletes. The article is based on a presentation to the Gatorade Sports Science Institute (GSSI) expert panel, and the GSSI, a division of PepsiCo, funded attendance and an honorarium for its preparation; the authors declare no conflicts of interest.
practicalImplications: Before advising a supplement, assess anthropometrics, blood markers, clinical history, diet and the athlete's environment. If supplementation is chosen, plan dose, timing, food and drug interactions, duration and the frequency of biochemical monitoring, and use batch-tested products. Iron screening guidance cited in the review suggests assessing female athletes' iron status at 6-month intervals, especially when iron compromise is known.
athleteDev: Performance staff should check energy intake and key blood markers such as iron and 25(OH)D before adding supplements to training programmes. In the cited meta-analysis, iron supplementation did not change performance in iron-deficient non-anaemic athletes.
rtp: This review cannot be used to set return-to-sport criteria. It mentions bone health, stress fracture and energy availability, but it gives no return-to-play protocol, and it says optimising energy intake is the primary intervention for poor bone health with low energy availability.

citation: Zapata-Linares J, Gervasini G. Contaminants in Dietary Supplements: Toxicity, Doping Risk, and Current Regulation. International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism. 2024 (ahead of print).
abstract: This narrative review describes undeclared contaminants found in dietary supplements, including anabolic steroids, stimulants, diuretics, selective androgen receptor modulators, growth hormone-releasing peptides and cobalt. It covers their health risks, doping implications and the current EU and US regulatory framework.
tldr: Supplements used by athletes can contain undeclared steroids, stimulants, diuretics and other drugs that cause health harm and can lead to doping violations. The authors judge regulation to be weakly enforced, so athletes should take supplements with caution.
methods: Narrative review. The authors state they conducted an exhaustive literature search for the most common contaminants, then summarized mechanism, clinical use, health risk and doping status for each. No databases, dates, selection criteria or quality appraisal are reported.
findings: The authors report that anabolic-androgenic steroids and stimulants are the most frequently found contaminants, and that many designer steroids and stimulants have never been tested in humans. In cited product testing, 23 of 24 UK fitness-shop supplements contained steroids (16 of those 23 mislabeled), and 11 of 19 products sold as erythropoiesis stimulants contained cobalt and nickel, nine of them undeclared. The authors also state that good manufacturing practice certification reduces contamination risk but does not test for doping agents.
limitations: A narrative review with no reported search protocol or quality appraisal, so selection and emphasis cannot be reproduced. Most contaminants are documented through product testing rather than measurement in athletes, and the authors note that the health effects of designer agents are largely untested in humans.
practicalImplications: Staff should advise athletes to confirm the need for any supplement with a doctor or dietitian before use, to prefer products with independent third-party testing, and to avoid online purchasing where anti-doping rules apply. The authors state that third-party testers greatly reduce contamination risk, and that good manufacturing practice certification alone does not test for doping agents.
athleteDev: The review does not test performance. Its relevance to performance is that products marketed as performance or fat-burning aids can contain stimulants or steroids the athlete did not know they took, which the authors link to doping violations.
rtp: This review cannot inform return to sport decisions. It covers supplement contamination and doping risk, and does not address injury, rehabilitation or clearance criteria.

citation: Owens DJ, Kasper AM, Close GL. Current Practice in the Measurement and Management of Vitamin D Status in Elite Sport and Parasport. European Journal of Sport Science. 2025;25:e12305.
abstract: This survey of practitioners in elite sport and parasport asked about vitamin D testing methods, supplementation decisions and information sources. Financial and logistical limits were the main barriers, venous blood was the most common sampling method, and many respondents did not know which analytical method their lab used. Supplementation decisions were usually collaborative, but criteria varied widely across practitioners.
tldr: A survey of 74 elite-sport practitioners found that vitamin D testing and supplementation vary widely, and that cost and logistics limit testing. Staff who test should confirm the lab's analytical method and agree shared criteria for supplementation.
methods: Practitioners in elite sport and parasport were surveyed using items validated by a Delphi panel of seven experts from 12 invited. The survey covered testing, supplementation decisions and information sources, and open-ended responses were analysed thematically.
findings: Of 74 respondents, about a quarter did not test athletes' vitamin D status, and all of these reported no budget or did not know whether one existed. Among those who tested, 94% (n = 53) used venous blood, and 89.5% (n = 51) did not know the analytical method, mostly sending samples to an external lab or hospital. Supplementation was reported as a joint support-team decision (47%) or the respondent's sole decision (44%), and 97% (n = 71) used academic literature as an information source.
limitations: The survey is self-reported and lab methods and test results were not verified. Recruitment was through social media and email, and the sample was skewed to UK respondents (48 of 74) and to nutritionists and dietitians (64 of 74). The results report 74 respondents but the discussion says 73, one percentage (n = , 20%) has no count, and a second breakdown of who makes the supplementation decision (club doctor 38%, combined team 30%, nutritionist 21%) does not match the 47% joint and 44% sole figures.
practicalImplications: Staff who test vitamin D should confirm the analytical method with their lab, because most respondents did not know it and immunoassays can misestimate 25(OH)D. The authors suggest that a single spot test does not capture seasonal change, so testing at high-risk points of the year may support more individual decisions. Clear, shared supplementation criteria are also recommended by the authors, but the survey did not test whether any criteria improve outcomes.
athleteDev: The survey does not measure performance. It shows that testing timing, supplementation thresholds and doses vary widely across elite teams, and open-ended responses named poor athlete adherence and a lack of perceived benefit as barriers to supplementation.
rtp: The survey does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot guide return-to-play decisions. It describes testing and supplementation practice only.

citation: Gillham SH, Cole PL, Owens DJ, Chester N, Bampouras TM, McCartney D, et al. Daily Use of a Broad-Spectrum Cannabidiol Supplement Produces Detectable Concentrations of Cannabinoids in Urine Prohibited by the World Anti-Doping Agency: An Effect Amplified by Exercise. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, Publish Ahead of Print, 2025.
abstract: Healthy, physically active adults took a broad-spectrum CBD oil (150 mg/day, with trace CBG) or a placebo for 10 weeks, then completed a fasted 90-minute moderate-intensity exercise bout with urine and blood sampling before and after. In the CBD group (n = 31), urinary CBD, CBG, CBDV and CBD metabolites were detected after 10 weeks, and several rose further after exercise. No delta-9-THC or its metabolites were found, and the authors advise athletes to avoid broad-spectrum CBD products.
tldr: Ten weeks of a broad-spectrum CBD oil produced urine levels of WADA-prohibited minor cannabinoids (CBG and CBDV) in healthy adults, and fasted moderate exercise raised several of them further. Athletes subject to testing should treat broad-spectrum CBD as an anti-doping risk.
methods: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled parallel trial with deliberately unbalanced groups. Participants took 150 mg/day of a broad-spectrum CBD oil (n = 31) or an MCT oil placebo (n = 5) for 10 weeks, then completed a fasted 90-minute cycling bout at about 55% of peak wattage. Plasma and urine cannabinoids were measured by UHPLC-MS/MS at baseline, pre-exercise and post-exercise, and only the CBD group was analysed, with repeated-measures ANOVA including sex.
findings: No cannabinoids were detected at baseline. After 10 weeks, urinary CBD and its metabolites were present, and CBG and CBDV were detected in 42% and 68% of pre-exercise samples, rising to 74% and 84% after exercise. Significant time effects were reported for urinary CBD, CBG, CBDV, 6-OH-CBD and 7-OH-CBD (P = 0.006 to 0.043) but not 7-COOH-CBD (P = 0.128), with no sex effect, and delta-9-THC and its metabolites were not detected in any sample.
limitations: Adherence was not monitored beyond self-report, pre-exercise concentrations varied widely, the placebo group was not analysed, and CBDV is not reported on the product's certificate of analysis. Reporting conflicts should be checked: abstract and results P values differ for CBG (0.0023 vs 0.023) and 7-OH-CBD (0.009 vs 0.010), plasma and urine CBD share the same statistic (F 4.501, P 0.043), plasma 7-OH-CBD is listed twice with different results, the reported mean urinary CBDV is lower after exercise (10 vs 26 ng/mL) despite a reported increase, and results repeatedly say 'both groups' increased although only the CBD group was analysed. The fat-release explanation was not tested, the lead author's lab was funded by a CBD manufacturer, and participants were not competing athletes.
practicalImplications: Athletes subject to anti-doping testing should know that a broad-spectrum CBD product can produce urine results for WADA-prohibited minor cannabinoids, and that a fasted exercise session may raise them further. The authors recommend that athletes abstain from CBD supplements until a batch-tested isolate free of minor cannabinoids is available or WADA policy changes. CBD isolates were not tested, so this study does not show their risk.
athleteDev: Performance outcomes were not measured, so the study says nothing about training or competition performance. Its relevance is to anti-doping risk when athletes use broad-spectrum CBD around training sessions.
rtp: The study did not include injured people or clinical outcomes, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. Its relevance is limited to anti-doping risk for athletes who use broad-spectrum CBD.

citation: Pelly FE, Thurecht RL, Slater G. Determinants of Food Choice in Athletes: A Systematic Scoping Review. Sports Medicine - Open. 2022;8:77.
abstract: This systematic scoping review maps the individual and interpersonal determinants of food choice in athletes aged 16 years or older. It describes the sports, methods and reported determinants of 15 studies and rates their reporting quality. Health, performance and nutritional attributes recurred across studies, and the authors call for more research, particularly in female athletes.
tldr: Athletes' food choices are shaped by health and performance goals, along with competition phase, experience, sport culture and the food environment. Most of the 15 included studies were surveys or interviews, and few linked food choice to diet quality.
methods: Scoping review following PRISMA-ScR, with a protocol registered on the Open Science Framework. Eleven databases were searched from September to November 2020 and updated in March 2021, with reference-list checks. Two reviewers screened and extracted data. Reporting quality was rated against SRQR (qualitative) and STROBE (quantitative) items.
findings: Fifteen studies published from 2001 to 2021 were included, most since 2018. Health and performance were common motives, and nutritional attributes, sensory factors, familiarity, convenience, mood and weight control also recurred. Competition season, athlete experience, sport culture, nationality and sex influenced priorities, but quantitative results were inconsistent. Only one study linked food choice to diet quality, and its competition meals generally lacked fruit and dairy and included discretionary foods.
limitations: No quantitative synthesis was done, and quality appraisal is limited to reporting scores. Most studies were cross-sectional surveys or interviews in small, often single-country samples, and only one focused on female athletes. The authors note that some relevant studies with generic food-choice questions may have been missed.
practicalImplications: When planning nutrition education or menus, find out which factors drive each athlete's food choices, such as health, performance, taste, convenience or weight control. Competition phase, experience level and sport culture changed priorities in the included studies, so food support may need to differ across these. The authors name the Athlete Food Choice Questionnaire as the most extensively validated tool, while noting it needs further testing in specific sports and cultures.
athleteDev: Frame nutrition advice around performance and health goals, since these were the most consistent influences on athlete food choice. Adjust food planning for competition season, experience level and sport culture, which changed priorities in the included studies.
rtp: The review covers food choice in healthy competing athletes and reports no injury, rehabilitation or recovery outcomes. It cannot guide nutrition during return to play. The authors list food choice through injury and illness as a topic for future research.

citation: Rawson ES, Miles MP, Larson-Meyer DE. Dietary Supplements for Health, Adaptation, and Recovery in Athletes. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2018.
abstract: This scholarly review describes dietary supplements that may help athletes train or compete more effectively through health, adaptation and recovery rather than direct performance gains. Creatine, omega-3, vitamin D, probiotics, gelatin or collagen and some anti-inflammatory products are discussed. The authors recommend creatine and probiotics for specific purposes, do not recommend HMB at present, and call for more research.
tldr: The review supports creatine for recovery and adaptation to intense training, and probiotics for reducing upper respiratory infections. HMB is not recommended, and the other supplements need more research before firm advice.
methods: Scholarly narrative review of human, animal and mechanistic studies for each supplement. The article does not describe a systematic search, inclusion criteria or quality rating.
findings: In one cited review, 7 of 15 studies found that creatine improved markers of exercise-induced muscle damage or recovery, and 8 found no effect. Most placebo-controlled probiotic trials in athletes reported lower incidence, duration or severity of upper respiratory tract infection, while performance effects were not established. Vitamin D supplementation effects on muscle function were described as equivocal; low vitamin D status was associated with more respiratory infections, and in one trial in female naval recruits vitamin D3 plus calcium reduced stress fracture incidence by 20%.
limitations: The review does not describe how studies were selected, so the evidence base cannot be reproduced. Many cited trials are small and differ in dose, duration and outcome, and the HMB-free acid findings have been challenged. The summary lists creatine for mTBI, although human data are limited to two open-label trials in children plus animal data. The text is an accepted manuscript with no printed volume or pages, so the year is taken from the 2018 copyright line.
practicalImplications: Creatine monohydrate is the supplement the review most supports for recovery and adaptation to intense training, and for periods of extreme inactivity. Check vitamin D status before supplementing, since the authors advise against indiscriminate high doses. For omega-3, the authors suggest fatty fish over fish oil at present.
athleteDev: For recovery between intense training, the review supports creatine monohydrate. Probiotics may be worth starting well before travel or competition for athletes who are prone to gastrointestinal problems.
rtp: The review suggests creatine may help limit muscle loss during immobilization or recovery from injury, based on seven studies with mixed outcomes. It does not address return-to-play decisions or the criteria for returning to sport.

citation: Walpurgis K, Thomas A, Geyer H, Mareck U, Thevis M. Dietary Supplement and Food Contaminations and Their Implications for Doping Controls. Foods. 2020;9:1012.
abstract: This narrative review summarizes published evidence on food and supplement contamination or adulteration with doping agents and its implications for sports drug testing. Anabolic agents and stimulants are the substances most often found as undeclared ingredients. The authors conclude that education is the main protection for athletes, supported by better laboratory methods.
tldr: Supplements, some medicines and contaminated meat have caused positive doping tests, sometimes at trace levels. Education and lists of tested low-risk products are the main protections for athletes.
methods: Narrative review of published case reports, administration studies, surveys and doping-control statistics. The authors do not describe a systematic search. The cited analytical evidence is based on chromatographic-mass spectrometric methods.
findings: Anabolic agents and stimulants were the substances most often found as undeclared contaminants or deliberate additions in supplements, with diuretics, higenamine and other classes in fewer cases. In a 2004 study, 14.8% of 634 non-hormonal supplements contained undeclared anabolic steroids, and only 0.7% of 597 products did in a later repeat study. Clenbuterol residues in meat and a contaminated ibuprofen tablet are also described as sources of positive tests, and Table 1 summarizes which confirmed sources plausibly explained adverse findings.
limitations: The review does not describe a systematic search, so the case selection may not be complete. The authors note that proof of causality between an adverse finding and contaminated food or supplements is difficult to provide in most instances. Contamination rates come from a few product surveys of different eras and markets, so they do not give a current overall contamination rate.
practicalImplications: Athletes who need supplements should use products from low-risk sources, such as independent lists of tested products. Education on the risk of contaminated supplements, meat and medicines is the main recommended protection. Athletes should act with caution when using supplements marketed for muscle gain, fat loss or mental enhancement.
athleteDev: Include education on supplement contamination in performance planning, since the review names education as the main protection. Where supplements are used, direct athletes to products from low-risk sources rather than unlisted products.
rtp: This review cannot inform return to sport. It addresses contamination and doping-control risk and does not assess injured or rehabilitating athletes.

citation: Lauritzen F. Dietary Supplements as a Major Cause of Anti-doping Rule Violations. Front Sports Act Living. 2022;4:868228.
abstract: This study reviewed 18 years of doping controls by the Norwegian national anti-doping agency to test how often supplement use caused analytical anti-doping rule violations. Athletes claimed supplements as the source in 26% of cases, and evidence supported this in about half of those. Stimulants were the most common substance group, and most high-risk products were multi-ingredient pre-workout supplements.
tldr: Supplements were a likely source in about 14% of Norwegian analytical doping violations from 2003 to 2020, mostly through stimulants in pre-workout products. Staff should treat multi-ingredient pre-workout and fat-burning products as a doping risk.
methods: Retrospective analysis of Anti-Doping Norway test statistics and case files for 192 analytical ADRVs from 2003 to 2020. Each case was reviewed using decisions by the Prosecution and Judiciary Committees, investigator and athlete documents, product evidence and laboratory reports. Supplements were categorized by Garthe and Maughan, with multi-ingredient pre-workout supplements added as a separate category.
findings: In 49 of 192 cases (26%), athletes claimed a supplement caused the finding. Evidence supported a causal link in 27 cases (14%), and the committees did not exclude a supplement in 9 more, giving an estimated 14 to 19%. Stimulants were linked to 24 of the 27 supported cases, mostly methylhexanamine, and multi-ingredient pre-workout supplements were the likely source in 20; in 15 of the 27 the label declared the prohibited substance, sometimes under another name such as geranium. Most supported cases involved men (25 of 27) and recreational athletes (17 of 27), none involved sports foods, medical supplements or natural products, and the yearly share ranged from 0 to 36% with no clear trend.
limitations: Data come from one national agency, so the author states results cannot be generalized, and the study did not measure supplement use prevalence. Attribution depended on documentary judgment, and athlete intent could not be established. The abstract and results text give 16 methylhexanamine cases, but Table 2 lists 17, and only 17 sums with the other stimulants to the reported 24.
practicalImplications: Athletes should assume that multi-ingredient pre-workout and fat-burning products may contain a banned stimulant, and check ingredients beyond the label. Anti-doping and support staff should help athletes judge the need, risk and consequences of each supplement. Independent quality-assured products are a reasonable option, though the paper notes they reduce rather than remove the risk.
athleteDev: Ask athletes which supplements they take before any performance plan starts, because pre-workout and fat-burning products were the most frequent source of supplement-linked violations. Treat a stimulant-containing product as a doping risk, not only a performance aid.
rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It covers the sources of prohibited substances in doping-control cases and does not address injured athletes or rehabilitation.

citation: Gillham SH, Starke L, Welch L, Mather E, Whitelegg T, Chester N, et al. Does a broad-spectrum cannabidiol supplement improve performance in a 10-min cycle ergometer performance-test? European Journal of Sport Science. 2024;1-8.
abstract: In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study, 22 healthy participants (11 men and 11 women) completed two 10-minute cycle ergometer trials separated by 3 weeks of daily broad-spectrum CBD (150 mg) or placebo. Mean power, heart rate, blood lactate and RPE did not differ significantly between groups, so the authors conclude that the supplement did not improve performance through changes in RPE.
tldr: Three weeks of a broad-spectrum CBD oil at 150 mg/day did not change mean power or perceived exertion in a 10-minute cycling time trial, compared with placebo, in 22 recreationally active adults. The result does not support a performance benefit for this product in this test.
methods: Healthy recreationally active adults (24 recruited; 22 analysed, CBD n = 10 and placebo n = 12) were matched on peak power and randomly assigned to 150 mg/day broad-spectrum CBD oil or placebo oil for 3 weeks. Two 10-minute WattBike time trials, before and after supplementation, recorded power, distance, heart rate, RPE and blood lactate. Two-way ANOVAs were used.
findings: Mean power did not change significantly pre to post (time effect p = 0.77; time by group p = 0.32), and RPE showed no time by group effect (p = 0.19). Heart rate and blood lactate also showed no time by group effects. Twelve of 22 participants (54%) correctly guessed their allocation.
limitations: The groups were small (10 CBD, 12 placebo) and mixed by sex without a sex analysis, and the test was a single 10-minute cycling trial, so other modes and intermittent sport cannot be assessed. Both excluded participants were in the CBD group (one illness, one non-compliance), so the analysis is per protocol. Pain and recovery were not measured, although analgesia was the basis of the hypothesis, and the manufacturer provided financial support; the product contained trace cannabinoids other than CBD (CBG, CBC, CBGA).
practicalImplications: Staff should not expect a performance gain from this broad-spectrum CBD oil in aerobic time-trial work, since 3 weeks at 150 mg/day did not change power or RPE in this sample. The authors also advise athletes to avoid off-the-shelf CBD products, because such products can contain other cannabinoids that may affect anti-doping status.
athleteDev: Performance staff should not expect a 10-minute cycling or similar aerobic gain from this supplement in recreational adults, since the study found no change in power or perceived exertion. The paper does not test intermittent team-sport or strength performance.
rtp: The study measured performance and perceived exertion in healthy recreational adults and did not measure pain, injury or recovery after exercise. It cannot inform return-to-sport decisions or support the use of CBD for pain management after injury.

citation: Kenefick RW. Drinking strategies: planned drinking versus drinking to thirst. Sports Medicine. 2018;48(Suppl 1):S31-S37.
abstract: Thirst is alleviated before full rehydration, so when sweat rates are high and ad libitum drinking does not replace sweat losses, cumulative body water deficits develop. Planned drinking is favoured for longer exercise, especially in heat, at high intensity or high sweat rates, and when carbohydrate intake of 1 g/min is desired, while drinking to thirst may suffice for shorter, cooler or lower-intensity exercise.
tldr: Drinking to thirst is often not enough during long, hot or intense endurance exercise, because thirst eases before fluid losses are replaced. A planned drinking strategy based on individual sweat rate is the author's recommendation for those conditions, while thirst-guided drinking may be sufficient for shorter or cooler sessions.
methods: Narrative review of programmed drinking and drinking to thirst during exercise, with operational definitions of each strategy. The review draws on the author's earlier review of 34 endurance dehydration studies (60 observations), ad libitum drinking studies in running and cycling, and fluid-loss predictions for 5 to 42 km runs. No systematic search method is described.
findings: Of 60 observations from 34 endurance studies, 41 (68%) showed significantly impaired performance at 2% or greater body mass loss. In several studies, ad libitum drinking replaced only about half of sweat losses, and in 14 marathon studies it commonly led to losses above 2%. Ad libitum and programmed drinking produced similar running and cycling performance in several studies, while one 30 km cycling study favoured prescribed drinking in the heat.
limitations: Most dehydration studies were laboratory-based, many ad libitum studies used low-intensity or cool conditions, and field studies often started exercise euhydrated, so the 2% threshold may not be reached until late in the event. Predicted sweat losses are conservative estimates from equations not designed for sport, and fluid-loss estimates for ultra-endurance events are hard to interpret because non-fluid mass losses occur. The author declares no conflicts, yet he received an honorarium from the Gatorade Sports Science Institute, a PepsiCo division that funded the supplement.
practicalImplications: Athletes doing long (over about 90 minutes to 2 hours), hard or hot sessions, or who need carbohydrate at about 1 g/min, should follow a planned drinking program tailored to their measured sweat rate. Thirst-guided drinking may be sufficient for shorter sessions below about 1 to 2 hours, lower intensity work or cool conditions, and athletes should never drink to the point of weight gain.
athleteDev: Use the duration, intensity and heat thresholds to decide when endurance athletes need a planned drinking plan, and have them measure sweat rate under conditions similar to competition. The review does not show a direct performance benefit of planned drinking in every sport or setting, so frame the 2% threshold as a risk marker.
rtp: This review does not address return to sport. It covers fluid intake during exercise in general and does not address injury, rehabilitation or medical clearance.

citation: Patel DR, Ergun-Longmire B. Drugs and Supplements in Athletic Injury Recovery and Performance: WADA Perspective. In: Doral MN, et al., editors. Sports Injuries. Springer Nature Switzerland; 2025. p. 243-259.
abstract: The chapter reviews the World Anti-Doping Agency's prohibited substances and methods, the Athlete Biological Passport, and sports nutrition guidance for performance and recovery. It concludes that only a handful of supplements have shown ergogenic effects to a variable degree, namely caffeine, creatine, nitrate, beta-alanine and sodium bicarbonate.
tldr: Of the many supplements sold to athletes, the chapter finds evidence of performance effects only for caffeine, creatine, nitrate, beta-alanine and sodium bicarbonate, and it describes the health risks of banned drug classes. Check the current WADA and sport-specific lists rather than rely on this summary.
methods: Narrative book chapter summarising the WADA prohibited list, the Athlete Biological Passport, and nutrition and supplement guidance from ACSM, the IOC, ISSN and other bodies. No systematic search method is described, and the chapter cites sources accessed in February 2023.
findings: The chapter reports that anabolic agents made up 40% of the adverse analytical findings in WADA's 2021 report, from 241,430 samples, with an overall adverse finding rate of 0.65%. It lists five supplements with evidence of performance effects: caffeine (about 2 to 6 mg/kg before exercise), creatine (about 20 g/day for 5 to 7 days, or 3 to 6 g/day without loading), nitrate from beetroot juice (about 500 ml/day), beta-alanine (4 to 6 g/day for 2 to 4 weeks, with equivocal endurance evidence) and sodium bicarbonate (about 300 mg/kg 1 to 2 hours before exercise). For most banned classes it reports weak or no ergogenic evidence, and it states that anabolic agents have not been shown to enhance endurance performance.
limitations: The chapter is a narrative summary with no described search method, and its sources were accessed in early 2023 while the chapter is dated 2025. The adverse finding figures come from one WADA report, which the chapter says can include Therapeutic Use Exemption findings and is not a list of adjudicated violations. Dose and timing advice is summarised from other societies' guidance rather than tested in the chapter.
practicalImplications: Check each athlete's current WADA prohibited list and sport-specific rules before recommending any drug, supplement or method, since the chapter notes restrictions such as beta-blockers in archery, shooting and golf. Where iron deficiency is suspected, test serum ferritin (below 20 micrograms per litre indicates deficiency) before supplementing, because the chapter finds no evidence of an ergogenic effect of iron in athletes without deficiency. Plan fluid replacement to keep losses under 2% of body weight, since the chapter links 2% fluid loss to impaired aerobic performance, especially in hot weather.
athleteDev: Performance programmes can rest on the five supplements the chapter identifies with evidence, each with dose and timing guidance, while the chapter finds little or no evidence for most banned agents. Carbohydrate and fluid planning follow the sports nutrition guidance the chapter summarises.
rtp: This chapter cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. Its recovery content is general protein, carbohydrate and fluid guidance, and it does not assess injury rehabilitation outcomes or any treatment given after injury.

citation: Sinnott AM, Kontos AP, Collins MW, Ortega J. Concussion Symptoms Among Athletes: Preinjury Factors Predict Postinjury Factors. Journal of Head Trauma Rehabilitation. 2020;35(4):E361-E371.
abstract: This retrospective analysis of 290 high school and collegiate-aged athletes tested whether preinjury Post-Concussion Symptom Scale factors predict postinjury symptom factors. In the combined sample, preinjury cognitive-sensory symptoms and female sex predicted cognitive-migraine-fatigue symptoms, and in age-specific models preinjury sleep-arousal symptoms predicted somatic and sleep factors in 14 to 17 year olds, while preinjury affective symptoms predicted affective and somatic factors in 18 to 21 year olds. The authors conclude that symptom factors may help clinicians interpret symptom clusters, particularly in adolescents.
tldr: Symptoms reported before the season predicted some post-concussion symptom patterns, and the pattern differed between high school and college-aged athletes. The study is retrospective and explains a modest share of the variation, so it supports better symptom interpretation rather than individual prognosis.
methods: Retrospective analysis of the 22-item Post-Concussion Symptom Scale (PCSS) embedded in ImPACT testing from a community surveillance programme in northern California (2008 to 2017). Preinjury and postinjury PCSS scores were grouped into four preinjury and four postinjury symptom factors from a previously published factor structure, and linear regressions tested whether preinjury factors, sex and prior concussion predicted postinjury factors in 14 to 17 and 18 to 21 year olds and combined, with a Bonferroni-corrected alpha of .0083.
findings: Of 772 subjects, 290 were analysed (mean age 16.99 years). In the combined sample, preinjury cognitive-sensory symptoms (P = .002) and female sex (P = .002) predicted the postinjury cognitive-migraine-fatigue factor, and prior concussion predicted the somatic factor (P = .005). In 14 to 17 year olds, preinjury sleep-arousal predicted postinjury somatic (P = .003) and sleep (P = .005) factors. In 18 to 21 year olds, preinjury affective symptoms predicted postinjury affective (P = .001) and somatic (P = .009) factors. Postinjury assessment took place on average 3 days after injury.
limitations: The design is retrospective, the analysis used raw PCSS scores rather than change scores, and lifestyle factors such as activity, sleep and medication were not controlled. The authors did not assess honesty or effort in symptom reporting, and did not record race, ethnicity, language or multisport status. The paper has internal inconsistencies: Methods exclude evaluations more than 8 days after injury but Results say 7; the 18 to 21 year old somatic result is P = .008 in the abstract and P = .009 in the Results, which is above the stated corrected alpha of .0083; and the Discussion and Conclusion describe predictions (cognitive-sensory for both age groups, affective to sleep in 18 to 21 year olds) that Table 5 does not show.
practicalImplications: When an athlete reports sleep or emotional symptoms before the season, clinicians can ask more detailed questions about onset and daily course, since these preseason patterns were linked to specific post-injury symptom groups. The paper gives no validated prognostic score, so the findings should prompt questions rather than set expected recovery.
athleteDev: For performance and wellbeing staff, preseason reports of sleep or mood complaints may flag athletes whose post-injury symptom profile needs closer watch. The paper does not assess training or performance outcomes.
rtp: The paper does not give return-to-play criteria or timing. Its finding that preseason symptom patterns relate to post-injury symptom profiles may help decide who needs closer symptom tracking after injury, but it should not be used to decide when an athlete can return to play.

citation: Rajaei AY, Neary JP, Thompson ES, Singh J, Mang CS. Considering the Effects of Cannabinoids and Exercise on the Brain: A Narrative Review. Sports. 2025;13:320.
abstract: This narrative review describes overlapping effects of cannabinoids and exercise on brain function through inflammation, vascular function and neuroplasticity, with attention to athletes. The authors conclude that combined effects could be additive, synergistic or opposing, and that direct study of the interaction is scarce.
tldr: A mechanistic review suggesting that cannabinoids and exercise act on shared brain-relevant pathways, with THC and CBD producing different effects. The combined effects in athletes have not been tested directly.
methods: Narrative review. The authors searched PubMed and Google Scholar with combined keywords, emphasizing work from 2010 onward, and two authors screened titles and abstracts. They included 243 references, judging quality informally by journal credibility and the alignment of methods, results and conclusions, with no systematic protocol, inclusion criteria or formal appraisal tool.
findings: The authors report that exercise and the endocannabinoid system both influence inflammation, cerebral blood flow and neuroplasticity. In the cited work, single bouts of treadmill running or cycling raised circulating anandamide, and THC-dominant cannabis use is described as disrupting neuroplasticity. In athletes, one cited trial reported that acute CBD improved peak oxygen consumption and lactate accumulation in endurance-trained men, and a cited female athlete study reported lower anaerobic performance in cannabis users.
limitations: Narrative design with a non-systematic search and no formal quality appraisal. Most mechanistic evidence comes from animal, cell and non-athlete studies, and the authors state that few human or athlete studies have tested cannabinoid-exercise interaction. The concussion and pain applications are described as largely unstudied.
practicalImplications: Staff should treat cannabinoid use in athletes as an unresolved question. The review gives no dosing, safety or return-to-play guidance, and its authors call for direct study before therapeutic use.
athleteDev: The review reports no performance outcomes. Staff can note the authors' view that habitual exercise might offset some effects of THC-dominant cannabis on neuroplasticity, but this is speculative and untested.
rtp: This review cannot inform return to sport. Concussion and pain are discussed only as speculative targets, and the only post-concussion cannabinoid evidence cited is a single small report in females with post-concussion syndrome.

citation: Roschel H, Gualano B, Ostojic SM, Rawson ES. Creatine Supplementation and Brain Health. Nutrients. 2021;13:586.
abstract: This short review updates evidence on creatine supplementation and brain health in humans. Creatine may improve cognitive processing, especially where brain creatine is low because of acute stressors such as exercise or sleep deprivation, or chronic conditions. The optimal protocol to raise brain creatine has not been established, and studies that measure brain creatine and cognition together are needed.
tldr: Creatine may help cognition when the brain is stressed, such as during sleep loss or hypoxia, but the dose and duration needed to raise brain creatine are not settled. Human evidence for concussion recovery is limited, so the authors describe high-risk use as a judgment rather than a proven treatment.
methods: Narrative review of human and animal studies on brain creatine, cognition and brain injury. No systematic search method is described. The authors summarize study protocols and outcomes in a table of cognitive studies and discuss findings on brain creatine uptake, sleep deprivation, mental fatigue, and mild traumatic brain injury.
findings: The authors report that of 12 studies of creatine and brain creatine or phosphocreatine, nine showed significant increases of about 5 to 10 percent, smaller than the muscle response. Cognitive results were mixed across studies, with clearer effects under stress such as hypoxia and sleep deprivation. In children with mild traumatic brain injury, creatine was associated with improvements in several symptoms, and the authors note that the mechanistic and animal evidence is much larger than the human evidence.
limitations: Studies differ in brain creatine measurement, dose, duration and population, which prevents direct comparison. The review has no described search, many cited trials did not measure brain creatine, and the authors state that human brain creatine rises only about 10 percent, which limits extrapolation from animal findings. Several authors have declared financial ties to creatine manufacturers.
practicalImplications: Creatine should not be presented to athletes as a proven way to protect the brain or speed concussion recovery. The authors argue that, given creatine's safety record, encouraging supplementation in populations at high risk of mild traumatic brain injury might be prudent, but they acknowledge this rests mainly on animal and theoretical data rather than clinical trials.
athleteDev: The review cites studies in which creatine reduced the effect of sleep deprivation on rugby passing accuracy and improved selected cognitive indexes in semi-professional mountain bikers, while two studies in non-stressed soccer players found no effect on passing accuracy. None of these studies measured brain creatine, and the authors say transfer to sport performance remains to be shown.
rtp: Not suitable for return-to-sport decisions after concussion. The authors describe the human mild traumatic brain injury evidence as scarce, with much of it from animal models, and they say it is difficult to generalize that evidence to athletes.

citation: Doohan MA, Watzek JT, King N, White MJ, Stewart IB. Does increased core temperature alter cognitive performance during exercise-induced heat strain? A narrative review. J Appl Physiol. 2023;135:35-52.
abstract: Thirty-one studies that measured cognitive performance and core temperature during exercise in heat were reviewed and grouped into inhibition, working memory and cognitive flexibility tasks. Core temperature change alone did not predict cognitive performance, and effects were more likely when heat strain was combined with dehydration, prolonged exercise or high core temperatures.
tldr: Heat-induced changes in core temperature alone were not a consistent predictor of cognitive decline during exercise. Impairments were more likely when heat was combined with dehydration, long exercise bouts or core temperatures near 39 C.
methods: Systematic search of CINAHL, Embase and PubMed (final search 11 May 2022) for adult human studies with control and experimental conditions that measured cognitive performance and core temperature during exercise-induced heat strain. Two reviewers screened studies, and 31 studies were included in the narrative review. Hedges' g was calculated for each cognitive task at the time point with the peak core temperature difference between conditions, and risk of bias was assessed with the Cochrane tool.
findings: Core temperature changes of 0 to 1.0 C (18 studies), 1.0 to 2.0 C (7 studies) and greater than 2.0 C (2 studies) were used. The authors report that changes above 1 C were needed to influence cognitive performance across all three domains. Accuracy was more affected than response time, and reaction time, memory recall and Stroop tasks were most likely to detect change. The greatest decrements typically occurred near 39 C.
limitations: Small samples (mean 16 participants per study), a modest number of studies with usable data (four of 31 could not have peak core temperature changes identified because data were not shared), and differing protocols and task designs. The authors judged a meta-analysis inappropriate for these reasons. All studies had a moderate overall risk of bias.
practicalImplications: When heat strain is a concern, staff should consider hydration status, exercise duration and core temperature together, not core temperature alone, when interpreting cognitive performance. Reaction time, memory recall and Stroop tasks are the measures the authors identify as most likely to detect change.
athleteDev: Performance Application: when testing decision-making or cognitive tasks in hot training or competition, record core temperature, hydration and exercise duration alongside the cognitive result. A small change in core temperature alone may not explain a change in performance.
rtp: This review cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It studied healthy participants in exercise heat and does not address concussion, injury or medical clearance.

citation: Verschueren J, Tassignon B, Proost M, Teugels A, Van Cutsem J, Roelands B, et al. Does Mental Fatigue Negatively Affect Outcomes of Functional Performance Tests? Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2020.
abstract: In 14 healthy adults, a 90-minute incongruent Stroop task increased subjective mental fatigue, and accuracy on the neurocognitive Reactive Balance Test fell after the task. Single-leg hop, countermovement jump and Y-Balance test results were not affected by mental fatigue.
tldr: A 90-minute mentally demanding task reduced accuracy on a reactive balance test, while traditional strength and balance tests were unchanged. Mental fatigue may affect adaptability and decision-making in ways standard functional tests do not capture.
methods: Randomized counterbalanced crossover design with 14 healthy adults. A 90-minute 100% incongruent Stroop task (mental fatigue) and a 90-minute documentary (control) were each followed by pre and post testing of single-leg hop, countermovement jump, Y-Balance test and the Reactive Balance Test (accuracy and visuomotor reaction time). Analysis used repeated-measures ANOVA and paired t-tests.
