findings: Subjective mental fatigue was higher after the Stroop task than after the control task (interaction p = 0.002). Reactive Balance Test accuracy was 86.16 +/- 1.22% post mental fatigue versus 91.62 +/- 1.56% post control, with a condition by time interaction (p = 0.023 in the results text; the abstract reports p = 0.024). No condition by time interaction was found for the single-leg hop, countermovement jump, Y-Balance test, or Reactive Balance Test reaction time; small condition effects favoured the control session for single-leg hop and countermovement jump. Stroop task accuracy and reaction time did not change over the 90 minutes.
limitations: Small sample of 14 healthy adults (four women), tested in a laboratory with one session per condition. No neurophysiological measures were taken. The Stroop task did not produce a behavioural decline, and the authors state that clinical applicability cannot be inferred from these first results. The abstract and results text give slightly different p-values for the Reactive Balance Test interaction (0.024 and 0.023).
practicalImplications: Where decision-making and reactive balance matter, staff may consider adding a reactive or neurocognitive test to standard functional tests when an athlete is mentally fatigued. Traditional single-leg hop, countermovement jump and Y-Balance results were not changed in this study, so they should not be read as detecting mental fatigue.
athleteDev: Performance Application: in healthy active adults, a 90-minute mentally demanding task lowered reactive balance accuracy but not jump, hop or Y-Balance results. If staff want to detect effects of mental fatigue, these data suggest reactive or decision-based tests are more sensitive than traditional jump and balance tests, though this has not been tested in athletes.
rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It used healthy adults, no injured participants, and no return-to-play outcome, and the authors state that the clinical use of neurocognitive tests is not yet established.

citation: Hashida K, Shirahata K, Furutani T, Tamura K. Clinically feasible dual-task detects residual post-concussion deficits after return-to-play. Journal of Sports Sciences. 2024.
abstract: A prospective cohort study compared a clinically feasible dual-task test (Expanded Timed Get Up and Go with an auditory odd-or-even task) with single-task performance in adolescent athletes with concussion and matched controls. The concussion group was tested 7 to 10 days after injury and again after completing a graduated return-to-play protocol.
tldr: After athletes were cleared to return to play, those with concussion were still slower than matched controls on the dual-task walk test, by about 5.7 seconds on average. Symptom checklists showed no group difference at that point, so this test may detect deficits that standard checks miss.
methods: Concussion and control groups each had 10 male and 10 female participants, matched by age, sex and sport. Each participant completed two single tasks (ETGUG and an auditory odd-or-even switch task) in randomized order, then the two combined as a dual task, with symptoms recorded before and after each session. Group, task and time effects were analysed with mixed-design ANOVAs and post-hoc tests.
findings: At 7 to 10 days, the concussion group was slower than controls on single-task ETGUG (2.61 s, p = 0.018) and dual-task ETGUG (3.49 s, p = 0.014). At return to play, the concussion group remained slower on single-task (2.85 s, p = 0.007) and dual-task (5.65 s, p < 0.001) ETGUG, the task-by-group interaction was significant, and only the concussion group still showed a significant dual-task cost (4.46 s, p = 0.008). Controls got faster between sessions on both tasks, while the concussion group did not, and symptom totals did not differ between groups at return to play.
limitations: The sample is small (20 per group), drawn from high school and university athletes at more than one test site, and the gap between the two sessions varied by person and was not controlled. The text and tables disagree slightly: the RTP task-by-group interaction is p < 0.001 in the text and p = 0.001 in Table 2, and the 95% CI for the RTP dual-task difference is 2.56 to 8.74 s in the text and 2.53 to 8.78 s in Table 3. The paper reports no reliability data in this population and did not test the deficits against later outcomes.
practicalImplications: The test needs only a chair, a cone set 10 m away, a phone timer and someone to call random numbers, so it can be run in an athletic training room. Because the paper leaves open whether baseline data are needed, an individual athlete's time should not be read against a norm without a local baseline or control comparison.
athleteDev: For performance staff, the test measures how well divided attention holds up while walking. The paper does not link dual-task speed to training load, readiness or performance output, so it cannot guide training prescription.
rtp: The authors recommend adding a dual-task walk-and-count test to concussion assessment, because athletes cleared to return still performed slower than matched controls as a group. The study does not show that the test should change individual clearance decisions, gives no cut-off, and does not test whether these deficits predict re-injury.

citation: Philipp NM, Scott AA, Caldwell BR, Cabarkapa D, Johnson QR, Fry AC. Comparing the maximal horizontal deceleration demands between a novel acceleration to deceleration assessment and the 505 change of direction test. Journal of Human Sport and Exercise. 2024;19(3):803-814.
abstract: Laboratory comparison of 19 recreationally trained, college-aged athletes performing a 10-m acceleration-to-deceleration assessment (ADA) and the 505 change of direction test, measured with an inertial measurement unit system. Six of 12 deceleration metrics differed between tests, with the 505 showing greater average deceleration and braking force, and the ADA showing shorter stopping time and distance, although these two stopping measures had insufficient reliability.
tldr: In 19 recreationally trained athletes, the 505 test produced greater average deceleration, braking force, stopping time and stopping distance than a 10-m acceleration-to-deceleration task with a cued braking point and no fixed stopping point. Stopping time and distance were not reliable enough to track small changes, so the two tests should be treated as measuring different braking demands rather than as interchangeable.
methods: Within-session comparison of ADA (three trials) and 505 (four trials, two per leg) using an Xsens MVN Awinda IMU suit sampling at 100 Hz, with metrics processed in Athlete Analytics. Between-test differences were tested with paired t-tests and Hedges' g, and reliability was assessed with ICC (2,k), SEM and minimal difference across trials.
findings: Average approach velocity and momentum did not differ between tests. The 505 showed greater average deceleration (4.10 vs 3.32 m/s2, ES -2.46) and braking force (313.6 vs 252.4 N, ES -1.61), longer stopping time (1.41 vs 1.20 s) and distance (5.38 vs 4.17 m), shorter brake-step contact time (0.18 vs 0.20 s) and brake steps placed closer to the centre of mass (36.1 vs 41.0 cm). Stopping time and distance ICCs were 0.51 and 0.56 for stopping time and 0.13 and 0.26 for stopping distance, with the authors describing these as insufficient.
limitations: The authors acknowledge that the sample had little prior experience with either test, which may inflate variability, and that deceleration phase COM drop had high SEM. The reliability of average deceleration was poor (ICC 0.34 for ADA and 0.47 for 505), and the Table 3 confidence interval for average deceleration (-0.91; 0.78) and ES interval (-3.33; 1.88) are not internally consistent with the reported means. The SEM is described as coming from an ANOVA across three trials although the 505 had four, and the abstract's 'reductions in velocity' is not a separately reported metric.
practicalImplications: When deceleration is quantified with IMUs, these results suggest that a 505 test with a fixed turn point and an ADA with a cued braking point but no fixed stopping point should not be treated as interchangeable, since braking force and stopping metrics differ. Because stopping time and distance were unreliable, staff should check the minimal difference values (for example 2.48 m for ADA stopping distance) before treating a change in these measures as real.
athleteDev: The paper suggests the predetermined turn in the 505 imposes a different braking demand from the ADA, with longer stopping time and distance, greater braking force and shorter brake-step contacts. The authors speculate that this demands different neuromuscular and skill qualities, but the study did not measure performance outcomes, so its use for training selection remains an inference.
rtp: The study tested healthy recreationally trained athletes and did not assess injury, rehabilitation or return-to-sport status, so it cannot be used to clear an athlete or set return-to-play benchmarks. The minimal-difference values reported, such as about 2.5 m for ADA stopping distance, suggest these metrics would miss small changes in braking capacity during rehabilitation.

citation: Chilmeran Z, Akhtar MU, Sharafeldin A-BK, Gaynor D. Concussion injuries in sports and the role of instrumented mouthguards: a mini review. Frontiers in Bioengineering and Biotechnology. 2025;13:1567429.
abstract: This mini review summarises concussion in contact sports, including mechanisms, prevalence and long-term effects, and examines the validity of instrumented mouthguards (iMGs) for measuring head impacts. The authors report that iMGs can measure linear and rotational acceleration with low error in several studies, but that accuracy depends on fit, sensor coupling and signal filtering. Citing a consensus statement, they describe iMGs as research tools that need further refinement and standardised validation before reliable clinical or field use.
tldr: Instrumented mouthguards measure head impacts with reasonable accuracy in some validation studies, but fit and sensor coupling strongly affect their readings. The review states that they are still research tools and cannot diagnose concussion on their own.
methods: Narrative mini review. The paper does not describe a systematic search or study selection criteria. It draws on prior work on concussion epidemiology and pathophysiology, mouthguard history, and iMG validation in headform, cadaveric, laboratory and field studies.
findings: The review cites an observational NFL study (1,302 concussions in 1,004 players, 2015 to 2019) and an NHL rate of about 5.8 to 6.1 concussions per 100 games. One high school football comparison of an iMG with the helmet-mounted HIT System (133 paired events) found low average error but significant variability in higher-impact events, and one headform study reported mean absolute errors as low as 7%. In 915 female youth soccer players, an iMG had 69.2% sensitivity and 80.3% positive predictive value, which the authors describe as confirming reliability for on-field use, while they also report that iMGs lack validity at high impact velocities and that fit, direct contact and filter cutoffs affect accuracy.
limitations: The review does not describe how the cited studies were selected, so the evidence is not systematically weighed. It notes that female and younger athletes are under-represented in iMG research and that validation and calibration protocols are not standardised. The authors also state that evidence on whether mouthguards reduce concussion is inconsistent and unclear.
practicalImplications: Before using iMGs, staff should check whether a device has been validated in their sport and age group, and should check fit and sensor coupling before trusting readings. The review advises that iMG data alone should not diagnose concussion, and that clinical assessment with SCAT-6 and expert judgement remain essential.
athleteDev: For performance staff, iMGs can record head impacts in real time, so they can support monitoring of impact exposure. The readings are sensitive to fit and comfort, and the review notes barriers to adoption, so the data should be treated as one monitoring signal. The review does not evaluate training load or performance outcomes.
rtp: The review does not study return to play and gives no return-to-play criteria. Its statement that iMG data alone cannot diagnose concussion, and that clinical assessment is still needed, means impact readings should not be used to clear an athlete to return.

citation: Arbogast KB, Caccese JB, Buckley TA, et al. Consensus Head Acceleration Measurement Practices (CHAMP): Origins, Methods, Transparency and Disclosure. Annals of Biomedical Engineering. 2022.
abstract: This consensus paper describes the origins and voting methods of the Consensus Head Acceleration Measurement Practices (CHAMP) group. It introduces reporting checklists for head kinematic measurement studies and for disclosing industry involvement.
tldr: Use the CHAMP 2022 checklists to report how a head-acceleration device was validated, verified, windowed and processed. Disclose sponsor and industry involvement so readers can judge bias.
methods: Expert working groups drafted best-practice chapters in six areas. Statements were voted on at a March 2022 consensus conference, with 80% agreement required for acceptance. The authors then built reporting checklists aligned with five methods and a disclosure table.
findings: At least 80% agreement was reached for every statement, often after discussion and revision, so no dissent statements were needed. The checklists list items such as sensor specifications, surrogate and mounting details, event verification, data processing, and reporting of validation metrics and false-positive rates. The paper also lists six types of industry involvement that should be disclosed, including funding, in-kind equipment, proprietary software and help with analysis.
limitations: The paper reports no measured data, so the checklists have not been tested for their effect on study quality. The authors state the checklists are not all-encompassing and will need updating, and not every item has a published example. Financial ties to the NFL and Football Research Inc. are disclosed for several authors, and conference support came from the same organisations.
practicalImplications: When reviewing or planning head-acceleration monitoring, check whether the study reports device validation, event verification, data processing and false-positive or false-negative rates before using its impact counts. Disclosure of sensor-company or league involvement should be read as a transparency requirement, not as proof of bias.
athleteDev: Staff who use head-impact sensors for monitoring should compare players or seasons only when the data are verified and processed in comparable ways. The paper provides reporting and methods guidance and no training-load or performance prescription.
rtp: This paper cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It contains no injury thresholds, clinical criteria or concussion diagnostic standards.

citation: Thorborg K, Branci S, Nielsen MP, Langelund MT, Hölmich P. Copenhagen five-second squeeze: a valid indicator of sports-related hip and groin function. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2017;51:594-599.
abstract: This validation study tested a five-second hip-adduction squeeze in 667 subelite male football players, who rated groin pain from 0 to 10 during the squeeze and completed the Copenhagen Hip and Groin Outcome Score (HAGOS). Construct validity, responsiveness, reliability and floor and ceiling effects were assessed.
tldr: The pain score from a five-second squeeze tracks sports-related hip and groin function in football players and was reliable in a small test-retest sample. A pain score of 6 or more indicated substantially impaired function in this study, which the authors suggest should prompt clinical assessment.
methods: Cross-sectional validation study following COSMIN guidance. Construct validity used 667 players at season start, responsiveness and floor and ceiling effects used 52 players tested again later in the season, and test-retest reliability used 10 players with stable status. Analyses used Spearman correlations, Kruskal-Wallis and Mann-Whitney tests, and Lin's concordance correlation coefficient for reliability.
findings: Squeeze pain correlated with lower HAGOS Sport scores at season start (rho -0.61, p<0.01, n=665) and in the 52-player subgroup early and later in the season (rho -0.79 and -0.76), and change scores correlated with HAGOS Sport change scores (rho -0.51). Median HAGOS Sport scores were 97 for pain 0 to 2, 69 for 3 to 5 and 47 for 6 to 10, and test-retest concordance was 0.90 (95% CI 0.67 to 0.97) in 10 players. Only 4 of 39 symptomatic players (10%) scored at the floor or ceiling, below the 15% threshold, so no floor or ceiling effect was declared.
limitations: The reliability sample was 10 players, and reliability analysis included only players whose scores changed by 10 points or less; the responsiveness sample was the 52 players who attended a clinical examination. Change scores correlated more strongly with HAGOS Symptoms (rho -0.64) than with HAGOS Sport, and the subgroup analyses by diagnosis were post hoc, with 24 and 15 players. The authors note that players may under-report pain when they know a high score could stop them playing, and the study did not test whether the cut-offs predict injury or return to play.
practicalImplications: Staff can use the five-second squeeze as a quick, equipment-free pain and function check for football players with groin pain. The authors' traffic-light scheme suggests stopping football and seeking clinical assessment at a pain score of 6 or more, clinical review at 3 to 5, and treating 0 to 2 as few restrictions rather than full clearance.
athleteDev: The paper does not measure performance. Its relevance to performance staff is as a rapid screen of sport-specific hip and groin function, which the authors suggest can inform participation decisions alongside clinical review.
rtp: The authors suggest the traffic-light categories can guide football participation, but say that players with a score of 0 to 2 may still need clinical review before return to play. The study does not test return-to-play outcomes, so it supports screening and monitoring rather than clearance decisions.

citation: Capling L, Gifford JA, Beck KL, Flood VM, Slater GJ, Denyer GS, et al. Development of an Athlete Diet Index for Rapid Dietary Assessment of Athletes. International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism. 2019 (accepted manuscript).
abstract: This study describes the development of an Athlete Diet Index (ADI), an electronic food-based tool for rapid dietary assessment of athletes. Items came from sports nutritionist focus groups, a modified Delphi survey and an athlete pilot. The final 68-item tool was rated easy to use and relevant by pilot athletes, and the authors report content and face validity. Scoring and criterion validation are still needed.
tldr: A 68-item electronic Athlete Diet Index was developed with sports nutritionists and tested with athletes for content and face validity. Pilot athletes found it easy to complete and relevant, but its scoring and accuracy against established dietary methods have not yet been tested.
methods: Mixed-methods study in three phases. Phase 1 used focus groups with 20 accredited sports nutritionists, coded thematically in NVivo. Phase 2 used a modified Delphi survey of 9 of these nutritionists over two rounds. Phase 3 piloted the electronic tool with 15 athletes, who rated comprehension and relevance on 5-point scales, and completion time was recorded.
findings: Focus groups identified athlete-specific features such as training load and injury status, food images and serve sizes, nutrition and hydration around training, meal patterns and supplement use. In the Delphi survey, 6 of 71 draft items were recommended for deletion and minor modifications were suggested for 54, with consensus for inclusion after a second round. The final tool has 68 items: core nutrition (45), performance nutrition (15) and personal information (8); all pilot athletes rated it easy (40%) or very easy (60%) to understand and relevant (37%) or very relevant (63%), and median completion time was 17.5 minutes (range 13 to 26).
limitations: Only content and face validity were tested, with no scoring matrix, no comparison with established dietary methods and no reliability testing. The pilot sample was small, mostly female, and drawn from water polo and rowing. The authors note that the researchers' own sports nutrition experience may have influenced responses.
practicalImplications: Sports nutrition staff could use a brief electronic screen to identify athletes whose intake needs follow-up and to see changes across training phases. The authors advise that it should not replace detailed dietary assessment or individual guidance. Scoring and validation are needed before it is used to judge diet quality.
athleteDev: The tool asks about training load, nutrition and hydration practices around training, and supplement use alongside usual food intake. Without a scoring matrix it cannot yet show whether intake matches training demands, and its items have not been tested against performance outcomes.
rtp: The study addresses dietary assessment in athletes in general, and only one of the 15 pilot athletes was injured. It does not evaluate nutrition for rehabilitation or return to play and cannot be used to set injury nutrition plans.

citation: Scott TJ, Thornton HR, Scott MTU, Dascombe BJ, Duthie GM. Differences Between Relative and Absolute Speed and Metabolic Thresholds in Rugby League. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2018;13(3):298-304.
abstract: This study compared relative speed and metabolic thresholds, derived from the 30-15 Intermittent Fitness Test, with absolute thresholds for quantifying match-play running in elite rugby league. Distances above relative thresholds correlated strongly with absolute thresholds, but differences were large by position and fitness. The authors conclude that absolute high-intensity speed thresholds underestimate high-intensity running load for many players.
tldr: Absolute speed thresholds (over 5.2 m/s) underestimate high-intensity running for many rugby league players, especially those with lower fitness. A threshold derived from a 30-15 IFT gives an individual reference that may suit squad monitoring.
methods: GPS match data were collected from 26 professional NRL players across the 2013 season (346 match files). The 30-15 IFT was repeated at four time points about six weeks apart to update individual thresholds. Distances above each threshold were compared using Pearson correlations and magnitude-based effect sizes.
findings: Distance above VT1IFT and MIRTh correlated at r = .94, VT2IFT and HIRTh at r = .94, and HPmetVT2 and HPmetTh at r = .93. Distance above VT2IFT was almost certainly greater than HIRTh for all positional groups (effect size 0.79 to 1.03), with the largest differences in middle forwards and outside backs. Absolute MIRTh over- or underestimated VT1IFT distance depending on position and fitness, and edge forwards covered moderately less distance above HPmetVT2 than HPmetTh.
limitations: Relative thresholds are estimated from the 30-15 IFT, and the authors note that the assumed link between this test and the ventilatory thresholds may vary between individuals. The abstract and results call the 138 to 167% values 'increases', but Table 2 means put VT2IFT distance at about 138 to 169% of HIRTh distance (for example, outside backs 809 m vs 535 m is about 151%, not the 144% reported), and the Practical Applications cite an absolute HIR threshold of over 5.5 m/s while the Methods use over 5.2 m/s. The discussion also describes adjustables and edge forwards as covering 'substantially less' distance above VT1IFT than MIRTh, while the results report most likely the same distances; only one season was observed.
practicalImplications: Squads can set individual high-intensity running references using a 30-15 IFT-based VT2 threshold without laboratory gas analysis. Absolute speed bands are likely to understate high-intensity load for lower-fitness players and to overstate moderate-intensity load for higher-fitness players. Repeat the field test across the season, because the authors changed thresholds when fitness changed.
athleteDev: Use individual relative thresholds when prescribing and monitoring high-intensity running in rugby league. Position-based absolute speed bands can misstate the work of players with different fitness levels. Treat the 30-15 IFT-derived values as estimates, as the authors do.
rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It describes match-play running in fit professional players and does not assess injured athletes or return-to-play criteria.

citation: James LP, Suppiah H, McGuigan MR, Carey DL. Dimensionality Reduction for Countermovement Jump Metrics. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2021 (ahead of print).
abstract: This brief report applies principal component analysis (PCA) and maximum likelihood factor analysis to countermovement jump (CMJ) variables from three cohorts recorded on three different devices. About 90% of the variance in each data set was explained by 3 or 4 principal components, and 2 to 3 factors explained the jump.
tldr: Applying PCA and factor analysis to three CMJ data sets showed that about 90% of the variance can be captured by 3 or 4 components, so a practitioner can report fewer CMJ variables. The method is demonstrated on three specific samples and devices and does not show which metrics matter most for performance.
methods: Three cohorts were tested on different devices: recreationally trained males (n = 16; force platform, 2000 Hz), competitive mixed martial arts athletes (n = 29; linear position transducer, 100 Hz) and junior elite Australian football players (n = 19; ForceDecks force platform, 1000 Hz). Three trials were performed per set and the best trial was analysed. PCA (singular value decomposition) and maximum likelihood factor analysis with varimax rotation were applied after checking factorability with Bartlett's test and the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin measure.
findings: Bartlett's test was significant and KMO was acceptable (0.51 to 0.65) for all sets. About 90% of variance was explained by 3 components in set 1 and 4 in sets 2 and 3, and scree plots suggested retaining 2 factors for sets 1 and 2 and possibly 3 to 4 for set 3. The authors note that the factors appeared to group variables into output-type (velocities and displacements), causal (force and impulse) and timing (time to peak) constructs.
limitations: The three samples are small (16 to 29 per set), use different devices and variable lists (Table 1), and the authors state that component contents may vary with population and time of season. The abstract reports over 90% of variance explained, whereas the results section reports about 90%; this record uses the results values. Sex is stated only for set 1, and health status is not stated for any set.
practicalImplications: Practitioners who collect many CMJ variables can run PCA or factor analysis on their own data to find a smaller set that holds most of the variance. Where interpretability matters, select one variable that correlates strongly with each component and prefer the most reliable option, as the authors suggest. Re-check the structure on the staff's own athletes and devices before fixing a variable set.
athleteDev: Use a reduced set of CMJ variables, one from each independent component, to track changes across training blocks. The paper's example choices (average power, average velocity and peak displacement from set 1) are illustrations from one device and sample, not recommendations. Confirm that the retained variables relate to the demands of the sport, since the paper does not test this.
rtp: Not applicable. The study covers variable reduction for CMJ data and includes no injured athletes and no return-to-sport outcome, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.

citation: Gómez-Carmona CD, Rojas-Valverde D, Ibáñez SJ, Pino-Ortega J. Does the operating temperature of accelerometers affect data measurement during static and dynamic conditions in sports? A randomized-control trial. Proc Inst Mech Eng Part P J Sports Eng Technol. 2023.
abstract: Two operating temperatures were compared for WIMU PRO inertial devices in a static trial and in a 60-minute U-16 soccer session. Internal temperature and resultant acceleration differed early in the sessions, while PlayerLoad did not differ significantly.
tldr: Accelerometers that had not warmed up to their operating temperature gave different acceleration values early in the session (up to about 30 minutes when static and about 13 minutes during play). PlayerLoad totals were not significantly affected in this study.
methods: Ecological design comparing devices switched on at manufacturer's optimal operating temperature (38-39 C) with devices switched on at session start. Static trial in a docking station and dynamic trial in a 60-minute U-16 small-sided game session with 14 male players wearing paired units in a harness at the interscapular level. Internal temperature, resultant acceleration and PlayerLoad (PLRT) were compared with repeated-measures t-tests in 1-minute averages.
findings: Internal temperature differed between the two temperature conditions for the first 31 minutes in the static trial and the first 20 minutes in the dynamic trial. Resultant acceleration differed for the first 29 minutes (static) and, per the results text, the first 13 minutes (dynamic), mostly with small effects during play. PLRT dynamics and accumulated PLRT did not differ significantly (static p = 0.06, d = 0.19; dynamic p = 0.71, d = 0.08), although the environmental-temperature group showed higher values.
limitations: Single device model and manufacturer, with proprietary filtering that prevents analysis of raw data. One session per condition at one environmental temperature (about 28 C), and 14 youth players in the dynamic trial. The procedures state 58 devices while the abstract and group sizes give 56, and the abstract reports dynamic resultant acceleration differences to minute 19 while the results text reports them to minute 13.
practicalImplications: Switch units on well before a session so that they reach the manufacturer's operating temperature, especially for measures that depend on the resultant acceleration vector. Use one standard warm-up protocol across sessions and devices, because the start-up period can bias early-session data.
athleteDev: Performance Application: when comparing training loads across days or devices, check that all units were switched on and stabilized the same way. A mismatch in device warm-up can change early-session acceleration values, though this study found no significant change in PlayerLoad totals.
rtp: This study does not inform return-to-sport decisions. It measured healthy youth soccer players in a training session and did not assess injured athletes, rehabilitation or return-to-play criteria.

citation: Harper DJ, Cohen DD, Rhodes D, Carling C, Kiely J. Drop jump neuromuscular performance qualities associated with maximal horizontal deceleration ability in team sport athletes. European Journal of Sport Science. 2021.
abstract: In 29 university athletes, drop jump (DJ) reactive strength index (RSI) and concentric mean force had the largest correlations with maximal horizontal deceleration (r = -0.54 to -0.61) and the largest differences between high and low deceleration groups (d = 1.20 to 1.40). Eccentric mean force from the 40 cm drop had a much larger difference between groups than at 20 cm (d = 1.11 vs 0.51), which led the authors to suggest DJ RSI as a proxy for deceleration ability and a higher drop height for assessing braking capacity.
tldr: In 29 university team-sport athletes, drop jump reactive strength index was strongly correlated with horizontal deceleration ability, and the authors suggest it as a quick field proxy. Sprint velocity was more strongly related to deceleration than the jump measures, and the cross-sectional design cannot show that training drop jump qualities improves braking.
methods: Cross-sectional study with three test sessions over two weeks. Participants completed drop jumps from 20 and 40 cm on force plates and maximal horizontal deceleration after a 20 m sprint, measured by radar. Pearson or Spearman correlations were used, and high and low deceleration groups were formed by a median split (15 vs 14) and compared with Cohen's d, with 90% confidence intervals.
findings: Drop jump RSI and concentric mean force at both heights had large correlations with average deceleration (r = -0.54 to -0.61) and with early-phase deceleration (r = -0.54 to -0.66), but smaller correlations with late-phase deceleration (r = -0.24 to -0.40). High deceleration players had larger RSI than low players at 20 cm (d = 1.28) and 40 cm (d = 1.20). Approach velocity correlated very strongly with average deceleration (r = -0.76), and the 40 cm eccentric mean force separated groups more clearly than the 20 cm version (d = 1.11 vs 0.51).
limitations: The study is cross-sectional with 29 participants (6 women), tested only in December during the competitive season, and the deceleration measures had moderate-to-good relative reliability (ICC 0.60 to 0.87). The authors note that actual drop height may vary within and between participants and that the findings still need testing in more highly trained athletes and in unanticipated decelerations; the injury-risk links discussed in the paper were not measured. The article reviewed is the accepted author version, so volume, issue and page details are not printed.
practicalImplications: Where radar or other deceleration testing is not available, drop jump RSI may serve as a quick field indicator of deceleration ability, as the authors suggest. Use a 40 cm drop when the aim is to separate players on braking capacity, since eccentric force differed more between groups at that height, and, as the authors recommend, profile deceleration alongside acceleration and top speed.
athleteDev: Use drop jump RSI and 40 cm eccentric force as part of a profile that includes sprint velocity, since the paper links braking ability to reactive strength and eccentric force. The paper does not test whether training these qualities improves deceleration, so treat the links as a basis for monitoring rather than proven training effects.
rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It tested team-sport athletes without recent injury that had kept them from sport in the previous three months, and it did not measure injury or recovery. Its suggested links to injury risk are not tested.

citation: Roe G, Whitehead S, Starling L, Allan D, Cross M, Falvey É, et al. Embracing the impact from instrumented mouthguards (iMGs): a survey of iMG managers' perceptions of staff and player interest into the technology, data and barriers to use. European Journal of Sport Science. 2024;24:670-681.
abstract: Forty-six instrumented mouthguard (iMG) managers from men's and women's rugby union and league completed an 18-question survey on staff and player interest, device use and barriers. Managers perceived medical staff as having the most interest in iMG data and found the devices easy to use but uncomfortable, with comfort, size and fit the main barriers to player use, and time constraints and limited understanding of data as barriers to engagement.
tldr: Rugby instrumented mouthguard managers see medical staff as the most interested group, and they find the devices easy to use but uncomfortable for players. Comfort, fit and inconsistent wear are the main player-side barriers, while time and limited understanding of the data restrict staff use.
methods: Cross-sectional online survey (Google Forms, May to July 2023) of iMG managers in men's and women's rugby union and league, with 46 of 54 eligible managers completing it. The survey had five-point Likert items and open-ended questions, analysed with descriptive Likert charts and inductive thematic analysis following Braun and Clarke's six phases.
findings: Medical staff were the group most often perceived as interested in iMG data (60% to 100% agreement across environments), while most men's league managers and many men's union managers disagreed that coaches or management were interested. Most managers found the devices easy to use on training and match days, but only 20% to 43% agreed that players found them comfortable, while 20% to 50% disagreed. Comfort, size and fit was the most identified barrier to players wearing iMGs, alongside inconsistent use of ordinary mouthguards and perceived negative effects on performance; lack of understanding of the data, time constraints, inconsistent wear and technology issues were barriers to data engagement, and 71% to 80% of managers in women's union, men's union and men's league said the data were rarely or never used for training load management.
limitations: This is a self-reported survey of 46 managers, so the findings describe managers' perceptions rather than measured player comfort, compliance or staff behaviour, and players and other staff were not surveyed. The authors' own survey was checked for content and face validity by discussion only, with no quantitative validation or reliability testing, and several authors are affiliated with World Rugby, which funded the study. The results are not linked to athlete welfare or performance outcomes, which the authors call for in future research.
practicalImplications: Staff introducing iMGs should address comfort, size and fit with players first, since managers named comfort as the most common barrier and inconsistent wear undermines the data. Time pressure and limited understanding of what the data mean were also barriers, so education on how the data can be used should accompany rollout before routine use is expected.
athleteDev: The paper measures technology adoption, not performance outcomes. The authors note that performance staff need to work with coaches to act on iMG data, and coach interest was low in the men's environments, so the data may stay with medical staff unless a shared strategy is agreed.
rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It surveyed practitioners about device use and did not test head acceleration data against injury, symptoms or recovery. Some managers described using iMG data to support graded return to play, but the survey did not test this use.

citation: O'Connor FK, Stern SE, Doering TM, Minett GM, Reaburn PR, Bartlett JD, et al. Effect of Individual Environmental Heat-Stress Variables on Training and Recovery in Professional Team Sport. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2020. Ahead of print.
abstract: Forty-five professional Australian Rules football players were monitored across 579 outdoor training sessions in an 8-week preseason. Solar radiation, relative humidity and ambient temperature were each related to GPS external load, heart rate, RPE, well-being and heart-rate variability using mixed-effects models.
tldr: In heat-acclimatized professional footballers, higher solar radiation was associated with less distance and high-speed running in training, and higher humidity with higher RPE and stress. Higher ambient temperature was associated with more work. Recovery links were weak.
methods: Prospective observational study of 45 male professional Australian Rules football players during an 8-week preseason. Ambient temperature, humidity and solar radiation were measured at each outdoor session. GPS (distance per minute, percentage of distance above 14.4 km/h), heart-rate zones, RPE, well-being and daily rMSSD were analyzed with mixed-effects linear models, with the player as a random effect and standardized coefficients reported.
findings: Solar radiation was associated with lower distance per minute (-19.7 m/min, P < .001) and lower percentage high-speed running (-10.1%, P < .001), and with lower rMSSD 48 hours after training (-16.9 ms, P = .019). Relative humidity was associated with lower high-speed running (-3.4%, P = .010), more time above 85% HRmax (+3.9%, P < .001), higher RPE (+1.8 AU, P < .001), greater body mass loss (-215 g, P < .001) and more stress 24 hours after training (-0.11 AU on the well-being scale, P = .002). Higher ambient temperature was associated with more distance (+19.2 m/min, P < .001) and high-speed running (+3.5%, P = .005), alongside higher mean heart rate (+4.8 bpm, P < .001) and slightly higher RPE (+0.3 AU, P = .019).
limitations: The design is observational, using a convenience sample of heat-acclimatized players from one club in one subtropical preseason, and the authors state they cannot ascribe cause and effect. The abstract gives the temperature effect on distance as 19.7 m/min while the results text gives 19.2 m/min (95% CI 18.0 to 21.4); the results value is reported here. Recovery links were mostly null, and heart-rate variability was measured once each morning with a smartphone application.
practicalImplications: In hot preseason training, staff should record solar radiation and humidity separately, because the study links each to different training outcomes. Use the associations to plan and interpret sessions in the heat, not as fixed thresholds or proven causes of lost work capacity.
athleteDev: The study measures training output in hot outdoor conditions, so it may guide how staff interpret GPS and heart-rate data across different weather. It does not test a training method or show that heat exposure improves performance, though the authors suggest higher temperature may relate to more work.
rtp: The study does not address injury rehabilitation or return to play. It describes training load and recovery in heat-acclimatized squads, so it does not set criteria for clearing players after injury.

citation: Rodríguez-Rosell D, Yáñez-García JM, Mora-Custodio R, Sánchez-Medina L, Ribas-Serna J, González-Badillo JJ. Effect of velocity loss during squat training on neuromuscular performance. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2021;00:1-15.
abstract: Thirty-three young men were randomly assigned to 8 weeks of velocity-based squat training with velocity losses of 10%, 30% or 45% allowed in each set, with identical loads, frequency and rest. All groups improved strength and muscle endurance. The 10% group showed the greatest countermovement jump and sprint improvements, and the authors conclude that a low velocity-loss limit gives similar strength gains with better jump and sprint gains than higher limits.
tldr: In 33 physically active young men training squats twice weekly for 8 weeks, limiting each set to 10% velocity loss gave strength gains similar to 30% and 45% limits with about a third to half the repetitions, and a larger jump gain than the 45% limit. Sprint differences between groups were not statistically confirmed, and the study used one exercise, so it does not show that 10% is optimal for all athletes.
methods: Randomized trial of three 8-week velocity-based squat programs, run twice weekly with 3 sets at 55 to 70% 1RM and 4 minutes of rest, differing only in the velocity loss allowed per set (10%, 30% or 45%). Sets ended when the target loss was reached, using a linear velocity transducer for feedback. Before and after training, participants completed a 20 m sprint, countermovement jump, progressive squat loading (estimated 1RM and load-velocity profile), a squat fatigue test and surface EMG of the vastus lateralis and medialis.
findings: All groups improved estimated 1RM, load-velocity measures and fatigue test performance. The only significant group by time interaction was for countermovement jump, where the 10% group's gain (11.9%, effect size 0.75) was significantly larger than the 45% group's; for 20 m sprint the 10% group improved significantly within group (-2.4% to -3.1% across 10 and 20 m), the 30% group improved at 20 m but not 10 m, and the 45% group did not improve, but no significant interaction was reported. The 10% group completed about 181 repetitions over the program compared with about 348 in the 30% group and 501 in the 45% group, and no EMG variable changed significantly in any group.
limitations: The study had no non-training control group, included only young men who were physically active students, and used one exercise (Smith machine squat), so its scope is limited to these conditions. The Abstract says the 10% group's jump gain was greater than both other groups and that its sprint change was greater, but the Results report a significant between-group difference in jump height only against the 45% group and a significant interaction only for jump. Strength was estimated from a load-velocity equation rather than measured as a direct 1RM, and the surface EMG findings cannot rule out changes in muscles not measured.
practicalImplications: For squat programs in young, moderately trained men, stopping each set at a 10% velocity loss gave similar strength gains to 30% or 45% limits with far fewer repetitions, and a larger jump gain than the 45% limit, in this 8-week study. Velocity monitoring can be used to stop sets at a chosen loss, but the study does not show that 10% is optimal for every athlete or sport, or that it improves sprinting more than higher limits.
athleteDev: Coaches can use a velocity-loss cap, set at 10% in this study, to limit fatigue and repetitions within squat sets while keeping strength gains and supporting jump improvement. The trial measured squat strength, jump and sprint outcomes in non-athletes, not sport-specific performance, and sprint differences between groups were not statistically confirmed.
rtp: The trial used healthy, injury-free young men and did not test rehabilitation or return to sport. It cannot support using velocity-loss limits to guide injury rehabilitation or return-to-play decisions.

citation: Merrigan JJ, Tufano JJ, Falzone M, Jones MT. Effectiveness of Accentuated Eccentric Loading: Contingent on Concentric Load. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2020 (ahead of print).
abstract: Crossover study of 21 resistance-trained men comparing a single accentuated eccentric repetition (120% 1-RM) with traditional loading during back-squat sets at 65% and 80% 1-RM. Eccentric velocity and power were greater after AEL, and the concentric benefit appeared only at the 65% load, where velocity and power were higher in later repetitions.
tldr: In resistance-trained men, one 120% 1-RM eccentric repetition improved later back-squat velocity and power at a 65% 1-RM working load but not at 80% 1-RM. Eccentric power was higher after AEL at both loads, so the concentric benefit depends on the working load.
methods: Four sessions, 48 h apart, in a counterbalanced crossover: AEL65 (3 x 5 at 120%/65% 1-RM), AEL80 (3 x 3 at 120%/80%), TRA65 and TRA80 at matched loads. Weight releasers disengaged after the first eccentric phase; a force plate and four linear position transducers measured kinetics and kinematics, analysed with repeated-measures ANOVA.
findings: At 65%, AEL produced higher eccentric peak velocity (-0.076 m/s, P = .01) and greater eccentric power than TRA65 (eccentric peak power -328.6 W, P < .01), and concentric peak force was 187.8 N higher (95% CI 58.5 to 317.1). Concentric velocity and mean power were higher only in repetitions 3 and 4. At 80%, concentric peak force was 133.8 N higher with AEL and eccentric mean and peak power were greater, but concentric velocity and power did not increase, and concentric mean velocity in repetition 1 was lower.
limitations: Only 21 men, one session per protocol, and lab measures only. The abstract gives P = .01 for the 65% concentric peak force difference, while the Results give P < .01; the Results value is reported here. The Results also show a significant protocol-by-repetition effect for concentric mean power at 80%, but the Discussion states no concentric power increase occurred at 80%; the Discussion statement is reported here.
practicalImplications: A single 120% eccentric overload before 65% 1-RM squat sets was followed by higher velocity and power in later repetitions in this sample, so it may be worth testing in that context. The study found no concentric velocity or power gain at 80% 1-RM, so the same protocol should not be expected to improve heavy sets. At 80% 1-RM the concentric mean velocity of the first repetition was lower after AEL, which the authors attribute to an altered pacing strategy when controlling the weight releasers.
athleteDev: In these resistance-trained men, a single 120% 1-RM eccentric overload improved later back-squat velocity and power at 65% 1-RM but not at 80% 1-RM. Staff should treat the load-dependence as the main finding, since the effects came from one acute session.
rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It tested healthy resistance-trained men in one acute session and included no injured or rehabilitating athletes.

citation: Macchi R, Hegyi A, Giroux C, Rabita G, Nordez A, Hollville E, et al. Effects of Resistance and Speed on Electromyographic Activity of Thigh and Gluteal Muscles in Elite Athletes throughout Resisted Sprint Running. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2025 (published ahead of print).
abstract: Within-session study of 37 elite athletes measuring surface EMG from eight thigh and gluteal muscles during unresisted sprints and sprints against resistance equal to 25% and 75% of body mass. Hamstring activity rose with speed and fell with resistance, the reverse of the quadriceps pattern, and the response differed between hamstring heads.
tldr: In elite track and field, rugby sevens and bobsleigh athletes, hamstring muscle activity rose with running speed and fell with added resistance, while quadriceps showed the opposite pattern. The response differed between hamstring muscles, but the study measured activation in one session and does not show any training benefit.
methods: Each athlete completed two trials of a 40 m unresisted sprint and sprints with robotic resistance equal to 25% and 75% of body mass (sled-equivalent; 25 m and 20 m sprints), with force plates, optoelectronic timing and EMG on eight muscles per leg. Generalized mixed models related EMG to normalised speed in stance and swing phases, statistical parametric mapping tested sprint phase and resistance across the stride, and binomial tests assessed between-athlete consistency.
findings: Hamstring stance-phase EMG rose with speed in the unresisted sprint (+17.9%, P < 0.001) and was lower at higher resistance for all hamstring muscles except short head biceps femoris, while quadriceps showed higher stance activity at higher resistance. Between-athlete consistency for hamstring stance-phase increases with speed was high in unresisted and low-resistance sprints (89% to 100% in Table 2), but fell to 60% to 66% for semimembranosus and semitendinosus at the highest resistance, which was not significantly different from 50%. In the unresisted sprint, biceps femoris long head was the only hamstring head with higher late-swing activity at maximum speed and late acceleration than in early acceleration.
limitations: Surface EMG may include cross-talk and cannot show neural drive directly, and the study used two resistance levels and compared conditions at normalised speed rather than absolute speed. The Discussion states consistent hamstring increases in 90% of athletes, but the Results give a range of 70% to 100% and Table 2 shows 60% to 66% for semimembranosus and semitendinosus at the highest resistance; the Table values are reported here. The authors' suggestion that resisted sprinting could be introduced earlier after hamstring injury was not tested in injured athletes.
practicalImplications: Resisted sprints produced a different muscle activation pattern from unresisted sprints, with relatively more quadriceps and less hamstring activation, so they could be considered for targeting early acceleration. Whether this improves acceleration or lowers hamstring load was not tested. The study's gluteus medius finding is EMG only and does not show that gluteus medius exercises improve sprinting.
athleteDev: Resistance and speed shifted hamstring and quadriceps activity in opposite directions, so the resistance level changes which thigh muscles are most active during a sprint. Whether matching resistance to a given acceleration phase improves performance was not tested; these are single-session EMG patterns.
rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It tested injury-free athletes in one session, and the suggestion that resisted sprinting could be introduced earlier after hamstring injury was not tested.

citation: Uthoff AM, Macadam P, Zois J, Nagahara R, Neville J, Cronin JB. Effects of forearm wearable resistance during accelerated sprints: From a standing start position. J Sports Sci. 2021.
abstract: Fourteen sprint-trained men completed 30 m sprints from a standing two-point start with and without 2 percent body mass of forearm wearable resistance. Sprint time at 10 m and 30 m did not change significantly, but step frequency fell in acceleration phases 2 and 3. The authors conclude that arm loading may provide a sprint-specific overload for two-point starts.
tldr: Adding 2 percent body mass to the forearms did not significantly change 10 m or 30 m sprint time in trained male sprinters, but it lowered step frequency in the early-middle acceleration phases. Whether this helps performance over time was not tested.
methods: Fourteen male track and field athletes completed three 30 m sprints from a standing two-point start over in-ground force plates: one unloaded and two with 2 percent body mass split between both forearms, with the loaded pair done before or after the unloaded trial in randomized order and the faster loaded trial analysed. Step kinematics and kinetics were averaged over four-step blocks from steps 1 to 16 and compared with a 2 x 4 repeated-measures ANOVA, with Cohen's d effect sizes.
findings: Sprint times were not significantly different at 10 m (2.22 versus 2.26 s, effect size -0.32) or 30 m (4.60 versus 4.64 s, effect size -0.24). Step frequency decreased significantly in phase 2 (4.39 to 4.24 Hz, effect size -0.81) and phase 3 (4.44 to 4.28 Hz, effect size -0.86). Contact time, flight time, step length and vertical impulse rose with small to moderate effect sizes, but these were not reported as significant and no kinetic difference was statistically significant.
limitations: This is a single-session, 14-man acute comparison with one unloaded trial and no training outcome, although the authors call it cross-sectional. The abstract reports a significant 3.6 percent step velocity drop in phase 4, but Table 2 shows no significant change (8.85 to 8.80 m/s, effect size -0.16); Table 1 percent-change intervals and several Table 2 contact time intervals exclude zero although the text calls them non-significant, while the starred step frequency effect size intervals include zero. One author is head of research at the garment manufacturer, though the authors state he was blinded from data collection and analysis.
practicalImplications: Forearm loads of about 2 percent body mass did not significantly slow 10 m or 30 m sprint time in these sprint-trained men in one session. The lower step frequency in early and mid acceleration suggests the loads change step mechanics, but this should be treated as a hypothesis to test in a training block before it is used to target specific mechanics.
athleteDev: Forearm wearable resistance at 2 percent body mass changed step frequency and contact and flight times in the first 16 steps without a clear loss of sprint time. Whether repeated training with these loads improves acceleration or sprint performance was not tested.
rtp: The study tested healthy, uninjured male athletes in a single session and does not address rehabilitation or return to sprinting after injury. It cannot be used to guide return-to-play decisions.

citation: Bartolomei S, Rosaci G, Latini D, Nigro F. Effects of horizontally versus vertically loaded resistance exercises on performance and muscle architecture. J Sports Med Phys Fitness. 2024.
abstract: Nineteen resistance-trained adults were randomly assigned to six weeks of horizontally loaded (n = 10) or vertically loaded (n = 9) lower-body training with equal total repetitions. Horizontal training produced larger gains in 1RM hip thrust and standing long jump, while vertical training produced larger gains in 1RM squat and vastus medialis thickness. Countermovement jump showed only a small time effect with no group difference, and 20 m sprint did not change in either group.
tldr: In resistance-trained adults, six weeks of hip-thrust-based training improved hip thrust strength and standing long jump more than squat-based training did, while squat-based training improved squat strength more. Neither program changed sprint time, and the study is too small, short and inconsistently reported to set training priorities.
methods: Nineteen resistance-trained adults were randomly assigned to horizontally loaded (hip thrust, reverse hyperextension, horizontal jumps) or vertically loaded (parallel squat, barbell step-up, countermovement jumps) lower-body programs, four sessions per week for six weeks, with the same upper-body exercises and equal total repetitions. Pre and post measures included 1RM squat and hip thrust, countermovement jump, standing long jump, 20 m sprint, and ultrasound muscle thickness and echo intensity of the vastus lateralis, vastus medialis and gluteus.
findings: Group by time interactions were significant for 1RM squat (P = 0.007), 1RM hip thrust (P = 0.004), standing long jump (P = 0.026) and vastus medialis thickness (P = 0.009). From Table III means, 1RM hip thrust rose 21.0 percent (horizontal) versus 1.8 percent (vertical) and 1RM squat rose 9.0 percent (vertical) versus -0.3 percent (horizontal); the text reports 17.9 versus 5.3 percent and 10.5 versus 0.1 percent. Countermovement jump had only a time main effect (P = 0.047; mean changes about 0.6 to 1.3 cm, below the stated 5.4 cm minimal difference), 20 m sprint did not change, and gluteus thickness rose over time without a group difference.
limitations: The groups were small (9 and 10 analyzed versus 11 per group planned) and the program lasted only six weeks. Text percentages differ from Table III and IV means, the Discussion gives gluteus thickness gains of 14.8 and 18.0 percent while Table IV implies about 14 and 3 percent, the abstract gives p = 0.004 for the standing long jump interaction while Results give P = 0.026, the 1RM squat interaction effect size is 0.998, and some p-values (gluteus echo intensity F = 10.9 with P = 0.050; r = -0.487 with P = 0.004 in 19 people) do not match their statistics. Group characteristics also differ between the abstract and Methods.
practicalImplications: If the goal is hip thrust strength or standing long jump, horizontally loaded exercises may be a useful choice, and squat-based work may suit squat strength and vastus medialis thickness. Neither program improved sprint time, and vertical jump changes were small in both. Given the small sample and reporting errors, these results should be tested in the target athletes before a program is chosen on their basis.
athleteDev: Horizontal lower-body exercises such as hip thrust and reverse hyperextension favored standing long jump and hip thrust strength, while squat and step-up work favored squat strength in this six-week trial in resistance-trained adults. Neither program changed 20 m sprint time, so this study gives no basis for using either to improve sprinting.
rtp: The participants were resistance-trained adults without an injury focus, and the study did not test injured athletes or rehabilitation outcomes. It cannot be used to guide loading after a hamstring, hip or knee injury or return-to-play decisions.

citation: Takarada Y, Sato Y, Ishii N. Effects of resistance exercise combined with vascular occlusion on muscle function in athletes. European Journal of Applied Physiology. 2002;86:308-314.
abstract: Elite rugby players completed 8 weeks of knee extension training at about 50% of 1RM with vascular occlusion (LIO, n = 6), the same load without occlusion (LI, n = 6), or no training (control, n = 5). The LIO group showed larger increases in isokinetic knee extension torque than the other two groups, a 12.3% increase in knee extensor cross-sectional area, and improved fatigue resistance, while the LI group showed no significant strength change.
tldr: In 17 elite rugby players, eight weeks of knee extension at about 50% of 1RM with vascular occlusion increased quadriceps size, strength and fatigue resistance. The same load without occlusion did not increase strength, but the groups were small and not described as randomized.
methods: Seventeen young male rugby players were assigned to LIO (about 50% 1RM with pneumatic thigh compression, mean 196 mmHg), LI (same load and repetitions without compression), or an untrained control group, all with more than 5 years of resistance-training history. Training ran twice weekly for 8 weeks, with four sets per session. Outcomes were isokinetic and isometric knee extension torque, knee extensor cross-sectional area by MRI (LIO only), fatigue indices over 50 contractions at 180 deg/s, and integrated EMG.
findings: Averaged across velocities, strength rose 14.3 +/- 2.0% in LIO and 3.2 +/- 2.3% in LI, with LIO significantly greater at all velocities. Knee extensor cross-sectional area rose 12.3 +/- 0.8% in LIO (p = 0.002), while flexor and femur areas did not change. Fatigue indices fell from 63.7% to 58.7% and from 61.3% to 53.7% after LIO (p = 0.002 for both), with no change in LI or controls. Integrated EMG did not change in either the LIO or control group, and maximal isometric torque per unit area did not change.
limitations: Five or six players per group, with no randomization described, and MRI measured only in the occlusion group. The control group was drawn from the same athlete pool and did not train, so the term 'untrained' refers to no study training. The results rest on one 8-week block of isokinetic and MRI measures, with no sport-specific performance, tendon or injury outcome. The Discussion's mechanisms (metabolic, hormonal, fibre-type) were not measured.
practicalImplications: In highly trained rugby players, twice-weekly low-load knee extension with occlusion increased strength and fatigue resistance where the same load without occlusion did not, and knee extensor size rose in the occlusion group (size was not measured in the other groups). Staff could consider it as a supplement in supervised training, with occlusion pressure monitored as in this study.
athleteDev: In elite rugby players, 8 weeks at about 50% 1RM with occlusion increased isokinetic strength and fatigue resistance more than the same load without occlusion, and knee extensor CSA rose 12.3% in the occlusion group. Size was measured only in the occlusion group, the groups were small, and sport performance was not measured.
rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It tested healthy trained athletes, included no injured participants, and measured no tendon load tolerance or rehabilitation outcome.

citation: Pedersen H, Saeterbakken AH, Vagle M, Fimland MS, Andersen V. Electromyographic Comparison of Flywheel Inertial Leg Curl and Nordic Hamstring Exercise Among Soccer Players. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2020. Ahead of print.
abstract: Fifteen male amateur soccer players performed five repetitions each of the Nordic hamstring exercise (NHE) and the flywheel inertial leg curl (FLC) in a randomised, counterbalanced order. Surface EMG of the biceps femoris and semitendinosus was recorded at three sites and analysed by lower and upper movement phases.
tldr: In amateur male soccer players, the flywheel inertial leg curl produced similar hamstring activation to the Nordic hamstring exercise in the lower eccentric phase and higher activation in the concentric phase. It may be a more individualised option for weaker players, but this is an activation study, not an injury study.
methods: Within-subject crossover design. Each player completed five maximal repetitions of the NHE (bodyweight) and of the FLC (load producing maximal power output), in randomised order. EMG was normalised to maximal voluntary contraction and root mean square values were compared between exercises by phase using paired t tests.
findings: In the lower eccentric phase there were no significant differences between exercises (P = .101 to .826), although activation was non-significantly higher in all sites for the NHE (ES 0.08 to 0.61). In the lower concentric phase the FLC produced higher activation in all sites of the biceps femoris (31% to 52%, P < .001) and the semitendinosus (20% to 35%, P = .001 to .023). The NHE showed higher proximal semitendinosus activation over the whole eccentric movement (23%, P = .016).
limitations: Only male amateur players were studied, so results may not generalise to elite players. Surface EMG is an estimate affected by cross-talk, and the authors note that the lack of significant differences in the lower eccentric phase may reflect limited statistical power with 15 participants. All players used their arms to push off in the NHE concentric phase, the FLC was unilateral on the dominant leg, and injury outcomes were not measured.
practicalImplications: If the goal is high hamstring activation in the concentric phase, the FLC produced clearly higher activation than the NHE. In the lower eccentric phase the two exercises were similar, so the FLC may suit weaker players as a more adjustable eccentric option. The study measured activation only, so it does not show that the FLC reduces hamstring injury.
athleteDev: The FLC load can be individualised to each player's maximal power output, and the authors suggest it may suit weaker players before progression to the NHE. The data show muscle activation, not strength or performance gains.
rtp: The study used healthy amateur players and did not include injured athletes, so it cannot guide return-to-sport loading. It does not show that either exercise reduces re-injury.

citation: Valenzuela PL, Amo C, Sánchez-Martínez G, Torrontegi E, Vázquez-Carrión J, Montalvo Z, et al. Enhancement of Mood but not Performance in Elite Athletes With Transcranial Direct-Current Stimulation. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2019.
abstract: Eight male elite triathletes completed a crossover, counterbalanced, sham-controlled, double-blind test of 20 minutes of anodal tDCS over the motor cortex or sham before an 800-m freestyle swim. Vigor was higher with active tDCS after stimulation and after swimming, while swim time did not differ between conditions (596 s active vs 599 s sham).
tldr: In 8 elite triathletes, one session of anodal tDCS raised self-rated vigor but did not improve 800-m swim time. Treat the mood result as a small-sample signal, not a performance aid.
methods: Eight healthy male triathletes (age 20 years, VO2max 71 mL/kg/min) completed two sessions one week apart, receiving either 20 minutes of active anodal tDCS (2 mA, anode at C3, cathode at Fp2) or sham. An 800-m freestyle swim test followed each session. Brunel Mood Scale, RPE, blood lactate, heart-rate variability and a CNS readiness score were recorded.
findings: Vigor (change from baseline) was higher with active tDCS than sham after stimulation (P = .018, g = 1.14) and after swimming (P = .022, g = 0.98); other mood domains showed no condition effect. Swim time was 596 s with active and 599 s with sham tDCS (P = .346), and peak lactate, RPE, pacing, heart-rate variability and CNS readiness did not differ significantly. Tingling was reported by all 8 athletes in both conditions, with no difference in adverse effects.
limitations: Eight men were studied, which the authors justify by the difficulty of recruiting elite athletes. The study used one stimulation protocol and a cephalic montage, and it did not measure cortical excitability or brain activity. Swim time was compared with a paired t test (P = .346) and with magnitude-based inference ('likely trivial'), and the authors note an extracephalic montage may work differently.
practicalImplications: In this study, one session of anodal tDCS raised self-rated vigor but did not improve 800-m swim time. Any use with athletes needs replication and should not be presented as an ergogenic aid.
athleteDev: A single tDCS session did not improve 800-m swim time in elite male triathletes (596 vs 599 s, P = .346). Its only signal was higher self-rated vigor, so it should not be presented as a performance aid.
rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It tested healthy athletes only and did not assess injury, pain, symptoms or recovery outcomes.

citation: Luders J, Gleadhill S, Garrett J, Bennett H. Enhancing athletic performance with complex contrast training: A Delphi study of elite strength and conditioning coaches. International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching. 2024.
abstract: Thirty-eight elite strength and conditioning coaches completed round one of a three-round Delphi survey on how they prescribe complex contrast training to team sport athletes. Of 139 statements, 31 reached 80% agreement, including use in the preparatory phase, in-season and in power blocks, four sets per pairing, 85-90% 1RM with two repetitions in reserve for the strength exercise, and bodyweight to 30% 1RM for the power exercise.
tldr: Expert coaches agreed on a set of complex contrast training settings for team sport athletes, including four sets, 85-90% 1RM for the strength exercise, and bodyweight to 30% 1RM for the power exercise. These are coaching consensus points, not tested training benefits.
methods: Three-round Delphi survey run in REDCap. Round one used 14 open-ended questions answered by 38 coaches with ASCA level 2 or equivalent accreditation and team sport experience, and the answers were analysed thematically into 139 statements. Rounds two (37 coaches) and three (34 coaches) rated agreement on a 9-point Likert scale, with consensus set at 80% agreement within one three-point band.
findings: Consensus (80% or more) was reached for 31 of 139 statements. Agreed items included use in the late pre-season preparatory phase, in-season and in power blocks, one in-season session per week, four sets per pairing, three or four repetitions at 85-90% 1RM with two repetitions in reserve for the strength exercise, bodyweight to 30% 1RM for the power exercise, and 2-3 minutes of rest from the power exercise back to the strength exercise. Consensus was not reached for general pre-season use (73.5%), rest from strength to power, or sex-specific prescription, and time efficiency and practicality as reasons reached 79%, below the threshold.
limitations: The results are coach opinion (38 at round one, 34 by round three), mostly from Australia and New Zealand, with a mixed sport background. Repetition results are internally inconsistent: Table 2 marks three and four repetitions as consensus for the strength exercise but neither for the power exercise (79.4% and 81.1% unmarked), whereas the Discussion says four power repetitions met consensus and the Conclusions reverse the two. The Discussion also says inter-set rest did not reach consensus while Table 2 marks 2-3 minutes as consensus, and the Abstract presents time efficiency as a reason although it reached only 79%.
practicalImplications: Coaches can use the consensus settings as a starting point: four sets, three or four repetitions at 85-90% 1RM with two repetitions in reserve for the strength exercise, bodyweight to 30% 1RM for the power exercise, and 2-3 minutes of rest back to the strength exercise, used in the preparatory phase, in-season or in power blocks. The study does not show these settings improve performance, so staff should track their own outcomes before relying on them.
athleteDev: Expert coaches agreed on four sets of paired exercises, 85-90% 1RM with two repetitions in reserve for the strength exercise, bodyweight to 30% 1RM for the power exercise, and 2-3 minutes of rest back to the strength exercise, with one session per week in-season. The consensus covers coaching practice, not measured performance gains.
rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It surveyed coaches about training prescription and did not address injury, rehabilitation or return-to-play criteria.

citation: Abade E, Rodrigues Costa A, Parraca JA, Tomas-Carus P, Clemente-Suarez VJ, Gonçalves B. Enhancing team sports performance: a case study of the optimal post-warm-up time window. Sport Sciences for Health. 2024.
abstract: In 19 college athletes, a team-sport warm-up was followed by tests of jump, 20-m sprint and handgrip, plus saliva markers, at 5 and 10 minutes after the warm-up. Jump and sprint improved from pre-warm-up to both time points, while handgrip did not change significantly. Salivary flux fell and alpha-amylase and protein rose, which the authors interpret as sympathetic activation.
tldr: In a single session of 19 college athletes, jump and sprint were better 5 and 10 minutes after a team-sport warm-up than before it. Mean sprint time was best at 5 minutes, but the 5 vs 10 minute difference was not significant and there was no control group.
methods: Single-day repeated-measures design with no control group. Nineteen injury-free college athletes completed a standard team-sport warm-up, then were tested before the warm-up and at 5 and 10 minutes after it. Measures were countermovement jump, 20-m sprint, dominant-hand handgrip and unstimulated saliva flux, alpha-amylase and total protein. Effects were analysed with repeated-measures ANOVA, Bonferroni post hoc tests and Cohen's d.
findings: Countermovement jump rose from 0.35 m pre-warm-up to 0.38 m at 5 minutes and 0.37 m at 10 minutes (F = 8.2, P < .001; small effects), with a trivial 5 vs 10 minute difference. The 20-m sprint improved from 3.83 s to 3.60 s at 5 minutes (large effect) and 3.68 s at 10 minutes (moderate effect); the 0.07 s slowing from 5 to 10 minutes had a 95% CI crossing zero (-0.01 to 0.16) and was not a significant post hoc difference. Handgrip did not change significantly (F = 2.1, P = .14), and salivary flux fell while alpha-amylase and total protein per litre rose, with amylase per mg of protein unchanged.
limitations: There was no control group, so the results cannot show that the warm-up caused the changes rather than time, test order, learning or measurement drift. The Abstract says all three performance measures changed significantly (P < .001), but Table 1 shows handgrip did not (P = .14), and the Results still describe a 'late small increase of ~2 kg'. The saliva markers are used as indicators of sympathetic activity, which the study did not measure directly, and the reported body mass of 6.787 ± 11.57 kg is implausible.
practicalImplications: Jump and sprint were still better than pre-warm-up values 10 minutes after a team-sport warm-up in this group, so a 5 to 10 minute gap before play did not erase the warm-up effect. Because responses varied between athletes and there was no control, check individual timing before changing a routine. The paper's suggestion of a re-warm-up is speculative and was not tested.
athleteDev: In this single-session study, sprint and jump performance were above pre-warm-up levels at both 5 and 10 minutes after a team-sport warm-up. The mean sprint time was slightly slower at 10 than at 5 minutes, but that difference was not significant, so it does not establish a decline.
rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It tested injury-free athletes only, and it did not assess injured athletes, pain or readiness criteria.

citation: Schroeder LH, Tyndall MC, McDaniel AT, Wang Y, Kale JL. Evaluating a 14-week neck strengthening protocol for neuromuscular indicators associated with head and neck trauma. Sports Medicine and Health Science. 2024.
abstract: This pilot study tested whether a 14-week neck-strengthening program using a helmet-mounted device increased isometric neck strength and rate of force development in young adults. The authors report increases in rate of force development in both rotation directions and in isometric strength in cervical extension and left lateral flexion. They suggest the protocol may help reduce traumatic brain injury, but the study did not measure injury outcomes.
tldr: A 14-week helmet-mounted neck program was followed by higher rate of force development on the device in healthy young adults, with less consistent evidence for isometric strength. There was no control group and no concussion outcome, so it cannot show an injury benefit.
methods: Twenty adults consented and 18 (aged 18 to 29 years) completed 14 weeks of staged training on the TopSpin360 device, which uses self-generated centripetal force, in sessions of about 10 to 15 minutes. Isometric neck strength was tested in four directions with a portable tool, and rate of force development and revolutions per minute were measured on the device. Linear models regressed post-program scores on pre-program scores, and mixed models tracked change across sessions.
findings: Rate of force development rose across sessions by 0.132 (clockwise) and 0.137 (counterclockwise) per session (both P < 0.001), and every participant's post value in Tables 5 and 6 exceeded the pre value. The pre-post analyses tested the slope of post on pre: slopes were 2.649 clockwise (one-sided P = 0.010) and 1.913 counterclockwise (one-sided P = 0.034), and the abstract's 4.344 and 5.978 come from the same model with one outlier removed. For isometric strength, slopes were significant for cervical extension (P = 0.010) and left lateral flexion (P = 0.009) but not flexion (P = 0.065) or right lateral flexion (P = 0.702); no mean pre-post change in kilograms is reported.
limitations: There was no control group, training was short, and the small sample was recruited during COVID-19 restrictions with a narrow age range. The analysis regresses post on pre scores, so its slopes and P values describe how pre predicts post rather than the magnitude of change, and the authors interpret slopes as 'times greater'; some P values are one-sided, the abstract values depend on removing one outlier, and residuals were non-normal for right lateral flexion. Participant counts conflict (20 consented and 18 completed in the results, 18 consented in the methods, 19 and 21 in the models), and reference 19 is a patent for the neck assessment tool held by two authors, which the conflict statement does not mention.
practicalImplications: Staff could treat the staged 14-week protocol as an option for building device-measured rate of force development in healthy adults and should test isometric strength before and after with their own data. The study does not show that the protocol reduces concussions or brain injury and should not be presented as injury prevention.
athleteDev: Rate of force development on the device improved over 14 weeks in healthy young adults, while isometric strength evidence was mixed across directions. The study does not measure sport performance or responses to contact.
