rtp: Not applicable to return to sport. Participants were healthy adults without neck or head injury, so the study cannot inform neck rehabilitation, concussion recovery or return-to-play decisions.

citation: Scott BR, Loenneke JP, Slattery KM, Dascombe BJ. Exercise with Blood Flow Restriction: An Updated Evidence-Based Approach for Enhanced Muscular Development. Sports Med. 2014.
abstract: Review of the evidence on blood flow restriction (BFR) combined with low-load resistance exercise, with low-workload aerobic exercise, and at rest. It gives practical guidance on cuff type and width, restrictive pressure, exercise type, load, volume, inter-set rest and training frequency for clinical, healthy and athletic populations.
tldr: Adding BFR to low-load resistance training (about 20 to 40% 1RM) enhances muscle and strength responses, and BFR alone can limit disuse atrophy. The authors give guidance on cuff width, pressure, volume and rest, and note that the pressure guidance needs more study.
methods: Narrative review with practical recommendations. No systematic search method is described. The authors summarize acute and adaptive studies of BFR, then present a summary table of recommendations and a flowchart for clinical, healthy and athletic populations.
findings: BFR combined with low-load resistance exercise enhances hypertrophy and strength, and BFR alone during cast immobilization can attenuate disuse atrophy. Low-workload walking or cycling with BFR gives small but significant gains in muscle size and strength. The summary table recommends wide cuffs for the legs and narrow cuffs for the arms, 50% to 80% of arterial occlusion pressure at rest, 30 to 45 s rest between sets, 50 to 80 repetitions per exercise, and 2 to 4 athletic sessions per week in addition to high-load training.
limitations: The review does not describe a search method, and much of the cited evidence comes from small samples, often of untrained or older participants. Some pressure guidance relies on unpublished laboratory data, the circumference-based pressures have not been tested for training adaptation, and the authors state that the mechanisms are not yet understood. Strength gains after BFR are not larger than muscle size gains, and the Conclusions give 30 to 60 s inter-set rest while Table 1 gives 30 to 45 s.
practicalImplications: Match cuff width to the limb, with wider cuffs for the legs, and set pressure for each limb rather than using one fixed value. Pair low loads (about 20 to 40% 1RM) with short rest (30 to 45 s, cuff kept on) and high total repetitions (50 to 80 per exercise), reducing intensity or lengthening rest rather than cutting set volume when the planned repetitions cannot be completed. Screen for contraindications such as a history of deep-vein thrombosis, pregnancy or varicose veins, and avoid regular training to failure for people new to BFR.
athleteDev: Gives athletes a low-load, lower-mechanical-stress option that the authors suggest should be added to high-load training, not used as the only method. The review notes that strength gains after BFR are closer to hypertrophy than to neural adaptation, so it may not replace heavy strength work for athletic development.
rtp: Relevant to rehabilitation, where the review suggests BFR at rest or with walking or cycling can limit disuse atrophy when high loads are not tolerated, following the four-phase progressive model of Loenneke et al. The review gives no return-to-sport criteria or outcome data showing when an injured athlete is ready to resume high-load training.

citation: Fritzlen JT, Martinez MW. Echocardiography in Athletes: the Ever-Evolving Assessment of Physiology Versus Pathology. Current Cardiology Reports. 2026;28:12.
abstract: This review summarizes the physiologic echocardiographic adaptations seen in athletes and updates the diagnostic criteria for conditions that overlap with exercise-induced cardiac remodeling. It covers apical hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, excessive trabeculation and arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, and it emphasizes comparing these updates with athletic adaptation.
tldr: Athlete echocardiograms need to be read against sport, position, sex, race and training history, because athletic remodeling can mimic cardiomyopathy. Newer criteria for apical hypertrophy, excessive trabeculation and arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy make this comparison more important.
methods: Narrative review, with no search strategy described. The authors summarize established athlete echocardiographic adaptations and recent diagnostic criteria, with figures and cited studies for each chamber, the valves, the coronary arteries and the aorta.
findings: The review describes wall thickness of 13 to 15 mm as a grey zone and says values above 15 mm make secondary causes more likely. It notes that endurance athletes commonly show left and right ventricular dilation, that systolic function usually stays preserved, and that an increase in ejection fraction of 10% or more with exercise has a low likelihood of pathology. It cites a study of 1146 athlete echocardiograms with trabeculation in 18.3% of athletes versus 7.0% of controls.
limitations: The review does not describe how studies were selected, and it does not grade the evidence behind its thresholds. The authors note that there is no exact established cut-off for spherical index, that the accepted strain value varies among vendors, and that there are limited data on whether detraining predictably reverses athletic changes.
practicalImplications: When an athlete's echo shows hypertrophy, dilation or reduced function, clinicians should check sport, sex, race, training history and the pattern of change before deciding it is pathologic. Cardiac MRI or exercise echocardiography may be needed when findings stay unclear.
athleteDev: The review is about cardiac safety and interpretation of echocardiograms, not training prescription or performance outcomes. It can inform how staff interpret cardiac findings in athletes but does not show that any training approach changes performance.
rtp: The review supports careful cardiac evaluation before an athlete is cleared after cardiac findings, including repeat imaging when pathology is suspected. It does not set return-to-play criteria, so it should be used with current sport cardiology guidance.

citation: Knapik JJ, Hoedebecke BL, Rogers GG, Sharp MA, Marshall SW. Effectiveness of Mouthguards for the Prevention of Orofacial Injuries and Concussions in Sports: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Sports Medicine. 2019.
abstract: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 26 studies on whether mouthguards reduce sports-related orofacial injuries and concussions. Orofacial injury risk was about 2.3 times higher in non-users in cohort and questionnaire studies, and the concussion effect was small and not statistically significant.
tldr: Athletes who wore mouthguards had lower orofacial injury risk in pooled cohort and questionnaire studies, though the evidence is of low quality and highly varied. The review found no clear evidence that mouthguards reduce concussion risk.
methods: Systematic review following PRISMA, searching PubMed, Embase and CINAHL to August 2018 for studies with quantitative injury data in sport and exercise groups with mouthguard users and non-users. Risk ratios were pooled with random-effects models for orofacial injury and a fixed-effect model for concussion, with Downs and Black quality scoring, funnel plots, Begg and Mazumdar tests and trim-and-fill analysis.
findings: Cohort and one-group ecological trials of orofacial injury (12) gave a summary risk ratio of 2.33 (95% CI 1.59 to 3.44), and questionnaire studies (11) gave 2.32 (1.04 to 5.13), both favouring mouthguards. Trim-and-fill in the cohort analysis imputed five studies and gave 1.68 (1.14 to 2.47). Concussion in five cohort studies gave 1.25 (0.90 to 1.74), a non-significant difference. Quality scores averaged 49% (range 34% to 68%), with only one randomized study (RR 2.44).
limitations: Heterogeneity was high (I2 88% for cohort and 98% for questionnaire orofacial analyses), and injury definitions, mouthguard types and designs varied widely. Questionnaire studies are prone to recall bias, compliance was reported in fewer than half of cohort studies, and the authors found evidence of publication bias for the concussion analysis.
practicalImplications: Mouthguards are supported for reducing orofacial injury in sports with significant risk, and staff should check that athletes wear them consistently during games and practices. Staff should not present mouthguards as a concussion-prevention measure based on this review.
athleteDev: The review addresses injury prevention, not training or performance outcomes, so it cannot support a performance claim. Its practical relevance is limited to protecting teeth and the mouth during sport.
rtp: The review covers injury prevention, not rehabilitation or return to play. It does not show that mouthguards change concussion recovery or return-to-play timing, so it should not be used to clear an athlete after injury.

citation: Soga T, Nishiumi D, Furusho A, Akiyama K, Hirose N. Effect of Different Slopes of the Lower Leg during the Nordic Hamstring Exercise on Hamstring Electromyography Activity. J Sports Sci Med. 2021;20:216-221.
abstract: Fifteen male volunteers performed the Nordic hamstring exercise (NHE) on lower-leg slopes of 0, 20 and 40 degrees. The 20 and 40 degree slopes increased biceps femoris long head and semitendinosus EMG at 0 to 20 degrees of knee flexion compared with the standard NHE and shifted the break point angle to a lower knee flexion angle. The authors conclude that a steeper slope may be a useful rehabilitation exercise to prevent recurrence of hamstring strain injury.
tldr: In 15 healthy young men, a steeper lower-leg slope during the Nordic hamstring exercise moved the point where control was lost to a shallower knee angle and raised hamstring muscle activity near full extension. The study measured muscle activity only, so it does not show injury or strength benefit.
methods: Crossover laboratory study. Participants performed the NHE on 0, 20 and 40 degree slopes in random order, two repetitions each, after a warm-up. Surface EMG from the biceps femoris long head and semitendinosus was normalized to a prone leg curl maximal voluntary isometric contraction and analyzed across five knee flexion phases from 0 to 50 degrees. The break point angle, where knee extension velocity exceeded 10 degrees per second, was measured from 2D video.
findings: EMG of both muscles was higher on the 20 and 40 degree slopes than on the standard NHE at 0 to 20 degrees of knee flexion (P < 0.05), while at 40 to 50 degrees the 40 degree slope gave much lower EMG than the standard NHE (BFlh 25.9% vs 96.3% MVIC). The break point angle was 57.75 plus or minus 13.28 degrees on the standard NHE, 36.27 plus or minus 9.89 on 20 degrees and 16.26 plus or minus 9.58 on 40 degrees (P < 0.05 for each step). The Discussion says only the 40 degree slope raised the BFlh to ST ratio at lower knee angles, but the Results report a non-significant interaction for that ratio and Table 1 shows the ratio was lower on the 40 degree slope than the standard NHE at 10 to 30 degrees.
limitations: All participants were male, none were described as competitive athletes, and the sample was small (n = 15), so the findings may not transfer to female or sporting groups. The study used one session, did not adjust for other training or sport activity, and measured no injury, recurrence, strength or sprint outcomes. Several reported ANOVA degrees of freedom (for example F(1,26) for the angle factor) do not match a 15-subject, three-condition, five-phase design and no sphericity correction is described, so the exact statistics cannot be confirmed.
practicalImplications: A steeper lower-leg slope (20 to 40 degrees) during the Nordic hamstring exercise can be used to shift hamstring loading toward the near-extended end of the range, where EMG rose, in exchange for less activity at the start of the descent, where the 40 degree slope lowered it. This does not show that the progression lowers injury or recurrence rates.
athleteDev: The slope gives coaches a practical way to increase the load on the hamstrings in the final part of the NHE range without changing the exercise. The study measured muscle activity only, not strength, sprint speed or training adaptation.
rtp: The study recruited uninjured men and did not test athletes with a hamstring injury or track recurrence. The authors suggest a steeper-slope NHE may be a rehabilitation exercise, but the data cannot show that it reduces re-injury or should guide return-to-play decisions.

citation: Loud D, Grimshaw P, Kelso R, Robertson WSP. Effect of Soccer Boot Outsole Configuration on Translational Traction Across Both Natural and Artificial Playing Surfaces. Orthop J Sports Med. 2024;12(8):23259671241259823.
abstract: A custom traction rig tested five soccer boot outsole configurations moving in four directions on natural grass and artificial grass. Longer and asymmetric studs gave significantly higher traction coefficients than the recommended configuration on 75% of natural-grass loading scenarios and 50% of artificial-grass scenarios. The authors conclude that some boots produce higher traction than the recommended configuration and that higher traction could increase foot-fixation and injury risk for players.
tldr: On a bench rig, longer and blade-shaped studs gave higher traction than the recommended boot on natural grass and on some artificial-grass loads, while turf boots gave the least. No players were tested, so the study cannot show that higher traction increases injury risk.
methods: A portable linear rig pulled a footform, fitted with a male US size 9 boot, at 4 m/min under a normal load of 148 N. Five Nike boots (soft-ground, firm-ground circular, firm-ground blade, artificial-grass and turf) were tested on natural grass and third-generation artificial grass at South Australian club pitches, moving in anterior, posterior, medial and lateral directions with 10 repeats per condition. Trials 2 to 10 were analyzed by three-way ANOVA with Tukey comparisons against the firm-ground circular boot (natural grass) or the artificial-grass boot (artificial grass).
findings: Surface type had the largest effect on traction coefficient (partial eta-squared 0.751), followed by outsole configuration (0.644), and artificial grass gave higher traction than natural grass in every movement. Soft-ground or blade studs gave significantly higher traction than the control boot in 3 of 4 directions on natural grass (anterior, medial, lateral) and 2 of 4 on artificial grass (anterior and medial, both soft-ground), while turf boots produced significantly less traction than the control boot for one or both surfaces in every movement. The first trial on each location gave higher traction than later trials, which the authors attribute to root zone or infill disturbance.
limitations: The study used one footform, one boot model per stud type, one slow speed (4 m/min) and one normal load, with no human participants, so it cannot show injury or performance effects. The statistics use trials 2 to 10 only, although the authors cite trial 1 as the peak most relevant to injury, and the normal load is given as 148 N in the Methods and 146 N in the Limitations. Appendix mean differences are expressed as control minus comparison (negative means more traction than the control); Table A2 lists an 'AG' row against the AG control, the Discussion claims higher anterior and posterior traction for blade studs on artificial grass that Table A2 shows as non-significant (P = .502 and .997), and the Discussion says no boot gave significantly more lateral traction while Table A1 shows soft-ground studs did on natural grass (P = .028).
practicalImplications: In this bench test, boot choice changed traction more on some surfaces than others, and turf boots gave the least traction on both surfaces. Coaches and medical staff can use this to discuss stud type by surface, but the study does not show that higher-traction boots cause injuries, so it should not be used to ban or prescribe boots on its own.
athleteDev: The study compares boot traction, not player performance. Its finding that studs with more length or asymmetric shapes give more traction may matter for acceleration, turning and braking, but no player performance was measured.
rtp: The study tested a footform and did not involve injured players, return to play or post-injury function. It cannot inform boot selection or return-to-sport decisions after an ACL or foot injury.

citation: Hu C, Du Z, Tao M, Song Y. Effects of Different Hamstring Eccentric Exercise Programs on Preventing Lower Extremity Injuries: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Int J Environ Res Public Health. 2023;20:2057.
abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis of 23 randomized controlled trials examined hamstring eccentric training programs for preventing lower extremity injury in sport. The authors report that programs reduced lower extremity injuries by 28%, hamstring injuries by 46%, and knee injuries by 34%. Subgroup results suggested the greatest effect with twice-weekly training and with 21-30 weeks of training.
tldr: Across 23 RCTs, programs that included hamstring eccentric exercise reduced lower extremity injuries overall, with the largest reduction for hamstring injuries. The subgroup results on frequency and duration come from few studies and are not firm dosing rules.
methods: Searched PubMed, Web of Science and EMBASE up to 20 August 2022 for RCTs, with 8 of the 23 trials added from other meta-analyses; two reviewers screened and extracted data, and risk of bias was rated with the Cochrane tool. Risk ratios were pooled with a random-effects model when I2 was 50% or more and a fixed-effects model otherwise (used for hip and groin and ankle), with subgroup analyses by exercise method, frequency, period and competition level (PROSPERO CRD42022352757).
findings: The overall pooled risk ratio for lower extremity injury was 0.72 (I2 = 83%), with 0.54 for hamstring, 0.73 for hip and groin, 0.66 for knee and 0.78 for ankle injury. Twice-weekly programs had RR 0.60 (95% CI 0.49-0.72, 5 studies) and once-weekly programs RR 1.00 (2 studies), while the 21-30 week subgroup had RR 0.62 (95% CI 0.38-1.01, 4 studies). Youth (RR 0.75), elite (RR 0.73) and amateur adult (RR 0.54, 2 studies, 271 participants) subgroups all favored the program.
limitations: The authors note high heterogeneity, possible publication bias (Peters test p = 0.28 with slight funnel plot asymmetry), and inability to blind participants and coaches. The abstract and results disagree on the overall sample (14,721 versus 15,049 injury participants), and the overall CI is 0.71-0.80 in the results but 0.60-0.88 in the discussion. Most subgroups have few studies.
practicalImplications: Hamstring eccentric exercise added to warm-up or strength work is supported as part of an injury prevention program for lower extremity injuries in soccer and similar sports. Twice-weekly sessions had the strongest subgroup estimate, but this should be read as a tentative guide given the small number of studies.
athleteDev: Hamstring eccentric exercise can be included in warm-up or strength programs for athletes as an injury prevention measure. The review does not establish a single best frequency or duration, and it does not test performance outcomes.
rtp: This review evaluates injury prevention in uninjured athletes and does not study return to sport after injury. It cannot be used to guide rehabilitation progression or return-to-play decisions.

citation: Romero V, Lahti J, Castaño Zambudio A, Mendiguchia J, Jiménez Reyes P, Morin JB. Effects of Fatigue Induced by Repeated Sprints on Sprint Biomechanics in Football Players: Should We Look at the Group or the Individual? Int J Environ Res Public Health. 2022;19:14643.
abstract: Fifty-one football players completed twelve maximal 30 m sprints with 20 s recovery to test the effects of fatigue on sprint kinetics and kinematics. Kinetic outputs, including maximal power, fell after the protocol, and individual kinematic changes differed widely. Cluster analysis identified five response patterns, with some players in patterns the authors estimate would increase or decrease hamstring length.
tldr: After a repeated-sprint protocol, average sprint power fell in amateur football players, but how each player changed their sprint posture varied widely. The hamstring implications are modeled estimates, not measured strain or injury outcomes.
methods: Fifty-one male amateur football players (sports science students) performed two sets of six 30 m maximal sprints with 20 s active recovery between sprints and 3.5 min between sets. Sprint force and velocity outputs were derived from radar, and touchdown joint angles were digitised from 240 Hz smartphone video of the same leg in the first two and last two sprints. K-means cluster analysis grouped individual kinematic changes, and hamstring length was inferred from these angles.
findings: Theoretical maximal velocity fell by 12.9 percent (effect size -1.99), maximal power by 18.9 percent (effect size -1.56), and 20 m sprint time rose by 9.0 percent. At touchdown, trunk angle (effect size 0.54), ipsilateral knee extension (0.43) and contralateral hip extension (1.16) increased at group level, while ipsilateral hip angle did not change. Five clusters were found, with 20 players in a cluster the authors estimate increases hamstring length and 11 in one they estimate decreases it.
limitations: The study has no control group and no injury outcome, and hamstring length and strain are inferred from 2D sagittal angles rather than measured. Pelvic tilt was not measured directly, only one leg sequence per sprint was analysed, and clusters 3 and 4 contain 1 and 3 players. Some changes are called significant at p = 0.067 and p = 0.072.
practicalImplications: Coaches may consider checking individual sprint posture under repeated-sprint fatigue, because the response to fatigue differed from player to player in this sample. The link to hamstring injury risk is an inference, so these results should not be used as an injury screening cut-off.
athleteDev: Repeated-sprint fatigue reduced maximal velocity and sprint power in amateur football players, and the kinematic response varied between players. Individual sprint kinematics under fatigue may help show how a player's running technique changes, but this study does not show that changing it improves performance.
rtp: The study tested uninjured amateur players in one fatigue session and did not study injured athletes or return to sport. It cannot be used to decide readiness to return to sprinting after a hamstring injury.

citation: Sugiura Y, Sakuma K, Fujita S, Aoki K, Takazawa Y. Effects of Various Numbers of Runs on the Success of Hamstring Injury Prevention Program in Sprinters. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. 2022;19:9375.
abstract: This study examined hamstring injuries in 613 collegiate male sprinters over 24 seasons, comparing high-volume submaximal and maximal running with low-volume supramaximal tow running. Injuries during supramaximal running fell significantly across three periods, while injuries during submaximal and maximal running did not decline.
tldr: In one collegiate sprint team over 24 seasons, hamstring injuries during low-volume supramaximal tow runs fell as the prevention program evolved. Injuries during high-volume submaximal and maximal running did not fall, and the historical design cannot separate the run count from the program changes.
methods: Historical records from one university sprint team coached by the same coach (613 male sprinters aged 18 to 24, 24 seasons) were divided into three periods of differing prevention programs. Hamstring injury was diagnosed by the team physician and defined as one that kept the athlete from training or competition for at least one week. Injury rates in each period were compared with chi-square tests, separately for supramaximal running (2 to 5 runs per day, 15 to 25 days per season) and for submaximal and maximal running.
findings: Supramaximal-run injury rates were 137.9 in Period I, 60.6 in Period II and 6.7 in Period III, a significant decline (chi-square = 31.78, p < 0.01). Submaximal and maximal-run rates were 103.4, 131.3 and 183.9, with no significant change (chi-square = 5.15, p = 0.07). Period I used only concentric leg curls, Period II added agility drills and a concentric hip extension machine, and Period III added Nordic hamstring and glute-ham raise exercises and dynamic stretching.
limitations: One team, no control group, and a non-randomized period comparison in which the prevention program changed alongside the run structure; the periods also differed in length (4, 8 and 12 seasons). The rates are labelled per athlete-season in the Results but values above 1 are impossible on that scale, and the Methods also describe incidence per 1000 sprinters, so the true denominator is unclear. The reported effect size of ES(w) = 19.09 is not a valid Cohen's w, and the Abstract's claim that a small number of runs works by limiting muscle fatigue is untested because fatigue was not measured.
practicalImplications: This team limited supramaximal tow runs to 2 to 5 per day and at most 50 per season (actual 20 to 30), scheduled after a day off, alongside a program that eventually included Nordic and glute-ham work, and injuries during tow runs fell over time. Because the program changed in the same periods, the data cannot show that the run cap itself prevented injuries, and injuries during high-volume usual sprint training did not fall.
athleteDev: In one collegiate sprint team, low-volume supramaximal tow runs combined with an evolving hamstring program were followed by fewer hamstring injuries, while high-volume submaximal and maximal running was not. These are observational training-period data, not a controlled test of performance outcomes.
rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It counted injuries in training sprinters and included no rehabilitation, recovery or return-to-play outcome.

citation: Ivanic B, Cronström A, Johansson K, Ageberg E. Efficacy of exercise interventions on prevention of sport-related concussion and related outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Br J Sports Med. 2024.
abstract: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 26 articles (RCTs, cluster RCTs and quasi-experimental studies) on exercise interventions and sport-related concussion outcomes, searched to 26 June 2023. Outcomes were concussion incidence, linear and rotational head acceleration and isometric neck strength, and reporting completeness was scored with the CERT.
tldr: Neck resistance training clearly increased isometric neck strength, but no included study tested its effect on concussion incidence. Neuromuscular warm-up programmes did not significantly reduce concussion incidence in the pooled data.
methods: PRISMA-guided review of six databases (PROSPERO CRD42023435033). Risk of bias was assessed with RoB 2, reporting completeness with CERT, and random-effects meta-analyses were run where two or more articles reported the same outcome.
findings: Neuromuscular warm-up programmes had a non-significant effect on concussion incidence (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.39 to 1.23; 3 articles, 4466 participants; low-quality evidence). Resistance training had a large effect on isometric neck strength (SMD 0.85, 95% CI 0.57 to 1.13; 20 articles; high-quality evidence), with non-significant effects on linear (SMD -0.43) and rotational (SMD 0.08) head acceleration.
limitations: Participants were 96% male and most athlete studies involved rugby, soccer or American football, and 6 of 26 articles enrolled non-athletes, so results may not generalise to women, other sports or all athlete groups. Half the articles had a high risk of bias, heterogeneity was moderate to substantial, and reporting completeness was low (median CERT score 11.5 of 19), which limits replication. RoB 2 was applied to quasi-experimental designs, and only English-language articles were included.
practicalImplications: Neck resistance training can raise isometric neck strength, so it can be included in programming for that goal. Staff should not present these strength gains as proof of concussion prevention, because the review did not measure concussion incidence after resistance training.
athleteDev: Dynamic and multimodal neck resistance programmes showed larger pooled effects on isometric neck strength than static programmes, and effects were larger in males and adults than in females and adolescents, although the authors attribute the subgroup gaps partly to unequal representation and differing prescriptions. These are strength outcomes, not performance outcomes.
rtp: Studies excluded athletes with current acute or chronic neck or head injuries, so the review cannot inform return-to-sport decisions after concussion or neck injury.

citation: Sebyani M, Minoonejad H, Shirzad E, Alizadeh MH, Sarvestan J. Electromyography activity of posterior oblique sling muscles during high-speed running in elite soccer players: risk factors for hamstring injury. BMC Sports Sci Med Rehabil. 2025. Article in press.
abstract: Twenty-four male soccer players were grouped by the timing of muscle activation during the prone hip extension test. Surface EMG of the gluteus maximus, hamstrings and contralateral lumbar erector spinae was recorded during treadmill running at 20 km/h, and time-series analysis compared the groups across the running cycle.
tldr: Players whose lumbar erector spinae fired before the gluteus maximus or hamstrings on a prone hip extension test showed different muscle activity patterns while running at 20 km/h. This is a laboratory pattern study and does not show that the pattern causes hamstring injury.
methods: Cross-sectional design. Players with no lower limb or back injury in the previous 24 months and no range of motion limitation were grouped by PHE pattern. Four EMG channels were recorded during two bouts of 30 strides; 20 cycles per player were averaged, normalised to MVIC, and compared between groups across 101 points using statistical parametric mapping (independent t tests).
findings: The delayed group had higher gluteus maximus activity at 55-62% of the running cycle (P < .001), while the non-delayed group was higher at 7-10% (P = .036). Biceps femoris activity was higher in the delayed group at 0-15% and 95-100% and higher in the non-delayed group at 45-62%. Semitendinosus activity was higher in the delayed group at 45-70% and in the non-delayed group at 95-100%, and lumbar erector spinae activity did not differ between groups.
limitations: The methods describe the sample as collegiate players, although the title and abstract say elite. The design is cross-sectional with no injury follow-up, so the pattern cannot be linked to injury, and effect sizes are reported only as thresholds (for example d>0.14). Running was at a constant 20 km/h on a treadmill, not during acceleration or overground running, which the authors note as a limitation.
practicalImplications: The prone hip extension test separated players with different running muscle activity patterns, but the study did not validate it as an injury screening tool. It tested no intervention, so the bridging, bird-dog and reactive training exercises proposed in its conclusion remain untested here.
athleteDev: The study gives no training prescription and no evidence that retraining this pattern improves running mechanics or performance. Use the test result as a discussion point, not a training target.
rtp: The players were healthy, with no hamstring injury in the previous 24 months, so the study cannot guide return-to-sport decisions. It does not show whether the pattern changes after hamstring injury or whether retraining it reduces re-injury.

citation: Krzywański J, Mikulski T, Krysztofiak H, Pokrywka A, Młyńczak M, Małek ŁA, et al. Elite athletes with COVID-19 - predictors of the course of disease. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2021. Pre-proof.
abstract: Observational screening of 111 RT-PCR-confirmed COVID-19 athletes from Polish national teams, examined 12 to 68 days after diagnosis with physical examination, resting ECG, blood tests and SARS-CoV-2 antibody assays. Symptom severity, asymptomatic status and antibody response were compared with age, sex, sport discipline and symptoms.
tldr: Most elite athletes with COVID-19 had mild or no symptoms, and 88% had detectable antibodies at screening. Asymptomatic athletes were younger and more often female, but the study had no control group and screening timing varied, so it cannot settle return-to-sport safety.
methods: Observational study. Between July and October 2020, 111 of 1425 screened national-team athletes were RT-PCR positive and were included. Screening took place 12 to 68 days after diagnosis and included examination, resting ECG, blood counts, CRP, high-sensitivity troponin T, a SARS-CoV-2 antibody assay and 25(OH)D. Comparisons used Wilcoxon, Kruskal-Wallis, correlation and chi-squared tests.
findings: Symptoms were reported by 84% (mild in 82%, moderate in 2%), and 16% were asymptomatic. Asymptomatic athletes were younger (18.5 vs 23.2 years, P < .001) and a larger share of females than males were asymptomatic (23.7% vs 7.7%, P < .05). At screening, 18% still reported symptoms; 9 had cardiac MR or chest CT for clinical reasons, cardiac MR showed no active myocarditis, and one CT showed pneumonia. Antibody response was found in 88%, and COI correlated with time since diagnosis (P < .001), fever, fatigue and conjunctivitis.
limitations: The study is retrospective and observational, without a non-athletic control group. Examination timing was long and unequal (median 20 days, range 12 to 68), screening was voluntary, and the sport groups were not similar in size. Cardiac MR was done only in symptomatic athletes with clinical indications, so cardiac involvement in the others was not assessed.
practicalImplications: Post-COVID screening can identify persisting symptoms, and antibody testing indicated past infection in most athletes. Because one in six infected athletes had no symptoms, staff should not assume that a lack of symptoms means no infection. The study does not show that heart screening can be skipped, since it was not designed to test that.
athleteDev: The study gives no training prescription. It reports that 18% of athletes still had symptoms at a median of 20 days after diagnosis, including 3% with subjectively decreased exercise tolerance.
rtp: The study describes post-COVID screening findings but had no control group, did not follow athletes after return, and did not test a return-to-play protocol. Its conclusions that athletes can return after two symptom-free weeks and that heart screening is usually not required go beyond the data and should not be used as a clearance rule.

citation: Vasireddi N, Hahamyan H, Salata MJ, Karns M, Calcei JG, Voos JE, et al. Emerging Use of BPC-157 in Orthopaedic Sports Medicine: A Systematic Review. HSS Journal. 2025.
abstract: Systematic review of English-language literature from database inception to 3 June 2024 on BPC-157 and its mechanism, musculoskeletal effects, metabolism and safety. Thirty-six studies were included: 35 preclinical and one clinical.
tldr: BPC-157 improved healing outcomes in animal muscle, tendon, ligament and bone models, but there is almost no human evidence. Because products are unregulated and human safety is unknown, clinicians should counsel athletes with caution and ask about supplement use.
methods: Systematic review per PRISMA of PubMed, Embase and Cochrane, with PROSPERO searched for current reviews. Two reviewers screened in three phases, with consensus and a third author for disagreements. Data were extracted and grouped by mechanism, musculoskeletal outcome, metabolism and safety. A meta-analysis was not possible.
findings: Fourteen studies measured musculoskeletal outcomes, mostly in rats with one rabbit model, cultured cells and one human series. BPC-157 improved muscle, tendon, ligament and bone structure, biomechanics and function in those models. In the single clinical study, 7 of 12 patients with unspecified chronic knee pain reported subjective improvement for more than six months after intra-articular injection. Animal safety studies up to 6 weeks showed no acute toxicity, no human safety data were found, and urinary metabolites were detectable for 4 days in one study and 5 days in another.
limitations: Heterogeneity in design and outcomes prevented a quantitative meta-analysis. The evidence is level IV and V and mainly preclinical, the one clinical study is a 12-patient retrospective series, and the only registered trial has had unknown status since 2016. The text is internally inconsistent: it gives 15 and 14 musculoskeletal-outcome studies and 4 and 3 safety studies, and its conclusion says detection up to 4 days although one included study reported 5 days.
practicalImplications: Clinicians who see athletes using BPC-157 should ask directly about peptides and supplements, because product quality is unregulated. Athletes should be told the substance is not approved, may be contaminated, and may be banned by their sport. The review does not support recommending it as treatment.
athleteDev: The review does not support a performance or healing protocol. BPC-157 is specifically banned by WADA, the NFL and the UFC and falls under non-specific peptide bans in other organisations including the NCAA, and products are unregulated for quality.
rtp: No clinical return-to-sport outcomes were studied, and no human safety data were found. The review cannot guide the use of BPC-157 in return to sport after musculoskeletal injury.

citation: Lemme NJ, Li NY, DeFroda SF, Kleiner J, Owens BD. Epidemiology of Achilles Tendon Ruptures in the United States: Athletic and Nonathletic Injuries From 2012 to 2016. Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2018;6(11):2325967118808238.
abstract: Using emergency department data from the NEISS database for 2012 to 2016 with national weights, this study estimated Achilles tendon rupture incidence in the US. The overall rate was 2.1 per 100,000 person-years, rising from 1.8 to 2.5; men had 3.5 times the rate of women, and 81.9% of ruptures were sport or recreational, most often in basketball.
tldr: In US emergency department data, Achilles tendon rupture rates rose from 1.8 to 2.5 per 100,000 per year between 2012 and 2016. Most cases were men, 81.9% happened in sport or recreation, and the largest rise in rate was in people aged 40 to 59.
methods: Retrospective analysis of NEISS emergency department records for lower-leg tendon or muscle ruptures coded from 2012 to 2016, with narratives reviewed to keep clear Achilles ruptures (854 of 5,564 cases; national estimate 32,906). Incidence per 100,000 person-years used US Census denominators with NEISS weights, and group comparisons used incidence rate ratios, ANOVA, chi-square and Bonferroni-adjusted post hoc tests.
findings: Incidence rose from 1.8 per 100,000 person-years in 2012 to 2.5 in 2016 (P < .01), with an overall rate of 2.1. Men had 3.2 and women 0.9 per 100,000 (IRR 3.5). The highest rate was in men aged 20 to 39 (5.6 per 100,000), and the largest rise was in those aged 40 to 59 (78%, from 2.0 to 3.5). Sport or recreation caused 81.9% of ruptures, and basketball was the most common sport-related cause (42.6%).
limitations: Only emergency visits were captured, so true incidence is likely higher, and diagnoses could not be confirmed from the narratives. Race was missing for 30.5% and location for 37% of cases, and BMI and level of play were not recorded. The Results give basketball's 42.6% as a share of sport-related ruptures, while the Discussion gives the same figure as a share of all ruptures; Table 1 counts suggest about a third of all ruptures were basketball-related.
practicalImplications: Staff can use the age, sex and sport pattern to prioritise Achilles injury-risk discussions for men aged 20 to 39, especially in basketball, and to note the rising rate in people aged 40 to 59. The study does not show that any prevention strategy reduces ruptures.
athleteDev: Injury-risk discussions can focus on men aged 20 to 39 in basketball, the group with the highest rate, and on people aged 40 to 59, where the rate rose most. The data come from the general population and cannot show which training loads or exposures cause ruptures.
rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It reports incidence and mechanism from emergency visits, and the return-to-play figures cited in its discussion come from other studies, not its own data.

citation: Prien A, Grafe A, Rössler R, Junge A, Verhagen E. Epidemiology of Head Injuries Focusing on Concussions in Team Contact Sports: A Systematic Review. Sports Medicine. 2018.
abstract: Prospective cohort studies of concussion in elite football, rugby union, ice hockey and American football were reviewed through June 2016; 70 were included and 47 pooled. Pooled match rates were highest in men's rugby, training rates were consistently far lower than match rates, and pooled rates were higher in women's than men's football and ice hockey.
tldr: In these elite contact sports, concussions were far more common in matches than in training, and highest in men's rugby. Data from women are thin, so the sex comparison is tentative.
methods: Systematic review and meta-analysis following MOOSE guidance. Four databases were searched for English-language prospective cohort studies of concussion incidence in players aged 17 years or older at national level or above, published from 2000 to June 2016. Quality was rated on a 20-point scale, and 47 studies were pooled with inverse-variance fixed-effects models for match and training rates per 1,000 hours or athletic exposures.
findings: Of 70 included studies, 47 were pooled. Pooled match rates were 3.89 per 1,000 hours in men's rugby (95% CI 3.51 to 4.28), 0.44 per 1,000 hours in men's football (0.36 to 0.53), and 2.52 per 1,000 athletic exposures in men's American football. Training rates were far lower (for example 0.01 per 1,000 hours in men's football), though the highest pooled training rate per 1,000 hours was in women's football (0.13). Pooled match rates were higher in women's football (1.76 vs 0.44 per 1,000 hours) and women's ice hockey (2.27 vs 1.63 per 1,000 athletic exposures), but these comparisons draw on different studies.
limitations: Heterogeneity was high (I-squared up to 98%) yet a fixed-effects model was used, low-quality studies were kept in the meta-analysis, and time-loss and medical-attention definitions were treated as equivalent. The Abstract states female players had higher concussion risk in ice hockey, but individual ice hockey studies were inconsistent (two found higher male match rates, one higher female) and no consistent sex difference was found for all head injuries. The stated total exposure of 92,715 hours is far below the hours summed in Table 3, the pooled men's rugby training rate rests mainly on one study, and older studies may inflate rates.
practicalImplications: Staff can use the match-versus-training gap to justify concussion surveillance in training as well as matches. The authors recommend weekly training data collection, a concussion-specific definition and a standard diagnostic procedure. The pooled rates are averages across heterogeneous studies, so they should not be used as a squad's own risk estimate.
athleteDev: Training concussions were far rarer than match concussions, but the authors say this may partly reflect less diagnosis during training, so training should not be assumed to be low-risk. Pooled rates should be used as context, not as a squad-specific prediction.
rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It estimates how often concussions occur and does not report recovery times, return-to-play decisions or rehabilitation outcomes.

citation: Quintana-Cepedal M, Maniar N, del Valle Soto M, Crespo I, Olmedillas H. Epidemiology of hip and groin injuries in sport: a systematic review with meta-analysis and meta-regression of 5914 injuries from over 9 million exposure hours. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2026.
abstract: Seventy-one prospective studies with 5,914 hip and groin injuries over more than 9 million exposure hours were pooled. The incidence was 0.71 per 1,000 hours, 11% of all injuries, and was higher in competition than in training and in older cohorts; male athletes had higher rates than female athletes; adductor-related injuries were the most common clinical entity.
tldr: Hip and groin injuries occur at about 0.7 per 1,000 hours of exposure, around 11% of all injuries in these sports. Competition carries about 6.5 times the rate of training, mostly in soccer data.
methods: Systematic review and meta-analysis following PRISMA, registered on PROSPERO (CRD42024573833). Six databases were searched to 14 September 2024 for prospective studies of competitive athletes reporting hip and groin injury incidence, burden, prevalence or proportion of all injuries. Random-effects multilevel models were run in R (metafor), with meta-regression on age, sex, anthropometrics, year, scenario and level, plus sensitivity analyses for small-study bias and reporting quality.
findings: Across 71 studies, the pooled incidence was 0.71 per 1,000 exposure hours (95% CI 0.59 to 0.86; 5,914 injuries). Adductor-related injuries had an incidence of 0.41 per 1,000 hours, and the injury burden for all hip and groin injuries was 11.5 days lost per 1,000 hours. Hip and groin injuries made up 11% of all injuries (95% CI 10% to 13%), and seasonal prevalence was 19% (95% CI 5% to 40%, 12 effect sizes). Incidence was 2.47 per 1,000 hours in competition vs 0.38 in training, rose by about 5% for each year of mean cohort age (P = .046), did not differ between elite and amateur cohorts (P = .89), and was 0.87 per 1,000 hours in male vs 0.47 in female athletes (rate ratio 1.8).
limitations: Most cohorts were soccer and 68% of effect sizes came from male-only studies, so the results may not transfer to other sports or to women. Small-study bias was detected, and the Results label the sex moderator as proportion of male athletes although its negative coefficient (-0.6) matches the female proportion shown in Figure 3f. Body mass (P = .004) and height (P = .024) were significant moderators in unadjusted meta-regression; the Abstract reports only the age-adjusted nulls (P = .52 and P = .87) without saying they are adjusted, and the Conclusions' statement that rates 'have not declined over the past 30 years' rests on a non-significant year effect (P = .127).
practicalImplications: Staff can plan for hip and groin injuries as a frequent and burdensome problem, since they made up 11% of injuries and 11.5 lost days per 1,000 hours. Competition carried about 6.5 times the training rate, and adductor-related injuries were the largest clinical group, which the authors use to support adductor strength work. The study does not test any prevention or screening programme, so the authors' call for routine groin-symptom screening remains untested.
athleteDev: Hip and groin injuries cost about 11.5 days per 1,000 hours of exposure, so they matter for availability. Competition carried a much higher rate than training, and the pooled data show higher rates in older athletes and in male athletes (0.87 vs 0.47 per 1,000 hours).
rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It reports incidence, burden, prevalence and the share of all injuries, and it does not report recovery times, return-to-play decisions or rehabilitation outcomes.

citation: Hardin S, Silverman R, Brophy R, Putukian M, Silvers-Granelli H. Epidemiology of Injury and Illness in North American Professional Men's Soccer: Comparing COVID-19 Lockdown With Previous Seasons. Sports Health. 2024.
abstract: This retrospective cohort study compared injuries and illnesses in Major League Soccer players during the 2020 COVID-19 season with the 2018 and 2019 seasons. Injury incidence rose to 10.8 per 1000 hours in 2020 from 5.4 and 5.0, with increases in training injuries, lower extremity muscle injuries, ACL injuries and concussions. The authors note the design cannot establish causation.
tldr: Injury rates in Major League Soccer roughly doubled in the 2020 COVID-19 season, driven by training injuries, muscle injuries, ACL injuries and concussions. Injured players also missed more time. Treat this as a warning about the period after a training stoppage, not as proof of what caused the increase.
methods: Club medical staff recorded time-loss injuries, illnesses and athletic exposure in a league-wide electronic medical record system. Incidence per 1000 hours was compared across the 2018, 2019 and 2020 seasons, and severity was measured as days missed. Exposure hours were calculated from rostered players and average weekly training time.
findings: Total injury incidence was 10.8 per 1000 hours in 2020 versus 5.4 (2018) and 5.0 (2019). Training injury incidence rose to 8.9 from 2.5 and 2.6, while match injury incidence fell to 18.3 from 24.0 and 22.7. Lower extremity muscle injuries (6.04 vs 2.50 and 2.36), ACL injuries (0.17 vs 0.07 and 0.05) and concussions (0.49 vs 0.27 and 0.22) per 1000 hours were higher in 2020. Non-COVID-19 illness was 3.93 per 1000 hours in 2020 versus 1.53 and 1.32.
limitations: The design was retrospective, so causality cannot be established. Exposure hours were estimated from roster size and average weekly training and game time reported by each club, reporting depended on individual club staff, and the authors did not account for COVID-19 exposure or infection, opt-outs, or increased illness screening in 2020. The data come from one league, the study received partial funding from Major League Soccer, and two authors report ties to the league.
practicalImplications: Plan closer monitoring of muscle, ACL and concussion risk during and after a league training stoppage. The paper suggests this period can carry a higher injury burden, but it does not test which return-to-training plan reduces that risk.
athleteDev: The study links a period of reduced training exposure with a higher training injury rate and more severe injuries. It does not identify the training loads or ramp rates that would prevent these injuries.
rtp: Supports closer attention to muscle injury, ACL and concussion risk after a stoppage, and to longer time loss. It cannot be used for individual return-to-play decisions, clearance criteria or timelines for a single athlete.

citation: Trojan JD, Meyer LE, Edgar CM, Brown SM, Mulcahey MK. Epidemiology of Shoulder Instability Injuries in Collision Collegiate Sports From 2009 to 2014. Arthroscopy: The Journal of Arthroscopic and Related Surgery. 2020;36(1):36-43.
abstract: This retrospective cohort study used NCAA Injury Surveillance Program data to describe shoulder instability injuries in collegiate collision sports from 2009-2010 to 2013-2014. Anterior subluxation was the most common type, contact with another player caused most injuries, and surgery and time loss differed by NCAA division. Male ice hockey and lacrosse players had a higher rate than female players, with the combined comparison reaching significance.
tldr: Shoulder instability in collegiate collision sports is mostly anterior subluxation caused by player contact. Nearly 30% of these injuries needed surgery, and time loss and surgery rates differed by NCAA division. Use these figures as broad benchmarks, since they are averages from a surveillance database.
methods: Athletic trainers at voluntarily participating schools reported time-loss and non-time-loss shoulder instability injuries and athlete-exposures to the NCAA Injury Surveillance Program. Incidence per 100,000 athlete-exposures was calculated for the four men's collision sports, practice and competition rates were compared with injury proportion ratios, men's and women's ice hockey and lacrosse were compared with rate ratios, and time loss and surgery were compared across divisions.
findings: Among 445 injuries in men's collision sports over 1,421,561 athlete-exposures, the rate was 31.30 per 100,000 (95% CI 28.40-34.21). Subluxation was 59.1% of injuries and anterior subluxation the most common type (35.3%); 80.8% of contact injuries involved contact with another player. Competition carried a higher rate than practice (IPR 4.43, 95% CI 3.66-5.35), 29.3% of injuries with known status required surgery, and time loss (Division I 4.77, II 20.52, III 11.23 days; P = .01) and surgery rates (32.9%, 38.1%, 19.4%; P = .04) differed by division. Men's ice hockey and lacrosse combined had a rate ratio of 2.17 versus the women's sports (95% CI 1.04-4.50), but neither sport alone was significant.
limitations: Diagnoses were recorded by athletic trainers or physicians and were not standardized or validated, and some data were submitted incompletely, leaving time loss unknown for 106 injuries. The database lacks demographic and treatment detail and long-term follow-up after college, so recurrence is likely underestimated. Women's sports and some divisions had few injuries, and the Table 1 total row appears to swap the competition and practice counts relative to the sport rows and text (264 practice injuries).
practicalImplications: Expect contact with another player to account for most shoulder instability injuries in these sports, and plan for surgery in a substantial minority of cases. Division-level differences in time loss and surgery mean that benchmarks from one competition level should not be applied directly to another.
athleteDev: Competition carried about four times the shoulder instability injury rate of practice in these sports (IPR 4.43). Load and contact planning for competition can therefore be a focus for collision athletes, though the study does not test any specific training or rule intervention.
rtp: Indicates that time-loss shoulder instability injuries averaged about 18 days missed, dislocations about 18 days, and about 35% of injuries were recurrent, which is relevant when estimating expected time loss. It cannot be used to set return-to-play criteria, since it does not measure strength, function or readiness after treatment.

citation: Turnbull MR, Gallo T, Carter HE, Drew M, Toohey LA, Waddington G. Estimating the cost of sports injuries: a scoping review. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2024.
abstract: This scoping review describes the methods used to estimate the cost of sports injuries in 31 studies published from 2000 to 2023. Most studies used bottom-up costing and reported a lack of explicit detail on costing method and on who bears the cost. The authors conclude that the field lacks methodological guidance and recommend applying a cost-of-illness checklist to sports injury studies.
tldr: Studies of sports injury cost use a wide range of injury definitions, cost types and costing methods, and most do not state their perspective. Read any single cost figure with its method in mind, because the same injury can be costed very differently.
methods: Scopus, MEDLINE and CINAHL were searched for 2000 to 2023 using cost, injury and sport terms. Two reviewers screened titles, abstracts and full texts independently, and data were charted on design, sport, injury definition, cost type, costing approach and perspective. The protocol was registered with the Open Science Framework. Results were synthesized narratively.
findings: Of 31 included studies, 12 examined direct costs, 10 indirect costs and 9 both. Twenty-one (68%) used a bottom-up approach, and seven (23%) used a top-down approach to estimate indirect salary cost from public salary data. Ten studies (32%) were classed by the review team as taking a sporting-organization perspective, but only one study explicitly stated its perspective. Only 10 studies (32%) reported a diagnostic coding system, and three did not clearly specify the injury diagnosis.
limitations: The authors note that costing approach and perspective were mostly inferred by the review team because studies did not state them. The review covers injuries only, excludes illness, and does not appraise study quality or risk of bias. The search began in 2000, which the authors justify by the recency of the topic.
practicalImplications: When reading or quoting a sports injury cost estimate, check the injury definition, which costs were counted, the costing approach and the perspective, since these change the result. Salary-based estimates from public data can over- or under-state the true cost of a player's absence.
athleteDev: Cost estimates for time-loss injuries can help a sports organization weigh the value of prevention, but salary-based figures depend on the team's salary and replacement assumptions. The review does not evaluate any prevention program, so it cannot show which programs are cost-effective.
rtp: Not applicable to return to sport. The review addresses how injury costs are estimated and does not study rehabilitation, clearance or return-to-play decisions.

citation: Thompson K, Kwon Y, Flatow E, Jazrawi L, Strauss E, Alaia M. Everything pectoralis major: from repair to transfer. Physician Sportsmed. 2020;48(1):33-45.
abstract: Review of pectoralis major rupture covering anatomy, evaluation, classification, nonoperative care, acute and chronic repair, reconstruction and tendon transfer, with outcome tables from the included studies.
tldr: Repair within about six weeks gives the best reported results for pectoralis major rupture. Nonoperative care often leaves strength and cosmetic deficits, and tendon transfer gives unpredictable but usually satisfactory results.
methods: Search of electronic databases using terms for pectoralis major rupture, repair, transfer and nonoperative treatment. Case reports, systematic reviews, and prospective and retrospective studies in English were included. The authors summarized results in tables and added expert opinion.
findings: Acute ruptures mostly affect young men aged 20 to 40, and the inferior sternal fibers tear first. Among studies that defined acute repair as under 6 weeks, 90% or more of patients had excellent or good outcomes, versus 63% to 90% for repair at 6 to 8 weeks; across 10 studies, 18% of repaired patients had complications and 7% needed reoperation. Nonoperative care gave lower strength and cosmetic satisfaction, delayed repair gave 50% to 100% excellent or good outcomes, and tendon transfer gave unpredictable but overall satisfactory results.
limitations: Mostly small retrospective case series with varying definitions of acute and chronic, and no test of classification reliability. The authors state there is no scientific evidence supporting a specific fixation method, and tendon transfer outcomes are unpredictable.
practicalImplications: Athletes with a suspected pectoralis major rupture should be assessed early, because repair within about six weeks has the best reported outcomes. Staff should counsel that nonoperative care usually restores function but often leaves strength and cosmetic deficits, and that chronic ruptures often need reconstruction.
athleteDev: Repair before about six weeks is the best-supported route for athletes who want to return to strength and contact work. Athletes should expect some residual strength or cosmetic difference after either route.
rtp: After repair, the cited protocol starts passive motion at 2 weeks, expects full motion by 12 to 16 weeks, and avoids lifting more than 50% of one repetition maximum until 6 months. Several studies report return to preinjury level before 6 months, some as early as 2 months. These timelines come from small series and are approximate.

citation: Smock CS, Twohey E, Johnson AJ, Sellon JL, Cabarcas BC, Nagelli C, et al. Evidence-Based Management of Patellar Tendinopathy in Athletes: A Narrative Review. Curr Phys Med Rehabil Rep. 2026;14:4.
abstract: Narrative review of non-operative and operative treatments for patellar tendinopathy in athletes, with a conceptual framework for in-season and off-season decisions.
tldr: Start with structured physical therapy. Tendon scraping and high-volume injection are reasonable in-season options, while tenotomy, PRP and surgery are better timed to the off-season or to refractory cases.
methods: Comprehensive search of MEDLINE/PubMed and EMBASE for studies from 2015 to May 2025, using terms for patellar tendinopathy, treatments and study designs. Of 241 abstracts screened, eligible studies were summarized by treatment, with reference-list checks.
findings: Physical therapy is first-line. Corticosteroid injection gave inferior VISA-P and pain outcomes at 6 months in a network meta-analysis, and should not routinely be used. Shockwave, PRP, hyaluronic acid, high-volume injection, scraping and tenotomy show mixed or preliminary results. Surgery reports high return-to-sport rates, with 89.8% in a 40-study systematic review.
limitations: The narrative format and article selection are subjective, many studies are small or single cases, and quality varies widely across treatments. Few studies report cost, adverse events, or in-season versus off-season outcomes. The authors also note that some studies included a few nonathletes.
practicalImplications: Begin with a structured physical therapy program, using eccentric or heavy slow resistance loading, before any injection or procedure. For athletes who do not respond, the review suggests tendon scraping or high-volume injection in season, tenotomy or PRP in the off-season, and surgical referral after 6 to 12 months of conservative care.
athleteDev: For athletes with patellar tendinopathy, eccentric or heavy slow resistance loading remains central, and the season shapes the choice of procedure. Procedures with longer recovery are better timed to the off-season.
rtp: Return-to-sport data are strongest for surgery, and reported return rates are high for PRP and tendon scraping, but these come from small or uncontrolled studies. Corticosteroid injection should not routinely be used in high-load athletes because of rupture risk.

citation: Pryor RR, Pryor JL, Vandermark LW, Adams EL, Brodeur RM, Armstrong LE, et al. Exacerbated heat strain during consecutive days of repeated exercise sessions in heat. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2019 (accepted manuscript).
abstract: Repeated-measures laboratory study of 17 healthy, recreationally active men who completed two 2-hour intermittent exercise sessions separated by 2 hours of rest in 40 °C heat, and a third session 24 hours later. The second same-day session produced higher core temperature and heart rate at minute 35, and fewer participants completed it.
tldr: In recreationally active men, a second 2-hour intermittent exercise session in 40 °C heat after only 2 hours of rest produced higher core temperature and heart rate at minute 35, and only 35% of participants finished it. The authors conclude that multiple sessions should be avoided on the first day of activity in a hot environment.
methods: Seventeen healthy, recreationally active men (age 22 ± 3 years, VO2max 54.6 ± 5.3 ml/kg/min) completed two sessions on day 1, separated by 2 hours of rest, and one session on day 2, in a chamber at 40 °C and 40% relative humidity. Each session was 2 hours of walking, jogging and running at 60% and 80% of VO2max, with rest between blocks. Rectal temperature, heart rate, perceptual scales and symptom questionnaires were recorded, and repeated-measures ANOVA and Friedman tests compared minute 0, minute 35 and immediate post-exercise values.
findings: Participants completed 100%, 35% and 71% of the full protocol in Bout 1, Bout 2 and Day 2, and averaged 120, 93 (p = 0.001) and 113 min (p = 0.032). Minute-35 rectal temperature was highest in Bout 2 (38.80 ± 0.47 °C) compared with Bout 1 (38.41 ± 0.52 °C, p = 0.001) and Day 2 (38.31 ± 0.35 °C, p < 0.001), and minute-35 heart rate was higher in Bout 2 than Bout 1 (189 vs 180 bpm, p = 0.004); Day 2 minute-35 values were not higher than Bout 1. Immediate post-exercise temperature and heart rate were similar across sessions despite the shorter durations, and resting fatigue was higher before Bout 2 and Day 2 than before Bout 1.
limitations: The Results give 5 Bout 2 terminations for reaching 40 °C but state that six participants reached 40 °C in Bout 2, and the Discussion says five; the text does not explain the difference. The authors' claim of greater heat strain on Day 2 rests on lower completion, shorter exercise time and higher resting fatigue, not on higher minute-35 temperature or heart rate, and participants arrived slightly hypohydrated on Day 2 (USG 1.021). The authors acknowledge the fixed work rate, the single hot condition, a 2-hour rest shorter than the 3 hours in current guidance, and no adjustment for multiple comparisons.
practicalImplications: In this protocol, 2 hours of rest between moderate-high intensity sessions in oppressive heat did not prevent rectal temperature reaching the 40 °C cut-off in several participants in the second session the same day. Participants also rated greater strain in the second session. The authors advise avoiding multiple sessions on the first day of activity in the heat and having medical staff watch body temperature and heat illness signs during consecutive sessions and the next day.
athleteDev: The study tested recreationally active men at a fixed intensity, so it does not show how football practice design should be set. It supports the authors' conclusion that multiple sessions should be avoided on the first day of activity in a hot environment.
rtp: The study tested healthy participants with no injury, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It does not address rehabilitation or return to play after injury.

citation: Kushner JN, Swickley T, Bandi R, Lian J, Knecht MK, Sacca L. Examining the Prevalence of Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries on Artificial Turf Surfaces Compared to Natural Grass Surfaces in Athletes: A Scoping Review. Cureus. 2024;16(7):e63770.
abstract: Scoping review of nine epidemiological and cohort studies comparing ACL injury rates on artificial turf and natural grass in athletes, mostly American football and soccer players, drawn from PubMed, Embase and Cochrane. Three studies found more ACL injuries on turf, one found more on grass, and the rest found no clear difference or did not report confidence intervals.
tldr: Across nine studies of athletes, the evidence is mixed on whether ACL injuries are more common on artificial turf than natural grass. In American football, turf may carry more risk, but the evidence is not conclusive enough to settle surface choice.
methods: Scoping review following PRISMA-ScR and Arksey and O'Malley's framework, with predefined keywords searched in PubMed, Embase and Cochrane in January and February 2023. Three reviewers voted independently on inclusion in Rayyan, and nine studies were retained after reference searching; bias was assessed with MINORS (scores 10 to 14). Results were charted and summarised narratively, because the studies used different ratios and could not be standardised.
findings: Dragoo (collegiate football), Hershman (NFL football) and Ngatuvai (high school football and female soccer) reported significantly more ACL injuries on artificial turf, while Howard et al. (2020, collegiate soccer) reported significantly more on natural grass (incidence rate ratio 1.26, 95% CI 1.14 to 1.38). Hagglund, Loughran and Powell reported no significant difference, Dodson reported no significant difference without a p-value or confidence interval, and Scranton reported a higher incidence on turf without a statistical test. Of the seven American football studies, three found significantly more injuries on turf, and the soccer evidence was inconsistent.
limitations: The studies used different injury measures and ratios, and the authors could not standardise them, so comparisons across studies are indirect. Most were descriptive epidemiology drawn from public surveillance databases, and two did not report confidence intervals. The Discussion states the results 'definitively conclude that there is not a greater risk of ACL injuries on natural grass', which conflicts with the Howard soccer result and with the Conclusion that there is 'no universal consensus'; the Conclusion matches the data better.
practicalImplications: Staff should not treat artificial turf as clearly more dangerous for ACL injury, or natural grass as safer, because the evidence supports neither conclusion firmly. In American football, three of seven studies found more ACL injuries on turf, but the authors judge this not conclusive. The soccer evidence points in both directions, including one large collegiate study with more ACL injuries on grass.
athleteDev: The review addresses injury risk by playing surface, not training or performance. It does not show that either surface improves or harms athletic performance.
rtp: The review addresses ACL injury incidence, not rehabilitation or return to sport. It cannot guide return-to-play decisions after ACL injury or surface choice during rehabilitation.

citation: Saarensilta A, Aufwerber S, Grävare Silbernagel K, Ackermann P. Early Tendon Morphology as a Biomarker of Long-term Patient Outcomes After Surgical Repair of Achilles Tendon Rupture: A Prospective Cohort Study. The Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2023;11(11):23259671231205326.
abstract: Achilles tendon rupture outcomes vary and are hard to predict. In 86 adults who had surgical repair, ultrasound tendon cross-sectional area and elongation were measured at 6 weeks, 6 months and 12 months. A larger CSA ratio at 6 weeks was associated with better heel-rise height symmetry at 12 months, and greater elongation at 12 months was associated with poorer total concentric work symmetry.
tldr: In surgically repaired Achilles ruptures, a larger tendon cross-sectional area on ultrasound at 6 weeks was linked to better heel-rise height symmetry at 12 months. Greater tendon elongation at 12 months was linked to poorer work symmetry. These are single-cohort associations, not validated clinical tools.
methods: Prospective cohort study using data from a randomized trial of early functional mobilization versus cast immobilization after acute Achilles tendon repair (2013 to 2018). Ultrasound measured CSA and tendon length at 6 weeks, 6 months and 12 months, with 12-month outcomes from the Achilles tendon Total Rupture Score, heel-rise endurance test limb symmetry indices, and multiple linear regression adjusted for age with AUC analysis.
findings: The 6-week CSA ratio was associated with LSI maximum heel-rise height at 12 months (n = 45, adjusted R2 0.35, P < .001; AUC 0.82 for LSI above 80%). Greater TE at 12 months was associated with lower LSI total concentric work measured at the same visit (n = 82, adjusted R2 0.21, P = .001; AUC 0.71, which the authors call diagnostic rather than predictive). CSA ratio at 6 months with ATRS, TE at 6 months with LSI total concentric work, and TE at 12 months with LSI heel-rise height were not significant after Bonferroni correction (threshold P < .0019).
limitations: Postoperative regimens differed between the trial groups, rehabilitation was not standardized after 6 weeks, only three time points were measured, and not all patients were measured at every time point. Only surgically treated patients were included, the predictive values were not externally validated, and the 12-month elongation finding is concurrent with the outcome, so its predictive value is unclear. The participants' athletic status is not described.
practicalImplications: Ultrasound tendon measures may be worth tracking in research on Achilles rupture recovery, but this study does not show they should set rehabilitation or return-to-sport decisions. Clinicians should not treat the 6-week CSA ratio as a validated prognostic tool based on this cohort alone.
athleteDev: The study does not measure athletes or sport performance, so it cannot inform training prescription. Its heel-rise and work outcomes are functional measures after rupture repair, and any use for athletes would be an inference beyond this data.
rtp: The study does not test return-to-sport criteria. It found that a larger 6-week CSA ratio and greater 12-month elongation were associated with heel-rise and work symmetry at 12 months, which may guide research but should not be used alone to clear or delay return to sport.

citation: Knobloch K, Kraemer R, Jagodzinski M, Zeichen J, Meller R, Vogt PM. Eccentric Training Decreases Paratendon Capillary Blood Flow and Preserves Paratendon Oxygen Saturation in Chronic Achilles Tendinopathy. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2007;37(5):269-276.
abstract: Twenty adults with chronic Achilles tendinopathy were randomized to 12 weeks of daily eccentric training (n = 15) or a control group (n = 5). Laser Doppler and spectroscopy measured paratendon microcirculation at 8 sites and 2 depths. Pain fell 48% in the eccentric group, and some superficial capillary flow measures decreased, while oxygen saturation was preserved.
tldr: In this small randomized trial, daily eccentric training reduced pain by 48% in chronic Achilles tendinopathy. Some paratendon blood flow readings fell within the training group, but the between-group flow difference was not significant. Oxygen saturation was preserved.
methods: Randomized controlled trial with 15 patients in eccentric training (3 sets of 15 repetitions daily for at least 12 weeks) and 5 controls who used cryotherapy and relative rest. Laser Doppler and spectroscopy (Oxygen-to-See) measured capillary blood flow, tissue oxygen saturation, postcapillary venous filling pressure and blood flow velocity at 8 paratendon locations and 2 depths before and after 12 weeks. Pain was rated on a 0 to 10 visual analogue scale.
findings: Within the eccentric group, pain fell from 4.1 to 2.1 on the VAS (48%, P < .05); in controls it fell from 8.0 to 5.5 (P = .123). Superficial (2 mm) capillary blood flow fell within the eccentric group at the medial distal midportion (-31%, P = .008) and lateral proximal midportion (-45%, P = .016 in the abstract and .04 in the results text), while controls showed similar or larger nonsignificant median drops at several sites, and there was no significant between-group difference in blood flow. Tissue oxygen saturation did not change in either group, and superficial postcapillary venous filling pressure rose within the eccentric group at the medial and lateral insertion sites.
limitations: The sample was small, with 5 controls, and the control group had higher baseline pain (not statistically significant, P = .086). The abstract reports a deep midportion blood flow decrease and reduced deep filling pressures, and the discussion reports a between-group flow difference, but the results and tables show only superficial within-group flow decreases, superficial filling-pressure increases at the insertions, and no between-group flow difference; the two text sections also give different P values for the lateral site. Laser Doppler outputs are uncalibrated arbitrary units, adherence to the home program was not verified, and the many within-group tests were not corrected for multiple comparisons.
practicalImplications: Pain fell within the group doing daily eccentric training for chronic Achilles tendinopathy, but pain was not formally compared with the small control group, and the trial does not show that eccentric training changes tendon blood flow relative to control. Clinicians should not use paratendon microcirculation measures to judge treatment response based on this study.
athleteDev: The study measured pain and tendon microcirculation in recreationally active patients with tendinopathy, not athletic performance or training adaptation. It does not support a performance claim.
rtp: The study does not test return-to-sport criteria or tendon load tolerance for sport. Its pain and microcirculation results cannot be used to judge readiness to return to sport.

citation: Afonso J, Olivares-Jabalera J, Fernandes RJ, Clemente FM, Rocha-Rodrigues S, Claudino JG, et al. Effectiveness of Conservative Interventions After Acute Hamstrings Injuries in Athletes: A Living Systematic Review. Sports Medicine. 2023.
abstract: Living systematic review of 14 studies (730 athletes) comparing conservative treatments for acute hamstring injury on time to return to sport or full training and reinjury. No intervention was superior for any outcome, and the only signal was limited, very low-certainty evidence that eccentric lengthening shortens time to full training. Platelet-rich plasma did not consistently shorten time or reduce reinjury.
tldr: For acute hamstring injuries, no exercise-based rehabilitation approach was shown to be better than another for return to sport or reinjury. PRP did not reliably speed recovery or reduce reinjury, and the eccentric lengthening signal is preliminary.
methods: Searches of seven databases to January 2022, plus manual searches, citation tracking and expert consultation; PRISMA 2020 and Cochrane methods. Risk of bias was judged with RoB 2 and ROBINS-I, exercise-program reporting with i-CONTENT, and certainty with GRADE. Results were synthesized narratively because the studies were too few and too heterogeneous to pool.
findings: Fourteen studies with 730 athletes were included; most were judged at high risk of bias, and only three had low risk of ineffectiveness for their exercise programs. Eccentric lengthening (L-protocol) was followed by a shorter time to full training than the C-protocol in two trials (28 vs 51 days; 49 vs 86 days), but these trials had selection and detection problems. PRP gave mixed results against placebo or no injection, with a faster time to full training in some trials, no difference in others and no consistent effect on reinjury; low-level laser therapy showed no difference in return to sport versus placebo.
limitations: Few studies per comparison, high risk of bias, and very low GRADE certainty for all outcomes; no pooled estimates were calculated. Several reinjury percentages in the text do not match the Table 2 counts (for example 0.8% and 3.6% for the C-protocol versus 1/38 (2.6%) and 2/28 (7.1%), and 6.7% and 8.0% for Hamilton et al. versus 2/26 (7.7%) and 3/28 (10.7%)), so the Table 2 counts should be used. Competitive level was unreported in three studies and sex was unreported for four participants.
practicalImplications: On this evidence no exercise-based rehabilitation approach should be prioritised for reducing reinjury risk, so protocol choice should rest on other factors. Eccentric lengthening was the only exercise approach with a signal for earlier full training, and it is worth testing as a hypothesis rather than a standard. PRP should not be expected to shorten return to training or reduce reinjury, and LLLT added no clinical benefit to exercise in the one trial that tested it.
athleteDev: This review gives performance staff no basis to choose one hamstring rehabilitation protocol over another for reinjury prevention. The one signal, eccentric lengthening for faster full training, comes from two trials from one group and is very low certainty.
