rtp: This review is directly about time to return to sport and full training after acute hamstring injury, but it supports no specific protocol for return to sport. It does not support PRP or LLLT as accelerators, and it cannot set return-to-play criteria because the included studies used inconsistent criteria.

citation: Baxter JR, Corrigan P, Hullfish TJ, O'Rourke P, Grävare Silbernagel K. Exercise Progression to Incrementally Load the Achilles Tendon. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2020.
abstract: Laboratory study of Achilles tendon loading across a battery of rehabilitation exercises, walking and running in healthy adults. The authors combine peak load, loading impulse and loading rate into a loading index and use it to propose an exercise progression that increases tendon loading in steps, with separate sequences for isolated ankle and multi-joint movements.
tldr: Achilles tendon load was measured across rehabilitation exercises in eight healthy adults and ranked into four tiers. Single-leg hopping produced the highest loads (up to 7.3 bodyweights), so the ranking may help order loading, but it has not been tested in patients.
methods: Eight healthy adults (6 male, 2 female) completed a battery of heel raises, squats, lunges, step ups and downs, jumps, hops and drop jumps, plus walking and running. Motion capture (100 Hz) and force plate (1,000 Hz) data were processed in an open-source musculoskeletal model. Tendon load was estimated as the plantar flexion moment divided by a 5 cm moment arm, and the authors combined peak load (50%), impulse (30%) and loading rate (20%) into a loading index.
findings: Loading index values rose from seated heel raises (0.100 for two-leg, 0.128 for one-leg) to single-leg hops (0.904 to 0.924). Walking scored 0.359 and running 0.600. Single-leg heel raises and two-leg drop jumps had similar indices (0.493 vs 0.519) but different peak loads (3.0 vs 3.6 bodyweights) and loading rates. For lunges, the trailing leg had a higher index than the leading leg (0.435 vs 0.285), mainly through longer time under load.
limitations: The study used eight healthy, recreationally active adults and did not measure patients, so the loads are not patient data. Tendon load was estimated from joint moments with a constant 5 cm moment arm, and the scaling weights were chosen from the authors' clinical experience, which they say could be debated. The Results text gives the seated heel raise indices the other way round (single-leg 0.100, double-leg 0.128) from Table 1 (two-leg 0.100, one-leg 0.128); Table 1 values are reported here. The Discussion refers to 25 exercises, while Table 1 has 30 rows that also count walking, running and leading and trailing legs separately.
practicalImplications: Use the tiers as a reference for ordering loads, for example moving from seated heel raises (Tier 1) toward single-leg hops (Tier 4). Single-leg heel raises and two-leg drop jumps have similar index values but different peak loads and loading rates, so they should not be treated as interchangeable. The authors suggest walking and running as milestones for adding exercises with similar index values, and lunges and step ups can be used to load one side more than the other.
athleteDev: Relevant to staff who reintroduce jumping and hopping, since single-leg hops produced the highest measured Achilles loads (peak 7.3 bodyweights). It reports tendon loading values for these movements, not performance outcomes.
rtp: Can inform the staged loading of the Achilles tendon during rehabilitation, with walking and running suggested as milestones. It does not show that any exercise or tier is safe for return to sport, and because the sample was healthy adults, the loads cannot be used directly to judge tendon tolerance after rupture or tendinopathy.

citation: Shaw AG, Chae S, Levitt DE, Nicholson JL, Vingren JL, Hill DW. Effect of Previous-Day Alcohol Ingestion on Muscle Function and Performance of Severe-Intensity Exercise. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2021. Ahead of print.
abstract: Twelve recreationally active adults completed morning-after testing after a standardized alcohol dose or placebo the previous evening. Time to exhaustion in a severe-intensity constant-power cycle test was shorter after alcohol, while jump, isometric strength, dynamic strength and fatigue measures were not significantly changed.
tldr: A standardized alcohol dose the evening before was associated with an 11% shorter time to exhaustion in a severe-intensity cycle test the next morning. Jump, isometric strength and biceps curl measures did not change significantly.
methods: Within-subjects crossover study with 12 participants (6 men, 6 women), with counterbalanced, randomly assigned placebo and alcohol visits at least 3 days apart. Beverage drinking began between 12:00 and 2:30 PM (the abstract describes evening visits) at 1.09 g/kg fat-free mass of vodka (mean 52 g ethanol, peak BAC about 0.09 g/dL) or flavored water, and morning tests 17 to 19 hours after arrival were countermovement jumps, isometric mid-thigh pulls, 15 maximal biceps curls, and a constant-power cycle test to exhaustion at peak incremental power with oxygen uptake and accumulated oxygen deficit. Paired t tests compared conditions.
findings: Time to exhaustion in the constant-power test was 181 (39) s after alcohol versus 203 (34) s after placebo (-11%, P = .03, Cohen d 0.61), with lower accumulated oxygen uptake (80.1 vs 95.8 mL/kg, P = .01). Peak oxygen uptake (P = .63), maximal accumulated oxygen deficit (P = .34) and mean response time (P = .07) were not significantly different, and hangover symptom counts were higher after alcohol (10 vs 3, P = .01). Countermovement jump (P = .08), isometric mid-thigh pull (P = .45), biceps curl (P = .41) and fatigue index (P = .16) showed no significant difference.
limitations: The sample was 12 recreationally active students, the study was not powered to test sex interactions, and the cycle test was a single laboratory protocol. Participants were generally aware of the alcohol condition, the abstract describes evening drinking while the methods state drinking began between 12:00 and 2:30 PM, and the authors describe any shared mechanism as speculative.
practicalImplications: In recreationally active adults, a standardized previous-day alcohol dose (about 3.8 standard drinks) was followed by an 11% shorter time to exhaustion in a severe-intensity cycle test the next morning, while jump and strength tests were not significantly changed. The paper does not test athletes or sport-specific performance, so any effect on a particular sport is an inference.
athleteDev: The authors recommend educating athletes whose events rely on anaerobic capacity or a rapid aerobic response, but this rests on one cycling test in non-athlete students, and anaerobic capacity (MAOD) itself was not significantly reduced. The study does not measure sport performance or training adaptation.
rtp: The study addresses performance after drinking, not recovery from injury or exercise, so it does not inform return-to-play decisions. It should not be used to clear or delay an athlete after injury.

citation: Huang YC, Chou TY, Chen TC, Chen HT. Effect of cold-water immersion treatment on recovery from exercise-induced muscle damage in the hamstring. Eur J Sport Sci. 2024;1-9.
abstract: Eighteen healthy adult women were randomly assigned to a cold-water immersion (CWI) group or a control group after 100 maximal eccentric hamstring contractions. The CWI group received a 14 minute immersion at 14 C at 1, 25, 49, 73 and 97 hours after exercise, while controls rested seated. The authors report that five consecutive days of CWI improved maximal isometric strength, soreness, straight leg raise and plasma myoglobin compared with the control group.
tldr: In this small trial of healthy adult women who were not described as athletes, repeated 14 C immersions after a hard eccentric hamstring bout reduced soreness and improved isometric strength and flexibility compared with seated rest. The trial does not test athletes, training adaptation or injury rehabilitation.
methods: Eighteen healthy adult women were randomly assigned to CWI (n = 9) or control (n = 9). All performed 10 sets of 10 maximal isokinetic eccentric contractions of the nondominant hamstring at 30 degrees per second. CWI was a 14 minute seated immersion at 14 C on days 1 to 5; outcomes were maximal voluntary isometric contraction, delayed-onset muscle soreness on a 100 mm visual analog scale, passive straight leg raise and plasma myoglobin, measured before and up to 120 hours after exercise.
findings: The CWI group had higher maximal isometric contraction than controls on days 4 and 5 (89.3% vs 77.6%, and 94.0% vs 82.1%, apparently percent of baseline) but not on days 1 to 3, and lower soreness from day 2 to day 5 (15.4 vs 52.4 mm on day 2). Straight leg raise was higher in the CWI group from day 2 to day 5 (for example 86.3% vs 78.8% on day 2). Plasma myoglobin was described as a greater 'rate of decline' in the CWI group, but the printed values (436.3% vs 4362.1% on day 3) look like percent of baseline, with a much smaller rise in the CWI group, and cannot be percentage declines, so this outcome is not interpretable as reported.
limitations: The sample was 18 healthy women, the protocol used one exercise bout, and no athlete or male group was studied, so generalizability is limited. The design is described as double-blind, which is not explained for an immersion intervention, the DOMS method describes pressing on the rectus femoris (a quadriceps muscle) rather than the hamstrings, and the Abstract describes MVC, DOMS and SLR values as increases or decreases where the Results give group values. No sample size calculation is reported, and long-term effects of repeated immersion on strength adaptation were not studied.
practicalImplications: In healthy adult women, a 14 C, 14 minute immersion repeated daily for five days after a damaging eccentric bout reduced soreness and sped recovery of isometric strength and flexibility compared with seated rest. Transfer to athletes, men or training blocks is untested here, and the authors note that repeated immersion has been linked to blunted strength and hypertrophy gains in men, which this study did not measure.
athleteDev: The trial does not test sport performance, sprint or jump outcomes, or training adaptation. It supports only that a 14 C immersion may reduce soreness and partly restore isometric strength after a single high-volume eccentric bout in healthy women who were not described as athletes.
rtp: The trial does not study injured people, return to sport, or re-injury risk. It cannot be used to set rehabilitation timelines, clear an athlete after a hamstring injury, or judge whether immersion protects against re-injury.

citation: Li S, Kempe M, Brink M, Lemmink K. Effectiveness of Recovery Strategies After Training and Competition in Endurance Athletes: An Umbrella Review. Sports Medicine - Open. 2024;10:55.
abstract: Umbrella review of 22 systematic reviews and meta-analyses on recovery strategies after training in endurance athletes, using 63 controlled studies with 1,100 athletes. No recovery strategy showed consistent benefit across outcomes. For the 8 to 24 hour training-recovery window, cryotherapy and compression garments showed the most positive results, but the evidence is limited.
tldr: For endurance athletes, no between-session recovery strategy was consistently effective across the reviews. Compression garments and cryotherapy looked most promising 8 to 24 hours after training, but that conclusion rests on eight studies.
methods: Umbrella review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses from PubMed, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews and Web of Science to December 2022, following PRISMA. Review quality was rated with AMSTAR 2 and reviews rated critically low were excluded; only endurance-athlete studies with a control or placebo group were analysed, and outcomes were classed as positive, negative, no effect or contradictory.
findings: Across 60 passive-recovery studies, compression garments showed positive effects on time to exhaustion or jump performance only twice against 12 non-significant results, and massage studies reported no performance outcomes and improved muscle soreness in two of four studies. For the eight studies measuring 8 to 24 h after training, the authors report cryotherapy effect sizes of 0.33 to 3.00 for strength and sprint (0.10 to 0.12 for endurance performance) and benefits of compression socks and tights for strength and jump at 24 h. In Table 3, only cold water immersion for cyclist sprint performance (ES 1.01, 95% CI 0.16 to 1.86) has a confidence interval excluding zero.
limitations: Most included reviews were of low to moderate AMSTAR 2 quality, and the training-recovery conclusions rest on a small number of studies with varied exercise protocols; results were not pooled into a single estimate. The Discussion describes compression garment benefits as consistent for runners, but several CG estimates in Table 3 have confidence intervals crossing zero, so consistency is not claimed here.
practicalImplications: On this evidence, no single between-session recovery strategy can be recommended for endurance athletes. Compression garments and cryotherapy may be worth trialling in the 8 to 24 hour window, using the athlete's own outcome measures, but the evidence does not justify routine use. Massage showed little effect beyond muscle soreness.
athleteDev: This review does not support choosing one between-session recovery strategy for endurance performance. Compression garments and cryotherapy showed the most positive training-recovery results, but the evidence is thin and staff should treat them as candidates to test, not proven tools.
rtp: This review cannot inform return to sport because it excluded injury recovery and studied healthy endurance athletes recovering from training. It gives no criteria or timelines for return after injury, illness, or time loss.

citation: Dáttilo M, Antunes HK, Nunes-Galbes NM, Mônico-Neto M, de Sá Souza H, Quaresma MVLS, et al. Effects of Sleep Deprivation on the Acute Skeletal Muscle Recovery after Exercise. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2019 (published ahead of print).
abstract: Sleep may influence muscle recovery through hormones and cytokines. In a randomized crossover study of 10 healthy men, an eccentric knee extensor damage protocol was followed by 48 h of total sleep deprivation or normal sleep. Isometric strength and creatine kinase changed similarly in both conditions, while IGF-1, cortisol and the cortisol to total testosterone ratio were higher over 24 h with sleep deprivation.
tldr: In 10 healthy men, 48 h of total sleep deprivation after eccentric muscle damage did not change the pattern of isometric strength recovery over 60 h. It did raise 24-h cortisol, IGF-1 and the cortisol to testosterone ratio, but the link to muscle recovery is not established.
methods: Ten recreationally active men completed two conditions separated by at least 4 weeks. Both began with 240 isokinetic eccentric knee extensor contractions; afterwards they either stayed awake for 48 h or slept normally for three nights. Isometric peak torque, serum creatine kinase, cytokines and hormones were measured over 60 h, and hormones were also summarized as 24-h areas under the curve.
findings: Isometric strength fell immediately after the damage protocol and partly recovered by 12, 36 and 60 h, with no difference between conditions. Serum creatine kinase rose over time and was highest at 60 h. IL-6 rose immediately after damage in both conditions with no between-condition difference, and its 24-h area under the curve tended to be higher with sleep deprivation (P = 0.08). IGF-1 (P = 0.02), cortisol (P < 0.01) and the cortisol to total testosterone ratio (P < 0.01) were higher during sleep deprivation, and testosterone did not differ.
limitations: Only 10 men were studied, and the sleep loss and damage model were extreme and not training-like. The abstract says that only IL-6 increased during sleep deprivation and that strength and creatine kinase increased, but the Results show no between-condition IL-6 difference and a strength decrease with partial recovery; the Results values are used here. The Discussion calls the IL-6 24-h effect a main finding, although it was not significant at P = 0.08.
practicalImplications: Based on this study, staff should not assume that 48 h of total sleep loss after heavy eccentric exercise slows isometric strength recovery in healthy young men. The hormone and IL-6 changes come from a small, non-training sample and should not guide recovery or training decisions.
athleteDev: This study measured isometric knee extension strength only, so it does not show how sleep loss affects athletic performance. Use it to understand possible recovery mechanisms, not as evidence for performance decisions.
rtp: The study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It tested healthy men after induced muscle damage, not injured athletes, and it did not measure function or readiness to play.

citation: Petit E, Bourdin H, Tio G, Yenil O, Haffen E, Mougin F. Effects of a 20-Min Nap Post Normal and Jet Lag Conditions on P300 Components in Athletes. International Journal of Sports Medicine. 2018 (published online).
abstract: Athletes often nap to offset the afternoon dip in alertness and expected sleep disruption. In 16 highly trained young men, a 20-minute post-lunch nap was compared with rest after a normal night and after a simulated 5-hour jet lag night. The authors report that the nap increased P300 amplitude in both conditions, shortened P300 latency and improved subjective alertness and divided-attention reaction time after normal sleep only.
tldr: In highly trained young men, a 20-minute post-lunch nap raised a brain marker of attention and made participants feel more alert after a normal night. After a simulated 5-hour jet lag night, only P300 amplitude improved, and reaction times did not.
methods: Twenty highly trained male athletes were recruited; four were excluded for reported sleep disturbances, leaving 16, and two more were excluded from the P300 analysis for poor signal quality (n = 14). After a habituation night, each completed four laboratory nights in randomized crossover order: normal sleep or a 5-hour phase advance, each followed by a 20-minute nap (13:00 after normal sleep, 08:00 after the advance) or one hour of rest in bed without sleep. Thirty minutes later, participants rated alertness on a visual analogue scale, completed an auditory oddball task with EEG recording of P300 amplitude and latency, and completed six reaction-time attention tests.
findings: After normal sleep, the nap increased P300 amplitude at Fz (11.14 vs 9.05 microvolts, P < 0.05) and shortened P300 latency at Pz (327.2 vs 344.9 ms, P < 0.01). Subjective alertness was higher after the nap (visual scale 19.7 vs 27.5, P < 0.05), and divided-attention reaction time was faster (645 vs 698 ms, P < 0.05). After the 5-hour phase advance, only P300 amplitude increased, at Fz (10.30 vs 7.54 microvolts, P < 0.01) and Cz (11.48 vs 9.77 microvolts, P < 0.05), with no change in latency or reaction time. Naps lasted about 21 to 22 minutes with sleep efficiency near 70%.
limitations: Only 16 of 20 recruited men took part, and the P300 analysis used 14 after exclusions (Table 4 n = 14). The nap by condition interaction for P300 latency was not significant, the nap was taken in darkness while rest was not, and no sport performance was measured. The authors' claims that vigilance is necessary for athletic performance and that naps should be planned for athletes needing fast decisions were not tested in this design.
practicalImplications: A 20-minute nap after lunch may improve brain-based attention measures in trained athletes who sleep normally. The study does not show that the nap improves sport performance, and the jet lag results were limited to P300 amplitude, so the same benefit should not be assumed after a shifted night without testing it in athletes.
athleteDev: The study measured brain responses and reaction times in a laboratory, not sport performance. Use it to support a short post-lunch nap for trained athletes who sleep normally, not as proof that naps improve competition or training output.
rtp: The study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It tested healthy athletes in a sleep laboratory and did not study injury, medical clearance or return to play.

citation: Souissi M, Souissi Y, Bayoudh A, Knechtle B, Nikolaidis PT, Chtourou H. Effects of a 30-min nap opportunity on cognitive and short-duration high-intensity performances and mood states after a partial sleep deprivation night. Journal of Sports Sciences. 2020 (published online).
abstract: Partial sleep deprivation is known to impair cognitive performance, short-duration exercise and mood. In 14 physically active male students, a 30-minute afternoon nap opportunity was compared with no nap after a normal night and after a partial sleep deprivation night. The authors report that the nap improved vigilance, reaction time, shuttle-run distance and mood after both nights, although in the Results vigour improved only after sleep deprivation.
tldr: A 30-minute afternoon nap opportunity was followed by better vigilance, reaction time, mood and shuttle-run distance at 18:00, after both a normal night and a partial sleep deprivation night, in 14 active male students. Shuttle-run gains ranged from trivial to moderate, and only one night of sleep loss was tested.
methods: Fourteen physically active male students completed four laboratory sessions in a within-subjects, counterbalanced design, separated by four days: normal sleep or partial sleep deprivation, each with or without a 30-minute nap opportunity at 13:00. At 18:00 participants completed a mood questionnaire (POMS-f), a digit cancellation vigilance test and a simple reaction time test, then six 30-second 5-m shuttle runs with 35-second recoveries. Blood lactate was measured before, just after and 3 minutes after the shuttle runs, and sleep was monitored by actigraphy and diaries.
findings: Vigilance was better after the nap than without it after normal sleep and after sleep deprivation (both P < 0.0005), and simple reaction time was faster after the nap in both conditions (P = 0.0008 and P < 0.0005). Total shuttle distance was higher after the nap after normal sleep (d = 0.17, trivial) and after sleep deprivation (d = 0.45, small); peak distance was higher after the nap after normal sleep (d = 0.6, moderate) and after sleep deprivation (d = 0.36, small), and the fatigue index was lower after the nap in both conditions. Anxiety, fatigue, confusion and depression were lower after the nap in both conditions, vigour was higher after the nap only after sleep deprivation (P = 0.0012), and after the shuttle runs blood lactate was higher after sleep deprivation than normal sleep without a nap and lower with the nap than without it after sleep deprivation.
limitations: Only 14 men completed the study (two withdrew with injuries), the sample was physically active students rather than athletes, and the sleep loss was one partial night. The abstract says vigour rose after the nap in both conditions, but the Results show this only after sleep deprivation; the Discussion and Conclusions say blood lactate did not change, although the Results report significant sleep and nap differences; the Results values are used here. Several effect sizes are implausibly large (d = 17.1 and 16.83 for vigilance), the fatigue index ANOVA values duplicate those for total distance, and nap sleep duration is not reported.
practicalImplications: A 30-minute early afternoon nap opportunity may help physically active people feel less sleepy, improve mood and keep short repeated shuttle performance closer to normal after one partial night of sleep loss. After normal sleep the gain in total shuttle distance was trivial (d = 0.17), so staff should expect modest physical effects.
athleteDev: The study suggests that a 30-minute early afternoon nap may help maintain alertness and short shuttle-run output after a partial night of sleep loss. Its performance test was a laboratory shuttle run in active men, so it does not show effects on sport-specific or competition performance.
rtp: The study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It tested healthy, physically active men after one partial night of sleep loss, not injured or rehabilitating athletes.

citation: Craven J, McCartney D, Desbrow B, Sabapathy S, Bellinger P, Roberts L, et al. Effects of Acute Sleep Loss on Physical Performance: A Systematic and Meta-Analytical Review. Sports Medicine. 2022.
abstract: Sleep loss may influence subsequent physical performance, which matters for athletes. In a systematic review of 69 publications (227 outcome measures, 89% male), acute sleep loss of 6 hours or less reduced exercise performance across all exercise categories when all protocols were combined. The authors report that deprivation and late restriction were the protocols with consistent negative effects, and that tasks performed in the morning were largely unaffected.
tldr: Across 69 publications, acute sleep loss of 6 hours or less reduced exercise performance by about 7.6% on average, with the largest drop in skill tasks and larger drops in afternoon than morning testing. Deprivation and late restriction (early waking) had the most consistent negative effects, and in restriction protocols the drop grew with hours awake before testing.
methods: The authors searched Web of Science, Scopus and PsycINFO to September 2020, with an update in December 2021, and followed PRISMA-P 2015 (PROSPERO CRD42020211824). Included studies were controlled repeated-measures trials in adults comparing performance after sleep of more than 6 hours with performance after 6 hours or less. Performance outcomes were pooled as percentage change using multilevel random-effects meta-analysis, with meta-regression on hours awake and subgroup analyses by sleep-loss type, time of day and limb strength. Quality was rated with the Rosendal scale (mean 67 plus or minus 9%).
findings: Across all categories, sleep loss reduced performance by 7.56% (95% CI -11.9 to -3.13%; 227 outcomes; I2 = 98.1%). Subgroup estimates were -5.25% for deprivation, -8.59% for restriction, -5.85% for early restriction (95% CI -13.4 to 1.66, not significant) and -7.39% for late restriction. Category estimates were -20.9% for skill, -9.85% for strength-endurance (unstable on one-out analysis), -6.26% for anaerobic power, -6.15% for high-intensity interval exercise, -5.55% for endurance, -2.90% for speed/power endurance and -2.85% for strength. Performance declined about 0.36 to 0.55% per hour awake for restriction and late restriction, and about 0.27% per hour for deprivation only after removing one influential outcome.
limitations: Heterogeneity was very high, about 98% of outcomes measured only sleep quantity, about 11% of participants were women, and training status could not be explored. The abstract says the roughly 0.4% hourly decline applied to deprivation, but the deprivation estimate was not significant (-0.30%, P = 0.051) and became significant only after removing one outlier, and the all-protocol meta-regression was not significant (-0.09%, P = 0.095). The abstract says morning tasks were largely unaffected, but the overall morning estimate was -5.42% (95% CI -9.66 to -1.17), the Results text describes a consistent negative effect in both AM and PM, and no direct morning-versus-afternoon test is reported.
practicalImplications: When sleep loss cannot be avoided, staff should expect a reduction in performance that is likely to grow with time awake before a task, so testing and training should be planned for soon after waking where practical. Staff should not assume that morning tasks are immune, because the pooled morning estimate was also negative.
athleteDev: When sleep loss before a session or event is unavoidable, the pooled data suggest scheduling key physical or skill work soon after waking rather than late in the day, and avoiding early waking where travel or schedules allow. The hourly decline (about 0.36% per hour for restriction and 0.55% for late restriction) varies widely by task and study, so treat it as a rough guide.
rtp: The review cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It pooled healthy adults in short laboratory performance tests and did not study injured athletes, medical clearance or rehabilitation.

citation: Moore E, Fuller JT, Bellenger CR, Saunders S, Halson SL, Broatch JR, et al. Effects of Cold-Water Immersion Compared with Other Recovery Modalities on Athletic Performance Following Acute Strenuous Exercise in Physically Active Participants: A Systematic Review, Meta-Analysis, and Meta-Regression. Sports Medicine. 2022.
abstract: Recovery methods after strenuous exercise have produced mixed results. This systematic review and meta-analysis of sport and physically active participants compared cold-water immersion with active recovery, contrast water therapy, warm-water immersion, air cryotherapy and massage. The authors report that cold-water immersion reduced muscle soreness more than other methods and was similar on power and flexibility.
tldr: Across 28 studies in sporting or physically active participants, cold-water immersion gave small reductions in muscle soreness at 24 and 48 hours compared with other recovery methods. Pooled effects on power, strength, flexibility, perceived recovery and creatine kinase were all non-significant.
methods: Seven databases were searched to September 2022 for English-language peer-reviewed randomized or crossover trials in sport or physically active participants that compared cold-water immersion with another recovery method after strenuous exercise and measured performance, perceived recovery or creatine kinase. Study quality was rated with the SIGN randomized trial checklist. Hedges g effect sizes were pooled with random-effects models at each time point, and water temperature and exposure duration were tested as meta-regression moderators.
findings: Against all other methods, cold-water immersion reduced muscle soreness at 24 h (SMD 0.29, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.56; moderate GRADE) and 48 h (SMD 0.31, 0.05 to 0.57; high GRADE), with a non-significant effect at 1 h. Pooled effects on power, strength, perceived recovery and flexibility were non-significant at all time points. Creatine kinase at 24 h favoured cold-water immersion without reaching significance (SMD -0.58, 95% CI -1.17 to 0.01). Against active recovery, cold-water immersion reduced soreness at 1 h, and against contrast water therapy it reduced soreness at 48 h, both as small significant effects. Air cryotherapy gave a significantly larger 1-hour power effect than cold-water immersion (moderate effect).
limitations: The abstract says air cryotherapy was significantly better than cold-water immersion for strength, but the strength comparison was non-significant at every time point, and the abstract and Key Points describe cold-water immersion as more effective than active recovery, contrast and warm-water immersion for most outcomes, although most of those stratified effects were non-significant; the Discussion also claims a soreness benefit at 1 h that was not significant in the pooled analysis (P = 0.12). The meta-regression is reported inconsistently: one section says temperature and duration never significantly moderated outcomes, while the active recovery section and the Key Points report a significant dose-response for 24 h power. Table 2 states that negative effect sizes favour other methods, yet the text describes the 24 h creatine kinase effect (-0.58) as favouring cold-water immersion.
practicalImplications: Cold-water immersion may be a reasonable option for reducing muscle soreness 24 to 48 hours after strenuous exercise in active people. Its effects on power, strength and creatine kinase are small or uncertain, and the authors note it may blunt adaptations after resistance training in preparation phases.
athleteDev: Cold-water immersion may help athletes feel less sore in the 24 to 48 hours after hard sessions or matches, but the review does not show a reliable gain in jump, sprint or strength recovery. The authors caution that it may blunt resistance training adaptations in preparation phases, which this review did not test.
rtp: The review cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It pooled physically active and sporting participants after exercise-induced damage or match play, not injured athletes, and it did not study rehabilitation or clearance.

citation: Blumkaitis JC, Moon JM, Ratliff KM, Stecker RA, Richmond SR, Sunderland KL, et al. Effects of an external pneumatic compression device vs static compression garment on peripheral circulation and markers of sports performance and recovery. Eur J Appl Physiol. 2022;122:1709-1722.
abstract: This randomized trial compared a single 30-minute partial-leg external pneumatic compression (EPC) treatment, a static compression (SC) garment, and no treatment (control) after 100 drop jumps in 30 healthy, active males. No between-condition differences were found for jump height, soreness, pressure pain threshold, blood flow, or isokinetic torque. Squat jump propulsive force and power were higher in EPC and SC than in control at 24 and 48 hours.
tldr: A single 30-minute partial-leg compression treatment did not change jump height or soreness after drop jumps in healthy active men. Squat jump propulsive measures at 24 and 48 hours were better maintained with EPC or static compression than with no treatment. The paper reports EPC and SC only against control, not against each other.
methods: Thirty healthy, active males performed 100 drop jumps from 0.6 m, then were randomized to a 30-minute partial-leg EPC device (110 mmHg at the lower sleeve), a static compression sock (20-30 mmHg), or no treatment. Jump tests, isokinetic plantar and dorsiflexion torque, soreness, pressure pain threshold, femoral blood flow, muscle oxygenation, lactate and muscle size were measured before, after treatment, and at 24 and 48 hours.
findings: Soreness, fatigue, pressure pain threshold, blood flow, blood lactate, muscle size and isokinetic torque showed no condition effect, and countermovement and squat jump height did not differ between conditions. For squat jump, average relative propulsive force and power were higher in EPC and SC than in control at 24 and 48 hours (large effects), and EPC power was also higher than control at 30 minutes after treatment. In the countermovement jump, average relative braking force fell from pre-exercise to 24 and 48 hours within control and SC but not EPC, with no significant between-condition difference at any timepoint.
limitations: The sample was 30 active men, not trained athletes or women, tested with one 30-minute treatment and one damaging protocol followed only to 48 hours. The abstract says EPC maintained countermovement jump braking force and propulsive power across all timepoints, but this is a within-condition finding and the results report no significant between-condition difference; the results text for the propulsive power interaction also describes braking power, so that result is ambiguous. Funding was provided by MAS Holdings, and the EPC device was made by MAS Design Inc.
practicalImplications: A single short compression treatment did not reduce soreness or change jump height after a drop jump session in this group. Squat jump propulsive measures were better maintained at 24 and 48 hours with EPC or a static garment than with no treatment, so compression may be considered as one option for jump recovery in similar healthy adults, not as a proven EPC-specific method.
athleteDev: Compression treatment may help maintain squat jump propulsive force and power in the 1 to 2 days after a damaging drop jump session in active adults. The study does not show that partial-leg EPC is better than a static garment, and it does not show gains in jump height or strength.
rtp: This study used healthy active men after an induced muscle damage protocol and did not study injured athletes. It cannot be used to guide rehabilitation or return-to-play decisions.

citation: Chen TC, Huang YC, Chou TY, Hsu ST, Chen MY, Nosaka K. Effects of far-infrared radiation lamp therapy on recovery from muscle damage induced by eccentric exercise. Eur J Sport Sci. 2023.
abstract: Two laboratory experiments tested 30-minute far-infrared (FIR) lamp therapy against sham treatment after maximal eccentric exercise of the elbow flexors (24 women) or knee flexors (24 women). Acute changes immediately after exercise were similar in both groups, but changes at 24 to 120 hours were smaller with FIR. The authors conclude that FIR lamp therapy accelerated recovery from muscle damage.
tldr: In two small sham-controlled studies of sedentary women, daily 30-minute FIR lamp treatment after eccentric exercise was followed by faster recovery of strength, soreness, creatine kinase and proprioception than sham. The studies used a laboratory damage model and did not measure performance or athletes.
methods: Study 1 (elbow flexors, 72 eccentric contractions) and Study 2 (knee flexors, 100 eccentric contractions) each enrolled 24 healthy sedentary women allocated to FIR or sham (12 per group) by matching baseline MVC. Treatments were given at 1, 25, 49, 73 and 97 hours after exercise, and MVC torque, soreness, plasma CK, and position sense and force matching were measured up to 120 hours.
findings: Changes at 0.5 hours (before the first treatment) were similar between groups in both studies. From 24 to 120 hours, changes in all measures were smaller with FIR than sham, with MVC torque back to baseline by 72 hours with FIR but still 19 plus or minus 6 percent (Study 1) and 17 plus or minus 12 percent (Study 2) below baseline at 120 hours with sham. Peak soreness and plasma CK were lower with FIR, with the Discussion reporting peak CK reductions of 89 percent (elbow flexors) and 83 percent (knee flexors).
limitations: Participants were young sedentary women, and allocation was by stratifying baseline strength rather than randomization, so results may not apply to athletes or men; the authors also did not record ovarian hormone status. One Methods sentence says 12 participants per study while the abstract and sample-size paragraph say 24 per study (12 per group), and soreness reductions are given as 55 to 60 percent in the highlights, about 60 percent and 40 to 42 percent for peak soreness in the Discussion. Outcomes are indirect damage markers, and the treating physical therapist knew the condition while participants wore an eye mask and headphones.
practicalImplications: In sedentary young women, a daily 30-minute FIR treatment after a standardized eccentric protocol was followed by faster return of strength and lower soreness than sham. Whether this applies to athletes after matches or training is not shown by this study, and the mechanisms are not tested.
athleteDev: This study does not measure sport performance, sprinting or jumping, so it cannot show that FIR lamp therapy improves athletic performance. Its finding is limited to faster recovery of isometric strength and soreness after a laboratory eccentric protocol in sedentary women.
rtp: The study used a laboratory damage model in healthy sedentary women and did not study injured or returning athletes. It cannot be used to guide hamstring rehabilitation or return-to-play decisions, although the authors suggest hamstring strains as a future question.

citation: Rossiter A, Comyns TM, Sherwin I, Nevill AM, Campbell MJ, Warrington GD. Effects of long-haul transmeridian travel on physiological, sleep, perceptual and mood markers in Olympic team support staff. Chronobiol Int. 2022;39(12):1640-1655.
abstract: Nine Irish Olympic team support staff were studied before and after an eastward flight across eight time zones to Japan. Perceived jet lag was elevated for six days, morning salivary cortisol was lower than baseline from day 1 to day 5, and actigraphy showed shorter sleep on days 2, 3 and 6. Evening mood showed more fatigue, confusion and depression and less vigour in the days after travel.
tldr: After an eight-time-zone eastward flight, nine Olympic support staff reported jet lag for about six days and had shorter sleep and lower evening vigour in the first few days. Most measures returned to baseline within about a week, but vigour stayed low.
methods: Nine staff collected morning and evening saliva samples and completed Liverpool jet lag questionnaires and Brunel Mood Scale ratings, and wore wrist actigraphy with sleep diaries, on two baseline days in the week before travel, the first eight days in Japan and day 15. Multilevel random-intercept models compared each post-travel day with the averaged baseline; there was no control group, and collection was not directly supervised because of Covid-19 restrictions.
findings: Morning perceived jet lag was higher than baseline on days 1 to 6, and evening fatigue and jet lag peaked on day 2. Morning salivary cortisol fell 66 percent on day 1 and stayed lower until day 5, then rose above baseline on day 7. Actigraphy showed shorter total sleep on days 2, 3 and 6, and evening confusion and fatigue were higher on days 2 and 3, evening depression was higher on days 3 and 7, and evening vigour was lower on days 2, 6 and 7.
limitations: The study had nine participants, no control group, no direct supervision of sample collection, and no record of work or social schedules, and baseline was taken in a week the authors say may already have involved high tension and poor sleep. The abstract says it took seven days for physiological circadian markers to normalize, while the Results show morning cortisol back to baseline on day 6. The Results report elevated salivary alpha-amylase on the evening of day 3 (and the Discussion also mentions day 5), which conflicts with the conclusion that travel did not change stress markers.
practicalImplications: The authors recommend that staff travelling eastward across eight time zones plan their work program around about a week of recovery and use sleep and mood strategies before and after such trips. The paper's suggestion to schedule key decision-making in the morning rests on mood changes, not on measured work performance.
athleteDev: Olympic support staff in this study had reduced sleep and mood in the first days after eastward travel, which may matter when they are supporting athletes. The study did not measure athlete performance, so it cannot show how staff recovery affects athlete outcomes.
rtp: The study followed healthy support staff after travel and did not test injured athletes or return-to-play decisions. It cannot be used to guide rehabilitation or return-to-sport timing.

citation: Normand-Gravier T, Solsona R, Dablainville V, Racinais S, Borrani F, Bernardi H, et al. Effects of thermal interventions on skeletal muscle adaptations and regeneration: perspectives on epigenetics: a narrative review. European Journal of Applied Physiology. 2024.
abstract: This narrative review examines how cold and heat interventions affect long-term training adaptations and muscle regeneration. Repeated cold after resistance exercise can blunt hypertrophy and isometric strength, while heat may mitigate atrophy and, in some trained athletes, improve strength or endurance.
tldr: This narrative review suggests repeated cold after resistance training can blunt muscle growth and isometric strength gains. Repeated heat may help limit atrophy and may benefit some trained athletes, but the human heat evidence is small and mixed.
methods: Narrative review of cold (cold-water immersion, whole-body cryotherapy, ice) and heat (sauna, hot-water immersion, diathermy, heat pads and sheets) interventions, covering acute and repeated exposures, training adaptations, muscle regeneration after injury, atrophy from immobilization, and epigenetic changes. Human and animal studies are summarized in tables; no systematic search or quality appraisal is described.
findings: Over 12 weeks of twice-weekly resistance training, post-exercise cold-water immersion produced smaller hypertrophy gains and blunted isometric strength gains (Roberts et al.), while several cold-water and whole-body cryotherapy studies found no blunting of endurance adaptations. In humans, repeated heat produced some gains in trained athletes (for example 20 min hot-water immersion at 40.3 degrees C, 4 days per week for 4 weeks, increased knee extensor isometric strength in elite short-track speed skaters) but not in others, including rugby players with no body composition or resistance performance gain, and it impaired shooting performance and postural stability in elite teen archers. During limb immobilization in humans, 2 h daily diathermy over 10 days maintained mitochondrial function and attenuated atrophy, and whole-body heat over 2 weeks prevented the loss of plantar flexor isometric strength and soleus CSA.
limitations: No systematic search, selection or quality appraisal is described, and much of the regeneration and mechanistic evidence comes from rodents. The studies differ in temperature, duration, population and training status, and the authors note that these differences may explain the conflicting heat results. The authors state that human studies of cryotherapy after muscle injury do not yet exist.
practicalImplications: Avoid routine cold-water immersion after resistance training when the goal is hypertrophy or isometric strength; the authors find less evidence that cold blunts endurance adaptations. If heat is used to support adaptation, the authors stress confirming that muscle temperature reaches about 39 degrees C, and caution with hot-water immersion in sports that depend on fine postural control.
athleteDev: For athletes building muscle or isometric strength, the review suggests avoiding repeated cold immersion after resistance training. Heat may add to isometric strength or endurance in some trained athletes, but the human evidence is small and mixed and no added effect on muscle mass has been shown in trained humans.
rtp: The review summarizes rodent injury studies and two human immobilization studies in which heat limited atrophy, and it notes there are no human studies of cryotherapy after muscle injury. It gives no validated return-to-sport protocol, so use it to frame questions about heat during immobilization rather than to set return-to-play timelines.

citation: Rossiter A, Comyns TM, Sherwin I, Nevill AM, Warrington GD. Elite athletes' and support staffs' experiences and perceptions of long-haul travel, and the self-management strategies they use. International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching. 2023.
abstract: Survey of 88 elite athletes and support staff who had flown more than 8 hours for training or competition in the previous two years. The online survey asked about symptoms in the three days after the flight, travel strategies, and perceived effects of travel on performance and injury risk.
tldr: Most elite athletes and staff in this Irish survey said long-haul travel hurt their physical performance and increased injury risk. Fatigue and sleep disruption were the most common symptoms, and in-flight movement and body-clock strategies were the most used.
methods: Cross-sectional online survey open from March to May 2019, with separate athlete and staff versions. Chi-squared or Fisher's exact tests linked symptoms and strategies to traveller and journey characteristics. Open responses were coded qualitatively.
findings: Long-haul travel was perceived to hinder physical performance (86.4%), mental performance (72.7%) and to increase illness or injury risk (86.4%), and 27.3% self-reported illness or injury after arrival. Daytime fatigue was more common in women (71.1% vs 44.0%, P = .011), early waking and general weariness were linked to crossing more time zones, and eastward travellers more often reported stiffness or soreness (53.8% vs 22.2%). Most participants (70.5%) perceived full recovery within three days, and more time zones crossed was associated with longer perceived recovery.
limitations: Data are retrospective self-report, covering flights up to two years earlier, which may introduce recall error, and the authors note surveys tend to show higher symptom reports in females. The analysed subset of 88 (50 athletes, 38 staff) came from Irish high-performance sport across 14 sports, symptoms were recorded only for the three days after travel, and the survey did not assess whether strategies were applied appropriately.
practicalImplications: Fatigue and sleep disruption were the most reported problems, so travel planning can prioritise them; the authors suggest scheduling work and training before travel to limit sleep loss. Women and those crossing more time zones reported more symptoms or longer recovery, but the study did not test whether any strategy works, and the authors' view that fast recovery shows strategies are effective is not supported by the design.
athleteDev: Fatigue, sleep disruption and perceived performance cost were common after long flights, so they can inform pre-travel load planning and in-flight sleep and movement plans. The survey does not show that these strategies improve performance.
rtp: The study measured symptoms and perceived recovery after travel and did not include injured athletes, so it cannot guide return-to-sport decisions after injury.

citation: Barnard J, Roberts S, Lastella M, Callahan DL, Aisbett B, Condo D. Evening Alpha-Lactalbumin Supplementation Alters Sleep Architecture and Reduces Morning Reaction Time in an Athletically Trained Population With Sleep Difficulties. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2025 (ahead of print).
abstract: Double-blind crossover trial of 40 g alpha-lactalbumin versus collagen taken before bed for three nights in 19 trained adults with sleep difficulties, with EEG sleep, mood, sleepiness and morning cognition outcomes.
tldr: Alpha-lactalbumin taken two hours before bed increased NREM stage 2 sleep, reduced REM sleep and sped up three of four morning reaction-time tests in trained adults with sleep difficulties. It did not shorten sleep onset or improve sleep efficiency.
methods: Randomized, double-blind, counterbalanced crossover trial. Participants had a familiarization night and a standardized diet, then took 40 g alpha-lactalbumin or 40 g collagen 2 hours before bed on three nights. Sleep was measured by a dry-EEG headband, plasma amino acids were sampled on night one, and a four-task cognitive battery was completed each morning.
findings: Compared with control, alpha-lactalbumin increased NREM stage 2 sleep (216.5 vs 205.9 min, P=.02) and reduced REM sleep (99.7 vs 110.8 min, P=.01). Reaction time improved in three of four morning tasks, while the primary outcome of sleep onset latency, sleep efficiency and total sleep time did not change. Subjective sleep quality was slightly lower and morning muscular and overall stress ratings were slightly higher with alpha-lactalbumin.
limitations: Nineteen participants in a controlled laboratory over three nights, with the first night excluded, and collagen may affect sleep through other pathways. Sleep onset was already short in the laboratory (median 13 min under control), and sport performance and longer use were not tested. The alpha-lactalbumin was provided in kind by its manufacturer.
practicalImplications: Trained people with sleep difficulties could trial 40 g alpha-lactalbumin about 2 hours before bed, separated from a low-protein evening meal, as in this protocol. Expect modest changes in sleep stages and morning reaction time, not faster sleep onset, which was the trial's primary outcome and did not change.
athleteDev: Alpha-lactalbumin before bed improved some laboratory reaction-time tests in trained adults with sleep difficulties. Its effect on sport performance has not been tested, so it should not be presented as a performance aid.
rtp: Not applicable. The trial studied trained adults with sleep difficulties, not injured athletes, and it did not measure return-to-sport outcomes.

citation: Markus I, Constantini K, Hoffman JR, Bartolomei S, Gepner Y. Exercise-induced muscle damage: mechanism, assessment and nutritional factors to accelerate recovery. Eur J Appl Physiol. 2021.
abstract: Narrative review of exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD) after endurance and resistance exercise in recreational and competitive athletes. It covers the mechanisms of damage, methods for assessing damage and recovery, sex and age differences, and nutritional factors including diet patterns, protein, creatine, beta-alanine and polyphenols.
tldr: Recovery from muscle damage is assessed in several ways, and the chosen marker can change the conclusion. Among nutritional strategies, protein, creatine and polyphenols have some support, while the evidence for diet patterns and beta-alanine is limited.
methods: Narrative review. No systematic search method is described. The authors review endurance and resistance EIMD, a table of invasive and non-invasive assessment methods, sex and age differences, and the effects of vegetarian, omnivore and ketogenic diets and of supplements (protein, creatine, beta-alanine, polyphenols) on recovery indices.
findings: Prolonged downhill running or eccentric cycling reduced knee extensor torque by 15% to 30%, and strength returned to baseline by about 7 days when the initial loss was under 50%. Several studies found faster strength recovery in women than in men after single bouts of resistance exercise, although findings conflict and most participants were untrained. The authors found no support for vegetarian diets improving recovery, limited evidence for ketogenic diets, and some support for protein, creatine and polyphenols, with mixed results between studies.
limitations: The review gives no search strategy, so the selection of evidence cannot be checked. Much of the cited work used untrained participants, and the authors identify gaps in research on women, especially resistance-trained women, and on sex and age comparisons. Diet and supplement conclusions rest on a few studies, some in rodents; the creatine mechanism is unclear and the beta-alanine antioxidant evidence comes mainly from animal models.
practicalImplications: Track recovery with more than one measure, such as strength or jump performance alongside blood markers, because the chosen marker can change the conclusion. The authors support protein after training for muscle repair and suggest that whey, with its faster absorption, may be the most useful protein immediately after a session. Creatine (for example 20 g per day for 5 days in several studies) and polyphenols may be considered by athletes who choose to use them, but results are inconsistent and no diet pattern has been shown to be superior for recovery.
athleteDev: Relevant to staff managing repeated high-volume sessions, since the review judges recovery by return of performance to baseline and not by blood markers alone. In one study of resistance-trained men, bench press throw power was reduced 24 h after a high-volume bench press and returned to baseline by 48 h, and countermovement jump was reduced for up to 48 h after high-volume squats.
rtp: Not a return-to-sport study. The review proposes that jump, strength and bench press throw measures can track recovery of performance, but it gives no return-to-play criteria, and the performance evidence it reviews comes mostly from studies of men, many of them untrained.

citation: Nath S, Bhattacharya S, Golla VB, Kumar R. Effect of Social Media on Diet, Lifestyle, and Performance of Athletes: A Review of Current Evidence. Current Nutrition Reports. 2024.
abstract: This review searched PubMed, Embase and Google Scholar and retained 22 articles on how social media influences the diet, lifestyle and performance practices of athletes. The authors describe social media as a powerful, but credibility-limited, source of nutrition and lifestyle advice, with links to supplement choices, dietary trends and body image concerns. They conclude that social media advice should be used with caution and checked against sports nutrition and coaching advice.
tldr: This review of 22 articles found that athletes often use social media for diet and supplement advice, and that the credibility of that advice is hard to judge. Trending foods and supplements should be checked with a sports dietitian and coach before use.
methods: Literature was searched in PubMed, Embase and Google Scholar using combined keywords for social media, athletes, diet, nutrition, lifestyle and athletic performance. The initial search returned 121 records, 102 after removing duplicates; titles and abstracts were screened, and 22 articles were retained after full-text review by at least three authors. The paper describes no formal quality appraisal of the included studies.
findings: Included studies report high social media use for nutrition information among athletes, for example 65% of 306 New Zealand athletes used it for nutrition needs in the past year, and 64% of 455 athletes in Lebanon relied on online social media for supplement information. Several studies link fitspiration and thinspiration content to body image concerns, mainly in non-athlete samples. The authors note that literature on social media effects on athlete lifestyle and performance is scarce, that a cited systematic review rated evidence for health behavior change interventions delivered through online social networks as modest, and that social-media-delivered dietary weight loss interventions were not consistently effective.
limitations: The search was limited to three databases and English-language journal articles, and no risk-of-bias or quality appraisal is reported. The included set mixes original research with viewpoints and commentaries, many studies are cross-sectional or qualitative, and several sampled non-athletes such as gym users, military personnel or young adults. The review does not pool or quantify effects, so the strength of its conclusions cannot be graded.
practicalImplications: Ask athletes which diet, supplement and lifestyle trends they follow online, and have those trends checked with a sports dietitian and coach before use. For supplements, check for doping risk, since the review cites evidence that some products contain doping substances. Watch for body image concerns in athletes who follow image-focused fitness or diet content, which the review links to disordered eating.
athleteDev: The review gives performance staff a reason to ask athletes where they get nutrition and supplement advice, and to route trending diet or supplement ideas through a sports dietitian. It contains no measured performance outcomes, so it cannot guide training or performance programming.
rtp: The review does not study return to sport or recovery from injury, so it cannot show whether social media nutrition advice helps or harms recovery. It supports only the general advice to verify online recovery-nutrition claims with a qualified sports dietitian.

citation: McCubbin AJ, da Costa RJS. Effect of Personalized Sodium Replacement on Fluid and Sodium Balance and Thermophysiological Strain During and After Ultraendurance Running in the Heat. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2023.
abstract: Nine ultraendurance runners completed two 5-hour treadmill runs in 30 C heat in a double-blind randomized crossover design, receiving sodium capsules that replaced 100% of their estimated sweat sodium losses or placebo. Sodium replacement did not change ad libitum fluid intake or heat strain during exercise, but it raised plasma sodium more than placebo. Over the next 24 hours, fluid intake and urinary sodium excretion were higher after sodium replacement, and the authors conclude that personalized replacement was not needed to limit body-water loss.
tldr: In 9 ultraendurance runners exercising 5 hours in 30 C heat, sodium capsules matched to sweat sodium losses did not change drinking or heat strain during exercise, but raised plasma sodium. Over the next day they increased fluid intake and reduced sodium conservation by the kidneys, so the effect on hydration needs careful reading.
methods: Double-blind randomized crossover trial. Nine runners (7 men, 2 women) completed two 5-hour runs at 60% VO2max in a 30 C climate chamber. Sodium chloride capsules replaced 100% of sweat sodium losses estimated from a familiarization run, or matched maltodextrin capsules were given as placebo; a fixed carbohydrate solution and ad libitum water were provided. Plasma sodium and osmolality, plasma volume, heart rate, rectal temperature, thermal comfort, and 24-hour fluid and urine measures were collected.
findings: Ad libitum water intake during exercise did not differ between trials (1,553 vs 1,216 mL; P = .07), nor did net water balance, heart rate, rectal temperature or perceived exertion. Plasma sodium rose more with sodium replacement at 2.5 and 5 hours (for example 4 vs 1 mmol/L at 2.5 hours), and postexercise urinary sodium was higher (66 vs 21 mmol). After exercise, total fluid intake (2,541 vs 1,998 mL, P = .04) and net water balance (+1,532 vs +774 mL, P < .01) were higher with sodium, giving a total net water balance across exercise and the 24-hour recovery of +265 vs -812 mL (P < .01); net sodium balance at 24 hours was positive with sodium and negative with placebo.
limitations: The sample was 9 runners (7 men and 2 women), one 5-hour session at one intensity, so the findings do not cover longer events, cooler conditions or sex-specific effects. Sweat sodium was estimated from one familiarization run and replacement ranged from 78% to 231% of actual losses, and sodium was given as capsules rather than in drinks. The authors conclude that sodium replacement did not substantially affect overall body-water balance, but Table 2 shows a significant difference in postexercise and total water balance, and the abstract labels postexercise total fluid intake as ad libitum intake.
practicalImplications: In about 5 hours of heat running, replacing estimated sweat sodium did not significantly change drinking during exercise in this small sample. Sweat sodium estimates varied between sessions, so an individual sodium plan should not be treated as precise. Over the next 24 hours, the sodium trial had higher total fluid intake and better water balance, so staff should not read this trial as showing that sodium is unneeded for hydration.
athleteDev: The trial measured hydration, plasma sodium and heat strain rather than running performance. Heart rate, rectal temperature and perceived exertion did not differ with sodium replacement over 5 hours, which suggests little effect on heat strain during a single run in these runners.
rtp: The trial used healthy runners and does not study injury, illness or heat-related injury recovery. It cannot inform return-to-sport timing or readiness after an injury or heat illness.

citation: Lis DM, Baar K. Effects of Different Vitamin-C Enriched Collagen Derivatives on Collagen Synthesis. International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism. 2019 (accepted manuscript).
abstract: Randomized double-blind crossover in 10 recreationally active men comparing placebo, vitamin C-enriched gelatin, hydrolyzed collagen, and a gummy, each taken before 6 min of jump rope. Amino acid levels rose similarly for all supplements, and PINP changes were positive for gelatin and hydrolyzed collagen, but no change reached statistical significance because of large variability.
tldr: A single 15 g dose of gelatin or hydrolyzed collagen taken before a short jump-rope bout did not produce a statistically significant rise in the bone collagen marker PINP. The study is too small and too affected by assay problems to show a real effect on collagen synthesis.
methods: Randomized, double-blind, crossover trial with four trials at least 48 h apart: maltodextrin placebo, 15 g gelatin, 15 g hydrolyzed collagen, or a gummy with about 7.5 g each of gelatin and collagen, all with blackcurrant cordial. Participants jumped rope for 6 min one hour after ingestion; serum PINP was measured by ELISA at baseline and 4 h, and a subgroup of four men had serum amino acids measured at 1 h.
findings: Mean PINP change from baseline at 4 h was 20.4% (± 52.9) for gelatin, 19.6% (± 47.5) for hydrolyzed collagen, -23.8% (± 30.5) for the gummy, and -6.8% (± 43.7) for placebo, none statistically significant (P > 0.05); the methods state data are mean ± SEM. In the four-man subgroup, serum glycine, lysine, proline, hydroxyproline and hydroxylysine rose at 1 h to a similar extent across the three collagen products, while leucine did not change.
limitations: The sample was ten men, five outlying PINP values were removed, and the amino acid arm had only four men. The authors report that vitamin C inhibits the PINP ELISA and that serum clotting time may have affected results, so the PINP data are weak. The text and Figure 2 caption describe increases and a 'strong trend' for gelatin, but the Results report no significant change; the Results are reported here.
practicalImplications: This study does not support using gelatin or hydrolyzed collagen to speed tendon or bone collagen synthesis after exercise. Staff could treat the 1-hour amino acid response as confirmation that the products are absorbed similarly, but that is not a training outcome. The authors suggest vitamin C co-ingestion may matter for the collagen response, which has not been tested.
athleteDev: This study measured no performance or tissue outcome, so it gives no evidence of a performance or tissue-strength benefit from gelatin or collagen before loading. Its only usable finding for staff is that the products raised circulating amino acids similarly, which does not show a training effect.
rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It tested recreationally active men after one 6-minute jump-rope session and measured no injured, rehabilitating, or tissue-load outcomes.

citation: Tuma C, Schick A, Pommerening N, Braun H, Thevis M. Effects of an Individualized vs. Standardized Vitamin D Supplementation on the 25(OH)D Level in Athletes. Nutrients. 2023;15:4747.
abstract: Vitamin D is important for athletes, and a 25(OH)D target of at least 40 ng/mL is often suggested. In a 10-week winter study in Germany, athletes with insufficient vitamin D were randomized to an individualized loading dose, a standard 2000 IU daily dose or no supplement. The authors report that the individualized group had higher 25(OH)D on its calculated target day than the standard group at 5 weeks (41.1 vs 32.5 ng/mL).
tldr: In winter, an individualized vitamin D loading dose gave higher 25(OH)D on its calculated target day than a standard 2000 IU daily dose at 5 weeks. By 10 weeks both groups had similar levels, and only 30% of the individualized group were at or above 40 ng/mL.
methods: Ninety athletes training at least 5 hours per week were enrolled in Germany from January to April. Athletes with 25(OH)D below 30 ng/mL were matched on baseline level and randomized to an individualized group (4000 IU per day until a calculated target day, from the Groningen formula, then 1000 IU per day), a standard group (2000 IU per day) or a control group with no supplement. Sufficient athletes were monitored without supplementation. Total 25(OH)D was measured from capillary VAMS samples at baseline, at a second time point and at 10 weeks, and a vitamin D questionnaire was completed.
findings: At the second measurement, the individualized group had 41.1 plus or minus 10.9 ng/mL at its calculated time (41 plus or minus 12 days), compared with 32.5 plus or minus 6.4 ng/mL in the standard group at 5 weeks (P < 0.001). At the final measurement the individualized and standard groups had similar means (37.9 plus or minus 10.3 vs 38.1 plus or minus 6.8 ng/mL); the individualized group declined by 3.2 ng/mL on the 1000 IU maintenance dose while the standard group kept rising. The unsupplemented control group fell from 21.9 to 18.1 ng/mL and the sufficient group fell by 8.7 ng/mL. Half of the individualized group reached 40 ng/mL at the calculated day and 30% did so at the end, compared with 17% and 38% of the standard group at 5 and 10 weeks, and baseline 25(OH)D correlated negatively with the rise over the study (r = -0.54, P < 0.001).
limitations: The abstract says all 90 athletes were insufficient and randomized, but only the 67 with levels below 30 ng/mL were randomized (28 INDV, 26 STAD, 13 CON), and the 23 sufficient athletes were monitored only. The key comparison used different time points (about 41 days for INDV versus 5 weeks for STAD), and final samples were taken at 77 and 78 days in the two supplemented groups rather than at 10 weeks. The reported weight difference between INDV athletes who did and did not reach 40 ng/mL has a 95% CI that includes zero (-0.21 to 18.66) yet is reported as P < 0.05; the abstract also says dried blood spots, while the Methods used VAMS whole-blood samples.
practicalImplications: Athletes with low winter vitamin D may need more than 1000 IU daily to hold a level near 40 ng/mL, so periodic measurement during the season is sensible. The study does not show that individualized loading gives better levels than a standard dose by the end of 10 weeks.
athleteDev: The study measured vitamin D status, not performance, and did not test jump, strength or endurance. Use it to guide winter vitamin D testing and supplementation, not as evidence that supplementation improves athletic performance.
rtp: The study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It enrolled healthy athletes with low vitamin D and did not study injury, stress fractures or rehabilitation outcomes.

citation: Farjallah MA, Graja A, Ben Mahmoud L, Ghattassi K, Boudaya M, Driss T, et al. Effects of melatonin ingestion on physical performance and biochemical responses following exhaustive running exercise in soccer players. Biology of Sport. 2022;39(2):473-479.
abstract: In a double-blind randomized study, 13 professional soccer players ran to exhaustion at 100% of maximal aerobic speed after either 6 mg melatonin or placebo. Melatonin attenuated the post-exercise rise in malondialdehyde and the rise in creatine kinase and lactate dehydrogenase, but physical performance was not affected.
tldr: In 13 professional soccer players, 6 mg melatonin before a running test to exhaustion did not change running time, but it blunted the rise in muscle-damage and lipid-peroxidation markers. These are acute, single-session findings and do not show a performance benefit.
methods: Thirteen players completed three sessions at least 48 hours apart: anthropometrics and a maximal aerobic speed field test, then a crossover comparison of 6 mg melatonin or lactose placebo, each followed by a running test at 100% of maximal aerobic speed until exhaustion. Blood was sampled at rest and 3 minutes after the test for oxidative stress, antioxidant and muscle-damage markers, and oral temperature and a vigilance test were also recorded.
findings: Physical performance did not differ between placebo (362.5 +/- 42.1 s) and melatonin (374.5 +/- 58.0 s; p = 0.19), nor did HR max or RPE. After the test, MDA rose only under placebo (1.55 to 2.89 umol/L), CK rose only under placebo, and post-exercise CK (310 vs 250 IU/L; p < 0.001) and LDH (272 vs 238 IU/L; p < 0.05) were lower after melatonin than placebo. SOD fell after the test in both conditions, GPx fell and uric acid and bilirubin rose only under placebo, and post-exercise oral temperature was lower after melatonin.
limitations: Thirteen players, one 6 mg dose given in the afternoon, and only a 3-minute post-exercise blood sample, so delayed biochemical responses were not measured. The sex of the sample is not stated. The Abstract says melatonin alleviated changes in uric acid and total bilirubin, but the condition by exercise interaction for both was not significant (p > 0.05); only within-condition post hoc changes differed.
practicalImplications: A single 6 mg afternoon dose did not improve running time to exhaustion in this group, so it should not be used for performance. Lower post-exercise muscle-damage markers suggest a possible recovery effect that needs testing over several days before staff act on it.
athleteDev: Melatonin did not change running time to exhaustion in this study, so it cannot be recommended to improve performance. The lower CK, LDH and MDA after one session are an acute finding and need multi-day replication.
rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It used healthy players without injury and measured no injury, rehabilitation or return-to-play outcome.

citation: Reis CEG, Loureiro LMR, Roschel H, da Costa THM. Effects of pre-sleep protein consumption on muscle-related outcomes - a systematic review. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2020.
abstract: Nine clinical trials were reviewed for the acute effects of pre-sleep protein on overnight muscle protein synthesis and the chronic effects on muscle mass and strength. Roughly 20 to 40 g of casein about 30 minutes before sleep raised overnight protein synthesis, and pre-sleep protein augmented resistance-training gains in young but not older men, with the caveat that protein intake was often unmatched.
tldr: In healthy adults, about 20 to 40 g of casein before sleep raised overnight muscle protein synthesis. Evidence that it adds to muscle size or strength over 10 to 12 weeks is limited, mostly to one young-men trial in which total protein intake was not matched.
methods: Systematic search of PubMed, ScienceDirect and Web of Science (December 2019, updated June 2020) following PRISMA, with two independent screeners and a third author for disagreements. Eligible studies were human clinical trials in apparently healthy adults or older adults comparing pre-sleep protein with placebo, carbohydrate or water, reporting overnight muscle protein synthesis or chronic changes in muscle mass or strength. Data were summarized in tables, with protein synthesis rates converted to common units; no pooled meta-analysis was performed.
findings: Acute: casein raised whole-body protein synthesis overnight in young men after evening resistance exercise (for example 41.5 vs 32.8 umol/kg/h in Res et al., p < 0.01) and in older men without exercise (Groen et al. +47.6%, p < 0.01; Kouw et al. +18.9%, p < 0.05). Fractional synthesis rose in both older-men studies but in only one of three young-men studies (Res et al., p = 0.05). Chronic: in young men on 12 weeks of resistance training, pre-sleep protein produced larger changes in quadriceps cross-sectional area (8.4 vs 4.8 cm2, p < 0.05), type II fiber area and strength (164 vs 130 kg, p < 0.01), but protein intake was about 1.9 vs 1.3 g/kg/day; with endurance training one study found greater whole-body lean mass gain (1.5 vs 0.4 kg, p < 0.01) and another no difference (p = 0.43), and in older men on resistance training muscle outcomes did not differ.
limitations: Nine trials with small samples, and the chronic trials did not match total daily protein between groups, so timing cannot be separated from total intake. The Abstract and Conclusions say pre-sleep protein improves protein synthesis, while the Discussion warns that these acute tracer measures may not translate to muscle mass. The review has no pooled estimate, the search used three databases with keyword terms only, and two of the chronic trials are endurance training studies rather than resistance training.
practicalImplications: A pre-sleep casein dose of about 20 to 40 g is supported for raising overnight protein synthesis in young adults after evening resistance exercise. Staff should present it as a way to raise total daily protein, because the chronic gains come from one trial in which the protein group also ate more protein overall.
athleteDev: Pre-sleep casein increased overnight muscle protein synthesis after evening resistance exercise in young men, but chronic muscle and strength gains rest on one trial with unmatched protein intake. The outcomes were muscle size and strength rather than sport performance.
rtp: This review does not inform return-to-sport decisions because it included apparently healthy or older adults and no injured participants or rehabilitation outcomes.

citation: Jakubowski JS, Wong EPT, Nunes EA, et al. Equivalent Hypertrophy and Strength Gains in A-Hydroxy-A-Methylbutyrate- or Leucine-supplemented Men. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2019;51(1):65-74.
abstract: This randomized, double-blind trial compared whey protein with HMB-calcium against whey protein with leucine during 12 weeks of periodized resistance training in young men. Both groups gained fat- and bone-free mass, muscle size, strength and power, and the authors found no differences between the two supplements. The authors conclude that HMB added to whey was no more effective than leucine added to whey.
tldr: In recreationally trained young men on a 12-week periodized program, whey with HMB produced the same gains in lean mass, muscle size, strength and power as whey with leucine. HMB does not add to a leucine-containing protein supplement in this setting.
methods: Thirty recreationally trained men were recruited and 26 completed the trial (one injured in training, one injured outside the study, one relocated, one non-adherent). Participants took twice-daily whey protein (25 g) plus 1.5 g HMB-calcium or whey protein plus 1.5 g leucine during an 8-week periodized phase, a 2-week overreaching phase and a 2-week taper. Outcomes were DXA fat- and bone-free mass, ultrasound muscle thickness and cross-sectional area, muscle fiber size, 1-RM strength, Wingate and Optojump power, blood hormones and creatine kinase.
findings: Fat- and bone-free mass rose in both groups (2.3 +/- 1.2 kg with HMB, 2.6 +/- 1.9 kg with leucine; P = 0.59), and muscle thickness (5% each) and cross-sectional area (2.2 vs 2.3 cm2) increased by similar amounts. Total 1-RM strength increased by 70 +/- 21 kg with HMB and 80 +/- 40 kg with leucine (P = 0.41), and peak Wingate power rose in both groups with no between-group difference (P = 0.39). Hormones and CK did not differ between groups at any phase. During overreaching (weeks 8 to 10), peak power fell by 39 +/- 74 W with HMB versus a change of 18 +/- 51 W with leucine, a significant group-by-time interaction (P = 0.03) that the abstract does not report.
limitations: There was no non-supplemented control group, and HMB dosing and timing differed slightly from the recommended 1 g three times daily before exercise. The abstract states no group differences in mass and strength but omits the larger peak-power decline with HMB during overreaching (P = 0.03) reported in the results. Figure 2 lists 12 leucine participants for muscle thickness while the methods report 13 per group, and the authors could not explain why their fat-free mass gains were 3 to 3.7 times smaller than earlier HMB trials using the same program.
practicalImplications: For resistance-trained young men who already take whey protein, this trial gives no reason to add HMB in place of leucine for muscle or strength gains over 12 weeks. The study does not test HMB against no supplement, so it cannot show whether HMB has any benefit on its own.
