athleteDev: Within a periodized program with adequate protein, HMB-calcium added to whey gave no greater gains in lean mass, muscle size, strength or power than leucine added to whey in trained non-athlete men. The single group-by-time difference, a larger peak-power decline with HMB during overreaching, comes from one small trial and needs confirmation before it informs load planning.
rtp: Not applicable to return to sport. The trial enrolled healthy recreational exercisers, so it cannot inform rehabilitation, return-to-play or load-progression decisions after injury.

citation: Estevan Navarro P, González-Díaz C, García Pérez R, Gil-Izquierdo A, García CJ, Giménez-Monzo D, et al. Ergogenic and Physiological Effects of Sports Supplements: Implications for Advertising and Consumer Information. Nutrients. 2025;17:2706.
abstract: This review summarizes the ergogenic and physiological effects of six Australian Institute of Sport category A sports supplements, drawing on position statements and systematic reviews with meta-analyses. It also examines how these supplements are regulated and marketed in Europe. The authors conclude that the evidence is strong for several supplements, that only caffeine and creatine have authorized health claims, and that regulation and labeling need updating.
tldr: Caffeine, creatine, beta-alanine, nitrates, sodium bicarbonate and glycerol have dose and protocol patterns that expert bodies largely agree on. Only caffeine and creatine have EFSA-authorized health claims, so marketing for the others should be checked against the evidence. Use the dose tables as reference points, adjusted for the athlete and event.
methods: The authors compiled sport, protocol, dose and reported effects for six AIS category A supplements from position or consensus statements (from 2015 onward) and systematic reviews with meta-analyses found with a PubMed keyword search and meta-analysis filter, prioritizing those from the last 2 years. Two reviewers extracted data independently with a predefined template, and a third resolved disagreements. The authors call it a narrative review that did not follow PRISMA or register a protocol.
findings: Caffeine (3-6 mg/kg, about 60 minutes before exercise) and creatine (loading of 20-30 g/day or 0.3 g/kg for 5-7 days, or maintenance of 3-5 g/day) are the only supplements with EFSA-authorized health claims. Beta-alanine, nitrates and sodium bicarbonate are described as having evidence-supported ergogenic effects, while glycerol has shown mixed results. Citing earlier label analyses rather than new data, the authors report that only 2.78% of caffeine products fully complied with EFSA criteria and that only 25% of products analyzed partially or fully complied.
limitations: The authors note that the work was not a formal systematic review, that secondary sources can carry publication bias and overrepresent male athletes, and that inter-individual response is not captured. The abstract describes the effects as supported by strong evidence, while the limitations call some effects, such as those of beta-alanine and glycerol, modest and context-dependent. The regulatory analysis covers only Europe, the product-compliance figures come from cited prior studies, and AIS category B supplements are excluded.
practicalImplications: Use the protocol and dose tables as starting references when advising on the six supplements, adjusting for the athlete, event and conditions the authors name. Check any product claim against the authorized EFSA claims, since only caffeine and creatine have them. The authors' labeling and advertising recommendations are proposals and are not established requirements.
athleteDev: The review summarizes doses, timing and sport contexts for caffeine, creatine, beta-alanine, nitrates, sodium bicarbonate and glycerol. It notes that caffeine response depends on individual factors, such as CYP1A2 genotype and time of day, and that sodium bicarbonate has gastrointestinal side effects. The effects of individual supplements in a specific sport still need to be confirmed with trials in that context.
rtp: Not applicable to return to sport. The review covers performance and recovery effects in athletes and does not study injured athletes or rehabilitation.

citation: Camera DM. Evaluating the Effects of Increased Protein Intake on Muscle Strength, Hypertrophy and Power Adaptations with Concurrent Training: A Narrative Review. Sports Medicine. 2021.
abstract: Narrative review of protein intake during concurrent resistance and aerobic training, covering muscle protein synthesis, lean mass, strength, and muscle damage and power outcomes.
tldr: Protein above standard intakes raises muscle protein synthesis after a single concurrent session and may add lean mass over long programs. It does not appear to restore the strength or power lost to concurrent training.
methods: Narrative review of acute and chronic studies, organized by outcome: muscle protein synthesis, lean mass and strength over longer programs, and muscle damage and power. No database search or formal selection process is described.
findings: Acute studies show that protein increases myofibrillar protein synthesis after concurrent exercise compared with placebo. Over longer programs, high protein may increase lean mass, but these gains do not consistently translate into more strength, and protein at twice the recommended intake does not reverse force and power decrements.
limitations: No search method is described, so study selection cannot be checked. Most trials are small and short, and few isolate the effect of protein against a resistance-only group. The author notes that running, a common aerobic mode in team sports, has been little studied with protein.
practicalImplications: Athletes doing high-volume concurrent training may gain lean mass from protein above standard intakes, especially in contact sports and pre-season blocks. Protein alone is unlikely to offset strength or power losses, so the review points to recovery time between sessions and power-based training as more important levers.
athleteDev: Protein above standard intakes may add lean mass for team-sport athletes doing concurrent training, but it does not add strength or power beyond that. Plan recovery time between endurance and resistance sessions and keep power-based work in the program.
rtp: The review concerns training adaptation in trained adults, not recovery from injury, so it cannot guide protein or training decisions in return to sport. Its muscle damage evidence is equivocal and does not support protein for faster return after injury.

citation: Peeling P, Binnie MJ, Goods PSR, Sim M, Burke LM. Evidence-Based Supplements for the Enhancement of Athletic Performance. International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism. 2018 (ahead of print).
abstract: Narrative review of performance supplements grouped by strength of evidence: established (caffeine, creatine, nitrate, beta-alanine, sodium bicarbonate), equivocal (sodium citrate, phosphate, carnitine) and developing. For each supplement it summarises the event type, proposed mechanisms and common protocols.
tldr: Caffeine, creatine, nitrate, beta-alanine and sodium bicarbonate have the strongest evidence for performance benefit when used at defined doses and timings. Citrate, phosphate and carnitine remain equivocal, and the developing products need more research before they can be recommended.
methods: Narrative scholarly review. No search strategy, inclusion criteria or appraisal method is described. Evidence is summarised from cited studies and earlier reviews and grouped into established, equivocal and developing categories.
findings: The review describes caffeine at about 3 to 6 mg/kg taken around 60 min before exercise, creatine loading of about 20 g/day for 5 to 7 days followed by a maintenance dose, and beta-alanine at 3.2 to 6.4 g/day for at least 2 to 4 weeks as having consistent benefit in the settings cited. Sodium bicarbonate benefits are mostly seen in efforts of about 60 s, with gastrointestinal upset common. Sodium citrate, phosphate and carnitine are described as equivocal, and polyphenols and N-acetylcysteine are discussed as developing options, mainly for training support and recovery.
limitations: The authors describe no search method, so the selection of studies cannot be verified and the review may favour positive findings. Several claims rest on single studies or small samples. The authors also note that sport-specific evidence is lacking for some supplements, including beta-alanine, and that nitrate evidence for exercise longer than about 40 min is limited.
practicalImplications: Staff should consider only supplements with a strong evidence base, and only after checking that the product is safe, legal and free of contamination risk. Any supplement should be trialled in training before competition use, because individual responses vary. The review frames supplements as an addition to a bespoke, periodised training and nutrition program built mainly on whole foods.
athleteDev: The review supports considering caffeine, creatine, nitrate, beta-alanine and sodium bicarbonate for specific performance demands, using the protocols it describes. Equivocal and developing supplements should be trialled in training first, because the evidence does not establish a performance benefit for them.
rtp: The review does not address injury rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot guide supplement choice during or after return to play.

citation: Roberts MD, Moulding B, Forbes SC, Candow DG. Evidence-based nutritional approaches to enhance exercise adaptations. Current Opinion in Clinical Nutrition and Metabolic Care. 2023;26.
abstract: Opinion review of dietary supplements that support resistance training adaptations or acutely enhance strength-power or endurance performance. It covers protein, creatine monohydrate, caffeine, beetroot juice (nitrate), sodium bicarbonate and beta-alanine, with a summary table of doses and documented benefits.
tldr: Protein, creatine and caffeine have the strongest support for strength, muscle and power outcomes, and caffeine, nitrate, sodium bicarbonate and beta-alanine have the most support for endurance and high-intensity efforts. Most of the evidence comes from male, non-competitive athletes over 6 to 12 weeks, so staff should adapt these protocols with care.
methods: Opinion review. No search strategy, inclusion criteria or appraisal method is described. The authors discuss supplements they consider well documented, drawing on prior meta-analyses, reviews and position stands, and summarise doses in a table.
findings: The authors state that protein intakes above the recommended 0.8 g/kg/day, with animal-based protein favoured, optimise muscle mass gains during resistance training, and that resistance-trained men may need more than 2.0 g/kg/day. Creatine monohydrate (20 g/day for 5 to 7 days, or 3 to 5 g/day) increased lean tissue by 1.1 kg more than placebo with resistance training in a meta-analysis of 35 trials with 1192 participants, and caffeine at 1 to 6 mg/kg taken about 60 min before exercise is described as improving strength, power and endurance (9 to 11 mg/kg may be ergolytic). For endurance and high-intensity work, the authors describe beetroot juice (6 to 8 mmol nitrate), sodium bicarbonate (about 0.3 g/kg 1 to 3 h before exercise) and beta-alanine (4 to 6 g/day for 4 weeks, with benefit possibly for efforts of 1 to 4 min) as beneficial.
limitations: The authors note that most chronic supplementation studies ran for 6 to 12 weeks, that nearly all studies examined non-competitive athletes, and that most data come from male participants. They also state that beta-alanine research has mostly not shown benefit for strength or power, and that the combined effects of these supplements are untested. The review does not describe how studies were selected.
practicalImplications: Protein, creatine and caffeine are the supplements the authors consider best supported for strength and power, with the doses and timing given in their table. For endurance and high-intensity work, nitrate, sodium bicarbonate and beta-alanine are the options described, with the authors noting side effects such as GI upset and paresthesia and suggesting split or multi-day dosing to reduce them. Staff should check the evidence against their own athletes' level and sex, because most of the data come from non-competitive males.
athleteDev: The review supports using the listed supplements as adjuncts to training for the performance demands it describes, with the doses and timing given in its table. It does not establish benefit for competitive female athletes or for athletes at the elite level, so staff should trial protocols in training before using them in competition.
rtp: The review does not address injury rehabilitation or return to sport. It cannot guide supplement use during or after return to play.

citation: Lee JKW, Tan B, Ogden HB, Chapman S, Sawka MN. Exertional heat stroke: nutritional considerations. Exp Physiol. 2022;1-14.
abstract: Narrative review of how nutrition and diet may influence exertional heat stroke (EHS) risk and pathophysiology in athletes, military personnel and workers. It covers carbohydrate, hydration, glutamine, bovine colostrum, antioxidants, probiotics and arginine as possible protective strategies, and ergogenic aids and low energy availability as possible harmful factors, with recommendations for future research.
tldr: Nutrition may influence exertional heat stroke risk. Regular carbohydrate intake during exercise is the one strategy the authors judge to consistently dampen the physiological features of EHS, while other supplements have mixed or limited evidence and some ergogenic aids may add risk.
methods: Narrative review with a conceptual model of the progression from exercise heat stress to EHS (Figure 1), and summary tables of protective strategies (Table 1) and ergogenic aids with possible harmful effects (Table 2). No systematic search method is described. Each nutritional factor is discussed for its effect on modifiable EHS pathways, including intestinal permeability, hydration, cellular thermotolerance and systemic inflammation.
findings: In subclinical exertional-heat studies, carbohydrate at 30 to 90 g per hour during exercise favourably affected intestinal permeability, plasma cytokines and leukocyte function, but did not change the rise in core temperature, and the authors note it could also raise risk by increasing central drive. Euhydration reduced intestinal and blood-brain barrier permeability and acute kidney injury compared with dehydration in the cited studies, yet dehydration was not a contributing factor in 83% of military EHS cases. Glutamine, bovine colostrum, antioxidants, probiotics and arginine gave inconsistent or limited human results, while sodium bicarbonate, oral menthol and dietary nitrate were flagged as possible risk factors and caffeine has no evidence of directly contributing to EHS.
limitations: The review notes that there is no universal definition of EHS and that the main protective candidates have not been directly tested for EHS outcomes in humans. Many protective findings come from rodent heat stroke models or subclinical exercise studies, and results for antioxidants, probiotics and colostrum are inconsistent. No search method is described, and the authors list youths, women, middle-aged and multi-ethnic populations among groups needing investigation.
practicalImplications: Regular carbohydrate intake during prolonged exercise in the heat, within the 30 to 90 g per hour range cited by the authors, is the most consistently supported nutritional measure, but it may also let athletes push harder in the heat. Athletes and workers should begin exercise euhydrated, avoid drinking beyond sweat losses, and avoid alcohol beforehand, since alcohol may increase intestinal permeability and diuresis. Use caution with high-dose glutamine, large carbohydrate doses that cause gastrointestinal distress, and ergogenic aids such as sodium bicarbonate and oral menthol, which may cause dehydration or reduce thermal sensation.
athleteDev: Relevant to staff who plan fueling and hydration for hot training and competition, since the carbohydrate and fluid strategies used for performance are the ones the review links to lower EHS-related strain. The review also flags sodium bicarbonate, oral menthol and nitrate as possible heat-risk factors when used in hot conditions.
rtp: Not a return-to-play study, and it gives no criteria for return to activity. The review notes that EHS can have long-term sequelae and that a recent viral illness may increase susceptibility, which may be relevant to clearance decisions but has not been tested as a clearance criterion.

citation: Ezzat B, Hrabarchuk E, Lemonick M, Rentzeperis F, Kalagara R, Ali M, et al. Effect of Sleep Duration and Concussion History on Neurocognitive Testing Symptoms for Post-injury States. Clin J Sport Med. 2024;00:1-7.
abstract: Retrospective observational study of 5,349 student-athletes aged 12 to 22 who had post-concussion ImPACT and PCSS assessments at urban concussion centers in Colorado and Florida (2009 to 2019). Multivariable linear regression related hours of sleep the night before testing to symptom scores, controlling for age, sex, ADHD, learning disability and number of prior concussions. Less sleep was associated with higher total symptom scores in athletes with and without a prior concussion, and the associations with specific symptoms were mixed.
tldr: In this registry of adolescent athletes, fewer hours of sleep before post-concussion testing went with higher total symptom scores, whether or not the athlete had a prior concussion. Specific symptom associations were inconsistent, so sleep and concussion history should be weighed alongside symptoms rather than used alone.
methods: Retrospective analysis of ImPACT and PCSS registry data, restricted to post-injury assessments. Athletes were grouped by no prior concussion (n = 2,671) or one or more prior concussions (n = 2,678), and sleep was categorized as under 7, 7 to 9, or over 9 hours. Multivariable linear regression tested sleep hours against neurologic, psychiatric and total symptom scores and against individual PCSS symptoms, controlling for age, sex, ADHD, learning disability and prior concussion count.
findings: Total symptom score was negatively associated with sleep hours in athletes without a prior concussion (b = -0.007, 95% CI -0.011 to -0.003; P = 0.0006) and with one (b = -0.009, 95% CI -0.012 to -0.005; P < 0.0001), while neurologic and psychiatric scores were not significantly associated. In Table 4, vomiting and difficulty concentrating were negatively associated with sleep in athletes without a prior concussion; in athletes with a prior concussion, headache, irritability and difficulty concentrating were negatively associated, but light sensitivity, numbness and feeling slowed down were positively associated (more symptoms with more sleep). Athletes without a prior concussion had higher total, neurologic and psychiatric symptom scores than those with one (total 21.5 vs 15.1; P < 0.0001).
limitations: The design is retrospective, sleep is self-reported for the night before testing, and concussion severity was not measured, so causal and clinical inference is limited. The Results text describes headache in the prior-concussion group as worsening with longer sleep despite a negative coefficient, and the Abstract gives a different light-sensitivity estimate (b = 0.10) and a malformed confidence interval for difficulty concentrating; this record uses the Table 4 values. Effect sizes are small, sleep was entered as the dependent variable, and the authors note the mean sleep difference between groups (7.7 vs 7.6 hours) is not clinically significant.
practicalImplications: When recording post-concussion symptoms, also record the night's sleep hours and the number of prior concussions, because both are associated with symptom scores in this study. Read symptom scores with that context rather than in isolation. The study does not show that changing sleep changes symptoms or recovery.
athleteDev: This is not a performance study. The applied point is that sleep hours and concussion history should be recorded alongside baseline or post-injury testing data so that symptom and cognitive scores are read in context.
rtp: The study supports considering sleep duration and concussion history when assessing post-concussion symptoms and planning management, as the authors conclude. It cannot show that longer sleep speeds recovery or that either factor should set return-to-play timing, because the design is retrospective and no return-to-play outcome is reported.

citation: McAllister-Deitrick J, Trbovich AM, Broglio SP, McCrea M, McAllister TW, Kontos AP. Effect of Diagnosed Sleep Disorders on Baseline Concussion Symptom, Cognitive, and Balance Assessments in Collegiate Athletes. Am J Sports Med. 2020;1-9.
abstract: In 666 NCAA student-athletes (333 with a reported diagnosed sleep disorder, 333 matched controls), athletes with a sleep disorder reported higher affective and concussion symptoms at baseline and scored lower on the Standardized Assessment of Concussion, while they had fewer errors on the Balance Error Scoring System. There were no group differences on ImPACT. The authors conclude that clinicians should consider reported sleep disorders when interpreting baseline and post-injury concussion assessments, while noting that the differences are small.
tldr: Among 666 collegiate athletes, those with a reported diagnosed sleep disorder had more baseline symptoms and emotional distress and scored slightly lower on a cognitive screen, but showed no ImPACT differences. The differences are small, so sleep disorder history should be noted when reading baseline and post-injury results.
methods: Cross-sectional study across 30 NCAA institutions in the CARE Consortium. Athletes with a self-reported diagnosed sleep disorder were matched by age, sex, sport and concussion history to controls without one. Baseline BESS, BSI-18, ImPACT, PCSS, SCAT5 and SAC were compared using one-way ANCOVAs adjusted for learning disability, ADHD and migraine history, with Bonferroni correction.
findings: Athletes with a sleep disorder reported higher BSI-18 global severity (4.85 vs 2.30), PCSS (8.84 vs 4.04) and SCAT5 symptom severity (9.46 vs 4.48), with significant ANCOVA results (P < .01). They also had fewer BESS errors (12.93 vs 14.52; P = .003) and lower SAC scores (26.86 vs 27.30; P = .037), and the authors state the SAC difference is under one point. There were no group differences on ImPACT composites, and reported sleep the night before testing did not differ significantly (6.41 vs 6.72 hours; P = .087).
limitations: The design is cross-sectional, so the associations cannot be read causally, and sleep disorder type, treatment and onset were not recorded. ImPACT data were available for 148 of 333 sleep-disorder athletes but 273 of 333 controls, so the null ImPACT result rests on unequal subsets. Effect sizes were small, the BESS result runs against the symptom findings and the authors call it anomalous, and the group differences in learning disability, ADHD and migraine history may influence the results.
practicalImplications: When an athlete has a reported diagnosed sleep disorder, record it alongside baseline results and note that symptom scores such as the PCSS, SCAT5 and BSI-18 may be higher at baseline. Compare post-injury symptoms with that athlete's own baseline rather than with a norm alone. Take learning disability, ADHD and migraine history at the same time, since they were also more common in the sleep-disorder group.
athleteDev: The paper concerns baseline testing rather than training or performance. It does not measure athletic performance, and its balance result (fewer BESS errors in athletes with diagnosed sleep disorders) was unexpected, so it should not be used to judge balance or training status.
rtp: The study measures baseline performance only and does not track recovery or return-to-play decisions. The authors suggest baseline results and sleep disorder history may influence return-to-play and return-to-learning decisions, but the study cannot show how sleep disorders change return-to-play timing.

citation: Caccese JB, Best C, Lamond LC, DiFabio M, Kaminski TW, Watson D, et al. Effects of Repetitive Head Impacts on a Concussion Assessment Battery. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2019 (published ahead of print).
abstract: Prospective study of 38 collegiate football and women's soccer players who completed a concussion assessment battery before and after one season, with head impacts recorded across the season. Few measures changed in a clinically meaningful way; the few significant associations were between high-magnitude impacts (above 98 g) and poorer visual memory, tandem gait and King-Devick performance.
tldr: Across one collegiate season, repetitive head impacts were not linked to clinically meaningful change on a concussion battery. A few exploratory associations with high-magnitude impacts were found, and these need confirmation before anyone acts on them.
methods: Pre-season and post-season testing of tandem gait, SAC, BESS, King-Devick, clinical reaction time and ImPACT composites in 15 male football and 23 women's soccer players, with impacts recorded by the HITS (football) or SIM (soccer) system. Direct-entry linear regressions tested impact exposure against change in each measure, with a group-by-time MANOVA; significance was set at P < 0.05 with no correction for multiple comparisons.
findings: Among women's soccer players, more impacts above 98 g predicted worse Visual Memory (R2 = 0.670, P = 0.002) and Tandem Gait (R2 = 0.636, P = 0.029); among football players, more impacts above 98 g predicted worse King-Devick time (R2 = 0.756, P = 0.013). Overall time effect was significant (P = 0.006), and most measures improved from pre- to post-season in both groups, with Tandem Gait and King-Devick improving more in women's soccer than football (P = 0.001 and 0.048).
limitations: There was no non-contact control group, and the two sports used different accelerometer systems, so impact magnitudes cannot be compared across sports. The authors ran 30 regression analyses without correction (Bonferroni would give P = 0.002), the football sample was 15 players, and impacts above 98 g were rare (mean 0.2, SD 0.4 per player in women's soccer and 1.1, SD 1.0 in football), so the significant associations rest on very few high-magnitude impacts. The authors state that the battery's learning effects may explain the post-season improvements.
practicalImplications: This study does not support changing concussion screening on the basis of season-long impact counts, because the only significant links were exploratory and the battery showed no clinically meaningful change. Staff tracking head impacts may note that high-magnitude impacts, rather than total exposure, were the variable linked to the few worse scores, and test this in a larger cohort with a control group before acting on it.
athleteDev: The paper gives no basis for changing training or performance programming. Season-long head impact exposure produced few significant associations with the concussion battery, and none that the authors call clinically meaningful.
rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-play decisions after a concussion. It tested athletes medically cleared for full participation who had no concussion in the prior 60 days, so the results do not apply to athletes after a diagnosed injury.

citation: Hunzinger KJ, Caccese JB, Mannix R, Meehan WP, Hafer JF, Swanik CB, et al. Effects of contact/collision sport history on gait in early to mid-adulthood. Journal of Sport and Health Science. 2022 (article in press).
abstract: Repetitive head impacts from contact and collision sports may affect later brain health, but evidence on gait in early and mid-adulthood is limited. This study compared single-task and dual-task gait in 113 adults across four groups, including former rugby players with prolonged head impact exposure. The authors report no significant group differences in gait after adjustment, and no prediction of gait from contact-sport career duration.
tldr: In mostly young, physically active adults, past contact-sport participation, including prolonged rugby, was not linked to differences in walking speed, stride length or double support. Career duration did not predict gait, but the study was small and cross-sectional.
methods: Participants were non-athletes who were not active, active non-contact athletes, active former high-risk contact-sport athletes, and active former rugby players with prolonged repetitive head impact exposure. Gait speed, stride length and double support were measured with three inertial sensors during single-task walking and walking with a cognitive task, and dual-task cost was calculated. Groups were compared with analysis of covariance adjusted for age, sex, concussion history and BMI, and career duration was tested with regression in the two contact-sport groups.
findings: After adjustment, no group differences reached significance for any single-task, dual-task or dual-task cost gait variable (all P > 0.05). Adjusted single-task gait speed ranged from 1.04 m/s in former rugby players to 1.12 m/s in non-contact athletes. Career duration did not significantly predict gait in the contact-sport groups; one single-task double support model was significant overall (P = 0.009), but career duration did not add to it (P = 0.058).
limitations: The sample was small (27 to 29 per group) and mostly under 50, with sex composition that differed considerably across groups (not statistically significant, adjusted for), career duration as a crude proxy for head impact exposure, and self-reported yes or no physical activity; survivor or volunteer bias is possible. The Table 3 footnote says there were significant group differences, which conflicts with the Results and abstract (all P > 0.05). The abstract conclusion generalizes to neurobehavioral function and the Conclusion refers to postural control, although only gait was measured, and the study did not include older or inactive former players.
practicalImplications: For physically active adults in early to mid-adulthood, this study does not show that past contact-sport participation changes walking or dual-task gait. Staff should not use these null results to rule out later effects, especially in older or inactive former players.
athleteDev: The study measured walking and dual-task gait, not sport performance, so it gives no basis for changing training loads or performance plans for current athletes. Its relevance is to neurobehavioral screening of former players.
rtp: The study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It excluded participants with a concussion in the prior 6 months and did not test athletes returning after concussion or injury.

citation: Tan XR, Stephenson MC, Alhadad SB, Loh KWZ, Soong TW, Lee JKW, et al. Elevated brain temperature under severe heat exposure impairs cortical motor activity and executive function. Journal of Sport and Health Science. 2023. Article in press.
abstract: Eleven healthy males were studied with MRI at rest and after four conditions: exertional hyperthermia, passive hyperthermia, exertional hyperthermia with blended ice ingestion, and a seated control. Brain temperature was measured by MR spectroscopy, with cerebral perfusion, motor task activation and Stroop task activation also assessed.
tldr: In healthy men, severe heat raised brain temperature and reduced motor cortex activity during a plantarflexion task, and passive heating reduced Stroop accuracy. Ice slurry ingestion lessened the rise in core and brain temperature, but the study is small and laboratory-based and did not measure sport performance.
methods: Crossover design with 11 males (VO2peak 59 mL/kg/min). Each completed a familiarisation session and then four trials at least 7 days apart. Scans before and after each trial measured brain temperature by MR spectroscopy, cerebral blood flow by ASL, motor cortex BOLD during plantarflexion at 60% and 80% maximal voluntary contraction, and BOLD during a Stroop task.
findings: Resting brain temperature was about 0.6 C higher than rectal temperature (37.3 vs 36.7 C) and rose to match rectal temperature after exertional heating, but stayed lower than rectal temperature after passive heating. Left precentral BOLD activity fell after exertional (P = .009) and passive (P = .006) heating but not after ice ingestion, and global grey matter perfusion fell after passive heating (P = .016). Stroop reaction times were faster after the exercise trials, while overall Stroop accuracy fell only after passive heating (P = .017).
limitations: Rectal temperature could not be held above 38.5 C during scans, and sweat losses were under 3% of body mass. The sample was small (n=11), all were healthy young males not described as athletes, and the trials were single acute exposures in a laboratory.
practicalImplications: Severe heat reduced motor cortex activity during a high-force plantarflexion task, and passive heating reduced Stroop accuracy. Ice slurry before and during exercise lowered rectal temperature and the left precentral activity drop was not seen in that trial. Whether these brain changes affect sport performance was not tested, and the sample was not athletes.
athleteDev: The findings suggest pre-exercise and in-exercise cooling may protect neural function under heat stress, but sport performance was not measured. Cooling should be tested in sport settings before it is planned as a performance strategy.
rtp: The study tested healthy volunteers, not injured players, and says nothing about return to sport after heat illness.

citation: Caccese JB, Iverson GL, Cameron KL, Houston MN, McGinty GT, Jackson JC, et al. Estimated Age of First Exposure to Contact Sports Is Not Associated with Greater Symptoms or Worse Cognitive Functioning in Male U.S. Service Academy Athletes. Journal of Neurotrauma. 2020;37:334-339.
abstract: This cross-sectional study examined whether estimated age of first exposure to contact sport was associated with pre-season ImPACT neurocognitive scores and symptom ratings in male service academy NCAA athletes. No association was found between early exposure, contact sport participation and cognitive or symptom outcomes. Learning accommodation history was linked to lower visual motor speed, and older age to faster reaction time and lower symptom severity.
tldr: In male collegiate athletes at US service academies, starting a contact sport before age 12 was not linked to lower baseline cognitive scores or higher symptom ratings. This is a single-time-point study, so it does not show that early exposure is harmless over a lifetime.
methods: Pre-season ImPACT baseline tests were collected from 891 male cadets, and 889 were analyzed for cognitive scores (826 for symptoms). Participants were split into contact (lacrosse, wrestling, ice hockey, soccer, rugby) and non-contact sports, and each group into estimated age of first exposure below or at least 12 years. Generalized linear models tested group, exposure, their interaction and covariates for learning accommodation, concussion history and age.
findings: The group-by-exposure interaction was not significant for verbal memory (P = 0.788), visual memory (P = 0.100), visual motor speed (P = 0.780), reaction time (P = 0.955) or symptom severity (P = 0.090). Learning accommodation history was associated with lower visual motor speed (B = -2.97, P = 0.013). Older age was associated with faster reaction time (P = 0.036) and lower symptom severity (P = 0.019).
limitations: Age of first exposure was estimated from self-reported years of participation and assumed continuous, the design is cross-sectional, and only men were studied. The authors note ImPACT and symptom reporting may be too insensitive to detect small differences and that pre-season under-reporting of symptoms is possible. The abstract and methods state N = 891, but the subgroup and sport counts sum to 889, which is the analyzed sample (826 for symptoms); one author reports research funding from ImPACT Applications.
practicalImplications: This cross-sectional result does not support using an early contact-sport start age to flag collegiate male athletes for lower baseline cognitive scores or higher symptom ratings. Learning accommodation history (a small subgroup) was linked to lower visual motor speed, which supports recording it when interpreting baseline ImPACT scores.
athleteDev: The study does not show that early contact-sport start age changes baseline cognition in these athletes, so start age should not be used alone to set cognitive expectations. It does not test whether exposure affects cognition or symptoms later in life.
rtp: Not applicable to return to sport. The study used pre-season baseline testing only, and it did not assess athletes after a concussion or track recovery over time.

citation: Willer BS, Tiso M, Haider MN, Hinds AL, Baker JG, Miecznikowski JC, et al. Evaluation of Executive Function and Mental Health in Retired Contact Sport Athletes. J Head Trauma Rehabil. 2018:E1-E7.
abstract: Comparison of 21 retired professional NFL and NHL players with 21 age-matched noncontact sport athletes on self-report, informant report, neuropsychological tests, and mood and personality measures.
tldr: Retired professional contact sport athletes reported some executive function problems, but objective tests and spouse reports showed no differences from controls. They did have more anxiety, which deserves follow-up.
methods: Case-control design. Executive function was measured with the BRIEF-A (self and spouse report), the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test, D-KEFS, Trail Making, digit span, list learning, verbal fluency and digit symbol. Mood and personality were measured with the BDI, BAI and PID-5. Group comparisons used unequal-variance t tests with Cohen's d.
findings: Players rated themselves more impaired on working memory and initiation subscales than controls, but spouse reports and objective executive tests showed no significant differences. Raw depression scores were higher in players (BDI 10.2 vs 3.8, P=.004), though within the normal range, and 7 of 21 players versus 0 of 21 controls met the anxiety threshold. Psychoticism was higher in players, driven by the unusual beliefs and experiences facet, and remained within norms.
limitations: Small sample of 21 per group, with volunteers who said worry about their mental health was a main reason for joining. No formal effort testing was done. The controls were endurance-trained noncontact athletes whom the authors describe as a superior aging population, and they scored below norms on psychoticism, which inflates some group differences.
practicalImplications: Clinicians seeing retired contact sport athletes should screen for anxiety, which was more common in this group, rather than assume broad executive decline. Self-reported working memory or task initiation problems should be checked with objective testing and informant reports.
athleteDev: Retired contact sport athletes in this study reported some working memory and task-initiation problems, but objective tests showed no differences from controls. Anxiety screening may matter more than assuming executive decline.
rtp: The study concerns retired players, not athletes recovering from injury, so it cannot guide return-to-sport or return-to-play decisions.

citation: Lempke LB, Howell DR, Eckner JT, Lynall RC. Examination of Reaction Time Deficits Following Concussion: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Sports Medicine. 2020.
abstract: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 60 studies (9,688 participants) on reaction time after concussion. Acute deficits were medium-to-large in both between-subject and within-subject designs, persisted to 21 to 59 days in the between-subject analysis, and were not significant at 80 to 365 days.
tldr: Reaction time is slower after concussion in the first 3 days, with medium-to-large effects in both study designs. Between-subject deficits lingered to about 59 days, beyond typical clinical recovery, but the clinical meaning of those lingering deficits is not yet established.
methods: PRISMA-guided searches of PubMed, CINAHL and EBSCOhost (January 2002 to March 2019) were screened independently by two reviewers. Hedges' d effects were calculated separately for between-subject (concussed vs control) and within-subject (post-injury vs baseline) designs. Mixed-effects multilevel models with restricted maximum likelihood accounted for nested effects, and moderators were examined in acute effects, with time since injury binned into acute, sub-acute, intermediate and long-term periods.
findings: Acute deficits were D+ = -0.73 (95% CI -0.99 to -0.46) between-subject and -0.75 (95% CI -0.91 to -0.59) within-subject. Between-subject deficits remained at 4 to 17 days (D+ = -0.57) and 21 to 59 days (D+ = -0.32, p = 0.025), with no significant deficit at 80 to 365 days (D+ = 0.35, 95% CI -0.48 to 1.18). Sex (% male) was the only significant between-subject moderator (about -0.017 per 1% male), while RT measure type (simple vs mixed) and computerized platform (ANAM, HeadMinder CRI, ImPACT) differed within-subject; all category estimates were negative, although the ANAM within-subject interval crossed zero (-0.37, 95% CI -0.77 to 0.03).
limitations: Pooled effects were highly heterogeneous, funnel and Q-Q plots showed asymmetry (Egger's test significant), and 22 studies were excluded for lacking numerical data. The within-subject analysis could not examine intermediate or long-term timeframes, and the intermediate-term between-subject result rests on 26 effects. Study quality was moderate (mean Newcastle-Ottawa scores 7.41 and 7.56), and most studies used high school or college athletes or military personnel.
practicalImplications: Reaction time should be one part of a multi-part concussion assessment, since it is slower in the first 3 days after injury and the authors say the method matters less than using reliable, valid tools. The authors state that these findings are not a reason to drop pre-injury baselines, because reaction time is only one component of the battery. Staff should avoid judging concussed athletes only against orthopaedic-injured controls, which the authors suggest may not be the best comparison.
athleteDev: The review does not address training or performance enhancement. Its relevance to performance is the authors' view that reaction time likely has not fully recovered when athletes return to sport, so staff should not assume reaction time has normalised at clearance.
rtp: The review directly addresses recovery timing, reporting that reaction-time deficits extend beyond typical clinical recovery and that reaction time likely has not truly recovered at return to sport. It cannot show when return is safe, because the clinical consequences of lingering deficits are unknown and return-to-play decisions were not studied.

citation: Iverson GL, Gaudet CE, Kissinger-Knox A, Gardner AJ. Examining Whether Loss of Consciousness Is Associated With Worse Performance on the SCAT5 and Slower Clinical Recovery After Concussion in Professional Athletes. Journal of Neurotrauma. 2023;40:2330-2340.
abstract: Video review of head impact events in three National Rugby League seasons identified possible loss of consciousness (LOC) in 99 of 1,706 events (5.8%). In diagnosed concussions, possible LOC was linked to worse Maddocks question scores but not to games missed or time to medical clearance.
tldr: Brief possible loss of consciousness seen on video may be more common than self-report studies suggest, and in diagnosed concussions it was linked to more Maddocks orientation and memory errors. It did not predict games missed or days to medical clearance in this professional league.
methods: Analysis of head impact events from 201 matches per season in the National Rugby League (2017 to 2019), with possible LOC defined from physician removal for suspected LOC plus video signs, or both video signs (no protective action in the fall, unresponsiveness or lying motionless), and duration timed on video by one senior author. Players removed for a Head Injury Assessment completed the SCAT5, including Maddocks questions, the Standardized Assessment of Concussion (SAC) and modified Balance Error Scoring System (mBESS). Groups were compared with chi-square and Mann-Whitney U tests, with odds ratios and Cohen's d as effect sizes and Benjamini-Hochberg correction (alpha 0.01).
findings: In the 255 medically diagnosed concussions, players with possible LOC scored lower on the Maddocks questions (mean 4.0 vs 4.6 of 5, p < 0.01), but did not differ on SAC total score, orientation, memory, concentration, mBESS errors or symptom endorsement. Possible LOC was not associated with missed games (21.5% vs 14.0% missed one or more games, p = 0.164) or days to medical clearance (7.8 vs 7.4 days, p = 0.486). In the full sample of 661 athletes with SCAT5 data, possible LOC was linked to more symptoms and lower SAC and Maddocks scores.
limitations: Possible LOC was judged from video rather than observed by a clinician, and duration was timed by stopwatch with uncertain reliability. The authors note possible circularity, because seeing LOC may raise the expectation of concussion and the SCAT5 is part of the diagnosis, and a single rater coded all videos. In the full sample the abstract lists worse concentration, but Table 2 gives p = 0.03 against the study alpha of 0.01; only 20 possible-LOC cases without a diagnosed concussion had SCAT5 data.
practicalImplications: The authors conclude that concussion should be managed on clinical evaluation and individual needs rather than differently because of LOC, since possible LOC did not predict games missed or days to clearance. Possible LOC was linked to more Maddocks errors on the sideline, although the authors note Maddocks questions have not shown high sensitivity for concussion in prior rugby research. Video signs indicate only possible LOC, because the authors state LOC can usually only be determined definitively by a provider who observes it.
athleteDev: The study concerns concussion assessment rather than training or performance, and it reports no performance outcome. Staff should not use it to judge an athlete's on-field performance after a head impact.
rtp: The study directly addresses return to play: in medically diagnosed concussions, possible LOC was not associated with games missed or days to medical clearance. Because it covers one professional league and relies on video identification, staff should not use this finding alone to shorten or lengthen a return-to-play timeline.

citation: Howell DR, Wingerson MJ, Smulligan KL, Magliato S, Simon S, Wilson JC. Exercising More Than 150 min/wk After Concussion Is Associated With Sleep Quality Improvements. J Head Trauma Rehabil. 2023.
abstract: Prospective observational cohort of adolescents with concussion, who wore a wrist-worn activity tracker between clinic visits about 1 and 5 weeks after injury. Participants who averaged more than 150 min/wk of aerobic exercise showed greater improvement in Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index scores than those who exercised 150 min/wk or less, and weekly exercise volume predicted sleep improvement after adjustment for age and migraine history.
tldr: Adolescents with concussion who averaged more than 150 minutes per week of aerobic exercise between visits showed greater sleep quality improvement than those who exercised less. The study is observational, so it cannot show that the exercise caused the improvement.
methods: Prospective cohort of adolescents aged 10 to 17 years with concussion, first assessed within 18 days of injury (mean 8 days) and again about 5 weeks later. Sleep was measured with the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index and symptoms with the Post-Concussion Symptom Inventory. Exercise was recorded with a wrist-worn activity tracker and grouped at 150 min/wk, and a multivariable regression used weekly exercise volume as a continuous predictor, adjusted for age and migraine history.
findings: Fifteen participants (42%) exercised more than 150 min/wk and 21 exercised 150 min/wk or less. The higher-volume group had greater improvement in PSQI scores (median change 5 [IQR 3, 7] vs 1 [0, 4]; P = .008; Cohen d 0.96), and PSQI scores did not differ significantly between groups at the first visit. Each additional hour of weekly exercise was associated with an expected 0.82-point greater PSQI improvement (95% CI 0.26 to 1.38; P = .005).
limitations: The observational design means causality and direction cannot be determined, because better sleep may also allow more exercise, although the abstract conclusion uses causal wording ('led to'). Sleep was self-reported and not measured objectively, and 7 of 43 enrolled adolescents were excluded for loss to follow-up or not wearing the tracker. The two groups differed in age, sex and migraine history at a trend level (P = .06 to .09), and preexisting conditions were self-reported.
practicalImplications: Counsel adolescents with concussion on both exercise and sleep habits, since higher weekly exercise was associated with better sleep recovery in this cohort. The study points to a volume above 150 min/wk, but it did not test exercise as a treatment, so the figure should be presented as an association and not as a prescription. Track sleep quality alongside symptoms during the subacute phase, since sleep quality changed differently between exercise groups in this cohort and the study measured it separately from symptom severity.
athleteDev: The study does not measure performance and does not show that more than 150 min/wk of aerobic exercise is appropriate for athletic training after concussion. It is only relevant to the return of training volume in that it links higher weekly exercise with better sleep quality in this group.
rtp: Limited direct relevance, since the study does not address return-to-play decisions. Time to symptom resolution did not differ significantly between the groups (23 vs 29 days; P = .31), but sleep quality may be an additional recovery domain to monitor during the subacute phase.

citation: Lievens E, Van de Casteele F, De Block F, Van Vossel K, Vandenbogaerde T, Sandford GN, et al. Estimating Muscle Fiber-Type Composition in Elite Athletes: A Survey on Current Practices and Perceived Merit. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2024 (ahead of print).
abstract: This cross-sectional survey asked 446 high-performance coaches and sport-science or sports-medicine staff how they estimate athletes' muscle fiber-type composition and whether they consider it useful. Most experts relied on experience and jump tests rather than biopsy, and most used the information to individualize training volume and intensity. The authors conclude that some of the estimation methods in use lack scientific validity.
tldr: Many high-performance staff use estimates of muscle fiber-type composition, mostly to individualize training volume and intensity. Most rely on experience, visual inspection and jump tests rather than biopsy, and some of these methods are not supported by validation evidence.
methods: An online questionnaire in four languages was started by 740 people between February and April 2021; 32 athletes and 262 who answered only the first questions were excluded, leaving 446 experts (290 individual-sport, 104 team-sport, 52 both). Items covered demographics, use of MFTC and attitudes to biopsy, the general and sport-specific methods used to estimate MFTC, and the decisions MFTC informs. Differences between sport groups were tested with chi-square, ANOVA and related tests.
findings: About 40% of experts used MFTC assessment for performance optimization, while 50% did not know their athletes' MFTC but would use it if they could assess it, and 10% saw no value in it. Experience or observation was the most common method (65%; 68% of individual-sport vs 51% of team-sport experts, P = .009), and jump tests were second (56%). Among current users, 87% used MFTC to individualize training volume and 84% to individualize training intensity. Fewer than 20% of experts thought their athletes would agree to a muscle biopsy.
limitations: The paper has no separate limitations section. Its discussion notes that the sample was 88.6% male, that the share using biopsy and MRS (13.2% and 11.8%) suggests close academic involvement, that about 7% had no training in exercise physiology, and that results may not generalize to all coaches. Only 60% of people who started the survey were analyzed, and the athletes these experts serve ranged from world class (38.2%) to trained (17.7%).
practicalImplications: Treat experience-based and visual estimates of fiber-type composition as unvalidated when planning athletes' training. The authors report that correlations between jump or strength tests and fiber type are often moderate, so most tests are not adequate estimators of fiber type.
athleteDev: The survey shows that most high-performance users apply fiber-type estimates to individualize training volume and intensity. The paper does not show that these estimates improve training outcomes, so the decision should be tested in the athlete's own monitoring data before it changes the program.
rtp: Not applicable to return to sport. The survey covers training and performance decisions and contains no injury, rehabilitation or return-to-play data.

citation: Mihalik JP, Lynall RC, Wasserman EB, Guskiewicz KM, Marshall SW. Evaluating the "Threshold Theory": Can Head Impact Indicators Help? Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2017;49(2):247-253.
abstract: Analysis of 283,348 head impacts recorded by the Head Impact Telemetry System in 185 Division I football players over eight seasons, with 24 physician-diagnosed concussions. The authors tested how well linear acceleration thresholds from 50 g to 120 g predicted concussion.
tldr: Head impact indicators based on linear acceleration thresholds flagged many impacts that did not cause concussion, so they should not be used alone to diagnose concussion. Positive predictive values were under 2% at every threshold tested.
methods: Prospective data from one Division I program across eight seasons (2004 to 2012). Impacts were matched to physician-diagnosed concussions by time stamp and video review. The authors calculated sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive value at each threshold, and repeated the analysis with concussion counts multiplied by five to allow for unreported cases.
findings: Sensitivity fell from 95.8% at 50 g to 16.7% at 120 g, while specificity rose from 90.4% to 99.6%. Positive predictive value was at most 0.39% on the recorded data and no more than 1.94% after the fivefold adjustment; negative predictive value was 99.9% at all thresholds. In one season with 48 players, up to 2,092 evaluations would have been needed, with one diagnosed concussion.
limitations: Only 24 concussions and one school, so sensitivity and predictive values are imprecise. Some unreported concussions may have been coded as noninjury. Many device thresholds are customizable or unpublished, and the study used HIT System data rather than the devices' own alerts.
practicalImplications: Head impact indicators should not be used alone to diagnose concussion, because most alerts would trigger evaluations in uninjured athletes. Staff can still use sensor data to track repetitive head impacts and to find practices and games with high impact exposure.
athleteDev: Impact sensors can show head-impact load and the practice and game situations that carry high exposure. They should not be used as a stand-alone measure of concussion or to replace the standard assessment.
rtp: The study does not support using head impact thresholds to decide return to play or to clear an athlete after concussion. It evaluated concussion diagnosis, not return-to-sport decisions.

citation: Nair VS, Hanelli FA, Moore C, Goodrum JM, Miller GD, Crouch A, et al. Evaluation of Minimum Reporting Limits to Determine In-Competition Use of Stimulants. Drug Test Anal. 2025;17(6):915-922.
abstract: Controlled administration of amphetamine, methylphenidate and modafinil to volunteers, with paired urine, serum, dried blood spot and oral fluid sampling, to test whether urinary minimum reporting limits can separate in-competition from out-of-competition use.
tldr: A urinary reporting limit of 50 ng/mL cannot reliably separate in-competition from out-of-competition use of these stimulants. Serum and dried blood spots show systemic presence better, but still cannot separate the two periods.
methods: Volunteers took one daily dose for five days, with urine, serum, dried blood spots and oral fluid collected during dosing and for 48 hours afterward. A single-dose group of two men was sampled to 96 hours. Analytes were measured by tandem mass spectrometry after validation for linearity, precision, accuracy and recovery.
findings: In the multidose cohort, urinary concentrations of all target analytes were above 50 ng/mL at 48 hours after the last dose; methylphenidate parent was the exception and fell below the limit about 24 hours after the last dose. After a single dose, urinary amphetamine fell below 50 ng/mL by 72 hours, while modafinil acid stayed above it at 96 hours. Serum and dried blood spots showed detectable amounts at 48 hours in most volunteers, and oral fluid results were hard to interpret because they could not be normalized for hydration and viscosity.
limitations: Volunteers were not athletes, and groups were small (4 to 6 per drug, two in the single-dose group). Dried blood spot results varied between spots in some samples, and oral fluid recovery was not estimated, so no matrix-specific cutoff could be set.
practicalImplications: Anti-doping decisions should not assume that a urine positive for these stimulants reflects in-competition use, because urine stayed above the limit for two days after use. Athletes taking prescribed stimulants near competition need a valid therapeutic use exemption, and the authors suggest reviewing whether these drugs need a different reporting limit or status.
athleteDev: Athletes taking prescribed stimulants can test positive days after their last dose, so a valid therapeutic use exemption matters. The study does not measure performance effects of these doses.
rtp: Not applicable. The study concerns anti-doping detection in volunteers and does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport.

citation: Kintz P, Gheddar L. Evidence of ostarine cross-contamination via sweat in 2 athletes sharing the same neoprene hamstring sleeves. An original situation of drug transfer where the anti-doping rule violation was suspended by the sport authorities. Clin Chim Acta. 2024;559:119688.
abstract: Case report of ostarine transfer from one athlete's neoprene hamstring sleeves to a second athlete, supported by hair, nail and sleeve analysis by tandem mass spectrometry.
tldr: Shared neoprene sleeves were a plausible route for ostarine to reach an athlete's urine. Hair and nail testing were key to the defense, but this single case does not show how common such transfer is.
methods: Case analysis. Ostarine was measured in head hair, fingernail and toenail clippings from both athletes, and in 12 pieces (six per sleeve) of the two hamstring sleeves, using ultra-performance liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry. The authors combined these results with the sport authority's investigation.
findings: Athlete A had urine findings of 0.035 to 0.086 ng/mL, with ostarine not detected in hair or fingernails. Athlete B had ostarine at 190 pg/mg in hair, 780 pg/mg in fingernails and 45 pg/mg in toenails. Ostarine was found in all sleeve samples at 3 to 142 pg/g, and the sport authority accepted drug transfer and gave athlete A no fault or negligence.
limitations: A single case with no controlled exposure, and the no-fault outcome is an authority decision reported by the authors, who also acted for the athlete's defense testing. The role of the medicinal skin cream in transfer is inferred, not measured.
practicalImplications: This case suggests athletes should not share sweat-soaked skin-contact accessories such as sleeves, because a banned substance on them may reach the body through the skin. When an athlete faces a positive test with a very low urine concentration, hair and nail testing can help show whether long-term use is likely.
athleteDev: Shared or sweat-soaked equipment can carry a banned substance and create an anti-doping risk. Athletes should not share sleeves or other skin-contact gear.
rtp: Not applicable. The case concerns contamination and anti-doping rules, not injury care or rehabilitation.

citation: Behrens M, Gube M, Chaabene H, Prieske O, Zenon A, Broscheid KC, et al. Fatigue and Human Performance: An Updated Framework. Sports Med. 2022.
abstract: Narrative review that updates the fatigue framework of Enoka and Duchateau. It separates trait fatigue from motor or cognitive task-induced state fatigue, and defines state fatigue as a decrease in motor or cognitive performance and/or an increased perception of fatigue. It adds cognitive performance fatigue and perceived cognitive fatigue to the taxonomy, adds determinants such as effort perception, affective valence and self-regulation, discusses how performance fatigue and perceived fatigue interact, and proposes research recommendations.
tldr: Task-induced fatigue has two interdependent parts, a drop in motor or cognitive performance and a rise in perceived fatigue, and no single factor determines either. When assessing fatigue, measure objective performance and perceived fatigue together, and account for task type, duration and motivation.
methods: Narrative review. The authors propose a revised taxonomy and framework and discuss the mechanisms of motor and cognitive performance fatigue and perceived fatigue, drawing on studies in healthy, older and clinical populations. The Methods section does not describe a search strategy or study selection process.
findings: In one cited comparison, a 90-minute AX continuous performance test and a 16-minute working-memory dual task both raised perceived cognitive fatigue; the largest visual analogue scale rise was in the individualised dual-task condition, while the AX test produced a larger rise in fatigue and drop in vigor on the Brunel Mood Scale. Perceived cognitive fatigue rose consistently with time on task, whereas cognitive performance declines were often missing when measured on the fatiguing task itself, and a boredom condition produced higher perceived fatigue than an active cognitive task despite lower effort ratings. In motor-cognitive dual-task studies, time to exhaustion in submaximal motor tasks was shorter with a concurrent cognitive task, tended to be shorter under high than low cognitive load, and knee extensor voluntary activation fell more in dual-task than single motor task conditions.
limitations: The review does not state how studies were selected, so the evidence base cannot be checked for completeness. The framework is a conceptual update, and the authors note that the interdependence of performance and perceived fatigue, and the relative weight of each determinant, remain to be quantified. Many cited studies used laboratory tasks or clinical and older-adult samples rather than athletes.
practicalImplications: Measure objective performance and perceived fatigue together when assessing fatigue, because the reviewed studies show perceived fatigue rising even when task performance does not decline. Consider the cognitive load, duration and the person's interest in a task when judging perceived cognitive fatigue. The cited dual-task and prior-cognitive-task studies suggest cognitive demands can shorten time to exhaustion in a motor task, though this evidence comes from laboratory tasks rather than sport.
athleteDev: For performance staff, the framework suggests that sessions which combine physical and cognitive demands may produce fatigue that a physical test alone would miss. The review gives no training prescription and does not test any athlete intervention.
rtp: The framework is not designed to guide return to sport, and it does not provide validated criteria for judging fatigue recovery after injury. Its use in return-to-sport decisions would be an extrapolation beyond the review.

citation: Blemker SS, Brooks SV, Esser KA, Saul KR. Fiber-type traps: revisiting common misconceptions about skeletal muscle fiber types with application to motor control, biomechanics, physiology, and biology. J Appl Physiol. 2024;136:109-121.
abstract: A review that brings together muscle research fields to examine three common fibre-type assumptions: that classification by myosin isoform and by oxidative capacity are equivalent, that fibre cross-sectional area is a surrogate for myosin isoform or oxidative capacity, and that muscle force-generating capacity can be inferred from myosin isoform. The authors find that none of these assumptions is universally valid and warn against generalising fibre-type findings across muscles, species or sex.
tldr: Fibre type, oxidative capacity, fibre size and force are related only loosely and vary by muscle, species and sex. Treat claims that infer fatigue resistance, fibre size or strength from a fibre-type label, or fibre type from imaging, with caution.
methods: Narrative review and perspective by four muscle researchers from biomedical engineering, physiology and mechanical engineering backgrounds. It traces the history of each assumption and discusses histochemical, antibody, imaging and mechanical evidence across species. No search strategy or study selection process is described.
findings: The authors report that myosin heavy chain antibody staining is the best available fibre-typing method but gives no information on metabolic properties, and that type IIX fibres have very low oxidative enzyme activity in humans but moderate or high activity in rats and mice. They report wide overlap in cross-sectional area between fibre types, including in human vastus lateralis, and sex differences such as larger type IIA fibres in males but larger type I fibres in females in one biopsy study. A cited meta-analysis of 61 human fibre studies found type IIa fibres produce about 24% higher specific force than type I, but variation between research groups exceeded variation between fibre types, and whole-muscle force depends on architecture, coordination and motor unit recruitment.
limitations: This is a perspective review without a described search method, so the evidence base cannot be checked for completeness. Much of the evidence is from animal muscle, and the paper does not test any of its points in athletes or training studies.
practicalImplications: When interpreting biopsy, imaging or marketing claims about fibre type, check how fibre type was measured and in which muscle, species and sex, because the authors show these change the result. Do not treat fibre cross-sectional area or imaging measures such as diffusion tensor imaging as a stand-in for fibre type.
athleteDev: The review cautions against predicting an athlete's strength, fatigue resistance or fibre size from a fibre-type label, noting that whole-muscle force depends on architecture, coordination and recruitment as well as fibre type. It gives no training prescription.
rtp: The review does not address injury or return to sport and cannot be used to guide return-to-play decisions.

citation: Banks NF, Berry AC, Rogers EM, Jenkins NDM. Flywheel resistance training promotes unique muscle architectural and performance-related adaptations in young adults. European Journal of Sport Science. 2024;1-14.
abstract: Randomized, non-exercise-controlled 10-week study in 31 physically active young adults comparing volume-matched total-body traditional resistance training (TRT), flywheel resistance training (FWRT) and a habitual-activity control (CON). TRT and FWRT both increased maximal isometric torque and fat-free mass compared with CON. FWRT increased fascicle length, countermovement jump and broad jump relative to CON, while TRT increased pennation angle and produced larger free-weight 1RM gains than FWRT.
tldr: In physically active young adults, 10 weeks of volume-matched flywheel or traditional resistance training gave similar gains in isometric strength and fat-free mass compared with control. Flywheel training also improved fascicle length and jump performance relative to control, while traditional training produced larger free-weight 1RM squat and bench gains.
methods: Thirty-one physically active adults were randomized to TRT, FWRT or CON. Both training groups completed three sessions per week for 10 weeks of a periodized total-body program (squat, bench press, deadlift, row plus assistance work), with load on FWRT prescribed from work in joules. Outcomes were isometric leg extension torque, 1RM free-weight squat and bench, 3-repetition flywheel work, ultrasound muscle size, fascicle length and pennation angle, body composition, and countermovement and broad jump; group by visit mixed linear models were used with Tukey post hoc tests.
findings: Compared with CON, TRT and FWRT both increased maximal isometric torque (TRT +78.6 Nm, p=0.014; FWRT +56.1 Nm, p=0.023) and fat-free mass (TRT +1.72 kg, p=0.008; FWRT +1.44 kg, p=0.032), with no difference between the two training groups. TRT increased free-weight squat 1RM more than FWRT (+43.3 kg, p<0.001) and CON (+79.3 kg), and bench 1RM more than FWRT (+15.6 kg, p<0.001) and CON (+21.8 kg); FWRT improved squat 1RM versus CON (+36.0 kg, p=0.002) but not bench 1RM (p=0.25), and improved flywheel squat and bench 3Wmax versus CON but not versus TRT. FWRT increased fascicle length (+1.33 cm vs CON, p=0.002), countermovement jump (+2.37 cm vs CON, p=0.048) and broad jump (+47.5 cm vs CON, p=0.007), while TRT increased pennation angle more than both CON (+3.01 deg) and FWRT (+1.81 deg); change in fascicle length correlated with change in broad jump (r=0.49, p=0.005) and, not significantly, countermovement jump (r=0.35, p=0.054). Proximal vastus lateralis size increased with TRT only versus CON (+3.71 cm2, p=0.02), and distal vastus lateralis size increased with FWRT only versus CON (+3.29 cm2, p=0.005).
limitations: Groups were small (8 to 12) and the authors state the study was not powered for all comparisons or for sex-specific effects. The direct FWRT versus TRT differences were not significant for distal vastus lateralis size (p=0.41), proximal vastus lateralis size (p=0.056), countermovement jump (p=0.19) or broad jump (p=0.22). Only isometric and flywheel-specific strength were tested; velocity was recorded for FWRT but not TRT, and FWRT received real-time work feedback that may have encouraged faster reps. Participants were physically active rather than trained athletes. The reported 95% CI for the FWRT versus CON isometric torque difference (-27.92 to 140.08 Nm) crosses zero despite p=0.023.
practicalImplications: For physically active young adults on a volume-matched total-body block, flywheel and free-weight training gave similar isometric strength and lean mass gains, so equipment access and preference can guide the choice. If free-weight squat or bench 1RM is the target, traditional training produced larger gains. Flywheel training improved jumps versus control, but its jump advantage over free weights was not statistically significant and should be tested in athletes before it is relied on.
athleteDev: Performance Application: flywheel training matched free-weight training for isometric strength and lean mass gains in physically active young adults, and improved jump performance versus control. Free-weight training gave larger squat and bench 1RM gains. The jump difference between the two training modes was not significant, and the sample was not athletes.
rtp: Not applicable. The study tested healthy, physically active adults and did not assess injury, rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.

citation: Verheul J, Harper D, Robinson MA. Forces experienced at different levels of the musculoskeletal system during horizontal decelerations. Journal of Sports Sciences. 2024. Published online 15 Nov 2024.
abstract: Team-sport athletes performed maximal-effort horizontal decelerations while full-body kinematics and ground reaction forces were recorded. A musculoskeletal model estimated whole-body, joint-level and tissue-level loads across the lower limb. The authors report large external forces, large hip, ankle and knee joint moments and contact forces, and high eccentric force requirements in several muscles, which they suggest helps explain why decelerations are among the most demanding movements in team sports.
tldr: Maximal horizontal decelerations load the hip, ankle and knee heavily, with peak hip and ankle contact forces of about 14 and 24 body weights and high eccentric demand on the tibialis anterior, soleus, quadriceps and gluteal muscles. The authors suggest these patterns may guide deceleration-focused training, but the sample is small and the muscle forces are modelled.
methods: Fifteen recreational team-sport athletes landed one foot on a force platform during the first or second braking step after a maximal sprint, completing at least ten valid trials, with 161 trials analysed. Ten cameras and 76 markers recorded kinematics, and an OpenSim full-body model with 80 muscle-tendon units was scaled to each athlete to estimate joint moments, contact forces and muscle forces by static optimization.
findings: Peak vertical and anteroposterior ground reaction forces were 4.48 plus or minus 1.11 and -1.67 plus or minus 0.27 body weights. Peak hip extension moment was -9.93 plus or minus 4.07 Nm/kg in the first quarter of contact, and mean peak ankle, knee and hip contact forces were 24.49, 12.86 and 13.76 body weights. Nine of twelve muscles acted eccentrically, with the quadriceps lengthening through the whole contact phase and the hamstrings not lengthening; peak tibialis anterior force was 2.95 plus or minus 1.07 body weights. Peak patellar and Achilles tendon forces were 7.42 and 5.58 body weights, which the authors judge no greater than those in common running. The Discussion reports vertical forces about 1.5 to 3 times, and horizontal forces up to about four times, those in accelerated or constant-speed running.
limitations: Only 15 recreational players were tested, and the authors note that sex and athletic experience may change the loading patterns. Muscle and contact forces are estimated with a Hill-type model and static optimization, which does not capture history-dependent muscle behaviour, so tissue loads are model estimates. The abstract states horizontal forces were up to six times those in running, while the Discussion gives up to four times; this summary uses the Discussion figure. Only the first or second braking step after a sprint was analysed.
practicalImplications: The authors suggest that eccentric capacity of the tibialis anterior, soleus and quadriceps, and maximal force capacity of the gluteus maximus, may be relevant for athletes who perform many horizontal decelerations. Their data do not identify which training changes improve deceleration performance, so these are hypotheses to test rather than prescriptions. The tendon forces were not higher than in common running, so decelerations alone do not clearly raise patellar or Achilles tendon load beyond running.
athleteDev: Performance Application: the authors describe horizontal deceleration as a key team-sport performance demand and suggest that the loading data can inform deceleration-specific training. They also state that which force characteristics to target, and whether targeted interventions improve deceleration, remain unresolved.
rtp: Limited application: the athletes were healthy and injury-free for at least six months, so the study does not describe return-to-sport loading. The authors suggest the high loads could contribute to injury risk, including ACL and shank injuries, but this is an inference from modelled loads, not a tested injury outcome, and it cannot guide return-to-sport decisions.

citation: Gabbett TJ, Oetter E. From Tissue to System: What Constitutes an Appropriate Response to Loading? Sports Med. 2024.
abstract: This narrative review describes the typical response of muscle, tendon, bone and cartilage to training load and the time each needs to recover before a similar load. The authors propose a conceptual framework with typical recovery timeframes, from about 30 minutes for cartilage to 48 to 72 hours or more for some high-stress loads. They conclude that load and response data should be interpreted together within an athlete monitoring framework.
tldr: Recovery time varies by tissue, from about 30 minutes for cartilage to 48 to 72 hours or more after high-stress muscle loading, so one rest rule does not fit every tissue. The authors suggest reading training load alongside athlete responses and readiness measures.
methods: Narrative review of PubMed searches using combinations of training, load, tissue, response and recovery terms, with hand-checking of related systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Only English-language, peer-reviewed studies in humans were included. The text describes no formal screening or quality-appraisal process.
findings: The review presents time courses rather than new data. Examples include bone mechanosensitivity falling after about 20 loading cycles and recovering over about 8 hours in a cited animal study, and reactive tendons benefiting from a 48-hour refractory period. A cited study reported that sprint-related performance decrements lasted 48 to 72 hours, and a cited meta-analysis reported tendon stiffness gains with contraction intensities of at least 70% of maximal voluntary contraction or 1RM (effect size 0.90 versus 0.04).
limitations: As a narrative review with no formal selection, appraisal or pooled analysis, the timelines are the authors' synthesis. The 20-cycle bone figure cites an animal study (reference 5), and the authors state that exact recovery durations are not established for some tissues, such as rapid eccentric muscle contractions. The example microcycles are described as illustrations, not tested programs.
practicalImplications: Separate high-stress sessions, such as maximal sprinting or heavy eccentric work, by at least 48 to 72 hours, as the review's example microcycles do. Schedule lower-body strength or plyometric work 4 to 8 hours after running when bone-centric loading is wanted. Interpret load alongside soreness, fatigue and readiness measures rather than judging a session from one number.
athleteDev: Use the review's tissue timelines to sequence high-stress and low-stress sessions, and check readiness data before repeating a high-stress dose. The polarized weekly plans are offered as examples of how to combine low-stress aerobic work with a small number of high-intensity sessions.
rtp: The review gives rehabilitation guidance, such as training around an injured tissue and maintaining systemic loading during unloading.
