It advises that athletes with bone stress injuries be pain-free during daily activity for 5 consecutive days before a return-to-run program, citing one source. It does not test return-to-sport outcomes, so its tissue timelines should not be used as return-to-play clearance criteria.

citation: Leońska-Duniec A, Borczyk M, Korostyński M, Massidda M, Maculewicz E, Cięszczyk P. Genetic variants in myostatin and its receptors promote elite athlete status. BMC Genomics. 2023;24:761.
abstract: Myostatin (MSTN) and its receptors ACVR2A and ACVR2B were sequenced by whole-genome sequencing in 102 elite Polish athletes and 41 controls. Two variants that were relatively common in athletes, MSTN rs11333758 and ACVR2A rs3764955, were then genotyped in 330 athletes and 365 controls. Genotypes were associated with competition level and discipline, most strongly in mixed-sport high-elite athletes, where a gene-gene interaction was also found.
tldr: A small Polish genetic association study reports that some MSTN and ACVR2A genotypes differ between elite athletes and controls, mainly in subgroup analyses. The results are hypothesis-generating and do not support genetic testing for athlete selection.
methods: Whole-genome sequencing of MSTN, ACVR2A and ACVR2B was done in 102 elite athletes (101 male, 1 female; sprint/power n = 53, endurance n = 49) and 41 controls (23 female, 18 male). Two SNPs were then genotyped by TaqMan assay in 330 athletes (endurance 101, mixed-sport 138, sprint/power 91) and 365 non-training students, tested under codominant, dominant, recessive and overdominant models with Bonferroni correction and epistasis tested with the W-test.
findings: No variant differed significantly between all athletes and controls, or between discipline groups, after correction in the sequencing analysis. In genotyping, ACVR2A rs3764955 heterozygotes were less common among elite athletes than controls (overdominant model, corrected p = 0.043), and MSTN rs11333758 deletion homozygotes (-/-) were more common among high-elite athletes (recessive model, OR 4.39, p = 0.004). In mixed-sport high-elite athletes, the MSTN -/- genotype was more common (recessive model, OR 8.53, corrected p = 0.0027), no athlete carried the ACVR2A GC plus MSTN AA combination (controls 28%; Fisher p = 0.005), and the interaction test was significant (p = 0.0057).
limitations: Whole-cohort and discipline-level comparisons were not significant, so the positive results rest on subgroup analyses with small cells; the mixed-sport high-elite group has 17 athletes (Table 6) and some genotype-combination cells hold 0 to 6 athletes. Bonferroni correction was applied for the two genotyped variants only, not for the four genetic models and multiple subgroups, and subgroups were far below the 329 per group from the authors' own sample size calculation. Athletes and controls differ in age (27.8 vs 22 years) and sex composition (25% vs 42% female), sex-specific effects were not tested, and the abstract's statement that CC and GG carriers were more likely to be high-elite rests on a non-significant result (overdominant p = 0.067).
practicalImplications: Do not use these genotypes to select, rank or predict athletes, because the study reports no predictive accuracy and the associations are subgroup-level in one Polish cohort. The paper is best used as a research lead on myostatin pathway variation in elite athletes.
athleteDev: These MSTN and ACVR2A variants should not be used to select or predict athletes. The associations are small subgroup findings that have not been replicated.
rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It examined genotype and competition level in healthy elite athletes and controls, not injury, rehabilitation or recovery outcomes.

citation: Collings TJ, Bourne MN, Barrett RS, Meinders E, Gonçalves BAM, Shield AJ, et al. Gluteal Muscle Forces during Hip-Focused Injury Prevention and Rehabilitation Exercises. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2023;55(4):650-660.
abstract: Eight hip-focused exercises were performed with body weight and with a 12RM load by 14 female footballers, and gluteal muscle forces were estimated with an EMG-informed neuromusculoskeletal model. Exercises were ranked and grouped into four tiers for each gluteal muscle. Loading at 12RM increased peak muscle force for all exercises, and the size of the increase varied by exercise and muscle.
tldr: In 14 female footballers, modelled gluteal forces were ranked across eight hip exercises, and adding a 12RM load raised peak force for each one. The forces are model estimates from a single session, and the study reports no training or injury outcomes.
methods: Eight hip-focused exercises were performed with body weight only and with a 12RM load by 14 female footballers aged 18 to 32. Motion capture, ground reaction forces and surface EMG from 12 muscles were used as inputs to an EMG-informed OpenSim model that estimated gluteus maximus, medius and minimus forces, with exercises grouped into tiers by k-means clustering and loaded versus body weight differences reported with 95% CIs.
findings: Tier 1 exercises for gluteus maximus were loaded split squat (95% CI 495 to 688 N), loaded single-leg RDL (500 to 655 N) and loaded single-leg hip thrust (505 to 640 N). For gluteus medius, the top tier was body weight side plank (338 to 483 N), loaded single-leg squat (278 to 422 N) and loaded single-leg RDL (283 to 405 N), and for gluteus minimus it was loaded single-leg RDL (267 to 389 N) and body weight side plank (272 to 382 N). Adding the 12RM load increased mean peak force for every exercise, by 48 to 150 N for gluteus maximus, 62 to 121 N for gluteus medius and 28 to 88 N for gluteus minimus, and peak force coincided with maximum fiber length in five of seven dynamic exercises.
limitations: The main limitation is the generic musculoskeletal model, whose moment arms come from a male model and were not personalized for female participants. The muscle forces were not validated against in vivo measures; the model was only checked against inverse-dynamics joint moments and surface EMG (median errors under 3.5 N·m and 16%). The sample is 14 female footballers from mixed codes, movement speed was fixed at about 30 degrees per second, and the outputs are model estimates from one session, not training or injury outcomes.
practicalImplications: The modelled tier rankings can help match exercises to the gluteal muscle being targeted, and adding external load raised modelled force for every exercise, although some loaded exercises still produced less force than other body weight exercises. The study does not show that these forces produce strength, hypertrophy or injury-reduction gains, so the rankings guide mechanical loading rather than prescribe a programme.
athleteDev: Use the tier rankings to choose exercises for the gluteal muscle being trained, and load them externally where possible. The study does not show that the forces produce strength or hypertrophy gains, and it was done in 14 female footballers.
rtp: The participants had no current lower-limb injury, and no post-injury data were collected, so the study cannot establish which exercises are safe or effective in rehabilitation. The authors suggest the rankings may inform rehabilitation goals, which would need to be tested in injured patients.

citation: Yoshida R, Sato S, Kasahara K, Murakami Y, Murakoshi F, Aizawa K, et al. Greater effects by performing a small number of eccentric contractions daily than a larger number of them once a week. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2022.
abstract: Thirty-six healthy adults were placed in three groups of 12 for four weeks of maximal eccentric elbow flexor training: one set of six contractions once a week, one set of six on five days a week, or five sets of six once a week. Strength rose significantly only in the five-day group, and muscle thickness rose in both the five-day and once-weekly 30-contraction groups.
tldr: In 36 young adults, only the group doing six maximal eccentric elbow flexor contractions on five days a week gained significant strength, while the group doing the same weekly total in one session did not, and muscle thickness rose in both of those groups. The study is small, non-randomized and limited to the elbow flexors over four weeks.
methods: Thirty-six healthy university students with no regular arm resistance training in the previous six months were placed into three groups of 12 for four weeks: six contractions once a week, six contractions on five days a week, or five sets of six once a week. Maximal isometric, concentric and eccentric elbow flexor torque on an isokinetic dynamometer, and biceps brachii plus brachialis thickness by ultrasound, were measured before and after training and compared among groups with split-plot ANOVA.
findings: Group-by-time interactions were significant for all averaged torque measures, and post hoc tests showed significant increases only in the six-contractions, five-day group: MVC-ISO 9.3 ± 5.5%, MVC-CON 11.1 ± 7.4% and MVC-ECC 13.5 ± 11.5% (d = 0.33 to 0.49). The once-weekly six-contraction and once-weekly 30-contraction groups showed no significant strength change, although the 30-contraction group did the same weekly number of contractions as the five-day group. Muscle thickness increased in the five-day group (10.3 ± 4.4% in Results) and the once-weekly 30-contraction group (8.0 ± 5.8%), with no significant difference between these two groups (p = 0.40).
limitations: Participants were placed into groups with no description of randomization, groups were 12 people each, 24 of the 36 participants were men, and post-training tests were taken 3 to 9 days after the last session because of COVID-19 restrictions. The Results give the five-day thickness change as 10.3 ± 4.4% while the Abstract and Discussion give 10.4%, and thickness change cannot separate hypertrophy from swelling without biopsy or echo-intensity data. The study covered once versus five times a week over four weeks, the elbow flexors only, used an isokinetic dynamometer, and had no neural measures.
practicalImplications: For untrained adults, spreading six maximal eccentric contractions across five days gave strength gains that once-weekly training did not, even with the same weekly total, so the spread of the work over the week may matter. The study does not test athletes or other muscle groups, and maximal eccentric work needs an isokinetic dynamometer or similar device.
athleteDev: Spreading a small number of maximal eccentric contractions across the week raised strength in untrained adults more than the same weekly total done once. The study does not test athletes, sport movements or lower-limb training, so it cannot be applied to athletic performance directly.
rtp: The participants were healthy young adults, and no injured or rehabilitating people were studied. The authors note that maximal eccentric contractions may be unsafe for older or clinical populations, so the study does not establish a rehabilitation or return-to-sport protocol.

citation: Lacome M, Avrillon S, Cholley Y, Simpson BM, Guilhem G, Buchheit M. Hamstring Eccentric Strengthening Program: Does Training Volume Matter? Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2019 (ahead of print).
abstract: Nineteen elite U19 soccer players were randomised to low-volume (one set, 10 repetitions per week) or high-volume (four sets, 40 repetitions per week) eccentric hamstring training, then crossed over during a 15-week in-season period. Knee-flexor eccentric strength and biceps femoris long head and semimembranosus fascicle length were measured with a NordBord and ultrasound at pre, mid and post-training. The authors conclude that low-volume training is as effective as high-volume training for strength and fascicle length in this group.
tldr: In elite youth soccer players, 10 eccentric hamstring repetitions per week gave strength and fascicle-length gains similar to 40 repetitions per week over 6 weeks. The trial was small, had no control group and did not measure injury.
methods: Nineteen U19 academy players were block-randomised into two groups that completed 6 weeks of either low-volume (1 set of 4 Nordic repetitions and 6 stiff-leg deadlifts) or high-volume (4 sets) training, then crossed over after a 1-week break. Eccentric knee-flexor strength was measured with a NordBord, and biceps femoris long head and semimembranosus fascicle lengths with panoramic ultrasound, at pre, mid (week 7) and post (week 15) testing.
findings: Knee-flexor eccentric strength rose about 11% from pre to mid-training in both groups (low volume +11.3%, high volume +11.4%), with biceps femoris long head fascicles about 4.5 to 4.8% longer and semimembranosus fascicles about 4.3 to 6.3% longer. There was no clear between-group difference in the changes. In the second block, strength and biceps femoris long head length did not change substantially, and the Results report a possibly slightly greater semimembranosus change in the high-volume group.
limitations: The sample was small (9 versus 10 players) with no no-training control group, so the study compares two eccentric doses rather than training against none, and both exercises were given together, so their separate effects cannot be determined. Fascicle length was measured with a panoramic ultrasound algorithm the authors say needs validation, and inference used magnitude-based probabilities rather than significance testing. The group baseline values in Table 1 and the phase 1 PRE values in Table 2 appear swapped between groups, and the abstract does not mention the possible phase 2 semimembranosus difference reported in the Results.
practicalImplications: In-season, a 10-repetition weekly eccentric dose can be considered when fixture congestion limits time for high-volume work, because it produced gains similar to the 40-repetition dose in this group. It should not be presented as a proven injury-prevention dose, since injuries were not measured.
athleteDev: Elite youth soccer players in season gained knee-flexor strength and fascicle length from a low weekly eccentric dose, with no clear between-group difference from four times the volume in this small sample. When the high-volume group dropped to 10 repetitions per week, strength and fascicle length did not change substantially over the next 6 weeks, which the authors read as maintenance.
rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It tested healthy players only, so it should not be used to set strength or fascicle-length criteria for clearance.

citation: Lazarczuk SL, Collings TJ, Hams AH, Timmins RG, Shield AJ, Barrett RS, et al. Hamstring Muscle-Tendon Geometric Adaptations to Resistance Training Using the Hip Extension and Nordic Hamstring Exercises. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2024;34:e14728.
abstract: Thirty recreationally active men were randomised to 10 weeks of Nordic exercise, hip extension or control training (10 per group), with MRI of both thighs before and after. Hip extension increased the biceps femoris long head muscle volume-to-interface area ratio, tendon and aponeurosis size changed little, and hamstring muscle size increased in specific regions.
tldr: Ten weeks of Nordic or hip extension training increased hamstring muscle size in specific regions but did little to tendon or aponeurosis size. Hip extension raised the biceps femoris long head muscle-to-aponeurosis ratio, which the authors suggest could affect strain at the musculotendinous junction.
methods: Secondary analysis of a three-arm randomised controlled trial. Thirty recreationally active men were allocated to control, Nordic or hip extension groups (10 each) and trained twice weekly for 10 weeks, with progressive loading. Thigh MRI was acquired about 1 week before and after training, with manual segmentation of muscle, free tendon and aponeurosis, linear mixed models, and statistical parametric mapping for regional cross-sectional area.
findings: Hip extension produced a larger increase in the BFlh muscle volume-to-interface area ratio than the Nordic (mean difference 0.10, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.19, p = 0.03) and control (0.12, 0.03 to 0.22, p = 0.009) groups, while change in BFlh interface area did not differ between groups. Compared with control, semitendinosus cross-sectional area increased in mid-muscle regions with both exercises, and BFlh increased in mid-muscle regions with hip extension. The only significant free tendon difference was a larger semimembranosus increase in the Nordic than the hip extension group (0.06 cm3, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.11), which the authors say was within the standard error of measurement.
limitations: The sample was small, the training dose was a single 10-week programme, and tendon material properties were not measured. MRI slices 10 mm thick could not resolve the proximal semitendinosus tendon. The abstract and Results disagree on the comparator for the semimembranosus free tendon result (control vs hip extension) and on one confidence limit (0.007 vs 0.01), and the Discussion describes BFlh mid-muscle hypertrophy after Nordic training that the regional Results do not show.
practicalImplications: Hip extension increased biceps femoris long head muscle size relative to its aponeurosis interface, whereas the Nordic exercise did not. Because 10 weeks of either exercise produced only limited tendon or aponeurosis change, programmes aiming at tendon adaptation may need longer or higher-strain loading.
athleteDev: Exercise choice changes the ratio between hamstring muscle size and its aponeurosis, and hip extension raised that ratio in this sample. Staff should not assume either exercise builds hamstring tendon or aponeurosis within a 10-week block.
rtp: The sample was uninjured recreationally active men, so the study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. Any injury-risk link through the musculotendinous junction remains a hypothesis.

citation: Presland JD, Opar DA, Williams MD, Hickey JT, Maniar N, Dow CL, et al. Hamstring strength and architectural adaptations following inertial flywheel resistance training. J Sci Med Sport. 2020.
abstract: Twenty recreationally active males completed 6 weeks of flywheel leg-curl training, either conventional (n=10) or with an eccentric bias (n=10), followed by 4 weeks of detraining. The eccentric-bias group showed a 14 +/- 5% increase in biceps femoris long head fascicle length after training, which fell by 13 +/- 4% after detraining. The conventional group showed no change in fascicle length, and neither group showed changes in eccentric or isometric knee flexor strength or rate of force development.
tldr: Eccentrically biased flywheel leg curls lengthened biceps femoris fascicles in 6 weeks, but the gain was lost after 4 weeks without training. Strength did not change in either group.
methods: Randomised, stratified trial with two training groups. The conventional group trained one leg concentrically and eccentrically; the eccentric-bias group trained both legs concentrically but only one leg eccentrically, with the other leg as a within-person control. Fascicle length, pennation angle and muscle thickness were measured by 2D ultrasound weekly, and eccentric Nordic strength, isometric strength and rate of force development were tested before, after training and after detraining.
findings: In the eccentric-bias group, the trained leg's fascicle length rose 14 +/- 5% (p<0.001, d=1.98) and was 1.4 cm longer than the concentric-only leg (95% CI 0.8 to 2.1 cm). This gain reversed by 13 +/- 4% after detraining. The conventional group showed no fascicle change (-0.5 +/- 0.8%). Eccentric strength, isometric strength and rate of force development showed no significant group-by-leg interaction, and pennation angle fell by 1.9 degrees in the eccentric-trained leg relative to the concentric-only leg.
limitations: The sample was 20 recreationally active men with no lower-limb injury in the previous 36 months, and no injury outcome was measured. Eccentric strength was tested bilaterally while training was unilateral, fascicle length was estimated from a 2D extrapolation equation, only the biceps femoris long head was measured, and the two groups used different flywheel inertias (0.05 vs 0.1 kg.m2). Two authors have a patent and commercial or research ties to the NordBord device used for testing.
practicalImplications: Where flywheel leg curls are used, adding an eccentric bias to one leg lengthened biceps femoris fascicles in this sample, while the conventional prescription did not. The gain was lost within 4 weeks without the eccentric stimulus, so the stimulus has to be maintained. The study did not show any strength change or injury effect, and it did not test athletes.
athleteDev: In recreationally active men, eccentrically biased flywheel leg curls changed fascicle length without changing strength or rate of force development. Whether athletes respond the same way is untested.
rtp: The study cannot inform return to sport: it measured no injured athletes, no rehabilitation outcomes and no time to return. It also does not show that fascicle lengthening reduces re-injury risk, only that the two are plausibly linked.

citation: Crawford SK, Sandberg C, Vlisides J, Thompson Q, Mosiman SJ, Heiderscheit BC, et al. Hamstrings muscle architecture and morphology following 6 weeks of an eccentrically-biased Romanian deadlift or Nordic hamstring exercise intervention. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2025. Published ahead of print.
abstract: Thirty-two physically active young adults were randomly assigned to a 6-week eccentrically biased Romanian deadlift or Nordic hamstring exercise programme, followed by 2 weeks of detraining. Biceps femoris long head fascicle length increased by 0.80 cm (9%) and pennation angle decreased by 1.2 degrees (10%) after training, and both returned to near baseline after detraining. Anatomical cross-sectional area of the hamstrings increased by 10% after training and remained elevated after detraining, with no differences between the two exercises on any measure.
tldr: Over six weeks, an eccentrically biased Romanian deadlift and a Nordic hamstring exercise produced similar changes in biceps femoris fascicle length, pennation angle and hamstring cross-sectional area. Fascicle length and pennation angle returned to baseline within two weeks of stopping, while cross-sectional area stayed slightly elevated.
methods: Single-blinded randomised trial. Participants were randomised to Romanian deadlift or Nordic hamstring exercise, trained twice weekly for 6 weeks with matched volume, eccentric tempo and RPE-based loading, and had a 2-week detraining period. Extended-field-of-view ultrasound measured biceps femoris long head fascicle length, pennation angle and muscle thickness at proximal, mid-belly and distal sites, and anatomical cross-sectional area of three hamstring muscles. Linear mixed models with intention-to-treat analysis were used.
findings: Across both groups, fascicle length increased by 0.80 cm (95% CI 0.6 to 1.0) after training and fell by 0.72 cm after detraining, with no difference from baseline at detraining. Pennation angle fell by 1.2 degrees after training. Hamstring cross-sectional area increased by 0.78 cm2 after training and was still 0.35 cm2 above baseline after detraining. No between-group differences were found for fascicle length (p=0.55), pennation angle (p=0.74), muscle thickness (p=0.48) or cross-sectional area (p=0.60). A location-by-group interaction for fascicle length (p=0.01) did not show differences at any individual site.
limitations: The sample was 32 physically active young adults, not defined as athletes, there was no non-training control group, and the study lasted only 6 weeks. The Romanian deadlift included a concentric return phase and so is less eccentric than the Nordic exercise. Some reported confidence intervals do not match their estimates (cross-sectional area decrease after detraining given as -0.43 cm2 [0.10, 0.76]; muscle thickness group difference -0.06 [-0.12, 0.25] cm), so these values should be checked against the final published version.
practicalImplications: Both exercises produced similar fascicle length, pennation angle and cross-sectional area changes in this sample, so either can be used for these adaptations; the study did not compare tolerance or soreness. Fascicle length and pennation angle changes were lost within two weeks of stopping, so the stimulus needs to continue to keep them. The study did not measure injury or strength.
athleteDev: Over six weeks, an eccentrically biased Romanian deadlift or Nordic hamstring exercise produced similar fascicle length, pennation angle and cross-sectional area changes in physically active adults. Muscle thickness did not change with either exercise, and no strength outcome was measured.
rtp: The study cannot inform return to sport. It included no injured participants and no return-to-sport or re-injury outcomes, and it measured only muscle architecture in healthy, physically active adults.

citation: Maeo S, Balshaw TG, Nin DZ, Mc Dermott EJ, Osborne T, Cooper NB, et al. Hamstrings hypertrophy is specific to the training exercise: Nordic hamstring versus lengthened state eccentric training. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2024. Published ahead of print.
abstract: Forty-two healthy young men completed 12 weeks of Nordic hamstring training or lengthened state eccentric training on a weight-stack machine, or served as controls. Lengthened state eccentric training produced larger increases in whole-hamstring and biceps femoris long head muscle volume and in biceps femoris aponeurosis area than Nordic hamstring training, while Nordic hamstring training produced larger increases in the knee flexors that do not extend the hip. Maximum eccentric torque rose by 17% after lengthened state eccentric training, compared with 4% in controls. The authors conclude that lengthened state eccentric training is superior for hamstring hypertrophy.
tldr: Twelve weeks of lengthened state eccentric training on a weight-stack machine grew the biceps femoris more than Nordic hamstring training, while Nordic training grew the knee flexors that do not cross the hip more. Neither sprint performance nor injury was measured.
methods: Participants were allocated to control (1:2 by schedule) or to training groups randomised to lengthened state eccentric training or Nordic hamstring training, for 34 sessions over 12 weeks with progressive load. Axial MRI measured volumes of seven knee flexors and the biceps femoris aponeurosis before and after training, and isometric, concentric and eccentric knee flexion torque were measured in duplicate sessions.
findings: Whole hamstring volume rose 18% after LSET and 11% after NHT, with no change in controls, and the change differed between all three groups (LSET>NHT>CON). BFlh volume rose 19% after LSET and 5% after NHT, and the NHT change in BFlh and semimembranosus did not differ from controls; BFlh aponeurosis area rose 9% after LSET, 3% after NHT and 2% in controls, with only LSET greater than the other groups. Maximum eccentric torque rose 17% after LSET (p=0.002), 11% after NHT (p=0.048) and 4% in controls (p=0.397); only LSET versus controls differed (p=0.009), and LSET versus NHT did not (p=0.237).
limitations: The two regimes differed in equipment, hip position, unilateral versus bilateral eccentric work and the presence of concentric work, so the study did not isolate one variable. Controls were allocated by schedule, not at random, and isometric and concentric torque also rose in controls, suggesting learning effects. Sprint performance and injury were not measured.
practicalImplications: In untrained young men, a machine-based lengthened-state programme grew the biceps femoris more than Nordic training over 12 weeks, while Nordic training grew the knee flexors that do not cross the hip more. Choose the exercise to match the muscle goal, and do not assume either one prevents injury or improves sprinting.
athleteDev: The study shows different hypertrophy patterns between two knee flexor programmes in untrained men. The authors suggest a sprint benefit, but the study did not measure sprinting.
rtp: The study cannot inform return to sport. It included no injured participants and measured no rehabilitation or return-to-play outcomes.

citation: Zurawlew MJ, Mee JA, Walsh NP. Heat acclimation by post-exercise hot water immersion in the morning reduces thermal strain during morning and afternoon exercise-heat-stress. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2018 (ahead of print).
abstract: Ten recreationally active men completed exercise-heat stress tests in the morning and afternoon before and after six days of morning post-exercise hot water immersion. Rest and exercise rectal temperature, heart rate, perceived exertion and thermal sensation fell after heat acclimation, and the reductions did not differ between morning and afternoon tests.
tldr: Six days of hot water immersion after morning exercise lowered core temperature and heart rate during heat stress, in both the morning and afternoon, in recreationally active men. The study does not show the same effect in trained athletes or compare it with exercise heat acclimation.
methods: Controlled laboratory study with 10 recreationally active men, who completed a 40-minute treadmill run at 65% VO2max in a 33 C chamber before and after six consecutive days of post-exercise hot water immersion (40 C, up to 40 minutes, performed 06:30 to 11:00). Exercise-heat tests were run at 09:45 and 14:45 on the same day. Paired t-tests and two-way repeated measures ANOVA were used, with a sample size estimate of eight participants plus dropout allowance.
findings: Heat acclimation reduced resting rectal temperature (P = 0.002), rectal temperature at sweating onset (P = 0.001) and end-exercise rectal temperature (AM -0.47 C, PM -0.43 C; P = 0.001), as well as end-exercise heart rate (P < 0.001), RPE (P = 0.01), thermal sensation (P = 0.005), skin temperature and VO2. There were no heat acclimation by time-of-day interactions, so the changes were similar in morning and afternoon tests. Whole-body sweat rate, RER and plasma volume did not change.
limitations: Small sample of 10 recreationally active men, with no women and no trained athletes. There was no concurrent control group; the comparison control data (thermoneutral immersion) come from an earlier study. The text lists mean RER both as having and as not having a time-of-day main effect, and the authors state that clock-time dependence of exercise heat acclimation still needs testing.
practicalImplications: Post-exercise hot water immersion after morning exercise may be considered as a heat acclimation option when the time of day of future heat exposure is unknown, as in some military or occupational settings. The authors suggest it could be fitted into post-exercise washing routines, but the study did not test this in athletes.
athleteDev: The study does not test sport performance or endurance outcomes. The authors call for trials in highly trained athletes that measure performance and heat illness.
rtp: Not applicable. The study used healthy recreational men and does not address return to sport or heat-related injury.

citation: Pritchard HJ, Barnes MJ, Stewart RJ, Keogh JW, McGuigan MR. Higher vs. Lower Intensity Strength Training Taper: Effects on Neuromuscular Performance. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2018.
abstract: Eleven strength-trained men completed a randomized crossover study with two four-week strength blocks, each followed by a one-week taper with about 70% lower volume and either higher or lower intensity. Countermovement jump height improved after training and again after the taper, isometric mid-thigh pull force improved after training, and there were no significant differences between the two tapers.
tldr: In 11 strength-trained men, jump height kept improving during a one-week taper that cut volume by about 70%, while isometric strength was maintained rather than increased. Higher- and lower-intensity tapers did not differ significantly, so the study does not show that a higher-intensity taper is better.
methods: Randomized crossover study in which 11 strength-trained men completed two four-week standardized strength blocks, each followed by a one-week taper that reduced volume by about 70%, with intensity increased by 5.9% (Taper A) or decreased by 8.5% (Taper B). Countermovement jump, isometric mid-thigh pull and isometric bench press were tested before training, after training and after the taper, with salivary hormones, creatine kinase and the DALDA questionnaire also measured; analysis used two-way repeated-measures ANOVA with effect sizes.
findings: Pooled countermovement jump height rose from 38.0 cm (pre-training) to 39.3 cm (post-training, p = 0.010) and 40.0 cm (post-taper, p = 0.001), with a further post-training to post-taper gain (p = 0.002, pooled ES 0.14). Isometric mid-thigh pull relative peak force rose from 34.7 to 35.9 N/kg after training (p = 0.013) with no significant change across the taper. There were no significant between-taper or time-by-taper effects; within each taper, pre-training to post-taper effect sizes were small for jump height (0.43 higher-intensity, 0.30 lower-intensity) and mid-thigh pull (0.37, higher-intensity only).
limitations: The study had only 11 participants and no untapered control group, so post-taper values reflect training and tapering together. The higher-intensity advantage was a non-significant trend based on within-taper effect sizes, the taper intensity changes (+5.9% and -8.5%) differed from the targets (+5% and -10%), accessory lifts were removed during tapers, and participants could continue their own aerobic or conditioning training. The manuscript is an accepted version without printed volume or page numbers, and dynamic strength was not measured.
practicalImplications: In a one-week strength taper, a volume cut of about 70% with removal of accessory lifts preserved isometric strength and allowed a small further gain in jump height. The authors suggest trialing a slight intensity increase, but no between-taper difference reached statistical significance, so intensity choice is not settled by this study.
athleteDev: In 11 strength-trained men, jump height improved slightly across a one-week taper that cut volume by about 70%, while isometric mid-thigh pull force, which rose during training, was maintained. A slightly higher-intensity taper showed a non-significant trend toward larger gains, and there was no untapered control.
rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It tested strength-trained men in a planned strength taper, with no injury, rehabilitation or return-to-training outcomes.

citation: Bramah C, Mendiguchia J, Dos'Santos T, Morin JB. Exploring the Role of Sprint Biomechanics in Hamstring Strain Injuries: A Current Opinion on Existing Concepts and Evidence. Sports Med. 2023.
abstract: The authors argue that hamstring prevention and rehabilitation have focused on increasing hamstring tolerance to strain while paying little attention to the mechanical strain itself, which sprint mechanics may influence. They review the proposed mechanistic links between sprint running mechanics and hamstring strain, along with the supporting evidence, and identify areas for further research.
tldr: Sprint mechanics such as anterior pelvic tilt, trunk control and over-striding are plausible, partly modifiable contributors to hamstring strain, but the injury evidence for most of them is limited. Staff should treat these as targets for further study, not as proven risk factors.
methods: Current opinion article that reviews functional anatomy, biomechanical modelling, and retrospective and prospective studies on sprint kinematics and hamstring strain injury. No systematic search method is described.
findings: The authors conclude that functional anatomy and modelling studies support a role for sprint mechanics in hamstring tissue strain, but no single biomechanical parameter has been identified as a driver of strain. Anterior pelvic tilt has mixed prospective evidence but a mechanistic link through elastography, and lumbo-pelvic control has supporting prospective and experimental evidence; the links for back-side mechanics, triple extension and lumbar extension are described as theoretical, maximal hip flexion findings conflict across three retrospective studies, and over-striding and forward trunk lean have plausible mechanisms but little injury data. The authors also state that no established in-field method or threshold for normal mechanics exists.
limitations: The review does not describe how its evidence was selected, and the prospective anterior pelvic tilt studies had only four injured players between them, so they are likely underpowered. The authors note that no biomechanical study of lumbar kinematics in hamstring injury exists, and that the evidence for back-side mechanics, triple extension, maximal hip flexion, over-striding and forward lean is conflicting, limited, or theoretical.
practicalImplications: Staff could assess sprint mechanics such as anterior pelvic tilt, trunk control and hip flexion during maximal-speed running as possible modifiable contributors to hamstring strain, alongside eccentric strength work. The authors note that interventions can reduce anterior pelvic tilt during sprinting, but no validated in-field screening method or threshold for normal technique exists, so any target would be provisional.
athleteDev: Sprint technique such as anterior pelvic tilt, trunk control and over-striding could be observed as possible modifiable contributors to hamstring strain in sprint-based training. No validated in-field assessment or threshold for normal technique exists, so any technique target would be provisional.
rtp: The authors suggest that targeting sprint mechanics may help hamstring rehabilitation, but they present this as an area for further study. The review reports no rehabilitation outcomes and sets no return-to-sport criteria, so it should not be used to judge return-to-sport timing or clearance.

citation: Ziedas A, Nasir M, Dubé M, Elagamy N, Gumma J, Shaheen P, et al. Full Return to Sport After Suture-Button Fixation for Syndesmotic Injuries in All Athletes; However, Faster Recovery Was Seen in National Collegiate Athletic Association Football Players Compared with National Football League Players. Arthroscopy, Sports Medicine, and Rehabilitation. 2025.
abstract: This retrospective cohort study included 21 ankles in 7 NCAA and 14 NFL football players treated with suture-button fixation for unstable syndesmotic injuries between 2017 and 2023, using public data. Only players who returned to NCAA or NFL play were included; NCAA players returned sooner, and postinjury game totals per season were similar in both groups.
tldr: In this small public-record series of football players who all returned after suture-button fixation for a syndesmotic ankle injury, NCAA players returned in about 39 days and NFL players in about 190 days. Because non-returners were excluded, the study gives return times for returners, not a return-to-play rate, and it cannot explain the NCAA versus NFL difference.
methods: Retrospective cohort study (Level III). NCAA and NFL players with in-season syndesmotic injuries treated with suture-button fixation were identified from public sources, and each injury was cross-referenced with at least two sources. Players were excluded if the injury or surgery could not be verified, if they had not played a game before the injury, or if they did not return to NCAA or NFL play. Time to first game, games played per season before and after injury, age, BMI and position were compared using t-tests and chi-square or Fisher's exact tests, with P < 0.05 as significant.
findings: All 21 included ankles returned to sport, as required for inclusion. Mean time from surgery to first game was 139.4 ± 123.6 days (range 12 to 427). Time to return was shorter in NCAA players (39.0 ± 20.4 days) than NFL players (189.6 ± 123.2 days; P = 0.005). Postinjury games per season were 8.6 ± 4.6 (NCAA, including later NFL games) and 11.2 ± 5.9 (NFL), P = 0.32. NCAA players were younger (20.0 ± 1.2 versus 27.3 ± 3.6 years, P < 0.001) and had fewer preinjury games per season (8.6 ± 1.7 versus 13.5 ± 2.0, P < 0.001).
limitations: Players who did not return to play were excluded, so the 100% return rate is built into the design and the Discussion's comparisons with return rates after ACL reconstruction are not valid. The sample is small (7 NCAA and 14 NFL players), and injury, surgery and return data came from public reports rather than medical records, so selection and inaccuracy bias are possible. The study did not measure individual performance statistics, PROMs or ankle function scores, did not control for rehabilitation, and the Discussion's claim that the procedure does not compromise athletic performance goes beyond what games played can show.
practicalImplications: This study cannot be used to say how likely a football player is to return after suture-button fixation, because only players who returned were studied. Among those who did return, time to first game ranged from 12 to 427 days and differed by about five months between NCAA and NFL players, so return timelines should be planned individually; the study cannot say which factors caused the difference.
athleteDev: Performance Application is limited. The study counts games played and does not measure sport-specific performance, so it cannot show that the technique preserves training or competitive output.
rtp: For players who do return after suture-button fixation, this series shows a wide range of times to first game (12 to 427 days) and similar games per season after return. It cannot give a return-to-play rate or set return criteria, because non-returners were excluded and rehabilitation, functional testing and PROMs were not recorded.

citation: Rooks LT, Bertò G, Pasquina PF, Broglio SP, McAllister TW, McCrea MA, et al. Factors Associated with Persisting Post-Concussion Symptoms Among Collegiate Athletes and Military Cadets: Findings from the NCAA-DoD CARE Consortium. Sports Medicine. 2025.
abstract: This analysis of 5,073 concussions from the NCAA-DoD CARE Consortium examined which pre-injury and post-injury factors were linked to slow recovery, defined as return to play after more than 29 days. A high early symptom score, three or more prior concussions, female sex and delayed reporting were associated with slower recovery in the adjusted model, while NCAA sport participation (compared with cadets) and injury at practice or competition (compared with outside sport) were associated with lower odds.
tldr: In this large collegiate and cadet concussion dataset, a high early symptom score, three or more prior concussions, female sex and delayed reporting were linked to return to play after more than 29 days. A prognostic model built from these factors missed 91% of athletes with slow recovery.
methods: Analysis of prospectively collected CARE Consortium data from 30 sites (2014 to 2019); nonsport cadets were excluded. Baseline histories and SCAT3 and BSI-18 scores were used with post-injury symptom scores taken within 48 hours. Outcomes were days to return to play (Cox models) and return to play after more than 29 days (PPCS, logistic models). Adjusted odds ratios came from stepwise logistic regression (stepAIC), checked with LASSO, with cadets and outside-of-sport injury as reference categories. Missing data were excluded from each analysis.
findings: Median and mean return to play were 15.2 and 22.2 days, and 891 athletes took more than 29 days. Adjusted odds ratios were: SCAT symptom total above 45 (OR 1.91, 95% CI 1.58 to 2.30), three or more prior concussions (OR 1.80, 1.29 to 2.52), female sex (OR 1.80, 1.53 to 2.13) and delayed reporting (OR 1.42, 1.20 to 1.67). Contact (OR 0.34), limited-contact (0.34) and noncontact sport (0.35) were lower relative to cadets, and injury at practice (0.64) or in competition (0.44) relative to injury outside sport; with cadets removed, noncontact (OR 1.79) and limited-contact (1.32) sport had higher odds than the reference and contact sport lower (0.62). Learning disability with a neurostimulant (unadjusted OR 0.44) and learning disability overall (0.59) were not retained in the adjusted model, and the nine-variable prognostic model had an AUC of 0.72, sensitivity 9% and specificity 98%.
limitations: Mental health, migraine, learning disability, prior concussion and LOC were self-reported, and the BSI-18 and SCAT symptom scores are subjective. Return to play depends on staff decisions and season timing, so it is a weak proxy for symptom resolution, and exposure was not measured. The high-symptom threshold is given as SCAT above 45 in the text but as SCAT 68 or higher in Figures 2 and 3, and the neurostimulant recommendation in the abstract and conclusions rests on unadjusted odds ratios that were removed from the adjusted model.
practicalImplications: A high SCAT symptom score within 48 hours, three or more prior concussions, female sex and delayed reporting can help flag athletes who may need closer follow-up. The prognostic model should not be used to predict individual outcome, since it detected only 9% of athletes with return to play after 29 days, and the study does not support medication decisions.
athleteDev: The study does not address training or performance outcomes. Its results relate to recovery timing after concussion and should not be used to judge performance load.
rtp: The findings can inform cautious return-to-play planning by showing which early factors were linked to longer times, but the study does not test a return protocol. The authors' outcome is clinician-cleared return to play after 29 days, so it cannot set clearance criteria for an individual athlete.

citation: Kajy M, Higginbotham DO, Ball G, Vaidya R. "Fantasy Points" associated with Professional Athlete Performance after Lumbar Discectomy or Microdiscectomy. Spartan Medical Research Journal. 2022;7(1).
abstract: This retrospective series of 38 professional players from the NFL, NBA, NHL and MLB who had a lumbar discectomy or microdiscectomy used fantasy points or WAR to compare performance before and after surgery. Return to play was 82% overall, with NFL players the least likely to return, and the authors report a long-term decline in performance after surgery.
tldr: Most professional players in this public-record series returned to play after a lumbar discectomy, but their fantasy points and WAR tended to fall in the years that followed. The series has no control group, so the decline cannot be attributed to surgery.
methods: Retrospective series of professional players who missed at least one game after a lumbar discectomy or microdiscectomy between 1993 and 2015. Data came from public sites including ESPN, Rotoworld and FanGraphs. Fantasy points (NFL, NBA, NHL) and WAR (MLB) were tabulated per season, with pre- and post-surgery averages compared. Return to play, career length after surgery, time to pre-surgery performance level and recovery time were summarised descriptively, with no statistical testing or control group.
findings: Of 38 players, 31 (82%) returned to play: NFL 9 of 14 (64%), NBA 6 of 7 (86%), NHL 8 of 9 (89%), MLB 7 of 8 (88%). Average recovery time was 6 months (NFL), 2.8 months (NBA), 4.7 months (NHL) and 12 months (MLB). Ten of 14 NFL players (71%) had fewer games played and lower fantasy scores after surgery, as did 4 of 7 NBA players, 4 of 9 NHL players (6 of 9 with lower fantasy value) and 7 of 8 MLB players. Twelve players (31%) improved in the first two years after surgery before declining.
limitations: The sample is small and male-only, has no age-matched controls, and relies on public sources that may be inaccurate; no statistical tests were run, and careers continuing after 2015 were cut short. Table 3 gives one example NFL player's averages (games 14.63 to 13.5, fantasy 73.94 to 43.63), but the Discussion presents these as averages for all players who returned, which the data do not support. The abstract calls the NFL career length (34.8 months) the lowest, but Table 4 shows NHL players lowest at 29 months.
practicalImplications: The study is useful as a description of return-to-play and performance trends in elite players after lumbar discectomy, and it suggests that performance may not return to pre-surgery levels in some players. Staff should not treat the performance decline as a surgical effect, since no controls were used.
athleteDev: The performance metrics in this study are measures of game production, not training outcomes. Staff could use the pattern of post-surgery change to set expectations for playing time, but the study does not address how training should change after surgery.
rtp: The return-to-play rates (82% overall, 64% in NFL players) and recovery times (2.8 to 12 months) in this series can inform expectations for elite players after lumbar discectomy. The study cannot set criteria for return, because the surgical and clinical details that drive clearance were limited and not controlled.

citation: Kellis E, Kekelekis A, Drakonaki EE. Fascia and Muscle Stiffness in Soccer Athletes with and Without Previous Hamstring Injury. J. Funct. Morphol. Kinesiol. 2025;10:48.
abstract: This cross-sectional study compared fascia and muscle stiffness, measured with shear-wave elastography, in 10 soccer players with a previous biceps femoris strain and 13 uninjured players. Active stiffness during submaximal contraction was higher in the injured group, while passive stiffness was similar, and the injured group had lower strength and biceps femoris cross-sectional area.
tldr: Soccer players about four months after a grade II biceps femoris strain had stiffer fascia and muscle than uninjured players, but only during contraction. They were also weaker and had less biceps femoris muscle area.
methods: Cross-sectional study of semi-professional soccer players recruited from eight Greek clubs. Ten players with an MRI or ultrasound-confirmed grade II biceps femoris long head strain within the past year who had returned to play (4 recurrent injuries; mean 34.8 days lost) and 13 age-matched uninjured players were tested. Shear-wave elastography of the semitendinosus and biceps femoris fascia and muscle was measured passively and at 60% MVC at 0, 45 and 90 degrees of knee flexion, with surface EMG and isometric MVC from a hand-held dynamometer. Cross-sectional area was measured in 8 injured and 12 uninjured players, and four-way ANOVA and t-tests were used.
findings: Group effect on SWE modulus averaged across conditions was significant (F1,21 = 4.91, P = 0.038), with the group by condition interaction significant (P = 0.018). Post hoc tests found higher stiffness in the injured group during active contraction only. Injured players had lower MVC at all three angles (for example 93.4 vs 122.8 Nm at 0 degrees) and lower biceps femoris cross-sectional area (13.2 vs 14.6 cm2, P = 0.012). Normalised EMG did not differ between groups (P > 0.05). Reliability of the SWE measures was high (ICC 0.86 to 0.94).
limitations: The sample is small and homogeneous (one sport, one injury grade, one muscle), the groups were matched only on age, and rehabilitation and injury mechanism were not controlled. The cross-sectional design cannot show whether stiffness was caused by the injury or existed before it. The Results text says MVC was greater in the injured group, but Table 3 and the abstract show it was lower, and the text says the semitendinosus was stiffer than the biceps femoris while Table 1 reports ST < BF.
practicalImplications: Players who return to play after a biceps femoris strain may show higher stiffness during active contraction, along with lower strength and muscle area. Staff may want to check strength and muscle size in addition to standard return-to-play measures. The study does not show that treating fascia stiffness reduces re-injury.
athleteDev: The study does not test any training intervention. Injured players had lower knee flexor strength and biceps femoris area, which the authors attribute to atrophy rather than lower activation, but the study cannot show that strength training restores fascia stiffness or performance.
rtp: Injured players in this study, at a mean of about four months after a biceps femoris strain and after returning to play, had higher active fascia and muscle stiffness, lower strength and lower biceps femoris area. The study does not provide return-to-play criteria, and the authors suggest that management may be needed for about six months after injury without evidence that it prevents recurrence.

citation: Zügel M, Maganaris CN, Wilke J, Jurkat-Rott K, Klingler W, Wearing SC, et al. Fascial tissue research in sports medicine: from molecules to tissue adaptation, injury and diagnostics. Br J Sports Med. 2018.
abstract: A consensus statement from the Second International CONNECT Conference and a follow-up expert meeting on fascial tissue in sports medicine. It reviews the fascial system from molecular and cellular responses to mechanical properties, the responses of fascia to exercise, disuse, injury, ageing and inflammation, the methods used to study fascia, and interventions that target fascial tissue in sport and exercise.
tldr: Fascial tissue responds to loading, injury and ageing, but the diagnostic methods for it have limited reliability and validity, and treatment evidence is still incomplete. Use the statement to frame fascia as a tissue to consider in injury and rehabilitation, and treat claims for specific fascia treatments with caution.
methods: Consensus statement developed from the Second International CONNECT Conference (Ulm, Germany, March 2017) and a follow-up meeting of conference speakers and experts. The Methods section does not describe a systematic search or formal consensus procedure.
findings: The authors report that tendon stiffness increases with chronic overloading and decreases with chronic unloading, with adaptations occurring within weeks, and that changes in tendon size and Young's modulus both contribute. They report that injury or overload triggers an inflammatory response that, if prolonged, can produce fibrosis and fatty change, and that resistance exercise is needed to reverse fatty change in chronic muscle conditions. They also report that manual palpation and bioimpedance have limited reliability, and that ultrasound-based stiffness estimates often disagree with in vitro material tests.
limitations: The statement does not describe how the consensus was reached, and only some claims carry an evidence grade (for example, moderate evidence for shockwave therapy and eccentric loading in tendon healing). Much of the mechanistic evidence comes from animal, cadaver or in vitro work, and the authors state that the contribution of myofascial force transmission under in vivo conditions remains to be elucidated.
practicalImplications: Treat fascial stiffness and tissue-change measures as limited in accuracy: the authors advise interpreting clinical soft-tissue data with caution and combining methods while no gold standard exists. They report that resistance exercise is needed to reverse fatty change in chronic muscle conditions, and that anti-inflammatory drugs used for overuse pathologies may impair regeneration and diminish tissue adaptation. Foam rolling may help short-term flexibility and soreness, but manual therapies such as massage, osteopathy and Rolfing are not yet validated.
athleteDev: The statement supports the view that tendons adapt to chronic loading and unloading within weeks, so progressive loading of connective tissue is the relevant mechanism. It gives no dose or programme for athletes, and it reports only short-term flexibility and soreness benefits for foam rolling.
rtp: The statement can support the view that fascial tissue changes after injury, such as fibrosis and fatty infiltration, may persist and affect function. It does not establish a return-to-sport threshold or validated tests for judging fascial recovery.

citation: Evangelidis PE, Shan X, Otsuka S, Yang C, Yamagishi T, Kawakami Y. Fatigue-induced changes in hamstrings' active muscle stiffness: effect of contraction type and implications for strain injuries. Eur J Appl Physiol. 2022.
abstract: The authors examined the effect of a submaximal fatiguing task on hamstring active muscle stiffness, measured by shear wave velocity, and whether contraction type (isometric, concentric or eccentric) changes this effect. Nine healthy males completed 99 submaximal knee flexions in each mode. Shear wave velocity was measured during contraction in the biceps femoris long head, semitendinosus and semimembranosus, and T2 relaxation was measured by MRI before and after the task. Stiffness responses differed by muscle and contraction type, and the authors report preliminary evidence that the biceps femoris long head is more fatigued during eccentric contractions.
tldr: Fatigue changed the stiffness of individual hamstring muscles differently depending on contraction type. In this small study of healthy men, biceps femoris long head stiffness fell after eccentric fatigue, a pattern that may be relevant to why that muscle is injured, but the study did not measure injury.
methods: Within-subject laboratory study. Nine healthy males (age 21.8 +/- 4.2 years) completed one session in each of isometric, concentric and eccentric modes, with 99 contractions at 50% maximal voluntary torque. Shear wave velocity was recorded during contraction for three hamstring muscles, and maximal voluntary torque and T2 MRI were measured before and after the task, with a 48-hour follow-up.
findings: Maximal voluntary torque fell after all three tasks: isometric -18.4%, concentric -33.6% and eccentric -30.9% (pre to post). Average relative torque during the task was lower in concentric (41.9% MVT) than isometric (49.1%) and eccentric (46.5%), while absolute torque was similar. Biceps femoris long head shear wave velocity fell after eccentric fatigue (-0.8 m/s, -7.7%, p < 0.01) and tended to rise after isometric fatigue (+0.4 m/s, +4.5%, p = 0.064). Semitendinosus (-1.1 m/s, -9.0%) and semimembranosus (-0.8 m/s, -8.1%) velocity fell after concentric fatigue. T2 rose after the task and returned to baseline by 48 hours.
limitations: The sample of nine was small and the authors state that they used a more qualitative interpretation of the data. Individual stiffness responses were highly variable, and the ANOVA found no significant pairwise differences between contraction types and no contraction type by muscle interaction, so the contrasts rest on within-condition changes. Relative torque during the task differed between conditions, the task intensity was moderate, and participants were healthy young men without hamstring injury history, with no injury outcomes measured.
practicalImplications: Staff who assess fatigue of the hamstrings may need to test contraction types that match the sport's demands, because the study found different responses by contraction type. Eccentric fatigue was associated with reduced biceps femoris long head stiffness in this sample, which the authors link to strain injury risk. The study does not show that any load management strategy reduces injury.
athleteDev: The study suggests that the same fatiguing work can change hamstring muscles differently depending on contraction type, so fatigue monitoring may need to consider eccentric demands. It does not test a training or recovery intervention, and its participants were healthy young men who were not described as athletes.
rtp: The study does not address return to sport, because it included no injured participants and no return-to-play outcomes. It suggests a possible mechanism that would need testing in injured athletes before it could inform return-to-play decisions.

citation: Beas-Jiménez JD, León Garrigosa A, Doñoro Cuevas P, Álvarez Recio MI, Cofré Bolados C, Alonso JM. Fibrosis and Sports Injuries: Concept and Implications. The GESMUTE-SETRADE Consensus Statement. Orthop J Sports Med. 2024;12(9):23259671241266604.
abstract: Consensus statement by the GESMUTE and SETRADE groups, based on a bibliographic review, that proposes a definition of musculoskeletal fibrosis in sport. The authors define fibrosis as an abnormal accumulation of extracellular matrix, usually a complication of injury, affecting muscles, tendons, ligaments, joint capsules and nerves, which impairs recovery, causes symptoms and can lead to relapse. The statement also lists sport-related entities in which fibrosis may be present and identifies gaps in epidemiology, diagnosis and treatment.
tldr: Fibrosis after sports injury has no agreed definition, and this statement proposes one: an abnormal build-up of extracellular matrix after injury that can impair recovery and cause relapse. Use it as a working definition for clinical discussion, not as a validated diagnostic standard.
methods: Expert consensus by a Spanish working group. The Methods section describes a bibliographic review of existing scientific evidence and consensus on fibrosis in sport; no search strategy or formal consensus procedure is reported.
findings: The authors report that only one tendon study and four muscle studies have examined fibrosis in post-injury scar tissue, with incidence ranging from 29.5% to 78% on MR or ultrasound. They list entities where fibrosis may be accepted in sport, including granulomas, encapsulated hematomas, tendon and ligament scars, and retractile capsulitis. They state that imaging by ultrasound or MR should confirm fibrosis, and that prior drug treatments (indomethacin, losartan, curcumin, chitosan) have shown very poor outcomes.
limitations: This is expert opinion built on a bibliographic review, with no primary data and no validation of the definition. The authors state that the epidemiology, diagnosis and treatment of sport-related fibrosis remain largely unstudied, and that the effects of exercise type and load programming on fibrosis are unclear.
practicalImplications: Staff can use the proposed definition to describe post-injury fibrosis and consider ultrasound or MR to confirm it. The authors' main prevention message is that preventing injury and treating it early and adequately are the most effective measures. No validated treatment for fibrosis is established.
athleteDev: The statement gives no training prescription. For performance staff, its relevance is that fibrosis can persist in muscle, tendon and ligament after injury and can compromise function and regeneration, which the authors link to recurrent injury. It does not show that any training method prevents fibrosis.
rtp: Supports imaging to confirm fibrosis after an injury when a clinician is assessing tissue recovery. It cannot set a return-to-sport threshold, and it does not show that fibrosis changes return-to-play outcomes.

citation: Miyazaki Y, Sugizaki R, Kawasaki M, Nakagawa T, Saho Y, Tateishi T. Fifth metatarsal strain distribution during cutting motions in soccer. Sports Biomechanics. 2023.
abstract: The authors determined fifth metatarsal strain generation during cutting motions in soccer using a finite element foot model. Five collegiate players performed side-step and cross-step cutting while three-dimensional foot kinematics, ground reaction force and plantar pressure were measured, and these were used as boundary conditions for simulations. During side-step cutting, maximum principal strain on the fifth metatarsal correlated with forefoot adduction during stepping out. During cross-step cutting, it correlated with plantar pressure at the distal end of the fifth metatarsal.
tldr: In five collegiate soccer players, a finite element foot model suggests that fifth metatarsal strain in side-step cutting tracks forefoot adduction, while in cross-step cutting it tracks plantar pressure under the distal fifth metatarsal. These are model-based mechanisms that have not been tested for injury prevention in athletes.
methods: Five male collegiate players performed side-step and cross-step cutting on long-pile artificial turf in a laboratory, with motion capture, force plates and insole pressure sensors. Three trials per player were analysed after two outliers were excluded. A CT-based foot model, with fifth metatarsal stiffness assigned from Hounsfield units across ten levels, was driven by each player's measured foot motion and plantar load. Cross-correlation and Kruskal-Wallis tests with Conover post hoc tests compared strain waveforms with plantar pressure in 13 areas and with forefoot adduction angle.
findings: In side-step cutting, forefoot adduction angle had the highest cross-correlation with fifth metatarsal strain (mean 0.965, SD 0.034). Plantar pressure correlations were lower than adduction, highest in Areas 5 and 6 under the first metatarsal and lowest in Areas 10 and 13 under the fifth metatarsal. In cross-step cutting, plantar pressure in Area 10 under the distal fifth metatarsal had the highest correlation (mean 0.971, SD 0.024), while the adduction angle correlation was low. Kruskal-Wallis tests showed differences among the 14 parameters for both steps (p = 1.96 × 10-5 for cross-step; p = 0.013 for side-step).
limitations: The sample was five players, and the finite element model was built from the CT image of one foot rather than each player's own foot. The study used training shoes without studs on one artificial turf, and stud placement, upper design and surface type were not varied. The authors note that wire-element ligaments concentrate stress at attachment points, that tangential loads were distributed in proportion to plantar pressure, and that bone stiffness was derived from CT values without a calibration phantom; validation used cadaver data from the first and second metatarsals and barefoot adduction in one participant.
practicalImplications: The authors propose that for side-step cutting, shoe uppers that limit forefoot bending and insoles or outsoles that reduce pressure under the first metatarsal may reduce strain. For cross-step cutting, they propose reducing pressure under the distal fifth metatarsal. These proposals come from model results and have not been tested in athletes.
athleteDev: Performance staff can see that footwear, insole and surface choices change forefoot plantar load, which the authors link to fifth metatarsal strain in simulation. The paper gives no training or conditioning prescription and does not show that any footwear or insole change lowers fracture rates.
rtp: Relevant to fifth metatarsal fracture mechanisms and prevention. It cannot guide return-to-play decisions after a fracture and does not test whether any footwear or insole change reduces re-injury.

citation: Bill K, Krosshaug T, Kersting UG. Foot strike angle as key predictor of multi-plane knee joint moments in sidestep cutting: implications for ACL injury prevention. Sports Biomechanics. 2025.
abstract: Investigates whether knee joint moments are related to foot strike angle at initial ground contact in pre-planned and unplanned handball sidestep cuts performed by 51 female handball players. Canonical correlation analysis on the three-dimensional knee moment vector field showed a relationship with foot strike angle in both conditions. The authors conclude that single-plane analyses only partly explain this relationship, and that changing foot strike may help reduce multi-plane knee loading linked to ACL injury.
tldr: In female handball players, a more forefoot foot strike angle was associated with knee moment patterns linked to ACL loading during sidestep cuts, most clearly when the three knee moment planes are analysed together. Because these are correlations from unmanipulated cutting, the result supports testing forefoot-strike technique work in prospective studies rather than confirming an injury benefit.
methods: Laboratory study in which 51 high-level female handball players performed at least five valid pre-planned and five unplanned sidestep cuts on a force plate, with a 24-camera motion capture system and full-body marker set. Knee moments were resolved into a three-component vector field over stance, and canonical correlation analysis (statistical parametric mapping) tested its relationship with foot strike angle, followed by post hoc analyses of moment couples and individual components.
findings: Foot strike angle was related to the knee moment vector field in pre-planned cuts during early (0 to 13.2% of stance, p=0.006) and late stance (p=0.029), and in unplanned cuts during early stance (0 to 22.9%, p<0.001) and late stance (p=0.048). The non-sagittal (Mxz) and non-frontal (Myz) moment couples explained most of the early-stance relationship in both conditions. Among individual components, the transverse plane moment (Mz) showed the strongest correlation with foot strike angle (early stance p=0.007 in both conditions), and the authors report that increasing foot strike angle toward a forefoot strike was related to lower internal rotation moments in the peak loading phase, while the abduction moment relationship was not significant.
limitations: No injury data were collected, and the authors state that prospective studies are needed to establish a causal link with injury risk. The study included only female handball players, so generalization to males or other sports is unknown. Foot strike angle was not controlled or manipulated, cutting angles and approach speeds varied, and the authors note that the reasons for larger discrepancies between the vector and single-plane analyses in the unplanned condition are unclear. The study was part of a larger project and the sample size was based on resource constraints rather than a power analysis. The authors consider the late-stance correlations most likely irrelevant to non-contact ACL injury, and the reported late-stance interval for the pre-planned Mz result is printed as '73.8-6.6%', an apparent typo.
practicalImplications: Coaches and clinicians can consider foot strike angle as one technique factor in cutting when assessing knee loading, while recognizing that these are correlations rather than effects of a training intervention. Because single-plane knee moments may understate the multi-plane loading linked to ACL injury, practitioners may need to interpret moment results with a three-dimensional view. Forefoot-strike technique work should be evaluated in intervention studies before it is relied on to reduce injury risk.
athleteDev: Performance Application: foot strike angle in sidestep cutting was linked to knee loading in female handball players. The authors suggest that the possible performance benefits of a forefoot strike, which this study did not measure, may help athletes accept the technique change; the study does not show that changing foot strike improves cutting performance or reduces injury.
rtp: Limited application: the study examined healthy, injury-free players and did not assess athletes returning from ACL or other injury. It cannot support return-to-sport decisions, although it may inform the technique side of later ACL prevention work.

citation: Nurse CA, Lewis CL, Shefelbine SJ. Frontal plane pelvic kinematics during high velocity running: Association with hamstring injury history. Phys Ther Sport. 2023;64:133-139.
abstract: This cross-sectional study compared frontal-plane pelvic motion during sprinting in 22 NCAA Division 1 sprinters and 17 controls who were not Division 1 athletes, using three inertial measurement units on the pelvis. Sprinters with a hamstring injury in the previous two seasons showed greater mediolateral pelvic motion and side-to-side pelvic asymmetry during stance than healthy sprinters. The authors suggest these differences may matter for rehabilitation, and they note the design cannot show whether they caused or resulted from injury.
tldr: In a small study, sprinters with a recent hamstring injury showed more side-to-side pelvic asymmetry and mediolateral motion during stance than healthy sprinters. The authors suggest postural control and stability work may be worth targeting in rehabilitation, but the design cannot show cause.
methods: Sprinters (12 with a hamstring injury in the previous two seasons, 10 healthy) and non-track controls (17, of whom 3 had a previous hamstring injury) each completed three 50 m sprints with three inertial measurement units on the sacrum and both iliac crests, sampled at 128 Hz. Mediolateral motion was the root-mean-square ratio of sacral mediolateral acceleration, and asymmetry was the difference in vertical acceleration between iliac crest sensors during single-leg stance. Groups were compared with a three-way repeated-measures ANOVA (sex, competitive status, injury history) and Cohen's d.
findings: The authors report higher mediolateral motion during stance in previously injured than in healthy sprinters (p = 0.02, d = 0.93) and more mediolateral motion in controls than in sprinters (p = 0.04, d = 0.41), with no significant sex difference. Pelvic asymmetry was higher in previously injured than in healthy sprinters (p < 0.001, d = 1.39), controls showed larger asymmetry than sprinters (p < 0.001, d = 0.25), and most sprinter outliers were previously injured. The p values come from the injury-history and competitive-status factors of a three-way ANOVA (Table 1).
limitations: The study is cross-sectional with small groups, and the authors state that it cannot show whether the differences contributed to or resulted from injury. Injury history came from a survey, controls were non-competitive participants with only 3 previously injured, so the injury effect rests mainly on the sprinters. The 128 Hz sampling rate may be low for ground contact in sprinting, though the authors argue the effect is small, and no rehabilitation history was available.
practicalImplications: IMU-based pelvic measures were collected in a track setting and may be used for on-the-spot screening, as the authors propose. Treat a high mediolateral motion or asymmetry reading as a prompt for a closer look at lumbo-pelvic strength and coordination, not as a diagnosis or clearance decision. Do not apply the group values to an individual athlete until the findings are confirmed in larger, longitudinal samples.
athleteDev: Side-to-side pelvic symmetry during sprint running may be one way to monitor stance mechanics in sprinters with a hamstring history. The study does not test whether changing these measures improves sprint performance, so pair them with sprint performance data.
rtp: The authors suggest that side-to-side lumbo-pelvic strength and coordination assessment could help confirm readiness to return to sport. The study did not test return-to-sport decisions or outcomes, so these pelvic measures should not be used as return-to-sport clearance criteria.

citation: Maemichi T, Matsumoto M, Okunuki T, Tsutsui T, Kumai T. Functional and anatomical characteristics of the heel fat pad based on different sports events. J Biomech. 2026;196:113148.
abstract: This cross-sectional study compared heel fat pad thickness and stiffness in 34 male university athletes from judo (barefoot), American football (shoe-based) and swimming (water-based), and in 12 male non-athlete controls. Ultrasound measured shallow and deep layer thickness at 0%, 50% and 100% loading, and shear-wave elastography measured stiffness. The authors report that swimmers had the thickest heel fat pads at no load and the largest thickness change with loading in the shallow layer, and conclude that sport-specific loading may shape heel fat pad morphology and mechanics.
tldr: In this small cross-sectional study, swimmers had the thickest heel fat pads at no load, and judo and American football athletes the thinnest. The authors suggest sport-specific loading may shape the heel fat pad, but they note that sport cannot be isolated as the only cause.
methods: Cross-sectional comparison of 34 male university athletes (12 judo, 10 American football, 12 swimmers) and 12 male students with no sport participation. Ultrasound (14 MHz linear probe) measured shallow and deep layer thickness at 0%, 50% and 100% loading, and shear-wave elastography measured stiffness in the prone position. Participants with heel pain, recent foot or ankle injury or surgery, or rheumatic or systemic disease were excluded, and group differences were tested with ANOVA.
findings: At no load, swimmers had the thickest shallow and deep layers (body-mass corrected), and the conclusions describe judo and American football athletes as thinnest; the discussion also reports controls thicker than judo and football, although one Results sentence reports the deep layer thicker in all three sports than in controls. Swimmers showed the greatest shallow-layer thickness change with loading, and judo and swimmers showed greater deep-layer change than American football from 0 to 50% load. Section 3.3 and the discussion report higher deep-layer stiffness in American football than in judo and swimmers and the highest shallow-layer stiffness in judo, which conflicts with the abstract and conclusions.
limitations: The design is cross-sectional with 10 to 12 participants per group, controls were older than the athletes, and competitive history and measurement timing were not uniform. The stiffness results conflict: the abstract and conclusions place the lowest shallow-layer stiffness in American football and the highest deep-layer stiffness in swimmers, while Section 3.3 and the discussion place the highest deep-layer stiffness in American football and the highest shallow-layer stiffness in judo; the values here follow Section 3.3. The methods also describe controls both as non-participants in sport and as club athletes, do not clearly map the shallow and deep layers to the macro- and microchamber layers, and the study measured no pain or injury outcome.
practicalImplications: Heel fat pad thickness and its response to load differed by sport in this small study, so sport-specific loading may be worth considering when heel pain is assessed in athletes. The study does not show that these differences predict pain or injury. Do not use the group values as reference ranges for individual athletes, given the small samples and the inconsistent stiffness results.
athleteDev: The study measured tissue characteristics only and tested no training or performance outcome, so it cannot guide training prescription. Its relevance for performance staff is that heel tissue differed by sport in this sample, which could be tested in future work on load planning or footwear, as the authors discuss shoe wearing as one factor.
rtp: The study compares athletes without heel pain or recent foot injury, and it does not evaluate injury, rehabilitation or return to sport. It should not be used to set return-to-sport criteria for heel pain.

citation: Manaseer TS, Gross DP, Dennett L, Schneider K, Whittaker JL. Gait Deviations Associated With Concussion: A Systematic Review. Clin J Sport Med. 2020;30(2 Suppl 1):S11-S28.
abstract: This systematic review identified quantifiable gait deviations associated with concussion across populations and time since injury. Six databases were searched from 1974 to 2016, and 21 analytic studies were included, all rated level 4 evidence with a median Downs and Black score of 12/33.
