The authors found consistent evidence of increased medial-lateral centre-of-mass displacement and inconsistent evidence of decreased gait velocity after concussion, with preliminary evidence that deficits may persist beyond 10 days.
tldr: Concussed individuals in these studies swayed more side to side and sometimes walked more slowly than controls, and some deficits may last beyond the typical 10-day recovery period. The evidence is low-level, so gait testing should not yet be used alone to make concussion or return-to-activity decisions.
methods: Systematic review following PRISMA guidance, with searches of six databases from January 1974 to September 2016. Two authors screened records independently and rated study quality with the Downs and Black checklist and the Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine levels. Meta-analysis was precluded by heterogeneity in gait parameters and in the timing of postconcussion testing.
findings: The 21 included studies enrolled 1120 participants, most of them athletes or athletic-like students, and most compared concussed people with healthy controls. Medial-lateral centre-of-mass displacement was reported as increased in concussed groups in multiple studies, and gait velocity was reported as decreased in some studies but not others. Several studies reported gait deviations after the typical 10-day recovery period, and three reported deviations after return to activity, but these findings rest on fewer studies.
limitations: Study quality was low, with a median Downs and Black score of 12/33 and the main threats being selection bias and poor adjustment for confounders. Fifteen studies (71%) had fewer than 50 participants, and 76% were conducted by three research teams, which limits generalisability. The authors also state that the timing of follow-up testing was not justified and that only two studies reported the measurement properties of their systems.
practicalImplications: Gait assessment may be considered as one part of a concussion evaluation, and the authors say a clinical gait test should include walking speed and side-to-side sway. Because the evidence is low-level and inconsistent, staff should not rely on a single gait measure to decide when an athlete is recovered. The authors note that the common Tandem Gait Test captures both elements, but its accuracy for detecting gait disturbance is unknown.
athleteDev: Not applicable. This review addresses concussion and gait in injury assessment and does not study training, performance or performance outcomes.
rtp: The authors state that no included study assessed gait parameters to inform return to activity, sport, recreation or work decisions. The review supports only the finding that some gait deficits may persist after the typical 10-day recovery period, and it should not be used to set return-to-play criteria.

citation: Leońska-Duniec A. Genetic Susceptibility to Sport-Related Muscle Injuries: Insights from the Literature and Novel Gene Candidates. Int J Mol Sci. 2025;26:11175.
abstract: This review summarises polymorphisms associated with susceptibility to sport-related muscle injury in physically active people, identified through a systematic search of PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science. The author reports that 37 single nucleotide polymorphisms in 32 genes have been linked to injury risk, recurrence, severity and recovery. The genes cluster into functional categories, and the review proposes candidate genes for future work.
tldr: Several gene variants, including ACTN3 R577X, ACE I/D and COL5A1 rs12722, have been associated with muscle injury in some studies, but findings are inconsistent and mostly come from case-control studies of one or a few SNPs. Nothing in the review validates a genotype or score for screening athletes or setting individual injury risk.
methods: Literature review with a described search of PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science using polymorphism, gene, SNP and muscle injury terms. Inclusion criteria were original English-language human studies in physically active people with documented muscle injuries, excluding people with additional disease. No search dates, study counts, selection flow, pooled analysis or formal quality appraisal are reported.
findings: The review reports 37 SNPs in 32 genes associated with muscle injury risk, incidence, severity or recovery time. It cites a systematic review in which the ACTN3 XX genotype was linked to noncontact muscle injury in 12 of 13 studies, while other studies found no association, and IL6 rs1800795 findings point in opposite directions (GG as the risk genotype in one study, CC in another). For ACE, the II genotype is linked to more muscle injuries in football players and the D allele to protection, and a 4-SNP total genotype score in 64 Italian footballers gave an injury odds ratio of 3.5 above a 56.2 a.u. cut-off.
limitations: Most of the included evidence comes from case-control studies of one or a few SNPs, which the author says do not support firm conclusions about combined effects. The review does not describe quality appraisal or pooled effect sizes, and the Table 2 candidate genes were selected mainly on biological plausibility rather than tested for muscle injury. COL5A1 rs12722 is described inconsistently (Table 1 lists the CT genotype with greater severity and TT as lower risk, while the text describes TT as stiffer and higher risk).
practicalImplications: Current findings do not support using a genotype to screen athletes or to predict an individual's muscle injury risk. The author suggests that multi-gene scores, genome-wide and sequencing studies, and epigenetic work could support personalised prevention in future. Until such work is validated, staff should treat genetic results as research information rather than as a basis for training or selection decisions.
athleteDev: The review links some variants to performance traits, such as the ACTN3 RR genotype in speed and power athletes and the ACE D allele with power and strength, but these links are not injury tools. Use this evidence as background only, and do not use genotype to select, rank or limit athletes.
rtp: The review does not evaluate return to sport or rehabilitation outcomes. Reported links between some variants and longer recovery time come from individual association studies and cannot be used to set rehabilitation or return-to-play timelines.

citation: Larruskain J, Celorrio D, Barrio I, Odriozola A, Gil SM, Fernandez-Lopez JR, et al. Genetic Variants and Hamstring Injury in Soccer: An Association and Validation Study. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2017. Published ahead of print.
abstract: This study investigated candidate SNPs associated with non-contact hamstring injury in elite soccer players and tested a risk model in an independent season. Five SNPs (MMP3, TNC, IL6, NOS3, HIF1A) and age were associated with hamstring injury in the discovery phase, with a C index of 0.74. The model did not predict injury in the validation season (C index 0.52), and the authors conclude that genetic testing for hamstring injury risk seems premature.
tldr: Five gene variants and age were associated with hamstring injury in one elite club over five seasons, but the resulting risk model could not identify injured players in the following season. Genetic testing for hamstring risk is not yet supported.
methods: Prospective cohort of 107 male outfield players from one elite club (First team, Reserves and U19), with time-loss hamstring injuries and exposure recorded over six seasons; saliva for genotyping was collected in 2014-2015. Players were genotyped for 37 SNPs, each tested under four inheritance models with the best chosen by minimum P, and variables with P of 0.25 or less entered a forward-selection Cox proportional hazards model with frailty terms in the discovery seasons (2010-2011 to 2014-2015). Discrimination was tested with Harrell's C index in the discovery phase and in the 2015-2016 validation season.
findings: In the discovery phase, MMP3 rs679620 (A vs G, HR 2.06, 95% CI 1.51-2.81), TNC rs2104772 (A vs T, HR 1.65, 95% CI 1.17-2.32), IL6 rs1800795 (GG vs GC+CC, HR 1.68, 95% CI 1.11-2.53), NOS3 rs1799983 (G vs T, HR 1.35, 95% CI 1.01-1.79) and HIF1A rs11549465 (CC vs CT, HR 2.08, 95% CI 1.00-4.29) were associated with hamstring injury in the multivariable model, as was age of 24 or older (HR 2.10, 95% CI 1.29-3.42). TNC and IL6 were not significant on their own (P = 0.12 and 0.25), and MMP3 rs679620 was the only SNP associated with acute, overuse, severe and recurrent injuries separately. The model had a C index of 0.74 in discovery and 0.52 in validation.
limitations: Only one club was studied, and the authors state that replication is needed. The validation phase included 31 injuries from 67 players, and the injury subtype analyses were underpowered. Preventive training was not recorded, and two SNPs (COL1A1 rs1800012 and COL5A1 rs12722) had 10% missing genotypes. The HIF1A confidence interval reaches 1.00, and no correction for multiple testing across 37 SNPs and several inheritance models is described. The study was funded by Baigene, a genetics company, and several authors are its members.
practicalImplications: Do not use these genotypes to identify hamstring injury risk in players. The model did not predict injury in an independent season, so the flagged variants should be treated as research leads. Hamstring prevention programmes should continue to be offered to all players, as the authors recommend, because screening tests are not yet accurate.
athleteDev: Not applicable. The study addresses injury susceptibility and does not examine performance outcomes or training adaptation.
rtp: The study models the risk of any hamstring injury, including recurrences, and does not examine rehabilitation or return to play. Its findings cannot be used to set return-to-play timelines or to guide rehabilitation decisions after injury.

citation: Ding H, Deng Q, Guo Z. Genetic and epigenetic determinants of injury risk and recovery in elite athletes: toward precision sports medicine. Gene. 2026;980:149957.
abstract: This review synthesises genetic and epigenetic determinants of injury risk and recovery in elite athletes. It covers candidate SNPs in COL1A1, COL5A1, ACTN3 and IL6, genome-wide association studies, polygenic risk scores (PRS), DNA methylation and exercise-responsive microRNAs. The authors conclude that current genetic associations should be viewed as probabilistic and require multi-ethnic validation before clinical translation.
tldr: Genetic and epigenetic markers such as COL5A1, MMP3, ACTN3 and some microRNAs have been linked to injury or recovery, but the review describes these links as probabilistic and much of the cited evidence is not from elite athletes. Polygenic risk scores are presented as research tools rather than ready-to-use screening instruments.
methods: Narrative synthesis of literature retrieved from PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science using keywords such as genetics, sports injuries, recovery, epigenetics and nutrigenomics. English articles from 2000 to 2025 were considered, with emphasis on elite athlete cohorts, and both candidate-gene and GWAS studies were reviewed. The authors state that heterogeneity led them to present a narrative synthesis rather than a systematic review, and no inclusion criteria, pooled analysis or formal quality appraisal is described.
findings: The review tabulates candidate variants and reports odds ratios from earlier meta-analyses, such as COL5A1 rs12722 TT vs TC+CC (OR 1.58, 95% CI 1.33-1.89; nine studies) for tendon and ligament injury. It describes a longitudinal pilot study of 64 professional Italian footballers in which injury risk was 3.5 times higher below a total genotype score cut-off of 56.2 a.u. It presents exercise-responsive microRNAs and DNA methylation as dynamic, context-dependent markers, and notes that existing PRS explain only 0.07% to 1.44% of variance in physical activity levels in UK Biobank data.
limitations: The authors note small cohorts, limited population diversity, a lack of sport-specific validation, inconsistent definitions of non-responders, and methodological heterogeneity in methylation and microRNA studies. The review does not describe inclusion criteria or quality appraisal, so study selection cannot be checked. Some details are internally inconsistent: Table 1 attributes the COL1A1 meta-analysis to a different source than the text, and the MMP3 Achilles tendinopathy result is reported for a cohort described as ACL ruptures.
practicalImplications: Current genetic and epigenetic results should not be used to screen athletes or to predict an individual's injury risk, since the authors describe PRS as research tools that are not ready for screening. Where genetic information is collected, the review says it should complement medical assessment and performance monitoring, not replace them. Staff should also plan for protection of athlete genetic data, which the review identifies as a privacy and discrimination risk.
athleteDev: The review proposes that genotype could inform periodisation and that microRNA or methylation markers could track training adaptation. These are the authors' proposals drawn from small or early studies, so they should not change training prescriptions yet. Athletes should not be selected or ranked on genetic profiles.
rtp: The review suggests that athletes with COL1A1 or COL5A1 variants might need longer recovery periods and that epigenetic markers could personalise rehabilitation. These are author proposals rather than tested findings, and they should not be used to set return-to-play timelines.

citation: Maestro A, Del Coso J, Aguilar-Navarro M, Gutiérrez-Hellín J, Morencos E, Revuelta G, et al. Genetic profile in genes associated with muscle injuries and injury etiology in professional soccer players. Front Genet. 2022;13:1035899.
abstract: This study examined the relationship between muscle injury-related genes and injury risk and etiology in 122 professional soccer players. Six polymorphisms were combined into a total genotype score (TGS), which was lower in injured players and had an odds ratio of 1.91 for injury at a cut-off of 45.83 a.u. The authors conclude that TGS may in future help predict injury risk in professional soccer players.
tldr: A combined score of six muscle-related gene variants was lower in injured professional soccer players, but it discriminated injured from uninjured players only weakly. The score is not yet a usable injury predictor, and the single-season, single-cohort design limits what it can show.
methods: Cohort of 122 Spanish male professional soccer players from five clubs during the 2021/2022 season, with a Caucasian-ancestry inclusion criterion and exclusion of players with incapacitating injuries in the previous 6 months. Six polymorphisms (ACE I/D, ACTN3, AMPD1, CKM, and two MLCK variants) were genotyped from buccal swabs, and a total genotype score was calculated. Non-contact injuries were recorded by club doctors using a consensus-based questionnaire, and TGS was compared between injured and non-injured players by t-test, chi-squared test, ROC analysis and logistic regression, with etiology analyses run across the 121 injuries.
findings: Non-injured players had a mean TGS of 57.18 a.u. and injured players 51.71 a.u. (p = 0.034). ROC analysis gave an AUC of 0.612 (95% CI 0.513-0.711), and in the results players below the 45.83 a.u. cut-off had an odds ratio of 1.91 for injury (95% CI 1.14-2.91). AMPD1 CC genotype frequency was 88.2% in non-injured and 57.7% in injured players (p < 0.001), and TGS did not discriminate musculoskeletal injury, place of injury or injury severity.
limitations: The study covers one season and five clubs, the sample is 122 players, the TGS cut-off was derived from the same data, and no correction for multiple testing is described. The abstract calls the design cross-sectional and the methods longitudinal, the abstract places higher risk beyond the cut-off while the results place it below, and the discussion gives a non-contact injury rate (16.6%) that conflicts with the results (58.2%). The discussion also compares MLCK CC in injured players (84.5%) with a 70.6% figure it attributes to AA players, though Table 5 gives 70.6% as CC in non-injured players, and it presents CKM GA and ACTN3 TT differences as findings although the overall tests were not significant (p = 0.131, 0.091 and 0.149).
practicalImplications: Do not use the TGS or the AMPD1 and MLCK genotypes to identify players at risk of injury, since discrimination was weak and the findings have not been validated. The authors themselves say it is still premature to use genetic testing to predict injury risk in professional soccer players. Any future use would need replication in larger, multi-season cohorts.
athleteDev: The study addresses injury susceptibility and not performance. The authors discuss muscle-performance genes, but the analysis does not measure performance, so the results should not be used to select or rank players.
rtp: The study does not examine rehabilitation or return to play. Its finding that injury severity was not linked to the TGS in a discriminatory way means the score cannot inform recovery timelines or return-to-play decisions.

citation: Kaynak M, Nijman F, van Meurs J, Reijman M, Meuffels DE. Genetic Variants and Anterior Cruciate Ligament Rupture: A Systematic Review. Sports Med. 2017.
abstract: This PRISMA systematic review summarised case-control evidence on genetic variants and anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) rupture. Sixteen studies examining 33 variants were included and rated with a best-evidence synthesis. The authors found conflicting evidence for COL1A1 rs1800012 and COL3A1 rs1800255, limited evidence of no association for some COL5A1 and COL12A1 variants, and concluded that larger and prospective studies are needed.
tldr: Sixteen case-control studies gave conflicting results for COL1A1 and COL3A1 variants and limited evidence against an association for some COL5A1 and COL12A1 variants. The authors conclude that the evidence does not yet show a clear genetic association with ACL rupture.
methods: PRISMA-reported systematic review searching Embase, MEDLINE, Web of Science, Scopus, PubMed Publisher, the Cochrane trials register and Google Scholar to 24 August 2015, with reference-list screening. Eligible studies were case-control, retrospective or prospective follow-up, or randomised designs comparing a genetic variant between ACL rupture cases and controls. Three reviewers assessed risk of bias with the Cochrane case-control tool, and pooling was not possible, so a best-evidence synthesis was used.
findings: Sixteen case-control studies (eight high risk of bias, eight unclear) examined 33 variants. For COL1A1 rs1800012, two studies reported lower odds of rupture with the TT genotype (OR 0.12, 95% CI 0.02-0.92; OR 0.08, p = 0.031), one reported an association for GG (p = 0.046) and one found none. For COL3A1 rs1800255, AA vs GA+GG gave odds ratios of 3.8 (95% CI 1.1-12.8) and 5.05 (95% CI 1.62-15.78) in two Polish cohorts but no association in a South African cohort, and single-study findings for DCN rs516115 (GG protective) and VEGFA rs1570360 (GA harmful) rest on nearly the same population.
limitations: Pooling was not possible because of heterogeneity in variants, outcome definitions and genetic contrasts. Many studies had small samples, 14 used partly or fully the same population for cases and controls, and eight were high risk of bias. Confounding by ethnicity is possible, and subgroup analyses by sex and injury mechanism could not be reported. The role of haplotypes remains unclear.
practicalImplications: Current evidence does not support screening athletes for ACL rupture risk using these variants, because each variant has insufficient or conflicting evidence. Any future use would need large prospective studies that show predictive value. The review suggests genome-wide studies and studies of tendon and osteoarthritis genetics as next steps.
athleteDev: Not applicable. The review addresses ACL rupture susceptibility and does not examine training, performance or performance outcomes.
rtp: The review does not evaluate rehabilitation or return to sport. Its findings on injury susceptibility cannot inform return-to-play timelines or post-injury decisions after an ACL rupture.

citation: Onori ME, Pasqualetti M, Moretti G, Canu G, De Paolis G, Baroni S, et al. Genetics and Sport Injuries: New Perspectives for Athletic Excellence in an Italian Court of Rugby Union Players. Genes. 2022;13:995.
abstract: ACE, ACTN3, COL1A1 and MCT1 genotypes were compared between 100 male professional and semiprofessional rugby union players and 100 non-athletic Italian men, and related to injury history in the players. The authors report no significant genotype-injury association for ACE, ACTN3 or COL1A1. They report that the MCT1 rs1049434 AA genotype was associated with total and bone injuries, but the chi-square values they print (0.115 and 0.603) are inconsistent with the p-values given (0.003 and 0.007).
tldr: In 100 rugby union players, the authors report that the MCT1 rs1049434 AA genotype was linked to total and bone injury history, while ACE, ACTN3 and COL1A1 were not. The result is small, unreplicated and internally inconsistent, so it does not support genetic screening of players.
methods: Genotypes for ACE I/D, ACTN3 R577X, COL1A1 rs1800012 and MCT1 rs1049434 were determined by PCR, RFLP or Sanger sequencing in 100 male professional and semiprofessional rugby union players and 100 non-athletic Italian men. Injuries from medical history and injury records were grouped as bone, muscle or tendon/ligament, with genotype frequencies compared by chi-square tests and injured versus non-injured players compared by unpaired t-tests under a dominant model, at p < 0.05.
findings: No genotype-injury association was reported for ACE, ACTN3 or COL1A1 (p > 0.05). For MCT1, the authors report that the AA genotype was associated with total injuries (reported chi-square 0.115, p = 0.003) and bone injuries (reported chi-square 0.603, p = 0.007), and allele frequencies did not differ between athletes and controls. The printed chi-square values do not correspond to the printed p-values, and no odds ratios or confidence intervals are given.
limitations: The sample is small and drawn from two teams, with 15 athletes reporting no injuries, and injury data come from retrospective medical history and injury records. Four genes and several injury categories were tested with no multiple-comparison correction, an unpaired t-test was used to compare injured and non-injured players by genotype, and the injury counts by type (129 muscle, 247 bone, 170 tendon; sum 546) do not match the total of 573 reported. The control group is 100 non-athletic men over 18 with no age data reported, and the Hardy-Weinberg result is printed as p < 0.05, which conflicts with the stated equilibrium.
practicalImplications: Do not use MCT1 genotype to screen players for injury risk or to set individual load, because the association is unreplicated and its statistics are inconsistent. Treat the MCT1 result as a hypothesis for prospective study in a larger squad with injuries recorded prospectively.
athleteDev: This study does not support genotype-based talent selection or training individualisation. The ACE, ACTN3 and COL1A1 results are null, and the MCT1 result needs confirmation in a larger, prospectively followed squad.
rtp: The study can speak to injury history by genotype, but not to return-to-sport decisions, since it does not assess rehabilitation, recovery time or return outcomes. Do not use the MCT1 result to set return-to-play timelines or clearance.

citation: Dupré T, Lysdal FG, Funken J, Mortensen KRL, Müller R, Mayer J, et al. Groin Injuries in Soccer: Investigating the Effect of Age on Adductor Muscle Forces. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2019 (published ahead of print).
abstract: Sixty healthy male academy players in four age groups (U12, U15, U16 and U23) performed submaximal inside passes in a Footbonaut while motion capture and inverse dynamics estimated adductor longus and gracilis forces. Forces increased across age groups, and lower limb mass was the best anthropometric predictor of the calculated forces. The authors link this to overuse groin injury risk, which the study did not measure.
tldr: In 60 academy players, modelled adductor forces during passing rose with age group, and lower limb mass tracked them best. No groin injuries were recorded, so the injury-risk link is an inference from the force estimates.
methods: Sixty healthy male academy players (mean ages 11.1, 14.7, 15.8 and 20.2 years for U12, U15, U16 and U23) each performed 10 analysed inside passes in a Footbonaut, with 71 markers and 16 infrared cameras recording kinematics. An AnyBody model with static optimization estimated adductor longus and gracilis forces, and linear regression related those forces to thigh and lower limb size and mass.
findings: Adductor longus and gracilis peak forces were significantly lower in U12 than in all older groups, and lower in U15 than in U16 and U23, while U16 and U23 did not differ significantly. Gracilis force rose 49% from U12 (92.4 N) to U15 (138.0 N), and adductor longus rose 22% from U15 to U16 and 6% from U16 to U23. Lower limb mass gave the highest R-squared for both muscles (0.70 for adductor longus and 0.73 for gracilis), above thigh mass (0.65 and 0.69) and lower limb length (0.51 and 0.54), and U15 players had lower hip flexion velocity than U12 and U16 and lower adduction velocity than U16 and U23.
limitations: The design is cross-sectional, maturity was not measured, and group sizes of 14 to 17 mean that age, size and growth stage are confounded. The regression pools all 60 players, so the R-squared values largely reflect between-group size differences, and the forces are static optimization estimates checked only against EMG in earlier work. The abstract, Discussion and conclusion describe injury risk, reduced training volume and Copenhagen adduction training that the study did not test, and the conclusion names thigh mass where the regression favoured lower limb mass.
practicalImplications: Lower limb mass should not yet be used as an injury-risk screen or to set training volume, because no injuries were recorded. The findings show that modelled adductor forces during passing rise through the academy years, which coaches could keep in mind when planning load changes; any screen would need testing against injury records.
athleteDev: Modelled adductor forces during passing rose sharply between under-12 and under-15 players, so the demands of passing change through the academy years. The study estimated forces only and did not test how training volume or coaching alters them.
rtp: The players were healthy, and no injured or rehabilitating players were studied, so the study cannot inform return-to-sport or rehabilitation decisions. It was not designed to test groin injury recovery.

citation: Heer ST, Callander JW, Kraeutler MJ, Mei-Dan O, Mulcahey MK. Hamstring Injuries: Risk Factors, Treatment, and Rehabilitation. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 2019;101(9):843-53.
abstract: This Current Concepts Review covers the anatomy, risk factors, diagnosis, imaging, nonoperative and operative treatment, and rehabilitation of hamstring injuries. It summarises the published literature, includes a level-of-evidence table of selected studies, and grades its treatment recommendations.
tldr: A previous hamstring injury is the strongest predictor of re-injury, and eccentric hamstring strengthening is recommended in both rehabilitation and prevention. Complete proximal avulsions with significant retraction are treated surgically, and other injuries are generally managed conservatively.
methods: Narrative review of the literature on anatomy, risk factors, diagnosis, imaging, treatment and rehabilitation, with a level-of-evidence table (Table II) and recommendation grades (Table III). No search strategy is described.
findings: Previous hamstring injury is the most predictive risk factor, with recurrence reported at 32% in American football, 21% in rugby and 16% in soccer. Eccentric physical therapy is recommended for rehabilitation, and Nordic hamstring exercise is cited as having a preventive effect in soccer players. Surgical repair of acute avulsions with retraction above 2.5 to 3 cm is graded B, and surgery for ischial tuberosity fractures displaced more than 1 cm is graded C.
limitations: The review does not describe how sources were searched or appraised, and it draws on mixed populations and many lower-level studies. The authors note that return-to-preinjury criteria are hard to assess objectively, especially for grade 1 and 2 injuries.
practicalImplications: For proximal tendon injuries, MRI is the most useful imaging study for injury extent and surgical planning. Eccentric hamstring tendon loading should be part of both nonoperative and postoperative rehabilitation, and the review cites Nordic exercise after training as preventive in soccer.
athleteDev: Prior hamstring injury is the strongest flag for re-injury risk, so it should shape prevention priorities. Eccentric hamstring tendon strengthening belongs in both prevention and rehabilitation, but the review gives no loading or progression parameters.
rtp: The review guides the choice between conservative and surgical care by injury type, favouring surgery for complete proximal avulsions with significant retraction. It states that return-to-preinjury criteria are hard to measure objectively, so it should not be the sole basis for clearance.

citation: Andrews MH, Shield AJ, Lichtwark GA, Pincheira PA. Hamstring Injury Mechanisms and Eccentric Training-Induced Muscle Adaptations: Current Insights and Future Directions. Sports Med. 2025.
abstract: This narrative review uses PubMed and SPORTDiscus searches to May 2025 to examine the causes of running-related hamstring injury, the effect of eccentric training on injury risk, and the contractile, non-contractile and neural adaptations to eccentric training. It argues that research has focused on resting fascicle length and that tendon, titin and neural adaptations need further study.
tldr: Running-related hamstring injuries mostly occur in late swing, when the hamstrings produce large eccentric force at long lengths. Eccentric training, especially the Nordic exercise, reduces injury risk in adherent athletes, but the muscle changes that explain this protection remain unclear.
methods: Narrative review with searches of PubMed and SPORTDiscus up to May 2025 using defined hamstring, injury mechanism, eccentric training and adaptation terms, followed by title and abstract screening and reference-list checks. Three predefined research questions shaped the scope.
findings: Over 80% of hamstring injuries occur during high-speed running, mainly to the biceps femoris long head, with injury proposed in late swing or early stance. Meta-analytic evidence cited by the review indicates that Nordic programmes reduce injury incidence by about 51%; one meta-analysis found no significant effect, which the authors attribute to poor adherence, and restricting to compliant participants gave reductions approaching 65%. One prospective cohort cited by the review links each 0.5 cm of longer resting fascicle to a 21% lower injury risk, while the link between sarcomere, titin, tendon and neural changes and protection remains unverified.
limitations: The review is narrative: it pools no data and does not grade the evidence. Several adaptation mechanisms rest on animal or non-hamstring studies, and the authors note that the link between resting fascicle lengthening and protection during active lengthening is theoretical.
practicalImplications: Eccentric hamstring training should remain a core prevention approach, and adherence matters because the protective effects were concentrated in compliant participants. The review notes that knee-dominant exercises such as the Nordic tend to activate and grow the semitendinosus more than the biceps femoris long head, while hip-dominant exercises activate the hamstrings more uniformly, although surface EMG findings are inconsistent.
athleteDev: Track adherence as a core metric for eccentric hamstring programmes, since protective effects were concentrated in players who completed them. Match exercise choice to the target region, although the review gives no dosing guidance.
rtp: The review addresses prevention and training adaptation in running sports, not rehabilitation or return to play. Its conclusions cannot be used to set return-to-sport criteria or timeframes.

citation: Palmieri-Smith R, Strickland M, Lepley LK. Hamstring Muscle Activity After Primary Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction: A Protective Mechanism in Those Who Do Not Sustain a Secondary Injury? A Preliminary Study. Sports Health. 2019.
abstract: This cross-sectional study compared surface EMG of the vastus lateralis, biceps femoris and lateral gastrocnemius during a single-leg hopping task at return to play in 7 patients who later had a second ipsilateral ACL injury, 7 matched patients with a single ACL injury, and 7 uninjured controls. Hamstring activity before landing was higher in the single-injury group than in the re-injury group, and vastus lateralis activity after landing was lower in both ACL groups than in controls.
tldr: At return to play after ACL reconstruction, patients who later re-injured the same knee used less hamstring activity before landing than those who did not, and all ACL patients used less vastus lateralis activity than controls. With 7 per group and a cross-sectional design, this is a hypothesis for prospective testing, not an established protective mechanism.
methods: Cross-sectional study. Seven patients who later had a second ipsilateral ACL injury were matched 1:1 for sex, age (within 2 years), graft type and Tegner score to patients with a single ACL injury, and 7 uninjured controls were matched for sex and age (within 3 years). Participants performed single-leg hopping at return to play, with surface EMG normalised to peak dynamic activity and analysed 100 ms before and 250 ms after ground contact using ANOVA with post hoc t tests.
findings: Pre-landing biceps femoris activity was 0.48 %max in the single-injury group and 0.20 %max in the re-injury group (P=0.018), with controls at 0.38 %max (not significant). After landing, vastus lateralis activity was 0.38 and 0.40 %max in the two ACL groups versus 0.58 %max in controls (P=0.016 and P=0.033). Quadriceps strength was lower in both ACL groups than in controls, and the groups did not differ on hamstring strength.
limitations: The groups are very small, and the control group was significantly older than both ACL groups, which the authors acknowledge may reflect maturation effects. Only one hop task was used, and the authors state that the findings need longitudinal confirmation.
practicalImplications: Rehabilitation after ACL reconstruction should keep targeting quadriceps (vastus lateralis) activity, since it was lower during landing in all reconstructed knees at return to play than in uninjured controls. Pre-landing hamstring activity is worth monitoring in future prospective studies, but this study does not show that training it reduces reinjury.
athleteDev: Landing EMG at return to play could be explored as a monitoring idea, but this preliminary study gives no training dose or target. Hamstring pre-activation should not be used as a training target until prospective data confirm it.
rtp: Landing muscle activity was lower in all ACL groups than in uninjured controls, which supports continued quadriceps-focused rehabilitation at return to play. The study does not establish clearance criteria, and the authors note that their return-to-play criteria differ from those recommended in the literature.

citation: Hajek M, Williams MD, Bourne MN, Roberts LA, Morris NR, Shield AJ, et al. Hamstring and knee injuries are associated with isometric hip and trunk muscle strength in elite Australian Rules and Rugby League players. J Sci Med Sport. 2023 (journal pre-proof).
abstract: This prospective cohort study measured isometric trunk and hip extensor strength (5 s maximal and 45 s endurance) and lumbar multifidus and quadratus lumborum cross-sectional area in AFL and NRL players during the 2020 preseason. Non-contact hamstring strain and knee ligament injuries were recorded over the season and analysed with logistic regression and decision trees.
tldr: In elite AFL and NRL players, lower preseason trunk and hip extensor strength and endurance were associated with more hamstring strains. Larger lumbar multifidus size was associated with more knee ligament injuries, but the knee model did not discriminate well.
methods: Prospective cohort. Isometric trunk and hip extensor strength was tested with a modified Biering-Sorensen protocol (5 s maximal and 45 s endurance), and lumbar multifidus and quadratus lumborum cross-sectional area was measured by ultrasound at the 2020 preseason. Injuries were recorded across the 2020 season, with univariable logistic regression (strength per SD) and decision trees with ROC analysis.
findings: Of 126 players with follow-up, 19 had a hamstring strain and 13 a knee ligament injury. Per SD, maximal strength (OR 0.55, P=0.039) and strength endurance (OR 0.42, P=0.004) were associated with lower hamstring strain odds. Larger LM L5 CSA (OR 1.66 per cm2) and LM-to-QL ratio (OR 1.57) were associated with knee ligament injury (P=0.008 each), and no strength variable was associated with knee injury. The Results report decision-tree AUCs of 0.75 for hamstring and 0.82 for knee injury, but the Limitations describe the knee model as not discriminating.
limitations: Injury numbers are small, 85 players declined the strength test, and the decision trees were not validated on held-out data; the Methods say no data were held back, while the Discussion mentions k-fold cross-validation. The Results give strength odds ratios per 1 N/kg while Table 2 gives them per SD, the Abstract gives a strength-endurance threshold in Nm while the Results give 3.42 N/kg, and the Results both state no differences and a higher BMI in players lost to follow-up.
practicalImplications: The modified Biering-Sorensen field test gives a preseason measure of trunk and hip extensor strength and endurance that may help identify players at higher hamstring strain risk. The knee-ligament findings are exploratory and should not be used to screen players.
athleteDev: Preseason trunk and hip extensor strength and endurance testing could support hamstring risk screening, since weaker players were more often injured here. The cut-offs are not validated, and lumbar muscle size should not be used to target knee injury screening on these data.
rtp: The study addresses preseason injury risk, not return to play. It does not indicate when a player with a hamstring or knee injury is ready to return.

citation: Malliaropoulos N, Mendiguchia J, Pehlivanidis H, Papadopoulou S, Valle X, Malliaras P, et al. Hamstring exercises for track and field athletes: injury and exercise biomechanics, and possible implications for exercise selection and primary prevention. Br J Sports Med. 2012;46:846-851.
abstract: This review considers hamstring strain injuries in track and field athletes, the role of eccentric training in prevention, and the strength and biomechanical factors involved. It proposes exercise classification criteria (hip or knee dominance, kinetic chain, location, targeted muscle and training parameters) to guide prevention and strengthening programmes.
tldr: Track and field hamstring prevention should emphasise eccentric strengthening, with exercises chosen by hip or knee dominance, kinetic chain and target muscle. The authors advise prioritising muscle length over strength or contraction speed, but the classification is a clinical proposal that has not been tested.
methods: Narrative review of injury mechanisms (late swing and early stance sprinting), strength as a risk factor, the properties of eccentric training, prevention studies and exercise biomechanics. The authors propose an exercise classification and training principles for track and field; no search strategy is reported.
findings: The review states that eccentric training consistently reduces hamstring injury rates, citing five prevention studies (four Nordic hamstring, one yo-yo curl) with over 1000 athletes, each reporting significant reductions. It recommends prioritising muscle length over strength and contraction velocity, combining open and closed kinetic chain and stretch-shortening exercises, and avoiding high-intensity, long-length eccentric work during key competition phases.
limitations: No literature search is described, and no study is cited that compares eccentric protocols for preventing track and field hamstring injury. The authors say much of the training advice derives from basic science and clinical experience and needs randomised testing.
practicalImplications: Include both hip-dominant and knee-dominant eccentric exercises, together with stretch-shortening exercises, rather than relying on a single exercise. Progress exposure to long-length strain gradually, and avoid high-intensity eccentric loading before key competitions, as the review recommends.
athleteDev: The review gives coaches a framework for choosing hamstring exercises by hip or knee dominance, kinetic chain and target muscle, and for progressing strain. Its volume guidance is general, since no published track and field dose comparisons exist.
rtp: The review addresses prevention and training design, not rehabilitation or return to sport, and it gives no clearance criteria.

citation: Brukner P. Hamstring injuries: prevention and treatment, an update. Br J Sports Med. 2015;49:1241-1244.
abstract: Narrative update on hamstring injuries. It reports that injury type (slow-stretch versus high-speed running) and central tendon involvement affect return-to-play time, that predictor evidence is conflicting, and that eccentric strength deficits may persist. It supports lengthened-position strengthening and NHE for prevention, and concludes that PRP is not yet supported for acute strains.
tldr: Hamstring injuries still recur at high rates. Lengthened-position eccentric work and Nordic hamstring exercises are the main strategies discussed, and PRP is not yet supported by the evidence.
methods: Narrative clinical review. No systematic search or appraisal method is described. The author discusses injury types, predictors of return to play, recurrence, rehabilitation programs, PRP trials and prevention studies.
findings: Slow-stretch injuries and injuries involving the central tendon are reported to need longer return to play. Evidence for individual predictors, including MRI findings, is conflicting. Eccentric hamstring strength may remain reduced after return to play, and the two PRP trials gave conflicting results: a placebo-controlled trial found no benefit, while a non-placebo trial reported faster recovery with PRP. NHE programs are cited as reducing hamstring injury incidence.
limitations: No search strategy or quality grading is given. The author acknowledges conflicting predictor evidence and few high-quality PRP trials, and some recommendations rest on mechanistic reasoning.
practicalImplications: Classify injuries by mechanism and location, and expect longer return to play for slow-stretch and central tendon injuries. Include lengthened-position eccentric strengthening and NHE in rehabilitation and prevention, and do not expect PRP to shorten recovery on the strength of this review.
athleteDev: Use injury type and recurrence risk to shape the return-to-running plan, and include NHE across the squad as a prevention method. Check eccentric hamstring strength after injury, since deficits may persist.
rtp: Make lengthened-position strengthening a central part of rehabilitation and check eccentric strength before clearance. The review gives no validated RTP criteria, so injury type and clinical tests should guide timing.

citation: Avrillon S, Lacourpaille L, Hug F, Le Sant G, Frey A, Nordez A, et al. Hamstring muscle elasticity differs in specialized high-performance athletes. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2020;30:83-91.
abstract: Compared passive shear modulus of the three hamstring muscles in elite athletes from seven sports with that of active controls, using shear wave elastography at 60 and 90 degrees of knee flexion. Semimembranosus stiffness was lower in four sports than in controls, while biceps femoris and semitendinosus did not differ.
tldr: Semimembranosus stiffness was lower in some elite sports than in controls, and the authors link the pattern to stretching demands in taekwondo, figure skating, fencing and soccer. Biceps femoris and semitendinosus did not differ.
methods: Cross-sectional study. Participants lay supine with the hip flexed to 90 degrees while the knee was held at 90 and 60 degrees on an isokinetic dynamometer. Shear modulus was measured by shear wave elastography, with inter-day reliability assessed in 12 controls (ICC 0.80 to 0.98). Athletes with a unilateral injury history contributed only their uninjured leg, and ANOVA models compared groups and muscles.
findings: At 60 degrees, semimembranosus shear modulus was lower than in controls in figure skating (mean difference -17.2 kPa, d = 1.8), taekwondo (-18.0 kPa, d = 2.1), fencing (-10.3 kPa, d = 1.0) and soccer (-9.0 kPa, d = 0.9). No difference was found for sprinters, field hockey or basketball players. Biceps femoris and semitendinosus did not differ between athletes and controls, and sex had no main effect.
limitations: The design cannot separate sport effects from innate properties, prior injury or stretching volume, which was not quantified. Group sizes are small, and basketball players were 9.7 years younger than controls. The conclusion says semimembranosus shear modulus is 'increased' in these athletes, which conflicts with the lower values in the abstract and results; this summary follows the results. Between-person variation is large, with SD up to 44% of the mean at 60 degrees.
practicalImplications: Interpret hamstring stiffness profiles against sport-specific norms, because semimembranosus values differed by sport. Do not compare an athlete's values with a general reference population without that sport context.
athleteDev: Sports with long stretching demands may show lower semimembranosus stiffness, which may be a training adaptation rather than a deficit. Whether it affects performance is not shown, so it should not set a training target.
rtp: Not for return-to-sport decisions or injury risk. The study excluded injured sides and did not follow athletes after injury, so it says nothing about stiffness during recovery.

citation: Kepir E, Demiral F, Akaras E, Paksoy AE, Sevindik Aktas B, Yilmaz Cankaya B, et al. Hamstring muscle stiffness in athletes with and without anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction history: a retrospective study. J Clin Med. 2024;13:4370.
abstract: Retrospective case-control comparison of passive hamstring stiffness, measured with shear wave elastography, in athletes with and without ACL reconstruction history. Stiffness of the biceps femoris long head, semimembranosus and semitendinosus did not differ between injured legs, uninjured contralateral legs and control legs.
tldr: Passive mid-belly hamstring stiffness did not differ between legs of athletes after ACL reconstruction and legs of uninjured athletes. The study is small and retrospective, and it measured only the mid-belly.
methods: Retrospective comparative case-control design. With the participant prone and relaxed, three mid-belly elastograms per muscle were averaged; groups were compared by one-way ANOVA. The injured group was 13 athletes aged 18 to 35 who had returned to sport after ACL reconstruction with a semitendinosus graft; the control group was 20 uninjured athletes contributing both legs.
findings: Mean stiffness was similar across groups for all three muscles, with reported p values of 0.291 or higher. For example, biceps femoris long head was 26.19 kPa in injured legs, 26.16 kPa in uninjured contralateral legs and 27.64 kPa in control legs. The hypothesis of higher semitendinosus stiffness from post-surgical scar tissue was not supported.
limitations: The design is retrospective, with an unblinded assessor, unmeasured probe pressure and no reliability study. Only male athletes were included, and rehabilitation details could not be recorded. The three small measurement points sat in the lowest-stiffness (blue) region, the sample size was based on an assumed large effect (0.8), and the discussion quotes a BFlh value of 9.91 kPa for this study that does not match the 26 to 28 kPa in Table 1.
practicalImplications: Mid-belly stiffness measured this way did not separate ACL-reconstructed athletes from uninjured athletes, so it should not be used as a marker of post-ACL hamstring change. Anyone using elastography should record probe pressure and region-of-interest size, and check reliability locally.
athleteDev: This study does not show a change in hamstring stiffness after ACL reconstruction, so it gives no performance target. It also did not link stiffness to performance or hamstring strain risk.
rtp: Do not use these results to set return-to-sport criteria after ACL reconstruction, since stiffness did not differ from controls and recovery was not tracked. The study cannot show whether elastography can monitor healing, which the authors suggest but did not test.

citation: Wangensteen A, Tol JL, Witvrouw E, Van Linschoten R, Almusa E, Hamilton B, et al. Hamstring reinjuries occur at the same location and early after return to sport: a descriptive study of MRI-confirmed reinjuries. Am J Sports Med. 2016;44(8):2112-2121.
abstract: This descriptive case series drew on 180 male athletes who had an MRI within 5 days of an acute hamstring injury, and analysed the 19 MRI-confirmed reinjuries in the same leg within one year of return to sport (18 football and 1 futsal player). Most of the reinjuries (15 of 19, 79%) occurred in the same location as the index injury, more than half (10 of 19) occurred within 25 days of return to sport, and all 7 reinjuries that were more severe on MRI grading occurred in the same location. The authors suggest the index injury may not have healed completely and recommend reinjury-prevention exercise after return to sport.
tldr: Most hamstring reinjuries in this series happened in the same place as the original injury and within weeks of return to sport. Keep hamstring-specific loading going after return to sport, because the injury may not have fully healed.
methods: Descriptive case series within a prospective cohort and randomised trial at Aspetar, Doha. An MRI was taken five days after the index injury in 180 athletes, and athletes were followed for one year after return to sport; reinjury required acute posterior thigh pain and MRI signal change. A single radiologist scored index and reinjury location and severity, and medians and proportions were reported.
findings: Of the 19 reinjuries, 15 (79%) were in the same muscle and location as the index injury, and the musculotendinous junction was the most common reinjury site (13 of 19). The median time from return to sport to reinjury was 24 days (range 4-311), and 10 of 19 reinjuries occurred within 25 days of return to sport. Seven of 19 reinjuries (37%) were graded more severe on MRI than the index injury, and all seven were in the same location; continuous MRI measures of injury extent did not differ between index injury and reinjury.
limitations: The study is single-centre with only 19 reinjuries and no comparison group, and percentages are of those 19 reinjuries rather than the 180 athletes. Return-to-sport decisions outside the study centre varied, 74 athletes were followed only passively so some reinjuries may have been missed, and the authors note that same-location MRI signal may partly reflect residual index injury rather than a new reinjury.
practicalImplications: After return to sport, continue specific hamstring loading and reinjury-prevention work, particularly in the first few weeks, because most reinjuries in this series were early and in the original location. Note that the paper cannot show whether a particular return-to-sport test or time frame prevents reinjury.
athleteDev: The paper has no performance outcomes. Its practical message is to keep hamstring-specific training going after return to sport, since reinjuries clustered in the original location early on.
rtp: The study can inform the period after return to sport, showing that reinjury risk was high in the first weeks and that reinjury was usually in the original location. It cannot be used to set a validated return-to-sport criterion, because the authors state that no objective validated criteria exist and this study did not test any.

citation: Gurchiek RD, Teplin Z, Falisse A, Hicks JL, Delp SL. Hamstrings are stretched more and faster during accelerative running compared to speed-matched constant-speed running. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2024. Published ahead of print.
abstract: Ten recreationally active adults ran at constant speeds and in accelerative flying sprints, and OpenCap markerless motion capture with a musculoskeletal model estimated biceps femoris long head muscle-tendon length and lengthening velocity. Peak length was greater in accelerative running below 75% of top speed, and lengthening velocity was greater in accelerative running at all speeds. Greater hip flexion drove the longer lengths and faster lengthening, and the knee's contribution was smaller during acceleration.
tldr: During acceleration from slower speeds, the modelled biceps femoris was stretched further and lengthened faster than at the same constant speed. Staff monitoring hamstring exposure may need to count acceleration, not only top speed.
methods: Ten recreationally active participants recorded overground trials at self-selected jogging and brisk speeds and prescribed speeds of 3, 4, 5 and 6 m/s, each as constant-speed running and as an accelerative flying sprint, with a 30 m maximal sprint to set top speed. OpenCap and a three-dimensional musculoskeletal model estimated peak muscle-tendon length and step-average lengthening velocity. Linear mixed models compared the conditions across running speeds.
findings: At top speed, peak muscle-tendon length was 111-112% of neutral length and did not differ between conditions (p=0.431). Below about 75% of top speed, accelerative running gave longer peak lengths (p<0.001), and the regression model predicted that accelerating from 50% of top speed produced the same peak length as constant running at 88%. Average lengthening velocity was greater during acceleration at all speeds, driven by faster hip flexion rather than knee extension. During acceleration, peak length occurred at an average hip flexion angle of 67 degrees regardless of speed, and at slower speeds both hip and knee were more flexed at peak length than in constant-speed running.
limitations: The sample was small (n=10, 5 men and 5 women) and not all participants were sprint specialists. Muscle length and velocity are model estimates from markerless video, OpenCap has not been validated for these specific tasks, speed order was not randomised, and 61 of 300 steps were removed in quality control. Only the swing-phase step was analysed, and the authors state that causal links between acceleration mechanics and hamstring injury are not established.
practicalImplications: Staff who track hamstring exposure with running speed alone may miss the high lengths and fast lengthening that occur when players accelerate from slower speeds. Consider counting acceleration as well as speed when planning exposure, while recognising that the link to injury has not been shown.
athleteDev: The paper gives no performance outcome. Its findings suggest that acceleration from slower speeds loads the hamstrings with longer, faster lengthening than constant running at the same speed, which may matter when designing acceleration training.
rtp: The study cannot inform return to sport, because it included no injured athletes and no rehabilitation or return-to-running outcomes. It can only describe modelled hamstring mechanics in healthy recreationally active adults.

citation: Encarnación-Martínez A, García-Gallart A, Sanchis-Sanchis R, Jimenez-Perez I, Priego-Quesada JI, Pérez-Soriano P. Higher Hamstrings Strength and Stability Are Related to Lower Kinematics Alteration during Running after Central and Peripheral Fatigue. Sensors. 2022;22:1990.
abstract: Eighteen male recreational runners had hamstring and quadriceps isokinetic strength and dynamic postural stability measured, then ran kinematic trials before and after central and peripheral fatigue protocols. Runners with higher hamstring strength and better stability showed smaller kinematic changes after central fatigue, and smaller ankle changes after peripheral fatigue.
tldr: In 18 male recreational runners, those with stronger hamstrings and better jump-landing stability showed smaller changes in running mechanics after fatigue. These are associations in a small laboratory study, so they do not show that strength training reduces fatigue-related changes.
methods: Within-subject laboratory study with 18 male recreational runners (no injury in the prior 6 months) who completed central fatigue (30 minutes of treadmill running at 85% of maximal aerobic speed) and peripheral fatigue (continuous isokinetic knee flexion-extension until peak torque fell below 50%) sessions in randomized order. Isokinetic peak torque, a jump-landing dynamic postural stability index, and treadmill kinematics before and after each fatigue protocol were analyzed with repeated-measures ANOVA or Friedman tests and Pearson correlations.
findings: After central fatigue, knee flexion at maximum knee flexion rose from 32.12 to 33.79 degrees (p < 0.01), stance time from 0.226 to 0.232 s (p = 0.025) and propulsion time from 0.127 to 0.133 s (p = 0.033). After peripheral fatigue, knee flexion at toe-off rose (p = 0.003) and ankle angle at initial contact moved toward plantarflexion (p = 0.035). Runners with greater hamstring torque had smaller knee-flexion change after central fatigue (r = -0.582), and a worse stability index was linked to larger knee-flexion change (r = 0.534).
limitations: Eighteen runners is a small sample, and most findings are Pearson correlations across many outcomes, so the results are exploratory. Several correlations are reported with p values smaller than a sample of 18 would usually give, and the unit of analysis for these correlations is not stated. The 113.6 N reduction in ground reaction force is estimated from earlier literature rather than measured, the sample size calculation refers to cyclists although runners were tested, and no training program or injury outcome was studied.
practicalImplications: Hamstring strength and jump-landing stability testing may help identify runners whose technique changes more when fatigued, which could guide monitoring. The study does not show that training these qualities reduces fatigue-related changes or injury risk, so present any training recommendation as untested.
athleteDev: For recreational runners, greater hamstring strength and better dynamic stability were associated with smaller fatigue-related changes in knee flexion and stance time. The study does not show that training these qualities would prevent those changes.
rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It tested healthy recreational runners with no injury, and it reports no rehabilitation or return-to-running outcomes.

citation: Taylor JB, Nguyen AD, Shultz SJ, Ford KR. Hip biomechanics differ in responders and non-responders to an ACL injury prevention program. Knee Surgery, Sports Traumatology, Arthroscopy. 2018.
abstract: Adolescent female athletes in the intervention arm of a cluster-randomized trial (43 reported, 42 in the responder analysis) completed drop vertical jump testing before and after a 6-week ACL injury prevention program. Athletes whose knee abduction moment fell beyond the minimal detectable change had greater hip adduction excursion at baseline and larger improvements in hip flexion and knee abduction measures, while the program overall did not reduce knee abduction moment relative to control.
tldr: Adolescent female athletes who reduced knee valgus loading most in a 6-week warm-up injury prevention program started with greater hip adduction and showed larger hip flexion changes. The comparison involved only eight responders, and the program as a whole did not outperform control, so this does not yet validate a test for who will respond.
methods: Secondary analysis of a cluster-randomized trial in which female basketball and soccer players aged 13 to 19 years completed a 20 to 25 minute warm-up-based program 2 to 3 times a week for 6 weeks. Within the intervention arm, responders were athletes whose knee abduction moment fell by more than 9.4 N m (the minimal detectable change) on a drop vertical jump, and baseline and change scores for 3D hip and knee kinematics and kinetics, performance tests and history variables were compared with MANOVA, t tests and chi-square tests.
findings: At baseline, responders showed greater hip adduction excursion than non-responders (5.3 vs 2.7 degrees, p = 0.02, d = 0.82), with no other baseline biomechanical differences. Responders reduced knee abduction moment by 17.8 N m versus an increase of 2.5 N m in non-responders (p < 0.001), and increased peak hip flexion angle (+5.1 vs -1.2 degrees, p = 0.02) and hip flexion moment (+37.8 vs +4.2 N m, p < 0.001). Responders attended about 22% more sessions and were more often soccer players, both trends (p = 0.07), and the intervention group as a whole did not differ from control in knee abduction moment change.
limitations: Only 8 responders were compared with 34 non-responders, and the analysis is a post-hoc sub-analysis of a trial powered for the overall comparison. Responders were defined by the same knee abduction moment change that is then compared between groups, so part of that difference follows from the grouping, and the authors note classification by one variable as a limitation. The tables sum to 42 athletes, while the abstract and methods report 43 in the intervention arm, and the text does not explain the difference.
practicalImplications: Before a warm-up injury prevention program, clinicians may record hip adduction excursion with frontal-plane video, as the authors suggest, to flag athletes who may need more individualized work. Because the baseline finding rests on eight responders and has not been tested as a predictor, treat it as a hypothesis rather than a screening cut-off.
athleteDev: In adolescent female basketball and soccer players, those whose knee abduction moment fell meaningfully after a 6-week warm-up program had started with greater hip adduction excursion and also increased hip flexion angle and moment. Team-wide warm-up programs may not change landing mechanics equally across players, but the study does not show effects on performance or injury.
rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It tested healthy adolescent athletes without a current lower-extremity injury, and it reports no rehabilitation or return-to-play outcomes.

citation: Caron JG, Cadotte G, Collict C, van Ierssel JJ, Podlog L. Exploring the Factors Involved in Being "Ready" to Return to Sport Following a Concussion. Clin J Sport Med. 2023;33(4):395-404.
abstract: Interviews with 22 sport-injury stakeholders described physical, behavioral, psychological and social factors that they believed affect whether an athlete is ready to return to sport after a concussion. The authors argue that the graduated return-to-sport strategy in the Concussion in Sport Group consensus statement focuses mainly on physical factors and does not address the other factors that participants raised.
tldr: Athletes, coaches and clinicians described readiness to return after concussion as more than symptoms and fitness, including avoidance, hesitant play, external pressure, mood and anxiety. These are interview themes rather than validated measures, so they show what to look for, not how to score it.
methods: Qualitative study with individual semistructured Zoom interviews (average 72 minutes) of 22 stakeholders in contact and collision sports, analyzed by thematic analysis following Braun and Clarke with NVivo 12. Member reflections were sought from the participants, and 7 of 22 responded and agreed the results reflected their experience.
findings: Participants described physical factors (concussion symptoms, 13/22; return to pre-injury fitness, 8/22), behavioral factors (avoiding contact, 4/22; malingering, 7/22; playing more passively, 9/22), psychological factors (cognitive appraisals, 22/22; mental health, 13/22; individual factors, 10/22) and social factors (external pressures, 21/22; social support, 11/22; isolation, 4/22; interactions between clinicians or coaches and the athlete, 8/22, or the athlete's teammates or roommates, 7/22). The authors conclude that these factors go beyond the physical emphasis of the graduated return-to-sport strategy.
limitations: Only four athletes were interviewed, and most participants were university-educated and involved in Canadian ice hockey, so the findings may not transfer to other athletes or sports. Interviews were conducted by videoconference by two interviewers, and the counts describe how many participants raised each theme rather than prevalence in any population.
practicalImplications: When judging readiness after a concussion, staff could look beyond symptoms and fitness to avoidance of contact, hesitant play, pressure from coaches, teammates or family, and mood or anxiety. Participants described athletes withholding information to be cleared and described asking directly, in private check-ins, about pressure and mood. These themes have not been validated as measures, so they should inform the clinical conversation rather than serve as clearance criteria.
athleteDev: Coaches and staff could note hesitant play, avoidance of contact, or passive play in practice as signs that an athlete may not be fully ready. The study describes these signs but does not establish how to measure them.
rtp: The study can inform how clinicians broaden their readiness assessment after concussion, but it does not validate any readiness test or set return-to-play timing or clearance criteria. Its findings are stakeholder perceptions, not measured outcomes, so they should not be used alone to make clearance decisions.

citation: Webster KE, Nagelli CV, Hewett TE, Feller JA. Factors Associated With Psychological Readiness to Return to Sport After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Surgery. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2018:1-6.
abstract: This cross-sectional study of 635 athletes after hamstring-graft ACL reconstruction, assessed about 12 months after surgery, examined which factors were associated with psychological readiness to return to sport measured by the ACL-RSI. Self-reported knee symptoms and function were the strongest correlate, with younger age also contributing.
tldr: Self-reported knee symptoms and function were the strongest factor linked to psychological readiness after ACL reconstruction. Only a quarter of this cohort had returned to competitive sport at about 12 months.
methods: Cross-sectional study of athletes who had primary hamstring-graft ACL reconstruction by 1 of 3 surgeons at one private clinic between May 2011 and February 2013, were cleared to return to sport, and were recruited at their routine 12-month review. The ACL-RSI was the outcome. Predictors were sex, age, injury-to-surgery interval, preinjury sport frequency, KT-1000 laxity, single-leg hop limb symmetry index and IKDC subjective score. Univariate and stepwise multivariate linear regression were run for the full cohort and by return-to-competition status.
findings: The ACL-RSI mean was 65 (SD 23). In univariate analysis for the full cohort, male sex (b = 5.8), younger age (b = -0.2), shorter injury-to-surgery interval (b = -0.1), higher preinjury sport frequency (b = 5.4), greater limb symmetry (b = 0.5) and higher IKDC score (b = 1.3) were associated with higher ACL-RSI scores. In the multivariate model, IKDC score (b = 1.2) and age (b = -0.3) remained significant and explained 37% of variance (r2 = 0.37). Laxity was not associated. Sex was significant only in the not-returned group in the univariate models (b = 5.1, P = .02).
limitations: Causal relationships cannot be established from a cross-sectional design. The cohort was relatively homogeneous and came from one clinic. The abstract's statement that female patients have a more negative outlook rests on univariate results, since sex did not stay in the multivariate model.
practicalImplications: Psychological readiness after ACL reconstruction tracks with how patients rate their knee symptoms and function, so staff can use the IKDC alongside the ACL-RSI when judging readiness. Because readiness was measured at one time point, the paper does not show that targeting interventions to female athletes would improve return rates.
athleteDev: The study does not address performance training. Its findings relate to how athletes perceive their knee after surgery and whether they are ready to compete again, and it does not measure sport-specific performance.
rtp: The study can inform the psychological side of return-to-sport discussions, showing that the ACL-RSI and IKDC are associated with each other at about 12 months. It cannot establish readiness criteria or safe return timing, and the authors note that high readiness does not show that return is safe.

citation: Webster KE, McPherson AL, Hewett TE, Feller JA. Factors Associated With a Return to Preinjury Level of Sport Performance After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Surgery. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2019:1-6.
abstract: This prospective cohort of 222 patients who had primary ACL reconstruction and had returned to their preinjury sport was followed to a mean of 3 years to see who reported being back to their preinjury level of performance. About 61% did, and psychological readiness at 12 months was the strongest factor associated with that self-rating.
tldr: Among athletes who had returned to sport after ACL reconstruction, about six in ten said 2 to 4 years later that they could perform as well as before injury. Psychological readiness measured at 12 months was the factor most linked to that self-rating, while age and sex were not.
methods: Prospective cohort from one private clinic (surgery June 2014 to July 2016, 1 of 3 surgeons). Eligibility required a sport-related ACL injury, primary hamstring (98%) or patellar tendon (2%) reconstruction, no prior contralateral ACL injury, 12-month review data and a return to preinjury sport. At 12 months, age, sex, return to competition, KT-1000 laxity, limb symmetry (single and triple crossover hop), flexion and extension deficits, ACL-RSI, IKDC subjective score and Marx activity score were recorded. At a minimum of 2 years, return to performance was a self-reported yes or no answer, analysed with univariate and stepwise multivariate logistic regression.
findings: Of 222 patients with complete data, 135 (61%) reported returning to preinjury performance (males 59%, females 63%). In univariate analysis, higher ACL-RSI (OR 1.03, P = .0001), limb symmetry (OR 1.03, P = .048), IKDC score (OR 1.03, P = .013) and Marx activity score (OR 1.07, P = .04) were associated with return to performance; age and sex were not. In the multivariate model only ACL-RSI remained significant (OR 1.03, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.04), and it correctly classified 87% of those who returned to performance but only 26% of those who did not (63% overall).
limitations: Return to performance was a single self-reported question, so it may not match objective performance, and the authors note that athletes can under- or overrate their performance. Follow-up was 2 to 4 years, the timing of return was not recorded, and 82% of the 272 patients who answered the performance question had complete data. The cohort came from one clinic and was homogeneous in sport and level, and factors not measured may matter.
practicalImplications: Higher ACL-RSI scores at 12 months were associated with later self-rated return to preinjury performance among athletes who resumed sport, so the score is worth tracking alongside knee function. It should not be used on its own to predict an individual's outcome, since it identified only 26% of those who did not return to performance, and the observational design does not show that raising readiness scores restores performance.
athleteDev: The study does not test training methods. It shows that athletes' own sense of readiness and confidence is associated with later perceived performance, which may matter when planning how athletes are reintegrated into training.
rtp: This study informs the performance end of the return-to-sport continuum: about 61% of athletes who had already returned to sport rated their performance as back to preinjury level by 2 to 4 years. It cannot be used to set return-to-play criteria, time frames or overall return rates, because only returners were studied and the timing of return was not recorded.

citation: Compagnin A, Della Villa F, La Rosa G, Patterson S, Read P, Herrington L, et al. Force and Power Testing During Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Rehabilitation: A World-Wide Survey of Current Practices. Sports Medicine. 2025.
abstract: International online survey of practitioners who assess patients after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction, examining which force and power testing devices are used across rehabilitation stages and how the number and type of devices relate to self-perceived testing quality. Practitioners used a mean of 3.6 devices with wide variation in combinations. Force plates, isokinetic dynamometers, Nordic hamstring devices and hand-held dynamometers were associated with higher self-perceived testing quality.
tldr: Practitioners test force and power after ACL reconstruction in very different ways, with 157 device combinations recorded in this survey. Those who used more devices, especially force plates and isokinetic dynamometers, rated their testing higher, but this is a self-report and does not show better patient outcomes.
methods: Anonymous international online survey of 100 items in 12 sections, developed by an expert team, piloted in two rounds and open from April to July 2024, promoted by direct contact, conferences and social media. Closed responses were analysed descriptively, with Spearman correlation between device number and self-perceived testing quality, stepwise multiple regression, and trend tests across rehabilitation stages.
findings: Of 1,154 respondents, 95.8% used multiple devices (mean 3.6 plus or minus 1.4), and 46.4% used device testing as criteria-based progression, 30.8% criteria- and time-based and 21.9% time-based only. Jump and hop devices without a force plate were used by 84.8%, hand-held dynamometers by 48.5%, isokinetic dynamometers by 45.7%, manual muscle testing by 44.7%, force plates by 35.7% and the Nordic hamstring device by 12.6%. Device number correlated weakly with self-perceived testing quality (rho=0.32, p<0.001), and force plates (coefficient 0.50), isokinetic dynamometers (0.44), the Nordic hamstring device (0.29) and hand-held dynamometers (0.21) were significant predictors (R2=0.21). Among the 1,072 respondents who did not rate their testing as excellent, equipment cost (77.2%), lack of space (34.2%) and managerial decisions (33.4%) were the most common barriers.
limitations: Responses are self-reported in an anonymous survey with no response rate, and the authors state that question validity and reliability were not established. Three-quarters of respondents came from Europe and North America and most worked in private practice, which limits generalization. The survey was in English, device categories may have overlapped, and the authors note that engaged practitioners may be overrepresented, so testing quality may be overestimated.
practicalImplications: Most surveyed practitioners used several devices, in 157 different combinations, and almost half used testing as criteria for progression, so local test batteries can be compared against this reported practice. Force plates and isokinetic dynamometers were associated with higher self-rated testing quality, but the survey does not show that they change rehabilitation decisions or outcomes. The authors advise caution when bodyweight, free-weight or machine tests estimate maximal strength from repetitions far from 1RM, and note that eccentric strength was assessed on the isokinetic dynamometer by only about 10% of the whole sample.
athleteDev: Performance Application: this is a rehabilitation testing survey, so its direct performance relevance is limited. It shows that jump and hop tests are the most common force and power measures after ACL reconstruction and that, among isokinetic dynamometer users, rate of force development and work were analysed by around a third, but it does not show that any device improves performance.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: the survey describes testing used to guide progression and return-to-sport decisions after ACL reconstruction, with 46.4% using criteria-based testing and 21.9% relying on time alone. It does not validate any test, cut-off or decision rule, so it describes practice rather than supporting a specific return-to-sport standard.

citation: Freiwald J, Javanmardi S, Hotfiel T, Engelhardt M, Rappelt L, Baumgart C. Fundamentals of individual loading for strength training after knee injuries. Sports Orthop Traumatol. 2023;39:368-377.
abstract: This narrative review describes how strength training after knee trauma and surgery should be adapted from principles developed mainly in healthy athletes. It covers arthrogenic muscle inhibition, the neuromuscular basis of eccentric actions, biochemical and sensor-based monitoring, and psychological factors such as fear of pain. The authors propose an extended table of load parameters for orthopedic rehabilitation, including avoiding maximal (1RM) testing in injured athletes and keeping early acceleration and movement speed low.
tldr: Strength training after a knee injury should be individualized, starting with low acceleration and loads, and maximal (1RM) testing should be avoided in injured athletes. The authors' load parameters are proposals, and the review does not test them against outcomes.
methods: Narrative review and special-issue article. The text describes no literature search, selection criteria or quality appraisal. The authors draw on their own earlier work on knee injury and strength training, together with cited literature, to build an extended table of load parameters (intensity, volume, density, frequency, movement speed, range of motion and termination criteria) for orthopedic rehabilitation.
findings: The review describes reduced neuromuscular activation after knee trauma from peripheral, spinal and central factors, and notes that eccentric actions need less activation to produce the same force.
