It advises against maximal (1RM) testing in injured athletes, against training to failure in early rehabilitation, and for low early acceleration and sensor-based monitoring. Table 2 lists general recovery times between sessions of about 72 to 84 hours for untrained people, about 48 hours for strength-trained athletes, and 24 to 48 hours for highly trained athletes.
limitations: No search or appraisal is described, so the selection of evidence cannot be checked. The load parameters are proposals that the text does not test against rehabilitation outcomes, and the authors note that much of the underlying training research uses mostly healthy athletes. Claims such as eccentric training significantly reducing injury likelihood are given without effect sizes.
practicalImplications: Start knee rehabilitation strength work with low acceleration, slow movement and low loads, and avoid 1RM testing and training to momentary muscular failure in the early phases, as the authors advise. Monitor joint pain, swelling, effusion and hyperthermia after sessions, and increase frequency and load gradually. Practice controlled movement reversal between concentric and eccentric actions, and keep deep squats out of rehabilitation in sports that do not need them.
athleteDev: When returning an athlete from knee trauma, the authors suggest matching strength work to the demands of the sport and training the uninjured limbs and trunk more often with explosive work. The review gives no performance outcome data, so progression should be checked against the athlete's own tests.
rtp: The review covers rehabilitation loading after knee injury and surgery, and notes that surgical, rehabilitation, social and psychological factors all affect return to sport. It gives no return-to-sport criteria or outcome data, so its load parameters should not be used as return-to-play clearance standards.

citation: Hoy MK, Stache S Jr, Roedl JB. Hamstring Injuries: A Paradigm for Return to Play. Semin Musculoskelet Radiol. 2024;28(2):119-129.
abstract: Narrative review of hamstring injury anatomy, classification, MRI and ultrasound imaging, treatment, return-to-play decisions and prevention in athletes, with a focus on professional soccer and American football. It also covers the Nordic hamstring exercise and emerging machine learning models for RTP prediction.
tldr: A radiology-led review that puts MRI grading, clinical tests and team context together when setting a return-to-play date after a hamstring injury. Imaging informs the decision but does not settle it alone.
methods: Narrative review. No systematic search method is described. The authors summarize anatomy, injury classification, imaging, rehabilitation, UEFA and NFL data, and recent machine learning studies.
findings: Grade 2 MRI injuries took on average about 6 more days to RTP than grade 1 injuries in a 255-injury UEFA cohort, as reported. Intramuscular tendon involvement was linked to longer time to full training (36 vs 24 days) and a higher reinjury rate (38% vs 12.5%) in English Premier League players. In the UEFA survey data, teams that used the Nordic hamstring exercise for all or most players had fewer hamstring injuries than teams that used it only for players with a current or prior injury.
limitations: The review gives no search strategy, and it draws on cohort and survey data from particular leagues and clubs. Its prognostic correlations are group-level associations, not individual timelines, and the authors state that imaging does not capture all factors in RTP.
practicalImplications: Use MRI grade and location as one input to RTP timing with clinical findings and sport-specific tests. When using the Nordic hamstring exercise for prevention, the cited UEFA survey data associate whole-squad use with fewer hamstring injuries than use limited to previously injured players.
athleteDev: Use injury grade and location to set expectations for training return, and plan prevention programs for the whole squad, not only for players with a prior injury.
rtp: Use MRI grade as one input to RTP timing, alongside clinical examination, strength and sport-specific tests. The review gives no validated RTP algorithm, so an MRI grade should not set a fixed return date.

citation: Vicens-Bordas J, Parvaneh Sarand A, Beato M, Buhmann R. Hamstring injuries, from the clinic to the field: a narrative review discussing exercise transfer. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2024. Ahead of print.
abstract: Brief narrative review of hamstring rehabilitation and training exercise selection. It asks which exercises improve eccentric knee flexor torque during the swing phase of sprinting, when the hamstrings are exposed to high strain, and compares eccentric, isometric, flywheel, lumbopelvic, sprint and bounding approaches.
tldr: Eccentric exercise, mainly the Nordic hamstring curl, is the only option with evidence of changes in running mechanics after training. Other methods are plausible but need kinematic and randomized trials.
methods: Narrative review. No systematic search is described. The authors discuss hamstring demands during acceleration and high-speed running, the transfer principle, and the evidence for each exercise type from training, cross-sectional and biomechanical studies.
findings: Nordic hamstring curl training increased eccentric hamstring strength by about 10 to 15% after 4 to 6 weeks in cited studies, and the one study that tested transfer linked the gains to larger terminal swing knee and hip moments. Flywheel training is described as more consistent with transfer principles but lacks kinematic studies. Lumbopelvic training reduced anterior pelvic tilt by about 5 degrees during swing in one study, but knee moments and injury risk were not shown to change, and bounding did not reduce injury incidence compared with a control group in one cluster RCT.
limitations: The review gives no search strategy. Its transfer conclusions rest on very few kinematic studies, and several cited injury-reduction studies are small or pilot-scale. The authors note that some studies find no link between eccentric strength and injury risk.
practicalImplications: Choose eccentric exercise, especially the Nordic hamstring curl, when the aim is to improve hamstring torque during running. Treat isometric, flywheel, lumbopelvic and bounding work as complements until kinematic or randomized evidence is available.
athleteDev: Select eccentric exercise, especially the Nordic hamstring curl, when the aim is to improve hamstring torque during running. Use progressive sprinting to expose athletes to near-maximal speeds, and treat flywheel or isometric work as additions with less direct evidence.
rtp: Use eccentric exercise and progressive high-speed running in late rehabilitation before return to competition. Individual muscle activity patterns may matter, but the review gives no validated EMG-based protocol, so exercise should not be individualized on that basis alone.

citation: Silvers-Granelli HJ, Cohen M, Espregueira-Mendes J, Mandelbaum B. Hamstring muscle injury in the athlete: state of the art. J ISAKOS. 2021;6:170-181.
abstract: State-of-the-art review of hamstring injuries in athletes. It covers incidence and time loss across sports, risk factors, injury classification, MRI and ultrasound use, platelet-rich plasma, exercise-based rehabilitation, return-to-sport criteria and prevention programs. It reports support for eccentric and lengthening exercise and for the FIFA 11 and 11+ programs when compliance is adequate, and states that PRP use is not substantiated.
tldr: Hamstring injuries remain common and recur often. Eccentric and lengthening exercise and the 11 and 11+ prevention programs have the best support, while PRP and MRI-based prediction of return to sport are not yet supported.
methods: State-of-the-art review by four authors. No systematic search or appraisal method is described. The review covers epidemiology, mechanisms, risk factors, diagnosis, treatment, return to sport and prevention, with boxed key articles and practical tips.
findings: In a cited meta-analysis, eccentric rehabilitation exercise significantly shortened time to return to sport but did not change recurrence risk. PRP trials gave conflicting results, and the authors do not consider PRP medically relevant at present. Prevention programs that include the Nordic hamstring exercise reduced hamstring injury rates, by up to 51% in a cited meta-analysis of 15 studies. MRI has not been shown to validly predict return to sport.
limitations: The review is not systematic, and the authors describe evidence on several topics as limited or inconclusive, including PRP, fatigue, muscle imbalance and ethnicity. Some recommendations on lengthened-position exercise and running progression rest partly on mechanism.
practicalImplications: Use classification, location and history to guide rehabilitation, combining eccentric and isometric hamstring work with a running progression. Include NHE or 11+ type programs in prevention, and monitor compliance, since the review reports that most professional soccer teams were not compliant.
athleteDev: Plan running exposure and high-speed progression, and keep eccentric hamstring strength work in the season plan as a prevention program. Congested fixtures and fatigue are discussed as possible risks, but the review says the evidence does not yet directly link fatigue to injury.
rtp: Use the review's return-to-sport domains (functional performance, strength, flexibility, pain and psychological confidence) rather than MRI alone. The review states that MRI does not reliably predict time to return or reinjury risk.

citation: Macdonald B, Mcaleer S, Kelly S, Chakraverty R, Johnston M, Pollock N. Hamstring rehabilitation in elite track and field athletes: applying the British Athletics Muscle Injury Classification in clinical practice. Br J Sports Med. 2019.
abstract: This two-part clinical review describes how British Athletics manages hamstring injuries in elite track and field athletes. It sets out general principles (early structural diagnosis with MRI, a shared decision-making model, targeted training of the muscles and movements involved, eccentric and isometric loading, and attention to fatigue resistance and lumbo-pelvic control) and class-specific progressions for myofascial, muscle-tendon junction and intratendinous injuries. The authors propose this as a structured approach but present no quantitative outcome data.
tldr: Match the rehabilitation plan to the BAMIC injury class, because myofascial injuries progress to running quickly while intratendinous injuries need a slower, longer tendon-loading progression. The approach is clinical reasoning from one national programme, not tested in a trial.
methods: Clinical narrative review of the British Athletics hamstring rehabilitation approach. The authors describe general management principles, class-specific guidance, and example running and strength progressions in tables, drawing on cited literature and clinical practice. No formal literature search method or patient dataset is reported.
findings: The paper reports no comparative or outcome data. It describes a diagnostic route with ultrasound and MRI within 72 hours, class-specific running and strength progressions, and return-to-full-training decisions based on clinical tests and shared team judgement. The authors state that their injury audit shows a marked reduction in previously published re-injury rates, but no figures are given.
limitations: The approach comes from one elite track and field setting and may not transfer to sports with lower tendon or muscle-tendon demand, as the authors acknowledge. The class-specific progressions have not been tested prospectively, and the audit improvement is not quantified in the paper.
practicalImplications: Use the BAMIC class to set the rehabilitation pace, with slower running progression and later eccentric loading for intratendinous (class c) injuries, which the authors estimate delays eccentric loading by about 3 weeks. Treat the progressions as a clinical framework to test locally, since the paper's evidence for them is expert reasoning.
athleteDev: Use the injury class to guide the strength and running progression. High-load isometrics can precede eccentric work, and fatigue resistance and lumbo-pelvic control are included in the plan. The paper gives no performance outcome data.
rtp: Return to full training is decided by clinical examination (range of movement, strength, palpation, Askling H-test), progression of high-intensity running, Nordbord strength at pre-injury level for MTJ and intratendinous injuries, and team shared decision-making, with repeat MRI as one input for intratendinous injuries. Table 3 gives approximate timeframes (about days 5-10 for 1a, days 14-28 for 2b, weeks 6-9 for 3c), but these are expert estimates, not outcome data, and no re-injury rates are reported.

citation: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, Carreira D, Martin RL, McDonough CM. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Clinical Practice Guidelines. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther. 2023;53(12):CPG1-CPG39.
abstract: This is the 2023 revision of the Academy of Orthopaedic Physical Therapy clinical practice guideline on heel pain and plantar fasciitis. It updates the physical therapy intervention recommendations from the 2014 revision, after systematic searches of MEDLINE, CINAHL, Cochrane Library and PEDro from December 2012 to March 2023. The authors state that the search found no new literature that required fundamental changes to earlier recommendations on risk factors, diagnosis and examination.
tldr: For plantar fasciitis, the guideline gives grade A support to manual therapy, plantar fascia and calf stretching, taping alongside other treatment, and 1 to 3 months of night splints for people with consistent first-step morning pain. It gives grade B support to resistance training for the foot and ankle and advises against orthoses used alone for short-term pain and against ultrasound to enhance stretching.
methods: Clinical practice guideline based on systematic literature searches (MEDLINE, CINAHL, Cochrane Library and PEDro; December 2012 to March 2023). Evidence was graded by level and recommendations were graded A to E. ESWT, corticosteroid injection and PRP were reviewed in scoping form only.
findings: Grade A: manual therapy to lower extremity joints and soft tissue, plantar fascia-specific and gastrocnemius/soleus stretching, rigid or elastic taping with other treatment for short-term pain and function, night splints for 1 to 3 months in people with consistent first-step morning pain, and no ultrasound to enhance stretching. Grade B: no isolated orthoses for short-term pain relief, low-level laser as part of rehabilitation for short-term pain, therapeutic exercise including foot and ankle resistance training, and dry needling of trigger points. Grade C: orthoses combined with other treatment and phonophoresis with ketoprofen gel; grade D (conflicting evidence): manual therapy, stretching and orthoses may be used instead of electrotherapy, with iontophoresis or interferential current as second line; grade E: education and counseling on maintaining lean body mass.
limitations: The recommendations depend on the trial evidence the panel reviewed, and the text does not report outcomes for athletes or sport-specific subgroups. The guideline is limited to interventions within physical therapy scope, so surgical, pharmacological and ESWT options are not graded.
practicalImplications: Staff managing plantar heel pain in athletes can use the grades to choose among manual therapy, stretching, taping, night splints and resistance training for the foot and ankle. Orthoses should be combined with other treatment rather than used alone for short-term relief. Ultrasound should not be used to enhance stretching.
athleteDev: Not directly applicable. The guideline addresses treatment of plantar fasciitis and does not report performance outcomes for athletes.
rtp: The guideline can inform rehabilitation of plantar fasciitis, including loading through resistance training for the foot and ankle. It does not give return-to-sport criteria or timelines for athletes.

citation: Whiteley R, Gregson W, Bahr R, Tabben M, Chamari K, Lolli L, et al. High-speed running during match-play before and after return from hamstring injury in professional footballers. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2022.
abstract: Match tracking and medical data from 38 professional male players in the Qatar Stars League were analyzed for maximal speed, high-speed running and sprint distance before and after a first hamstring strain. Post-injury values were modestly lower, but the authors state the differences were within normal match-to-match variability for these measures.
tldr: Professional players returning from a hamstring strain ran slightly less at high speed in matches, but the drop was within normal match-to-match variation. The finding describes match output after return and does not establish readiness or re-injury risk.
methods: Retrospective cohort analysis of multi-camera tracking data from 38 male outfield professionals (1,426 match observations) in one league, who played at least 45 minutes in at least 10 consecutive official matches as starters before and after their first hamstring injury in a calendar year (38 of 306 screened injuries). Multivariable random-effects generalized additive models compared pre- and post-injury maximal speed (km/h), high-speed running (>20 km/h) and sprint distance (>25 km/h), interpreted against match-to-match variability estimated from 265 players in one full season.
findings: Post-injury minus pre-injury differences were -0.25 km/h for maximal speed (95% CI -0.38 to -0.12), -43 m for high-speed running (95% CI -56 to -30) and -22 m for sprint distance (95% CI -29 to -16). The authors state these could not be distinguished from the within-player match-to-match variation of 1.67 km/h, 102 m and 60 m. Median layoff was 14 days (IQR 4-21).
limitations: Only players who met the 10-consecutive-start criteria were included, so the sample is likely a best-case group and results should not be extended to players who did not meet these criteria. The study covers one league, men only, and no standardized pre- and post-injury fitness tests, and it did not account for layoff length. The variability benchmark comes from league-wide data rather than an established anchor for meaningful change.
practicalImplications: When players return from a hamstring injury, small drops in match maximal speed, high-speed running and sprint distance are expected and in this cohort sat within each player's normal match-to-match range. Match data alone did not capture capacity, so the authors recommend adding standardized high-speed running assessments during rehabilitation.
athleteDev: For professional male players, returning from a hamstring strain was associated with small reductions in match speed and high-speed running that the authors judged within normal match-to-match variation. Coaches can use these values as context for expected match output after return, but the study does not set a target or threshold.
rtp: This study can inform expectations for match running after return from hamstring strain in male professionals in one league. It cannot establish when a player is ready to return to play, or whether reaching high-speed running targets reduces re-injury, which the authors leave to future research.

citation: Hegyi A, Csala D, Péter A, Finni T, Cronin NJ. High-density electromyography activity in various hamstring exercises. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2018.
abstract: Nineteen amateur athletes without a history of hamstring injury performed nine hamstring exercises while high-density EMG recorded the biceps femoris long head and semitendinosus. Activity patterns between the two muscles and along each muscle were exercise-dependent and, in some exercises, changed with contraction mode.
tldr: Across nine common hamstring exercises, overall EMG activity varied widely, and the 45-degree hip extension was the only exercise with slightly higher biceps femoris long head than semitendinosus activity. Activity also differed between proximal, middle and distal regions in an exercise-specific way, but this single-session EMG study does not show training or injury effects.
methods: Within-subject laboratory study in which 19 young male amateur athletes (soccer, Gaelic football, rugby) completed nine hamstring exercises at 12-repetition maximum in random order, with six repetitions each. Surface EMG was recorded from two 15-channel high-density arrays, normalized to maximal voluntary isometric contractions, and compared between muscles and between proximal, middle and distal regions for the eccentric and concentric phases.
findings: Overall activity ranged from 17 to 54% MVIC (eccentric) and 32 to 83% (concentric) for the biceps femoris long head, and from 19 to 51% and 33 to 85% for the semitendinosus. Hip extension at 45 degrees was the only exercise with higher biceps femoris long head activity (d = 0.28 eccentric, 0.33 concentric; significant only in the concentric phase). Semitendinosus activity was lower distally than in the middle and proximal regions in bent-knee bridge, prone leg curl and slide leg curl (d = 0.53 to 1.20).
limitations: The study had 19 men, all amateur and without hamstring injury history, and the authors state the results may not apply to injured or professional athletes. Surface EMG is prone to cross-talk, exercises used 12-repetition maximum loads, and no strength, adaptation or injury outcomes were measured. The abstract gives the biceps femoris long head regional range as 0.00 to 1.28 while the results give 0.02 to 1.28, and the results text reverses the eccentric and concentric order of the 45-degree hip extension effect sizes relative to Table 1 and the abstract; this review uses the table values.
practicalImplications: When a specific hamstring emphasis is the goal, choose exercises by the muscle balance they produce. Hip extension at 45 degrees favored the biceps femoris long head, while straight-knee bridge, bent-knee bridge and one-leg Romanian deadlift showed no clear muscle difference in the eccentric phase. The authors suggest exercises with high overall hamstring activity, such as straight-knee bridge, upright hip extension and leg curls, may support adaptation, but this was not tested.
athleteDev: For amateur soccer, Gaelic football and rugby players, hamstring exercises differed in overall activity and in how evenly they loaded the two muscles, so exercise selection can be matched to a muscle goal. These are single-session EMG patterns and do not show strength gains or reduced injury risk.
rtp: This study can inform exercise selection in hamstring rehabilitation only as a hypothesis about muscle activity, since it tested healthy amateur players and no injured people. It cannot show which exercises speed recovery or reduce re-injury risk, which the authors recommend testing in future studies.

citation: Nishida M, Yamamoto K, Murata Y, Ichinose A, Shioda K. Exploring the Effect of Long Naps on Handball Performance and Heart Rate Variability. Sports Med Int Open. 2021;5:E73-E80.
abstract: Eleven male collegiate handball players completed a handball-specific test (turnaround runs, a loaded 10-m run and ball shooting) after no nap, a 20-min nap and a 60-min nap. Nap condition had no significant effect on performance, but after the long nap higher heart rate variability (RMSSD) during the nap correlated with faster loaded run time. After the long nap, poorer habitual sleep quality (higher Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index score) also correlated with higher shooting accuracy.
tldr: A 60-minute nap did not change handball-specific performance on average in this small group of collegiate players. Any link between nap length, sleep quality and shooting accuracy is exploratory and should not guide individual nap plans yet.
methods: Eleven male collegiate handball players were randomly assigned, in a crossover design with at least one week between sessions, to a no-nap, 20-min nap or 60-min nap condition before a test of three 20-m turnaround runs, a 10-m run carrying a load and three shots at a 45 cm target. Naps and heart rate were recorded with Actiheart 5 monitors, HRV was analyzed in 5-min epochs, and the analysis used linear mixed-effects models and Spearman correlations.
findings: Linear mixed models showed no significant condition effect or condition-by-trial interaction for the 20-m turnaround run, the 10-m load run or shooting accuracy. In the long-nap condition only, PSQI score (higher means poorer sleep) correlated positively with average shooting accuracy (rho = 0.658, p = 0.039) and RMSSD correlated negatively with average 10-m load run time (rho = -0.929, p < 0.001); neither correlation was significant after the short nap. HRV indices did not differ between short and long naps, and post-nap sleepiness (KSS) did not differ across the three conditions.
limitations: The study had 11 men, one participant's nap data were excluded, and the authors state the results cannot be extrapolated to women. The abstract gives the PSQI correlation as rho = 0.636 with 'r = 0.048', while the Results and Table 3 give rho = 0.658 and p = 0.039; the abstract also claims a significant benefit of long naps for poor sleepers, and the Discussion says longer naps were 'likely more beneficial for 10-m turnaround runs', but Table 2 shows no significant condition effects and a slightly slower average turnaround time after the long nap (12.52 s) than the short nap (12.35 s). The tasks were simplified, habituation and day-to-day variability were noted, and several correlations were tested in a very small sample.
practicalImplications: A single 60-minute nap did not change handball-specific performance compared with no nap or a 20-minute nap, so a nap should not be expected to produce a measurable performance gain by itself. The PSQI-accuracy correlation after long naps is a single exploratory finding in about 10 athletes, so it is a hypothesis for a larger controlled trial, not a basis for prescribing long naps to poor sleepers.
athleteDev: A 60-minute nap did not improve handball-specific sprint, loaded run or shooting performance on average in these 11 collegiate players. The signals that poorer sleepers shot more accurately after a long nap, and that higher nap RMSSD went with faster loaded runs, are exploratory correlations that need a larger controlled trial before a nap plan is based on them.
rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It tests no injured or rehabilitating athletes and does not measure return-to-sport readiness, so it should not be used for that purpose.

citation: Mohr M, Ermidis G, Jamustas AZ, Vigh-Larsen J, Poulios A, Draganidis D, et al. Extended Match Time Exacerbates Fatigue and Impacts Physiological Responses in Male Soccer Players. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2022.
abstract: In 20 competitive male players, the 30-minute extra-time period of 120-minute games was associated with lower running output, maximal speed and accelerations per minute than the first 90 minutes, with further declines in repeated-sprint and jump performance and muscle glycogen. The authors also report lower blood glucose and higher plasma ammonia and glycerol after extra time, and they conclude that metabolic disturbances are a major part of the fatigue response.
tldr: Running output per minute, maximal speed and post-match sprint and jump performance were lower after 30 minutes of extra time than after 90 minutes, and muscle glycogen fell to very low levels in most fibers. Staff should plan for lower late-game output in 120-minute matches, but this analysis does not test fueling strategies.
methods: Analysis of the first 120-minute game in each of two trials of a pre-registered crossover project (40 player observations, 30 with complete data), before any diet intervention, comparing the 90-minute and 120-minute time points within the match. Match tracking used 10 Hz GPS and heart rate, with countermovement jump, repeated-sprint tests, knee strength, blood sampling and vastus lateralis biopsies at baseline, 90 and 120 minutes, analyzed by repeated-measures ANOVA.
findings: In Table 2, total distance per minute was 9.7% lower, maximal speed 10.1% lower and accelerations and decelerations per minute 18.3% and 16.8% lower in extra time than in the first 90 minutes, and successful passes and duels won also fell; high-intensity running per minute was 11.6% lower but is not flagged as significant in the table, and sprint distance per minute was essentially unchanged (-0.8%). Countermovement jump fell 19% at 90 minutes and 27% at 120 minutes against baseline, and muscle glycogen fell from 266 +/- 64 to 186 +/- 56 mmol/kg dry weight, with 82% of slow-twitch and 78% of fast-twitch fibers completely or almost empty after 120 minutes. Blood glucose fell 13% after extra time against baseline and 90 minutes, and plasma ammonia (+191% vs baseline) and glycerol (+137%) rose further, which the authors link to fatigue.
limitations: Extra time is compared with the same match's first 90 minutes, so the effect is confounded with cumulative time on the pitch, and players knew extra time was coming, which the authors acknowledge. The repeated-sprint test and biopsies before extra time may have lowered glycogen (the authors' own caveat), up to 30 observations pooled from 20 players are analyzed as if independent, and sample sizes vary by outcome (n = 30, 25, 19 and 11). Reported values conflict in places: the Results text gives high-intensity running and sprinting as p < 0.01 while Table 2 does not flag them and their effect sizes are trivial to small; maximal speed is 11% in the abstract versus 10.1% in Table 2; depleted fibers are about 75% (abstract), 76% (Discussion) or 82% and 78% (Results); and the Results report glycogen correlated with the sprint fatigue index (r = -0.56) while the Discussion says no such association was shown.
practicalImplications: Staff could expect lower running output, slower maximal speed and weaker post-match sprint and jump performance in the final 30 minutes of a 120-minute game, and plan recovery and substitutions with that in mind. Because glycogen and blood glucose were low at 120 minutes, recovery planning for players who play extra time could account for fuel status, but this analysis did not test any fueling intervention.
athleteDev: Total distance per minute fell about 10% and maximal speed about 10% in the extra-time period, with fewer accelerations and decelerations and weaker post-match sprint and jump tests. Performance staff planning for 120-minute matches or cup schedules could expect lower late-game output and plan rotation and recovery around it.
rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It enrolled players free of recent injury and tests match fatigue in healthy players, so it does not assess rehabilitation or readiness after injury.

citation: Robson-Ansley PJ, Gleeson M, Ansley L. Fatigue management in the preparation of Olympic athletes. J Sports Sci. 2009;27(13):1409-1420.
abstract: Narrative review of practical methods for monitoring and managing fatigue in Olympic athletes. The authors assess the scientific merit of self-assessed training load, self-scored questionnaires, saliva and blood diagnostic markers, nutrition and hydration strategies, and short-term recovery methods. They conclude that sufficient nutrition, hydration and rest are the best-supported strategies for optimising recovery in Olympic athletes.
tldr: For Olympic athletes, the best-supported fatigue management is adequate rest, sleep, carbohydrate intake and hydration. Session RPE and brief questionnaires are practical monitoring tools, but no single blood or saliva marker reliably identifies overreaching.
methods: Narrative review of training-load methods, questionnaires, performance tests, blood and saliva markers, nutrition, hydration and recovery modalities, drawing on studies in trained and elite athletes. The Methods section does not describe a search strategy or study selection.
findings: The authors describe session RPE multiplied by duration as a simple training-load method that gives similar results to TRIMP except at high intensity, citing a recommendation to keep weekly load below 4000 to 5000 arbitrary units. They report that POMS and DALDA questionnaires are practical indicators of training stress, and that no single reliable diagnostic marker of overreaching or underperformance syndrome exists, although the plasma cortisol to testosterone ratio is considered a good indicator of the overreached state. They give carbohydrate targets from 5 to 7 g/kg/day for light to moderate training up to 10 to 12 g/kg/day for extreme training, and report that active recovery speeds lactate removal but its benefit for subsequent performance is questionable, with little evidence supporting massage.
limitations: The review has no described search method, so it cannot be checked for completeness. The authors note that there is little literature on recovery strategies in elite athletes, and that the outcomes used in recovery studies (lactate clearance or muscle soreness) may not apply to them. Evidence on long-term daily questionnaire use is scarce.
practicalImplications: Track session RPE and a brief mood or stress questionnaire over several days rather than relying on one score. Schedule at least one passive rest day per week, protect sleep, and use earplugs or quieter rooms where noise disturbs sleep. Match carbohydrate intake to training load, and use urinary ketones and urine colour as practical checks on carbohydrate intake and hydration. The authors find no evidence of benefit for massage, stretching, cryotherapy alone, hydrotherapy or active recovery, and some evidence that compression garments may help.
athleteDev: Session RPE and questionnaires can show whether training load is being absorbed, and the review's guidance on rest, sleep and carbohydrate intake can be used to adjust the load. The paper gives no sport-specific training prescription and no outcome data from a training intervention.
rtp: The review concerns fatigue after training and competition, not recovery from injury, and it gives no return-to-sport criteria. Its general guidance on rest, sleep and nutrition cannot be used to clear an athlete to return to play.

citation: Driller M, Leabeater A. Fundamentals or Icing on Top of the Cake? A Narrative Review of Recovery Strategies and Devices for Athletes. Sports. 2023;11:213.
abstract: This narrative review ranks recovery strategies by the strength of their evidence, from meta-analyses to case reports. The authors report a high level of positive evidence for foam rolling, compression garments, cryotherapy, photobiomodulation, hydrotherapy and active recovery. Sauna, recovery boots or sleeves, occlusion cuffs and massage guns have lower-level and mixed evidence, and the review offers guidance for using strategies across season phases.
tldr: Foam rolling, compression garments, cold water immersion, cryotherapy, photobiomodulation and active recovery have the strongest evidence in this review. Sleep, nutrition and periodisation should be optimised before adding recovery devices.
methods: Narrative review. No search strategy is described. Recovery strategies were grouped by the level of evidence available, from meta-analyses and systematic reviews down to small trials and case reports.
findings: Foam rolling and compression garments are reported to reduce soreness and improve range of motion, but few studies link these to athletic performance. Cold water immersion supports acute recovery, while the cited meta-analysis of eight studies found that regular use after resistance training may attenuate maximal strength adaptations. Sauna, recovery boots or sleeves, float tanks, occlusion cuffs and massage guns have limited or mixed evidence, and two case reports describe serious illness or injury after massage gun use.
limitations: The review does not describe how sources were selected, so its evidence grading cannot be reproduced. The authors acknowledge that many strategies have been tested only in small trials or case reports, that performance evidence is sparse, and that the chronic effects of most modalities are largely unknown.
practicalImplications: Check sleep, nutrition and training periodisation before adding recovery devices, since the authors position these as the foundation. Foam rolling, compression garments and cold water immersion can be used for soreness and perceived recovery, with timing adjusted to the season. Sauna, massage guns, occlusion cuffs and recovery boots have weaker evidence and should be used with caution.
athleteDev: Use strategies with stronger evidence for soreness and perceived recovery, and do not expect them to raise performance on their own. The review suggests cold water immersion may suit in-season or competition periods, while repeated use after resistance training may blunt strength adaptation.
rtp: This review does not study return to sport or injury rehabilitation, so it cannot guide return-to-play decisions. Its mention of sauna for injury rehabilitation is a cited claim, not evidence from the review.

citation: Fowler PM, Knez W, Crowcroft S, Mendham AE, Miller J, Sargent C, et al. Greater Effect of East versus West Travel on Jet Lag, Sleep, and Team Sport Performance. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2017;49(12):2548-2561.
abstract: Ten physically trained men were tested for four days before, and four days after, a 21-hour westward trip from Australia to Qatar and a return eastward trip across eight time zones. Measures included countermovement jump, 20-m sprint, Yo-Yo IR1, sleep monitoring, and jet lag, fatigue and motivation ratings. The authors report that east travel had a greater detrimental effect on sleep, jet lag, fatigue, motivation and maximal and intermittent sprint performance, particularly within 72 hours of arrival.
tldr: In 10 trained men, travelling east across eight time zones reduced sleep and sprint performance more than travelling west did, and jet lag and fatigue lasted longer. The authors suggest arriving about 96 hours before competition, a recommendation from a small, non-counterbalanced study.
methods: Ten physically trained men (age 20.6 ± 2.7 years) were tested at 0900 and 1700 h on four days before outbound travel (BASE), for four days after a westward trip from Australia to Qatar (WEST), and for four days after the eastward return (EAST), with a pre-return day used as an internal control. Countermovement jump, 20-m sprint and Yo-Yo IR1 performance, jet lag, fatigue, motivation and physical feeling ratings, and wrist-monitor and diary sleep data were analysed with linear mixed models.
findings: Across the four days, sleep duration and time in bed were reduced after east travel compared with BASE and WEST (P < 0.05), with later sleep onset and offset, and mean jet lag, function (fatigue and mental performance) and motivation ratings were worse after east than west travel. Yo-Yo IR1 distance fell after east travel on day 1 but rose after west travel (P < 0.001), and 20-m sprint times were slower on day 2 after east than west travel (P = 0.03). Countermovement jump and sprint performance were reduced after both directions, with CMJ deficits greatest on day 3, and after west travel mean jet lag, function and motivation ratings were also worse than at BASE.
limitations: The direction order was not counterbalanced, which the authors acknowledge, so the east-west difference cannot be separated from order effects, and arrival time of day also differed (morning after west, 2220 h after east). The group is 10 men, interindividual variation was large, and only large effect sizes are reported. The Discussion calls the effects of west travel negligible and says west travel had no effect on sleep, but the Results report worse jet lag, function and motivation after west travel than at BASE, and the 96-hour arrival recommendation is extrapolated from CMJ recovery rather than tested.
practicalImplications: Expect the largest sleep, motivation and sprint decrements after east travel, mainly in the first 48 to 72 hours, but do not treat west travel as harmless, since CMJ and sprint performance and perceived jet lag were also worse than baseline after it. The authors' suggestion of arriving at least 96 hours before competition was not tested in this study and should be treated as a hypothesis to check locally.
athleteDev: Expect sprint and sleep decrements after eastward travel, mainly in the first 48 to 72 hours after arrival, and lower-body power deficits for up to about 3 to 4 days after travel in either direction. The 96-hour arrival suggestion is the authors' untested recommendation from 10 trained men, not a validated threshold for elite players.
rtp: The participants were healthy trained men and no injury, rehabilitation or return-to-sport outcomes were measured. The study cannot guide clearance or return-to-play decisions.

citation: Pimenta R, Correia JP, Vaz JR, Veloso AP, Herzog W. Hamstrings passive and active shear modulus: implications of conventional static stretching and warmup. J Sci Med Sport. 2024.
abstract: Forty physically active men without hamstring injury history were tested before and after a 5-minute static stretching protocol or a running-style warm-up, using shear wave elastography at rest and at 20% of maximal isometric contraction. After stretching, knee flexion strength fell by 18.3%, passive shear modulus did not change, and active shear modulus rose in biceps femoris short head and fell in semimembranosus. After the warm-up, passive shear modulus did not change, and active shear modulus fell only in semitendinosus, a change within measurement error.
tldr: Five minutes of static stretching changed the active stiffness of two hamstring muscles in opposite directions and reduced knee flexion strength by 18%. A running-style warm-up left passive stiffness unchanged and changed active stiffness only trivially.
methods: Two separate experiments in 40 physically active men (20 per experiment), each completing one laboratory session with pre and post measures and no control condition. Shear modulus of the biceps femoris long and short heads, semimembranosus and semitendinosus was measured by shear wave elastography at rest and at 20% of maximal isometric knee flexion, before and after passive static stretching (five 60-second repetitions) in one experiment or a warm-up of treadmill running, calisthenics and skipping in the other. The authors describe the design as an observational cross-sectional study.
findings: After stretching, knee flexion maximal torque fell from 98.9 to 80.8 Nm (18.3%, p<0.001), and passive shear modulus showed no change (p=0.996). At 20% contraction, active shear modulus fell in semimembranosus and rose in biceps femoris short head, and the pre-post difference between them rose from 3.8 to 39.3 kPa (p<0.001, d=1.66). After warm-up, maximal torque rose 1.4% (p=0.03, d=0.06), passive shear modulus was unchanged, and semitendinosus active shear modulus fell from 65.3 to 60.3 kPa (p=0.035, d=0.4), within a standard error of measurement of 10.54 kPa.
limitations: Stretching and warm-up were tested in different groups with no control condition, so the two protocols cannot be compared directly. The authors state that the active measurement was made at one contraction level, that muscle temperature was not measured after warm-up, and that other synergists crossing the knee were not measured; passive measures were taken with the hamstrings slack (hip neutral, knee 30 degrees).
practicalImplications: Five minutes of static stretching changed active shear modulus in opposite directions for the biceps femoris short head and semimembranosus, and reduced knee flexion strength by 18%. Do not expect the running-style warm-up to change hamstring passive or active stiffness in this sample. The functional meaning of these shifts is not known, so do not use them as a training or injury-prevention target.
athleteDev: The study shows that a running-style warm-up did not meaningfully change hamstring shear modulus in physically active men, and that stretching reduced knee flexion torque for the period tested. No performance outcome was measured.
rtp: The study cannot inform return to sport. It included no injured participants and measured no return-to-play or rehabilitation outcomes, so it cannot show when hamstring stiffness returns to normal after injury.

citation: Stevenson S, Suppiah H, Ruddy J, Murphy S, Driller M. Higher Levels of Morning and Daytime Light Exposure Associated with Positive Sleep Indices in Professional Team Sport Athletes. Nature and Science of Sleep. 2024;16:1279-1290.
abstract: Seventeen professional male Australian football players wore a wrist actigraph and a wearable light sensor for 14 days, and completed sleep questionnaires at the end. Morning light was linked to longer total sleep time, daytime light to higher subjective sleep quality, and evening light to higher Athlete Sleep Screening Questionnaire scores. The authors conclude that athletes should be educated on optimizing light exposure.
tldr: Elite Australian football players with more light in the morning and during the day recorded longer sleep or better sleep quality, while brighter evening light went with more sleep-problem scores. These are correlations in 17 players over two weeks, so they support sleep education rather than showing that light changes sleep.
methods: Observational study of 17 male professional players at one club during pre-season. Wrist actigraphy and collar-worn melanopic light sensors recorded sleep and light for 14 days, with questionnaires (ASBQ, ASSQ, B-PSQI) completed at the end; light was summed into morning, daytime and evening windows. Repeated-measures correlation was used for nightly sleep measures and Pearson correlation for questionnaire and well-being measures.
findings: Morning light was correlated with total sleep time (repeated-measures r = 0.26, p = 0.001). Daytime light was correlated with subjective sleep quality (r = 0.48, reported as p = 0.05), and evening light with ASSQ global score (r = 0.52, p = 0.04). Other light and sleep or well-being correlations were not significant, and the sample had a mean sleep latency of about 7 minutes and mean sleep regularity index of 79.
limitations: The sample was small and came from one club, and the design is correlational, so causation cannot be inferred. Light was measured by a collar-worn sensor that may not reflect light at the eye, its validity rests on unpublished laboratory observations, and sleep came from a consumer wrist device. The abstract reports morning light with total sleep time as r = 0.31, while Table 3 and the results give r = 0.26; this review uses the table value. The daytime sleep-quality result sits at p = 0.05 against a stated p < 0.05 threshold, and the athletes trained mostly outdoors, which may not apply to indoor-based athletes.
practicalImplications: Use these results to support education on getting light in the morning and during the day and reducing light before bed, as the authors recommend. The findings are correlations and do not show that changing a player's light exposure will improve their sleep, so do not present them as a validated sleep intervention.
athleteDev: In 17 elite Australian football players during pre-season, more morning and daytime light went with longer sleep and better self-rated sleep, while brighter evening light went with more sleep-problem scores. Use these links to frame light habits as part of sleep education rather than as a proven sleep intervention.
rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It measured sleep and light exposure in pre-season players and includes no injury, rehabilitation or return-to-play outcomes.

citation: Baker LB, De Chavez PJD, Nuccio RP, Brown SD, King MA, Sopeña BC, et al. Explaining variation in sweat sodium concentration: effect of individual characteristics and exercise, environmental, and dietary factors. J Appl Physiol. 2022;133:1250-1259.
abstract: In a retrospective analysis of 1,944 whole-body sweat sodium tests from 1,304 athletes and recreational exercisers, stepwise regression explained 17-23% of the variation in sweat sodium concentration. Energy expenditure and season of the year (a proxy for heat acclimatization) were the most important factors, while sex, exercise mode, air temperature and whole-body sweating rate contributed in some models. Age group, race/ethnicity, fluid balance and sodium intake were not associated with sweat sodium.
tldr: Higher energy expenditure was associated with higher whole-body sweat sodium and warm-season testing with lower sweat sodium, but all measured factors together explained only about a fifth of the variation. The authors conclude that predicting sweat sodium without individualized sweat patch testing is difficult.
methods: Retrospective multiple regression (stepwise, P < 0.05 for entry) of sweat tests compiled from Gatorade Sports Science Institute service and research testing from 2000 to 2020. Whole-body sweat sodium was estimated from forearm patches in models 1 and 2 and measured by whole-body washdown in a controlled 90-min cycling subset (model 3, n = 48).
findings: Model 1 (1,944 tests, 1,304 subjects, adjusted R2 0.17) retained warm season, cycling, male sex, whole-body sweating rate and body mass, and model 2 (1,003 tests, 607 subjects, adjusted R2 0.19) retained warm season, energy expenditure, cycling, air temperature and male sex. Warm-season tests were associated with lower sweat sodium, while higher energy expenditure, cycling, male sex and higher air temperature were associated with higher sweat sodium; in the laboratory cycling subset (model 3, unadjusted R2 0.23), energy expenditure was the only significant predictor. Age group, race/ethnicity, relative humidity, exercise duration, urine specific gravity, fluid balance, relative VO2max, and dietary or exercise sodium intake were not significant in any model.
limitations: The data are a retrospective convenience sample from one laboratory, with a male-majority sample, and race/ethnicity was dropped from model 2 for limited diversity. Heat acclimatization was estimated only from season, and field energy expenditure came from GPS or accelerometer devices with limited accuracy. The models explained only 17-23% of the variation, and model 3 rests on 48 tests from one controlled protocol.
practicalImplications: Repeat sweat testing when training or competition changes meaningfully in intensity, air temperature, exercise mode or season, because these factors shifted sweat sodium in the models. Athletes with higher energy expenditure had higher sweat sodium, so heavy-output blocks should not be assumed to share one sweat sodium value. Do not use age group, race/ethnicity or fluid balance as a shortcut to estimate sweat sodium, since they were not significant predictors.
athleteDev: Repeat sweat testing when training or competition differs in sweating demand, environment, exercise mode or season, because these factors shifted sweat sodium in the models. Higher energy expenditure was associated with higher sweat sodium, so sessions with high energy output should not be assumed to share one sweat sodium value.
rtp: This study does not inform return-to-sport decisions. It includes no injured or rehabilitating athletes and does not test any return-to-sport criteria, so it should not be used for those decisions.

citation: Di C, Jia W. Food-derived bioactive peptides as momentous food components: Can functional peptides passed through the PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathway and NF-κB pathway to repair and protect the skeletal muscle injury? Critical Reviews in Food Science and Nutrition. 2023.
abstract: Skeletal muscle injury from overuse or trauma is common in sport, and the authors review food-derived bioactive peptides as nutritional aids for muscle repair. They summarise the proposed mechanisms (PI3K/Akt/mTOR protein synthesis, oxidative stress, inflammation, cartilage, tendon and connective tissue) and list peptide sources from meat, fish, dairy, egg, plants and fruit.
tldr: Food-derived peptides are proposed to support muscle repair through protein synthesis, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory pathways. Most of this evidence is preclinical, so it is not yet a basis for recovery prescriptions.
methods: Narrative review. No systematic search, selection criteria or risk-of-bias appraisal is described. Evidence is drawn from cell, animal, in vitro and selected human studies.
findings: The authors propose that peptides may act on the PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathway, oxidative stress and NF-κB-linked inflammation after muscle injury. Human examples cited include a 14-week collagen peptide plus resistance training trial in 40 healthy young men (tendon and muscle hypertrophy outcomes) and a crossover study of protein and carbohydrate after exercise in 35 men that reported changes in serum cytokines. The authors state that most peptide research is still at the laboratory stage and call for human studies, yet they also conclude that peptide intake is "a good and safe way to improve the skeletal muscle function", which goes beyond the human evidence they cite.
limitations: The review does not describe how studies were searched or selected, so the evidence base cannot be audited. Most mechanistic and peptide data are from cell and rodent work, and the human studies are few and small. The authors list open problems themselves: separation methods for industrial production, possible allergic reactions, and the need for in vivo activity and safety testing.
practicalImplications: Peptide-containing foods or supplements should not be presented to staff as proven recovery aids for injured athletes on the strength of this review. Protein-based nutrition after muscle-damaging exercise is supported in general terms by the human studies cited, and any specific peptide use would need trial-level evidence in athletes.
athleteDev: The review gives no performance training protocol. Its human examples concern exercise-induced muscle damage and training adaptation in healthy or physically active young men, and the authors call for more human data before any performance claim.
rtp: This review cannot be used to set return-to-sport criteria or nutrition timelines. Its tendon and cartilage examples come from Achilles tendinopathy patients, healthy men and rodent models, and none tests a return-to-play outcome in athletes.

citation: Close GL, Kasper AM, Walsh NP, Maughan RJ. 'Food first but not always food only': Recommendations for using dietary supplements in sport. International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism. 2022. Ahead of print.
abstract: Narrative review proposing a working definition of 'food first' as meaning that, where practical, nutrients come from whole foods rather than isolated components or supplements. It sets out six reasons a food-only approach may not be optimal for athletes, including nutrients that are hard to obtain, variable nutrient content of foods and food contamination concerns. It then summarizes evidence for specific supplements and advises that any supplement use be batch tested and risk-managed.
tldr: Food first should mean that nutrients come from whole foods where practical, but it is not always food only. A small set of supplements with good evidence, such as caffeine, creatine, nitrate and beta-alanine, can be justified when food cannot supply the dose, and only if they are batch tested and used with a risk-management plan.
methods: Narrative review in which the authors explore the food first concept and give guidance on delivering it safely. No systematic search, inclusion criteria or evidence grading are described.
findings: The authors propose six criteria for when a food-only approach may not be optimal: nutrients that are hard to obtain in sufficient amounts, nutrients found only in foods athletes avoid, variable nutrient content of foods, high doses needed to correct deficiency or promote tolerance, foods that are hard to eat around exercise, and food hygiene or contamination concerns. For creatine, beta-alanine and nitrate the review states that the required doses are difficult or impractical to reach from food alone, and for caffeine the problem is that the dose in coffee is too variable to control (15 to 254 mg per serving); for sodium bicarbonate, food-based loading would need a high-carbohydrate, low-protein diet that is not optimal for other aspects of performance. For immune health, the authors note that supplements aimed at boosting immune resistance have shown little if any benefit in athletes, but suggest that vitamin D, vitamin C and probiotics may reduce illness during the common cold season and that zinc lozenges taken within 24 hours of onset may shorten a cold, citing meta-analyses and Cochrane reviews that are partly from non-athlete populations.
limitations: This is a narrative review with no described search, so the choice of evidence cannot be checked. Many supporting claims are taken from cited meta-analyses and consensus statements rather than from new analysis. Several immune recommendations rest on general or military population data. The author disclosures list consultancy, honoraria or research funding from sports organizations and nutrition companies, including the Gatorade Sports Science Institute.
practicalImplications: Treat food first as the default, and consider a targeted supplement only when the review's criteria apply, for example when a creatine or nitrate dose cannot realistically come from food or a known caffeine dose is needed. Any supplement should be independently batch tested and used with a risk-management plan, because batch testing reduces but does not remove contamination and labelling risk. Immune supplements such as vitamin D, vitamin C, probiotics or zinc lozenges are framed for specific high-risk scenarios (cold season, foreign travel, onset of a cold), not as routine immune boosters.
athleteDev: Performance Application: the review supports targeted supplements such as creatine, caffeine, nitrate, beta-alanine and sodium bicarbonate when food cannot supply the required dose, provided they are batch tested and risk-managed. It presents carbohydrate and protein products as practical options around training and competition when whole foods are hard to consume.
rtp: Limited application: the review mentions collagen and iron deficiency in relation to tissue repair and performance, based on the studies it cites. It gives no return-to-sport protocol and cannot guide return-to-sport decisions.

citation: Wickham KA, Spriet LL. Food for thought: Physiological considerations for nutritional ergogenic efficacy. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2023.
abstract: Brief narrative review of the physiological considerations that determine whether an orally ingested nutritional ergogenic aid can improve athletic performance. The authors discuss first-pass metabolism, rises in systemic concentration and interaction with target tissues, and explore mouth rinsing as a route that bypasses these barriers. They also cover practical factors that alter efficacy, including human variability, dosing, training status, sex differences and placebo effects.
tldr: An orally taken supplement should survive first-pass metabolism, raise circulating levels for a useful period and reach its target tissue, as creatine, beta-alanine and nitrate do. Study designs should control dose, training status, sex, placebo and blinding, because these can change whether an effect appears.
methods: Narrative review in which the authors build a framework of three physiological considerations for oral ergogenic aids and illustrate it with examples. No systematic search or study selection criteria are described.
findings: The authors state that an oral aid is likely to be effective only if it survives first-pass metabolism in sufficient quantities, produces a substantial rise in systemic concentration for a reasonable time, and interacts with or is taken up by the target tissue. Creatine and beta-alanine are presented as raising muscle stores, and dietary nitrate is reported to reduce the oxygen cost of submaximal exercise in recreationally trained males, with benefits described as mostly limited to recreationally active people and stop-and-go team sport athletes rather than elite endurance athletes, and emerging evidence of no benefit in women. Taurine raised plasma levels without changing human muscle taurine or cycling performance, carnitine raised plasma only modestly (about 30%) with no change in muscle content after 14 days, and pyruvate and microhydrin did not rise in the blood or improve performance. Carbohydrate mouth rinsing is described as consistently ergogenic through the central nervous system, while performance effects of caffeine rinsing are mixed.
limitations: The authors state the review is not meant to cover all potential ergogenic aids, and it does not grade the strength of the cited studies. The examples are selected to illustrate the framework, so the review does not give a complete or systematic picture of any one supplement. The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
practicalImplications: Before assuming a supplement will help, check whether there is evidence it reaches the target tissue at a useful concentration. Trials should standardize dose, co-ingestion (such as carbohydrate with creatine), training status and blinding, and should not assume an aid that works in recreational athletes will work in elite athletes. Staff should expect the size and direction of a supplement effect to vary with training status, sex and the demands of the sport.
athleteDev: Performance Application: the review provides a checklist for judging whether an oral supplement is plausible (first-pass metabolism, circulating rise, target tissue). It notes that benefits can differ by training status, sex and sport, for example nitrate effects appearing more in stop-and-go team sport athletes than in elite endurance athletes. It gives no dosing protocol for staff use.
rtp: Not applicable: the review addresses ergogenic efficacy and does not discuss injury, rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.

citation: Burd NA, Beals JW, Martinez IG, Salvador AF, Skinner SK. Food-First Approach to Enhance the Regulation of Post-exercise Skeletal Muscle Protein Synthesis and Remodeling. Sports Medicine. 2019.
abstract: Review of protein quality, the food matrix and post-exercise muscle protein synthesis. The authors argue that meal-based protein recommendations are built on isolated proteins, while whole foods contain non-protein components that may modulate the anabolic response. They conclude that a food-first approach is likely beneficial for both muscle adaptation and diet quality, but the food matrix hypothesis still requires rigorous testing.
tldr: The authors argue that whole protein foods, with their other nutrients, may support post-exercise muscle protein synthesis as well as or better than isolated proteins, so a food-first approach is likely beneficial for most people. This remains a hypothesis, because current meal-level protein guidance comes mainly from studies of isolated proteins such as whey and casein.
methods: Narrative review of protein quality scores (PDCAAS and DIAAS), the leucine trigger hypothesis, food matrix effects and exercise-induced gut permeability. No literature search, selection criteria or evidence grading are described, and the review draws on the authors' own studies and cited work.
findings: The authors report that post-exercise MPS plateaus at about 0.25 g protein/kg per meal in healthy young men when isolated protein is consumed, and that whole foods can stimulate MPS despite a slower rise in leucine. In the cited studies, skim milk gave greater MPS than beef during early (0 to 2 h) recovery, and whole eggs gave a greater post-exercise MPS response than an isonitrogenous amount of egg white. The authors also summarize that exercise increases intestinal permeability, which returns to baseline faster when food is consumed afterwards, and suggest this may allow food components to reach the circulation. The authors state that which food components or mechanisms drive the matrix effect is not known.
limitations: No search method is described, so the choice of evidence cannot be checked. The matrix case rests on a few acute MPS comparison studies, and studies that co-ingested casein with single milk components (milk fat, carbohydrate, milk serum) were done at rest and showed no added MPS response, so the authors suggest an exercise stimulus may be needed. The supplement was supported by the Gatorade Sports Science Institute, and the first author reports honoraria from that institute and research support from the National Cattlemen's Beef Association and the Alliance for Potato Research and Education.
practicalImplications: Dietitians should consider an athlete's eating pattern (animal- or plant-based), travel and training schedule when deciding between whole foods and supplements. In the cited studies, whole-food protein sources such as milk and eggs supported a post-exercise MPS response, so they are reasonable choices when they suit the athlete's diet. The advantage of the food matrix over an equivalent isolated protein is not established.
athleteDev: Performance Application: the review argues that whole foods such as milk and eggs may support the muscle protein synthesis response to training through components beyond protein. Dietitians should plan post-exercise protein around the athlete's diet and schedule, while treating the matrix advantage as a hypothesis.
rtp: Not applicable: the review addresses post-exercise muscle protein synthesis and remodeling in healthy adults and athletes, and does not discuss injury, rehabilitation or return-to-sport nutrition. It cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.

citation: Wang L, Meng Q, Su CH. From Food Supplements to Functional Foods: Emerging Perspectives on Post-Exercise Recovery Nutrition. Nutrients. 2024;16:4081.
abstract: This narrative review covers post-exercise recovery nutrition, from traditional supplements (protein, carbohydrate, creatine, BCAAs, electrolytes) to functional foods with bioactive compounds such as tart cherry juice, turmeric, omega-3 sources, and probiotics. The authors searched PubMed, Web of Science and Google Scholar for English-language studies from 2000 to 2024. They conclude that functional foods and personalized nutrition may support recovery alongside a balanced diet, and that dosage, nutrient interactions and long-term effects need more research.
tldr: Protein, carbohydrate and electrolyte intake are presented as core recovery needs, with dairy, tart cherry and omega-3 foods as complements. The authors note that evidence for BCAAs, bromelain and long-term supplement use is mixed or limited.
methods: Narrative review of PubMed, Web of Science and Google Scholar searches (English-language, 2000 to 2024) using keyword Boolean combinations. Studies were selected for relevance to recovery outcomes and grouped by theme. The authors describe the quality review as informal, with no structured risk-of-bias assessment.
findings: The review summarizes protein and carbohydrate timing, electrolyte replacement, and functional foods such as dairy, tart cherry juice, turmeric and omega-3 sources. It reports that plant-based protein supplements outperform low or no protein but are generally less effective than whey or milk protein, citing a Bayesian meta-analysis. It describes the evidence for BCAAs on soreness and fatigue, and for bromelain, as inconclusive or mixed.
limitations: The review has no quantitative synthesis and no structured appraisal, and the study selection is not reproducible from the text. Its own appendix notes short follow-up, small and non-randomised samples, self-reported intake, and few analyses by sex or age across the cited studies. Some statements go beyond the cited evidence, such as describing inflammation as a causal mechanism for recovery.
practicalImplications: Build recovery nutrition on a balanced diet and use supplements where intake is insufficient, such as protein or electrolytes after high sweat losses. Choose third-party tested products, because the review notes that supplement labels can be inaccurate and some products contain unauthorized pharmaceuticals. Treat functional foods as complements to whole-food intake, not replacements for it.
athleteDev: Use protein and carbohydrate intake after training to support repair and glycogen restoration, and note that strict timing matters less if daily needs are already met. The cited evidence suggests animal and plant protein sources differ in effectiveness, so check that total daily protein intake is adequate.
rtp: This review does not evaluate return-to-sport or rehabilitation outcomes, so it cannot be used to set a rehabilitation nutrition protocol. Its mentions of injury risk rest on the mixed BCAA and omega-3 evidence it cites.

citation: Bowtell J, Kelly V. Fruit-Derived Polyphenol Supplementation for Athlete Recovery and Performance. Sports Med. 2019.
abstract: This narrative review summarizes evidence on fruit-derived polyphenol supplementation for exercise performance and recovery. The authors report that acute doses of about 300 mg polyphenols 1 to 2 hours before exercise may improve endurance and repeated-sprint performance, based on a small number of studies with methodological limitations. They also report that more than 1000 mg per day for 3 or more days before and after exercise is associated with better recovery from exercise-induced muscle damage, mainly through antioxidant and anti-inflammatory mechanisms.
tldr: Acute doses of about 300 mg of fruit polyphenols before exercise may help endurance and repeated-sprint performance, but the evidence is small and mixed. The authors report a larger body of evidence that more than 1000 mg a day for 3 or more days helps recovery from muscle damage, much of it from Montmorency cherry trials.
methods: Narrative review with no described search strategy, inclusion criteria or quality appraisal. The authors organize studies into acute and chronic performance trials and into recovery-from-muscle-damage trials, and summarize them in tables by population, dose, protocol and outcome. The review was published in a supplement supported by the Gatorade Sports Science Institute.
findings: For performance, acute trials of pomegranate, cherry, cocoa and other extracts gave mixed results, with some showing better time to exhaustion or power output and others showing no difference, and chronic blackcurrant, grape and pomegranate studies also varied. For recovery, five of nine Montmorency cherry trials reported favorable effects on muscle function or performance, and those trials provided at least 1200 mg polyphenols per day, while soreness was reduced in half of eight cherry studies. Pomegranate trials mostly reported faster recovery of isometric strength but reduced soreness in only one study, and one blueberry trial reported faster recovery of knee extensor strength.
limitations: The review has no search strategy, inclusion criteria or quality appraisal, so the evidence base cannot be reproduced. The authors note that polyphenol composition varies by batch, that most studies did not measure plasma phenolics, and that serum markers may not reflect processes inside muscle. The first author received an honorarium from the Gatorade Sports Science Institute for writing the review.
practicalImplications: For an acute performance aim, the authors suggest about 300 mg polyphenols 1 to 2 hours before exercise. For recovery, they suggest more than 1000 mg per day for 3 or more days before and after heavy or repeated sessions, which they estimate 300 g of Montmorency cherries would provide. Check the polyphenol content of each product batch, since composition varies, and expect the clearest support for recovery of muscle function and soreness rather than for performance.
athleteDev: The authors suggest polyphenols may help time-trial and repeated-sprint performance when taken 1 to 2 hours before competition or for 1 to 6 weeks beforehand, but they describe this as early evidence. They also suggest they may be considered during repeated-sprint or high-intensity interval training, while noting that a training benefit has not been demonstrated and that evidence in resistance training is lacking.
rtp: The review covers recovery from exercise-induced muscle damage in trained or recreationally active adults, not injury or return to sport. It does not test rehabilitation after injury, so it should not be used for return-to-play or rehabilitation decisions.

citation: Zuhl M, Specht J, Beatty S, Mermier C. Glutamine Supplementation: A Possible Strategy to Help Mitigate Health Risks of Heat-Related Illness. Journal of Nutrition and Metabolism. 2024;2024:1638244.
abstract: The authors review the literature on glutamine during heat stress and exertional heat illness. They cover intestinal barrier damage, immune and cytokine responses, antioxidant defence, hydration and fatigue, and conclude that glutamine may be a useful adjunct to cooling and work-rest strategies.
tldr: This narrative review proposes that glutamine may help protect the gut, immune system and antioxidant defences during exertional heat stress. Most of the mechanistic support comes from animal and cell studies, and the human trials give mixed results.
methods: Narrative review with no described search strategy, date range or selection criteria. It draws on animal, cell and human studies of glutamine during heat stress, together with surveillance reports of heat illness among workers, military personnel and athletes.
findings: The review reports that 7 days of 0.90 g/kg/day glutamine, or a single 0.90 g/kg dose, prevented the rise in intestinal permeability after 60 min of high-intensity treadmill running in the heat in the authors' earlier work. A low dose of 0.30 g/kg/day did not change permeability or IFABP after about 22 min of exhaustive running in heat or 80 min of walking, and other human results are mixed: one 0.15 g/kg dose raised plasma total antioxidant capacity at 4 h after 78 min of heat stress, and a 0.60 g/kg dose before exercise in heat increased only T-lymphocyte mobilization. The review also cites a glutamine-enriched hydration mix that increased sodium and water absorption in healthy adults.
limitations: The review is narrative with no described search or selection method, so its evidence base cannot be audited, and much of the cited human work is from the authors' own group. Most mechanistic evidence is from animal and cell models, and the human trials differ in dose, timing and sampling, which the review itself notes. The suggested 0.15 to 0.30 g/kg/day range is justified by raised plasma glutamine without adverse effects, is lower than the 0.90 g/kg doses behind the clearest gut-permeability results, and no cited study measured heat illness as an outcome.
practicalImplications: Glutamine should not replace cooling, hydration, acclimation and work-rest measures, because no cited study shows that it prevents exertional heat illness. If staff consider it, the review's split doses before and after heat exposure, with large single boluses avoided because doses at or above 0.90 g/kg have been linked to GI discomfort, are the authors' own proposals based on plasma glutamine responses.
athleteDev: Glutamine is not a substitute for heat acclimation, hydration and cooling in heat training. The human performance benefit is not established, since the review notes limited data suggesting improved performance.
rtp: The review does not address return to sport after heat illness, so it cannot guide return-to-play decisions. It concerns prevention and mechanisms, and does not show that glutamine speeds recovery from exertional heat illness.

citation: Kasper AM, Sparks SA, Hooks M, Skeer M, Webb B, Nia H, et al. High prevalence of cannabidiol use within male professional rugby union and league players: a quest for pain relief and enhanced recovery. International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism. 2020 (ahead of print).
abstract: An anonymous online survey of 517 male professional rugby union and league players found that 26% had used or were still using cannabidiol (CBD). Use was higher in union than league and rose with age, with the main reasons given being pain relief, recovery and sleep. The authors call for player education on CBD risks and for research on its efficacy.
tldr: About a quarter of professional rugby players surveyed had used CBD, mainly for recovery, pain and sleep, and use was highest in older players. Players most often perceived a sleep benefit, and the study did not test whether CBD works or whether products contained THC.
methods: Cross-sectional anonymous online survey of 15 multiple-choice questions, sent to professional male players from 30 invited teams (English Premiership, Pro14 and Super League) in the 2019 to 2020 season, with 25 teams responding. Responses were coded in Excel and analysed with goodness-of-fit and independence chi-square tests, Cramer's V, Bonferroni post hoc tests, and Kruskal-Wallis tests for team differences.
findings: Of 517 respondents, 91% (472) were aware of CBD and 133 had used it, reported as 26% (8% current, 18% previous). Use was higher in union than league (chi-square 8.29, p = .004), did not differ by position (p = .760) and differed by age (p < .001), with fewer users than expected aged 18 to 23 and more aged over 28; team-level use ranged from 5% to 70%. Users cited recovery or pain (80%) and sleep (78%), 67% perceived a benefit (sleep 41%, recovery or pain 14%), no adverse effects were reported, and 79% believed their product was batch tested although only one listed product appeared to be.
limitations: The survey is self-reported and anonymous, products were not tested and the authors note perceived benefits may be placebo. Figures are inconsistent: the abstract reports 41% use in players 28 and older and 68% perceived benefit, while the Discussion gives 39% ("almost 40%") and 67%; the 26% use rate is described as a share of the 472 aware players, but 133 users is 26% of all 517 respondents and 28% of 472. The abstract attributes the information sources (Internet 73%, teammate 61%, nutritionist 16%) to CBD users, while the Results report them for all 472 aware players.
practicalImplications: Staff should ask players directly about CBD, since few players reported getting information from a nutritionist (16%) or other staff (4%). The authors call for education on anti-doping risk and product quality, because THC may exceed legal thresholds in some products and most users wrongly assumed their product was batch tested. The reported benefits should not be treated as evidence of effect.
athleteDev: Not applicable to training prescription. The study does not test performance outcomes.
rtp: Not applicable. The study does not test pain or recovery outcomes after injury, so it cannot inform return to play.
