citation: Hevia-Larraín V, Gualano B, Longobardi I, Gil S, Fernandes AL, Costa LAR, et al. High-Protein Plant-Based Diet Versus a Protein-Matched Omnivorous Diet to Support Resistance Training Adaptations: A Comparison Between Habitual Vegans and Omnivores. Sports Medicine. 2021.
abstract: Nineteen habitual vegans and 19 omnivores (untrained young men) completed a 12-week supervised lower-limb resistance training program. Habitual protein was adjusted to 1.6 g/kg/day with soy (vegans) or whey (omnivores). Leg lean mass, muscle and fiber cross-sectional area, and leg-press 1RM rose in both groups with no between-group differences.
tldr: Untrained vegan and omnivorous young men gained similar muscle size and strength over 12 weeks of leg training when both reached about 1.6 g protein/kg/day. The vegan group needed large soy protein supplements to get there, so the result does not show that plant foods alone would perform the same way.
methods: Non-randomized parallel-group study: 19 habitual vegans and 19 omnivores completed twice-weekly supervised leg-press and leg-extension training for 12 weeks. Protein was topped up to 1.6 g/kg/day with soy (vegans) or whey (omnivores) supplements, and outcomes were DXA leg lean mass, ultrasound muscle cross-sectional area, muscle biopsy fiber area (11 per group), and leg-press 1RM, analyzed with mixed models. The power calculation required 17 per group, and 23 per group were targeted to allow for dropouts.
findings: Both groups increased leg lean mass by 1.2 kg (vegans 18.9 to 20.1 kg; omnivores 19.1 to 20.3 kg), with no group difference in change (p = 0.99). Vastus lateralis area rose by 2.2 cm2 in vegans and 2.8 cm2 in omnivores, and leg-press 1RM rose from 258 to 354 kg (vegans) and 261 to 383 kg (omnivores), with no group-by-time interaction (p = 0.10). Type I and type II fiber areas increased in both groups, with no group-by-time interaction.
limitations: Groups were self-selected by habitual diet, not randomized, the trial was registered retrospectively, fiber data come from 11 per group, dietary intake relied on 24-h recalls, and physical activity was not reassessed at the end. The abstract and results disagree: the abstract gives 1RM changes of 97 and 117 kg and an omnivore rectus femoris change of 0.9 cm2, while the reported pre and post values give 96 and 122 kg and 0.7 cm2, and the results values are used here. Baseline leg lean mass for vegans is 18.1 kg in Table 1 but 18.9 kg in the text, and the discussion gives omnivore supplement intake as about 41 g/day versus 39 g/day in the results.
practicalImplications: For untrained young adults doing resistance training, a vegan diet providing about 1.6 g protein/kg/day produced muscle and strength gains similar to a protein-matched mixed diet over 12 weeks. Achieving that target required about 58 g/day of supplemental soy protein in the vegan group compared with about 39 g/day of whey in the omnivore group, so staff should plan for the extra protein and not assume a food-only vegan plan would match these results.
athleteDev: In untrained young men, protein source did not change 12-week gains in muscle size or leg strength when total protein was about 1.6 g/kg/day, which supports a plant-based diet for these adults only if protein intake is actively managed. The study did not test trained athletes, women, or whole-food-only diets.
rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It involved healthy untrained men and measured no injury, rehabilitation or return-to-play outcomes.

citation: Candow DG, Forbes SC, Ostojic SM, Prokopidis K, Stock MS, Harmon KK, et al. "Heads Up" for Creatine Supplementation and its Potential Applications for Brain Health and Function. Sports Med. 2023.
abstract: This narrative review summarizes research on creatine supplementation and brain health and function, and discusses possible sex and age differences in response. The authors report that creatine can increase brain creatine stores, which may explain some benefits for cognition and memory, especially in aging adults or during metabolic stress such as sleep deprivation. They also describe promise for TBI (including concussion in children), muscular dystrophy, depression and anxiety, while noting that sex and age differences are largely unknown.
tldr: Creatine may support cognition under stress such as sleep deprivation and may help some brain conditions, but most of the evidence is from animals, older adults or patients. Brain creatine rises only with high doses (about 20 g per day) over weeks, and athlete data are very limited.
methods: Narrative review with no described search strategy, inclusion criteria or quality appraisal. Sections cover brain bioenergetics, cognitive function, TBI, neurodegenerative diseases (Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, multiple sclerosis, ALS, muscular dystrophies, Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease) and mood disorders, drawing on animal and human studies. The paper is based on a presentation to the Gatorade Sports Science Institute Expert Panel.
findings: The authors cite evidence that high-dose creatine (about 20 g per day or more) is needed over several weeks to raise brain creatine, for example an 8.7% rise in total brain creatine after 20 g per day for 4 weeks in 9 healthy people. Human cognitive results are mixed; benefits appear more often under sleep deprivation, hypoxia or mental fatigue, including attenuated loss of passing accuracy in 10 sleep-deprived elite male rugby players given 50 or 100 mg/kg before testing. For TBI, animal studies show reduced cortical damage, and an open-label trial in 39 children and adolescents (0.4 g/kg/day for 6 months) reported shorter post-traumatic amnesia and better recovery; trials in Parkinson's disease and ALS were largely negative.
limitations: The review gives no search or selection method, so the evidence summarized may be selective. Much of the evidence is from rodents or patient populations, sex-specific responses come mainly from animal models, and the pediatric TBI trial was open-label with no sex-based analysis. The authors declare creatine-industry relationships and the supplement was funded by GSSI, a division of PepsiCo.
practicalImplications: Practitioners should not expect standard muscle-loading doses to change brain creatine, since the review cites about 20 g per day for several weeks as needed. Creatine's possible cognitive benefit during sleep loss is supported by a few small studies, including one in rugby players, and should be presented as preliminary. The review does not support creatine as a concussion treatment for athletes.
athleteDev: Evidence that creatine protects skill or cognitive performance during sleep deprivation comes from a few small trials, including one in 10 elite male rugby players. It is not enough to set doses or expected effects for athletes.
rtp: The review cannot inform return-to-play decisions after concussion. The human TBI evidence is one open-label pediatric trial in hospital TBI patients, and the authors call for more research before conclusions are drawn.

citation: Sone JY, Lamb SCK, Techar K, Dammavalam V, Uppal M, Williams C, et al. High prevalence of prior contact sports play and concussion among orthopedic and neurosurgical department chairs. J Neurosurg Pediatr. 2018.
abstract: This survey compared high school and college contact sport participation and lifetime concussion history among US orthopedic and neurosurgery department chairs with historical population norms. Chairs reported much higher rates of contact sport and football play and of at least one concussion (about 42%) than the general population. The authors conclude that individuals in careers requiring high motor and cognitive function frequently played contact sports, and call for study of both long-term benefits and risks.
tldr: Surgical department chairs reported playing youth contact sports and having concussions far more often than historical population norms. The study shows these histories did not preclude high-level surgical careers, not that contact sport or concussion is harmless.
methods: Cross-sectional email survey of 107 orthopedic and 74 neurosurgery department chairs at ACGME-accredited US programs, asking about high school and college contact sport play (American Academy of Pediatrics definition) and lifetime concussion. Responses were compared with male norms derived from 1970 to 1980 high school and 1981 to 1990 NCAA and census data and a 12% concussion prevalence, using one-proportion Z-tests, chi-square tests and binary logistic regression. Analyses were repeated assuming all nonrespondents had not played contact sport or had no concussion.
findings: High school contact sport play was 65.3% (orthopedic) and 47.9% (neurosurgery) against a 27.74% norm, and high school football 46.9% and 33.3% against 10.91%; college contact sport was 44.7% and 21.7% against 1.44%, and college football 21.3% and 6.5% against 0.758%. At least one lifetime concussion was reported by 42.6% and 42.4% of chairs against a 12% norm, and most chairs who described a cause attributed it to contact sports, mainly football. High school contact sport play was associated with higher odds of prior concussion after adjusting for specialty (OR 10.6, 95% CI 3.7 to 30.8).
limitations: Self-report and recall bias, moderate response rates (about 44 to 65%) and possible response bias toward sport-interested chairs; the authors also note physicians may recognize concussion more readily than laypeople. There were no standard definitions of sport participation or concussion, the 12% norm is a general adult TBI prevalence, norms were male-only and era-specific, and only one respondent was female. The worst-case model gives a much larger odds ratio (35.5) because nonrespondents were coded as having neither exposure nor concussion.
practicalImplications: The findings can inform discussion that youth contact sport participation does not by itself preclude later high-level cognitive and motor careers. They do not show benefit from contact sport, and the authors stress that the risks of head impacts and their sequelae cannot be dismissed. High school contact sport play was associated with a much higher self-reported lifetime concussion rate in this group.
athleteDev: Not applicable to training or performance. The study describes past sport participation and career attainment in surgeons.
rtp: The study cannot inform concussion management or return-to-play decisions. It measured self-reported concussion history only, with no injury details, recovery data or clinical outcomes.

citation: Manzi V, Savoia C, Padua E, Edriss S, Iellamo F, Caminiti G, et al. Exploring the interplay between metabolic power and equivalent distance in training games and official matches in soccer: a machine learning approach. Front Physiol. 2023;14:1230912.
abstract: In 21 elite male Serie A players over one season, four machine learning classifiers separated training games from official matches using metabolic power and equivalent distance index, although overall external load intensity did not differ between the two. Training load calculated from metabolic power metrics correlated with Edwards' heart-rate-based training load (individual r = 0.59 to 0.87). The authors conclude that these metrics can indicate differences between the two session types.
tldr: Metabolic power and equivalent distance index separated training games from official matches in one elite soccer squad even though overall intensity was similar, and load built from these metrics tracked Edwards' heart-rate load. Because games and matches were measured with different tracking systems and training games made up most of the data, the classification result is a weak basis for redesigning training games.
methods: Retrospective analysis of 4,269 training games and 380 official matches from 21 elite male players in Serie A over the 2021-2022 season; training was tracked with GPEXE 18-Hz GPS and matches with the STATS SportVU multicamera system. Metabolic power and equivalent distance index were used to build KNN, decision tree, random forest and SVM classifiers with 3-fold stratified cross-validation, and Pearson correlations compared Edwards' training load with metabolic-power-based load.
findings: The four classifiers discriminated training games from matches, with AUC of 0.89 to 0.98 and classification accuracy of 0.93 to 0.98 across playing positions in Table 2. There was no significant difference in overall intensity between training games and matches (mean difference 0.01 AU), and metabolic-power-based training load correlated with Edwards' training load at r = 0.59 to 0.87 within players and r = 0.75 for the team (p < 0.001). Metabolic power and equivalent distance index were not significantly correlated with each other (r = 0.017), and area per player was not correlated with training-game intensity.
limitations: The sample is a retrospective convenience sample from one squad, and the authors state the study should be read as a case study. Training games came from GPS and matches from optical tracking, and with 4,269 training games against 380 matches a classifier that always predicted 'training game' would already be about 92% accurate, so the reported accuracy is less informative than it appears; the paper does not report metabolic power or equivalent distance values for each session type. The abstract and Results give AUC of 0.90 to 0.96 and accuracy of 0.89 to 0.98, while Table 2 gives AUC of 0.89 to 0.98 and accuracy of 0.93 to 0.98, and the cross-validation description does not state whether folds were split by player.
practicalImplications: Metabolic-power-based training load tracked heart-rate training load within players in this squad, which supports its use as one external load measure alongside others. The claim that training games differ from matches in how intensity is produced rests on a classifier that may reflect different tracking systems and class imbalance, so it should not drive training-game design on its own. The authors' suggestion to copy exact percentages of high-speed metabolic power was not tested in this study.
athleteDev: Staff using GPS metabolic power can expect it to track heart-rate training load reasonably well within individual players (r = 0.59 to 0.87 in this squad). Whether training games reproduce how match intensity is produced is not settled by this study, because the paper does not report the session-type values and the classification may be confounded by measurement system.
rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It analyzes training and match load in a squad and does not assess injury, rehabilitation or readiness after injury.

citation: Junge N, Lundsgaard A, Hansen MF, Samozino P, Morin JB, Aagaard P, et al. Force-velocity-power profiling of maximal effort sprinting, jumping and hip thrusting: Exploring the importance of force orientation specificity for assessing neuromuscular function. Journal of Sports Sciences. 2021.
abstract: The authors compared force-velocity-power (FVP) profiles from maximal sprint acceleration, squat jump and hip thrust in 41 professional male footballers. They tested whether the profiles are linked across these tasks, to judge whether hip thrust profiling reflects sprint-specific neuromuscular function.
tldr: In elite footballers, maximal power (Pmax) was shared between sprinting and squat jumping, but the force and velocity components were not. Hip thrust Pmax was not related to sprint Pmax, so hip thrust profiling should not be read as a direct measure of sprint profile.
methods: Cross-sectional correlational design in 41 male professional footballers from two Danish Super League teams. Sprint FVP was derived from three 30 m sprints timed with photocells (time-shift method); squat jump FVP from unloaded and loaded jumps (+30 and +60 kg); hip thrust FVP from five loads (+40 to +120 kg) with high-frequency video. Pearson correlations were calculated between matching F0, V0, Pmax and SFv across tasks, with n = 26, 29 and 32 for the paired comparisons.
findings: Sprint and squat jump Pmax were correlated (r = 0.73, 95% CI 0.47 to 0.87, P < 0.001; n = 26). Squat jump and hip thrust Pmax were correlated (r = 0.44, P = 0.01; n = 32). Sprint and hip thrust Pmax were not correlated (r = 0.18, P = 0.36; n = 29). No significant correlations were found for F0, V0 or SFv between any two tasks (r between -0.19 and 0.20). The authors report that these findings are consistent with task specificity in neuromuscular function.
limitations: Sprint profiles were computed from split times and the hip thrust from video, and the authors note that the validity of the hip thrust FVP is not well established. Sub-sample sizes differ across the three comparisons (n = 26 to 32) because of player transfers and minor injuries. The population was a homogeneous group of male professional footballers, so the findings may not generalise to other sports, sexes or training levels.
practicalImplications: Staff who profile footballers should not assume that a hip thrust FVP profile reflects sprint acceleration capacity, since Pmax was not related between these two tasks in this group. Squat jump and sprint Pmax were moderately correlated (r = 0.73, n = 26), but F0 and V0 were not, so one test cannot substitute for the other when force or velocity capacity is the question.
athleteDev: Profiling the hip thrust separately from sprinting and jumping may give extra information on individual neuromuscular constraints. The study does not show that hip thrust training improves sprint capacity, and the authors state that transfer from hip thrust to sprint-specific function may be limited in high-level players.
rtp: This study does not address injury or return to sport. Its participants were free of injury at testing, so the findings cannot be used to judge recovery of sprint or jump capacity after injury.

citation: Rebelo A, Martinho DV, Valente-dos-Santos J, Coelho-e-Silva MJ, Teixeira DS. From data to action: a scoping review of wearable technologies and biomechanical assessments informing injury prevention strategies in sport. BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation. 2023;15:169.
abstract: This scoping review maps 21 studies on wearable and biomechanical technologies used in athletes to inform training adaptation and injury prevention. The authors searched PubMed/Medline, Scopus, SPORTDiscus and Web of Science to June 2023, following PRISMA-ScR. They report that Player Load, change-of-direction measures and the acute:chronic workload ratio were the most used metrics for injury-related decisions, and that force plates helped assess fatigue and rehabilitation.
tldr: GPS, accelerometers and force plates are widely used in sport, and Player Load is the most common metric. The authors see these tools as useful for individualizing loads and assessing fatigue, but they note that device validity and reliability are reported in fewer than half of the studies.
methods: Scoping review following PRISMA-ScR, with a protocol registered on the Open Science Framework (June 2023). The authors searched PubMed/Medline, Scopus, SPORTDiscus and Web of Science (last run June 15, 2023), limited results to English-language journal articles, and had each source charted by at least two reviewers. A basic quality check was done during charting but did not affect inclusion, and no formal risk-of-bias assessment was performed.
findings: Of 735 records, 21 studies were included: 10 in male athletes only, 8 in female athletes only, and 3 in both sexes. One cited American football study reported that a greater proportion of injuries occurred at an acute:chronic workload ratio above 1.6, and force plate studies in female volleyball, handball and basketball examined biomechanical variables linked to ACL injury risk. The authors describe these as mapped findings, not pooled conclusions about injury prediction.
limitations: No formal risk-of-bias assessment was done, so study quality was not critically appraised, and the review says it may have missed newer or less frequently studied technologies. Only 9 of 21 studies (43%) reported device validity or reliability, and the authors note that device heterogeneity limits comparison. The search was limited to English-language journal articles.
practicalImplications: Monitor Player Load and acute:chronic workload alongside position-specific drill demands, as the included soccer, volleyball and American football studies did. Confirm a device's validity and reliability before using it for decisions, because fewer than half of the included studies reported these. Use force plate jump and landing tests to track mechanics over time, as several studies did, rather than as stand-alone injury predictors.
athleteDev: Use GPS and accelerometer data to compare positional and drill demands and to set individual loads, as several included studies did. Pair device data with athlete-reported and performance measures, because the authors note that privacy concerns, discomfort and limited data-interpretation skills can reduce uptake.
rtp: The review cites rehabilitation uses, such as force plate tests during hamstring and ankle rehabilitation and workload management during recovery in professional soccer. These come from individual studies, and the review sets no pass criteria, so the findings cannot be used as return-to-play clearance standards.

citation: Kupperman N, Hertel J. Global Positioning System-Derived Workload Metrics and Injury Risk in Team-Based Field Sports: A Systematic Review. J Athl Train. 2020;55(9).
abstract: This systematic review of PubMed studies from January 2009 to May 2019 evaluated whether GPS-derived workload metrics are associated with musculoskeletal injury risk in team-based field-sport athletes. Total distance, high-speed running and acute:chronic workload ratios were the most common metrics. Many metrics were associated with injury in individual studies, but the authors concluded the evidence was inconclusive for any metric across sports.
tldr: Workload metrics such as total distance, high-speed running and acute:chronic workload ratios were linked to injury in some individual studies, but no metric predicted injury consistently across sports. Treat these metrics as descriptive associations until injury definitions and methods are standardised.
methods: Systematic review of PubMed records (January 2009 to May 2019) using search terms for GPS, workload, injury and team field sports. Eligible studies were original research that used GPS-derived variables as predictors and injury as the main outcome in team field-sport athletes only. Two independent raters graded study quality with the NIH observational-study tool, and a meta-analysis was not possible because of heterogeneity.
findings: Across 22 studies, results for the same metric often conflicted. For example, high one-week total distance was linked to higher injury risk in some studies and to lower risk in others. Acute:chronic workload ratios above about 2.0 were associated with higher injury risk in several studies, but these findings used different ratio methods and varied in strength, and five studies relied on magnitude-based inference, which the review describes as mathematically refuted.
limitations: The review could not pool results, and most included studies covered one team over one season. None of the included studies involved female athletes, and the authors note that none came close to the sample sizes needed for the number of predictors modelled. The per-sport counts in the text (10 Australian football, 6 soccer, 5 rugby, 1 Gaelic, 1 American football) add to 23 for 22 studies and do not match Table 2 (9 Australian football), and some in-text study citations appear misnumbered.
practicalImplications: Do not use a single GPS workload metric or acute:chronic ratio threshold to predict injury in an individual athlete, because the authors say unvalidated models offer descriptive associations, not prediction. Record injury definitions and load thresholds consistently so results can be compared. The authors recommend a four-tier daily availability classification that captures partial participation, which binary time-loss injury records miss.
athleteDev: Use GPS workload data to describe training and match loads, not as validated targets for performance. Avoid applying one squad's cut-offs as universal load limits, since the review found that the thresholds did not transfer consistently across teams.
rtp: This review studies injury risk in athletes who were participating in team sport and does not evaluate return to sport or rehabilitation. Its findings cannot be used to set return-to-play decisions or GPS-based rehabilitation loads.

citation: Pinto MD, Blazevich AJ, Andersen LL, Mil-Homens P, Pinto RS. Hamstring-to-quadriceps fatigue ratio offers new and different muscle function information than the conventional non-fatigued ratio. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2017.
abstract: Thirty-five professional soccer players completed a 30-repetition isokinetic knee extension and flexion fatigue test. The conventional hamstring-to-quadriceps ratio was calculated for the non-fatigued state and in fatigue, and several fatigue index methods were compared. Knee flexor and extensor moments fell significantly by the sixth repetition, and fatigue-state ratios were significantly higher than the conventional ratio but only weakly correlated with it. The authors suggest the fatigue ratio gives different information and needs prospective testing for injury prediction.
tldr: A hamstring-to-quadriceps ratio taken during fatigue gave larger values that were only weakly related to the usual non-fatigued ratio. It is a new measure that has not been shown to predict injury or return to sport.
methods: Thirty-five professional soccer players performed 30 continuous concentric knee extension and flexion repetitions at 300 deg/s on a Cybex Norm dynamometer in preseason. Conventional and fatigue-state hamstring-to-quadriceps ratios were calculated, along with fatigue indices using several published and new methods. Relationships were tested with Pearson and Spearman correlations and paired comparisons with effect sizes.
findings: Knee extensor and flexor moments were significantly reduced by the sixth repetition and fell further to the end. The fatigue-state ratios were 1.25-1.38 compared with 0.70 for the conventional ratio (p<.01 for repetitions 28 and 30; repetition 29 was not significant but had a large effect size). The conventional ratio correlated weakly with the repetition-30 fatigue ratio (r=.39, p=.02) and not significantly with the repetition 28 and 29 ratios (rs=0.25-0.27), so player rankings differed. The decline in the conventional ratio was strongly correlated with knee flexor fatigue in repetitions 28-30 (r=.80-.84).
limitations: Reliability was not measured, because players had limited time for laboratory visits in preseason. Eccentric hamstring strength was not tested. The authors note that the fatigue index method and angular velocity affect the results, and the test is untested as a predictor of injury or return to sport.
practicalImplications: A fatigue-state ratio calculated from a 30-repetition isokinetic test gives different values and different player rankings from the conventional ratio, so the two should not be used interchangeably. Staff should not treat the fatigue ratio as an injury-risk threshold until prospective data exist.
athleteDev: The paper suggests knee flexor fatigue may explain changes in the conventional ratio more than knee extensor fatigue. Staff could use this to guide fatigue-resistance work for the hamstrings, but the study did not test training effects.
rtp: The fatigue ratio has not been shown to inform return to sport. The authors suggest it may help return-to-sport decisions in future studies, but this study had no injured players and no return-to-sport outcomes.

citation: Flores G, Monteiro D, Silva F, Duarte-Mendes P. Heart rate variability activity in soccer athletes after a musculoskeletal injury. J Rehabil Med. 2024;56:jrm24969.
abstract: This study measured heart rate variability (HRV) in 15 semi-professional male soccer players within 72 hours of a musculoskeletal injury and again 5 to 7 days after full return to play. Low-frequency power and the LF/HF ratio were lower after injury, and high-frequency power was higher. The authors conclude that HRV may help detect autonomic imbalance and support safer return to play, and they call for controlled studies and baseline values.
tldr: In 15 injured semi-professional soccer players, HRV measured within 72 hours of injury differed from HRV measured after return to play, with lower LF power and LF/HF ratio and higher normalized HF power soon after injury. With no control group or pre-injury baseline, this is a within-group change only.
methods: Longitudinal study of 15 male semi-professional soccer players with a recent musculoskeletal injury, from three clubs in central Portugal; one further athlete was excluded as a statistical outlier. After 5 minutes seated rest, HRV was recorded standing for 8 minutes with a Polar H10 strap and m200 watch, and minutes 2 to 8 were analysed in the frequency domain at T1 (within 72 hours of injury) and T2 (5 to 7 days after full return to play). Paired t-tests or Wilcoxon tests were used, with an a priori power analysis requiring n = 15.
findings: At T1 compared with T2, LF power (n.u.) was lower (69.5 vs 83.7, p = 0.001), HF power (n.u.) was higher (30.5 vs 16.3, p = 0.001) and the LF/HF ratio was lower (median 2.81 vs 5.42, p = 0.001). HF power in ms2 differed between time points (p = 0.017), although the reported medians were similar (205 vs 218 ms2), and LF power in ms2 did not differ (p = 0.233).
limitations: No control group or pre-injury baseline, injuries of nine types including traumatic ones, and 6 athletes with a prior similar injury; stress and pain were not controlled. One athlete was excluded as a statistical outlier, but the number recruited is not reported in the text (the abstract says 15 were recruited). The higher HF power after injury conflicts with earlier studies, which the authors note were mostly in concussion, and the abstract's 'high values after injury' for HF power does not match the ms2 medians in Table II.
practicalImplications: HRV could be explored as one monitoring signal during recovery from musculoskeletal injury, alongside clinical assessment. The study suggests individual pre-injury baseline values would be needed before a post-injury change could be interpreted.
athleteDev: Not applicable to training prescription. The study measures autonomic changes after injury and does not test training or performance outcomes.
rtp: The study compares HRV in the acute phase with HRV after full return to play, and the authors suggest it could help identify a safer return. It does not test return-to-play decisions or show that HRV predicts re-injury, so it cannot set return-to-play criteria.

citation: Hintz C, Presley DM, Butler CR. Heat Stroke Burden and Validity of Wearable-Derived Core Temperature Estimation during Elite Military Training. The Physician and Sportsmedicine. 2023.
abstract: A retrospective case series and device validity study of exertional heat stroke among elite Air Force Special Warfare trainees wearing a Zephyr Bioharness. Of 10 confirmed heat stroke cases, 8 had estimated core temperature below the 39.7 C alert threshold, giving 20% sensitivity and 98.9% specificity. The authors conclude that the device had substantial false-positive and false-negative rates and should be used with extreme caution.
tldr: In elite military trainees, a chest-strap estimate of core temperature missed 8 of 10 confirmed heat stroke cases and produced 499 alerts, only 2 of which were heat stroke. The authors say medical staff, not the device, should be the first line of detection.
methods: Retrospective study of 1,364 trainees whose estimated core temperature was monitored in real time during strength and conditioning, running and rucking from January to September 2021, with peak ECT recorded per session. Trainees reaching 39.7 C stopped and were assessed; those with CNS dysfunction had rectal temperature measured, and heat stroke was diagnosed by an on-site physician and treated with cold water immersion. Incidence, sensitivity, specificity, likelihood ratios and Bland-Altman limits of agreement for the 10 cases were calculated in R.
findings: Of 47,058 daily peak ECT readings, 499 (1.1%) were flagged above 39.7 C, and only 2 of the flagged trainees had confirmed heat stroke. Ten heat stroke cases were confirmed (0.8 per 1,000 person-months), with peak rectal temperatures of 39.4 to 42.2 C and peak ECT of 37.8 to 40.6 C; sensitivity was 20%, specificity 98.9%, positive likelihood ratio 18.93 and negative likelihood ratio 0.81. The Bland-Altman plot showed low agreement between ECT and rectal temperature.
limitations: Retrospective design with only 10 cases, one of them a recurrence in the same trainee, and no reference temperature for trainees without CNS signs. The paper is inconsistent on sex: the abstract and Table 2 report 9 men and 1 woman, while the Results describe the cases as 100% male, and the Results call the trainees athletes. The abstract describes 499 flagged trainees, while the Results describe 499 flagged measurements, and the Bland-Altman bias and limits are shown only in a figure.
practicalImplications: This device's core temperature alert should not be relied on to detect heat stroke, because most cases occurred below the alert threshold. The authors recommend that medical staff on site remain the first line of detection, with rectal temperature and CNS assessment to confirm suspected cases, and they note that reviewing frequent false alerts takes staff time.
athleteDev: Not applicable to training prescription. The study does not test performance outcomes.
rtp: The study does not address return to activity after heat stroke. Table 2 lists a gradual return to training for all 10 cases, but the protocol is not described.

citation: Willer J, Allen SJ, Burden RJ, Folland JP. How Humans Run Faster: The Neuromechanical Contributions of Functional Muscle Groups to Running at Different Speeds. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2024;34(8):e14690.
abstract: Eleven male middle-distance runners ran on an instrumented treadmill at six speeds from 2.78 to 8.33 m/s. Inverse dynamics quantified the positive and negative work of flexor and extensor moments for each functional muscle group, and EMG was recorded from eight muscles per leg. Ankle plantar flexors were the largest stance-phase contributor at all speeds. Hip extensors and knee flexors became the dominant whole-stride contributors at higher speeds.
tldr: At higher running speeds, hip extensors and knee flexors carry most of the stride's work, while plantar flexors remain the main contributors during stance. Plantar flexor stance kinetics track step length, and hip extensor swing kinetics track step frequency.
methods: Eleven male middle-distance runners ran at six treadmill speeds with kinematics, ground reaction forces and surface EMG from eight muscles per leg. Joint moments and the positive and negative work of flexor and extensor moments were summed by functional muscle group. Linear mixed-effect models related kinetic variables to step length and step frequency.
findings: Ankle plantar flexors contributed more than 60% of stance positive and negative work at all speeds, but their share of whole-stride work declined with speed. Hip extensors became the largest whole-stride positive-work contributor above 5 m/s, and knee flexors became the largest whole-stride absorber above 7.22 m/s. Plantar flexor peak moment and positive stance work explained 97% and 96% of the variance in step length. Hip extensor peak moment and positive swing work explained 98% and 99% of the variance in step frequency.
limitations: The sample was 11 men with a relatively homogeneous middle-distance profile, and the top speed was below elite sprint speed. Net joint moments may understate muscle group forces because of co-contraction. EMG was limited to eight muscles, and some sample sizes were reduced to n = 7. The across-speed correlations do not show that changing plantar flexor kinetics would change step length.
practicalImplications: Coaches can use the finding that plantar flexors carry most stance work at all speeds, while hip extensors and knee flexors carry most whole-stride work at high speeds, to set conditioning priorities. The associations come from one treadmill protocol, so they should guide, not dictate, training choices.
athleteDev: Plan conditioning around the muscle groups that carry the most work at the speeds an athlete trains. Plantar flexor capacity may matter most for lower-speed running, and hip extensor and knee flexor capacity for high-speed running.
rtp: This study of healthy runners on a treadmill cannot guide return to sport after injury. It does not show that any muscle group is weak or injured, so it cannot set return-to-run criteria.

citation: Tourillon R, Michel A, Fourchet F, Edouard P, Morin JB. Human foot muscle strength and its association with sprint acceleration, cutting and jumping performance, and kinetics in high-level athletes. J Sports Sci. 2024.
abstract: In 52 high-level athletes, the authors tested the association between maximal MTP flexion torque and sprint acceleration, cutting and jumping performance and ground reaction force kinetics, and whether adding other foot and leg variables improved the models. MTP torque was moderately associated with maximal-speed sprint kinetics, where models including MTP torque explained 28% and 35% of variance, while acceleration and cutting performance were explained mainly by plantarflexor and quadriceps strength.
tldr: In this group of injury-free athletes, forefoot (MTP) flexion strength was moderately linked to maximal-speed sprint kinetics and to 10 m time in the high-acceleration condition. It was not linked to cutting or vertical jump performance, and higher gripping strength went with lower horizontal jump power, so its training value is untested.
methods: Cross-sectional study of 52 injury-free athletes (47 men, 5 women) at national level in five sports. MTP flexion torque was measured with a custom dynamometer, and sprint acceleration, 90-degree cutting, vertical and horizontal countermovement jumps and foot-ankle hops were recorded on force platforms with timing gates. Pearson correlations and stepwise backward multiple regressions were used, with foot posture, foot deformation, ankle plantarflexor and quadriceps torque, and reactive strength added to the models.
findings: Relative MTP pushing and total torque were moderately associated with 10 m sprint time in the high-acceleration condition (r = -0.33, p = 0.02) and with relative effective vertical impulse (r = 0.42, p = 0.03) and contact time (r = -0.41, p = 0.04) at maximal speed. Higher gripping torque was associated with lower horizontal jump peak power (r = -0.35, p = 0.01), and no MTP torque variable was associated with vertical jump height or cutting time. Models combining MTP torque with foot deformation or foot-ankle reactive strength explained 28% and 35% of variance in maximal-speed impulse and contact time; acceleration (27% to 36%) and cutting (35%) models did not retain MTP torque, and jump models (26% to 38%) retained only gripping torque, for horizontal power.
limitations: The design is cross-sectional and correlational, so causal effects cannot be inferred. Strength was measured at one joint angle only, the hip was not measured, and the sample was young (mean age 20.1 years), 90% male and from five sports. The sample size was calculated for an assumed r of 0.70, which no observed correlation reached, so the authors note possible underpowering. Sprint data came from several trials with different starting points. The Discussion gives 37% of variance for contact time, while the Results give an adjusted r2 of 0.35. The explained variance comes from models that include other variables, not from MTP torque alone, and the Discussion attributes 23% and 26% of vertical jump variance to quadriceps torque and foot flexibility, while the Results report 26% to 38% for jump models.
practicalImplications: Forefoot (MTP) flexion strength can be considered as one part of a profile when assessing sprint and jump capacity, mainly for maximal-speed sprint kinetics. The authors suggest adding MTP flexion and foot-ankle reactive strength exercises to development programmes, but this study did not test training, so treat it as a hypothesis to trial and measure. Keep ankle plantarflexor and quadriceps strength in view: together they explained acceleration performance, plantarflexor torque contributed to cutting, and quadriceps torque contributed to jumping.
athleteDev: Consider testing forefoot flexion strength as part of a performance profile for sprinters and field athletes. The study links it to maximal-speed sprint kinetics, but not to cutting or vertical jump height. Pair any forefoot work with reactive strength and plantarflexor strength, and track changes in sprint outcomes to test whether the link holds in your athletes.
rtp: The sample was injury-free and the study did not assess return to sport or rehabilitation. It cannot inform return-to-play decisions or set strength targets for injured athletes.

citation: Scott BR, Slattery KM, Sculley DV, Dascombe BJ. Hypoxia and Resistance Exercise: A Comparison of Localized and Systemic Methods. Sports Medicine. 2014;44:1037-1054.
abstract: Narrative review of resistance exercise under localized hypoxia (blood flow restriction, BFR) and systemic hypoxia (intermittent hypoxic resistance training, IHRT). The authors summarize adaptive, perceptual and mechanistic evidence for each method and compare their practical limits. They suggest IHRT may suit athletic populations but state that few studies allow firm recommendations.
tldr: Low-intensity BFR training can build muscle and strength more than the same training without BFR, but its mechanisms are not settled. Resistance training in systemic hypoxia looks promising for athletes, but the evidence is thin.
methods: Narrative review, with no described search method, of published studies on resistance exercise with BFR and with systemic hypoxia. It covers morphological, strength, perceptual, hormonal, metabolic and signalling responses. Tables 2 and 3 summarize acute and training studies of systemic hypoxia.
findings: BFR studies report larger gains in muscle cross-sectional area and strength after low-intensity training (about 20 to 50 percent 1RM) than the same training without BFR, with inconsistent responses for IGF-1, testosterone and myostatin. For systemic hypoxia, the review cites a 5-week study in netball athletes in which both IHRT and BFR gave greater strength and muscle size gains than normoxic training, and a 4-week study with no advantage for hypoxia.
limitations: The review does not describe how studies were selected or how evidence quality was judged. The authors note that IHRT research is limited, that the mechanisms remain poorly understood, and that low-intensity BFR does not produce the same motor unit activation as high-intensity training taken to failure.
practicalImplications: BFR may suit people who cannot tolerate moderate or high loads, such as older adults, rehabilitation patients, or athletes managing total training load. The authors suggest IHRT may suit athletes because multi-joint lifts can be trained at higher intensity, but they say current understanding does not allow firm recommendations. Cuffs must be applied with experience, since inappropriate use can cause petechiae, numbness and dizziness.
athleteDev: Low-intensity BFR can add a muscle and strength stimulus when heavy loads are not suitable, for example when managing total training load. Resistance training in systemic hypoxia may suit athletes because multi-joint lifts can be trained at higher intensity, but the review says the evidence is too thin for firm training recommendations.
rtp: The review mentions rehabilitation patients as a possible BFR population and proposes that BFR could reduce joint stress, but it does not test return-to-sport outcomes or injury rates. It cannot set return-to-sport loading or clearance criteria.

citation: Husmann F, Mittlmeier T, Bruhn S, Zschorlich V, Behrens M. Impact of Blood Flow Restriction Exercise on Muscle Fatigue Development and Recovery. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2018;50(3):436-446.
abstract: Laboratory study of 17 resistance-trained, physically active males comparing four sets of low-intensity knee extension with and without blood flow restriction. The authors tracked maximal voluntary torque, electrically evoked twitch torque and voluntary activation during and after exercise. BFR produced faster and larger fatigue during exercise, and the effect diminished within about 2 minutes of reperfusion.
tldr: Low-intensity knee extension with blood flow restriction causes more muscle fatigue than the same work without restriction, mainly through reduced contractile torque. The extra loss of maximal torque was gone within 2 minutes of cuff release, although some twitch-torque differences persisted longer.
methods: Within-subject, randomized, counterbalanced design with two sessions. Participants did four sets (30, 15, 15 and 15 repetitions at 30 percent 1RM) with BFR at 60 percent of arterial occlusion pressure, or without BFR. Neuromuscular tests (MVC, interpolated twitch, paired stimuli at 10 and 100 Hz, single stimuli) were done before, after each set, and at 1, 2, 4 and 8 minutes of recovery, with EMG, RPE and leg pain recorded.
findings: After the first set, BFR caused larger reductions in MVT, PS100 twitch torque and the PS10:PS100 ratio than control. At exercise termination, MVT fell 44.5 percent with BFR and 24.3 percent in control, and voluntary activation fell more with BFR (10.2 vs 3.2 percent). Twitch torque recovered substantially within 2 minutes after BFR, while voluntary activation was reduced in both conditions at 1 minute and MVT had not fully recovered by 8 minutes.
limitations: Only men were tested and the sample was small, so sex differences in fatigability are not addressed. Peripheral nerve stimulation cannot show whether spinal or supraspinal factors caused the impairment in neural drive, and the authors infer group III/IV afferent mechanisms without measuring them.
practicalImplications: Low-intensity BFR produces large fatigue within a session, so set loads and rest periods with that in mind. The authors suggest low-intensity BFR may suit high-frequency hypertrophy training because much of the torque loss recovers within minutes of cuff release, but this single-session study tested no training outcomes and MVT was still about 13 percent down at 8 minutes.
athleteDev: Within a session, low-load BFR produced large early torque loss and higher perceived effort, so set loading should account for that. The authors propose low-intensity BFR for high-frequency hypertrophy work, but the study measured acute fatigue only, not performance or adaptation.
rtp: The study measured acute fatigue in healthy men and did not include injured people or return-to-sport tests. It cannot show whether BFR work is safe after injury or set loading for return to sport.

citation: Hegyi A, Lahti J, Giacomo JP, Gerus P, Cronin NJ, Morin JB. Impact of Hip Flexion Angle on Unilateral and Bilateral Nordic Hamstring Exercise Torque and High-Density Electromyography Activity. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2019;49(8):584-592.
abstract: This laboratory study compared knee flexion torque and high-density EMG of the BFLH and ST during bilateral and unilateral Nordic hamstring exercise performed with neutral hips and with 90-degree hip flexion. Thirteen amateur football and rugby players completed the four exercise variants at an eccentric 1-repetition maximum load. Hip flexion to 90 degrees produced higher torque and lower EMG in both muscles.
tldr: Hip position changes how the Nordic hamstring exercise loads the hamstrings. Flexing the hips to 90 degrees gave more knee flexion torque with less muscle activity, while neutral hips gave more activity, especially in the BFLH near full knee extension.
methods: Thirteen amateur football and rugby players performed bilateral and unilateral Nordic hamstring exercise with neutral hips (NHE0) and with 90-degree hip flexion (NHE90) at an eccentric 1-repetition maximum load, with knee motion paced at about 15 degrees per second. Torque came from a load-cell device, and 15-channel high-density EMG was recorded from each of the BFLH and ST. Curves were compared with statistical parametric mapping.
findings: NHE90 produced higher knee flexion torque than NHE0 across most of the movement in the bilateral mode (0% to 87%) and throughout the unilateral movement. Both BFLH and ST were more active in NHE0 than in NHE90, and bilateral and unilateral modes gave similar peak torque and EMG when load was matched. Bilateral NHE0 produced higher torque than unilateral NHE0 only in the midrange (52% to 78%).
limitations: The sample was small (13 amateur male players), and the authors state that this may have raised the false-negative rate and biased the effect sizes. Surface EMG is prone to cross-talk, knee angle came from the device potentiometer rather than direct measurement, and torque and EMG were recorded from the dominant leg only. One author is the inventor and patent owner of the load-cell device used, the results may not apply to other populations, and only acute responses were measured.
practicalImplications: Choose hip position deliberately: NHE90 gave more knee flexion torque with less hamstring EMG, which may suit long-length eccentric loading and selective ST activation, while NHE0 gave more EMG, especially BFLH near full extension. Unilateral and bilateral versions gave similar peak torque and EMG at matched load, so single-leg work is a reasonable option. The study did not test whether unilateral work reduces side-to-side strength imbalance.
athleteDev: Hip position changes the torque and EMG profile of the NHE. Use NHE90 when the goal is higher eccentric torque and selective ST activation at long hamstring lengths, and NHE0 when the goal is higher BFLH activity near full knee extension. Unilateral and bilateral NHE gave similar peak torque and EMG at matched load, so the choice between them did not change these measures.
rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions or hamstring injury risk. It measured acute torque and EMG in healthy amateur players and did not test injured athletes. The authors suggest, but do not test, that NHE90 may reduce injury risk.

citation: Cook CJ, Kilduff LP, Beaven CM. Improving Strength and Power in Trained Athletes With 3 Weeks of Occlusion Training. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2014;9:166-172.
abstract: Twenty male semiprofessional rugby union players each trained for two 3-week blocks, with and without intermittent 180 mmHg occlusion of the lower limbs, using 5 x 5 bench press, squat and pull-up at 70% 1RM. Occlusion produced greater gains in bench press, squat, sprint time, jump power and repeated-sprint maintenance, and larger acute salivary testosterone and cortisol responses, with the cortisol response attenuated over the block.
tldr: In a small crossover study of 20 semiprofessional rugby players, adding lower-limb occlusion to moderate-load (70% 1RM) lifting gave larger strength, sprint and jump gains than the same training without occlusion over three weeks. The result comes from one squad over two short back-to-back blocks.
methods: Twenty male semiprofessional rugby union players were split into two matched groups of 10 and completed two counterbalanced 3-week blocks of nine sessions, one with 180 mmHg intermittent occlusion on both thighs during exercise and one without. Sessions used 5 x 5 at 70% 1RM for squat, bench press and weighted pull-up. Outcomes were 1RM strength, countermovement-jump power, 40 m sprint time, repeated-sprint performance maintenance, and salivary testosterone and cortisol.
findings: Occlusion gave larger improvements than control for bench press (5.4 vs 3.3 kg, P = .0044), squat (7.8 vs 4.3 kg, significant), best sprint time (-0.03 vs -0.01 s, P = .0162), countermovement-jump power (168 vs 68 W in the abstract, P = .0003) and repeated-sprint maintenance (0.74%, P = .0023). Acute salivary testosterone rose more after occlusion sessions, resting testosterone rose 8% across the occlusion block, and the acute cortisol response to occlusion was attenuated over the block. Acute testosterone response correlated with strength gains (r = .68 for squat).
limitations: All 20 players came from one club in one preseason, and the two blocks ran consecutively within an 8-week preseason with no washout described, so carry-over between blocks is possible. Outcomes were strength, jump and sprint tests rather than muscle size or competition performance, and the hormone correlations do not show cause. The methods describe the players as semiprofessional but the practical applications call them elite, and the abstract reports changes in kg, s and W while the results report percentages. The text is an OCR scan with several garbled characters, including the squat P value.
practicalImplications: For trained athletes in a short preseason block, adding intermittent lower-limb occlusion to 70% 1RM lifting may add strength, sprint and jump gains compared with the same lifting alone. The effect is shown for three weeks in one group of rugby players, so it should be trialed and monitored before it becomes a routine part of a program.
athleteDev: Within a three-week preseason block, adding 180 mmHg lower-limb occlusion to moderate-load lifts produced larger gains in squat, bench press, sprint time and jump power than the same lifts without occlusion. The study shows the effect in trained semiprofessional rugby players only, over one short block.
rtp: The authors suggest occlusion training may suit athletes returning from injury or who cannot tolerate high loads, but the study tested players in normal preseason training and did not include injured athletes or measure rehabilitation outcomes. It should not be used to set return-to-play loads or criteria.

citation: Thompson SW, Olusoga P, Rogerson D, Ruddock A, Barnes A. "Is it a slow day or a go day?": The perceptions and applications of velocity-based training within elite strength and conditioning. International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching. 2023;18(4):1217-1228.
abstract: Velocity-based training (VBT) is used in strength and conditioning for programming, testing and monitoring, but research procedures do not always reflect applied practice. This study interviewed 14 high-performance strength and conditioning coaches about their experiences of implementing VBT and analysed the interviews using reflexive thematic analysis. Three central themes emerged: technology, applications and reflections. Coaches perceived VBT as a beneficial and flexible tool, while noting drawbacks and challenges in some settings.
tldr: Elite strength coaches value velocity-based training for objective load prescription, readiness tracking and driving intent, but they weigh it against cost, usability and the risk that chasing velocity harms technique. Their practice often differs from the research literature, which they seldom cite.
methods: Semi-structured interviews, conducted remotely by Zoom, with 14 male high-performance strength and conditioning coaches recruited by purposive and opportunity sampling until data saturation. Transcripts were analysed using Braun and Clarke's six-phase reflexive thematic analysis with an inductive, realist approach, and the authors used Tracy's big-tent quality criteria, triangulation and member reflections to support credibility.
findings: Coaches described buying technology on the basis of logistics, usability, data quality, cost and whether it suited performance or recruitment goals. They used velocity-based training mainly for key lifts, load-velocity profiling, velocity-loss thresholds, velocity zones and feedback to drive intent. They reported benefits such as individualised training, objective programme evaluation and readiness tracking, and drawbacks including chasing velocities, time demands, erroneous data and the risk of becoming an "iPad coach". Most coaches used simple methods rather than full load-velocity profiles, and few described relying on peer-reviewed research for their decisions.
limitations: This is an interview study with 14 male coaches, so the themes reflect their perceptions and self-report rather than observed sessions or outcomes. The paper has no separate limitations section, but it states the principal investigator is a VBT researcher and practising coach, and the purposive and opportunity sample limits how far the findings generalise.
practicalImplications: When choosing VBT technology, weigh usability, set-up time and cost alongside reliability, because coaches reported that ease of use and budget shaped purchases even though most saw data quality as essential. Velocity targets should be paired with technique cues, because coaches reported that chasing velocity can degrade lift technique, and load-velocity profiling should be kept to key exercises given its time cost.
athleteDev: Coaches used velocity-based training to prescribe load and volume in key lifts, to autoregulate sets using velocity loss, and to drive intent with live feedback. Performance staff should set velocity targets with technique standards in place, and use simpler protocols such as velocity zones or velocity-loss cut-offs where time within sessions is limited.
rtp: The study concerns elite strength and conditioning practice and does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.

citation: Pryer ME, Cronin J, Neville J, Uthoff A. Kinematics and kinetics of pick-up acceleration. International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching. 2025:1-9.
abstract: Narrative review that defines pickup acceleration (maximal acceleration from a submaximal, non-static entry) and proposes a step-analysis framework. It discusses the kinematics, kinetics and technical demands of the pickup steps, summarizes normative data, and outlines practical applications and future research directions.
tldr: Accelerating from a moving start is a distinct motor quality that is under-studied. Most of the evidence comes from walking-entry studies with small samples, and jogging-entry data are largely missing.
methods: Narrative review. The authors define pickup acceleration, name the steps of the transition (approach steps -2 and -1, transition step 0, pickup steps 1 and 2), and summarize kinematic and kinetic findings from gait-transition and sprint studies. No database search strategy is described.
findings: The transition step shows the largest step-to-step velocity change (up to about 30 percent from walking), with accelerations of 2.62 to 3.63 m/s2. Vertical ground reaction force in pickup step 1 averages 174.93 percent of body weight, a 34 percent increase from the transition step. Kinetics for a jogging entry are described as largely unstudied, and the authors' own testing (Figure 1) showed athlete rankings for maximal acceleration changing between a static start and 1.5 or 3.0 m/s entries.
limitations: Several cited studies had athletes hold a steady pace before accelerating to a controlled submaximal speed, so maximal acceleration may not have been measured. Normative data come from small groups, entry velocities differ across studies, and the authors call for more video and force-plate work before the step variables can be relied on.
practicalImplications: Sprint drills for team sport athletes should be matched to the entry speed the athlete actually uses. The review suggests watching trunk lean and lower-body flexion in walking entries, recovery mechanics and stretch-shortening cycle use in jogging entries, and including lower-body range of motion work. These are the review's suggestions and have not been tested as a program.
athleteDev: Test and train pickup acceleration as its own quality, because an athlete's rank for a static start can differ from their rank at a 1.5 or 3.0 m/s entry. Use the step framework to look for excessive braking and collapse in the approach steps and weak propulsion at the transition step.
rtp: The review does not address return to sport or injury outcomes. It mentions tracking pickup mechanics as a possible way to judge readiness after injury, but gives no data, so it cannot be used to set return-to-play criteria.

citation: Windt J, Gabbett TJ. How do training and competition workloads relate to injury? The workload-injury aetiology model. Br J Sports Med. 2016.
abstract: The authors review injury aetiology models and workload-injury studies, then propose an updated model in which training and competition loads influence injury risk through exposure, fitness and fatigue. Total workload and acute:chronic workload spikes are linked to injury in the cited studies. The model is presented as a conceptual framework for future research.
tldr: Workloads should be treated as the vehicle through which athletes are exposed to injury risk, and as a driver of both fitness and fatigue. Monitoring workload changes, not only total load, is likely to matter for injury risk.
methods: Narrative review and conceptual model. No systematic search method is described. The authors discuss previous injury aetiology models and workload-injury studies, then propose the workload-injury aetiology model.
findings: Previous aetiology models did not include training and competition workloads. The authors propose that workloads affect injury risk through exposure, fitness and fatigue. The review reports that acute:chronic workload spikes are strongly associated with injury in several sports, but the mechanisms remain unclear.
limitations: The model is conceptual and has not been tested in a prospective study. The review does not describe how studies were identified, so the evidence it draws on cannot be checked for completeness. The authors acknowledge that many risk-factor interactions are unknown.
practicalImplications: Staff can use the model to frame workload monitoring as part of injury prevention, tracking both total load and how quickly it changes. The cited evidence favours building high chronic loads while keeping week-to-week changes within about 10% and avoiding acute:chronic spikes, though these figures come from a small number of team-sport cohorts.
athleteDev: Build training loads gradually and keep acute increases from outpacing chronic preparation, so that fitness gains are not offset by fatigue and injury risk. Track workload over time as well as total volume.
rtp: The review cites data from cricket, rugby league and Australian football linking acute:chronic workload ratios to injury risk during return to play, so it can frame how load is rebuilt after injury. It does not provide validated return-to-play thresholds and should not be used alone to clear an athlete for full training.

citation: Schwellnus M, Soligard T, Alonso JM, Bahr R, Clarsen B, Dijkstra HP, et al. How much is too much? (Part 2) International Olympic Committee consensus statement on load in sport and risk of illness. Br J Sports Med. 2016;50:1043-1052.
abstract: An IOC expert group reviewed evidence on how training, competition, psychological and travel load relate to acute illness and overtraining in athletes. The statement summarises the load-illness evidence and sets out practical guidelines for load management, illness monitoring and illness prevention. It also identifies urgent research priorities.
tldr: Very high training loads can raise illness risk in recreational and subelite athletes, and the pattern may differ in top elite athletes. Staff should monitor external and internal load, change loads gradually, manage psychological stress and plan recovery, while recognising that illness risk cannot yet be quantified.
methods: Consensus statement by an IOC expert group that met in November 2015. Members reviewed the literature independently, and a post hoc search of four databases (1980 to March 2016) identified 796 unique studies after duplicates were removed. Two reviewers screened titles and abstracts, 30 publications were included in the load-illness analysis, and recommendations were agreed by consensus.
findings: Absolute training load showed a J-shaped relationship with illness in recreational and subelite athletes, while high-level elite athletes may show a different pattern with lower illness risk at high loads. Increases in training volume were associated with more illness in several studies, and competition was an independent risk factor for illness (odds ratio 2.9) in one cohort of elite cross-country skiers. In one study of elite rugby union players, travel across more than four time zones was associated with two to three times the risk of illness. The authors state that the data are not yet sufficient to quantify illness risk for a given load or load change.
limitations: This is an expert consensus document, so recommendations reflect judgement applied to heterogeneous studies that are mostly observational. Most illness data were self-reported, all studies measured external load but only some measured internal load or load changes, and few used multiple risk factor modelling, as the authors acknowledge. The weekly increase limit of under 10% is drawn from the injury literature rather than from illness data.
practicalImplications: Medical staff can build an illness-prevention plan covering hygiene, sleep, nutrition, vaccination and early symptom monitoring, and track both external and internal load. Training loads should change in small weekly steps, with planned recovery after intense blocks, competitions and travel. Because quantitative thresholds are not established, these measures are a framework for judgement rather than fixed limits.
athleteDev: Plan training and competition loads in gradual steps, and build in recovery after congested competition blocks and long-haul travel. Track how athletes respond as well as the volume they complete, because the same external load can produce different internal responses.
rtp: The statement addresses illness prevention and load management, not return to sport after injury, and it gives no return-to-sport criteria. Its principle of gradual load increase could inform a return to training, but the paper sets no thresholds for that use.

citation: Soligard T, Schwellnus M, Alonso JM, Bahr R, Clarsen B, Dijkstra HP, et al. How much is too much? (Part 1) International Olympic Committee consensus statement on load in sport and risk of injury. Br J Sports Med. 2016;50:1030-1041.
abstract: The International Olympic Committee convened an expert group to review evidence linking load (training and competition load, calendar congestion, psychological load and travel) to health outcomes in sport. The consensus summarises the links between load and injury, gives practical guidelines for prescribing and monitoring load, and identifies research priorities.
tldr: Rapid increases in load, relative to what an athlete is prepared for, are a major injury risk factor. Load should be prescribed and monitored individually, using a combination of external and internal measures, because no single marker has been validated.
methods: Expert consensus meeting, followed by a post hoc literature search of PubMed (including MEDLINE) and SPORTDiscus limited to English-language studies published before June 2016. The consensus group included 104 publications in the review and agreed the final guidelines by consensus.
findings: Studies on absolute load gave mixed results: high load was linked to injury in several sports but was not, or was protective, in others. Studies in several team sports associated large week-to-week load increases with higher injury risk. In data from Australian football, cricket and rugby league, injury likelihood was below 10% with an acute:chronic load ratio of 0.8 to 1.3 and more than doubled when the ratio exceeded 1.5. In football, two matches per week compared with one was associated with higher match injury risk, and no link to injury was established for travel.
limitations: The authors note heterogeneity in sports, samples, load and injury definitions, and designs. Many congestion studies used small single-team samples, ignored player rotation, or used retrospective cross-sectional designs, and the acute:chronic ratio was validated in only three sports. No single marker has been validated to identify maladaptation.
practicalImplications: Avoid rapid increases in load. Based on evidence from Australian football, cricket and rugby league, the statement suggests limiting weekly increases to under 10% or keeping the acute:chronic load ratio within 0.8 to 1.3. In football, consider squad rotation when two matches fall in one week, and monitor load with a combination of external and internal measures, including subjective well-being scales.
athleteDev: Keep week-to-week load increases modest and use an acute:chronic load ratio of 0.8 to 1.3 as a monitoring reference rather than a hard threshold. Prescribe and adjust load individually, combining external load data with subjective measures, because no single marker has been validated. In football, consider squad rotation when two matches fall in one week.
rtp: The statement does not address return to sport or rehabilitation criteria. Its load ranges come from injury studies in healthy athletes, so they should not be used to set return-to-play loads for an injured athlete.

citation: Luan L, Witchalls J, Ganderton C, Adams R, El-Ansary D, Han J. Is chronic ankle instability associated with contractile thickness of gluteus medius and gluteus maximus during functional movement and exercise? A systematic review and meta-analysis. J Sports Med Phys Fitness. 2024;64.
abstract: Systematic review and meta-analysis of ultrasound-measured contractile thickness of the gluteus medius and gluteus maximus during functional movement and exercise in people with chronic ankle instability (CAI). Six observational studies with 176 participants were identified, and four were pooled. The authors report lower gluteus medius activity in CAI, no significant difference in gluteus maximus, and a weaker correlation between the two muscles in CAI than in controls.
tldr: People with chronic ankle instability may recruit the gluteus medius less during functional movement than people without it, while gluteus maximus activity looks similar. Few studies, high heterogeneity and graph-derived values mean this should be treated as a trend.
methods: Systematic review following PRISMA, searching six databases to 15 January 2024 for observational studies of ultrasound-measured gluteal thickness in CAI versus controls during physical activity. Included studies were scored with the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale and graded with GRADE. Outcomes were functional activity ratios (thickness during activity divided by thickness at rest), pooled in RevMan, and GMed and GMax correlations and differences were analysed in CAI and control groups.
findings: Across four pooled studies, gluteus medius FAR was lower in CAI than in controls (WMD -0.08, 95% CI -0.11 to -0.04; P < 0.00001; I2 74%), and it was also lower in both the walking and the elementary movement or resistance-exercise subgroups (I2 0% in each). Gluteus maximus FAR did not differ (WMD 0.02, 95% CI -0.01 to 0.05; P = 0.25; I2 71%). In the CAI group, GMed and GMax FAR were only weakly correlated (PCC 0.397) and differed from each other (t-test P = 0.029), whereas in controls the correlation was moderate (PCC 0.627) with no difference (P = 0.354).
limitations: Only four studies were pooled, the samples were small, and the included participants differed in sex, height, weight, age and control-limb choice. Some FAR values were digitized from graphs, which the authors say may reduce precision. The GRADE table lists '15 (528)' trials and participants for each overview, which appears to count task-level comparisons rather than the 6 studies and 176 participants reported in the abstract and text.
practicalImplications: Clinicians could assess gluteus medius recruitment during functional tasks in people with CAI, and the authors suggest prioritizing gluteus medius strengthening. The studies do not show that gluteus medius training corrects recruitment deficits or reduces instability, so any program should be judged on patient outcomes.
athleteDev: The review does not measure performance. Its one practical suggestion is to consider gluteus medius recruitment and strengthening in people with CAI, since pelvic and single-leg control matter in sport; gluteus maximus activity looked similar to controls.
rtp: The review addresses people with chronic ankle instability, a common outcome of ankle sprain, but it does not study return to sport or re-injury. It cannot be used to set return-to-play criteria or to show that gluteal retraining reduces re-injury.

citation: Bordalo M, Serner A, Yamashiro E, Al-Musa E, Djadoun MA, Al-Khelaifi K, et al. Imaging-detected sports injuries and imaging-guided interventions in athletes during the 2022 FIFA football (soccer) World Cup. Skeletal Radiology. 2023.
abstract: Retrospective analysis of all radiology examinations at the central medical facility for players during the 2022 FIFA World Cup in Qatar. Of 143 examinations in 94 athletes, MRI accounted for 67%, and 112 injuries were recorded, mostly muscle and tendon (42%), ligament (25%) and cartilage (21%) injuries. Image-guided interventions were 8% of examinations, and imaging was used for 11% of players.
tldr: At the 2022 World Cup, about 11% of players needed imaging at the central facility, mostly MRI. Muscle and tendon injuries, mainly acute grade 1 and 2 tears in the thigh, were the most common imaging findings.
methods: Retrospective cohort of all radiology examinations for players who attended the Aspetar central medical facility from 10 November to 19 December 2022. Two musculoskeletal radiologists independently reviewed MRI, ultrasound, radiography and CT, with a third reader resolving disagreements, and classified injuries using IOC tissue categories and imaging grading systems. Image-guided procedures were recorded from the same images and reports.
findings: Of 143 examinations for 94 players, 112 injuries were found, most often in the thigh (27%), ankle and foot (23%) and knee (23%). Muscle and tendon injuries were 42% of injuries, and 95% of muscle injuries were acute, with grade 1 and grade 2 tears making up most cases. Eleven players had imaging-guided injections, and eight of them (72%) returned to play during the tournament.
limitations: Clinical information was limited and there was no clinical or surgical correlation, and return-to-play data were incomplete. The authors also had no access to ultrasound performed by team medical staff or to imaging done outside the facility.
practicalImplications: Staff planning imaging for a major tournament should expect MRI to be the main modality, with muscle injuries and ankle ligament and cartilage findings common. The central-facility model gave one overview of imaging use, but the authors do not show that it improved outcomes.
athleteDev: Imaging at this tournament was mostly MRI for thigh, groin and knee problems, and the common findings were muscle tears, ankle ligament tears and cartilage lesions. The study does not show whether these injuries or imaging choices affected performance.
rtp: The study reports that 8 of 11 players who received imaging-guided injections returned to play during the tournament, but it has no return-to-play timelines or outcomes. It cannot be used to set return-to-play timing or to show whether injections or MRI findings predict return.

citation: Asken BM, Bauer RM, Guskiewicz KM, McCrea MA, Schmidt JD, Giza CC, et al. Immediate Removal From Activity After Sport-Related Concussion Is Associated With Shorter Clinical Recovery and Less Severe Symptoms in Collegiate Student-Athletes. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2018;46(6):1465-1474.
abstract: Cohort analysis of CARE Consortium data on 506 concussions in collegiate and military-academy athletes across 18 sports. Athletes removed from activity immediately (n = 184) lost about 3 fewer days from sport than delayed-removal athletes (n = 322), had shorter symptom duration, and had lower risk of needing 14 or 21 days to full clearance. They also had fewer and less severe acute symptoms, and the authors describe immediate removal as a protective factor.
tldr: Athletes removed from play immediately after a concussion recovered faster and had milder early symptoms than those who kept playing. The design is observational, so the result may partly reflect injury severity and reporting patterns.
methods: Cohort analysis of the NCAA-DoD CARE Consortium concussion database. Athletes were classified as immediate or delayed removal from activity using two clinician questions. Outcomes were time lost from sport, symptom duration, and acute clinical scores (SCAT3, BSI-18, SAC, BESS), analysed with three-step hierarchical regression, 20 multiple imputations, and multivariate and univariate tests.
findings: Immediate removal was the only factor that significantly predicted time lost, with about 3 fewer days lost (pooled B = 2.95) and about 2 days shorter symptom duration (pooled B = 2.02). Immediate removal was also linked to lower risk of needing 14 days (RR 0.614) or 21 days (RR 0.534) to full clearance, and to fewer and less severe SCAT3 symptoms at 0 to 6 hours and 24 to 48 hours and lower BSI-18 scores at 24 to 48 hours. SAC and BESS scores did not differ, and loss or alteration of consciousness was more common in the immediate-removal group.
limitations: The main limit is missing data: only 506 of 815 concussions had complete data, and the authors assume the included cases represent the full set. Removal timing and symptom report relied on clinician and athlete recall, and some athletes with delayed symptom onset may have been classified inconsistently. The abstract lists 25 institutions, while the Methods list 22.
practicalImplications: Athletes, coaches and clinicians should be taught to report concussion symptoms and stop activity immediately, since the study links immediate removal with shorter recovery. The paper supports education about symptom reporting rather than a specific removal protocol, and it cannot show that stopping play sooner causes faster recovery.
athleteDev: The study is about concussion recovery rather than performance. For performance and athletic staff, the message is to make immediate reporting and removal from practice or games routine, because delayed removal was linked to longer time out of sport.
rtp: The study bears directly on return to sport, since immediate removal was associated with shorter time to full clearance. It does not set clearance criteria, and its outcome is time to clearance rather than the safety of return, so it should not be used alone to decide return to play.

citation: Doucette MM, du Plessis S, Webber AM, Whalen C, Garcia-Barrera MA. In it to Win it: Competitiveness, Concussion Knowledge and Nondisclosure in Athletes. The Physician and Sportsmedicine. 2020.
