abstract: This cross-sectional survey of 161 Canadian athletes aged 14 to 32 years examined concussion knowledge, attitudes and competitiveness in relation to past concussion nondisclosure and intention to keep playing with symptoms. Competitiveness was associated with both outcomes, and concussion knowledge was not.
tldr: Among 161 young athletes, more competitive athletes were more likely to report having kept playing after a suspected concussion and more likely to say they would keep playing with symptoms. Concussion knowledge did not explain either outcome.
methods: Cross-sectional paper survey completed anonymously and under supervision by athletes from teams recruited through coaches. The survey included a modified Rosenbaum Concussion Attitude and Knowledge Survey, the 25-item Sport Orientation Questionnaire for competitiveness, a yes/no item on past nondisclosure and a 5-point item on continuing to play with a headache from a minor concussion. Binomial (past nondisclosure) and ordinal (intention) logistic regressions included competitiveness, knowledge, age, sex and sport.
findings: Of the 161 athletes, 44% reported having received what they thought was a concussion and kept playing without telling anyone. Higher competitiveness was associated with past nondisclosure (OR 1.03 per point, p = .03) and with intention to play with symptoms (OR 1.05 per point, p < .01), and rowers were less likely than collision-sport athletes to report past nondisclosure (OR 0.13). Concussion knowledge, age and sex were not significant in either model. Soccer players and females scored higher on knowledge, but the authors describe these differences as small and possibly not clinically meaningful.
limitations: The design is cross-sectional, the sample was male-majority (71%), only one non-collision contact sport and one noncontact sport were recruited, recruitment was through coaches, and each model explains about 18% of variance. The Results text gives the 97.5% CI for the intention model as 1.003 to 1.06, but Table 3 and the abstract give 1.03 to 1.08 (1.003 to 1.06 is the past-nondisclosure CI). Some Table 3 standard errors look like typing errors (age 2.20 and sex .05 in the past-nondisclosure model). The intention outcome is a single Likert item, and the file is the accepted author manuscript.
practicalImplications: Programs that aim to improve concussion reporting could be designed to reach highly competitive athletes, as the authors suggest, rather than relying on knowledge campaigns alone. The study does not show that this targeting reduces nondisclosure, and it can only support asking about competitive drive as a risk marker in a conversation.
athleteDev: The study is about concussion reporting, not performance outcomes. Its relevance for performance staff is limited to how the athlete's competitive drive may affect honest symptom reporting during training and competition.
rtp: The study does not measure recovery, return-to-play decisions or post-concussion symptom management. It may help flag athletes at higher risk of hiding symptoms, but it cannot set return-to-play criteria or clearance steps.

citation: Maniar N, Carmichael DS, Hickey JT, Timmins RG, San Jose AJ, Dickson J, Opar D. Incidence and prevalence of hamstring injuries in field-based team sports: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 5952 injuries from over 7 million exposure hours. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2022.
abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis of 63 prospective cohort studies in six field-based team sports pooled 5952 hamstring injuries over about 7.26 million exposure hours. The pooled hamstring injury incidence was 0.81 per 1000 hours, and the 9-month prevalence was 13%. Incidence was higher in matches than in training and on grass than on artificial turf, and it rose with average cohort age.
tldr: Hamstring injuries made up about 10 percent of all injuries in these team sports, with about 13 percent of athletes injured over a 9-month period. Matches carried a much higher injury rate than training, and the findings suggest the rate has not fallen over 30 years.
methods: Systematic search of six databases from inception to August 2020, limited to prospective cohort studies of hamstring injury with total exposure hours in field-based team sports. Two authors screened titles and abstracts, three assessed full texts, and two rated quality with the JBI Critical Appraisal Tool for prevalence studies. Random-effects (multilevel) meta-analysis and meta-regression were used, with a protocol registered on PROSPERO.
findings: Pooled hamstring injury incidence was 0.81 per 1000 hours (95% CI 0.66 to 0.98; prediction interval 0.18 to 3.70) and prevalence was 13% over 9 months (95% CI 9.5% to 17.6%). Match incidence was 3.85 vs 0.41 per 1000 hours in training (p < 0.001), and grass incidence was 0.72 vs 0.48 per 1000 hours on artificial turf in soccer (p < 0.001). Incidence rose 6.4% per year of average cohort age (p = 0.003), and sport, body mass, stature and year of data did not significantly moderate incidence. Hamstring strain injury alone had an incidence of 0.67 per 1000 hours.
limitations: Heterogeneity was very high, and the included studies used different injury definitions (hamstring injury, hamstring strain injury and posterior thigh injury). Most data came from soccer and rugby union, many cohorts reported one pooled value for multiple seasons, previous injury could not be modelled, and women contributed only about 310,000 exposure hours. The abstract attaches p = 0.003 to the 9.4-fold match vs training difference, but the results give p < 0.001 for match vs training and p = 0.003 for age, and hamstring strain prevalence is 9.8% in the results but 9.7% in the discussion.
practicalImplications: Staff in these sports can expect more hamstring injuries in matches than in training, and the authors suggest that training may not reproduce the high-intensity running demands of matches, so match-specific preparation deserves attention. The surface result is based on limited exposure hours, so it supports checking surfaces rather than treating artificial turf as a proven preventive measure.
athleteDev: The study reports injury epidemiology, not performance outcomes. Its most useful point for performance staff is that match exposure carries a much higher hamstring injury rate than training, which should inform how match running demands are planned.
rtp: The study does not evaluate rehabilitation or return-to-play decisions. It gives context on how often hamstring injuries occur, which can inform injury planning, but it cannot set return-to-play criteria or timelines.

citation: Bayrak A, Patlar S. Increased anterior pelvic tilt angle elevates the risk of hamstring injuries in soccer player. Research in Sports Medicine. 2024.
abstract: This study examined whether anterior pelvic tilt (APT) angle is associated with hamstring injury in male professional football players followed over five years. Injured and non-injured players were compared with t-tests, regression and ROC analysis to find an APT cut-off. The authors report that higher APT was associated with more hamstring injuries, with a cut-off of 13 degrees.
tldr: In 76 male professional footballers followed for five years, higher standing anterior pelvic tilt was associated with hamstring injury, and the authors derived a 13 degree cut-off. The cut-off comes from the same players and has not been validated, so it is a hypothesis for screening and not a clinical threshold.
methods: Retrospective study of first-team players from one Premier Division club over five seasons. Standing APT (caliper inclinometer), knee posture, Q angle and tibial torsion were measured by one physiotherapist, and the authors state that APT was documented before injury; hamstring injuries causing at least three days out were confirmed by MRI. Analyses used independent t-tests, multiple linear regression and ROC analysis to set a cut-off.
findings: Injured players (n = 33) had higher right and left APT than non-injured players (n = 43), about 14.1 and 14.2 degrees vs 9.7 degrees. The ROC cut-off was 13 degrees for both sides, with AUC 0.87 (right) and 0.88 (left), sensitivity of 69.7 to 72.7 percent and specificity of 93.0 percent. Q angle, tibial torsion and knee posture were not significant for overall hamstring injury.
limitations: The Discussion states that 'a lower APT angle increases hamstring injuries' and gives a pooled mean APT of 14.54 degrees, both of which conflict with the Results tables (higher APT in injured players; injured about 14.1 to 14.2 degrees, non-injured about 9.7 degrees), so the table values are reported here. The Methods describe t-tests but Table 8 reports z values, Table 5 coefficients are garbled, and the 13 degree cut-off was derived and tested on the same players. The retrospective design, single male club sample and lack of exposure, strength or training-load data limit causal and general conclusions.
practicalImplications: Staff could record standing APT in pre-season screening as one possible risk marker, alongside other factors such as strength and flexibility. Because sensitivity was about 70 percent, a 13 degree threshold would miss many injured players, so it should not be used alone to decide who receives prevention work until it is validated in an independent group.
athleteDev: The study does not measure performance. Its discussion cites other work suggesting that higher pelvic tilt can aid sprint speed while increasing hamstring strain, and this study does not test that trade-off.
rtp: The study cannot show that adjusting pelvic tilt reduces hamstring injury, and it does not test any intervention or return-to-play outcome. It should not be used to set return-to-play criteria or to clear players for training or matches.

citation: Hegyi A, Gonçalves BAM, Finni T, Cronin NJ. Individual Region- and Muscle-specific Hamstring Activity at Different Running Speeds. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2019.
abstract: This laboratory study measured proximal-distal and muscle-specific activity of the biceps femoris long head and semitendinosus during treadmill running at three speeds in 13 healthy amateur male athletes, using high-density surface EMG. EMG rose with running speed in all regions of both muscles, and each individual kept a similar activity pattern across speeds. The authors conclude that individual hamstring activity patterns are highly variable but consistent across speeds, which may support early submaximal running after hamstring injury.
tldr: During treadmill running, hamstring EMG rose with speed and peaked in late swing, with large differences between individuals and little group-level difference between muscles or regions. The study tested healthy amateur men at submaximal speeds, so the authors' suggestion about early running after injury is a hypothesis, not a tested result.
methods: Repeated-measures laboratory study of 13 male athletes from football and Gaelic football. Participants ran at 4.1, 5.4 and 6.8 m/s (about 45, 60 and 75 percent of maximum speed) while high-density surface EMG, kinematics and foot contact timing were recorded. EMG was normalised to maximal voluntary isometric contraction and analysed with two-way repeated-measures ANOVA using statistical parametric mapping.
findings: EMG activity increased with running speed in all regions of both muscles, peaking in late swing (BFlh about 63, 90 and 115 percent MVIC; ST about 69, 102 and 121 percent at the three speeds, as mean with 95 percent confidence limit). Group-level differences between proximal, middle and distal regions, and between BFlh and ST, were not significant at any speed. Individual activity patterns were highly variable between people but similar across speeds, and changes in muscle-tendon length in late swing were small.
limitations: The sample was 13 healthy amateur men, the fastest speed was submaximal, and running was on a treadmill, so the results may not generalise to sprinting, overground running, women or injured athletes. Surface EMG is affected by cross-talk, and the authors note that the EMG normalisation could influence absolute values, although speed trends are unaffected. The authors also report that the cost and benefit of individual hamstring profiling is unclear.
practicalImplications: Staff could expect hamstring EMG to rise steeply with running speed, with high late-swing activity at sprint-related speeds in healthy amateur athletes. The authors suggest that early submaximal running after hamstring injury may support neuromuscular recovery, but this was not tested in injured players and should be treated as a hypothesis for monitoring and trial designs.
athleteDev: Hamstring EMG reached about 115 to 121 percent of MVIC in late swing at the fastest speed, and each athlete showed a consistent but individual activation pattern. Staff could consider individual hamstring activation profiles when choosing hamstring exercises, but the study does not test any training or performance outcome.
rtp: The study tested healthy amateur men, so it cannot show that submaximal running after hamstring injury restores normal neuromuscular function or lowers reinjury risk. It should not be used alone to set running progressions or return-to-sport criteria.

citation: Mayfield CK, Bolia IK, Feingold CL, Lin EH, Liu JN, Hatch GFR, et al. Injectable Peptide Therapy: A Primer for Orthopaedic and Sports Medicine Physicians. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2026;54(1):223-229.
abstract: This narrative review examines the current evidence for six injectable peptides marketed for regenerative medicine and sports performance: BPC-157, TB-4, TB-500, CJC-1295 with ipamorelin, tesamorelin and GHK-Cu. It summarizes preclinical, case-level and clinical data for each peptide. The authors conclude that the evidence does not yet support clinical use and that dosing, frequency and duration are unknown.
tldr: Injectable peptides such as BPC-157 and TB-500 are widely sold for injury recovery, but the review finds only animal data and one uncontrolled human knee series. Several of these peptides are on anti-doping lists, so athlete use raises doping and safety questions as well as clinical ones.
methods: Narrative review of PubMed-indexed biochemical and clinical studies on six popular injectable peptides. The paper does not report search terms, date limits or screening steps, and it does not appraise study quality.
findings: BPC-157 improved tendon, ligament, muscle and bone healing in animal models, but no randomized orthopedic trials exist. A 12-patient case series reported knee pain improvement in 11 patients after intra-articular BPC-157, with no control group and no quantitative outcome. TB-4 and TB-500 showed tissue repair in preclinical models, and no human orthopedic studies were found. CJC-1295 with ipamorelin and GHK-Cu have animal or non-orthopedic data only, and tesamorelin has no orthopedic studies. The authors state that BPC-157, TB-4/TB-500 and tesamorelin are on the WADA Prohibited List, and that FDA has placed several of these peptides in category 2 for compounding safety concerns.
limitations: The review is narrative, with no reported search strategy or quality appraisal, and it relies on mostly animal and preclinical evidence. The only human orthopedic data is one uncontrolled case series with flawed methods, and the authors note that dosing, frequency and duration are unknown.
practicalImplications: Check WADA and USADA status before discussing any injectable peptide with an athlete, and refer doping questions to the team physician and anti-doping staff. Explain that BPC-157 and TB-500 have no human orthopedic trial data, and that the single human BPC-157 series had no control group. Record the product source, since the review notes that peptides are sold as research chemicals and that compounding impurities are a concern.
athleteDev: The review describes proposed muscle and performance effects for CJC-1295 with ipamorelin and GHK-Cu, but it finds no human data showing muscle growth or performance gains from these peptides. Staff should not recommend these peptides for performance use.
rtp: The review gives no return-to-sport guidance. It cannot be used to decide whether an injured athlete can return to play or to support peptide use as a recovery aid, because the only human injury data is one uncontrolled knee injection series.

citation: Stickels MW, Brazier B, Parmar R, Cronen A, Hui C, Shah A. Injectable Testosterone Replacement Therapy Within 1 Year Before ACL Reconstruction Is Associated With Increased Revision Rates. The Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2026;14(1):23259671251399845.
abstract: This retrospective cohort study compares anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) revision rates in patients who received injectable testosterone replacement therapy (TRT) before surgery with matched controls. TRT use within 1 year before the primary ACLR was associated with a higher revision rate, while TRT exposure at any time showed no difference. The authors suggest that counseling about this risk may be warranted in shared decision-making.
tldr: Injectable testosterone in the year before ACL reconstruction was linked to a 3.3-fold higher revision rate (17.05% vs 5.17%) in a matched claims cohort. The study is retrospective, has no dose data and shows large baseline imbalances, so it supports counseling rather than a firm rule.
methods: Retrospective PearlDiver claims cohort of patients with primary ACLR from 2015 to 2022 and at least 2 years of follow-up, using ICD-10 and CPT codes. Injectable TRT users were propensity-matched to non-users on age, sex and Charlson score, and revision was compared in three exposure intervals with univariate tests and log-rank analysis.
findings: Injectable TRT within 1 year before ACLR was associated with revision in 66 of 387 patients (17.05%) vs 20 of 387 controls (5.17%), relative risk 3.30 (95% CI 2.04 to 5.33, P < .001). The Kaplan-Meier difference appeared at about 400 days. Distant use (more than 1 year before surgery) had 23 revisions among 160 patients (14.38%), but controls had too few revisions for a valid comparison. Any TRT exposure before or after surgery showed 6.36% vs 6.21% revision (P = .82).
limitations: The study is retrospective and claims-based, with no dose, formulation detail, indication, graft type, surgical technique or activity level, and the authors note that people seeking TRT may be more physically active. Table 2 shows the groups still differed on hypogonadism (55.8% vs 3.4%), obesity, osteoarthritis and erectile dysfunction after matching. The distant-use and post-operative subgroups are underpowered, the Results text gives n = 2,614 for the any-exposure group while Tables 1 and 4 give 2,641, and the fold-change in the extracted conclusion is garbled ('.3-fold'), so rely on the reported relative risk of 3.30.
practicalImplications: When counseling a patient who is on injectable testosterone and facing ACL reconstruction, present the reported association (17.05% vs 5.17% revision with exposure in the prior year) and its uncertainty. The authors suggest considering stopping TRT up to a year before elective ACLR, and delaying surgery where feasible, but the study did not test whether this changes outcomes. The any-exposure analysis found no difference, so do not extend the finding to post-operative use.
athleteDev: The paper measures no performance outcome. Its relevance for athletes is a possible graft-outcome risk for those on injectable testosterone before ACL surgery, which should be raised with the team physician rather than used to guide training or performance decisions.
rtp: The study bears on return to sport only indirectly, since revision is a major setback. It gives no return criteria or timelines, and the authors note that the revision code does not confirm graft failure.

citation: Roberts SP, Stokes KA, Williams S, West SW, Kemp S, Cross M, et al. Injury in Starting and Replacement Players from Five Professional Men's Rugby Unions. Sports Medicine. 2024.
abstract: This study compares the incidence, severity and burden of time-loss injuries in starting and replacement players across professional men's teams in five rugby unions. It also tests whether one team's use of replacements is associated with injuries to the opposing team. The authors find no overall difference in incidence, a lower replacement incidence in the second half of matches, and a higher injury burden for replacements.
tldr: Across five professional rugby unions over three seasons, starters and replacements had similar overall injury rates, but replacement injuries cost more days lost. Replacements were injured less often than starters in the last two match quarters, which suggests fatigue or interaction effects but does not prove them.
methods: Cross-sectional analysis of time-loss match injuries and player minutes for starters (shirt numbers 1 to 15) and replacements (16 to 23) from English Premiership, Welsh Pro14 and Super Rugby teams, 2016 to 2019. Incidence, severity and burden were compared using rate ratios, and generalised linear mixed models tested whether one team's replacement use predicted injuries to the opponent.
findings: Overall incidence was 78.2 per 1000 hours for starters and 77.0 for replacements (rate ratio 0.98, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.10), and concussion incidence did not differ. Mean burden was higher for replacements (rate ratio 1.31, 95% CI 1.17 to 1.46), with median injury severity 14.5 vs 12.0 days. Replacement incidence was lower in the third quarter (rate ratio 0.68, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.92) and fourth quarter (0.78, 0.67 to 0.92), with the fourth-quarter difference driven by forwards. Burden met the authors' both-mean-and-median rule for lower-limb injuries (mean rate ratio 1.24, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.46) and for the tackled player (1.30, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.66), and head and neck injury severity was higher for replacements (median 11 vs 9 days). The number of replacements or replacement minutes a team used did not change the injury count or burden of the opposing team.
limitations: The design is observational, and the study does not capture injury mechanism, activity intensity or replacement entry reason, such as blood or head injury assessment. Data collection tools varied between unions. The lower-limb median burden rate ratio is printed as 1.19 (95% CI 1.00 to 1.40), and it counts as significant only because the unrounded lower limit is 1.003, so the lower-limb burden result is borderline. The authors note limited ability to extrapolate to teams with fewer replacements.
practicalImplications: Plan for replacement injuries to cost more time, since mean burden was about 31% higher, rather than assuming a replacement carries more injury risk over a full match. The second-half pattern (fewer replacement injuries) is an observational finding, so use it to inform discussion, not to change rotation rules. The authors' finding that opponents' replacement use did not change injury counts also argues against treating substitutions as a clear injury-risk lever.
athleteDev: The study measures match injuries and minutes, not performance. The authors cite other studies reporting higher early running intensity in replacements, but they did not measure intensity here, so the link to performance and load is untested.
rtp: The study bears on return to sport only indirectly, through the higher days lost for replacement injuries (median severity 14.5 vs 12.0 days). It gives no return criteria or protocols and cannot guide return-to-play decisions for individual players.

citation: Elliott J, Heron N, Versteegh T, Gilchrist IA, Webb M, Archbold P, et al. Injury Reduction Programs for Reducing the Incidence of Sport-Related Head and Neck Injuries Including Concussion: A Systematic Review. Sports Medicine. 2021.
abstract: This systematic review of six studies examined whether neck strength is linked to sport-related concussion (SRC) and whether neck exercise programs reduce head and neck injuries and SRC in athletes. Higher neck strength was associated with lower SRC risk in one observational study, and neck exercise programs were associated with lower injury rates in the intervention studies, with the strength of evidence varying by study.
tldr: Six studies suggest that higher neck strength may be linked to lower concussion risk and that neck exercises within injury-prevention programs may reduce head and neck injuries. The authors describe this as limited evidence, and the clearest result comes from one adult rugby trial.
methods: A PRISMA systematic review, registered on PROSPERO (194217), searched five databases to May 2020 for athlete studies that measured neck strength or included a neck exercise intervention. Methodological quality was rated with the Downs and Black checklist, and risk ratios and incidence rate ratios were calculated from raw counts. A meta-analysis was not done because the designs, sports, ages and programs were too heterogeneous.
findings: Of the two observational studies, the larger (6,662 high school athletes) found that composite neck strength predicted concussion after adjusting for sex and sport (OR 0.95 per pound, 95% CI 0.92-0.98, p = 0.004), while a study of 130 university athletes found no link between deep neck flexor endurance and concussion. Using the reviewers' calculated risk ratios, a cluster trial of 1,355 adult rugby players showed fewer head and neck injuries (RR 0.34, 95% CI 0.18-0.64) and fewer concussions (RR 0.36, 95% CI 0.19-0.69), whereas in a cluster trial of 2,452 adolescent rugby players neither reduction was significant (head and neck RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.61-1.09; concussion RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.55-1.17). Two pre-post studies used historical controls: 119 high school athletes had 2 concussions against 11 expected (RR 0.15, 95% CI 0.04-0.62), and 27 professional rugby players had fewer match-related cervical injuries but no significant change in total cervical injuries (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.30-1.87).
limitations: The authors note few included studies, varied designs, small samples and heterogeneous sports and age groups, and adverse events and missing data were rarely reported. Each intervention outcome rests on only three studies (Tables 3 and 4), not four, and only the adult rugby trial gave a certain effect for head and neck injury. The Abstract says four intervention studies showed reductions, which overstates the non-significant adolescent trial and the uncertain professional rugby result.
practicalImplications: The authors suggest considering neck exercises within multi-component injury-reduction programs for contact-sport athletes, and they flag adolescent and female athletes as the groups most in need of further study. Because the evidence is limited, staff should treat neck training as one part of a broader program and track adherence, which the authors link to program effect.
athleteDev: Neck strengthening can be included in contact-sport injury-reduction programs, with attention to adherence and dose. The review does not measure performance outcomes, so it does not show any performance benefit.
rtp: This review concerns injury prevention and does not address return to sport after concussion. It should not be used to set return-to-play timelines or clearance decisions.

citation: Sharma A, Smith DR, Slutsky-Ganesh AB, Diekfuss JA, Hogg JA, Foss KDB, et al. Integrating intramuscular fat radiomics with hamstrings-to-quadriceps structure and function ratios to predict future hamstring strain injury. PLOS Digit Health. 2025;4(12):e0001144.
abstract: A prospective longitudinal study of 93 professional American football players, nine of whom sustained a hamstring strain injury during the season, tested whether MRI radiomic features of thigh intramuscular fat could predict future injury. The authors also tested whether adding muscle imbalance and injury history improved prediction, using a K-nearest neighbour classifier.
tldr: In 93 professional football players, MRI texture features of hamstring fat combined with strength ratios and injury history predicted in-season hamstring strain injury with a cross-validated AUC of about 0.79. With only nine injuries, the authors say the models need validation in larger, independent groups.
methods: A prospective cohort in which thigh IDEAL MRI, isokinetic knee strength at 180 deg/s and the Hamstring Outcome Score were collected from 112 athletes, with 93 having complete data. Radiomic features were extracted from hamstring and quadriceps fat-contrast images, reduced by correlation and minimum-redundancy selection, and classified with K-nearest neighbour models using 250 repetitions of three-fold cross-validation.
findings: The best model, combining hamstring radiomics, muscle imbalance and injury profile, had an AUC of 0.79 (95% CI 0.78-0.80; sensitivity 78.4%, specificity 67.9%), above hamstring radiomics alone (AUC 0.68) and quadriceps radiomics alone (AUC 0.55). The hamstring-to-quadriceps torque ratio alone also had an AUC of 0.79, and it was lower in injured players (0.39 vs 0.49, p = 0.006). Injury profile alone gave an AUC of 0.67, while the HaOS score alone gave an AUC of 0.49.
limitations: Only nine injuries occurred, there was no independent holdout test set because of the small event rate, and the sample was single-site, male and from one sport. The Results text gives hamstring radiomics alone as AUC 0.67 while Table 2 and the Abstract give 0.68 (0.6789), and the Abstract gives the injury profile model as 0.68 while Table 2 gives 0.67. Limb-identification models performed poorly on right-side injuries (specificity 20-25%).
practicalImplications: Hamstring fat texture, the hamstring-to-quadriceps torque ratio and injury history are candidate risk markers worth testing in larger cohorts. The paper does not support using these models to flag individual players, since the best model misclassified 22% of injured players and 32% of uninjured players.
athleteDev: Injured players had lower hamstring torque and a lower hamstring-to-quadriceps torque ratio, but the paper does not test whether training changes these measures or affects performance.
rtp: The study predicts future injury and does not evaluate return to sport. The authors suggest baseline scans could later help judge injury severity and guide clinical decisions after injury, but this was not tested and should not guide clearance.

citation: Davis GA, Makdissi M, Bloomfield P, Clifton P, Echemendia RJ, Falvey EC, et al. International study of video review of concussion in professional sports. Br J Sports Med. 2018.
abstract: This survey of medical personnel from six professional sports compared how video review is used to identify and manage possible concussion, including the video signs, definitions, reviewer roles and protocols. Lying motionless and motor incoordination were video signs common to all six sports, and impact seizure and tonic posturing were included in the criteria for all sports except the NHL. The authors conclude that video review is well established, that the diagnostic criteria and reviewer expertise are not clearly established, and that sports should work towards a common standard.
tldr: Professional sports use video review for concussion in different ways, and the signs and removal rules differ between codes. Only lying motionless and motor incoordination are common to all six sports, so one sport's protocol should not be assumed to transfer to another.
methods: Senior medical advisers and chief medical officers from seven major codes were invited, and all seven responded; MLB was excluded because it does not use video review, leaving six sports. Each sport completed a standardised questionnaire on video source, video signs, definitions, biomechanical criteria, reviewer qualifications, spotters, time limits, equipment, education and compliance between November and December 2017. Two researchers extracted the data independently, and a narrative synthesis compared definitions across sports.
findings: All six sports use live in-game video review. Lying motionless and motor incoordination are common to all six sports, and impact seizure and tonic posturing are in the criteria for all sports except the NHL. Only three sports include a biomechanical video criterion, and most sports mandate permanent same-game removal for some video signs; the NHL does not mandate permanent removal from video alone and instead uses a standardised assessment.
limitations: This is a descriptive census of protocols reported by medical personnel from six codes, with no athlete data and no data on how accurately reviewers identify video signs. The authors note that there is no validated biomarker of concussion, so video studies carry the risk of false positives and false negatives. The paper reports practice as of 2018 and does not examine whether private viewing areas change reviewer performance.
practicalImplications: Medical staff should know which video signs trigger permanent removal and which trigger removal and assessment under their own governing body's protocol, because these differ between codes. Where possible, reviewers should have access to multiple camera angles and variable-speed playback, as the authors recommend. The paper supports a conservative approach to lying motionless, tonic posturing, impact seizure and motor incoordination on video, but does not show that any of these signs confirms a concussion.
athleteDev: This is not a performance paper. It may help performance and sports science staff understand the game-day video review process they support, but it does not address training or performance outcomes.
rtp: It can inform on-day decisions about permanent removal versus removal and assessment after a suspected concussion. It cannot be used to set return-to-play timelines or recovery criteria, because it reports protocols and does not evaluate recovery.

citation: Kellis E. Intra- and Inter-Muscular Variations in Hamstring Architecture and Mechanics and Their Implications for Injury: A Narrative Review. Sports Med. 2018.
abstract: This narrative review examines intra- and inter-muscular variation in the architecture and mechanical properties of the hamstrings. The biceps femoris long head has the shortest and most pennated fibres, the semimembranosus differs in proximal attachment and moment arm, and the semitendinosus shows less relative strain for the same joint motion. The author concludes that some architectural variations may help explain why some muscles are injured more than others, and that interventions targeting specific muscles or regions should be tested.
tldr: The hamstring muscles differ in fibre length, pennation, tendon and moment arm, so one exercise is unlikely to load all of them in the same way. These differences may help explain injury patterns, but the link to injury has not been tested directly.
methods: This narrative review drew on studies found by searching SPORTDiscus and MEDLINE from 1966 to October 2017 with terms for hamstring architecture, anatomy, mechanics, strain and injury. Studies were included if they related to hamstring architecture, anatomy or mechanical properties. The review summarises findings by muscle, tendon, muscle-tendon unit mechanics and fascicle-tendon interaction, with tables of architecture values reported across studies.
findings: The biceps femoris long head has the shortest and most pennated fibres and is injured more often than the other hamstrings, while the semitendinosus has the longest muscle-tendon unit and fascicles and the least relative strain for the same joint motion. Values for the same parameter vary widely between studies; for example, the reported pennation angle of the biceps femoris long head ranges from 0 to 28 degrees. The semitendinosus is divided into two compartments by a tendinous inscription, but the functional role of these compartments in humans is unclear.
limitations: Most of the evidence comes from cadaver, imaging and modelling studies, and the author attributes much of the variation in reported values to where and at what joint position measurements were taken. Several conclusions rest on assumptions, such as that fibre length governs excursion and pennation governs force, and the tendon and aponeurosis properties of each hamstring are not fully known. The search covered two databases only, and no quality appraisal of the included studies is described.
practicalImplications: Practitioners should recognise that the hamstrings do not all respond the same way to one exercise, which the author suggests may justify exercises or rehabilitation aimed at specific muscles or regions. This is a hypothesis for future research and not a proven prescription, because the review does not show that targeted programmes reduce injury or speed recovery. When interpreting published architecture values or individual imaging, staff should allow for the wide variation between studies.
athleteDev: The review suggests that different hamstring exercises may load each muscle differently, which could matter when designing strength work for sprinting and high-speed running. It does not test any training programme or measure performance outcomes.
rtp: It can inform the question of whether rehabilitation after a hamstring injury should target the specific muscle or region involved, as the author suggests. It cannot be used to set return-to-play criteria, because the review contains no outcome data on rehabilitation, recovery or re-injury.

citation: Grassi A, Napoli F, Romandini I, Samuelsson K, Zaffagnini S, Candrian C, et al. Is Platelet-Rich Plasma (PRP) Effective in the Treatment of Acute Muscle Injuries? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Sports Medicine. 2018.
abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials evaluated platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injections for acute muscle injuries compared with placebo injection or physical therapy. Six trials with 374 patients were included. The authors found that PRP shortened time to return to sport across all trials, but that this effect was not supported when only double-blind trials or hamstring-only trials were considered, and that re-injury and complication rates were similar between groups.
tldr: Across six randomized trials, PRP for acute muscle injuries shortened time to return to sport only when all trials were pooled, and the effect was not significant in blinded trials. PRP did not reduce re-injury, and the evidence was rated low to very low quality.
methods: Systematic review and meta-analysis following PRISMA, searching PubMed, CENTRAL and Web of Science, plus grey literature and reference lists, to 1 November 2017. Randomized trials of PRP for acute muscle injuries with a placebo or physical therapy control were included. Return to sport was pooled as a mean difference and re-injury and complications as risk differences, with sensitivity analyses by blinding and injury site, risk of bias assessed with the Cochrane tool, and evidence graded with GRADE.
findings: Across all six trials, PRP shortened time to return to sport (mean difference -7.17 days, 95% CI -12.26 to -2.08; I2 = 95%). This was not significant in the two double-blind trials (mean difference -5.65 days, 95% CI -12.14 to 0.84) or in the three hamstring-only trials (mean difference -5.95 days, 95% CI -12.48 to 0.57). Re-injury (risk difference -0.03, 95% CI -0.10 to 0.05) and complications (risk difference 0.01, 95% CI -0.05 to 0.06) did not differ, and pain was reported as better with PRP in three of five trials, mostly in the first three weeks.
limitations: The review includes only six trials with 374 enrolled patients, and the authors state the time-to-return data were not normally distributed, which may bias the parametric analysis. Reporting is inconsistent: Table 1 and the abstract show four trials without patient blinding while Section 3.6 says three, and the text's analysed group sizes (145 PRP, 191 control) do not match the Table 2 totals (163 and 170 included, 157 and 161 at follow-up). The review was not registered in PROSPERO.
practicalImplications: The authors conclude that the large and indiscriminate use of PRP for acute muscle injuries is not justified and that use should be limited to controlled trials until better evidence emerges. Because adverse effects were negligible, PRP is low risk, but the faster return it suggests should not be relied on, since it was not significant in blinded trials.
athleteDev: Four studies found no strength difference at final follow-up, and only one small trial reported early strength and range-of-motion gains with PRP, so PRP should not be expected to improve physical performance on return. Staff should not plan return-to-play timelines around a PRP-related gain, because the time benefit was not significant in the blinded trials.
rtp: The review addresses return to sport after acute muscle injury and found a shorter time to return across all trials, but this was not significant in the double-blind trials, which the authors rate as moderate-quality evidence of no difference. It should not be used to set a faster return-to-play timeline, and it does not support PRP for reducing re-injury, which did not differ between groups.

citation: McGeown JP, Hume PA, Kara S, Neary JP, Gardner W. Is it really the result of a concussion? Lessons from a case study. Sports Medicine - Open. 2019;5:8.
abstract: This case study used an interdisciplinary assessment to determine the cause of persistent symptoms in a man with multiple sports-related concussions. The Neary neurophysiological protocol and a concussion clinic assessment showed no impairment in the neurophysiological tests, and specialist assessment identified peripheral vestibular and otolithic dysfunction seemingly unrelated to his concussion history. The authors conclude that persistent symptoms that patients attribute to concussion may have unrelated causes with similar symptoms, and that multi-disciplinary assessment with repeated testing is important.
tldr: In one 40-year-old man with persistent symptoms and a history of 10 self-reported sport concussions, a full multi-disciplinary work-up identified a vestibular and otolith cause that seemed unrelated to his concussion history. The authors argue persistent symptoms should not be assumed to come from concussion without a complete assessment.
methods: Single-case short communication with ethics approval and written consent for publication. The participant completed the Neary protocol twice (7 and 20 March 2018), which assesses neurophysiological responses over about 60 minutes, followed by a concussion clinic assessment, neurology review with structural MRI, and a dizziness and balance centre assessment including vestibular and audiology tests.
findings: The Neary protocol assessments showed no notable impairment, and he performed within normative limits on all concussion clinic tests; his concussions had all occurred before age 30, resolved within days or weeks, and his current symptoms began at 33. The MRI and neurological examination were normal apart from a minor note of fluid in the inner ear, and specialist testing found unilateral tinnitus, an asymmetric hearing profile and otolithic dysfunction that reproduced his symptoms during gait with large head movements. He was diagnosed with peripheral vestibular disturbance and started an exercise programme to load the otolith, with follow-up every three to four weeks; outcomes are not reported.
limitations: This is a single case with no control group, and the authors state that the attribution of his symptoms to a non-concussion cause cannot be made with absolute certainty. The discriminatory value of the Neary protocol is not established, blood pressure monitoring was not performed, and the response to the exercise programme is not reported.
practicalImplications: When an athlete with prior concussions reports persistent symptoms, staff should not assume that concussion is the cause without a multi-disciplinary assessment that checks for other causes, such as vestibular or otolith problems. Referral to a neurologist, vestibular therapist or other specialist should be considered when the symptoms do not fit a concussion pattern, and the assessment should be repeated.
athleteDev: The case does not bear on performance training. For staff, the point is that symptoms an athlete attributes to past concussions may need medical assessment before any change to training load is based on them.
rtp: The paper gives no return-to-play criteria and reports no outcome from the exercise programme, so it cannot inform a return-to-sport timeline. Its message for return-to-sport decisions is that persistent symptoms in an athlete with prior concussions should be assessed for other causes before they are attributed to concussion.

citation: Andrade R, Wik EH, Rebelo-Marques A, Blanch P, Whiteley R, Espregueira-Mendes J, et al. Is the Acute:Chronic Workload Ratio (ACWR) Associated with Risk of Time-Loss Injury in Professional Team Sports? A Systematic Review of Methodology, Variables and Injury Risk in Practical Situations. Sports Medicine. 2020.
abstract: This PROSPERO-registered systematic review summarised the methods used to calculate the acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR) and its association with time-loss injury in adult professional or elite team sport athletes. Twenty longitudinal studies with 2,375 injuries from 1,234 male athletes were included. The majority of studies found a higher injury risk at a higher ACWR relative to a lower or moderate ACWR, but the methodological approaches varied widely and limit the strength of recommendations.
tldr: Across 20 studies of professional male team-sport athletes, a higher acute:chronic workload ratio was usually linked to more time-loss injuries, but the methods varied so much that no cut-off could be set. Staff should manage workload spikes and build chronic load, not apply a fixed ACWR threshold.
methods: PRISMA systematic review (PROSPERO CRD42017067585) searching PubMed, EMBASE and OpenGrey from inception to 31 May 2019 for longitudinal studies of ACWR and time-loss injury in adult professional or elite team sport athletes. Two reviewers screened and extracted data, and a third resolved disagreements. Study quality was rated with a modified Downs and Black checklist, and results were summarised by workload metric, without a meta-analysis.
findings: Ninety percent of studies showed a positive association between a higher ACWR (relative to a low or moderate ACWR) and a higher risk of injury, and two studies found no significant association. A low ACWR was linked to higher risk in only a few studies, and when combined with low chronic load, high or low ACWR was associated with increased risk in four studies. Most studies used a coupled ACWR with weekly blocks, a 1-week acute and 4-week chronic window, and the subsequent week as the injury lag, and none used time-to-event analysis. In one example, a high total distance ACWR above 2.0 was associated with about a fivefold increased risk, corresponding to a 4% injury likelihood versus 1% at a moderate ACWR.
limitations: The review could not pool results because the studies used different sports, ACWR calculations, binning methods and injury definitions, and it excluded adolescents, recreational players and non-time-loss injuries. Most included studies did not adjust for confounders, did not report power calculations, and did not describe how missing data or transferred players were handled, and all included studies used male athletes.
practicalImplications: The ACWR can be used as a planning tool to flag sharp workload spikes during the season, after injury and after the off-season, but it should not be used alone to judge individual injury risk. Staff should report the ACWR method they use, including coupling, averaging method and window lengths, because the results depend on these choices. The authors do not support a single cut-off, and staff should note that a large relative increase can still mean a low absolute injury risk.
athleteDev: The review supports monitoring workload spikes using the ACWR, but it does not support a single prescribed cut-off. The authors argue that developing higher chronic load helps athletes tolerate the acute loads of competition, so chronic load building should be planned alongside spike management.
rtp: The authors suggest the ACWR could help plan load when athletes return to competition after injury, but no included study tested this and the review reports no return-to-play outcomes. It cannot establish safe return-to-play thresholds.

citation: Martin HD, Khoury A, Schröder R, Palmer IJ. Ischiofemoral Impingement and Hamstring Syndrome as Causes of Posterior Hip Pain: Where Do We Go Next? Clin Sports Med. 2016;35:469-486.
abstract: No structured abstract is printed. The key points state that deep gluteal syndrome can be associated with ischiofemoral impingement and hamstring syndrome, that six physical examination tests help diagnose these conditions, and that non-operative and operative treatment depend on the differential diagnosis and contributing anatomy.
tldr: Posterior hip pain can come from deep gluteal syndrome, ischiofemoral impingement or hamstring syndrome, and these can coexist. A structured history, a set of hip examination tests and imaging help separate them before treatment is chosen.
methods: Narrative clinical review by the authors, who describe anatomy, biomechanics, history and examination, imaging, and non-operative and operative treatment. No systematic search is described. Test accuracy values are taken from cited studies.
findings: The review reports the cited accuracy of several tests: long stride-walking test sensitivity 0.94 and specificity 0.85; IFI test sensitivity 0.82 and specificity 0.85; active piriformis test sensitivity 0.78 and specificity 0.80; piriformis stretch test sensitivity 0.52 and specificity 0.90. It also describes an endoscopic lesser trochanteroplasty series in which modified Harris Hip Score, VAS and return to sport improved at 2 years.
limitations: No described search method and no evidence grading. The IFI validation cited uses 17 patients with IFI. The authors' own clinical observation on lesser trochanter version is noted as needing further study. The text does not report the issue number.
practicalImplications: When posterior hip pain is reported, the review advises a full hip examination that includes the long stride-walking test, the IFI test and piriformis tests, with imaging to rule out intrapelvic causes. Non-operative care combines physical therapy, guided injections and a home programme for sciatic nerve mobility.
athleteDev: For performance staff, the review explains how to tell IFI, proximal hamstring syndrome and deep gluteal syndrome apart when an athlete reports sitting pain or pain lateral to the ischium. It gives no athlete performance or load data.
rtp: The review gives no return-to-sport criteria. It cites one endoscopic IFI series that reported return to sport, and its post-operative tables give rehabilitation timelines (for example 12 weeks for IFI, and 24 weeks to 2 years for deep gluteal syndrome). These are clinical planning guides, not validated return-to-sport tests.

citation: Bullock GS, Mylott J, Hughes T, Nicholson KF, Riley RD, Collins GS. Just How Confident Can We Be in Predicting Sports Injuries? A Systematic Review of the Methodological Conduct and Performance of Existing Musculoskeletal Injury Prediction Models in Sport. Sports Medicine. 2022.
abstract: Systematic review of the methodological conduct and completeness of reporting of musculoskeletal injury prediction models in sport. Thirty studies (204 models) were included. Most used regression and some used machine learning. None externally validated a model, and most were rated high or unclear risk of bias. The authors conclude no model can be recommended for practice.
tldr: Most published sports injury prediction models were poorly developed, have a high risk of bias and have not been externally validated. None can be recommended for practice yet.
methods: Systematic review using PRISMA and CHARMS, with PROBAST risk of bias. Medline, EMBASE, CENTRAL, SPORTDiscus and CINAHL were searched from inception to 24 June 2021, with two reviewers screening and extracting data. Studies needed a sport injury prediction model using regression, machine learning or deep learning.
findings: Of 30 studies, 18 used regression only, 4 machine learning only, 7 both, and 1 regression, machine learning and deep learning. No model was externally validated. Two studies (7%) were rated low risk of bias overall and 28 (93%) high or unclear. Internal validation was performed in 14 studies, calibration was reported in 3, and 2 studies cited or discussed TRIPOD. No machine learning study reported tuned hyperparameters or code. The median events per parameter was 2.7.
limitations: The Methods list five databases, but the flow diagram shows three and the Discussion says only three were included. The Discussion names studies 42 and 39 as low risk while Results and Table 3 list 37 and 39, the count of studies using both regression and machine learning is given as seven and as eight, calibration is reported in two studies (abstract) or three (Results), and the Key Points say 79% of studies were high risk versus 93% high or unclear in the Results. The review was limited to English-language, peer-reviewed articles.
practicalImplications: Do not use the reviewed injury prediction models to make load or training decisions for athletes. If a model is considered, check its development, reporting and external validation first, using the review's criteria, and be cautious where sample sizes are small.
athleteDev: The review gives no model to use for injury-risk decisions in performance programmes. Screening outputs from small, unvalidated models should not drive training load changes without checking how they were built.
rtp: Not applicable to return-to-sport decisions. The reviewed models predict new injury rather than readiness after injury, and the review finds none suitable for practice.

citation: Picot B, Lempereur M, Morel B, Forestier N, Rémy-Néris O. Lack of Proprioceptive Strategy Modulation Leads to At-Risk Biomechanics for Anterior Cruciate Ligament in Healthy Athletes. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2024;56(5):942-952.
abstract: Forty-seven handball players performed anticipated and unanticipated side-cutting, and were classified as flexible or rigid by their proprioceptive postural strategy on firm and foam surfaces. Pelvic and lower-limb kinematics, kinetics and EMG of seven muscles were compared between profiles and between cutting conditions using statistical parametric mapping.
tldr: Handball players who could not shift their balance control away from the ankle (rigid profile) showed muscle activity and ankle rotation patterns linked to ACL injury risk during side-cutting. These are laboratory markers, not injury outcomes.
methods: Forty players (aged 15 to 25, with at least two years of high-level experience) were grouped as flexible or rigid from their postural response to muscle vibration on firm and foam surfaces. They then performed three anticipated and five unanticipated side-cutting trials, interspersed with straight runs. Kinematics and kinetics were recorded with a 3D motion system and force plates, and EMG was recorded from seven muscles, with two-way statistical parametric mapping for group and condition effects.
findings: Rigid players showed less semitendinosus (P<0.001) and less vastus lateralis (P<0.05) preactivity 200 to 100 ms before initial contact, more gluteus medius preactivity, and more ankle internal rotation before contact. About 70 ms after contact they showed higher vastus lateralis activity (P<0.001) and more ankle internal rotation (-8.49 vs -3.17 degrees at 75 ms). Knee moments and kinematics did not differ between profiles, and unanticipated cuts showed less ipsilateral pelvic tilt before contact and more vastus lateralis activity about 50 ms after contact, with no interaction between profile and condition.
limitations: Laboratory tasks may not reproduce match conditions. EMG was normalized to the anticipated-cut peak and interpreted as activation, not force, and only the dominant limb was analysed. Seven players were removed by the 95 to 105 percent cut-off, and no injury outcomes were measured. The abstract reports higher vastus lateralis activity in rigid players (P=0.032), while the results text reports lower vastus lateralis preactivity before contact and higher activity after it; the results values are used here.
practicalImplications: Screening for proprioceptive strategy with vibration and foam-surface testing could identify players whose cutting patterns may need attention. The authors propose a targeted neuromuscular program for rigid players and cues to keep the ankle in neutral rotation during stance. These are proposals and were not tested in this study.
athleteDev: Cutting drills for handball and other field sports could target ankle rotation and hamstring preactivation in side-cutting, which the authors identify as the key differences in rigid players. The study did not test whether training changes these patterns, so treat the drills as a hypothesis to monitor.
rtp: No injured or post-operative players were studied and no return-to-sport outcomes were measured. The study cannot be used to set return-to-sport criteria or to judge readiness after ACL reconstruction.

citation: Kenneally-Dabrowski CJB, Brown NAT, Lai AKM, Perriman D, Spratford W, Serpell BG. Late swing or early stance? A narrative review of hamstring injury mechanisms during high-speed running. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2019;29:1083-1091.
abstract: Narrative review of biceps femoris long head musculotendon mechanics and muscle excitation during high-speed running, and how they may relate to injury timing. It contrasts a late-swing mechanism (large eccentric force, peak strain and negative work) with an early-stance mechanism (high hamstring loads from ground reaction forces), and concludes that late swing is the most likely injury phase while noting that direct evidence is lacking.
tldr: Most of the evidence points to late swing, when the hamstring lengthens under large force and strain, as the likely injury phase in high-speed running. Direct evidence is still lacking, and early stance remains a plausible alternative.
methods: Searches of Scopus, Web of Science and PubMed using combinations of hamstring, injury, sprint, run, EMG, activity, kinematic and kinetic terms, plus manual checks of reference lists. The review synthesises hip and knee kinematics and kinetics, EMG excitation, musculoskeletal-model estimates of musculotendon length and force, and the few prospective and case-based injury studies. No pooled analysis is reported.
findings: Model estimates show the biceps femoris long head reaches peak length and strain at about 112 percent of upright muscle length in terminal swing, and musculotendon force peaks at 10.5 to 26.4 N/kg in late swing, with a smaller early-stance peak of 3 to 11.6 N/kg. Excitation in late swing is reported as two to three times that in early swing and late stance. The one prospective study (Schuermans et al, soccer players) found kinematic differences in later-injured players only during the swing phase.
limitations: Musculotendon findings depend on model assumptions and on filtering choices that may under-estimate early-stance force. The injury-timing conclusions rest partly on speculative mechanisms and on a few injury cases, and the authors state that direct evidence is lacking. The paper is labelled a narrative review, and the search terms and databases are reported without a formal appraisal of study quality.
practicalImplications: A late-swing focus supports prioritizing exercises that lengthen the hamstring fascicles, a principle the authors cite from other literature. The review does not test any specific exercise or program, and the authors call for prospective musculoskeletal-model studies before the timing question can be settled.
athleteDev: Use the late-swing framework when reviewing sprint mechanics, paying attention to hip flexion, then knee and hip extension, in terminal swing. The review gives no validated screen, so any such assessment remains a coaching judgement.
rtp: The review addresses injury mechanism only. It does not evaluate return to sport, reinjury or rehabilitation outcomes, so it cannot be used to decide when an athlete is ready to sprint after a hamstring strain.

citation: Moghadam N, Hieda M, Ramey L, Levine BD, Guilliod R. Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy in Sports Musculoskeletal Injuries. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2019.
abstract: The authors review the mechanisms, adverse effects and current evidence for hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) in sports musculoskeletal injuries. They conclude that human evidence is scarce and that HBOT should be tested in rigorous human trials before it is accepted as a way to speed return to play.
tldr: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy is popular with injured athletes, but human evidence is small and inconsistent, mostly on induced soreness. There are no human trials in muscle strain or contusion, so it should not be relied on to speed return to play.
methods: Narrative review with no search method described. The authors discuss HBOT indications and mechanisms, adverse effects, and human trials in delayed-onset muscle soreness, muscle injury, and ligament and tendon injury, with animal and in vitro studies. They also review trial design limitations, including selection, performance and detection bias.
findings: Eight human trials are summarised, including DOMS, ankle sprain, and medial collateral ligament injury studies with groups of about 6 to 16 participants. Some DOMS trials reported faster torque recovery or less pain with HBOT, but a prior systematic review reported higher pain at 48 and 72 hours with HBOT and no differences in longer-term pain, swelling or muscle strength. The authors found no human trials in muscle strain or contusion, and the ligament and tendon human studies were small and inconclusive. Half of the human trials used blinded outcome assessors. The authors conclude that the last systematic review and meta-analysis, which found HBOT ineffective for DOMS, still stands.
limitations: The review has no described search, so selection of studies may be incomplete. Most human trials were small, with some lacking baseline comparisons, and sham designs used different pressures, which may weaken blinding. The authors note that basic and animal studies far outnumber human trials, and that these studies do not establish clinical benefit.
practicalImplications: Do not use HBOT as an assumed way to speed recovery from muscle, ligament or tendon injury, since the human evidence is small and mixed. Before offering it, review the sham and blinding design of any trial you rely on, and monitor for barotrauma and oxygen toxicity (central nervous system and, with prolonged exposure, pulmonary), which the authors name as the two main concerns. Record outcomes carefully if you use it, given the uncertain benefit.
athleteDev: The review addresses treatment of musculoskeletal injury and soreness, not training adaptation or performance enhancement, so it cannot inform performance programming.
rtp: The authors state that rigorous human trials are needed before HBOT can be concluded to help athletes return to play. Current human evidence does not support using HBOT to set return-to-play timelines, and no clinical criteria are given.

citation: Markström JL, Grip H, Schelin L, Häger CK. Individuals With an Anterior Cruciate Ligament-Reconstructed Knee Display Atypical Whole Body Movement Strategies but Normal Knee Robustness During Side-Hop Landings: A Finite Helical Axis Analysis. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2020;48(5):1117-1126.
abstract: This controlled laboratory study compared landing control during standardized side-hop landings in 32 people with an ACL-reconstructed knee and 32 matched asymptomatic controls. Dynamic knee robustness was measured with a finite helical axis method, and whole-body movement strategies were compared with multivariate analyses. Knee robustness was similar between groups, but the reconstructed group used different trunk, hip and knee strategies and the reconstructed leg showed a knee flexor strength deficit.
tldr: People with a reconstructed ACL landed differently from matched controls, with more hip and knee flexion at contact, even though knee robustness and most hop scores looked similar. Staff should consider whole-body landing strategy as well as limb symmetry when assessing these patients.
methods: Controlled laboratory study with 32 people with an ACL-reconstructed knee and 32 matched asymptomatic controls. Participants performed standardized rebound side hops on force plates while motion capture recorded joint angles and moments, and knee robustness was measured with a finite helical axis approach. Groups and legs were compared with MANOVA, and one-leg hops and isometric knee strength were also recorded.
findings: Knee robustness was lowest in the first 10 degrees of helical motion after initial contact and did not differ between groups or legs. Compared with controls, the reconstructed group had greater hip and knee flexion at initial contact (16 and 24 percent) and greater peak hip flexion, knee flexion and knee internal rotation moments, while the injured leg had greater trunk and hip flexion at contact and a 7 percent lower knee flexion moment than the noninjured leg. Hop distance was similar, the injured leg's one-leg vertical hop height was 8 percent lower than the noninjured leg, and knee flexor strength was 12 percent lower.
limitations: The study is a single-session comparison, mainly recruited from one clinic, so causal links to reinjury cannot be drawn. Knee robustness was low in both groups right after landing, which the authors note is when injury risk is highest. The authors also note that the lack of knee abduction differences conflicts with earlier work and needs further research.
practicalImplications: Staff could assess landing after ACL reconstruction using whole-body measures, such as trunk, hip and knee flexion at contact and knee moments, rather than relying only on limb symmetry in hop tests. Because knee robustness was low right after landing in both groups, the authors suggest training to improve control at initial contact, but this was not tested in the study.
athleteDev: The study does not test performance outcomes. Its relevance to performance is that landing technique and whole-body control after reconstruction may matter for sport-specific side-hop tasks, which staff may consider when planning change-of-direction work.
rtp: The study can inform return-to-sport assessment by showing that most hop and knee extensor measures met common symmetry criteria while the reconstructed group still used atypical landing strategies and had lower knee flexor strength. It cannot show that these strategies predict reinjury or that a particular test should clear athletes to return to sport.

citation: Summers SJ, Chalmers KJ, Wallwork SB, Leake HB, Moseley GL. Interrogating cortical representations in elite athletes with persistent posterior thigh pain - New targets for intervention? J Sci Med Sport 2021;24:135-140.
abstract: This cross-sectional study compared tactile, proprioceptive and spatial processing in 14 male professional athletes with persistent posterior thigh pain after hamstring injury and 14 matched pain-free athletes. Patients were less accurate at localising touch on the affected leg and slower on left/right judgements of lower-limb images matching the affected leg, while two-point discrimination did not differ; auditory detection near the affected leg was lower on visual inspection but was not statistically tested. The authors conclude that leg-specific deficits exist and may contribute to persistent pain, which warrants further study.
tldr: Elite athletes with persistent hamstring-related thigh pain showed leg-specific deficits in touch localisation and limb judgement on the affected side, with a possible, untested deficit in sound detection near that leg. The study cannot show that these deficits cause the pain to persist, so they are a reason to investigate, not a treatment target yet.
methods: Fourteen male professional athletes with persistent posterior thigh pain after a grade 1 to 3 hamstring injury were compared with 14 pain-free athletes matched for age, sport, BMI and level, with data collected between 2007 and 2017 by a blinded examiner. Outcomes were two-point discrimination thresholds, tactile localisation error, left/right judgement response time for upper and lower limb images, and accuracy in detecting auditory clicks around each thigh. Groups were compared with independent t tests and legs with paired t tests (or non-parametric equivalents) under a prospectively published plan; the planned Wilcoxon test for the auditory task was not run, and an ultrasound post hoc test was added.
findings: Two-point discrimination thresholds were similar between patients and controls (p = 0.70). Patients were less accurate at localising touch on the affected leg than on the unaffected leg (p = 0.004) or the matched leg of controls (p = 0.009), and slower on lower-limb left/right judgements when the image matched the affected leg than the unaffected leg (p = 0.001) or the matched leg of controls (p = 0.008); upper-limb judgements did not differ. Patients scored 86.4 +/- 17.6% on auditory detection for the affected leg and 100% for the unaffected leg, and controls scored 100% on both legs, but no test was reported because the lack of variance made the Wilcoxon test unsuitable.
limitations: The sample is small and drawn from very elite athletes, so findings may not generalise to the wider athletic population. The tasks are indirect measures of cortical representation, no corrections were made for multiple comparisons, and the design cannot show whether deficits cause or follow persistent pain. The abstract reports p < 0.01 for the auditory task while the Results report no statistic for it. Ultrasound also showed grade 1 changes in 4 patients' unaffected legs and 4 controls, which the authors suggest may be false positives.
practicalImplications: Clinicians treating persistent posterior thigh pain after hamstring injury may wish to assess touch localisation, limb judgement and sound detection as part of the picture, since leg-specific deficits were found in this group. Because the study cannot show that these deficits drive persistent pain, any training of cortical representations should be treated as untested in sport and monitored as such.
athleteDev: This paper is about rehabilitation of a persistent injury, not performance development, so it has limited direct use for training prescription. It may be relevant to staff who work on movement and body awareness in athletes returning from hamstring injury.
rtp: It can inform the question of why some hamstring injuries stay painful beyond expected recovery time, but it cannot be used to set return-to-play criteria or timelines. The study had no outcome data on recovery, re-injury or return to competition.

citation: Severini G, Holland D, Drumgoole A, Delahunt E, Ditroilo M. Kinematic and electromyographic analysis of the Askling L-Protocol for hamstring training. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2018;1-11.
abstract: Eleven healthy individuals performed the three Askling L-Protocol exercises (extender, diver, glider) with EMG from four muscles and motion capture. The glider elicited peak hamstring activation of up to 60% MVC at a work point the authors liken to the running swing phase. Hamstring activation did not differ between the diver and glider, while the extender stretched the hamstrings with minimal engagement.
tldr: The glider and diver exercises load the hamstrings at a joint position similar to the running swing phase, while the extender mainly stretches them. This describes muscle activity only and does not show how the protocol performs in rehabilitation.
methods: Eleven participants did 10 repetitions of each exercise in random order. Surface EMG was recorded from biceps femoris, semitendinosus, rectus femoris and gluteus maximus, normalised to MVC tests, with motion capture of hip and knee angles. Root-mean-square EMG was compared across exercises, and muscle synergy analysis was used as a co-activation index.
findings: In the glider, biceps femoris and semitendinosus peaked at 55 to 60% MVC at the start of the concentric phase, with eccentric-phase peaks reported as about 35% (Results) or 40% (Discussion). In the diver, hamstring peaks were below 50% MVC (about 40% in the Discussion) and gluteus maximus averaged about 48% MVC with peaks near 84%. The extender kept biceps femoris at a tonic 11.7% MVC with semitendinosus negligible, and hamstring RMS was significantly higher in the glider and diver than the extender, with biceps femoris higher in the glider than the diver during the eccentric phase.
limitations: Eleven participants of mixed sex and activity level, EMG from the right leg only, and one session of 10 repetitions. The authors say the synergy analysis is not a neurophysiological measure, and eccentric-phase peak values differ between Results and Discussion. The study did not test strength, hypertrophy or return to sport.
practicalImplications: The glider and diver produce submaximal hamstring activation during lengthening, lower than reported for the Nordic hamstring exercise (close to 100% MVC) and likely lower than in sprinting, with peaks as the hip begins to extend. The extender is mainly a flexibility exercise with low hamstring activation. Do not infer strength or injury-prevention effects from these EMG values.
athleteDev: The glider and diver load the hamstrings at a joint position the authors liken to the running swing phase, but at lower activation than sprinting or the Nordic exercise. The extender is not a strength exercise in these data.
rtp: The participants were healthy and uninjured, so the study cannot show how the L-Protocol performs in rehabilitation or set return-to-sport timing. The lower re-injury and shorter return to sport reported by Askling et al. were not tested here.

citation: Chennaoui M, Vanneau T, Trignol A, Arnal P, Gomez-Merino D, Baudot C, et al. How does sleep help recovery from exercise-induced muscle injuries? J Sci Med Sport. 2021.
abstract: This narrative review describes how sleep and the circadian system regulate hormonal and immune responses, and how sleep relates to injury risk in athletes and soldiers. It then reviews the phases of muscle regeneration and the effects of sleep deprivation and sleep extension on muscle tissue. The authors propose that sleep extension could aid recovery from exercise-induced muscle injury through higher local IGF-I and better control of local inflammation.
tldr: Sleep loss shifts hormones and inflammation in ways that could slow muscle repair after injury. Sleep extension is a plausible recovery strategy, but the authors state that human evidence on sleep and muscle injury recovery is lacking.
methods: Narrative review. No systematic search method is described. The authors summarise sleep physiology, sleep in athletes and military personnel, muscle regeneration, and the effects of sleep deprivation and sleep extension on muscle repair.
findings: Acute and chronic sleep loss raise catabolic hormones and markers of systemic inflammation, and in a rodent model it impaired muscle regeneration after injury. In humans, extending sleep by under 1 hour a day for seven days increased circulating IGF-1 in healthy young men. The authors state that there is no data in healthy humans on sleep interventions and inflammation after muscle injury.
limitations: The review is narrative and does not describe a systematic search, so the sources selected cannot be checked. Most of the muscle-repair evidence comes from rodent models, and the human sleep-extension data come from healthy young men without muscle injury. The authors call for direct studies before clear guidelines are possible.
practicalImplications: Staff can explain to athletes that poor sleep may slow recovery and raise injury risk, and promote sleep hygiene, such as limiting bright light and noise and controlling bedroom temperature. Sleep extension may be worth considering as part of recovery, but the review does not give dosing or timing for injured athletes.
athleteDev: Protect sleep during heavy training blocks and travel, since sleep loss is linked to altered hormones, inflammation and muscle damage markers in athletes. Sleep hygiene is the practical lever the review discusses.
rtp: The review does not provide evidence that sleep extension speeds return to sport or lowers re-injury risk. It can support sleep as part of recovery planning, but it should not be used to set return-to-play timelines.

citation: Sargent C, Lastella M, Halson SL, Roach GD. How Much Sleep Does an Elite Athlete Need? Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2021.
abstract: Elite athletes' self-assessed sleep need was compared with an objective measure of habitual sleep duration in 175 athletes from 12 sports over about 12 nights of normal training. Athletes needed 8.3 hours of sleep to feel rested but averaged 6.7 hours, and only 3% obtained enough sleep to meet their stated need. Habitual sleep duration was shorter in individual than team sport athletes.
tldr: Most elite athletes in this sample slept about 1.6 hours less than the sleep they said they needed to feel rested. Earlier sleep onset and later wake times were associated with longer sleep, and the authors suggest the data can serve as normative sleep targets.
methods: Participants were 175 elite athletes (30 women) aged 22.2 (3.8) years from 12 sports, excluding those who were injured, at altitude, had a sleep disorder or had recent transmeridian travel. Sleep need was asked as a single question, and sleep was recorded over an average of 12 nights with sleep diaries and wrist activity monitors. A sleep deficit index was calculated as sleep need minus habitual sleep duration, and mixed models compared sports, sport types and sexes.
findings: Athletes reported a sleep need of 8.3 (0.9) hours and habitual sleep of 6.7 (0.8) hours, a deficit of 96.0 (60.6) minutes, and only 3% met their need. Habitual sleep was shorter in individual than team sport athletes (d = 0.6), although sleep need did not differ (d = 0.2). Earlier sleep onset and later wake times were associated with longer sleep, and female athletes went to bed earlier than male athletes, with no sex difference in sleep duration.
limitations: Sleep need came from a single question, and wrist monitors can over- or underestimate sleep by tens of minutes. Daytime naps were not recorded, so total sleep may be underestimated. Only 30 women were included, and sex comparisons were across sports rather than within sport. The text describes 12 sports, but Table 1 lists 14 (including one alpine skier and one diver).
practicalImplications: Use the 8.3-hour self-reported sleep need as a reference, recognising that individual need ranged from 5.5 to 11 hours. Earlier sleep onset and later sleep offset were associated with longer sleep, so the authors suggest reviewing training start times (especially sessions before 6 AM) and allowing later wake times after evening sessions.
