Their suggested targets of sleep starting 22:00 to 22:30 or ending 09:00 to 09:30 come from these associations and were not tested as interventions.
athleteDev: Use the athlete's self-reported sleep need and sleep logs to set practical sleep targets, and check whether training start times leave enough time for sleep. Individual sports athletes in this sample slept less than team sport athletes, so monitor them closely. Sleep schedule changes were not tested for performance benefit in this study.
rtp: The study did not include injured athletes and does not address return to sport. It should not be used to set sleep requirements for rehabilitation or return-to-play decisions.

citation: Janse van Rensburg DC, Jansen van Rensburg A, Fowler P, Fullagar H, Stevens D, Halson S, et al. How to manage travel fatigue and jet lag in athletes? A systematic review of interventions. Br J Sports Med. 2020.
abstract: The authors systematically reviewed exercise, sleep, light, nutrition, and pharmacological interventions for travel fatigue and jet lag in athletes, using studies from athletes and, where none existed, healthy populations. They found no studies on travel fatigue and 12 athlete-specific jet lag studies, with the evidence graded as low quality for successful jet lag management in athletes.
tldr: There is no research-based evidence on managing travel fatigue in athletes, and the athlete jet lag evidence is low quality. Judiciously timed exercise may help, and melatonin may be important, but both need larger athlete studies before they can be recommended.
methods: Systematic review following PRISMA, registered on PROSPERO, searching PubMed, MEDLINE, CINAHL, Google Scholar and SPORTDiscus from inception to March 2019. Eligible studies were RCTs and non-randomised trials of interventions in travel-based or laboratory-based phase shifts, with athlete-specific studies preferred. Risk of bias was assessed with the Cochrane tool (RCTs) and Downs and Black (non-RCTs), and certainty was graded with GRADE. A meta-analysis was judged not feasible.
findings: No studies on travel fatigue were found. For jet lag, 12 athlete-specific studies were found (6 non-randomised, 6 randomised). Exercise (4 studies) suggested that timing matters. Napping had some positive influence in two laboratory studies and a breathing and sleep CD intervention had no benefit, but the authors concluded the evidence does not support sleep interventions. Light gave contrasting results: an uncontrolled multifactorial study reported faster resynchronisation, while an RCT in 22 elite female soccer players found no clear benefit. That multifactorial study (melatonin, light and exercise) reported 2.13 days to resynchronise against an expected 6 days. Athlete-specific evidence was graded very low to low; stimulant and melatonin analogue findings (graded moderate) and nutrition findings (very low) came only from healthy non-athlete studies.
limitations: No meta-analysis was possible because of heterogeneity in populations, flight direction, protocols, outcomes and circadian phase measurement. Athlete-specific studies had small samples, and many had no control group. The melatonin and light studies were multifactorial, so the effect of each component cannot be separated. The search was expanded to healthy populations for some interventions. The abstract describes the athlete evidence as low quality, while most athlete-specific GRADE ratings in the tables are very low (the sleep RCTs and the light RCT were rated low).
practicalImplications: Do not treat any travel fatigue intervention as evidence-based for athletes yet. If a team tries judiciously timed exercise for jet lag (the authors suggest outdoor sessions, since appropriate exercise and light timing appear to coincide), it should record outcomes carefully, since the athlete evidence is low to very low quality. The authors are hesitant to recommend sedatives for regular jet lag management and do not recommend first-generation antihistamines or glucocorticoids. Melatonin use is restricted in some countries, and athletes must follow WADA rules.
athleteDev: Use the review as a map of what has and has not been tested, not as a protocol. Judiciously timed exercise is the most-studied athlete option for jet lag (four small studies), while light gave contrasting results, and all of this evidence is low to very low quality. Any intervention used in athletes should be checked against current WADA rules before use.
rtp: The review does not address return to sport or rehabilitation. Its findings relate to travel fatigue and jet lag in athletes who are competing and should not be used for injury return decisions.

citation: Souissi MA, Gouasmia C, Dergaa I, Faleh J, Trabelsi O, Weiss K, et al. Impact of evening blue light exposure timing on sleep, motor, and cognitive performance in young athletes with intermediate chronotype. Biology of Sport. 2025;42(3):61-68.
abstract: Randomized crossover study of 16 healthy male adolescent athletes with intermediate chronotype, exposed to a tablet video in four evening conditions: no exposure, 19:30 to 21:00, 21:00 to 22:30, and 22:30 to 00:00. Later exposure reduced total sleep time, lengthened sleep onset, and worsened dart-throwing accuracy, movement duration and selective attention. The authors conclude that evening blue light, especially after 21:00, harms sleep, motor and cognitive performance in young athletes.
tldr: Watching a tablet in the late evening, especially after 9 PM, shortened self-reported sleep and worsened next-morning dart accuracy and attention in 16 adolescent male athletes. The study is small and tested single nights, so it does not show longer-term or training effects.
methods: Randomized crossover design with four conditions in random order and 72-hour washouts. Participants watched the same neutral video on an 11-inch tablet during each exposure window, with a fixed bedtime of 00:00 and wake-up at 08:30. Outcomes were the Spiegel and Vis-Morgen questionnaires, dart-throwing accuracy and movement duration (video-analysed), and the Bells Test; analysis used one-way repeated-measures ANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc tests.
findings: Total sleep time was lower after exposure from 21:00 to 22:30 (442 minutes) and from 22:30 to 00:00 (428.5 minutes) than in control (465.5 minutes), and sleep latency was longest after the latest window (31.4 vs 20.1 minutes). Dart-throwing accuracy and selective attention were lower after the two later exposures, and movement duration was longer, with partial eta squared of 0.47 to 0.51 for accuracy and movement duration. Subjective sleep freshness did not differ between conditions.
limitations: The authors acknowledge the small sample, the brief exposure, and that training schedules and diet were not controlled. Sleep outcomes were questionnaire-based with no objective sleep measure, and bedtime was fixed at midnight right after the latest exposure. The paper reports F(2,26) for selective attention where F(3,45) would be expected, contains a leftover generated sentence in the reference list ('Here are the remaining references (21-45)...'), and cites references by numbers that do not match the list (for example Phillips et al. [39] is absent and [39] is the Bells Test paper).
practicalImplications: Coaches and athletes could limit tablet and phone use after about 21:00 before next-morning skill sessions, because exposure in the 21:00 to 00:00 windows reduced self-reported sleep and next-morning performance in this sample, while 19:30 to 21:00 exposure did not differ from control. The authors also suggest blue-light filters or blue-light-blocking glasses, but the study did not test those interventions.
athleteDev: Late-evening tablet use was linked with less sleep and worse next-morning dart accuracy and attention in this small sample of adolescent athletes. A screen curfew before about 21:00 is a low-cost sleep habit to try, but the study does not show that it improves sport-specific skill beyond this task.
rtp: The study used healthy adolescents with no injuries, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. Its sleep findings may matter for recovery, but they do not test injured athletes or return to play.

citation: Botonis PG, Toubekis AG, Hill DW, Mündel T. Impact of long-haul airline travel on athletic performance and recovery: A critical review of the literature. Experimental Physiology. 2025;1-19.
abstract: This narrative review summarizes studies of athletes and physically active participants who travelled west or east across four or more time zones. The authors cover aerobic, anaerobic, strength and power, perceptual, sleep and jet lag outcomes, and discuss travel, testing, timing, team, trait and tournament factors. They conclude that anaerobic and strength measures are negatively affected, endurance evidence is equivocal, and no particular recovery time can be established.
tldr: After long-haul travel across four or more time zones, anaerobic power, muscle power and strength can be reduced for several days, and eastbound travel is generally more disruptive. The authors state that no single recovery time applies to every athlete.
methods: Narrative review with no described systematic search. The authors limited the evidence to athletes or physically active participants travelling west or east across four or more time zones. They organized the findings by aerobic power, anaerobic power and capacity, strength and power, perceptual and psychophysiological variables, and sleep and jet lag, and summarized the included studies in a table.
findings: Anaerobic power, muscle power and strength were reduced after transmeridian travel in several studies, with deterioration estimated at up to about 3 days after westbound and 4 days after eastbound travel. Endurance results were inconsistent, and sleep was disrupted after eastbound travel across seven or eight time zones. Eastbound travel produced more severe and longer jet lag symptoms, and one study reported jet lag persisting for up to 13 days after a seven-zone trip.
limitations: No search strategy, databases or inclusion process are described, so study selection cannot be checked. The authors note that sex differences and chronotype were rarely examined, that sprint and jump tests may not reflect all sport demands, and that only one study measured anaerobic capacity after travel, and it is over 30 years old. The authors' views on teams, traits and tournaments are presented as perspectives rather than tested findings.
practicalImplications: Plan for performance and sleep disruption to last several days after long-haul travel rather than assuming it resolves on arrival. The authors estimate that anaerobic and strength decrements may last up to about 3 days after westbound and 4 days after eastbound travel, and conclude that recovery may need more than 3 days, with eastbound travel generally more disruptive. Protect sleep after arrival, since sleep loss was linked to larger performance and jet lag effects, and test at a matched time of day because testing time can confound results.
athleteDev: Expect anaerobic power, muscle power and strength to be reduced for several days after long-haul travel, with eastbound travel generally more disruptive. Use sprint and jump tests at a matched time of day when monitoring readiness after travel. Do not assume endurance performance is affected, since the evidence is inconsistent, and do not use the 0.5 or 1 day per time zone rule as a fixed timeline.
rtp: This review does not address injury, rehabilitation or return-to-play decisions, and it cannot set clearance criteria. Its findings describe performance changes in healthy athletes after travel, not after injury.

citation: Naughton M, Miller J, Slater GJ. Impact-Induced Muscle Damage and Contact Sports: Etiology, Effects on Neuromuscular Function and Recovery, and the Modulating Effects of Adaptation and Recovery Strategies. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2018.
abstract: This brief review compares impact-induced muscle damage (IIMD) from collisions in contact sports with exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD). The authors summarize the etiology of both, their effects on neuromuscular function and recovery, the repeated-bout effect, and recovery strategies. They conclude that IIMD appears distinct from EIMD, that its time course is not established, and that recovery evidence is largely drawn from EIMD and animal studies.
tldr: Collisions in contact sports can cause muscle damage that differs from eccentric exercise damage. Controlled studies with simulated collisions show reduced power and sprint performance, but the time course of this damage and the best recovery strategies are not established.
methods: Narrative review with no described systematic search. The authors reviewed human contact-sport studies, animal contusion and drop-mass models, and EIMD research, and used EIMD recovery studies to inform strategies where IIMD data were lacking.
findings: Controlled simulated-collision studies in contact-sport athletes found decrements in power and mean sprint time after IIMD compared with nonimpact control conditions, while blood marker and soreness responses were inconsistent. In a rugby match study, the number of tackles was strongly associated with peak myoglobin (r = .852) and peak creatine kinase (r = .922). Animal drop-mass models reported reductions in isometric force, power and submaximal work at 1 hour (28% to 33%) and 48 hours (28% to 38%), and the authors judge the evidence on adaptation to IIMD equivocal.
limitations: Most controlled human IIMD studies included wrestling, high-intensity running or other exercise that may have produced EIMD, which the authors note may confound results. Recovery strategies for IIMD are supported only by animal contusion models, and the authors state that anti-inflammatory approaches need caution because inflammation is needed for regeneration. The text describes no search strategy.
practicalImplications: Do not assume that EIMD recovery timelines apply to collision exposure, since the authors state the IIMD time course is undefined. After collision-heavy sessions, monitor power, sprint and soreness responses over several days, because controlled studies show decrements in these measures. Use caution with anti-inflammatory recovery strategies after contact, because the review notes that inflammation supports regeneration.
athleteDev: Expect power and sprint performance to decline after simulated collision work, and track these measures after collision-heavy training. Do not assume that EIMD recovery timelines describe collision exposure, since the time course of IIMD is not established. Strategies with EIMD support, such as cold-water immersion and tart cherry juice, have not been tested against collision damage in athletes.
rtp: This review cannot define when a contact athlete is ready to return to play after collision-induced muscle damage, because the IIMD recovery timeline is undefined and controlled human data are limited. It does not provide return-to-sport criteria, and its animal and EIMD evidence cannot be used to set clearance timing.

citation: Fusi J, Scarfò G, Di Silvestro R, Franzoni F. Improving Sleep Quality to Enhance Athletic Activity, the Role of Nutrition and Supplementation: A Mini-Short Review. Nutrients. 2025;17:1779.
abstract: This mini-short narrative review summarizes how sleep loss affects athletes and how nutrition, supplements and exercise may influence sleep. It covers caffeine, magnesium, melatonin, tryptophan, ashwagandha and apigenin, and it concludes that the evidence in athletes is conflicting and needs more study.
tldr: Sleep loss can impair athletic recovery and some kinds of performance, but this short review finds the evidence for specific supplements and exercise strategies for sleep in athletes limited and conflicting. Its firmest points are that evening caffeine disrupts sleep and that a low-glycemic, tryptophan-rich diet is the authors' preferred dietary approach.
methods: Narrative review with no described search strategy, inclusion criteria or appraisal method. The authors summarize sleep physiology, sleep loss and performance, dietary carbohydrate and macronutrients, and six supplements, drawing mainly on individual trials and meta-analyses.
findings: The review reports that sleep loss can reduce endurance and some skill performance and can slow recovery. It cites evidence that evening caffeine reduces sleep quantity and quality, and that high-glycemic meals have different effects in sedentary people and in athletes after training. It reports that melatonin, tryptophan (at 1 g or more), magnesium and ashwagandha improved some sleep outcomes in some non-athlete trials, while magnesium supplement users did not differ in sleep duration in one large survey. The authors conclude that a Mediterranean diet with low-glycemic and tryptophan-rich foods seems best for sleep, and that regular exercise can improve sleep.
limitations: The review has no described search method, so the evidence base cannot be reproduced. It relies heavily on non-athlete populations, and several supplement claims rest on single small trials or on animal and mechanistic work. The authors acknowledge that the findings on nutrition, supplements and sport are conflicting.
practicalImplications: Staff can use the review to support advising athletes to avoid caffeine in the evening before sleep. Staff should not treat the supplement doses in the review as validated sport protocols, since they come mainly from non-athlete trials. The authors suggest, without testing it, that a final taper session with sleep-promoting exercises could be included in a training program.
athleteDev: The review links sleep loss to slower recovery, higher perceived exertion and, in some tasks, lower performance, which supports prioritizing sleep in athlete programs. It does not provide a validated supplement or meal plan to improve performance through sleep.
rtp: The review does not address injury rehabilitation or return-to-play decisions. It may inform general recovery advice, but it should not be used to set sleep or nutrition criteria for clearance after injury.

citation: Knowles OE, Drinkwater EJ, Urwin CS, Lamon S, Aisbett B. Inadequate sleep and muscle strength: Implications for resistance training. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2018; article in press.
abstract: This systematic review of 17 studies examined the effects of sleep deprivation and sleep restriction on resistance exercise performance and on hormonal markers of muscle protein metabolism. One night of deprivation had little effect on strength, consecutive nights of restriction reduced multi-joint force output, and hormonal results conflicted.
tldr: Losing one night of sleep did little to maximal strength in most of the studies reviewed, while the one study of three nights of 3 h sleep found lower 1RM in multi-joint lifts. Caffeine, group training and training before long waking periods are suggested to protect performance, but each rests on very few studies.
methods: Systematic search of five electronic databases for English-language studies of sleep deprivation or restriction with resistance exercise performance or hormonal outcomes, following PRISMA. Two reviewers screened, extracted data and rated quality with the EPHPP tool. Seventeen studies were included, covering athletes, military personnel and other adults; no shiftwork studies met the criteria.
findings: Seven studies examined one night of restriction and one examined three consecutive nights. In the multi-night study (8 trained men, 3 h sleep), 1RM fell for leg press, deadlift and bench press but not biceps curl. After one night of restriction, total resistance-training workload fell in professional rugby players and strength fell only with afternoon testing after early waking in judo athletes, while other studies found no change. One night of total deprivation had little or no effect on maximal strength in most studies, and cortisol and testosterone findings were inconsistent.
limitations: The authors rated 13 studies as moderate and 4 as weak quality, and none reached strong quality because blinding of participants is not possible. Only one study tested consecutive nights of restriction and only two used a resistance training session, athlete studies were few and mostly used severe sleep loss, and only four studies included women. The abstract states that inadequate sleep impairs compound-movement strength, which is firmer than the evidence base the authors themselves describe as limited.
practicalImplications: Staff who schedule heavy compound lifts after several very short nights may plan for lower force output, though this rests on one small study. Caffeine, group sessions and training before long waking periods are suggested as ways to protect performance, but they rest on very few studies and should be tested in the athletes staff work with.
athleteDev: Multi-joint strength may fall after several nights of very short sleep, but a single night of sleep loss had little effect on maximal strength in most studies. The review suggests that caffeine, group training or training before long waking periods may help, but these were tested in very few studies.
rtp: The review does not study injured athletes or rehabilitation. It cannot set return-to-play strength criteria, although it may inform how sleep loss is considered when interpreting strength tests during rehabilitation or return.

citation: Kemp S, Spence AL, Keller BS, Ducker KJ, Gucciardi DF. Intraindividual variability in sleep among athletes: A systematic review of definitions, operationalizations, and key correlates. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2023.
abstract: This systematic review with narrative synthesis examined how researchers have defined, measured and studied intraindividual variability in athlete sleep across 16 eligible studies. Few studies defined the concept, and most measured variability as deviation from each athlete's typical sleep, usually with standard deviation or coefficient of variation. The authors rate the overall quality of the evidence as moderate and propose a working definition of sleep variability to guide future research.
tldr: Research on athlete sleep variability rarely defines the concept, and the methods used to measure it vary widely. Anyone tracking night-to-night sleep variability should state how it was calculated, because the result depends on the measure chosen.
methods: This preregistered review followed PRISMA 2020 and searched six databases from inception to April 2022, plus reference lists and citations. Two authors screened titles and abstracts together using a machine-learning ranking tool; eligible studies sampled athletes and recorded sleep daily for at least three nights by self-report or wearable device, and polysomnography-only studies were excluded. Data were extracted by one author, with a random 30% checked by a second, and study quality was rated on a bespoke eight-item tool.
findings: From 1,209 records, 16 observational studies met the criteria, published between 2015 and 2022 and sampling 937 athletes. Only four studies gave an explicit definition of sleep variability, and all but one study measured variability as deviation from a typical level, most often with intraindividual standard deviation (n = 8) or coefficient of variation (n = 6). Sample size justification was absent in all studies, and missing data were not reported in 62.5%. The authors propose a working definition: the magnitude of temporally heterogeneous deviations, for each 24-hour sleep cycle, from one's typical level of sleep indicators across a finite period.
limitations: The search did not seek unpublished work such as preprints, was limited to English, and quality was rated with a bespoke tool. The synthesis is narrative, the included studies are small and observational, and the authors describe knowledge of determinants and outcomes of sleep variability as in its infancy, so the proposed definition is not yet tested. The authors also note that standard deviation and coefficient of variation indices have known weaknesses (poor reliability, correlation with the mean), and found no consensus on the minimum number of nights needed.
practicalImplications: Staff who monitor athlete sleep may consider night-to-night variability alongside average sleep duration, because the authors argue that averages alone can hide meaningful differences between athletes. The review does not provide thresholds for harmful variability, so variability should be treated as an additional indicator to watch, not a validated cut-off. Any internal report should state the measure used (standard deviation, coefficient of variation or z score), the number of nights and how missing data were handled.
athleteDev: The review supports tracking how far an athlete's sleep moves from their own typical pattern, as well as average sleep, when planning training and performance. It did not synthesise links between sleep variability and performance, so its value for training decisions is not yet established.
rtp: The review does not examine injury, recovery or return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions. It cannot say whether a given level of sleep variability is safe for an athlete to return at.

citation: Driller MW, Suppiah H, Rogerson D, Ruddock A, James L, Virgile A. Investigating the sleep habits in individual and team-sport athletes using the Athlete Sleep Behavior Questionnaire and the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index. Sleep Sci 2022;15(1):112-117.
abstract: This cross-sectional survey compared sleep behaviours and self-reported sleep in 137 individual-sport and 270 team-sport elite adult athletes using the ASBQ and PSQI. Individual-sport athletes reported slightly longer sleep and higher sleep efficiency, while PSQI global scores did not differ. Team-sport athletes scored worse on the ASBQ global score and on several items, including stimulant use, alcohol before bed and travel disrupting routines.
tldr: Team-sport athletes in this sample reported more maladaptive pre-sleep behaviours than individual-sport athletes, and slightly shorter, less efficient sleep. The differences are small and self-reported, so they point to behaviours worth addressing rather than a reliable group-level sleep problem.
methods: A convenience sample of 407 elite athletes from 16 sports and nine countries, who were at least four weeks into the in-season phase, completed the ASBQ (18 items) and PSQI (19 items) online for the past four weeks. Independent t tests compared individual-sport and team-sport athletes for each questionnaire and item, with Cohen's d for effect sizes. Athletes were classed as individual-sport (n = 137) or team-sport (n = 270).
findings: Individual-sport athletes reported longer total sleep time (7:57 vs 7:40 h:mm, p = 0.04, d = 0.28) and higher sleep efficiency (91.1% vs 88.6%, p = 0.009, d = 0.29). PSQI global scores did not differ (team 5.4, individual 5.2, p = 0.51). The ASBQ global score was higher in team-sport athletes (44.3 vs 42.6, p = 0.004, d = 0.30), who also reported more stimulant use with training or competition (p = 0.0001), alcohol within 4 hours of bed (p = 0.005) and travel disrupting their routine (p = 0.03). Team-sport athletes also reported more night waking and feeling too hot.
limitations: This is a self-reported, cross-sectional convenience sample across nine countries, with the team-sport group dominated by rugby union. The effect sizes are small, the design cannot show causes, and no correction for multiple comparisons is described. The authors note that the sports differ in training time and style, so the team and individual split may hide differences between endurance and strength or power sports.
practicalImplications: Practitioners working with team-sport squads could review stimulant use, alcohol timing and travel schedules, since these were the items where team-sport athletes scored worst. Pre-sleep screen use, going to bed sore and worrying in bed were common across the whole cohort and are reasonable targets for education. Because the group differences are small and self-reported, individual sleep assessment should guide any specific plan rather than assuming a whole squad needs the same intervention.
athleteDev: Staff could use the ASBQ items where team-sport athletes scored worst, such as stimulant use, late alcohol and travel disruption, to plan targeted sleep education in training camps and competition schedules. The study did not measure performance outcomes, so any performance benefit is not shown.
rtp: The study is not about injury or return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions. Sleep behaviours such as worry in bed or late stimulant use may be relevant to recovery after injury, but no recovery or injury outcomes were measured.

citation: Wilson SMB, Jones MI, Draper SB, Parker JK. Irregular sleep/wake patterns in student-athletes exposed to early morning training. J Sports Sci 2025.
abstract: This observational study measured sleep and sleep regularity in 21 male student rugby union players over two weeks using wrist actigraphy. Nights before morning training were shorter and started and ended earlier than nights before free mornings, and the Sleep Regularity Index was low overall. The authors conclude that early morning training contributes to irregular sleep in student-athletes and should be scheduled at another time where feasible.
tldr: Student-athletes who start training at 06:30 to 07:00 slept about 1.8 hours less the night before and had irregular sleep timing across the week. The authors recommend later training where feasible, but this single-team study cannot show that a later start would improve sleep.
methods: Twenty-eight male players from one university rugby union team were recruited, and 21 with at least five days of valid actigraphy were analysed. Sleep was measured for two weeks in October 2023 with GENEActiv wrist monitors and a sleep diary that recorded naps and training attendance. The Sleep Regularity Index (SRI) was calculated, and nights before morning training were compared with free mornings using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, with Friedman tests and Bonferroni post-hoc tests across days, and with correlations against SRI. Players also completed the Athlete Sleep Screening Questionnaire for sleep screening and chronotype.
findings: Nights before morning training (n = 109) had a shorter median total sleep time (5.86 vs 7.66 h, r = 0.67), a shorter sleep period, and earlier sleep onset (23:07 vs 00:00, about 0.9 h earlier) and offset (05:45 vs 08:57, about 3.2 h earlier) than nights before free mornings (n = 121); 85.3% of nights before training had under 7 h of sleep, against 33.8% before free mornings. The median SRI was 67.0 (IQR 17.0), and 9 of 21 players (42.9%) had an SRI in the lowest 10th percentile of UK Biobank data (below 65.1). Lower SRI was associated with more cumulative sleep including naps (r = -0.62), later sleep onset (r = -0.50) and offset (r = -0.60) and a later chronotype (r = 0.52), but not with nocturnal sleep time, and nappers had lower SRI than non-nappers (57.9 vs 73.6, p = 0.004).
limitations: The sample is 21 male players from one team over two weeks, so the findings may not apply to women, other sports or a full season. Sleep was measured by wrist actigraphy and diaries, and the actigraphy device cited has a specificity of 45% against polysomnography. The authors did not control academic timetables or off-campus travel, which may have affected sleep, and the design cannot show that early training causes the irregularity.
practicalImplications: Where feasible, coaches and performance staff could move morning sessions later, as the authors recommend, because nights before morning training were much shorter and most fell under 7 hours. Staff could monitor sleep regularity as well as duration, since sleep timing shifted by up to about 3 hours between training and free days. Any change to training times should be checked for its effect on sleep, because the study did not test whether a later start improves sleep.
athleteDev: Early training starts were associated with about 1.8 hours less sleep the night before, which may affect recovery and training quality, so training schedules are a practical lever for performance staff. The study did not measure performance, and the authors say the link between sleep regularity and sports performance is unclear.
rtp: The study did not examine injury or return to sport, and players with a concussion since the start of the season were excluded, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions. Its findings on sleep timing may be relevant to sleep planning during rehabilitation, but this was not tested.

citation: Le Mansec Y, Dorel S, Nordez A, Jubeau M. Is reaction time altered by mental or physical exertion? European Journal of Applied Physiology. 2019;119:1323-1335.
abstract: This study assessed the effects of mental effort and muscle effort on simple reaction time and its components, premotor time and electromechanical delay (EMD). Thirteen men completed a mental arithmetic task, an isometric biceps fatiguing protocol, and a control task. Reaction time and premotor time remained stable in all conditions, and EMD increased only after muscle effort, mainly due to the passive part of the series elastic component. The authors conclude that neither mental nor muscle effort has a negative effect on simple reaction time during voluntary contractions.
tldr: Fourteen minutes of mental arithmetic or a short biceps fatiguing protocol did not slow simple reaction time in healthy active men. Muscle fatigue did lengthen the electromechanical delay and reduce force production, so the reaction time result should not be read as full explosive readiness.
methods: Randomised crossover design with three sessions at least one week apart: mental effort (14 minutes of serial subtraction), muscle effort (intermittent elbow flexor contractions to task failure) and a control movie. Simple visual reaction time was split into EMG-based premotor time and voluntary EMD, and EMD was also measured with electrical stimulation using ultrafast ultrasound. Maximal voluntary torque, voluntary activation, contractile properties, rate of force development and NASA-TLX scores were measured before and after each session and analysed with repeated-measures ANOVA.
findings: Reaction time and premotor time did not change in any condition (all P > 0.05). After muscle effort, EMD rose during electrically evoked contractions (10.5 to 12.3 ms, P = 0.001), mainly due to an increase in the passive part of the series elastic component, and voluntary EMD rose by 25.6% without statistical significance. Maximal voluntary torque fell by 17.7% after muscle effort, and rate of force development over 50 to 100 ms fell by 31% to 42%.
limitations: The study had 13 men, and the authors acknowledge that it may have been too small to detect small changes, creating a risk of a type 2 error. Reaction time was measured with only two or three trials to limit recovery, which reduces reliability, and only the biceps was recorded, so other elbow flexors could have driven the response.
practicalImplications: A short mental task or a brief elbow flexor fatigue protocol did not slow simple reaction time in healthy active men, so an unchanged reaction time should not be taken as proof that a person is unaffected by fatigue. After heavy muscle work, staff should check explosive force capacity, because rate of force development fell substantially even though reaction time did not change.
athleteDev: For performance staff, the study suggests that a simple reaction time test after fatiguing work may look normal even when force production is reduced. Rate of force development should be checked alongside reaction time when explosive actions matter.
rtp: The study used healthy, active men after short, non-injurious protocols, and it does not assess injured athletes or any return-to-sport criteria, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.

citation: Maughan RJ, Burke LM, Dvorak J, Larson-Meyer DE, Peeling P, Phillips SM, et al. IOC Consensus Statement: Dietary Supplements and the High-Performance Athlete. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2018.
abstract: IOC consensus statement on dietary supplements for high-performance athletes. It explains why supplement use is widespread, which products have good evidence for performance in specific situations, and where evidence is absent or weak. It also covers nutrient deficiencies, immune support, physique products, product contamination, anti-doping risk, and a decision-tree approach to supplement choice.
tldr: Only a few supplements, including caffeine, creatine, nitrate, sodium bicarbonate and possibly beta-alanine, have good evidence of performance benefit in specific situations. Before use, confirm a real need, trial the product in training, and assess the risk of contamination with prohibited substances.
methods: Expert consensus statement by IOC-affiliated authors that groups supplements by purpose and reviews the evidence for each category, using a hierarchy of evidence. The authors state they rely mainly on studies of healthy adults relevant to athletes, and they cite supporting reviews and position stands. No new data or systematic search are reported.
findings: Caffeine, creatine monohydrate (loading about 20 g/day for 5 to 7 days, then 3 to 5 g/day), nitrate, sodium bicarbonate (0.2 to 0.4 g/kg) and possibly beta-alanine are the performance supplements with adequate support, with benefits reported in specific tasks. Evidence for most immune, weight-loss and fat-burning products is weak or absent, and the authors name vitamin D and probiotics as the most promising immune options. Some products contain undeclared prohibited substances, which can cause anti-doping violations.
limitations: The statement is not a systematic review, and it does not describe how studies were selected beyond a general evidence hierarchy. The authors note that much supplement research uses small or unrepresentative samples, that individual responses vary, and that elite-athlete data are almost entirely absent.
practicalImplications: Before choosing supplements, complete a nutritional assessment and use supplements to fill identified gaps, such as iron, vitamin D, calcium or energy intake. For performance, trial caffeine, creatine, nitrate, sodium bicarbonate or beta-alanine in training before any competition use, and check whether the product has third-party testing for prohibited substances.
athleteDev: Only a few supplements have good performance evidence in specific situations: caffeine, creatine, nitrate, sodium bicarbonate and possibly beta-alanine. The statement advises trialing them in training that mimics competition and weighing any marginal gain against the risk of an anti-doping violation from contaminated products.
rtp: The statement mentions injury-related uses, such as vitamin D for stress-fracture risk and creatine for recovery, but it does not test return-to-sport decisions. It cannot show that any supplement speeds return from injury or should guide clearance.

citation: Chan DKC, Yip LMH, Tang TCW, Yung PS-H, Gucciardi DF, Hagger MS. Implicit doping attitude and athletes' accuracy in avoiding unintentional doping when being offered beverages with banned performance-enhancing substances. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2025.
abstract: This cross-sectional study tested whether athletes' implicit doping attitude, measured with a smartphone implicit association test, predicted accuracy in a canned-beverage sorting task for banned substances. In 681 athletes from Hong Kong, Australia and the United Kingdom, a more positive implicit doping attitude was associated with lower sorting accuracy, and the association held after adjusting for society and demographics. The authors propose both tasks as objective measures for anti-doping education.
tldr: Athletes with more positive implicit attitudes toward doping were slightly less accurate at sorting drinks that might contain banned substances. The association is small and cross-sectional, and the new sorting task still needs validation.
methods: Cross-sectional real-time experimental design. Athletes completed a demographic survey, a smartphone single-category implicit association test that produced a D-score, and a 32-item canned-beverage sorting task in which they chose can drink or cannot drink. Hierarchical linear regression entered society, gender, age, education, sport type and sport level in step 1 and implicit doping attitude in step 2.
findings: Implicit doping attitude was a significant negative predictor of sorting accuracy (beta = -.09, t[641] = -2.35, p = .02), with R2 = .029 at step 2. Society, gender, age, education, sport type and sport level were not significant predictors of accuracy. The authors describe the effect size as small.
limitations: The single-occasion cross-sectional design cannot show causal or temporal links, and this is a journal pre-proof whose final version may differ. Most athletes competed at regional or state level, and the beverage task used broad banned-substance categories rather than technical names, so it tests label vigilance more than knowledge of specific substances. The authors also note that other psychological factors were not measured, that implicit association tests are open to practice and familiarity effects, and that the explained variance was small (about 3%).
practicalImplications: The authors propose the smartphone implicit test and the beverage sorting task as objective measures for anti-doping education, although only one small association is shown so far. Athletes should still check the ingredients of unfamiliar drinks and supplements and consult a team physician or sports dietitian before using new products. Label checks alone are not sufficient, because contamination can occur even when the label is clean.
athleteDev: This study does not measure performance. Its practical relevance is that athletes varied in how accurately they spotted banned ingredients, and lower accuracy was linked to more positive doping attitudes, which supports anti-doping education on unfamiliar drinks and supplements.
rtp: The study does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport, and it has no clinical outcome. Its findings cannot inform medical clearance or return-to-play decisions.

citation: Boro TL, Rezaei S, Kavoura IE, Kooima P, Wasserbeck A, Schott KD, et al. Improved Postexercise Rehydration With a Milk Permeate-Based Sports Drink. International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism. 2026;36(1):30-41.
abstract: This randomized crossover trial compared rehydration after exercise-induced dehydration with a milk permeate-based sports drink, a traditional sports drink, a high-potassium sports drink and water. Twelve young adults lost 2% of body weight in the heat and then drank 150% of the loss over the first hour. The milk permeate drink gave higher net fluid balance at 3 and 4 hours and lower cumulative urine volume, and the authors conclude it is more effective than the other drinks for postexercise rehydration.
tldr: A milk permeate-based sports drink retained more fluid than a traditional sports drink, a high-potassium drink or water over 4 hours after 2% body weight loss in heat. Fluid balance stayed negative in every trial, and the effect was modest in 12 adults.
methods: Randomized crossover trial in which 12 young adults completed four trials, each with a 2-hour exercise-induced dehydration to 2% of body weight in 29.9 degrees C heat and a 4-hour rehydration. Participants drank 150% of body weight loss in four doses during the first hour, using one of four drinks in block-randomized order. Outcomes included net fluid balance, urine volume and osmolality, osmotic and free water clearance, plasma volume, plasma osmolality and electrolytes, and perceptual ratings.
findings: Net fluid balance was higher with MPSD than with the other drinks at 180 min (-0.38% +/- 0.3%) and 240 min (-0.66% +/- 0.3%), although balance remained negative in all trials. Cumulative urine volume was 1,268 +/- 173 mL with MPSD, 1,796 +/- 459 mL with the high-potassium drink, 1,493 +/- 211 mL with the traditional drink and 1,565 +/- 501 mL with water; the results section reports MPSD as significantly lower than the high-potassium drink and water. Plasma volume at 60 min rose with the traditional drink (1.5% +/- 5%) but fell with MPSD (-3.7% +/- 6.5%) and the high-potassium drink (-5.5% +/- 7.8%), and MPSD was rated less pleasant in taste than the traditional drink.
limitations: The sample was small (12 healthy adults, 4 women, not described as athletes) and the protocol was a single heat exposure. Drink osmolality, sugar type, erythritol and potassium differ at once, so the cause of the effect cannot be isolated, and stomach fluid and insulin were not measured. The abstract reports MPSD urine volume as lower than all drinks, but the results text reports it as lower than the high-potassium drink and water only. The study was funded by the National Dairy Council, and the senior author reports consulting for several beverage companies.
practicalImplications: A milk permeate-based drink may help retain fluid over 3 to 4 hours of rehydration after heat-induced losses, compared with a traditional sports drink, a high-potassium drink or water. Fluid balance remained negative in every trial, so total fluid volume still needs to match losses. If fast early plasma volume restoration is the priority, the traditional sports drink performed better in the first hour of this study.
athleteDev: After heat-induced losses of about 2% of body weight, a milk permeate-based drink gave a modest advantage in net fluid balance at 3 and 4 hours compared with a traditional sports drink, a high-potassium drink or water. Fluid balance stayed negative in every trial, so total intake still needs to match losses.
rtp: This is a laboratory rehydration study in young adults after exercise-induced dehydration. It does not address injury, rehabilitation or return-to-play decisions and reports no clinical outcome.

citation: Souza DB, Duncan M, Polito MD. Improvement of Lower-Body Resistance-Exercise Performance With Blood-Flow Restriction Following Acute Caffeine Intake. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2019.
abstract: In a double-blind crossover design, 22 trained men took 6 mg/kg caffeine or placebo one hour before unilateral knee extension at 30% of 1RM with blood flow restriction, performed to exhaustion over three sets. Caffeine increased total repetitions (44.5 vs 35.0), post-exercise blood lactate (7.8 vs 6.0 mmol/L) and reduced pain ratings in the second and third sets.
tldr: A single dose of caffeine allowed trained men to do more repetitions in a knee-extension set with blood flow restriction, and the work felt less painful in the later sets. Whether this adds to strength or muscle gains over time was not tested.
methods: Twenty-two trained men, low habitual caffeine users and new to BFR training, completed four visits. On two randomized, double-blind visits they took 6 mg/kg caffeine or maltodextrin placebo 60 minutes before three sets of unilateral knee extension at 30% 1RM to failure, with cuff pressure at 80% of the restriction value. Repetitions, perceived exertion, pain and blood lactate were recorded.
findings: Caffeine increased repetitions in set 1 (28.3 vs 23.7, p = .005), set 2 (11.6 vs 8.9, p = .03) and in total (44.5 vs 35.0, p = .001; Cohen d 1.17), while set 3 did not differ. Post-exercise lactate was higher with caffeine (7.8 vs 6.0 mmol/L, p = .03), which the authors say may reflect the greater work done. Pain was lower with caffeine in set 2 (6.9 vs 8.4, p = .04) and set 3 (8.7 vs 9.5, p = .01). Perceived exertion did not differ between conditions.
limitations: The sample was resistance-trained men, not competitive athletes, and the test was a single unilateral knee-extension protocol in an acute session. Plasma caffeine was not measured and test reliability was not assessed. The correct-versus-incorrect identification analysis was post hoc with 9 and 13 participants. Table 1 reports a 1RM standard deviation of 61.1 kg, which looks like a typographical error.
practicalImplications: Where BFR knee-extension or similar low-load work is used to add repetitions, a caffeine dose of about 6 mg/kg taken an hour before may increase the work done in the session. Practitioners should not assume that the extra repetitions will change strength or muscle size, because the study measured only acute repetitions and did not follow training over time.
athleteDev: In this study, acute caffeine increased repetitions to failure in one unilateral knee-extension exercise performed with blood flow restriction. It does not show gains in maximal strength, power or sport performance, and it tested one exercise in trained men rather than athletes.
rtp: The study cannot inform return to sport. It used healthy trained men, an acute single-exercise test, and no injured participants, so it should not guide rehabilitation loading or clearance decisions.

citation: Burke LM, Castell LM, Casa DJ, Close GL, Costa RJS, Desbrow B, et al. International Association of Athletics Federations Consensus Statement 2019: Nutrition for Athletics. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2019.
abstract: An International Association of Athletics Federations consensus statement on nutrition for track and field athletes. It covers periodisation, energy availability, protein, fluid, carbohydrate for training and racing, health, injury, supplements, special environments, special populations, travel and special diets.
tldr: This consensus statement sets practical nutrition targets for track and field athletes, including protein of 1.3-1.7 g/kg/day for athletes aiming to maintain or gain weight, and carbohydrate during long races. It stresses periodised, individual plans, screening for low energy availability and iron deficiency, and caution with supplements.
methods: A consensus statement prepared for the IAAF, drawing on event-group reviews and 12 themed sections written by the authors. The paper describes no systematic literature search, evidence grading or consensus voting procedure.
findings: The statement advises periodised nutrition matched to training and competition, and recommends protein of 1.3-1.7 g/kg/day for athletes aiming to maintain or gain weight, 1.6-2.4 g/kg/day during high-quality weight loss, and 0.3-0.4 g/kg per meal, with intakes above 2.5 g/kg/day offering no adaptive advantage. It gives glycogen normalisation targets of 7-12 g/kg/day for 24 hours, in-race carbohydrate typically of 30-60 g/h (up to 90 g/h in races over about 2.5 hours), and states that fluid losses above 2-3% of body mass are associated with reduced performance in warm conditions. It identifies low energy availability as a major risk factor for bone stress fractures, recommends regular iron screening for females, endurance athletes and vegetarians, and lists five evidence-based performance supplements (caffeine, creatine, nitrate, beta-alanine, bicarbonate) whose value depends on the event.
limitations: The statement does not grade its evidence or describe a consensus procedure, and the authors list areas where evidence is lacking, including event-specific protein needs for body composition change, long-term benefits of high-quality weight loss, and dose responses to food-based protein. Several sections, such as tendon and ligament nutrition and the role of melatonin and meal timing in travel, are described as early or still needing investigation.
practicalImplications: Use the targets as starting points for individual plans, adjusting protein and carbohydrate to training load, body-composition goals and race distance, with input from accredited sports nutrition experts. Screen for low energy availability, check iron status regularly in females, endurance athletes and vegetarians, and use intravenous or intramuscular iron only under medical supervision. Trial any supplement before competition, and use only those with a strong evidence base for the event.
athleteDev: Periodised fuelling, carbohydrate intake during long events, and protein spread across the day are presented as performance-supporting strategies in track and field. The statement says most performance products lack evidence and that five evidence-based supplements may give a marginal gain depending on the event, and it does not quantify performance effects for most strategies.
rtp: The statement covers nutrition for injury prevention and rehabilitation, including energy availability for stress fracture prevention, protein to limit lean mass loss during rehabilitation, and early data on collagen and micronutrients for tendon and ligament injury. It gives no return-to-sport criteria and should not be used to clear athletes to compete.

citation: Rogers DL, Tanaka MJ, Cosgarea AJ, Ginsburg RD, Dreher GM. How Mental Health Affects Injury Risk and Outcomes in Athletes. Sports Health. 2023.
abstract: This clinical review summarises how mental health disorders and symptoms occur in athletes, and how they relate to injury risk and recovery. It also reviews evidence that injury can worsen mental health and describes barriers to care such as stigma and limited clinical resources. The authors conclude that physical and mental health are closely linked in athletes and that screening and support systems need to improve.
tldr: Athletes with anxiety, depression or high life stress appear to have higher injury risk and slower recovery, and injuries can in turn worsen mental health. Screening and access to clinicians with sport experience are the practical priorities the review identifies.
methods: Clinical review. The authors state they searched PubMed for pertinent peer-reviewed studies. No inclusion criteria, screening process or quality appraisal are described.
findings: In a cohort of 307 athletes at the 2015 IAAF World Championships, reporting a physical illness symptom that caused anxiety was associated with about five times the odds of injury during the event (odds ratio 5.6, 95% CI 1.3-23). In a preseason cohort of collegiate athletes, preseason anxiety was associated with higher subsequent injury rates (rate ratio 2.3, 95% CI 2.0-2.6). The review also reports that depression and stress were associated with poorer performance and with delayed or reduced return to sport in cited studies.
limitations: This is a narrative clinical review with a single-database search and no described selection or quality criteria. The injury-link studies it cites are mostly observational cohorts and surveys, and the authors note that the true prevalence of mental health disorders is hard to measure. Causal direction between mental health and injury cannot be established from these data.
practicalImplications: Sports medicine staff can add brief mental health screening to preseason and injury-rehabilitation pathways, and make a clinician with sport experience accessible. Because anxiety, stress and depression were linked to later injury in several cohorts, staff should consider mood and stress alongside injury monitoring, while recognising that the associations are observational.
athleteDev: Depression was associated with performance failure in cited studies of elite swimmers, and depressive symptoms or perceived stress with later time lost to illness in Australian Olympic athletes. Mental wellbeing therefore belongs in performance planning, with concerns routed to a qualified clinician rather than handled through performance monitoring alone.
rtp: Psychological readiness and preinjury stress were associated with return to sport and rehabilitation outcomes in cited surgical studies, so mental state is worth assessing during rehabilitation. The review does not provide validated psychological criteria for return to sport, so it cannot set a clearance threshold.

citation: Proost M, Habay J, De Wachter J, De Pauw K, Rattray B, Meeusen R, et al. How to Tackle Mental Fatigue: A Systematic Review of Potential Countermeasures and Their Underlying Mechanisms. Sports Med. 2022.
abstract: The authors systematically reviewed acute countermeasures against mental fatigue, classified by timing (before, during or after the fatiguing task) and type (behavioural, physiological or psychological). Of 33 included studies, most countermeasures improved behavioural or subjective markers of mental fatigue, but the neurophysiological evidence was inconclusive.
tldr: Caffeine, odours, music and extrinsic motivation are the most evidenced countermeasures for mental fatigue, based on small trials in healthy adults. The effects on brain and physiological markers are not yet clear, so these results should guide testing rather than set protocols.
methods: PRISMA-guided systematic review searching PubMed, Web of Science and PsycINFO to 7 March 2022, with backward and forward citation screening. Eligible studies were RCTs or non-randomised controlled trials in healthy adults aged 18 to 50, with mental fatigue induced by a task of at least 30 minutes, placebo or control groups, and at least two of behavioural, subjective and physiological markers. Risk of bias was assessed with RoB 2 and RoB 2 for crossover trials.
findings: Of the 33 studies, 8 tested behavioural, 22 physiological, 1 psychological and 2 combined countermeasures. Most reported positive effects on behavioural or subjective markers, for example caffeine at 5 mg/kg improving endurance or time-trial performance in two small studies (n = 8 and n = 12). Neurophysiological markers were measured in 19 studies, with heterogeneous results, so no firm conclusion was reached. Risk of bias was high in 25 studies, some concerns in 3, and low in 5.
limitations: Heterogeneous fatigue-inducing tasks and markers prevented a meta-analysis. Most studies had small samples and high risk of bias. Several outcomes were cognitive tasks rather than sport performance, and three studies did not report participant sex. Some supporting studies were industry-supported, such as the two chicken essence trials.
practicalImplications: Caffeine taken before a mentally demanding task, odours during the task, and music or motivational incentives are the most promising options to test in your own setting. Caffeine carries gastrointestinal and tremor risks at higher doses, and modafinil is banned in competition. Test any countermeasure with your own athletes and tasks before relying on it, since the evidence comes mostly from small laboratory trials in healthy adults.
athleteDev: Caffeine given relative to body mass, odours during a fatiguing task, and music or extrinsic motivation are the most promising options in this review for managing mental fatigue. Use them as hypotheses to test, since the trials used healthy adults and laboratory tasks. Check WADA rules before using any substance.
rtp: The review addresses acute mental fatigue in healthy adults and does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport. It cannot inform return-to-play decisions.

citation: Tawil S, Kassis V, Bassil T, Farhat K, Hourani E, Massoud L, et al. Intermediary role of mental toughness beliefs on the relationship between pain self-efficacy and fear avoidance in Elite injured athletes. BMC Sports Sci Med Rehabil. 2025;17:124.
abstract: This cross-sectional study of 172 injured elite and competitive athletes in Lebanon examined relationships between fear avoidance, pain self-efficacy and mental toughness. Fear avoidance was negatively correlated with both mental toughness and pain self-efficacy, and mental toughness was positively correlated with pain self-efficacy.
tldr: Among 172 injured athletes, lower fear avoidance went with higher mental toughness and higher pain self-efficacy. The design is cross-sectional, so these are associations, not evidence that mental toughness mediates recovery.
methods: An online cross-sectional survey, completed February to June 2024, of injured elite and competitive athletes recruited through a university sports federation. Participants completed the Athletic Fear Avoidance Questionnaire, Pain Self-Efficacy Questionnaire and Sports Mental Toughness Questionnaire, analysed with t-tests, ANOVA and Pearson or Spearman correlations.
findings: Of 172 athletes, 57.6% had returned to sport less than a month earlier, and fear avoidance was negatively correlated with mental toughness (r = -0.47) and pain self-efficacy (r = -0.44). Mental toughness differed by sport, highest in boxers (43.5) and lowest in futsal players (35.9). Athletes who had returned within a month scored higher on pain self-efficacy (39.9 vs 35.3, p = 0.016) and mental toughness (42.4 vs 40.3, p = 0.037) and lower on fear avoidance (24.3 vs 27.3, p = 0.009) than those who had not returned.
limitations: The authors note a small, non-random sample limited to elite or competitive athletes, with possible recall and social desirability bias. The Abstract says age and training hours 'predicted' higher mental toughness, but only bivariate tests were run, and in Table 4 the youngest group scored highest, contrary to the Discussion's claim that mental toughness rises with age. The Table 4 age and training-hours means (about 37-39) do not fit the overall mean of 41.5, and the training-hours row repeats the same values under fear avoidance, so those rows look erroneous; the Abstract gives the mental toughness and pain self-efficacy correlation as 0.36 and Results as 0.37.
practicalImplications: Staff working with injured athletes may find it useful to ask about fear avoidance, pain self-efficacy and mental toughness together, since they were associated in this sample. The authors conclude that mental toughness and pain self-efficacy training yield benefits, but no training was tested, so any mental-skills programme should be evaluated rather than assumed to help.
athleteDev: Mental toughness differed by sport and was highest in boxing. The reported higher score in athletes training 10 or more hours a week comes from a table row that appears inconsistent, and the study measured no performance outcome, so the Discussion's link to sports performance is not shown.
rtp: Athletes who had returned to training within a month scored lower on fear avoidance and higher on pain self-efficacy and mental toughness than those who had not returned. The cross-sectional design cannot show that these scores predict return to sport, and the paper should not be used to set return-to-play timing or clearance.

citation: Boltz AJ, Memmini AK, Brett BL, Snedden TR, Yengo-Kahn AM, Chandran A, et al. Intersection of Race and Socioeconomic Status on Concussion Recovery among NCAA Student-Athletes: A CARE Consortium Study. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2023;55(12):2180-2193.
abstract: This CARE Consortium cohort study described race and household income in 22,819 NCAA varsity athletes and compared time to return to learn, start of the RTP protocol, RTP protocol completion and unrestricted RTP among athletes with a concussion. Race was not associated with return to learn or start of the RTP protocol, but non-Black/non-White athletes were less likely to complete the RTP protocol and Black athletes were more likely to reach unrestricted RTP than White athletes. The authors conclude that clinicians should be aware of how implicit or preconceived biases may influence concussion management.
tldr: In this large NCAA cohort, most athletes were White and from higher-income households, and race had little relationship with time to return to learn. Small race-related differences were seen in RTP protocol completion and time to unrestricted RTP, and the paper does not explain why.
methods: Data came from the CARE Consortium, a 30-site study of NCAA and military academy athletes, with baseline assessment and post-injury follow-up between 2014 and 2020. Race and household income were self-reported, and SRC was diagnosed by local medical teams using a common definition. Kaplan-Meier curves and multivariable Cox models estimated time to return to learn (n = 1,724), time to start the RTP protocol, RTP protocol duration and time to unrestricted RTP, adjusting for sex, contact level, SRC history, symptom change and time to asymptomatic.
findings: Most athletes were White (75%), and 53% reported household income above $120,000, whereas 41% of Black athletes reported income below $60,000. In adjusted models, race was not associated with return to learn or start of the RTP protocol (overall p = 0.09). Non-Black/non-White athletes had lower hazard of RTP protocol completion (HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.71 to 0.97), and Black athletes had higher hazard of unrestricted RTP (HR 1.17, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.31) than White athletes, with Kaplan-Meier medians differing by about 1 day. In both return-to-learn models, stratified by symptom change, taking more than 7 days to become asymptomatic was linked to slower return to learn (HR 0.35), and in the higher symptom-change stratum male athletes returned faster than female athletes (HR 1.31, 95% CI 1.11 to 1.53).
limitations: Race was self-reported and grouped into three categories that combine several different groups, ethnicity was not analysed, and household income was self-reported and not modelled in the recovery analyses. Most SRC in the sample occurred in White athletes, the authors state the findings may not be relevant to the general population, and the analyses did not control for individual sport. The Methods text reports a final dataset of 2,464 SRC for the RTP analyses, whereas the abstract and Tables 1C and 2B give N = 2,646 (with 2,334, 2,083 and 2,267 per outcome), so the exact analytic sample is unclear.
practicalImplications: Clinicians should not assume that race predicts how quickly an athlete will return to learn after a concussion, since no race difference was found in the adjusted return-to-learn models. The small race differences in RTP protocol completion and unrestricted RTP timing support the authors' call to examine how bias may affect concussion care, but they do not show which athletes need different management. Taking more than 7 days to become asymptomatic was consistently linked to slower return to learn, so prolonged symptoms are a reasonable flag for academic support planning.
athleteDev: This paper addresses concussion recovery and social factors rather than performance development, so it has limited direct use for training or performance programming. It may matter for staff who make decisions about academic and sport workload after concussion.
rtp: It can inform the understanding of time to return to learn, RTP protocol start and completion, and time to unrestricted RTP in collegiate athletes after SRC. It cannot be used to set individual return-to-play criteria or timelines, and the paper does not show that race should change how an individual athlete is managed.

citation: Fuller CW. Implementing exposure limits for players in contact team sports: review of principles and practices. Frontiers in Sports and Active Living. 2025;7:1593766.
abstract: This mini review applies occupational exposure-limit principles to professional contact team sports such as football and rugby union. It covers how workplace limits are defined, the criteria for prescribing occupational disease, and the evidence on post-career neurological disease and knee osteoarthritis. The author concludes that current evidence cannot confirm or reject these health concerns, and recommends research designed to support evidence-based sport exposure limits.
tldr: Post-career neurological disease and knee osteoarthritis in contact sport players are not confirmed as occupational health concerns, so current exposure limits are precautionary. The author recommends research designed to meet occupational health criteria before limits are set.
methods: Narrative review with no described systematic search. The author reviews UK occupational health principles for workplace exposure limits and the criteria for prescribing occupational disease, then considers the evidence on post-career health in professional football and rugby players.
findings: Studies of retired UK professional players have reported more lower-limb osteoarthritis in footballers and more neurological disease in rugby and football players than in the general population, but three Industrial Injuries Advisory Council reviews judged the evidence insufficient to prescribe these conditions as occupational diseases. Two studies of retired footballers suggested a possible exposure-response relationship between heading and neurological concerns, but the author judges that no study alone was sufficient to confirm exposure-related health concerns or set limits. The 30 game-involvement season limit in English professional rugby from 2024/25 was based on a study that found no association between previous-season match exposure and current-season match injury incidence, and the 10 high-force headers per week limit in English football was introduced under the Precautionary Principle.
limitations: The author notes that few sport-related studies were designed to examine post-career health, and that definitions of osteoarthritis vary across studies, which limits cross-study comparison. The review gives no search strategy, and it does not establish exposure limits or their effect on long-term health.
practicalImplications: Treat sport exposure limits as policy decisions rather than evidence-confirmed requirements, since the author states that the evidence cannot confirm or reject the health concerns. Record training and match exposures alongside injury data in a consistent format, because the author argues that this would help future studies test exposure-response relationships. Present exposure caps as policy decisions when discussing them with players or staff.
athleteDev: Sport exposure limits, such as the game-involvement and heading limits discussed, are policy decisions rather than established performance or load standards. The author argues that consistent exposure data would help future studies set evidence-based limits, so collecting such data is worthwhile now.
rtp: This review does not address injury rehabilitation or return-to-play criteria. Its discussion of injury burden and post-career health concerns does not support any clearance decision for injured players.

citation: Athanasiadou I, Voss SC, El Saftawy W, Al-Jaber H, Dbes N, Al-Yazedi S, et al. Hyperhydration Induced Decrease in Urinary Luteinizing Hormone Concentrations of Male Athletes may be Compensated by Specific Gravity Adjustment in Doping Control Analysis. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2018.
abstract: This study tested whether hyperhydration lowers urinary luteinizing hormone (LH), a marker used in doping control, and which volume adjustment corrects it. Seven healthy, recreationally active men drank 20 mL/kg of water or a sports drink on 3 consecutive days. Urinary LH fell after fluid loading, and adjustment by specific gravity to 1.020 restored values close to the baseline profile.
tldr: Drinking large volumes dilutes urine and can push LH below the old 1.0 IU/L doping-control threshold for several hours. Adjusting LH to a urine specific gravity of 1.020, the WADA method, corrected most of this effect in 7 recreational men.
methods: Seven healthy, recreationally active, non-smoking men (38.4 +/- 8.2 years) completed a 24-hour baseline urine collection, then two 72-hour hyperhydration phases (20 mL/kg water, then a 6% carbohydrate sports drink, each taken daily for 3 days) separated by a 4-day washout. Every void was analysed for LH (IMMULITE immunoassay), specific gravity, creatinine, pH, conductivity and urine flow rate. Five adjustment methods (specific gravity, SG(z), urine flow rate, creatinine and creatinine regression) were compared using pooled Mann-Whitney and Wilcoxon tests.
findings: Mean non-adjusted LH was 4.24 IU/L (water) and 4.74 IU/L (sports drink), significantly lower than baseline (P < 0.001), and values returned near baseline about 10 hours after each intake; the cumulative 24-hour LH amount did not differ from baseline (P = 0.87 and 0.84). In the first 24 hours, 24.6% and 15.6% of samples were below 1.0 IU/L without adjustment, falling to 3.08% and 1.56% after specific gravity adjustment. Specific gravity, SG(z) and flow-rate adjustment changed values significantly, SG-adjusted values did not differ from baseline (P = 0.08 and 0.86), and creatinine-based methods gave no significant correction.
limitations: The sample was 7 recreationally active men and diet was not controlled, as the authors note. Statistics were run on pooled samples rather than per participant. Baseline LH is given as 7.11 +/- 5.42 IU/L in the abstract and first results paragraph but 7.72 +/- 5.42 IU/L later in the results; neither value is used here as the primary comparison.
practicalImplications: Medical and anti-doping staff should expect a very dilute urine sample (specific gravity below 1.005) to show low LH for some hours after heavy fluid intake. The authors suggest applying specific gravity adjustment to LH regardless of the sample's specific gravity, which differs from the WADA rule current at the time (adjustment only above 1.020).
athleteDev: The study measured no performance outcome. Its relevance to athletes is that large fluid boluses before a test dilute urine and can change how an endogenous hormone result is read.
rtp: The study does not involve injury, illness or return to sport and cannot inform return-to-play decisions.

citation: Ryan C, Uthoff A, McKenzie C, Cronin J. Inertial measurement unit analysis for providing greater diagnostic value during the modified 5-0-5 change of direction test. Journal of Sport and Exercise Science. 2023;7(2):54-61.
abstract: This study examined the inter-session reliability of a foot-mounted inertial measurement unit (IMU) insole for peak acceleration, peak deceleration, maximum speed and ground contact time during a modified 5-0-5 change-of-direction test. Ten elite female netball athletes completed the test on three sessions, and IMU variables were correlated with timing gate splits. The authors report moderate to excellent relative consistency, acceptable absolute consistency, and peak acceleration as the variable most strongly associated with total time.
tldr: A foot-mounted IMU insole gave mostly consistent measures across three sessions in elite netball players, and peak acceleration tracked total change-of-direction time closely. The study did not test validity against a gold standard, so coaches should treat the insole as a reliable supplement to timing gates rather than a replacement.
methods: Test-retest and correlation study in 10 elite female netball athletes who performed three maximal trials per leg of a modified 5-0-5 test on three sessions one week apart. Plantiga insole IMUs were worn with dual-beam timing gates set at 0, 2 and 4 m. Reliability used CV and two-way random ICC, and Pearson correlations linked IMU variables to timing splits and total time.
findings: Inter-session CVs were 1.8 to 9.5 percent for most variables (left ground contact time between sessions 1 and 2 was 14.4 percent), and ICCs were 0.81 to 0.96 except left peak deceleration between sessions 1 and 2 (0.57). In Table 2, higher peak acceleration was associated with shorter total time (r = -0.95), and higher maximum speed with shorter total time (r = -0.91), while ground contact time had weak correlations with the other variables. The authors state that the IMU variables add diagnostic information beyond total time.
limitations: Only 10 athletes were tested, and left and right legs were pooled after no side differences were found. The paper reports reliability and association, not validity against a criterion. Reporting conflicts: the abstract gives ICC 0.57 to 0.94 while Table 1 runs to 0.96, the abstract and some text report the peak acceleration and total time correlation as r = 0.95 while Table 2 and one Discussion passage give r = -0.95, split 5 is r = 0.68 in the text but -0.68 in the table, and the left ground contact time CV is 14.4 percent in Results but 14.5 percent in the Discussion; table values are reported here.
practicalImplications: Coaches could use a foot-mounted IMU insole alongside timing gates to track peak acceleration, maximum speed and ground contact time in change-of-direction testing, since most measures were consistent across three sessions. The study does not show that these measures predict performance change or injury, so decisions about training should rest on repeated testing in the same athletes.
athleteDev: Peak acceleration and maximum speed were strongly associated with total 5-0-5 time, and ground contact time at the turn gave different information. Staff could use these variables to look for why a change-of-direction time changed, but the study does not test any training intervention.
rtp: The study does not address return to sport or injury rehabilitation, and its athletes were healthy elite netball players. It should not be used to set return-to-play criteria.

citation: Hillen B, Pfirrmann D, Nägele M, Simon P. Infrared Thermography in Exercise Physiology: The Dawning of Exercise Radiomics. Sports Medicine. 2020;50:263-282.
abstract: This review asks how infrared thermography (IRT) can be used to measure changes in body surface radiation temperature during exercise. The authors summarise endurance, incremental and resistance-exercise studies and add their own high-resolution camera case experiments. They describe a fine surface radiation pattern (Psr) during endurance and incremental exercise and argue that skin temperature measures are confounded by environmental, technical and individual factors.
tldr: Infrared thermography during exercise shows a consistent early drop in skin temperature in endurance and incremental work, but the results for resistance work conflict across small, varied studies. A single average skin temperature from one body region is not a reliable basis for comparison.
methods: Narrative review of peer-reviewed English-language studies with human exercise, found in PubMed and Google Scholar using infrared thermography and exercise search terms for 1992 to 2018, plus reference lists. The authors also report their own case experiments with a 640 x 480 pixel IRT camera on one to three participants per figure.
findings: In constant-load endurance exercise, skin temperature fell at the start and then stabilised or slowly rose. In incremental testing, skin temperature generally fell progressively to exhaustion and rose during recovery. In resistance exercise, reported changes were inconsistent: seven studies reported a rise, three a fall and one no change. The authors describe a fine surface radiation pattern (Psr) during endurance and incremental exercise, a different venous pattern in their own resistance-exercise cases (not previously reported in the literature), and an athlete case showing different forearm and thigh patterns within one test.
limitations: The review uses one search string, no formal quality appraisal and no pooled analysis. The studies are small and heterogeneous in camera resolution, regions of interest, exercise protocols and timing points. The case experiments include one to three participants each, and the link between Psr and cutaneous blood flow is the authors' interpretation, not a tested result.
