practicalImplications: Do not compare average skin temperature across body regions, studies or camera systems unless the region, distance, ambient conditions and timing are the same. Treat the surface radiation pattern as an exploratory research signal, not a validated measure of fatigue, core temperature or training load. Any IRT session data should be collected with a fixed camera setup and a reference object to check for environmental bias.
athleteDev: Thermal imaging could eventually help staff track individual responses to training, but the authors do not provide validated thresholds or a proven link to training load. Use IRT only for comparing the same athlete under identical conditions and treat any pattern change as a prompt for further checks.
rtp: This review does not evaluate injury, inflammation or return to sport. It cannot be used to judge recovery readiness or return-to-play decisions, because the paper addresses dynamic exercise measurement in healthy participants.

citation: Beausejour JP, Knowles KS, Wilson AT, Mangum LC, Hill EC, Hanney WJ, et al. Innovations in the Assessment of Skeletal Muscle Health: A Glimpse into the Future. Int J Sports Med. 2024.
abstract: This concise review highlights innovative or overlooked in vivo approaches for assessing skeletal muscle health. Topics include dynamic ultrasound imaging, tensiomyography, blood flow restriction occlusion pressure, serological neoepitope biomarkers, ultrasound echo intensity, body composition and bioimpedance, and skeletal muscle pain assessment.
tldr: Several low-cost, non-invasive tools, including dynamic ultrasound, tensiomyography, echo intensity and bioimpedance phase angle, may help practitioners assess muscle function and quality outside the laboratory. The authors note that many of these methods still need reliability and validity work before routine use.
methods: A narrative review using PubMed and Google Scholar to identify recent publications on dynamic imaging, neuromuscular assessment, echogenicity, blood flow restriction, biomarkers, muscle quality, body composition and pain. No systematic search strategy, eligibility criteria or screening process is reported.
findings: Dynamic ultrasound and tensiomyography are presented as feasible, non-invasive ways to measure muscle thickness, activation and contractile properties, with reliability data drawn largely from small samples. One study of 10 participants reported high test-retest reliability for an algorithm-based blood flow restriction device (ICC above 0.953), but the authors note its validity was not examined. The authors report that echo intensity is associated with functional outcomes and age-group differences, and that bioimpedance phase angle is higher in athletes than controls in a systematic review they cite.
limitations: As a narrative review without a stated search strategy or quality grading, the choice of methods reflects the authors' judgement. Most cited reliability studies are small (n = 13 and n = 10), and the authors note that tensiomyography does not measure neural activation or force and that tensiomyography and echo intensity are affected by skin impedance, probe tilt and participant position. Neoepitope biomarker research is described as being in its infancy, and the evidence for MRI of trigger points is unclear.
practicalImplications: Dynamic ultrasound, tensiomyography and echo intensity may suit practitioners who need muscle function and quality measures without MRI, but staff should first check reliability in their own setting and protocol. Algorithm-based occlusion pressure devices are described as not without error and lacking validity data, and the authors favour raw bioimpedance values (resistance, reactance, phase angle) over prediction-equation estimates of body composition.
athleteDev: Echo intensity and bioimpedance vector analysis are presented as possible ways to track muscle quality and body composition, and the authors say vectors can separate competitive levels and types of athletes. The review does not present evidence that these measures predict performance or respond to training.
rtp: The review mentions return-to-play contexts for localized bioimpedance, but it gives no return-to-sport criteria or validated thresholds. It should not be used to make return-to-play or clearance decisions.

citation: Thorsson S, Rayner D, Palm G, Lindberg F, Carlström E, Börjesson M, et al. Is Physiological Equivalent Temperature (PET) a superior screening tool for heat stress risk than Wet-Bulb Globe Temperature (WBGT) index? Eight years of data from the Gothenburg half marathon. Br J Sports Med. 2020.
abstract: Wet-Bulb Globe Temperature (WBGT) is a common heat-stress screening tool at sporting events, but it has known limitations. This study used eight years (2010-2017) of meteorological and ambulance transport data from the Gothenburg half marathon to identify which thermal index best predicts ambulance-required assistances and collapses. The authors report that Physiological Equivalent Temperature (PET) showed the strongest correlation with both outcomes, followed by the Universal Thermal Climate Index (UTCI), with WBGT performing substantially worse.
tldr: In eight years of data from one city half marathon, PET predicted ambulance calls and collapses better than WBGT, the standard race heat screen. The authors suggest PET could be considered alongside WBGT, but they do not recommend replacing WBGT yet.
methods: Race-level analysis of eight half marathons (2010-2017). Ambulance transport and medical records were linked to hourly meteorological data, and WBGT, PET and UTCI were calculated, with WBGT estimated because on-site sensors were not available. Linear regression with Monte Carlo simulation and leave-one-out cross-validation was used to compare how much variance each index explained in ambulance-required assistances and collapses per 1000 starters.
findings: PET explained 72% of the variance in ambulance-required assistance rates (R2 = 0.72, p = 0.008) and 71% for collapses (p = 0.008), versus 56% for WBGT (p = 0.031 and 0.033). The Monte Carlo confidence that PET correlated more strongly than WBGT was 0.74 for both outcomes. Collapses were 1.10 per 1000 starters in 2010 when the maximum PET rose sharply from the day before, and 0.66 in 2013 when it did not, with a similar maximum PET on both days. The authors note that WBGT underestimated heat stress, most markedly at high radiant heat load.
limitations: The study covers eight race-years at one event, so the regression is based on very few data points and the authors state more data are needed. WBGT was estimated from modelled globe temperature, and the authors acknowledge that PET and UTCI are not designed for athletes and may underestimate heat stress in runners.
practicalImplications: Race medical planners could consider PET-based heat stress stages as an additional screen alongside WBGT, especially when radiant heat load is high. The authors suggest a large rise in PET from the day before the race may raise collapse rates, but this rests on a comparison of two race-years and should be treated as a hypothesis. Do not replace WBGT with PET on the basis of this study alone, because the authors call for further comparison before any change.
athleteDev: The paper concerns heat-stress screening at a mass endurance race, not training prescription. For performance staff, the finding that WBGT read lower than PET as radiant heat load rose suggests a single WBGT reading may understate heat stress on sunny, low-wind days.
rtp: This study addresses exertional collapse and ambulance need among race participants and cannot inform return-to-sport decisions for injured athletes.

citation: Ahn N, Kim H, Krzyszkowski J, Roche S, Kipp K. Joint-level determinants of the dynamic strength index: implications for testing and monitoring. Sports Biomechanics. 2022.
abstract: Compares a traditional ground reaction force dynamic strength index (DSI) with joint-level DSIs from net joint moments in eight female NCAA Division I lacrosse players. Only the hip joint-level DSI correlated with the force-based DSI, and joint-level values were generally higher. The authors conclude the joint-level ratio may not give practitioners intuitive or useful data.
tldr: In a small group of female lacrosse players, the hip joint-level strength index tracked the usual force-based index, but the joint-level values were much higher and hard to interpret. The authors suggest the joint-level index may not give coaches intuitive or useful data.
methods: Eight female lacrosse players did three maximal isometric mid-thigh pulls and three countermovement jumps. Motion capture and force plates gave ground reaction force and net joint moments at the hip, knee and ankle, normalised to body mass. Ratios of jump to pull peaks gave the force and joint DSIs, compared with Pearson correlations, paired t-tests and Hedges g.
findings: The hip joint-level DSI correlated with the force-based DSI (r = 0.738, p = 0.037; bootstrapped 95% CI 0.147 to 0.976), while ankle (r = -0.349) and knee (r = 0.139) did not. Joint-level DSIs were higher than the force-based DSI at all joints (mean differences: ankle 34.3, knee 62.1, hip 111.5; Hedges g 1.35 to 2.49). Reliability was excellent (ICC 0.960 to 0.993; CV 3.2% to 6.8%).
limitations: Very small sample (8 of 10 recruited players, data from two discarded), a single sex and sport, and peak net joint moment in the pull measured at one position only. Countermovement depth was self-selected and varied, and net joint moments ignore co-contraction.
practicalImplications: The force-based DSI was not associated with ankle or knee joint-level DSI, so it should not be read as a measure of joint-specific strength use. The authors conclude that joint-level DSI values, which mostly exceeded 100%, are hard to contextualise and may not be practical for evaluating strength or monitoring adaptations.
athleteDev: In this sample the force-based DSI tracked hip-level DSI but gave little information about the knee and ankle. The authors question the practical usefulness of joint-level DSI, so it should not be used to choose between maximal strength and speed-strength training.
rtp: No return-to-sport data. Players' injury or health status was not reported, and the study cannot be used to judge readiness after injury.

citation: Silverman R, Knapik DM, Smith MV, Baker JC, Napier K, Matava MJ, et al. Limited Agreement on ACL Tear Location Between Arthroscopy and MRI: A Prospective Evaluation. Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2025;13(12):23259671251397389.
abstract: Prospective cohort of 174 patients with full-thickness ACL tears (2022 to 2024) who had preoperative MRI and arthroscopy at one institution. Tear location was classified on the modified Sherman scale by MRI and at arthroscopy, and the study compared agreement and examined associations with age, sex, BMI and injury mechanism.
tldr: MRI matched arthroscopic ACL tear location in only 43 percent of cases overall, although it identified 95.5 percent of tears that arthroscopy called midsubstance (type III). MRI called far more tears midsubstance than arthroscopy did (67.2 vs 25.8 percent), and arthroscopy found more proximal tears.
methods: Prospective cohort at one institution. Tear location was classified on MRI by two musculoskeletal radiologists (disagreements resolved by the senior author) and during surgery by one of four sports surgeons, using the modified Sherman classification. Agreement and tear-type distributions were compared by sex, BMI, injury mechanism and age using chi-square, ANOVA, Fisher exact and ordinal logistic regression tests.
findings: Arthroscopic distribution was type II 44.8 percent, type I 26.4 percent, type III 25.8 percent and type IV 3.4 percent, with no type V tears. MRI distribution was type III 67.2 percent, type II 22.4 percent, type I 9.8 percent and type IV 0.6 percent. Overall agreement was 43.1 percent (75 of 174) and 95.5 percent for type III tears. Interobserver kappa between radiologists was 0.41. Age was significantly associated with tear type on both assessments (arthroscopy P=.009; MRI P=.0001), with type I tears in older patients.
limitations: Single-center cohort of ACL reconstruction patients with athletic status not reported; surgeon arthroscopic classification was not video-recorded and surgeons were not blinded to the MRI scans, and radiologists disagreed on 28.7 percent of MRIs. Types IV and V were too rare for reliable comparison. The abstract reports no significant association with injury mechanism, but the results text reports one significant clustered comparison (arthroscopic type III tears, indirect contact versus direct contact or noncontact, odds ratio 0.35, P=.038).
practicalImplications: Do not rely on preoperative MRI alone to decide whether a tear is proximal enough for repair, because MRI agreed with arthroscopy in only 43 percent of tears and identified fewer proximal avulsions (9.8 vs 26.4 percent). The 95.5 percent figure is the share of arthroscopic midsubstance tears that MRI also called midsubstance; MRI labelled many more tears midsubstance than arthroscopy confirmed, so an MRI midsubstance read is not reliable on its own.
athleteDev: The study measures diagnostic agreement, not athletic performance or training, so it has no direct performance application. For sports medicine teams planning ACL surgery, it indicates that MRI and surgical tear-type calls disagree in most cases.
rtp: Indirectly relevant, because tear location bears on whether primary repair or reconstruction is considered. The study reports no return-to-sport outcomes, so it cannot be used to set return-to-sport timelines or readiness criteria.

citation: Fitzwilliam E, Steventon-Lorenzen N, Opar D, Schache AG, Maniar N. Lower Limb Joint Mechanics during Maximal Accelerative and Decelerative Running. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2024. Published ahead of print.
abstract: This laboratory study compared hip, knee and ankle joint moments and work in 20 recreationally active adults performing maximal-effort accelerations and unanticipated decelerations. Net joint work was positive during acceleration and negative during deceleration, with the ankle contributing most positive work in acceleration and the knee and hip contributing most negative work in deceleration. Peak joint moments were generally larger during deceleration, except for the ankle plantarflexion and hip flexion moments.
tldr: In recreationally active adults, maximal acceleration relied mainly on positive work from the ankle and hip, while deceleration relied on negative work from the knee and hip. Peak moments were generally greater in deceleration, which may inform training, but the study measured mechanics rather than performance or injury.
methods: Laboratory study. Twenty recreationally active adults (10 men, 10 women; age 25 +/- 4 years; mass 70 +/- 10 kg; at least 150 minutes of moderate activity per week) performed three maximal acceleration trials and three deceleration trials, in which a light at a second timing gate randomly signalled stop or continue. Marker-based motion capture, two force plates and OpenSim inverse dynamics with a 31 degree-of-freedom model gave hip, knee and ankle moments, power and work. Linear mixed models with participant as a random effect were used, with p < 0.01 as the significance threshold; 118 of 120 trials were analysed after two non-decelerative trials were excluded.
findings: Net joint work was positive in acceleration (hip 0.48, knee 0.37, ankle 0.74 J/kg) and negative in deceleration (hip -0.73, knee -0.65, ankle -0.54 J/kg), and net work differed between tasks at every joint (p < 0.001). Positive work was greater in acceleration at the hip and ankle (p < 0.001) but not at the knee (p = 0.014, above the 0.01 threshold), and negative work was greater in deceleration at all three joints (p < 0.001). The peak hip extension moment was -1.88 N m/kg in acceleration and -4.97 N m/kg in deceleration, the peak knee extension moment was -1.66 and -2.30 N m/kg, and the peak ankle plantarflexion moment was larger in acceleration (-2.86 versus -1.76 N m/kg).
limitations: Twenty recreationally active adults in a laboratory, with the authors noting that sprint and deceleration mechanics may differ in elite or previously injured athletes. No sex-specific analysis was possible, and deceleration strategies varied across participants. Joint angles from skin markers are subject to soft-tissue artefact, and the laboratory setting differs from field play; forward velocity at foot strike differed by 5% between tasks, and the authors report that a covariate-adjusted model did not change any conclusion. The design is cross-sectional, so injury mechanisms in the discussion are inferences. One co-author holds interests in Vald Performance, which supplied the timing gates.
practicalImplications: Deceleration placed larger negative work and peak extension demands on the knee and hip than acceleration did, so eccentric knee and hip extensor strength may be relevant to deceleration performance, as the authors propose. The mechanics should not be assumed to indicate injury risk, because injury was not measured. Findings from recreational adults should be checked against athletes before they inform training prescription.
athleteDev: Performance Application: Maximal acceleration depended mainly on ankle plantarflexor and hip extensor work, while deceleration depended on knee and hip extensor work. These are mechanical descriptions in recreational adults rather than performance outcomes, so they do not show that training these muscles improves sprint or change-of-direction performance.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: The study does not include injured athletes or return to sport. The authors suggest that the high eccentric hip and knee demands of deceleration may relate to hamstring, groin and ACL injury mechanisms, but they state that injury risk was beyond the scope of the study, so this paper cannot inform return-to-play loading or clearance.

citation: May AK, Russell AP, Warmington SA. Lower body blood flow restriction training may induce remote muscle strength adaptations in an active unrestricted arm. European Journal of Applied Physiology. 2018.
abstract: Twenty-four recreationally active young men were randomised to 8 weeks of leg resistance training with or without blood flow restriction, while both groups trained the dominant arm with bicep curls. The BFR group gained more elbow flexion 1-RM in the trained arm than the untrained arm and the controls' trained arm, and more knee extension 1-RM than controls. Muscle cross-sectional area changes did not differ between groups, and the authors attribute the remote strength effect mainly to neuromuscular adaptation.
tldr: Adding light-load blood flow restriction to leg training was associated with a larger strength gain in a concurrently trained arm than arm training alone in 24 young men. Muscle size did not differ between groups, and the study did not test athletes, injured people or women.
methods: Randomized two-group trial of 24 recreationally active young men (BFR group n = 12; non-BFR control n = 12) over 8 weeks, with 20 sessions three times per week. The dominant arm performed three sets of 10 unilateral bicep curls at 50% 1-RM, and both groups performed knee extension and flexion at 30% 1-RM. The BFR group used individually set cuff pressure at 60% limb occlusion pressure during leg exercise. Strength was measured by 1-RM in both arms and legs, and muscle cross-sectional area by peripheral quantitative CT at one leg site (25% femur length) and at 50% humerus length. Results are mean +/- SEM with mixed-model ANOVA and ANCOVA, with significance at p < 0.05.
findings: Elbow flexion 1-RM increased by 2.5 +/- 0.4 kg in the BFR group's trained arm, compared with 0.8 +/- 0.4 kg in its untrained arm and 0.6 +/- 0.3 kg in the controls' trained arm (p < 0.05 for both comparisons). Knee extension 1-RM rose 16.3 +/- 1.3 kg in the BFR group and 8.3 +/- 1.6 kg in controls (p < 0.01). Knee flexion 1-RM and leg muscle cross-sectional area increased similarly in both groups, and trained-arm cross-sectional area did not differ between groups. The untrained arm did not change significantly in cross-sectional area.
limitations: Only 12 men per group, all young and recreationally active, and the authors caution against generalising to women or clinical populations. Muscle size was measured at one leg site and by pQCT, so the null hypertrophy result is limited, and the authors suggest MRI at several sites in future work. The trained arm was always the dominant arm, and baseline elbow flexion strength was higher in the controls' trained arm than their untrained arm (p < 0.001). The abstract describes 7 weeks of training while the methods describe 20 sessions with post-testing in week 8. Participants gripped the machine handles during leg exercise, which the authors suggest may have recruited arm muscles more in the BFR group but judge to be negligible, and sitting on the cuffs during knee flexion may have reduced the restriction stimulus. The conclusion that the effect is neuromuscular rests partly on the null size result.
practicalImplications: In this study, adding BFR to leg training produced a larger elbow flexion strength gain in a concurrently trained arm than arm training alone. The untrained arm did not differ from controls, and the authors suggest that a local mechanical stimulus in the arm may be needed, so leg BFR should not be expected to strengthen an arm that is not trained. The evidence rests on one small trial, so it should be treated as a hypothesis for athletes rather than a protocol.
athleteDev: Performance Application: In recreationally active young men, leg BFR training combined with arm training increased trained-arm elbow flexion strength more than arm training alone over 8 weeks, which may be relevant to programmes that develop an arm alongside lower-body work. The study did not test athletes or sport performance.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: The study does not include injured people or return-to-sport outcomes. The authors suggest the approach may help people with localised movement disorders in early rehabilitation, but clinical groups were not tested, so the paper cannot guide load, cuff pressure or clearance in rehabilitation.

citation: Thosar SS, Herzig MX, Roberts SA, Berman AM, Clemons NA, McHill AW, et al. Lowest perceived exertion in the late morning due to effects of the endogenous circadian system. Br J Sports Med. 2018.
abstract: This research letter describes a forced desynchrony study of ten healthy adults that tested whether rate of perceived exertion (RPE) changes with the internal circadian clock when workload and behaviour are held constant. RPE was lowest in the late morning and highest during the biological night for the same mild-intensity cycling.
tldr: In healthy adults, the same mild cycling workload felt least demanding in the late morning and most demanding in the biological night, independent of sleep, activity and meal timing. The study did not include athletes or high-intensity work.
methods: Ten healthy adults (six female, mean age 52 years) went through a forced desynchrony protocol in dim light with repeated 5 hour 20 minute behavioural cycles. About one hour after each sleep episode they cycled for 15 minutes at 50% predicted maximal heart rate, and Borg RPE was recorded at 3, 8 and 13 minutes. RPE was Z-scored within each participant, grouped into 60 degree circadian phase bins and compared with repeated measures ANOVA, with circadian phase set from dim light melatonin onset.
findings: The circadian system significantly affected RPE for the same workload, with the lowest RPE at circadian phase 210 degrees (about 10:45 AM) and the highest at 90 degrees (about 3:45 AM). The size of the circadian variation was about 1 Z-score unit (1 SD).
limitations: The sample was small (n = 10) and was not made up of athletes. Only mild-intensity cycling was tested, and RPE was rated at only three time points within each bout. The authors' suggestion about athletes performing high-intensity exercise is untested in this study, and the text does not report a p-value.
practicalImplications: Under controlled, mild cycling in healthy middle-aged adults, RPE for the same workload varied with circadian phase. Staff who compare RPE across sessions held at very different times of day may want to record session time, but the study did not test athletes or normal daytime training windows. It does not justify changing athlete session times or using light exposure to shift circadian timing.
athleteDev: This study cannot be used to set athlete session times. It suggests that RPE for a fixed workload may be lower in the late morning, so RPE comparisons across different times of day should be interpreted with that in mind.
rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It included no injured participants and no return-to-play outcomes.

citation: Champion L, Middleton K, MacMahon C. Many Pieces to the Puzzle: A New Holistic Workload Approach to Designing Practice in Sports. Sports Medicine - Open. 2023;9:38.
abstract: The paper argues that representative learning design should weigh how closely training matches competition (fidelity) against the cognitive and physical load it imposes. It proposes a total workload approach with four characteristics and five training categories, linked to the perception-action cycle.
tldr: The authors argue that highly match-like training should aid transfer but also adds cognitive and physical load that can contribute to fatigue, injury or burnout. They propose planning fidelity and load together across a week or cycle, alternating high and low demand.
methods: Narrative conceptual review drawing on representative learning design, ecological dynamics and meshed control theory, with examples mainly from team sport. The paper describes no search strategy, database or appraisal method, and collects no data.
findings: The authors state that representative training improves transfer but can add substantial cognitive and physical load, and that existing models do not quantify cognitive demand in training. They propose four characteristics and five training categories, and show a hypothetical seven-day microcycle in which cognitive and physical emphasis alternate. No validation or athlete outcome data are reported.
limitations: The framework has no empirical testing, and the authors note that it does not dictate how fidelity or load should be measured. They also state that EEG, MEG and pupillometry can estimate cognitive workload but restrict movement, so practical measurement remains unresolved.
practicalImplications: Plan match-like training together with its recovery demands rather than by volume alone, and consider cognitive as well as physical load when programming. The authors suggest that, until better measures exist, simpler tools such as session RPE and subjective fidelity ratings may be used, especially at sub-elite levels.
athleteDev: Performance staff can use the framework to balance match-like drills against their load across a microcycle, treating cognitive demand as a planning variable. The framework is not validated and should be trialled before it changes programming.
rtp: The paper does not address rehabilitation or return to sport. Its overload concerns apply to healthy training design, and it gives no return-to-play criteria.

citation: Roberts MD, McCarthy JJ, Hornberger TA, Phillips SM, Mackey AL, Nader GA, et al. Mechanisms of mechanical overload-induced skeletal muscle hypertrophy: current understanding and future directions. Physiol Rev. 2023;103:2679-2757.
abstract: The review traces the history of hypertrophy research and summarises the mechanisms linked to overload-induced muscle growth. It highlights mTORC1 signalling, translational capacity, satellite cells and myonuclear accretion, and it proposes directions for future research.
tldr: Resistance training increases muscle mass through a few well-supported mechanisms, including mTORC1 signalling, ribosome biogenesis and satellite cell activity. Many other proposed mechanisms remain unproven, so the mechanistic picture is incomplete.
methods: Narrative review with no search strategy reported. The authors present a historical account, a summary of mechanisms with a table of current role and knowledge gaps for each, and a discussion of methodological issues in hypertrophy research.
findings: The authors identify enhanced mTORC1 signalling, expansion of translational capacity through ribosome biogenesis, and satellite cell-mediated myonuclear accretion as the mechanisms with the most support. They present other candidates (mTORC1-independent signalling, genetic variants, DNA methylation, proteolysis, myostatin, extracellular matrix remodelling, angiogenesis, microRNAs and prostaglandin signalling) as contributors with mixed or incomplete evidence, and rate testosterone signalling, endogenous beta-adrenergic signalling, angiotensin II, the muscle circadian clock and microtubule networks as not well elucidated. They also note that preliminary human data suggest individuals may differ in how they hypertrophy, with some gaining mainly through fascicle length and others through fibre cross-sectional area.
limitations: The review does not describe a search or appraisal method, and the authors' own table marks several mechanisms as not well elucidated or as possibly only coinciding with hypertrophy. Much of the mechanistic evidence comes from rodent models, including the synergist ablation model that the authors say does not resemble progressive resistance training, and the review covers sex, race and ageing only briefly. Some authors report industry funding, including dairy industry grants.
practicalImplications: Resistance training programmes should be built on progressive mechanical overload, which the authors describe as the stimulus that best achieves hypertrophy. The review reports that transient post-exercise rises in circulating hormones do not correlate with hypertrophy, and that high-dose ibuprofen (1,200 mg/day) and cold-water immersion may blunt hypertrophy-related responses, although findings are mixed and appear age dependent. Individual molecular mechanisms should not be treated as training targets.
athleteDev: Use the review to explain why progressive overload is the core of hypertrophy work for athletes, while treating individual mechanisms as research questions rather than training targets. Individual responses may differ, so track each athlete's own change over time.
rtp: The review concerns hypertrophy mechanisms during loading in healthy and general adult populations and does not address rehabilitation after injury, return-to-sport loading or tissue healing. It should not be used to set return-to-play criteria.

citation: Staiano W, Salazar Bonet LR, Romagnoli M, Ring C. Mental Fatigue Impairs Repeated Sprint and Jump Performance in Team Sport Athletes. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2023.
abstract: In 18 male team-sport players, a 30-minute Stroop task increased mental fatigue and rating of perceived exertion compared with a documentary. Mental fatigue impaired directional repeated sprint performance and repeated jump performance, but not linear sprinting, peak performance or a single countermovement jump.
tldr: A 30-minute Stroop task made team-sport players slower and less consistent in directional repeated sprints and repeated jumps. Linear sprints and single jumps were not affected, and the effect was linked to higher perceived effort rather than blood lactate or heart rate.
methods: Eighteen male amateur basketball, handball and football players completed a familiarization session and then two counterbalanced conditions at least 10 days apart: a 30-minute Stroop task or a documentary. Afterwards they completed 12 maximal 20-m sprints (10 m linear plus 10 m directional), 12 maximal repeated countermovement jumps and a countermovement jump test, with mental fatigue, psychomotor vigilance, RPE, heart rate and lactate measured.
findings: Mean directional sprint time was longer after the Stroop task (P = 0.032) and sprint decrement was greater (P = 0.027). In the repeated jump test, mean jump height was lower (P = 0.009, d = 0.60) and decrement greater (P = 0.034) after the Stroop task. Peak sprint time, peak jump height, countermovement jump height, heart rate and lactate did not differ, while RPE was higher and psychomotor vigilance reaction time was slower than control (P = 0.002).
limitations: The authors note the lack of biomechanical measures of postural control, so their proposed mechanism is speculative. The sample was 18 amateur men at one performance level (no women could be tested), and the study tested a single 30-minute Stroop protocol against a documentary control.
practicalImplications: Demanding cognitive work before a session may reduce the quality of repeated directional sprints and repeated jumps, and the authors advise coaches in sports with repeated sprinting and jumping to plan strategies to limit mental fatigue. They suggest power naps, self-talk, caffeine and brain endurance training, but this study tested none of them.
athleteDev: Mentally fatiguing work before a session may reduce the quality of directional repeated sprints and repeated jumps in team-sport athletes, so the timing of cognitive load matters. Linear sprinting and single jumps were not affected in this study.
rtp: The study tested healthy players and did not measure injury or return-to-play readiness, so it cannot be used to clear an athlete to return to sport.

citation: Davidow D, Smith M, Ross T, James GL, Paul L, Lambert M, et al. Mental Fatigue Impairs Tackling Technique in Amateur Rugby Union Players. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2023.
abstract: Twenty male amateur rugby union players tackled a simulator on both shoulders in a control condition and after a 30-minute Stroop task. Tackling proficiency was lower after the Stroop task, mainly on the non-dominant shoulder, with small effect sizes.
tldr: Mental fatigue reduced the technical quality of tackles, most clearly on the non-dominant shoulder. The effects were small, and the study used a tackle simulator rather than live tackles.
methods: Twenty players completed a four-set tackle protocol (three tackles per shoulder per set) on a tackle contact simulator at two counterbalanced visits at least 72 hours apart. One visit included passive reading and the other a 30-minute Stroop task with 5-minute top-ups after sets 1 and 2. Each tackle was video-scored by one assessor against 11 technical criteria, and mental fatigue, physical fatigue, RPE and mental effort were rated on visual analogue scales.
findings: Across both shoulders, tackle proficiency was lower in the Stroop condition at set 2 (6.91 vs 7.30 AU, P = 0.009) and set 3 (6.88 vs 7.34 AU, P = 0.002). On the non-dominant shoulder the difference was significant at set 2 (P = 0.047) and set 3 (6.61 vs 7.14 AU, P = 0.007), while the dominant shoulder showed no between-condition difference. Explosiveness on contact was the component most impaired on both shoulders, and mental fatigue and physical fatigue ratings were higher after the Stroop task.
limitations: Baseline tackle proficiency was higher in the Stroop condition (7.47 vs 7.08 AU, P = 0.009), which may affect the between-condition comparison. The authors note the simulator has only moderate ecological validity, the Stroop task's ecological validity has been questioned, and effects at junior, elite or female levels are unknown.
practicalImplications: The authors recommend including a mental fatigue component in tackle training, for example by asking players to tackle while performing a demanding cognitive task. This study did not test that training approach, so its benefit is untested.
athleteDev: Mentally fatiguing demands may reduce the explosive, on-contact quality of tackles, especially on the non-dominant shoulder, so technical training under cognitive load may be worth trying. The effect came from one 30-minute Stroop protocol in a simulator, so it should be treated as a hypothesis for training design.
rtp: The study did not measure injury, live tackling or return-to-play readiness, so it cannot decide when a player can return to contact. Its link to tackle injury risk comes from the literature the authors cite, not from a finding of this trial.

citation: Andrews MH, Anoosha Pai S, Gurchiek RD, Pincheira PA, Chaudhari AS, Hodges PW, et al. Multiscale hamstring muscle adaptations following 9 weeks of eccentric training. Journal of Sport and Health Science. 2024.
abstract: Twelve recreationally active adults completed 9 weeks of Nordic hamstring exercise (NHE) training followed by 3 weeks of detraining. Biceps femoris long-head fascicle length increased (19% central, 33% distal) and serial sarcomere number increased (25% central, 49% distal), with muscle volume (8%) and knee flexion strength (40%) also rising. Fascicle length partly reverted after detraining.
tldr: Nine weeks of Nordic hamstring training lengthened hamstring fascicles and increased muscle volume and eccentric strength in a small group of recreationally active adults. The sarcomere-level results are indirect, and the study does not show injury protection.
methods: Longitudinal single-group design with 3 NHE sessions a week for 9 weeks, then 3 weeks of detraining, and no control group. Fascicle length was measured with 3D freehand ultrasound, sarcomere length with second harmonic generation microendoscopy, muscle volume with MRI, and eccentric knee flexor torque with load cells on the ankle straps.
findings: Fascicle length increased significantly over training, with a larger change distally, and serial sarcomere number increased significantly (per the abstract, 25% central and 49% distal). Sarcomere length did not change significantly (p = 0.083). Muscle volume and eccentric strength increased, strength stayed above baseline after detraining, and fascicle length fell by 12% (central) and 16% (distal) during detraining.
limitations: Twelve participants, no control group, and sarcomere measurements were sparse, so the detraining sarcomere data were excluded from the statistics. Serial sarcomere number is a calculated value, and the abstract's statement that sarcomeres were added in series rests on that calculation and on a sarcomere length change that was not significant.
practicalImplications: A 9-week NHE programme lengthened biceps femoris fascicles and increased strength in recreationally active adults, so the exercise is a reasonable option for building hamstring architecture. Fascicle gains partly reversed within 3 weeks of detraining and strength fell (p = 0.006) while staying above baseline, so the stimulus needs to be maintained if the changes are to last.
athleteDev: Shows that 9 weeks of NHE lengthened biceps femoris fascicles and increased muscle volume and eccentric strength in recreationally active adults. It does not test sprint or sport performance.
rtp: Can inform that eccentric hamstring training changes muscle architecture and strength over weeks, but it cannot clear anyone to return to sport or estimate injury risk. It included no injured participants and no return-to-sport outcome.

citation: Van Hooren B, Vanwanseele B, van Rossom S, Teratsias P, Willems P, Drost M, et al. Muscle forces and fascicle behavior during three hamstring exercises. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2022.
abstract: Ten male athletes performed the Nordic hamstring curl, single-leg Roman chair hold and single-leg deadlift while kinematics, ground reaction forces, surface EMG and biceps femoris long-head fascicle length were recorded. The Nordic curl produced the highest peak hamstring forces and the greatest fascicle excursion, and the authors suggest it may be the most effective of the three for increasing fascicle length.
tldr: Across three popular hamstring exercises, the Nordic curl produced the highest peak hamstring forces and the largest fascicle lengthening in a single session. These acute mechanics do not show which exercise produces the best long-term change.
methods: Cross-sectional laboratory study with 10 male athletes performing the three exercises in random order in one session. Full-body 3D motion capture, force plates, surface EMG and B-mode ultrasound of the biceps femoris long head were used, and muscle forces were estimated with inverse dynamics and optimisation in a modified OpenSim model.
findings: Fascicle excursion over the whole exercise was highest in the Nordic curl, significantly greater than in the deadlift. Mean fascicle length was highest in the deadlift, then the Roman chair, then the Nordic curl. Peak forces were higher in the Nordic curl than in both other exercises for the biceps femoris short head, semitendinosus and semimembranosus, and higher than the deadlift for the biceps femoris long head.
limitations: One session, 10 men, and forces estimated by a model rather than measured. Fascicle lengthening velocity during the Nordic curl had poor reliability (ICC 0.42), and the study did not measure training adaptations. The abstract says fascicle lengthening was higher in the Nordic curl than in both other exercises, but Table 1 shows whole-exercise excursion was significantly greater only versus the deadlift (Nordic vs Roman chair 12.6 mm, 95% CI -1.6 to 26.7). The authors' suggestions about which exercise builds which muscle are inferences from acute mechanics rather than results of training.
practicalImplications: The Nordic curl produced significantly more acute fascicle excursion than the deadlift and higher peak forces in three hamstring muscles than both other exercises, while mean eccentric forces were mostly similar between the Nordic curl and Roman chair. This is a useful mechanical comparison when selecting exercises. Training studies are needed before choosing an exercise for a specific adaptation.
athleteDev: Shows how three hamstring exercises differ acutely in fascicle lengthening and hamstring force, which may help exercise selection. It does not measure sprint or sport performance, so the performance link is untested.
rtp: Can inform that the Nordic curl and Roman chair load the hamstrings differently from the deadlift, but cannot show that any exercise reduces re-injury or is safe for return to sport. No injured athletes were included.

citation: Kawama R, Takahashi K, Tozawa H, Obata T, Fuji N, Arai A, et al. Muscle morphological changes and enhanced sprint running performance: a 1-year observational study of well-trained sprinters. Eur J Sport Sci. 2024.
abstract: Measured 100 m and split sprint velocities and MRI muscle volumes in 23 male collegiate athletes before and after one year of their own daily training. Sprint velocity increased, and relative volumes of the tensor fasciae latae, sartorius, biceps femoris long and short heads, semitendinosus and iliacus increased. Among the hypertrophied muscles, only the change in semitendinosus volume correlated with the change in 50-60 m velocity.
tldr: Over one year of ordinary daily training, collegiate athletes' sprint speed rose along with several thigh muscles, and only semitendinosus growth tracked the gain in top-end speed. This is an association in one group without a control, not a tested training prescription.
methods: Longitudinal observational study without intervention. Twenty-three male collegiate athletes had 100 m sprint splits from timing gates and high-speed video, and T1-weighted MRI of 14 trunk and thigh muscles, before and after one year of daily training. Changes were tested with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, and changes in muscle volume were correlated with changes in sprint velocity with Spearman correlations and a false discovery rate correction.
findings: The 100 m time improved from a median of 11.69 s to 11.49 s (p < 0.001), and 50-60 m velocity rose from 9.52 to 9.71 m/s (p = 0.018). Relative volumes increased for the TFL, sartorius, biceps femoris long and short heads, semitendinosus and iliacus, and decreased for the rectus femoris. The change in relative semitendinosus volume correlated with the change in 50-60 m velocity (rho = 0.591, p = 0.018), and no other muscle-speed correlation was significant.
limitations: No control group, two sprint tests only, and wind was higher at the second test, so the conditions were not comparable. The false discovery rate correction is described for the correlations, while the muscle-volume comparisons across 14 muscles are reported without it, and the semitendinosus link did not appear in any spatiotemporal sprint variable, leaving the mechanism unclear.
practicalImplications: Training that combined sprint, jump and resistance work was followed by faster speed and larger size in several thigh muscles, so staff can monitor muscle size and split times together over a season. The semitendinosus link should be treated as a hypothesis to test, not a rule for choosing exercises.
athleteDev: Shows that a year of ordinary sprint, jump and resistance training was followed by faster 100 m and 50-60 m speed and larger thigh muscles in collegiate athletes. The semitendinosus association is a lead for testing, not a prescription.
rtp: Not designed for return to sport: the athletes were healthy by inclusion and no injured athletes were studied. It cannot be used to judge when an athlete is ready to return to sprinting after injury.

citation: Nobari H, Azarian S, Saedmocheshi S, Valdés-Badilla P, García Calvo T. Narrative review: The role of circadian rhythm on sports performance, hormonal regulation, immune system function, and injury prevention in athletes. Heliyon. 2023;9:e19636.
abstract: Review of circadian rhythm (CR) and its links to sports performance, endocrine homeostasis, sex differences and immune function in athletes. The authors searched PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science for English-language peer-reviewed studies to July 2023. They report that performance measures tend to peak in the afternoon, that CR can be shifted by light, exercise and feeding, and that sleep loss and time of day interact to affect performance, a point drawn from cited studies rather than new data.
tldr: A review arguing that time of day affects athletic performance, hormones, immune function and recovery, and that sleep and diet can shift circadian timing. Much of the evidence is mechanistic, animal-based or from non-athletes, so the practical recommendations are suggestions rather than tested protocols.
methods: The authors call this a narrative review, but it describes a database search, so the library codes it as a systematic review by precedent. PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science (core collection) were searched with the terms circadian rhythm, sports performance, hormonal regulation, immune system and injury prevention, limited to English, peer-reviewed studies published up to July 2023 that examined CR in athletes, and the authors say the search followed PRISMA. No counts of records screened, quality appraisal or pooled analysis are reported, and synthesis was narrative.
findings: The review states that many performance measures peak in the afternoon or early evening, with anaerobic performance usually described as peaking in the evening, although one passage places muscle power and anaerobic capacity peaks in the early morning, and it calls evidence for aerobic performance inconsistent. It cites a study of 11 endurance runners during Ramadan in which glucose peaked around 20:00 and 04:00, and a study in which lactate after the Wingate test was higher in the evening than the morning. It reports that lack of sleep seems to affect evening performance more than morning performance, and it cites one study in which a 30-minute afternoon nap after a short night improved running performance. For injury, the text gives inconsistent figures for adolescent athletes sleeping under 8 hours (1.7 times more injuries in one section, OR 2.1 in another), and a Swedish study reporting OR 0.39 for more than 8 hours.
limitations: The authors say the review lacks signaling-pathway and molecular evidence, has limited evidence on training models, and relies on mechanistic and rodent studies for several claims. Study selection, screening and quality appraisal are not described in enough detail to reproduce the search. The Discussion's injury figures conflict (1.7 times vs OR 2.1), the review places muscle power and anaerobic capacity peaks in both the evening and the early morning, and the abstract's claim that the sleep-by-time-of-day interaction was 'established in this study' is unsupported because the paper contains no original data.
practicalImplications: Staff can use the review to prompt timing questions, for example scheduling key high-intensity or power sessions in the afternoon where feasible and checking athletes' sleep before early training or travel. Claims about specific foods, supplements and melatonin doses should not be adopted without checking the primary studies and the athlete's medical and anti-doping status.
athleteDev: The review supports considering time of day and individual chronotype when scheduling sessions, testing and competition. It gives conflicting timing for power and anaerobic peaks, and its performance claims are largely drawn from short-term or mechanistic studies, so they should be tested in the local squad before they change training plans.
rtp: The review does not address return-to-sport testing or rehabilitation timing. Its injury and sleep associations come from observational adolescent data with conflicting figures, so they should not be used to decide when an injured athlete can return to play.

citation: Del Vecchio A. Neuromechanics of the Rate of Force Development. Exercise and Sport Sciences Reviews. 2023;51(1):34-42.
abstract: A review of how neural drive and muscle properties determine the maximal rate of force development (RFD) in healthy individuals. The author hypothesizes that differences between people are mainly due to how fast motor units are recruited, and supports this with previously published motor unit recordings from 20 men, computer simulations, and a reanalysis of spike frequency adaptation in 242 motor neurons.
tldr: Differences between people in how quickly they develop force appear to be driven mainly by how fast motor units are recruited. Early motor unit discharge rate also contributes, while muscle properties play a smaller part in this account.
methods: A review article with new analyses of previously published data. The author reports motor unit discharge in 20 men, a reanalysis of spike frequency adaptation across 242 motor neurons from 20 subjects, computer simulations using data from 25 people, and force data from three muscle groups. No literature search method is described.
findings: The fastest of 20 men reached a peak motor unit discharge rate of about 200 Hz, compared with about 100 Hz in the slowest, and had about twice the recruitment rate. In simulations, varying the recruitment interval had a more than fourfold greater effect on RFD than varying initial discharge rate, and the author describes a faster nervous system as about six times more efficient than a faster muscle. After 4 weeks of high-force training, maximal force increased but RFD and early (first 50 ms) force impulse did not change, which the author links to unchanged recruitment interval and initial discharge rate.
limitations: Most motor unit data come from tibialis anterior, and the author notes that other muscles could differ. The recruitment-rate measure depends on how many motor units are detected, which the author acknowledges. Subject characteristics are given only by reference to earlier studies, and the author notes that muscle properties may dominate after injury or disuse.
practicalImplications: Staff analysing rapid force tests could treat the force-time curve as a continuous signal, as the author recommends, rather than relying only on fixed time windows, which he describes as arbitrary thresholds. The author reports that early and late rapid force are strongly related, so early and late phases should not be read as purely neural or purely muscular.
athleteDev: The modelled 4-week heavy strength training study raised maximal force without changing RFD, so maximal strength gains alone may not improve rapid force in this account. These findings come from healthy adults, mostly one muscle, and simulations, so they should not alone be used to design athlete RFD training.
rtp: The paper does not address return to sport, injury or rehabilitation. It notes that some individuals may have weaker muscle after injury, disuse or other factors, but it provides no return-to-play criteria and should not be used for return-to-play decisions.

citation: Grange S, Reurink G, Nguyen AQ, Riviera-Navarro C, Foschia C, Croisille P, et al. Location of Hamstring Injuries Based on Magnetic Resonance Imaging: A Systematic Review. Sports Health. 2022.
abstract: From 2788 records in five databases, the authors included 34 MRI studies of 2761 acute hamstring injuries. The long head of the biceps femoris was most often affected (70%) and the myotendinous junction was the most common tissue (52%). The abstract describes the proximal, central and distal distribution as homogeneous and notes that MRI reports of hamstring injuries are often poor.
tldr: Across 34 MRI studies of 2761 acute hamstring injuries, the long head of the biceps femoris and the myotendinous junction were most often involved. Reporting of injury location was inconsistent, so the even proximal-central-distal split should not be assumed to apply to every squad.
methods: The review was registered in PROSPERO (CRD42018107580) and searched PubMed, SPORTDiscus, Scopus, Web of Science and the Cochrane Library on March 1, 2020. Included studies reported MRI-based location of acute indirect hamstring injuries performed within 8 days of injury, and case reports and reviews were excluded. Two reviewers screened titles, abstracts and full texts, one reviewer rated risk of bias with a 14-item checklist (75% cut-off), and the data were summarized descriptively.
findings: Of 34 studies, 26 were prospective and 8 retrospective, with 97.4% of injured participants men and 83.3% high-level athletes. The long head of the biceps femoris was involved in 69.8% of 1068 injuries (20 studies) and was the primary lesion in 76.9% of 2438 injuries (30 studies) in the text, and the myotendinous junction was the most common tissue (51.9% of 1286 injuries, 18 studies). Proximal, central and distal shares were 34.0%, 33.4% and 32.6% in 8 studies (344 injuries), while 7 other studies (713 injuries) reporting only proximal versus distal found lesions mostly proximal (62.8%). Sprinting accounted for 55.3% and stretching for 3.0% of 788 injuries with a reported mechanism (9 studies); of the 24 stretching injuries, 14 involved the semimembranosus and 13 its proximal tendon.
limitations: The abstract presents the even proximal-central-distal split as describing 'all lesions', but it rests on 8 studies with 344 injuries; 7 other studies with 713 injuries found mostly proximal lesions, and the body's own conclusion calls the location distribution 'inhomogeneous'. The abstract's claim that the stretching mechanism leads to a longer time out from sport is not supported by any time-loss data in the text, and the primary-lesion share for the long head of the biceps femoris is 76.9% in the text but 79.6% in Table 2. Table 1 notes that some studies may involve identical or overlapping populations that were included separately, and only 2 studies described tissue within each muscle head, English-language studies only were included, and a single reviewer rated risk of bias.
practicalImplications: Recording muscle head, tissue and location on early MRI, as the authors advise, can make a hamstring injury more specific for staff reporting and rehabilitation planning. The most common pattern (long head of the biceps femoris, myotendinous junction) is a useful starting point, but no single injury classification is agreed, so staff should state the classification they use.
athleteDev: Sprinting accounted for 55.3% of acute hamstring injuries where mechanism was reported (9 studies, 788 injuries), which points to high-speed running as the main context in these sports. The review is descriptive and does not test training changes, so it cannot show which sprint or conditioning loads reduce injury.
rtp: The review describes where injuries sit on early MRI, which can help classify a hamstring injury, but it does not report time to return to play or recurrence rates. It should not be used to set return-to-sport timing.

citation: Paton BM, Court N, Giakoumis M, Head P, Kayani B, Kelly S, et al. London International Consensus and Delphi study on hamstring injuries part 1: classification. Br J Sports Med. 2023.
abstract: This modified Delphi study combined a narrative evidence review with expert surveys and a consensus meeting on how to classify hamstring injuries. Experts agreed that MRI is the preferred imaging, that classification should use one agreed terminology, and that systems should separate individual hamstring muscles and include mechanism and functional criteria. The authors note that no current classification predicts time to return to sport or reinjury.
tldr: An international expert panel agreed that MRI is the preferred imaging for hamstring injuries and that one agreed terminology is needed, with the BAMIC system the most used. The authors state that current classifications do not predict return to sport or reinjury, so they should be used to describe injury anatomy rather than set timelines.
methods: This was a modified Delphi study with a narrative evidence review. Round 1 was a digital survey of 46 invited experts (35 responded), followed by a two-day face-to-face consensus meeting with 15 experts and a round 2 survey of 99 respondents (of 112 invited) voting on 18 statements. Statements were accepted at 70% or more agreement, and athletes were not included as participants.
findings: In the round 2 survey, MRI was judged the preferred imaging for diagnosis and classification (89.5%), agreed terminology was supported (91.8%), and one main classification system was supported (84.8%). Imaging was judged vital for classification (70.5%), but the statement that anatomical classification is essential for diagnosis reached only 62.0%, and the statements on surgical criteria (52.1%) and a registry (68.7%) did not reach the 70% threshold. The BAMIC system was the most used (56 of 96 votes, 58%), ahead of Munich and Barcelona.
limitations: Only 15 of 35 first-round respondents attended the meeting, women were few (18 of 99 in the final survey; Table 2 gives 2 of 35 in round 1 although the text says 2 of 39), and experts from Asia, Africa and South America were under-represented; athletes were not included. Several agreement levels in the discussion differ from Table 7, which is reported here: anatomical, radiological parameters 95.1% in text vs 95.9% in Table 7, free vs central tendon 86.1% vs 86.9%, surgical criteria 51.2% vs 52.1%, ultrasound as primary imaging after 48 hours 21.8% vs 25.8%, and BAMIC use 57% vs 58% in Table 3; the text also cites 70.3% and 56.6% for imaging being essential for classification and diagnosis, against 70.5% and 62.0% for the closest Table 7 statements. Respondents chose which survey domains to answer, and most classification systems lack validity or reliability data.
practicalImplications: Staff should record the affected muscle, tissue, location and mechanism of a hamstring injury in one agreed terminology, as the panel recommends. Clinical signs such as bruising, loss of muscle tension, palpable defect or significant weakness should prompt imaging, and the panel's recommended MRI timing is 24 to 48 hours after injury. Functional criteria and patient-reported outcome measures should be used alongside any classification.
athleteDev: The consensus supports consistent recording of injury site, tissue and mechanism so that staff can compare injuries across a squad and season. It does not provide training load thresholds or performance targets.
rtp: The panel recommends that functional criteria and patient-reported outcomes run alongside classification in rehabilitation decisions. The authors state that no current classification predicts time to return to sport or reinjury, so the classification should not be used to set return-to-sport timing.

citation: Plastow R, Kerkhoffs GMMJ, Wood D, Paton BM, Kayani B, Pollock N, et al. London International Consensus and Delphi study on hamstring injuries part 2: operative management. Br J Sports Med. 2023.
abstract: A literature review and modified Delphi process were used to produce consensus statements on operative management of hamstring injuries. Experts agreed on surgical indications for proximal avulsions with gapping or loss of tension, symptomatic displaced bony avulsions and proximal free tendon injuries with functional compromise, and agreed that corticosteroid injections have no role for undisplaced avulsions. Agreement was not reached on surgery reducing recurrence or on endoscopic fixation.
tldr: An international expert panel agreed on several indications for surgery on hamstring injuries, mainly high-grade proximal avulsions with gapping or loss of tension, and agreed that corticosteroid injections should not be used for undisplaced avulsions. Agreement was not reached that surgery reduces reinjury, and the authors describe that benefit as unproven.
methods: This was a modified Delphi study built on a literature search of PubMed, CINAHL, Cochrane and EMBASE up to January 2020, which identified 1626 articles and used 146 after screening, with no quality appraisal tool. Round 1 surveyed 46 invited experts (35 responded), a consensus meeting drafted statements, and a round 2 online survey of 99 respondents (of 112 invited) voted true, false or undecided, with 70% agreement as the threshold. Athletes were not included as survey participants.
findings: Round 2 statements reaching 70% agreement (Table 1) included surgery for gapping at the zone of tendinous injury (87.2%), loss of muscle tension (70.7%), loss of muscle and tendon tension producing a gap in proximal free tendon injuries (83.5%), risk of functional loss or performance deficit with non-operative management (72.2%) and symptomatic displaced bony avulsions of the ischium (72.8%), plus indications depending on anatomy, athlete demands and expected outcome (87.1%) and surgery's capacity to restore anatomy and function (87.1%). Corticosteroid injections for undisplaced avulsions were agreed to have no role (80%). Agreement was not reached that surgery reduces recurrence (48.2% overall, 70% among surgeons), speeds recovery (36.0%), that fixation should be endoscopic (9.5% in Table 1) or that avulsed ischial bone should be resected (31.2% in Table 1).
limitations: Counts conflict within the paper: the text reports 15 of 35 round 1 respondents at the meeting and women as 2 of 39, while Table 2 lists 38 round 1 respondents and 14 meeting members but sex splits summing to 35 and 15; the discussion gives 9.8% and 29.3% agreement for endoscopic fixation and bone resection where Table 1 gives 9.5% and 31.2%, and it says six statements were agreed although Table 1 shows eight above 70%. The evidence base is small uncontrolled case series and expert opinion, the literature search used no quality appraisal, and non-surgeons were allowed to vote on surgical statements. The panel had few women, no athletes and limited representation from Asia, Africa and South America.
practicalImplications: For complete proximal avulsions with gapping or loss of tension, surgery should be considered and weighed against the athlete's sporting demands and expected function, with early repair preferred once surgery is chosen. Corticosteroid injections should not be used for undisplaced avulsions, and endoscopic fixation or a claimed reduction in reinjury should be treated as unproven. Lower-demand patients whose daily function is not significantly affected may consider non-operative care.
athleteDev: The authors state that high-demand athletes cannot accept decrements in strength or performance, so surgery for a high-grade proximal avulsion should be discussed early in those athletes. The consensus gives no training load, sprint or performance targets.
rtp: The authors cite uncontrolled case series reporting return to pre-injury sporting level after surgical repair in high-level athletes, but the panel did not establish return-to-sport timelines or reinjury rates after surgery. The paper should not be used to set return-to-sport timing for operative or non-operative care.

citation: Buhmann R, Trajano GS, Kerr GK, Shield AJ. Lower knee flexion and hip extension rate of torque development in athletes with previous hamstring strain injury. Journal of Sports Sciences. 2021.
abstract: In 10 male athletes with a previous unilateral hamstring strain and 10 without, previously injured limbs had slower rate of torque development (-31%, p = 0.02) and slower biceps femoris sEMG rise (p = 0.003) during intended eccentric knee flexion than control limbs. Both injured and uninjured limbs had slower hip extensor rate of torque development than control limbs. The authors suggest these findings may reflect lower descending input to hamstring motoneurons in previously injured athletes.
tldr: Ten male athletes with a past hamstring strain had slower rate of torque development and biceps femoris EMG rise during intended eccentric knee flexion than controls, and both legs were slower in hip extension. The retrospective design cannot show whether these deficits cause or result from injury.
methods: Retrospective comparison of 20 recreationally active males who played soccer, sprinting, rugby league or rugby union. Ten had a unilateral hamstring strain 3 to 24 months earlier (all biceps femoris long head, self-reported grade 2), and ten had no history. Participants completed two familiarisation sessions, then isokinetic dynamometry with intended isometric, concentric and eccentric knee flexion (order randomised) and isometric hip extension, with surface EMG on the biceps femoris and medial hamstrings. Control limbs were averaged across dominant and non-dominant limbs. Rate of torque development and sEMG rise were calculated over 50 and 100 ms and analysed with two-way ANOVA (limb by time) and Bonferroni post hoc tests.
findings: During intended eccentric knee flexion, rate of torque development was lower in previously injured limbs than in control limbs (-204 Nm/s, -31%, 95% CI -377 to -32, p = 0.02, d = 0.62) and uninjured limbs (-187 Nm/s, -29%, p = 0.03, d = 0.59). Biceps femoris sEMG rise was lower in injured limbs than in controls (-181% per second, 95% CI -308 to -54, p = 0.003, d = 1.10). During isometric hip extension, rate of torque development was lower in injured limbs (-323 Nm/s, -29%, p = 0.01, d = 0.85) and in uninjured limbs (-337 Nm/s, -31%, p = 0.007, d = 0.73) than in controls. Concentric and isometric knee flexion showed no limb difference, and time since injury was unrelated to any outcome.
limitations: Ten men per group, a retrospective design, and self-reported injury grade, so causation cannot be established. The 'eccentric' contractions were largely isometric for the first 100 to 150 ms before the dynamometer lever moved, and the authors note that surface EMG cannot establish voluntary activation. The analysis is described as a two-way ANOVA with no stated handling of each injured participant contributing two limbs. The authors could not separate hamstring from other hip extensors such as adductor magnus or gluteus maximus. Within-participant coefficients of variation for rate of torque development were 8 to 15%.
practicalImplications: Staff could consider measuring rate of torque development in both limbs during rapid knee flexion and hip extension when assessing athletes after hamstring injury, since this study found about 30% differences between previously injured and control limbs. The uninjured limb was also slower than controls in hip extension, so a limb-symmetry comparison could miss this deficit. The study does not test whether training changes these measures or whether they predict re-injury, so they should not be used as a clearance threshold on their own.
athleteDev: Performance Application: Explosive torque production and biceps femoris activation were lower in previously injured limbs, which may matter for sprinting and deceleration. The study did not measure sprint or sport performance, so the link to performance is inferred.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: Deficits in rate of torque development and EMG were still present 3 to 24 months after strain injury, which suggests they may persist after rehabilitation. The design cannot show whether they cause or result from injury, and no return-to-sport outcomes were recorded, so the findings cannot set a clearance criterion.

citation: Ertelt T, Gronwald T. M. biceps femoris - A wolf in sheep’s clothing: The downside of a lower limb injury prevention training. Med Hypotheses. 2017;109:119-125.
abstract: This hypothesis article proposes that lower limb injury prevention training may change biceps femoris activation patterns and insertion-dependent knee mechanics, which could raise hamstring injury susceptibility. The proposal is supported by a single simulated one-legged stopping maneuver in an 80 kg model.
tldr: A simulated stopping maneuver suggests that biceps femoris insertion site and activation level change knee mechanics, which could in theory affect hamstring injury risk after prevention training. The idea has not been tested in athletes.
methods: The authors built a simplified muscle-driven forward dynamics model of an 80 kg male performing a one-legged stopping maneuver after running at 2 m/s, using MATLAB/SimMechanics. Biceps femoris was set to a tibial or fibular insertion configuration and activated at 0%, 50% or 100%, and knee extension or flexion was compared across these conditions.
findings: With biceps femoris activated at 100% and a tibial insertion, the model showed noticeable knee extension during the stop, whereas with a distal fibular insertion it showed noticeable knee flexion over the same time frame. At 0% activation, knee extension was produced by rectus femoris and vastus intermedius. The authors describe the effect of a minor increase in activation as large for the tibial insertion, based on a lever ratio of about 4:1 in one case and 2:1 in the other. No statistical analysis is reported.
limitations: The results come from one simulated subject and a simplified six-muscle model, with no experimental, EMG, MRI or athlete data. The authors acknowledge that the findings must be verified in a controlled experimental setting. The hypothesis that training increases injury risk is not tested, and the paper contains no statistical analysis.
practicalImplications: The paper does not support changing current hamstring prevention programmes. It proposes that insertion geometry and individual activation patterns could be assessed in future studies, and that these might inform individualised programmes. Staff should treat this as a hypothesis for research, not a basis for changing athlete programmes.
athleteDev: This paper cannot guide athlete training prescription. It suggests that individual differences in biceps femoris activation could in theory affect knee mechanics, which is a question to test rather than a basis for changing programmes.
rtp: This paper cannot inform return to sport decisions. It includes no injured athletes and no return-to-play outcomes; the only re-injury figures are background citations from other studies.

citation: Simunic-Briski N, Vrgoc G, Knjaz D, Jankovic S, Dembic Z, Lauc G. MMP3 single-nucleotide polymorphisms are associated with noncontact ACL injuries in competing high-level athletes. J Orthop Res. 2024;42:109-114.
abstract: This case-control genetic association study compared Croatian athletes with noncontact ACL rupture against retired professional athletes without ACL injury. Three MMP3 single-nucleotide polymorphisms were associated with ACL rupture status, with the rs591058 TT, rs650108 GG and rs679620 AA genotypes and the T-G-A haplotype over-represented in the ACL group.
tldr: In a small Croatian case-control study, three MMP3 genotypes and one haplotype were more common in athletes with noncontact ACL rupture than in retired athletes without ACL injury. The association is unreplicated and the reported odds ratios need checking.
methods: A case-control study recruited 95 athletes with MRI and arthroscopically confirmed noncontact ACL rupture (2016-2017) and 92 retired professional athletes with no ACL injury during their careers. Three MMP3 SNPs (rs591058, rs650108, rs679620) were genotyped by pyrosequencing, and allele, genotype and haplotype frequencies were compared using odds ratios, with Hardy-Weinberg and linkage analyses and false discovery rate adjustment. No power analysis was performed.
findings: Genotype frequencies differed for all three SNPs: TT for rs591058 was 29.4% (28/95) in cases and 9.8% (9/92) in controls (p = 0.0012); GG for rs650108 was 54.7% (52/95) vs 33.7% (31/92) (p = 0.0051); and AA for rs679620 was 27.4% (26/95) vs 9.8% (9/92) (p = 0.0030). The T-G-A haplotype was more frequent in cases (97 vs 68 haplotypes, p = 0.0104, OR 1.71, 95% CI 1.13-2.59) and C-A-G was more frequent in controls (OR 0.55). The printed genotype odds ratios (38.541, 23.338 and 34.750) lie outside their printed 95% CIs (1.7024-8.7254, 1.2899-4.2226 and 1.5266-7.9101), and the text does not resolve which value is correct.
limitations: The sample is small, controls were older (39.0 vs 25.8 years) and heavier and were not matched on age or weight, and no replication cohort was used. The text has internal number conflicts: genotype odds ratios lie outside their own confidence intervals, rs591058 allele frequencies print as 48.9% and 52.1% (summing to 101%), and haplotype counts in Table 3 sum to 182 controls and 192 cases rather than 184 and 190. The abstract describes professional athletes while the methods describe recreationally competing or professional athletes, and injury mechanism was self-reported.
practicalImplications: The study does not support using MMP3 genotype to screen, select or rank athletes for ACL risk, because no screening tool was tested and the association is unreplicated. Current practice should not change on the basis of this paper. The authors' suggestion of future screening is a research question.
athleteDev: This study does not inform athlete training or performance programming. Staff should not use these genotypes to classify athletes' ACL risk or to guide training decisions.
rtp: This study compares athletes with ACL rupture to controls and reports no return-to-sport outcomes, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions.

citation: Hayward G, Gaborini L, Robinson N, Stuart M, Mottram D. Mapping of the Pharmacological Effect of Prohibited Substances and Methods to Athletic Physiological Characteristics. Drug Testing and Analysis. 2025.
abstract: The authors built a physio-pharmacological scoring framework that maps the expected performance effects of WADA Prohibited List categories onto the physiological demands of 160 Olympic disciplines. They propose that the framework can inform anti-doping risk assessment and test distribution planning.
tldr: Expert ratings estimate which prohibited substances and methods could most help each Olympic discipline, based on its physiological demands. The authors propose using these estimates to plan anti-doping testing, though the ratings are theoretical and expert agreement was low.
methods: Eight experts rated 31 pharmacological categories on six athletic demands using a 5-point scale, and a gene and cell doping category was excluded because of disagreement. Ratings were aggregated by majority vote, mapped to each discipline's demands with a calibrated scoring function and bilinear interpolation, and reliability was assessed with Krippendorff's alpha.
findings: Krippendorff's alpha was 0.55 (95% CI 0.49 to 0.61), which the authors describe as low agreement. The mapping gives strong potential advantages to anabolic agents for strength and power disciplines and to erythropoietin and blood manipulation for aerobic endurance, while narcotics and cannabinoids show negative effects. Diuretics show limited direct performance effects, which the authors attribute to their masking role.
limitations: The scores are not compared with International Federation testing or sample data, so the authors cannot show that high-scoring substances are the ones detected. The authors also note that non-performance motives for doping are outside the scope of the study.
practicalImplications: Anti-doping test planning could weight testing toward substances with high estimated benefit for a discipline's physiological demands, as the authors propose. Staff should treat the scores as a hypothesis for risk planning, not as evidence of use by any athlete.
athleteDev: The paper links physiological demands to theoretical performance effects by discipline, which helps explain anti-doping risk. It gives no training or performance guidance, and it should not be used to judge an athlete's performance.
rtp: The paper does not address rehabilitation or return to sport. It covers performance effects only, and it does not assess health harms of the listed substances.

citation: Delahunt E, Farrell G, Boylan A, Kerin F, Tierney P, Hogan H, et al. Mechanisms of acute ankle syndesmosis ligament injuries in professional male rugby union players: a systematic visual video analysis. Br J Sports Med. 2020.
abstract: The authors used retrospective video analysis to describe how acute ankle syndesmosis ligament injuries occurred in male professional rugby union players at one club. Three physiotherapists independently assessed the videos, reached a consensus, and described each injury mechanism.
tldr: Most of the 13 included syndesmosis injuries happened while players were being tackled or were tackling. The study describes a common limb position at injury, but it is small and comes from one club.
methods: Retrospective review of 30 time-loss syndesmosis injuries from one professional club's surveillance database, with video available for 27 and the mechanism visible in 13. Three physiotherapists assessed the videos independently, reached consensus, and wrote a qualitative description of each mechanism.
findings: Six injuries (46%) were direct contact and seven (54%) indirect contact injuries, with seven sustained while being tackled and six while tackling. The anterior inferior tibiofibular ligament was injured in all 13 cases, and the most common limb position was hip and knee flexion, knee valgus, ankle dorsiflexion, pronation and external rotation of the foot. The authors judged tackle mechanics suboptimal in all six tackling injuries, and ten cases were managed surgically with a mean time to unrestricted training of 61 days (SD 25).
limitations: Only 13 injuries from one club were analysed, because the injury event was not visible in 14 of the 27 videos. The moment of injury was estimated by subjective consensus, and video quality, resolution and camera angle limited the analysis.
