The paper's counts are internally inconsistent: it reports 6 direct and 7 indirect contact injuries, but the case descriptions classify 5 as direct and 8 as indirect (case #9 is labelled both), and it reports 8 right and 7 left ankles for 13 injuries while Tables 1 and 2 list 8 right and 5 left.
practicalImplications: Clinicians assessing a rugby player with an ankle injury should consider a syndesmosis injury when the history includes external rotation of the foot, forced pronation or forced dorsiflexion. Coaches can use the tackle examples to review footwork and tackle technique, but the study cannot show how often each mechanism causes injury.
athleteDev: Use the described tackling situations to review tackle technique and footwork with professional players, recognising that the evidence is descriptive and comes from a small sample.
rtp: The study reports a mean time to unrestricted training of 61 days for these 13 cases, but it sets no return-to-play criteria and tests no readiness measures, so it should not be used to decide when a player can return to play.

citation: Huygaerts S, Cos F, Cohen DD, Calleja-González J, Guitart M, Blazevich AJ, et al. Mechanisms of hamstring strain injury: interactions between fatigue, muscle activation and function. Sports. 2020;8:65.
abstract: The authors review evidence on sprint-type hamstring strain injury mechanisms, focusing on the late swing and early stance phases of running. They also discuss how neuromuscular fatigue may change hamstring activation, coordination and function, and how this could relate to injury risk.
tldr: Hamstring injury mechanisms during sprinting are still unclear, and most mechanical evidence comes from non-fatigued athletes. Fatigue may alter muscle coordination and running mechanics in ways that could raise strain risk, but this link has not been tested in injury data.
methods: Narrative critical review with no search method reported. The authors summarise biomechanical modelling, EMG and fatigue studies, and tabulate 13 modelling or EMG studies that measured non-fatigued participants, plus two case reports.
findings: The authors conclude that the late swing and early stance phases are the points at which sprint-type injury is most likely, while stating that the evidence on which phase carries the greatest risk is inconclusive. They propose fatigue-related changes that could raise strain risk, including altered hamstring coordination, earlier fatigue of biceps femoris and rectus femoris than of other lower limb muscles during high-speed running, reduced horizontal force after repeated sprints, increased anterior pelvic tilt, and reduced lower limb stiffness with a 'Groucho' running pattern. These links are drawn from separate studies and have not been tested as injury predictors.
limitations: No search or appraisal method is described, and the review does not grade the strength of the evidence it cites. Most mechanical evidence comes from simulation models and small samples of non-fatigued athletes, and the authors note that these models omit tissue complexity and fatigue effects.
practicalImplications: Staff should not treat the late swing and early stance phases as established injury windows, because the authors describe the evidence as inconclusive. Fatigue monitoring during high-speed running work can be framed as a hypothesis to test, since the review gives no thresholds or validated tests for practice. Hamstring and synergist strength-endurance work is presented as an area for further study rather than a proven intervention.
athleteDev: Use the review to frame questions about how fatigue changes sprint mechanics and hamstring coordination, not as a basis for fatigue thresholds or sprint prescriptions. Check any speed or fatigue monitoring against each player's own baseline.
rtp: The review addresses mechanisms of hamstring strain during sprinting. It does not evaluate rehabilitation, return-to-sport testing or re-injury criteria, so it should not be used to set return-to-running or return-to-play decisions.

citation: Schmidt JD, Weber Rawlins ML, Lynall RC, D'Lauro C, Clugston JR, McAllister TW, et al. Medical disqualification following concussion in collegiate student-athletes: findings from the CARE Consortium. Sports Med. 2020.
abstract: The authors compared premorbid and postmorbid factors between NCAA student-athletes who were and were not medically disqualified after concussion, using CARE Consortium data. Disqualification was uncommon and was associated with prior concussions, headaches, a more immediate initial presentation and a longer, more complicated recovery.
tldr: Medical disqualification after concussion was uncommon (2.9%) in this collegiate sample. Disqualified athletes more often had prior concussions, recent headaches, immediate removal from play and longer, more complicated recoveries, but the study is exploratory and cannot set a disqualification rule.
methods: Prospectively collected CARE Consortium data from 1,832 NCAA varsity student-athletes diagnosed with concussion across 29 sites, using each athlete's most recent concussion. Baseline and serial symptom, cognitive and balance assessments, and clinician case report forms were compared between 53 medically disqualified and 1,779 non-disqualified athletes with chi-square, Fisher's exact, ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis tests, and unadjusted odds ratios were calculated for factors that were significant or trending.
findings: Two prior concussions (OR 3.2) and three or more (OR 7.4) were associated with disqualification, as were one or more headaches in the past three months (OR 1.8) and immediate removal from play (OR 2.4), while delayed symptom onset was linked to lower odds (OR 0.43). Clinician-reported prolonged recovery due to mental health alterations (OR 5.3), motivation or malingering (OR 7.5) or other injuries (OR 3.7) was also associated, as were alcohol (OR 2.6), tobacco (OR 3.3) and marijuana (OR 5.4) use since injury, and disqualified athletes took longer to become asymptomatic (23.5 vs 10.6 days, p < 0.001). Sex, sport, division, loss of consciousness and amnesia did not differ, and some athletes were disqualified with few prior concussions while others with three or more were not.
limitations: The authors describe the study as exploratory. Only 53 athletes were disqualified, the odds ratios are unadjusted with wide confidence intervals, and several recovery factors reflect the clinician's impression. Disqualification included season-only decisions, formal disqualification may miss athletes whose eligibility ended, and site practices were not recorded. The results text assigns the substance-use odds ratios to different substances than the abstract (the abstract matches Table 5 counts), and the discussion says 32.1% of disqualified athletes had one prior concussion while Table 3 gives 32.1% with none.
practicalImplications: Staff managing collegiate concussion should record prior concussion and recent headache history, because these were the only premorbid factors that differed. A prolonged recovery with mental health alterations, substance use or apparent motivation problems should prompt closer clinical management, and the authors suggest exploring treatments such as cognitive behavioural therapy before a final disqualification decision. The authors state that no set number of concussions should force disqualification and that immediate removal should not be treated as predictive, so these factors should inform rather than determine the decision.
athleteDev: This study describes clinical disqualification decisions and has little direct performance application. It can support conversations with athletes about why concussion history and recovery course feature in eligibility decisions, without implying a fixed concussion limit.
rtp: The study describes who was medically disqualified after concussion, not who can safely return. It sets no return criteria and should not be used to decide whether an individual athlete is cleared or disqualified after concussion.

citation: Carey DL, Crossley KM, Whiteley R, Mosler A, Ong KL, Crow J, et al. Modeling training loads and injuries: the dangers of discretization. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2018;50(11):2267-2276.
abstract: This simulation study compared discrete and continuous models of the relationship between workload (ACWR) and injury risk, using workload data from an Australian football club and a soccer league. Injuries were simulated from three predefined risk profiles. Discrete models produced more false discoveries (16% to 21%) than continuous models (3% to 7%), and AUC selected a discrete model in more than 30% of simulations, while Brier and logarithmic scores selected discrete models in 6% or fewer.
tldr: Splitting a continuous training load variable such as ACWR into categories gave poorer injury risk models than spline or fractional polynomial methods in simulated data. Calibration measures such as the Brier score are more informative than AUC when comparing injury risk models.
methods: Simulated 100 studies per condition at 1000 and 5000 observations, with ACWR values resampled from pooled Australian football and soccer data and injuries generated from U-shaped, flat or S-shaped risk profiles. Models were compared using RMSE against the true risk, false discovery and false rejection rates, and AUC, Brier and logarithmic scores estimated by 10-fold cross-validation. A longitudinal extension simulated correlated repeated observations (50 observations from 20 participants, or 100 from 50) and compared naive logistic regression with GEE.
findings: Discrete models had higher RMSE than restricted cubic splines and fractional polynomials under the U-shaped and S-shaped profiles, and they fitted the true curve poorly. With a flat profile and 5000 observations, discrete models produced 16 to 21 false discoveries per 100 studies, against 7 for splines and 3 for fractional polynomials; false rejections at 1000 observations were high for quantile and cut-point models (59 and 57 of 100) but low for the z-score model (5 of 100). AUC selected a discrete model in 38 of 100 studies (U-shaped) and 31 of 100 (S-shaped), whereas Brier and logarithmic scores selected discrete models in 6 of 100 or fewer, and naive logistic regression missed the weakened longitudinal signal more often than GEE (47 vs 18 of 100).
limitations: All injuries were simulated, and only a single covariate was modelled, so the multivariable and real-world behaviour of these methods was not tested. The risk profiles were assumed, and the U-shape was chosen to match the hypothesised relationship rather than estimated from injury data. The ACWR was calculated with one method (1-week acute, 4-week chronic, overlapping windows), and other calculation methods would change the value distribution.
practicalImplications: When modelling training load against injury, avoid splitting continuous load into categories, and consider spline or fractional polynomial models. Judge candidate injury risk models with calibration measures such as the Brier or logarithmic score, not AUC alone. Where several observations come from the same athletes, account for the correlation (for example with GEE), since assuming independence inflated false rejections in the simulations.
athleteDev: The paper does not test any training programme or performance outcome. Its use for staff is in how workload-injury models are built: keep load as a continuous variable rather than binning it, and do not treat a model's AUC as proof that one model is better for prescribing training.
rtp: Not applicable to return-to-sport decisions. The study used simulated injuries on squad training-load data and cannot set ACWR thresholds or return-to-play load limits for rehabilitating athletes.

citation: Grassi A, Macchiarola L, Lucidi GA, Stefanelli F, Neri M, Silvestri A, et al. More than a 2-fold risk of contralateral anterior cruciate ligament injuries compared with ipsilateral graft failure 10 years after primary reconstruction. Am J Sports Med. 2020;48(2):310-317.
abstract: In 244 consecutive patients followed for a mean of 10 years after hamstring ACL reconstruction, contralateral ACL reconstruction was more common than ipsilateral revision (7.8% vs 3.4%). Patients younger than 18 years with a preoperative Tegner level of 7 or higher had the lowest survival (61.1% at 10 years for either knee).
tldr: After hamstring ACL reconstruction, contralateral ACL reconstruction was more common than revision of the operated knee, with a significant difference from about year 6 onward. Young patients with a high preoperative activity level had the highest risk.
methods: Retrospective analysis of a prospectively collected database from one centre, with all patients receiving the same single-bundle over-the-top reconstruction with lateral plasty using hamstring tendons. Follow-up was at a minimum of 10 years, with medical chart review and patient interview to identify further ACL surgery. Survival curves, log-rank tests, hazard ratios and stepwise logistic regression were used to test age, sex, BMI, smoking, preoperative Tegner level and timing of reconstruction.
findings: Ipsilateral revision occurred in 8 patients (3.4%) and contralateral reconstruction in 19 (7.8%), and the 10-year survival free of a second ACL rupture was 89.3%. Patients younger than 18 (OR 4.0 for contralateral reconstruction) and those with preoperative Tegner level 7 or higher (OR 16.2) had higher risk, and the combination had 61.1% survival at 10 years. From year 6 onward, contralateral reconstruction was more likely than ipsilateral revision (hazard ratio 3.6 at 6 years, 95% CI 1.4 to 9.6, and 2.4 at 10 years, 95% CI 1.1 to 5.3).
limitations: This was a retrospective single-centre series of one graft technique, and 15.1% of eligible patients were lost to follow-up. Injuries were identified by chart review and interview without objective examination, so subclinical failures may have been missed. Subgroup estimates are imprecise (for example the OR for Tegner level 7 or higher has a 95% CI of 2.1 to 124.0), and no return-to-sport data were collected.
practicalImplications: Counsel patients that the uninjured knee may be at higher risk of ACL injury than the reconstructed knee in the years after surgery. Rehabilitation should address both knees, with particular attention to patients younger than 18 and those with high preoperative activity, as the authors recommend. The 40% figure for second injury in young, high-activity patients should be treated as a hypothesis to test, not a settled estimate.
athleteDev: The paper has no performance outcomes. Its relevance for staff is injury prevention: the authors argue that the uninjured knee needs as much attention as the operated one in young athletes who take part in demanding sport.
rtp: Relevant to return to sport because it argues for rehabilitating both knees, but the study did not record return to sport or any return-to-play test. It cannot be used to set clearance criteria or to judge readiness for sport.

citation: Murray IR, Makaram NS, Geeslin AG, Chahla J, Moatshe G, Crossley K, et al. Multiligament knee injury (MLKI): an expert consensus statement on nomenclature, diagnosis, treatment and rehabilitation. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2024.
abstract: An international Delphi consensus of 39 experts agreed 50 statements on the nomenclature, diagnosis, treatment and rehabilitation of multiligament knee injury. The panel recommended a clear definition, a need for an updated classification, and individual decisions on surgery, with a multicentre registry and core outcome set as research priorities.
tldr: An international expert panel reached agreement on 50 statements covering the definition, classification, imaging and treatment of multiligament knee injuries. It gives a clear definition and recommends MRI for suspected cases, but its timing and rehabilitation advice rests largely on expert opinion.
methods: Modified Delphi consensus following British Journal of Sports Medicine guidelines and the ACCORD reporting checklist. Thirty-nine experts from 14 countries (31 men, 8 women), selected partly by publication count, completed three anonymous online rounds rating statements on a 5-point Likert scale; consensus required more than 75% agreement and fewer than 10% disagreement in the final round.
findings: Experts agreed a definition of multiligament knee injury as a high-grade partial or complete tear of at least two major knee ligaments verified by examination or stress radiography (agreement 97.4%), and that most of these injuries are not caused by knee dislocation (agreement 79.5%). They recommended MRI for all suspected cases where available and a low threshold for CT angiography in high-energy injuries, and agreed single-stage surgery should be used whenever possible (agreement 80.6%) with decisions made on an individual basis. Early surgery was defined as within 21 days (agreement 76.3%), and a 4 to 6 week period of restricted weight-bearing was considered acceptable on low-order evidence (agreement 92.1%).
limitations: The panel was weighted toward men, with 25 of 39 from North America and 28 orthopaedic surgeons, and expertise was judged by publication count, so the consensus may reflect that group; ethnicity and race were not collected. Many recommendations rest on expert opinion or low-order evidence, and rehabilitation timelines and content were not addressed. The abstract gives levels of agreement for operative management in young patients (100%) and single-stage surgery (92.3%) that differ from the agreement values in the tables (89.7% and 80.6%).
practicalImplications: Medical and rehabilitation staff can adopt the consensus definition and classification principles when recording these injuries, and should avoid equating knee dislocation with multiligament injury unless a dislocation is confirmed. Surgical and staging decisions should be individual, based on injury pattern, associated injuries and patient factors, rather than on a fixed timeline.
athleteDev: The statement does not address training load, performance or conditioning, so performance staff should use it only to inform communication with the medical team after a knee injury.
rtp: The statement covers timing of surgery, single or staged surgery, and early range-of-motion work that bear on recovery time, but it sets no return-to-sport criteria, testing thresholds or timelines. Its weight-bearing period rests on low-order evidence and it does not address rehabilitation timelines, so return-to-play decisions still depend on the treating team's judgment.

citation: Nuñez FJ, Ritzmann R, Hernandez-Abad F, Martinez JC, Suarez-Arrones L. Muscle architecture, morphology, and mechanical and functional properties of biceps femoris long head in professional soccer players with a prior healed injured hamstring. J Clin Med. 2022;11:7222.
abstract: Compared fascicle length, pennation angle, muscle thickness, stiffness and eccentric hamstring strength in 20 elite soccer players, 10 with a healed hamstring injury and 10 without. The injured limb had shorter biceps femoris long-head fascicles and higher proximal stiffness than the uninjured players' limbs. No significant differences were found between the injured and uninjured limbs of injured players, or in eccentric strength.
tldr: In elite soccer players, a healed hamstring injury was associated with shorter biceps femoris long-head fascicles and stiffer proximal muscle, but the two limbs of injured players did not differ. Strength was not reduced, so this snapshot cannot show which players will re-injure.
methods: Cross-sectional comparison of players from two squads, one in Switzerland and one in Italy. Fascicle length and pennation angle were measured with extended field-of-view B-mode ultrasound, stiffness with MyotonPRO, and eccentric strength by Nordic hamstring exercise on a NordBord and, in injured players only, by isokinetic dynamometry at 30 and 120 deg/s. Groups were compared with one-way ANOVA and Bonferroni post hoc tests.
findings: The injured limb had a shorter BFlh fascicle (8.18 cm vs 9.41 and 9.46 cm in uninjured players' limbs; overall p = 0.039) and higher proximal stiffness (308 vs 269 and 260 N/m; overall p = 0.038). Injured and uninjured limbs of injured players did not differ on fascicle length, pennation angle, muscle thickness, stiffness or eccentric strength. NHE strength did not differ significantly between the injured limbs and the limbs of uninjured players. Isokinetic strength was measured only in injured players, so no between-group isokinetic comparison exists.
limitations: The abstract describes muscle thickness as substantially lower in injured players, but Table 1 marks no significant difference for thickness (2.23 and 2.19 cm vs 2.42 and 2.39 cm). The Discussion says both legs of injured players had shorter fascicles and higher proximal stiffness, but only the injured-limb comparison is reported with a test. Sex is not reported, the sample is 20 players, the choice of players from the two squads is not explained, and only injured players completed the isokinetic test.
practicalImplications: The authors suggest that individual fascicle length and stiffness may be worth considering when designing prevention for players with a past hamstring injury. These data do not show that these measures predict re-injury, and no fascicle length threshold can be set from this study.
athleteDev: Does not measure performance. Eccentric hamstring strength did not differ between groups, so the study gives no performance-based guidance.
rtp: Can inform that players with a healed hamstring injury may show different muscle architecture and stiffness, but not that they are ready to return or at greater risk. It cannot be used as a return-to-play test, because the injured and uninjured limbs of injured players did not differ in fascicle length or strength.

citation: McPherson AL, Nagai T, Webster KE, Hewett TE. Musculoskeletal injury risk after sport-related concussion: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Am J Sports Med. 2018.
abstract: Ten studies of athletes with sport-related concussion and controls were reviewed, and eight were pooled with random-effects models. Athletes with concussion had 2.11 times the odds of a musculoskeletal injury after return to sport (95% CI 1.46 to 3.06) and a pooled incidence rate ratio of 1.67 (95% CI 1.42 to 1.96). The raised odds were seen in both male and female athletes.
tldr: Athletes who had a concussion had about double the odds of a musculoskeletal injury after return to sport in pooled observational studies. The association held for both sexes, but the studies are small and mixed in design, and they cannot show that concussion causes the injuries.
methods: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis following PRISMA. PubMed and Google Scholar were searched from January 2000 to November 2017 by two reviewers, with reference-list checks. Study quality was rated with the NIH tool for cohort and cross-sectional studies (6 to 11 of 14 items), and odds ratios and incidence rate ratios were pooled with the I2 index for heterogeneity.
findings: Pooled odds ratio 2.11 (95% CI 1.46 to 3.06; I2 = 59%; 661 concussed and 1757 control athletes). Pooled incidence rate ratio 1.67 (95% CI 1.42 to 1.96; I2 = 0%). Sex-stratified odds ratios were 2.23 for female athletes (95% CI 1.40 to 3.57) and 2.06 for male athletes (95% CI 1.26 to 3.37), with no significant difference between the sexes (OR 1.53, 95% CI 0.86 to 2.70; p = 0.15).
limitations: Included studies were mostly retrospective or prospective cohorts (level 3 evidence) with small samples, and control groups varied: matched non-concussed athletes in five studies, athletes with another injury in three, and none in one. Some studies reported athlete exposures poorly and had short follow-up, and two survey studies that could not establish the order of concussion and injury were excluded.
practicalImplications: Staff managing return to sport after concussion should know that pooled odds of musculoskeletal injury after return were about twice those of controls in both male and female athletes, with no significant difference between the sexes. The authors recommend adding neuromuscular risk screening to return-to-sport protocols, but this review does not test whether such screening reduces injuries.
athleteDev: Shows higher musculoskeletal injury rates after return from concussion, which bears on how closely staff monitor athletes once they are back in training. It does not measure performance outcomes.
rtp: Can inform that athletes with a recent concussion had higher musculoskeletal injury rates after return, which is relevant to return-to-sport monitoring. It cannot set a return-to-play time, and it does not show that neuromuscular screening prevents injury.

citation: Juginović A, Kekić A, Aranza I, Biloš V, Armanda M. Next-Generation Approaches in Sports Medicine: The Role of Genetics, Omics, and Digital Health in Optimizing Athlete Performance and Longevity: A Narrative Review. Life. 2025;15:1023.
abstract: Review of genetics, pharmacogenomics, digital health and multi-omics for precision sports medicine. Literature was searched in MEDLINE, EMBASE, Web of Science and Cochrane Library for January 2018 to April 2024. The authors summarize gene variants linked to endurance, power, strength and injury, pharmacogenomic guidance for common sports medications, wearable and telemedicine tools, and multi-omics approaches, and propose a clinical framework.
tldr: A review that proposes a staged framework for precision sports medicine: wearable monitoring through the season, genetic testing early in a career, pharmacogenomic testing before medication, and multi-omics profiling in the off-season. Most of the evidence is early-stage and qualitative, so the framework should be treated as a proposal rather than a validated protocol.
methods: The authors call this a narrative review, but it describes a database search, so the library codes it as a systematic review by precedent. The Methods list MEDLINE (PubMed), EMBASE and Web of Science for January 2018 to April 2024 (the abstract also names Cochrane Library), using terms such as precision medicine, sports medicine, genomics and multi-omics, with forward and backward citation tracking. The synthesis was qualitative, with no screening counts or quality appraisal, and organized into four domains: genomics, pharmacogenomics, digital health and multi-omics.
findings: The review links gene variants such as ACTN3, AMPD1, PPARGC1A and COL5A1 with performance or injury traits in the cited studies, and summarizes CPIC and DPWG dosing guidance for drugs metabolized by CYP2C9, CYP2D6 and CYP2C19. It reports that an acute-to-chronic workload ratio above 1.7 was associated with almost fivefold higher odds of contact injury in the cited work, and cites a study of eight NCAA Division I teams reporting a 60% injury decrease. Its multi-omics sections describe early associations rather than validated tools.
limitations: The authors acknowledge possible bias in article selection and interpretation, and there is no quality appraisal or count of studies screened and included. The 60% injury-reduction claim is cited to a WHOOP press release (ref 102), not a peer-reviewed study. The authors also state that many genetic association studies are small and limited to specific populations, and the abstract names Cochrane Library while the Methods list only MEDLINE, EMBASE and Web of Science.
practicalImplications: Use the framework as a discussion guide rather than a protocol. Before ordering genetic or pharmacogenomic tests for an athlete, confirm the specific gene-drug guideline and the governance and consent process for the test. Wearable load data can flag changes in training load, but the injury-reduction figure cited here comes from a commercial source and should not be assumed for a local program.
athleteDev: The paper presents genetic profiling and multi-omics as early-stage ways to individualize training and nutrition, and treats wearable load metrics such as the acute-to-chronic workload ratio as useful for managing load. The genetic performance associations it cites are small, population-specific and not validated for selecting or programming individual athletes.
rtp: The review suggests pharmacogenomic testing could make analgesic and other medication choices during recovery safer, and describes monitoring of recovery status. It gives no return-to-sport criteria or clearance tests, and its genetic injury-risk markers should not be used to decide return to play.

citation: Chia L, De Oliveira Silva D, Whalan M, McKay MJ, Sullivan J, Fuller CW, et al. Non-contact Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury Epidemiology in Team-Ball Sports: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis by Sex, Age, Sport, Participation Level, and Exposure Type. Sports Med. 2022.
abstract: Systematic review with meta-analysis of 45 cohort studies of non-contact ACL injuries in team ball-sports, searched in six databases to July 2021. Non-contact injuries made up 55% of all ACL injuries (95% CI 48-62), and the overall incidence was 0.07 per 1000 player-hours (95% CI 0.05-0.10). Incidence was 0.14 per 1000 player-hours in females and 0.05 in males, and 0.48 during competition versus 0.04 during training, with high heterogeneity across studies.
tldr: Across team ball-sports, non-contact ACL injuries account for a little over half of all ACL injuries, and most occur in competition rather than training. Female athletes had a significantly higher incidence per player-hour than males, but no significance test is reported for the sex difference in the proportion of non-contact injuries.
methods: Systematic review and meta-analysis following PRISMA 2020 and registered in PROSPERO (CRD42020179475). Six databases (MEDLINE, EMBASE, Web of Science, CINAHL, Scopus, SPORTDiscus) were searched from inception to July 2021, and cohort studies reporting ACL injuries by mechanism were included. Pooled proportions and incidences used random-effects models, with meta-regression for sex, age group, sport, participation level and exposure type.
findings: Forty-five studies reported 2,748 non-contact ACL injuries. The pooled proportion of non-contact to total ACL injuries was 55% (95% CI 48-62, I2 = 82%), with 63% in females and 50% in males, a difference the authors did not report as significant. Incidence per 1000 player-hours was 0.14 in females and 0.05 in males, a significant difference by meta-regression, and 0.48 in competition versus 0.04 in training, also significant. Incidence per 1000 player-hours was 0.06 in elite, 0.10 in intermediate and 0.13 in amateur athletes.
limitations: Study quality was assessed with a modified six-item Newcastle-Ottawa scale, and authors of 22 of 46 included studies had to be contacted for non-contact data (the paper reports 45 included studies elsewhere). Heterogeneity was high, and many included studies defined non-contact mechanisms loosely, possibly including indirect contact. The abstract and conclusion state the proportion was higher in females without a reported significance test, and the participation-level results conflict by unit (amateur is higher per player-hour, intermediate higher per player-exposure). The amateur-level CI in Section 3.4.4 reads 45-767, which appears to be a typographical error.
practicalImplications: Use the finding that most non-contact ACL injuries in these sports occur in competition as a prompt to review competition-specific risk factors, not as proof that training is safe. The sex difference in incidence per player-hour is a reason to examine female athletes' exposure and mechanisms, but staff should not assume the proportion of non-contact injuries differs by sex.
athleteDev: For performance staff, the review supports reporting injury data by mechanism, sex and exposure type so that ACL risk-reduction work targets the right settings. The participation-level and sport-level findings are inconclusive, so they should not be used to set training priorities for a specific squad.
rtp: The review does not address return to sport, rehabilitation or clearance decisions after ACL injury. Its incidence and proportion figures describe injury occurrence, so they should not be used to judge an individual athlete's readiness or re-injury risk.

citation: Wilke J, Groneberg D. Neurocognitive function and musculoskeletal injury risk in sports: a systematic review. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2021.
abstract: A systematic review of the relationship between cognitive function and musculoskeletal injury in athletes. Nine cohort and case-control studies were included, most in college athletes in open-skill sports. Seven of nine studies suggested that lower-order cognitive function (visuomotor reaction time) was associated with injury, and none examined executive function.
tldr: Nine studies suggest slower visuomotor reaction time may be linked to sport injury, mostly in college open-skill athletes. The evidence is limited and the authors call for prospective studies, including executive function, before any recommendations.
methods: Systematic review following PRISMA, with searches of PubMed, Web of Science and Google Scholar in March 2021 and reference-list checks. Two reviewers screened and rated studies with a modified Downs and Black checklist, giving a mean of 12 of 17 points.
findings: Of nine eligible studies (seven cohort, two case-control), seven reported an association between lower-order cognition and injury, mainly slower reaction time. Examples include Dvorak et al. (injured soccer players with higher baseline reaction time than uninjured players, 128 ms and 134 ms vs 108 ms) and Wilkerson et al. (low performers with odds ratio 2.94 for lower extremity sprain or strain). Two studies (Faltus et al. in adolescent skiers and snowboarders, and Ha et al. in collegiate athletes) found no association.
limitations: The authors note that the studies used different populations, outcomes and injury definitions, and most measured only lower-order functions. The text gives a reaction-time cut-off of 550 ms for one study, while the table gives 545 ms. Several included studies were retrospective, and one (Taimela et al.) gave no effect size.
practicalImplications: The authors suggest exercise professionals may consider developing screening measures addressing neurocognitive function, such as reaction time, as part of a multifactorial injury risk assessment. They state that several gaps must be addressed before definitive recommendations can be made, and that executive function needs further research.
athleteDev: Performance staff could consider reaction time as one measure in a broader assessment, but the review does not show that reaction time training improves performance. The authors note that intervention studies improved reaction time, and that it is unclear whether these gains translate into fewer injuries.
rtp: The review does not address return to sport. Its findings relate to injury risk in healthy athletes, not to decisions after an injury, so it should not be used for return-to-play clearance.

citation: Howell DR, Lynall RC, Buckley TA, Herman DC. Neuromuscular Control Deficits and the Risk of Subsequent Injury after a Concussion: A Scoping Review. Sports Medicine. 2018.
abstract: A scoping review of 32 studies in two linked areas: musculoskeletal injury risk after concussion (10 studies) and dual-task gait deficits after concussion (22 studies). The authors conclude that athletes appear more likely to sustain a musculoskeletal injury after concussion, and that dual-task neuromuscular deficits may persist after symptoms and clinical tests have recovered. The mechanism linking these findings is not yet tested.
tldr: Athletes appear more likely to be injured after a concussion, and walking while performing a cognitive task can reveal deficits after symptoms and standard tests have recovered. The authors propose these deficits as one possible explanation, but it has not been tested directly.
methods: Scoping review following PRISMA, with two searches of PubMed, Web of Science and Academic Search Premier from database inception to 9 December 2016, and reference-list checks. Two authors screened records independently and resolved discrepancies by consensus. No data quality assessment, effect size calculation or meta-analysis was performed.
findings: Most of the 10 injury-risk studies reported a higher musculoskeletal injury risk after concussion, mainly for lower extremity injuries. For example, Brooks et al. reported odds of 2.48 and Herman et al. reported odds of 3.39 for lower extremity injury within 90 days in college athletes. The 22 dual-task gait studies generally reported altered gait under dual-task conditions for up to about two months after concussion, although some found no differences, for example in children.
limitations: Results were not uniform: Nyberg et al. found no increased risk in professional ice hockey players compared with players with knee injuries, and some studies used injured comparison groups that could mask an effect. Injury definitions, follow-up periods and exposure differed across studies. The authors note that most dual-task gait studies came from a single laboratory, and that only one injury-risk study reported specifically on a female population (a sub-analysis of 25 cases).
practicalImplications: The authors suggest that combined motor and cognitive tests may better reflect sport demands, and that including them in post-concussion examinations may help identify athletes at higher risk. Clinicians should treat this as a hypothesis, since the review does not show that these tests predict later injury.
athleteDev: Performance and conditioning staff could consider cognitively loaded movement tasks when rebuilding athletes after concussion, since the authors argue these tasks resemble sport demands. The review reports no performance outcomes.
rtp: The review addresses return to play directly. It reports that some athletes show dual-task gait deficits at return to activity and that injury risk may be higher after return, but the authors describe the link as a hypothesis. It should not be used to set clearance criteria, because no study has shown that dual-task testing predicts injury after return.

citation: Morrissey MC, Szymanski MR, Grundstein AJ, Casa DJ. New Perspectives on Risk Factors for Exertional Heat Stroke. Kinesiology Review. 2020;9(1):64-71.
abstract: Narrative review of new perspectives on risk factors for exertional heat stroke (EHS), focusing on hydration, heat acclimatization, medical conditions, climate change and heat policies, medications, and strength and conditioning sessions. The authors state that EHS is survivable with appropriate care and that most cases should not occur in the first place.
tldr: A narrative review of EHS risk factors. Heat acclimatization, fitness, hydration, weather-based activity modification and gradual return to training after inactivity are presented as the most practical controls. Several medication and supplement effects rest on small or animal studies.
methods: Narrative review with no described search strategy. It draws on the Rav-Acha et al. (2004) case series of more than 130 EHS cases, a 2019 meta-analysis of heat-mitigation strategies, data on NCAA and high school heat-acclimatization guidelines, and a Georgia high school football heat-policy study cited as in press.
findings: The authors report that low fitness was present in 71% of the Rav-Acha cases and overweight in 64.7%. The 2019 meta-analysis ranked aerobic fitness as the most important protective factor, followed by heat acclimatization, pre-exercise cooling and hydration. After NCAA heat-acclimatization policies, EHS-related deaths fell by 95% from 2003 to 2016 (Adams et al., 2016). In the Georgia study, rates of heat syncope and heat exhaustion fell by 35% to 100% after the heat policy, depending on the WBGT category. The authors cite studies suggesting that each 1% of body-mass loss during exercise in the heat raises internal temperature by about 0.15 to 0.22 degrees C. In one cycling study, prescribed drinking gave a 5.1% (plus or minus 4.8%) speed advantage over ad libitum drinking (Bardis et al., 2017).
limitations: This is a narrative review with no described search method, so study selection and the strength of each claim are not systematic. Much of the evidence comes from case series, observational studies, small trials and rodent work. The authors state that human NSAID evidence is limited and that the effects of creatine and caffeine are inconclusive. The Georgia policy study is cited before its publication.
practicalImplications: Build fitness and heat acclimatization into preseason plans before athletes train in hot conditions, since the cited evidence links both to lower heat-illness risk. Use weather-based activity modification, and bring athletes back to training after inactivity in graded steps rather than at full workload. For hydration, start sessions euhydrated, and match the fluid strategy to the sport: programmed drinking where fluid cannot be taken during play, and drinking to thirst may suit cycling-type events.
athleteDev: Use the review's points on fitness, heat acclimatization and gradual workload increases when planning training-camp and preseason heat exposure. The review states that untrained athletes are more susceptible to heat illness, so new or returning athletes need graded loading. Stimulant medications and dehydrating medications should be reviewed before hot-weather training.
rtp: The review addresses EHS prevention and does not give return-to-play criteria for an athlete who has had a heat stroke. Its guidance on returning to training after a break is about prevention, and it notes that prevention strategies differ from the treatment of EHS. It cannot be used to clear an athlete after EHS.

citation: Buckley TA, Howard CM, Oldham JR, Lynall RC, Swanik CB, Getchell N. No Clinical Predictors of Postconcussion Musculoskeletal Injury in College Athletes. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2020;52(6):1256-1262.
abstract: In 66 NCAA athletes with concussion and a matched subset of 36 non-concussed teammates, concussed athletes had a higher hazard of lower-extremity musculoskeletal injury in the year after return to play (HR 1.78, 95% CI 1.12 to 2.84). Demographic, injury and acute concussion assessment measures did not predict which concussed athletes were later injured.
tldr: Athletes who had a concussion were about 1.8 times as likely to sustain a lower-extremity musculoskeletal injury in the following year as matched teammates. Standard concussion measures and demographics did not identify which concussed athletes were at risk, so they cannot yet be used to target prevention.
methods: Cohort study of 66 intercollegiate athletes with a diagnosed concussion who completed a baseline and an acute (within 48 hours) battery: symptom checklists, SAC, BESS, ImPACT, clinical reaction time and the King-Devick test. Change scores (acute minus baseline) and demographic and injury variables were entered into two logistic regression models for subsequent lower-extremity MSK injury. A matched subset of 36 concussed athletes was compared with 36 non-concussed teammates, with time to injury analysed by Cox proportional hazards over one year before and after return to play.
findings: Concussed athletes had a hazard ratio of 1.78 for subsequent lower-extremity MSK injury compared with matched controls (95% CI 1.12 to 2.84; P = .015), with no difference in the year before concussion. Among athletes who were injured, mean time to injury was 160 days in the concussion group and 244 days in controls (P < .001). Neither the demographic and injury model (P = .318) nor the clinical concussion model (P = .461) predicted subsequent injury, and no individual predictor was significant.
limitations: The matched subset is small (36 concussed athletes and 36 controls), and the authors state that the study was underpowered to identify individual predictors. The sample followed CARE protocols with a mean time loss of 18.4 days, which the authors note is well beyond the commonly reported 7 to 10 days, and included one university's NCAA athletes only. The year-before comparison is reported inconsistently: Results give a between-group HR of 0.858 (95% CI 0.52 to 2.09, P = .910), but the Discussion cites P = .795, Exp(B) = 0.858, which are the Table 4 logistic-regression values for prior injury (95% CI 0.270 to 2.723) within concussed athletes only; the Results CI is also not centred on 0.858, so one of these figures is likely a reporting error.
practicalImplications: Treat the year after return from concussion as a period of raised lower-extremity injury risk: in this matched cohort the hazard was 1.78 times that of teammate controls. Standard concussion measures, demographics and injury presentation did not identify who was at risk, so they should not be used alone to select athletes for prevention work. The authors recommend considering injury prevention strategies at return to play, but this study did not test any intervention.
athleteDev: Lower-extremity injury risk was higher in the year after concussion in this cohort, and injuries came sooner (mean 160 vs 244 days). The study did not test monitoring, load management or any prevention program, and it does not identify which athletes are at greatest risk, so it cannot guide individual training decisions.
rtp: This study is directly relevant to return to play after concussion. Athletes in the cohort had returned to baseline and completed a progressive protocol, and the concussed group still had a higher lower-extremity injury risk over the following year. It does not test whether any concussion measure can clear an athlete to return, and it cannot be used to judge readiness to return.

citation: Paton BM, Read P, van Dyk N, Wilson MG, Pollock N, Court N, et al. London International Consensus and Delphi study on hamstring injuries part 3: rehabilitation, running and return to sport. Br J Sports Med. 2023.
abstract: A modified Delphi process with an international expert panel produced consensus statements on hamstring injury rehabilitation, running and return to sport. The panel recommends individualised rehabilitation based on sporting demands, the involved muscle and injury severity, with pain-free sprinting, running progression and a multidisciplinary, athlete-involved return-to-sport process. Agreement was not reached on flexibility and strength benchmarks or on adjuncts such as blood flow restriction.
tldr: An international expert panel agreed that hamstring rehabilitation should be individualised to sporting demands, muscle and injury type, and that running, sprinting and an athlete-involved return-to-sport process are central. Benchmarks for flexibility and strength, and the use of adjuncts such as blood flow restriction, were not agreed.
methods: This was a modified Delphi study with a literature review. Round 1 was an open-ended survey of 46 invited experts (35 responded), a consensus meeting of 15 experts drafted statements with facilitated debate and anonymous voting, and a round 2 online survey of 99 respondents (of 112 invited) voted true, false or undecided. The threshold was 70% agreement, and athletes were not included as survey participants.
findings: Statements reaching 70% or more included that the order and speed of exercise progression should depend on the adaptation required (96.2%), symptoms (88.9%) and stage of tissue healing (90.7%), that on-pitch running is a significant part of rehabilitation (98.4%) and that running dosage should be increased to full sprinting (100%). Pain-free running was agreed as a criterion for sprinting (85.5%) and pain-free sprinting as a criterion for return to play (96.7%), and a full unrestricted training session (93.3%) and a multidisciplinary return-to-sport process involving all stakeholders (98.3%) were also supported. Agreement was not reached for flexibility as a progression criterion (67.9%), range of motion as a return-to-sport consideration (45.0%), strength benchmarks within 10% (66.1%), the Askling H-test (57.6%) or adjuncts such as blood flow restriction (68.9%), all values from Tables 1 to 3.
limitations: The meeting included 15 of 35 round 1 respondents, women were few (Table 4 gives 2 of 35, 1 of 15 and 18 of 99, while the text says 2 of 39 in round 1), no athletes were included, and experts from Asia, Africa and South America could not attend. Several figures conflict within the paper: the abstract gives 88.2% for round 2 response (99 of 112 is 88.4%) and 40% for flexibility benchmarks (Table 3 gives 45.0%), and the discussion gives 67.8% for adjuncts, 56.1% for the Askling H-test and 98.6% for athlete apprehension where the tables give 68.9%, 57.6% and 98.3%; table values are reported here. The authors note that the background rehabilitation literature is small (six studies with about 386 athletes) and heterogeneous.
practicalImplications: Staff should individualise hamstring rehabilitation to the sport's demands, the injured muscle and the tissue type, and should progress loading by symptoms, healing stage and response to previous loading. Running and sprinting should be included in late rehabilitation, with pain-free sprinting before return to play and a full training session as a criterion. Benchmarks for flexibility and strength, and adjuncts such as blood flow restriction, should not be treated as agreed standards.
athleteDev: The panel supports building running and sprinting dosage toward game-level intensities and volumes before return to play, and using GPS data to guide running load. The consensus does not give specific load, speed or sprint-volume thresholds.
rtp: The panel's criteria include pain-free sprinting, a full unrestricted training session, peak isometric and eccentric strength at length and athlete self-assessment, decided by a multidisciplinary team. The consensus did not establish validated return-to-sport tests, strength benchmarks or reinjury rates, so it cannot set a fixed return-to-sport timeline.

citation: Johnston CD, Dewig DR, Pietrosimone B, Padua D, Ryan ED, Hart J, et al. Longitudinal Changes in Quadriceps Morphology over the First 3 Months after Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2024;56(5):933-941.
abstract: This prospective cohort compared quadriceps echo intensity (a marker of poorer muscle quality) and cross-sectional area in 20 people with ACL reconstruction and 12 healthy controls at baseline, 1 month and 3 months. Echo intensity was higher in the ACLR limb than baseline and the contralateral limb at 1 and 3 months, while muscle size fell and then increased from 1 to 3 months without a matching change in echo intensity. The authors conclude that muscle quality declines rapidly after ACLR and does not recover within 3 months.
tldr: Quadriceps muscle quality, measured by ultrasound echo intensity, worsened within the first month after ACL reconstruction and did not improve by 3 months, even as muscle size began to recover. From 1 to 3 months size and quality changed independently, so size alone may not show the full picture.
methods: Prospective cohort in which 20 people with ACL reconstruction (15 men, 5 women) and 12 healthy controls were tested before surgery or at baseline, at 1 month and at 3 months, with 32 of 54 recruited completing all sessions. Ultrasound images of the vastus lateralis and rectus femoris were used to calculate echo intensity, corrected for subcutaneous fat, and anatomical cross-sectional area, and mixed-model ANOVAs compared the ACLR limb with controls and with the contralateral limb.
findings: In the ACLR limb, echo intensity increased from baseline at 1 month (vastus lateralis +11.45%, rectus femoris +9.83%) and at 3 months (+11.50% and +9.40%), with no change between 1 and 3 months. Vastus lateralis cross-sectional area fell 25.1% at 1 month and rose 17.9% from 1 to 3 months, while rectus femoris area returned to baseline by 3 months; the baseline to 1 month changes in size and echo intensity were correlated for the vastus lateralis (r = -0.584, P = 0.007) but not the rectus femoris, and no changes were correlated from 1 to 3 months. Echo intensity did not differ significantly between the ACLR and control groups at any time point (Bonferroni-adjusted alpha 0.006), although the differences exceeded the control-derived minimal clinically important difference at 1 and 3 months.
limitations: The sample is small: 32 of 54 recruited participants (20 of 30 ACLR, 12 of 24 controls) completed all three visits, and the COVID-19 pandemic stopped the planned 6-month assessment. The abstract states that changes in quality and size were not correlated, but the results report a significant first-month correlation for the vastus lateralis, and the Figure 5 caption says the ACLR limb did not differ from control while the text reports smaller vastus lateralis area than controls at 1 and 3 months. Echo intensity may be affected by hydration and probe orientation, rehabilitation was not standardized, control-group physical activity was not measured, only the vastus lateralis and rectus femoris were imaged, and no strength or functional outcome was reported.
practicalImplications: Clinicians may consider tracking echo intensity alongside muscle size during early rehabilitation after ACL reconstruction, since size recovered from 1 to 3 months while echo intensity did not. The findings do not show that current rehabilitation should change, and the authors state that further work is needed on how to reverse the shift in muscle composition.
athleteDev: The study did not measure strength, power or performance, so it does not show what this muscle quality change means for an athlete's training or load decisions.
rtp: The study covers the first 3 months after ACL reconstruction and reports no return-to-sport criteria or outcomes. It cannot be used to judge readiness to return to sport, though the authors suggest echo intensity could give an objective progress marker that size measures do not.

citation: Maestrini V, Penza M, Filomena D, Birtolo LI, Monosilio S, Lemme E, et al. Low prevalence of cardiac abnormalities in competitive athletes at return-to-play after COVID-19. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2022.
abstract: In 219 competitive athletes evaluated for return to play after COVID-19, all had good exercise capacity and normal echocardiographic systolic and diastolic function. Two cases of acute myocarditis (0.9%) were found on cardiac MRI, and uncommon premature ventricular contractions were found in about 9% of athletes. The authors conclude that exercise testing has additional value in return-to-play evaluation, but the study had no comparison group and was not designed to measure the yield of CPET or Holter.
tldr: Among 219 competitive athletes screened for return to play after COVID-19, 0.9% had myocarditis on cardiac MRI and about 9% had uncommon ventricular ectopy at exercise testing. The study had no control group, so these figures describe one screening protocol rather than the risk caused by infection.
methods: Single-centre cross-sectional study of competitive athletes evaluated between October 2020 and May 2021 before resuming training, using the Italian return-to-play protocol: 12-lead ECG, blood tests including high-sensitivity troponin, pulmonary function, transthoracic echocardiography, maximal symptom-limited CPET, and 24-hour Holter ECG. Cardiac MRI with late gadolinium enhancement and T1/T2 mapping was performed on clinical indication. Results are descriptive; no control group was included.
findings: Of 219 athletes (59% male, median age 23), none had cardiovascular or respiratory limitation on CPET, and echocardiography showed normal systolic and diastolic function in all. Uncommon PVCs were found at CPET in 20 athletes (9%), and 13 of the 16 with a prior evaluation (81%) had newly diagnosed arrhythmia after COVID-19. Two female athletes (0.9%) had acute myocarditis on CMR, with raised troponin and increased T1 and T2 mapping values. Five athletes (2%) were temporarily not eligible for sport and were followed up.
limitations: Single centre, no comparison group, and pre-infection data for only about half the cohort. The authors state that a defined association between infection and arrhythmia cannot be proved. CMR was not performed in all athletes, so tissue abnormalities are likely undercounted. Several figures conflict: the abstract reports 9.5% (21 athletes) with ectopy at CPET or Holter, while the text reports 9% (20) at CPET; the abstract says three athletes were restricted from sport, while the results describe five; the abstract reports one new pericardial effusion, while echocardiography in the results shows mild effusion in four; and non-sustained VT is 1.4% in the text but 1.6% in Table 2.
practicalImplications: The authors argue that CPET adds value to return-to-play screening after COVID-19, because the athletes withdrawn from sport had uncommon PVCs at CPET and Holter, but the study was not designed to measure the diagnostic yield of CPET or Holter and had no comparison group. Myocarditis was uncommon in this group, but the 0.9% figure should not be used as a general risk estimate. The authors suggest CMR when myocarditis is likely, such as with symptoms, suspicious findings or uncommon PVC morphology.
athleteDev: Performance Application: Athletes showed good exercise capacity on CPET after recovery, with no functional limitation reported. The study did not measure training or performance outcomes, so it cannot show how training load should change after infection.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: Two athletes with myocarditis were withdrawn, and two athletes with newly diagnosed uncommon PVCs were withdrawn temporarily and resumed about three months later when the arrhythmias had disappeared. The protocol is not validated outside this cohort, so the 0.9% figure should not be used as a clearance criterion, and because CMR was done only on clinical indication the study cannot show that a normal CPET or Holter excludes myocarditis.

citation: Zaffagnini S, Vannini F, Di Martino A, Andriolo L, Sessa A, Perdisa F, et al. Low rate of return to pre-injury sport level in athletes after cartilage surgery: a 10-year follow-up study. Knee Surgery, Sports Traumatology, Arthroscopy. 2018.
abstract: In 31 competitive male athletes treated with arthroscopic MACT for focal knee cartilage lesions, IKDC scores improved markedly and stayed stable to 10 years. Overall, 64.5% returned to a competitive level and 58.1% to the same pre-injury level, with return rates falling over time. Previous surgery was the most influential factor for returning to the same level (p = 0.010), and the authors conclude that the chondrocyte-based approach has limits for sport-related outcomes.
tldr: In 31 competitive male athletes treated with cartilage repair for knee lesions, clinical scores stayed improved for 10 years, but only about 3 in 10 were still at their pre-injury level at 10 years. Previous knee surgery, degenerative or OCD lesions and higher BMI were linked to poorer sport return.
methods: Prospective case series of 31 male competitive athletes (34 enrolled, 3 lost) with focal grade III to IV osteochondral lesions of the distal femur, treated with arthroscopic hyaluronan-based MACT between 2000 and 2006. Patients completed IKDC subjective, Tegner and EQ-VAS scores before surgery and yearly for up to 10 years. Return to sport was recorded by competitive level (Tegner 8 to 10) and by pre-injury level, and factors were examined with Friedman, Mann-Whitney, ANOVA and backward logistic regression. No control group was included.
findings: IKDC subjective score rose from 40.3 +/- 13.4 to 81.7 +/- 14.4 at 12 months, 89.5 +/- 11.3 at 2 years and 87.3 +/- 13.6 at 10 years. The Tegner score rose from 1.9 pre-treatment to 6.7 +/- 2.3 at 10 years, which remained below the pre-injury mean of 9.1 +/- 2.3. Return to a competitive level was 61.3%, 45.2% and 35.5% at 2, 5 and 10 years, and return to the same pre-injury level was 54.8%, 38.7% and 29.0%. Return to competitive level was 84% without previous surgery and 33% with it (p = 0.007), 87% for traumatic lesions versus 33% for degenerative and 50% for OCD lesions (p = 0.035), and 92.3% in athletes under 20; higher BMI was also linked to lower return (p = 0.001). In multivariate analysis previous surgery and BMI were the factors retained. Only one failure was recorded, in a 19-year-old who needed further surgery at 6 years.
limitations: Uncontrolled series with 31 patients and level IV evidence, and no imaging assessment of the repaired tissue. The time to return is not reported in the results despite being listed as an outcome. The logistic regression odds ratios (for example 139.7 for previous surgery on competitive level) are unstable for this sample size. Comparisons with other studies (73% to 84% return rates) mix different populations and definitions. The title's 'low rate' refers to same-level return, while the abstract describes the outcome as satisfactory and the overall return to sport as successful. The surgery was performed 2000 to 2006 with a specific hyaluronan scaffold, so the 10-year data may not reflect current techniques.
practicalImplications: Discuss realistic expectations before cartilage surgery: in this series about 6 in 10 athletes returned to competitive play at some point, but fewer than 3 in 10 were at their pre-injury level by 10 years. Previous surgery, degenerative or OCD lesions, older age and higher BMI were linked to lower return, so these should shape counselling. Clinical scores can remain high while sport level falls, so staff should track sport level as well as symptom scores.
athleteDev: Performance Application: The study measures sport level by the Tegner scale, not performance. It shows that competitive athletes' activity level stayed below pre-injury levels at 10 years (6.7 versus 9.1), but no performance metrics were recorded.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: Around 58% of these athletes returned to their pre-injury level at some follow-up point, falling to 29% at 10 years. Previous surgery, degenerative or OCD lesions, older age and higher BMI were associated with lower return, so these factors should inform return-to-sport expectations. The results do not report time to return, so this study cannot set a timeline for return.

citation: Palermi S, Vittadini F, Vecchiato M, Corsini A, Demeco A, Massa B, et al. Managing Lower Limb Muscle Reinjuries in Athletes: From Risk Factors to Return-to-Play Strategies. J Funct Morphol Kinesiol. 2023;8:155.
abstract: This narrative review covers the epidemiology, risk factors, clinical management, imaging, prevention and artificial intelligence applications for lower limb muscle reinjury, with a focus on football players. Reinjury is defined as recurrence of the same injury type at the same site within 2 months, or up to 1 year in other definitions.
tldr: Muscle reinjury remains common, and the authors argue for a multidisciplinary plan that combines individualized rehabilitation, return criteria beyond elapsed time, eccentric training and training-load monitoring.
methods: Narrative review of PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science literature, selected by keywords and by the authors' judgement of relevance, limited to peer-reviewed English-language articles. The authors state that, unlike systematic reviews, it does not follow a strict inclusion protocol or appraise study quality and risk of bias in depth.
findings: Reinjury rates are reported as 12% to 43% across sports, with a meta-analysis cited for a risk ratio of 4.8 for recent hamstring strain. The authors describe eccentric exercise as having the strongest evidence for secondary prevention and cite an acute-to-chronic workload ratio of 0.8 to 1.3 as a target. They describe robust evidence for physical therapies and platelet-rich plasma as limited or elusive.
limitations: The review may omit relevant studies and may not match the depth of systematic reviews, and the search window is not stated. Table 2 lists higher reinjury risk for high-grade muscle injuries, while the text cites Malliaropoulos et al. for higher reinjury risk after low-grade hamstring lesions, and the review does not reconcile the two.
practicalImplications: Return-to-play decisions should combine clinical, strength, flexibility and sport-specific tests, because the authors argue that elapsed time alone can allow return before tissue maturity. Eccentric strengthening and training-load monitoring belong in prevention plans for athletes with prior muscle injury.
athleteDev: Performance staff can include eccentric hamstring work and training-load monitoring in prevention planning for athletes with prior muscle injury. The review reports no performance outcome data.
rtp: The review supports individualized return-to-training and return-to-play criteria based on clinical, strength and sport-specific tests rather than time alone. It gives no validated cut-off values and notes that no MRI finding has strong evidence for predicting reinjury at return, although one retrospective study linked some features to risk.

citation: Sano Y, Kawabata M, Kenmoku T, Watanabe H, Takahira N. Maximum-Speed Single-Leg Bridge Test for Concentric Functional Assessment and Exercise in an Athlete with Recurrent Hamstring Strain Injuries: A Case Report. International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy. 2025;20(5):716-726.
abstract: The authors describe a rugby player on a fourth hamstring strain recurrence, whose residual high-speed deficits were found by the maximum-speed single-leg bridge test. The same test was then used as a home intervention, with reported gains in speed, height, isometric knee flexor strength and flexibility, and ultrasound changes in the muscle.
tldr: A high-speed single-leg bridge test identified deficits that conventional strength and flexibility tests did not, and the test was then used as a training exercise. For practitioners, this is a single-case signal that speed-based hamstring testing may be worth trialling in rehabilitation.
methods: Single case of a 21-year-old rugby player with a fourth semitendinosus recurrence, tested monthly with the maximum-speed single-leg bridge test, VAS pain, active knee extension, isometric knee flexor strength and ultrasound. The test was then used as a two-month daily home exercise, with a 1.5-month detraining follow-up and compliance of 94.3% tracked by exercise videos.
findings: At one month after injury there was no reported side-to-side difference in isometric knee flexor strength or flexibility, and at two months the injured side showed lower buttock-raising height (0.19 m vs 0.22 m) and speed (0.83 vs 1.01 m/s) than the uninjured side. After the two-month intervention, height was 0.35 m and speed 1.46 m/s, and both were largely maintained after 1.5 months of detraining (0.36 m, 1.36 m/s), with ultrasound showing fewer muscle fibre irregularities.
limitations: The paper describes one athlete with no control group and a short follow-up, and the authors state it is uncertain whether resolving these deficits prevents recurrence. Because testing ran from two to four months after injury, the gains cannot be separated from natural healing. The injury involved the semitendinosus rather than the more commonly injured biceps femoris, and Table 1 lists Active Knee Extension values of 23.0 degrees uninjured versus 14.0 injured at one month although the text reports no flexibility difference.
practicalImplications: A speed-based single-leg bridge test may reveal hamstring deficits that strength and flexibility tests miss in an athlete who has met standard criteria. Keep sets short enough to preserve high-speed movement, since the authors reduced the protocol after fatigue slowed movement speed and consistency.
athleteDev: Performance staff could add a high-speed hamstring test to monitoring for athletes with recurrent strain, since this case showed speed deficits that conventional tests missed. The authors compare the athlete with a reference average of 0.98 m/s from 26 healthy recreational athletes, but a single case cannot set norms.
rtp: The authors suggest the test could become part of return-to-play criteria, because the athlete still had deficits after standard criteria were met. Its value for predicting re-injury is untested, so it should be used alongside established criteria, not in place of them.

citation: Baida S, King E, Gore S, Richter C, Franklyn-Miller A, Moran K. Movement Variability and Loading Characteristics in Athletes With Athletic Groin Pain: Changes After Successful Return to Play and Compared With Uninjured Athletes. The Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2022;10(10):23259671221125159.
abstract: This laboratory study compared 36 athletes with athletic groin pain and 36 uninjured athletes during a continuous lateral hurdle hop, and retested the injured group after rehabilitation. At baseline the injured athletes had longer ground contact times and lower peak vertical ground reaction force, and these differences were no longer significant after rehabilitation.
tldr: In a hurdle hop test, athletes with groin pain had longer ground contact and lower peak vertical force than controls, and these loading differences were no longer significant after rehabilitation. Movement variability did not differ at any point, and the authors suggest rehabilitation that targets trunk and pelvis control.
methods: Pre- and post-rehabilitation laboratory cohort: 36 athletes with athletic groin pain were tested before and after a three-level exercise program focused on intersegmental control, and 36 uninjured athletes matched for age, level and sport were tested once. Each athlete made 10 continuous side-to-side hops over a 15 cm hurdle on force plates with 3D motion capture, and group comparisons used statistical parametric mapping, t tests and a permutation analysis of 30-athlete random samples.
findings: At baseline, the groin pain group had longer ground contact time (P = .025, d = 0.43), greater concentric impulse (P = .028, d = 0.52) and lower peak vertical force (P = .025, d = 0.36) than controls; lower eccentric peak force (P = .029) and eccentric rate of force development (P = .049) were only trends that did not meet the 85% permutation criterion, and no movement variability or joint-level differences were found. From pre to post rehabilitation, the injured group's ground-force changes were not significant (small effect sizes), while trunk, pelvis and hip kinematics and hip kinetics changed significantly (for example, pelvic contralateral drop, d = -0.53). At return to play, ground-force measures no longer differed significantly from controls (ground contact time P = .755, peak force P = .589, concentric impulse P = .478).
limitations: The uninjured group was tested only once and the injured group had no untreated comparison, so change over time, test familiarity and any rehabilitation effect cannot be separated. The abstract and discussion describe reduced rate of force development as a baseline finding, but the results report it as a trend that did not reach the 85% permutation criterion (P = .049, d = 0.34), and the pre-to-post ground-force changes were themselves non-significant; the abstract also gives a mean age of 27.5 years for the injured group where Table 1 gives 25.9. The rehabilitation was prescribed by two of the authors and the study was funded partly by the clinic.
practicalImplications: Ground contact time and peak force from a continuous lateral hurdle hop on force plates differed between athletes with groin pain and controls at baseline, and the authors suggest that ground contact time, measurable with force plates or jump mats, may be a simple clinical measure; the within-group change in these measures after rehabilitation was not significant, so single-athlete change should be read cautiously. The authors suggest including trunk and pelvis control work during explosive, sport-specific movements, because pelvis and trunk kinematics changed with rehabilitation.
athleteDev: For performance staff, athletes with groin pain had longer ground contact and lower peak force in a fast hop, and these differences were no longer significant after rehabilitation. The test was run in a laboratory with no training or competition outcomes, so it cannot show that these loading measures predict performance.
rtp: Athletes were tested at return to play after clinical milestones were met, and their ground-force measures were no longer significantly different from controls, but this does not show equivalence and the study did not track re-injury or later sport participation. It cannot set return-to-play thresholds, and all HAGOS subscales except Symptoms, and the Marx activity score, remained significantly below the uninjured group at return.

citation: Rafols Parellada L, Linde X, Solà J, Fort A, Brau J. Muscle activation during rehabilitation on artificial turf vs. sand after cruciate ligament surgery: a case series. Apunts Sports Medicine. 2020.
abstract: Describes surface EMG data from two female youth soccer players recovering from ACL surgery, recorded over six rehabilitation sessions on artificial turf and sand. The authors report increased activation of the cross pattern (left hamstring and right gluteus) in player 1 and of the left quadriceps in player 2, and conclude that the muscle most activated in both players was the antagonist of the injured leg, regardless of surface.
tldr: Two case reports of ACL rehabilitation on turf and sand show surface EMG patterns that are worth describing but cannot yet guide practice. The authors themselves call for more cases before a common pattern is claimed.
methods: Case series of two female youth soccer players after ACL surgery: player 1 had ACL and patellar tendon surgery on the left leg, and player 2 had ACL surgery with a semitendinosus plasty on the right leg. Surface EMG (Myontec Mbody AllSport 6-channel mesh) was recorded during six rehabilitation sessions, three on artificial turf and three on sand, for anterior and posterior chain muscles on both legs.
findings: Player 1 showed higher left than right hamstring activation on five of six days, peaking at 36.7% on the first turf session. Player 2 showed higher left than right quadriceps activation on five of six days, with the largest difference (8.7 percentage points) on the first sand session. The authors conclude that the antagonist of the injured leg was the most active group in both players, regardless of surface.
limitations: Two players, no statistics, and EMG values given as absolute percentages with no described normalisation. The text says player 1's left hamstring exceeded the right in all six posterior-chain sessions, but Table 1 shows the reverse on day 3, and the 'most active muscle is the antagonist' claim is not borne out in Table 1 on days 2, 3 and 5. Player 2's left quadriceps is called the antagonist of her injured leg, although her injured leg was the right.
practicalImplications: Surface EMG on both legs can help staff describe muscle activity during ACL rehabilitation on different surfaces. Two cases cannot set a rehabilitation rule, so any surface choice should rest on the clinical picture and on more data.
athleteDev: Does not measure performance. The sessions describe muscle activity during rehabilitation running on turf and sand in two players, with no performance outcome.
rtp: Can describe muscle activity patterns during ACL rehabilitation on turf and sand, but cannot show that either surface improves return-to-play readiness. It contains no strength, hop or return-to-play criteria, so it cannot be used to clear an athlete to return to sport.

citation: Nagelli CV, Wordeman SC, Di Stasi S, Hoffman J, Marulli T, Hewett TE. Neuromuscular Training Improves Biomechanical Deficits at the Knee in Anterior Cruciate Ligament-Reconstructed Athletes. Clinical Journal of Sport Medicine. 2021;31(2):113-119.
abstract: A cohort study of 18 athletes after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) and 10 uninjured control athletes, all of whom completed a 12-session neuromuscular training program. Sagittal-plane knee biomechanics during drop vertical jumps improved in the ACLR group after training. After training, the groups had comparable sagittal-plane mechanics, and controls landed with a larger knee abduction angle than the ACLR athletes, who landed in slightly more adduction.
tldr: Athletes after ACL reconstruction who completed a 12-session neuromuscular training program landed with a more flexed knee and lower flexion moment at initial contact during a drop jump. Frontal-plane knee measures did not change with training, and after training the ACLR athletes landed with less knee abduction than uninjured controls, not more.
methods: Cohort study in a controlled laboratory. Athletes with ACLR (hamstring autograft, about 8 months post-surgery) and uninjured controls passed a clinical screen, and both groups completed 12 sessions of neuromuscular training in four phases. Knee kinematics and kinetics were recorded with 12-camera motion capture and force plates during three double-leg drop vertical jumps from a 30.5 cm box, before and after training in the ACLR group and after training in both groups, analysed with repeated-measures and two-way ANOVA.
findings: In the ACLR group, knee flexion angle at initial contact increased from 17.2 to 24.3 degrees (session effect P=0.001), and knee flexion moment at initial contact decreased from 0.48 to 0.36 Nm/kg (P=0.008). Knee abduction angle and moment did not change significantly, limb symmetry for the sagittal variables did not change, and the uninvolved limb had a greater peak knee flexion moment than the involved limb (P=0.005). After training, controls had a larger knee abduction angle at initial contact than ACLR athletes, who landed in more adduction (group effect P=0.002), with no other group or limb effects.
limitations: No untrained ACLR group was included, so the sagittal changes cannot be separated from time or natural recovery. The control group was small (n=10) and was analysed only after training. Screening excluded athletes with poor single-leg hop mechanics or joint effusion, so the cohort was higher functioning than typical, which the authors suggest may explain the lack of frontal-plane change. Exercise progression was based on trainer judgment, so athletes did not all complete the same exercises. The group means for knee abduction angle in the Results text and Table 3 do not match cleanly in the extracted text, so only the direction of the difference is reported here.
practicalImplications: Rehabilitation and performance staff could consider a structured neuromuscular training program in the late stage of ACL rehabilitation to improve sagittal-plane landing mechanics, since knee flexion at landing increased. Frontal-plane measures did not change with training in this high-functioning cohort, which had been screened to exclude athletes with medial knee collapse, so the program's effect on valgus cannot be judged from this study.
athleteDev: Performance staff could use drop vertical jump knee flexion and flexion moment at initial contact to track landing mechanics in athletes returning from ACL reconstruction. The paper does not show that these landing changes improve sport performance.
