rtp: The study concerns athletes before return to sport and suggests neuromuscular training can improve sagittal-plane landing mechanics before return. It does not show that this program reduces second ACL injury, and the authors state that future work must test re-injury outcomes. Landing-mechanics improvement alone should not be used as a clearance criterion.

citation: Calabro RS, Calderone A, Fiorente N. Neurosciences and Sports Rehabilitation in ACLR: A Narrative Review on Winning Alliance Strategies and Connecting the Dots. Journal of Functional Morphology and Kinesiology. 2025;10:119.
abstract: A narrative review of neuroplasticity, motor control and sensorimotor retraining in rehabilitation after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR). The authors propose a conceptual model with three neuroplastic pathways and summarize robotics, virtual reality and biofeedback as tools to address neurocognitive deficits, with reinjury rates after ACLR of 9% to 29% in most studies cited. The review concludes that long-term monitoring and interdisciplinary work are needed.
tldr: A narrative review argues that rehabilitation after ACL reconstruction should address brain-level changes, proprioception and fear of reinjury, not only strength. It proposes a conceptual model and summarizes technologies whose long-term effects, the authors say, are still being studied.
methods: Narrative review of peer-reviewed literature from PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science, organised around a conceptual framework (the Neuroplastic Adaptation Trident Model) that the authors cite to Machan and Krupps (2021). Search terms, date limits and inclusion criteria are not reported, and study quality is not appraised or pooled.
findings: The authors argue that ACL injury alters motor cortex activity, cerebellar and prefrontal activation, and proprioceptive processing, and they cite neuroimaging studies of ACLR patients. They cite a biofeedback study in young, physically active females (not stated to be ACLR patients) that reported a reduced peak knee abduction moment after six weeks, and a virtual reality study in which ACLR patients' knee biomechanics became more similar to healthy controls. Reported reinjury rates after ACLR range from 1.5% to 37.5%, with most studies reporting 9% to 29%.
limitations: The review does not report search terms or inclusion criteria, and it does not appraise study quality. The authors acknowledge that robotic systems are costly and may not mimic multiplanar sport movements, that virtual reality can cause motion sickness, and that biofeedback needs skilled interpretation. They also state that long-term efficacy of these technologies remains under investigation.
practicalImplications: Rehabilitation staff could add proprioceptive and dual-task drills, such as counting during drills or responding to unexpected cues, as the review suggests, while noting that much of this evidence comes from individual studies. The review also suggests biofeedback and force plate feedback for loading symmetry, but these need trained staff and equipment.
athleteDev: Performance staff could consider reaction and dual-task drills in the later phases after ACL reconstruction, as the review proposes. The review presents the link to athletic performance as a claim and does not provide performance outcome data.
rtp: The review proposes neuroplasticity-based and cognitive-motor training as ways to reduce reinjury risk around return to play. It presents these within a conceptual framework rather than as tested criteria, and it states that long-term efficacy is still under investigation, so it should not be used to set return-to-play clearance.

citation: Reurink G, Almusa E, Goudswaard GJ, Tol JL, Hamilton B, Moen MH, et al. No Association Between Fibrosis on Magnetic Resonance Imaging at Return to Play and Hamstring Reinjury Risk. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2015;43(5):1228-1234.
abstract: In 108 athletes with grade 1 or 2 hamstring injuries, MRI fibrosis at return to play was present in 38% of athletes. Over one year, reinjury occurred in 24% of athletes both with and without fibrosis (HR 0.95, 95% CI 0.43 to 2.1), so fibrosis was not associated with reinjury in this cohort.
tldr: Fibrosis on MRI at return to play was common after grade 1 or 2 hamstring injuries (38%), but it did not predict one-year reinjury (24% in both groups). With 26 reinjuries, the study could not detect a small or moderate association.
methods: Cohort study pooling athletes from two double-blind randomized trials of platelet-rich plasma in hamstring injury, a Dutch cohort and a Qatari cohort, recruited from November 2009 to July 2014. MRI was performed within 5 days of injury and again within 1 week of return to play; each MRI was scored by one of two experienced radiologists, blinded to scan timing, for intramuscular low signal (fibrosis) on T1, T2 and fluid-sensitive images. Reinjury was recorded for one year and analysed with univariate and multivariable Cox proportional hazards models, the latter adjusted for prior ipsilateral hamstring injury and cohort.
findings: Fibrosis was present at return to play in 41 of 108 athletes (38%), with a median longitudinal length of 5.8 cm. There were 26 reinjuries in total (19 of 63 in the Dutch cohort and 7 of 45 in the Qatari cohort). Reinjury occurred in 10 of 41 athletes with fibrosis (24%) and 16 of 67 without (24%), giving HR 0.95 (95% CI 0.43 to 2.1; P = .898). After adjustment, the HR was 1.3 (95% CI 0.55 to 2.8; P = .591).
limitations: With 26 reinjuries the confidence interval (0.43 to 2.1) includes a doubling of risk, and the authors state only a moderate to strong association could be detected. The athletes came from platelet-rich plasma trials, the two cohorts used different MRI protocols and return-to-play criteria, fibrosis scoring had no reliability or histological data, and no MRI was done at reinjury. Two reporting conflicts: the abstract gives a fibrosis volume IQR of 1.5 to 3.9 cm3 while Table 3 gives 0.5 to 3.9 cm3 (Table 3 used here), and the Table 2 Qatari grade column repeats the whole-sample counts (45/63) although the Qatari cohort had 45 athletes.
practicalImplications: Expect MRI fibrosis in about 4 in 10 athletes at return to play after grade 1 or 2 hamstring injuries; in this cohort it was not associated with reinjury, so it should not be treated alone as a reinjury marker. Because the study could only detect a moderate to strong association, it does not show that fibrosis is harmless, and it should not be used to set an MRI-based clearance rule either way.
athleteDev: The study does not address training load or performance, so it gives no basis for changing training volume or intensity. Its only relevance is that fibrosis at return to play, which is common, was not associated with reinjury in these athletes.
rtp: The study is directly about return to play after grade 1 or 2 hamstring injuries. Fibrosis was present in 38% of athletes at return to play (median 30 days after injury), and it was not associated with one-year reinjury here. It cannot identify a safe fibrosis threshold, cannot support clearance on MRI alone, and says nothing about grade 3 injuries.

citation: Kim K, Monroe JC, Gavin TP, Roseguini BT. Local Heat Therapy to Accelerate Recovery After Exercise-Induced Muscle Damage. Exerc Sport Sci Rev. 2020;48(4):163-169.
abstract: This review tests the hypothesis that local heat therapy speeds functional recovery after strenuous eccentric exercise by aiding glycogen resynthesis, reversing vascular dysfunction, improving mitochondrial function and stimulating muscle protein synthesis. The authors summarize cell, animal and human evidence and conclude that localized heating is a promising recovery tool that needs further study.
tldr: Local heat therapy may speed recovery of muscle function after eccentric exercise through better blood flow, glycogen resynthesis and mitochondrial function. The mechanisms are mostly supported by non-athlete and cell or animal work, so they remain unproven in athletes.
methods: This is a narrative review with no described literature search method. It organizes evidence from cultured cells, rodents, pigs and humans around heat-induced signaling, muscle blood flow, glycogen resynthesis, microvascular function, mitochondria, protein turnover and soreness.
findings: In the authors' own earlier study (Kim et al., 2019), one thigh heated for 90 minutes immediately after maximal eccentric knee-extensor exercise and daily for 4 days recovered fatigue resistance faster than the thermoneutral control thigh (main effect of treatment, P = 0.02), and soreness tended to resolve faster. Cited human studies report faster glycogen resynthesis with local heat after exhaustive cycling, and mechanistic studies show heat-related increases in muscle blood flow, eNOS, angiogenic factors and mitochondrial proteins, although one cited study found 20 minutes of 46 C leg immersion did not increase myofibrillar protein synthesis. The authors note the glycogen studies did not use eccentric exercise and that most human evidence comes from exercise-naive or recreationally active people.
limitations: The review does not describe how sources were selected, so its coverage cannot be judged. Much of the evidence is from cell, rat, mouse and pig models, and the authors state it is unclear whether the findings apply to competitive athletes. The review also states that the optimal timing of heat (before or after exercise) is not yet defined and that effects on connective tissue repair are unexplored.
practicalImplications: Localized heat is a possible recovery option after strenuous eccentric exercise, but the review does not establish a protocol, dose or timing for athletes. Staff should treat the proposed mechanisms as hypotheses and should not expect the same recovery gains in trained athletes until the authors' call for further study is answered.
athleteDev: Heat therapy may be considered as a recovery aid after high-volume eccentric training, but the review does not show that it improves later training adaptation or competitive performance. Its proposed effects on glycogen and mitochondria come mainly from non-athlete or non-eccentric studies.
rtp: The review discusses recovery after muscle damage in general and does not assess return-to-sport decisions or injured athletes. It cannot be used to judge readiness to return to sport, though it notes heat is used in sports rehabilitation settings.

citation: Janse van Rensburg DC, Jansen van Rensburg A, Fowler PM, Bender AM, Stevens D, Sullivan KO, et al. Managing Travel Fatigue and Jet Lag in Athletes: A Review and Consensus Statement. Sports Medicine. 2021.
abstract: The authors review circadian physiology, travel fatigue and jet lag in athletes, and give consensus recommendations for managing both. The recommendations are organized as travel toolboxes for pre-flight, in-flight and post-flight phases, with the authors noting that research is needed to strengthen them.
tldr: Travel fatigue and jet lag can affect sleep, performance and illness risk, but evidence for specific management is limited. The panel's toolbox favors protecting sleep, planning recovery windows, timed light exposure and avoidance, and sensible melatonin use, with caution about unvalidated tools.
methods: Expert panel of 26 that ran literature searches in PubMed, MEDLINE, CINAHL, Google Scholar and SPORTDiscus, then used Qualtrics voting on terminology, travel fatigue management and jet lag management. Consensus thresholds were 80% for terminology and travel fatigue and 75% for jet lag, with average author response rates of 96.2% and 92.3%.
findings: The authors report no research on interventions that specifically manage travel fatigue in athletes, and a cited systematic review found low-quality evidence for jet lag interventions. Consensus recommendations include protecting sleep before and during travel, timed light exposure and avoidance, and exogenous melatonin, with the authors noting that inappropriate light exposure can be counterproductive. The authors caution against jet lag calculators and apps until their efficacy in athletes is tested.
limitations: The recommendations rest mainly on opinion, collective experience and laboratory or community studies rather than athlete trials, and the authors say this limits the strength of recommendation. The extracted text does not include the content of Table 4 or the figure dosing schedules, so specific timing advice could not be checked against the source.
practicalImplications: Plan training load and recovery around travel so athletes have time to adjust, and protect sleep before and during long journeys. Use the light and melatonin guidance only with individual supervision, because the authors say inappropriate light can be counterproductive and app-based timing advice is unvalidated.
athleteDev: Performance staff can use the toolbox to plan training load and recovery windows around travel, and can track sleep and fatigue with subjective tools such as the Total Quality of Recovery scale. The authors say no single marker captures travel fatigue, so these are monitoring aids rather than performance tests.
rtp: The paper does not address return to sport after injury. Its guidance applies to fit, travelling athletes, and it should not be used to make return-to-play decisions.

citation: Baird MB, Asif IM. Medications for sleep schedule adjustments in athletes. Sports Health. 2018;10(1):35-39.
abstract: The authors review evidence for melatonin, caffeine and nonbenzodiazepine sleep aids used to shift athletes' sleep schedules around travel and competition. They give timing recommendations for sports medicine providers and note that most supporting data come from non-athlete populations.
tldr: Melatonin, caffeine and nonbenzodiazepine sleep aids may help athletes shift sleep schedules, but very few studies test them in athletes. Most guidance comes from shift workers and travellers, so timing should be individualised and checked against anti-doping rules.
methods: Clinical review using MEDLINE keyword searches on sleep aids, circadian adjustment, athletes, caffeine and melatonin. The authors extracted and discussed pertinent articles, with no stated inclusion criteria, and assigned a level of evidence of 2.
findings: Melatonin is presented as the best-studied agent, with benefits for sleep phase advancement such as eastward travel and early competition. Early-day caffeine may help re-entrainment and alertness, but caffeine taken for late afternoon or evening competitions may impair sleep. Sedative-hypnotics are described as second-line agents for phase advance, with short-acting agents preferred, benzodiazepines discouraged, and at least 8 hours of sleep advised before competition. In a trial of 12 soccer players, morning melatonin reduced physical performance at 08:00 with no differences at 12:00 or 16:00, and a second athlete trial found no likely effect on morning performance after night-time melatonin.
limitations: The review uses a keyword MEDLINE search with no inclusion criteria, and the authors state that few studies involve athletes. Much of the guidance is inferred from shift workers, aircrew and other travellers, and caffeine tolerance was not adjusted for in the cited studies. The cited soccer trial's authors concluded morning melatonin had no unfavourable effects even though performance fell at 08:00.
practicalImplications: Sports medicine providers can time melatonin to the direction of travel as the review's table sets out, and use sedative-hypnotics only when at least 8 hours of sleep is available before preparation and competition. The review accepts caffeine shortly before competition for its ergogenic effect, but staff should weigh its cost to sleep after late afternoon or evening events. Melatonin supplements and energy drinks are not regulated to prescription standards, so contamination and anti-doping risk should be checked, and the authors note ramelteon as a prescription alternative.
athleteDev: Plan sleep timing, naps and light exposure around travel and competition before turning to medication, as the review recommends non-drug strategies first. Any sleep aid plan should be individualised, because the authors note that each athlete's circadian physiology differs.
rtp: The review addresses sleep schedules and jet lag, not injury, so it cannot inform return to sport. It should not be used to decide when an injured athlete can return to training or competition.

citation: Heidari J, Beckmann J, Bertollo M, Brink M, Kallus W, Robazza C, et al. Multidimensional Monitoring of Recovery Status and Implications for Performance. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2018.
abstract: This invited brief review describes recovery monitoring in athletes across biological, psychological and social approaches. It argues that these approaches should be combined rather than relying on a single measure, and that monitoring should use individual reference values.
tldr: Recovery monitoring should combine biological, psychological and social tools rather than rely on one measure, with individual baselines and the smallest meaningful change used to judge results. The review does not test these recommendations, so treat them as a framework.
methods: Invited brief review; the article does not describe a literature search, study selection or quality appraisal. It summarizes biological markers (resting HRV, heart rate recovery, creatine kinase, testosterone/cortisol ratio, immune markers), psychological questionnaires (MTDS, POMS and BRUMS, RESTQ-Sport and RESTQ-Sport-36, ARSS and SRSS) and a social stress tool (DALDA).
findings: The authors suggest combining five minutes of resting HRV with submaximal exercise heart rate as the most feasible cardiac measures, but say the response to underrecovery is hard to generalize across sports. They state that no single biological marker is a gold standard, that links between hormones and performance are weak, and they cite a testosterone/cortisol ratio drop of more than 30% as a sign of overtraining from one older source. They recommend a multimodal approach with individual reference values, the smallest meaningful change, and key assessments at set points combined with brief regular checks.
limitations: This narrative review has no described search or quality appraisal, so its claims cannot be checked against a defined evidence base. The authors note that no consensus exists on the optimal biological parameter, that biological markers vary widely between and within athletes, and that the logistics of blood sampling limit daily use.
practicalImplications: Staff setting up recovery monitoring should choose tools by goal and time budget: the review suggests key assessments at set points, such as preseason and postseason, with brief regular measures such as the MTDS between them. Judge changes against each athlete's own reference values and the smallest meaningful change, and use blood or saliva markers only where laboratory turnaround and resources allow.
athleteDev: For performance staff, the review supports combining a few brief self-report measures with periodic fuller assessments and individual baselines to detect changes in recovery. It also says the link between hormonal markers and performance is weak, so its performance-related advice is a framework rather than tested evidence.
rtp: The review covers recovery monitoring in athletes and does not address injury rehabilitation or return-to-play decisions. Its note that RESTQ-Sport includes an injury scale and that underrecovery can precede injury does not give return-to-play criteria, so it should not be used to clear an athlete to return.

citation: Pereira R, Hartescu I, Jackson RC, Morgan K. Napping behaviour, daytime sleepiness, and arousal in high performance athletes and non-athlete controls. J Sports Sci. 2023.
abstract: Cross-sectional online survey of 158 high-performance athletes and 82 non-athlete controls to examine napping in relation to sleep quality, daytime sleepiness and pre-sleep arousal. Athlete and non-athlete nap prevalence did not differ significantly, and athletes had longer self-reported sleep and lower cognitive arousal. Among athletes, higher daytime sleepiness was associated with napping (OR 4.91), and each point higher on cognitive arousal was associated with lower odds of napping (OR 0.95).
tldr: Athletes nap about as often as active non-athletes, and napping among athletes is linked to daytime sleepiness and lower pre-sleep cognitive arousal rather than to poorer night sleep. About half of athletes did not nap, and many non-nappers said napping would hurt their night sleep or that they could not fall asleep when they tried.
methods: Cross-sectional online survey (Qualtrics) of athletes at least semi-elite and non-athlete controls who were active at WHO activity levels but not competitive. Measures included the PSQI, Pre-sleep Arousal Scale, Epworth Sleepiness Scale, GAD-7, FIRST and rMEQ, plus single items on napping. Analyses used age-adjusted ANCOVA, chi-square and logistic regression in SPSS 27.
findings: Nap prevalence was 51.3% in athletes and 36.6% in non-athletes, a non-significant age-adjusted difference (OR 0.63, 95% CI 0.35-1.13). Athletes had longer self-reported total sleep time (456 vs 419 minutes, p<0.001) and lower cognitive arousal, but PSQI global scores did not differ. Among athletes, higher daytime sleepiness predicted napping (OR 4.91, 95% CI 2.38-10.13) and each 1-point rise in cognitive arousal lowered the odds of napping (OR 0.95, 95% CI 0.89-0.99); in the combined athlete and non-athlete sample, nappers with lower sleepiness had lower cognitive arousal than non-nappers (difference 4.2 points, p=.005). Team and individual sport athletes had similar nap prevalence (51.9% vs 50.6%), but individual sport athletes had higher somatic and cognitive arousal and higher sleep reactivity.
limitations: The sample was recruited through convenience methods and was not random, and women were over-represented. The authors note the large number of comparisons, though they used Bonferroni post-hoc tests. The Discussion gives the female share of athletes as 61.7% while Table 1 gives 64.6%, the team (76) and individual (80) groups sum to 156 rather than 158, and the single napping item and self-report measures limit what the data can show.
practicalImplications: Staff should not assume that athletes who avoid napping have adequate night sleep, because about half of athletes in this sample did not nap, many non-nappers gave a concern about night sleep as their reason, and non-nappers reported lower daytime sleepiness. Before recommending a planned nap, staff could ask athletes about daytime sleepiness and whether they can fall asleep in the day, then monitor the effect on night sleep.
athleteDev: For performance staff, the findings suggest that nap programs should account for individual differences in sleepiness and arousal, rather than assuming all athletes will benefit. Individual sport athletes in this sample reported higher arousal and sleep reactivity, so they may need different support for daytime sleep.
rtp: The study does not address return to sport or injury rehabilitation and included no injured athletes. Its nap and sleepiness findings should not be used to judge readiness to return to training or competition.

citation: Gupta L, Morgan K, North C, Gilchrist S. Napping in high-performance athletes: sleepiness or sleepability? Eur J Sport Sci. 2020.
abstract: Daytime napping in high-performance athletes is widely assumed to reflect sleepiness from sleep debt, but this has not been tested against a control group. In a two-trial laboratory study, elite (n=10), sub-elite (n=10) and non-athlete (n=10) participants had polysomnography-measured sleep latency during a single 20-minute nap opportunity. Elite athletes had shorter sleep latencies than controls on both trials, and Table 2 shows these elite differences remained significant after separate adjustment for 15:00 sleepiness and prior-night total sleep time; sub-elite results were less consistent, which the authors interpret as a gradient in sleepability.
tldr: Elite athletes fell asleep faster than matched controls during a daytime nap opportunity, and this was not fully explained by how sleepy they felt. The authors suggest some athlete napping may reflect a capacity to sleep on demand rather than sleep debt, but the sample of 30 is small.
methods: Two laboratory visits (adaptation and experimental trial) with a single polysomnography nap opportunity at 15:00 and a 20-minute maximum. Groups were elite and sub-elite athletes and active non-athlete controls recruited from a university population, with actigraphy screening for insomnia and sleep duration. Sleep latency and Karolinska Sleepiness Scale scores were compared using regression models adjusted for pre-trial sleepiness or total sleep time, with Fisher's exact tests for the proportion with high sleep tendency.
findings: Elite athletes had shorter sleep latencies than controls in both trials (10.4 vs 16.3 minutes on the adaptation trial, p=0.02; 7.9 vs 13.7 minutes on the experimental trial, p=0.02), and Table 2 shows adjusted elite differences of about 6 minutes, all p<0.05. Sub-elite athletes had shorter latencies than controls on the adaptation trial (8.0 vs 16.3 minutes, p=0.001) but not significantly on the experimental trial (9.1 minutes, p=0.055 unadjusted; p=0.07 after adjustment for total sleep time). High sleep tendency (latency 8 minutes or less) was reached by 2, 8 and 5 of 10 controls, sub-elite and elite athletes in the adaptation trial and by 2, 6 and 8 of 10 in the experimental trial (both Fisher's exact p<0.05).
limitations: Only 10 participants per group, and the authors note reduced power and unstable group means in the experimental trial; pre-trial training was not controlled. The abstract's 'all p<0.05' applies only to the elite group: the sub-elite TST-adjusted experimental difference was p=0.07 and the KSS-adjusted experimental model overall was p=0.07. Table 2 prints high-sleep-tendency percentages as shares of all high-tendency participants (for example 13.3%, 53.3%, 33.3%) rather than of each group of 10, and some adjusted confidence intervals are printed without negative signs.
practicalImplications: Staff should not assume that a teammate who naps easily is sleep-deprived, since in this small study elite athletes fell asleep quickly without being sleepier than controls. The results suggest that athletes who settle quickly into a new sleep environment may cope better with travel and camps, but this needs replication before it is used to select or monitor athletes.
athleteDev: The study does not test performance, so its implications for training are indirect. It suggests that the ability to fall asleep on demand may differ between athletes, which could matter for nap scheduling around training loads, but the study does not show whether naps help performance.
rtp: The study does not involve injured athletes, and it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. Sleep latency during a lab nap should not be used to judge an injured athlete's recovery or readiness.

citation: Thomas K, Brownstein CG, Dent J, Parker P, Goodall S, Howatson G. Neuromuscular Fatigue and Recovery after Heavy Resistance, Jump, and Sprint Training. Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise. 2018;50(12):2526-2535.
abstract: In 10 male athletes, heavy-resistance, jump and sprint sessions performed with maximal intent produced neuromuscular fatigue that took up to 72 hours to resolve. Potentiated twitch force remained reduced for 48 hours after all sessions, and voluntary activation was reduced for 24 to 48 hours. The authors conclude that this fatigue is multifactorial and not primarily central.
tldr: Heavy strength, jump and sprint sessions performed with maximal intent reduced maximal force and twitch force for 48 hours in ten male athletes, with recovery by 72 hours. Central fatigue recovered faster than peripheral fatigue, and the authors give partial support to separating such sessions by at least 48 hours when peak performance matters.
methods: Crossover design in which 10 male athletes completed three sessions a week apart in randomized order: 10 sets of 5 back squats at 80% 1RM, 10 sets of 5 jump squats, and 15 sprints of 30 m. Before, immediately after, and at 24, 48 and 72 hours, the authors measured maximal isometric force, voluntary activation, twitch force, corticospinal excitability and intracortical inhibition, plus soreness, perceived fatigue and creatine kinase.
findings: All three sessions reduced maximal isometric force for 48 hours, with average decrements of 8% (strength), 7% (jump) and 6% (sprint), and values were back to baseline at 72 hours. Potentiated quadriceps twitch force was reduced at 48 hours after every session, and was lower immediately after the strength session than after the jump and sprint sessions. Voluntary activation was reduced for 24 hours after jump and sprint sessions and for 48 hours after the strength session, while corticospinal excitability and intracortical inhibition did not change.
limitations: The sessions could not be matched for training load, so between-session differences should be treated with caution, and the authors note that the jump session may have differed in muscle damage and work. The sample was small and all male, and the exercises were limited to high-volume sessions that may not reflect typical training. The authors also note that measurement tools for central fatigue have limited validity.
practicalImplications: When peak performance is the priority, the authors give partial support to separating maximal-intent strength, jump or sprint sessions by at least 48 hours, since most measures took up to 72 hours to return to baseline. Monitoring should include peripheral and perceptual measures, because the authors found the residual fatigue to be multifactorial.
athleteDev: Performance staff can use the time course (force and twitch deficits at 48 hours, recovered by 72 hours; perceived fatigue raised for 24 hours after jumps and 48 hours after strength and sprints; soreness raised for 48 hours) when planning maximal-intent lower-body sessions. Because the study used high-volume, single-exercise sessions, these timings should not be applied directly to varied programs.
rtp: The study uses healthy trained men and does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport. Its fatigue timeline may inform load planning, but it should not be used for return-to-play or clearance decisions.

citation: Juliff LE, Peiffer JJ, Halson SL. Night Games and Sleep: Physiological, Neuroendocrine, and Psychometric Mechanisms. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2018. Ahead of print.
abstract: In 12 netball athletes, sleep after a night game was shorter, less efficient and ended earlier than sleep on a time-matched rest day. Adrenaline and noradrenaline were higher around the game, but they did not correlate with sleep, while higher trait hyperarousal was associated with lower sleep efficiency.
tldr: After a 6 pm netball game, these 12 athletes slept less, woke earlier and had lower sleep efficiency than on a rest day. Catecholamine and cortisol changes did not track with the sleep loss, but higher trait hyperarousal was linked to poorer sleep efficiency.
methods: Observational crossover design in 12 netball athletes, comparing an evening international game (6 pm start) with a time-matched rest day that took place 10 days later. Sleep was monitored for two weeks with diaries and Actiware-scored wrist actigraphy. Measures included core temperature by ingestible telemetry pill, salivary cortisol at eight time points, 24-hour urinary adrenaline and noradrenaline, the Pre-Sleep Arousal Scale, the Karolinska Sleep Questionnaire, and a trait hyperarousal scale. Analysis used paired t tests, two-way repeated-measures ANOVA and Spearman correlations.
findings: Compared with the rest day, the night game produced a shorter sleep duration (P = .02, d = 1.13), lower sleep efficiency (P < .001, d = 0.73) and earlier wake times (P <= .01, d = 0.959). Eleven of 12 athletes had objectively shorter sleep, with reductions of 15 to 140 minutes. Adrenaline (main effect P = .02) and noradrenaline (main effect P < .01) were higher across the game day, and cortisol was higher on the morning of the game, immediately after the game and one hour after it. Bedtime cortisol and bedtime core temperature did not differ between conditions. Trait hyperarousal was negatively correlated with sleep efficiency (rs = -0.611, P <= .01), while the catecholamine and cortisol measures were not correlated with sleep variables.
limitations: Twelve athletes is a small convenience sample, which the authors acknowledge may limit significance. The rest day always followed the game by 10 days, so the order of conditions was not counterbalanced, and match-day load was not analysed. Inference: the hyperarousal correlation is reported with 23 degrees of freedom, which does not match 12 athletes, so the unit of analysis is unclear.
practicalImplications: Plan for shorter, lower-quality sleep after evening games, and build recovery time around the likely earlier wake-up. The authors suggest targeting hyperarousal in susceptible athletes, since higher trait scorers slept less efficiently. Bedtime cortisol and core temperature (about 3 hours after the game) and catecholamines did not correlate with sleep here, so they should not be used to predict post-game sleep.
athleteDev: Evening competition shortened and reduced the quality of sleep in these netball athletes, which can cut into recovery between games in a tournament. The hyperarousal result suggests that athletes with higher trait arousal may need individual sleep support after night games. The findings come from one game in a small group and are not a basis for fixed training rules.
rtp: The study does not address return to sport after injury or illness, and it cannot be used to judge readiness to play. It describes sleep after a single night game in athletes who were in national age-group teams, so it may inform recovery planning after a late game, but not medical clearance.

citation: Margolis LM, Pasiakos SM. Low carbohydrate availability impairs hypertrophy and anaerobic performance. Current Opinion in Clinical Nutrition and Metabolic Care. 2023;26(4):347-352.
abstract: This narrative review summarises mechanistic, acute and short-term studies of dietary carbohydrate restriction on muscle protein regulation, body composition, strength and anaerobic performance. The authors conclude that low-carbohydrate intake increases branched-chain amino acid oxidation and may blunt hypertrophy, while muscle strength does not appear to be impaired. They also report that low muscle glycogen impairs supramaximal exercise capacity.
tldr: Carbohydrate restriction appears to increase amino acid oxidation and may blunt hypertrophy, but most of the evidence is acute or confounded by energy deficit. Strength does not appear to be reduced, and low muscle glycogen reduces high-intensity and sprint capacity.
methods: Narrative review in Current Opinion in Clinical Nutrition and Metabolic Care. The authors summarise acute, mechanistic and short-term studies on carbohydrate restriction and muscle protein regulation, and draw on a systematic review by Coleman et al. (13 studies, 21 to 84 days), a narrative review of glycogen and high-intensity exercise, and a systematic review of strength outcomes. No literature search method is described.
findings: Acute 24-hour low-carbohydrate feeding increased branched-chain amino acid oxidation and reduced myogenic regulator transcription compared with mixed feeding. In Coleman et al., low-carbohydrate diets with exercise training produced greater losses of body and fat mass than mixed diets, and fat-free mass fell by 0.3 kg versus a gain of 0.7 kg on the mixed diet, a 1 kg difference. Across studies of 2 to 84 days, strength was not reduced, and glycogen below about 200 mmol/kg dry weight reduced time to exhaustion and repeated sprint performance.
limitations: No search method or quality appraisal is described, and the review is a narrative synthesis rather than a systematic one. Most mechanistic data come from acute human studies, cell culture and mouse models, and the authors note there is no consensus on the effect of glycogen on mTORC1 signalling. Many studies did not control energy intake, so body composition changes may reflect energy deficit, and the Coleman fat-free mass difference is described by the authors as modest and heterogeneous. The Summary states that restriction impairs hypertrophy, while the body of the text says it may blunt hypertrophy. The sample size of the 8-week bodybuilder study is not given in the text.
practicalImplications: The review supports advising athletes who need high-intensity exercise to avoid severe or prolonged carbohydrate restriction, because low muscle glycogen reduces supramaximal capacity. Short-term strength does not appear to be reduced by low-carbohydrate diets, but this should not be read as evidence that hypertrophy is unaffected over the long term.
athleteDev: Performance Application: The review links glycogen below about 200 mmol/kg dry weight to reduced repeated-sprint and time-to-exhaustion performance, which is relevant to sport. Strength does not appear to be impaired in studies of 2 to 84 days, but long-term effects on hypertrophy and performance are unclear.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: The review suggests from acute markers that low carbohydrate availability may impair muscle remodelling and repair, but it did not study injured athletes or return to sport. It cannot inform return-to-play timing, rehabilitation nutrition targets or clearance.

citation: Witard OC, Bannock L, Tipton KD. Making Sense of Muscle Protein Synthesis: A Focus on Muscle Growth During Resistance Training. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2021 (ahead of print).
abstract: This narrative review examines whether acute muscle protein synthesis responses to resistance exercise and nutrition predict chronic muscle hypertrophy during resistance training. The authors discuss physiological and methodological factors that limit this relationship and offer practical implications for practitioners.
tldr: A single acute muscle protein synthesis response to exercise and protein does not reliably predict an individual's muscle growth, especially early in training. It can still help compare nutrition strategies at group level, but not by quantity.
methods: A narrative review with no described search strategy. The authors evaluate studies that measured acute muscle protein synthesis after resistance exercise and nutrition, mostly with stable isotope methods, and related these to hypertrophy after resistance training. They also discuss physiological factors (training status, individual variability and translational capacity) and methodological factors (timing of biopsies, the measurement method and the different definitions of hypertrophy).
findings: Mitchell et al. (23 untrained young men, 16 weeks) found no correlation between myofibrillar synthesis measured over 6 hours after the first session and the change in quadriceps volume (r = .10). Mayhew et al. (36 untrained men and women, 16 weeks) found no correlation between mixed-muscle synthesis and muscle mass change. In Damas et al. (10 untrained young men, 10 weeks), synthesis at week 1 did not correlate with muscle change, whereas synthesis at week 3 correlated with change in vastus lateralis cross-sectional area (r = .9, p = .002). The authors conclude that acute synthesis responses do not predict individual hypertrophy, noting that individual responses can vary by as much as 100%, but can predict average hypertrophy at group level.
limitations: The review describes no search method, so study selection cannot be checked, and it relies on a small number of studies with 10 to 36 participants. All Table 1 studies enrolled untrained participants, so the authors' practical statement that MPS 'will translate to chronic adaptations in muscle mass only in trained individuals' is not tested directly in trained athletes. The authors also note measurement limits of both synthesis and hypertrophy methods.
practicalImplications: Staff should not use a single acute synthesis result to predict how much muscle an individual athlete will gain. The authors suggest acute synthesis studies remain useful as a starting point for comparing protein sources and interventions at group level, with expectations managed because some athletes will not respond. Quantitative differences in synthesis should not be converted into predicted differences in hypertrophy.
athleteDev: For athlete programming, the review supports treating acute protein-synthesis findings as a starting point for trying a nutrition or training strategy, with the individual athlete's response checked over time. It does not support using these findings as a guarantee of muscle gain.
rtp: The review does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport. Its material on muscle damage concerns healthy adults after unaccustomed eccentric exercise, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions.

citation: Pușcaș A, Buț MG, Vari CE, Ősz BE, Ștefănescu R, Filip C, et al. Meldonium supplementation in professional athletes: career destroyer or lifesaver? Cureus. 2024;16(7):e63634.
abstract: The authors describe meldonium's proposed effects on carnitine metabolism, mitochondrial function, oxidative stress and inflammation. They discuss whether these effects could protect the heart of athletes, while noting that meldonium is on the WADA prohibited list.
tldr: Meldonium is banned for competing athletes, and its proposed mechanisms, such as reduced fatty acid oxidation and less oxidative stress, come mostly from animal and cell studies. The review does not show improved endurance or heart health in athletes.
methods: Narrative review of animal, cell and clinical literature on meldonium, with no search method reported. The authors describe its carnitine-related mechanisms, its effects in animal models of mitochondrial dysfunction and inflammation, and its use in cardiac patients.
findings: Meldonium inhibits the enzyme that makes carnitine and shifts fatty acid oxidation toward peroxisomes, which the authors propose reduces acyl-carnitine build-up and oxidative stress. In animal models it reduced mitochondrial DNA damage, oxidative stress and inflammation, including in a rat sepsis model. The human evidence cited comes from trials in patients with heart failure and in a phase 2 trial of 512 patients with stable angina, where exercise tolerance improved in a dose-dependent way, and the authors state that few human studies link meldonium to sports performance.
limitations: The review gives no search or appraisal method, and most mechanistic evidence comes from animal, cell and fish studies. The cited human trials are in heart failure and angina patients rather than athletes, and no athlete performance or cardiac data are reported. The authors' claims that meldonium improves endurance and that no negative effects have been shown in athletes are not supported by data presented in the review.
practicalImplications: Staff should treat meldonium as a WADA-listed prohibited metabolic modulator (S4 list since 2016) and confirm its current status before advising any athlete. It should not be presented as a cardioprotective supplement, because the review's support for that is mechanistic, animal-based or from cardiac patients. The review notes that athletic heart changes can be hard to distinguish from cardiomyopathy, which is a reason for clinical assessment rather than self-treatment.
athleteDev: Performance staff should not plan around meldonium as an endurance or recovery aid, because the performance claims rest on mechanistic and animal evidence and the substance is prohibited in competition.
rtp: The review concerns the metabolic and cardiac mechanisms of a prohibited substance and does not evaluate rehabilitation or return to sport after injury or illness. It should not be used to decide when an athlete can return to training or competition.

citation: Burke LM, Peeling P. Methodologies for Investigating Performance Changes With Supplement Use. International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism. 2018.
abstract: This scholarly review sets out how performance supplement studies should be designed, controlled and interpreted so that claims about sports performance can be tested. It covers crossover and parallel designs, blinding, confounding variables, combined and repeated supplement use, and whether small changes are meaningful in competition.
tldr: Supplement studies need well-trained athletes, reliable performance tests, good controls and realistic protocols before their results can guide practice. Combined and repeated supplement use have been poorly studied.
methods: Narrative scholarly review. The authors discuss design options (crossover, parallel, stratified and matched allocation), blinding and presentation of treatments, confounding variables, and interpretation of individual responses and small performance changes, with examples from several supplements. No systematic search method is described.
findings: The authors state that the supplement evidence base is limited by small samples, weak methods and few studies of combined or repeated use. They note that crossover designs need fewer athletes but may need washout periods. They recommend reporting percentage change with 90 to 95% confidence limits and a smallest worthwhile change, warn that apparent individual responses are often confused with day-to-day variability, and note that gains of about 0.5 to 1% may matter in competition.
limitations: The authors describe the review as brief and acknowledge that many supplement studies are small and of limited quality. The examples are illustrative rather than a systematic synthesis.
practicalImplications: When judging a supplement study, check whether it used well-trained athletes, a reliable performance test, a placebo and a protocol that matches the event, and whether claims about responders account for normal day-to-day variability. The review also notes that combined and repeated use are poorly studied, so benefits seen with a single use may not carry over.
athleteDev: Before a supplement is added to a program, check whether the evidence used a test that matches the event and whether any claimed individual responses were confirmed with repeated trials. The review does not show that any particular supplement improves performance.
rtp: This review concerns performance supplements in competition and does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions.

citation: Wardenaar FC, Burns SF, Campos M, Chan Y, Claassen-Smithers A, Dunshea-Mooij C, et al. Navigating the Risks Beyond the Label: Unpacking Global Nutritional Supplement Safety. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2025 (ahead of print).
abstract: Global overview of nutritional supplement use among athletes, relevant authorities, legislation and safety measures, with a focus on third-party testing (TPT). Data were drawn from peer-reviewed studies, government sources and regional expert contributions across six world regions. Reported use ranged from 7% to 100%, higher-risk products such as herbal blends, preworkouts and weight-management products were reported in all regions, and TPT was concentrated in Europe, North America and Australia/New Zealand.
tldr: Supplement use among athletes is widespread, and products such as preworkouts, herbal blends and weight-loss products carry a higher risk of banned substances in every region. Third-party tested products are concentrated in a few countries, so athletes in other regions face greater anti-doping and health risks.
methods: Scholarly review with six regional sections written by two to three co-authors per region, combining desk research with local performance nutrition input. Co-authors listed relevant studies from PubMed and Google Scholar, preferring studies from 2014 to 2025 of elite adult athletes, and classified athlete tiers using the McKay et al. framework. The authors also listed national authorities, legislation and TPT programs, and included anecdotes from stakeholders. No systematic search protocol, screening or quality appraisal is reported.
findings: Reported supplement use ranged from 7% (Nepal national athletes) to 100% (several studies), with protein, multivitamins, creatine, caffeine and sports drinks most common. The authors cite analytical studies in which 14% to 50% of tested supplements were positive for prohibited substances, and a Duiven et al. study in which at least one in five supplements contained ingredients not on the label. TPT use among athletes was reported at 18% to 85%, mostly in Western countries. The text also cites an estimate that about 9% of US doping cases involved nutritional supplements.
limitations: The review acknowledges that studies on supplement use lack methodological standardization, differ in recall period and assessment method, and that TPT use data come mainly from Western countries. The anecdotes are described by the authors as subjective and drawn from memory, and several authors disclose supplement-industry ties, including one author employed by a company that sells dietary supplements. Recommendations, such as a food-first approach and harmonized TPT standards, are author consensus rather than tested interventions.
practicalImplications: Staff should ask athletes to check whether any product they use is third-party tested for banned substances, and to record the batch or lot number. Preworkouts, fat burners, herbal blends and products bought from unregulated sources or compounding pharmacies should be treated as higher risk, and athletes should be warned that supplements may contain ingredients not listed on the label.
athleteDev: For performance staff, the review supports choosing supplements through a team policy and a food-first approach, with TPT products where a supplement is needed. Performance benefits are not assessed in the review, so the choice of supplement should rest on evidence for the specific purpose and on anti-doping risk.
rtp: The review does not address rehabilitation or return to sport. Its concern with contaminated and undeclared ingredients is relevant to medications and recovery products used after injury, so medical staff should check any product used during rehabilitation against the anti-doping rules.

citation: Martin K, Meeusen R, Thompson KG, Keegan R, Rattray B. Mental Fatigue Impairs Endurance Performance: A Physiological Explanation. Sports Medicine. 2018.
abstract: This theoretical review proposes that extracellular cerebral adenosine accumulates during demanding cognitive work and increases perceived exertion and reduces motivation during later endurance exercise. The authors review evidence to support and extend this hypothesis, noting that heart rate, lactate and neuromuscular function are generally unaffected by mental fatigue.
tldr: Mental fatigue appears to impair endurance mainly by raising perceived exertion, and the authors propose that adenosine built up during demanding cognitive work is the cause. This remains a hypothesis that has not been tested directly in humans.
methods: Theoretical narrative review. It draws on animal pharmacology, human caffeine and sleep deprivation studies, and brain imaging work. No systematic search method is described.
findings: The review states that mental fatigue impairs endurance performance and that heart rate, lactate and neuromuscular function are generally unaffected. It proposes that adenosine acting in the anterior cingulate cortex raises perceived exertion and impairs motivation through an interaction with dopamine. The authors note that adenosine has not been directly evaluated for effects on perceived exertion during exercise in humans.
limitations: The authors acknowledge that adenosine is probably one of several contributors and that direct measurement of adenosine in humans is not currently possible. The review contains no new data, and its mechanism depends on animal and indirect pharmacological evidence.
practicalImplications: The review suggests that reducing adenosine build-up during mental exertion might lessen the effect of mental fatigue on endurance, but this has not been tested. The authors note that self-report is the only available measure of motivation and is prone to social desirability bias, so motivation ratings should be read with caution.
athleteDev: The review suggests that mentally fatigued athletes may fail endurance efforts through higher perceived exertion, while heart rate and lactate are not affected. The adenosine mechanism remains a hypothesis and should not yet change training or competition plans.
rtp: The review does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions.

citation: Habay J, Arenales Arauz YL, Proost M, Schampheleer E, Lathouwers E, De Pauw K, et al. Mental Fatigue Negatively Impacts Cognitive and Physical Performance Outcomes: A Large-Scale Randomized Crossover Trial. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2026;58(2):225-241.
abstract: A randomized crossover trial in 117 healthy adults compared a 45-minute Stroop task with a documentary before a GoNoGo task and a 20-minute cycling time trial. The Stroop task slowed GoNoGo reaction time and increased mental fatigue, RPE and sleepiness during the time trial, and cadence was lower after it. The time-trial distance difference was only a trend (P = 0.059).
tldr: In healthy adults, 45 minutes of a Stroop task slowed a GoNoGo reaction time task and raised perceived fatigue and effort during a cycling time trial. The effect on time-trial distance was small and not statistically significant, so the physical effect is weaker than the title suggests.
methods: Healthy adults aged 18 to 50 completed a familiarization visit and then two counterbalanced visits, one with a 45-minute individualized Stroop task and one with a documentary. Outcomes were GoNoGo performance, a 20-minute cycling time trial and subjective ratings, analysed with paired t tests, mixed models and non-parametric tests.
findings: Go reaction time after the task was slower in the Stroop condition (380.45 vs 367.30 ms; interaction P < 0.001). Time-trial distance was 12.6 vs 12.8 km (P = 0.059, d = 0.20) and cadence was 87 vs 88 rpm (P = 0.042, d = 0.22). Power output, workload, heart rate, lactate, motivation and Go and NoGo accuracy did not differ, while mental fatigue, physical fatigue and RPE (P = 0.002) were higher during the time trial and sleepiness was higher overall in the Stroop condition.
limitations: The distance and cadence effects are small and vary widely between individuals, and the authors say the 45-minute induction may not have been long enough to show the full cognitive effect. The analysed sample is unclear (117 in the baseline table versus 104 who completed all steps), and only one induction protocol in healthy adults aged 18 to 50 was tested.
practicalImplications: A demanding cognitive task before a hard effort may make the effort feel harder and slightly reduce cadence, so cognitive load is worth considering before testing or hard sessions. The physical effects were small and the distance result was not statistically significant, so the study does not justify large changes to training or competition plans.
athleteDev: A prolonged demanding cognitive task before exercise may raise perceived effort and reduce cadence in a cycling time trial, with only a small and non-significant effect on distance. The study used a laboratory Stroop task in healthy adults, so its effect size should be read as an estimate for this design, not a sport-specific prediction.
rtp: The study tested healthy adults and did not assess injured athletes or return-to-sport tasks, so it cannot guide return-to-play decisions.

citation: Zivadinov R, Polak P, Schweser F, Bergsland N, Hagemeier J, Dwyer MG, et al. Multimodal Imaging of Retired Professional Contact Sport Athletes Does Not Provide Evidence of Structural and Functional Brain Damage. Journal of Head Trauma Rehabilitation. 2018.
abstract: This 3 tesla multimodal MRI study compared 21 retired professional football and hockey players with 21 age-matched noncontact sport athletes. It found no significant group differences in white matter abnormalities, brain volumes, diffusion, susceptibility, spectroscopy or perfusion measures.
tldr: In 21 retired professional football and hockey players compared with 21 noncontact athletes, a multimodal MRI battery found no significant differences in brain structure, diffusion, iron, metabolism or perfusion. The sample was too small to rule out smaller effects, so the result is not evidence that contact sport is safe for the brain.
methods: Substudy of a larger project of retired athletes; 21 retired contact sport athletes and 21 age-matched noncontact athletes were scanned on a 3 tesla scanner with proton-density/T2, FLAIR, 3D T1, diffusion (tract-based spatial statistics), susceptibility (QSM and microbleeds), single-voxel spectroscopy and perfusion sequences. Group differences were tested with ANCOVA adjusted for age, body mass index and education, with Cohen's d and Cramer's V effect sizes.
findings: Twelve of 21 contact athletes (57.1%) and 11 of 21 controls (52.4%) had white matter signal abnormalities, with no significant differences in lesion measures or in global and regional brain volumes. No diffusion, susceptibility, spectroscopy or perfusion measures differed significantly between groups, and microbleeds were present in 2 of 21 contact athletes (9.5%) versus 7 of 21 controls (33%; P = .067). The authors report the effect sizes and 95% confidence intervals so readers can judge the size of the differences, which were not significant.
limitations: The authors state that the sample was too small to detect differences in the brain measures and refer other limitations to the companion paper. Several perfusion and susceptibility comparisons show moderate to large effect sizes (for example, accumbens mean transit time d = 0.97) and 95% confidence intervals that exclude zero while the covariate-adjusted P values are non-significant, Table 2 gives a globus pallidus mean diffusivity of 0.5 for controls against 0.87 for athletes (effect size 6.95), which looks like a reporting error, and the mild cognitive impairment subgroup comparison mentioned in the discussion is not shown.
practicalImplications: Staff should not present this study as evidence that retired contact athletes have normal brains, because it was too small to detect moderate differences. It tested group differences, not individual diagnosis, so it gives no basis for using these MRI measures to judge an individual athlete's brain health.
athleteDev: The study measures brain structure and perfusion, not performance, so it has no direct training or performance application. The paper does not report cognitive test results, so staff should not cite it as reassurance about long-term cognitive performance.
rtp: The study compares retired athletes and does not examine current players or those after a head injury, so it cannot guide return to play or clearance after concussion. A normal-appearing MRI in this study does not support clearing an injured athlete.

citation: Ng T, Sanders H, Merrill S, Faustin M. Media's effect on athletes' mental health. Clin Sports Med. 2023.
abstract: The authors review how traditional and social media affect athletes' mental health. They cover media obligations, coverage of female and minoritized athletes, social media use, and the pressure of media attention on elite athletes.
tldr: Media attention can add real stress for elite athletes, female athletes receive less and more appearance-focused coverage, and athletes from minoritized backgrounds can face stereotyped coverage and online abuse. Research on athletes' mental health and social media is still limited.
methods: Narrative clinical review with no search method reported. The authors describe media obligations by competition level, summarise studies of media coverage and social media, and draw on high-profile cases and small qualitative studies of athletes.
findings: Professional and Olympic athletes are usually required by written agreements to speak to the media, and collegiate athletes often need administrative approval. The authors report that female athletes receive less media coverage than male athletes, and that coverage often focuses on appearance. Qualitative studies describe media attention as a source of stress for elite athletes, including a study of four male and six female athletes who had each won at least two gold medals. The authors also cite a systematic review of 13 studies linking social media use to depression, anxiety and distress in the general population, and state that no major studies address athletes' mental health and social media directly.
limitations: The review gives no search or appraisal method, and the authors note that little research addresses athletes' mental health and social media directly. Much of the cited evidence comes from general-population or small qualitative studies, and several examples are high-profile news cases.
practicalImplications: Sports medicine staff can check whether athletes understand their media obligations and have media training, particularly collegiate athletes who face NIL-related pressure to build an online presence. Periods of heavy media attention, such as major events, title wins and difficult losses, are reasonable times to check in, since the cited qualitative studies link them with stress. The review does not offer screening tools or thresholds.
athleteDev: Include media preparation and a check on media pressure in athlete support planning, especially around major events and for athletes building a social media profile. Treat coverage of female and minoritized athletes as a context factor rather than a predictable effect on any individual.
rtp: This review covers media effects on the mental health of competitive athletes. It does not address concussion, injury recovery or return-to-play decisions and should not be used to guide return to sport after injury.

citation: Hoare E, Reyes J, Olive L, Willmott C, Steer E, Berk M, et al. Neurodiversity in elite sport: a systematic scoping review. BMJ Open Sport and Exercise Medicine. 2023;9:e001575.
abstract: A systematic scoping review of 23 studies on neurodivergence (mainly ADHD, also autism and specific learning disorders) in elite sport, searched to May 2023. The studies were 10 observational studies, 4 reviews, 6 commentary or position statements and 3 qualitative studies. The authors found very limited research, mostly on ADHD in US college athletes, and no intervention studies.
tldr: Research on neurodivergent athletes in elite sport is very limited and mostly concerns ADHD, concussion and medication rules. The authors conclude that neurodiversity-inclusive practice is not yet evidence-based in elite sport.
methods: Systematic scoping review following PRISMA-ScR, with six databases searched through the EBSCOhost platform to 12 May 2023 and reference lists checked. Title and abstract screening was done by one author, a second reviewer checked 10% of articles, and a third reviewer resolved discrepancies.
findings: Of 23 included studies, 10 were observational, mostly in US college athletes, and most focused on ADHD as a risk factor for concussion and its management. Other work covered ADHD prevalence, stimulant medication under anti-doping rules, and lived experience from three qualitative studies, one of which examined autism in elite French athletes. The authors found no studies of interventions or environmental practices for neurodivergent athletes.
limitations: The authors note small sample sizes and self-report measures of neurodevelopmental differences, which are open to individual bias. Grey literature was not searched, and the authors acknowledge that relevant studies may have been missed. The definition of athlete populations varied across studies.
practicalImplications: The authors state that coaches and performance staff need education on the sensory, emotional and cognitive needs of neurodivergent athletes, and that healthcare staff would likely benefit as well. Staff should note that evidence-based inclusive practices are limited in elite sport.
athleteDev: Performance and coaching staff may need to understand neurodivergent athletes, since learning and skill development are central to performance. The review found no studies of performance outcomes or coaching approaches for neurodivergent athletes, and any performance advantage linked to ADHD or autism is unconfirmed.
rtp: The review does not address return to sport or rehabilitation. It reports that ADHD may affect baseline concussion screening performance and that findings on prolonged concussion recovery remain mixed. It provides no return-to-play criteria and should not be used to set return-to-play decisions for neurodivergent athletes.

citation: Pérez-Castilla A, Jukic I, Janicijevic D, Akyildiz Z, Senturk D, García-Ramos A. Load-Velocity Relationship Variables to Assess the Maximal Neuromuscular Capacities During the Back-Squat Exercise. Sports Health. 2022.
abstract: Twenty-four male national-level wrestlers completed 1RM and load-velocity testing during concentric-only and eccentric-concentric back squats on a Smith machine. Aline was highly reliable, L0 and v0 had acceptable CVs but lower ICCs, and L0 and Aline were strongly associated with 1RM and Pmax. The authors conclude that load-velocity variables are a quick, simple estimate of maximal force and power capacity during the back squat.
tldr: A short load-velocity test on the back squat gave reliable estimates of maximal strength and power in national-level male wrestlers. The area under the line (Aline) was the most reliable variable, and the velocity-axis intercept (v0) was the least reliable.
methods: Twenty-four male wrestlers completed a 1RM session and four experimental sessions (two concentric-only and two eccentric-concentric back squats) on a Smith machine, with at least 48 hours between sessions. Each session used 3 repetitions at 45%, 55%, 65%, 75% and 85% of 1RM, followed by 1RM attempts, with velocity recorded by a linear position transducer. Reliability was assessed with CV and ICC between sessions, and validity with correlations of L0 with 1RM and of Aline with Pmax.
findings: Aline had high between-session reliability (CV 2.58% to 4.37%; ICC 0.97 to 0.99, Table 1). L0 (CV 5.25% to 9.01%; ICC 0.77 to 0.91) and v0 (CV 5.08% to 8.66%; ICC 0.45 to 0.72) had CVs within the acceptable range, but all v0 ICCs and the eccentric-concentric average-score L0 ICC were below 0.80 and are flagged in Table 1 as unacceptable; no significant between-session differences were found (P >= 0.23). L0 correlated very largely with 1RM (r = 0.87 to 0.88) and Aline nearly perfectly with Pmax (r = 0.98 to 0.99; all P < 0.001), and all three variables were more reliable with the concentric-only variant (CV ratio 1.49 to 1.65).
limitations: The sample was 24 male national-level wrestlers (age 19.1 +/- 3.4 years, some under 18) tested on a Smith machine, which restricts the bar to vertical movement and may limit generalizability to free-weight squatting and other athletes. The abstract gives ICC ranges of 0.98 to 0.99 for Aline and 0.45 to 0.96 for L0 and v0, but Table 1 gives 0.97 to 0.99 and 0.45 to 0.91, so table values are reported here. The authors call L0 and v0 reliability acceptable, but by their own stated criteria (ICC >= 0.80) v0 ICCs were unacceptable in every condition; v0 validity was not tested and L-V variables lack a clear physiological meaning.
practicalImplications: Staff can use L0 and Aline from a Smith-machine back squat load-velocity profile as a quick estimate of maximal strength and power. The concentric-only variant gave more reliable values for all three variables, and v0 should not be tracked on its own given ICCs of 0.45 to 0.72.
athleteDev: The load-velocity profile can estimate maximal strength (L0) and maximal power (Aline) in male athletes using only velocity data and a few submaximal loads. Changes in v0 are less reproducible here (ICC 0.45 to 0.72), so they should not be used alone to judge training effects.
rtp: The study tested healthy wrestlers and did not assess injured athletes or rehabilitation outcomes, so it cannot be used to judge return-to-sport readiness.

citation: Picot B, Fourchet F, Lopes R, Rauline G, Freiha K, D'hooghe P, et al. Low Ankle-GO Score While Returning to Sport After Lateral Ankle Sprain Leads to a 9-fold Increased Risk of Recurrence: A Two-year Prospective Cohort Study. Sports Medicine - Open. 2024;10:23.
abstract: In 54 of 64 active patients followed for two years after a lateral ankle sprain, a two-month Ankle-GO score was lower in those who had a recurrent sprain (5.4 vs 9.1 points, p = 0.002; AUC 0.75). A score below 8 points was associated with higher recurrence odds (OR 8.6, 95% CI 2 to 37.2) in multivariable logistic regression. The authors report a non-significant trend toward higher recurrence in women (OR 3.8, 95% CI 0.9 to 15.5, p = 0.065).
tldr: A low Ankle-GO score two months after a lateral ankle sprain was associated with a later recurrence in this small cohort. Scores below 8 points gave an odds ratio of about 9 for recurrence, but the estimate is imprecise and has not been tested in a separate sample.
methods: Prospective cohort. Sixty-four active patients with a recent lateral ankle sprain completed the Ankle-GO score, which combines two questionnaires and four functional tests for 25 points, about two months after injury. Two years later a blinded assessor asked about recurrence, and 54 responded. Groups were compared with chi-square, t and Mann-Whitney tests, a Youden-index cut-off was derived, and stepwise logistic regression was used.
findings: Eighteen of 54 (33.3%) had a recurrent sprain, all non-contact. The two-month Ankle-GO score was 5.4 +/- 2.8 points in patients with recurrence and 9.1 +/- 4.5 without (p = 0.002), with AUC 0.75 (95% CI 0.62 to 0.88). The 8-point cut-off gave 83% sensitivity and 64% specificity. In the multivariable model the score was the only significant predictor, with OR 8.6 (95% CI 2 to 37.2) for a score below 8 points.
limitations: Only 18 recurrences, a cut-off chosen on the same data, and 15% loss to follow-up limit precision and generalisability. The nine-fold figure is an odds ratio, not a risk ratio. The p value for the odds ratio is 0.001 in the abstract and 0.004 in the results. Sex labels conflict: Methods give 36 women and 28 men, Table 1 header gives men/women as 36/28, and Table 3 lists 4 women and 14 men among reinjured patients. On the Table 3 counts, the reinjury proportion was lower in women (4 of 23) than in men (14 of 31), which contradicts the authors' sex conclusion; the reported women OR of 3.8 (95% CI 0.9 to 15.5, p = 0.065) is not significant. Rehabilitation content, injury severity and other known risk factors were not analysed.
practicalImplications: Use the Ankle-GO as one objective input alongside clinical judgement when deciding return to sport, rather than as a threshold that clears or blocks an athlete. A low score at two months may justify closer follow-up and rehabilitation of the deficits the patients showed, such as the SEBT and FAAM-ADL results, but an 8-point cut-off needs external validation before it is used as a fixed rule.
athleteDev: Performance Application: The study measured recurrence, not performance, so it does not show that the score predicts athletic performance. It may help identify which balance and hop deficits to address during late-stage rehabilitation.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: A score below 8 points at two months was associated with later recurrence, so it may flag athletes who benefit from further rehabilitation before full return. The study cannot show that a score of 8 or above makes return safe, and it does not establish a validated clearance threshold.

citation: Torres-Velazquez M, Wille CM, Hurley SA, Kijowski R, Heiderscheit BC, McMillan AB. MRI radiomics for hamstring strain injury identification and return to sport classification: a pilot study. Skeletal Radiol. 2023.
abstract: This pilot study tested whether MRI radiomics from the hamstring muscles of 32 collegiate athletes with a hamstring strain injury can separate injured from uninjured limbs and classify time to return to sport. Support vector classifiers were cross-validated using DTI, T2-weighted and T1-weighted features, and the best-performing combinations were reported for each task.
tldr: In a 32-athlete pilot, MRI radiomics features classified injured limbs and return-to-sport timing well in cross-validation. The approach is unvalidated on an external sample, so it is not ready for clinical decisions.
methods: MRI from 32 collegiate athletes (2017-2020) with an acute hamstring strain was analyzed, using T1-weighted, T2-weighted and diffusion tensor imaging, with four hamstring muscles segmented in each limb. A total of 101 PyRadiomics features per muscle and modality were extracted and fed to L1-penalized logistic regression feature selection (up to 25 features) and a radial basis function support vector classifier. Performance was assessed with 10-fold (binary) or 7-fold (multiclass) cross-validation repeated 10 times, using accuracy, AUC and weighted F1 scores; return to sport was defined by medical clearance, split at 25 days for the binary task and into under 14, 14 to 42 and over 42 days for the multiclass task.
findings: For involved versus uninvolved limbs, combined DTI and T2w features gave the highest mean test accuracy (0.842, SD 0.163) and AUC (0.844, SD 0.163), but were not significantly better than all DTI features or all features combined. For the binary return-to-sport task at 25 days (16 athletes per group), all radiomics combined gave accuracy 0.953 (SD 0.158) and AUC 0.958 (SD 0.150), and DTI alone gave accuracy 0.933. For the three-class task (7, 14 and 11 athletes), DTI features gave the highest weighted one-vs-rest AUC (0.809, SD 0.162); Table 4 prints a weighted F1 of 0.721 (SD 0.227) for this model, while the results text prints 0.93 (SD 0.19).
limitations: The sample was small (n = 32), and the authors acknowledge overfitting risk because there was no separate test dataset; the 25-day cutoff was chosen to balance groups and the multiclass groups were very small. Clinical return-to-sport tests were not compared, and the authors note clearance-based return to sport may be premature. The text has internal conflicts: the multiclass weighted F1 is 0.93 in the text but 0.721 in Table 4, the 14 to 42 day class is labelled '2-4 weeks', and Table 1 lists 26 primary injured muscles although 28 athletes had a BAMIC grade above 0.
practicalImplications: Radiomics should not be used to set return-to-sport dates for individual athletes on the basis of this study. Clinicians may note that MRI texture features from DTI and T2-weighted images separated injured from uninjured limbs in this cohort, and that larger, longitudinal datasets are needed before any clinical use.
athleteDev: This paper does not address training or performance. Its MRI features are not a validated performance or readiness measure and should not be used as one.
rtp: The study models time to return to sport, but only in cross-validation on 32 athletes, with clearance timing as the reference standard. It cannot be used to guide return-to-play decisions and provides no comparison with clinical return-to-sport tests.

citation: Haischer MH, Krzyszkowski J, Roche S, Kipp K. Maximal Strength in Relation to Force and Velocity Patterns During Countermovement Jumps. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2021.
abstract: The study examined how isometric midthigh pull peak force relates to time-series patterns of ground reaction force and center-of-mass velocity during countermovement jumps in female college lacrosse players. Principal components analysis was used to extract the patterns from the full jump waveforms.
tldr: In 19 female collegiate lacrosse players, stronger athletes showed countermovement jump patterns with higher eccentric rate of force development and higher peak force, while jump height did not correlate with strength. Waveform patterns may be more informative than discrete variables, but this needs replication.
methods: Nineteen female Division I lacrosse players completed up to three maximal countermovement jumps and three maximal isometric midthigh pulls in one session at the start of an off-season period. Force-plate data were time-normalized to 101 points and analysed by principal components analysis, and Spearman correlations with bootstrapped 95% CIs linked midthigh pull peak force to discrete jump variables and principal component scores.
findings: Midthigh pull peak force correlated with a ground reaction force pattern (PC2, rho 0.544, P = .016) that reflected higher eccentric rate of force development, higher peak force and a unimodal profile. It also correlated with a center-of-mass velocity pattern (PC2, rho 0.634, P = .004) that reflected higher concentric velocity, while it did not correlate with jump height (rho 0.308, P = .199) or other discrete jump variables.
limitations: The sample is 19 women from one team, the design is cross-sectional, and the authors state it is unknown whether the relationships change over a season or with training. The paper describes no correction for the many correlations tested, and the authors note that linear time normalization could change results.
practicalImplications: Coaches who test strength with the midthigh pull may find that jump waveform patterns relate to strength when jump height does not, so waveform analysis may add information to jump monitoring. The authors suggest the findings frame directional hypotheses for training studies rather than settled measures.
athleteDev: Performance staff can consider force-plate waveform analysis alongside peak-force testing to see how athletes produce jumps, which the authors suggest may help monitor change. The study does not test whether these patterns change with training or fatigue.
rtp: The study includes no injured athletes and does not address return to sport. Its jump waveform patterns have no established return-to-play thresholds.

citation: Osgnach C, di Prampero PE, Zamparo P, Morin JB, Pavei G. Mechanical and metabolic power in accelerated running Part II: team sports. Eur J Appl Physiol. 2024;124:417-431.
abstract: The authors discuss how velocity and acceleration together set mechanical and metabolic power in team sports. They use GPS data from 38 official matches of one Italian Serie B team to compare acceleration-count and power-based event counts, and they track metabolic power events across 15-minute periods.
tldr: Counting accelerations above a fixed 2.5 m/s2 threshold undercounts high-intensity efforts, and the undercount differs by position. Power-based and metabolic event counts describe match demands more completely, but they come from one team in one season.
