methods: Retrospective analysis of GPS data sampled at 18.18 Hz from 29 outfield players (549 match observations) over 38 official matches. Individual acceleration-speed profiles were built in situ from match data (320 profiles from 24 players; role averages for the other 5), and events were counted when external power exceeded 80% of each player's estimated maximal power (#burst) and when metabolic power exceeded an assumed VO2max of 18 W/kg (#MPE).
findings: For players who completed the full match, mechanical power events were 1.61 times the number of acceleration events above 2.5 m/s2 (2.30 for midfielders and 1.36 for attackers). Metabolic power events averaged 151.9 per match, and in full-match players their number fell from 28.1 to 21.4 per 15-minute period while the recovery between them rose from 25.5 s to 36.5 s.
limitations: The study covers one team and one season, with retrospective data and no outcome validation against performance or injury. The authors acknowledge that substitutions and tactical changes affect the late-match trends, and the thresholds (80% of maximal power, 2.5 m/s2, an assumed 18 W/kg for VO2max) were chosen by the authors. Two authors are scientific consultants for the company that supplied the GPS units.
practicalImplications: Staff profiling match demands should not rely on acceleration counts alone, because those counts undercount intense efforts unevenly across positions. Mechanical and metabolic power counts can be reported alongside them, with the threshold choices stated. Results from one squad should not be used as positional norms for other teams.
athleteDev: Use power-based event counts alongside acceleration counts when describing match demands by position, and compare each player with their own acceleration-speed profile rather than with a fixed threshold.
rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It describes match demands in professional players and gives no clinical or return-to-play criteria.

citation: di Prampero PE, Osgnach C. Metabolic Power in Team Sports - Part 1: An Update. International Journal of Sports Medicine. 2018;39:581-587.
abstract: Team-sport energy expenditure is estimated from GPS speed and acceleration by treating accelerated running as uphill running, and the update includes walking and air resistance. The updated model gives whole-match energy expenditure about 14% lower than the original approach, with air resistance about 2% of the total. The paper is theoretical and contains no new comparison with measured values.
tldr: A GPS-based model can estimate energy cost in team sports by treating accelerated running as uphill running, and the update separates walking from running. The authors' example suggests the earlier method overestimates match energy expenditure by about 14%.
methods: Theoretical update of an existing model, with equations for the energy cost of running and walking on an equivalent slope, a walk-to-run transition speed, and an air-resistance term. An illustrative average 90-minute match from 497 Serie A players is used, with the data cited as in preparation.
findings: In the example, air resistance accounts for about 1.7% of total energy expenditure and walking for about 25%. Treating all locomotion as running gives about 13.7% higher overall energy expenditure than the updated approach. The authors state that acceleration data need a sampling rate of at least 10 Hz, careful filtering and validation before the estimates are reliable.
limitations: The authors say the approach omits jumps, backward running, ball carrying, kicking and contact, and that it uses a linear extrapolation beyond the slopes Minetti et al. measured. They also assume the same energy cost of level running and the same coefficients for all players, and acknowledge these assumptions may not hold for individuals.
practicalImplications: The paper states that GPS acceleration data sampled below 10 Hz are highly questionable and that signal filtering and algorithms must be appropriately chosen and validated before the model is used. Practitioners should read the energy values as model estimates that depend on fixed assumptions for all players.
athleteDev: The model may allow drills and matches to be compared by energy demand, including walking, running and air resistance, using only GPS speed and acceleration. Its outputs are estimates that assume the same energy cost for every player and ignore jumps, kicking and contact, so they should not be read as measured energy expenditure.
rtp: The paper addresses match and training energetics and does not cover injury, rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions.

citation: Osgnach C, di Prampero PE. Metabolic Power in Team Sports - Part 2: Aerobic and Anaerobic Energy Yields. International Journal of Sports Medicine. 2018.
abstract: A GPS-based method estimates metabolic power and oxygen uptake in team sports, and this paper tests it against a portable metabolic cart and reports aerobic and anaerobic energy yields. Estimated oxygen uptake was close to measured values on average but varied by protocol, and match data show fewer high-intensity efforts later in a soccer match.
tldr: A GPS-based model estimated oxygen uptake fairly closely overall, but errors ranged from about 15% under to 20% over depending on the activity. Serie A match data suggest fewer high-intensity bouts later in the game, with longer low-intensity periods between them.
methods: A preliminary set of shuttle-run data from 9 subjects and a later experiment (subject number not stated) compared model-estimated oxygen uptake with breath-by-breath measurement from a portable metabolic cart during walking, constant running and three sprint protocols (straight, L-shaped and shuttle), with blood lactate sampled. A separate analysis applies the model to match data from 497 outfield players in 71 Serie A matches, cited as in preparation.
findings: Estimated oxygen uptake matched measured values for constant-speed walking, was about 20% higher for constant-speed running and about 15% lower for intermittent running. For one typical subject over a 47-minute trial, measured oxygen use was about 10% below estimated energy expenditure. In matches, the number of high-intensity bouts fell from 30 in the first 15 minutes to 23 in the last, with mean high-intensity power about 22 W/kg, while mean low-intensity power fell from about 5.8 to 4.8 W/kg.
limitations: The model assumes the same energy cost and oxygen kinetics for all players and does not correct for individual differences, and measured resting oxygen uptake rose by about 46% over the session. Match data and the detailed validation analysis are cited as in preparation, so they cannot be checked from this paper.
practicalImplications: The authors suggest that low-intensity periods and the recovery between high-intensity bouts deserve as much attention as the high-intensity bouts themselves. Practitioners should keep in mind that estimated oxygen use is approximate and that pre-exercise oxygen uptake rises during a session.
athleteDev: Match data in this paper suggest that high-intensity bouts become less frequent later in a match, with recovery between bouts lengthening, which may matter for late-game conditioning and recovery planning. The authors describe the estimates as reasonable but variable, so they are best used as approximate guides rather than exact physiological prescriptions.
rtp: The study uses soccer match and sprint protocols and does not measure injury or return to play, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.

citation: Kozhuharov VR, Ivanov K, Ivanova S. Monitoring dietary supplements for undeclared diuretics as a strategy for preventing unintentional doping. Processes. 2025;13:79.
abstract: This study developed and validated a gradient HPLC-UV method to screen dietary supplements for furosemide, torasemide and hydrochlorothiazide, as a way to reduce unintentional doping. Applied to 10 supplements, the method detected an undeclared diuretic (furosemide, 1210 µg per capsule) in one product.
tldr: A low-cost HPLC-UV method can screen supplements for three diuretics, and it found undeclared furosemide in one of the 10 products tested. It is a laboratory screening method, and the paper does not show how often supplements used by athletes are contaminated.
methods: Reversed-phase gradient HPLC with UV detection at 272 nm on a C18 column, with a 12-minute run. Validation followed ICH guidance for linearity, accuracy, precision, LOD and LOQ, and robustness (column temperature 32 to 38 °C). Ten randomly selected, purchased supplements, all promoted for weight loss and detoxification, and three diuretic medicines were analysed in triplicate, with spiked-recovery tests on two supplements.
findings: Calibration was linear from 3.125 to 50 µg/mL (R2 above 0.999). Intra-day CVs were 0.18 to 1.48% and inter-day CVs were 0.52 to 2.04%, and recovery in spiked supplement samples was 95.5 to 102.7%. Of the 10 supplements, only Sample 6 contained an undeclared diuretic, furosemide at 1210 µg per capsule (about 2420 µg per day at the recommended two capsules). The product was a herbal supplement labelled with cassia tora, hawthorn and water lily leaves and advertised for weight loss.
limitations: No athletes or human samples were tested, the products were weight-loss and detox supplements rather than sports supplements, and the nine other products showed no detected diuretic. The detection limits (0.69 to 0.99 µg/mL) are higher than those of LC-MS/MS, which the authors describe as more sensitive, and the paper reports no mass-spectrometry confirmation of the furosemide finding. The validation was carried out in a single laboratory with a small number of products.
practicalImplications: Laboratories that check supplement quality can use this HPLC-UV method as a low-cost screen for furosemide, torasemide and hydrochlorothiazide. Teams that supply supplements to athletes should consider independent quality testing before use, since one of the 10 products here contained an undeclared diuretic. Because the method is less sensitive than LC-MS/MS, a negative screen should not be read as proof that a product is free of diuretics.
athleteDev: The paper has no performance outcome. Its relevance for staff is supplement quality: the contaminated product was sold for weight loss, and the authors link undeclared diuretics to electrolyte imbalance, dehydration and unintentional anti-doping violations.
rtp: Not applicable to return-to-sport decisions. The study has no athlete or patient sample and gives no guidance on medicine or supplement use during rehabilitation.

citation: Golberg E, Pinkoski A, Beaupre L, Rouhani H. Monitoring external workload with wearable technology after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: a scoping review. Orthop J Sports Med. 2023;11(8):23259671231191134.
abstract: This PRISMA-ScR scoping review summarised 20 studies that used wearable technology to measure external workload after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR). Accelerometers were the most common device, and daily steps and moderate to vigorous physical activity were the main outcomes, with deficits reported against healthy controls and between limbs in some studies.
tldr: Wearable accelerometers can track daily activity after ACLR outside the clinic, and several studies found lower step counts or activity in ACLR groups than in controls. The evidence comes mostly from small cross-sectional studies, and the review found no evidence that these measures predict future ACL injury.
methods: Scoping review following the Arksey and O'Malley framework, JBI guidance and PRISMA-ScR. Eight databases were searched in February 2023, giving 2831 unique records after duplicates were removed; 175 full texts were reviewed and 20 included. A single reviewer screened titles and abstracts, two reviewers did full-text selection and extraction (agreement 91.39%, Cohen's kappa 0.66), and no formal quality assessment was made.
findings: Daily step count from accelerometers or pedometers was the most common outcome (15 studies), and MVPA was reported in 10. Several studies found fewer daily steps or less MVPA in ACLR groups than controls, others found no difference, and adolescents with ACLR had 26% fewer daily steps and 33% less MVPA than adults with ACLR. Plantar insoles in one study showed lower daily loading of the surgical limb than the non-surgical limb (d = 0.63, P < .001), elite rugby players with ACLR covered less match distance than controls in one study, and MVPA was not associated with new or recurrent ACL injury in one follow-up study.
limitations: No quality appraisal was conducted, and the review did not assess the validity or reliability of the outcomes it lists, although the authors state that the devices have acceptable criterion validity for step counting and activity monitoring. Most of the 20 studies were cross-sectional, several had very small groups, and most participants were physically active rather than competitive athletes (23% athletes, 1% elite). Most of the evidence comes from accelerometers, with only one GPS study and one insole study.
practicalImplications: Wearable accelerometers can give rehabilitation teams step and activity data from daily life over periods that a single clinic test cannot cover. The authors advise caution when interpreting these outcomes because their validity and reliability after ACLR were not assessed. Use them alongside clinical return-to-sport testing rather than in place of it, because the review found no evidence that they predict future ACL injury.
athleteDev: The review covers activity and workload during rehabilitation rather than performance. It reports very little wearable data on training or competition after ACLR (only a few studies, including one case report and one rugby study), so it offers little evidence for sport-specific load decisions.
rtp: Relevant to return to sport because the included studies measured activity from about 2 weeks to 5 years after ACLR, and some report between-limb asymmetry. The review does not set return-to-sport criteria, and it found no evidence that these measures predict future ACL injury, so they cannot support a clearance decision on their own.

citation: Neupert E, Holder T, Gupta L, Jobson SA. More than metrics: The role of socio-environmental factors in determining the success of athlete monitoring. Journal of Sports Sciences. 2024.
abstract: This cross-sectional survey asked 30 UK elite sport practitioners (a 40% response from 75 invited) how they rated their athlete monitoring systems. Practitioners were divided on whether their athlete self-report measures were sensitive, and a scientific basis for the measures was linked to feedback to athletes and to stakeholder responsiveness. Socio-environmental factors such as buy-in and feedback were highlighted alongside metric quality.
tldr: Practitioners were split on whether their self-report measures were sensitive, and about half thought performance would suffer without monitoring. Feedback to athletes was associated with adherence, so the social side of monitoring needs as much attention as the metrics.
methods: Online closed survey, completed in 2017/18, sent to 75 practitioners working with tier 3 to 5 Olympic and Paralympic athletes in the UK; 30 responded, and most (83%, n = 25) used a custom system. Likert and checkbox items were analysed with Spearman correlations and a Bonferroni-corrected alpha of 0.017, and free-text answers were grouped into themes.
findings: Fifty-two percent (n = 13) were confident in the sensitivity of their athlete self-report measures, and 64% (n = 16) said the measures had a scientific underpinning. A scientific underpinning correlated with feedback to athletes (rS(23) = 0.487, p = 0.014) and feedback correlated with athlete adherence (rS(22) = 0.675, p < 0.001); the link to confidence (rS(23) = 0.398, p = 0.049) did not meet the corrected threshold and is described as a trend. Fifty-two percent (n = 13) felt performance might be compromised without monitoring, while 56% (n = 14) had worked with internationally successful athletes who did not complete it.
limitations: Only 30 of 75 invited practitioners responded, the sample is UK-based and self-selected, and the data are perceptions from 2017/18, so non-response bias is likely and the correlations do not show causation. Several percentages match a denominator of 23 to 25 rather than 30, and the discussion gives 58% for the item the results report as 56%.
practicalImplications: Staff who doubt that their self-report measures are scientifically grounded should review the evidence behind them, because the survey linked a scientific basis to feedback to athletes. Adherence planning should include what athletes are told about their data, since feedback was correlated with adherence, and coach buy-in should be treated as part of the system, not a separate issue.
athleteDev: The study suggests that monitoring value depends on feedback to athletes and on coach buy-in as well as on the metric. The correlations do not show whether better feedback causes better adherence.
rtp: The study did not measure injury, rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot guide return-to-play decisions or the choice of a return-to-play measure.

citation: Adlou B, Wilburn C, Weimar W. Motion Capture Technologies for Athletic Performance Enhancement and Injury Risk Assessment: A Review for Multi-Sport Organizations. Sensors. 2025;25:4384.
abstract: This review compares optical marker-based, inertial (IMU) and markerless motion capture for athlete use across indoor court, aquatic and outdoor field settings. It draws on peer-reviewed studies from 2015 to 2025, 82 of 234 full-text articles, and proposes a phased purchasing framework for multi-sport organizations.
tldr: Each motion capture technology trades accuracy against practicality: optical systems are most accurate in the lab, while IMU and markerless systems suit field and team use but with larger errors. Verify accuracy on the sport's own movements before buying, rather than relying on vendor claims.
methods: Narrative review of PubMed, SPORTDiscus and Web of Science searches (January 2015 to January 2025) using motion capture and validation keywords. Of 953 unique articles, 234 were screened at full text and 82 met the eligibility criteria, which covered validation, comparative and implementation studies; no formal risk-of-bias appraisal or pooled analysis is reported.
findings: Optical systems were sub-millimeter accurate in controlled settings, but IMU joint-angle errors varied widely: Xsens RMSEs were about 3 to 10 degrees for knee, ankle and hip in walking and running, while APDM Opal RMSEs in jumps, squats, lunges and cuts were 8.11 to 28.37 degrees sagittal and up to 116.75 degrees transverse. Theia3D markerless sagittal RMSEs were 3.20 to 15.66 degrees, and GNSS-integrated IMU units had positional accuracy of about 0.3 m under optimal conditions, which degraded in stadiums with high stands. Waterproof IMU orientation error was 6.1 degrees in water versus 4.4 degrees dry, and cited studies reported 99.7 to 100% lap-counting accuracy.
limitations: The review applies no formal quality appraisal. Its abstract states IMU angular accuracy of 2 to 8 degrees, but in the body that figure is attributed to Xsens MVN multi-sensor validation studies, while other cited IMU validations report much larger joint-angle errors in some joints, planes and dynamic tasks. The authors note that most validation samples were male and that long-term reliability data are lacking, so accuracy figures are ranges across studies rather than guarantees for any one system.
practicalImplications: Organizations should match validation evidence to their own sports and movements rather than to vendor specifications, which the review says can differ substantially from field performance. Its foundation phase is either a team IMU system for workload or a multi-camera markerless system for controlled technique analysis, with optical systems added later for research or clinical work.
athleteDev: For performance staff, the review pairs a team IMU or GNSS system for workload with a markerless system for technique analysis. Because joint-angle errors can be large for some movements and planes, the review advises conservative interpretation thresholds so that differences within known measurement error are not read as real change.
rtp: The review suggests a multi-sensor IMU system and a mid-range optical system for return-to-play validation, but it tests no injured athletes and reports no return-to-play outcomes. It cannot show that these systems detect return-to-play readiness, which would need validation in the injury-relevant movements.

citation: Collins N, White R, Palczewska A, Weaving D, Dalton-Barron N, Jones B. Moving beyond velocity derivatives; Using Global Positioning System data to extract sequential movement patterns at different levels of rugby league match-play. European Journal of Sport Science. 2022.
abstract: This observational study applied the sequential movement pattern (SMP) framework to GPS data from 11 rugby league matches at three competition levels. It identified 121 movement patterns, mostly built from walk and jog units, and nine of 17 movement units differed between levels, mainly between international and regular Super League matches.
tldr: A movement-pattern method applied to GPS data shows that rugby league match play is built mostly from low-speed walk and jog actions, and these differ most between international and regular Super League matches. The study describes match demands; it does not test whether training to match these patterns changes outcomes.
methods: Observational analysis of 2019 GPS data (Catapult Optimeye S5, 10 Hz) from 11 matches, covering four regular Super League, three semi-finals or finals and four international matches. Movement patterns were tested with linear discriminant analysis (accuracy 0.81), and the 17 movement units used in the patterns were compared with Kruskal-Wallis tests, Dunn post-hoc tests and Cohen's d effect sizes.
findings: The framework found 121 movement patterns, and no pattern was unique to one competition level. Nine of 17 movement units differed between levels: all nine differed between international and regular Super League matches, three differed between international and finals, and four differed between the two domestic levels. The authors report that the units that differed were mainly low velocity, and that walk and jog patterns were the most prevalent.
limitations: The sample is small (11 matches), and the international data come from a single team set against several domestic teams, so tactics and squad differences may explain the results as much as competition level. The authors' claim of more high-velocity patterns in international matches (units T, S and y) is descriptive, since those units showed no significant difference (p = 1.000), and the conclusion overstates the domestic comparison because only three units differed from the finals. Match outcome and context were not analysed, and the text cites unit h as significant although Table 1 has no row for it.
practicalImplications: Staff preparing players for rugby league could use movement-pattern analysis to check whether training includes the walk and jog sequences, with their acceleration and turning changes, that occur in match play, rather than relying on total distance or speed bands alone. Any move toward more high-speed work for international preparation should await a study that links these patterns to outcomes, because the high-velocity claim here is descriptive.
athleteDev: The study suggests that movement sequences, not only speed thresholds, can describe match demands and differ by competition level. The authors infer that international players need more high-speed exposure, but that inference rests on descriptive counts and was not tested.
rtp: The study covers match demands in players and does not include injury, rehabilitation or return to play, so it cannot guide return-to-play decisions. Any use in return-to-play planning would be the reader's inference, since no injured players were studied.

citation: Walpurgis K, Agricola J, Thomas A, Thevis M. Myostatin inhibitory peptides in sports drug testing. Drug Test Anal. 2023.
abstract: Myostatin inhibitors are potential muscle-building agents and are prohibited under section S4 of the WADA Prohibited List. The authors developed and characterized a protein precipitation and LC-HRMS/MS method to detect six myostatin inhibitory peptides in doping control serum, with detection down to 3 to 9 ng/mL, and identified possible metabolites of DF-3, DF-25 and Peptide 7 as complementary targets.
tldr: An anti-doping lab built and validated a blood test for six experimental myostatin-blocking peptides that are not clinically approved but can be bought for research. It shows the assay works on spiked samples; how long real use stays detectable is still unknown.
methods: Six custom-synthesized peptides and two internal standards were measured in serum after acidification and acetonitrile protein precipitation, using an Orbitrap LC-HRMS/MS system. Selectivity, linearity, detection limit, recovery, carryover, matrix effects, robustness in plasma and stability were assessed per WADA guidelines with commercial serum and samples from 10 healthy volunteers, and metabolites were sought after 2 h incubation of each peptide in serum.
findings: No interfering signals were found in 10 blank sera, responses were linear to 100 ng/mL (r above 0.97), and estimated detection limits were 3 to 9 ng/mL. Recovery was 20% to 48% for most peptides but about 8% for Peptide 8a. At room temperature Peptide 7, DF-3 and DF-25 degraded within 1 h while Peptide 8a was detectable for 14 days, and N-terminally shortened metabolites were found for Peptides 7 and 3d, DF-3 and DF-25.
limitations: All validation used fortified serum or plasma; the peptides are in preclinical development and have not been tested in humans, so authentic post-administration samples were not available to confirm sensitivity, detection windows or in vivo metabolites. Several targets were unstable in serum even when refrigerated, and the identified metabolites were also unstable, which may limit detection after sample transport.
practicalImplications: For anti-doping education, the paper documents that myostatin inhibitory peptides are prohibited, are sold for research and on the black market, and are now targeted by a validated serum assay. It gives no evidence of performance benefit or safety in humans.
athleteDev: Does not measure performance. Muscle mass and strength gains cited for these peptides come from mouse studies described in the introduction, not from this study.
rtp: Not relevant to return to sport. It is a laboratory detection method and cannot inform injury management or clearance decisions.

citation: Retzky JS, Koff MF, Nwawka OK, Rodeo SA. Novel Noninvasive Imaging Techniques to Assess Structural, Functional, and Material Properties of Tendon, Ligament, and Cartilage: A Narrative Review of Current Concepts. Orthop J Sports Med. 2025;13(2):23259671251317223.
abstract: Narrative review of quantitative MRI (qMRI) and shear wave elastography (SWE) for soft tissue of the knee and shoulder, including meniscus, ACL graft, articular cartilage and rotator cuff. A PubMed search was run in October 2022 using four keyword phrases, and clinical studies and reviews were included. The authors report that qMRI and SWE may improve early detection of pathology and help evaluate tissue after treatment, while conventional MRI and ultrasound have limited ability to assess material properties.
tldr: Quantitative MRI and shear wave elastography can measure soft tissue composition and stiffness that standard MRI and ultrasound do not show, with early uses in ACL graft maturity, meniscal healing and cartilage degeneration. The evidence is mostly early-stage, animal-based or small, and the authors say these tools are not yet established for routine clinical decisions.
methods: The authors call this a narrative review, but it describes a database search, so the library codes it as a systematic review by precedent. A PubMed search was performed in October 2022 with four keyword phrases (quantitative MRI tendon, ligament and cartilage, and shear wave elastography tendon). Cohort studies, systematic and narrative reviews, book chapters and randomized trials on clinical applications were included, editorials and technique papers were excluded, and no screening counts or quality appraisal are reported.
findings: The review describes T2 mapping and UTE-T2* imaging for ACL graft maturity, with one human study reporting that UTE-T2* values changed mostly in the first 6 months and decreased between 1 and 2 years after reconstruction. In a goat meniscal repair model, T1rho relaxation times were sensitive to healing, and in a human cohort a T2 decrease of 22.3 ms was associated with complete healing confirmed by second-look arthroscopy. For SWE, torn tendons were reported to be softer, and in a pilot study Achilles stiffness rose at 6 weeks, plateaued, then rose again at 3 to 6 months after rupture, but the authors note that SWE was not associated with rotator cuff tear size, retraction or fatty infiltration in one study.
limitations: The authors identify variability between MRI hardware and software, magic-angle effects, and contrast-agent concerns for qMRI. For SWE they note user dependence, sensitivity to patient position, sex and age, reduced reliability beyond about 7 cm depth, and cutoff values that differ between ultrasound systems. The review does not appraise study quality or sample sizes, and it cites a human meniscal pilot (Sneag) that found no significant T2* difference between repaired and meniscectomy groups. Several authors report industry ties, including a research agreement with GE Healthcare and Siemens Healthineers and consulting fees from Samsung.
practicalImplications: Treat qMRI and SWE as research-stage tools for staff discussions, not as a basis for graft, meniscus or tendon clearance decisions. If a team considers SWE for tendon monitoring, the same operator, machine, transducer and positioning protocol should be used at each time point, because the authors report that these factors change readings.
athleteDev: The review offers no performance outcomes or athlete-specific measurement norms. The tendon stiffness example in a college basketball player is illustrative only, so staff should not use these measures to set training loads.
rtp: The review suggests that qMRI could help judge ACL graft maturity and meniscal healing, and SWE could help judge tendon healing, which may inform rehabilitation timing. It does not provide return-to-sport criteria or validated cutoffs, so these measures should not be used alone to clear an athlete to return to play.

citation: Alt T, Severin J, Komnik I, Nodler YT, Benker R, Knicker AJ, et al. Nordic Hamstring Exercise training induces improved lower-limb swing phase mechanics and sustained strength preservation in sprinters. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2021.
abstract: Twelve regional-to-national class male sprinters completed a 22-week longitudinal study that included a 4-week high-intensity Nordic Hamstring Exercise (NHE) block. The 4-week NHE block improved camera-based isokinetic hamstring and thigh muscle balance measures, small improvements in sprint velocity and late-swing mechanics, and effects on hamstring function remained at 3 months. Adaptations in isokinetic parameters were related to changes in late-swing sprint joint moments, and the weakest participants showed the largest isokinetic gains.
tldr: In sprinters with no prior NHE experience, a 4-week high-intensity NHE block improved eccentric hamstring strength and late-swing joint moments, and these strength gains remained above baseline about 3 months later. Sprint velocity changed only slightly (+1.4%).
methods: Twelve male sprinters completed a within-subject design with 4 weeks of baseline, a 4-week NHE block (assisted and unassisted sessions with live video feedback), 2 weeks of adaptation and 12 weeks of retention, with no control group. Isokinetic knee tests were recorded with four high-speed cameras, maximal sprints with a 10-camera 3D motion capture system, and lower-limb inverse dynamics were computed from the sprint data.
findings: Peak eccentric hamstring moment at 150 deg/s rose 15.5% (d = 1.14) and peak power rose 14.6% (d = 0.89), while sprint velocity rose 1.4% (d = 0.26). Gains in peak eccentric hamstring moment were associated with changes in late-swing sprint knee and hip peak moments (r = .909 and .849; R2 = 82.6% and 72.1%), and hamstring function (+6% to +14%) and thigh muscle balance (+8% to +10%) remained significantly above baseline at retention.
limitations: The study had no control group and a small sample (n = 12) with variable training history and performance level. The authors note that the inverse dynamic model has limited ability to estimate muscle function in the swing phase.
practicalImplications: A short block of supervised high-intensity NHE training with live feedback improved eccentric hamstring strength in these sprinters, and much of the gain persisted for about 3 months. Sprint velocity gains were small, so staff should not expect large speed changes from this block alone. The authors suggest that sprint-specific strength programs should also include hip-dominant exercises.
athleteDev: In sprinters with no prior NHE experience, a 4-week high-intensity NHE block improved eccentric hamstring strength and late-swing knee and hip moments, and the strength gains remained above baseline at about 3 months. Expect small sprint velocity gains (+1.4%) from this design, which had no control group.
rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. All participants were free of thigh muscle and knee injury for the previous two years, and injured athletes, return-to-play criteria and injury outcomes were not studied.

citation: Bell L, Ruddock A, Maden-Wilkinson T, Rogerson D. Overreaching and overtraining in strength sports and resistance training: a scoping review. J Sports Sci. 2020;38(16):1897-1912.
abstract: This scoping review searched SPORTDiscus, Scopus and Web of Science and included 47 studies of overreaching and overtraining in strength sports and resistance training. Short-term high-volume or high-intensity training can produce functional overreaching, and chronic high-volume or high-intensity training can lead to non-functional overreaching. The authors find minimal evidence that true overtraining syndrome has occurred in these populations.
tldr: Short-term planned overreaching in weightlifting and resistance training usually produces functional overreaching, while chronic high loads can tip athletes into non-functional overreaching. Evidence of true overtraining syndrome is minimal, and no current test identifies the transition point.
methods: Scoping review following PRISMA-ScR and Joanna Briggs Institute guidance, with the protocol registered on the Open Science Framework in July 2019. SPORTDiscus, Scopus and Web of Science were searched in June 2019 using overreaching and overtraining terms combined with resistance, strength, weight training or weightlifting terms. Of 1170 records, 137 underwent full-text review and 47 studies were included, with data charted by the principal investigator and assessed by the team.
findings: In strength sports (13 studies, 12 in weightlifters and 1 in collegiate throwers), short-term increases in training volume often improved weightlifting- or throwing-specific performance, while testosterone and cortisol changes did not consistently track performance. In resistance training (34 studies), a daily 10 x 1-RM squat protocol for two weeks reduced strength in several studies by one research group, and in one of them normal training could only be resumed after 2 to 8 weeks; the authors note this extreme protocol is unlikely to reflect practice. The authors state that no single performance test, hormone or biomarker identifies the point at which functional overreaching becomes non-functional.
limitations: As a scoping review, the paper maps the literature and does not pool effects, and no risk-of-bias appraisal is described. Evidence is heterogeneous and based on small samples, 92.3% of strength-sport studies involve weightlifters, 23.5% of resistance-training studies share one first author, and many studies predate the 2013 ACSM/ECSS overtraining definitions. The authors advise caution with the lean-mass results of two supplement studies (Lowery et al., 2016; Wilson et al., 2013) because other researchers have raised concerns about their data.
practicalImplications: The review describes planned overreaching over about 2 to 4 weeks as common practice in strength sports that often led to functional overreaching in the included studies, but it gives no threshold for when this turns non-functional, so athletes need monitoring through and after such blocks. Because testosterone and cortisol changed independently of performance in several studies, hormone results should not be used alone to identify non-functional overreaching. The authors describe the evidence for supplements during overreaching as less than conclusive.
athleteDev: Jump and force measures such as rate of force development and maximal force appeared sensitive to training load during overreaching, so they can be paired with performance tests to monitor fatigue. Practitioners should account for typical error in jump measures before interpreting an individual change.
rtp: The review does not address return to sport or clearance after injury, so it cannot guide return decisions. One case study in the review described a knee overload injury after a two-week high-intensity protocol in one male participant, which shows only that overreaching can be associated with joint injury in that case.

citation: Grandou C, Wallace L, Impellizzeri FM, Allen NG, Coutts AJ. Overtraining in resistance exercise: an exploratory systematic review and methodological appraisal of the literature. Sports Med. 2019.
abstract: This systematic review searched PubMed, Web of Science and SPORTDiscus to June 2019 for resistance-training studies that tried to induce overreaching or overtraining in healthy participants. Of 22 included studies, eight showed performance decrements with follow-up testing, four showed decrements without follow-up, and ten showed no decline. The authors conclude that few studies have properly established functional overreaching, non-functional overreaching or overtraining syndrome in resistance exercise.
tldr: Few resistance-training studies have properly established functional overreaching, non-functional overreaching or overtraining syndrome, mainly because performance was not retested during follow-up. Frequent, high-intensity and monotonous training appears to raise the risk, but no biomarker other than a sustained performance decrease is validated.
methods: Systematic review following PRISMA and registered on the Open Science Framework. PubMed, Web of Science and SPORTDiscus were searched from inception to June 2019 using resistance-training terms combined with overtraining and overreaching terms, and reference lists were screened. Two authors independently screened titles, abstracts and full texts, and two authors extracted data. Because the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool did not reflect overtraining methodology, the authors used an adapted appraisal that included follow-up duration and frequency of performance testing.
findings: Twelve of 22 studies showed a decline in at least one performance measure, and 8 of these included follow-up testing. Where reported, performance returned to baseline after 1 week (2 studies), after 2 to 8 weeks by survey or interview (Fry et al.), and was not restored after 2 days of rest in one study; for Margonis et al., Table 2 says 1RM returned to baseline after 3 weeks of recovery, while the discussion says 1RM was not restored after a 6-week taper and suggests OTS. Every study that used daily sets of one repetition at 100% 1RM for two weeks produced a performance decrease. Overload groups showed exacerbated cortisol, creatine kinase and noradrenaline responses and blunted T:C ratio responses versus controls, but the authors state that biochemical markers could not separate normal training, acute fatigue, FOR, NFOR and OTS.
limitations: A meta-analysis was not possible because of heterogeneous methods and outcomes, and most included studies came from one author group. The paper gives conflicting time-course data for Margonis et al. (Table 2 says 1RM returned to baseline after 3 weeks of recovery, but the discussion says it was not restored after a 6-week taper). The risk-of-bias tool was adapted by the authors, and the review's search terms and exclusion decisions may carry bias.
practicalImplications: When planning an overload block, staff should track performance during the block and in a follow-up period, since most included studies did not measure recovery of performance. The authors associate high training frequency, high intensity and low exercise variety with performance decline, so exercise selection and recovery time are worth considering when programming an overload period. Biochemical and psychological markers should not be used alone to diagnose overtraining, and the authors recommend combining them with performance measures.
athleteDev: Maximal strength appeared resilient to large acute increases in training load in these studies, so a maximal strength test alone may not detect overreaching. The authors suggest secondary performance measures, such as jump or sprint tests, may help early detection, but the evidence for them is inconsistent, so the test should reflect competition demands.
rtp: The review contains no return-to-play criteria and studied healthy participants, so it cannot guide return from injury. Follow-up periods in the included studies ranged from 2 days to 8 weeks across different protocols, and these cannot be generalised to clearance decisions for an individual athlete.

citation: Biro P, Walker SG. Parametric modeling and analysis of NFL run plays. Journal of Sports Analytics. 2023.
abstract: A skew-t regression model of yards gained on NFL run plays from the 2017 and 2018 regular seasons estimates a league-average run distribution by down, distance and line of scrimmage, and team-specific shifts from that average. Team variance and skewness parameters were correlated with team yards per attempt, and in a matched-pairs analysis running outside was associated with more yards gained.
tldr: Run-play yardage can be modeled by game situation and by team, and the team-level variance and skewness parameters track with how well teams run the ball. Outside runs gained about 0.5 more yards in matched plays, but this is observational and depends on an external run-gap label.
methods: Play-by-play data from the 2017 and 2018 regular seasons (nflscrapR), filtered to 19,881 run plays, with outside runs defined by the nflfastR run-gap labels 'tackle' or 'end'. A Bayesian skew-t mixture model with down, distance and line-of-scrimmage covariates was fit by MCMC, and team adjustments were estimated by weighted maximum likelihood. Team parameters were correlated with yards per carry, and a Mahalanobis-matched comparison of 2,628 inside and outside run pairs estimated the yardage difference.
findings: The skew-t fit for the most common 1st and 10 state was not rejected (chi-squared 83.46, df 80, p = 0.374). The printed correlations of the team variance and skewness parameters with yards per carry are -0.432 and -0.515 (p = 0.0135 and 0.00257). The team share of outside runs correlated with the variance parameter (r = .448), and outside runs gained 0.503 more yards on average in matched pairs (95% CI 0.160 to 0.846).
limitations: Two NFL regular seasons only, and outside runs are defined by a run-gap field that the authors note does not reflect the play scheme. The authors call the matched-pairs difference a causal effect, but it is an observational comparison. The yards-per-carry correlations are printed as negative (-0.432, -0.515), while the text, Figure 8 caption and the EPA comparison (r = 0.411 and 0.418) describe higher variance and skewness as linked to better running teams; this sign conflict is unresolved in the source, which is an uncorrected author proof.
practicalImplications: Situational yardage distributions by down, distance and field position can serve as an external reference for expected run gain and downside risk. The outside-run result should be checked against a team's own personnel and scheme before it changes run selection.
athleteDev: The model describes team offensive run output, not individual athlete development. It can inform which run situations a unit practices, but it does not measure athlete capacity.
rtp: Not applicable. The study uses team and play-level NFL data without injury or return-to-play outcomes, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.

citation: Johnson QR, Yang Y, Cabarkapa D, Sealey D, Stock S, Gleason D, et al. Periodization for success: in-season external training loads relative to competition load in American football. Front Sports Act Living. 2025;7:1662240.
abstract: GPS training loads of 27 NCAA Division II American football players were compared across 32 in-season practices and 11 games, by position group and practice day. Several load measures were higher in practices three and four days before games than in games, and the study describes weekly load patterns but tests no performance or injury outcome.
tldr: For this team, practices three and four days before games carried more volume and load than games, the practice two days before was shorter, and practice work rate was above game level. This describes one NCAA Division II team and does not test whether the pattern helps performance.
methods: Observational study using 10 Hz GPS units worn in a vest during 32 practices and 11 conference games in the regular season. Players had to play in at least 60% of games. Duration, distance, yards per minute, hard running distance and efforts, and 2D and 3D load were compared with a 4 (day) by 3 (position group) factorial ANOVA, Bonferroni post hoc tests and subgroup t-tests.
findings: Practices on GD-4 and GD-3 had higher duration, distance and 2D and 3D load than games, GD-2 duration was lower than games (102.9 vs 117.4 min), and yards per minute was higher than in games on each practice day (39.8 to 41.4 vs 35.8). Starters had higher yards per minute but non-starters had higher hard running distance and efforts. The five players who went on to play professionally had higher yards per minute, hard running and load than the 22 who did not, an association within one team.
limitations: The sample is one team, with only three linemen, and repeated sessions are analysed as a between-subjects factorial ANOVA; the reported error df (1,562) cannot be reconciled with 27 players and 43 sessions, and the position groups listed in Table 3 (3, 9 and 14) sum to 26, not 27. The abstract gives practice ranges as 'GD-4 to GD-1' although GD-1 was a walkthrough with no GPS recorded, and it gives yards per minute as '+15% to -11%' while the results text gives '+15% to +11%' and Table 2 shows every practice day above game level; values here follow the results and tables as printed. Hard running thresholds were the manufacturer's and differ from other studies.
practicalImplications: For this team, practice loads were highest three to four days before games and lower two days before, and practice work rate was at or above game level. Position groups had different load profiles, which supports looking at loads by position group, but the study does not test whether any planning approach improves performance or reduces injury.
athleteDev: The data describe one NCAA Division II team's practice loads against games, and show that practice work rate was at or above game level on the recorded days. Use the position-group profiles as a reference rather than a prescription, since the study does not test whether any load pattern improves performance.
rtp: The study does not include injury, return-to-play or rehabilitation outcomes, so it cannot guide return to sport. It describes in-season load in healthy players only.

citation: Finnegan E, Daly E, Pearce AJ, Ryan L. Nutritional interventions to support acute mTBI recovery. Front Nutr. 2022;9:977728.
abstract: The authors systematically review human nutritional interventions given within 14 days of mild traumatic brain injury. They conclude that certain therapies, especially omega-3 fatty acids, show potential, but that heterogeneous, small studies do not allow definitive recommendations.
tldr: Nutrition for acute concussion has promising but weak evidence, with the strongest signal for omega-3 DHA in small trials. Most included studies are not in athletes, so the findings cannot yet set a concussion nutrition protocol.
methods: PRISMA systematic review registered on PROSPERO (CRD42021226819). Five databases were searched to 6 January 2021 for human studies of nutrition or nutritional interventions in mild TBI within 14 days of injury, with screening of titles, abstracts and full texts, and quality rating against the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics checklist. Eleven studies were included and were synthesised qualitatively because data were insufficient for meta-analysis.
findings: In a sports concussion trial of 40 adolescents, DHA (2,000 mg) for 12 weeks gave symptom resolution in 16.1 days versus 20.9 days for placebo (p=0.082, not significant). In an NCAA trial of 55 student athletes, 2,200 mg DHA for 30 days gave return to play in 9.1 days versus 10.7 days for placebo (p=0.397, not significant). In 81 military personnel with blast-related mTBI, N-acetyl cysteine (early and delayed groups combined) gave higher day-7 symptom resolution than placebo (OR 3.6, p=0.006), and in 17 adolescents magnesium oxide reduced post-concussion symptom scores at 48 hours (p=0.016) with 50% loss to follow-up. A 5-day cerebrolysin infusion improved CASI scores from baseline within the treated group in a 32-person pilot, with no significant between-group MMSE difference (p=0.111), and the citicoline phase III trial (n=1,213) found no benefit over placebo at day 90.
limitations: Included trials are small, use different doses, timings and outcomes, and the three omega-3 trials are abstracts with incomplete data. In the NCAA trial, 7 of 62 athletes (6 DHA, 1 placebo) who did not return to play within 30 days were excluded from the analysis. The abstract's claim that patients who met calorie and protein needs within 96 h had a reduced hospital length of stay is not supported by the reported data: the only nutrition-intake study was observational, found intakes below requirement, and did not compare length of stay; the discussion presents reduced length of stay only as a possible benefit. The 'positive' labels are quality ratings, and the count of nine positive outcome studies is not consistent with the cited studies' results.
practicalImplications: The one observational study found hospitalised TBI patients ate about 23% of estimated calorie needs and 15% of protein needs on day 1, so monitoring early food intake in admitted patients is reasonable. Do not start omega-3, N-acetyl cysteine or magnesium as standard post-concussion care on the basis of this review; the athlete trials did not show statistically significant benefit. The vitamin D evidence comes from one retrospective study of mostly mild to moderate TBI with benefits at 12 weeks, not in the acute phase.
athleteDev: The review does not assess athletic performance or training outcomes. Its only sport-specific trials are small and did not show statistically significant differences in return to play.
rtp: The review cannot be used to shorten concussion management or to set a return-to-play timeline. The authors state that no nutritional recommendations exist for post-mTBI recovery, and the two athlete trials did not show statistically significant return-to-play differences.

citation: Waller G, Domingue GA, Kintada JR, Box MW, Steinmetz G, Rowles D. Observation of risk for concussion following 'lowering the helmet to initiate contact' penalties in the NFL. Journal of Orthopaedic Reports. 2024;3:100347.
abstract: Observational study of NFL players diagnosed with concussion from 2015 to 2022 and of 'lowering the helmet to initiate contact' penalties from 2018 to 2020, using publicly reported league injury and play data. The authors compared penalty-linked concussions with the overall per-play concussion rate and tested trends across years.
tldr: Three of 86 'lowering the helmet' penalties in 2018 to 2020 were followed by a concussion (3.5%), above the league's 0.45% per-play rate, although the two rates use different denominators. The overall NFL concussion rate fell over 2015 to 2022, but the study cannot show the penalty caused that fall.
methods: Retrospective descriptive study using NFL.com injury reports, penalty records and team play counts for 2015 to 2022. Online game recordings and play tracking were used to identify the player hit on each penalized play, and a second researcher verified the records. Friedman tests compared years, Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Bonferroni correction compared pairs of years, and linear regression and Pearson correlation assessed trends.
findings: Mean regular-season concussion incidence was 0.45% of plays (SD 0.08%). Three of 86 penalties (3.5%) from 2018 to 2020 were followed by a concussion; in each case a defensive player was penalized and the concussed player was an offensive player. The Friedman test showed differences across years (chi-square = 16.0, p = 0.0003), but no pairwise year-to-year difference was significant after Bonferroni correction. The concussion rate per play showed a significant negative linear trend from 2015 to 2022 (R² = 0.575, p = 0.029).
limitations: Only three concussions followed penalties, and the paper is inconsistent on details: the discussion refers to four concussions on these plays, and the penalty is said to have been grouped under unnecessary roughness in 2020 and in 2021. The 3.5% rate is per penalty and the 0.45% rate is per play, and no statistical test compares them, so the paper's conclusion that penalized plays carry a higher incidence is a descriptive comparison of unlike rates. Data were collected retrospectively from public NFL reports, equipment, practice, reporting and protocol changes could explain the trend, and the authors note possible underreporting of concussions.
practicalImplications: Because athletes underreport concussions, the authors advise thorough medical evaluation after head-first contact whether or not a foul is called. They also suggest teaching players to avoid lowering-the-helmet positions, a recommendation that rests on three events. The data cannot show whether the penalty itself reduces concussions, so staff should not assume it does.
athleteDev: The authors recommend coaching tackling and contact positions that do not lead with the helmet, but the supporting data are three concussions in 86 penalties. Track head-first contact in your own data, and do not use the 3.5% figure as a per-play risk benchmark.
rtp: The study covers concussion occurrence and penalty records and does not assess recovery time, symptom management or return-to-play criteria. It cannot be used to make return-to-sport decisions.

citation: Lynall RC, D'Lauro C, Kerr ZY, Knight K, Kroshus E, Leeds DD, et al. Optimizing Concussion Care Seeking: The Influence of Previous Concussion Diagnosis Status on Baseline Assessment Outcomes. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2022.
abstract: Cross-sectional analysis of 29,934 college athletes and military cadets in the CARE Consortium at preseason baseline. Participants reporting at least one undiagnosed concussion (5.3%) had higher symptom severity and BSI-18 scores and mixed neurocognitive results, with no differences in mental status or balance, compared with those with no concussion history or only diagnosed concussions.
tldr: In nearly 30,000 college athletes and cadets, those reporting at least one undiagnosed concussion had more symptoms and psychological distress at baseline, along with mixed neurocognitive results. Mental status and balance were unchanged, and the design cannot show whether the undiagnosed injuries caused these differences.
methods: Participants completed a baseline questionnaire on concussion history and diagnosis status, followed by the SCAT3 symptom checklist, BSI-18, SAC, BESS and one of four computerized neurocognitive tests depending on site (ImPACT, CNS Vital Signs, ANAM or CCAT). Three history groups were compared using multiple linear regression for continuous outcomes and negative binomial models for symptom and BSI-18 scores, adjusted for sex, race, ethnicity, sport contact level, concussion count and clustering by site. Differences counted as meaningful only if the 95% CI excluded the null and the effect was at least small (effect size 0.20 or IRR 1.10).
findings: Compared with no concussion history, at least one undiagnosed concussion was associated with higher SCAT symptom severity (IRR 1.39, 95% CI 1.20 to 1.61) and BSI-18 scores (IRR 1.31, 95% CI 1.16 to 1.48), with similar IRRs against the all-diagnosed group (1.38 and 1.39). The authors report worse performance for the undiagnosed group on 6 neurocognitive comparisons (CNS Vital Signs visual memory, processing speed and reaction time; ANAM simple reaction time test 1 and procedural reaction time) and better performance on 2 (ANAM matching to sample, CCAT learning). Participants with only diagnosed concussions did not differ from those with no history on symptoms or BSI-18, and no group differences were found on the SAC or BESS.
limitations: Concussion history and diagnosis status were self-reported, diagnosis categories were collapsed, and medical records were not reviewed, so some injuries may be missed or misclassified; the authors also note that a more thorough history reporter may report symptoms more thoroughly at baseline. The cross-sectional design cannot show causation, and neurocognitive results were inconsistent across platforms, each tested at only 1 to 25 sites (CNS Vital Signs n=1087, ANAM n=875, CCAT n=1407). The Results list ANAM simple and procedural reaction time as worse in the undiagnosed group, but the Discussion calls them faster; the abstract gives a symptom IRR of 1.38 where Table 3 gives 1.39 against no history; and minus signs in the extracted Table 3 mean differences are garbled, so only the text and IRRs are reported here.
practicalImplications: The authors suggest previous concussion diagnosis status is another factor that may affect baseline performance, so recording whether past concussions were diagnosed can help when interpreting baseline symptom and BSI-18 scores. Their main recommendation is interventions that increase timely concussion diagnosis.
athleteDev: The study measured baseline symptoms and neurocognitive scores, not athletic performance, and the differences were modest. A history of undiagnosed concussion may be worth noting when a baseline is used as a reference, but the study does not support performance decisions.
rtp: The study does not measure recovery or return-to-play timing, so it cannot show that undiagnosed concussions slow recovery or change when an athlete can return. Its relevance to return to play is indirect: a history of undiagnosed concussion may mean that baseline symptom or cognitive scores differ, which can affect how post-injury scores are read.

citation: Madi NS, Parekh TJ, Parekh SG. Outcome of Turf Toe Injuries in NFL Players. The Journal of Foot & Ankle Surgery. 2022.
abstract: Retrospective study of 67 NFL players with 71 turf toe injuries during the 2011 to 2014 seasons. Among 16 offensive skill players, power ratings did not differ significantly before versus after injury, or compared with uninjured running backs and wide receivers.
tldr: In NFL players with turf toe injuries, a yards-and-touchdowns power rating did not change significantly after injury, either compared with before injury or with uninjured running backs and wide receivers. The performance group was small (16 players), and the study does not show whether injury grade matters.
methods: Turf toe injuries from the 2011 to 2014 seasons were identified from online NFL injury reports, player registries and news sources. For offensive skill players with at least 200 total power-rating points over six seasons, the power rating (total yards divided by 10 plus touchdowns times 6) was calculated for three seasons before injury, the index season and two seasons after, and compared with 149 uninjured running backs and wide receivers from 2012 using two-sided t tests.
findings: Sixty-seven players had 71 turf toe injuries; 9 (13%) were placed on injured reserve, 8 (12%) had operative repair, and the average time missed was 3.2 games. Among the 16 offensive skill players, power rating was 105.7 per season before injury, 87.3 in the index season and 115.5 afterward (P=.53), and 7.3, 6.9 and 8.1 per game (P=.4). Post-injury values did not differ from controls (115.5 vs 99.2 per season, P=.24; 8.1 vs 7.2 per game, P=.27).
limitations: Data came from public online sources without clinical records, and injury grade and playing surface were not analysed in the performance comparison. The performance cohort was only 16 players and required at least 200 power-rating points over six seasons, which favours players who returned and produced (inference); the authors acknowledge a few productive post-injury seasons could skew results. The Discussion describes 'improvements in play' and a return to preinjury level, but the differences were not significant (P=.53 and P=.4), so they show no detectable change rather than gains.
practicalImplications: For NFL running backs and wide receivers with turf toe, staff can note that power ratings were not significantly lower after injury in this small sample, but should not extend that to other positions. Injury grade was not analysed, and 8 of the 67 players in the cohort had operative repair.
athleteDev: The study tracks a yards-and-touchdowns power rating for running backs and wide receivers, and found no significant change after turf toe injury in 16 offensive skill players. It does not measure speed, cutting or push-off power, so it should not be used to judge performance in other positions or sports.
rtp: The study shows only that 16 productive offensive skill players had similar power ratings after injury; one of them was placed on injured reserve and did not return the next season. It does not give return-to-play rates or timelines by injury grade or treatment, and the authors state that grade-specific studies are needed.

citation: Laitano O, Murray KO, Leon LR. Overlapping mechanisms of exertional heat stroke and malignant hyperthermia: evidence vs. conjecture. Sports Med. 2020.
abstract: This review compares exertional heat stroke (EHS) and malignant hyperthermia (MH) in pathophysiology, incidence, diagnosis and treatment. The authors find that the two conditions share clinical features, but the evidence that they share a calcium-dysregulation mechanism is limited. They conclude that dantrolene's effect in EHS is uncertain, while rapid cooling remains the most effective EHS treatment.
tldr: Exertional heat stroke and malignant hyperthermia look alike, but the review finds no robust evidence that they share a mechanism. Rapid cooling remains the treatment for heat stroke, and dantrolene's benefit in EHS is unproven.
methods: Narrative review that draws on case reports of awake MH (Table 1), the EMHG and NAMHG in vitro contracture test protocols (Table 2), and a small number of EHS incidence and cohort reports. The paper describes no systematic literature search.
findings: Awake MH during exercise or heat exposure shares symptoms with EHS, but EHS patients usually show muscle flaccidity on collapse while MH causes rigidity. In a triathlon series, 12 of 68,557 starters (1.74 per 10,000) were diagnosed with EHS. In a French military cohort of prior EHS cases, 45.6% tested positive on IVCT, but the authors note the test has never been validated for EHS. Dantrolene tested in EHS has shown either a lack of clinical efficacy or mixed results, while rapid cooling is described as the most effective EHS treatment.
limitations: The paper is a narrative review with no described search method, so evidence selection cannot be checked. Table 1 gives 466 EHS patients for the French cohort while the text gives 454. The authors note that IVCT results have low specificity (Table 2 lists 78% for NAMHG and 93.6% for EMHG). Much of the evidence is from case reports.
practicalImplications: Staff should treat an athlete who collapses with hyperthermia as an emergency and start rapid cooling, which the authors identify as the most effective EHS treatment. Staff should not assume dantrolene helps EHS, since the authors describe the evidence as mixed and note possible side effects. Rigidity, a core temperature that keeps rising after exercise stops, and family history are features the review links to awake MH, so these should prompt medical review.
athleteDev: Exertion in hot, humid conditions can trigger both EHS and awake MH, so performance staff can use the awake-MH risk factors the review lists (family history of MH, pre-existing muscle conditions, large muscular build, recent or concurrent illness, prior psychological or environmental stress) to flag athletes for medical attention during hot training. The review does not validate any screening tool for these factors.
rtp: The review does not give return-to-play criteria. It cannot be used to decide whether an athlete with a prior EHS or MH episode can return to hot-weather training, since the authors describe this as a matter still under debate.

citation: Patel H, Polam S, Joseph R. Overview of treatment options for mild traumatic brain injury: a literature review. Cureus. 2024;16(4):e59021.
abstract: This literature review summarizes concussion diagnosis and treatment options for athletes, including rest, a jugular vein compression collar, osteopathic manipulative medicine, herbal and pharmacological treatments, hyperbaric oxygen therapy, blood-flow-restricted interval training, aerobic exercise and vestibular rehabilitation. It also reviews the Amsterdam 2022 consensus statement. The authors state that there is no definitive treatment for concussion and that the evidence for most options is limited.
tldr: There is no definitive concussion treatment, and care relies on brief relative rest followed by a stepwise return to activity with medical clearance before contact. The best athlete-specific evidence summarized is one adolescent trial of early aerobic exercise; the other options rest on small, pilot or non-athlete studies.
methods: Literature review of PubMed, Embase and Medline for April 2012 to April 2022, limited to peer-reviewed English-language human studies of athletes with diagnosed concussion and treatment approaches. The search returned 163 articles, and 24 were included. The Amsterdam 2022 consensus statement was added to cover recent developments. No quality appraisal method is described.
findings: In one trial of adolescents with sport-related concussion, aerobic exercise started within 10 days was reported to improve symptoms within four weeks and to lower the risk of long-term symptoms by 48%. In a trial of patients after traumatic brain injury, group vestibular rehabilitation improved dizziness and mobility, but control and treatment groups reached the same level by the second follow-up; the review also states, citing that trial, that starting within 30 days leads to earlier return to play. Hyperbaric oxygen in persistent post-concussion syndrome, methylphenidate or galantamine in PTSD and/or TBI patients, the herbal product MLC901 in a pilot TBI trial, and blood-flow-restricted interval training in a pilot study were each reported to improve symptoms, and one cited study found people who did not rest after concussion recovered faster than those who rested.
limitations: The paper gives only a brief search description and no quality appraisal, so selection cannot be checked. Several trials cited are in traumatic brain injury, PTSD or post-concussion patients rather than athletes, and the interval training (ref 20) and MLC901 (ref 9) studies are pilot studies, yet Table 1 says interval training 'can be used to aid athletes in recovery'. Table 1 and the Discussion say galantamine can be used with methylphenidate, but the body text and reference title describe the McAllister trial as testing methylphenidate or galantamine, and the conclusion mentions optometry, which the body text does not discuss.
practicalImplications: Staff should follow a stepwise return-to-activity progression after 24 to 48 hours of relative rest, with at least 24 hours between steps and medical clearance before full-contact practice. Athletes with signs such as loss of consciousness, seizures, ataxia, confusion or amnesia should be removed from play immediately and returned only after medical clearance. The review, summarizing the Amsterdam statement, says dizziness, neck pain or headache beyond 10 days warrants cervicovestibular rehabilitation; the hyperbaric, herbal, drug and blood-flow-restriction options should not be treated as established athlete treatments on this evidence.
athleteDev: Graded aerobic work is part of the review's recovery approach, so performance staff can plan conditioning during a concussion only under the direction of the medical team. The review warns that weightlifting or sprinting can raise heart rate rapidly, which is not advised when symptoms are being assessed.
rtp: The review describes a stepwise progression (rest, light aerobic, sport-specific, non-contact, full-contact practice, then return) with at least 24 hours between steps, and says the process applies regardless of age or level of sport. It also says the steps should allow at least one week and that timing depends on age, sport and history, so it gives no fixed return-to-play timeline.

citation: Hazzard S, Bacevich B, Lustig M, Lonati D, Asnis P. Preferences Including Graft Choice, Lateral Augmentation, and Rehabilitation After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Among National Football League Team Orthopaedic Surgeons. Arthroscopy, Sports Medicine, and Rehabilitation. 2025;7(4):101161.
abstract: A multiple-choice survey was sent to NFL team physicians who perform sports medicine knee surgery, and 51 of 97 (53%) responded. Patellar tendon autograft was the favored graft for the three hypothetical athletes, with quadriceps tendon second. Most respondents would not recommend primary ACL repair, outpatient physical therapy beyond team staff, or a brace for return to play.
tldr: Among 51 NFL team knee surgeons who responded to a survey, patellar tendon autograft was the most common graft choice in three hypothetical ACL reconstruction scenarios, with quadriceps tendon second. These are stated surgeon preferences, not outcome data, and do not show that one graft performs better.
methods: An 11-question online survey was emailed four times in May 2023 to 97 NFL team physicians identified through public web searches as performing sports medicine knee surgery, with NCAA physicians excluded. The survey was designed to resemble a 2014 NFL and NCAA survey and asked about graft choice for three hypothetical athletes, primary repair, femoral tunnel drilling, lateral augmentation, return-to-sport criteria and bracing. Responses were summarized by question with no advanced statistical analysis.
findings: Of 51 respondents, the mean experience with ACL surgery was 19.6 years (SD 11.4) and the mean number of ACL reconstructions in 2022 was 103.9 (SD 46.6). Patellar tendon autograft was chosen by 48 (94%) surgeons for the 20-year-old running back, by 33 (65%) for the 25-year-old recreational athlete and by 20 (39%) for the 35-year-old. Two surgeons (4%) would choose primary repair for the running back, 43 (84%) would add lateral augmentation only if certain findings were present, 38 (76%) did not recommend a brace and 38 (75%) recommended team staff rehabilitation alone. Compared with the 2014 survey, the authors report hamstring autograft preference fell from 42.3% to 8% for the 25-year-old, and transtibial femoral drilling fell from 25% to 14%, while anteromedial portal drilling was 71% and retrograde drilling 16%.
limitations: The survey was not validated, had no advanced statistical analysis and reached 53% of identified surgeons, so responder bias is possible. NCAA physicians were excluded, which limits direct comparison with the 2014 survey, and the text dates the survey to May 2023 while the results label it 2024. The abstract gives 96% for lateral augmentation, but the results report 43 (84%) and the discussion '>80%', so this record uses the results figure; the brace question also totals 50 answers (12 yes, 38 no), so 76% is of 50 rather than 51 respondents.
practicalImplications: The results describe how NFL team knee surgeons approach ACL graft choice and rehabilitation, including that patellar tendon autograft is the most common choice and that bracing is not routinely recommended. Because the findings are hypothetical preferences, they should not be applied as a protocol for an individual athlete, and decisions should rest on the injury, the surgeon's assessment and local rehabilitation practice.
athleteDev: The study reports surgeon preferences for ACL reconstruction, not athlete performance. It cannot show how graft choice or lateral augmentation affects speed, strength or other performance measures.
rtp: The study can be used only to describe surgeon return-to-sport criteria. Fifteen surgeons (29%) required passing strength and agility tests, 13 (25%) also required at least 9 months after surgery, and 38 (76%) did not recommend a brace. It cannot show which return criteria reduce reinjury, so it should not be used as evidence for return-to-play decisions.

citation: Esteve E, Casals M, Saez M, Rathleff MS, Clausen MB, Vicens-Bordas J, et al. Past-season, pre-season and in-season risk assessment of groin problems in male football players: a prospective full-season study. Br J Sports Med. 2021.
abstract: A prospective full-season cohort of 245 male amateur football players examined past-season groin pain, pre-season adductor squeeze strength, age and in-season HAGOS (Sport) scores as risk factors for in-season groin problems. Past-season groin pain and lower pre-season long-lever adductor squeeze strength were associated with higher risk, while short-lever strength, age and HAGOS (Sport) were not associated in the main models.
tldr: Players with groin pain in the previous season had about 2.4 times the risk of a groin problem in the new in-season. Higher pre-season long-lever adductor squeeze strength was linked to lower risk, but this comes from one cohort of amateur players.
methods: Prospective cohort of 245 amateur male players from 17 teams (tiers IV to VI), followed for a 39-week competitive in-season. Pre-season measures were past-season groin pain (yes/no), age, and short- and long-lever adductor squeeze strength normalised to body mass and lever length. In-season groin problems were recorded as time-loss injuries or as self-reported groin pain without time loss, with HAGOS (Sport) every 4 weeks. Two-part Bayesian logistic models (INLA) estimated relative risks adjusted for football exposure, with team and player random effects.
findings: Of 245 players, 99 (40.4%) had a groin problem, covering 233 in-season problems (35 with time loss, 198 without). In the long-lever model, past-season groin pain was associated with higher risk (RR 2.40, 95% credibility interval 1.52 to 3.74), and each 1 N·m/kg increase in long-lever squeeze strength with lower risk (RR 0.65, 0.42 to 0.99); short-lever strength (RR 0.72, 0.39 to 1.30), HAGOS (Sport) and age (RR 1.05, 0.99 to 1.11) were not associated. In the split analysis, past-season pain was associated with problems without time loss (RR 2.60, 1.63 to 4.20) but not with time-loss problems (RR 1.55, 0.72 to 3.29), and long-lever strength was associated with time-loss problems (RR 0.50, 0.26 to 0.94) but its interval crossed 1 for problems without time loss (RR 0.67, 0.43 to 1.04).
limitations: Convenience sample of amateur players, 69 players (28.2%) dropped out, and exposure was estimated for two teams with incomplete records. The abstract's 'Players (n=245) suffering from groin pain during the past-season' can be read as 245 players with past-season pain, but Table 1 shows 245 is the whole sample and 77 (31.4%) reported past-season pain; the results text also gives the past-season interval as 1.52 to 3.54 while Table 2 gives 1.52 to 3.74. The abstract says age was not associated, yet Table 3 shows a borderline age association for problems without time loss (RR 1.05, 1.00 to 1.11).
practicalImplications: Pre-season screening should record past-season groin pain whether or not it caused time loss, since it was the clearest risk marker here. Long-lever adductor squeeze strength is a reasonable pre-season baseline for flagging players for closer in-season monitoring. The study did not test whether training to raise strength reduces groin problems.
athleteDev: Pre-season long-lever adductor strength can serve as a baseline measure within individual planning for amateur players. The study did not measure performance outcomes, so it does not show that changing strength improves performance.
rtp: Limited. The study models the risk of new in-season groin problems, not recovery or return to play after an injury, so it cannot guide return-to-play decisions.

citation: Sahota S, Gibbs DB, Lawton CD, Balderama ES, Chambers CC, Mack CD, et al. Pectoralis major injuries in the National Football League. Sports Health. 2019.
abstract: A retrospective review of NFL Injury Surveillance System data over 15 seasons identified 211 pectoralis major injuries, 132 strains and 79 ruptures. Ruptures treated operatively missed significantly more days than ruptures treated without surgery or with unknown treatment.
tldr: Pectoralis major injuries are uncommon in the NFL, and most occur in games. Ruptures repaired surgically kept players out for about 147 days on average versus about 77 days for the no-surgery or unknown group, which helps frame expected time loss.
methods: Retrospective review of primary pectoralis major strains (grades 1 and 2) and ruptures (grade 3) in the NFL Injury Surveillance System, 2000 to 2014, excluding offseason and conditioning injuries, with game injuries used for position, activity and contact-type analyses. Incidence was expressed per 10,000 athlete-exposures, calculated by assuming 53 players per team and 105 practices per year rather than counting actual participation. Rates were compared with exact Poisson tests and days missed with t tests.
findings: Of 211 injuries, 132 were strains and 79 were ruptures. Strain incidence was 0.41 and rupture incidence 0.25 per 10,000 athlete-exposures, and game rates were far higher than practice rates (strains 1.91 versus 0.12; ruptures 1.33 versus 0.03).
