Of 69 ruptures with treatment data, 52 (75.4%) were treated surgically and missed 146.7 ± 55.0 days versus 77.2 ± 72.9 days for no surgery or unknown treatment (P < 0.01); among 130 strains, the 10 treated surgically missed 151.2 ± 62.9 days versus 18.1 ± 28.7 days (P < 0.01). Defensive players had more in-game injuries than offensive or special teams players for both types.
limitations: Retrospective surveillance data depend on club reporting, and the 2014 move to the clinical EMR changed how injuries were captured. Exposure denominators were assumed (53 players per team in every practice and game), which the authors note overstates exposure because fewer players are actually exposed, so incidence rates are estimates and likely understated. Days missed can be underestimated because injuries without a return date by the June 2015 data cutoff were excluded, the 'no surgery' groups include unknown treatment, the surgical strain group is small (10 cases), and no performance or functional outcomes were available.
practicalImplications: Players with a rupture that needs operative repair should be counselled to expect a substantially longer absence, around 5 months on average in this cohort. Because the data show time missed rather than performance after return, and the comparison group includes unknown treatment, they cannot by themselves settle whether surgery or nonoperative care gives the better result. Most in-game injuries occurred in defensive players and during contact with another player, especially tackling.
athleteDev: Performance Application is limited. The study does not measure performance after injury, but its position and contact-type patterns can inform where injury-prevention work is focused.
rtp: Relevant to return-to-play counselling on expected time missed. Operatively treated ruptures missed about 147 days on average, compared with about 77 days for the no-surgery or unknown group, and strains averaged 28 days. The study reports no strength, functional or performance outcomes, so it cannot show whether players return to their previous level.

citation: Wise PM, Ptasinski AM, Gallo RA. Pectoralis major ruptures in the National Football League: incidence, RTP, and performance analysis. Orthop J Sports Med. 2021;9(6):23259671211018707.
abstract: Season-ending pectoralis major ruptures in NFL players from 2010 to 2018 were identified from public reports. Most injured players were defensive, linebackers were most affected, and 54 of 63 ruptures were followed by an NFL return, with no significant change in Pro Football Focus grades among 35 players with a full season before and after injury.
tldr: Pectoralis major ruptures in the NFL were concentrated in defensive players and mostly occurred in games, and most injured players returned to the league. Grades were unchanged on average in 35 players with a full season before and after injury, but the sample is small and drawn from public reports.
methods: Season-ending pectoralis major ruptures in NFL players from 2010 to 2018 were identified from public injury reports, team statements and news articles. Position, age, treatment, setting, NFL Combine bench-press percentile and performance-enhancing drug suspension history were recorded. For the performance analysis, players needed at least 4 games in the season before and after their first rupture, and Pro Football Focus season grades were compared with paired t tests.
findings: There were 63 ruptures in 58 players. Defensive players made up 79.3% of players (46/58; linebackers 36.2%), 76.2% of ruptures (48/63) occurred in games and 11.1% (7/63) in training, lifting or offseason activities, and 53 players had surgery while treatment was undetermined for 10 injuries. Return to NFL play was 85.7% (54/63), lowest in defensive backs (10/13). Among 35 players analysed, the mean Pro Football Focus grade was 65.10 ± 3.04 before and 65.08 ± 3.52 after injury (difference -0.02 ± 3.68; P = 0.99), with no position showing a significant change; 4 of 58 players (6.9%) had a performance-enhancing drug suspension.
limitations: Injuries came from public reports, so grade, mechanism, concurrent injuries and exact treatment are unknown, some cases may have been missed, and rates could not be normalised for position or exposure. The authors' '769% increase' divides their 7.0 ruptures per year by 0.91 per year from a separate 2000 to 2010 study with different case finding, uses raw counts rather than exposure rates, and the 7.7-fold ratio would be a 669% increase. The return rate uses ruptures as the denominator (54/63) but is labelled as players, the discussion's 84.6% defensive share of ruptures does not match the counts (52/63 is 82.5%; 84.6% is the defensive return rate), and time to return could not be determined.
practicalImplications: The high return rate can inform counselling for NFL players with this injury, but the small performance sample is not a guarantee of an individual's outcome. The study reports no treatment comparison, so the unchanged grades should not be read as showing that surgery restores performance. The authors link the injuries to tackling and blocking, which points prevention work toward those contact situations.
athleteDev: Performance Application is limited to the pre- and post-injury comparison in NFL players. Grades were unchanged on average for 35 players, which describes a group pattern rather than individual development.
rtp: Relevant to return-to-play counselling. 54 of 63 ruptures (85.7%) were followed by an NFL return, with defensive backs lowest at 10 of 13 (76.9%). The study cannot give an expected time to return and reports no strength or isokinetic outcomes.

citation: Rishiraj N, Taunton JE, Regan W, Woollard R, Lloyd-Smith R, Niven B. Performance effects of functional knee brace removal and prolonged use in healthy male athlete: Lower extremity power, acceleration, speed, and agility. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2025.
abstract: Prospective crossover study of 27 healthy male athletes wearing a functional knee brace (FKB) for up to 21 hours. Vertical jump, 2 m acceleration, 10 m sprint and agility were compared after brace removal at 17.5 hours and after continued use for 21 hours. The authors report percentage improvements in most tests, but none of the comparisons reached statistical significance.
tldr: Healthy male athletes showed no statistically significant change in jump, acceleration, sprint or agility after removing a functional knee brace at 17.5 hours or continuing it to 21 hours. The percentage changes are small, and the reported improvements should not be read as a performance effect.
methods: Repeated-measures crossover study in 27 healthy male provincial basketball and national field hockey players. After 17.5 hours of brace use, athletes were randomly selected to remove the brace (n = 12) or continue it (n = 15), and four performance tests were compared with earlier sessions using unpaired t tests and Cohen's effect sizes.
findings: Vertical jump changed by +2.7% after brace removal (P = 0.704) and +3.1% after continued use (P = 0.661). Across the four tests, changes ranged from 0.5% slower to 3.1% better, with effect sizes from trivial to small, and none of the comparisons was statistically significant. The authors describe the changes as performance improvements, although the results report no significant difference.
limitations: The removal and continued-use groups were small (12 and 15) and were compared with different earlier sessions (S5 and S11), so time, fatigue and familiarization are confounded, and fatigue was not measured. By the authors' own a priori power table, groups of 10 to 20 had power below 0.80 for vertical jump and agility, so small effects could have been missed. Every comparison was non-significant, so the abstract's conclusion of improved performance overstates the findings, and results may not apply to women or athletes at risk of ACL injury.
practicalImplications: In healthy male athletes, removing a functional knee brace after 17.5 hours or continuing it for 21 hours did not produce a significant change in vertical jump, acceleration, sprint or agility. Brace decisions for healthy athletes should not rest on expected performance gains or losses from these data alone. Because the study did not test injured knees, these results do not settle brace decisions after ACL injury.
athleteDev: For performance staff, the study shows no significant change in jump height, 2 m acceleration, 10 m sprint or T-test agility in healthy male athletes after 17.5 to 21 hours of functional brace use. The changes were small and not significant, so the study shows neither a performance benefit nor a cost.
rtp: The study cannot inform return to sport, because it tested healthy athletes with intact knees rather than athletes returning from ACL reconstruction or other injury. It also does not show whether brace use changes re-injury risk.

citation: Cricco R, Segreti A, Stirpe E, Ferro A, Ciancio M, Cipriani F, et al. Performance-Enhancing Effects of Inhaled Medications: Implications for Heart, Muscle Function, and Doping Detection in Athletes. J Funct Morphol Kinesiol. 2025;10:462.
abstract: Narrative review of how inhaled bronchodilators and corticosteroids may affect the heart, skeletal muscle and performance in athletes, and how WADA thresholds and detection methods apply. The authors conclude that ergogenic effects are mainly seen at supratherapeutic doses, and that urinary thresholds remain hard to interpret.
tldr: Inhaled asthma and exercise-induced bronchoconstriction medicines can affect heart rhythm and, at high doses, muscle performance. Athletes who need these medicines should stay within WADA dose limits and use the TUE process when they must exceed them.
methods: Narrative review with no described search method; the article states that no new data were created or analysed. It draws on cited trials, WADA documents and news reports of doping cases, and summarises cardiovascular, muscle and detection evidence in tables.
findings: The review reports that high or supratherapeutic inhaled doses (for example terbutaline) raised strength, sprint performance and lean mass in some trials of trained men, while standard inhaled salbutamol doses had limited or no effect on strength or sprint performance in non-asthmatic athletes. It lists tachycardia, arrhythmia, QTc prolongation and hypokalaemia as cardiovascular risks, mainly with overuse, and reports that inhaled corticosteroids have little ergogenic effect.
limitations: The review does not describe how sources were selected, so its coverage cannot be checked. Many of the ergogenic and mechanistic studies it cites are small trials, and the authors describe the findings as dose-dependent and mixed. Its regulatory details cite both the 2025 and the 2026 WADA Prohibited Lists, so current dose and urine limits need checking against the official list.
practicalImplications: Inhaled beta-2 agonists at standard doses are reported to have little performance effect in non-asthmatic athletes, and effects appear mainly above therapeutic use. Athletes using inhalers for asthma or EIB should keep to WADA dose limits and apply for a TUE when they need more, noting the cited finding that exercise and dehydration raised urinary salbutamol above 2000 ng/mL after 1600 micrograms inhaled. Check the current Prohibited List before advising on any inhaled medicine.
athleteDev: Inhaled beta-2 agonists at supratherapeutic doses may improve sprint and strength outcomes in some trials, but standard inhaled doses show little benefit in non-asthmatic athletes. The review does not support using inhalers to improve training adaptation or performance.
rtp: The review does not address return to sport, injury or rehabilitation, so it cannot inform clearance decisions. Athletes returning from asthma or EIB treatment would need their own clinical assessment and TUE status checked.

citation: Carollo A, Corazza O, Mantovani M, Silvestrini N, Rabin O, Esposito G. Performance-enhancing substances in sport: A scientometric review of 75 years of research. Drug Test Anal. 2024.
abstract: Scientometric review of doping research using Scopus records (search run March 2023) and document co-citation analysis. It maps the main countries, journals, authors and seven research clusters in performance-enhancing substance research from 1948 to 2023.
tldr: Doping research has concentrated on established classes such as anabolic agents and peptide hormones, and detection methods have advanced. Research on contaminated supplements and newer substances is comparatively thin, so athlete and staff education needs to keep pace.
methods: Scientometric review: a Scopus title and abstract search (English-language documents, run 9 March 2023) returned 4,330 documents, analysed with bibliometrix and CiteSpace. A PRISMA flowchart is provided, and among g-index, TOP N and TOP N% networks the TOP N (N=7) document co-citation network was chosen for its structural properties. There is no quality appraisal of the documents.
findings: The collection contained 4,330 documents from 1948 to 2023, led by Drug Testing and Analysis (399 documents), with mainly German, US and UK affiliations. The co-citation network had 363 nodes, 1,092 links and seven clusters (largest: athlete biological passport, detection of peptide hormone abuse, image and performance enhancers). Of 51 documents with citation bursts, six were duplicates; the strongest bursts were Ntoumanis et al. (2014, 25.66) and Lasne and Ceaurriz (2000, 17.66), with Catlin et al. (2004) at 16.61 in Table 2.
limitations: The authors note that a Scopus-only, English-only search run in 2023 may miss relevant publications and search terms. Co-citation and citation burst measure influence in the literature, not clinical or analytical quality. The text and tables disagree in places: Catlin et al. burst strength is 17.61 in the text but 16.61 in Table 2, and cluster #10 silhouette is 0.996 in the text but 0.986 in Table 1; table values are reported here.
practicalImplications: For anti-doping and athlete education planning, the review supports continued education on doping risks, with attention to contaminated supplements and emerging substances that the authors find under-studied. Use it as a map of the research landscape rather than as a ranking of substance risk.
athleteDev: The performance application is indirect: the research base is strongest on anabolic agents and peptide hormones and thinner on contaminated supplements. The review does not evaluate the performance effect of any substance.
rtp: This review does not address return to sport, injury or rehabilitation, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions.

citation: Smith MJ, Hoffman NJ, San Jose AJ, Burke LM, Opar DA. Nutritional Interventions to Attenuate Quadriceps Muscle Deficits following Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury and Reconstruction. Sports Medicine. 2025.
abstract: This narrative review describes how quadriceps atrophy after anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury and reconstruction may arise from disuse, altered mTOR and myostatin signalling, and inflammation. It then reviews nutritional supplements that might support hypertrophy alongside rehabilitation, and proposes a phase-based nutritional strategy. The authors state that the ACL-specific evidence is limited and that their strategy needs testing in ACL populations.
tldr: Quadriceps atrophy after ACL reconstruction may respond to nutrition used alongside rehabilitation, but only seven ACL-specific supplement studies exist and they are mixed. The phase-based supplement plan in the review is preliminary.
methods: Review based on Medline, Embase and CINAHL searches (earliest dates to 2023) with manual reference checks; the authors state that a systematic search strategy was not employed and no appraisal method is described. It is coded Systematic Review / Meta-analysis under the library rule for reviews that describe a database search. The review covers muscle atrophy and hypertrophy signalling, energy and carbohydrate availability, protein and amino acids, creatine, omega-3, collagen and caffeine, and summarises supplement studies in tables.
findings: Myostatin was reported to be about 50% higher in ACL-injured patients than in uninjured patients, and disuse atrophy can reach 0.5% of muscle per day. Of the seven ACL-specific supplement studies cited, three (Laboute et al. 2013, Holm et al. 2006 and Shaw et al. 2019) reported some benefit with rehabilitation, and four reported no effect. The authors propose matching supplements to rehabilitation phases, such as whey protein after pre-operative exercise and 10 g collagen peptides during rehabilitative loading, but describe this as preliminary.
limitations: The search was not systematic and study quality was not appraised, and the authors acknowledge that some relevant literature may be missing. The ACL evidence is small: one cited study had only two professional rugby players. The text reports Lopez-Vidriero et al. (2019) as showing no benefit, while Table 1 reports a higher IKDC score at 60 days in the supplement group, so the three-versus-four count of positive and null ACL trials depends on which is correct. The first author owns a company (Straight Up Performance) that produces supplements including collagen peptides, which the review suggests considering during rehabilitation.
practicalImplications: Supplements should not be expected to replace rehabilitation for quadriceps atrophy after ACL reconstruction, because the ACL-specific trials are few and mixed. Meeting energy and protein needs is the review's base recommendation, since 5 days of low energy availability reduced muscle protein synthesis by about 30% in young trained volunteers (cited study). Any supplement trial with a patient should be agreed with the treating clinical team, given that the phase-based suggestions are preliminary.
athleteDev: For athletes rehabbing from ACL reconstruction, the review's link between nutrition and quadriceps strength is mechanistic and preliminary. Energy and protein intake are presented as the foundation for recovering muscle, and the review does not test any sprint or performance outcome.
rtp: The review addresses quadriceps recovery after ACL reconstruction and suggests nutrition as an adjunct to the clinical milestones that rehabilitation phases already use. It does not set return-to-play criteria, and it states that return-to-play nutrition is sport-specific and outside its scope, so it should not be used to judge readiness to return to sport.

citation: Giraldo-Vallejo JE, Cardona-Guzmán MÁ, Rodríguez-Alcivar EJ, Kočí J, Petro JL, Kreider RB, et al. Nutritional Strategies in the Rehabilitation of Musculoskeletal Injuries in Athletes: A Systematic Integrative Review. Nutrients. 2023;15:819.
abstract: The authors update nutritional strategies for rehabilitation from musculoskeletal sports injuries in elite athletes, using a systematic integrative review of 18 studies. They conclude that energy balance, high protein and carbohydrate intake are the most supported strategies, and that evidence for supplements such as collagen, omega-3, creatine and vitamin D needs more clinical research.
tldr: Rehabilitation nutrition for injured athletes should focus first on keeping energy availability adequate and protein intake high. Supplement evidence is limited to a few small trials, so supplement use after injury cannot yet be firmly recommended.
methods: PERSiST-based systematic integrative review using the Whittemore and Knafl framework, searching PubMed/Medline, Scopus, PEDro and Google Scholar for English or Spanish studies published 2012 to 2022, with a protocol posted on Figshare. Risk of bias was assessed with RoB 2 for trials and AMSTAR 2 for reviews. Eighteen of 3,736 records were included: five randomized trials, one cross-sectional study and 12 reviews.
findings: Five randomized trials were included. Leucine (1.2 g/day, n=45 high-performance athletes after ACL reconstruction) was reported to favour recovery of the injured muscle, and creatine (n=18 adolescent fin swimmers with tendon overuse injury) was reported to support rehabilitation. Glucosamine (n=30 men after ACL reconstruction) did not improve outcomes, vitamin D (6000 IU/day for 12 weeks, n=21 wheelchair athletes with spinal cord injury) corrected status with an unclear effect on strength, and HMB (n=8, 4 per group, patellar tendinopathy) may improve power. Most included reviews advise avoiding energy availability below 30 kcal/kg fat-free mass per day and a high-protein diet of about 1.6 to 3 g/kg/day with 20 to 30 g of leucine-rich protein per meal.
limitations: The evidence base is small and mostly narrative reviews with high risk of bias, and several included studies fall outside the stated inclusion criteria (adolescents, spinal cord injury rather than musculoskeletal injury, an injury-history survey rather than a rehabilitation intervention). The review excludes trauma such as concussion and focuses on treatment rather than prevention. Two authors hold supplement industry roles, including creatine-specific ties (science product manager for a supplement company that sells creatine, honoraria for creatine talks, and membership of the 'Creatine for Health' advisory board for Alzchem), and the article processing charge was partly funded by Galascreen Laboratories and DBSS International, both author affiliations; the review recommends creatine while declining to recommend HMB.
practicalImplications: Monitor energy intake against energy availability during rehabilitation, since the authors advise avoiding values below 30 kcal/kg fat-free mass per day. Aim for high protein intake of roughly 1.6 to 3 g/kg/day spread across 4 to 6 meals, and check vitamin D status and correct deficiency. The review does not support a routine supplement protocol after injury: HMB cannot be confidently recommended, and collagen, omega-3 and creatine need injury-specific trials, so any creatine use should be weighed with the authors' disclosed industry ties in mind.
athleteDev: Performance is mentioned only as background. The review notes that low energy availability can impair health and physical performance, but it does not test performance outcomes.
rtp: The review is relevant to nutrition during rehabilitation from musculoskeletal injury, but it cannot set return-to-sport timing or doses for an individual athlete. The authors state that clinical trials in injured athletes are too few to confirm supplement doses.

citation: Holwerda AM, Weijzen MEG, Zorenc A, Senden J, Jetten GHJ, Houben LHP, et al. One Week of Single Leg Immobilization Lowers Muscle Connective Protein Synthesis Rates in Healthy, Young Adults. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2023 (published ahead of print).
abstract: Within-person study of 7 days of one-leg knee immobilization followed by 14 days of ambulant recovery in 30 healthy young men. Deuterium-labeled muscle biopsies measured connective protein synthesis, and extracellular matrix gene expression, muscle collagen, plasma collagen markers and leg strength were also assessed.
tldr: A week of single-leg immobilization lowered muscle connective protein synthesis in healthy young men, and synthesis rose during two weeks of normal activity. The study measured the tissue response but did not test any rehabilitation program.
methods: Thirty healthy young men had one knee immobilized in a full leg cast for 7 days, with crutches allowed and no weight-bearing on that leg, followed by 14 days of free-living recovery. Deuterium oxide was given throughout, and biopsies from both legs measured connective protein fractional synthesis, mRNA expression and collagen content. Two-way repeated-measures ANOVA compared legs and time periods.
findings: During immobilization, connective protein synthesis was lower in the immobilized leg (1.07 ± 0.30 %/day) than in the non-immobilized leg (1.48 ± 0.44 %/day; P < 0.01). During recovery, synthesis in the previously immobilized leg rose to 1.48 ± 0.64 %/day (P < 0.01 versus immobilization) and did not differ from the other leg (1.32 ± 0.59 %/day). Leg extension 1RM fell from 56.7 to 49.5 kg and rose to 52.9 kg after recovery, still below baseline. Muscle collagen content and plasma PINP and CTX-I did not change, while collagen III, fibronectin and fibromodulin mRNA fell after immobilization and collagen I, collagen III, fibronectin, fibromodulin, tenascin-C and decorin mRNA rose after recovery.
limitations: The immobilization lasted only 7 days, and the 14-day recovery is reported as an average, so the time course cannot be read from the study. Only healthy young men who were not resistance training were studied, and all received milk protein or peptide supplements from the parent trial (no group differences were found). Some samples were lost (collagen analyses in 25 men, synthesis in 28), and the parent study was supported by Nuritas Ltd.
practicalImplications: The study supports the idea that a week of unloading lowers connective tissue remodeling in muscle, and that two weeks of normal activity brings synthesis back to the level of the other leg, while leg extension strength was still below baseline. It does not test any exercise, nutrition or loading protocol, so staff cannot set a rehabilitation dose from it. The authors speculate that resuming daily activity drives the early recovery, which was not tested here.
athleteDev: The study gives a physiological reason to avoid unnecessary disuse, since leg extension strength fell from 56.7 to 49.5 kg in one week in these young men. It does not measure performance outcomes in athletes, so it cannot predict how much strength or training time is lost in a given sport.
rtp: The participants were healthy young men with a cast on one leg, not injured athletes, and the study did not test rehabilitation or return-to-sport criteria. It cannot be used to set return-to-sport timing or loading, though it helps explain why short disuse affects muscle tissue.

citation: Nudelman B, Gardner BB, Bryant SA, Lansdown DA, Feeley BT, Pandya NK. Open Fractures in National Football League Athletes: Analyzing Performance and Return to Sport. Spartan Medical Research Journal. 2023;8(1).
abstract: Retrospective study of 95 NFL athletes who had surgery for forearm, tibial shaft or ankle fractures between 2009 and 2018 (10 open, 85 closed), built from public injury reports and performance data. Open and closed fractures showed similar return-to-sport rates (90% vs 83.5%), career durations and performance changes, but the open group was small.
tldr: In 95 NFL players who had surgery for forearm, tibial shaft or ankle fractures, open fractures (n=10) had return-to-sport rates and performance changes similar to closed fractures (n=85). The open group is too small to rule out a meaningful difference.
methods: Injury, return-to-sport and career data were compiled from public team and media reports for NFL players with surgically treated forearm, tibial shaft or ankle fractures. Return to sport was defined as playing at least one regular-season game after injury, and performance was measured with Pro-Football-Reference approximate value (AV) against a two-season pre-injury baseline. Groups were compared with Fisher's exact, Mann-Whitney U and two-sample t-tests.
findings: Return to sport was 90% (9 of 10) for open and 83.5% (71 of 85) for closed fractures (P>0.99). Median time missed was 48.9 weeks (range 35.1 to 117.4) for open and 43.0 weeks (range 2.4 to 108.0) for closed injuries, which was not statistically significant (P=0.17). Career duration (7.7 vs 8.0 years, P=0.78) and AV change in the first post-injury season (-0.6 vs +0.4, P=0.91) did not differ significantly, and the two-season post-injury AV change was -2.1 vs -0.5 (P=0.60).
limitations: This retrospective design relies on public reports, and with only 10 open fractures the study had limited power, so a meaningful difference cannot be ruled out; fracture pattern and soft-tissue severity could not be classified. The Results attribute extra open-tibia time missed to a preseason re-fracture and an unrelated shoulder injury, while the Discussion names a serious infection and the shoulder injury; without these outliers the authors estimate a 46.0-week median (range 35.1 to 59.9). Text and tables conflict in places (closed first-season AV change described as a 0.4 decrease vs +0.4 in Table 4; 22 vs 20 closed forearm returners in Table 2; post-injury seasons 2.4 vs 2.0 in the Discussion vs 2.4 vs 2.9 in Table 3), so table values are reported here.
practicalImplications: For NFL players with surgically treated open forearm, tibial shaft or ankle fractures, counseling can state that return-to-sport rates were similar to closed fractures in this sample. Expectations should also note the small open group, the wide time-to-return range and that complications may increase return time.
athleteDev: Average AV changes after open and closed surgical fractures did not differ significantly, which suggests similar performance outcomes for professional players in this sample. The result is a broad expectation only, since it rests on 10 open fractures and one public performance metric.
rtp: Supports counseling that open and closed surgically treated forearm, tibial shaft and ankle fractures in NFL players had similar return rates in this cohort. It cannot predict an individual athlete's return date, since time missed ranged from 2.4 to 117.4 weeks, and the authors note results may differ in lower-level athletes or high-energy injuries.

citation: McHale KJ, Rozell JC, Milby AH, Carey JL, Sennett BJ. Outcomes of Lisfranc injuries in the National Football League. Am J Sports Med. 2016;44(7):1810-1817.
abstract: This case-control study compared 28 NFL players with Lisfranc injuries (2000 to 2010) with same-position controls from 2005. Of the 28 players, 26 (92.9%) returned to NFL competition at a median of 11.1 months (IQR 10.3 to 12.5). Median change in power rating per season was -34.8 (IQR -64.4 to 1.4) vs -18.8 (IQR -52.9 to 31.5) in controls for offensive players (P = .33) and -13.5 (IQR -30.9 to 4.3) vs -5.0 (IQR -22.0 to 14.0) for defensive players (P = .21), so the declines did not differ significantly from controls.
tldr: Most NFL players in this series (26 of 28) returned to NFL play after a Lisfranc injury, at a median of 11.1 months. Their power ratings fell after return, but not significantly more than controls in this small sample.
methods: Injuries were identified from NFL game summaries, weekly team injury reports and player profiles for 2000 to 2010. Offensive players were compared with running backs, wide receivers and tight ends, and defensive players with linemen, linebackers and defensive backs who competed in 2005. Yearly power ratings (offense: yards and touchdowns; defense: tackles, sacks and interceptions) were compared for 3 seasons before and after the injury season using Mann-Whitney U tests with a Bonferroni-adjusted threshold of P = .001.
findings: 26 of 28 (92.9%) players returned to regular-season play at a median of 11.1 months (IQR 10.3 to 12.5) and missed a median of 8.5 regular-season games. Nonoperatively treated players (n = 6) returned at a median of 6.2 months vs 11.6 months for operative cases (n = 22, P = .02), which the authors call a trend and attribute more likely to injury severity than to surgery. The median change in power rating per season was -34.8 vs -18.8 for offensive players and controls (P = .33) and -13.5 vs -5.0 for defensive players and controls (P = .21); games played after the injury season did not differ from controls (offense 48 vs 53, P = .61; defense 50 vs 46, P = .78). Fourteen of 28 players exceeded their preinjury power rating in at least one postinjury season.
limitations: Injuries were identified from public NFL reports without physical examination or imaging, so the diagnosis and injury severity were not confirmed. Severity, surgical technique and rehabilitation programmes were not assessed, and the sample was small (11 offensive and 17 defensive players; only 6 managed nonoperatively), so the authors note the study may have been underpowered to detect a mild decline. The extracted abstract text drops the minus signs on the change scores and IQRs (for example '234.8 (IQR, 264.4 to 1.4)'); the tables and discussion print them as -34.8 (-64.4 to 1.4), and those values are used here. Injured defensive players also had higher preinjury production than controls (median DPR 61.0 vs 44.0, P = .02).
practicalImplications: Staff can tell athletes that most NFL players with a Lisfranc injury in this cohort returned to play, at a median of about 11 months, and that half exceeded their preinjury production in at least one later season. Expectations of a performance drop should be framed as uncertain, since the observed declines did not differ significantly from controls in this small sample. The shorter return after nonoperative care should not be read as an effect of treatment choice, since the authors suggest it likely reflects milder injuries.
athleteDev: Performance staff can use a season-level production rating as a simple outcome measure after a midfoot injury in football. The study did not find a significant change after return, so it should not be used to predict an individual player's performance decline.
rtp: The study supports telling an NFL player that return to at least one regular-season game occurred at a median of 11.1 months in this cohort. It does not set clearance criteria or show whether specific rehabilitation or surgical approaches change return timing, and it should not be applied to non-football athletes or to midfoot sprains.

citation: Gulgosteren E, Yuksel O, Gurol B, Yildirim O, Atar O, Soylu C, et al. Persistent neuromuscular deficits in the posterior kinetic chain following hamstring strain injury: EMG insights from Nordic hamstring curl, kettlebell swing, and supine sliding leg curl. BMC Sports Sci Med Rehabil. 2025.
abstract: Cross-sectional study of 42 male football players (21 with a hamstring strain in the previous 6 months, 21 healthy controls) comparing surface EMG activation of the biceps femoris, gluteus maximus, latissimus dorsi and iliocostalis lumborum during three posterior chain exercises. The injured group had lower activation in all four muscles across the Nordic hamstring curl, kettlebell swing and supine sliding leg curl, with effect sizes from medium to large.
tldr: Football players with a recent hamstring strain showed lower EMG activation in the hamstring, gluteal and trunk muscles than healthy controls during three strengthening exercises. The design cannot show whether this deficit causes or results from injury, so treat it as a finding to check, not a proven target.
methods: Cross-sectional laboratory study comparing 21 male football players with a unilateral hamstring strain within the previous 6 months against 21 controls with no strain in the past 6 months and a straight-leg raise under 80 degrees; players with a professional sports background were excluded. Surface EMG (8-channel Noraxon, SENIAM placement, blinded analysis) was normalised to maximal voluntary isometric contraction (%MVIC) during three randomised exercises of three repetitions each: Nordic hamstring curl, kettlebell swing and supine sliding leg curl. Groups were compared with independent t-tests (Mann-Whitney U if normality failed), with no correction for multiple comparisons.
findings: Injured players had lower activation than controls in all four muscles for all three exercises. Biceps femoris was 52.3 vs 76.8 %MVIC (Nordic hamstring curl, d = 2.08), 58.7 vs 82.4 (kettlebell swing, d = 2.06) and 48.6 vs 70.5 (supine sliding leg curl, d = 2.07), all p < 0.001; gluteus maximus gaps were largest in the kettlebell swing (68.9 vs 92.6, d = 1.87). Latissimus dorsi and iliocostalis lumborum differences were smaller (d 0.86 to 1.07, p 0.001 to 0.008).
limitations: The cross-sectional design cannot establish causation. Inclusion only required a strain within the previous 6 months, and return-to-play status was not reported, so the abstract's claim of deficits 'even after return to play' was not measured. Injured players were tested on the injured limb and controls on the dominant limb, and no multiple-comparison correction was applied. The abstract's percentage reductions for the Nordic hamstring curl and supine sliding leg curl (for example, biceps femoris -23.9% and -20.8%) do not match the reported group means (about -32% and -31%), so the results values are used here; the abstract's claim that the largest deficits were in hip-dominant exercise holds for gluteus maximus but not biceps femoris (24.5 %MVIC gap in the Nordic hamstring curl vs 23.7 in the kettlebell swing).
practicalImplications: Because injured players showed lower activation in both knee-dominant and hip-dominant exercises, staff could include both types when assessing or training athletes after a recent hamstring strain. The study does not show that restoring activation reduces reinjury or that a particular exercise sequence improves outcomes.
athleteDev: Lower posterior chain activation after a recent hamstring strain suggests that the hamstring, gluteal and trunk muscles may not work fully in these exercises for some players. Performance staff can use these results as context for exercise choice, but the study did not measure strength, sprinting or change-of-direction outcomes.
rtp: The study did not report return-to-play status or test readiness, so it cannot be used as a clearance criterion or as evidence that deficits persist after return to play. The authors suggest sEMG benchmarks could guide return-to-play decisions, but this was not tested.

citation: Scattone Silva R, Song K, Hullfish TJ, Sprague A, Silbernagel KG, Baxter JR. Patellar tendon load progression during rehabilitation exercises: implications for the treatment of patellar tendon injuries. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2024;56(3):545-552.
abstract: Twenty healthy adults performed 35 rehabilitation and sport-movement exercises while motion capture and force plate data were collected. A patellar tendon loading index, weighted 50% loading peak, 30% impulse and 20% loading rate, was used to rank the exercises, with the single-leg decline squat highest (0.747) and walking lowest (0.106).
tldr: Patellar tendon load was highest in single-leg decline squats, run-and-cut and single-leg hops, and lowest in walking, low step-ups and 60-degree squats. The tiers offer an ordered loading progression, but they come from healthy adults and a model-estimated tendon force.
methods: Twenty healthy adults (10 women, 10 men) with no lower-limb or spine injury in the previous 6 months performed 35 exercises. Twelve-camera motion capture (100 Hz) and three force plates (1000 Hz) fed a constrained sagittal-plane knee model, and patellar tendon force was estimated as knee moment divided by a knee-angle-dependent moment arm. Loading peak, impulse and rate were normalised and combined into a loading index, and exercises were grouped into three tiers (index of 0.33 or less, 0.33 to 0.66, and 0.66 or more).
findings: The single-leg decline squat had the highest loading index (0.747; peak 5.2 body weights), followed by run-and-cut (0.725) and single-leg countermovement hop (0.711). Walking (0.106), low step-up (0.187), 60-degree double-leg squat (0.224), low step-down (0.288) and high step-up (0.321) were tier 1. The Spanish squat scored 0.563, mostly from loading impulse. Single-leg squats did not double the peak load of double-leg squats, and 60-degree squats produced about half the peak load of full squats (1.8 versus 3.4 body weights).
limitations: Participants were young healthy adults, not patients with patellar tendinopathy or ACL reconstruction, and the authors caution against generalising to patients. Patellar tendon force was estimated from net knee moment with a sagittal-plane knee model, not measured, so frontal and transverse plane effects and hamstring coactivation were not modelled, and the Spanish squat relied on an assumed equal belt force. The weights and scaling of the three loading parameters rest on the authors' judgment, changing them changes the ranking, and the tiers have not been tested in intervention studies.
practicalImplications: Clinicians can use the tiers to sequence loading, for example starting with lower-tier step-ups and 60-degree squats before full squats. The authors suggest the single-leg decline squat is not the best first exercise for tendinopathy, and that jumps and landings can enter at an intermediate stage, excluding the highest-tier hops. They also note the Spanish squat produces anterior tibial translation, which they consider contraindicated in the early phase after bone-patellar tendon-bone graft.
athleteDev: The tiers can help order jump and landing loads within a conditioning progression. The study did not measure performance outcomes or use athletes.
rtp: Limited to load ordering. The authors suggest ranking exercises by loading rate near return to sport, but the study did not test this or any return-to-sport criterion.

citation: Girdwood MA, Crossley KM, Patterson BE, Rio EK, Whitehead TS, Morris HG, et al. People are more variable than their hop test would suggest: hop performance and self-reported outcomes over 11 years following ACL reconstruction. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2024;34:e14727.
abstract: A cohort of 124 adults followed for 11 years after hamstring-autograft ACL reconstruction showed stable self-reported knee pain and quality of life on average, with wide individual variation. Better single-forward and side hop performance at one year was modestly related to better later KOOS pain, but hop performance was not related to subsequent knee events.
tldr: Self-reported knee pain and quality of life after ACL reconstruction stayed broadly stable for 11 years, with large differences between individuals. One-year hop performance showed only small, group-level links to later knee pain and no link to later knee injury or surgery.
methods: Prospective cohort of 124 adults aged 18 to 50 at ACL reconstruction with a hamstring autograft, assessed at 1 year, with follow-up at 3 years (n = 114), 5 years (n = 89) and 11 years (n = 72). Single-forward, triple-crossover and side hop tests were done at 1 year, but only single-forward and side hop were used as predictors because the two forward tests were highly correlated (r = 0.90); KOOS pain and quality of life were collected at each follow-up. Ordered beta mixed models estimated hop-outcome relationships, and Cox models related hop performance to subsequent knee events, adjusted for age, sex, BMI and concomitant injury with return to preinjury sport as a time-varying covariate.
findings: Mean KOOS pain changed by 3 points or less and KOOS quality of life by up to 10 points (at 5 years) across follow-up, with large individual variation (ICC 0.67 for pain). Each additional cm of single-forward hop was associated with a 0.06% better KOOS pain score (95% CI 0.02 to 0.10), and each side hop repetition with 0.10% (0.02 to 0.19); for quality of life the single-forward hop relationship was present below 108 cm (0.36% per cm, 0.19 to 0.52) but not above it. There were 21 index-knee and 11 contralateral subsequent knee events, and hop performance was not related to their risk (index-knee HR 0.99, 0.98 to 1.02).
limitations: Single-centre cohort with about 40% dropout by 11 years, and men were more likely than women to be lost (OR 3.55), so attrition bias is possible. Rehabilitation was not controlled, return-to-sport testing was not routine, knee events were recalled by participants, and sport type and competitive level were not reported. The text gives 11 contralateral events while Table 2 totals 12 (one participant injured both knees), and the abstract gives age as 31 ± 8 years while Table 1 gives 30.8 (8.7); table values are reported here.
practicalImplications: Hop testing remains useful for judging readiness to return to sport and for setting rehabilitation goals. For long-term prognosis, the authors suggest that the patient's current self-reported knee status at 1 year may be a better guide than hop performance. Hop results should not be used to tell an individual patient what their knee outcome will be.
athleteDev: Not applicable to athlete development. The study concerns knee outcomes after ACL reconstruction, not performance improvement.
rtp: Relevant to return-to-sport testing, but the study does not show that passing hop criteria reduces reinjury risk. Return to preinjury sport was not associated with later knee injury, and the authors say the impact of passing return-to-sport criteria could not be measured.

citation: Cotton MO, Sliepka JM III, Klavas DM, McCulloch PC, Harris JD, Jack RA II. Performance and Return to Sport After Open Fracture in National Football League Players. The Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2021;9(9):23259671211027862.
abstract: Retrospective comparative series of 37 NFL players who sustained an open fracture between 1970 and 2018, each compared with one matched control. Thirty players (81%) returned to at least one NFL game after a mean of 9.3 ± 8.2 months. Career length, games per season and performance scores were similar to matched controls, and upper-extremity fractures were associated with faster return and better postinjury performance than lower-extremity fractures.
tldr: Most NFL players with open fractures (81%) returned to play, at an average of about 9 months, with career length and performance similar to matched controls. Upper-extremity fractures returned faster than lower-extremity fractures, but that difference disappears when hand and finger injuries are excluded.
methods: Retrospective comparative series using public NFL records and pro-football-reference statistics. Each injured player was matched to one control by position, age (±1 year), experience (±1 year) and preinjury performance, and a position-specific performance score was compared using paired t tests.
findings: Of 37 players, 30 (81%) returned, with a mean time to return of 9.3 ± 8.2 months. Postinjury career length (4.3 vs 4.4 seasons), games per season (11.5 vs 11.3) and performance score (5.0 vs 4.7) did not differ from controls, and performance was similar to preinjury levels (5.0 vs 5.5). Upper-extremity fractures returned faster than lower-extremity fractures (4.0 ± 4.8 vs 14.6 ± 7.4 months, P = .00007) and scored higher postinjury (6.4 ± 4.3 vs 3.3 ± 2.1, P = .03), but these differences were not seen after hand and finger fractures were excluded.
limitations: Data came from public online records, which carry selection, reporting and observer bias, and fracture details, classification and treatment were largely unavailable. The sample of 37 players is small, the authors note possible beta error, and offensive linemen performance scores, players still active and patient-reported outcomes were not assessed.
practicalImplications: Staff can use the 81% return rate and the similar postinjury career length and performance scores to set realistic expectations for NFL players with open fractures. Four hand or finger fractures in this series were managed without surgery and those players returned, so nonoperative management may be considered case by case. The findings come from NFL players and may not transfer to other sports or levels.
athleteDev: Performance scores in players who returned were close to their preinjury levels overall, which gives performance staff a reference for expected output after this injury at NFL level. The paper contains no training, load or monitoring data, and it does not score offensive linemen.
rtp: The study can inform return-to-sport expectations: 30 of 37 NFL players (81%) played again, typically after about 9 months. It cannot set a return-to-play date for an individual athlete, because fracture grade, treatment and surgery timing are not available.

citation: Bodendorfer BM, DeFroda SF, Shu HT, Knapik DM, Yang DS, Verma NN. Performance and Survivorship of National Football League Players with Pectoralis Major Injuries. Arthroscopy, Sports Medicine, and Rehabilitation. 2021:e1-e8.
abstract: This study used publicly available NFL data from the 1998 to 2020 seasons to examine return to play, performance and career length after pectoralis major injuries. It compared injury grades and operative with nonoperative management in 258 injuries. Most players returned to play, but return was lower and slower after surgical repair, and some defensive positions and wide receivers had lower performance scores after injury.
tldr: NFL players with pectoralis major injuries returned to play less often and later after surgical repair, likely because repaired injuries were higher grade. Performance scores fell for some defensive positions and wide receivers after return, and career length did not differ by treatment.
methods: Injuries were identified from weekly NFL injury reports and Pro-Football-Reference, verified with press releases, and graded from news reports or inferred from treatment and return. Player Efficiency Rating (PER) and Pro Football Focus (PFF) scores were compared for the season before injury and two seasons after, with Kaplan-Meier survival and log-rank tests for return to play and career length.
findings: Of 258 injuries, 126 (48.8%) were repaired, 95.2% of them grade III, while none of the 116 nonoperatively treated injuries were grade III. Return to play was 85.3% overall, with 78.6% after repair vs 95.7% nonoperatively (P < .005), and mean return of 289.5 vs 47.4 days. PER was lower in the first postinjury season for overall defense (.32 to .28, P = .046) and defensive backs (.35 to .25, P = .049), and in the second season for defensive linemen (.38 to .27, P = .019) and wide receivers (6.68 to 3.58, P = .030); defensive linemen also had lower PFF grades in season 2 (P = .044), and career length did not differ by management (P = .980).
limitations: Injuries came from public databases and some 'chest' or 'undisclosed' reports could not be confirmed, while grade was inferred from news reports and treatment. Operatively treated players had lower preinjury PER (P = .004), and the subgroup sizes are small. The abstract reports shorter career length for tears than strains (P < .001), but the results report no difference by degree of injury (P = .540), and the Discussion says only defensive linemen and wide receivers declined although Table 5 also shows first-season declines for overall defense and defensive backs; this summary follows the results and tables.
practicalImplications: Staff can expect a lower return-to-play rate and a longer time to return after surgical repair of pectoralis major injuries in NFL players, which in this sample mostly reflects higher-grade tears. Defensive players, especially defensive backs in the first season and defensive linemen in the second, and wide receivers in the second season showed lower PER or PFF scores, so their performance may be worth following after return. Career length did not differ by management in this sample.
athleteDev: Performance staff can use the position-specific PER and PFF declines (defensive backs and overall defense in season 1, defensive linemen and wide receivers in season 2) to plan follow-up after pectoralis major injury. PER is not defined for offensive linemen, and the paper reports no training, load or strength data.
rtp: The study can inform return-to-sport expectations for NFL players: 85.3% returned overall, 78.6% after repair vs 95.7% nonoperatively, with mean return of 289.5 vs 47.4 days. It cannot set an individual return date or support a repair decision, because injury grade was inferred, the sample is NFL-only, and strength outcomes were not measured.

citation: Harty PS, Cottet ML, Malloy JK, Kerksick CM. Nutritional and Supplementation Strategies to Prevent and Attenuate Exercise-Induced Muscle Damage: a Brief Review. Sports Medicine - Open. 2019;5:1.
abstract: This brief narrative review summarises nutritional and supplementation strategies that have been studied for exercise-induced muscle damage, grouped by nutrient source. It states that many strategies have been tested with varying results, and it focuses on acute damaging-exercise studies. The authors state that effective strategies matter to athletes whose training quality and performance are affected by muscle damage.
tldr: Several foods and supplements, including tart cherry, pomegranate, protease and chronic n-3 fatty acids, show some benefit for muscle damage symptoms, but results are mixed and often depend on the damaging exercise used. The review offers no firm dosing guidance.
methods: Brief narrative review by four authors, organised into fruit, vegetable, herb, amino acid and protein, vitamin, and other supplement sections. Only strategies tested in at least two well-controlled studies were included, acute damaging-exercise studies were the focus, and oxidative stress outcomes were excluded. No systematic search method is described.
findings: Chronic tart cherry juice or concentrate is described as effectively modulating muscle damage symptoms, and pomegranate juice as improving functional measures and reducing markers of damage in several studies. Protease supplements improved muscle function and soreness in some studies, but effects on biomarkers were less clear. Vitamin D3 may improve outcomes, whereas vitamin D2 may increase damage in one study, and caffeine mainly reduces soreness rather than biomarkers.
limitations: The review is brief and selective, and it describes no systematic search or risk-of-bias assessment. Some cited studies used damage protocols that the authors judged insufficient to produce a clear effect, and the authors note that the effects of combined strategies and the potency of many strategies in female participants remain unclear.
practicalImplications: Athletes who need quick recovery between damaging sessions could trial tart cherry or pomegranate products, and staff can track soreness and function to judge individual response. The authors warn that long-term use of some nutrients may impair training adaptations, so chronic use should be weighed against the need for recovery. Staff should not assume that any one supplement is proven, because the review rates many results as mixed.
athleteDev: For athletes who must recover quickly between damaging training or competition, the review describes some supplements, such as tart cherry and protease, as promising for soreness and muscle function. The review states that these effects are inconsistent, and long-term use may blunt training adaptations, so they should be trialled and monitored rather than assumed to improve performance.
rtp: This review cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It covers recovery from exercise-induced soreness and muscle damage in healthy or active people, and it does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to play.

citation: Gratwicke M, Miles KH, Pyne DB, Pumpa KL, Clark B. Nutritional Interventions to Improve Sleep in Team-Sport Athletes: A Narrative Review. Nutrients. 2021;13:1586.
abstract: The authors review nutritional interventions for sleep quality and quantity in team-sport athletes. They found few athlete studies and report that selected interventions improve sleep in general populations, with dose, source and timing still to be defined for athletes.
tldr: Sleep nutrition evidence in athletes is limited to four small studies with mixed results. Most supporting evidence comes from healthy adults and poor sleepers, so the timing and doses in this review should be trialled with individual athletes.
methods: Narrative review with a semi-systematic search of PubMed, Scopus, CINAHL, EMBASE, SPORTDiscus and Google Scholar to November 2020. Athlete studies were prioritised, and healthy adult and poor-sleeper trials were included because athlete data are scarce.
findings: The four athlete studies were mixed: high-carbohydrate drinks during intensified training reduced total sleep time by 19 minutes in 10 cyclists (Table 2), a high-glycemic-index evening meal gave a non-significant 26.5-minute increase in 8 basketball players, 40 g alpha-lactalbumin had no effect in 6 track cyclists, and beetroot juice improved PSQI sleep quality in 30 male athletes. In non-athletes, a high-glycemic-index meal after evening exercise increased total sleep time by 62 minutes in 10 healthy active males, two kiwifruit an hour before bed added 55 minutes in 24 poor sleepers, 20 g alpha-lactalbumin added 55 minutes in 10 healthy males, and tart cherry juice added 29 to 39 minutes in two trials.
limitations: Only four athlete studies were included, with 6 to 30 participants each, and no formal risk-of-bias assessment is reported. The text and tables disagree on several attributions, so Table 1 values are used here: the text assigns cycling to refs 21 and 22 and basketball to ref 23, while Table 1 lists ref 22 (Daniel) as basketball, ref 23 (Shamloo) as unspecified male athletes and ref 24 (MacInnis) as track cyclists; Table 2 labels Daniel as ref 24 and Inagawa as ref 30; and the tart cherry discussion swaps the healthy-adult (Howatson, ref 27) and insomnia (Pigeon, ref 31) studies. The text also does not discuss the athlete carbohydrate study that Table 2 shows reducing total sleep time.
practicalImplications: For an athlete with sleep trouble after late training, competition or travel, the authors suggest options such as a high-glycemic-index meal 2 to 4 hours before bed, 3 g of glycine before bed, kiwifruit, or tart cherry juice, based mainly on non-athlete data. Their suggested 20 to 40 g alpha-lactalbumin 2 hours before bed is the protocol that showed no effect in the only athlete trial. The review also advises avoiding caffeine, alcohol and excess fluid before sleep.
athleteDev: The review does not measure performance outcomes that would support a performance claim. Its sleep findings come from small athlete samples and from non-athletes.
rtp: The review does not address return to sport or injury recovery, and it excluded participants with concussion. It cannot be used to set a sleep or nutrition plan during concussion or post-injury rehabilitation.

citation: Langan-Evans C, Hearris MA, Gallagher C, Long S, Thomas C, Moss AD, et al. Nutritional Modulation of Sleep Latency, Duration, and Efficiency: A Randomized, Repeated-Measures, Double-Blind Deception Study. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2023;55(2):289-300.
abstract: Randomized, repeated-measures, double-blind crossover study in 16 healthy adults testing whether a blend of tryptophan, glycine, magnesium, tart cherry powder and L-theanine improves sleep under free-living conditions. Participants were told the study was about fat oxidation; 75% did not identify sleep as the true outcome. The blend shortened sleep onset latency, increased total sleep time and sleep efficiency, and reduced morning sleepiness compared with placebo.
tldr: In 16 healthy non-athlete adults, a pre-bed blend of tryptophan, glycine, magnesium, tart cherry and L-theanine helped them fall asleep about 24 minutes faster and sleep about 22 minutes longer over 3 nights than placebo. It has not been tested in athletes or for performance.
methods: After a 3-day familiarization period to record habitual sleep, diet, activity and light exposure, participants completed 3-day intervention and placebo trials in random order, 4 days apart, taking opaque pills 2 h before bed. Sleep was measured with wrist actigraphy (MotionWatch 8), the Consensus Sleep Diary and the Karolinska Sleepiness Scale, and diet was replicated using weighed food records and photographs with 100% reported compliance. Conditions were compared with paired t-tests or Wilcoxon tests, and urine metabolomics were analysed in a random subgroup of 8.
findings: Sleep onset latency was 16 +/- 6 min with the blend versus 40 +/- 25 min with placebo (P = 0.002, ES 1.29), total sleep time 422 vs 400 min (P = 0.01, ES 0.55), and sleep efficiency 83.3% vs 80.9% (P = 0.03, ES 0.48). Wake after sleep onset (49 vs 51 min) and time in bed did not differ, and morning but not evening sleepiness was lower with the blend (P = 0.02). In the 8-person metabolomic subgroup, urinary 6-sulfatoxymelatonin and D-serine were higher and L-glutamic acid lower with the blend.
limitations: The sample was small, not athletes, and each trial lasted only 3 nights, so longer-term effects are unknown. Actigraphy cannot assess sleep stages, the blend cannot isolate individual ingredients, and magnesium status was not measured. Half the sample were poor sleepers by PSQI and 14 of 16 had short or inefficient sleep by actigraphy at baseline, which may not reflect well-rested athletes; the study was funded by Science in Sport and one author consults for the company, which the authors state had no role in the study.
practicalImplications: For staff working with athletes who report trouble falling asleep, this blend taken 2 h before bed is one option with controlled evidence of shorter sleep onset over a few nights in healthy young adults. Any use with athletes should be checked for anti-doping certification and monitored individually, since the study did not include athletes.
athleteDev: The study measured no training, performance or recovery outcomes, so it cannot show that the sleep changes improve athletic performance. The authors' links to exercise performance are discussion only.
rtp: The study did not involve injured athletes or rehabilitation, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.

citation: Nobari H, Banihashemi M, Saedmocheshi S, Prieto-González P, Oliveira R. Overview of the impact of sleep monitoring on optimal performance, immune system function and injury risk reduction in athletes: a narrative review. Sci Prog. 2023;106(4):1-18.
abstract: This narrative review examines how sleep quantity and quality affect performance, recovery, immune function and injury risk in athletes, and how sleep can be monitored. The authors state that athletes may experience lower sleep quality and quantity than is needed. They describe questionnaires, sleep diaries, actigraphy and polysomnography as monitoring options, with nutrition and bedtime routines as improvement strategies.
tldr: The review argues that athletes often sleep less and worse than they need and that sleep should be monitored alongside training load. Its specific injury and performance figures are attached to mismatched or missing references, so treat it as a general overview, not a source of numbers.
methods: Narrative review with no described search strategy, selection criteria or quality appraisal. It covers sleep physiology, hormones and immune function, sex differences, sleep monitoring tools (questionnaires, diaries, actigraphy and polysomnography), nutrition and supplements, and sleep-hygiene tips.
findings: The review's clearest sourced content is on monitoring: it reports that actigraphy showed 81 to 90% agreement and 81 to 92% sensitivity against polysomnography in athletes, that software thresholds change its bias, and that it performs poorly in people with fragmented sleep. It also states that sleeping under 8 hours was linked to a 65% higher injury risk in 122 athletes, that adolescent athletes sleeping under 8 hours were injured 1.7 times as often, and that extending sleep to about 8.4 hours improved endurance performance; these are not established findings here, because the first and third cite references on consumer sleep devices and the second has no citation. It lists tryptophan, melatonin (5 to 8 mg) and other supplements in Table 1, noting no demonstrated benefit for valerian or L-theanine.
limitations: The paper does not describe how sources were selected or appraised. Several claims cite references that do not match them: the 65% injury figure cites a review of consumer sleep devices (ref 22), the soccer sleep-deprivation and injury claim cites a paper on betatrophin in type 1 diabetes (ref 23), the endurance sleep-extension result cites a review of consumer trackers (ref 26), and the sex-difference figures cite supplement and meal studies (refs 43, 44). Several passages are garbled, including the sex-difference sentence, the kiwifruit paragraph, 'octopography' for actigraphy, 'I require 12 hours of sleep every night' in Table 2, and a nap limit of 'half an afternoon', and the conclusion mentions wearable ultrasound monitors that the body text does not discuss.
practicalImplications: Staff can track sleep alongside training load, using low-cost questionnaires such as the Hooper index sleep item or sleep diaries routinely and research-grade actigraphy for multi-day tracking. General sleep-hygiene habits the review lists include a consistent bedtime and wake time, a dark, cool and quiet room, no screens in bed, avoiding caffeine close to bedtime, and avoiding late-afternoon or evening naps. The review's injury-risk and performance numbers should not be used to set policy without checking the original studies.
athleteDev: The review states that short sleep is linked to lower speed, anaerobic power and attention, so performance staff can monitor sleep next to training load when planning sessions. It gives no validated thresholds, and it notes that smartphone sleep apps still need validation.
rtp: The review does not address return to sport or injury clearance. It notes that athletes may need extra sleep to recover from injuries caused by intense training, but it gives no sleep target or criteria for return to play.

citation: Falkenberg E, Aisbett B, Lastella M, Roberts S, Condo D. Nutrient intake, meal timing and sleep in elite male Australian football players. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2020.
abstract: This cohort study tracked sleep with actigraphy and sleep diaries, and dietary intake with photo food diaries, in 36 elite male Australian Football League players across 10 pre-season days. Higher total daily protein intake was associated with more wake after sleep onset and lower sleep efficiency, and higher evening sugar intake was associated with less total sleep time and less wake after sleep onset. A longer gap between the evening meal and bedtime was associated with less total sleep time.
tldr: In elite Australian football players, evening sugar intake and the time gap between the last meal and bedtime were the dietary factors most linked to sleep. These are observational associations, not tested dietary changes.
methods: Prospective cohort study of 36 male players from one professional club over 10 consecutive pre-season days. Sleep was measured with wrist actigraphy (medium threshold) and sleep diaries, and food intake with the MealLogger photo app and FoodWorks analysis; generalised linear mixed models adjusted for training load, previous-night sleep, travel, chronotype, alcohol, caffeine, age and body mass.
findings: Higher total daily protein (g/kg) was linked to more wake after sleep onset (+4.0 min, P = 0.013) and lower sleep efficiency (-0.7%, P = 0.006). Higher evening sugar (g/kg) was linked to less total sleep time (-5.1 min, P = 0.027), less wake after sleep onset (-1.0 min, P = 0.005) and slightly higher sleep efficiency (+0.2%, P = 0.021), and higher evening energy was linked to longer sleep onset latency (+5.0 min per MJ, P = 0.011). Each extra hour between the main evening meal and bedtime was linked to 8.1 min less total sleep time (P = 0.042) and 2.3 min less wake after sleep onset (P = 0.015).
limitations: The study is observational, with a single club and 36 players, and sleep and food intake were estimated by actigraphy, diaries and a photo app that has not been validated against weighed food records. The abstract attributes the sleep-onset-latency association to total daily energy intake, but Table 1 shows no such association (0.7 min, P = 0.116); the association is for evening energy intake (5.0 min, P = 0.011, Table 2). For evening protein (g/kg) and sleep onset latency, the abstract gives P = 0.02 and the Discussion a 4-min decrease, while Table 2 and the Results give -2.2 min (P = 0.016).
practicalImplications: Practitioners could raise evening sugar intake and the timing of the last meal with players who sleep poorly, since these were the factors most linked to sleep in this group. The authors' advice to take whey protein before bed is not supported by these data, because protein type was not analysed and no intervention was tested. Eating closer to bedtime was linked to longer sleep time but more wake time after sleep onset, so staff should not assume that a later meal is simply better or worse for sleep.
athleteDev: In elite male Australian football players, higher evening sugar intake and a longer gap between the evening meal and bedtime were linked to less total sleep, and higher total daily protein was linked to more wake time after sleep onset. These findings suggest topics to review with players, but they do not show that changing these intakes would improve sleep or performance.
rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It did not study injured players, and it did not measure sleep or nutrition during rehabilitation, return-to-play clearance or re-injury.

citation: Halson SL, Burke LM, Pearce J. Nutrition for Travel- from Jetlag to Catering. International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism. 2018.
abstract: This scholarly review covers the travel challenges of high-performance athletes, mainly track and field athletes, including jetlag, fatigue and gastrointestinal comfort, travel hygiene and illness, and catering in unfamiliar environments. It discusses melatonin, caffeine and meal timing and composition for jetlag, and it sets out shared responsibilities among athletes, team management and caterers for food and water safety and eating behaviour.
tldr: Traveling athletes face jetlag, travel fatigue, illness and catering problems that planning can reduce. The evidence for melatonin, caffeine and meal timing against jetlag is limited, and the review treats food safety and eating behaviour as shared responsibilities.
methods: Scholarly narrative review. The authors cover jetlag, travel fatigue and eating en route, travel hygiene and catering, and provide checklists for caterers, teams and athletes. No systematic search or study-selection method is described.
findings: Melatonin shifts the body clock in a direction that depends on the timing of intake, and a cited systematic review found it reduced subjective jetlag compared with placebo. A cited study found 300 mg of slow-release caffeine at 08:00 destination time for 5 days resynchronised faster than placebo. The review reports that illness rose two- to threefold with travel across more than five hours' time difference, citing earlier work.
limitations: The review has no described search or appraisal method, so its selection of evidence cannot be checked. The authors note that meal composition and timing effects on jetlag have not been well studied in athletes, and that melatonin product content varied from 18% to 478% of the labelled amount in one cited survey.
practicalImplications: Plan meals, snacks and fluids around the travel itinerary, and for athletes prone to motion sickness the review lists avoiding large meals, caffeine and alcohol before and during travel. Agree team food and hygiene protocols before departure and check destination food and water safety. Check supplements such as melatonin for content and banned substances before use, because the review reports that product content varies.
athleteDev: For traveling track and field athletes, planned meal timing, food access and fluid intake before and during travel are presented as ways to limit jetlag and fatigue effects on performance. The review's evidence for melatonin, caffeine and meal timing against jetlag is limited, so these tools should be trialled rather than assumed to work.
rtp: This review cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It covers travel nutrition, illness prevention and catering for traveling athletes and does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to play.

citation: Rotovnik Kozjek N, Tonin G, Gleeson M. Nutrition for optimising immune function and recovery from injury in sports. Clinical Nutrition ESPEN. 2025;66:101-114.
abstract: This educational narrative review describes how nutrition relates to immune function, sports injury, detraining and rehabilitation in athletes. It sets out nutritional targets for energy, protein, carbohydrate, fat and micronutrients, and tabulates supplement recommendations. The authors conclude that a quality whole-food diet comes first and that supplements are mainly indicated for documented deficiencies.
tldr: Injured or training athletes need adequate energy, protein and carbohydrate from quality whole foods, and supplements are generally limited to documented deficiencies such as vitamin D. The supplement tables give specific doses, but many carry limited or no clear evidence.
methods: Educational narrative review with learning objectives, written by three authors. It covers injury terminology and stages, detraining, immunometabolism, immunodepression and moderating factors, and nutritional targets, drawing on cited literature. No search strategy or study-selection method is described.
findings: The review notes that immobilisation causes muscle mass loss of about 0.5-0.6% per day. It gives post-injury targets of 1.6-2.5 g/kg/day protein and carbohydrate of 3-5 g/kg/day, and says low energy availability (<30 kcal/kg fat-free mass/day) should be avoided. Supplement tables rate glutamine as having no clear benefit for infection incidence, and report that vitamin C at 0.25-1.0 g/day may reduce the incidence, duration and severity of common colds in athletes.
limitations: The review has no described search or appraisal method, so the evidence base and the strength of each recommendation cannot be checked. Several recommendations are extrapolated from immobilisation, non-athlete or small studies, and the authors state that evidence for immune-supporting supplements is limited.
practicalImplications: For injured athletes, the review recommends individually adjusted energy and protein intake, with whole-food sources spread across the day, before supplements are considered. It recommends a seasonal check of serum vitamin D as part of routine medical examination, with treatment of deficiency, and says iron deficiency should be treated only under medical supervision. Antioxidant supplements are not recommended in the review, which cites evidence that high vitamin C plus vitamin E intake can impair training adaptation, and third-party testing is advised for any supplement.
athleteDev: The review's performance-related content is limited to energy availability, and to protein and carbohydrate targets for training and immune health. It frames a quality diet as the first line of immune support, and it does not test performance outcomes.
rtp: The review gives nutrition targets during immobilisation and rehabilitation and states that nutritional support can aid the return to activity. It did not study return-to-sport outcomes and sets no return-to-play criteria, so it cannot be used to decide whether an athlete is ready to return.

citation: Rocha-Rodrigues S, Leão C, Marinho M, Afonso J. Nutritional approaches applied to recovery of skeletal muscle injury immobilization: a review of nutrition aid for sport trauma. J Sports Med Phys Fitness. 2024 Sep 17.
abstract: The authors review current evidence on nutritional approaches to skeletal muscle injury recovery in athletes, covering energy intake, proteins, carbohydrates, vitamins and omega-3 fatty acids. They conclude that evidence from injured athletes is scarce, so specific guidelines cannot yet be established.
tldr: Evidence on nutrition for recovering from a muscle injury in athletes is thin. Most of it comes from healthy people with immobilization or induced soreness, so it cannot yet support specific guidelines for injured athletes.
methods: Narrative review of the literature on nutrition and skeletal muscle injury recovery. No systematic search method is described.
findings: The authors report that energy needs after injury are variable and recommend monitoring body fat percentage rather than relying on energy expenditure estimates. Creatine results during immobilization in healthy young people were mixed: one small crossover study (n=7, arm cast) and one trial (n=22, leg immobilization) reported preserved or restored muscle mass, while another trial (n=30, leg immobilization) found no effect on muscle mass or strength. A 5-day hydrolysed whey study in young professional soccer players (n=24) reported lower creatine kinase (-42%) and lactate dehydrogenase (-30%) than maltodextrin, and the authors describe evidence for vitamin C, omega-3 and carbohydrate in injured athletes as absent or indirect.
limitations: Most cited data come from healthy or non-injured people, soreness models, or two case studies of soccer players after anterior cruciate ligament injury. No specific guidelines for injured athletes could be formed, and the review does not describe how studies were selected.
practicalImplications: Energy and protein intake during injury recovery should be individualized by the athlete's immobilization level, activity and body composition. Staff should not treat the reviewed supplement findings as an established protocol for injured athletes.
athleteDev: The review offers no performance-enhancement recommendation. Its supplement findings come from healthy or non-injured people.
rtp: Cannot be used to set a nutrition protocol or a return-to-play timeline for injured athletes. The authors state that specific guidelines for injured athletes cannot yet be established.

citation: Bongiovanni T, Genovesi F, Nemmer M, Carling C, Alberti G, Howatson G. Nutritional interventions for reducing the signs and symptoms of exercise-induced muscle damage and accelerate recovery in athletes: current knowledge, practical application and future perspectives. Eur J Appl Physiol. 2020.
abstract: The authors review nutritional strategies for the signs and symptoms of exercise-induced muscle damage and group them by level of supporting evidence. They conclude that the evidence is mixed and suggest a periodised approach to supplementation until more is known about effects on adaptation.
tldr: The authors place vitamin D, omega-3, creatine, tart cherry, beetroot and pomegranate in their best-researched group, but they say this does not mean the supplements are clearly effective, and for vitamin D they find no clear recovery benefit. Where these are used, the authors suggest periodising them around high-stress phases rather than using them all the time.
methods: Invited review. The authors report searching PubMed, EMBASE, Scopus and Web of Science using combinations of EIMD and nutrition terms. No study count, inclusion criteria or risk-of-bias method is reported.
findings: The good-evidence group is defined by the amount of research, and results within it are mixed. For vitamin D, one trial in 20 deficient, moderately active men found better recovery of muscle function after 6 weeks of 4000 IU/day, while other trials found no effect, and the authors conclude there is no clear benefit for recovery after damaging exercise.
