Creatine trials show both lower creatine kinase (for instance, 84% lower in one 5-day study of 14 untrained men) and no effect (for instance, 40 g loading then 10 g daily); vitamins C and E show limited ability to reduce EIMD signs, and a cited Cochrane review rates antioxidant evidence for soreness as moderate to low quality.
limitations: Study designs, doses, timing and outcome measures vary widely, and many trials use untrained or recreationally active participants rather than well-trained athletes. The tiering is internally inconsistent for vitamin D, which is placed in the good-evidence group and Table 1 with a 2000 to 4000 IU daily dose although the text finds no clear recovery benefit. The authors also note that cross-over designs can mask effects through the contralateral repeated bout effect and that most redox measures are mechanistically limited.
practicalImplications: The authors suggest a regular, varied diet without added supplements during preseason adaptation phases, and carefully planned interventions when fast recovery is the priority, such as congested fixture schedules. Vitamin D should be used to maintain sufficient status rather than as a recovery aid, since the review finds no clear recovery benefit.
athleteDev: The authors raise a theoretical concern that antioxidant or anti-inflammatory supplements could blunt training adaptation, while stating there is no evidence yet that these interventions do so; this is the basis for their periodised approach. The review does not show that any intervention improves performance or adaptation.
rtp: The review concerns recovery from exercise-induced muscle damage, not injury. It cannot be used to set a return-to-play nutrition plan after a musculoskeletal injury.

citation: Carey CC, Doyle L, Lucey A. Nutritional priorities, practices and preferences of athletes and active individuals in the context of new product development in the sports nutrition sector. Front Sports Act Living. 2023;5:1088979.
abstract: The authors surveyed athletes and active individuals on their nutrition priorities, supplement and functional food use, and preferred product formats. They conclude that a food-first approach and evidence-based functional foods, focused on recovery, endurance and strength, should guide new sports nutrition products.
tldr: Athletes in this Irish survey most wanted products that support muscle recovery and rated nutritional quality as the top purchase factor. Whole-food formats were the most preferred, though the survey measured preferences rather than product effects.
methods: Online Qualtrics survey of 34 questions, developed from a literature review, two focus groups and a review of products on the Irish and online markets. Recruitment used social media, university email lists and clubs, and analyses were descriptive with Mann-Whitney U tests by gender, competition level and weekly activity time.
findings: Enhanced muscular recovery was the top product claim (first choice 25%, n=101; top three 73%, n=295), ahead of improved endurance (top three 58%) and improved strength and power (57%). Nutritional profile was rated the most important purchase feature (3.37 ± 0.65 out of 4), ahead of taste (3.15 ± 0.80) and ease of access (3.09 ± 0.72). Fifty-eight percent reported taking supplements, 43% used bioactive functional foods, and whole-food products received the most first-choice rankings for both recovery (186) and performance (180) products.
limitations: Recruitment was by convenience sampling in Ireland, the focus groups used to build the questionnaire did not reach saturation, and no health, performance or efficacy outcome was measured. The authors state that rank-order questions could not be compared statistically across gender or competition level; only the 1 to 4 rating questions were tested with Mann-Whitney U, so the discussion's claim that gender influenced the 'rank importance' of product features refers to ratings, not rankings. Some figures differ between text and tables, for example 202 top-three rankings for smoothie or juice in the results text versus 220 in Table 4, and 87% rating scientific proof at least 3 of 4 versus 86% in Table 3.
practicalImplications: Most respondents who changed their recovery routine used stretching (n = 230) and foam rolling (n = 166), which the authors note have little effect on muscle damage recovery, while only 4% used dietary nitrate and 6% polyphenol foods. This points to an education gap staff can address, and to whole-food formats as the options athletes say they prefer.
athleteDev: The survey covers performance-related product priorities, including endurance and strength claims, but it does not show that any product improves performance. Its findings describe preferences, not effects.
rtp: The survey does not address injury or return to sport. It cannot be used to choose a recovery product or plan for an injured athlete returning to training.

citation: Naderi A, Rothschild JA, Santos HO, Hamidvand A, Koozehchian MS, Ghazzagh A, et al. Nutritional Strategies to Improve Post-exercise Recovery and Subsequent Exercise Performance: A Narrative Review. Sports Medicine. 2025.
abstract: Narrative review of nutritional strategies used to speed recovery and improve performance when athletes face short gaps between exercise bouts. It covers carbohydrate type and timing, protein, carbohydrate-protein co-ingestion, fluids and electrolytes, sodium bicarbonate, creatine, caffeine, fats and micronutrients.
tldr: For the first 4 h after exercise, carbohydrate at about 1 to 1.2 g/kg/h, preferably with glucose and fructose in a 2:1 ratio, is the core recovery strategy. Protein, creatine, caffeine and sodium bicarbonate can help in some settings, but their performance effects are inconsistent.
methods: Narrative review. The authors searched PubMed/MEDLINE and Google Scholar using keyword and Boolean combinations, then graded each strategy as strong, moderate or limited evidence. The paper does not report study counts, inclusion criteria or a formal quality appraisal.
findings: Carbohydrate at 1 to 1.2 g/kg/h is recommended for the first 4 h, and glucose-fructose co-ingestion is preferred for gastrointestinal comfort and liver glycogen replenishment. The authors conclude that adding protein to carbohydrate during recovery shorter than 24 h likely has a small positive effect on performance (0.6 to 1.6%), although for glycogen resynthesis the benefit appears only when carbohydrate intake is suboptimal. Sodium bicarbonate may improve subsequent exercise when recovery is about 30 to 90 min, and creatine and caffeine can increase glycogen storage in some studies, though performance results are mixed. Fats have no clear effect on subsequent performance, and micronutrients reduce muscle damage without a clear performance benefit.
limitations: The authors note a sex bias toward male participants, variable exercise protocols, and individual differences by training status and genetics. Several supplement effects are not additive, and the review does not describe a systematic search protocol or study quality appraisal.
practicalImplications: When the next bout is less than 4 h away, athletes can take 1 to 1.2 g/kg/h of carbohydrate in small, frequent doses, preferably glucose-fructose at a 2:1 ratio. Adding 20 to 40 g of protein is reasonable when there is time for digestion. Caffeine or sodium bicarbonate can be considered for specific schedules, with attention to gastrointestinal discomfort and sleep disruption.
athleteDev: Use 1 to 1.2 g/kg/h of carbohydrate in the first 4 h after training when the next session is less than 24 h away, with 20 to 40 g of protein added. Caffeine or sodium bicarbonate may suit athletes with multiple sessions in one day, but the review does not support them as a routine add-on.
rtp: The review covers recovery between training or competition bouts within 24 h. It does not study injury or return to sport and cannot inform return-to-play decisions.

citation: Tomczyk M. Omega-3 Fatty Acids and Muscle Strength: Current State of Knowledge and Future Perspectives. Nutrients. 2024;16:4075.
abstract: Narrative review of the effects of EPA and DHA supplementation on muscle strength in healthy adults and older adults, with a summary of trials and of the limitations that prevent firm conclusions. It also covers the proposed neuromuscular and inflammation-related mechanisms and supplement safety.
tldr: Omega-3 (EPA and DHA) supplementation may produce a small strength gain in healthy and older adults, but the trials are few and inconsistent and most were not in athletes. It is not a proven strength strategy for athletes.
methods: Narrative review with no described search strategy, selection criteria or quality appraisal. Trials are summarized in a table by population, supplement dose, duration and outcome, and meta-analyses are described from the published literature.
findings: Three of six adult trials reported higher strength with omega-3 than placebo (Heileson 2023 in bench press and squat 1RM, Philpott 2019 in leg extension 1RM, Crestani 2017 in knee extension 1RM). In the two athlete trials, Lewis 2015 (30 male athletes) found an unclear effect on quadriceps MVC force with higher vastus lateralis EMG, and Gravina 2017 (soccer players) found no strength difference; Lewis 2017 in active men also found no difference. Among older adults, Xu 2022 (187 participants, 6 months) reported higher grip strength and better Timed Up and Go times than placebo, while Krzymińska-Siemaszko 2015 (53 participants, 12 weeks) found no difference. Cited meta-analyses describe a very small but significant strength effect with low certainty (14 studies), and a network meta-analysis found the highest efficacy above 2.5 g/day.
limitations: The author notes that many trials did not control training or diet, and that dose and duration affect how much omega-3 reaches tissues. The review does not describe how studies were selected. Adverse effects include a higher atrial fibrillation risk in some meta-analyses at high doses, and fishy aftertaste or burping.
practicalImplications: Omega-3 supplementation is unlikely to produce more than a small strength gain, and the trials are small and mixed. If it is used, plan for a long enough period at a standardized dose, since the review cites about 12 weeks at 1000 to 1500 mg/day EPA and DHA to reach an omega-3 index of 8% (Dempsey et al., as cited). The author advises considering atrial fibrillation risk before starting, particularly at high doses or in high-risk individuals.
athleteDev: The strength evidence comes mostly from recreationally trained and older adults, and the two athlete trials in the review found no clear strength gain. If omega-3 is trialled alongside resistance training, expect at most a small effect, track strength and tolerance, and do not treat it as a substitute for training or basic nutrition.
rtp: The review does not study injured athletes or return-to-sport outcomes and cannot guide return-to-play decisions. Its injury remarks refer to general links between strength and injury rates from other studies.

citation: Singh M, Givens M, Singh T, Rao P. Performance Enhancing Supplements and Cardiovascular Health. Current Treatment Options in Cardiovascular Medicine. 2025;27:29.
abstract: This narrative review covers performance enhancing supplements used by recreational athletes, including anabolic-androgenic steroids, testosterone and hormone therapy, caffeine and pre-workout products, and creatine. It summarizes mechanisms, reported benefits and cardiovascular risks, and proposes a risk-stratified approach based on education, screening and shared decision-making.
tldr: The review links anabolic-androgenic steroid misuse to serious cardiovascular and metabolic harm. It describes low to moderate caffeine and creatine intake as carrying minimal cardiovascular risk in healthy athletes, and notes that the long-term effects of creatine still need study.
methods: Narrative review with an opinion statement, drawing on prior trials, registry studies, meta-analyses and reviews. No search strategy, selection criteria or quality appraisal is described.
findings: In 100 men on an AAS cycle, systolic and diastolic blood pressure rose by 6.87 and 3.17 mmHg, and LDL cholesterol rose by 0.45 mmol/L; many of these changes reversed after cessation. In the TRAVERSE trial, testosterone was noninferior to placebo for major adverse cardiac events but increased pulmonary embolism, acute kidney injury and non-fatal arrhythmias. Creatine at 10 g/day in healthy athletes did not alter creatine clearance or glomerular filtration rate over 10 months to 5 years, and the review states that caffeine above about 6 to 9 mg/kg may add little performance benefit while posing serious cardiovascular risk.
limitations: This is a narrative review with no described search, selection or risk-of-bias method. The registry estimate is subject to confounding, and the TRAVERSE trial had low adherence (39% completed the full study drug duration), which the review says biases results toward the null. The creatine safety data are short- to medium-term, and the authors call for longer prospective trials.
practicalImplications: The review recommends regular checks of hormone levels, hematocrit, lipids, blood pressure and echocardiography for people using AAS. It advises low to moderate caffeine use, notes that many pre-workout products contain 200 mg or more per serving, and says excessive stimulant use warrants screening for comorbidities, genetic heart disease and symptoms. Creatine at about 5 g/day is described as largely safe, with weight gain and fluid retention to consider in people with hypertension or left ventricular dysfunction.
athleteDev: The review describes creatine as improving high-intensity efforts under 30 seconds and supporting strength and power. Caffeine may improve endurance at low to moderate doses, but the benefit is not consistent, and high doses add little.
rtp: This review does not address return to sport after injury, so it cannot set return-to-play timelines or medical clearance. Cardiovascular screening is relevant for athletes who use these supplements, but the review does not define clearance criteria.

citation: Jeukendrup AE. Periodized Nutrition for Athletes. Sports Med. 2017;47(Suppl 1):S51-S63.
abstract: Narrative review defining periodized nutrition (nutritional training) and summarising methods that manipulate carbohydrate availability, gut training, hydration and supplements to shape training adaptation. The author concludes that the methods differ in evidence strength and that most have little performance evidence so far.
tldr: Nutrition can be timed and planned around training to shape adaptation, but most of these methods have little performance evidence yet. Choose methods to fit the goal, such as gut training for race fuelling, and treat the others as untested for performance.
methods: Narrative review with no described search strategy. The author defines periodized nutrition, then categorises methods in a table covering train low, train high, training the gut, training dehydrated and supplements, drawing on earlier reviews and selected primary studies.
findings: Train-low methods such as twice-daily training, fasted training and sleep low have generally changed signalling and oxidative markers, but few have shown performance benefit; two cycling studies of twice-daily training found no performance difference after 3 weeks. In the only sleep-low study with a performance outcome, 10 km running improved within the sleep-low group (n=11) but not the control group (n=10), and in a 3-week study of elite endurance athletes the ketogenic diet group did not improve high-intensity performance (-1.6%) while high-carbohydrate (6.6%) and mixed (5.5%) groups did. The author also reports that caffeine and sodium bicarbonate improve performance within the durations studied and that high-dose antioxidants may blunt training adaptation.
limitations: The review is selective and gives no search, quality appraisal or grading of evidence. Several examples are small early studies in untrained or recreational participants, the sleep-low evidence rests on two studies and the dehydrated-training evidence on one study of 10 recreationally active people. The article was published in a supplement supported by the Gatorade Sports Science Institute (a division of PepsiCo), and the author received an honorarium from GSSI for the meeting and for writing the manuscript.
practicalImplications: Match nutrition methods to the goal: gut training or race-nutrition practice fits endurance athletes with gastrointestinal problems, and caffeine (studied mostly in exercise of about 1 hour) or sodium bicarbonate (about 1 to 10 minutes) fit efforts of those durations. Treat train-low and dehydrated training as unproven for performance, note that the ketogenic diet studies cited showed no performance benefit, and avoid high-dose antioxidants if the goal is training adaptation.
athleteDev: The review frames nutrition as a planned part of training, but finds few performance benefits so far for train-low, sleep-low or ketogenic approaches. It gives no clear guidance yet on fasted or dehydrated training.
rtp: The review does not discuss injury, rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot inform clinical recovery decisions after injury.

citation: Cheuvront SN, Kenefick RW. Personalized fluid and fuel intake for performance optimization in the heat. J Sci Med Sport. 2021.
abstract: Review of how individual sweat rate, thirst and sports-drink fuel targets interact during prolonged exercise in the heat. Using modelled sweat losses for 50 and 90 kg runners, the authors show that drinking to match sweat loss and meeting carbohydrate targets with one sports drink often cannot both be achieved.
tldr: In the heat, drinking enough to limit dehydration and meeting carbohydrate targets from one sports drink often conflict. For longer runs the authors suggest food or more concentrated fuel, and a fluid plan based on individual sweat rate.
methods: Narrative review with worked calculations. Evaporative heat balance and energy-cost equations estimate sweat rates for 50 and 90 kg runners at 0.5, 1.0 and 1.5 L/h over 1, 2 and 4 hours, and the drinking rates needed to hold dehydration at or below 2% of body mass. Fuel targets are 30, 60 and 90 g/h carbohydrate, and thirst-based intake is modelled at 50% of sweat loss.
findings: With no drinking, the modelled runners reach more than 2% dehydration in 11 of 18 scenarios, and drinking a typical sports drink (about 60 g carbohydrate per litre) to meet fluid needs would rarely meet fuel targets. Meeting the 90 g/h fuel target over 4 hours from sports drink alone would require substantial over-drinking. A modelled drink-to-thirst strategy (50% replacement) gave too much or too little fluid in 14 of 18 cases and missed fluid or fuel needs in 28 of 36, but never over-drank relative to sweat rate.
limitations: This is a model with no participants and no measured sweat losses. Its results depend on the assumed 2% threshold, the 50% thirst replacement and the chosen sweat rates. The authors note that 50% is at the high end of reported thirst-driven intake, with others reporting around 20%, so thirst-based results may differ. The source is an accepted manuscript before copyediting, and the authors note that production errors may be found.
practicalImplications: Athletes running long events in the heat need a fluid and fuel plan tested in training, because one sports drink may not meet both needs. Knowing individual sweat rate helps set drinking volumes, and for exercise of about 2 hours or more the authors suggest food or concentrated carbohydrate sources, tested for tolerance, to meet fuel needs without over-drinking.
athleteDev: For performance in the heat, the review suggests planning fluid and carbohydrate targets together, using individual sweat-rate estimates and gels or food for longer efforts. The modelled figures are not tested in athletes, so they guide planning rather than set targets.
rtp: The paper does not address return to sport, heat illness after injury or rehabilitation. Its dehydration threshold concerns exercise performance in healthy runners, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions.

citation: Barber R, Fahey JT, Comfort P, Ripley NJ. Normalization of rapid force to peak force in an isometric hamstring assessment using force plates. Apunts Sports Medicine. 2024;59:100450.
abstract: Twenty elite female soccer players completed three maximal 90-90 isometric hamstring contractions on a force plate. Force at 100 ms and 200 ms, normalized to peak force, showed good absolute and moderate relative reliability, and the authors propose a quadrant method for combining peak force with normalized rapid force to guide training.
tldr: Rapid force at 100 and 200 ms, expressed as a percentage of peak force, was measured reliably in a 90-90 isometric hamstring test on a force plate in elite female soccer players. Whether the proposed quadrant method changes training or detects fatigue is not tested here.
methods: Observational reliability study of 20 elite female soccer players tested once, 72 h after a match. Each player completed three maximal isometric 90-90 hamstring trials per leg on a 1000 Hz force plate, and the mean of three trials was used. F100 and F200 were expressed as a percentage of peak force, with reliability calculated using CV% and ICC.
findings: In Table 1, normalized F100 and F200 had CV 6.12-7.62% and ICC 0.689-0.721. Peak force had CV 3.05% and ICC 0.887 for the left limb and CV 2.25% and ICC 0.917 for the right limb, and no significant difference was found between limbs (P = 0.826-0.919, Hedges g 0.11-0.24). The authors describe a quadrant plot of peak force against normalized rapid force for identifying training priorities.
limitations: Only one test session is described, so between-day reliability was not assessed, and the sample was a single squad of elite female players. The quadrant thresholds are the group means, and the authors state that the 90-90 position may lack specificity to the hamstring injury mechanism and that the fatigue and injury-risk applications need further research. The abstract gives ICC 0.689-0.703 for normalized rapid force, while Table 1 gives 0.689-0.721.
practicalImplications: Normalized rapid force can be measured with acceptable consistency using a single-plate 90-90 test, so a practitioner could track it over time. The quadrant plot is the authors' proposal for choosing between maximal-strength and explosive-strength emphasis, and it has not been tested against training outcomes.
athleteDev: In elite female soccer players, rapid force at 100 and 200 ms normalized to peak force was reproducibly measured in a 90-90 hamstring test on a force plate. The authors propose using peak force and normalized rapid force together to choose between maximal-strength and explosive-strength work, but this use is untested.
rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It included only uninjured players, and the normalized measures have not been shown to track recovery, readiness or re-injury risk.

citation: McKay BA, Delaney JA, Simpkin A, Larkin T, Murray A, Daniels D, et al. Objective Measures of Strain and Subjective Muscle Soreness Differ Between Positional Groups and Season Phases in American College Football. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. Ahead of print, 2023.
abstract: Repeated-measures study of 23 male American college football players across off-season, fall camp and in-season phases, comparing oxidative stress markers, countermovement jump variables and subjective muscle soreness by position group. In 'Bigs' (offensive and defensive linemen), redox markers, jump variables and soreness were higher in the off-season than in the other phases, and 'Skills' showed no significant phase differences in redox markers.
tldr: In one college football team, linemen ('Bigs') showed the highest oxidative strain and soreness in the off-season, a phase where their share of high-speed running was descriptively higher. Position groups should be reviewed separately rather than as one squad.
methods: Weekly point-of-care capillary blood tests (FORT, FORD and derived OSI), countermovement jumps on force plates and a subjective soreness questionnaire were collected over 10 weeks. Linear mixed models with athlete as a random effect compared phases and position groups. GPS data were described but not included in the statistical analysis because about 25% was missing.
findings: In the off-season, FORT, FORD, OSI and soreness were higher in 'Bigs' than in fall camp and in-season, and their jump flight time and RSImod were also highest then (for soreness, the in-season value was also higher than fall camp). 'Combos' showed lower FORT and OSI in the off-season than in the later phases. Between groups, FORT was higher in 'Bigs' than 'Combos' in all three phases, OSI was higher in 'Bigs' than 'Combos' and 'Skills' in the off-season, and FORD was higher in 'Skills' than 'Bigs' in the off-season. The authors report that 'Skills' showed no significant phase differences in FORT, FORD or OSI.
limitations: The study covers one team of 23 players, with 3 off-season and 3 in-season weeks of data, so it does not capture a full season. GPS data were about 25% missing and were not statistically tested. The authors note that CMJ has not been validated as a fatigue measure in American football and that the wellness questionnaire is not formally validated.
practicalImplications: Analyze position groups separately when reviewing team strain data, because the groups differed in redox markers and soreness within the same phase. The authors suggest individual adaptive ranges across season phases to identify maladaptation. They also suggest that rising FORT or FORD with falling CMJ performance may indicate detrimental fatigue, though this was not tested against outcomes.
athleteDev: Review FORT/FORD, CMJ and soreness by position group and season phase, using each athlete's own history rather than one team norm. In this team the largest strain signal for linemen coincided with off-season conditioning, so staff can check off-season running load for that group first, though the study did not test load as a cause.
rtp: The players were tracked during training and competition, and the paper does not assess injured players or return to play. It cannot be used to make return-to-sport decisions.

citation: Di Paolo S, Gokeler A, Benjaminse A, Zaffagnini S, Bragonzoni L. On-field kinematics of cut maneuvers in football players: Are wearable sensors reliable for assessing anterior cruciate ligament injury risk? Journal of Sports Sciences. 2025.
abstract: Cross-sectional study of youth academy soccer players (47 enrolled: 27 male, 20 female) performing a planned Agility T-test and an unplanned football-specific cut, measured with eight wearable inertial sensors. It reports test-retest and side-to-side reliability of joint kinematics and normative values by sex, for use in ACL injury prevention work.
tldr: Wearable inertial sensors gave moderate-to-excellent test-retest reliability for most joint measures during on-field cutting, with weaker side-to-side reliability. Female youth players cut with different knee and trunk patterns than males, but the study does not show that these patterns predict ACL injury.
methods: Players performed two trials per side of a planned 90-degree Agility T-test and an unplanned deceiving cut on artificial turf, with eight MTw Awinda sensors recording at 100 Hz. Intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC 3,1), root mean square error and pooled T-scores assessed test-retest and side-to-side reliability. Male and female values were compared with t-tests or Mann-Whitney tests and Cohen's d. The sample size was estimated a priori at 44 players.
findings: Test-retest reliability was moderate to excellent for most parameters (r = 0.40 to 0.92 in the Agility T-test), while side-to-side reliability was poorer, with excellent values mainly for pelvis and trunk flexion. Sagittal-plane measures were the most reliable, and the authors judged pelvis and trunk frontal-plane values not sufficiently reliable. In the Agility T-test, females had lower knee, pelvis and trunk flexion at peak knee flexion (d = 0.50 to 0.58) and greater frontal-plane range of motion at knee, pelvis and trunk (d = 0.57 to 0.59, from the text); in the deceiving cut, females had lower knee flexion (d = 0.39) and lower trunk lateral tilt (d = 0.73). Females also had lower approach velocity and lower high-intensity acceleration and deceleration percentages (d up to 1.53).
limitations: The design is cross-sectional, so day-to-day reliability and change over time were not measured. Only one sensor type was used, the deceiving cut could not be standardized for speed or angle, and all players were healthy youth, so the findings may not apply to adults or injured players. The text reports four excluded players while Table 1 lists 47. Several sex differences cited in the text (peak knee external rotation d = 1.1, frontal ROM) are in appendices not in the main table, and for the deceiving cut the text reports greater female knee internal rotation while Table 3 shows more external rotation at peak knee flexion (-2.2 vs -0.7 degrees).
practicalImplications: Check the reliability of each joint measure before using wearable data for an individual player, and treat side-to-side differences and pelvis or trunk frontal-plane values with caution. Use sex-specific values as reference points rather than injury-risk cut-offs. The authors advise against judging ACL risk from single peak values and suggest multi-plane analysis of whole-movement patterns.
athleteDev: For academy testing, rely more on sagittal-plane knee and hip measures from wearables than on frontal or transverse-plane values, which the study found less reliable. Compare players with sex-specific reference values, and where possible test cutting in game-like conditions, as the authors recommend.
rtp: The study included healthy youth players only and did not compare injured or post-surgical players. It cannot be used to make return-to-sport decisions, although the authors suggest future studies in cleared ACL-injured players.

citation: Slutsky-Ganesh AB, Baup S, Bharadwaj UU, Slaton JA, Valencia M, Diekfuss JA, et al. Optimizing MRI annotation workflows for high-accuracy deep learning thigh muscle segmentation in athletes. Radiology Advances. 2026;3(1):umag005.
abstract: Thigh muscle MRI from 94 male professional football athletes and 67 athletes with acute ACL injury was used to train nnU-Net deep learning models on 5 to 120 annotated subjects, tested on a fixed set of 41 subjects. Twenty training subjects reached a mean Dice of 0.94 against assisted manual segmentation, and fat fraction and diffusion measures agreed closely with manual values.
tldr: In single-site 3 T MRI of football and ACL-injured athletes, a deep learning model trained on 20 annotated thigh scans reached a Dice of 0.94 against assisted manual masks on 41 held-out scans. Agreement was measured against the same semi-automatic ground truth, so the model is not yet validated on other scanners or populations.
methods: Fourteen thigh muscles were segmented on IDEAL water images with semi-automatic 3D propagation followed by manual correction, and these assisted manual masks served as ground truth. nnU-Net models were trained on 13 training-set sizes from 5 to 120 subjects and evaluated on a fixed test set of 41 subjects (34 athletes, 7 ACL). Accuracy was assessed with Dice, relative volume difference, Hausdorff distance, HD95 and average symmetric surface distance, and fat fraction and DTI values from automatic and manual masks were compared by ICC and Bland-Altman analysis.
findings: At 20 training subjects the grand-total results were Dice 0.94 ± 0.02, relative volume difference 4.9% ± 5.2%, ASSD 0.8 ± 0.4 mm and HD95 3.2 ± 2.0 mm, meeting the authors' a priori reliability thresholds. The authors report that 50 subjects first met the stricter thresholds (Table 1: Dice 0.95 ± 0.02, RVD 3.5%, ASSD 0.7 mm, HD95 2.8 mm), and 120 subjects gave Dice 0.95 ± 0.02. Volume ICC was 0.995 and fat fraction ICC was 0.989 at 20 subjects, and the open-source MuscleMap model scored a Dice of 0.65 ± 0.21 on the same test set.
limitations: All data came from one site on a single 3 T GE system, and the cohort was largely male and young (the ACL group had a mean age of 17.0 years, with 23 of 67 male), so generalization to other scanners, protocols and populations is untested; five of 41 test subjects were also excluded from DTI analyses. Agreement is measured against assisted manual masks rather than an independent gold standard, and the 20-subject operating point was identified from learning curves computed on the same fixed test set used to report accuracy. Text and tables conflict: the abstract gives HD95 as 3.2 ± 2.8 mm against 3.2 ± 2.0 mm in Table 1, and the Results say Dice was 'consistently >0.95 with Ntrain = 30 or more' while Table 1 shows 0.95 ± 0.02 at 50 and 120, so table values are reported here.
practicalImplications: Labs with a similar 3 T IDEAL and DTI protocol could build a site-specific model from roughly 20 carefully annotated scans, which reached the authors' reliability thresholds on held-out data. Local validation against manual masks is still needed before the outputs are used for athlete decisions, and the released model is licensed for research use only (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0).
athleteDev: Automated thigh segmentation with fat fraction and diffusion outputs could support repeated measurement of muscle size and composition in athletes, with less manual annotation time. The paper tests segmentation accuracy and biomarker agreement only, not whether these measures detect changes in performance, so it supports a measurement method rather than a training decision.
rtp: The study supports quantitative muscle MRI as a measurement method in ACL-injured athletes, but the ACL group was used only for segmentation accuracy and not for recovery outcomes. It cannot show that these measures track rehabilitation or inform return-to-sport decisions.

citation: Kotsifaki R, Sideris V, King E, Bahr R, Whiteley R. Performance and symmetry measures during vertical jump testing at return to sport after ACL reconstruction. Br J Sports Med. 2023.
abstract: This cross-sectional study used dual force plates to test vertical jumps in athletes at return to sport after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) and in healthy professional football players. Athletes after ACLR remained asymmetrical in the concentric phase and during landing from bilateral jumps, and most performance metrics were still lower than in controls. Normative jump data for professional football players are also reported.
tldr: Athletes cleared to return to sport after ACL reconstruction still showed concentric and landing asymmetries in vertical jumps, and most jump performance metrics had not returned to control values. Vertical jump testing, especially single-leg drop jump metrics, may help identify deficits that standard discharge criteria do not show.
methods: Cross-sectional comparison of 126 male professional or recreational athletes after ACLR, tested within 2 weeks of clearance to return to sport, with 532 male professional soccer players as controls. Four jumps (countermovement, single-leg countermovement, double-leg drop jump and single-leg drop jump) were analysed with ForceDecks software, and between-group differences were tested using mixed-effects models; performance metrics were compared only between professional ACLR athletes and controls.
findings: Concentric impulse symmetry was lower after ACLR in all four jumps (P < 0.001). Peak landing force asymmetry was greater than in controls for the countermovement jump (mean difference -11.6 percentage points, 95% CI -15.4 to -7.9) and the double-leg drop jump (-8.9, 95% CI -14.9 to -2.8), and eccentric impulse asymmetry was greater in the single-leg drop jump only (-3.8, 95% CI -5.8 to -1.7, P = 0.018). Among professional athletes, jump height after ACLR was below controls in the countermovement jump (33.3 vs 36.3 cm) and in the single-leg jumps, and the single-leg drop jump showed the most residual deficits.
limitations: The study used a single-institution, male-only sample, the ACLR group is mostly professional (94 of 126) and its sport is not reported. Sample sizes differ by test, and the controls differ in activity level, so the comparisons are not matched. The Discussion states there were no eccentric deceleration impulse differences at return to sport, but the abstract and Table 2 report a significant eccentric impulse difference in the single-leg drop jump (P = 0.018); this summary follows Table 2, and Table 3 also reports a recreational drop-jump height of 27.3 ± 56.7, which looks like a typographical error.
practicalImplications: The authors suggest that vertical jumps, including single- and double-leg tests, should be part of periodic and return-to-sport testing after ACLR. Clinicians should track jump height, reactive strength index and contact time as well as symmetry, and plyometric training should be part of rehabilitation because single-leg drop jump deficits remained. These suggestions follow from the residual asymmetries observed, but the study does not show that addressing them lowers re-injury risk.
athleteDev: The study gives normative vertical jump values for professional football players, such as a countermovement jump height of 36.3 ± 5.4 cm (Table 3), which performance staff can use as reference points. It shows that concentric impulse and reactive strength index remained lower after ACLR, so these metrics are worth tracking in return-to-performance testing.
rtp: The study informs return-to-sport testing: athletes cleared under standard criteria (including quadriceps and hop limb symmetry above 90%) still showed jump asymmetries at about 9 months after surgery. It cannot show that these deficits predict re-injury or that jump tests should decide clearance, because no injury outcomes were followed.

citation: Amundsen R, Møller M, Bahr R. Performing Nordic hamstring strength testing with additional weight affects the maximal eccentric force measured: do not compare apples to oranges. BMJ Open Sport Exerc Med. 2023;9:e001699.
abstract: In 140 football players (84 women, 56 men), maximal eccentric hamstring force measured on a Nordic device rose when 5 kg or 10 kg of added weight was used, compared with no added weight. The rise occurred in players who could and could not control the final phase, so that criterion should not decide whether weight is used.
tldr: Adding weight to the Nordic hamstring test raises the force measured, whether or not the athlete can control the final phase. Use the same test load for pre and post testing, and do not use the control criterion to choose load.
methods: Female (n=84) and male (n=56) football players performed three maximal Nordic test sets with 0, 5 and 10 kg vests, and 10 men were also tested at 15 and 20 kg. Control of the final phase (about the last 20 degrees) was judged by visual inspection, and differences were analysed with repeated-measures ANOVA and independent t-tests.
findings: Maximal force was higher with 5 kg (women +8 N, 2%; men +18 N, 4%) and 10 kg (women +17 N, 5%; men +27 N, 6%) than with no added weight, in players who could (n=65) and could not (n=75) control the final phase. For men, the extra rise with 10 kg was larger in players who could control the phase (17 N, p=0.004), but this difference was not seen in women.
limitations: Control of the final phase was judged by visual inspection, and its reliability was not tested. Loads were always applied in the same increasing order (0, 5, then 10 kg), so order effects such as learning cannot be ruled out, and the 15 and 20 kg analysis includes only 10 men with low power and unadjusted multiple comparisons. Women and men were tested in different squads and seasons (2021 and 2022), so sex and test season cannot be separated.
practicalImplications: Use the same added weight for pre and post Nordic testing, or test all players with the same load, and do not choose load by whether the athlete can control the final phase. If weight is used, increase it until force plateaus, as the authors recommend.
athleteDev: Keep the Nordic test protocol, including any added load, identical across pre and post testing so that changes are not produced by the protocol. The 2 to 8% rise with load is similar to the test's measurement error, so changes in individual athletes need care when interpreted.
rtp: The study does not address return to sport, injury risk or hamstring rehabilitation criteria. Its load-consistency point may help if the same test tracks strength during rehabilitation, but it sets no return-to-play threshold.

citation: Dello Iacono A, Hillan J, Watson K. Personalizing Resistance Training Mitigates Neuromuscular and Perceived Fatigue: The Autoregulation Cluster Training Method. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2023. Ahead of print.
abstract: Twenty-six resistance-trained men completed bench press and back squat sessions at 75% 1RM, matched for load, volume (24 repetitions) and total rest (240 s), using traditional sets (3 x 8 with 120 s rest), interset rest redistribution (6 x 4 with 48 s between clusters) and autoregulation cluster training (ACT), in which the cluster structure was adjusted during the session to a 20% velocity loss target. IRR and ACT produced less velocity loss than TRA, and ACT produced less velocity loss and rate of fatigue than IRR. The authors conclude that cluster structures reduced neuromuscular and perceived fatigue and that ACT was the most effective.
tldr: In resistance-trained men, cluster-set structures reduced within-session velocity loss and perceived fatigue compared with traditional sets at the same load, volume and total rest. An autoregulated cluster method reduced both more than a fixed cluster structure, but this was a single-session study.
methods: Randomized crossover design with 26 resistance-trained men (mean age 26.7 years). Each man completed three sessions in randomized order (TRA, IRR, ACT) with bench press and back squat at 75% 1RM, 24 repetitions and 240 s total rest, separated by 48 to 72 hours. Mean propulsive velocity was measured with a linear encoder and rate of fatigue was rated on an 11-point scale (0 to 10) within 5 minutes of each exercise. Linear mixed-effects models tested training structure and exercise.
findings: Velocity loss was lower for IRR and ACT pooled than TRA (b = -2.09, P < .001) and lower for ACT than IRR (b = -2.31, P < .001), with no significant structure by exercise interaction; the back squat had greater velocity loss than the bench press (b = 1.83, P < .001). Mean velocity loss was 19.8%, 15.9% and 11.3% for bench press (TRA, IRR, ACT) and 23.3%, 16.6% and 12.6% for back squat (Table 2). Rate of fatigue was lower for IRR and ACT than TRA (b = -0.64, P < .001) and for ACT than IRR (b = -1.05, P < .001). In ACT, 87% of bench press and 82% of back squat repetitions were within the 20% velocity loss target.
limitations: Only men were studied, with two exercises, one load (75% 1RM) and one comparator cluster structure. Lactate and other metabolic markers were not measured, so the mechanisms are speculative. Dello Iacono and Watson declare a conflict of interest as part of the team that developed the ACT mobile app. The Results text prints the pooled IRR and ACT vs TRA velocity loss contrast as b = 2.09, but the abstract, Table 3 and the printed 95% CI (-2.46 to -1.72) all give -2.09, so the text sign is a typo. The first Results paragraph is labelled as rate of fatigue but reports the velocity loss interaction values from Table 3 (b = -0.81 and 0.34, not significant). Outcomes are acute, within-session measures only.
practicalImplications: ACT is a reasonable option for personalized cluster-set prescription in resistance-trained men when the goal is to limit within-session velocity loss and perceived fatigue. It requires velocity measurement during the session, which many staff will not have. Total rest and volume were matched across conditions, so ACT did not add training time in this study.
athleteDev: Within a session, cluster-set structures reduced velocity loss and perceived fatigue compared with traditional sets at matched load, volume and total rest, and the autoregulated version reduced both most. Use this to manage within-session fatigue. The study does not show gains in strength, power or sport performance.
rtp: Not applicable. The sample was healthy, resistance-trained men and no injured or rehabilitating participants were studied, so the study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.

citation: Jones AM, Kirby BS. Physiological Resilience: What Is It and How Might It Be Trained? Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2025;35(3):e70032.
abstract: Physiological resilience is proposed as an additional factor in endurance performance, reflecting how VO2max, efficiency and metabolic thresholds deteriorate during prolonged exercise. The authors describe the physiological basis, practical testing approaches, and the available evidence on training. They suggest that long-term training consistency and volume, prolonged sessions including high-intensity or progressive efforts, and heavy strength and plyometric training may enhance resilience, while noting that the data are scant.
tldr: Physiological resilience (how well VO2max, economy and thresholds hold up during prolonged exercise) may be a separate determinant of endurance performance. Evidence on training is limited, so long-term volume, prolonged sessions with race-pace or progressive efforts, and heavy strength and plyometric work are candidates to test rather than established methods.
methods: Narrative review and perspective by two authors. No search strategy, inclusion criteria or appraisal method is described. The review draws on the Joyner model, data from Clark et al. (critical power after 2 hours of heavy cycling, 36 participants pooled from three studies), and observational and small training studies, including one unpublished doctoral thesis.
findings: After 2 hours of heavy-intensity cycling, critical power fell by about 10% at group mean, with individual declines from 1% to 33%, and the decline was not explained by baseline VO2max or fresh critical power. Substrate shifts toward fat accounted for about 30% of the rise in VO2 over that period. Unhjem reported smaller increases in O2 cost in trained runners than in active adults. Zanini et al. (ref 44) reported a 2.4% change in O2 cost in the higher-performing group versus 4.5% in the lower group. Heavy strength training improved performance after prolonged exercise in cyclists (Ronnestad et al.) and in cross-country skiers (Ofsteng et al.). The authors state that no longitudinal study has targeted training for resilience.
limitations: Narrative review with no described search or appraisal method. The Clark studies used non-elite participants, and the authors caution about extrapolation to highly trained athletes. The Figure 1 model adds a generic resilience factor based on another dataset, so its accuracy gain is illustrative. Several training claims rest on an unpublished thesis (ref 59) and on speculation about super-shoe effects, which the authors label as tempting but untested. One author is affiliated with the Nike Sport Research Lab, and the paper declares no conflicts of interest.
practicalImplications: Coaches of endurance athletes can consider long-term training consistency and volume, some race-pace or progressive long sessions, and regular heavy strength and plyometric work as candidates for building resilience. These are hypotheses rather than validated methods, so staff could track fatigued-state performance or economy to see whether a programme is working. Added training should be balanced against recovery, because the authors note the risk of overreaching.
athleteDev: Resilience, the decline in fresh-state capacities during long efforts, may matter for endurance performance. Long-term consistent volume, race-pace and progressive long sessions, and heavy strength and plyometric training are plausible ways to build it, but none has been tested for resilience directly. Fatigued-state testing of athletes could show whether a programme is working.
rtp: Not applicable. The review covers performance physiology in endurance athletes and does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport.

citation: He C, Zhu D, Hu Y. Physiological adaptations and practical efficacy of different blood flow restriction resistance training modes in athletic populations. Frontiers in Physiology. 2025;16:1683442.
abstract: This review compares three blood flow restriction resistance training (BFRT) modalities in athletes: low-load training with BFR (BFR-LIRT), high-load training supplemented with BFR (S-BFRRT), and periodized combined high-load and BFR training (C-BFRRT). It links each modality to a proposed mechanism and training phase, and it offers a framework for rehabilitation, competitive and preparatory periods. The authors describe the framework as preliminary rather than a definitive prescription.
tldr: Blood flow restriction training comes in three forms for athletes, and the review links each to a different mechanism and training phase. These links are the authors' proposed framework, drawn from 14 small studies, and are not validated prescriptions.
methods: The authors searched CNKI, PubMed and Web of Science, identified 412 articles, and included 14 studies of athletes with structured BFRT and control groups; they also state that Table 1 was selected to give a representative overview rather than an exhaustive systematic inventory. Table 1 summarizes the included studies by modality, sport, load, pressure, duration and outcome. Table 2 gives programming ranges that the authors state come from a qualitative synthesis of targeted database searches and should be read as practical guidelines rather than unequivocal prescriptions.
findings: For BFR-LIRT at 20 to 30% 1RM, the text states that Korkmaz et al. (n = 23 football players, 6 weeks) found greater rectus femoris thickness and knee strength gains than high-load training (p < 0.05), but Table 1 marks only the rectus femoris change as better than the control group and the strength change as within-group only. The review cites a meta-analysis reporting moderate strength gains (effect size 0.65) for BFR-LIRT, although the reference title describes BFR combined with high-load training, and it notes two studies with weaker or null results. For C-BFRRT, small studies (Che et al. 2022, n = 16; Sarfabadi et al. 2023, n = 16; Zhu 2021, n = 20) reported gains superior to conventional training, while for S-BFRRT the text reports that Scott et al. 2017 found no added benefit in preseason; the review gives no pooled estimates comparing modalities.
limitations: The authors call this a narrative review, and the included studies are small (6 to 32 athletes) with varied pressures, durations and outcomes. Table 1 conflicts with the text for Korkmaz et al. 2022 (table: strength change within-group only; text: strength gains surpassing high-load training), Scott et al. 2017 (table: superior to HLRT over 6 weeks; text: no added benefit over 5 weeks) and Yamanaka et al. 2012 (table: rectus femoris CSA increased; text: no limb hypertrophy). The review also gives no statistical detail for most comparisons and states that the most effective load range is 20 to 50% 1RM without a citation.
practicalImplications: Within this review's framework, BFR-LIRT at 20 to 30% 1RM may suit rehabilitation and in-season maintenance, and combined periodized BFR may suit hypertrophy blocks, but the authors present these as proposals. The proposed phase plan (8 to 12 weeks of preparation, 4 to 6 weeks of competition, 2 to 4 weeks of transition) and the pressure and duration ranges in Table 2 should not be treated as established protocols. The review notes that thrombosis risk and long-term safety are under-studied, and it recommends keeping total occlusion within the 15 to 30 minute range it describes.
athleteDev: The review proposes BFR-LIRT for strength maintenance and tissue-sparing hypertrophy, S-BFRRT for concurrent strength and hypertrophy in competitive phases, and C-BFRRT for hypertrophy in preparation phases. This phase plan rests on small studies and the authors' hypotheses, and the review does not test it against sport performance outcomes.
rtp: The review suggests BFR-LIRT may support rehabilitation after injury, but its examples come from case-level reports, including a two-decathlete case report on patellar tendinopathy (Cuddeford and Brumitt, 2020) per the reference title. It gives no return-to-play criteria, so it cannot be used to set return-to-sport decisions.

citation: Lima BM, Amancio RS, Gonçalves DS, Koch AJ, Curty VM, Machado M. Planned load reduction versus fixed load: a strategy to reduce the perception of effort with similar improvements in hypertrophy and strength. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2018;13(9):1164-1168.
abstract: Twenty-one recreationally resistance-trained men were randomized to constant 10RM load (CON), 5% load reduction after each set (RED 5) or 10% load reduction after each set (RED 10) during 16 weeks of biceps and Scott curl training, with each set taken to volitional fatigue. Muscle thickness and 10RM increased in all groups with no between-group differences, and volume load did not differ. RED 10 gave a lower average daily RPE than CON for the biceps curl and than CON and RED 5 for the Scott curl.
tldr: In recreationally trained men, a 10% load reduction across sets gave muscle and strength gains similar to constant-load training while lowering perceived effort. The study used two elbow flexor exercises with 7 men per group, so it does not show whether the effect holds for multijoint lifts.
methods: Three groups (CON, RED 5, RED 10; n = 7 each) trained 3 days per week for 16 weeks, performing 3 sets of biceps and Scott curls to volitional fatigue with 1 minute of rest between sets. Muscle thickness of the elbow flexors was measured by B-mode ultrasound before and after training, and 10RM was retested every 2 weeks from week 2 to week 14. Volume load and average daily RPE were calculated for each condition and compared between groups by one-way ANOVA.
findings: Muscle thickness increased in all groups (P < .001) with no group x time difference (P = .976). The 10RM biceps curl and Scott curl increased in all groups (P < .001) with no between-group differences (Scott curl P = .238; biceps curl P = .401). Volume load did not differ between groups (biceps curl P = .649; Scott curl P = .094). Average daily RPE was lower for RED 10 than CON for the biceps curl (6.8 [0.3] vs 7.3 [0.9]; overall P = .002) and, for the Scott curl, lower for RED 10 than CON (6.8 [0.1] vs 7.0 [0.1]; P < .001) and RED 5 (7.1 [0.1]; P = .001). Pooled correlations between biceps-curl volume load and change in biceps curl 10RM were modest and negative (r = -.522, P = .015).
limitations: Only 7 men per group, two single-joint elbow flexor exercises and 3 sets per exercise. The authors suggest total volume may have been too low to detect hypertrophy differences. The RPE differences were 0.2 to 0.5 points, and the correlations pool all groups, so they are not group comparisons. Multijoint lifts were not tested, as the authors note. The abstract reports the Scott-curl volume values as total volume and gives P = .001 for the biceps-curl RPE difference, whereas the results give P = .002 for the overall biceps-curl RPE test; the results values are used here.
practicalImplications: In this 16-week elbow flexor program, a 10% load reduction after each set did not change total volume, muscle thickness or 10RM compared with constant load, but it lowered perceived effort. Staff should use it as a way to reduce effort during training, not as a method to add volume or extra gains, and it has not been tested on squats or other multijoint lifts.
athleteDev: In recreationally trained men doing biceps and Scott curls, a 10% load reduction after each set produced hypertrophy and strength gains similar to constant load while lowering perceived effort. The study did not include athletes or multijoint exercises, so transfer to those settings is untested.
rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It enrolled healthy recreationally trained men with no injured participants and tested no rehabilitation outcome.

citation: Davidow D, Paul L, Jones B, Hohlfeld A, Rasenyalo S, Dane K, et al. Player-level tackle training interventions in tackle-collision sports: a systematic scoping review. Sports Med Open. 2025;11:103.
abstract: A systematic scoping review (PRISMA-ScR, four databases to May 2024) of 13 studies that tested player-level tackle training in American football and rugby, with 503 athletes in total. The authors report that all interventions produced favorable changes in their outcome measures, which were mainly tackle technique, kinematics and head impact measures.
tldr: Player-level tackle training has a small, mostly short-term evidence base in American football and rugby. Two randomized trials of helmetless tackle training reported fewer head impacts than controls, but no included study reported injury incidence as an outcome.
methods: The authors followed the Arksey and O'Malley scoping review framework with Levac et al. refinements and PRISMA-ScR, and registered the protocol with OSF. PubMed, EBSCOhost, Web of Science and Scopus were searched from January 2000 to 30 May 2024, two reviewers screened records, and one reviewer charted the data with corroboration by a second. Study quality was rated with JBI checklists for quasi-experimental studies and randomized trials, and no study was excluded on quality.
findings: Of 5,656 records, 13 full-text studies met the criteria: seven in American football (360 athletes), and six in rugby union and rugby league (143 athletes), with eight studies including only males. Interventions were mostly tackler-focused instruction or feedback delivered by video or expert coach, plus an 8-week strength and power program, helmetless training, and data-informed practice design. In the two randomized trials of helmetless training, the authors report 30% fewer head impacts per athlete exposure than controls in college players (Swartz 2015, n=50) and 26% to 33% fewer game-related head impacts in youth players (Swartz 2019, n=180).
limitations: Because this is a scoping review, the authors did not pool or grade effects. The abstract calls study quality 'good', but the results report only JBI checklist scores with no stated cutoff for 'good' (quasi-experimental studies averaged 7 of 9, range 4 to 9; the two randomized trials scored 10 and 11 of 13). Most studies were small, short-term and in youth or amateur players, one was a single-player case study and another had three participants, and outcomes were technique, kinematics or head impacts rather than injury incidence, which the authors list as a need for future studies.
practicalImplications: When planning tackle training, staff can use video feedback combined with expert instruction and standardized technique criteria, which the authors recommend based on the included studies. The review does not establish which program reduces match concussion or injury risk, so these methods should be monitored in the team's own technique and head-impact data rather than presented as proven injury prevention.
athleteDev: Video feedback with instruction and standardized scoring improved tackle technique or proficiency scores in several small studies in youth, amateur and college players. The review does not show that these methods improve performance at higher levels of play.
rtp: Not applicable: the review contains no injured-player samples and no return-to-play outcomes, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions.

citation: Dengel DR, Evanoff N. Positional Differences in Muscle-to-Bone Ratio in National Football League Players. International Journal of Sports Medicine. 2023.
abstract: DXA scans of 346 NFL players were compared with 228 age-matched healthy male controls to examine total and regional muscle-to-bone ratio (lean mass divided by bone mineral content), and the ratio was compared across positions.
tldr: NFL players had a slightly lower total muscle-to-bone ratio than controls despite more lean mass and bone, and the total ratio did not differ by position. Leg ratio did vary by position, but its link to performance or injury was not studied.
methods: Retrospective analysis of whole-body and regional DXA scans (GE Lunar iDXA, enCore 16.2) from 2006 to 2011. Muscle-to-bone ratio was lean mass divided by bone mineral content; group comparisons used t-tests and position comparisons used ANOVA with Tukey HSD.
findings: NFL players had a lower total (18.50 vs 19.12, P < .001) and trunk muscle-to-bone ratio than controls, a higher arm ratio (17.70 vs 16.48, P < .0001), and no difference in leg ratio (16.72 vs 16.85, P = .34). The total ratio did not differ across positions. Leg ratio was lowest in punters and kickers (15.7) and quarterbacks (15.8) and highest in offensive linemen (17.9) and defensive linemen (17.7).
limitations: The design is cross-sectional and retrospective (2006-2011 data), and controls were drawn from population studies rather than athletes. The abstract describes NFL players' percent body fat as 'significantly lower' than controls, but the reported P = .053 is not significant at .05. The Methods state paired t-tests for two independent groups, and the authors' explanation of the lower total ratio (greater height and skeleton size) was not tested; no performance or injury outcomes are included.
practicalImplications: A DXA scan gives total and regional lean mass and bone values that staff could use for body composition profiling, but the paper reports position averages only and gives no thresholds for individual decisions. Staff should not read a player's ratio against these averages as a bone-health or performance marker without outcome data.
athleteDev: Leg muscle-to-bone ratio varied by position, which may describe position-specific body composition, but the paper does not link it to speed, strength or game performance.
rtp: Cannot inform return to sport. The study has no injury, rehabilitation or return-to-play outcomes.

citation: Sanchez E, Weiss L, Williams T, Ward P, Peterson B, Wellman A, et al. Positional Movement Demands during NFL Football Games: A 3-Year Review. Applied Sciences. 2023;13:9278.
abstract: Player tracking data from 768 NFL regular-season games (2018-2020) were used to quantify on-field distance, maximum velocity, high-velocity efforts, and acceleration and deceleration efforts by position, using position-specific velocity thresholds.
tldr: Game movement demands differ clearly by position: receivers and defensive backs cover the most distance and reach the highest speeds, receivers make the most accelerations, and linemen have the lowest totals on every load measure. These averages can serve as position benchmarks, but they describe games and not injury risk.
methods: Retrospective analysis of Next Gen Stats tracking (10 Hz) during on-field play from kickoff to the end of each game, summarized per player-game. High-velocity efforts used 85% of each position's 75th-percentile maximum velocity; acceleration and deceleration efforts used 3.5 m/s^2. One-way ANOVA and Bonferroni post hoc tests compared positions.
findings: In-game maximum velocity was highest for cornerbacks (31.4 km/h), safeties (30.8 km/h) and receivers (30.7 km/h) and lowest for offensive linemen (20.4 km/h). Linebackers had the most high-velocity efforts (5.1 per game) and distance (98.5 m), and offensive linemen the fewest (1.4 efforts). Receivers had the most acceleration efforts (65.7 per game) and safeties the most deceleration efforts (23.5 per game); nearly all between-position differences were significant.
limitations: Only on-field tracking was used, with no collision data, injury or performance outcomes; the authors note that blocking and tackling are not captured. The Discussion says safeties had the most acceleration efforts on defense with linebackers close behind, but Table 2 gives cornerbacks 42.3, linebackers 41.1 and safeties 40.4; the abstract's statement that receivers and defensive backs had more acceleration efforts than other positions also conflicts with Table 2, where tight ends (49.6) exceed both defensive back groups. Table 2 values are reported here.
practicalImplications: Position averages and the 85%-of-positional-maximum thresholds can help performance staff benchmark practice and preseason targets for each group, especially for sprint, acceleration and deceleration volume. The authors also suggest the data may help plan return-to-play loads, but this study did not test that use.
athleteDev: Gives position-level benchmarks for in-game sprint, acceleration and deceleration volume that can guide training design. The authors state that run and pass plays should be analyzed separately before firm conclusions are drawn.
rtp: Can give game-demand context for return-to-play planning, but the study does not measure injury, rehabilitation progress or readiness, so it cannot set return criteria. The authors' suggestion that it may help return-to-play protocols is untested here.

citation: Freeman BW, Talpey SW, James LP, Rayner RJ, Young WB. Preseason and In-Season High-Speed Running Demands of 2 Professional Australian Rules Football Teams. Sports Health. 2024.
abstract: GPS data from 55 male athletes at two professional Australian Rules football clubs were used to compare high-speed running volume in the 2019 preseason and the first eight in-season rounds. Weekly running in the 71 to 80% and 81 to 90% Vmax bands was greater in preseason, with large individual variation in distance at each speed band.
tldr: Preseason high-speed running volume in professional Australian Rules football was higher than in the early season for mid-to-high speed bands. Individual exposure varied widely, so team averages hide athletes with very low sprint exposure.
methods: Observational cohort study using Catapult GPS data (10 Hz) from training and matches. Individual Vmax came from the first four preseason weeks and was updated if higher. Weekly distance in absolute and relative speed bands was compared with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, with Benjamini-Hochberg correction, and individual variation was summarized as coefficients of variation.
findings: Weekly distance in the 71 to 80% Vmax band (P < 0.01, r = 0.56) and 81 to 90% Vmax band (P < 0.01, r = 0.58) was greater in preseason than in-season; the 91 to 100% Vmax band did not differ significantly (P = 0.10, r = 0.22). Club A differed in all three bands, but Club B differed only in the 71 to 80% band. Mean weekly total distance was 30,967 m in preseason and 29,909 m in-season, and 6 athletes did not reach 95% Vmax in preseason.
limitations: Two clubs, one season, and a sample of 55 athletes limit generalizability. No injury or performance outcomes were analyzed, and the authors state that the link between this volume and injury risk is unknown. The abstract labels the bands as above 70% and above 80% Vmax with P = 0.01, while the Results report the 71 to 80% and 81 to 90% Vmax bands with P < 0.01, and the Discussion states that all three bands were significantly lower in-season although the Results report P = 0.103 for 91 to 100% Vmax. Weekly values were calculated as the summed session distance divided by the number of sessions that week, so they are per-session averages rather than weekly totals.
practicalImplications: Review individual speed-band exposure rather than team averages when planning preseason and early-season running, because some athletes covered very little distance above 90% Vmax. Track each athlete's maximum speed through the season, since 36 athletes recorded a higher Vmax in the first eight rounds than in preseason. The study does not establish a dose that reduces injury.
athleteDev: The study describes preseason and in-season high-speed running volume and shows that it varies widely between athletes. It does not show that any running dose improves performance.
rtp: The study does not include injured athletes or return-to-play outcomes, so it cannot guide return-to-play running progressions or clearance. It does not establish a sprint dose that prevents soft-tissue injury.

citation: Dello Iacono A, Beato M, Unnithan VB, Shushan T. Programming high-speed and sprint running exposure in football: beliefs and practices of more than 100 practitioners worldwide. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2023 (ahead of print).
abstract: An online survey of 102 football practitioners from 22 countries asked about the importance, timing, monitoring, training methods and perceived effectiveness of high-speed and sprint running exposure. Respondents agreed on importance, scheduled exposure differently for starting and nonstarting players, and lacked consensus on how to define and monitor these metrics.
tldr: A survey of 102 football practitioners found broad agreement that high-speed and sprint running exposure matters, but wide variation in how it is defined, monitored and scheduled. Respondent beliefs do not establish which practices work.
methods: Cross-sectional online survey (Qualtrics) of football practitioners recruited by convenience sampling, covering five domains: who, why, when, what and how, with data collected March 9 to July 5, 2022. Analyses used descriptive statistics, a mixed-effects logistic model for exposure timing by player status, and multinomial logistic models for match-outcome targets.
findings: Practitioners agreed that exposure is important for physical development, competition preparation and injury prevention. Most ranked official matches as the greatest exposure for starting players and complementary training for nonstarters, and the authors report that nonstarters' odds of training-based exposure were 2.74 times those of starters (95% CI 2.09 to 3.72). Using a 100% match-outcome target, predicted probabilities were 33%, 48% and 19% for single, two-microdose and multiple-microdose HSR strategies, but the match-outcome odds ratios were not significant (p = .108 and .227 for HSR). Conditioning and drill-based training were rated most effective, while game-based formats were rated at least moderately effective.
limitations: The sample is a convenience sample dominated by Italian and male respondents, and players' level and sex were not fully represented, so the results may not reflect other clubs or leagues. Table 3 is hard to interpret because it is labelled by exposure timing while the text describes player status, so the 2.74 odds ratio should be checked against the table. The authors acknowledge the evidence base is level 5 and that the match-outcome predictions are uncertain.
practicalImplications: Staff could use the finding that starters and nonstarters are exposed to sprinting at different times as a prompt to plan separate compensatory sessions for nonstarters. The authors' suggestion of two sessions roughly 48 hours apart between MD+2 and MD-2 is a practical option for them to test, not a tested standard.
athleteDev: The paper addresses how practitioners plan high-speed and sprint running exposure within the microcycle, including scheduling and the use of microdosed sessions. It does not measure physical adaptation, performance or injury outcomes, so it cannot show that any scheduling choice improves development.
rtp: The paper does not address return to sport, rehabilitation or injury recovery, so it cannot guide return-to-play decisions. Its injury-prevention comments are the practitioners' views, not measured outcomes.

citation: Dornelles MP, Fritsch CG, Sonda FC, Johnson DS, Leal-Junior ECP, Vaz MA, et al. Photobiomodulation therapy as a tool to prevent hamstring strain injuries by reducing soccer-induced fatigue on hamstring muscles. Lasers in Medical Science. 2019.
abstract: Twelve male amateur soccer players completed a randomized, crossover, double-blinded, placebo-controlled trial with photobiomodulation (300 J per thigh) or placebo before a simulated soccer match. Isokinetic hamstring and quadriceps torque and countermovement jump height were measured before and after the match. Hamstring eccentric peak torque, hamstring-to-quadriceps torque ratio and jump height fell less after PBMT than after placebo, and the authors conclude that PBMT attenuated hamstring fatigue and may be a tool to prevent hamstring strain injury.
tldr: In amateur soccer players, PBMT applied to the hamstrings before a simulated match reduced the fall in hamstring eccentric strength compared with placebo. The study measured strength and jump outcomes in 12 players over one simulated session, not injuries.
methods: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial in 12 male amateur soccer players. Each player had two sessions at least 7 days apart, in randomized order, receiving PBMT (LED device, 880 nm, 300 J per thigh over 60 s) or an identical placebo before a 45-minute simulated match (three modules of the SAFT90 protocol). Isokinetic knee torque and countermovement jump were measured before and after; the outcomes were percent change and effect sizes, analysed with magnitude-based inference.
findings: Hamstring eccentric peak torque fell 4.85% after PBMT (P = .005) and 8.72% after placebo (P = .001). The H:Q torque ratio fell 3.60% after PBMT (P = .056) and 7.75% after placebo (P = .008). Countermovement jump height did not change significantly in either condition (-1.77% PBMT, P = .531; -5.47% placebo, P = .085). Magnitude-based inference gave 75%, 69% and 53% chances of a beneficial PBMT effect versus placebo for eccentric torque, H:Q ratio and jump height. Quadriceps torque was not affected.
limitations: Twelve amateur players, one PBMT dose (300 J) and one 45-minute simulated match, with acute outcomes only, and isokinetic testing on the dominant limb only. Between-treatment effects were judged by magnitude-based inference rather than a significance test of the difference, and the CMJ chance (53%) falls in the 'possibly' band; jump height did not change significantly within either condition. Two authors have links to the device maker, Multi Radiance Medical, which supplied the prototype device: Leal-Junior receives research support from it and Johnson is an employee and shareholder. The authors state that neither took part in data collection or analysis. No injury outcomes were recorded.
practicalImplications: In amateur players, one 60-second application of 300 J to each hamstring before a simulated match reduced the fall in eccentric hamstring strength. This does not show fewer hamstring injuries, so any injury-prevention use would be experimental and should be tracked against injury data. The single dose and short simulation limit how far the dose can be transferred to other players or match formats.
athleteDev: In a 45-minute simulated match, PBMT before play reduced the loss of hamstring eccentric strength and H:Q ratio compared with placebo in amateur players. Jump height changes were not significant in either condition. The study did not measure match performance or recovery over time.
rtp: Not applicable. Participants were healthy players with no recent lower-limb injury, and no injured or rehabilitating players were studied. The study did not measure re-injury, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions.

citation: Ross B, Trojian T, Cushman DM. Physician Perceptions of Cannabidiol (CBD) and Cannabis in Sports Medicine and Performance. Translational Sports Medicine. 2023;2023:8824466.
abstract: Physician members of the American Medical Society for Sports Medicine completed an anonymous survey on demographics, CBD and cannabis recommendations, and attitudes toward cannabinoids in sports medicine. Of 333 responses, 40.8% had recommended CBD and 24.8% cannabis for therapeutic purposes. Age, female sex, rural practice and academic setting were associated with several recommendation and attitude outcomes, and the authors conclude that sports medicine physicians hold varying views on cannabinoids.
tldr: Among 333 AMSSM sports medicine physicians, about 41% had recommended CBD and 25% cannabis, mostly for musculoskeletal and neuropathic pain. Attitudes varied by age, sex and practice setting, but the survey did not measure athlete outcomes.
methods: Cross-sectional anonymous online survey (REDCap) emailed to AMSSM physician members in 2022, with a reminder. Of about 4,910 emails sent, 3,079 were opened and 333 surveys were completed. Demographic, practice and attitude items were analysed with logistic and ordinal regression in Stata 17.0.
findings: 40.8% of respondents had recommended CBD and 24.8% cannabis for therapeutic purposes. Pediatricians were less likely to recommend CBD than family medicine physicians (OR 0.28, P = .016), and community or private practice physicians were more likely to recommend CBD than academic physicians (OR 1.76, P = .030). Rural physicians were less likely to recommend cannabis than urban physicians (OR 0.23, P = .029). Older, female and rural respondents were less likely to favour recreational cannabis legalisation. Male physicians were less likely to rate cannabis as performance-enhancing (OR 0.38, P = .013). Only 9.9% of respondents rated CBD as detrimental to performance and integrity of sport, compared with 39% for cannabis.
limitations: Physician self-report only, with no athlete data and no measure of what physicians tell athletes. The response rate was 10.8% of opened emails, and the sample was 69% family medicine. The authors describe the study as a single data point. The abstract conflicts with the Results in two places: it says rural physicians were less likely to recommend CBD, but the Results report the rural effect only for cannabis (OR 0.23); and it says younger physicians were less likely to rate cannabis as performance-enhancing, but the Results report only the male effect (OR 0.38). This record uses the Results values. The text says 98% of respondents agreed to learn more through continuing education, but Figure 1 labels the CME item 93. The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
practicalImplications: Physician views on cannabinoids differ by age, sex and practice setting, so staff advising athletes on CBD or cannabis should not assume a consistent position from sports medicine colleagues. Cannabis remains prohibited in competition, while CBD was removed from the WADA list in 2018 (author statement). The survey does not show that either product improves performance or is safe for athletes.
athleteDev: The survey reports that many sports medicine physicians recommend CBD or cannabis for pain, but it does not measure performance effects. The authors state that the ergogenic or ergolytic effects of CBD and cannabis in athletes remain largely unknown, so perceived performance effects should not guide athlete use.
