rtp: Not applicable. The survey does not address rehabilitation or return-to-sport decisions. The authors note that only very few physicians recommended cannabinoids for sport-related concussion, which is physician behaviour rather than evidence of benefit.

citation: Buchheit M, Settembre M, Hader K, McHugh D. Planning the microcycle in elite football: to rest or not to rest? International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2023.
abstract: Retrospective data from 18 elite football teams (56 team seasons, 2018 to 2021) were used to examine how the timing of days off within 3- to 8-day turnarounds relates to noncontact injury rates (injuries with at least 3 days of time loss in the 15 main players per team). For 3- and 7-day turnarounds, a day off-feet at D+2 was associated with 2 to 3 times lower noncontact injury rates than the other sequences. For the other turnaround lengths, differences between sequences were unclear.
tldr: Across 56 elite soccer team seasons, a single off-feet day placed two days after a match was associated with lower noncontact injury rates than other day-off patterns, mainly in 3- and 7-day turnarounds. The analysis is observational and univariate, so it shows an association with injury rate and not a causal benefit.
methods: Injury and exposure records from a shared sports data platform were analyzed for 56 team seasons, with days off-feet inferred from days without a recorded session for the 15 main outfield players (511 players, 559 noncontact time-loss injuries). Turnarounds of 3 to 8 days were grouped by length, and injury rates were compared by the timing of the off-feet day, using noncontact injuries causing at least 3 days of time loss. Results are means with 95% CIs, differences were judged substantial when CIs did not overlap, Cohen d gave effect magnitudes, and only sequences with at least 10 occurrences were analyzed.
findings: Overall injury rate was about 5 times higher during matches than during training, and the presence of a day off-feet per se showed no clear difference in injury rate. For 3- and 7-day turnarounds, sequences with the day off-feet at D+2 were associated with 2 to 3 times lower noncontact injury rates per day than no day off or a day off at D+1; differences between the main sequences were unclear for 4-, 5-, 6- and 8-day turnarounds. Only 18 of the 655 three-day turnarounds used the x/o/x pattern, and the authors report no match injuries and no noncontact training injuries in that pattern, so the 3-day estimate rests on a very small count.
limitations: The study is observational and univariate, and the authors state that it does not show causal relationships. Days off were estimated from missing exposure records, so true rest days cannot be separated from off-feet days or unrecorded light work, and the D+2 sequences consistently had the fewest observations. The effect size wording differs across the text (abstract: overall rates with Cohen d 0.9 to 2.7; results: per-day rates with moderate to very large effects; discussion: large to very large; conclusion: moderate to large), and turnaround counts differ (1871 extracted in the methods, 2203 in Table 1, 2005 in Table 2).
practicalImplications: In 3- and 7-day turnarounds, placing the only off-feet day at D+2 was associated with lower noncontact injury rates than no off-feet day or an off-feet day at D+1 in this dataset. Because the association is observational, staff should treat it as a reason to review day-off timing, not as proof that D+2 prevents injuries.
athleteDev: The study covers injury rates, not performance or readiness, so it does not show any performance effect of day-off timing. Where a team uses one off-feet day in a 3- or 7-day turnaround, the D+2 timing was associated with fewer noncontact injuries here.
rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It counted injuries that caused at least 3 days of time loss across the squad and did not examine rehabilitation or return-to-play criteria.

citation: Seow D, Shimozono Y, Tengku Yusof TNB, Yasui Y, Massey A, Kennedy JG. Platelet-rich plasma injection for the treatment of hamstring injuries: a systematic review and meta-analysis with best-worst case analysis. Am J Sports Med. 2020.
abstract: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 10 clinical studies (published 2013 to 2018) of platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injection for hamstring injuries, with best- and worst-case scenario analyses for reinjury. The authors found no statistically significant difference in return to play or reinjury between PRP plus physical therapy and physical therapy alone, and complication rates were low.
tldr: Across 10 heterogeneous studies of hamstring injuries, adding PRP to physical therapy did not significantly shorten return to play or reduce reinjury compared with physical therapy alone. Complications were uncommon, but the evidence is weak and short-term.
methods: Two reviewers searched PubMed, Embase and the Cochrane Library from inception to August 2018 following PRISMA guidance, grading level of evidence (Oxford) and study quality (Coleman Methodology Score). Pooled results used fixed-effect models when heterogeneity was low (I2 below 25%) and random-effects models otherwise. Reinjury was also analyzed with best-case and worst-case scenarios, which assigned patients lost to follow-up to the favorable or unfavorable outcome.
findings: The 10 studies included 207 hamstring injuries in the PRP group and 149 in the control group (as protocol). Time to return to play was not significantly different for PRP plus PT versus PT alone (random-effects mean difference -5.67 days, 95% CI -12.62 to 1.28; I2 36%; P=.11), and reinjury risk ratios were 0.88 (95% CI 0.45 to 1.71; P=.70), 0.82 (best case) and 1.13 (worst case, favoring PT alone), none significant. Mean reinjury rates were 11.7% (PRP) and 12.8% (control); four complications occurred across four studies (mean rate 5.2%, range 2.7% to 9.1%), all post-injection discomfort, pain or sciatic nerve irritation.
limitations: Five of the 10 studies lost more than 2 patients to follow-up and five did not state losses, which the authors say may overestimate PRP's benefit. Most studies lacked a sham arm, PRP preparation and injection protocols varied widely and were poorly reported, and the data were too sparse for subgroup analysis by injury grade or PRP type. The abstract reports a significant fixed-effects return-to-play result (-5.70 days), which conflicts with the results section's non-significant random-effects result (-5.67 days, P=.11); the results-section values are reported here, and reinjury was not defined or confirmed by imaging.
practicalImplications: Staff should not expect PRP plus physical therapy to shorten return to play or reduce reinjury for hamstring injuries on the basis of this review, because neither difference reached statistical significance. Complication rates were low, but the authors grade the evidence as C, so PRP should not be presented as a proven way to speed hamstring recovery.
athleteDev: The review measured only time to return to play, reinjury and complications in injured athletes, so it cannot show that PRP improves performance or training capacity after a hamstring injury.
rtp: Return to play was not significantly shorter with PRP plus PT (random-effects mean difference -5.67 days, 95% CI -12.62 to 1.28), so PRP should not be used to shorten a return-to-play timeline. Reinjury estimates were imprecise (risk ratio 95% CI 0.45 to 1.71) with short follow-up, so the review cannot show that PRP makes an earlier return safer.

citation: Bradley JP, Lawyer TJ, Ruef S, Towers JD, Arner JW. Platelet-rich plasma shortens return to play in National Football League players with acute hamstring injuries. Orthop J Sports Med. 2020;8(4):2325967120911731.
abstract: A retrospective single-team cohort of NFL players with acute grade 2 hamstring injuries, comparing leukocyte-poor PRP plus rehabilitation with rehabilitation alone. The authors found no significant difference in days or practices missed, but PRP-treated players missed fewer games (1.3 vs 2.9, P<.05).
tldr: In one NFL team's retrospective cohort, PRP plus rehabilitation was associated with one fewer game missed after grade 2 hamstring injury, but not with fewer days or practices missed. Treatment was not randomized, so the result is hypothesis-generating.
methods: Players with MRI-confirmed grade 2 hamstring injuries from 2009 to 2018 were retrospectively reviewed. Those who received leukocyte-poor PRP (Arthrex ACP, given within 24 to 48 hours of injury, 1 to 3 injections) were compared with those treated with rehabilitation alone, using Fisher exact and Student t tests, with P<.05 as significant. All players followed the same physical therapy and return-to-play testing protocol.
findings: Of 108 players with hamstring injury, 69 had grade 2 injuries: 30 received PRP and 39 did not. Mean time missed was 22.5 days, 18.2 practices and 1.3 games with PRP versus 25.7 days (P=.81), 22.8 practices (P=.68) and 2.9 games (P<.05) without PRP, and the in-season subset showed the same pattern (only games missed significant). Each group had one recurrence, and no injection complications were recorded.
limitations: The study was retrospective with non-random allocation: injection was more common for in-season and playoff injuries and for more severe MRI findings, and the PRP group had more in-season injuries (19 vs 16) and fewer preseason injuries (6 vs 20). It was underpowered for days and practices, the number of injections varied (1 to 3), player position was not compared, and no follow-up MRI was obtained. The senior author, who gave the injections, reports royalties from Arthrex, the maker of the PRP system used, and the title and conclusion emphasize faster return to play although the only significant difference was one game missed.
practicalImplications: Staff should not expect PRP to reduce days or practices missed after grade 2 hamstring injury on the basis of this study, since those differences were not significant. The one-game difference in games missed is a hypothesis to test in controlled studies, not a basis for routine use.
athleteDev: The study measured games, practices and days missed in NFL players, and only games missed differed significantly. It does not show that PRP improves training availability or performance.
rtp: The only significant return-to-play difference was 1.3 vs 2.9 games missed (P<.05), with days and practices not significantly different. Because treatment was chosen by players and staff, there was one recurrence per group, and no follow-up MRI was done, the study cannot establish that PRP makes return to play safer or reduces reinjury.

citation: McCunn R, Fullagar HHK, Williams S, Halseth TJ, Sampson JA, Murray A. Playing experience and position influence injury risk among NCAA Division I collegiate footballers. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2017.
abstract: A prospective cohort of 76 male NCAA Division I football players over two seasons, examining how playing experience and position relate to injury incidence in training and games. The authors report that seniors were at greatest risk in training, while sophomores, juniors and wide receivers showed the highest game-related risk.
tldr: In one NCAA Division I football program, senior players had higher time-loss injury risk in training than freshmen, and wide receivers had higher non-time-loss injury risk in games. Most other comparisons were unclear because of small numbers.
methods: Injuries from two consecutive seasons (2014 and 2015) were recorded by athletic training staff and confirmed by a sports physician, and were classed as training or game related and as time loss or non-time loss. Exposure was training minutes or game snaps. A Poisson generalized linear mixed model with offsets for exposure estimated relative risks against freshmen and defensive linemen, and effects were assessed against smallest worthwhile effects of 0.90 and 1.11 using 90% confidence limits.
findings: Overall rates were 0.6 time-loss and 2.1 non-time-loss game injuries per 1,000 snaps, and 7.1 time-loss and 26.0 non-time-loss training injuries per 1,000 hours. Compared with freshmen, seniors were likely at higher time-loss training risk (RR 1.79, 90% CL 1.04 to 3.10), and sophomores (RR 4.43, 90% CL 0.77 to 25.49) and juniors (RR 5.08, 90% CL 0.88 to 29.41) were likely at higher time-loss game risk, while experience did not clearly affect non-time-loss game injuries. Wide receivers were likely at higher non-time-loss game risk (RR 1.84, 90% CL 1.01 to 3.36), running backs were likely at higher time-loss training risk (RR 1.62, 90% CL 0.86 to 3.07), and quarterbacks and tight ends were likely at lower training risk than defensive linemen.
limitations: This is one program over two seasons, with 76 players, 27 games and small position groups, so most inferences are unclear and the sophomore and junior game estimates have very wide limits. The injury definition included any physical complaint, with no contact, tissue or severity categories, and the authors' comparison with rugby union (3.0 per 1,000 training hours) is across studies with different definitions. The abstract's game-related wide receiver finding applies to non-time-loss injuries only (no position effect for time-loss game injuries), and the 'likely' effects are magnitude-based probability statements whose P values ranged from 0.07 to 0.21, with several 90% confidence limits crossing 1.0.
practicalImplications: The authors suggest that coaches consider limiting senior players' exposure to the most injurious training elements, such as contact drills, and that staff monitor recovery for seniors. Because the training estimates are imprecise and the authors call the mechanisms speculative, these should be treated as hypotheses to check within the team's own injury records rather than as a basis for changing training.
athleteDev: The study measures injury risk by player experience and position rather than performance, so it can prompt closer monitoring of senior players and running backs in training but does not show effects on performance.
rtp: The study records time-loss injuries but does not examine rehabilitation or return to play, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions.

citation: Baker HP, Lee CS, Qin C, Fibranz C, Rizzi A, Athiviraham A. Playing rule article eight decreases the rate of sport related concussion in NFL players over two seasons. Physician Sportsmed. 2020.
abstract: A retrospective review of NFL players placed on public injury reports for concussion across four regular seasons, comparing the two seasons before and after playing rule article 8 took effect. The authors report a lower concussion rate after the rule (RR 0.60), with no significant change in average games missed or players placed on injury reserve.
tldr: Across two NFL seasons after a helmet-hit rule was introduced, reported concussion rates were about 40% lower than in the two seasons before. Games missed and injured-reserve placements did not change, and the design cannot establish that the rule caused the drop.
methods: Concussions were identified from public injury reports and cross-checked with at least two sources and with absence from game statistics, for regular-season games only, from 2016 to 2019. Players were assigned to pre-rule (2016 and 2017) or post-rule (2018 and 2019) cohorts by date of injury. Rates were calculated per 1,000 athlete exposures, with relative risks and 95% confidence intervals, and games missed and injured-reserve placements were compared with t tests and chi-squared tests at P of 0.05 or less.
findings: There were 479 concussions, 299 before and 180 after the rule, with rates of 5.2, 5.8, 2.9 and 3.7 per 1,000 athlete exposures across 2016 to 2019 (pre 5.5, post 3.3; RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.73). Average games missed per concussion (1.02 to 1.33 across the four seasons, P=0.63 between cohorts) and the share of players placed on injury reserve (P=0.45) did not differ between cohorts. By position, the authors report decreases for running backs, linebackers and cornerbacks (t-test P=0.05, 0.02 and 0.05 on seasonal counts, with no multiplicity correction) and no clear change for wide receivers (68 concussions, P=0.45); recalculated from NFL-published data, the rate ratio was 0.77 (95% CI 0.66 to 0.90).
limitations: Public injury reports may omit concussions that resolve before the next report, and the authors' rates were lower than the NFL's own published rates for the same seasons (5.5 vs 6.6 pre, 3.3 vs 5.1 post). Diagnosis, severity, imaging and medical clearance were not available for all players, and only newsworthy injuries may have been reported. There was no control group, an educational program ('NFL Way to Play') ran alongside the rule, and the position comparisons were t tests on two seasonal counts per cohort, not exposure-adjusted rates, with no correction for multiple comparisons, which the authors acknowledge raises type 1 error risk.
practicalImplications: Staff who track concussion trends from public injury reports should expect them to undercount relative to league-published data, so these sources are not a substitute for internal medical records. The lower post-rule rate is consistent with league data showing fewer concussions after the helmet-hit rule, but the study cannot separate the rule from concurrent education, and the position-specific results are too fragile to guide position-specific concussion planning.
athleteDev: The study measures concussion incidence and games missed in NFL regular seasons and does not address performance, so it does not show whether the rule affected performance outcomes.
rtp: The study reports games missed and injured-reserve placement after concussion, not clinical return-to-play or clearance decisions, and found no significant change in average games missed (P=0.63), so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions.

citation: Miyamori T, Nagao M, Sawa R, Tumilty S, Yoshimura M, Saita Y, et al. Playing football on artificial turf as a risk factor for fifth metatarsal stress fracture: a retrospective cohort study. BMJ Open. 2019;9:e022864.
abstract: Football players completed a computer-based survey covering demographics, injury history, annual playing hours and the share of playing time on artificial turf and clay over the prior 24 months. Of 1,854 players, 41 had a physician-diagnosed MT-5, an incidence of 0.02 per 1,000 player hours. Higher artificial turf exposure was associated with MT-5 in adjusted models.
tldr: In this survey of 1,854 Japanese football players, a larger share of playing time on artificial turf was linked to higher odds of fifth metatarsal stress fracture, and clay time was linked to lower odds. The design is observational and recall-based, so it supports asking about surface exposure rather than proving that turf causes the fracture.
methods: Retrospective cohort using a computer-based questionnaire completed under supervision of coaches, physicians or physiotherapists. Generalized estimating equations were adjusted for age, sex, BMI, years of play, annual playing hours, MT-5 history and spike cleat type, with univariate logistic regression for comparison; test-retest reliability was checked in 50 players.
findings: The MT-5 incidence was 0.02 per 1,000 player hours (95% CI 0.013 to 0.027). Playing more than 80% of time on artificial turf was associated with higher adjusted odds of MT-5 than 0-20% (OR 3.44, 95% CI 1.65 to 7.18), and 61-80% clay time was associated with lower odds (OR 0.25, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.59). The other clay categories were not statistically significant, and higher BMI was also associated with MT-5 (adjusted OR 1.15, p=0.048).
limitations: Surface-time estimates and injury history were self-reported over 24 months, with recall bias, and only 41 cases were available; confounders such as vitamin D and calcium intake were not modeled. The Discussion says the MT-5 group was significantly younger, but Table 1 shows it was slightly older and not significantly different (19.68 vs 18.64 years, p=0.088). The Discussion's clay comparison (OR 0.42 at more than 80% clay time) was not significant (p=0.084).
practicalImplications: Staff whose teams train or play mostly on artificial turf could record surface exposure alongside other MT-5 risk factors such as foot alignment and vitamin D status. The study does not test any surface change or prevention program, so it does not show that moving players off turf reduces fractures.
athleteDev: Limited direct performance application. Surface exposure can be logged as a context variable when planning field-based loads on turf, but the study measured fracture risk, not performance.
rtp: Cannot inform return to sport. The study does not assess rehabilitation, return timing or re-fracture after return to play, so it should not set return criteria.

citation: Silva A, Narciso FV, Soalheiro I, Viegas F, Freitas LSN, Lima A, et al. Poor Sleep Quality's Association With Soccer Injuries: Preliminary Data. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2019 (ahead of print).
abstract: Twenty-three elite male soccer players from two Brazilian clubs wore wrist actigraphs and kept sleep diaries for 10 preseason days. Club medical teams recorded injuries over the following 6 months, and the authors compared sleep variables and injury characteristics between players with good and poor sleep quality.
tldr: In this small cohort, players with lower sleep efficiency and more wakefulness after sleep onset had more injuries, more severe injuries and longer time lost. The study is preliminary, so it supports monitoring sleep as a risk factor rather than proving that poor sleep causes injury.
methods: Prospective cohort with 10 days of actigraphy (Actiwatch 2) and sleep diaries in preseason, followed by 6 months of injury records using a consensus injury definition. Players were grouped as good sleepers (duration 7 h or more, efficiency above 85%, latency under 30 min) or poor sleepers (the opposite thresholds), and analyzed with Mann-Whitney U tests, Spearman correlations and linear regression.
findings: Sleep efficiency correlated negatively with absence time (r = -0.49, P = .01), injury severity (r = -0.69, P < .01) and number of injuries (r = -0.67, P < .01). WASO correlated positively with injury severity (r = 0.49, P = .02) and number of injuries (r = 0.55, P = .03), and sleep latency with number of injuries (r = 0.45, P = .03); sleep duration showed no significant correlation. Poor sleepers (n = 18) had 2.56 injuries on average versus 1.00 for good sleepers (n = 5), and 29.4 versus 4.6 days absent (Table 3, P < .01).
limitations: Only 23 players remained after excluding 19 of 42 invited, with just 5 in the good-sleep group, so the between-group results and the regression R2 values rest on very small numbers. Psychological, hormonal, biomechanical and training-load factors were not measured, yet the Discussion describes the associations as 'cause and effect'. The Discussion's absence figures (17.5 and 5.0 days) do not match Table 3 (29.4 and 4.6 days); the Table 3 values are reported here.
practicalImplications: Staff could add a sleep check, such as actigraphy or a simple sleep diary, to injury risk screening for elite soccer players, particularly where sleep efficiency is low or wakefulness after sleep onset is high. The authors also suggest a multifactorial risk review and sleep-improvement strategies, but this study cannot show that improving sleep reduces injuries.
athleteDev: In this sample, poorer sleep was associated with more time lost to injury, which bears on availability for training and matches. The study does not measure performance or test whether sleep interventions improve it.
rtp: Supports sleep monitoring as part of injury risk and availability planning only. The study does not assess return-to-play decisions, rehabilitation progress or re-injury, so it cannot set return criteria.

citation: Fritsch CG, Dornelles MP, Oliveira GS, Baroni BM. Poor hamstrings-to-quadriceps torque ratios in male soccer players: weak hamstrings, strong quadriceps, or both? Sports Biomechanics. 2020 (published online 8 June 2020).
abstract: Concentric quadriceps and hamstring torques and eccentric hamstring torque were measured with isokinetic dynamometry at 60 degrees per second in 101 male soccer players (202 legs). The authors compared legs above and below conventional (0.50, 0.55, 0.60) and functional (0.80, 0.85, 0.90) hamstrings-to-quadriceps cut-points and examined correlations between torques and ratios.
tldr: Players with low hamstring-to-quadriceps ratios mostly had weaker hamstrings, especially eccentric hamstring strength, rather than simply strong quadriceps. Staff should read the ratio alongside the raw torque values rather than the ratio alone.
methods: Cross-sectional isokinetic testing on a Biodex System 4 during the first two weeks of preseason, with two sets of three maximal contractions in concentric and eccentric modes at 60 degrees per second. Legs above and below each cut-point were compared with paired t-tests and Cohen's d, and Pearson correlations linked torques to the ratios.
findings: Legs below the conventional cut-points had lower concentric hamstring torque (effect sizes 0.73 to 0.94, P < .001) and higher concentric quadriceps torque (effect sizes 0.57 to 0.63, P < .01). Legs below the functional cut-points had lower eccentric hamstring torque (effect sizes 1.23 to 1.39, P < .001), with a quadriceps difference only at the 0.80 cut-point. Eccentric hamstring torque correlated moderately with the functional ratio (r = 0.66).
limitations: Testing was at one angular velocity and one time point, with no injury follow-up, so the findings describe muscle balance rather than injury risk. The Discussion's firm statement that hamstring deficit is 'the key factor' goes beyond a cross-sectional comparison. Table 2 has internal errors at the 0.90 functional cut-point (group sizes sum to 223 rather than 202, the balanced quadriceps values repeat the 0.60 conventional row, and a 0.51 effect size sits beside P = .522), so that row should not be relied on.
practicalImplications: When screening soccer players with isokinetic testing, staff should look at hamstring and quadriceps torques alongside the ratio, because a low ratio can come from either side. The authors suggest hamstring-focused training, such as eccentric or Nordic-type work, for players with low ratios, but this study did not test whether any program changes the ratio.
athleteDev: A low ratio here reflected weaker eccentric hamstring torque, which is relevant when programming eccentric hamstring strength for sprinting and kicking. The study does not measure sprint or kicking performance, and it does not show that changing the ratio improves performance.
rtp: Cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. The study tested preseason squad players and did not assess rehabilitation, return criteria or re-injury, so the authors' prevention suggestions are untested in this context.

citation: Álvarez-Herms J, González A, Corbi F, Odriozola I, Odriozola A. Possible relationship between the gut leaky syndrome and musculoskeletal injuries: the important role of gut microbiota as indirect modulator. AIMS Public Health. 2023;10(3):710-738.
abstract: This review examines the proposed link between gut microbiota, leaky gut and musculoskeletal injury, pain and recovery in athletes. The authors conclude that improving gut health may indirectly influence musculoskeletal homeostasis through systemic inflammation, immune response and nociceptive pain. The evidence cited is largely observational and mechanistic, and the authors describe the mechanisms as not fully understood.
tldr: A review based on a keyword database search proposes that gut permeability and microbiota shape systemic inflammation, pain and musculoskeletal recovery, but the supporting evidence is mostly observational or animal-based. Treat the proposed gut-injury pathway as a hypothesis, not a validated intervention target.
methods: Literature review with a described keyword search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science and SPORTDiscus using combinations of gut, leaky, microbiota, athletes, sport, performance and injury. No inclusion criteria, number of included studies, pooled analysis or risk-of-bias grading is reported, and the authors say their strategies also draw on their own practical experience.
findings: The review states that exercise, heat, splanchnic ischemia and dehydration can increase intestinal permeability, and that dysbiosis can raise circulating lipopolysaccharide and systemic inflammation. Associations between specific bacteria and osteoarthritis pain, bone density and tendon healing are described, mainly from observational and mouse studies. Its authors describe the causal role of these bacteria in leaky gut as unproven.
limitations: Most cited studies are observational, which limits causal inference, and the authors note that the evidence is heterogeneous in populations, interventions and outcomes. Athlete-specific data are limited, and the authors state that the mechanisms are not fully understood. The review does not describe a structured quality assessment of the included studies.
practicalImplications: The review's practical suggestions, including prebiotics, probiotics, reduced ultra-processed food and NSAID use, sleep, stress management and rest periods, are the authors' recommendations and are not tested in the review's own data. Staff should treat them as hypotheses for further study in athletes rather than injury-prevention protocols.
athleteDev: The review does not provide performance outcome data. Its links between gut microbiota and muscle performance rest on mouse data and an observational study in older adults, so it cannot guide training or nutrition decisions for performance.
rtp: The review cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It describes gut-related pain and inflammation hypotheses for musculoskeletal injury, but no return-to-play or recovery-timing data are reported.

citation: Chang RC, Singleton M, Chrisman SPD, Giza CC, Cuneo AZ, Murinova N, et al. Postinjury Alcohol Use Is Associated With Prolonged Recovery After Concussion in NCAA Athletes. Clin J Sport Med. 2023.
abstract: This prospective observational study compared time to unrestricted return to play in NCAA athletes with and without self-reported alcohol use after concussion. Among 484 athletes with complete data, those who drank after injury had longer adjusted recovery, at 23.3 versus 17.7 days. Alcohol use was not associated with SCAT3 symptom severity.
tldr: In NCAA athletes, self-reported alcohol use after concussion was linked to about one-third longer time to unrestricted play, but not to symptom severity. The observational design means this association does not show that alcohol causes slower recovery.
methods: Prospective observational analysis of NCAA athletes in the CARE Consortium (29 sites, 2014 to 2021). The alcohol group reported at least one drink per week since injury, asked at clearance to return to play. The primary outcome, days to unrestricted return to play, was analyzed with multivariable negative binomial regression adjusted for the confounders retained by a purposeful selection procedure (age, delayed symptom reporting and contact level); return to baseline on SCAT3 total severity, headache, concentration and memory was analyzed with logistic regression.
findings: Athletes who reported postinjury alcohol use (n=104) had an adjusted mean of 23.3 days (95% CI 20.0 to 27.2) to unrestricted play, compared with 17.7 days for those who did not (n=380), IRR 1.32 (95% CI 1.12 to 1.55, P<0.001). The unadjusted IRR was 1.33. Odds of returning to baseline SCAT3 symptom severity did not differ between groups (OR 0.96, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.07). The number of drinks per week correlated weakly with days to clearance (rho=0.169, P<0.001).
limitations: Alcohol, tobacco and marijuana use were self-reported, drink size and timing were not standardized, very few athletes reported more than 5 drinks per week, and the authors cannot determine causality. Only 484 of 4,802 concussed athletes had complete data, and they differed from the full cohort in age, sex, previous concussions and baseline symptom scores. Loss of consciousness (10.6% vs 3.7%), premorbid drinking and postinjury marijuana and tobacco use differed between groups in Table 1 but were not retained in the return-to-play model. The no-alcohol adjusted CI is 16.1 to 19.3 days in the Abstract and 16.2 to 19.4 in Results; the Results values are reported here, and the Abstract's symptom P value is printed as '<0.05' although all symptom comparisons were non-significant (P=0.47 to 0.98).
practicalImplications: Asking athletes about alcohol use during concussion recovery matches the association found, and staff may use this to counsel athletes who drink. The authors conclude that avoiding alcohol acutely after injury may shorten time to unrestricted play, which is their inference from an observational association and was not tested. Inference: the data do not show how much delay to expect per drink, so the association should not be used to set individual clearance dates.
athleteDev: The study does not measure performance outcomes. It addresses time to return to unrestricted play and symptom recovery in collegiate athletes, not training or competition performance.
rtp: This study is directly relevant to return to play. It found longer time to clearance after postinjury drinking, but it cannot show that alcohol causes the delay and it does not set a clearance criterion, so it should inform counseling and monitoring rather than clearance decisions.

citation: Ross S, Ripley NJ, McMahon JJ, Comfort P. Practices and perceptions in hamstring training for injury risk mitigation: A survey-based mixed-methods analysis. International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching. 2025.
abstract: An anonymous online survey of 47 practitioners examined how they use the Nordic hamstring exercise (NHE) and high-speed running for hamstring injury risk mitigation across seasons. Most programme both in-season and off-season, and the authors report higher high-speed running and NHE volumes off-season, although the NHE volume differences were not statistically significant. The authors conclude the reported NHE volumes are likely still above the smallest effective doses in the literature. Main challenges were athlete compliance, multidisciplinary team coordination and time.
tldr: Practitioners in this survey program the Nordic hamstring exercise and high-speed running in both seasons, with more volume off-season for most measures. Compliance, team coordination and time were the main barriers. The survey describes practice and does not test whether these approaches reduce injury.
methods: Anonymous online survey (27 fixed-response and 21 open-ended questions) distributed on social media to practitioners whose focus includes hamstring injury risk reduction. Fixed-response data were analysed by frequency counts and Hedges g estimation statistics, and open-ended responses by six-stage thematic analysis.
findings: Of 47 respondents, most programmed the Nordic hamstring exercise and high-speed running in both seasons. Upper-end weekly NHE repetitions were 45.5 in the off-season and 37.5 in-season (g = -0.44, p = 0.100), and the difference was not significant. Upper-end non-NHE resistance repetitions were significantly lower in-season (55.6 vs 77.4; g = -0.70, p = 0.014). The most frequent intervention codes were exposure to high-speed running (16 responses) and eccentric strength training (13).
limitations: The sample was self-selected through social media, and several off-season versus in-season differences were not significant; the discussion itself describes NHE volume as 'consistent' across seasons, which conflicts with the abstract's claim of higher off-season NHE volume. Methods describe paired-samples t-tests, but the reported comparisons are Hedges g from unequal-sized groups, and the claim of higher off-season high-speed running rests on frequency counts and non-numerical responses without a statistical test. Weekly NHE totals were calculated from Likert-scale ranges, so the upper-end values may overstate volume.
practicalImplications: The authors suggest that programmers compare their weekly NHE totals with lower doses, citing an earlier meta-analysis in which about 8 repetitions per week improved fascicle length, and check whether high volumes are affecting compliance. They also recommend better multidisciplinary planning of high-speed running exposure and education on micro-dosing and expected soreness. The survey does not test whether lower NHE volumes keep the injury benefit.
athleteDev: The survey reports practitioners pairing maximal running exposure with hamstring strength work, with an aim of building capacity and exposing athletes to maximal efforts. It does not measure performance outcomes, so it describes practice rather than showing which approach improves performance.
rtp: The study does not examine return to sport or rehabilitation outcomes, so it cannot set return-to-play criteria or loads. Its findings concern hamstring training for injury risk mitigation in athletes.

citation: Schroeder GD, Lynch TS, Gibbs DB, Chow I, LaBelle M, Patel AA, et al. Pre-existing Lumbar Spine Diagnosis as a Predictor of Outcomes in National Football League Athletes. American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2015;43(4):972-978.
abstract: A retrospective review of NFL Scouting Combine medical records from one franchise (2003 to 2011) compared players with a pre-existing lumbar spine diagnosis with matched drafted controls. Diagnosed players were less likely to be drafted, and drafted diagnosed players had fewer years and games played but no difference in performance score. Two drafted players who had a lumbar fusion went on to long NFL careers.
tldr: In this retrospective NFL combine cohort, athletes with a pre-existing lumbar diagnosis were drafted less often and had slightly shorter careers than matched drafted controls, with no difference in performance score. Two players with lumbar fusion had long careers, but that is only two cases.
methods: Retrospective cohort using written medical evaluations and imaging reports from one franchise's NFL Scouting Combine (2003 to 2011). Athletes with a lumbar diagnosis on appropriate imaging were matched to drafted controls by position, age, year and round. Career years, games and starts came from public sources, and a position-specific performance score was calculated; continuous variables used paired t tests and categorical variables chi-square tests.
findings: Of 414 athletes with a lumbar diagnosis, 253 were drafted (61.1%) compared with 80.2% of athletes without one. Among drafted athletes, the diagnosed group had fewer years played (4.0 vs 4.3), games played (46.5 vs 50.8) and games started (28.1 vs 30.6), with no difference in performance score (1.4 vs 1.8, P = .13). Among drafted athletes, spondylosis, herniated disc and spondylolysis were not associated with lower performance scores, and defensive backs with a diagnosis had fewer years and games but a higher performance score (0.3 vs 0.2, P = .003). Two drafted athletes with posterior lateral lumbar fusion played 108 and 125 games.
limitations: The study is retrospective, relies on imaging reports rather than standardised classification, and uses one franchise. Controls may have undetected radiographic findings, and offensive linemen have no performance score. The paper reports the spondylolysis longevity effect as P = .01 in the abstract and text, but Table 6 gives P = .32 for years played and P = .11 for games played, so the table values are reported here. The years played P value is .001 in the text and .0001 in Table 4. Table 10 also shows quarterbacks with a diagnosis were drafted more often than those without (80.0% vs 59.6%), and some draft percentages (for example 99.6% for linebackers without a diagnosis) look implausible.
practicalImplications: For draft evaluation, the authors' data suggest a lumbar diagnosis is associated with lower draft rates and modestly shorter careers in this sample, although overall performance did not differ. The authors suggest spondylolysis or spondylolisthesis, and a lumbar diagnosis in a defensive back, may signal a poorer career prognosis, but the longevity result for spondylolysis conflicts with Table 6, so that claim should be weighed cautiously.
athleteDev: The study concerns draft outcomes and career length, not training or development. In this sample, a pre-existing lumbar diagnosis was linked to lower draft rates and slightly shorter careers, while performance score was largely unchanged, which suggests the main cost was to draft status.
rtp: The study does not assess return-to-play decisions after treatment. Two drafted players with lumbar fusion had long careers (108 and 125 games), and operative and nonoperative herniation groups did not differ in longevity, but these are small, retrospective findings and the authors state that restrictions after fusion remain controversial, so the paper cannot set return-to-play or contact clearance.

citation: Hosokawa Y, Racinais S, Akama T, Zideman D, Budgett R, Casa DJ, et al. Prehospital management of exertional heat stroke at sports competitions: International Olympic Committee Adverse Weather Impact Expert Working Group for the Olympic Games Tokyo 2020. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2021.
abstract: This International Olympic Committee expert group statement summarises prehospital management of exertional heat stroke (EHS) at sports competitions. It sets out a designated on-site heat deck with equipment and staffing, rectal temperature confirmation, whole-body cold water immersion before any hospital transfer, and algorithms for diagnosis and treatment. It also covers coordination with hospitals and infection control during the COVID-19 pandemic.
tldr: For suspected exertional heat stroke at sports events, the IOC expert group recommends a designated on-site heat deck, rectal temperature confirmation, and whole-body cold water immersion before any hospital transfer. The aim is cooling within 30 minutes of collapse, with cooling completed on site before the athlete is transported.
methods: Members of the IOC Adverse Weather Impact Expert Working Group for Tokyo 2020 summarised current best practice for prehospital EHS management. The document reports no new data, and its recommendations draw on cited race-medicine studies and earlier consensus statements.
findings: The statement describes a heat deck with three zones (temperature assessment, cold water immersion and observation) and a recommended equipment list. It recommends rectal temperature confirmation, with EHS generally defined as a core temperature of 40.5°C or higher with central nervous system dysfunction, and cold water immersion at 5 to 15°C. Athletes should be cooled first and transported second, with at least four trained providers per athlete and a 15-minute stable temperature before transport.
limitations: The statement does not address Paralympic athletes, for whom the authors say classification-specific cooling strategies are needed. The cooling end point is written both as 39 C and as below 39 C. All authors are members of the IOC expert working group, and the statement reports no honoraria. Inference: the journal labels it 'Original research', but its Methods describe an expert group summarising best practice, so it is coded here as a consensus statement.
practicalImplications: Event medical teams at high-heat or high-demand events can set up a heat deck with a cold water tub, a rectal probe and point-of-care blood analysis, and staff it with at least four trained providers. The statement says to exclude a cardiac cause first, and to keep cooling collapsed athletes with confirmed hyperthermia below 40.5°C using rotating ice-wet towels while monitoring rectal temperature. The authors recommend pre-arranged hospital communication and hands-on scenario training before competition.
athleteDev: The statement is written for medical and event teams and says little about performance. Staff who support athletes in hot events can use it to check that the heat-illness plan includes a cooling area, trained staff and hospital links.
rtp: The statement covers acute emergency management of exertional heat stroke, not rehabilitation or return to sport. It leaves the return-to-competition decision to the athlete's team physician, guided by hospital and event medical advice, so it cannot set return-to-sport timing.

citation: Putukian M, Riegler K, Amalfe S, Bruce J, Echemendia R. Preinjury and Postinjury Factors That Predict Sports-Related Concussion and Clinical Recovery Time. Clinical Journal of Sport Medicine. 2021;31(1):15-22.
abstract: A prospective cohort of collegiate athletes tested preinjury risk factors and baseline measures, then followed athletes for concussion and clinical recovery. Only sport type and self-reported concussion history were associated with a later concussion. No preinjury factor or baseline measure was associated with days to symptom-free or return to play, while post-injury symptom number and severity and some ImPACT measures were associated with longer recovery.
tldr: In Ivy League athletes, preseason risk factors and baseline tests did not track how long concussion symptoms or return to play lasted. Post-injury symptom count and severity, and some ImPACT measures, were linked to longer recovery.
methods: Prospective cohort of 1,152 athletes (69% male) assessed before the season with the SCAT3, GAD-7, PHQ-9, ImPACT, and a self-reported history of concussion, ADHD, learning disability, migraine, depression and anxiety. After concussion, the SCAT3 was given a mean of 0.83 days and ImPACT a mean of 2.48 days after injury (range 0 to 13 days for both), and athletes were followed to symptom-free and full return to play. Associations were tested with chi-square tests, logistic regression, and Spearman and partial Spearman correlations, with significance set at P < 0.01.
findings: Concussion was associated with sport type (men's ice hockey 33.3% vs 11.6% for other athletes, P < 0.001) and with self-reported concussion history (10%, 16% and 21% concussed with none, one, and two or more prior concussions). Among 138 athletes followed to symptom resolution, days to symptom-free averaged 9.84 +/- 11.11 (range 1 to 86) and days to full return to play averaged 20.21 +/- 19.17 (n = 98, range 4 to 150), and no preinjury factor or baseline measure was associated with either (all P > 0.05). Post-injury SCAT3 symptom total (rs 0.31) and severity (rs 0.33) correlated with days to symptom-free but not significantly with days to return to play, whereas ImPACT symptom score, visual motor and reaction time correlated with both (Table 6).
limitations: Ivy League-only sample, which the authors say may limit generalizability, with self-reported risk factors and few women among the concussed athletes (34 of 138). The concussed-athlete count appears as 145 (Abstract and aim 1), 143 (Table 2) and 163 (aim 2). The printed median for days to return to play (20.21) repeats the mean and cannot be checked. Inference: the post-injury results are concurrent correlations in one cohort, not a validated prediction model. Two authors report consulting roles with professional leagues (MLS and NHL).
practicalImplications: Preseason risk-factor history and baseline testing did not add predictive value for recovery in this cohort. The authors support multidomain assessment after injury, including the SCAT5 and neuropsychological testing, and highlight symptom number, symptom severity, and ImPACT reaction time and visual motor scores as post-injury information that relates to longer recovery.
athleteDev: The paper is about concussion, not performance. Performance staff can note that prior concussion and playing men's ice hockey were the only markers linked to a later concussion in this cohort, which is a reason to watch athletes with a concussion history more closely.
rtp: The study addresses recovery and return to play directly. The authors do not propose a return-to-play rule, and their correlations cannot set a return date, but they support multidomain post-injury assessment, and post-injury symptoms and ImPACT results were associated with longer recovery.

citation: Grooms DR, Diekfuss JA, Criss CR, Anand M, Slutsky-Ganesh AB, DiCesare CA, et al. Preliminary brain-behavioral neural correlates of anterior cruciate ligament injury risk landing biomechanics using a novel bilateral leg press neuroimaging paradigm. PLoS ONE. 2022;17(8):e0272578.
abstract: Thirty-one high school female athletes performed a novel bilateral leg press during fMRI and a drop vertical jump assessed with 3D motion analysis. Peak knee abduction moment was used as a covariate in the fMRI analysis, and athletes were also grouped into high- and low-risk groups by knee abduction thresholds. Higher landing knee abduction moments were associated with greater activity in visual and sensory integration regions, and the high-risk group showed greater activity in motor and visual regions.
tldr: In adolescent female soccer players, greater knee abduction loading during a landing test was linked to greater brain activity in visual and spatial-processing regions during a bilateral leg press in the scanner. These results are preliminary and come from very small groups.
methods: Thirty-one female high school soccer players completed a drop vertical jump with 3D motion analysis and a bilateral leg press during fMRI, with peak knee abduction moment entered as a covariate. One athlete was removed for excess head motion, leaving 30 for the correlation analysis. A high-risk group (25.25 Nm or more, n = 4) was compared with a low-risk group (6.0 Nm or less, n = 5, matched for age and BMI) using a group analysis with cluster correction at z > 3.1 and p < .05.
findings: Greater knee abduction moment was associated with greater activity in the right lingual gyrus and intracalcarine cortex, and in bilateral lingual gyrus, posterior cingulate and precuneus (all z > 3.1, p < .05, cluster corrected). The high-risk group showed greater activity than the low-risk group in bilateral primary and premotor cortex, left posterior cingulate and lingual gyrus, and bilateral intracalcarine cortex, precuneus and lingual gyrus. Group peak knee abduction moments were 32.88 +/- 6.10 Nm and 2.80 +/- 2.54 Nm (Table 1), and no effect sizes were reported.
limitations: The injury-risk groups are very small: Table 1 gives four high-risk athletes, but Table 2 gives five per group. The low-risk cut-off is 6.0 Nm in the Table 1 row and text but 10.6 Nm in the Table 1 caption. The group peak knee abduction values in the text (33.19 +/- 5.33 and 2.84 +/- 1.58 Nm) differ from Table 1. The sample is female only, the fMRI task is a simplified supine bilateral leg press, and cognition and visual attention were not measured. The author Myer is an inventor of a patented biofeedback technology for injury prevention, receives licensing royalties, and consults with commercial entities.
practicalImplications: The study tests no screening or training method, so it is a basis for planning rather than a guide to practice. The authors propose that external-focus instructions, augmented visual biofeedback and stroboscopic visual perturbation might target the visual and proprioceptive activity they describe, but these are proposals that were not tested.
athleteDev: This study concerns ACL injury risk in adolescent girls, not sport performance. Staff who assess landing mechanics can note the authors' link between knee abduction loading and brain activity in visual and spatial regions, but the study does not show that changing that activity changes performance.
rtp: The sample reports no injured or reconstructed athletes, and the authors frame the findings as injury-risk correlates, not recovery markers. The study therefore cannot inform return to sport after ACL reconstruction.

citation: Memmini AK, Mosesso KM, Perkins SM, Brett BL, Pasquina PF, McAllister TW, et al. Premorbid Risk Factors and Acute Injury Characteristics of Sport-Related Concussion Across the National Collegiate Athletic Association: Findings from the Concussion Assessment, Research, and Education (CARE) Consortium. Sports Medicine. 2023.
abstract: Prospective cohort of 1,804 NCAA student athletes with a sport-related concussion and 21,702 without, from 22 sports in the CARE Consortium (2014 to 2021). Odds of SRC were higher with prior SRC, ADHD, learning disorder, migraine, and Black or multiracial identity. Altered mental status, loss of consciousness, amnesia and delayed symptom onset differed by sex and contact level.
tldr: In collegiate athletes, a prior concussion, ADHD, learning disorders, migraine and Black or multiracial identity were each associated with higher concussion odds. Injury presentation varied by sex and contact level, and loss of consciousness and amnesia were uncommon.
methods: Prospective cohort analysis of CARE Consortium data from NCAA student athletes in 22 sports with at least 30 SRCs. Independent unadjusted logistic regression models gave odds ratios for SRC by demographic and medical history, stratified by sex and contact level. Chi-square and Kruskal-Wallis tests compared post-injury characteristics.
findings: Female athletes had lower overall odds of SRC (OR 0.78, 95% CI 0.71 to 0.86), but higher odds than male athletes in limited-contact (OR 1.91) and non-contact (OR 1.86) sports, with no difference in contact sports (OR 1.01). Among SRCs, 54.9% of male and 40.4% of female athletes had altered mental status, and delayed symptom onset was reported in 38.8% of female and 26.8% of male athletes. Loss of consciousness (4.7%), post-traumatic amnesia (10.5%) and retrograde amnesia (5.4%) were infrequent overall.
limitations: Sports with fewer than 30 SRCs and military academy cadets were excluded, and American football (34% of SRCs, male only) drives the contact-sport results. Analyses are unadjusted for sport, exposure and race-by-sport mix, and history was self-reported. The authors state that the race findings do not show a causal relationship.
practicalImplications: Prior concussion, ADHD, learning disorder and migraine history can be used as risk context when planning prevention and evaluation in collegiate athletes. Because loss of consciousness and amnesia were uncommon in this sample, a concussion evaluation should not depend on them. Education on early symptom reporting is supported, especially for delayed symptoms.
athleteDev: This study addresses injury risk and post-injury presentation only and does not measure performance. It does not inform performance development.
rtp: The study does not measure recovery or return-to-play timing, so it cannot set return-to-play criteria or clearance. It reports that delayed symptom onset (31.2%) was common and that only 54.9% of athletes were removed from play immediately, while loss of consciousness and amnesia were uncommon, so removal decisions should not wait for those signs.

citation: Tu LA, Knapik DM, Sheehan J, Salata MJ, Voos JE. Prevalence of Jones Fracture Repair and Impact on Short-Term NFL Participation. Foot Ankle Int. 2017.
abstract: Fixation was performed for 41 Jones fractures in 40 of 1,311 athletes invited to the NFL Combine from 2012 to 2015 (3.1%). Athletes with a repair were not significantly different in draft status, games played or games started during their first NFL season compared with athletes without repair.
tldr: Among NFL Combine invitees from 2012 to 2015, 3.1% had a Jones fracture repair, and the repair group did not differ significantly from other athletes in draft status or early NFL playing time. The study is small and retrospective, so it cannot show long-term participation.
methods: Retrospective review of NFL Combine database records for 1,311 athletes, with radiographs reviewed by two senior authors to confirm Jones fracture and fixation type. Repair athletes were compared with all other invitees on draft status, games played and games started in the first NFL season, using t tests, chi-square tests and Fisher exact tests.
findings: Repair athletes were drafted in 70% (28 of 40) vs 66% (841 of 1,271) of others (P = .61). Mean games played were 8.8 vs 7.4 (P = .23) and games started 3.0 vs 2.7 (P = .76). Incomplete union was present in 3 fractures (8%), and none of the athletes reported a strength or range-of-motion limit in the operative foot. Of the repair group, 75% played a regular season game and 38% started one in the first season.
limitations: The data were retrospective, from a single Combine visit, and did not include operative reports, injury mechanisms, injury dates or complications. The repair group was small, so the analysis had limited power, and athletes with failed repairs were likely not invited to the Combine. The comparison group of 1,271 includes the 7 athletes excluded for diaphyseal stress or avulsion fracture fixation, and the authors describe the NFL outcomes as prospective, though they were collected retrospectively from NFL.com.
practicalImplications: For elite football athletes with Jones fracture fixation, staff can counsel that draft status and early NFL playing time were not significantly different from those without repair in this sample. The authors suggest clinical examination matters alongside radiographic union, based on 3 athletes with incomplete union who reported no strength or motion limit at a single Combine exam. The sample was selected for athletes who reached the Combine, so it should not be used to estimate fixation success.
athleteDev: The study measures draft status and game participation rather than performance, and it does not show whether fracture repair affects playing quality.
rtp: Most repair athletes (75%) played a regular season game in their first NFL season, and nonunion athletes had no reported strength or motion deficit on examination. The study did not report time to return to play, timing of return to full activity or refracture rates, so it cannot set return-to-play criteria.

citation: Mannava S, Frangiamore SJ, Murphy CP, Sanchez A, Sanchez G, Dornan GJ, et al. Prevalence of Shoulder Labral Injury in Collegiate Football Players at the National Football League Scouting Combine. Orthop J Sports Med. 2018;6(7):2325967118783982.
abstract: MRI-confirmed shoulder labral tears were identified in 377 shoulders (340 of 2,285 players, 14.9%) at the NFL Combine from 2009 to 2015. Linebackers had the highest rate, linemen had higher odds of a tear in at least one shoulder, and more than half of the affected shoulders had previous surgery on imaging.
tldr: Labral tears on MRI were found in 14.9% of NFL Combine players from 2009 to 2015, most often in linebackers and linemen. Anterior and posterior involvement were both common, and more than half of the affected shoulders showed prior surgery.
methods: Retrospective review of NFL team injury registry data for 2,285 Combine players from 2009 to 2015. Players with suspected labral tears were imaged, and MRIs were reviewed by two fellowship-trained orthopaedic sports medicine surgeons with a radiologist consulted for consensus. Prevalence was compared by position, and odds ratios with Fisher exact tests assessed linemen vs nonlinemen.
findings: MRI-confirmed labral tears occurred in 377 shoulders (340 players, 14.9%), with 37 players bilateral. Linebackers had the highest position rate (19.2%), and linemen had a higher rate than nonlinemen (17.2% vs 13.7%; OR 1.31, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.67, P = .029). Anterior involvement was present in 246 shoulders (65.3%), posterior in 262 (69.5%) and SLAP tears in 120 (31.8%), and 203 shoulders (53.8%) had previous surgery on imaging.
limitations: MRI was not obtained for all players and was required for diagnosis, so some labral injuries were likely missed and prevalence may be underestimated. The 14.9% uses all 2,285 Combine players as the denominator, although only players with a shoulder injury history and imaging were assessed. Symptoms were not correlated with imaging, MRA was not consistently available, selection bias favors healthier elite players, and the findings may not generalize to other football cohorts.
practicalImplications: When evaluating linemen and linebackers with shoulder complaints, staff should expect a labral tear to be possible and review the imaging for both anterior and posterior involvement. More than half of the affected shoulders had prior surgery on imaging, so surgical history should be checked when assessing these players.
athleteDev: The study describes injury prevalence and does not measure performance or draft outcome, so it does not inform performance development. The authors call for future work on how labral tears affect draft position and NFL performance.
rtp: The study does not follow players through rehabilitation or return to play, so it cannot guide return-to-play decisions. It reports that many affected shoulders had prior surgery, but outcomes after surgery were not measured.

citation: Cushman DM, Carefoot A, Corcoran B, Vu L, Fredericson M, Fausett C, et al. Prevalence of Sonographic Achilles Tendon, Patellar Tendon, and Plantar Fascia Abnormalities in Division I Collegiate Athletes From a Variety of Sports. Clin J Sport Med. 2023.
abstract: Ultrasound was used to scan the Achilles tendon, patellar tendon and plantar fascia of 243 collegiate athletes from 14 sports at three Division I institutions. Abnormalities were found in 10.1%, 37.2% and 3.9% of the respective structures and were associated with current pain in all three.
tldr: Ultrasound abnormalities were common in collegiate athletes across 14 sports, most often in the patellar tendon (37%), and were associated with current pain. Most abnormal tendons were painless, so an abnormal scan alone should not be used to screen athletes or label a tendon as injured.
methods: Cross-sectional ultrasound study of athletes recruited at preseason physical examinations at three Division I institutions. Each tendon was imaged in long and short axis, and a blinded sonographer scored hypoechogenicity, thickening and neovascularity, with a second sonographer re-scoring 20% of images. Relative risks for pain were estimated with a binomial generalized linear model using cluster-robust errors, and logistic regression examined demographic and sport factors.
findings: Any abnormality was found in 49 of 485 Achilles tendons (10.1%), 175 of 470 patellar tendons (37.2%) and 19 of 486 plantar fasciae (3.9%), and abnormality was associated with current pain (Achilles RR 4.25, 95% CI 2.05 to 8.84; patellar RR 5.69, 95% CI 2.31 to 14.00; plantar fascia RR 5.17, 95% CI 1.76 to 15.25). Neovascularity was associated with pain in the Achilles (RR 9.99), patellar (RR 6.16) and plantar fascia (RR 18.94), with the plantar fascia estimate based on very few cases. In logistic models, older age was associated with Achilles (OR 1.30) and plantar fascia (OR 1.41) abnormality, while younger age (OR 0.76) and running (OR 4.27) or explosive (OR 5.08) sport compared with aquatic sport were associated with patellar abnormality.
limitations: The study is cross-sectional, so the pain associations are not causal and the correlations were imperfect, since few athletes had pain. Sonographer agreement was not perfect, 58% of athletes were female, and 11.1% of athletes played more than one sport, so the sport driving each finding cannot be identified. Tendon counts for abnormality differ between Table 2 (49 Achilles, 19 plantar fascia) and Table 3 (51 Achilles, 17 plantar fascia).
practicalImplications: Tendon and fascia abnormalities on ultrasound were common in this collegiate sample, with patellar tendon abnormality present in more than a third of tendons. Abnormal findings were usually painless, so ultrasound should not be used alone as a screening tool or to diagnose injury. The authors state that the pain association provides a basis for improving preventive training and rehabilitation.
athleteDev: The study measures tendon and fascia imaging and pain, not performance, so it does not inform performance development.
rtp: The cross-sectional design does not follow athletes through injury or recovery, so the study cannot guide return-to-sport decisions. It does not show when a tendon abnormality should delay return to training or competition.

citation: Davies MAM, Kerr ZY, DeFreese JD, Arden NK, Marshall SW, Guskiewicz KM, et al. Prevalence of and Risk Factors for Total Hip and Knee Replacement in Retired National Football League Athletes. Am J Sports Med. 2019.
abstract: Cross-sectional study of retired NFL players who completed a general health survey in 2001 to 2002. It estimates the prevalence of hip and knee replacement after retirement and examines playing-career and injury factors associated with replacement, including the link between specific knee injuries and knee replacement.
tldr: In a survey of 2,432 retired NFL players, 11.4% reported a hip or knee replacement after retirement, and knee replacement (7.7%) was more common than hip (4.6%). Age, current weight and knee injury count were associated with knee replacement, but this cross-sectional design cannot show that injury or weight causes replacement.
methods: Cross-sectional analysis of a general health questionnaire sent to members of the NFL Retired Players Association, with nonrespondents followed by telephone (response rate 69.3%). Outcomes were self-reported hip and knee replacement after retirement, and exposures were years of play, playing position and self-reported severe hip or knee injuries; prevalence ratios were estimated by Poisson regression with robust variance, adjusted for age, weight and injury in staged models.
findings: Of 2,432 players, 277 (11.4%) reported a replacement: 7.7% knee, 4.6% hip and 1% both. In full multivariable models, knee replacement was associated with age (PR 2.23 per 10 years), current weight (PR 1.10 per 10 lb) and knee injury count (PR 3.44 for three injuries vs none), and hip replacement with age (PR 1.86 per 10 years), lineman position (PR 1.62 vs big skill players) and hip injury count (PR 2.77 for two injuries vs none). Total years of play was not associated with either replacement after adjustment (univariable knee PR 0.96 per year, 95% CI 0.93-0.99, became 1.01 in the full model).
limitations: The design is cross-sectional, so temporal order and causation cannot be inferred; the abstract labels it a case-control study, but the Methods and Discussion say cross-sectional, and it is coded here as cross-sectional. Injury history and replacement are self-reported and not validated against records. The abstract's 'majority of participants reported previous severe knee injury (53%)' refers to the named specific knee injuries (ACL, MCL, LCL, PCL, meniscus, dislocation), while Table 2 and the Results give 71.8% (1,747) for any severe knee injury. The survey was in 2001 to 2002, the parent study is funded in part by the NFL Players Association, NFL Charities and several corporations, and the authors note that surgical details were not available.
practicalImplications: Knee injury history and body weight can be used to flag retired players for long-term joint health follow-up, because both were associated with knee replacement in this survey. The study did not test whether preventing injury or reducing weight lowers later replacement rates, so these should not be presented as proven prevention targets.
athleteDev: The paper does not address training or performance. Among playing-career factors, injury history and lineman position were associated with later replacement, and total years of play was not.
rtp: The authors suggest the knee injury findings may matter for return-to-sport decisions for players with multiple knee injuries. The study cannot show that any return-to-play decision changes later replacement, because it contains no injury management or surgical data.

citation: Morrissey CD, Knapik DM. Prevalence, Mechanisms, and Return to Sport After Isolated Popliteus Injuries in Athletes: A Systematic Review. Orthop J Sports Med. 2022;10(2):23259671211073617.
abstract: Systematic review, following PRISMA and registered with PROSPERO, of published studies from January 1988 to August 2021 on athletes with isolated popliteus injuries sustained during sport. It describes mechanisms, sports, tear characteristics, treatment, outcomes and return to sport.
tldr: Isolated popliteus injury is rarely reported in athletes and is described only in case reports and small series, here 27 athletes from 19 studies. Most had a traumatic or contact mechanism and a lateral condyle avulsion, and the 13 athletes whose return was reported went back to sport at a mean of about 11 weeks.
methods: Seven databases (PubMed, OVID, MEDLINE, Biosis Previews, SPORTDiscus, PEDRO and EMBASE) were searched for English-language studies of athletes with isolated popliteus injuries sustained in competitive sport, with two reviewers screening independently. Studies with associated posterolateral corner, cruciate or meniscal injury were excluded, and the data were summarised descriptively because the reporting was too heterogeneous for statistical analysis.
findings: Mechanisms were traumatic or contact in 67% (18 of 27), noncontact in 15% (4), and unreported in 19% (5). Avulsions off the lateral femoral condyle occurred in 67% (18) and 85% (23) had swelling; 52% (14) were managed non-operatively and 48% (13) operatively, and complications were reported in 3 non-operatively managed athletes and none managed operatively. Athletes with intrasubstance tears returned to sport at a mean of 5.6 weeks compared with 15.4 weeks for avulsions; return timing was not compared by management type.
limitations: The authors could not run statistical analyses because outcomes were heterogeneous and inconsistently reported, and, because of the small number of studies, they included athletes with less than 2 years of follow-up. The sample is small and mostly male, and the title's 'prevalence' is a count of 27 published cases, not a rate in any athlete population, so it cannot show how common the injury is. D.M.K. reports grant support from Arthrex and education payments from Medwest and Smith & Nephew.
practicalImplications: Isolated popliteus injury should be considered in athletes with posterolateral knee pain and effusion after forced external tibial rotation, particularly when ligamentous examination is stable. Management should be individualised because the review found no definitive algorithm, and athletes can be told that reported return to sport was about 11 weeks, with intrasubstance tears returning sooner than avulsions.
athleteDev: The review addresses diagnosis, management and return to sport after a knee injury, not performance, and it reports no performance outcomes. Its only performance-relevant point is the reported return-to-sport timeline.
rtp: The 13 athletes whose return was reported all returned to sport at a mean of 10.8 weeks, with intrasubstance tears returning at 5.6 weeks and avulsions at 15.4 weeks. The review has no standard return criteria, and the short and inconsistent follow-up means these timings can be used as context, not as a rule.

citation: Anderson SA, Eichner ER, Bennett S, Boden BP, Elkins GA, Judge LW, et al. Preventing Exertional Heat Stroke in Football: Time for a Paradigm Shift. Sports Health. 2024.
abstract: Clinical review of exertional heat stroke (EHS) in football, using case series from the National Registry of Catastrophic Sports Injuries and a PubMed search. It argues that prevention should focus on position-specific conditioning, linemen, heat load, and eliminating punitive exertion, rather than on uniform, hydration and acclimatization rules alone.
tldr: Football heat stroke deaths in the registry cluster in linemen during conditioning, and the authors argue that prevention should shift to position-specific, intensity-limited training. The recommendations are expert opinion built on case series and have not been tested as interventions.
methods: Case series of youth, high school and collegiate football deaths were drawn from the National Registry of Catastrophic Sports Injuries (1955 to 2021), whose sources are media reports, newspaper clippings, autopsy reports, death certificates, school investigations and published literature. Articles were identified through a PubMed search using the terms football, exertional heat stroke and prevention, with no screening counts or appraisal reported. The paper is a Level 5 clinical review and its recommendations are expert opinion drawn from this material.
findings: Citing earlier registry analyses, the authors report that 97% of football EHS deaths from 1998 to 2018 were linemen, that 100% of high school and college deaths in a retrospective study occurred during conditioning drills and none in games, and that 37% of recent deaths involved exercise as punishment. Of deaths from 1998 to 2018, 70% occurred in shorts and a T-shirt, and the environment in recent deaths averaged a maximum of 90.8 F (32.7 C) with a wet-bulb globe temperature of 76.7 F (24.8 C). The registry shows a mean of 2 deaths per season from 1955 to 2021, rising to nearly 3 per season from 2000 to 2021, with 9 deaths in summer 2021.
limitations: Registry cases are drawn largely from media and school sources, the paper has no denominator of exposed athletes, the key percentages are cited from earlier analyses rather than re-derived here, and the positional movement data in Table 1 come from 12 regular-season college games (adapted from another study) rather than from heat stroke cases. Jon K. Davis, listed in the full author section, is an employee of the Gatorade Sports Science Institute (PepsiCo) and holds PepsiCo stock options, and another listed author sits on a medical advisory board for BOA; the paper argues that dehydration contributes little to fatal EHS, and the authors state the views are not PepsiCo's.
practicalImplications: Football staff should check that linemen's conditioning is position-specific and that sustained high-intensity sprints, timed conditioning tests and punitive exercise are removed, particularly in the first 7 to 10 days of a conditioning cycle. The authors also suggest adjusting activity to the heat load and considering air-conditioned spaces for linemen during hot practices, but these are expert recommendations rather than tested interventions.
athleteDev: The paper argues that linemen's conditioning should match their game demands, which are short efforts at low work-to-rest ratios, and it uses positional movement data from 12 college games to support this. It reports no performance outcomes, so the training recommendations are not tested for performance effects.
rtp: The paper does not address clearance after heat illness or return to sport after injury. Its one relevant point is that transition periods, including return to activity after injury, are high risk for heat stroke, so exercise intensity should be built up with appropriate work-to-rest ratios.

citation: Cantu RC, Sills AK, Alosco ML, Arbogast KB, Bazarian JJ, Bieniek KF, et al. Prevention of concussion and long-term effects of repetitive traumatic brain injury: Unanimous consensus from the Cantu Concussion Summit. PM&R. 2025;1-4.
abstract: A December 2023 summit convened clinicians and researchers to share findings and identify research gaps on brain injury and long-term cognitive disorders in athletes. After participants' advance statements and a conference discussion, the group reached unanimous agreement on six consensus statements aimed at player safety and health. The summit was supported by an unrestricted NFL educational grant.
tldr: An expert summit reached unanimous agreement on six statements that call for limiting avoidable head impacts in practices and games, safer contact technique, and further research on CTE signs and TES criteria. The statements are expert consensus, not tested interventions.
methods: No formal consensus method is reported beyond participants submitting three mitigation ideas in advance, aggregation of those ideas, multidisciplinary conference sessions, and a final discussion. The text does not describe how the statements were voted on or weighted.
findings: The six statements are: eliminate intentional and avoidable head impacts in practices and games; limit the number, duration and intensity of head impacts; reinforce safer techniques to avoid head contact at all levels of play; penalize intentional and avoidable contact to the head and neck; investigate clinical signs and symptoms associated with CTE neuropathology; and improve TES criteria through research. The paper reports no effect data for any statement.
limitations: The statements are expert opinion with no reported evidence grading or outcome data, and the head-impact limits are not quantified. The summit received an unrestricted NFL educational grant, and several authors report NFL-related roles or payments in the disclosures.
practicalImplications: Staff can use the statements as a policy framework for reducing avoidable head contact in practices and games and for reinforcing safer technique. The CTE and TES statements are research priorities, not clinical criteria staff can apply.
athleteDev: The statements bear on practice design, particularly limiting the number, duration and intensity of head impacts in practice. The paper gives no thresholds for these limits and no performance outcomes.
rtp: The paper does not address concussion diagnosis, recovery or return-to-play decisions, so it cannot guide return to sport.

citation: Krill MK, Hoffman J, Yang J, Hodax JD, Owens BD, Hewett TE. Previous foot injuries associated with a greater likelihood of Achilles tendon ruptures in professional American football players. The Physician and Sportsmedicine. 2018;46(3):342-348.
abstract: A retrospective review of NFL injury records from 2010-11 to 2016-17 identified 109 Achilles tendon ruptures. Injury rates in the season before rupture were compared with the NFL cohort, and only foot injuries were higher in the rupture group.
tldr: NFL players who ruptured an Achilles tendon had prior-season injury rates similar to the league overall and for lower-extremity injuries, but a higher foot injury rate. The foot finding rests on 6 injuries and should be treated as a hypothesis to test prospectively.
methods: Retrospective online review of team injury reports, media and video for NFL seasons 2010-11 to 2016-17, with ruptures confirmed from public reports and player participation records. Injury was defined as a missed game, and injury rates per 1000 athlete-exposures (games) were compared with the NFL cohort using rate ratios with 95% CIs.
findings: Among 31 analyzed players (35 game injuries in the prior season), the overall injury rate was 36.57 per 1000 AE versus 38.83 for the NFL cohort (IRR 0.94, 95% CI 0.68-1.31, p = 0.73). Lower-extremity injury IRR was 1.10 (0.76-1.58), while foot injury IRR was 2.58 (1.16-5.77, p = 0.02), with 6 foot injuries in the rupture group. Eleven players had two ruptures, and all 11 second ruptures were contralateral. The authors report more identified ruptures than the 31 reported for 1997-2002, but they give no denominator for the earlier period.
