It states that no firm recommendations for sport are possible at present, so staff should not present these compounds as performance aids on the basis of this review. The author advises avoiding nicotine because of its addictive properties, and identifies low-dose caffeine combined with other phytochemicals, such as guarana, as an area needing more research.
athleteDev: The review finds very few sport-context trials: one study of 15 athletes found a triterpene extract improved reaction times before and during graded cycling, and one study of 30 participants found peppermint essential oil improved reaction times and some physical performance measures. It reports that caffeine's ergogenic effects in endurance, high-intensity and intermittent exercise are well established, but that little research links caffeine's effect on alertness or attention to sport performance.
rtp: The review does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.

citation: Okoh AK, Amponsah MKD, Cheffet-Walsh S, Patel M, Carfagno D, Linton D, et al. Prevalence of Cardiovascular Disease and Risk Factors Among Former National Football League Players. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2024;83(19):1827-1837.
abstract: HUDDLE was a multicity cross-sectional study of NFL alumni and family members aged 50 and over who had health history reporting, blood pressure, ECG and transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) screening, with a 30-day follow-up call. This report covers the former NFL players, estimates the prevalence of hypertension and structural cardiac abnormalities, and tests hypertension as a predictor of abnormal TTE findings.
tldr: In 285 former NFL players aged 50 and over, hypertension was found at screening in 89.8% although only 37.5% reported it, and 61.8% had structural cardiac abnormalities on echocardiography. Screening hypertension was associated with these abnormalities, but the study has no comparison group and no outcome follow-up.
methods: Players were recruited through NFL Alumni Association chapters and screened at 9 events in 8 US cities between August 2021 and August 2022. Each participant completed a self-reported health history, blood pressure readings, a 12-lead ECG and a TTE, read by a central core lab, and a physician follow-up call at 30 days. Hypertension was defined as a reported history, medication use, or a screening reading of 130/80 mm Hg or higher, and multivariable logistic regression was used to identify predictors of structural abnormality on TTE.
findings: Hypertension prevalence was 89.8% (255 of 284), and 81.5% (145 of 178) of players without a reported history had a screening BP of 130/80 mm Hg or higher. Structural abnormalities on TTE were present in 61.8% of the 285 evaluable players, and 46.1% had abnormal ECG findings. In the multivariable model, hypertension at screening was associated with structural abnormalities on TTE (OR 2.02, 95% CI 1.03 to 3.96; P=0.04), and investigators recommended further follow-up for 76.7% (207 of the 270 players with follow-up reasons recorded).
limitations: The study was sponsored by Edwards Lifesciences, which funded it, organised the screening events, collected health histories and was involved in study design, data management and statistical analyses; nine authors are sponsor employees and others report consulting, proctoring or grants from the sponsor. In the multivariable model abnormal ECG was borderline (OR 1.68, 95% CI 1.00 to 2.82, P=0.05), and the authors report it as no longer significant. Self-report, volunteer recruitment through alumni chapters, no comparison group, mainly southern US sites, clinician-judged follow-up and no long-term outcomes all limit generalisation.
practicalImplications: For former players aged 50 and over, the study supports checking blood pressure at routine contact, because hypertension was common in this sample and largely unreported beforehand. Players with hypertension may benefit from echocardiographic assessment, since hypertension was associated with structural abnormalities in this sample, but the study does not show that screening improves outcomes.
athleteDev: The study covers former players and does not address training, performance or active players. Its relevance to current athletes is limited to the idea that hypertension and cardiac remodelling can occur in athletes and persist after retirement.
rtp: The study does not address return to sport or return to play. Its findings about elevated blood pressure and structural abnormalities in retired players do not establish clearance criteria for active players.

citation: Drew M, Vlahovich N, Hughes D, Appaneal R, Burke LM, Lundy B, et al. Prevalence of illness, poor mental health and sleep quality and low energy availability prior to the 2016 Summer Olympic Games. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52:1-8.
abstract: Cross-sectional study of Australian Olympic athletes from 11 sports, surveyed about 3 months before the 2016 Rio Olympic Games. It estimates the prevalence of illness symptoms, sleep quality, mental health symptoms, low energy availability and stress-recovery state, and their associations with recent illness.
tldr: In 132 Australian Olympic athletes surveyed 3 months before Rio 2016, 49% had poor sleep quality, 40% of LEAF-Q responses were above the low energy availability cut-off, and low energy availability was associated with several self-reported illness symptoms. Symptoms were self-reported at one time point, so these are associations and not causes.
methods: Athletes from 11 sports were invited to complete questionnaires between 20 April and 31 May 2016, about 3 months before the Games, covering illness and injury, depression, anxiety and stress (DASS-21), resilience, recovery-stress (REST-Q), sleep (PSQI and Epworth), low energy availability (LEAF-Q), probiotic use and travel. Associations between each health domain and recent illness were estimated as odds ratios with attributable fractions, and exploratory factor analyses were run on the questionnaire scores.
findings: Of 206 athletes who consented (from an estimated 317 eligible), 132 had sufficient data (47 men aged 25.8 years and 85 women aged 24.3 years). In the previous month, 46% reported upper respiratory symptoms, 36% fatigue and 20% bodily aches, 49% had poor sleep quality on the PSQI, and 14% to 19% screened positive for depression, anxiety or stress. In Table 4, low energy availability was associated with upper respiratory symptoms (OR 3.8, 95% CI 1.3 to 12), bodily aches (OR 5.8, 1.6 to 24), gastrointestinal symptoms (OR 3.8, 1.3 to 12) and head symptoms (OR 4.4, 1.4 to 14), and the Results report poor sleep quality as associated only with gastrointestinal symptoms (OR 2.8, 1.2 to 6.9).
limitations: The design is cross-sectional and was analysed as a case-control with no healthy controls, so no causal inference is possible, all data are self-reported, and 74 of the 206 consenting athletes had no health data (the abstract's 42% response rate is 132 of 317; the Results give 65% for consent). The text and tables disagree in places: the abstract gives the upper respiratory OR interval as 1.2 to 12 (Table 4 and Results: 1.3 to 12); Table 4 shows significant PSQI with upper respiratory symptoms (OR 2.8) and probiotic use with fatigue (OR 3.6, 1.5 to 8.5) that the Results do not mention, and the upper respiratory and gastrointestinal columns of Table 4 are identical in every row, which suggests a table error; and the LEAF-Q row (36 of 90 responses) exceeds the 85 women analysed. The LEAF-Q is validated in endurance athletes and dancers, not Summer Olympic sports.
practicalImplications: Preparation-period screening for female athletes can include a low energy availability questionnaire, with a positive result prompting individual nutrition and training review rather than a diagnosis. Sleep quality is worth screening because poor sleep was common, although apart from gastrointestinal symptoms it was not associated with illness, and the study does not show that acting on any of these screens reduces illness.
athleteDev: The paper addresses illness and health in the run-up to competition rather than performance, and the authors note that illness can lead to training modification and affect performance outcomes. Performance staff can use the low energy availability association as a reason to monitor nutrition and training load in female athletes, but the study has no performance data.
rtp: The authors suggest the patterns may inform return-to-sport decisions, and they estimate illness symptoms last about 2 to 7 days. The study has no return-to-sport outcomes and no data on recovery after illness, so it cannot set return criteria.

citation: Nocera A, Sbrollini A, Romagnoli S, Morettini M, Gambi E, Burattini L. Physiological and biomechanical monitoring in American football players: a scoping review. Sensors. 2023;23:3538.
abstract: This scoping review maps biomedical engineering research in American football, screening 1629 records and including 112 studies in topics such as concussion biomechanics, footwear, injury prediction, heat monitoring and training load. Safety-driven work on helmets and footwear dominates, and performance-driven work covers training-load monitoring and catch and kick aerodynamics. The authors identify gaps in internal load monitoring and in shoulder pad innovation.
tldr: This PRISMA scoping review of 112 studies finds most work on concussion biomechanics and training-load monitoring, with little on internal load or shoulder pads. The map shows where wearable monitoring has been applied, but most included studies are laboratory or small-sample sports science.
methods: PubMed, Web of Science and Scopus were searched from 1995 to July 2022 following PRISMA and scoping review guidance, and 1629 records were screened down to 112 research studies in American football players. Studies were classified by topic and design, appraised with design-specific checklists, and tabulated by sample, aim, outcome and quality score.
findings: Concussion biomechanics was the largest topic (55 studies, including 18 head impact telemetry and 16 laboratory reconstruction studies), and in one telemetry cohort head impacts were skewed toward low severity, with a median peak linear acceleration of 20.5 g. Training-load studies (25) measured external load in all cases and internal load in eight, and four papers by Flatt et al. (2018 to 2021) reported heart rate variability (vagal tone) falling across the season in linemen. In injury prediction (8 studies), one preseason model reported sensitivity 0.79 and specificity 0.83 at a threshold of 21 touches on the upper extremity stability test, while two Y-balance test studies gave conflicting results.
limitations: The review notes that its keyword choices and exclusion criteria may have removed relevant papers, and that the injury prediction studies were small and not internally validated. Its own counts disagree in places: heat monitoring is given as 8 in the abstract but 9 studies are listed in the body, and the total of 112 matches the body count. Table 9 labels the prediction-model studies 'High Bias', and the review states that the contradictory injury prediction results were tested on small samples.
practicalImplications: Helmet and footwear claims in this review rest mainly on laboratory and simulation tests, so staff should read them as lab results rather than field outcomes. For load monitoring, the review supports tracking external load with wearables and heart rate variability as an emerging internal load measure, but it finds internal load work limited. Injury prediction tests from the review should not be used alone for screening decisions, given their small samples and contradictory results.
athleteDev: The training-load studies in this review track external load such as distance, speed zones and accelerometer player load, and one group's heart rate variability work reports declining vagal tone in linemen across the season. The review does not link these measures to better on-field performance, so performance benefit remains untested.
rtp: The review does not give return-to-play criteria. One study cited in the review found that head impact biomechanics were not associated with symptom resolution or return-to-play time, so impact data alone should not set return-to-play timing. The review's heart rate variability work includes a single concussed player case report, which cannot guide return to play.

citation: Saita Y, Hattori K, Hokari A, Ohyama T, Inoue J, Nishimura T, et al. Plasma myoglobin indicates muscle damage associated with acceleration/deceleration during football. The Journal of Sports Medicine and Physical Fitness. 2023;63.
abstract: Fifteen male professional football players had fingertip myoglobin, laboratory creatine kinase and GPS load measured before one official match and at 2, 16 and 40 h afterwards. Myoglobin peaked at 2 h and was most strongly associated with acceleration and deceleration metrics rather than sprint or high-speed running distance. Creatine kinase rose after the match but did not reach statistical significance.
tldr: In 15 male professional footballers after one match, fingertip myoglobin peaked at 2 h and tracked acceleration and deceleration counts, while CK did not change significantly. The study is small, observational and from one club, and it does not test recovery or performance outcomes.
methods: Whole-blood myoglobin was measured with the portable IA-100 immunoassay at baseline and at 2, 16 and 40 h after one official match, and CK was measured in a clinical laboratory. GPS (Catapult Vector X7) recorded total distance, high-speed running, sprint distance, accelerations, decelerations and PlayerLoad for 15 field players. Repeated-measures ANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc tests compared time points, and partial correlations adjusted for baseline linked GPS metrics to myoglobin and CK.
findings: Mean myoglobin was 38.3 ng/mL at baseline, 140.1 at 2 h, 61.9 at 16 h and 43.2 at 40 h (95% CIs given in the text), and only the 2 h value differed significantly from the other time points; three players remained more than 1.5-fold above baseline at 16 h and one at 40 h. CK rose to a mean of 1188.3 U/L at 2 h from 234.3 at baseline, but no time point differed significantly. At 2 h, myoglobin correlated with accelerations (r = 0.87), total distance (0.82), decelerations (0.81) and total PlayerLoad (0.78), while high-speed running (0.66) and sprint distance (0.58) were not significant; CK at 2 h and 16 h correlated only with accelerations (r = 0.77 and 0.76).
limitations: The study covers one club, 15 players and one match, and it measured no physical performance or recovery outcome. Playing time ranged from 10 to 90 minutes, and correlations were adjusted only for baseline biomarker values, so volume of play may drive the associations; total distance (0.82) correlated almost as strongly as accelerations, and the difference from high-speed running was not tested formally. The authors describe myoglobin as back to baseline within 16 h, but the 16 h mean (61.9 ng/mL against 38.3) was only not significantly different, and the Results report full-match distance for five players although the Methods list six full-time players.
practicalImplications: Post-match myoglobin tracked acceleration and deceleration load in these players, so it may be worth testing alongside GPS as a check on post-match muscle damage. The study did not measure recovery, readiness or performance, so it does not show that myoglobin should guide return to training.
athleteDev: In these players, acceleration and deceleration counts were correlated with post-match myoglobin, while high-speed running and sprint distance were not marked significant, which suggests that load monitoring could include these acceleration metrics. The study did not measure physical performance, so any link to lower performance is untested.
rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It measured post-match muscle damage in squad players and did not address injured athletes, return-to-play criteria or clearance.

citation: Hulin BT, Gabbett TJ, Johnston RD, Jenkins DG. PlayerLoad variables are sensitive to changes in direction and not related to collision workloads in rugby league match-play. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2018.
abstract: Examines how change-of-direction workload and collision workload relate to PlayerLoad variables, using three 60 m drill protocols in junior players and match-play collision and distance data from professional rugby league players. The authors report that PlayerLoad variables rose with change-of-direction demands and were distinct from collision counts, but related strongly to total distance.
tldr: In rugby league, PlayerLoad variables rise when players change direction more often and track total distance closely, while relating only moderately to collision counts. The authors conclude that no PlayerLoad variable is a valid stand-alone measure of collision workload.
methods: Part one: 16 junior players (age 16.8 years) completed three crossover drills of 10 repetitions of 60 m in 15 s, with 0, 1 or 3 changes of direction, and changes of direction were compared by factorial ANOVA with Cohen d effect sizes. Part two: 25 professional players (270 appearances) wore GPS-based microtechnology, and collisions (12,039 events, detected with a device algorithm) were correlated with PlayerLoad variables and distance using Pearson correlations and R2. Two players were excluded from part one for repetitions faster than 15 s.
findings: In part one, PlayerLoad per minute was greater with three changes of direction than straight running (PLVM d=1.50, large; PL2D d=1.38, large; PLSLOW d=1.69, large), and PLSLOW was the only variable with a large difference from one change of direction to three (d=1.29). In part two, collisions per minute correlated with PLVM (R2 0.30, r=0.55) and PL2D (R2 0.37, r=0.61) at distinct levels below R2 0.50, while total distance per minute correlated with PLVM at R2 0.62 (r=0.79, very large).
limitations: Part one used 16 junior players in a controlled drill, and the authors did not test progressive increases in collision demand. In part two, collision counts came from a device algorithm (cited as detecting 97.6% of collisions in an earlier study), not video, and the R2 below 0.50 criterion for 'distinct' relationships is an interpretive threshold. The accepted manuscript has no printed volume or page numbers, so the final citation details need checking against the published issue.
practicalImplications: Staff monitoring rugby league should not use a PlayerLoad total as a measure of collision or contact load on its own, because it rises with change-of-direction demands. For change-of-direction work, the authors suggest PLML and PLV over PLAP and PL2D, and PLSLOW was most sensitive to change of direction but also tracks contact and wrestling at low speed, so it should be interpreted with collision counts.
athleteDev: In junior players, PlayerLoad variables increased with change-of-direction demands at matched distance, so they may help quantify change-of-direction work in training. The study does not show that these measures improve performance or training outcomes.
rtp: Not applicable: the study measured external workload in players and did not examine injury, rehabilitation or return-to-play outcomes, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions.

citation: Thompson SW, Rogerson D, Ruddock A, Banyard HG, Barnes A. Pooled Versus Individualized Load-Velocity Profiling in the Free-Weight Back Squat and Power Clean. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2021 (ahead of print).
abstract: Ten competitive weightlifters completed 1RM tests and three incremental load-velocity profiles in the back squat and power clean, with mean and peak velocity measured by a linear position transducer. The authors compared pooled and individualized profiles, linear and second-order polynomial fits, and between-subject variability and within-subject reliability at each relative load.
tldr: Load-velocity relationships varied widely between lifters, especially in the back squat. Individualized profiles were more strongly correlated than pooled profiles, and the power clean was reliable across loads while the back squat was not at heavier loads.
methods: Within-subject repeated-measures design with four sessions 48 to 72 hours apart: 1RM testing in each lift, then three profiles at 30-100% of 1RM. GymAware recorded mean and peak velocity per repetition; linear and second-order polynomial models were fitted to pooled and individual data, and reliability was assessed with CV, ICC, typical error and limits of agreement.
findings: Pooled and individualized profiles both showed strong inverse load-velocity relationships, and individualized profiles gave stronger correlations. Between-subject CVs were 8.2-27.8% in the back squat and 4.6-8.5% in the power clean. The power clean met the a priori reliability criteria (ICC above .70, CV below 10%) at all loads, while the back squat did not at heavier loads (MV at 95% or more, PV at 90% or more of 1RM); linear and polynomial models did not differ significantly (back squat P = .45, power clean P = .50).
limitations: Only 10 athletes (2 women) were tested in one laboratory with one transducer. The abstract gives back squat CVs of 13.1-20.5% for loads of 90% of 1RM or more, while the Results give the thresholds as 95% or more for MV (13.1-20.6%) and 90% or more for PV (11.8-15.6%). The claim that individualized profiles are preferable rests on correlation size and reliability rather than a direct test of pooled against individual profiles.
practicalImplications: If profiling is used, the paper supports building an individual profile for each athlete and reading velocity changes against the reported smallest worthwhile change values (for example, 0.02 m/s MV in the back squat). For the back squat, the authors suggest using MV across 30-90% of 1RM rather than heavy-load velocities, and they advise keeping 1RM testing alongside profiling because of time and logistics.
athleteDev: Usable for monitoring strength-speed status in weightlifting-style training, using individual profiles and the reported smallest worthwhile change values. Power clean velocities were reliable across loads, while heavy back squat velocities were not and should not be used to judge progress.
rtp: Not applicable to return to sport. The study tested healthy weightlifters and measured no injury, rehabilitation or return-to-training outcomes.

citation: Pérez-Castilla A, Piepoli A, Garrido-Blanca G, Delgado-García G, Balsalobre-Fernández C, García-Ramos A. Precision of 7 Commercially Available Devices for Predicting the Bench Press 1-Repetition Maximum From the Individual Load-Velocity Relationship. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2019.
abstract: Eleven men performed an incremental Smith machine bench press test at 45, 55, 65, 75 and 85% 1RM, followed by 1RM attempts. Seven commercial devices measured mean velocity, and 1RM was predicted from the individual load-velocity relationship using 5 loads or only 2 loads. Five devices (T-Force, Chronojump, Speed4Lift, Velowin and PowerLift) gave acceptable and comparable estimates, while the PUSH band and especially the Beast sensor were less accurate.
tldr: For Smith machine bench press, five of the seven devices estimated 1RM accurately from velocity, and two loads (45% and 85% 1RM) were as accurate as five. The two inertial sensors tested were the least accurate.
methods: Participants completed two sessions 48-72 h apart. Session 1 measured anthropometrics and 1RM. In session 2, they performed 3 repetitions at each of the 5 loads followed by 1RM attempts, with all seven devices recording at the same time. Accuracy was assessed with paired t-tests, Hedges' g, Pearson's r, standard error of the estimate and a device by method ANOVA on absolute errors.
findings: Five devices (T-Force, Chronojump, Speed4Lift, Velowin, PowerLift) showed ES <= 0.40, r >= 0.94 and SEE <= 4.46 kg with both methods, although all except Chronojump significantly overestimated the actual 1RM (Table 1, p 0.001 to 0.045; small ES). PUSH band (ES 0.70-0.83, r 0.93-0.94, SEE 4.45-4.80 kg) significantly underestimated 1RM, and Beast sensor had the lowest accuracy (ES 0.36-0.84, r 0.50-0.68, SEE 9.44-11.2 kg). The ANOVA on absolute errors found a main effect of device (p < 0.001) but no effect of method (p = 0.609).
limitations: The authors state no limitations section. Inference: the sample was 11 men experienced with the bench press, tested on a concentric-only Smith machine bench press with 1RM estimated at a fixed velocity of 0.17 m/s, so results may not transfer to free-weight or touch-and-go lifting, other exercises, women or trained athletes. Even the better devices showed small but significant systematic overestimation of 1RM.
practicalImplications: On a concentric-only Smith machine bench press, T-Force, Chronojump, Speed4Lift, Velowin or PowerLift can estimate 1RM from the velocity at about 45% and 85% 1RM, with the two-point method as accurate as five loads in this sample. Expect small overestimates of a few kilograms with most of these devices, and the authors conclude the PUSH band and Beast sensor are not accurate enough for this use.
athleteDev: Staff wanting a quick 1RM estimate for bench press can use the two-point method (45% and 85% 1RM) with the five devices the paper supports. The study measured prediction accuracy only and did not test training outcomes.
rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It tested men on a Smith machine bench press and reports no injured participants or return-to-play outcomes.

citation: Jaspers A, Op De Beéck T, Brink MS, Frencken WGP, Staes F, Davis JJ, et al. Predicting Future Perceived Wellness in Professional Soccer: The Role of Preceding Load and Wellness. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2019.
abstract: The authors used gradient boosted regression trees to predict next-day perceived wellness (fatigue, sleep quality, muscle soreness, stress and mood) in professional male soccer players over one season. Predictors were GPS external load, session RPE internal load and pre-session wellness, summed over 1 to 7 day windows. Models with pre-session wellness plus load beat a per-player average baseline for fatigue, soreness, stress and mood, while load alone and cumulative load gave no meaningful gain.
tldr: Pre-session wellness combined with recent training or match load gave the best next-day wellness predictions in professional soccer players, but the gains over a player's own average were small. Load alone and cumulative load added little.
methods: Data came from 26 professional male players in the 2015-2016 season, using 10 Hz GPS and accelerometry, session RPE and a five-item morning wellness questionnaire. Each player had an individual gradient boosted regression tree model trained on the first 80% of their data and tested on the last 20%, compared with a baseline of the player's own mean. Models were built for 14 players with at least 80 usable instances, and missing pre-session wellness was filled with the value from two days earlier.
findings: Pre-session wellness combined with external and/or internal load gave small effect sizes over baseline for fatigue, muscle soreness and stress levels across most time frames. For mood, only acute external load with pre-session wellness and the three-way combination gave a small effect. External load, internal load and their combination alone gave trivial effect sizes, cumulative load did not improve prediction, and sleep quality was trivial for almost all models.
limitations: The abstract says only the combination of external load, internal load and pre-session wellness gave non-trivial effects, but the Discussion reports small effects for pre-session wellness combined with either load measure alone. The Discussion states the models beat 'average player thresholds', but the baseline was each player's own average, so no threshold comparison was tested. The effect-size values appear only in figures not present in the text, match and rest days are excluded, and the direction of effects is not reported.
practicalImplications: The authors suggest that daily pre-session wellness alongside GPS and session RPE may help predict next-day fatigue, soreness and stress in a squad. They also suggest comparing predicted and reported wellness to flag players for closer review, but the study did not test whether this changes training decisions. Sleep quality was poorly predicted and mood only in some combinations, so the models add little for those items, although the authors still regard them as useful for assessing a player's status.
athleteDev: Staff could use daily wellness scores with load data to flag players whose reported wellness falls outside their predicted range for closer review. The paper does not show the direction of load effects or that acting on predictions improves performance, so it cannot set individual load targets.
rtp: The study has no injury or return-to-play outcomes, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. The authors also state that the wellness questionnaire's reliability and validity have not been extensively studied.

citation: Mortensen BB, Mitchell UH, Johnson AW, Fellingham GW, Feland JB, Myrer JW. Preseason Screen Cannot Predict Injury over Three Years of College Football. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2020;52(11):2286-2292.
abstract: Functional Movement Screen (FMS) total score, item scores and asymmetries were tested as predictors of noncontact injury in 208 NCAA Division I football players over three seasons (343 observations), with analyses by position group and adjustment for exposure. Total score and asymmetries did not predict injury. Push-up stability in the combo group was the only item associated in the expected direction, and rotary stability was associated in the opposite direction for the team and skill group.
tldr: In three seasons of NCAA Division I football, the preseason Functional Movement Screen total score and asymmetry count did not predict noncontact injury. Only one item result (push-up stability in linebackers and tight ends) ran in the expected direction, and rotary stability ran the opposite way, so the screen should not be used alone to judge injury risk.
methods: Three-year prospective descriptive epidemiology study of one NCAA Division I football team. FMS was scored before preseason practice, and noncontact injuries were recorded daily and coded by athletic trainers. Generalized linear mixed models (binomial and Poisson) related FMS total scores, individual item scores and asymmetry counts to injuries by team and position group, with and without adjustment for exposure, using alpha of 0.0167.
findings: Total FMS score was not associated with injury for the team (P = 0.130) or any position group, and asymmetry count was not associated with injury for the team (P = 0.472). Push-up stability was inversely associated with injury in the combo group (P = 0.001), with an estimated injury risk of 13.44% at a score of 2 and 3.67% at a score of 3 (not adjusted for exposure). Rotary stability was positively associated with injury for the team (P < 0.001) and skill group (P = 0.011), the opposite of the expected direction.
limitations: Coaching and strength staff changed across the study, and play volume dropped in year 3 (1,770 plays vs 2,059 and 1,792), which the authors note may have affected FMS scores. Many item-by-group tests were run with alpha set at 0.0167, and the authors note that large samples can produce statistically significant results with little practical meaning. The abstract notes only the push-up stability result as being in the expected direction and does not report the rotary stability results shown in Table 4.
practicalImplications: In this NCAA Division I football sample, preseason FMS total scores and asymmetry counts did not identify athletes at higher noncontact injury risk, so they should not be used alone to screen for injury. Isolated item results, including the rotary stability association in the opposite direction, should be interpreted cautiously. The authors suggest that other assessments be considered or developed.
athleteDev: The study measured injury, not performance, and does not inform performance development.
rtp: The study addresses preseason screening for future noncontact injury, not recovery or return to play, so it cannot guide return-to-play clearance or rehabilitation decisions.

citation: Pozzi F, Plummer HA, Shanley E, Thigpen CA, Bauer C, Wilson ML, et al. Preseason shoulder range of motion screening and in-season risk of shoulder and elbow injuries in overhead athletes: systematic review and meta-analysis. Br J Sports Med. 2020.
abstract: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 15 prospective cohorts of overhead athletes testing whether preseason shoulder range of motion (ROM) predicts in-season shoulder and elbow injury. Throwing-arm external rotation insufficiency was associated with injury in professional baseball pitchers, while absolute ROM and internal rotation deficit were not pooled as predictors and evidence in other overhead sports was limited.
tldr: In overhead athletes, preseason shoulder range of motion generally did not predict in-season shoulder or elbow injury. The exception was a throwing-arm external rotation shortfall (less than 5 degrees more than the non-throwing arm) in professional baseball pitchers, which rests on three studies.
methods: Systematic review (six databases to September 2018) and random-effects Mantel-Haenszel meta-analysis of prospective cohorts that tracked shoulder and elbow injuries in overhead athletes. Study quality was scored with a modified Downs and Black checklist (mean 14.9 of 21 points, range 11 to 18). Pooled odds or risk ratios were calculated for absolute ROM and ROM deficit variables.
findings: Throwing-arm external rotation insufficiency was associated with injury in pooled data from three professional baseball studies (OR 1.90, 95% CI 1.24 to 2.92, P < 0.01; I2 = 0%). Absolute shoulder ROM and internal rotation deficit of 20 degrees or more were not associated with injury, and shoulder flexion deficit of 5 degrees or more was not associated with injury in the pooled analysis. In single studies outside the meta-analysis, absolute external rotation below 93 or above 100 degrees was associated with shoulder injury in 74 swimmers (unadjusted OR 24.9 and 23.0, with very wide confidence intervals), and softball, volleyball and tennis cohorts showed no association.
limitations: Only three studies contributed to each ROM meta-analysis, and heterogeneity was high across age, position, competition level and injury definitions. Four studies did not describe how they selected their sample, only five adjusted for confounders, and the funnel plot suggested missing negative studies for external rotation deficit. The review reports 3,314 athletes enrolled but uses 3,750 (after counting athletes followed over several seasons and loss to follow-up) as the denominator for the 17% injury rate, with different sport counts in each, and most included studies did not adjust for previous injury or exposure.
practicalImplications: For professional baseball pitchers, preseason screening should record whether throwing-arm external rotation is at least 5 degrees greater than the non-throwing arm, since the shortfall was associated with in-season injury (OR 1.90). Absolute shoulder range of motion or internal rotation differences of 20 degrees should not be used alone to flag injury risk. The evidence is too limited to rely on ROM screening in handball, softball, volleyball or tennis, and youth and high school pitchers did not show a consistent association.
athleteDev: The review addresses shoulder and elbow injury risk and does not measure performance, so it does not inform performance development.
rtp: The review did not assess return to play or rehabilitation, so its preseason ROM findings cannot set return-to-throw criteria after injury.

citation: Nair VS, Heybroek M, Boyle E, Rogers M, Campbell T, Eichner D, et al. Prevalence of carboxy-Δ8-tetrahydrocannabiniol in antidoping samples. Drug Test Anal. 2024.
abstract: Δ8-THC products have become widely available with little oversight, and a Δ9-THC-COOH assay may overestimate Δ9-THC-COOH if the Δ8 isomer is present and not resolved. This study used LC-MS/MS to separate the Δ8 and Δ9 THC-COOH isomers in 1,000 routine anti-doping samples with a presumptive THC-COOH finding, and reports that about 12% contained Δ8-THC-COOH.
tldr: In 1,000 routine anti-doping urine samples that screened positive for THC-COOH, about 12% (119) also contained Δ8-THC-COOH. Because the samples were limited to screen-positive results, this is not a prevalence of Δ8-THC use across tested athletes.
methods: Routine anti-doping urine samples with a presumptive THC-COOH screen above 5 ng/mL, from Olympic sports (in and out of competition) and professional sports, were reanalysed by a modified LC-MS/MS confirmation method that resolves the Δ8 and Δ9 isomers. The method was validated over 0.5 to 500 ng/mL, with limits of identification of 0.5 ng/mL for both isomers and limits of quantitation of 2 ng/mL (Δ8) and 0.5 ng/mL (Δ9).
findings: Of 1,000 samples with screening concentrations between 5 and 450 ng/mL, 119 contained Δ8-THC-COOH. In these samples, Δ8 made up 5% to 100% of the combined Δ8 and Δ9 isomer signal. The authors note that the screening method does not separate the isomers and therefore measures total THC-COOH.
limitations: Single laboratory and single testing programme, with samples drawn only from those screening positive for THC-COOH. The text gives no athlete numbers, sex, sport or in- versus out-of-competition breakdown, and does not say how many Δ8-positive samples would have exceeded the Δ9-THC-COOH threshold. The abstract describes the 5% to 100% range as a share of total carboxy-THC, while Figure 3 expresses it as a ratio to the sum of the two isomers. The conclusion that Δ8-THC use has increased among athletes is not tested by this single time-point dataset, and applying the Δ9 threshold to the sum of both isomers is the authors' proposal, not a tested rule.
practicalImplications: Testing programmes that apply Δ9-THC-COOH thresholds may need an isomer-resolving method, because a screen can overstate Δ9-THC-COOH when Δ8 is present. The authors state that rules for reporting Δ8-THC-COOH are unclear, so programmes need their own written policy for it.
athleteDev: The paper reports no performance outcomes and has no direct use for training or performance decisions. Its relevance to performance staff is awareness that Δ8-THC products are in use and that Δ9-only testing cannot separate the isomers.
rtp: The paper does not address return to sport, injury or clinical care. It cannot inform return-to-play decisions, and the authors state that the potential for abuse or side effects is outside the scope of the study.

citation: Herberts T, Slater GJ, Farley A, Hogarth L, Areta JL, Paulsen G, et al. Protocol standardization may improve precision error of InBody 720 body composition analysis. International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism. 2023 (ahead of print).
abstract: Eighteen recreational athletes (10 men, 8 women) completed two within-day and one between-day InBody 720 bioelectrical impedance scans, with diet and physical activity replicated over the 24 hours before the first scan. Within- and between-day precision error did not differ significantly for fat-free mass, fat mass or total body water. The authors conclude that 24-hour standardization may minimize precision error, but the study has no unstandardized comparison day.
tldr: After 24-hour diet and activity replication, the gap between within-day and between-day precision error was within the 1% bound for fat-free mass and total body water, but not for fat mass. Without a comparison day, the study cannot show that this standardization beats current best practice.
methods: Test-retest study in 18 healthy recreationally active adults (10 men, 8 women, aged 18-40 years). Each participant had two consecutive within-day InBody 720 scans and a third scan on a randomly assigned day before or after, with food and activity from the 24 hours before the first scan replicated the next day and recorded in diaries. Precision was expressed as RMS-SD, %CV and least significant change (2.77 x RMS-SD), with paired t tests (alpha .025) and two one-sided equivalence tests using a 1% bound.
findings: Within-day RMS-SD was 411 g for FFM and 400 g for FM, and between-day LSC was 1,243 g for FFM, 1,053 g for FM and 881 ml for TBW. Within- and between-day %CV did not differ significantly (FFM p = .36, FM p = .82, TBW p = .20). The equivalence tests placed the difference in %CV inside the 1% bound for FFM (delta 0.14, 95% CI -0.013 to 0.29) and TBW (delta 0.17, 95% CI -0.14 to 0.48), but not for FM (delta 0.20, 95% CI -1.71 to 2.11). The diet diaries showed no significant difference in energy or macronutrient intake between the two days.
limitations: There was no randomized or unstandardized comparison day, so the authors state that effectiveness versus best practice cannot be concluded. Eighteen participants is below the ISCD-recommended 30 for LSC, diet was self-replicated, incidental activity was not recorded, and menstrual status and posture were not controlled. The results text describes the FFM and TBW confidence intervals as 'exceeding' the 1% bound although they lie inside it (upper limits 0.29 and 0.48), and the discussion quotes different upper limits (0.365%, 0.437%, and 2.143% for FM), so exact values should be checked against Figure 3.
practicalImplications: A 24-hour diet and training diary is a low-cost option practitioners can trial before InBody scans, although this study did not compare it against usual preparation. Fat-mass precision was poorer than FFM or TBW (%CV about 3.2 to 3.4%) and its between-day difference could not be shown to be within the 1% bound, so fat-mass change should be read against the reported between-day LSC of about 1,053 g.
athleteDev: The paper addresses measurement precision in recreational athletes, not training or performance. It can inform how body-composition change is tracked, but it does not show that changes in body composition improve performance.
rtp: The sample was healthy recreational athletes, and the study does not include injured athletes or return-to-play decisions. Its data should not be used to judge readiness to return to sport or to set body-composition targets for returning athletes.

citation: Driller MW, Dunican IC, Omond SET, Boukhris O, Stevenson S, Lambing K, et al. Pyjamas, Polysomnography and Professional Athletes: The Role of Sleep Tracking Technology in Sport. Sports. 2023;11:14.
abstract: This narrative review summarizes the importance of sleep for athletes, the sleep-monitoring tools used in sport, and the reliability and validity of sleep trackers. It also covers the limitations of trackers, their use to guide behaviour change, and practical recommendations for practitioners.
tldr: Consumer sleep trackers are reasonably good at estimating total sleep duration but are weak at detecting wake and sleep stages. The review advises choosing a tool to fit the monitoring goal and reading trends over at least 7 to 28 nights.
methods: Narrative review of polysomnography and home sleep tests, wrist-, finger- and head-worn wearables, nearables, smart pyjamas, questionnaires and diaries, and the sleep metrics trackers report, with a table comparing tools. No systematic search or inclusion criteria are described.
findings: Wearables were sensitive for sleep periods (91-96%) but had low specificity for wake (18% to 80%, averaging about 50%) against polysomnography, and a 2020 expert consensus was cited as finding insufficient evidence for accurate sleep staging by commercial wearables. Device-level figures varied: the Oura ring showed 96% sensitivity for sleep, with agreement of 65%, 51% and 61% for light, deep and REM sleep; the Somfit head-worn device correctly classified 92% of sleep epochs and 57% of wake epochs (kappa 0.48). The Phyjama smart pyjamas have been validated for sleeping position but not yet for sleep metrics.
limitations: No search strategy or inclusion criteria are described, and the review does not grade the strength of the evidence it cites. The Dreem accuracy figure comes from a manufacturer validation, and the review notes that many algorithms are proprietary, that not all wearables show acceptable agreement with polysomnography, and that validation is lacking for some rings and for smart pyjama sleep metrics. Two authors are employees of Cerebra, a sleep technology start-up, and Table 1 lists the Cerebra Sleep System as an example home polysomnography tool.
practicalImplications: The review recommends wearing a tracker for at least 7 nights, and preferably 2 to 3 weeks, and reading rolling averages over 14, 21 or 28 nights. It suggests using wearables mainly for duration and timing trends and not for stage data, and using polysomnography for sleep-disorder diagnosis. It also cautions against proprietary readiness scores and notes that feedback can be turned off around key competitions.
athleteDev: Sleep trackers can show trends in sleep duration and timing across a squad or season, and the review presents them mainly as an awareness tool for behaviour change. Stage data and proprietary readiness scores are not validated enough to set training or competition decisions. The review cites a sham-feedback study in people with insomnia (not athletes) showing that falsely reported poor sleep impaired daytime cognition. In professional rugby league players, a sleep-hygiene seminar gave about 20 minutes more sleep, but this had returned to baseline a month later.
rtp: The review does not address return to sport, injury or clinical clearance, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions. It cautions against using tracker readiness or recovery scores for elite athletes because these measures are often unvalidated.

citation: Hadley B, Kim JW, Magnusen M, Kim KT. Redefining the draft pick valuation in the National Football League. Frontiers in Sports and Active Living. 2025;7:1628223.
abstract: Regression models of 1993 to 2012 draft picks suggest late-round picks are undervalued by Jimmy Johnson's Pick Value Chart, and first-round trade-ups are associated with lower career wAV, games played and seasons started. The authors report a recalibrated pick value chart and a Day 3 emphasis.
tldr: Late-round NFL picks produced more career value than the classic pick value chart predicts, and first-round trade-ups were linked to weaker player outcomes. Front offices may want to test these findings against their own draft records before changing how they trade picks.
methods: Archival data from pro-football-reference.com for 4,996 draft picks from 1993 to 2012. Model 1 averaged each of 262 pick slots and fitted fifth-order polynomial regressions to wAV, GP and ST. Model 2 used player-level data with seven round-specific trade-up dummies. The results are from ordinary regression with the outcome measures as reported on the source site.
findings: Model 1 R2 was 0.90 for wAV, 0.82 for GP and 0.90 for ST. The last first-round pick was valued at about 56% of the first pick on GP, versus 20% on the chart. In Model 2, first-round trade-ups had significantly lower wAV (coefficient -5.44, P = .013), GP (-13.33, P = .018) and ST (-0.82, P = .008). Round 4 trade-ups had a significant positive effect on ST (0.92, P = .011), and other rounds were not significant. Model 2 R2 was 0.31 for wAV, 0.22 for GP and 0.31 for ST.
limitations: Outcomes are career totals from a single league, and the models do not adjust for position, team, injuries, or contract status. Model 2 explains little variance, and the round-specific effects are inconsistent (only Round 1 and Round 4 reach significance, with Round 4 effects visible only on ST). The paper does not test whether a recalibrated chart improves real draft results. The authors note that financial constraints can also shape draft behaviour.
practicalImplications: Draft boards may want to give more weight to later-round picks than the classic chart does, and first-round trade-ups should be checked against the lower average outcomes reported here. These are average patterns across the league, so each draft decision still needs player-level evaluation.
athleteDev: The paper gives no development or training data. Its relevance is to how teams value young players drafted from college and how they assess career output across positions.
rtp: Not applicable. The study does not examine injury, rehabilitation or return to play.

citation: Murray NB, Gabbett TJ, Townshend AD. Relationship Between Preseason Training Load and In-Season Availability in Elite Australian Football Players. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2017;12(6):749-755.
abstract: In 46 elite male AFL players from one club, the share of preseason sessions completed was linked to higher GPS training loads, more in-season training and match availability, and lower injury rates that were not statistically significant. Players who completed less than half of preseason training had the highest injury rate (26.8 per 1000 h versus 14.2 in the high-completion group).
tldr: Elite AFL players who completed more of their preseason training carried higher training loads into the season and played a larger share of matches. The availability and injury differences were not statistically significant, and low-completion players had spent much more of preseason in rehabilitation, so completion is a useful monitoring signal rather than a proven cause.
methods: Single-cohort observational study of 46 male AFL players. Players were grouped by the percentage of main preseason sessions completed (high >85%, medium 50 to 84.9%, low <50%). A 10-Hz GPS unit with accelerometer recorded total, low, moderate, high and very-high-speed distance and player load in training and matches. Injuries that caused a missed match were logged by club medical staff and expressed per 1000 h. Group and phase effects were analysed with two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, magnitude-based inferences and chi-square tests.
findings: Preseason training loads were about 1.3 times higher than in-season (P=.02). In the first half of the season, high and medium groups covered significantly more total distance (P=.03 and P=.02) and had higher player load (P=.03 and P=.02) than the low group. Match availability was 76.7% (high), 76.1% (medium) and 52.7% (low); these differences were not statistically significant (P>.05) but were rated very likely meaningful by magnitude-based inference. Injury rates were 14.2, 17.7 and 26.8 per 1000 h, a difference that was not significant (chi-square=3.48, P=.17), across 50 in-season injuries.
limitations: Data come from one club and one season with 50 injuries, which limits power and generalizability. Groups were not randomized, and low-completion players spent far more of the preseason in rehabilitation, so causation cannot be inferred. Internal load was not measured.
practicalImplications: Strength and conditioning staff can use preseason completion as a monitoring signal, since players who completed less preseason training had lower in-season loads and fewer match appearances. Strategies that keep players in the main program during preseason, rather than in rehabilitation or modified sessions, are the practical target.
athleteDev: Performance Application: players who completed more of the planned preseason program had higher GPS distance and player load in the first half of the season and a higher share of matches played, so preseason completion is worth tracking as an early marker of in-season load capacity. The design cannot separate the effect of training completed from the injury or rehabilitation status that limited it.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: the study does not measure return-to-play criteria or rehabilitation outcomes. Because the low-completion group had far more rehabilitation time, it cannot be used to set return-to-play timelines.

citation: Bellinger P, Bourne MN, Duhig S, Lievens E, Kennedy B, Martin A, et al. Relationships between Lower Limb Muscle Characteristics and Force-Velocity Profiles Derived during Sprinting and Jumping. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2021;53(7):1400-1411.
abstract: In 19 subelite male rugby league players, estimated muscle fibre type and specific muscle volumes explained much of the variation in maximal power, force and velocity derived from jumping and sprinting force-velocity profiles.
tldr: Estimated fibre type and the size of key thigh muscles were associated with maximal power, force and velocity in jumping and sprinting in these players. This is a cross-sectional association, not a training result.
methods: Nineteen subelite male rugby league players performed loaded and unloaded squat jumps and two 30 m sprints to derive vertical and horizontal force-velocity-power profiles. Fascicle length, pennation angle and thickness were measured with B-mode ultrasound, muscle volumes with MRI, and gastrocnemius medialis fibre typology estimated from carnosine with proton MR spectroscopy. Univariable regression screened predictors, then stepwise regression identified the best combinations.
findings: Vertical maximal power was best explained by gastrocnemius fibre typology and vastus lateralis volume (adjusted r2 = 0.440, p = 0.006), and horizontal maximal power by gastrocnemius fibre typology plus adductor and vastus intermedius volume (adjusted r2 = 0.634, p = 0.001). Vertical and horizontal maximal velocity were best explained by gastrocnemius fibre typology (adjusted r2 = 0.580) and fibre typology plus biceps femoris short head volume (0.590), both p < 0.001. Maximal force was explained by rectus femoris and vastus lateralis volume (vertical, r2 = 0.430) and adductor and vastus medialis volume (horizontal, 0.432); architecture explained little variation.
limitations: Small sample of 19 subelite male players, cross-sectional, with many correlations raising type I error risk. Fibre typology was estimated from carnosine in one muscle, and architecture was measured at single sites with extrapolated fascicle length. The abstract lists adductor and vastus medialis volume in the horizontal power model with p = 0.032, whereas the results and Table 4 give adductor and vastus intermedius volume with p = 0.001; this record uses the table.
practicalImplications: Muscle volume and estimated fibre type are associated with jump and sprint force-velocity variables and could be considered when interpreting power profiles in rugby players. Their value for guiding training change has not been tested here.
athleteDev: Specific muscle volumes and estimated fibre type explained much of the variation in jump and sprint power in these players, which supports considering muscle characteristics when interpreting force-velocity profiles, though not as a direct training prescription.
rtp: This study does not inform return-to-sport decisions. It was done in uninjured subelite players and does not test whether muscle characteristics or force-velocity profiles indicate readiness to return after injury.

citation: Thurlow, F., McLaren, S. J., Townshend, A., Morrison, M., Cowley, N., Weakley, J. Repeated sprint training: The effects of session volume on acute physiological, neuromuscular, perceptual and performance outcomes in athletes. European Journal of Sport Science. 2024;1-13.
abstract: The authors examined how repeated sprint training session volume (set by sprint distance and number of repetitions) affects acute physiological, perceptual, sprint and neuromuscular responses in 14 trained athletes. The 800 m protocol produced the greatest physiological and perceptual demands, while the 200 m protocol produced the lowest. Neuromuscular recovery was unclear, with large inter-individual variation.
tldr: Session volume drives the acute load of repeated sprint training. At 400 m, the sprint distance chosen changes the external load more than the internal load. Coaches can use 200 m sessions to introduce maximal sprinting and 800 m sessions for the largest aerobic stimulus.
methods: Fourteen healthy trained athletes (10 male, 4 female) completed four repeated sprint protocols, each two sets of 10 x 40 m, 5 x 40 m, 10 x 20 m or 5 x 20 m, one per week in a Latin-square crossover design, with 30 s inter-repetition rest and 3 min inter-set rest. Heart rate and oxygen consumption were measured, with differential RPE, session RPE, sprint decrement and GPS acceleration and high-speed sprint distance. Countermovement jump, leg stiffness and isometric hamstring strength were measured before, immediately after, and at 24 and 48 h. Protocols were compared with ANOVA and effect sizes.
findings: The 10 x 40 m protocol (800 m) averaged about 89% of maximal heart rate and 72% of VO2max, had the greatest sprint decrement and time above 90% VO2max (large effects), and had a very large higher session RPE training load than all other protocols; its heart rate exceeded only the 5 x 20 m protocol, and VO2 differences were not definitive. The 5 x 20 m protocol (200 m) had the lowest training load. At 400 m, heart rate, VO2, session RPE load, leg RPE and sprint decrement were similar between 5 x 40 m and 10 x 20 m, and acceleration load was greater with 10 x 20 m (large effect). The 40 m protocols gave over 100 m above 90% of maximal sprint speed per session vs 67 m for 10 x 20 m, though the 5 x 40 m vs 10 x 20 m difference was not reported as definitive. Neuromuscular changes at 0, 24 and 48 h were unclear, with decrement, no change or potentiation across athletes.
limitations: The sample was small (n = 14) and the authors describe the analysis as exploratory. Changing sprint distance also changed work-to-rest ratios, which limits comparisons. The neuromuscular measures were jump, leg stiffness and isometric hamstring tests, and eccentric hamstring function was not measured. Volumes were limited to 200 to 800 m, and the study did not measure training adaptations over time.
practicalImplications: Session volume and sprint distance change acute load in different ways. Practitioners can use 200 m (5 x 20 m) to introduce maximal sprinting and 800 m (10 x 40 m) for the largest acute demand. At 400 m, the authors suggest 5 x 40 m for more high-speed running and 10 x 20 m for more acceleration load. Adding repetitions at a fixed sprint distance did not greatly raise aerobic demand, so longer sprints may be a better way to increase the stimulus.
athleteDev: Use sprint distance and volume to set the acute load of repeated sprint training. Use 200 m at the start of a block, and 400 m with 40 m sprints when maximal running exposure is the goal. Use 800 m when the aim is the highest session demand.
rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It tested healthy athletes who had been injury-free for at least 3 months, and it did not include injured or rehabilitating athletes or any return-to-play criteria.

citation: Dennis, M. C., Goods, P. S. R., Binnie, M. J., Girard, O., Wallman, K. E., Dawson, B., et al. Repeated-sprint training in heat and hypoxia: Acute responses to manipulating exercise-to-rest ratio. European Journal of Sport Science. 2022.
abstract: The authors compared two exercise-to-rest ratios (1:2 and 1:4) during repeated-sprint cycling in hot, hypoxic conditions in 12 male team-sport athletes. The 1:4 ratio gave higher mechanical power and core temperature, while the 1:2 ratio gave greater muscle oxygen extraction, which the authors suggest may be used to target different outcomes.
tldr: In hot, hypoxic conditions, 10 sprints of 5 s with longer rest (1:4) produced slightly more power and a higher core temperature than 5 sprints of 10 s (1:2). The 1:2 format caused more muscle deoxygenation. These are single-session responses, not training effects.
methods: Twelve trained male team-sport athletes completed a familiarisation session and two randomised experimental sessions in an environmental chamber at 40 C, 50% relative humidity and a simulated altitude of about 3000 m (FiO2 0.144). Sessions were 3 sets of 5 x 10 s sprints (1:2, 5 min between sets) or 3 sets of 10 x 5 s sprints (1:4, 2.5 min between sets), matched for sprint and session duration. Mean and peak power, total work, muscle oxygenation (near-infrared spectroscopy), core and skin temperature, heart rate, blood lactate and RPE were recorded. Data were analysed with linear mixed models.
findings: The 1:4 protocol had higher mean power output and total work (both 5.2% higher) and peak power (4.4% higher) than the 1:2 protocol (condition effects p = 0.002 to 0.007). Muscle deoxygenation during sprints was greater with 1:2 (28.2 vs 22.4%, p < 0.001), and minimum muscle oxygenation was lower with 1:2 (p = 0.034). Peak core temperature was higher with 1:4 (38.44 vs 38.20 C, p = 0.028), and session core temperature was also higher with 1:4 (38.10 vs 37.89 C, p < 0.001); neither reached the roughly 38.5 C cited for heat acclimation. RPE was higher with 1:2 throughout the protocol (p = 0.019), and blood lactate rose more with 1:2 (14.5 vs 11.8 mmol/L at end of exercise, interaction p = 0.027). Muscle reoxygenation during recovery, heart rate and sweat loss did not differ between protocols.
limitations: Twelve men were tested once per protocol in one environment with no airflow, and a thermoneutral control was not tested, so the findings may not apply to other conditions, women or other populations. The participants were tier 4 trained athletes under the McKay et al. framework, and the authors note that more highly trained athletes may respond differently. The study measured acute responses only and did not assess training adaptation. Muscle oxygenation came from a single near-infrared site. The trials were conducted in a season when some heat acclimatisation may have been present.
practicalImplications: In hot, hypoxic sprint sessions, a 1:4 exercise-to-rest ratio with 5 s sprints produced more power and a higher core temperature than a 1:2 ratio with 10 s sprints. A 1:2 ratio produced more muscle deoxygenation. Coaches can use the ratio to shape the stimulus, but the study does not show which ratio gives better long-term results.
athleteDev: Use the exercise-to-rest ratio to change the acute stimulus in heat and hypoxia sessions. A 1:4 ratio with short sprints gives more power and a higher core temperature with lower RPE, while 1:2 gives more muscle deoxygenation, higher RPE and more blood lactate.
rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It tested healthy trained athletes in a single laboratory session, with no injured or rehabilitating athletes and no return-to-play outcomes.

citation: Angleri V, Damas F, Phillips SM, et al. Resistance training variable manipulations are less relevant than intrinsic biology in affecting muscle fiber hypertrophy. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2022.
abstract: Twenty resistance-trained men had one leg assigned to standard progressive training and the other to a variable program for 8 weeks. Both legs gained similar muscle fiber size, and individual differences were larger than differences between programs.
tldr: In trained men training to or near failure, changing load, volume, muscle action and rest between sessions did not add fiber growth beyond standard progressive training. Individual differences in fiber growth mattered more than the choice of program.
methods: Twenty resistance-trained young men had each leg randomly assigned to a standard progressive program (RT-CON) or a variable program (RT-VAR) for 8 weeks, two sessions per week. Vastus lateralis biopsies were taken before and after training, and a 17th session was biopsied acutely at 0 and 24 h to assess gene expression.
findings: Type I and II fiber cross-sectional area rose about 12 to 13% in both legs, with no difference between programs. Satellite cell and myonuclei numbers did not change. Most gene expression changes were similar between programs, except a larger acute MyoG increase after RT-VAR, and the between-leg correlation for fiber area change was r = 0.89.
limitations: Baseline biopsy came from one leg only, and histology used 19 of 20 participants. The sample was young resistance-trained men over one 8-week block, and accumulated volume load was 12.6% higher in the variable leg. Gene expression was sampled at limited time points, which the authors note may explain its poor alignment with individual fiber growth.
practicalImplications: For trained lifters training to or near failure, variation in load, volume, muscle action and rest did not add fiber growth over standard progressive loading. Variation may still suit people who find a varied program more motivating, but it should not be expected to change hypertrophy in this population.
athleteDev: Standard progressive loading produced the same fiber growth as the variable scheme in trained men, so variation alone is not a reason to change a hypertrophy program. Individual gains varied widely under both programs, so one program may produce very different results across athletes.
rtp: Not applicable. The study tested hypertrophy in healthy trained men and cannot inform return to sport, injury rehabilitation or return-to-play decisions.

citation: Heuberger JAAC, Cohen AF. Review of WADA Prohibited Substances: Limited Evidence for Performance-Enhancing Effects. Sports Med. 2018.
abstract: Review of the evidence for performance enhancement across the 23 substance classes on the 2018 WADA Prohibited List, using PubMed searches. Only 5 of 23 classes showed evidence of enhancing actual sports performance, with growth hormone showing similar evidence only in untrained subjects, and the evidence base is 11 studies with 266 subjects.
tldr: Most of the substances on the WADA Prohibited List have no convincing evidence of improving athletic performance in trained athletes. The few classes with evidence improve strength, sprint or accuracy tasks, and the authors found no studies showing benefit on reliable markers of endurance performance.
methods: Narrative review with a PubMed search using keyword combinations for each substance class, supplemented by reference lists. Evidence was graded by study design (double-blind randomized trials as level 1) and by training status (untrained, trained or highly trained), with actual performance tests preferred over surrogate markers.
findings: Five classes showed evidence of enhancing actual performance in trained subjects: anabolic agents (strength, three studies with 91 volunteers), beta2-agonists (peak sprint power and muscle strength, three studies with 39 volunteers), stimulants (muscle strength, sprint performance and 1500 m run time, 58 trained subjects in Table 1), glucocorticoids (one study with 10 subjects, 11% gain in one-legged hopping force, a surrogate marker) and beta-blockers (13.4% better shooting, one study of 33 subjects). Growth hormone improved sprint performance in untrained subjects only, 11 classes had no well-designed studies, and 6 classes had evidence of no relevant effect.
limitations: The search used PubMed only with keyword combinations, and no formal appraisal or PRISMA reporting is described. The authors note that trials of banned substances in elite athletes are very hard or impossible to run, so the target population is largely missing, and that endurance surrogates such as VO2max have limited predictive value for performance.
practicalImplications: Staff who advise athletes on prohibited substances should treat the evidence as limited, and should not assume that a listed substance improves performance in a given sport. The authors note that clear evidence of no effect for a class would be useful to share with athletes, and that research to fill the gaps in the evidence base could be done in many areas.
athleteDev: Performance staff should not use this review to judge whether a listed substance helps a specific athlete, since most evidence concerns strength or sprint tasks in small trials. Any discussion of performance-enhancing claims should refer to the specific substance class and the study population.
rtp: Not applicable. The review does not address return to sport or injury rehabilitation, and it cannot inform clearance decisions after injury.

citation: Karnovsky SC, Rosenbaum AJ, DeSandis B, Johnson C, Murphy CI, Warren RF, et al. Radiographic Analysis of National Football League Players' Fifth Metatarsal Morphology Relationship to Proximal Fifth Metatarsal Fracture Risk. Foot Ankle Int. 2019;40(3):318-322.
abstract: This Level III case-control study compared radiographic fifth metatarsal morphology and foot type in 15 fractured feet with 81 non-fractured feet from NFL players and NFL Combine participants. Fractured feet differed on several AP and lateral measurements. The authors concluded that long, narrow, straight fifth metatarsals with an adducted forefoot were associated with fracture.
tldr: In a small retrospective comparison of NFL players, proximal fifth metatarsal fractures were associated with a longer, narrower and straighter fifth metatarsal and an adducted forefoot. The findings are hypothesis-generating and need a larger study before they guide screening or footwear.
methods: Retrospective case-control study of NFL players with zone 2 fifth metatarsal fractures treated by the senior authors from 1992 to 2012, and 2014 NFL Combine participants with foot radiographs, using a convenience sample of 96 feet from 51 athletes. Two orthopedic foot and ankle fellows independently measured nine AP, eight lateral and two oblique parameters, averaged per foot. Fractured and non-fractured feet were compared with Student t tests, with P less than .05 considered significant.
findings: Of the AP measurements, nine were tested and four differed significantly. Apex medullary canal width (4.7 vs 5.5 mm, P = .001), fourth-fifth intermetatarsal angle (6.3 vs 7.9 degrees, P = .003), fifth metatarsal angle (3.9 vs 2.6 degrees, P = .004) and talar head uncovering (18.0 vs 22.7, P = .008) were different. On lateral views, five of eight differed: fifth metatarsal length (90.0 vs 86.1 mm, P = .040), distance to apex (53.6 vs 50.1, P = .010), apex height (4.6 vs 5.3 mm, P = .020), fifth metatarsal angle (6.2 vs 8.0 degrees, P = .010) and talocalcaneal angle (39.0 vs 41.8 degrees, P = .010). On oblique views, apex height differed (4.5 vs 5.5 mm, P = .002). The authors report that fractured feet were longer, straighter and narrower, and that metatarsus adductus was more common in fractured feet.
limitations: Small sample, especially the 15 fractured feet, and a retrospective convenience design. Data from the Combine database were incomplete for some players. Many comparisons were run without correction, and the authors note possible selection bias. The authors also note that their findings conflict with some earlier studies.
practicalImplications: The findings suggest that athletes with an adducted forefoot or long, narrow, straight fifth metatarsals may be at higher risk of Jones fracture, which could prompt staff to review foot radiographs in high-risk players. Any footwear, orthosis or off-loading intervention based on these features is untested here.
athleteDev: For performance staff, the paper gives a radiographic risk profile for Jones fracture, but the risk is not quantified and no intervention was tested. It could guide a conversation with the medical team about foot structure, not a training change.
rtp: The study addresses fracture risk and does not assess return to play. The authors suggest the morphology could help teams identify players at higher risk of refracture, but this was not tested, and it cannot be used to decide when a player can return.

citation: Green B, Bourne MN, van Dyk N, Pizzari T. Recalibrating the risk of hamstring strain injury (HSI) - A 2020 systematic review and meta-analysis of risk factors for index and recurrent HSI in sport. Br J Sports Med. 2020.
abstract: This systematic review updated a 2013 review of risk factors for index and recurrent hamstring strain injury (HSI) in sport. Eight databases were searched from 2011 to December 2018 and combined with the original review's studies. Seventy-eight prospective studies were included, with a random-effects meta-analysis for 21 factors and a best evidence synthesis for the rest. Older age, any history of HSI, a recent HSI, previous ACL injury and previous calf strain were significant risk factors, while the strength measures tested were not significantly associated in the meta-analysis.
tldr: Older age and any previous hamstring strain are the strongest risk factors for a new hamstring strain, and a recent strain in the same season carries the highest risk. Previous ACL or calf strain injuries also raised risk, while strength measures were not significantly associated in the meta-analysis.
methods: Systematic review update of a 2013 review, using eight databases from 2011 to December 2018, plus citation tracking and ahead-of-print searches. Prospective studies of index or recurrent HSI in athletes were included. Risk of bias was rated with a modified QUIPS tool, and random-effects meta-analyses were run where data allowed, with best evidence synthesis for the remaining factors.
findings: Across 78 studies (8,319 HSIs, 967 recurrences, 71,324 athletes), older age (SMD 1.6, 95% CI 0.6 to 2.6, p=0.002), any history of HSI (RR 2.7, p<0.001), a recent HSI (RR 4.8, p<0.001), previous ACL injury (RR 1.7, p=0.002) and previous calf strain (RR 1.5, p<0.001) were associated with greater HSI risk. None of the 13 strength-related variables was significantly associated with risk in the meta-analysis. The best evidence synthesis found strong evidence that playing position affects risk in football, linked increases in high-speed running exposure with index HSI, and found that clinical findings at return to play, rather than MRI findings, were associated with recurrence.
limitations: Study quality was mixed (40% low risk of bias), injury definitions varied, and recurrence was often based on participant recall. Many HSI samples were too small for the methods used, and publication and language bias were possible. The abstract and conclusion describe strength as a consistently associated factor, but the meta-analysis found no significant strength association, so the strength finding rests on limited evidence.
practicalImplications: Age, previous HSI, previous ACL or calf strain injury, and a recent HSI are useful flags for closer attention to load and return-to-play planning. A single strength or flexibility test should not be used to predict an individual athlete's risk, since the strength associations were not significant in the meta-analysis.
athleteDev: Manage high-speed running exposure and avoid sudden increases in it, because the paper links sudden rises in high-speed running (within the previous 7 to 14 days) with subsequent HSI. Hamstring testing is better used as ongoing monitoring than as a single baseline screen.
rtp: Use recent HSI history and clinical findings at return to play (strength, range of motion and tenderness to palpation) to judge recurrence risk. MRI findings at baseline or return to play did not accurately predict recurrence, so MRI should not be used alone to clear an athlete or set their risk. Intervention studies were excluded, so this review cannot show that any rehabilitation approach reduces risk.

citation: Baumann JR, Garlapaty AR, Cook JL, DeFroda SF. Recent Trends in Quadriceps Tendon and Patellar Tendon Injuries in the National Football League. Orthop J Sports Med 2025;13(2):23259671241304437.
abstract: Quadriceps tendon (QT) and patellar tendon (PT) tears were reviewed in the NFL from the 2009-2010 to 2022-2023 seasons using publicly available injury reports, with performance measured by Pro Football Focus grades in the season before injury and the first 2 seasons after. Eighty extensor tendon tears were identified (24 QT, 56 PT). Risk factors for QT tears were BMI of 31, age 26 years and 4 years of NFL experience, with higher QT risk in linemen; RTP was 58.3% after QT and 55.4% after PT tears.
tldr: Extensor tendon tears in the NFL were uncommon but seriously affected careers: most were season ending, and only about one in five players with a patellar tendon tear returned to prior performance within 2 seasons. Quadriceps tendon tears were more common in linemen and in players aged 26 or older.
methods: Descriptive epidemiology study using public NFL injury reports (Pro-Football-Reference, NFL injury reports) and Pro Football Focus season grades. All QT and PT tears in the 2009-2010 to 2022-2023 seasons were identified and classified by grade, timing and side. Return to play, games played and started, and relative performance were compared for the season before injury and the first 2 seasons after. Risk factors were tested with chi-square, Fisher exact or McNemar tests.
findings: Eighty tears were identified in 77 players (24 QT, 56 PT), with 96.3% season ending. QT tears were more likely in players with BMI 31 or more (OR 3), age 26 or older (OR 11) and 4 or more years of experience (OR 3), and were more common in offensive and defensive linemen than skill players (OR 5.2). PT tears were more likely in offensive linemen (OR 2.0). Both tear types occurred mostly in games and in the regular season. Return to play was 58.3% (14/24) for QT and 55.4% (31/56) for PT tears, and return to prior performance within 2 seasons was 33.3% (8/24) and 21.4% (12/56). Among PT tears, players with more than 4 years of experience were more likely to return to play (P=.033, OR 3.4).
limitations: Public databases may have missed injuries, and tear grade and side were classified from news reports. The sample is small, with no comparison group. The abstract and results describe a quicker return to performance after QT tears, but the mean time to return to play was 345.6 days for QT and 357.0 days for PT with wide SDs, and no test of that difference is reported. The authors note that prior NFL rates were 50% (QT) and 79% (PT), so the comparison with earlier years is not a direct trend test.
practicalImplications: For an NFL player with an extensor tendon tear, the expectation should be that most will miss the season and that about one in five patellar tendon tears (21.4%) and one in three quadriceps tendon tears (33.3%) will return to prior performance within 2 seasons. Quadriceps tendon tears in this sample clustered in linemen and in players aged 26 or older with BMI of 31 or more.
athleteDev: The paper offers no training or prevention data, so it cannot guide conditioning choices. The quadriceps tendon risk pattern (linemen, age 26 or older, BMI 31 or more, 4 or more years of experience) is descriptive context from a small sample, not a validated screening tool.
rtp: Use the return-to-play rates as a planning benchmark for extensor tendon repair in professional football players: about 55 to 58% returned to play at all, and about 21 to 33% returned to prior performance within 2 seasons. The data cannot show which rehabilitation approach or surgical technique improves these outcomes, and they cannot predict the return of an individual player.
