citation: Stuhlman CR, Owens CJ, Samuelson EM, Vermillion RP, Shermansky MD, King KB, et al. Recurrent Anterior Cruciate Ligament Tears in the National Football League: A Case-Control Study. Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2019;7(12):2325967119891413.
abstract: Among NFL draftees with a prior successful ACL reconstruction, 25% sustained a subsequent ACL injury in the NFL, compared with 9% of position- and draft-matched controls without prior ACL injury (P < .001).
tldr: NFL players who had a successful ACL reconstruction before the draft sustained a subsequent ACL injury at almost three times the rate of matched draftees without a prior ACL injury. Prior reconstruction should be part of the risk conversation with collegiate players aiming for the NFL.
methods: NFL Combine participants from 2006 to 2012 with a prior successful ACL reconstruction who were later drafted (n = 100) were identified from orthopaedic evaluations. Each was matched 2:1 by position, draft round and draft year to controls without prior ACL injury (n = 200). Subsequent ipsilateral or contralateral ACL injury during NFL play was traced through public internet sources, and groups were compared with the Fisher exact test.
findings: Subsequent ACL injury occurred in 25 of 100 reconstructed players (26 injuries: 12 ipsilateral, 14 contralateral) versus 18 of 200 controls (9%; P < .001). Injuries occurred at a mean of 22.1 months after the draft in the study group.
limitations: Retrospective design with internet-based outcome ascertainment. Graft type, concurrent knee injuries, depth chart position, team success and playing surface were not accounted for. Only Combine invitees who were later drafted were included, so players drafted without a Combine invitation were missed, and the 2006 to 2012 sample may not reflect current surgical, rehabilitation or return-to-play practice.
practicalImplications: Collegiate players with a history of ACL reconstruction who aspire to the NFL face a higher subsequent ACL injury risk during their NFL career than matched drafted peers without prior ACL injury. Physicians can use this figure when counselling these athletes.
athleteDev: For collegiate players with a prior ACL reconstruction, the study supports discussing a higher ongoing ACL injury risk when planning for an NFL career. It does not identify any training or conditioning method that reduces that risk.
rtp: The study shows NFL-level ACL re-injury risk after a successful reconstruction and return to play, which is relevant to return-to-play counselling. It cannot be used to set a return-to-play criterion or to judge when an individual athlete is safe to return.

citation: Bitchell CL, Varley-Campbell J, Robinson G, Stiles V, Mathema P, Moore IS. Recurrent and Subsequent Injuries in Professional and Elite Sport: a Systematic Review. Sports Medicine - Open. 2020;6:58.
abstract: Reporting of recurrent and subsequent injuries in professional and elite sport was inconsistent across 51 extracted surveillance studies, and few used subsequent injury categorisation models. In studies using those models, most subsequent injuries were to a different body part and unrelated to the index injury.
tldr: More than a third of eligible professional-sport injury surveillance studies did not report recurrent injuries at all, and few used a subsequent injury model. Staff should not assume published injury rates separate new injuries from re-injuries of the same tissue.
methods: PRISMA systematic review of prospective injury surveillance studies in professional or elite sport that followed a published consensus statement. Searches of SCOPUS, Embase and Medline covered articles published after 2005, up to 23 July 2020. Eighty-one studies met criteria, and 51 (one article containing two studies) were eligible for data extraction after excluding 30 that did not report recurrent injuries. Quality was rated with an amended Downs and Black checklist, and results were summarised narratively.
findings: Of the 51 studies, 44 reported recurrent injuries as a number, percentage, incidence or a combination, with proportions ranging from 5.5% to 48% and incidence from 0.5 to 2.55 per 1000 h. Seven studies used subsequent injury terminology, and 51 to 80% of subsequent injuries were classed as different and unrelated to the index injury. Specific subsequent injury categorisation models were used in only three studies.
limitations: Only one level of sport (professional or elite) and English-language studies were included, so amateur, collegiate and non-English data were excluded. Many studies pooled injuries across several seasons without reporting the number of new participants each season, and quality scores were often low. The review did not pool effect sizes.
practicalImplications: Injury reports from professional sport should be checked for whether they separate recurrent from new injuries, and for how many players and seasons they cover. Where a subsequent injury model is available, it gives more specific information on which injuries follow an earlier one.
athleteDev: The review does not evaluate any training intervention. Its relevance for athlete development is limited to how injury data are recorded and interpreted when comparing squads or seasons.
rtp: The review reports how recurrent and subsequent injuries are recorded in professional sport, but it does not give return-to-play timelines, criteria or outcomes. It cannot be used to decide whether an athlete is ready to return or how long recovery should take.

citation: Moreno-Pérez V, Del Coso J, López-Del Campo R, Resta R, Romero-Sangüesa J, Courel-Ibáñez J, et al. Reduced Match Exposure in the Previous 2 Matches Accounts for Hamstring Muscle Injury Incidence in Professional Football Players. Sports Health. 2023.
abstract: Hamstring strain injuries in 37 professional players were associated with lower playing time, total running and high-speed running in the one and two matches before injury, compared with paired uninjured controls. Playing time of 64 minutes or less in the match before injury was one practical cut-off.
tldr: In professional football, a hamstring strain was more likely after a player had very little match exposure in the two games before it. Playing minutes are a simple metric that staff can track to flag players with recent low match load.
methods: Prospective controlled observational study of 144 outfield players from two LaLiga teams over three seasons. Thirty-seven noncontact hamstring strains were each matched 1:1 to an uninjured starter in the same team and position. Playing time, total distance and high-speed running (above 24 km/h) were taken from a video tracking system for the four matches before injury. Generalized estimating equations gave relative risks, and ROC analysis gave diagnostic accuracy.
findings: Injured players had lower playing time, distance and high-speed running in the match before injury (for example, 65.4 vs 88.5 min playing time) and in the two matches before injury. Playing time relative risk was 1.41 per 10 min in one match and 1.14 per 10 min across two matches. Cut-offs in the match before injury were high-speed running of 328 m or less (sensitivity 64%, specificity 84%) and playing time of 64 min or less (sensitivity 36%, specificity 97%). Windows of three and four matches showed no significant differences in playing time.
limitations: Training exposure and internal load were not recorded, and injuries from training were included. Only two teams were studied, and the match-based cut-offs have high specificity but low sensitivity, so they miss many players who go on to be injured. The 3- and 4-match windows were not significant for playing time, and the authors suggest underexposure need not be sustained over longer periods to matter, but the study does not test a mechanism. The time taken to complete the four matches before injury differed between players, although the match before injury was 3 to 7 days before it for all players.
practicalImplications: Staff could record playing minutes for each player's last two matches and flag players with very low recent minutes for closer monitoring and individual load planning. The cut-off of about 64 minutes in the previous match was the most specific measure in this sample, but it misses many injuries and should be tested in other squads before being used as a rule.
athleteDev: The study supports tracking match minutes and high-speed running in the previous two matches as part of individual load management for players with reduced match involvement. It does not test training programmes that prevent hamstring injury.
rtp: The study does not assess return-to-play criteria and did not study players returning from injury. It cannot be used to set how quickly match minutes are reintroduced after an injury.

citation: Volpi A, Haselman W, Photopoulos C, Banffy M. Regular-Season Injury Rates in the National Football League After an Attenuated Preseason Due to COVID-19. Orthop J Sports Med. 2022;10(11):23259671221133776.
abstract: After the 2020 NFL preseason was cancelled because of COVID-19, the authors compared musculoskeletal injuries across all 32 teams in the 2019 and 2020 regular seasons using public records. Total injuries rose from 632 to 765 (P=.0324), with significant increases in calf or Achilles strains, groin injuries and ACL tears.
tldr: Musculoskeletal injuries in NFL regular-season games rose after the 2020 preseason was cancelled, with the largest increases in calf and Achilles strains, groin injuries and ACL tears. Staff should treat this as a signal to plan conditioning for disrupted preseasons, not as proof of cause.
methods: Descriptive epidemiology study of publicly reported NFL injuries for all 32 teams across the 2019 regular season and the 2020 regular season, which had 16 games. Players who missed a regular-season game or were placed on injured reserve with a musculoskeletal injury were included. COVID-19 injured-reserve cases, non-musculoskeletal injuries and undiagnosed injuries were excluded. Season totals and per-team counts were compared with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests at P<.05.
findings: Total musculoskeletal injuries were 632 in 2019 and 765 in 2020 (P=.0324); median injuries per team were 20.5 and 22.5. Calf or Achilles strains (17 vs 39, P=.0091), groin injuries (25 vs 46, P=.0177) and ACL tears (14 vs 29, P=.0157) increased significantly. Hamstring injuries increased from 87 to 114 but not significantly (P=.0847). Torn Achilles tendons (4 vs 10) rose but not significantly.
limitations: Public databases may omit or misreport injuries, and diagnosis, severity and time lost were not available. Counts were not normalized to player exposure. Practice-squad players were excluded, 332 COVID-19 injured-reserve placements were excluded, and possible unorganized preseason training could not be measured. Only one season pair was compared, so the findings are associations.
practicalImplications: Staff planning for a shortened or cancelled preseason could prioritize structured team conditioning before the first games, since the authors found more calf or Achilles, groin and ACL injuries in the season that followed a missed preseason. The increase is a count-based association and should not be read as a fixed per-player risk.
athleteDev: Performance Application: the findings are consistent with organized preseason conditioning having a protective role, because the authors saw more soft-tissue injuries in the season after one was cancelled, but the design cannot isolate the preseason as the cause. The paper does not test a specific training program.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: the study counts injuries and does not report time loss, rehabilitation or return-to-play outcomes, so it cannot be used to set return-to-play timelines or criteria for any injury.

citation: Grange S, Plancher R, Reurink G, Croisille P, Edouard P. Relationship Between the Pain Intensity at the Time of the Hamstring Muscle Injury and the Hyperintense T2 Weighted Volume of the Hamstring Muscle Lesion Measured by MRI. Clin J Sport Med. 2024.
abstract: In 61 athletes with suspected acute hamstring injury, pain at the time of injury (NPRS 0 to 10) showed a significant but weak correlation with the hyperintense T2 volume on MRI (r=0.287, P=0.025). Pain did not differ by Peetrons grade or by the muscle head involved.
tldr: Pain felt at the time of a hamstring injury is only weakly related to how large the MRI lesion is. Staff should not rely on pain alone to judge injury extent, and should order MRI when lesion size matters for management.
methods: Retrospective analysis of a prospective, multicenter, noninterventional cohort (HAMMER). Athletes aged 18 to 50 with suspected acute hamstring injury from sport had thigh MRI, with lesion volume estimated from three maximal dimensions and graded by the Peetrons classification. Pain at injury was recorded with a 0 to 10 Numeric Pain Rating Scale in a self-completed questionnaire. Pearson correlation and one-way ANOVA were used, with P<0.05 as significant.
findings: Across 61 patients, pain at injury correlated significantly but weakly with the hyperintense T2 volume (r=0.287, P=0.025), explaining about 8% of variance. Pain did not differ by Peetrons grade (F(3,57)=0.982, P=0.408) or by muscle head (F(3,57)=1.013, P=0.394). The MRI was done a mean of 7.8 days after injury (SD 5.7, range 1 to 24).
limitations: The sample is small and pain was assessed retrospectively, which may introduce recall bias, although the short delay limits this. Pain is subjective and only one clinical examination variable was studied. Table 1 percentages do not match the counts (for example, 6 patients with no injury given as 14.6%), and the text states 81% single lesions while the table gives 72.1%. Grade 3 had only four patients.
practicalImplications: Pain at the time of injury can be recorded during the clinical assessment, but a low or high pain score should not be used to predict lesion size. If the extent of edema matters for the management decision, the study indicates that MRI is needed, since pain alone explained only a small part of the variance.
athleteDev: Performance Application: not addressed. The study examines injury imaging and pain at injury, not training, load or performance outcomes.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: the study does not measure time to return to sport or recovery trajectories, so it cannot be used to predict return timing from pain or MRI lesion size.

citation: Fukuda T, Yamazaki K, Zhou B. Relationship between Neck Musculature and Head Kinematics during a Collision in University American Football Players. Asian J Kinesiol. 2026;28(1):11-18.
abstract: Head kinematics during collisions in American football may relate to neck muscle strength and neck size. In 22 players from one university team, neck strength and neck circumference were measured and head acceleration was recorded in game collisions across seven competition games.
tldr: In this small team study, players with stronger and thicker necks tended to have slightly lower head acceleration in collisions, but the correlations were weak. This is not evidence that neck training prevents concussion.
methods: Twenty-two players from one university team in the Kanto collegiate association second division had isometric neck strength measured in flexion, extension and left and right lateral flexion with a handheld dynamometer, and neck circumference measured, one month before the season. Head linear and angular acceleration were recorded in collisions over seven competition games using an impact-sensing mouthguard, with impacts defined as over 10 G. Spearman rank correlations were used.
findings: A weak negative correlation was found between the top 10% of head linear acceleration and neck flexor strength (r = -0.344, p < 0.05). Neck circumference had very weak to weak negative correlations with head linear and angular acceleration (r = -0.133 to -0.354). Neck lateral flexor strength had a very weak positive correlation with angular acceleration in the top 50% of impacts (r = 0.121).
limitations: Small single-team sample with mostly very weak or weak correlations and no adjustment for confounders. The authors note that preseason training data were analysed together with competition data, that circumference was not equated with muscle volume, and that concussion history and muscle activation timing were not considered. The discussion describes some correlations as positive where the results report them as negative, so the reported directions should be checked against Table 2.
practicalImplications: Neck strength and neck size can be tracked alongside impact data in collegiate football, but the weak associations here do not support using them to predict an individual player's head acceleration. Whether neck strength training lowers concussion risk needs prospective intervention studies.
athleteDev: Neck flexor strength and neck size were weakly associated with lower head acceleration in collisions in this group. This is consistent with, but does not test, the use of neck strengthening in collegiate football preparation.
rtp: This study does not inform return-to-sport decisions. It cannot be used to judge whether a player with a concussion is ready to return, or to set neck strength thresholds for play.

citation: Chyi T, Lu FJH, Hsieh Y-C, Hsu Y-W, Gill DL, Fang B-B. Relationship Between Athletes' History of Stressors and Sport Injury: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Percept Mot Skills. 2023.
abstract: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 19 studies on whether a history of stressors in athletes is associated with later sport injury. The pooled correlation was small (r = .12), with moderation by age, region, sport type, competition level and type of stress measure.
tldr: Athletes with a history of stressors are somewhat more likely to be injured, but the association is small. Use it to support a psychosocial screen, not to identify individual injury risk.
methods: Systematic search of seven databases (SPORTDiscus, PsycINFO, Academic Search Premier, Ovid, Scopus, Web of Science and PubMed) from January 2000 to September 2023, plus reference lists; 11 of the 19 included studies came from an earlier review by Ivarsson et al. (2017). Study quality was rated with the Kmet checklist and only studies meeting at least 60% of criteria were kept. A random-effects meta-analysis was run with moderator analyses by age, region, sport type, stress measure and competition level.
findings: The pooled correlation between stress history and sport injury was small but significant (r = .12, 95% CI .08 to .16; Q(18) = 106.71, I2 = 83.13). Correlations were r = .14 in adults vs .09 in adolescents, .10 in contact vs .01 in non-contact sports, .13 in non-elite vs .06 in elite athletes, and .22 for general vs .12 for sport-specific stress measures. The fail-safe N (314) and Begg test suggested no publication bias, but Egger's test was significant (bias = 2.41, p < .001).
limitations: Pooled effect is small, heterogeneity is high and subgroup analyses rest on few studies; gender, training load and resilience could not be examined. The abstract reports different values from the results (Q(17) = 98.61 and Z = 7.74 vs Q(18) = 106.71 and Z = 8.20; adolescents r = .14 and contact r = .09 vs adolescents r = .09 and contact r = .10); this record uses the results values. Included studies are observational, so the association cannot be read as causal.
practicalImplications: A brief stress history check could be included in psychosocial screening alongside injury monitoring. Its value as a stand-alone predictor is limited by the small pooled effect.
athleteDev: Athlete stress history is a small correlate of sport injury, which supports including stress monitoring as one input in athlete welfare and injury-prevention planning rather than as a standalone risk flag.
rtp: This review does not inform return-to-sport decisions. It cannot be used to decide whether an injured athlete is ready to return, or to delay or clear a return based on stress history.

citation: Avedesian JM, Covassin T, Baez S, Nash J, Nagelhout E, Dufek JS. Relationship Between Cognitive Performance and Lower Extremity Biomechanics: Implications for Sports-Related Concussion. Orthop J Sports Med. 2021;9(8):23259671211032246.
abstract: In 20 collegiate athletes with prior sports-related concussion and 20 matched controls, slower functional visuomotor reaction time was correlated with reduced knee flexion, and greater dominant-limb knee abduction moment was correlated with poorer ImPACT visual memory and ImPACT reaction time in the concussion group. Most computerised cognitive measures were not associated with the functional reaction time.
tldr: In athletes with a prior concussion, slower reaction time and poorer visual memory went with knee mechanics linked to injury risk during cutting. Standard computerised concussion tests did not track the sport-specific reaction measure well.
methods: Controlled laboratory study with a single testing session. Twenty NCAA Division I athletes with physician-diagnosed collegiate concussion (9 men, 11 women) and 20 matched controls from seven sports completed unanticipated land-and-cut tasks on dominant and non-dominant limbs, with motion capture and force plates over the first 100 ms of contact and a light-cued functional visuomotor reaction time. Athletes also completed ImPACT and three Senaptec Sensory Station tasks, and Pearson correlations were run for all athletes and for each group.
findings: In the concussion group, slower functional reaction time was moderately correlated with reduced dominant-limb knee flexion (r = -0.514) and slower non-dominant reaction time with reduced non-dominant knee flexion (r = -0.500). Increased dominant-limb knee abduction moment was moderately correlated with lower ImPACT Visual Memory (r = -0.539) and ImPACT Reaction Time (r = 0.515), and Go/No Go score with non-dominant vGRF (r = -0.700). Apart from MOT, computerised cognitive measures were not associated with functional reaction time in any cohort, and some correlations seen in controls were absent in the concussion group.
limitations: Small sample of 20 per group, cross-sectional, with many uncorrected correlations. Pre-collegiate concussion history, ADHD status and the reliability of the functional reaction time and Senaptec measures were not addressed, and mean time since concussion was 461 days. The abstract gives r = -0.512 for dominant knee flexion (table and text: -0.514; -0.512 is knee extension moment) and calls the ImPACT reaction time finding 'slower' where the results text says 'faster'; this record uses the table values.
practicalImplications: Reaction time and working memory may be worth assessing alongside landing and cutting mechanics in athletes with a concussion history. Computerised concussion tests alone may not reflect sport-specific cognitive processing.
athleteDev: In athletes with a prior concussion, poorer reaction time and visual memory were related to knee mechanics during cutting, which supports pairing cognitive and movement screening when profiling these athletes. The data do not show that training either one changes the other.
rtp: This study cannot be used to clear an athlete to return to sport. Its sample was already cleared and a mean of 461 days post-concussion, and it was not designed to test readiness to return after an acute injury.

citation: Aso T, Tamura M, Kaji N, Akiyama S, Maeda T, Takahashi Y, et al. Relationship between trunk and pelvic rotation angles during throwing and the Kerlan-Jobe Orthopedic Clinic score in American football quarterbacks. JSES Int. 2026.
abstract: In 11 healthy quarterbacks, trunk and pelvic rotation during throwing correlated with specific items of the KJOC shoulder and elbow function score. Significant correlations were positive and moderate to strong, at both the 20- and 30-yard throw distances.
tldr: Quarterbacks with more trunk and pelvic rotation at key points of the throw reported better scores on some KJOC shoulder and elbow items. This is a very small correlation study with an app-based measure.
methods: Eleven healthy quarterbacks without prior shoulder or elbow surgery completed five maximum-effort throws at 20 and 30 yards. A side-on iPad video at 240 Hz was analysed with PitchAI, a markerless app, for trunk rotation, pelvic rotation and hip-shoulder separation at stride foot contact, maximum shoulder external rotation and ball release. These angles were correlated with each KJOC item and the total score using Spearman rank correlation.
findings: At 20 yards, trunk rotation at maximum external rotation correlated with KJOC item 3 on weakness or fatigue (rs = 0.709, p = 0.015). At 30 yards, hip-shoulder separation at stride foot contact correlated with item 3 (rs = 0.662, p = 0.026) and pelvic rotation at ball release with item 4 (rs = 0.760, p = 0.007). Further significant positive correlations were reported for items 5, 7 and 10 (rs = 0.616 to 0.839).
limitations: Eleven participants from two teams, against an a priori sample size of 84, with many correlations tested. KJOC scores were mostly very high (ceiling effect), and PitchAI has been validated in baseball pitching but not quarterback throwing. Pre-proof article that has not completed copyediting; cross-sectional design in healthy players only.
practicalImplications: Trunk and pelvic rotation are candidate variables to study in quarterback throwing assessments alongside the KJOC score. The findings do not show which mechanic to change to reduce injury.
athleteDev: Trunk and pelvic rotation were related to some self-reported shoulder and elbow function items in healthy quarterbacks. This is hypothesis-generating and does not by itself justify changing a quarterback's throwing technique.
rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It included only healthy quarterbacks and does not test whether throwing mechanics or KJOC scores indicate readiness to return after injury.

citation: Whalan, M., Lovell, R., Steele, J. R., Sampson, J. A. Rescheduling Part 2 of the 11+ reduces injury burden and increases compliance in semi-professional football. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2019;29:1941-1951.
abstract: The authors randomised 25 semi-professional clubs to perform the FIFA 11+ with all three parts at the start of training, or with Part 2 moved to the end of training. Injury incidence was similar between groups, while the rescheduled group completed more 11+ sessions, had fewer severe injuries and fewer total days lost to injury.
tldr: Moving the strengthening part of the 11+ to the end of training kept injury incidence unchanged, while players completed more sessions and lost fewer days to injury. The authors suggest the gain is tied to the higher dose, so coaches can consider this schedule for semi-professional squads.
methods: This cluster randomised controlled trial allocated 25 semi-professional clubs (806 male players, 2017 season) to the Standard 11+ (all three parts at the start of training) or P2post (Parts 1 and 3 at the start, Part 2 at the end). Both groups aimed for at least two sessions per week. On-site primary data collectors recorded 11+ doses, exposure hours, and time-loss injuries. Injury incidence in a subset of 411 players was compared with their 2016 surveillance season with no prevention programme. Generalised estimating equations with Poisson distribution accounted for club clustering, and clinical inferences were derived from incidence rate ratios.
findings: Injury incidence was similar between groups (P2post 11.8 vs Standard 12.3 injuries per 1000 h; IRR 1.0, clinically likely trivial). The P2post group had more 11+ sessions (29.1 vs 18.9, p < .001). Table 1 shows fewer severe injuries (over 28 days lost) in P2post (33 vs 59, p = .012) and fewer total days lost (4303 vs 5815, p = .026), with fewer days lost to hamstring, non-contact and recurrent injuries. Ankle injury incidence was lower in P2post (IRR 0.7, 95% CI 0.4 to 0.9, possibly beneficial, p = .132). Quadriceps injuries (IRR 1.8, possibly harmful) and contusions (IRR 1.5, likely harmful) were more frequent in P2post. In the 2016 comparison subset, both groups had lower injury incidence than the 2016 season (38% and 35% lower). The authors say the sub-classification findings need caution.
limitations: The abstract and Table 1 disagree on several values: the severe-injury count is 58 in the abstract and 59 in Table 1, and the p-values for severe injuries (< .002 vs .012) and total days lost (< .001 vs .026) differ. The P2post reduction from 2016 is 35% in the Results but 40% in the Discussion. The 11+ dose differed between groups, so timing and dose cannot be separated. Quality of exercise performance was not recorded, and Part 2 progression could not be fully standardised. Injuries were recorded by several data collectors across clubs, which may have caused under- or over-reporting. Many sub-group tests were run on the same data, and the authors note this increases the risk of false findings. Only male semi-professional players were studied.
practicalImplications: Scheduling the 11+ with Part 2 at the end of training kept injury incidence the same as the standard order while players completed more sessions. Fewer severe injuries and days lost were seen, though the abstract and table disagree on those values. Coaches should not expect a lower injury rate overall, and higher quadriceps and contusion counts were seen with this schedule. The results apply to male semi-professional squads in one season.
athleteDev: Place Part 2 of the 11+ at the end of training when the aim is to get players to complete the full programme more often, because compliance rose with this schedule. Expect possible trade-offs by injury site: the trial showed lower ankle incidence and fewer hamstring days lost, but more quadriceps and contusion injuries.
rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It recorded injury counts and days lost in healthy players during a season and did not assess rehabilitation, clearance or return-to-play decisions after injury.

citation: Van Hooren B. Rethinking Acute Sports Injuries: Evidence for an Overuse Mechanism in Hamstring and ACL Injuries. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2025;35:e70146.
abstract: This narrative review argues that hamstring strain and ACL injuries may partly be overuse injuries caused by mechanical fatigue rather than single acute events. It draws on human, animal and cadaveric studies and states that further research is needed to test the idea.
tldr: Hamstring strains and ACL tears may partly come from repeated submaximal loading that weakens tissue, not only from one moment of overload. The idea is plausible but not yet proven, and it points toward tissue-load monitoring and recovery planning.
methods: Narrative review with no structured search or quality appraisal described. The author discusses human kinematic and modeling studies, animal and cadaveric fatigue-failure experiments, and ACL explant analyses.
findings: Three case studies found no notable kinematic or kinetic deviation in the stride when a hamstring injury occurred, compared with preceding strides. Repeated simulated landings caused ACL failure in cadaveric knees at loads below ultimate strength. ACL explants from noncontact injury showed collagen damage similar to that in repetitively loaded cadaveric ligaments.
limitations: Hamstring case studies estimated whole-muscle forces with generic muscle-tendon parameters. Fatigue-failure work used mostly animal calf muscles and middle-aged cadavers, and cadaveric ACL models do not reproduce unplanned movements or fatigue. Current imaging cannot detect the nano- and microscale damage the hypothesis depends on.
practicalImplications: If these injuries partly come from accumulated load, monitoring tissue load and allowing recovery between high-load bouts could reduce risk, as is already done for overuse in baseball pitching. The author proposes wearable load estimates, but notes these tools are not yet validated for hamstring or ACL load.
athleteDev: Tracking high-speed running, accelerations and change-of-direction loads, together with recovery time, could be one way to manage hamstring and ACL risk if the overuse model is confirmed. The review does not show that such load limits reduce injuries.
rtp: The review suggests mechanical fatigue could inform training and rehabilitation, but it tests no rehabilitation or return-to-play protocol. It cannot set return-to-sport timing, load progressions or readiness criteria.

citation: Mack CD, Herzog MM, Solomon G, Putukian M, Lee RY, Matava MJ, et al. Return to Full Participation Following Concussion in the National Football League, 2015 Through 2020. Clinical Journal of Sport Medicine. 2022.
abstract: This retrospective cohort study quantified days missed, games missed and time to return to full participation after concussion in NFL players from 2015 to 2020. Players missed a median of 9 days, 59% missed at least one scheduled game, and no player returned on the day of injury.
tldr: NFL players missed a median of 9 days after a concussion, and about 59% missed at least one game. No player returned to competition on the day of injury under the league's graduated protocol.
methods: Retrospective observational cohort of team-related NFL concussions from 2015 to 2020, drawn from the league's electronic health record and participation data. Days missed, games missed and injury burden were summarized by year, season, activity, roster position and day of week, with Wilcoxon and Kruskal-Wallis tests for group comparisons.
findings: There were 1,480 concussions in 1,121 players. The median days missed was 9 (mean 15.0, SD 23.7), with an average of 3,639 player-days and 255 games missed per year. Offensive linemen (median 10 days), tight ends, running backs and linebackers missed the most days per concussion, and quarterbacks and special teams players missed the fewest. Practice and game concussions had similar median days missed (8 and 9, P = 0.40). Of players concussed in preseason or regular season games, 41% returned without missing a game, 37% after one game, and 22% after two or more.
limitations: The study has no comparison group and does not account for symptom severity, concussion history or neuropsychological results. Missing return dates were imputed for 8% of concussions in the days analysis and 13% in the games analysis, and time missed depends on when in the season the injury occurred and on roster decisions. The 2020 season was shortened by COVID-19, and the authors note that some concussions may go undetected.
practicalImplications: Staff planning for a concussed professional football player can use the median of about 9 days out and the likelihood of missing at least one game as a league-level benchmark. Clinical teams should not expect same-day return, since the league protocol prohibits it, and individual timelines should follow symptom-based progression.
athleteDev: Performance Application: Planning for a concussion absence in football should assume a median of about 9 days out of full participation and a substantial chance of missing a game. The paper measures no performance, workload or readiness data after return, so it cannot guide training loads once the player is back.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: The league protocol requires graduated phases, symptom resolution and clearance by the team physician and an independent neurologist, with no same-day return. The study describes the outcome of that protocol but does not identify factors that predict longer recovery, so it cannot forecast an individual player's return date.

citation: Choi HR, Elattar O, Dills VD, Busconi B. Return to Play After Sports Hernia Surgery. Clinics in Sports Medicine. 2016;35:621-636.
abstract: This clinical review covers the definition, presentation, diagnosis, imaging, nonoperative and surgical treatment, and rehabilitation of sports hernia in athletes. It reports high return-to-sport rates after surgery, with laparoscopic repair generally returning athletes sooner than open repair, and outlines a phased rehabilitation protocol.
tldr: Sports hernia causes chronic groin and lower abdominal pain in athletes and is often diagnosed on history and examination. Surgery usually returns athletes to sport, with laparoscopic repair typically faster than open repair.
methods: Narrative clinical review of sports hernia, drawing on published case series, comparative studies and a randomized trial, with the authors' institutional rehabilitation approach described. No systematic search method is reported.
findings: Diagnosis rests on history and examination, since no imaging modality is sensitive and specific; MRI is preferred for soft tissue, with reported sensitivity of 68% for rectus abdominis injury and 86% for adductor injury. In a randomized trial, 27 of 30 operated athletes (90%) returned to sport at 3 months versus 8 of 30 (27%) treated without surgery. Case series reported return rates of 80% to 100% after surgery, with about 2 to 6 weeks to return after laparoscopic repair and 1 to 6 months after open repair. The authors' phased rehabilitation covers rest for 1 to 2 weeks, then progressive strength and mobility, then sport-specific work from about weeks 5 to 8.
limitations: The review is narrative, reports no search method, and relies mostly on uncontrolled case series with heterogeneous surgical techniques and outcome definitions. The authors state there is little research guiding return-to-sport timing, and direct comparison of outcomes is difficult because populations and techniques differ. The rehabilitation phases reflect one institution's practice and have not been tested against outcomes.
practicalImplications: In athletes with chronic groin pain, staff should consider sports hernia alongside hip and adductor causes, and a 4 to 8 week trial of nonoperative care is the usual first step in season. Athletes who keep pain after that may be considered for surgery, and return timing should be planned around the repair type.
athleteDev: Performance Application: In the authors' protocol, sport-specific plyometric and agility work starts about 5 to 8 weeks after surgery, so training after repair should build through the rehabilitation phases in that order. The review gives no load or performance measures for those phases.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: Return timing in the reviewed series ranged from about 2 to 6 weeks after laparoscopic repair to 1 to 6 months after open repair, and nonoperative care often ran about 10 to 12 weeks before return. The review sets no objective clearance criteria beyond pain-free progression, so return should be individualized and cannot be read as a fixed timeline.

citation: Swiatek PR, Nandurkar T, Maroon J, et al. Return to Play Guidelines after Cervical Spine Injuries in American Football Athletes: A Literature-based Review. Spine. 2021.
abstract: Study design: literature-based review. Objective: to review clinical and case studies on return to play after cervical spine injury in elite American football athletes and formulate guidelines. Methods: observational and case-based articles from PubMed and EMBASE, published before 1 December 2019, involving NFL or NCAA athletes. Results: 28 studies; stingers and burners were the most common injury, with transient quadriplegia, cervical stenosis, disc herniation and fractures having the greatest effect on long-term health and career length. Conclusion: return-to-play decisions should weigh average return time, recurrence risk, position played and imaging pathology.
tldr: Return to play after a cervical spine injury in football should be individualised, weighing return time, recurrence risk, position and imaging. The evidence is mostly case-based, so these principles are guides rather than validated rules.
methods: Literature-based review of PubMed and EMBASE for English-language studies published by 1 December 2019 on return to play after cervical spine injury in NFL or NCAA football athletes. Two independent reviewers screened titles and abstracts; reviews, editorials and opinion pieces were excluded. Twenty-eight studies met inclusion, and the authors combined them with consensus opinion to propose principles.
findings: Stingers and burners were the most common cervical injury, accounting for 46% of NFL and 65% of collegiate cervical injuries, and 97% of collegiate athletes with a stinger missed fewer than 21 days. In NFL players, single-level surgery for disc herniation was followed by return to play in 72% of players (average 29 games), compared with 46% of nonoperatively treated players (average 15 games). The authors cite canal-diameter thresholds for stenosis, but they describe the evidence on congenital stenosis and transient quadriplegia as controversial.
limitations: Most included studies are case series, case reports, panel discussions and injury surveillance with limited clinical detail, and the authors call several recommendations controversial. The review pools no data and describes no formal quality appraisal. The NFL and collegiate figures come from different periods and databases and are not directly comparable.
practicalImplications: Decide return to play on the combined picture of symptoms, neurological and range-of-motion examination, position, sport demands and MRI findings rather than a single test. Players with persistent neurological symptoms, neck pain or range-of-motion loss should not return. After a first stinger with significant physical findings, imaging is advised, and return to full contact should wait for symptoms to resolve.
athleteDev: Use the return-to-play criteria to gate the return to full contact: pain-free full cervical range, normal strength and an intact neurological exam. The authors' anecdotal experience is that recurrence rises when players return to full contact before symptoms fully resolve, so build contact back in stages after a stinger.
rtp: The review gives return-to-play information for strains, stingers, disc herniation after surgery, fractures and stenosis, but most of it is expert opinion. It cannot set a validated clearance standard for any single diagnosis. It must not be used to clear a player with persistent neurological symptoms, which the authors list as an absolute contraindication.

citation: White MD, Hersh AM, Weber-Levine C, et al. Return to play in professional football players following traumatic cervical spine injury: expert opinions from the National Football League spine surgeons. J Neurosurg Spine. 2024.
abstract: Objective: to report NFL team spine consultants' management and return-to-play decisions after cervical spine injury. Methods: a cross-sectional online survey of five clinical vignettes (radiculopathy, myelopathy, unilateral facet fracture, unilateral facet dislocation, and neck pain with ligamentous STIR signal), using multiple-choice and open-ended questions. Results: 26 physicians from 21 of 32 teams responded. Anterior surgery was most common for disc herniation with radiculopathy (73%) or myelopathy (88%); a rigid orthosis was preferred for nondisplaced facet fracture (68%), and single-level anterior fusion for facet dislocation (56%). Common clearance criteria were a normal examination, pain-free range of motion and radiographic fusion or fracture healing. Conclusions: decisions are complex and vary, and the results show how team consultants may counsel players.
tldr: NFL team spine consultants mostly favour anterior fusion for disc herniations with radiculopathy or myelopathy and a rigid orthosis for nondisplaced facet fractures. Clearance criteria vary; a normal or improved neurological exam was the most cited, and imaging evidence of fusion or healing was cited by about a quarter to two thirds of respondents.
methods: Cross-sectional online survey (SurveyMonkey) sent to 49 NFL spine consultants on all 32 teams, with five hypothetical vignettes built from non-NFL patient images. Responses were summarised descriptively, and chi-square or Fisher exact tests compared return-to-play timing by management choice. Of 26 respondents, one who stopped after the second vignette was excluded from later analyses.
findings: Anterior cervical discectomy and fusion was the most common choice for disc herniation with radiculopathy (73%) or myelopathy (88%), and the most common time to full professional play was 6 months (42% and 38%), although 8 respondents (31%) would never return the myelopathy/incomplete spinal cord injury case. For clearance after disc herniation with radiculopathy, respondents cited a normal examination (85%), radiographic fusion (58%) and pain-free range of motion (50%), and listed persistent stenosis (35%) and instability (31%) as contraindications. For facet fractures and dislocations, all but one respondent in each management group suggested waiting 6 to 12 months before return to play.
limitations: The results are expert opinion and self-reported practice from 26 of 49 invited consultants, not player outcomes or a formal consensus. Vignettes are hypothetical and use non-NFL images, and the survey cannot capture all injuries, treatments or clinical nuances. Respondents may read instability and healing on imaging differently, and the authors note the survey is a framework for later Delphi work.
practicalImplications: Expect team consultants to weigh a normal or improved neurological examination most heavily, with pain-free motion and, after surgery, imaging evidence of fusion also commonly required. For facet fractures and dislocations, consultants commonly expect 6 to 12 months before full play; disc herniation timelines varied more, with 3 to 12 months chosen. Players with myelopathy or spinal cord injury may not be cleared at all, as about a third of respondents would never return that case.
athleteDev: Use these clearance criteria to set the gate for progressing a player back to full contact after a cervical injury: normal neurological exam, pain-free full neck range of motion and, after fusion, imaging evidence of healing. Performance staff should not treat the 6 to 12 month timelines as training benchmarks, because they describe clearance for full professional play.
rtp: The survey shows the criteria NFL spine consultants commonly cite for clearing players after disc herniation, facet injury and ligamentous injury. These include a normal or improved neurological exam (68% to 88% across vignettes) and pain-free full range of motion (31% to 50%). It cannot set a return-to-play standard, because the cases are hypothetical and no player outcome data are reported.

citation: Abed V, Fine R, Fine R, et al. Return to Play, Performance, and Economic Analysis of National Football League Players After Lisfranc Injury. Orthop J Sports Med 2023;11(4):23259671231159935.
abstract: Background: a Lisfranc injury to the ligament or bone causes instability during strength and balance tasks. Purpose: to analyse return to play (RTP) and performance after Lisfranc injury in the NFL, and to estimate the economic impact. Study design: case series, level 4. Methods: NFL players with Lisfranc injuries from 2009 to 2020 were identified from public records; snap counts, approximate value (AV), games played and started were compared before and after injury, and salary loss was estimated. Results: 33 players were identified, 27 (81.8%) returned at a median of 11.0 months, AV fell significantly at 1 year (P = .022), and cost of recovery was $104.7 million, with quarterbacks accounting for $32.6 million. Conclusion: the RTP rate was higher than hypothesised, with a significant AV decrease at 1 year and quarterbacks responsible for almost one-third of costs.
tldr: Most NFL players with a Lisfranc injury (27 of 33) returned to play at about 11 months, but their approximate value fell in the first season back. The salary cost of missed games was large, driven mainly by quarterbacks.
methods: Case series of NFL players with Lisfranc injuries, identified by cross-referencing official injury reports, press releases and sports websites, with each case confirmed by at least two sources. Performance data came from Pro Football Reference for 3 seasons before and after return, and non-parametric Wilcoxon tests were used. Salary loss was calculated from Spotrac earnings divided by 17 weeks, multiplied by games missed, and adjusted to 2022 dollars.
findings: Of 33 players, 27 (81.8%) returned to play at a median of 11.0 months; players who did not return were significantly older (median 31 vs 26 years) with longer NFL careers, and 23 of 26 players injured through 2019 remained in the NFL two seasons after injury. Snap counts and games played and started did not change significantly, but AV fell at 1 year (median 6.0 to 5.0; P = .022), and the 3-year AV change was not significant (P = .080). The estimated salary cost of missed games for returning players was $104.7 million, with quarterbacks at $32.6 million from four players.
limitations: Players were identified from public sources, so unreported injuries are missing. The AV metric is not validated, and per-position groups are very small, so the study is underpowered. Injury type (soft tissue or bony), surgery details and rehabilitation were not assessed, and preseason and playoff games and the cost of travel and rehabilitation were excluded from the cost analysis.
practicalImplications: Counsel players that most returned to NFL play after about 11 months, but plan for a drop in performance in the first season back. Use the cost estimate to inform roster and contract planning, while recognising that it reflects salary for games missed, not a complete financial cost.
athleteDev: Build the return-to-performance plan around role-specific output, not only time to first game. Across 22 returning players with data, mean AV fell by about 23% and snap counts by about 9% after return, but these percentage changes were not tested for significance and position estimates rest on 2 to 4 players each.
rtp: Of players who were injured, 81.8% returned to at least one regular-season snap at a median of 11.0 months, which is a minimal definition of return. The study cannot show whether operative or nonoperative care, injury type or rehabilitation changes this outcome, so it cannot set a clearance standard for a specific case.

citation: Wörner EA, Nagel M, Kodde IF, Eygendaal D, The B. Return to sports following distal biceps tendon repair: a current concepts review. Journal of ISAKOS 2023 (accepted pre-proof).
abstract: The abstract states that distal biceps tendon ruptures are rare but occur in active and athletic populations, especially weightlifting and contact sports, and that the review aimed to determine the rate, time and level of return to sport after repair. Most included athletes were NFL players, with weightlifters and a few recreational athletes. The return-to-play rate was high, performance was similar to matched players and most returned to the same level, but most could not return within the same season, which should be discussed with the athlete and coach before surgery.
tldr: About 95% of athletes in the reviewed studies returned to sport after distal biceps tendon repair and about 82% to the same level, but the mean time to return was about 39 weeks, so return within the same season is unlikely in many sports. The evidence is small and retrospective.
methods: Narrative review of studies on return to sport after distal biceps tendon repair in athletes. The text does not describe a search strategy, databases, inclusion criteria or appraisal method. The included studies are summarised in a demographics table and a logistic regression table from one study.
findings: Return to sport was 100% (10 of 10) in the weightlifter series, 93.4% (57 of 61) in Gowd et al, 94% (33 of 35) in the NFL series by McGinnis et al (Table 1 gives 95%), and 84% in Pagani et al (reported against 21 of 22 players in Table 1, which does not compute to 84%). The authors report a mean return time of 6.0 months in Gowd et al and similar NFL performance scores to matched controls, but a shorter career length for defensive backs in Pagani et al. In Gowd et al, a single-incision approach and dominant-side surgery were associated with a longer time to return, and suture anchor fixation with a lower chance of returning at the same or higher level.
limitations: The review has no described search or appraisal, and it relies on four small retrospective studies with different outcomes, sports and rehabilitation protocols. The authors state that cohorts were not controlled for confounders and that athletes with complications may have been lost to follow-up. Several numbers conflict: the pooled 95.3% is not reproducible from per-study counts (121 of 128 by simple sum), McGinnis is 94% in the text but 95% in Table 1, Pagani's 84% does not match 21 of 22, and the dominant-side odds ratio is 6.370 in the text but 0.749 in Table 2. This is a pre-proof version that may change before publication.
practicalImplications: Discuss with the athlete and coach before surgery that the chance of return is high but usually not within the same season, with a mean of about 39 weeks. Surgical choices such as a single-incision approach or suture anchor fixation are associated with differences in return, but the authors say the evidence is not decisive. Early mobilisation may help return time, though this is not yet proven.
athleteDev: Plan the post-repair progression over a full season rather than weeks, because the authors report a mean of about 39 weeks to return. Only two included studies reported their rehabilitation protocol, with resisted strengthening from about 6 weeks and sport-specific work over the following 12 weeks in one, and the authors state current protocols are not evidence based.
rtp: The review reports that about 95% of athletes returned to sport after distal biceps repair, about 82% to the same level, at a mean of about 39 weeks, with a range of 27.6 to 50 weeks. It cannot set clearance criteria or a safe-return timeline for an individual athlete, because the source studies are small, retrospective and use no standard criteria.

citation: Ito N, Martin JA, Joachim MR, Blemker SS, Opar DA, Kliethermes SA, et al. Quantifying Muscle Volume Deficits Among 38 Lower Extremity Muscles in Collegiate Football Athletes After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction. Am J Sports Med. 2025.
abstract: Quadriceps dysfunction is common after ACL reconstruction (ACLR). This exploratory cross-sectional study used MRI with machine-learning segmentation to quantify volume deficits across 38 lower extremity muscles in 30 male Division I football athletes after primary unilateral ACLR. The largest deficits were in the uniarticular quadriceps, followed by the gastrocnemii. The fibularis group was larger in the surgical limb, and most other muscles showed no difference between limbs.
tldr: In collegiate football players about two years after ACL reconstruction and back to full play, quadriceps volume remained lower on the surgical side. Gastrocnemius volume was also lower, which suggests plantarflexor work deserves consideration.
methods: Secondary analysis of a prospective cohort of Division I football athletes with primary unilateral ACLR and lower extremity MRI at full participation. Volumes were segmented automatically from 3-T MRI, normalized to body weight and height, converted to Z scores, and compared between limbs with paired t tests, with a forest plot ranking muscles by standardized mean difference. A separate analysis excluded hamstring autografts (n = 25).
findings: The three uniarticular quadriceps muscles showed the largest surgical-limb deficits, and the biarticular rectus femoris showed a similar deficit that was not significant. The medial and lateral gastrocnemii were lower in the surgical limb, while the soleus was not. The combined fibularis muscles were greater in the surgical limb. Semitendinosus did not differ overall (mean difference -0.15 mL/kg/m, 95% CI -0.32 to 0.02, P = .080). Across athletes, vasti volume symmetry was positively associated with time from surgery (R2 0.19 to 0.49), but rectus femoris and gastrocnemius symmetry were not.
limitations: Cross-sectional design, so causation and change over time cannot be inferred. Small single-team sample with no power analysis and many comparisons, so some findings (notably the fibularis result) may be type I errors and null results may be type II errors. Muscle volume was not paired with strength or function measures.
practicalImplications: Quadriceps volume deficits were still present in high-level athletes who had returned to sport, which supports keeping isolated quadriceps strengthening in rehabilitation and beyond. The gastrocnemius deficit suggests that isolated plantarflexion strengthening could be considered, but this study does not show that it changes outcomes.
athleteDev: Quadriceps volume deficits persisted for years in returned-to-play collegiate players, so strength plans should keep the quadriceps as a priority. The study did not test whether training closes these deficits.
rtp: The study shows that muscle volume asymmetries can persist after athletes return to full participation. It cannot establish readiness to return to sport, because it did not link the deficits to re-injury or performance.

citation: Simonsson R, Sundberg A, Piussi R, Högberg J, Senorski C, Thomeé R, et al. Questioning the rules of engagement: a critical analysis of the use of limb symmetry index for safe return to sport after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction. Br J Sports Med. 2024.
abstract: This observational cohort study used Project ACL registry data from 233 athletes aged 15 to 30 years with a pre-injury Tegner score of 6 or higher after ACL reconstruction. Limb symmetry index (LSI) from knee strength and three hop tests was evaluated against a safe return to sport, defined as no second ACL injury within 2 years. LSI cut-offs, continuous LSI and deviation from symmetry did not reliably differentiate athletes with a safe return from those without, although 80% or 85% LSI on all tests was associated with lower odds of a safe return.
tldr: In young athletes after ACL reconstruction, limb symmetry index from strength and hop tests did not reliably separate those who returned to sport safely from those who had a second ACL injury within 2 years. LSI should be one part of return-to-sport decisions, not the only one.
methods: Observational cohort using prospectively collected data from the Project ACL rehabilitation registry in Gothenburg. Athletes aged 15 to 30 with pre-injury Tegner of 6 or higher and a completed muscle function test battery at return to sport were included. LSI was tested with ROC and AUC for best cut-offs, with logistic regression for predefined cut-offs (80% to 90%), for each 1% increment in LSI, and for deviation from 100% symmetry. Outcome was a second ACL injury within 2 years of return.
findings: Of 233 athletes, 37 (16%) had a second ACL injury within 2 years of return. Best-differentiating LSI cut-offs had poor discrimination (AUC 0.50 to 0.59; the vertical hop cut-off was significant at P = .04 but had no useful discrimination). Meeting 80% LSI on all tests (OR 0.32, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.87) or 85% (OR 0.39, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.84) was associated with lower odds of a safe return, with poor AUCs of 0.60 to 0.61. Meeting 90% was not significant (OR 0.65). Each 1% change in LSI or in deviation from symmetry had no significant association with a safe return, except the vertical hop LSI (OR 0.97 per 1%, P = .04).
limitations: Return to sport was defined by a self-rated Tegner score recorded only at scheduled follow-ups, so the true return date may differ and the rating does not show training exposure. Concomitant cartilage and meniscal injuries were not recorded, second injuries were self-reported, and absolute limb values were not considered. The abstract reports no effect of a 1% increase in LSI, while Table 1 shows a significant vertical hop association (P = .04); the authors note the cut-offs require replication in another cohort.
practicalImplications: LSI from knee strength and hop tests should not be the only basis for clearing an athlete to return to sport. The study does not show a cut-off that identifies a safe return, so LSI results should sit alongside time since surgery, psychological readiness and other measures. The finding that 80% or 85% LSI on all tests was linked to lower odds of a safe return should be treated as a weak signal with poor discrimination.
athleteDev: For performance staff, the study does not support using a single LSI score to predict who is ready to play. Strength and hop testing can still help track progress and motivation, but the results do not identify which athletes will avoid a second ACL injury.
rtp: The study addresses return-to-sport testing directly and finds that LSI cut-offs from strength and hop tests cannot reliably separate athletes with a safe return from those who later re-injure. It cannot be used to certify a safe return to sport on LSI alone, and it does not show that any particular test battery is sufficient for clearance.

citation: Power D, Haddad F, Wallis S, Baar K. Ramping Isometrics for Accelerated Return to Play following Hamstring Tendon Repair: A Case Study. Journal of Elite Sport Performance. 2023.
abstract: This case study describes an elite international rugby union player with a retracted semimembranosus tear, combined with biceps femoris and semitendinosus injury, treated with surgical repair. The authors used a low-jerk ramping isometric protocol early in rehabilitation, alongside progressive loading and nutrition support. The player returned to team training at 10 weeks, returned to play at 12 weeks after surgery, and had no reinjury over the following two seasons.
tldr: One elite rugby player returned to play 12 weeks after a surgically repaired semimembranosus tear, using early ramped isometrics within a bundled rehabilitation and nutrition plan. This single case shows the protocol was tolerated without reinjury, not that it speeds recovery.
methods: Clinical case description of one player's post-surgical rehabilitation. Isometric loading began in the first session as 5-second ramps, a 20-second hold and a 5-second release, with a load sensor and phone app used for feedback. Strength was tracked with isometric heel-dig tests on a force platform and Nordic eccentric tests, and MRI was repeated at 8 weeks after surgery.
findings: Nordic eccentric strength improved steadily with exposure; a 17.5% eccentric limb symmetry deficit remained at week 9 and the player returned to training with a 14% eccentric deficit. The authors report absolute eccentric strength above pre-injury baseline at return to play, and a between-limb imbalance they describe as moderate. Over the 16-week period, the summed eight skinfolds fell by 18.6 mm and body mass by 0.9 kg, and high-speed running distances after return were above pre-injury levels.
limitations: This is a single uncontrolled case, and the protocol was one part of a multimodal program, so no effect of the isometric protocol can be isolated. The authors note that eccentric tests after running were fatigued, and that the isometric and eccentric results did not agree.
practicalImplications: This case supports discussing early, pain-free ramped isometric loading with the surgeon after proximal hamstring tendon repair, with close monitoring of symptoms and tendon status. It does not establish a standard timeline, and the isometric dose and ramp rate should not be assumed to transfer to other injuries.
athleteDev: Performance Application: The case shows a staged progression from isometrics to eccentric, reactive and high-speed work, with Nordic and isometric tests tracked as limb symmetry. Running was built from partial body-weight treadmill sessions to pitch-based high-speed running with GPS-based targets.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: The 12-week return came from one player who passed the other criteria and still had a 14% eccentric deficit. It cannot set a return timeline for other players or injury grades, and it cannot show that ramped isometrics shorten recovery. Reinjury data cover only the two seasons reported.

citation: Bashaireh KM, Yabroudi MA, Logerstedt D, Snyder-Mackler L, Nawasreh ZH. Reasons for Not Returning to Pre-injury Sport Level After ACL-Reconstruction. Int J Sports Med. 2024.
abstract: The study surveyed athletes about 2 years after hamstring-autograft ACL reconstruction to find whether they had returned to their pre-injury sport level and, if not, why, and which factors were linked to the main reasons. Only 10% of the 91 athletes had returned to their pre-injury level. Lack of confidence or fear of re-injury and post-surgical knee impairment were the most common reasons, and knee giving-way was the only significant predictor of knee impairment.
tldr: Only 10% of 91 athletes had returned to their pre-injury sport level two years after hamstring-graft ACL reconstruction. Fear of re-injury, low confidence and knee impairment were the main reasons given, and giving-way episodes were the only factor tied to ongoing knee impairment.
methods: Cross-sectional survey of athletes aged 14 to 50 who had a primary hamstring-autograft ACL reconstruction 1 to 5 years earlier and played level I or II sports, carried out between July 2017 and August 2018. Athletes completed a self-administered questionnaire on pre-injury sport, return to sport, knee giving-way and second knee injuries, and chose and ranked reasons for not returning, with injuries confirmed by MRI and surgical reports. Univariate logistic regression tested predictors of the two most common reasons.
findings: Nine of 91 athletes (10%; 95% CI 4.6 to 17.9%) had returned to their pre-injury level at a mean follow-up of 1.8 years. Among the 82 who gave reasons, lack of confidence or fear of re-injury was most common (56 athletes, 68.3%), followed by post-surgical knee impairment (43 athletes, 52.4%), and little time or work and family obligations (each 23.2%). Knee giving-way was the only significant predictor of knee impairment as a reason (OR 8.3, 95% CI 2.48 to 27.42, p = 0.001), and no variable significantly predicted fear or lack of confidence.
limitations: The cross-sectional, self-report design carries recall bias, and about 30% of eligible athletes did not respond or were lost, although the authors found no demographic differences. Only two women took part, so results cannot be generalised to women, and rehabilitation was not standardised. Knee giving-way was not confirmed by clinical tests or MRI, and the sample is small. The abstract reports 48.8% and 39% for the two main reasons, which are the shares naming each as the only or primary reason; the Results values for any mention (68.3% and 52.4%) are reported here.
practicalImplications: Rehabilitation should check fear, confidence and knee impairment, for example by assessing psychological status, explaining expected timelines and gradually exposing athletes to higher knee demands. Athletes who report giving-way should have dynamic knee stability addressed before high-demand sport, and their own view of knee impairment should be asked about during rehabilitation.
athleteDev: Performance Application: Reported giving-way was tied to ongoing knee impairment, so performance staff should watch for it during return-to-training and build dynamic knee stability work before high-demand sessions. Fear and low confidence were the leading reasons athletes had not returned, and the authors suggest addressing them with psychological checks and graded exposure.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: The study explains why athletes 1 to 5 years after reconstruction had not returned, so it can guide which psychological and knee-stability items to check before clearance. It did not identify criteria that predict return, and it cannot show that addressing these reasons raises return rates.

citation: Buckthorpe M, Danelon F, La Rosa G, Nanni G, Stride M, Della Villa F. Recommendations for Hamstring Function Recovery After ACL Reconstruction. Sports Med. 2020.
abstract: The authors discuss deficits in hamstring function after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR), particularly with ipsilateral hamstring autograft, and how to restore them within the functional recovery process. They cover training principles such as optimal loading, eccentric and longer-length strengthening, balance of knee- and hip-dominant exercises, functional strength, and a stage-by-stage programme. They also propose return-to-sport hamstring testing and criteria.
tldr: After ACL reconstruction with a hamstring graft, knee flexor strength often stays below the other leg at return to sport and for years afterwards. The authors propose a staged hamstring programme that moves from low-load isometrics to high-speed running, and they recommend testing knee flexor strength before return to sport.
methods: Narrative review and recommendation paper by a multidisciplinary group, with no systematic search described. The authors combine hamstring injury prevention and rehabilitation research, ACLR studies, and their own staged rehabilitation framework (Table 2) to set out training principles, stage goals, exercise choices and return-to-sport criteria.
findings: Knee flexor strength deficits after ACLR are common and are usually 0 to 20% at return to sport, with larger deficits after hamstring tendon grafts. Reported knee flexor isometric LSI after hamstring grafts was 54%, 70% and 76% at 4, 8 and 12 weeks. The proposed training principles include periodised resistance training, eccentric and long-length work, a balance of knee-dominant and hip-dominant exercises, and high-speed running in the late stage. The recommended return-to-sport screen is a knee flexor LSI of 90% or more, a knee flexor to extensor ratio of 60% or more, and a knee flexor peak torque of 1.5 Nm/kg at 90 degrees per second.
limitations: As a narrative review with no described search, the selection of evidence cannot be checked. Much of the supporting evidence comes from hamstring injury populations rather than ACLR, and the authors state that evidence is missing on several points, including whether to delay hamstring loading after graft harvest, the timing of stage transitions, and the choice of exercises in the presence of tendon regeneration problems.
practicalImplications: Test knee flexor strength, and not only the standard knee extensor and hop tests, before clearing an ACLR athlete for return to sport. Progress from isometric and low-load work early, to moderate-load hypertrophy and strength work in mid stage, to high-load eccentric, long-length and high-speed running work late in the programme. Use both knee-dominant exercises, such as the Nordic hamstring exercise, and hip-dominant exercises.
athleteDev: Build hamstring work into the late-stage block with heavy eccentric and long-length exercise and high-speed running, then add explosive and sport-specific work as the athlete tolerates it. Where a hamstring graft was used, balance knee-dominant and hip-dominant exercises to address both the knee flexors and the medial and lateral hamstring muscles.
rtp: Use the knee flexor LSI of at least 90%, knee flexor to extensor ratio of at least 60%, and knee flexor peak torque of about 1.5 Nm/kg at 90 degrees per second as the authors' proposed screening standard, with eccentric testing (for example NordBord LSI above 90% and peak force above 350 N) where available. These thresholds are proposals, not outcomes shown to reduce re-injury, so they cannot prove an athlete is ready to return. The review cannot say whether these criteria reduce re-injury rates.

citation: Brukner P, Nealon A, Morgan C, Burgess D, Dunn A. Recurrent hamstring muscle injury: applying the limited evidence in the professional football setting with a seven-point programme. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2014;48:929-938.
abstract: A professional footballer with five hamstring injuries in five months was managed with a seven-part programme and returned to play at 42 days, then missed no games due to hamstring problems. The paper reviews the limited evidence for each intervention and states that which component caused the outcome cannot be determined.
tldr: A single professional player with repeated hamstring injuries recovered with a multi-part programme that combined biomechanical correction, neural mobilisation, eccentric strengthening and a high-speed running overload. Clinicians should treat it as a case example, not as a tested protocol.
methods: Clinical case description of one 26-year-old professional footballer with five hamstring episodes over five months. Management after the fifth episode combined orthotics for a 5 mm functional leg length difference with osteopathic manual therapy, more aggressive neural mobilisation and lumbar manual therapy, core stability work, a 1-in-3-day eccentric strength programme, an eight-cycle high-speed running overload programme tracked with GPS, local anaesthetic, Traumeel and Actovegin injections, and yoga-based stretching and relaxation. Two L4-5 epidural steroid injections had been given earlier, after the third episode and between the fourth and fifth, and the evidence base for each intervention was reviewed.
findings: The player returned to full-team training 33 days and was available for selection at 39 days after the fifth episode, then returned to play at 42 days. He played 33 of 42 possible games to season end, missing seven games with a ruptured plantaris but none for hamstring problems. The overload running programme gave 49.8% more high-speed running distance than the previous standard rehabilitation, with 16.8% more training time, and the player reported subjective improvement in hamstring freedom.
limitations: Single case with no control group, so no causal attribution is possible. Seven interventions were applied together, and the authors state that the key component cannot be identified. Outcomes after the return are described only as games played and absence, and the subjective improvements are self-reported. The authors note there have been no controlled trials of Actovegin or Traumeel for hamstring injury. Table 1 lists 28 days to team training and 38 days to play for episode 5, which differs from the 33 and 42 days given in the Outcome section.
practicalImplications: For a recurrent hamstring injury with neural or lumbopelvic symptoms, the paper suggests assessing those factors alongside the muscle, and it describes how a high-speed running overload block was used to build running load before return. It supports individualised, multi-component management with planned monitoring, but not a fixed protocol.
athleteDev: The paper describes monitoring a player's training and match running with GPS, heart rate and HRV, and using that data to shape a high-speed running overload block and conditioning. It does not test whether these methods improve performance in athletes without injury.
rtp: The player returned to full training at 33 days and to play at 42 days after the fifth episode, and then had no further hamstring absence. The paper can illustrate one return-to-play pathway for a recurrent hamstring injury, but a single case cannot set return-to-play criteria or a safe timeline for other athletes.

citation: Gadbois WJ, Cohn H, Vaidya R. Reframing Recovery: Fantasy Sports Metrics as Scalable Tools for Measuring Post-injury Athletic Performance. Cureus. 2025;17(9):e91602.
abstract: Return to play does not show whether athletes regain their pre-injury performance. This review used a targeted PubMed search to find six studies that used fantasy scores or WAR to measure post-injury performance in the NFL, NBA, MLB and NHL. Fantasy scores and WAR fell after injury in 14 of 15 sport-specific cohorts, and the authors propose them as a basis for a standardized return to pre-injury performance (RPIP) measure.
tldr: Across six small studies of professional North American athletes, fantasy scores and WAR usually dropped after injury. Staff can use them as a candidate performance outcome alongside return to play, but not yet as a validated measure.
methods: Narrative review with a targeted PubMed search for studies using fantasy scores or WAR to measure post-injury performance in the four major North American leagues. Studies were required to stratify by injury type and use publicly available scoring data. Six studies met criteria, and each was appraised with the STROBE checklist.
findings: Six studies (15 cohorts, 785 athletes) were included. Fantasy scores or WAR declined after injury in 14 of 15 cohorts, including NFL ACL cohorts where running backs and wide receivers declined (p<0.05) and NFL ankle injury cohorts (p<0.0001). The one exception was an MLB tibial fracture cohort (n=9) that improved by 8.1%. Only two studies referred to RPIP.
limitations: Seven of 15 cohorts had fewer than 20 athletes. Most studies were retrospective and excluded players who retired after injury, which may underestimate declines. Few studies reported inferential statistics or effect sizes, the search was limited to PubMed, and scoring systems varied across platforms. The authors call the design narrative, although a defined search was used.
practicalImplications: Fantasy scores and WAR are public, game-by-game and comparable across seasons, so they could be tracked to see whether an athlete is producing at a pre-injury level after return. Because the evidence is small and retrospective, any such use should be a supplementary check next to clinical measures.
athleteDev: Performance Application: a player's fantasy or WAR output before and after a lower-limb or spine injury can serve as a longitudinal performance reference, but the review does not provide thresholds or benchmarks for judging readiness.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: the review supports the idea that return to play does not capture performance recovery, but it cannot be used to set return-to-play criteria, clearance thresholds or expected percentage recovery, because no RPIP standard or validated cut-off exists.

citation: Mayer MA, Deliso M, Hong IS, et al. Rehabilitation and Return to Play Protocols After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction in Soccer Players: A Systematic Review. Am J Sports Med. 2024.
abstract: This systematic review of 23 studies (874 soccer players after ACL reconstruction) looked for rehabilitation protocols and functional tests that support return to play in soccer. The authors found no consensus, with wide heterogeneity in protocols and test batteries, return-to-play times of 3 to 8 months, and few reports of complications or long-term follow-up.
tldr: Rehabilitation and return-to-play testing after ACL reconstruction in soccer lack standardization, and the evidence is small, mostly retrospective and male-dominated. Staff should document and justify their own test batteries and progression criteria rather than adopt a protocol from this review.
methods: Systematic review of PubMed, Embase and CENTRAL following PRISMA, with two independent reviewers for selection and data extraction. Original studies at level of evidence 1 to 4 that reported rehabilitation protocols, knee rehabilitation metrics or clinical outcomes in soccer players after ACL reconstruction were included. Non-randomized studies were appraised with MINORS and the two RCTs with RoB 2. Weighted means and pooled percentages were calculated for participant characteristics.
