findings: Twenty-three studies (874 players) were included, with 5 accelerated and 7 criterion-based protocols and 11 unclassified. Two studies used all three test batteries (strength, hop and movement quality), eight used two, twelve used one and one used none. Mean surgery-to-return-to-play times ranged from 3 to 8 months. Only one study reported a return rate (95% returned to the same professional level), two reported complications, and all nine studies reporting PROMs showed significant improvement.
limitations: Heterogeneity in sample size, protocols and outcomes limited pooling, and long-term follow-up was lacking (mean follow-up ranged from 4 to 19.2 months). Most studies were retrospective, female players were under-represented, and the authors note the findings may not apply to other sports. Risk of bias was rated by a single reviewer, and the review did not assess the predictive value of any test.
practicalImplications: Clinicians can see that strength, hop and movement-quality batteries are common, but no single battery or criteria set has been shown to predict safe return. Programs should set and record their own progression criteria, and test results should be interpreted alongside clinical examination and the athlete's history.
athleteDev: Performance Application: the review supports using multi-domain test batteries during rehabilitation, but it does not give validated thresholds or identify which tests predict on-field performance, so any cut-off has to come from the program itself.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: the study reports mean surgery-to-return-to-play times of 3 to 8 months, but it reports return rates in only one study and complications in two, so it cannot be used to set a clearance date, a return-rate target or the claim that a specific test makes return safe.

citation: Gokeler A, Dingenen B, Hewett TE. Rehabilitation and Return to Sport Testing After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction: Where Are We in 2022? Arthroscopy, Sports Medicine, and Rehabilitation. 2022;4(1):e77-e82.
abstract: Athletes after ACL reconstruction often aim to return to preinjury sport, but few do, and second ACL injury rates are high after return. This clinical commentary reviews the current literature on RTS testing after ACL reconstruction and concludes that the validity of RTS criteria remains uncertain.
tldr: Current return-to-sport test batteries after ACL reconstruction have uncertain validity, and common cut-offs such as a 90% limb symmetry index do not capture knee function. Staff should treat a passed test battery as one input to a clinical decision, not as clearance on its own.
methods: Clinical commentary giving a critical overview of the literature on RTS testing after ACL reconstruction. The paper describes no systematic search, and its evidence is drawn from the cited studies and meta-analyses. Sections cover strength, hop tests, movement quality, psychological factors, rehabilitation approach, timing and consequences of testing.
findings: The authors cite a meta-analysis in which only 23% of patients passed RTS test batteries before return, and report that passing criteria reduced subsequent graft rupture risk by 60% but raised contralateral rupture risk by 235%. Only 14% of patients reached an LSI of 100% for strength at two years, and 60% of patients showed abnormal landing kinematics even though 72.3% passed an LSI above 90% on hop tests. A test battery with an 80% pass rate per test falls to 64% for two tests and 51% for three.
limitations: The commentary offers a critical narrative rather than a formal evidence grade, and its key claims depend on the cited studies. The abstract's 40% second ACL injury rate for athletes under 20 differs from the body, which attributes the 40% figure to men's Australian football. Exposure to high-risk activity after testing is often unreported, so test validity cannot be judged fully from these studies.
practicalImplications: Use a multi-domain battery (strength, hop and movement quality) but do not rely on a single limb symmetry cut-off, because a passed LSI can coexist with abnormal landing mechanics. Record the athlete's exposure after clearance, since the authors argue that second-injury risk depends on what athletes do after testing.
athleteDev: Performance Application: the commentary supports measuring absolute strength and movement quality as well as limb symmetry during rehabilitation, because symmetry can mask deficits in both limbs. It does not provide validated performance thresholds.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: the paper shows that current RTS batteries have uncertain validity and that passing them does not reliably identify athletes at risk of second ACL injury. It cannot be used to set a specific LSI threshold, a clearance date or a required test pass rate as a standalone decision rule.

citation: Robins RJ, Daruwalla JH, Gamradt SC, et al. Return to Play After Shoulder Instability Surgery in National Collegiate Athletic Association Division I Intercollegiate Football Athletes. Am J Sports Med. 2017.
abstract: Retrospective case series of 153 NCAA Division I football players with 177 shoulder instability surgeries from seven programs. Return to play was 85.4% after isolated arthroscopic surgery with no difference by repair type, and returning players played a larger share of games than before their injury.
tldr: In Division I football players, about 85% of those who had arthroscopic shoulder stabilization without other procedures returned to play, and returners often played in a larger share of games than before injury. Starters and scholarship players returned most often.
methods: Retrospective case series of athletes from seven Division I football programs in the Pac-12, ACC and SEC, covering the 2004-2013 seasons. Data included instability direction, type of surgery, time to resume play, and games played and depth-chart status before and after surgery. Return to play required clearance from medical and athletic training staff and a return to the roster, and chi-square and Fisher exact tests were used.
findings: Of 177 procedures in 153 athletes, 168 were arthroscopic and 9 were open bone-block operations. Return to play was 85.4% after isolated arthroscopic surgery, with no significant difference by repair type (82.4% anterior, 92.9% posterior, 84.8% combined), and games played rose from 49.9% before injury to 71.5% after surgery (P < .0001). Among returners, 15.6% later had a shoulder injury causing missed practices or games and 10.3% had recurrent instability requiring reduction or revision surgery.
limitations: Retrospective design with possible recall or exclusion bias, no control group, and games-played data missing for two of seven schools (only 142 players analyzed for that outcome). Open-surgery numbers were small (9), and instability episodes that did not need reduction or revision were not recorded. The authors state the results should not be used to judge recurrent instability, because return to play, depth chart and games played do not measure it.
practicalImplications: For a collegiate football player with shoulder instability, surgery led to a high return rate in this series. Expect lower return odds for players who rarely played before injury (75.7%) and for non-scholarship players (65.5%), and discuss later shoulder problems, which affected 15.6% of returners, with 10.3% having recurrent instability needing reduction or revision.
athleteDev: Players who returned often played a larger share of games and kept or improved their depth-chart role after surgery, which can serve as a benchmark when planning roles. The study has no control group, so it cannot show that surgery itself caused these changes.
rtp: The series gives return-to-play rates after shoulder stabilization in collegiate football, with 85.4% returning after isolated arthroscopic surgery and 10.3% of returners having recurrent instability needing reduction or revision. It does not set safe timing or readiness criteria, and it missed milder instability episodes, so it is weak evidence for clearing an individual athlete.

citation: Rosenthal MD, Wellsandt M, Specht Z. Return to Play After Shoulder Stabilization: What If This Isn't Going Well? Oper Tech Sports Med. 2024:151134.
abstract: Clinical review of return to play after shoulder stabilization in athletes who are struggling to return. It covers the wide variation in return rates, the lag in performance after return to sport, and the impairments and interventions that may explain poor outcomes.
tldr: Return to play after shoulder stabilization varies widely, and clearance by time alone misses impairments that matter. Rehabilitation should check range of motion, strength, neuromuscular control, kinetic chain mobility and psychological readiness before and during the return-to-sport progression.
methods: Clinical review chapter. No systematic search or appraisal method is described. The chapter draws on published consensus statements, rehabilitation guidelines, return-to-sport studies and assessment methods, and sets out a phased framework with assessment techniques and exercise examples.
findings: The chapter reports return-to-sport rates of 63% to 100% after stabilization, with performance lagging return to sport by 6% to 25%, most in throwing athletes. Time was the sole clearance criterion in 75% of studies it cites. It reports that athletes who did not undergo criterion-based return-to-sport testing were 4.85 times as likely to have recurrent instability after return, with a 22% recurrence rate versus 5% for those required to pass it.
limitations: Narrative review with no described search or appraisal method. Several thresholds it presents come from studies of throwers and swimmers, and the chapter itself notes there is no consensus on return-to-play criteria or on the use of ER/IR ratios in collision sports.
practicalImplications: Base the return-to-play decision on a test battery that covers range of motion (including total rotation arc asymmetry above 5 degrees in throwers), strength and endurance, neuromuscular control, kinetic chain mobility and psychological readiness, rather than time since surgery alone. Track workload with the acute:chronic ratio, while noting that the chapter's sources link ratios above 1.3 to injury in swimmers and overhead throwers.
athleteDev: Returning to sport does not mean returning to performance. The chapter reports that performance lags return to sport by 6% to 25%, so staff should track strength, rate of force development, endurance and workload through the advanced phase, not only clearance.
rtp: Clearance by time alone is not enough. The chapter recommends criterion-based return-to-sport testing and reports that athletes who did not undergo it had more recurrent instability. It gives reference thresholds rather than validated pass or fail cut-offs, so it cannot clear an individual athlete by itself.

citation: Read CR, Aune KT, Cain EL Jr, Fleisig GS. Return to Play and Decreased Performance After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction in National Football League Defensive Players. Am J Sports Med. 2017;45(8):1815-1821.
abstract: Matched case-control and cohort study of 38 NFL defensive players after ACL reconstruction, compared with 38 matched controls. Players who returned were above-average before injury and were about average after returning, and fewer than two-thirds returned for at least half a season.
tldr: About 61% of NFL defensive players who had ACL reconstruction returned for at least half a season, and those who did were above-average players before injury. After returning, their starts and solo tackles fell to about the level of average players, so counseling should cover both return and performance.
methods: Retrospective matched case-control and cohort study. Defensive players with ACL reconstruction from 2006 to 2012, identified from public injury reports, were matched to controls on position and years of NFL experience, with performance statistics taken from the NFL database for seasons before and after injury. Successful return was defined as at least 8 games after surgery, and analyses used t tests, chi-squared tests, repeated-measures ANOVA and Kaplan-Meier survival analysis.
findings: Of 38 injured players, 74% (28/38) played at least one NFL game after surgery and 61% (23/38) played at least 8 games. Before injury, returners started more games (80.9% vs 52.3% for non-returners) and made more solo tackles per game (3.44 vs 1.77) than non-returners, and after surgery their starts fell to 57.0% and solo tackles to 2.38 per game while matched controls did not decline significantly. Returners also showed a trend toward earlier retirement that did not reach significance (P = .064).
limitations: The retrospective design relies on public media and the NFL database, so some injuries may be missed, and concomitant injuries, graft type, technique and rehabilitation were not recorded; position subgroups were small and no multivariable adjustment was made. The abstract describes retirement as significantly sooner and more frequent, but the results give P = .064. The abstract's comparison values do not match the tables (non-returners 54% starts and 1.82 solo tackles vs Table 1 52.3% and 1.77; controls 52% and 1.77 vs Table 3 60.5% and 2.50), and the table values are reported here.
practicalImplications: In preoperative counseling, expect that about 6 in 10 NFL defensive players will return for at least half a season. Players who started often before injury were the most likely to return, and those who do return may not keep their pre-injury share of starts or tackles, so expectations for role and production should be set accordingly.
athleteDev: Track games started and solo tackles through the first seasons after surgery, since returners declined on both while matched controls did not. In position subgroups, defensive backs significantly lost starts and interceptions, but these subgroups were small (only 3 linemen returned), so position-specific planning rests on thin data.
rtp: The study gives return rates (61% played 8 games) and the timing of return (mean 47.0 weeks after surgery, range 29 to 101 weeks), but it cannot set readiness criteria or safe loading. It has no rehabilitation, graft or concomitant injury data, so it cannot guide the clearance decision for an individual athlete.

citation: Boufadel P, Daher M, Lopez R, Fares MY, Lawand J, Khan AZ, et al. Return to Sport After Distal Biceps Tendon Repair: A Systematic Review. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2025.
abstract: This systematic review pooled 42 clinical studies (1,093 patients) of distal biceps tendon repair to estimate return to sport, functional outcomes and complications. The overall return-to-sport rate was 91.5% at a mean of 6.3 months, and athletes alone returned at 96.4%.
tldr: Most patients return to sport after distal biceps tendon repair, at a pooled rate of 91.5% around six months. Athletes returned at a similar rate of 96.4%, but took a mean of 9.4 months.
methods: PRISMA systematic review of PubMed, Embase and Google Scholar, searched to December 2023, for clinical studies reporting return to sport after distal biceps repair. Two reviewers screened the studies independently, and outcomes were summarized descriptively in Stata across incision, fixation and rehabilitation groups.
findings: The overall return-to-sport rate was 91.5%, and 506 of 594 patients (85.2%) returned to preinjury level or higher. Athletes had a return rate of 96.4% at a mean of 9.4 months. Complications occurred in 19.2% of patients, most often sensory neurapraxia, and 2.2% needed reoperation. Bone tunnel fixation, two weeks of immobilization and early active motion were associated with higher return rates, but only as trends in pooled data.
limitations: All studies were level 3 or 4 evidence, outcome measures and protocols varied widely, and many studies did not report time to return. Incision, fixation and rehabilitation comparisons were not formally tested. The sample was 99.2% male and only 15.5% athletes, so the pooled rate is mainly a patient estimate.
practicalImplications: Injured athletes can be told that return to sport after distal biceps repair is common, at about six months across the pooled sample and about nine months in athletes. Fear of rerupture and poor mental health were reported as reasons some patients did not return, so these should be discussed during rehabilitation.
athleteDev: The review gives a realistic timeline for athletes who rely on elbow flexion and forearm supination, but it reports no strength or performance benchmarks, so training targets need other sources.
rtp: Athletes returned in 96.4% of cases at a mean of 9.4 months, and early active motion and bone tunnel fixation showed trends toward higher return rates. These trends were not tested statistically, so they cannot justify choosing one protocol over another.

citation: Wulf MW, Mackey AL, Kjær M, Bayer ML. Return to Sport, Reinjury Rate, and Tissue Changes after Muscle Strain Injury: A Narrative Review. Translational Sports Medicine. 2024;2024:Article 2336376.
abstract: This narrative review examines how resistance training in rehabilitation affects return to sport, reinjury rate and tissue changes after acute muscle strain. Across the studies, mean time to return ranged from 15 to 86 days and reinjury from 0% to 70%, and structural changes appeared to persist after injury.
tldr: Eccentric work at long muscle lengths and an early start to rehabilitation shortened return time in some trials. Reinjury rates varied widely, and the muscle and tendon changes after a strain may not fully resolve.
methods: Narrative review of randomized controlled trials that included a resistance training component in strain rehabilitation, and observational studies of tissue morphology after muscle strain. No systematic search strategy is described.
findings: Mean time to return to sport ranged from 15 to 86 days across eight studies, and mean reinjury rates from 0% to 70%. In the Askling studies, the long-length eccentric protocol reduced time to return by 45% and 38%, with low reinjury in all groups. In Bayer et al., early rehabilitation (day two) returned athletes in 63 days versus 83 days for delayed rehabilitation (day nine), with no difference in strength or muscle mass at return. Several other trials found no difference in return time between programs. Imaging-based injury severity was linked to longer return time in some studies, and muscle atrophy and aponeurosis changes were reported to persist for months to years.
limitations: The review is narrative with no described search method, and the sample is largely hamstring strains in young athletes (mean age about 25). Trials differed in return-to-sport criteria, injury grading and follow-up length, and most had small samples, so their findings are not directly comparable.
practicalImplications: For acute hamstring or calf strains, staff can start rehabilitation early and include eccentric work at long muscle lengths, which these studies associate with shorter return time. Return dates should be treated as individual, since the cross-study range was wide and reinjury risk did not always fall as return time lengthened.
athleteDev: Performance Application: Eccentric loading at long muscle length is the element the review supports most strongly for rebuilding hamstring capacity after strain, but it gives no sprint, power or load targets for the return phase.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: Early rehabilitation start and long-length eccentric work were linked to shorter time to return in some trials, but the review cannot predict an individual return date from injury severity. The authors note a gap between subjective readiness, physical tests and tissue state at return, so clearance should not be read as full tissue recovery.

citation: Mohtadi NG, Chan DS. Return to Sport-Specific Performance After Primary Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction: A Systematic Review. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2017.
abstract: This systematic review identified 15 prognostic studies of sport-specific performance after primary ACL reconstruction in competitive athletes and rated their risk of bias. Most high-level athletes returned to sport, the bulk of evidence showed a measurable decline in performance statistics that was highly sport-specific, and the literature was judged highly biased.
tldr: Many elite athletes return to sport after ACL reconstruction, but performance data are sparse, sport-specific and mostly biased. Expect a possible performance decline, not a fixed figure.
methods: Systematic review of Ovid MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane databases and PubMed, with hand searching of reference lists, for prognostic studies of sport-specific performance after primary ACL reconstruction. Two authors independently selected and extracted the studies, and each was rated on six QUIPS bias domains, with the overall rating based on participation, prognostic factor and confounding domains.
findings: Return to sport ranged from 63% (NFL players) to 97% (NHL players) across studies. Most studies reported no change or a decline in performance statistics after reconstruction, while three reported better performance in the ACLR group than in controls (hockey, soccer and alpine skiing). Most control-group comparisons favored the controls, but many lacked the numbers to show a difference and few corrected for multiple testing. Twelve of 15 studies were rated high risk of bias, mostly for how athletes were identified, and the two NHL studies reached different return and performance results depending on how injured players were found.
limitations: Only high-performance or professional athletes were studied, and no meta-analysis was possible because the outcomes and performance measures varied by sport. Most studies were small, did not correct for multiple testing, and used a case-control design that is closer to a retrospective cohort. Non-returning athletes were not measured, so performance among returners may be overstated.
practicalImplications: Staff counseling athletes about ACL reconstruction can say that many elite athletes return to sport, but that measured performance after return has generally declined or not changed, with large variation by sport. Because the data are biased, performance expectations should be presented as uncertain rather than as a fixed number.
athleteDev: Performance Application: The review gives no performance benchmark for returning athletes, so programs can only use it to justify tracking sport-specific output before and after injury, which the authors themselves recommend.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: Most high-performance athletes returned to sport after ACL reconstruction (63% to 97%), but the review cannot show whether returners reach preinjury performance, because non-returners were not measured and the studies are rated highly biased. Return to sport alone should not be treated as evidence of a return to preinjury performance.

citation: Pecci J, Sánchez-Trigo H, Mancha-Triguero D, Sañudo B, Reverte-Pagola G, del Ojo-López JJ, et al. Return to performance: machine learning insights into how absence time following muscle injuries affects match running performance in LaLiga soccer players. Biology of Sport. 2025;42(4):275-286.
abstract: This retrospective study of 110 muscle injuries in LaLiga players examined how absence time relates to changes in match running performance, using regression and random forest models. Maximal speed was the variable most strongly associated with longer absence, with maximal acceleration and deceleration also affected, while sprint count was not related to absence time.
tldr: Longer time out after a muscle injury goes with a larger drop in maximal speed, and to a lesser extent acceleration and braking, in match play. Sprint count did not follow absence time, so it should be checked regardless of how long a player was out.
methods: Retrospective design using match external-load data from the 2022-2023 LaLiga season, comparing four pre-injury and four post-injury matches for 110 lower-limb muscle injuries in 90 male players. Pre- and post-injury differences were tested with paired t-tests or Wilcoxon tests, then Pearson correlations with absence time were calculated, and multiple linear regression and random forest models with SHAP values were fitted to absence time using an 80/20 train-test split.
findings: Mean absence was 34.6 days (SD 27.9), with 51 hamstring injuries. Time played, total distance, maximal acceleration, maximal deceleration, maximal speed, sprint distance, relative sprint count and the composite index differed significantly after injury. Maximal speed fell by a mean of 0.48 km/h and showed the strongest correlation with absence (r = -0.355), followed by time played (r = -0.328) and maximal acceleration (r = -0.303). Test-set R2 was 0.348 for linear regression and 0.442 for random forest, and maximal speed was the top feature in both models. Relative sprint count showed the weakest relationship with absence time in both models (r = -0.149).
limitations: The sample is 110 injuries from one season, with a small test set and modest explained variance, and the training-set linear model R2 was only 0.12. The design is observational, so absence time cannot be separated from injury severity, tendon involvement, age or playing role, and no correction for multiple testing is reported.
practicalImplications: After a muscle injury with a longer absence, staff should expect larger drops in match maximal speed and acceleration, so return-to-play criteria should include specific tests of maximal speed and acceleration or braking before clearance. Sprint count did not track absence time, so it should be checked regardless of how long the player was out.
athleteDev: Performance Application: Players returning after longer absences tended to show larger losses of top speed and acceleration in matches, so reconditioning should include speed and acceleration work targeted at those outputs. The paper reports no load prescriptions, so volumes must come from elsewhere.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: The study supports checking maximal speed, acceleration and deceleration before return to play, with more emphasis on those tests after longer absences. It cannot set a return date or a performance threshold for an individual player, and the authors' recommendation to check sprinting regardless of absence time also applies.

citation: Pieters D, Wezenbeek E, Schuermans J, Witvrouw E. Return to Play After a Hamstring Strain Injury: It is Time to Consider Natural Healing. Sports Medicine. 2021.
abstract: This review argues that current return-to-play criteria for hamstring strain injury ignore biological healing time, since muscle and scar tissue are still immature when athletes return at 11 to 25 days. The authors propose a minimum of 4 weeks before return after grade 1 or 2 injuries, alongside a comprehensive functional test battery.
tldr: Athletes are usually cleared for return to play within 2 to 3 weeks of a grade 1 or 2 hamstring strain, before the muscle and scar tissue are mature. The authors propose a minimum 4-week period alongside the usual functional tests.
methods: Review article combining prior return-to-play reviews and consensus statements with a PubMed search (August 2020) for hamstring return-to-play studies, plus a search of reviews on muscle healing. The authors used the findings to describe muscle healing phases, the timing of collagen and adhesion maturation, survey data on return criteria, and imaging evidence.
findings: Average return to play after grade 1 and 2 hamstring strains was 11 to 25 days across criteria studies. In a worldwide survey of 131 premier league football teams, absence of pain, strength, training load and functional tests were the most used criteria, with an 'other' category (including time and imaging) chosen by only 1 to 2%. Basic science reports that muscle regeneration peaks around 2 weeks, type III collagen dominates through 2 to 3 weeks, and a firm attachment between regenerated fibers and scar forms around day 21. One study found about 25% of re-injuries in the first week after return, all at the index location.
limitations: The review is not a systematic synthesis of clinical outcomes, and the 4-week threshold has not been tested in trials. The healing timeline comes from basic science studies of muscle healing, and the authors acknowledge that the proposed minimum may be longer than needed for some grade 1 injuries. Individual healing variability and the role of tendon involvement are unresolved, and the review applies mainly to grade 1 and 2 injuries in football.
practicalImplications: For grade 1 or 2 hamstring strains, staff can treat four weeks from injury as a minimum before clearance, and still apply the functional test battery. The authors suggest that a player who passes functional tests before 4 weeks should still wait, and that a player who fails them after 4 weeks needs further assessment.
athleteDev: Performance Application: The review gives no load, speed or strength targets for the return phase. Its main point for performance staff is that good functional test scores can come before tissue maturity, so early test success should not be read as tissue readiness.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: The review supports a 4-week minimum before clearance for grade 1 and 2 hamstring strains, combined with functional tests and an individual assessment. It cannot show that the 4-week rule reduces re-injury, because that outcome has not been tested, and it does not apply to intratendinous or higher-grade injuries.

citation: van der Horst N, Backx FJG, Goedhart EA, Huisstede BMA, on behalf of the HIPS-Delphi Group. Return to play after hamstring injuries in football (soccer): a worldwide Delphi procedure regarding definition, medical criteria and decision-making. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2017.
abstract: This Delphi consensus study of 58 experts from FIFA Medical Centres of Excellence defined return to play after hamstring injury in football and agreed the medical criteria and decision-makers. The panel defined return to play as criteria-based medical clearance and mental readiness for full availability, and excluded MRI as a criterion.
tldr: Expert consensus defines return to play after hamstring injury as criteria-based clearance plus mental readiness. The criteria include pain-free palpation and tests, field performance and psychological readiness, and MRI is excluded.
methods: Delphi procedure with four online rounds between July 2015 and July 2016, using 58 experts selected from 28 FIFA Medical Centres of Excellence. Items were drawn from a prior systematic review, and consensus was defined as at least 70% agreement, with response rates of 84% to 93%.
findings: The panel agreed that return to play means criteria-based medical clearance and mental readiness for full availability for match selection and/or full training. Agreed criteria were medical staff clearance, absence of pain on palpation, pain-free strength, flexibility and functional testing, similar hamstring flexibility (0% to 10% difference), field performance testing and psychological readiness; similar eccentric hamstring strength was added as a potential criterion only in round 4, with the panel still divided. Field tests with at least 70% agreement were repeated sprint ability (76%), deceleration drills (71%), single-leg bridge (71%) and position-specific GPS-targeted match rehabilitation (82%). The sports physician was made ultimately responsible for the medical decision, with the physiotherapist, fitness trainer, athlete and team coach consulted. MRI findings were excluded.
limitations: The consensus is expert opinion and has not been validated against re-injury or return outcomes. The 70% threshold is a convention, eccentric strength was added only in the final round, and the panel was drawn from elite football centres. Apart from the flexibility range, the criteria have no cut-offs, and the authors note that opinions may change as new evidence appears.
practicalImplications: Clinicians can use the agreed criteria, pain on palpation, strength and flexibility checks, field tests including repeated sprints, deceleration and position-specific match rehabilitation, and psychological readiness, with MRI excluded from the decision. Return should be a multidisciplinary decision led by the sports physician, with the athlete and coaching staff involved.
athleteDev: Performance Application: The panel's field tests (repeated sprint ability, deceleration drills, single-leg bridge and position-specific GPS-targeted match rehabilitation) give sport-specific checks of performance before full training. The consensus gives no pass thresholds for these tests.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: The consensus defines return to play and lists the criteria clinicians should check, including pain on palpation, strength, flexibility, field tests, and psychological readiness, with MRI excluded. It is expert opinion without validated cut-offs, so it cannot show that following it lowers re-injury risk.

citation: Longstaffe R, Leiter J, Gurney-Dunlop T, McCormack R, MacDonald P. Return to Play and Career Length After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Among Canadian Professional Football Players. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2020.
abstract: This retrospective study followed anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstructions in Canadian Football League players from two teams between 2002 and 2017. Most reconstructions used hamstring tendon autograft, and about 70 percent of players returned to play with a mean career of about 2.8 seasons after injury.
tldr: Nearly 70 percent of Canadian professional football players in this series returned to play after ACL reconstruction, similar to NFL reports. A concomitant MCL injury was the only significant factor linked to not returning in the adjusted model.
methods: Team physicians and head athletic trainers recorded ACL injuries from two CFL teams from 2002 to 2017, including position, graft and concomitant injuries. Return to play and career length came from public sources, and returning and non-returning players were compared with t tests and a binomial logistic regression.
findings: Of 43 analysable injuries, 30 (69.8%) returned to play after a mean of 316 days. Returning players averaged 2.8 seasons (34.4 games) after injury, with preinjury career length similar between groups. Hamstring grafts were followed by return in 64.5% (20 of 31) and patellar tendon grafts in 87.5% (7 of 8), and graft type was not a significant predictor. Meniscal injury was linked to lower return (61.5% vs 82.4%) and shorter careers, but this was not significant.
limitations: Small sample, with return and career data from public sources that may contain errors, and no control group of uninjured players. The raw return rates were almost the same with and without an MCL injury (70% vs 69.7% in Table 5), so the MCL odds ratio comes only from the adjusted model and has a very wide confidence interval (1.1 to 32.8). The Discussion gives 58.3% for early-season injuries, while the Results give 56.8% (25 of 44), and the subgroup analyses are underpowered.
practicalImplications: In this small series, hamstring grafts did not show a lower chance of return than patellar tendon grafts, so graft choice should not be decided on return rates alone. A concomitant MCL injury was the only significant predictor of not returning in the adjusted model, and all 3 players with a grade III MCL injury did not return. More than half of the injuries occurred early in the season, which the authors suggest warrants study of prevention strategies.
athleteDev: The 2.8-season average career after return gives performance staff a rough benchmark for long-term planning in professional football players. Early-season clustering of injuries (56.8% in the Results) supports closer attention to preseason readiness, but the study does not test any training programme.
rtp: The 69.8% return rate and 316-day mean time to return can serve as a benchmark for professional football players, but they cannot predict an individual's outcome. A concomitant MCL injury lowered the odds of return in the adjusted model and should be considered when planning. The study cannot show that any graft is safer, and it does not measure on-field performance after return.

citation: Mody KS, Fletcher AN, Akoh CC, Parekh SG. Return to Play and Performance After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction in National Football League Players. Orthop J Sports Med. 2022;10(3):23259671221079637.
abstract: This study compared return to play and performance after ACL reconstruction across positions in 312 NFL players injured between 2013 and 2018. Players played fewer games, started fewer games, and had lower approximate value and snap counts after injury, and only 28.5% remained in the league three years later.
tldr: Only about half of NFL players in this database returned to play after ACL reconstruction, and fewer than one in three were still in the league three years later. Running backs, defensive linemen and linebackers showed the largest performance drops.
methods: NFL players with ACL reconstruction from 2013 to 2018 were identified from the FantasyData injury database. Games, starts, snap counts and AV were taken from Pro Football Reference for three seasons before and after injury, and pre- and postinjury values were compared with Wilcoxon and Kruskal-Wallis tests, with percentage change used to compare positions.
findings: Of 312 players, 174 (55.8%) returned to play, and 59 of 207 (28.5%) remained in the league three years after injury. Within three years, players averaged 8.7 games versus 13.7 before injury, 3.0 starts versus 8.3, an AV of 1.5 versus 4.3, and 259 snaps versus 619. Quarterbacks had the highest return rate (92.9% vs 53.7%) and the smallest AV decline (2% vs 50%), while running backs had the largest AV decline (90.5%); in pairwise tests only quarterbacks versus running backs differed significantly, and snap-count change did not differ across positions after correction (P=.1113).
limitations: The sample relies on public databases with no uninjured comparison group. The performance analysis covers only the 135 players who returned, and the 3-year analysis includes only players who stayed in the league. The text reports a 55.4% return (173 of 312) and the abstract 55.8% (174), while Table 2 gives 51.3% at one year; quarterback return is 92.9% in the text but 10 of 14 (71.4%) in Table 2, so the figures should be checked against the tables.
practicalImplications: For professional football players, an ACL injury was followed by fewer games, starts and snaps, and fewer players were still in the league three years later. Return planning should account for the chance that players will not regain their pre-injury workload. The study does not show that any rehabilitation approach changes these outcomes.
athleteDev: Performance staff can use the position-level declines in AV and snap count as a broad benchmark for the level of workload that returning players may reach. Only the quarterback versus running back difference in AV change was statistically significant, so the other position rankings are descriptive. The study does not measure training or conditioning inputs.
rtp: The 55.8% return rate and the 12.4-month average time to return can inform expectations for NFL players, but the study cannot predict an individual player's return. It does not show whether a specific rehabilitation protocol improves return, so it should not be used alone to set a return-to-sport date or criteria.

citation: Pagani NR, Leibman MI, Guss MS. Return to Play and Performance After Surgical Repair of Distal Biceps Tendon Ruptures in National Football League Athletes. Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery. 2020 (online pre-proof).
abstract: This case series of NFL players treated surgically for distal biceps tendon rupture compared return to play, performance and career length with position-matched controls. Most players returned to at least one game, but careers and games per season were shorter than for controls, and performance scores were not significantly different.
tldr: Most NFL players in this series returned to at least one game after surgical repair of a distal biceps rupture, but only 56% were still in the league at two years. In a small scored subgroup, returning players' performance scores did not differ significantly from matched peers.
methods: NFL players who had surgical repair of a distal biceps tendon rupture from 1998 to 2017 were identified from public injury databases and cross-checked with team and player sources. Each case was matched to a control by position, age and experience, and performance scores per game were compared with paired t tests, with Kaplan-Meier survival using final game played as the endpoint.
findings: Of 25 cases in 22 players, 21 (84%) returned to play, at a mean of 321 days, with 1-year and 2-year survival of 76% and 56%. Post-injury career length averaged 2.8 years versus 3.4 years for controls (P=0.049), and games per season averaged 11 versus 13 (P=0.02). Post-injury performance scores did not differ significantly from pre-injury or matched-control values in any position group, although defensive linemen fell from 3.2 to 2.4 points per game (P=0.06, n=9).
limitations: The sample is small, relies on public data without injury severity, technique or rehabilitation details, and offensive linemen were excluded from performance scoring, so only 16 cases were scored. The authors note that the lower career and games findings are likely confounded by factors such as trades and coaching changes, and they judge the career-length difference unlikely to be clinically significant. Time to return depends heavily on when in the season the injury occurred.
practicalImplications: Surgical repair in this series was followed by return to at least one NFL game in 84% of players, but not all returned, so players and staff should not assume a full return. Returning players' performance scores were not significantly different from matched peers, though the scored sample is too small to rule out a decline. Expectations about career length and games per season should be discussed with caution because of confounding.
athleteDev: Returning players in this series played somewhat fewer games per season than matched controls (11 vs 13), but the authors say this finding is likely confounded. The performance comparison involved only 16 defensive players and showed a non-significant drop in defensive linemen, so it cannot confirm that pre-injury performance standards will be met.
rtp: The 84% return to play and the mean of 321 days to return can inform expectations, though the authors note that time to return depends heavily on the point in the season when the injury occurred. The study does not identify rehabilitation protocols or predict an individual player's return, so it should not be used alone to set return criteria.

citation: Jeffers KW, Shah SA, Calvert DD, et al. Return to Play and Re-Injury Rates in NCAA Division I Football Players Following Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Using Hamstring Autograft. Arthroscopy: The Journal of Arthroscopic and Related Surgery. 2021 (online pre-proof).
abstract: This retrospective case series followed NCAA Division I football players who had ACL reconstruction with quadrupled hamstring autograft at a single institution between 2001 and 2016. Most players returned to play, the re-injury rate was low, and most reported good knee function years later.
tldr: Most NCAA Division I football players in this series returned to play after hamstring-graft ACL reconstruction, and few re-injured their knee. Mean Tegner-Lysholm scores were high at a follow-up of about eight years.
methods: Medical records of male varsity football players who had quadrupled hamstring ACL reconstruction by one surgeon from 2001 to 2016 were reviewed. Return to play, re-injury and eligibility used were taken from institutional records, and a survey provided Tegner-Lysholm scores, with t tests used for comparisons.
findings: Of 34 players, 29 (85.3%) returned to play after a mean of 318 days, and 2 of those 29 (6.9%) re-injured their knee, both running backs with direct-blow contact injuries. Players with eligibility remaining used 79.5% of it, and the mean Tegner-Lysholm score was 90.7 plus or minus 14.2 among 33 respondents. Players with multiligament injuries did not differ significantly from isolated ACL injuries in time to return (348 vs 273 days, P=0.709).
limitations: The study is retrospective, has no comparison arm, and includes a heterogeneous group of positions in a small sample. The Abstract gives return times of 306 days for isolated ACL and 353 and 324 days for multiligament injuries, which differ from the Results (348 vs 273 days), so the Results were used here; the Discussion also calls the 85.3% return 'the following season' while Results count any return with a mean of 318 days.
practicalImplications: In this series, hamstring autograft was followed by return to play in most players and a low re-injury rate, so it is a reasonable option to consider in collegiate football players. Because there was no comparison group, the study does not show that hamstring grafts are as safe as patellar tendon grafts. About one in four players needed a second procedure on the same knee, which should be part of counselling.
athleteDev: Performance staff can expect many collegiate players to use most of their remaining eligibility after hamstring-graft reconstruction, with 25 of 30 eligible players playing again. The study does not measure strength or performance outcomes after return.
rtp: The mean 318-day return (range 115 to 628 days) and the 85% return rate can inform expectations for collegiate football players after hamstring-graft reconstruction. Clearance was a joint athletic training staff and surgeon decision using criteria that included 80% isokinetic strength, so the timeline should not be transferred to other protocols without checking them.

citation: Green B, Lin M, McClelland JA, Semciw AI, Schache AG, Rotstein AH, et al. Return to Play and Recurrence After Calf Muscle Strain Injuries in Elite Australian Football Players. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2020.
abstract: This study used Australian Football League registry data on calf muscle strains to examine whether clinical and MRI findings were associated with time to return to play and with recurrence. A running-related mechanism and aponeurotic disruption on MRI were linked to longer return to play, while older age and prior calf or ankle injury were linked to recurrence, and index MRI findings were not.
tldr: In elite Australian Football players, calf strains with aponeurotic disruption on MRI and running-related mechanisms took longer to return to play. Recurrence was better predicted by age and prior calf injury than by the index MRI.
methods: Clinical and MRI data on 149 calf muscle strain injuries were collected in the AFL Soft Tissue Injury Registry from 2014 to 2017. Two blinded radiologists classified MRI findings, and return to play, functional progression and recurrence within two seasons were analysed using Kaplan-Meier curves, Mann-Whitney and Kruskal-Wallis tests, and Cox regression.
findings: Injuries with severe AD took 31.3 plus or minus 12.6 days to return to play, compared with 19.4 plus or minus 10.8 days with no AD (P=.003). A running-related mechanism was associated with longer return across all injuries (adjusted HR 0.59, P=.02), and AD was associated with longer return for soleus injuries (adjusted HR 0.6, P=.025), but not for all calf strains once adjusted (P=.11). Older age (adjusted HR 1.1, P=.013) and a previous calf strain (adjusted HR 6.7, P=.002) were associated with recurrence, while index MRI findings were not.
limitations: The study has no uninjured comparison group and relies on registry data, with club staff not blinded to MRI results. Recurrent injuries were few (35 overall, 19 early), so the recurrence and subgroup estimates are imprecise, and the mechanism categories overlap. The authors also note that MRI may miss some structural damage, so injuries without visible AD may still have longer recovery.
practicalImplications: For soleus strains with visible aponeurotic disruption, and for calf strains with running-related mechanisms, planning should allow for a longer return to play than for injuries without these features. Players with a previous calf strain or older age may carry a higher risk of recurrence, which should shape rehabilitation and return planning. Index MRI findings alone should not be used to predict recurrence.
athleteDev: Performance staff can use the longer return-to-full-training times for soleus strains with AD to set expectations for training reintroduction. Older players and those with prior calf strains may warrant closer attention during return to running, but the study did not test any monitoring method.
rtp: Mean return-to-play times were 19.4 days with no AD and 31.3 days with severe AD, with wide spread, so the figures are group benchmarks rather than individual predictions. The study does not validate functional criteria for clearance, and the timelines come from one league, so they should not be applied to other sports without checking.

citation: Barton D, Manoharan A, Khwaja A, Sorenson J, Taylor M. Return to Play Following Achilles Tendon Rupture in NFL Players Based on Position. Foot & Ankle Specialist. 2021.
abstract: This retrospective cohort study examined return to play and pre- and post-injury performance in NFL skill-position and linebacker players after Achilles tendon rupture and repair. Just over half of the players returned to at least one game, with rates varying by position, and returning players had more pre-injury games than those who did not.
tldr: About 57 percent of NFL skill-position and linebacker players in this series returned to at least one game after Achilles repair, with tight ends and linebackers highest and wide receivers and running backs lowest. Players who returned were more experienced before injury than those who did not.
methods: NFL injury reports and team rosters from the 2009-2010 to 2015-2016 seasons were used to identify players with Achilles tendon rupture and primary repair. Return to play was defined as playing in at least one NFL game after repair, and each returning player was matched to a same-position control from the same team, with pre- and post-injury statistics compared using paired and unpaired t tests.
findings: Of 63 players, 36 (57.1%) returned to play, with rates of 71% for tight ends, 70% for linebackers, 62% for defensive backs, 40% for running backs and 38% for wide receivers. Returning players had more career games than non-returners (78.3 vs 25.4 for offensive players, P=.0072; 93.6 vs 33.1 for defensive players, P=.0043). In the returning group, passes defended fell from 5.04 to 2.79 (P=.0306) and other categories showed no significant within-group change, while against controls the returning players had fewer receptions per game (P=.01), tackles (P=.0069) and passes defended (P=.0452).
limitations: The study is retrospective and built from public data, with concomitant injuries and surgical technique not recorded and small position groups that limit comparisons; running backs could not be tested statistically. The authors state that returning players declined in all categories, but Table 3 shows only one significant within-group change, the abstract counts fumbles forced/recovered (P=.0751) as significant, and the Discussion says passes defended increased significantly when Table 3 shows a fall. The Discussion's RTP rate of 58% and its claim that tight ends had the longest time to return (14.33 months) differ from the Results (57% and 11.25 months).
practicalImplications: Expected return after Achilles repair varies by position in this NFL series, with wide receivers and running backs returning less often, so position demands should be considered when counselling players. Players who returned had more career games and starts before injury, which suggests that established players had better odds of returning. The performance data are too small and inconsistent to say how much returning players decline.
athleteDev: Performance staff can use the reported position return rates and the mean 12.6-month return as broad benchmarks for players returning from Achilles repair. The performance comparisons are small and partly inconsistent with the text, and the study does not test any training programme.
rtp: Use the position-specific return rates (38% to 71%) and the mean time to return of 12.6 months as group benchmarks, not individual predictions. The return criterion here was a single NFL game, and the study cannot show whether any rehabilitation or operative technique changes that outcome.

citation: Khair M, Riboh J, Solis J, Maurer J, Brown JB, Vandermeer RD, et al. Return to Play Following Isolated and Combined Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction: 25+ Years of Experience Treating National Football League Athletes. Orthop J Sports Med. 2020;8(10):2325967120959004.
abstract: This case series reports two surgeons' experience treating NFL players with ACL injuries over more than 25 years, using both the standard return-to-game-play definition and a broader return-to-previous-participation definition. Return to previous participation was higher than return to game play, and age 25 years or younger predicted success.
tldr: Most NFL players in this single-centre series returned to their previous level of participation after ACL reconstruction, and the rate was higher than return-to-game-play figures from earlier series. Players aged 25 or younger were most likely to return.
methods: Retrospective review of prospectively collected data on NFL roster players who had ACL reconstruction by one of two surgeons at one centre. Return to game play (one regular-season game) and return to previous participation (passing a dynamic functional assessment, at least six weeks of position-specific activity, clearance by the NFL physical, and return at the same level) were recorded, and univariate and multivariate logistic and linear regression were used to identify predictors.
findings: Return to game play after primary reconstruction was 73% (27 of 37 knees), and return to previous participation was 87.8% (36 of 41 primary reconstructions). Age 25 years or younger predicted return to previous participation (adjusted OR 10.8, 95% CI 1.4 to 233, P=.02), with 96.2% of players in that group returning compared with 76.2% of older players. Offensive players (adjusted 1.18 more seasons, P=.009) and players drafted in rounds 1 to 4 (adjusted 1.48 more seasons, P=.008) played more seasons after surgery, and later ACL tears occurred in 12.8% (graft rupture 4.3%, contralateral 8.5%).
limitations: This is a single-centre series with two surgeons who also made return decisions, which may introduce selection bias, and follow-up duration was not recorded. The revision and multiligament groups are very small. The abstract gives 47 players while the Results give 47 reconstructions in 43 players, and its overall game-return rate of 67.6% differs from Table 4 (29 of 43, 67.4%); the claimed lower return after revision or bicruciate-plus-collateral reconstruction is not significant in Table 3 (P=.999 and P=.32), the text calls the primary versus revision game-return difference significant although Table 4 gives P=.07, and offensive position did not reach significance for return in the multivariate model (P=.07).
practicalImplications: For NFL players after ACL reconstruction, age 25 or younger was linked to returning to previous participation, and draft round and offensive position were linked to more seasons played after surgery, so these should be part of counselling. The return rate depends on the definition used, so clinicians should state which definition they are using when comparing outcomes. The study does not support a claim that revision reconstruction or multiligament surgery lowers return with any confidence.
athleteDev: Performance staff can use the 2.6-season average participation after surgery and the higher seasons played by higher draft picks and offensive players as context for long-term planning. The study does not measure strength, speed or other performance outcomes after return.
rtp: The 73% return to game play and 87.8% return to previous participation can serve as group benchmarks for NFL players after primary ACL reconstruction, with the authors' broader definition counting players who returned to their previous level without playing in a game. The study does not show that any rehabilitation protocol changes these rates, and the outcomes come from one centre, so the figures should not be applied to other levels without checking.

citation: Brelin AM, Rue JP. Return to Play Following Meniscus Surgery. Clin Sports Med 2016;35:669-678.
abstract: The article has no abstract. Its key points state that meniscectomy gives a faster return to play but carries degenerative risk, that meniscus repair should be performed when possible in young active athletes, that accelerated repair rehabilitation gives equivalent functional outcomes, and that meniscal allograft transplantation is a viable salvage option, with contact or collision sport return weighed carefully.
tldr: Meniscectomy returns athletes to sport fastest, but repair and transplant preserve the knee at the cost of longer, staged rehabilitation. Repair is favoured in young active athletes when the tear allows it.
methods: Narrative review. The authors summarise prior studies and tables and describe their institution's rehabilitation protocols for repair (Box 1) and transplant (Box 2). No literature search method is reported.
findings: Partial lateral meniscectomy returned 98% of 41 athletes to sport at an average of 55 days in one early series, and four NFL players who had midseason lateral meniscectomy returned at either 19 or 29 days. Accelerated repair protocols gave functional outcomes equivalent to standard regimens in the cited trials, and repair series report return to sport at roughly 5 to 6 months. In one allograft series, 10 of 13 athletes returned to their previous sport, with release to full training at about 4 months but a mean of 16.5 months to previous athletic level.
limitations: The paper reports no search method and no pooled analysis. Most cited athlete series are small and differ in procedure, follow-up and return-to-sport definitions. The authors note there is little literature validating postoperative repair protocols, and the protocols shown are one institution's practice. The abstract is replaced here by the key points because none is printed.
practicalImplications: Meniscectomy suits an in-season athlete who needs the fastest return, but the long-term osteoarthritis risk should be weighed and as much tissue as possible conserved. Repair is preferred in young, active athletes when the tear pattern allows, and accelerated rehabilitation can be used with the athletic trainer guiding progression. Allograft transplant is a salvage option, and the athlete should be told that return to collision or contact sport carries added risk.
athleteDev: Use the surgery type to set the rehabilitation pace. The cited protocols return athletes to running and sport-specific work at about 6 weeks after meniscectomy and begin sport-specific and run/jump work at 16 weeks after repair. One cited repair protocol (Kozlowski and colleagues) advances athletes by criteria after a time-protected first 6 weeks.
rtp: After meniscectomy, cited series report an average of 55 days to return to sport. After repair, roughly 5 to 6 months is typical in the cited series. After allograft transplant, full training at about 4 months does not mean return to previous level, which averaged 16.5 months. The review cannot set a clearance standard, because it describes no criteria-based testing and its cohorts are small.

citation: Dunlop G, Ardern CL, Andersen TE, et al. Return-to-Play Practices Following Hamstring Injury: A Worldwide Survey of 131 Premier League Football Teams. Sports Med 2020;50:829-840.
abstract: Purpose: to determine whether premier-league teams worldwide follow a return-to-play (RTP) continuum, which criteria they use, and how decisions are made after hamstring injury. Methods: a structured online survey sent to practitioners at 310 professional teams from 34 premier leagues. Results: 131 teams responded (42%); 124 (95%) used a continuum assessing clinical, functional and psychological criteria, and 105 (80%) used shared decision-making. Team hierarchy, match and player factors were common perceived challenges. Conclusions: practice appears broadly consistent with general research recommendations, but specific criteria, metrics and thresholds, and the roles of staff in decisions, are unclear.
tldr: Most professional football teams in this survey used a criteria-based return-to-play continuum with shared decisions after hamstring injury. The specific tests, metrics and thresholds they used were not clear, so the survey cannot show which ones work.
methods: Cross-sectional online survey of 29 items (10 closed, 19 open) across four sections, adapted from a return-to-play continuum model. The survey was piloted for content validity, translated into six languages and sent to 310 teams from 34 leagues between October 2017 and March 2018, with up to three reminders. Open responses were analysed by content analysis, and two authors reviewed the coding.
findings: 124 of 131 responding teams (95%) followed a return-to-play continuum, and 27 (21%) did not report a return-to-performance phase. Absence of pain, hamstring strength, training load and functional performance tests were the most frequently reported top criteria, and 68 teams (52%) reported always (100% of the time) meeting all their intended criteria before clearing players to high-speed running, with typical achievement of criteria at least 90% of the time. Medical staff were consulted at every phase, but the reported involvement of science staff, coaches and players depended on whether a medical or science practitioner answered the survey.
limitations: Results are self-reported by 131 of 310 invited teams, so they may not represent non-responding clubs. The survey covers one muscle group and one sport, and it does not describe the metrics or thresholds used, or whether accelerated return led to re-injury. The authors classify the design as level 5 evidence and note that different staff roles gave different accounts of involvement.
practicalImplications: Teams can use a criteria-based continuum with a shared decision, which the survey shows is common practice. Because the survey found no consistent metrics or thresholds, each team should define and record its own criteria and cut-offs. The survey also suggests the medical and science staff should agree on who is involved in each decision.
athleteDev: Set progression criteria for each phase (running, team training, match play, return to performance) and track whether they are met. The survey shows training load and functional tests are commonly used, so build a training-load plan into the progression, but no specific thresholds are supported by this study.
rtp: The survey describes how professional teams make return-to-play decisions after hamstring injury, including a continuum and shared decisions. It cannot show that these criteria or thresholds reduce re-injury, and it cannot be used to set a clearance standard for other muscle groups or injuries.

citation: Meredith SJ, Rauer T, Chmielewski TL, et al. Return to Sport After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury: Panther Symposium ACL Injury Return to Sport Consensus Group. Orthop J Sports Med 2020;8(6):2325967120930829.
abstract: Background: a precise and consistent definition of return to sport (RTS) after ACL injury is lacking. Purpose: to define RTS, describe the RTS continuum and give guidance on RTS testing and decisions. Study design: consensus statement. Methods: an international multidisciplinary group used a modified Delphi method, with a literature review. Results: RTS is achieved when the preinjury level of sport is reached, through criteria-based progression from return to participation to RTS and return to performance. Purely time-based decisions should be abandoned; decisions should be made by a multidisciplinary group using objective examination data and validated, peer-reviewed RTS tests that include functional and psychological assessment, and should consider biological healing, context and concomitant injuries. Conclusion: research is needed on the ideal test battery, psychological readiness testing and biological assessment of healing.
tldr: Return to sport after ACL injury should mean regaining the preinjury level of sport, reached through criteria-based stages. Time alone should not decide clearance, and the decision should use examination data, validated tests and psychological readiness.
methods: International consensus group of 26 ACL experts convened at a symposium in June 2019. A modified Delphi process ran three rounds (internet survey, structured in-person discussion and a final vote), with 80% agreement set in advance as consensus. Two liaisons completed a MEDLINE search (June 2019; anterior cruciate ligament, return to sport and return to play; 5 to 10 years) to support the statements.
findings: Consensus was reached on 11 statements. Return to sport was defined as the preinjury level of sport (24 of 26, 92%), and purely time-based decisions should be abandoned (26 of 26). Objective physical examination was required (26 of 26), with validated tests (23 of 26) and a validated psychological readiness scale (22 of 26). Cited data from the Delaware-Oslo cohort show that patients who passed a criteria-based test at 6 months returned to their previous level at 81% (1 year) and 84% (2 years).
limitations: The statements are consensus opinion built from an expert panel and a single MEDLINE search, not a systematic review or meta-analysis. The authors note that the best test battery, the psychological tools to use, and how to assess biological healing are not yet known. Some statements, such as the role of the coach, did not reach consensus, and the cited RTS outcomes come mainly from one cohort.
practicalImplications: Use criteria-based progression through return to participation, return to sport and return to performance, with a documented clearance by the health care provider before unrestricted training. Include objective examination, a validated test battery and a psychological readiness measure, and consider contextual factors such as position, sport and concomitant injury. Avoid clearing an athlete on time alone, and treat RTS before about 6 months as likely high risk.
athleteDev: Apply the RTS continuum to sport-specific training: clear unrestricted training first, then full participation in practice, then competition, with serial testing at each stage. Measure readiness with objective tests of strength, hop and movement quality before progressing, and do not use the calendar as the trigger.
rtp: The statements describe a criteria-based return to sport after ACL injury, requiring objective examination, a validated test battery and psychological readiness, with time used as a guide to graft healing rather than the decision. The paper cannot specify the exact test battery or thresholds, and it cannot be used as a validated clearance protocol or as a guarantee of return to the preinjury level.

citation: Taberner M, O'Keefe J, Dunn A, Cohen DD. Return to sport and beyond following intramuscular tendon hamstring injury: A case report of an English Premier League football player. Physical Therapy in Sport 2022;56:38-47.
abstract: Background: hamstring strains are the most common injury in elite football and carry a high reinjury risk, especially when the intramuscular tendon (IMT) is involved, and rehabilitation data for these injuries are limited. Case scenario: an elite player suffered a grade 2c hamstring injury in an EPL match and was managed with early care, progressive off-pitch physical preparation and the control-chaos continuum for on-pitch rehabilitation, with objective and subjective load-response monitoring. Outcomes: on-pitch rehabilitation at 11 days, full team training at 35 days, match play at 40 days, and no reinjury for the rest of the season. Conclusion: knowledge of the IMT and expected return timeframes, with performance and load-response monitoring, communication and practitioner experience, may help to guide return to sport.
tldr: A single elite player with an intramuscular tendon hamstring injury returned to full team training at 35 days and played at 40 days without reinjury. Isometric strength monitoring and load tracking guided each step, but this is one case.
methods: Single case report of one 23-year-old male player managed by the club's medical and sports science staff. Care followed a modified return-to-sport continuum with the control-chaos continuum for on-pitch work. Isometric posterior chain peak force (unilateral test on a force platform at 1000 Hz) and interlimb asymmetry were measured weekly and before most training sessions. GPS load and MRI and ultrasound were used at set points, and the player gave informed consent.
findings: Interlimb asymmetry in isometric posterior chain peak force fell below 10% by day 11, and the player reached his pre-injury weekly running load before full team training at day 35. He then played as a substitute for about 40 to 45 minutes in five matches and started one 90-minute match, where his high-speed running was 1.26 times his typical pre-injury game load, with no reinjury for the rest of the season. Authors note that the largest force decline came about 48 hours after match play, and it was symmetrical across both limbs.
limitations: Findings come from one player, one club and one injury, without a control group. The authors state that the injury presentation, loading progressions, response to load and return timeframes are player-specific and may not transfer to other elite footballers, and that partial team integration may not always be feasible. The case cannot show whether the monitoring reduced reinjury risk.
practicalImplications: Use an isometric strength test and load data before each stage of return, and combine them with pain response and player feedback. Consider an early phase of controlled loading and partial team involvement, as the authors describe, but expect the timeline to vary by injury and player. Keep monitoring after return to play, since the authors judged the reinjury risk after this injury type to be high.
athleteDev: Use the control-chaos continuum to build back to match demands: progress high-speed running and maximal speed exposure against the match demand, and check strength asymmetry the morning after sessions. The case suggests that matching training volume to the player's pre-injury weekly running load was a practical target before full team training.
rtp: The case describes one player who returned to team training at 35 days and to match play at 40 days after an intramuscular tendon hamstring injury, without reinjury for the season. It cannot set a return-to-play timeline for this injury, because the authors recommend an individual approach and the case involves no comparison.

citation: Solie BS, Tollefson LV, Doney CP, O'Keefe JMJ, Thompson WC, LaPrade RF. Return to the Pre-Injury Level of Sport after Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction: A Practical Review with Medical Recommendations. Int J Sports Med. 2024.
abstract: Return to sport after ACL reconstruction is complex, with return to the pre-injury level observed to be below athlete expectations and knee re-injury rates remaining high. The authors review graft, rehabilitation, objective testing, and psychological readiness factors and make medical recommendations for rehabilitation and return-to-sport decisions.
tldr: Return to pre-injury sport after ACL reconstruction varies widely by league, position and graft, and the authors recommend bone-patellar tendon-bone grafts for high-demand athletes, prehabilitation, a structured return-to-sport program, and repeated testing with psychological screening. Single test criteria should not be treated as proof of safe return.
methods: A practical review of 158 unique articles found in Google Scholar, Medline and SPORTDiscus (June to November 2023), with at least two authors screening titles, abstracts and full texts and with reference checking. The search was not conducted to PRISMA or scoping-review standards, and each author was assigned writing sections based on clinical expertise.
findings: Reported return to pre-injury level of sport varied by cohort, including 97% in the NHL, 80% in MLB, 77% in MLS, 92% in NFL quarterbacks, 86% in the NBA, 64.3% for NFL linemen and 69.5% in the WNBA. In a cited cohort, a BPTB autograft gave a higher return rate than a hamstring autograft (74% vs 53%), and an ACL plus MCL reconstruction gave 10% return against 48.9% after isolated ACLR (Svantesson et al.). Only 17% of athletes after ACLR, and 24% of non-injured athletes, met a 90% between-limb symmetry standard on a return-to-sport test battery, and the authors conclude that current criteria do not appear valid for predicting safe return.
limitations: The review has no formal risk-of-bias appraisal and was not conducted to PRISMA or scoping-review standards. Most included evidence comes from retrospective or registry cohorts, outcome definitions differ across studies, and several medical recommendations rest on expert judgement rather than direct comparative trials.
practicalImplications: Use the return rates as league-specific context rather than a prediction for an individual athlete, and treat passing a test battery as one input to a shared decision. The authors recommend prehabilitation, a comprehensive rehabilitation program, quadriceps strength and hop testing, ACL-RSI psychological screening, and a return-to-sport program before unrestricted participation.
athleteDev: For athletes returning to high-demand sport, the review supports tracking quadriceps strength, hop performance and ACL-RSI scores through rehabilitation and before clearance. Performance staff should not assume a passed test battery means a safe return, and should keep secondary injury-reduction work in place throughout.
rtp: The review can inform return-to-sport planning, including graft and concomitant-injury considerations, test selection and psychological readiness. It does not establish a validated clearance threshold, and it cannot tell staff what minimum time frame or test score makes return safe for a specific athlete.

citation: Schallmo MS, Fitzpatrick TH, Yancey HB, Marquez-Lara A, Luo TD, Stubbs AJ. Return-to-Play and Performance Outcomes of Professional Athletes in North America After Hip Arthroscopy From 1999 to 2016. Am J Sports Med. 2018.
abstract: Descriptive epidemiology study of 227 hip arthroscopy procedures in 180 professional MLB, NBA, NFL and NHL athletes from 1999 to 2016. Each player was compared with his own pre-surgery season, with return to play defined as at least one professional regular-season game.
tldr: Most professional athletes in this public-source cohort returned to at least one game after hip arthroscopy, but performance and playing time often fell in the following season. Hockey players returned most often and quickest but showed the largest first-season performance drop.
methods: Retrospective case identification from public sources (LexisNexis searches, player profiles, team reports and press releases), with at least two sources required per case. Each player was his own control, using the season before surgery as baseline, and performance scores were sport-specific (for example, player efficiency rating for basketball, on-base plus slugging for hitters, and position-specific formulas for NFL and NHL players). Comparisons across sports were adjusted for season and career length.
findings: Return to play occurred in 84.6% of procedures (192/227). NHL players returned at 91.8% against 81.2% for other sports (P = .048), and NFL offensive linemen at 61.1% (P = .010), with mean return time of 209 days. Across the 170 players with performance data, performance scores fell 15.8% in postoperative season 1 (P = .022) and 14.4% in seasons 2 and 3 (P = .008). Only NHL players showed a significant season-1 drop (-35.1%, P = .002), and lead-leg MLB hitters showed a 12.7% reduction (P = .041). MLB pitchers who had surgery on their lead leg showed a 1.3% fall in fastball velocity (P = .004) and a 60.7% fall in pitch count in season 1 (P = .007), with both recovering by seasons 2 and 3.
limitations: The authors state that a retrospective design, public-source capture and missing clinical data (imaging, rehabilitation, clearance, complications) limit interpretation. Revision and bilateral cases were pooled in the headline return rate, and sample sizes for individual sports and positions were small. The authors' hypothesis of consistently high performance return was only partly supported, because performance changes varied by sport and position.
practicalImplications: When discussing return after hip arthroscopy with professional athletes, staff can expect high return rates in these leagues, but should also plan for lower playing time and performance in the first season, especially for hockey players. Positional demands, such as the lead-leg loading in baseball and the line play of NFL linemen, should be part of return planning. The authors also note that medical clearance does not equal game readiness, so game participation should be assessed separately.
athleteDev: For professional athletes returning after hip arthroscopy, the study suggests tracking playing time, starts and sport-specific output across the first postoperative season rather than relying on return alone. The study's own findings show performance changes were not uniform across sports, so position-specific measures should inform progression.
rtp: The study can support expectations for return to professional game play after hip arthroscopy in these four leagues, including the lower return rate for NFL offensive linemen. It cannot define a minimum time from surgery to safe return, because the dose-response analysis found no significant link between return time and performance change, and the study does not include clinical clearance criteria.

citation: Schaefer JJ, Kang LS, Ward GH, Graden NR, Levy BA, Hevesi M, et al. Return-to-Sport Rates and Functional Outcomes After Hip Arthroscopy for Femoroacetabular Impingement in Young Football Athletes: A 9.8-Year Follow-up. Orthop J Sports Med. 2026;14(3).
abstract: Case series of 36 hips in 27 young male football players who underwent primary hip arthroscopy with labral repair for femoroacetabular impingement, with a mean follow-up of 9.8 years. Return to sport and patient-reported outcomes were assessed, with 84% of players who returned to football at the same or higher level and significant improvements in all reported PROMs.
