tldr: Most young football players who attempted a return after hip arthroscopy with labral repair went back to competitive football at the same or higher level, with lasting improvements in hip scores. Non-medical reasons, such as graduation, accounted for many players who did not return.
methods: Retrospective review of a prospectively maintained institutional database. Football players aged mostly under 25 with primary arthroscopic labral repair for FAI between 2010 and 2019 were contacted at least 5 years after surgery, and return to football, Modified Harris Hip Score, HOS-ADL, HOS-Sport, Tegner, VAS pain and satisfaction were collected. Predictors of return were examined with univariate logistic regression, and the authors note the sample was too small for formal power analysis.
findings: Of 27 players (36 hips), 16 of 19 who attempted to return did so (84%) at the same or higher level, and the overall return rate was 16 of 27 (59%) after counting eight players who stopped for non-medical reasons. At a mean 9.8-year follow-up, mHHS improved from 68.5 to 90.5, HOS-ADL from 73.9 to 94.5 and HOS-Sport from 49.7 to 91.1 (all P less than .002 or .001). Two hips (8%) were reoperated, with no revisions, and no logistic regression predictor (BMI, age, level of play, alpha angle or position) of return reached significance.
limitations: The study is a single-institution retrospective case series with no control group, and PROMs were available for only 19 of 27 players. The authors note that attrition (11 of 36 hips) and the small cohort may bias results, and that the predictor analysis was underpowered. The abstract gives reoperation as 2 patients (7%), whereas the results give 2 hips (8%); the figures differ because of the patient and hip denominators.
practicalImplications: When counseling young football players about hip arthroscopy with labral repair, staff can share the favorable 5-year-plus function and satisfaction data, and should also discuss non-medical reasons such as graduation and changing priorities, which accounted for many non-returns. Clinicians should plan for a return rate below 84% when all players are counted.
athleteDev: For young football players returning after hip arthroscopy, the study supports planned progression through the rehabilitation criteria (limb symmetry targets at week 12 and 16) before full football. Performance staff should also account for school and college transitions, since non-medical reasons drove most non-returns.
rtp: The study shows that most players who attempted a return after labral repair went back to competitive football, but it cannot predict an individual's return, because no tested factor predicted return and the sample is small. It also cannot show that outcomes would match those in professional or older athletes, whose return rates were reported in other studies.

citation: Perna P, Kerin F, Greig N, Beato M. Return-to-play criteria following a hamstring injury in professional football: a scoping review. Res Sports Med. 2024.
abstract: Scoping review of the criteria used to determine return to play after a hamstring strain injury in professional male football. Four databases were searched, and 19 studies were included and grouped into clinical, strength and performance criteria, with clinical criteria further split into absence of pain, flexibility, medical clearance, psychological readiness, surgeon's opinion and imaging.
tldr: Return-to-play after hamstring injury in professional football is guided by a mix of clinical, strength and performance criteria, but no criterion set has been validated. Staff should combine criteria in their battery and involve several disciplines in the decision.
methods: Scoping review following PRISMA 2020 and PRISMA-ScR, with a protocol registered on OSF in June 2023. Two reviewers screened PubMed, MEDLINE, Web of Science and SPORTDiscus records (1026 identified, 573 screened after duplicates removed, 19 included), and extracted design, sample, injury type and criteria. No risk-of-bias tool was applied.
findings: Of the 19 studies, absence of pain was used as a criterion in seven, hamstring flexibility in five, psychological readiness in seven, strength in nine and performance in six. Imaging was a criterion in three studies, and the surgeon's opinion in one. One randomized trial (Tol et al.) found that 67% of players had at least one isokinetic deficit over 10% at return. MRI grade and the BAMIC classification were reported as predictors of time to return, with a 3-day rise in return time per BAMIC grade in one cohort.
limitations: The review did not appraise study quality, and the authors note the evidence is weighted toward surveys, Delphi studies and case reports. Only English-language studies were included, and the review does not assess test validity or the optimal test for each injury type and stage. The text and flow diagram disagree on the number of full texts screened (52 vs 51).
practicalImplications: Staff should use a combination of clinical, strength and performance criteria, and make the return decision with several disciplines involved. Strength testing should include hamstring isokinetic or isometric tests, and the authors note that the choice of test is not settled. Psychological readiness should be assessed, although no validated tool exists in this population.
athleteDev: For professional footballers returning from hamstring injury, the review supports a criteria-based battery that includes absence of pain, hamstring strength and flexibility, sport-specific performance and load monitoring. Performance staff should plan for the high re-injury risk noted in the introduction, rather than relying on a single test.
rtp: The review can inform the clinical, strength and performance criteria used in return-to-play planning after hamstring injury in professional football. It cannot be used to set a validated pass or fail threshold, and the authors state it does not provide clinical practice guidelines.

citation: Vernon A, Joyce C, Banyard HG. Readiness to train: return to baseline strength and velocity following strength or power training. Int J Sports Sci Coach. 2020;15(2):204-211.
abstract: The study tracked the return to baseline of back-squat mean and peak velocity, 1RM and countermovement jump peak velocity over 96 h after a strength-oriented session and a power-oriented session in strength-trained men. Velocity at 60% 1RM and above was meaningfully reduced at 24 and 48 h after the strength session and had recovered by 72 h, while 1RM and jump measures did not change meaningfully. The authors conclude that velocity monitoring may be a more practical guide to full recovery and readiness to train than 1RM or jump testing.
tldr: After a heavy back-squat session, the authors report bar speed at 60% 1RM and above stayed below baseline at 24 and 48 h and was back by 72 h, while 1RM and jump peak velocity showed no meaningful change at any time. Velocity may be a more sensitive readiness check than 1RM or a jump test, though this rests on one protocol in 14 to 15 men.
methods: Repeated-measures crossover study in which strength-trained men completed a strength session (five sets of five at 80% 1RM) and a power session (six sets of three at 50% 1RM) in random order, one week apart. After a baseline 1RM and load-velocity profile, back-squat mean and peak velocity, 1RM and countermovement jump peak velocity were measured at 24, 48, 72 and 96 h using a linear position transducer. Cohen's d of 0.60 or more was treated as a meaningful change from baseline.
findings: The authors report moderate reductions in mean and peak velocity at 60%, 80% and 90% 1RM at 24 and 48 h after the strength session, no meaningful change at 72 or 96 h, and only trivial to small velocity changes after the power session. Maximal strength (1RM) and countermovement jump peak velocity showed only trivial to small changes at all times after either session. The effect-size flags in Tables 1 and 2 do not fully match this text: several 24 h strength-session reductions are flagged large, peak velocity at 80% 1RM is flagged medium at 72 h, and velocity at the 1RM load is flagged medium to large at several points after the power session.
limitations: The sample is small, all male, and studied with one back-squat protocol, so findings do not apply to other lifts or to athletes without this training history. The authors state the countermovement jump may not be sensitive enough to detect strength-session fatigue. The abstract gives the power session as three sets of six and 14 participants, the Methods six sets of three and 15 recruited, and the table effect-size flags conflict in places with the text's summary of which changes were meaningful.
practicalImplications: After a heavy strength session, a coach could delay heavy (60% 1RM and above) velocity-based work until about 72 h, and check bar speed at fixed loads before loading rather than relying on 1RM or jump tests. The study does not show that velocity checks improve later training results.
athleteDev: Performance Application: Bar speed at 60% 1RM and above recovered by 72 h after a heavy back-squat session, so coaches could use a fixed-load velocity check to decide when to repeat heavy lower-body work. The study did not test whether timing heavy work this way improves later strength gains.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: The men had no current musculoskeletal injury and the study did not include injured athletes, so it cannot inform return to sport. It cannot show that velocity recovery signals readiness after injury.

citation: Kellmann M, Bertollo M, Bosquet L, Brink M, Coutts A, Duffield R, et al. Recovery and Performance in Sport: Consensus Statement. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2018.
abstract: Recovery and fatigue and their effect on performance were reviewed at an international symposium in 2016. The statement defines central terms, describes how recovery and fatigue can be assessed, outlines training-recovery-performance models, and gives recommendations on monitoring training and recovery and on individualising recovery activities. It also identifies important questions for future research.
tldr: Recovery and fatigue should be monitored as a continuum, using several measures rather than one, and recovery should be planned as part of training. The statement stresses that the value of many monitoring tools and recovery methods is still unclear, so athletes need individualised decisions.
methods: Consensus statement from an invited international symposium on recovery and performance, held at the Technical University of Munich Science and Study Center Raitenhaslach in September 2016. Experts from several disciplines discussed definitions, frameworks and practical implications, and the statement summarises the current knowledge. The text does not describe a formal consensus or evidence grading process.
findings: The statement treats recovery and fatigue as a continuum, with underrecovery, non-functional overreaching and overtraining syndrome as possible outcomes of an imbalance. It advises assessing recovery against the demands of the sport, using performance measures where possible and recognising that proxy tests are often used. It recommends monitoring both external and internal load and using change criteria such as the smallest worthwhile change or Z-scores. It notes that single measures show only one aspect of recovery, so combined physiological and psychological measures are advised. It says short-term recovery interventions can help during heavy training, but their long-term effect on performance is unknown, and that cold water immersion results conflict, with some studies reporting blunted resistance-training adaptations. It also reports that coaches tend to overestimate athletes' need for recovery.
limitations: This is expert opinion with no new data and no described grading of evidence. The authors say the regular-use value of markers such as creatine kinase and urea nitrogen is unclear and that the use of blood lactate is debated. The text is the accepted manuscript, so volume, issue and page numbers are not printed, and the year is taken from the copyright line.
practicalImplications: Plan recovery around the season phase, the type of stress (muscle damaging, mentally fatiguing or metabolically demanding) and the competition schedule, rather than adding fixed recovery treatments after every session. Monitor with a small set of measures chosen for validity and reliability, combine performance, physiological and psychological data, and judge changes against each measure's typical error. Reduce load before competition to dissipate fatigue.
athleteDev: Programme recovery as a planned part of training, for example recovery microcycles and tapers before competition, and match the method to the stress. Use psychological strategies after mentally fatiguing work and recovery aimed at soreness after high muscle-damage sessions. Avoid routinely using short-term recovery methods such as cold water immersion in blocks where resistance-training adaptation is the goal, since the statement notes that these may blunt adaptation.
rtp: The statement does not address injury rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot be used to set return-to-play criteria. It can inform how recovery and readiness are monitored in athletes, but it gives no validated thresholds for clearing an athlete to play after injury or illness.

citation: Field A, Corr LD, Thompson CJ et al. Recovery following the extra-time period of soccer: practitioner perspectives and applied practices. Biol Sport. 2022;39(1):171-179.
abstract: An online survey of soccer practitioners explored perceptions and practices for recovery after matches that go to extra time (ET). Of 72 included practitioners, 63 (88%) believed ET delays recovery, and 49 (68%) reduced training loads and intensities for up to 48 hours after ET matches. Inductive content analysis identified five themes: conditioning, player monitoring, recovery practices, training and future research. Practitioners ranked tracking physiological and physical responses, nutritional interventions to accelerate recovery and changes in acute injury risk as the most important research areas.
tldr: Most soccer practitioners think extra time slows recovery and adjust training and recovery for up to 48 hours afterwards, but practice varies widely and the surveyed approaches have not been tested for effectiveness. Monitoring player responses after extra time is a clear research priority.
methods: Online survey sent to 208 club and federation representatives between January and June 2020, with 87 returned and 72 complete responses analysed. The survey had 14 main questions with sub-items, using 5- and 7-point scales, rankings and open-ended questions. Frequencies were calculated for closed items, and open responses were coded inductively by two researchers. The survey followed the CHERRIES reporting checklist.
findings: Eighty-two percent agreed that practices should be adapted after extra time compared with a 90-minute match, and 88% agreed that extra time delays recovery. Conditioning for extra time was not standard: 49% said they did not condition players outside peak periods, 36% did and 15% sometimes did. Seventy-two percent allowed players to return to training based on fatigue markers after extra time. Training loads and intensities were adapted by 46% at 24 hours, 68% at 24 to 48 hours and 39% at 48 to 72 hours. Common adaptations included longer cool-downs, extra rest days, changes to carbohydrate and protein intake, and longer or more intense massage and cold-water immersion.
limitations: The sample is convenience-based and self-selected, with a 42% response rate and possible bias towards this topic because respondents knew it in advance. Most respondents worked in English leagues and at professional level (44 of 72), and the instrument was not validated. The results describe perceptions and reported practice, not measured recovery, so the paper cannot show that any adapted practice improves recovery or reduces injury.
practicalImplications: Most surveyed practitioners reduced training loads and intensities for up to 48 hours after extra time and used fatigue markers to return players to training, which gives a common reference point for planning. The survey does not show which choices work, and the authors note that longer cool-downs have shown no effect on muscle soreness or glycogen resynthesis, so use player monitoring data to judge any adaptation.
athleteDev: Some practitioners prepared for extra time with longer training matches or a load increase 4 to 5 days before a knockout match, but the authors judge that such short-term preparation is unlikely to produce the needed adaptation. After extra time, practitioners commonly limited high-speed running, accelerations and decelerations in drills for the next 24 to 48 hours. The paper does not show that any of these steps improve recovery or readiness.
rtp: The study does not address rehabilitation or return to sport after injury, and no injured players were studied. It describes how uninjured players were returned to training after extra-time matches, so it cannot be used to set return-to-play criteria. Injury risk after extra time is named as a research priority, but this paper does not measure it.

citation: Wiewelhove T, Schneider C, Kellmann M, Pfeiffer M, Meyer T, Ferrauti A. Recovery management in sport: Overview and outcomes of a nine-year multicenter research program. Int J Sports Sci Coach. 2024.
abstract: The REGman project (2012 to 2021) aimed to advance understanding of recovery management in elite sport. It used a two-stage framework: first, investigating monitoring measures for short-term fatigue and recovery, and second, assessing recovery interventions, including psychological strategies, sleep, cooling, heating, compression, active recovery, stretching, massage and foam rolling. Recovery interventions had inconclusive or marginal group-level effects with possible individual differences. Individualised reference ranges improved classification accuracy compared with group-based ranges.
tldr: Across nine years of work, recovery interventions produced mostly small or uncertain group-level effects, so the authors put training planning, sleep and nutrition first. They recommend monitoring individual responses over time, with individual reference ranges for blood markers, before adding recovery strategies.
methods: Research note linking the outputs of a nine-year, two-phase multicentre programme funded by the German Federal Institute of Sport Science. The authors list 65 publications (original research, reviews and meta-analyses) mapped to project modules, outline the conceptual framework, and summarise the main findings on monitoring and recovery interventions. No systematic search is described.
findings: In the first phase, a diagnostic inventory of monitoring measures found acceptable sensitivity to change in several self-report, performance-based and physiological measures during short overload microcycles, with the ARSS and SRSS developed and validated. Changes in monitoring measures correlated poorly with performance changes. In the second phase, the recovery interventions showed low to trivial statistical evidence of effect at group level, although some athletes may benefit more than others. A Bayesian approach using individual reference ranges for creatine kinase and urea improved classification accuracy compared with group-based ranges. The authors also note that regular cold water immersion may attenuate strength and muscle gains after resistance training, so it should be avoided straight after strength or hypertrophy sessions.
limitations: The paper is an overview by the programme's own investigators and does not describe a systematic search or appraisal. It gives no per-study sample sizes or effect sizes, so the conclusions cannot be checked here. The authors state that monitoring changes did not reliably predict performance outcomes, and that individual response patterns need replicated measurement, which is hard to do in elite settings.
practicalImplications: Put training planning, sleep and nutrition ahead of recovery products. Monitor individual responses over time with repeated measures, use individual reference ranges when interpreting blood markers, and treat changes in monitoring data as a prompt to review training. Use recovery interventions as optional additions once the basics are in place, matched to the type of stress.
athleteDev: During strength or hypertrophy blocks, avoid cold water immersion or cryotherapy straight after training sessions, since the authors note it may blunt gains, and reserve it for competition or intensified periods where it is needed. Use sensitive monitoring tools such as the ARSS, SRSS, submaximal tests and individually referenced blood markers to decide when to adjust load.
rtp: The programme studied recovery and monitoring after training and competition loads, not injury rehabilitation or return to sport, so it does not provide return-to-play criteria. Because the authors report uncertain group-level effects for most recovery interventions, the findings should not be used as a basis for clearing an injured athlete to play.

citation: Murray A, Fullagar H, Turner AP, Sproule J. Recovery practices in Division 1 collegiate athletes in North America. Phys Ther Sport. 2018;32:67-73.
abstract: This study established current recovery practice and attitudes in 152 Division 1 collegiate athletes across basketball, American football and soccer, using an online questionnaire. Sleep, cold water immersion and nutrition were perceived as the most effective modalities. CWI was the most used modality, and only 24% of athletes both believed in and used sleep as a recovery method. The authors conclude that there is a discrepancy between perception and use of recovery modalities in collegiate athletes.
tldr: Collegiate athletes rate sleep as the most helpful recovery method, yet only about one in four both believes in it and lists it as a recovery practice, while cold water immersion is the most used method. Most athletes said they chose methods on evidence and experience together, and only 5% cited evidence alone.
methods: Cross-sectional online survey of 152 student-athletes (men's basketball n=10, men's American football n=116, women's soccer n=26) at a North American Division 1 university, from 161 invited (94% response), completed over two months in 2016. The 16-item questionnaire covered demographics, current practice after training and competition, beliefs about 8 modalities rated on a 5-point scale (coded as benefit or not), and the basis for choices. Group differences used chi-square, ANOVA or t tests, and clustering was used to group athletes by modality choice.
findings: Sleep had the highest overall rating (4.54 out of 5; 87.5% believed it helps), followed by CWI (83.6%) and nutrition (79.6%). Over half (53.9%) did not believe compression helps. CWI was the most used modality after training (55.9%) and competition (65.8%), and stretching was next. Sleep was used by 22.4% after training and 20.4% after competition. Among all athletes, 24.3% believed in and used sleep, 63.2% believed in sleep but did not list it as a recovery practice, and 65.1% both believed in and used CWI. Also, 65.1% believed in nutrition but did not list it as a recovery practice. Athletes chose their methods on evidence and experience together (74%), and 59% judged recovery by how they felt. The number of modalities used did not differ between post-training and post-competition.
limitations: The study uses self-reported beliefs and use, with no objective measure of modality use or effect. The sample comes from one institution and three teams, with more than three-quarters from American football, and the authors say a larger sample is needed to examine differences between sports. The sleep item may have been interpreted as night sleep only, so naps may have been missed. The abstract describes a 16-item questionnaire while the methods describe 17 questions.
practicalImplications: Collegiate staff should not assume that athletes who value sleep are using it as part of recovery, so sleep education deserves attention alongside other modalities, as the authors recommend. Because CWI is the most used modality despite what the authors describe as mixed support in the literature, staff can review why it is being used. Staff should also check whether athletes who believe in nutrition for recovery are putting that belief into practice.
athleteDev: Sleep was rated the most helpful method but listed as a recovery practice by fewer than a quarter of athletes, so sleep education and planning are a low-cost target; the authors suggest schedules and academic stress may limit sleep but call this speculative. The paper notes that CWI is used widely even though its benefits for team sport performance appear small, so its use should be a deliberate choice rather than a default.
rtp: The study describes recovery practice in healthy collegiate athletes after training and competition, and does not address injury rehabilitation or return to sport. It cannot inform return-to-play decisions. Its beliefs-versus-use findings describe what athletes do, not whether a modality helps an injured athlete recover.

citation: Jajtner, A. R., Pinzone, A. G., Abu-Amara, Y., Gant, R. W., Rivera, J., Tagesen, E. C., et al. Relative Rest Correlates to Winning Percentage in 2022 National Football League Season: A Preliminary Study. International Journal of Strength and Conditioning. 2025.
abstract: The authors examined whether season-average relative rest (the difference in days of rest between a team and its opponent in each game) relates to winning percentage across the 2022 NFL regular season. A significant positive correlation was found, and teams that won more often or made the playoffs had higher average relative rest.
tldr: In the 2022 NFL season, teams that had more rest than their opponents, on average, won a larger share of games. The link is a single-season correlation, so it describes schedule context rather than a cause.
methods: All 271 regular-season games of 2022 were analysed from public schedule data. Rest intervals were calculated per team per game, relative rest was averaged over the season, and it was correlated with winning percentage. Teams were split into thirds by relative rest and compared with ANOVA, and winning and playoff teams were compared with independent t-tests.
findings: Season relative rest correlated positively with winning percentage (r = 0.338, p = 0.029), accounting for about 11.4% of the variance. Winning teams (mean relative rest 0.183) and playoff teams (0.206) had higher relative rest than losing teams (-0.175) and non-playoff teams (-0.153), both p = 0.022, with moderate effect sizes (d about 0.71). Winning percentage did not differ between the high, middle and low relative-rest groups (p = 0.133).
limitations: Only one season was studied, so results may not hold in other years. The analysis is team-level and correlational. It did not include travel, time-zone change, sleep, training load, injuries or individual players. The three-group comparison of winning percentage was not significant.
practicalImplications: Relative rest across a season was associated with winning. Coaches could look at rest disadvantage when planning load management in the weeks a team has less rest than its opponent, as the authors suggest. The study does not show that managing rest changes results.
athleteDev: Use relative rest as one schedule factor when planning training load and recovery in weeks when a team has less rest than its opponent. Do not treat the finding as evidence that a specific load plan improves performance, because the study did not measure training or athlete outcomes.
rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It has no injury, rehabilitation, or individual athlete return data, and its team-level results should not be applied to decisions about a single athlete.

citation: Armstrong LE, Stearns RL, Huggins RA, Sekiguchi Y, Mershon AJ, Casa DJ. Reference Values for Hydration Biomarkers: Optimizing Athletic Performance and Recovery. Open Access Journal of Sports Medicine. 2025;16:31-50.
abstract: The authors compile reference values for body mass change, urine specific gravity and thirst rating from 16 field studies across competitions, training, weight-making and daily life. They propose using these values alongside an individual's own baselines within a personalized hydration plan.
tldr: When athletes lost body mass during exercise, urine specific gravity and thirst rating rose in every compiled field study, so a combination of these three measures is more useful than one threshold. Use the compiled values as a comparison point against each athlete's own baseline, not as a diagnostic cut-off.
methods: Narrative review with a described search of PubMed and Google Scholar (English, full-text, peer-reviewed, adult participants, to May 1, 2024) plus reference-list checks. From 3,224 records, 385 full texts were assessed and 16 field studies were included. Values were tabulated for outdoor competition and training (Table 1), weight-making in combat sports (Table 2), exertional hyponatremia cases (Table 3), morning versus afternoon free-living (Table 4) and 24-hour water restriction (Table 5). Correlations were calculated on group means from Tables 1 and 2.
findings: Table 1 shows body mass losses of 0.1% to 2.7% across outdoor events, with urine specific gravity and thirst rating rising in every study. For example, collegiate American football players lost 1.2% body mass with urine specific gravity from 1.020 to 1.024 and thirst from 4 to 6. In combat sports, a 48-hour weight-cut in judo lost 4.9% body mass with urine specific gravity from 1.014 to 1.026. In 14 men on 24 hours of water restriction, body mass fell 2.1% and urine specific gravity rose from 1.020 to 1.030, with thirst rating on a visual analog scale rising from 55 to 88. Body mass change correlated with urine specific gravity (r = 0.50, P = .013) and thirst (r = 0.68, P = .001). Two cyclists with exertional hyponatremia showed biomarker responses that differed from the comparison group.
limitations: The paper has no separate limitations section. The reference values come from 16 small studies, and the authors do not pool them statistically beyond the group-mean correlations. Several studies did not report standard deviations, thirst was measured on two different scales, and combat sport data were limited to a few studies. The correlations are calculated across group means, which may overstate agreement within individuals. The search was limited to two databases and English-language articles.
practicalImplications: Staff can record body mass, urine specific gravity and a thirst rating before and after sessions and compare changes with the ranges in Tables 1 to 5 and with each athlete's own baseline. The authors advise measuring at consistent times of day and seeking medical review if body mass rises or urine specific gravity stays unusually low after exercise.
athleteDev: The compiled values can help coaches and athletes build an individual hydration plan from measured sweat rate and event length. The paper does not test whether any hydration plan improves performance.
rtp: Not applicable. The review does not study injury, rehabilitation or return to play.

citation: Lempke LB, Walton SR, Brett BL, et al. Relating American Football Age of First Exposure to Patient-Reported Outcomes and Medical Diagnoses Among Former National Football League Players: An NFL-LONG study. Sports Med. 2022.
abstract: In a cross-sectional survey of 1,784 former NFL players, earlier age of first exposure to football was associated with higher PROMIS scores for anxiety, depression, sleep disturbance, pain interference and emotional-behavioral dyscontrol, but with small effect sizes. AFE was not associated with self-reported anxiety, depression, dementia or mild cognitive impairment, and no AFE-by-age interaction was found.
tldr: Among former NFL players, starting football earlier was linked only weakly to worse self-reported mood, sleep and pain scores and to none of the listed diagnoses. Age had much stronger associations with every outcome than AFE did.
methods: Cross-sectional survey of former NFL players recruited through the NFL Alumni Association and team contacts (2019 to 2020). The questionnaire recorded AFE, football history and self-reported diagnoses. PROMIS and Neuro-QOL measures were analysed with multivariable linear regression, and diagnoses with Poisson regression for prevalence ratios, both including AFE, age and an AFE-by-age term that was dropped when not significant. Concussion history and total years of football were not adjusted for, as the authors judged them endogenous.
findings: Among 1,784 players, one-year-later AFE was associated with lower PROMIS anxiety (B=-0.22, p=0.016), depression (B=-0.22, p=0.010), sleep disturbance (B=-0.16, p=0.007), pain interference (B=-0.19, p=0.014) and Neuro-QOL emotional-behavioral dyscontrol (B=-0.22, p=0.019). AFE showed no main effect on PROMIS cognitive function (p=0.116) or physical function (p=0.860) in Table 2, or on any diagnosis (anxiety, depression, dementia, mild cognitive impairment; all p>=0.449). Age was associated with all outcomes and diagnoses, and no AFE-by-age interaction was found (p>=0.066 for PROMIS, p>=0.147 for diagnoses).
limitations: Outcomes and diagnoses were self-reported, participation was voluntary, and the sample was recruited through networks, so selection and survivorship bias are likely. Concussion history and total years of football were not adjusted for. Effects were small (R2 0.03 to 0.06). The results text gives p>=0.168 for cognitive and physical function while Table 2 gives p=0.116 and 0.860, and the conclusions list both as associated with AFE; the table values (not significant) were used here. The abstract says binomial regression while the methods describe Poisson regression.
practicalImplications: Clinicians counselling former players can say that age of first exposure had at most a small association with self-reported mood, sleep and pain, and no measurable association with the listed diagnoses in this sample. The authors point to prior work in this cohort on modifiable factors such as exercise, diet and sleep, but those factors were not tested in this analysis.
athleteDev: Performance Application: the study does not address performance. It shows that age of first exposure is a weak correlate of later self-reported function in retired professionals, so it cannot establish a safe or unsafe starting age for tackle football.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: not applicable. The study covers retired players and does not examine injury, rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions.

citation: Bastgen, T., Evers, J., Oedekoven, C., Weide, C., Herzog, L., Ashton, N., et al. Repetitive head injuries in German American football players do not change blood-based biomarker candidates for CTE during a single season. Neurological Research and Practice. 2024;6:13.
abstract: The authors measured seven blood-based candidate biomarkers for chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) in 18 American football players before and after one season, and in 18 matched controls. Biomarker levels did not change significantly over the season. Phosphorylated tau was generally higher in players, and several biomarkers correlated with depression, quality of life, career length, training participation and headache after concussion.
tldr: Across one football season, blood levels of the candidate CTE markers did not change significantly. Phosphorylated tau was higher in players than controls, but the study is too small to show what this means.
methods: Eighteen male American football players gave blood before (T0) and after (T1) a season, and 18 sex- and age-matched controls gave blood once. Seven markers were measured (total tau, phosphorylated tau, neurofilament light, GFAP, amyloid-beta 40 and 42, and S100-B) with Simoa or ELISA-based assays. Apathy (AES-C), depression (BDI-II), EQ-5D-5L quality of life and a questionnaire on career, training and concussion history were collected. Group and time comparisons used Wilcoxon, Mann-Whitney and t-tests, and clinical correlations used Pearson correlation.
findings: Phosphorylated tau was higher in players than controls at T0 (10.87 vs 6.39 pg/ml) and T1 (10.12 pg/ml), with no change across the season. Total tau rose slightly across the season but was not significant. Amyloid-beta 40 and 42 were lower in players, not significantly. GFAP, S100-B and neurofilament light did not differ significantly between groups or across the season. Correlations included lower amyloid-beta 42 with depression (T0 and T1) and with high training participation (T1), higher neurofilament light with depression (T1), higher total tau at T1 in players with 6 or more seasons, a positive correlation between GFAP and quality of life, and higher S100-B when players continued to play with headache after concussion in at least half of cases. Some correlations were based on very small subgroups (for example n = 3 for depression).
limitations: The sample was small and the correlations used subgroups of as few as three players. The Methods report that three players dropped out after T0 with listwise deletion, yet the Results report n = 18 at T1, so the handling of dropouts is unclear. The training-participation threshold is 85% in the Results and 80% in the Discussion and Table 1. The text reports a positive GFAP and quality-of-life correlation, while Table 1 marks GFAP as decreased with higher quality of life. The authors describe the findings as indicative only, and blood markers may differ from cerebrospinal fluid markers, where earlier changes were reported.
practicalImplications: Candidate CTE blood markers did not change over one season in this small group of players, so the study gives no basis for using a single-season blood check to track CTE risk. Phosphorylated tau was higher in players than controls, but the study does not show that this has any clinical meaning. These markers should not be used for diagnosis or return decisions, and repeated long-term monitoring is the authors' suggested next step.
athleteDev: This paper does not inform performance training. It measured no performance, training-load or physical outcomes, and its only training link is an exploratory correlation between training attendance and amyloid-beta 42, which is too small to act on.
rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It did not assess return-to-play decisions or recovery after concussion, and its headache-after-concussion correlation is exploratory and based on a small sample.

citation: Schaffert, J., Datoc, A., Sanders, G. D., Didehbani, N., LoBue, C., & Cullum, C. M. Repetitive head-injury exposure and later-in-life cognitive and emotional outcomes among former collegiate football players: a CLEAATS investigation. International Review of Psychiatry. 2024;36(3):233-242.
abstract: The authors examined how head-injury exposure measures relate to later-life subjective and objective cognition and emotional symptoms in 216 former collegiate football players aged 50 to 87. The cumulative exposure index did not predict any outcome. Diagnosed concussions had small associations with depression and subjective cognitive symptoms, and emotional symptoms were strongly associated with subjective cognitive complaints.
tldr: In older former college players, cumulative head-injury exposure did not predict cognition or mood. Current mood symptoms were strongly linked to self-reported memory and thinking complaints, so mood should be considered when a former player reports cognitive problems.
methods: Former male collegiate football players (n = 216, aged 50 to 87) from the CLEAATS study completed a survey on playing history, diagnosed concussions and symptomatic hits, and a head-injury exposure index was calculated from high school and college contact practice, games and position. Subjective cognition was measured with the Cognitive Functioning Instrument (CFI), objective cognition with the modified Telephone Interview for Cognitive Status (TICS-m, n = 157), and mood with the PHQ-8, GAD-7 and NQoL Emotional and Behavioral Dyscontrol scale. Hierarchical linear regressions were adjusted for age and education, and a p < .01 threshold was used.
findings: The head-injury exposure index did not predict TICS-m, CFI, PHQ-8, GAD-7 or NQoL EBD (all p > .169). Each diagnosed concussion was associated with a small increase in PHQ-8 depressive symptoms (b = 0.50, p = .002, R2 change 0.052) and CFI subjective cognitive symptoms (b = 0.38, p = .002, R2 change 0.051). The emotional index was strongly associated with CFI scores (b = 0.69, p < .001, R2 = 0.36) but not with TICS-m scores (p = .052). When emotional symptoms were controlled, the concussion and CFI association was no longer significant (p = .078). Symptomatic hits were associated only with the NQoL EBD measure of emotional dysregulation (p = .006, R2 change 0.042).
limitations: The design is cross-sectional and survey-based, so reverse causation is possible, as the authors note, since depression may increase reports of past concussions and symptoms. Concussion history and playing exposure are self-reported and recalled. The sample is male, well-educated and mostly White, and the cognitive measure was a brief telephone screen rather than full neuropsychological testing. Some analyses had missing data, and the authors describe the effects as small. The abstract and Results disagree on mean age (63.4 vs 64.1) and percentage White (91% vs 92%).
practicalImplications: Self-reported subjective cognitive complaints in former players were strongly linked to current mood symptoms and were not significantly related to objective screening scores. Clinicians assessing a former player's cognitive complaints should consider current mood symptoms and objective testing, and should not rely on self-report alone. Head-injury exposure measures did not predict later cognition or mood in this group.
athleteDev: This study does not inform performance training. Its participants were former collegiate players aged 50 and older, and none of its measures concerned current training, load or performance.
rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It did not assess current injury, rehabilitation or return-to-play decisions, and its concussion results concern long-term symptoms and mood in retired players, which should not be applied to a current athlete's return decision.

citation: Iverson GL. Retired National Football League Players are Not at Greater Risk for Suicide. Arch Clin Neuropsychol. 2020;35:332-341.
abstract: Narrative review of the literature from 1928 to 2018 on suicide in former NFL players and its association with CTE. Epidemiological studies show lower suicide rates than in the general population, while a minority with depression and chronic pain appears to be at higher risk.
tldr: Former NFL players as a group have lower suicide rates than men in the general population, so CTE should not be assumed to drive suicide risk. A subgroup with depression, chronic pain or financial stress is at real risk and should receive standard depression and suicide care.
methods: Narrative review of the literature published from 1928 to 2018. No systematic search strategy is described. The review covers historical CTE case series, proposed clinical criteria, epidemiological cohorts of former NFL players and surveys of their mental health.
findings: Suicide was not a recognized clinical feature of CTE in the literature before 2010. In a cohort of former NFL players followed to 2013, suicide was less common than expected against the US population (standardized mortality ratio 0.47; 12 of 537 deaths from intentional self-harm). Surveys show that a substantial minority of former players have depression, chronic pain and opioid use, which the author links to higher risk of suicidal thoughts.
limitations: Narrative review with no described search or appraisal method, so study selection could be biased. The conclusions rest on cited case series, surveys and cohorts, and the review does not test whether CTE pathology changes suicide risk.
practicalImplications: Treat former players with chronic pain, depression, substance abuse problems, life stress or financial difficulty as at increased risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors, and offer evidence-based treatment. Avoid assuming that depression or suicidality is caused by CTE, because the author warns a CTE diagnosis could adversely affect treatment.
athleteDev: No performance application. The review covers the mental health of retired players and does not test training, performance or readiness.
rtp: Not applicable to return to sport. The review concerns retired players rather than active injury management, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions after concussion or other injury.

citation: McCrea M, Broglio S, McAllister T, Zhou W, Zhao S, Katz B, et al. Return to play and risk of repeat concussion in collegiate football players: comparative analysis from the NCAA Concussion Study (1999-2001) and CARE Consortium (2014-2017). Br J Sports Med. 2019.
abstract: This comparative analysis of two cohorts of concussed NCAA football players (1999-2001 and 2014-2017) examined symptom recovery, the symptom-free waiting period, return to play and repeat concussion. Current players had longer symptoms, waiting periods and return times, and very few had a repeat concussion within 10 days of the first.
tldr: Collegiate football players in the CARE Consortium were held out of play for longer than players in the earlier NCAA study, and far fewer had a repeat concussion within 10 days. The overall repeat-concussion rate difference was not statistically significant.
methods: Concussed NCAA football players from the NCAA Concussion Study (n=184) and CARE Consortium (n=701) were compared for symptom duration, symptom-free waiting period (SFWP), return-to-play time and same-season repeat concussion. Missing values were handled by multiple imputation for CARE, and groups were compared with t tests, Wilcoxon tests and chi-square or Fisher exact tests.
findings: Median symptom duration was 5.92 days in CARE and 2.00 days in the NCAA Study, median SFWP was 6.00 and 0.98 days, and mean return to play was 16.08 and 6.67 days (all P<0.0001). Same-season repeat concussion was 3.85% (27 of 701) in CARE and 6.52% (12 of 184) in the NCAA Study (P=0.17), while repeat concussion within 10 days was 1 of 27 in CARE and 11 of 12 in the NCAA Study (P<0.0001).
limitations: The cohorts are non-randomised and about 15 years apart, so the effect of specific clinical practices cannot be isolated from changes in awareness, reporting, diagnosis, rules or equipment. Acute injuries looked more severe in the NCAA Study (LOC or PTA 28.3% vs 17.9%), recovery relied on athlete self-report, and the samples cover NCAA football players only. The overall repeat-concussion difference was not significant (P=0.17), so the 41% lower rate should not be read as a firm reduction.
practicalImplications: The findings are consistent with international consensus advice to use a symptom-free waiting period and graded return, since repeat concussions within the first 10 days were rare in the CARE cohort, though the design cannot prove that the longer hold-out caused this. The overall same-season repeat rate did not differ significantly between eras.
athleteDev: Performance staff can expect current collegiate players to be out for about two weeks on average after concussion, which should be built into training and competition planning. The findings are about clinical management, and the study does not evaluate training load or performance after return.
rtp: The median return-to-play time of 12.23 days in CARE (IQR 8.04 to 18.92) and the finding that over 97% of CARE athletes had a symptom-free waiting period of at least one day can inform return timelines. The study shows group patterns in an observational setting and cannot set an individual's return date, so it should be used alongside the athlete's symptom and clinical assessment.

citation: Dunne EM, Striley CW, Mannes ZL, Asken BM, Ennis N, Cottler LB. Reasons for prescription opioid use while playing in the National Football League as risk factors for current use and misuse among former players. Clin J Sport Med. 2020;30(6):544-549.
abstract: This secondary analysis examined whether the reasons former NFL players gave for prescription opioid use during their careers were linked to opioid use and misuse in retirement. Among 336 retired players who had used prescription opioids in the NFL, 26.2% reported use in the past 30 days, including 11.9% who misused them. Using opioids in the NFL to function was associated with any current use, and using them to reduce stress was associated with current misuse.
tldr: Among 336 former NFL players who had used prescription opioids in their careers, using them to function in the NFL was linked to any opioid use after retirement, and stress-relief use was linked to misuse. Sedative and risky alcohol use were common among current users, so screening should cover both.
methods: Secondary analysis of a telephone survey of retired NFL players conducted in 2010, restricted to the 336 players who had used prescription opioids during their careers (from a parent sample of 644). Players reported reasons for in-career use (to function, change mood, relax or relieve stress, sleep, pain), past-30-day use and misuse, and alcohol and sedative use. Logistic regression tested the reasons as predictors of any current use and of misuse versus use as prescribed, with pain use, alcohol and sedatives included in the models.
findings: Of the 336 players, 14.3% reported use only as prescribed and 11.9% reported misuse in the past 30 days. Use to function in the NFL was reported by 56.8% of current users and 28.2% of non-users (OR 1.30, 95% CI 1.12 to 1.50). Among current users, misusers were more likely than those using as prescribed to report stress-relief use in the NFL (35.0% vs 14.6%; OR 1.45, 95% CI 1.01 to 2.11) and risky drinking (32.5% vs 12.5%; OR 3.25, 95% CI 1.05 to 10.00). Current users were also far more likely to report sedative use (30.7% vs 4.8%; OR 1.67).
limitations: The sample was restricted to former players who used opioids in the NFL and belong to the players' association, so it may overestimate health and underestimate substance use. The cross-sectional design and self-report data cannot establish cause, and the authors note possible social desirability bias. The findings apply only to professional American football and to 'to function' as a broad category. The Results text gives 35.2% of misusers reporting stress-relief use, while Table 3 gives 35.0%; the table value is reported here.
practicalImplications: Medical and team staff could ask players why they use opioids, with particular attention to use to function and to relieve stress, and screen current users for sedative and risky alcohol use. The authors recommend referral to evidence-based pain management for players with chronic pain or misuse.
athleteDev: Performance Application: Opioid use 'to function' during the NFL career was associated with current use in retirement, so staff who prescribe for players should ask why the medication is being taken and record those reasons alongside prescriptions. The study cannot show that changing practice reduces later misuse.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: The sample was retired players and the study did not measure return to play after injury, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions or opioid use during rehabilitation. It shows only that in-career reasons for use are associated with later use.

citation: Place N, Millet GY. Quantification of Neuromuscular Fatigue: What Do We Do Wrong and Why? Sports Med. 2020;50:439-447.
abstract: This opinion paper highlights pitfalls in quantifying neuromuscular fatigue with voluntary and evoked contractions. Problems can arise from the definition of fatigue and the index chosen (for example power vs isometric torque), the delay between exercise termination and testing, the stimulation technique and the way data are analyzed. The authors discuss alternatives proposed in the literature and give best-practice recommendations.
tldr: How neuromuscular fatigue is measured can change the answer: the index chosen, the delay before testing and stimulation settings all bias results. Lab testing should familiarize participants first and combine several fatigue measures.
methods: Narrative review with no described search, published as a Current Opinion article. It discusses published studies, mainly from the authors' groups, under four headings: the definition of fatigue, single-joint vs whole-body exercise, surrogates of nerve electrical stimulation, and other stimulation, recording and analysis issues.
findings: After a Wingate test, maximal power fell relatively more than isometric MVC force, while the opposite occurred after severe and moderate intensity cycling, so which task looks most fatiguing depends on the index. Typical delays of 1 to 4 min before testing after whole-body exercise allow recovery to begin, and the authors describe a cycling ergometer that permits testing within 1 s with good to excellent reliability. Muscle stimulation through large proximal electrodes gave maximal twitch and M-wave amplitudes similar to femoral nerve stimulation with less discomfort, and TMS outcomes depended on the stimulation intensity used.
limitations: The paper is labeled an opinion piece and does not describe a systematic search. Most supporting evidence comes from the authors' own laboratory studies, and some points rest on unpublished personal data, such as heart rate variability after an ultra-marathon.
practicalImplications: Teams that use MVC and evoked-force testing should familiarize athletes in a separate session, test as quickly as possible after exercise, and combine isometric force with other indices such as maximal power or time to task failure. These are expert recommendations rather than tested protocols.
athleteDev: A sprint power test and an isometric MVC can rank the same fatiguing session differently, so performance staff should not treat any single measure as fatigue. The authors also note that neuromuscular fatigue explains performance only in part.
rtp: The paper does not address return to sport and cannot be used to set clearance criteria. Its example that MVC and evoked forces had recovered 16 days after a 166-km ultra-marathon while other signs suggested incomplete recovery is anecdotal.

citation: Sclafani C, Smith P, McHugh T, Crane P. Resident Case Series: The Utility of the Athletic Shoulder Test Using Wireless Portable Force Plates for Measuring Peak Force in NCAA Division One Collegiate Quarterbacks. Int J Sports Phys Ther. 2025;20(7):1039-1049.
abstract: This case series explored the feasibility of the Athletic Shoulder (ASH) test using portable force plates to measure upper extremity isometric strength in three NCAA Division I quarterbacks. Testing was done weekly over nine weeks in the Y and T shoulder positions. The dominant shoulder produced greater peak force than the non-dominant shoulder in both positions, and athletes averaged at least 14% of body weight in force.
tldr: Sport-specific isometric shoulder testing on portable force plates was practical to run weekly in collegiate quarterbacks. Dominant-arm force was about 13 to 14% higher than the non-dominant arm, which gives staff a baseline for monitoring.
methods: Case series of three NCAA Division I quarterbacks, the top three on the depth chart and the only scholarship quarterbacks on the roster, with no current or prior upper extremity injury at pre-season screening. Weekly testing before practice on non-game days over nine weeks, using the ASH test in the prone Y (135 degrees abduction) and T (90 degrees) positions on VALD ForceDecks portable force plates, three trials per position, with peak force normalized to body weight and limb symmetry index calculated from dominant to non-dominant arm.
findings: Mean peak force in the Y position was 142.33 N dominant and 128.00 N non-dominant (LSI 1.13). In the T position it was 134.04 N dominant and 119.44 N non-dominant (LSI 1.14). Peak force was higher in the Y than the T position within each arm. Across both positions and arms, average peak force was at least 14% of body weight. The authors report only descriptive statistics.
limitations: Only three athletes from a single team were tested for nine weeks, so the findings cannot be generalized, and no validity, reliability or normative data were established. The authors did not test the athletes on the same day of each week. Standard deviations differ between the text (all trials) and Table 2 (athlete averages), and the text gives a Y-position dominant advantage range of 4% to 16% while Table 2 ratios run from 1.04 to 1.19. The case series has no comparison group and no link to injury or performance outcomes.
practicalImplications: Force-plate ASH testing in throwing-specific positions is feasible to run weekly within a practice routine. Teams could use a pre-season baseline and in-season comparisons to see whether a quarterback's force falls below their own baseline, but the 14% of body weight figure is only a local reference from three athletes and should not be treated as a normative standard.
athleteDev: For strength and conditioning staff, the ASH test gives a sport-specific measure of shoulder force that can be tracked weekly against each athlete's own baseline. The paper shows feasibility and describes how the team used the data, but it does not show that acting on the data improves performance.
rtp: The paper suggests that force-plate ASH testing could eventually inform return-to-play decisions for overhead athletes, but it does not show this. No athlete in the study was injured or returning from injury, and no criteria for return were tested.

citation: Varela-Olalla D, del Campo-Vecino J, Leyton-Román M, Pérez-Castilla A, Balsalobre-Fernández C. Rating of perceived exertion and velocity loss as variables for controlling the level of effort in the bench press exercise. Sports Biomechanics. 2022;21(1):41-55.
abstract: The study examined how RPE and velocity loss relate to the percentage of possible repetitions completed in a Smith machine bench press, and whether combining them improves prediction. Seven men completed three repetition-to-failure tests at loads set to target mean velocities of about 1.00, 0.70 and 0.50 m/s. Both RPE and velocity loss showed strong quadratic relationships with %REP, and a multiple regression using both variables fitted better than either alone.
tldr: In seven men doing Smith machine bench press to failure, both RPE and velocity loss tracked the share of possible repetitions completed, and using both gave the best estimate. Coaches can pair the two measures to estimate effort per set, but the equation is specific to this exercise and sample.
methods: Cross-sectional study in which seven physically active men completed three repetition-to-failure tests on a Smith machine bench press, at loads set from an individual load-velocity profile to target mean velocities of about 1.00, 0.70 and 0.50 m/s. Mean velocity was measured with a linear position transducer, RPE (Borg 1-10) was reported verbally at set intervals, and quadratic and multiple regressions were used to predict %REP.
findings: Quadratic fits were strong for RPE with %REP (r2 = 0.89) and for velocity loss with %REP (r2 = 0.91). The multiple regression with both variables improved fit (r2 = 0.94, SEE 7.18%), giving %REP = 0.76 x VL + 4.27 x RPE - 2.07. For the separate RPE and velocity loss equations, predicted and actual %REP correlated at r = 0.94 to 0.95 across the 140 observations, with trivial systematic bias and random errors of 9.78% (RPE) and 8.89% (velocity loss).
limitations: The sample is small (n = 7), with mixed training backgrounds that the authors flag as a possible confounder. Findings apply to a paused Smith machine bench press and should not be generalised to free-weight lifts or other exercises. The abstract gives an SEE of 9.85% for the velocity loss model, while the Discussion gives 8.96%, and the same data were used to fit and validate the equation.
practicalImplications: A coach using velocity-based training can ask athletes for an RPE at set intervals and read velocity loss alongside it to estimate how much of the possible repetitions has been completed. The equation should be checked before use with other lifts, other people or free-weight bars.
athleteDev: Performance Application: For bench press sets, the study supports pairing velocity loss with a 1-10 RPE scale to estimate the share of possible repetitions completed and to control effort. It does not show that controlling effort this way improves strength or performance.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: The study tested healthy, physically active men, so it cannot inform return to sport, rehabilitation loading or effort targets for injured athletes. It should not be used to set loads after injury.

citation: Jones B, Tooby J, Weaving D, Till K, Owen C, Begonia M, et al. Ready for impact? A validity and feasibility study of instrumented mouthguards (iMGs). Br J Sports Med. 2022.
abstract: This four-phase study assessed the laboratory validity, on-field validity, player feasibility and practitioner feasibility of four instrumented mouthguard systems in rugby league. Laboratory kinematics were compared with a headform reference, on-field events were checked against video, 18 players rated fit, comfort and function, and four practitioners rated usability. Total concordance was high for three systems and low for ORB, on-field performance differed between systems, and player and practitioner ratings favoured HitIQ and Prevent.
tldr: The four mouthguard systems differed widely: Biocore-FRI, HitIQ and Prevent matched the laboratory headform closely, and Prevent gave the best combined on-field performance. Teams should check mouthguard events against video before using the counts for player welfare or research.
methods: Four-phase study. Phase I compared peak linear and angular kinematics from each system with a headform reference at 25 to 100 g. Phase II compared triggered events in 80 player-match observations (51 male players, nine matches) with video verification to calculate positive predictive value and sensitivity. Phase III had 18 players rate fit, comfort and function after two training sessions, and Phase IV had four practitioners complete the System Usability Scale.
findings: Total concordance correlation coefficients were 0.986 (Biocore-FRI), 0.965 (HitIQ), 0.525 (ORB) and 0.984 (Prevent). Positive predictive values were 0.98, 0.90, 0.53 and 0.94, and sensitivity was 0.51, 0.40, 0.71 and 0.75. Counting off-camera and inactive assumed false positives lowered positive predictive values to 0.81, 0.60, 0.37 and 0.89. Player fit was highest for HitIQ (88%) and Prevent (85%), and practitioner usability scores were 83.8 and 80.0 for Prevent and 71.3 and 78.8 for HitIQ (preparation and management), against 51.3 and 50.6 for Biocore-FRI.
limitations: Only one camera view followed the ball, so some events could not be verified and were classed as assumed false positives. Recording thresholds were set by each company and affected sensitivity, and the on-field kinematics were not validated. The authors note that the study may have favoured systems previously tested in the laboratory or used in rugby league, and several authors have ties to Prevent Biometrics.
practicalImplications: When choosing an instrumented mouthguard, staff should weigh false positives and false negatives together rather than one alone, and check on-field events against video before using counts for welfare or research decisions. Kinematic values differ between systems, so peak values from one system should not be compared directly with another's.
athleteDev: Performance Application: Head acceleration counts from these mouthguards depend heavily on the system used, so a monitoring team should pick one system, check its events against video, and avoid comparing counts across brands. The study does not link the data to any performance outcome.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: The study did not link mouthguard data to concussion diagnosis or return-to-play decisions. The authors state that kinematic data in isolation may not support clinical decisions, so this study cannot show that these devices can guide return to play.

citation: Majano C, García-Unanue J, Hernandez-Martin A, Sánchez-Sánchez J, Gallardo L, Felipe JL. Relationship between Repeated Sprint Ability, Countermovement Jump and Thermography in Elite Football Players. Sensors. 2023;23:631.
abstract: In 20 male professional football players, high hamstring thermal asymmetry (0.2 degrees C or more) was associated with a larger sprint 2 slowdown and lower countermovement jump height after a repeated sprint test. Thigh and calf asymmetries showed no such differences.
tldr: Players with hamstring skin temperature asymmetry of 0.2 degrees C or more jumped lower after repeated sprints in this small study, but their jump drop was not significantly larger. Thigh and calf asymmetry did not separate players.
methods: Twenty male professional players had resting lower-limb thermography (thighs, calves, hamstrings) after 48 h rest, following the TISEM consensus. Players were grouped as low (below 0.2 degrees C) or high (0.2 degrees C or more) asymmetry separately for each muscle group. Each performed three countermovement jumps before and after a repeated sprint test (6 x 30 m, 20 s recovery), analysed with mixed two-way ANOVA and Bonferroni post hoc tests.
findings: Thigh and calf asymmetry had no significant effect on any sprint or jump variable (p > 0.05). For hamstrings, the high-asymmetry group had a higher percentage slowdown from sprint 1 in sprint 2 (p = 0.013), while the low-asymmetry group had larger differences from its best sprint in sprints 2 to 4 (p = 0.001 to 0.026). The low hamstring asymmetry group jumped higher after the sprint test (37.23 vs 32.78 cm, p = 0.013, ES = 0.28), with no significant group difference before the test or in jump change.
limitations: Small sample of 20 male players with subgroup sizes not reported. Single thermography session and a low cut-off set by club policy rather than evidence; the authors say a higher cut-off might show stronger relationships. Fatigue was inferred from performance measures, and the non-significant pre-test jump difference (40.80 vs 37.79 cm) may partly explain the post-test difference.
practicalImplications: Hamstring thermal asymmetry may be worth exploring as a monitoring input alongside sprint and jump tests. It should not be used as a fatigue threshold or to change training without replication in larger samples.
athleteDev: Hamstring thermal asymmetry was associated with sprint 2 slowdown and post-sprint jump height in professional players. This is preliminary support for studying thermography as a monitoring tool, not for using it in place of performance tests.
rtp: This study does not inform return-to-sport decisions. It was done in players without recent injury or pain, and it cannot be used to judge injury status, tissue healing or readiness to return.

citation: Joodaki H, Bailey A, Lessley D, Funk J, Sherwood C, Crandall J. Relative Motion between the Helmet and Head in Football Impact Test. J Biomech Eng. 2019.
abstract: Seven helmet-to-helmet impact configurations were simulated with helmeted crash test dummies. Helmets translated 12 to 41 mm and rotated up to 37 degrees with respect to the head, and helmet peak linear acceleration was 2 to 5 times the head's. The authors conclude that head motion must be measured independently of the helmet.
tldr: Helmets move noticeably relative to the head during football impacts, so video tracking of the helmet alone does not capture head biomechanics. Head motion needs its own measurement.
methods: Laboratory impact experiment. Two sled systems propelled Hybrid III dummies wearing large Riddell Speed Classic and Schutt Air XP Pro helmets into each other in seven front, side and oblique configurations at 8 to 11 m/s closing speed. Helmet and head kinematics were measured with helmet-shell and head-centre sensor packages and an 18-camera optical motion capture system, analysed from 10 ms before contact to 20 ms after loss of contact.
findings: Helmets translated 12 to 41 mm, mostly downward, and rotated up to 37 degrees relative to the head. Peak resultant linear acceleration of the helmet was about 2 to 5 times that of the head. Peak resultant angular velocity of the helmet ranged from 37 percent less to 71 percent more than the head, depending on the impact condition.
limitations: Crash test dummies, which lack biofidelity in some impacts, rather than human heads or players. Each of the seven configurations was run once with two helmet models, and helmet fit, chin strap tension, hair and friction were not varied. One helmet sensor package failed and one dummy's data were missing for one test.
practicalImplications: Helmet-mounted sensors or video of helmets are not enough to estimate head motion in football impacts; the authors estimate helmet-based angular velocity could be in error by up to 71 percent. Head-mounted or independent head measurement should be used where head kinematics are needed.
athleteDev: Staff using helmet video or helmet-based impact data to estimate head motion should treat it as a measure of helmet movement, not the head, which matters for how impact data are interpreted across football practice and games.
rtp: This study does not inform return-to-sport decisions. It uses crash test dummies and cannot be used to judge whether an injured player is ready to return.

citation: Omcirk, D., Vetrovsky, T., O'Dea, C., Ruddock, A., Wilson, D., Maleček, J., et al. Reliability of Three Landmine-Punch-Throw Variations and Their Load-Velocity Relationships Performed With the Dominant and Nondominant Hands. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2024. (Ahead of print)
abstract: The authors assessed the reliability and load-velocity profiles of three landmine punch throw variations (seated without trunk rotation, seated with trunk rotation, and standing whole body) at three loads with the dominant and nondominant hands in 14 boxers. Most variations were highly reliable, the nondominant hand was as reliable or more reliable, and group-average load-velocity relationships were very strong. Individual data gave more accurate profiles than group averages.
tldr: The landmine punch throw is a reliable unilateral upper-body ballistic test when used across both hands and three loads. Load-velocity profiles should be built and read for each athlete, not compared with a group average.
methods: Fourteen trained boxers completed one laboratory visit. In a quasi-randomised order they performed three repetitions of each of three landmine punch throw variations, at 20, 22.5 and 25 kg, with each hand, and peak velocity was recorded with a GymAware linear position transducer. Intraclass correlation coefficients, coefficients of variation and standard error of measurement were calculated for reliability, and repeated-measures ANOVA was used to compare slopes, intercepts and peak velocity.
findings: Most combinations had good reliability (lower 95% CI 0.75 to 0.89), and the nondominant hand was as reliable as or more reliable than the dominant hand. Group-average load-velocity regressions were very strong (R2 0.96 to 0.99). Slopes and intercepts did not differ by variation or hand. Peak velocity was highest for the whole-body variation, was greater with the dominant hand (mean difference 0.091 m/s), and fell as load increased. The area under the line differed by variation (greatest for the whole-body variation). The abstract states most ICCs exceeded 0.91, but Table 2 shows 8 of 18 ICCs below 0.91 (lowest 0.77, dominant hand), so the table values are reported here.
limitations: The sample was small and its sex and competitive level are not described. The load range was narrow (20 to 25 kg), and the authors note that a wider range could change the profile. The abstract's ICC summary (above 0.91) does not match Table 2, where 8 of 18 ICCs fall between 0.77 and 0.89. The text says the seated without-rotation variation had higher peak velocity than the seated-with-rotation variation, but Table 1 shows the opposite at each load, so the table is used here. Results reflect healthy boxers in one session, not repeated testing over time.
practicalImplications: The landmine punch throw can be used as a unilateral upper-body ballistic test, with both hands and a set of loads. Practitioners should track each athlete's own load-velocity profile over time and compare the two hands within the same athlete, rather than using the group average as a benchmark.
athleteDev: Use the landmine punch throw as a unilateral upper-body power test across both hands at 20 to 25 kg, and keep the same variation and hand in each session. Build individual load-velocity profiles to track progress and check limb asymmetry, rather than comparing athletes to the group average.
rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It tested healthy boxers with no injured athletes and no return-to-play criteria, so its reliability values should not be used as return-to-sport thresholds for an injured athlete.

citation: Escamilla-Galindo V-L, Felipe JL, Alonso-Callejo A, et al. Return-to-play criteria based on infrared thermography during anterior cruciate ligament rehabilitation in football players. Biol Sport. 2025;42(2):161-167.
abstract: Descriptive longitudinal study of knee skin temperature asymmetry measured by infrared thermography in 30 football players (male 23, female 7) during rehabilitation and return-to-play after ACL reconstruction, from day 2 to day 365. A linear mixed model with athlete as a random effect was used, and asymmetry decreased over time after surgery, with no significant sex effect.
tldr: Knee skin temperature asymmetry after ACL reconstruction fell steadily over the first year, which may help staff track healing between rehabilitation stages. The study does not show that any temperature value marks a safe return to play.
methods: Thermal images of the anterior legs were taken at days 2, 9, 20, 35, 63, 126, 187, 274 and 365 after surgery, using a FLIR T530 camera and standard room conditions. Knee regions of interest were extracted with ThermoHuman software, and the injured minus healthy knee asymmetry was modelled with linear mixed models (Day and Sex as fixed effects, athlete as random effect), with the best model selected by AIC.
findings: Asymmetry decreased with time after surgery (-0.01 degrees C per day, P < 0.01, Table 2), with a model intercept of 1.92 degrees C. Sex was not significant (estimate 0.14, P = 0.18). The authors report a model-based estimate of 2.52 degrees C at surgery and 1.62 degrees C at day 90, and a final asymmetry of 0.46 +/- 0.13 degrees C, still above healthy-knee values. The study did not record actual return-to-play dates, so the temperature values were not linked to return outcomes.
limitations: The study has no return-to-play dates or reinjury outcomes, and no other rehabilitation or performance measures were collected. Clubs used different rehabilitation protocols, leagues were heterogeneous, and only players who met functional criteria in the first year were included. The abstract states both predictors were significant, but Table 2 shows sex was not (P = 0.18).
practicalImplications: Staff can track the injured minus healthy knee temperature asymmetry at set time points after ACL reconstruction, and look for a steady decline over the first year. A single asymmetry value should not be read as a clearance threshold, and combining knee with thigh temperature asymmetry is only proposed by the authors as future research.
athleteDev: Thermography could give performance staff an extra monitoring point in the year after ACL reconstruction, where the study shows a gradual decline in knee asymmetry that was still above healthy-knee values at day 365. It should sit alongside strength, hop and load data rather than replace them.
rtp: The study can support monitoring of knee inflammation and recovery between rehabilitation stages after ACL reconstruction. It cannot be used as a return-to-play clearance criterion, because it has no outcome data linking thermal asymmetry to safe return or reinjury, and the authors did not validate any threshold.

citation: Cross R, Lovell R, Marshall PW, Norris D, Siegler JC. Scheduling Concurrent Training 48 versus 72 h after Simulated Match Play: Effects on Neuromuscular Function and Fatigue. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2023;55(2):301-310.
abstract: Ten male recreational team sport athletes completed two 5-day microcycles that began with a simulated soccer match, with concurrent training scheduled 48 h (MD+2) or 72 h (MD+3) later. Neuromuscular function recovered within 24 h in both conditions. Fatigue was higher at 48 and 72 h in MD+2, while fatigue remained above baseline at 96 h after concurrent training on MD+3.
tldr: Scheduling concurrent training 48 h after a simulated match did not slow neuromuscular recovery compared with 72 h. Training at 72 h left athletes more fatigued at 96 h, the day before the next match in a 5-day microcycle.
methods: Within-subject comparison in 10 male recreational team sport athletes across two counterbalanced 5-day microcycles, with concurrent training (an intermittent sprint protocol followed 1 h later by a lower limb resistance session) on MD+2 or MD+3. Maximal voluntary force, potentiated twitch, voluntary activation, EMG, POMS fatigue and quadriceps soreness were measured at baseline, after the simulated match, every 24 h to 96 h, and around the training session. Repeated-measures ANOVA was used.
findings: Immediately after the simulated match, maximal voluntary force fell 14.6% and potentiated twitch force fell 31.5%, recovering by 48 h and 24 h respectively. Neuromuscular function was back at baseline before both training sessions; immediately after concurrent training, force and twitch fell again (about 21% and 47%), with no difference between conditions, and returned to baseline by 24 h. Fatigue was higher in MD+2 than MD+3 at 48 h (5.6 vs 3.3 AU) and 72 h (7.5 vs 2.0 AU), and higher in MD+3 at 96 h (7.9 vs 4.7 AU).
limitations: The sample was small (n=10), the match was a non-contact simulation, and there was no control condition. Voluntary activation and twitch were estimated with 10-Hz doublets, which the authors note may not summate fully. The authors also note that effects below ES 0.71 may have gone undetected.
practicalImplications: In a short in-season microcycle, a concurrent training session 48 h after a match did not impair neuromuscular recovery in these recreational athletes. Athletes felt more fatigued on the day of that session, so their fatigue and soreness reports should be checked when it is scheduled.
