findings: Operated-leg speeds of 130% to 170% increased early-stance peak knee moment and peak vertical force in both limbs, while 30% and 50% decreased them. Slower speeds (30% to 90%) raised midstance knee moment and vertical load, and faster speeds lowered them. Simple linear models fitted the peak and midstance relationships, which the authors describe as dose-response, while second peak vertical force fitted a fourth-order polynomial.
limitations: Participants did not show the expected baseline loading asymmetry. The 2-minute washout may not have cleared prior effects, although speeds were randomised. Most participants had patellar tendon grafts, and the design cannot show aftereffects or transfer to overground walking.
practicalImplications: Split-belt speed is a dose that can be set to raise or lower knee and limb loading during treadmill walking. The authors suggest slower (30% to 50%) or faster (150% to 170%) operated-leg speeds as options to explore, not as proven protocols.
athleteDev: Performance Application: No performance outcome was measured. The findings concern loading during rehabilitation walking only.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: The study suggests split-belt speed can change knee loading during rehabilitation, but it cannot show that the effect lasts after training or transfers to overground walking or return to sport. The acute loading changes should not be used as a return-to-sport criterion.

citation: Paterno MV, Flynn K, Thomas S, Schmitt LC. Self-Reported Fear Predicts Functional Performance and Second ACL Injury After ACL Reconstruction and Return to Sport: A Pilot Study. Sports Health. 2017.
abstract: Prospective cohort pilot of 40 patients cleared to return to sport after ACL reconstruction. Fear was measured with the TSK-11 at return to sport and compared with activity level, single-leg hop and quadriceps limb symmetry, and second ACL injury over 24 months. High-fear patients (TSK-11 of 17 or more) were more likely to have lower activity and hop and quadriceps asymmetry. A TSK-11 score of 19 or more was associated with a higher risk of ipsilateral second ACL tear within 24 months.
tldr: Athletes returning from ACL reconstruction who reported high fear at clearance were less active, had more hop and quadriceps asymmetry, and had more same-side second ACL injuries. The paper suggests fear may belong in discharge criteria, but this 40-patient pilot cannot set a release threshold.
methods: Forty patients aged 10 to 25 who had been cleared to return to pivoting and cutting sports after primary ACL reconstruction were tested within four weeks of clearance. Testing included the TSK-11, the Marx Activity Rating Scale, four single-leg hop tests and isometric quadriceps strength on a Biodex dynamometer. Patients were split at a TSK-11 score of 17, and second ACL injuries were tracked for 24 months with chi-square analysis.
findings: High-fear patients (n = 19) had lower Marx activity in 73.7% versus 42.9% of low-fear patients (OR 3.73, 95% CI 0.98 to 14.23), single-leg hop for distance LSI of 95% or less in 55.6% versus 15% (OR 7.1, 95% CI 1.5 to 33.0), and quadriceps LSI of 90% or less in 50% versus 14.3% (OR 6.0, 95% CI 1.3 to 27.8); fear was not associated with the other hop tests. Fifteen patients (37.5%) had a second ACL injury; the ipsilateral group had higher TSK-11 scores than those without (19.8 vs 16.4, P = 0.03), and a score of 19 or more had RR 13.0 (95% CI 2.1 to 81.0) for ipsilateral tear. The TSK-11 had an AUC of 0.740 for ipsilateral injury, with sensitivity 0.75 and specificity 0.81, and was not associated with contralateral injury (P = 0.652).
limitations: Only 40 patients from one institution, a pilot study with very few ipsilateral (8) and contralateral (7) injuries, so the RR and AUC are unstable. The activity association is not statistically clear (CI crosses 1), and the 90% and 95% LSI cut-offs are debated. The abstract Methods say patients were tracked for 12 months, but the Injury Tracking section and Results report 24 months. The population was young and active athletes planning to return to cutting and pivoting sports, and the authors did not control rehabilitation or surgeon return-to-sport criteria.
practicalImplications: Asking athletes to complete the TSK-11 at clearance is quick and may flag those with higher fear who also show asymmetry or lower activity. The authors suggest fear may be worth considering in discharge planning, alongside hop and strength tests, but they do not give a validated cut-off for release.
athleteDev: Higher fear scores at clearance went with lower self-reported activity at that time, though this association was not statistically clear. The data are not enough to change the training plan for an individual athlete.
rtp: The paper directly informs return-to-sport decisions by suggesting that fear at clearance may be a discharge criterion for pivoting and cutting sports. The authors say this needs further study, and the study cannot establish a causal link or set a score that clears an athlete.

citation: Vitharana TN, King E, Welch N, Devitt B, Moran K. Sensorimotor Dysfunction Following Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury (Part 1): What Is It? How Can Clinicians Assess It? Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2025.
abstract: Clinical commentary asking what sensorimotor dysfunction follows ACL injury and how clinicians can assess it. Dysfunction is described across afferent pathways (pain and swelling, increased central processing, reduced proprioception, increased visual-motor reliance) and efferent pathways (reduced cortical and descending motor excitability, spinal reflex excitability acutely reduced then chronically increased). The authors propose practical tests of proprioception, pain, swelling, visual-motor reliance and processing, strength and voluntary activation.
tldr: Sensorimotor dysfunction after ACL injury spans pain, swelling, proprioception, visual reliance and quadriceps activation, and most of it can be screened with simple clinic tests. The battery is expert-proposed and has not been validated against reinjury.
methods: Narrative clinical commentary by five authors from sports medicine and university settings. The authors summarise mechanistic and clinical studies by subsystem (somatosensory, visual, efferent) and tabulate clinical tests with their equipment, facilitators and barriers. No literature search or appraisal method is described.
findings: The authors cite knee proprioception deficits after ACLR compared with both the uninjured limb and healthy controls, including a joint position error of 7.2 degrees in the ACLR limb versus 1.9 degrees in the uninjured limb in 10 elite athletes. They cite increased visual cortex activity after ACLR and quadriceps voluntary activation deficits up to four years after surgery. For their own adapted stepdown test they report ICCs of 0.71 to 0.96 (unpublished) and that healthy athletes improved time to stability by 17% with eyes closed.
limitations: No search or appraisal method, and the authors describe their recommendations as driven by clinical practice. The stepdown reliability and healthy-athlete data are unpublished, the suggested retest intervals (joint position sense every 4 to 6 weeks, strength every 6 to 8 weeks, EMG every 2 weeks) are practice-based, and the neurocognitive and sensory-station tests have no reliability data in ACLR patients. Most numbers quoted come from cited studies, not from new data.
practicalImplications: Clinicians can track pain (VAS or NRS) and effusion (sweep or ballottement test) each session, joint position sense with an image-based method, quadriceps and hamstring strength by isokinetic or handheld dynamometry, and between-limb quadriceps activation with surface EMG. The authors cite isokinetic peak torque values for elite field-based athletes (quadriceps and hamstrings 3.19 and 1.78 Nm/kg in males, 2.32 and 1.36 Nm/kg in females) and a between-limb EMG difference above 22% to 30% as possibly clinically relevant.
athleteDev: The cited strength values for elite field-based athletes can help frame late-stage strength targets after ACL injury. The article does not test whether reaching these values improves performance.
rtp: The paper informs which sensorimotor domains to assess during ACL rehabilitation but proposes no return-to-sport criteria or cut-offs, and the visual-motor tests have no normative values or link to reinjury yet. It cannot be used as a clearance test battery.

citation: Vitharana TN, King E, Welch N, Devitt B, Moran K. Sensorimotor Dysfunction Following Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury (Part 2): How Can Clinicians Rehabilitate It? Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2025.
abstract: Clinical commentary reviewing methods to rehabilitate sensorimotor dysfunction after ACL injury and reconstruction. Rehabilitation should prioritise efferent function and somatosensory function while reducing reliance on the visual-motor system. Proprioceptive training should start within the first six weeks and be progressed by task, visual information, cognitive load and perturbation; cryotherapy and TENS are suggested early, and high-intensity strength training, NMES and EMG biofeedback throughout.
tldr: Restore quadriceps drive with high-intensity strength work plus NMES and EMG biofeedback, and progress proprioceptive drills by task, vision, cognitive load and perturbation. These are expert recommendations from a narrative review, not tested protocols.
methods: Narrative clinical commentary by the same author group as Part 1, combining cited intervention and mechanistic studies with the authors' sports medicine practice. It presents a framework for progressing proprioceptive drills and summary dosing guidance. No literature search or appraisal method is described.
findings: The authors cite TENS reducing knee pain by 36% at specified settings, and cryotherapy with compression reducing pain by 50% with 83% of patients stopping pain medication by 6 weeks, versus 23% with standard ice packs. They cite increased corticospinal excitability when training at 75% but not 25% of maximum voluntary contraction, better quadriceps strength when NMES is added to exercise, and a progressive program building to over 90% of 1RM that brought ACLR athletes' strength to control levels by 7 months after surgery.
limitations: No search or appraisal method, and recommendations combine cited evidence with clinical practice and mechanistic research. Several doses are extrapolated (stroboscopic dosing from skill-acquisition studies, excitability data from uninjured people), the three-sessions-per-week stroboscopic schedule is the authors' experience, and proprioceptive training after ACLR has not been tested. The summary calls the evidence for strength training, NMES and EMG biofeedback strong without any formal grading.
practicalImplications: Early after surgery, the authors suggest cryotherapy with compression (ideally three times daily) for the first 6 weeks and daily 20-minute TENS for 4 to 6 weeks, with any medication prescribed by the treating physician. Throughout rehabilitation they recommend progressive strength training above 75% of 1RM, high-intensity NMES (15 to 20 s on, 15 to 50 s rest) and EMG biofeedback during strength sessions, plus proprioceptive drills progressed by task type, vision (including stroboscopic glasses), cognitive load and perturbation.
athleteDev: The framework for adding visual, cognitive and perturbation challenges to landing, deceleration and change-of-direction drills can shape late-stage on-field rehabilitation. It has not been tested as a performance intervention.
rtp: The paper guides rehabilitation content after ACL injury but gives no return-to-sport criteria or timelines and does not show that these methods reduce reinjury. It should not be used to decide clearance.

citation: Nagelli CV, Hewett TE. Should Return to Sport be Delayed Until 2 Years After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction? Biological and Functional Considerations. Sports Medicine. 2016.
abstract: The authors argue that young, active athletes returning to high-level sport after ACL reconstruction have their highest second-injury risk in the first two years, and that the knee does not regain baseline biological and functional status until about two years. They postulate that delaying return to unrestricted sport to about two years would significantly reduce second ACL injuries.
tldr: Young, active athletes after ACL reconstruction carry their highest second-injury risk in the first two years, while bone, graft, proprioception and strength are still recovering. The authors propose a return-to-sport delay of about two years for high-risk athletes.
methods: This is a narrative review and opinion article (Sports Medicine) with no described search strategy or inclusion criteria. It draws on prospective and registry cohorts, imaging, proprioception, gait, hop-test and isokinetic strength studies after ACL reconstruction.
findings: Second ACL injury risk is highest in the first two years after ACLR in young, active athletes, and the authors cite a second-injury rate of nearly one in three in the younger cohort. Bone bruises, graft ligamentization and proprioceptive and strength deficits are reported to approach baseline around two years, although the review notes conflicting evidence on proprioception and bone bruise relevance.
limitations: The review has no described search method, so study selection cannot be reproduced. The two-year figure is an argued position, presented as a postulate, and the authors acknowledge that the relative contribution of sensory loss to second injury is unclear. Much of the cited evidence comes from observational cohorts and small samples.
practicalImplications: Clinicians and staff can use the review to judge why early return may carry more risk for young athletes, and to weigh graft, bone and strength status in return-to-sport decisions. It does not establish a fixed two-year rule, because the delay is the authors' postulate and has not been tested as an intervention.
athleteDev: Performance staff should note that the review's argument for delayed return is about joint health and second-injury risk, not performance. The review does not provide training or performance outcomes for athletes returning from ACLR.
rtp: The review directly addresses return to sport after ACLR, arguing for a delay of about two years for young, high-risk athletes. It should not be used to set a fixed date for an individual athlete, because it does not give validated readiness criteria or test the delay in a trial.

citation: van Dyk N, Wangensteen A, Vermeulen R, Whiteley R, Bahr R, Tol J, et al. Similar Isokinetic Strength Preinjury and at Return to Sport after Hamstring Injury. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2019.
abstract: The study compared isokinetic strength of the injured hamstring at return to sport with pre-injury screening values in 41 professional male soccer players with MRI-positive hamstring injury. Injured-limb strength at return to sport averaged over 95% of pre-injury strength, and side-to-side differences were similar at return to sport and pre-injury. The authors conclude that isokinetic cut-off values are not useful for guiding strength restoration as a return-to-sport criterion.
tldr: Hamstring-injured professional soccer players were about as strong at return to sport as before injury, and a greater than 10% strength difference was about as common before injury as at return. Isokinetic cut-offs should not be used alone to clear players to return.
methods: Pooled data from two single-site randomized trials, including 41 players with MRI-positive hamstring injury who had pre-injury isokinetic screening. Concentric knee flexion and extension at 60 and 300 degrees per second and eccentric knee extension at 60 degrees per second were tested pre-injury, within seven days of injury (uninjured limb only) and before the return-to-sport assessment.
findings: Injured-limb strength at return to sport averaged above 95% of pre-injury strength. The proportions with a >10% difference were similar at return to sport and pre-injury, and the only statistically significant changes (quadriceps and hamstring concentric strength at 60 degrees per second, differences of 4.9% and 5.3%) were small and within the minimal detectable change. Of the 41 injuries, 21 were grade I and 20 grade II, and one re-injury occurred in the completed trial.
limitations: Testing was done at the end of a training session, so players may have been fatigued, and physicians were not blinded to the isokinetic results. Only grade I and II injuries were included, re-injury data are incomplete (one re-injury in the completed trial), and the population was homogeneous professional male soccer players. The authors suggest a 20% cut-point may be more realistic but say this needs further study.
practicalImplications: Isokinetic strength should not be used alone as a return-to-play criterion or against a fixed 10% cut-off. Expect both deficits and surpluses in the injured leg at return, and interpret any difference against test variability, which the authors put above 20% for these measures.
athleteDev: This study cannot guide training choices for performance. Its use is limited to reading isokinetic tests: differences of 10% are common in healthy and injured limbs alike, so small asymmetries should not be over-interpreted.
rtp: Supports keeping isokinetic testing as one part of return-to-sport decisions, not a stand-alone criterion. It did not link strength at return to re-injury risk, because the re-injury data were incomplete.

citation: Zuckerman SL, Yengo-Kahn AM, Tang AR, Bailes JE, Beauchamp K, Berger MS, et al. Sport-Related Structural Brain Injury and Return to Play: Systematic Review and Expert Insight. Neurosurgery. 2021.
abstract: Combines a focused PRISMA systematic review of sport-related structural brain injury from 2012 onward with a cross-sectional survey of 31 international sports neurosurgeons on operative management and return to play. The authors conclude that return-to-play decisions are heterogeneous and that level of play matters.
tldr: Return to play after sport-related structural brain injury has no evidence-based guidance, and expert opinion varies widely. Experts allowed earlier return at higher levels of play, and most allowed high-contact sport at 6 to 12 months after resolved hemorrhage.
methods: Focused systematic review following PRISMA, using PubMed MeSH terms and keywords; titles and abstracts from 2012 onward were screened, full texts reviewed by one author and verified by a senior author, and the protocol was not registered. A cross-sectional online survey covered 3 experience questions and 13 multiple-choice questions on operative indications and return timing in four scenarios at high school, collegiate and professional levels.
findings: Of 241 records, 27 studies were included. Nine articles (12 athletes) reported return-to-play information, and 10 of those 12 cases were high school athletes or younger. Among 31 responding neurosurgeons, 12 (38.7%) would not operate on an acute, asymptomatic structural injury; midline shift over 10 mm (63.2%) and hemorrhage over 10 mm (52.6%) were the most common operative indications among those who would. For resolved hemorrhage, most experts allowed return to high-contact sport at 6 to 12 months, and about 80% did not endorse return to high-contact sport with persistent hemorrhage. After craniotomy, 40% to 50% considered return at 6 to 12 months. Linear regression found that experts allowed earlier return at higher levels of play (beta -0.58, P = .033).
limitations: The systematic review yields little (27 studies, 12 athletes with return data), and the survey reflects opinion rather than outcomes. The regression is printed as beta -0.58 with 95% CI -0.111 to -0.005, which places the point estimate outside its own interval; this inconsistency appears in both the abstract and the results and should be checked against the source. The authors also note heterogeneity in both the literature and the survey responses.
practicalImplications: Use the paper as a structured aid for individualized decisions rather than a return-to-play protocol. Note the authors' finding that experts were more lenient at higher competition levels, and that they were more conservative after craniotomy or with persistent hemorrhage.
athleteDev: Performance Application: The review does not inform training load. Its only performance-relevant point is that expert views on return timing varied with level of play, so athletes at higher competition levels need individual planning with the treating neurosurgeon.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: Use it to frame the range of expert opinion on operative indications and return timing, such as 6 to 12 months for high-contact sport after resolved hemorrhage and no return for persistent hemorrhage in about 80% of experts. It cannot replace individual neurological and imaging assessment, and the evidence base is 12 athletes plus opinion.

citation: Teece A, Beaven CM, Suppiah H, Argus CK, Gill N, Driller MW. Routine, Routine, Routine: Sleep Regularity and its Association with Sleep Metrics in Professional Rugby Union Athletes. Sports Medicine - Open. 2024;10:51.
abstract: The study examined the relationship between sleep onset and offset variability, measured with the sleep regularity index (SRI), and sleep and well-being measures in 23 professional male rugby union players over a three-week pre-season period. Players with a higher SRI (regular sleepers) had significantly longer total sleep duration than irregular sleepers (about 24 minutes more per night), with non-significant trends toward higher sleep efficiency and fewer wake episodes. The authors conclude that minimizing variability in sleep onset and offset is beneficial for increasing sleep duration in elite male rugby players.
tldr: In 23 professional rugby players over three pre-season weeks, those with more regular sleep and wake times slept about 24 minutes more per night. Because the study is observational, treat this as a link to address through sleep-routine education rather than proof that routine adds sleep.
methods: Observational study with wrist actigraphy and a daily wellness questionnaire during a three-week pre-season block, plus the ASBQ and PSQI sleep questionnaires at the end. The SRI was calculated for each player and players were split at the cohort median (76.4) into regular and irregular groups, compared with independent-samples t-tests and effect sizes, and related to other measures with Pearson correlations.
findings: Median SRI was 76.4 (range 61.0 to 86.1). Regular sleepers averaged 7:42 vs 7:18 h:min per night (P=0.03) and had 169:28 vs 160:07 h:min of total sleep over three weeks (P=0.02, d=0.97), and spent more time in bed (9:09 vs 8:28 h:min per night, P<0.01, d=1.84). Sleep efficiency (85.2% vs 83.1%, P=0.09, d=0.69) and wake episodes (2.9 vs 3.8 per night, P=0.09, d=0.71) favored regular sleepers without reaching significance. Wellness and PSQI scores did not differ, and weekly running load was similar between groups (23.3 vs 23.9 km, P=0.74).
limitations: The observational design cannot show that regular timing causes longer sleep, and regular sleepers also spent more time in bed, which may explain much of the extra sleep. The three-week, no-competition window missed travel and match-day effects, only night-time sleep was measured, and the cohort was 23 men from one team. The abstract swaps the effect sizes for sleep efficiency and wake episodes relative to Table 1, and the ASBQ bedtime-variation item differed while overall questionnaire scores did not.
practicalImplications: Staff running pre-season sleep education could include consistent sleep and wake times, since the more regular players in this squad slept longer. The authors suggest that asking athletes about bedtime variation may identify irregular sleepers without monitoring, though this was not validated against the actigraphy here.
athleteDev: Performance staff can treat a consistent sleep-wake routine as a pre-season target, because regular sleepers in this sample slept longer while carrying similar running loads. The study does not test an intervention, so it cannot show how much a routine change would add to sleep or training adaptation.
rtp: The study covers sleep in healthy pre-season players and excludes injured athletes, with no return-to-sport outcomes, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions.

citation: Flatt AA, Allen JR, Keith CM, Martinez MW, Esco MR. Season-Long Heart-Rate Variability Tracking Reveals Autonomic Imbalance in American College Football Players. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2021 (ahead of print).
abstract: Resting heart rate and LnRMSSD were tracked through preseason and about three times a week up to the national championship in 20 NCAA Division 1 football players. Linemen showed suppressed LnRMSSD from playoff preparation onward, and resting heart rate rose at the same times in the combined group, while nonlinemen showed no significant LnRMSSD changes. The authors describe a progressive autonomic imbalance in linemen and suggest a downward LnRMSSD pattern as a red flag for staff.
tldr: Linemen in one college team had lower heart-rate variability and higher resting heart rate from the playoff run onward, while other players changed little. Serial smartphone tracking picked up individual drops that could guide staff checks.
methods: Prospective observational study across one NCAA Division 1 season, including preseason and regular-season weeks, conference championship, playoff preparation, the national semifinal and the national championship. Resting heart rate and LnRMSSD were measured by a finger-sensor smartphone application for 55 seconds, around noon, usually Tuesday to Friday. Analysis used linear mixed models with position and time, with Hedges g effect sizes against preseason, individual regression slopes, and correlations with preseason body mass.
findings: Linemen had lower LnRMSSD than preseason at playoff preparation (P=.041, ES -1.01), the national semifinal (P<.001, ES -1.27) and the national championship (P=.005, ES -1.16). Resting heart rate rose for the combined group (P<.001), with effect sizes of 1.03 to 1.10 in linemen and 0.48 to 0.59 in nonlinemen at these points. Nonlinemen had no significant LnRMSSD differences, though the semifinal effect was moderate (ES -0.66). All 8 linemen had rising resting heart rate and falling LnRMSSD slopes over the season, and preseason-to-postseason change in LnRMSSD correlated with body mass (r=-0.68).
limitations: Twenty players were analysed from 32 volunteers, after excluding those who missed competitions through injury or had too few HRV samples. Data came from one team, and no performance or clinical cardiovascular markers were measured. HRV was measured at the training facility rather than on waking, and no data were collected the day after matches. The playoff-preparation LnRMSSD effect size for linemen is -1.01 in the abstract and text but -1.05 in Table 1.
practicalImplications: Serial smartphone HRV tracking can show individual players whose LnRMSSD falls below their own preseason baseline during a season. A sustained downward pattern, particularly in linemen from the playoff run-in onward, may warrant a check on load, recovery and health before a formal decision is made.
athleteDev: For performance staff, the study suggests tracking resting heart rate and LnRMSSD several times a week across a season, and reviewing linemen closely as the late-season matches approach. Individual downward trends appeared before group averages changed, which supports individual decisions over group ones, although the study cannot show whether a player is overreaching.
rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. Two linemen with upper-extremity injuries appear only as descriptive case examples, and no return-to-play criteria or outcomes were studied.

citation: Fowler PM, Knez W, Thornton HR, Sargent C, Mendham AE, Crowcroft S, et al. Sleep Hygiene and Light Exposure Can Improve Performance Following Long-Haul Air Travel. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2020.
abstract: In a randomized matched-pairs study of 20 trained males flying 21 hours eastward across 8 time zones, a combined light exposure and sleep hygiene intervention was compared with a control group. The intervention group had better countermovement jump power and sprint times for 4 days after travel, longer sleep during and after travel, and better mood and motivation.
tldr: A light and sleep hygiene plan during and after an eastward flight improved jump power, sprint times and sleep for about four days after arrival in trained males. It did not change agility or Yo-Yo performance, and this is one small study.
methods: Twenty physically trained males were matched on age and baseline performance, then randomized to an intervention (n = 10) or control (n = 10) group before a 21-hour eastward flight across 8 time zones. The intervention group used earplugs, eye masks and neck pillows, scheduled sleep to night in the departure city, and followed a set schedule of outdoor or artificial light and light avoidance after arrival. Countermovement jump, 20-m sprint, T-test and Yo-Yo IR1 were tested for 4 days after travel and compared with baseline, with sleep measured by actigraphy and diaries.
findings: Over the 4 days after travel, the intervention group had very likely greater countermovement jump peak power than controls (ES 1.10, ±0.55) and likely faster 5-m (ES 0.54, ±0.67) and 20-m (ES 0.74, ±0.71) sprint times at 17:00 testing. Sleep duration was most likely greater during travel (ES 1.61, ±0.82; 6:18 vs 3:54 h) and greater across the nights after travel (ES 0.99, ±0.55), with more time in bed (ES 1.28, ±0.58) and earlier sleep onset in the intervention group. Mood and motivation were likely worse in the control group, and T-test and Yo-Yo IR1 showed no substantial between-group difference.
limitations: The sample was 20 males, and the intervention ran for only 4 days after one eastward flight. Adherence was confirmed verbally, sleep was not measured by polysomnography, and no circadian phase measure was taken, so the authors could not confirm circadian adaptation. The abstract gives ES 1.28 for sleep duration across the 4 nights after travel, but the results give 1.28 for time in bed and 0.99 for sleep duration across the 3 nights after travel; the results values are used here.
practicalImplications: For eastward long-haul trips, practitioners could use sleep hygiene (earplugs, eye mask, device limits, sleep timed to night at the departure city) together with scheduled light use after arrival. The likely benefit in this study was for jump and sprint performance and mood over about four days, not for agility or repeated sprints.
athleteDev: Performance staff could use this as a travel plan for eastward trips, since jump and sprint measures were better for about four days after arrival. Do not expect gains in agility or Yo-Yo performance, and treat this as a single small study to test with your own squad.
rtp: This study does not inform return-to-sport decisions, because it tested healthy trained males after travel rather than injured athletes. It cannot be used to plan rehabilitation or return timing.

citation: Bonnar D, Bartel K, Kakoschke N, Lang C. Sleep Interventions Designed to Improve Athletic Performance and Recovery: A Systematic Review of Current Approaches. Sports Med. 2018.
abstract: This PRISMA systematic review identified 10 sleep intervention studies with 218 competitive athletes aged 18 to 24 years. Sleep extension had the most beneficial effects on subsequent performance, while napping, sleep hygiene and post-exercise recovery strategies gave mixed results, and the authors outline a structured athlete sleep program for future testing.
tldr: In the studies reviewed, sleep extension gave the clearest performance benefit for athletes, and napping, sleep hygiene and recovery strategies gave mixed results. The evidence base is small, so use these findings to shape individual sleep plans and not as a fixed protocol.
methods: Systematic search of PubMed, PsycINFO and Web of Science (May 2016, updated September 2017) following PRISMA guidelines. Ten studies were included if they tested a sleep intervention in competitive athletes and reported performance, recovery, sleepiness or fatigue outcomes, and each was rated on a modified 8-item quality scale.
findings: Sleep extension in basketball and tennis players improved outcomes such as sprint time, shooting and serving accuracy, reaction time and daytime sleepiness, with the basketball study using 5 to 7 weeks of extended sleep. Acute sleep hygiene increased sleep duration without improving later performance, and in a one-month sleep hygiene leaflet study, soccer players who made more changes reported greater subjective performance gains. Post-exercise recovery studies (whole-body cryostimulation and evening red light) improved sleep measures, with minor performance improvements.
limitations: Only 10 studies with 218 athletes were reviewed, several with very small samples, and most used male athletes only. Quality ratings were mostly moderate, and the review reports no pooled effect size, so the strength of the conclusions is limited.
practicalImplications: For athletes with partial sleep restriction, increasing time in bed is the best-supported option in this review, with sleep diaries or actigraphy to check the effect. Sleep hygiene and recovery strategies can be introduced, but the evidence for performance gains from them is mixed.
athleteDev: Performance staff could prioritize extra time in bed for athletes with short sleep and, when extended night sleep is not possible, schedule naps at least 2 hours after training, as the authors suggest. The structured sleep program in the paper was not tested, so treat it as a proposal to pilot with your own squad.
rtp: This review does not inform return-to-sport decisions, because the included studies used healthy competitive athletes and did not assess injured athletes or recovery from injury. It can support general sleep planning in healthy athletes only.

citation: Kaczmarek F, Bartkowiak-Wieczorek J, Matecka M, Jenczylik K, Brzezińska K, Gajniak P, et al. Sleep and Athletic Performance: A Multidimensional Review of Physiological and Molecular Mechanisms. J Clin Med. 2025;14:7606.
abstract: This narrative review covers sleep physiology, the hormonal and molecular effects of sleep loss, sleep assessment methods, travel, diet and caffeine, sleep disorders, pharmacological and non-drug treatment, and sleep-based recovery strategies in athletes. The authors conclude that optimal sleep is a key recovery window for performance and that non-drug approaches should come first.
tldr: Sleep is a core part of athlete recovery: poor sleep impairs strength, power, endurance and skill, and sleep extension or naps can help some performance outcomes. The review favors behavioral and environmental measures first and reserves sedating medication for clear medical need because of performance and anti-doping risks.
methods: Narrative review using PubMed/Medline and Cochrane searches with combinations of athlete, sleep and performance terms, mostly limited to the last five years. About 7,700 records were screened, 178 articles were selected, and reference lists of key papers were added, with the findings grouped into physiology, molecular mechanisms, assessment tools, external factors, sleep disorders, treatment and recovery.
findings: Sleep loss raises cortisol and lowers testosterone and growth hormone, and a 24-hour sleep deprivation study in 20 healthy men raised pro-apoptotic markers (BAX, CCAR2) while lowering BCL2 and BMAL1 in blood mononuclear cells. Cited sleep extension studies report better sprint times and shooting or serving accuracy in several sports, and short naps of about 30 to 60 minutes helped physical performance after sleep loss. The review also cites a Major League Baseball analysis in which eastward travel reduced home-team win percentage by about 3.5%, and a study in which more than 1.5 caffeinated cups a day was linked to poorer sleep quality in endurance athletes.
limitations: The authors treat athletes as one group, select a subset of sleep factors, and do not comprehensively review sleep measurement methods. The included studies are heterogeneous and often small, few female athletes were studied experimentally, and much of the drug evidence comes from non-athlete trials.
practicalImplications: Start with non-drug measures: fixed bed and wake times, a sleep hygiene routine, light and caffeine management, and short early-afternoon naps of about 20 to 30 minutes, avoiding long or late naps. Reserve sedating antidepressants and hypnotics for clear medical need with monitoring, and check supplements for undeclared or prohibited ingredients.
athleteDev: Performance staff could build an individual sleep plan with fixed bed and wake times, a pre-sleep routine and a short planned nap on high-load days. For athletes who report poor sleep, add an objective check such as actigraphy with a diary, and review evening caffeine and any sleep products with the medical team before use.
rtp: The review gives no return-to-sport guidance and does not study injured athletes or rehabilitation. Its relevant point for rehab staff is that poor sleep is linked to injury risk and slower recovery, which supports screening injured athletes' sleep, though no rehabilitation protocol is tested.

citation: Walsh NP, Halson SL, Sargent C, Roach GD, Nedelec M, Gupta L, et al. Sleep and the athlete: narrative review and 2021 expert consensus recommendations. Br J Sports Med. 2020 (published online 3 November 2020).
abstract: Elite athletes are susceptible to sleep inadequacy, characterised by habitual sleep under 7 hours and poor sleep quality. Performance falls after a night or more without sleep, but the effect of partial restriction over one to three nights is unclear. The panel reviews the evidence, notes weaknesses in the research (poor control, few female athletes, weak sleep measures), and provides a practical sleep toolbox for practitioners.
tldr: Elite athletes often sleep under 7 hours and sleep poorly, mainly because of training, travel and competition schedules. Screen for sleep problems, educate athletes, and use naps and sleep planning where schedules limit night sleep.
methods: Narrative review by an international expert panel with a consensus process. The panel's selection and voting method is not described in the text. Topics include sleep measurement tools (Table 1), sleep and performance, sport-specific and general risk factors, travel and jet lag, nutrition and caffeine, and a practitioner toolbox.
findings: A night or more without sleep has a detrimental effect on sport-specific and physical performance, while the effect of partial restriction over one to three nights is mixed. Sleep disturbance affects 50% to 78% of elite athletes, and 22% to 26% have highly disturbed sleep. Caffeine typically increases sleep onset latency and reduces sleep duration and efficiency. Naps of 20 to 30 minutes improved sprint and peak jump velocity in cited studies. Sleep education sessions of 30 to 60 minutes increased sleep duration by an average of 20 to 90 minutes, but in one study the gains were not maintained at one-month follow-up.
limitations: The authors state that the quality of sleep and athletic performance research is poor, with inconsistent, unreliable and invalid methods, few female athletes and few controlled trials. Several sleep-extension findings come from studies without control groups, so parts of the toolbox rest on expert judgement.
practicalImplications: Screen athletes for sleep problems with a validated questionnaire and refer those with moderate or severe problems to a sleep specialist. Educate athletes about sleep, use naps under 30 minutes (or a 15 to 20 minute mid-afternoon coffee nap) to cover short nights, and limit caffeine, alcohol and heavy meals close to bedtime. Use sleep monitors with care, since they can increase worry about sleep.
athleteDev: Schedule training and travel to protect sleep, plan naps when night sleep is short, and use caffeine with care because it delays sleep onset and shortens sleep. Sleep banking before a key competition is an option for individual athletes, not a universal rule.
rtp: The paper addresses sleep in elite athletes in general and does not cover injured athletes or return-to-sport decisions. It cannot be used to set return-to-play criteria.

citation: Vitale JA, Galbiati A, De Giacomi G, Tornese D, Levendowski D, Ferini-Strambi L, et al. Sleep architecture in response to a late evening competition in team-sport athletes. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2022;17(4):569-575.
abstract: Purpose: to assess the effect of a late evening competition on sleep characteristics and perceived recovery in team-sport players using a validated portable polysomnographic device. Methods: sixteen players recorded sleep for four consecutive nights, two before and two after an evening match played between 6:00 and 9:00 pm. Results: bedtime on the first night after the match (mean 02:29) was 88 to 100 minutes later than on the other nights, and wake-up was later, while total sleep time, sleep efficiency, sleep onset latency, WASO, arousals, sleep stages, recovery and subjective sleep quality did not differ across nights. Conclusions: the later wake-up seemed to protect sleep efficiency and duration against the later bedtime.
tldr: After a late evening match, these players went to bed and woke up later, but total sleep, sleep efficiency and recovery scores did not change. The later wake-up appeared to offset the later bedtime.
methods: Observational study over four nights (two before and two after an evening match at 6 to 9 pm) in 16 male players from field hockey, volleyball and basketball. Sleep was recorded with a portable forehead device that provides EEG-based sleep staging, alongside sleep diaries and the Total Quality Recovery scale. Repeated-measures ANOVA or Friedman tests were used.
findings: Bedtime was about 88 to 100 minutes later on the first night after the match than on the two pre-match nights and the second post-match night (P < .0001). Wake-up time was about 85 minutes later than on two of the other nights (P = .049 to .050). Total sleep time was about 6.0 hours after the match and did not differ between nights (P = .253). Sleep efficiency, sleep stages, arousals, sleep quality and recovery scores did not change significantly.
limitations: Sixteen men from three sports at regional and national level. The authors note that the sample was small and that sport and chronotype subgroups could not be compared. Only one match and four nights were recorded. The device was uncomfortable, which limits longer use, and lifestyle factors such as caffeine, alcohol and device use were not controlled.
practicalImplications: In these players a later bedtime after an evening match did not appear to harm sleep. The authors suggest that forcing players to bed straight after a match could be counterproductive, and that the morning after a night match should be free of training or social commitments so athletes can extend sleep.
athleteDev: Protect the morning after an evening match from early training or commitments so players can sleep later, and avoid forcing an early bedtime straight after the match. Track sleep across the nights around a match, since this study sampled one fixture.
rtp: The study is in healthy athletes during a competitive season and does not address injured athletes or return-to-sport decisions. It cannot inform return-to-sport timing.

citation: Uchiyama K, Peeling P, Halson SL, Reid M, Wallman K, Walsh J, et al. Sleep architecture is altered with travel and matches in professional rugby union players. J Sports Sci. 2025.
abstract: This study compared sleep quantity, quality and architecture during home and away matches in professional male rugby union players. Twenty athletes had home-based polysomnography over three nights per condition: two before the match, the match night and the night after. Away travel (eastbound, three time zones) increased sleep onset latency and reduced light sleep. Match days delayed bedtime, reduced sleep duration and altered sleep architecture, with more deep and less REM sleep. Sleep duration, light sleep and REM sleep rebounded on the following night.
tldr: Matches and travel shortened and reshaped sleep in professional rugby players, with later bedtimes and less REM sleep on match nights and a partial rebound the next night. Plan sleep opportunity after travel and match days.
methods: Prospective observational study across the first two rounds of the 2023 Super Rugby Pacific season. Twenty players (age 27.5 +/- 4.1 years) wore a wireless home polysomnography device (Somfit) on three nights per fixture (MD-2, MD and MD+1). The away fixture involved a 3.6 h eastbound flight across three time zones. Linear mixed-effects models with Tukey-adjusted post hoc tests were used.
findings: Away compared with home: sleep onset latency was 12 min longer (P = .003) and light sleep proportion was 6.2% lower (P = .002). Match day compared with MD-2: bedtime was about 71 min later, total sleep time 94 min shorter (P = .016), deep sleep proportion 9.8% higher (P = .014) and REM proportion 6.9% lower (P = .026). On MD+1, total sleep rebounded by 96 min, and light and REM sleep rose by 52 and 39 min. Sleep efficiency did not differ by day or condition.
limitations: Conflict to note: the abstract gives the MD+1 light-sleep change as +52 +/- 44 min, while the Results text gives +/- 94 min; the mean is the same. The sample was small (69 of 120 planned nights), the design was non-randomised with home always first, there was no MD-1 night, and only one fixture pair was studied. The device was uncomfortable for some players, and sleep before the match was not measured.
practicalImplications: Plan sleep opportunity after away travel and match days. The authors suggest avoiding early return flights after an away match, creating dark, quiet and cool hotel rooms, and later training starts after travel. Read rebound sleep with caution, because it can hide accumulated sleep debt.
athleteDev: Protect sleep after travel and match days with later training starts, sleep-friendly hotel rooms and, where possible, no early-morning return flights. Read post-match rebound sleep in context, since the authors warn it can make players look recovered when residual fatigue remains.
rtp: The study looks at healthy players during the season and does not address injured athletes or return to sport. It cannot guide return-to-sport decisions.

citation: Leeder J, Glaister M, Pizzoferro K, Dawson J, Pedlar C. Sleep duration and quality in elite athletes measured using wristwatch actigraphy. Journal of Sports Sciences. 2012;30(6):541-545.
abstract: Wristwatch actigraphy was used to quantify individual nights of sleep in 47 Olympic athletes from four sports and 20 non-athletic controls. Athletes differed from controls on all measures except time asleep, with lower sleep efficiency and higher fragmentation, but remained within the range for healthy sleep. Males had more time awake and lower sleep efficiency than females.
tldr: Elite athletes in this home-based actigraphy study slept about as long as controls but with lower sleep efficiency and more fragmented sleep, though still within the healthy range. The data serve as descriptive reference values for elite athlete sleep.
methods: Four nights of Actiwatch wristwatch actigraphy (1-minute epochs) were recorded at home during an out-of-competition training phase in athletes from canoeing, diving, rowing and short-track speed skating. Athletes were compared with an age- and sex-matched non-athletic control group, and data from long-haul travel and altitude nights were excluded. Mean values across the four nights were analysed with two-way ANOVA, including the effects of sex.
findings: Time asleep did not differ between athletes and controls (p = 0.27). Athletes had lower sleep efficiency (80.6 +/- 6.4% vs 88.7 +/- 3.6%) and a higher fragmentation index (36.0 +/- 12.4 vs 29.8 +/- 9.0), with significant differences on every measure except time asleep. Across athletes and controls combined (23 males, 43 females), males had 12 minutes more time awake (95% likely range 3 to 21) and about 2.4 points lower sleep efficiency than females, and male athletes spent 54 minutes longer in bed than female athletes. Athletes showed larger between-person spread on every variable, and the authors note that some athletes had restricted sleep.
limitations: Cross-sectional, descriptive design with a small control group (n = 20) and no training-load or recovery measures, so the cause of the differences cannot be identified. The abstract reports 47 athletes, while the Methods and Table II report 46, and the lower 95% bound for the sex difference in sleep efficiency is 0.1 in the abstract but 0.05 in the Results. The authors suggest the absent sex difference in time in bed among controls may reflect a type 2 error. Actigraphy is an estimate of sleep, and the device model limits comparison with other studies.
practicalImplications: Elite athletes in this sample did not sleep shorter than controls, but their sleep was less efficient and more broken, so a staff check on sleep efficiency and wake time is worth making during training. Because the sample is small and single-phase, use these values as a rough reference rather than as targets for an individual athlete.
athleteDev: In a home-based training phase, Olympic athletes slept a similar total amount to controls but with lower sleep efficiency and more fragmentation. Actigraphy values for these athletes give practitioners a descriptive reference for sleep in their own environment.
rtp: This study does not measure injury or return-to-play outcomes, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It describes sleep in elite athletes during a training phase only.

citation: Erlacher D, Ehrlenspiel F, Adegbesan OA, El-Din HG. Sleep habits in German athletes before important competitions or games. Journal of Sports Sciences. 2011;29(8):859-866.
abstract: 632 German athletes from various sports reported their sleep on the night(s) before an important competition or game. 65.8% had poor sleep before a sports event at least once in their lives and 62.3% in the previous 12 months. Athletes in individual sports reported more sleep difficulties than team-sport athletes. Falling asleep was the main problem, and nervousness and thoughts about the competition were rated highest as causes. Most athletes said disturbed sleep had no influence on performance, though some reported a bad mood, daytime sleepiness and worse performance.
tldr: About two-thirds of German athletes in this survey had poor sleep before an important competition at least once, mostly with trouble falling asleep. Competition-related nervousness and thoughts were the main reasons cited.
methods: A questionnaire on sleep before important competitions was completed by 632 athletes recruited through contacts and coaches, of whom 368 were in the German national supported team system. Athletes were classed as team (n = 225) or individual (n = 407) sport. Percentages of athletes reporting poor sleep were compared by sex and sport type with chi-square tests and effect sizes (w), and follow-up questions on problem type, causes, consequences and coping strategies were asked of the 416 athletes who reported poor sleep.
findings: Poor sleep before a competition was reported by 65.8% of athletes at least once in their lives and by 62.3% in the previous 12 months. Individual-sport athletes reported poor sleep more often than team-sport athletes for lifetime experience (69.3% vs 59.6%, p = 0.01, w = 0.20). Sex did not differ for poor sleep. Women reported more unpleasant dreams than men (17.4% vs 7.0%, p < 0.01), and more often cited nervousness (69.2% vs 54.1%, p < 0.01) and thoughts about the competition (80.8% vs 71.7%, p = 0.03) as reasons. Among the 416, 79.7% had trouble falling asleep, 56.6% used no special strategy to sleep better, and 1.3% used sleeping pills.
limitations: The sample is not representative, mixes squad and non-squad athletes aged 14 to 55, and comes from one country, and the survey relies on retrospective recall with no sleep diary or objective measure. The 12-month sport-type comparison reports a chi-square of 3.40 with a p-value printed as 0.40, which does not match; the significance of that comparison is therefore unclear. The authors also note that the hypothesis of more sleep problems in female athletes was not supported.
practicalImplications: Poor sleep before competition is common, so staff could ask athletes about falling asleep before important games. The main reasons given were competition-related thoughts and nervousness, which suggests routines, relaxation and similar pre-competition strategies may be worth discussing with athletes. The study does not test any intervention, so it does not show that these approaches improve sleep.
athleteDev: Many competitive athletes in this sample reported trouble falling asleep before important competitions, linked mostly to thoughts and nerves about the event. Staff can use this to check pre-competition sleep routines with individual athletes, especially those in individual sports.
rtp: The study samples athletes in general and does not involve injured athletes or return-to-sport outcomes, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.

citation: Sim JE, Leota J, Mascaro L, Hoffman D, Facer-Childs ER. Sleep patterns before and after competition: A real-world examination of elite athletes. Journal of Sports Sciences. 2024.
abstract: Sleep of elite AFL and NRL male athletes (N = 85) was measured with actigraphy and sleep diaries across 1,808 nights and compared between nights before and after competition and free days. Before competitions, athletes advanced sleep timing and increased total sleep time, while after competitions they delayed sleep, slept less and reported worse sleep quality. Sleep after night competitions was especially disrupted. The authors suggest sleep strategies may be lacking after competitions.
tldr: Elite Australian footballers and rugby league players slept earlier and longer before matches, but slept later, shorter and reported worse sleep after matches. The post-match sleep loss was the clearest pattern and was largest after night games.
methods: Wrist-worn GENEActiv actigraphy and electronic sleep diaries were collected at home across 2 to 3 week blocks from 85 male athletes (AFL = 51, NRL = 34). Nights were classed by the next or current day as competition, training or free day, and analysed with linear mixed models that included participant and day-type random effects. Competition day start times were either afternoon (16:05 to 16:35) or evening (19:25 to 19:50) and were compared in a separate model.
findings: Before competition, sleep onset was earlier (diary, d = 0.63) and total sleep time longer (diary, d = 0.65) than before free days, and subjective sleep quality was higher (6.94 vs 6.28). Excitement and nerves were also higher before competition. Sleep efficiency and wake after sleep onset did not differ. After competition, sleep onset was delayed (diary d = 1.64), total sleep time shorter (diary d = 1.28; actigraphy d = 1.11), sleep efficiency lower and subjective sleep quality lower than after free days. Nights after evening competitions had later onset (diary 25.21 vs 24.46 h, p = .013) and shorter actigraphy sleep (5.69 vs 6.17 h, p = .049) than nights after day competitions; other evening-day differences were not significant.
limitations: The sample is male, from two clubs in one country, and collected in a real-world setting without a control group, so the findings are associations. Actigraphy tends to underestimate sleep onset latency and overestimate wake after sleep onset, and the authors did not measure performance or recovery or assess sleep complaints directly. The evening-versus-day comparison has modest statistics (several non-significant results), so the abstract's wording that sleep was 'especially worse' after night games rests on limited evidence, and the abstract's d = 0.71 for worse sleep quality matches the diary sleep-efficiency row in Table 4, while subjective sleep quality versus free days is d = 0.65.
practicalImplications: Staff can expect athletes to sleep later and shorter after matches, especially after evening games, and can plan recovery sleep and post-match routines with that pattern in mind. Because the study tested no intervention, staff should treat it as a reason to monitor post-match sleep rather than as proof that a particular strategy helps.
athleteDev: For elite footballers and rugby league players, sleep was shorter and later after matches and shorter after evening games, while sleep before matches was earlier and longer. Monitoring sleep after match days in the season may show where recovery is being lost.
rtp: Performance and recovery outcomes were not measured, and injured athletes were not analysed separately, so the study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. Injury is discussed only as a possible contributor to post-match sleep disruption.

citation: Pitchford NW, Robertson SJ, Sargent C, Cordy J, Bishop DJ, Bartlett JD. Sleep quality but not quantity altered with a change in training environment in elite Australian rules football players. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2017;12(1):75-80.
abstract: Nineteen elite Australian Rules football players wore wrist activity devices and completed sleep diaries across 8-day home and 8-day camp periods during preseason. Time in bed and wake after sleep onset increased on camp, total sleep time was similar, and sleep efficiency fell significantly. Players with higher sleep efficiency at home showed larger declines on camp. The authors conclude that the camp compromised sleep quality through longer time in bed without more sleep, and that individual interventions are needed.
tldr: Elite footballers spent about 34 minutes longer in bed on a preseason camp but slept no longer, so their sleep efficiency fell. Players responded differently, so camp sleep is best assessed one player at a time.
methods: Nineteen professional players from one AFL club wore Actiwatch 2 or ActiGraph wGTX3 devices and completed daily sleep diaries and wellness questionnaires across 8-day home and 8-day camp periods during the preseason. Home sleep was in players' own beds, and camp sleep was in a 4-star hotel with air conditioning and shared rooms. Repeated-measures ANOVA compared sleep, session RPE and wellness between periods (Bonferroni-adjusted p = .006), and correlations accounted for repeated observations within players.
findings: On camp, bedtime (21:40 vs 22:25, p < .001) and wake time (06:31 vs 06:51, p = .003) were earlier, and time in bed was longer (530.6 vs 496.5 min, p < .001, d = 1.21). Wake after sleep onset was higher (96.5 vs 68.9 min, p < .001, d = 0.87) and sleep efficiency lower (78.7% vs 84.7%, p < .001, d = -0.93). Total sleep time did not differ (417.0 vs 419.4 min, p = .846, d = -0.07). Subjective sleep quality and mean session RPE did not change. Players with higher sleep efficiency at home had larger falls on camp (r = -.46), and the relation between daily load change and total sleep time differed between periods.
limitations: The sample is 19 players from one club, and the study is non-randomised with home and camp differing in location, bedding, room-sharing, daylight and daytime temperature (29.0 vs 23.6 C). Two home subgroups were tested in different months. Sleep-onset latency was judged unreliable and not analysed. The WASO increase is given as 26 min in the abstract and about 30 min in the discussion, while the table means differ by about 28 min. The mechanism behind the load-sleep relationship on camp is unclear, as the authors note.
practicalImplications: When a camp changes where players sleep, staff could check time in bed, wake after sleep onset and sleep efficiency for each player, since the change differed between players. The study does not test an intervention, so it cannot show which measures would protect sleep on camp.
athleteDev: On preseason camp, these players spent longer in bed without sleeping longer and lost sleep efficiency, mainly through more time awake. Staff can use individual home-baseline sleep data to anticipate which players are most affected when a training environment changes.
rtp: The players were injury-free during the study and no return-to-sport outcome was measured, so the study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.

citation: Samuels C. Sleep, recovery, and performance: the new frontier in high-performance athletics. Neurologic Clinics. 2008;26:169-180.
abstract: No abstract is printed in the text. The article reviews the links between sleep length, sleep quality and circadian timing and recovery and performance in elite athletes. It describes three clinical cases and pilot questionnaire surveys of adolescent and adult athletes, and it calls for better-designed research on sleep and training, recovery and performance.
tldr: This review argues that sleep length, sleep quality and circadian timing should be measured in athletes, since each can affect recovery and performance. Pilot questionnaires suggested poor sleep quality was common among the athletes surveyed.
methods: This is a narrative review. It describes the theoretical basis of sleep length, quality and timing, presents three clinical case descriptions, and reports pilot surveys in which adolescent National Sport School athletes (n = 46) completed the PSQI and the Athlete Morningness/Eveningness Scale (AMES), and Bobsleigh Canada Skeleton athletes (n = 24) completed the same questionnaires after an education programme. The review does not describe a literature search method.
findings: In the National Sport School group, 85.7% of valid PSQI responses (36 of 42) scored 5 or more and 21.4% (9) scored 8 or more, with scores ranging from 2 to 16. Most of the adolescents were mid-range or morning types on the AMES, with 13.3% moderate evening types and no extreme evening types. In the Bobsleigh Canada Skeleton group, 78.3% of valid PSQI responses (18 of 23) scored 5 or more and 26.1% (6) scored 8 or more. In the adult group, more than 85% of AMES responses were mid-range or morning types, and 14% were moderate evening types. The clinical cases describe a delayed sleep phase treated with light therapy, a sleep-disordered breathing problem treated with positive airway pressure, and chronic sleep restriction from early training.
limitations: The article is a narrative review with no described search method, and the two questionnaire surveys are small convenience samples with no comparison group. The PSQI has not been validated for adolescents, and the author notes that its standard cut-off probably understates poor sleep in that group. The AMES is not validated. The case reports are individual examples, including treatment responses to light therapy and autoPAP, and cannot show population effects. The author states that studies linking sleep to training response, recovery and performance are still needed.
practicalImplications: The author supports screening athletes for sleep length, sleep quality and circadian phase, and assessing individual athletes who show sleep difficulty or early-morning training conflicts. Because the survey tools are unvalidated and the samples small, the results are a reason to screen and refer, not evidence of how common sleep disorders are in the wider athlete population.
athleteDev: The surveys suggest that many young and adult athletes in these two groups reported poor sleep quality, so staff can include sleep length, quality and timing in routine athlete check-ins. Early-morning training in athletes with a late sleep preference may restrict sleep, which staff can check individually.
rtp: The review does not study injured athletes or return-to-sport outcomes, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. Its clinical cases concern training fatigue and sleep disorders, not injury recovery.

citation: Halson SL, Johnston RD, Piromalli L, Lalor BJ, Cormack S, Roach GD, et al. Sleep regularity and predictors of sleep efficiency and sleep duration in elite team sport athletes. Sports Medicine - Open. 2022;8:79.
abstract: Sleep was monitored for at least seven consecutive nights in 203 elite team sport athletes (1,975 nights) using activity monitors and sleep diaries. The median sleep regularity index was 85.1. Regular sleepers had higher sleep efficiency and less variability in total sleep time, sleep efficiency, sleep onset and sleep offset than irregular sleepers, with similar total sleep time. Sleep offset time was the strongest predictor of total sleep time, and bedtime and sleep onset variability were the strongest predictors of sleep efficiency.
tldr: Elite team-sport athletes whose sleep timing was more regular from night to night had better sleep efficiency and steadier sleep, though not longer sleep. Later sleep offset mattered most for total sleep time, and an earlier bedtime with steadier sleep onset mattered most for efficiency.
methods: Athletes from netball, Australian rules football, rugby league and soccer wore wrist activity monitors (Actiwatch-64 or Actical Z-series) and completed sleep diaries for at least 7 nights outside competition, in their usual training and sleep environments. Sleep regularity index (SRI) was calculated from day-to-day sleep and wake shifts. Regular (top quintile, n = 42) and irregular (bottom quintile, n = 46) sleepers were compared with Wilcoxon tests, and total sleep time and sleep efficiency were modelled with several machine-learning methods, with linear regression giving the best fit on the hold-out set.
findings: The median SRI was 85.1 (IQR 81.4 to 88.8). Regular sleepers had higher sleep efficiency (87.7% vs 85.0%, p = 0.006, r = 0.31, medium) and less variation in sleep efficiency (2.7% vs 4.2% per night, p = 0.001). They had less variation in total sleep time (33 vs 77 min per night, p < 0.001, r = -0.69) and in sleep onset (27 vs 75 min) and offset (23 vs 62 min). Median total sleep time did not differ (8 h 18 min vs 8 h 22 min, p = 0.506), and neither did bedtime (22:44 vs 22:55, p = 0.604) or sleep onset (22:54 vs 23:03, p = 0.701). The model explained 78% of variance in total sleep time on the hold-out set, with sleep offset time the most important predictor, and 22% of variance in sleep efficiency, with bedtime and sleep onset variability most important.
limitations: The observational, cross-sectional design cannot show that regularity causes better sleep. Sleep efficiency was narrowly distributed, which limits prediction, and the authors state that sleep behaviour explained only 22% of its variance. The Key Points and Discussion say regular sleepers had significantly earlier sleep onset and offset, but Table 1 shows no significant difference (p = 0.70 and 0.68), and the Key Points give a median SRI of 85 (80 to 88.3) against 85.1 (81.4 to 88.8) in the Results. The abstract gives 73% variance explained for total sleep time, while the Results give R2 = 0.78 on the hold-out set. Competition periods, travel, altitude, medication, bed partners and daytime naps were not included.
practicalImplications: Coaches and staff can help by setting training times that leave athletes enough time in bed on most nights, and by encouraging consistent bedtimes and sleep onset. Because the study cannot show that changing regularity improves outcomes, these steps are a reasonable target to monitor rather than a proven intervention.
athleteDev: Elite team-sport athletes who kept their sleep timing steady had better sleep efficiency, though total sleep time was similar. Staff can review the regularity of athletes' sleep timing alongside their training schedules, and watch for late bedtimes and large changes between training and rest days.
rtp: Athletes were excluded if they were injured, so the study does not cover injury recovery or return to sport, and it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. The authors suggest that future work link sleep regularity to injury and illness, but this was not measured here.

citation: Kölling S, Duffield R, Erlacher D, Venter R, Halson SL. Sleep-related issues for recovery and performance in athletes. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2018.
abstract: The abstract, as printed in the accepted manuscript, states that sleep research in high-performance sport is growing and that many athletes have short or poor-quality sleep, often linked to training and competition schedules, pre-competition arousal, electronic devices and travel. It recommends behavioural strategies such as sleep hygiene, extending night-time sleep or napping, restricts pharmacological treatment to clinical cases, and recommends routine individual sleep monitoring.
tldr: Athletes often get short or poor sleep because of training and competition schedules, travel and pre-competition arousal. The review recommends routine individual sleep monitoring, with behavioural strategies such as sleep hygiene, extra sleep or naps, and medication only for clinical need.
methods: This is an invited brief review. It summarises the definition and measurement of sleep, the main challenges to athlete sleep, and intervention options, drawing on laboratory studies, actigraphy and questionnaire surveys. No systematic search method is described.
findings: The review reports that sleep disruption is common among athletes, citing actigraphy of 124 elite athletes averaging 6.8 hours of sleep with 86% efficiency, with individual-sport athletes sleeping less than team-sport athletes. It cites a survey in which 50% of 175 elite or highly trained team-sport athletes were poor sleepers, 28% had clinically significant daytime sleepiness, and 38% showed signs of obstructive sleep apnoea, based on self-defined snoring. Among 107 professional ice hockey players, 22% reported sleep problems off-season and 46% in season. It notes that sleep before competition is often worse and that early training reduces sleep time. Behavioural options include consistent sleep-wake times, screen-free pre-bed routines, extra night-time sleep, and short early-afternoon naps of under 30 minutes, with medication limited to clinically indicated use.
limitations: The review does not describe a search method, and many of the cited studies are questionnaire-based, small, or laboratory-based. The authors state that evidence for sleep extension, napping and sleep medication in athletes is limited, and that effects on performance are often indirect. Reported percentages come from specific cited samples and cannot be treated as general prevalence.
practicalImplications: Staff can routinely monitor sleep for each athlete, using both objective and subjective measures, and act early when schedules, travel or illness disrupt it. Behavioural options such as consistent sleep-wake times and screen-free bedtime routines can be offered, with extra sleep or naps tried individually and monitored. The review advises against self-administered sleep medication.
athleteDev: The review supports routine individual sleep monitoring for athletes in performance settings, with education on sleep habits, consistent sleep-wake routines and screen use before bed. Extra sleep of 30 to 60 minutes a night, or a short afternoon nap, can be trialled as an individual self-experiment with staff support.
rtp: The review focuses on sleep, recovery and performance in elite athletes and does not study injury rehabilitation, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. Its medication guidance concerns sleep, not injury treatment.

citation: de Blasiis K, Joncheray H, Elefteriou J, Lesenne C, Nedelec M. Sleep-wake behavior in elite athletes: a mixed-method approach. Frontiers in Psychology. 2021;12:658427.
abstract: Fifteen elite athletes were monitored for a 20-day in-season training period with actigraphy and sleep diaries and completed semi-structured interviews. Three influences on sleep emerged from the interviews: sleep environment, training and study requirements. Half the athletes complained about their sleep environment, and these athletes had lower sleep efficiency and more wake after sleep onset. Daily training load was weakly correlated with wake after sleep onset and sleep onset latency, and student athletes had later bedtimes, earlier wake times and shorter sleep. The authors recommend individualised sleep assessment combining actigraphy and interviews.
tldr: In 15 elite individual-sport athletes, interviews revealed sleep environment, training and study demands as the main influences on sleep, alongside actigraphy. The authors recommend assessing each athlete's sleep individually with both methods.
methods: Fifteen international-level individual-sport athletes wore a wrist actigraph (Camntech, 60-second epochs, medium threshold) and completed sleep diaries, the Spiegel Sleep Inventory, a sleepiness scale, a screen-use question and the PSQI and MEQ questionnaires over about 20 in-season days, with a session RPE used for training load. Each athlete also took part in one semi-structured interview of about 53 minutes, and content analysis produced the three factors. Athletes were then split into complainers and non-complainers about their sleep environment, and into student and non-student athletes, and compared with t-tests or Wilcoxon tests. Within-person correlations linked sleep to training load.
findings: Mean total sleep time was 418 min (95% CI 380 to 445), sleep efficiency 88.3% (95% CI 84.6 to 90.2), and wake after sleep onset 9.5% of time in bed (95% CI 8.5 to 10.4). Seven of 15 athletes had a PSQI of 5 or more. Eight athletes complained about the sleep environment, and they had lower sleep efficiency (87.6% vs 89.2%, p < 0.05, d = 0.31), more wake after sleep onset (47.4 vs 37.5 min, p < 0.001, d = 0.45), a lower SSI score and later wake times. Screens were used in the hour before bed on 63% of nights. Training load correlated weakly with wake after sleep onset (r = 0.30) and sleep onset latency (r = 0.20). Ten student athletes had later bedtimes, earlier wake times, less total sleep (6 h 50 min vs 7 h 06 min, p < 0.05, d = 0.20) and more wake after sleep onset (47 vs 39 min, p < 0.001) than five non-students.
limitations: The sample is 15 individual-sport athletes from one centre, and team sports were not included. The qualitative split into groups was based on interview content, and subgroup sizes were 5 to 10. Several comparisons were made without correction. The Spiegel Sleep Inventory has no published psychometric validity, and no baseline sleep values were collected. The authors present the work as a real-world applied example, and the qualitative findings are preliminary.
practicalImplications: Staff can assess each athlete's sleep with actigraphy and a short interview covering the bedroom environment, screen use before bed, early training and study load. The study does not test any intervention, so the sleep-hygiene and environment steps it suggests should be trialled and monitored rather than assumed to work.
athleteDev: For individual-sport athletes in this centre, sleep was affected by noise, heat, mattress and light, by screen use before bed, and by early training and study demands. Staff can combine actigraphy with an interview to find each athlete's main sleep barriers and plan changes for them.
rtp: Athletes with health problems were excluded and no injury outcome was measured, so the study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. The interviews mention sleep disturbance after hard training, but this was not linked to injury recovery.

citation: Renaghan E, Wishon MJ, Wittels HL, Hecocks D, Galasso PJ, Ren T, et al. Solving Heat Stress in Sport: Intermittent Cold Air Exposure Mitigates Deterioration of the Autonomic Nervous System in American Football Athletes. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2025.
abstract: Objectives: To test whether intermittent cold air exposure weakens the link between training duration, elevated core temperature and next-day autonomic nervous system (ANS) changes in collegiate football players. Methods: Fifty Division I male athletes in 2023 had cold air exposure before and during training. Baseline heart rate, heart rate recovery and heart rate variability were measured 24 hours later and compared with the 2022 season without cooling. Results: The 2023 cohort trained longer, spent less time at 38°C and 39°C or higher, and showed no significant association between training duration and ANS measures at those thresholds. Conclusions: Cold air exposure during training in high heat and humidity may mitigate heat-related ANS deterioration.
tldr: In collegiate football players training in heat and humidity, cold-air exposure before and during practice cut time at 38°C and 39°C or higher, and next-day autonomic measures did not show the decline seen in the previous season. The comparison is across two seasons, so the result is promising rather than proven.
methods: Prospective cohort analysis. The 2023 season (50 athletes, 128 sessions) included two cold-air exposures per session: 45 to 60 minutes of warm-up and sport-specific drills in an indoor facility air-conditioned to 15.6°C at the start of the session, and a 5-minute seated break indoors after the first outdoor block. It was compared with the 2022 season (50 athletes, no cooling). Core temperature was recorded during training with an armband monitor, morning baseline heart rate, rMSSD and SDNN were recorded about 24 hours after training, 30-second heart rate recovery was taken in the next day's session, and linear regressions were run within each cohort at 37, 38 and 39°C thresholds.
findings: The 2023 cohort trained longer (187.4 vs 161.1 min) and spent less time at 38°C or higher (9.7 vs 19.5 min) and 39°C or higher (0.9 vs 10.5 min), but more time at 37°C or higher (52.5 vs 30.4 min, marked significant in Table 1). Next-day rMSSD (82.1 vs 72.0 ms) and SDNN (125.6 vs 106.7 ms) were higher in 2023, while baseline heart rate and heart rate recovery were similar. In 2023 time above 38°C and 39°C was not associated with any ANS measure (all p of 0.68 or higher), whereas in 2022 the same associations were significant.
limitations: The control is a separate season, not a concurrent group, the cold-air arm could not be split into pre-cooling only or per-cooling only groups, and the authors note the longer 2023 sessions may partly reflect training variation and transition time. Skin temperature and hydration were not measured, core temperature was estimated by an armband infrared sensor, and time at 37°C or higher was higher in 2023, which the text does not discuss. The sample is one male collegiate team in Florida, and five authors are paid employees of Tiger Tech Solutions, which owns the monitor used.
practicalImplications: Where an air-conditioned facility exists, a cold-air warm-up and a mid-practice cold-air break may be worth trialling in hot, humid football practice, since time at 38°C and above fell. The study cannot say whether pre-cooling or the mid-session break did the work, so track core temperature during any trial.
