athleteDev: For football staff, the cold-air plan was linked to longer practices with less time above 38°C and 39°C, which helps plan heat exposure. The next-day autonomic result is a comparison across seasons, not a controlled effect.
rtp: Cannot inform return to sport. The cohort was healthy players in training, with no injured athletes and no return-to-play outcome. Its relevance to heat management during rehabilitation sessions in hot conditions was not tested.

citation: Jędrejko K, Lazur J, Muszyńska B. Risk Associated with the Use of Selected Ingredients in Food Supplements. Chem Biodivers. 2021;18:e2000686.
abstract: This review covers four newer categories of food supplements sold in Europe, the US, Australia and parts of Asia. It describes contamination, unauthorized and synthetic ingredients, and WADA-prohibited substances, and it links several ingredients to adverse effects and legal issues. The authors conclude that pre-workout, fat burner, brain booster and hormone booster products have the highest risk of harmful content.
tldr: Pre-workout, fat burner, brain booster and hormone booster supplements carry the highest risk of harmful or prohibited ingredients. Athletes should check products carefully before use, especially where doping rules apply.
methods: A narrative review of the chemical, regulatory and doping literature on selected supplement ingredients, with reference to EFSA novel food rules and WADA lists. No systematic search method is described.
findings: Products in the four categories may contain stimulants, plant ingredients used to disguise stimulants, medicines or synthetic compounds, and substances prohibited by WADA. Some products contain combinations of active ingredients that may cause adverse effects, and some have led to doping sanctions, such as methylsynephrine and higenamine cases traced to supplements.
limitations: No systematic search method is described, and evidence of harm comes from case reports, small volunteer studies and regulatory notifications rather than systematic outcome data. Prevalence figures come from heterogeneous surveys, and product contents vary by brand and batch.
practicalImplications: Athletes and staff should check pre-workout, fat burner and hormone-related products against WADA lists and be cautious about unlabelled stimulants. The review supports caution over these categories rather than proof of harm from any single product.
athleteDev: Athletes using pre-workout or fat-burning supplements should check ingredients against WADA lists and be aware that products may contain stimulants or hormone-related compounds not clearly declared on the label.
rtp: Not applicable to return-to-sport decisions. The review contains no rehabilitation or injury-recovery data.

citation: Bowler AL, Polman R. Role of a Ketogenic Diet on Body Composition, Physical Health, Psychosocial Well-Being and Sports Performance in Athletes: A Scoping Review. Sports. 2020;8:131.
abstract: This scoping review, conducted under JBI methodology, searched several databases and reference lists for studies of ketogenic diets (under 5% of energy from carbohydrate, at least 21 days) in trained athletes. From 814 articles screened, 12 studies met the criteria and covered body composition, physical health, well-being and performance. The authors report beneficial effects on body weight and fat mass, mixed effects on physical health, conflicting results for performance, and well-being benefits only after week two.
tldr: Across 12 small studies of trained athletes, body weight and fat mass fell and fat oxidation rose on a ketogenic diet, but in the one randomized body-composition study the non-KD group lost similar weight. Performance results were mixed and some physical-health markers moved unfavorably, and the authors say the evidence is too limited for firm recommendations.
methods: Scoping review following JBI methodology, searching PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science, Scopus, SPORTDiscus and the Cochrane database from inception to June 2020, plus citation indexes and reference lists. Included studies used a ketogenic diet (under 5% of energy from carbohydrate) for at least 21 days in trained or well-trained athletes, and each was critically appraised with a JBI or related checklist.
findings: The 12 studies included 101 athletes (84 men, 17 women) from seven sports, and the diets ran from three to twelve weeks. Body weight and fat mass fell within the KD groups of the two body-composition studies, but in the randomized taekwondo study the reductions were similar in the non-KD group, and lean mass was unchanged in gymnasts while fat-free mass fell in the taekwondo athletes. Fat oxidation rose in several studies, dietary iron intake was lower in the KD group, and bone resorption markers rose and formation markers fell after three weeks in one study. Performance results conflicted: VO2 peak rose in one study but exercise economy worsened, a 2000 m time improved within the KD group in one taekwondo study, and time to exhaustion was similar in others. Well-being fell in the first two weeks and then improved in one study of endurance athletes.
limitations: The included studies were small (5 to 37 participants), low quality, and mostly cross-sectional or non-randomized, and several reported on the same elite race-walker cohort, which limits generalizability and may over-weight negative findings. Performance was assessed in laboratory conditions rather than competition, and the review does not pool results quantitatively.
practicalImplications: Staff advising athletes who are considering a ketogenic diet should note that body weight and fat mass fell in small studies, while lean-mass, performance and immune effects are unresolved. The authors suggest the diet may suit athletes who struggle to make weight, but that rests on the small body-composition studies, and they recommend monitoring lean mass and consulting each athlete before starting.
athleteDev: Performance staff should not assume a ketogenic diet improves performance, since endurance and exercise-economy results were mixed and the one strength study showed no change. If the diet is used, the authors suggest tracking lean mass and adding protein or supplements to protect it, and this review does not test whether those steps work.
rtp: The review contains no injury, rehabilitation or return-to-sport outcomes, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.

citation: de Oliveira EP, Artioli GG, Burini RC. Safety of beta-alanine supplementation in humans: a narrative review. Sport Sciences for Health. 2023.
abstract: Narrative review of the safety of beta-alanine supplementation, covering paresthesia and the evidence on liver, kidney, taurine and long-term outcomes.
tldr: Beta-alanine appears safe at recommended doses in healthy people for up to about six months. The main side effect is tingling (paresthesia), which can be reduced by smaller or slow-release doses.
methods: Narrative review rather than a systematic search. The authors summarise clinical and safety studies, a systematic review and meta-analysis, a review on military personnel and the International Society of Sports Nutrition and Australian Institute of Sport positions.
findings: No adverse events were linked to beta-alanine in the reviewed literature. Paresthesia is the main side effect, is dose-related, and can be reduced with single doses under 800 mg or sustained-release forms. A meta-analysis found no effect on skeletal muscle taurine and only a small rise in alanine aminotransferase that stayed within clinical reference ranges.
limitations: Most studies were not designed to assess safety, some lacked key safety information, and none ran beyond 6 months; the clinical-marker studies used 3.2 g per day or less for 12 weeks or less. The paresthesia dose threshold is given as under 1.6 g in the abstract but under 800 mg in the body and conclusion. One author declared links to a beta-alanine supplement company (Natural Alternatives International).
practicalImplications: The evidence supports safety at recommended doses for up to 6 months. Splitting doses or using slow-release products reduces tingling, but the safety of chronic high-dose use or use beyond 6 months has not been studied.
athleteDev: Performance Application: Athletes can use beta-alanine within recommended doses, and split or slow-release forms reduce paresthesia. The review notes that the ergogenic effect applies to exercise of about 0.5 to 10 minutes.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: The review does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions.

citation: Książek A, Zagrodna A, Lombardi G, Słowińska-Lisowska M. Seasonal changes in free 25-(OH)D and vitamin D metabolite ratios and their relationship with psychophysical stress markers in male professional football players. Front Physiol. 2023;14:1258678.
abstract: Free 25-(OH)D, bioavailable 25-(OH)D, vitamin D metabolite ratios and stress markers were measured six times in 20 male professional football players over half a year. Total 25-(OH)D, bioavailable 25-(OH)D, vitamin D binding protein and several metabolites showed a seasonal rhythm, while free 25-(OH)D and the stress markers did not. Free and total 25-(OH)D were not correlated with the stress markers, so free measurement showed no advantage in this group.
tldr: In one club of professional footballers, total and bioavailable vitamin D were higher in summer than winter. Free vitamin D and the stress markers did not follow a seasonal pattern and were not linked to each other.
methods: Longitudinal observational study of 20 male professional players from one club, after excluding injured players, those missing more than two draws, and regular calcium or vitamin D supplement users. Blood was drawn in June (V1), July (V2), August (V3), October (V4), December (V5) and January (V6) across pre-season, competitive season and off-season. Total 25-(OH)D metabolites were measured by LC-MS/MS, VDBP by ELISA, and free and bioavailable 25-(OH)D were calculated. Stress markers included ferritin, liver enzymes, CK, testosterone, cortisol and T/C ratio. Mixed models, cosinor rhythm analysis and Pearson correlations were used.
findings: Cosinor analysis showed a seasonal rhythm for VDBP (P=0.003), total 25-(OH)D (P<0.001), bioavailable 25-(OH)D (P<0.001), 24,25-(OH)2D3 (P<0.001), 3-epi-25-(OH)D3 (P<0.001), and the 25-(OH)D3:24,25-(OH)2D3 and 25-(OH)D3:3-epi-25-(OH)D3 ratios. Summer values were higher than winter for VDBP (P=0.013), total 25-(OH)D (P<0.001), bioavailable 25-(OH)D (P=0.006) and 24,25-(OH)2D3 (P<0.001); mean total 25-(OH)D fell from 48.6 ng/mL in August to 33.7 ng/mL in January. Free 25-(OH)D showed no rhythm (P=0.082) and no seasonal difference (P=0.12). No stress marker showed a rhythm, although AST (P=0.027) and ALT (P=0.018) were higher in summer than winter. A strong correlation between 25-(OH)D3 and 24,25-(OH)2D3 was present in each period.
limitations: Twenty of 42 recruited players were analysed, and the data cover only half of a year. Free 25-(OH)D was calculated from total 25-(OH)D and binding constants rather than measured. Training load was described by session type and duration only, so the claim that loads did not affect metabolites is weakly supported. Sporadic vitamin D intake was allowed, and the authors name sunlight exposure as a major driver of vitamin D levels without reporting measuring it. The text and Table 4 also differ on one p-value.
practicalImplications: In this club at 50 to 54 degrees N, total and bioavailable vitamin D fell from summer to winter, although group means stayed above 30 ng/mL. The study did not test monitoring or supplementation, and it does not show that free vitamin D or the stress markers are useful for guiding intake or training.
athleteDev: This study has limited direct performance application. It suggests that total and bioavailable vitamin D in professional footballers tend to be lower in winter, which may matter for planning vitamin D monitoring across the year, and it does not show that stress markers or free vitamin D add to training decisions.
rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It excluded injured players and did not measure rehabilitation, injury recovery or return-to-play outcomes.

citation: Crewther B, Witek K, Zmijewski P, Obmiński Z. Short-Term D-Aspartic Acid Supplementation Does Not Affect Serum Biomarkers Associated With the Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Gonadal Axis in Male Climbers. International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism. 2018 (ahead of print).
abstract: In a two-period crossover trial, 16 male climbers took 3 g/day of D-aspartic acid or placebo for two weeks. D-aspartic acid did not change serum testosterone, free testosterone or LH, and the only hormonal time effects were a rise in SHBG and a fall in cortisol.
tldr: In 16 male climbers, 3 g/day of D-aspartic acid for two weeks did not change testosterone, free testosterone or LH compared with placebo. Hormone findings in this small group do not support its use to raise testosterone in similar athletes.
methods: Sixteen male climbers (mean age 35.4 years) completed a randomised, single-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial with 3 g/day of D-aspartic acid or placebo for 2 weeks, a 2-week washout, then the reverse order. Serum testosterone, LH, SHBG and cortisol were measured before and after each block, with calculated free testosterone, hand-grip strength, body mass and blood chemistry. Analysis used two-factor repeated-measures ANOVA and Pearson correlations.
findings: D-aspartic acid had no treatment or treatment-by-time effect on testosterone, free testosterone, LH, body mass, grip strength or blood chemistry. Time effects across both conditions were a 6.8% rise in SHBG, a 13.6% fall in cortisol and a 3.1% rise in left-hand grip strength (p=.025). Pre-treatment testosterone was negatively related to its change under placebo but not under DAA, although these correlations did not differ between treatments.
limitations: The study used 16 participants, a two-week dose, a short washout and uncontrolled diet, and the authors note that endogenous DAA was not measured. Performance was assessed only by grip strength and body mass, so the authors' conclusion that DAA gives no ergogenic benefit goes beyond the data.
practicalImplications: Staff advising climbers or similar trained men should know that 3 g/day of D-aspartic acid for two weeks did not change testosterone or LH in this group. The study does not show that the supplement is ineffective for other athletes, doses or durations.
athleteDev: This study does not show a performance benefit or harm, because the only performance-related outcome was hand-grip strength. Its hormone findings suggest no short-term change in testosterone-related markers in trained climbers, which is limited evidence for a training-focused decision.
rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. Participants were healthy and injury-free, and no injured athletes or rehabilitation outcomes were studied.

citation: Page J, Erskine RM, Hopkins ND. Skeletal muscle properties and vascular function do not differ between healthy, young vegan and omnivorous men. Eur J Sport Sci. 2021.
abstract: The study compared vascular and skeletal muscle properties between young, healthy, recreationally active habitual vegan (n = 9) and omnivorous (n = 16) men. Vegans consumed less protein, saturated fat and cholesterol. There was anecdotal Bayesian evidence for no differences in FMD, cIMT, vastus lateralis thickness, pennation angle, knee extension MVIC or VO2max, and the authors conclude that a healthy vegan diet is neither beneficial nor detrimental for vascular and muscle health in young untrained men.
tldr: In young untrained men, habitual vegans had similar muscle size, strength, VO2max and vascular function to omnivores despite eating less protein. The sample was small and the evidence for no difference was weak, so it does not settle the question for athletes.
methods: Single-centre cross-sectional study of 25 young men (16 omnivores, 9 vegans of at least six months) with no resistance or endurance training in the prior six months and no more than two hours a week of structured exercise. Measures were brachial FMD and carotid IMT by ultrasound, vastus lateralis thickness and pennation angle, knee extension MVIC on a dynamometer, and VO2max on a cycle ergometer with gas analysis. Diet came from a three-day food diary, and groups were compared with Bayesian independent-groups analysis.
findings: Vegans ate less protein (64 vs 98 g/d; 0.9 vs 1.4 g/kg/d), saturated fat, cholesterol and vitamin B12, and more fibre, iron and vitamin C. Between-group differences in muscle thickness (-1.72 mm, BF01 2.726), pennation angle (BF01 2.844), absolute MVIC (75.93 N, BF01 1.656) and relative VO2max (4.81 mL/kg/min, BF01 1.218) gave only anecdotal evidence for no difference, as did the vascular measures (BF01 1.557 to 2.591). Vegans were older than omnivores (24 vs 21 years, strong evidence).
limitations: The sample was small and limited to young, healthy, untrained men, and diet was recorded over only three days without amino acid analysis. Some abstract values differ from the tables (for example FMD is 3.37% vs 4.58% in the abstract but 6.54% vs 5.32% for vegans vs omnivores in Table 3), and this record uses the table values. The authors note that the lack of age-related decline in this cohort may explain the absence of vascular differences.
practicalImplications: In untrained young men, a habitual vegan diet providing about 0.9 g/kg/d protein was not linked to smaller or weaker thigh muscles or lower VO2max. The study does not test athletes or training adaptation, so it cannot set protein targets for vegan athletes.
athleteDev: This study cannot show how a vegan diet affects training adaptation, because participants were not resistance or endurance trained. The authors themselves suggest protein quality may matter more after resistance exercise in athletes, which this design did not test.
rtp: Cannot inform return to sport: the study involved healthy, uninjured, untrained men and measured no injury, rehabilitation or recovery outcomes.

citation: Aragón-Vargas LF, Garzón-Mosquera JC, Montoya-Arroyo JA. Skimmed, lactose-free milk ingestion postexercise: rehydration effectiveness and gastrointestinal disturbances versus water and a sports drink in physically active people. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2024.
abstract: This study compared rehydration after moderate-intensity cycling in the heat with water, a sports drink or skimmed lactose-free milk in 16 physically active college students, measuring net fluid balance, diuresis and gastrointestinal symptoms over 3 hours. Milk showed higher fluid retention (about 69%) than water (about 40%), and the sports drink (about 56%) did not differ from either. Gastrointestinal symptoms were mild and did not differ among drinks.
tldr: After a 2% body-mass loss in heat, skimmed lactose-free milk retained more fluid than water over 3 hours, with mild gut symptoms similar to the other drinks. It was not significantly different from a sports drink on fluid retention.
methods: Randomized crossover design in which 16 physically active college students each completed three sessions of cycling in a heat chamber (32 degrees C, 70% relative humidity) to lose about 2% of body mass. They then drank 150% of the loss in three aliquots over 90 minutes, with water, a sports drink or skimmed lactose-free milk, and fluid balance, urine output and gastrointestinal symptoms were measured for 3 hours.
findings: Fluid retention was about 69.8% for milk, 55.6% for the sports drink and 39.6% for water, with only milk versus water significant. Net fluid balance at 3 hours was -0.26 kg for milk, -0.42 kg for the sports drink and -0.67 kg for water; both milk and the sports drink differed from water, while milk and the sports drink did not differ (-0.15 kg, p = .126). Accumulated urine at 3 hours was lower with milk than with the sports drink (313 ml, p < .001) and water (611 ml, p < .001), and gastrointestinal scores were low.
limitations: The sample was small and recreationally active rather than trained athletes, and only one heat exposure with about 2 L of fluid was tested. Milk produced significantly less urine than the sports drink, yet fluid retention and net fluid balance did not differ significantly between them, and the authors report no gastrointestinal differences among drinks although the model's condition main effect was significant (p = .025). The drinks differed in protein, carbohydrate, fat and potassium, so the study cannot say which component drives retention.
practicalImplications: After a moderate sweat loss in heat, skimmed lactose-free milk may be a practical rehydration option if it is tolerated, since it retained more fluid than water and produced less urine than both water and the sports drink. On retention and net fluid balance, milk and the sports drink did not differ significantly, so tolerance and preference remain reasonable deciding factors between them.
athleteDev: In physically active adults rehydrating after exercise in the heat, milk gave better fluid retention than water, so it is a reasonable option for athletes who tolerate it. The study did not test athletes, carbohydrate or electrolyte goals, or later performance, so it does not settle drink choice for performance needs.
rtp: Cannot inform return to sport: the participants were physically active students without injury, and the study measured only post-exercise hydration.

citation: Luetkemeier MJ, Hanisko JM, Aho KM. Skin tattoos alter sweat rate and Na+ concentration. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2017;49(7):1432-1436.
abstract: The study compared sweat rate and sweat Na+ concentration from tattooed and nontattooed skin in 10 healthy men, using pilocarpine iontophoresis. Tattooed skin produced less sweat (0.18 vs 0.35 mg/cm2/min) and sweat with more sodium (69.1 vs 42.6 mmol/L) than nontattooed skin. The authors conclude that tattooed skin altered sweat function, and the changes did not relate to tattoo age.
tldr: Tattooed skin sweated about half as much as untattooed skin and gave sweat with higher sodium when stimulated at rest. Whether this changes sweat loss or heat tolerance during exercise has not been tested.
methods: Within-person comparison in 10 apparently healthy men with a tattoo of at least 5.2 cm2 on one side of the body and untattooed skin at the contralateral site. Sweat was stimulated by two 5-minute cycles of pilocarpine iontophoresis, collected for 20 minutes on a sweat collection disk, and analyzed for rate (by weight) and sodium (by flame photometry). Tattooed and nontattooed sites were compared with paired t-tests, and tattoo age was correlated with the ratios.
findings: Sweat rate from tattooed skin was 0.18 +/- 0.15 vs 0.35 +/- 0.25 mg/cm2/min for nontattooed skin (p = 0.001), with all 10 men sweating less on the tattooed side (ratio 0.53). Sweat Na+ was 69.1 +/- 28.9 vs 42.6 +/- 15.2 mmol/L (p = 0.02), with nine of ten men higher on the tattooed side. Tattoo age explained less than 1% of the variance in the sweat rate ratio and about 6% of the sodium ratio.
limitations: The sample was 10 men, the stimulus was pilocarpine at rest in a room controlled at 19 to 21 C, and no heat load or exercise was applied. The authors state the mechanism is unclear, that the results are preliminary, and that it is unknown whether similar changes occur with heat stress or internal heat production.
practicalImplications: Under pilocarpine stimulation at rest, tattooed skin produced less sweat with a higher sodium concentration, so heavily tattooed athletes may warrant attention in hot conditions. This has not been tested during exercise or heat stress, so it should not change current hydration plans yet.
athleteDev: This study does not give a performance or training prescription. It suggests tattooed skin may sweat differently, which could matter for heat-training planning, but that needs testing during exercise before it informs practice.
rtp: Cannot inform return to sport: participants were healthy non-athletes with no injury, and the study measured sweat function at rest only.

citation: Doherty R, Madigan S, Warrington G, Ellis J. Sleep and Nutrition Interactions: Implications for Athletes. Nutrients. 2019;11:822.
abstract: This narrative review explores the relationship between sleep and nutrition. Various nutritional interventions have been shown to improve sleep, including high carbohydrate, high glycaemic index evening meals, melatonin, tryptophan-rich protein, tart cherry juice, kiwifruit and micronutrients. The authors state that functional food-based interventions designed to enhance sleep and recovery warrant further investigation.
tldr: Several foods and nutrients have improved sleep in small studies, mostly outside athletic groups. For athletes they are options to test, not proven interventions.
methods: Narrative review with no described search strategy. It covers sleep physiology, the sleep-nutrition link and specific nutrients: carbohydrate, melatonin, tryptophan-rich protein, antioxidants, tart cherry, kiwifruit, B vitamins and magnesium.
findings: In one study, a high glycaemic index meal eaten four hours before bed cut sleep onset latency to 9.0 min, against 17.5 min after a low glycaemic index meal. In one study of healthy adults, tart cherry juice increased total sleep time by 34 min. In 25 volunteers with sleep disturbance, two kiwifruit an hour before bed for four weeks increased actigraphy sleep duration by 16.9%, with no control group. In six healthy men, melatonin at 0.3 mg or 1 mg shortened sleep onset latency when taken at 6 pm or 8 pm, but 0.3 mg taken at 9 pm lengthened it.
limitations: No systematic search or quality appraisal is described. Several cited trials are small or uncontrolled. The review notes that most antioxidant studies have been done in healthy adults, and that a melatonin, magnesium and zinc supplement will most likely only help where there is a deficiency or insufficiency.
practicalImplications: Evening meal timing and content are low-risk options to test with athletes who struggle to fall asleep. Late caffeine and alcohol are reasonable to limit, given their documented effects on sleep onset, duration and REM sleep. Magnesium and zinc supplements are likely to help only where there is a deficiency, and any supplement should be checked for banned substances.
athleteDev: Use evening food timing and content, plus limits on late caffeine and alcohol, as first sleep steps for athletes. Treat tart cherry, kiwifruit and tryptophan-rich protein as options to trial and track with individual athletes, not as proven interventions.
rtp: The review does not address injured athletes or return to sport, and its sleep findings come mostly from non-athletes. It should not guide return-to-sport decisions.

citation: Jerger S, Centner C, Lauber B, Seynnes O, Friedrich T, Lolli D, et al. Specific collagen peptides increase adaptions of patellar tendon morphology following 14-weeks of high-load resistance training: A randomized-controlled trial. Eur J Sport Sci. 2023;23(12):2329-2339.
abstract: This placebo-controlled study tested 5 g a day of specific collagen peptides (SCP) combined with 14 weeks of resistance training in 50 healthy, moderately active men. The SCP group showed a significantly greater increase in patellar tendon cross-sectional area than placebo at 60% and 70% of tendon length. Both groups increased tendon stiffness, muscle cross-sectional area and strength without significant group differences. Trial registration: DRKS00029244.
tldr: In moderately active men doing 14 weeks of high-load leg training, 5 g a day of collagen peptides enlarged the patellar tendon more than placebo at two sites, but did not change strength or stiffness gains. Treat it as a size effect, not a performance or injury-prevention result.
methods: Monocentric, prospective, placebo-controlled, double-blind trial with block randomisation on baseline tendon area. Participants trained three times a week for 14 weeks at 70% to 85% of 1RM. Patellar tendon cross-sectional area was measured by MRI at 10% intervals along the tendon, and stiffness, knee extension strength and rectus femoris size were also measured before and after training.
findings: Patellar tendon cross-sectional area rose 10.7% with SCP and 6.5% with placebo within groups, and the time by group interaction was significant only at 60% (P = .019) and 70% (P = .010) of tendon length. Tendon stiffness rose about 20% in both groups, and leg press and knee extension 1RM rose 31% to 37% in both groups with no group difference. Rectus femoris cross-sectional area rose about 5% in both groups with no group difference.
limitations: 19 of 50 recruited men dropped out (9 SCP, 10 placebo), so the analysis rests on the 31 completers, although the abstract says 50 participants completed the program. Only two of eleven tendon sites showed a significant group difference, the study covered men aged 18 to 40 only, and results apply only to this collagen product at 5 g a day for 14 weeks. Part of the costs were paid by Gelita AG, the product's maker.
practicalImplications: Adding 5 g a day of collagen peptides to a 14-week high-load leg training block may increase patellar tendon size more than placebo, at 60% and 70% of tendon length. Stiffness and strength gains were similar in both groups, so no extra strength benefit should be expected.
athleteDev: For athletes doing heavy knee-extensor work, the study suggests a possible extra tendon-size benefit from collagen peptides, but no extra strength or stiffness benefit, and it used non-athletes.
rtp: Cannot inform return to sport. It tested healthy men with no tendon injury, so it does not show whether collagen peptides help tendon healing or rehabilitation. The authors say clinical trials in patients with tendon injury are needed.

citation: McCubbin AJ, Allanson BA, Caldwell Odgers JN, Cort MM, Costa RJS, Cox GR, et al. Sports Dietitians Australia Position Statement: Nutrition for Exercise in Hot Environments. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2020 (ahead of print).
abstract: Position of Sports Dietitians Australia that exertional heat stress challenges athletes' nutritional status, health and performance. Recommended strategies include heat acclimation, starting exercise euhydrated, pre-exercise hyperhydration by sodium or glycerol loading, monitoring fluid balance and gastrointestinal tolerance, cold beverages and menthol, with tailored plans for youth, endurance and para-sport athletes.
tldr: Heat stress makes hydration, fuelling and gut comfort harder, so athletes should start euhydrated, practise their drinking plan in training and acclimatize where possible. Cold drinks, menthol and hyperhydration can help in some situations and should be tested in the athlete's own setting.
methods: Position statement developed by the authors, who review the physiology of heat stress and summarize practical strategies. No systematic search or formal evidence grading is described.
findings: The statement recommends heat acclimation and starting exercise euhydrated, and says pre-exercise hyperhydration may be desirable in some scenarios, achieved by acute sodium or glycerol loading. It recommends assessing fluid balance, gastrointestinal tolerance and thirst responses. Ice-slurry and cold beverages may help in hot, humid, still conditions but may not in warm, dry, windy settings, and menthol can alter thermal sensation. Table 3 gives sport-specific advice: endurance athletes should practise fluid plans in training and keep carbohydrate intake steady, and para-sport athletes should avoid overhydration.
limitations: The statement is a consensus document with no new data and no described grading system. Its recommendations depend on individual sweat rates, gut tolerance and event rules, and the authors note that sweat characteristics explain less than 20% of the variation in sweat sodium losses between athletes, so generic plans may fall short.
practicalImplications: Measure sweat losses and hydration status in training that mimics the hot event, and practise the fluid and carbohydrate plan there. Use cooling strategies such as cold beverages, ice slurry and pre-cooling where practical, and avoid large fluid volumes for para-sport athletes with impaired sweating.
athleteDev: Performance Application: Heat acclimation, starting euhydrated and practised fluid and carbohydrate plans are the main performance steps. Cold beverages and menthol can improve perceived comfort, though the statement says their value depends on conditions.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: Not addressed. The statement covers hot-weather nutrition and hydration and gives no guidance on return after illness or injury, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions.

citation: Williams K, Zeoli T, Allen JH, Jo J, Yengo-Kahn AM, Terry DP, et al. Risk of Two Sport-Related Concussions in the Same Year: Is the Second Concussion Worse? Clin J Sport Med. 2024;34(1):38-43.
abstract: The study assessed how often same-year repeat concussions occur among adolescent athletes, what predicts them, and how outcomes compare with a single concussion. Of 834 athletes with a sport-related concussion, 56 (6.7%) sustained a repeat concussion within 365 days, and personal and family migraine history and family psychiatric history were associated with repeat injury. Recovery timelines did not differ between groups, although initial symptom scores were higher at the second concussion.
tldr: About 1 in 15 adolescents with a sport-related concussion at this clinic had another within a year, and migraine or family psychiatric history was more common among them. Recovery times were similar after a repeat concussion, so the authors suggest managing it the same way as a first concussion.
methods: Retrospective case-control analysis of electronic medical record data for athletes aged 12-23 seen at a regional sports concussion center between 2017 and 2020. Athletes with a repeat concussion within 365 days were compared with single-concussion athletes using chi-square, t and Mann-Whitney tests, and within the repeat group the second concussion was compared with the first (initial-concussion data available for 31 of the 56) using chi-square and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests.
findings: Among 834 athletes, 56 (6.7%) had a same-year repeat concussion, which occurred a mean of 151 days after the first. Personal migraine history, family migraine history and family psychiatric history were associated with repeat concussion (P=.02, .03 and .01). Symptom resolution (median 15 vs 17 days), return to learn (4.5 vs 4 days) and return to play (18.5 vs 18 days) were similar for repeat and single concussions. Within the repeat group, the initial symptom score was higher at the second concussion (median 29.5 vs 20, P=.02), while amnesia was more common after the first (P=.03).
limitations: Migraine, psychiatric and concussion histories were self-reported, and symptom resolution was taken from provider notes, which may overestimate resolution times. The repeat group was small and came from a single specialty center, and the within-group comparison used different sample sizes (31 initial and 56 repeat). Mechanism, BMI and prior concussion count were not analyzed, and the authors did not adjust for multiple comparisons.
practicalImplications: Clinicians can note migraine and family psychiatric history as factors linked to repeat concussion when counseling athletes, while recognizing these are unadjusted associations. Because recovery timelines were similar, the authors suggest managing a repeat concussion the same way as a first.
athleteDev: Staff should not assume a second concussion needs a longer plan, since recovery times were similar in this sample. Athletes with a migraine history were more often in the repeat group, so they may warrant closer attention to concussion risk, though the study tests no intervention.
rtp: Median time to return to play was 18.5 days after a repeat concussion and 18 days after a single one, so the study can inform expected timelines in similar settings. It cannot set return-to-play criteria, because the sample is small and clearance was recorded from clinic notes.

citation: Stevens DJ, Alghwiri A, Appleton SL, Rogers JM, Plummer SL, Grant C, et al. Should We Lose Sleep Over Sleep Disturbances After Sports-Related Concussion? A Scoping Review of the Literature. Journal of Head Trauma Rehabilitation. 2022;37(3):E206-E219.
abstract: This scoping review searched four databases for studies of sleep after sports-related concussion in adults and included ten studies of 896 concussed adults. Most subjective measures found sleep disturbance after concussion, and the only polysomnography study found no differences from non-concussed controls.
tldr: Sleep disturbance is commonly reported after sports-related concussion in adults, but the evidence is preliminary and mostly subjective. The authors suggest asking about sleep in concussion assessments and screening for sleep disorders, while noting that intervention studies are lacking.
methods: Scoping review following PRISMA-ScR, with systematic searches of Scopus, MEDLINE, SportDiscus and Web of Science in November 2019 and September 2020. Included English-language cohort studies and RCTs of adults with athletic concussion that reported subjective or objective sleep outcomes, and ten studies were synthesised in a table without risk-of-bias ratings.
findings: Eight of nine studies that used subjective sleep measures reported some sleep disturbance after concussion. Two actigraphy studies found large coefficients of variation in sleep duration, and one study with 10 concussed and 11 control participants found no polysomnography differences despite worse self-rated sleep quality (PSQI 7.7 vs 3.5). Female athletes reported more sleep disturbance in one study, and no studies tested sleep interventions after concussion.
limitations: The authors note that the search was broad, which added methodological heterogeneity, and that the concussion and sleep measures were inconsistent. Several studies did not control for mental health problems or medication, and three studies used unvalidated probing questions with no objective corroboration. The review covered only adults in sport, so findings may not transfer to children or to non-sport concussion.
practicalImplications: Staff can consider asking athletes about sleeping more than usual after a concussion, because current assessment tools such as the SCAT ask only about trouble falling asleep. The authors suggest that a positive sleep finding should lead to a fuller assessment with validated questionnaires or a sleep diary, and that ongoing disturbance or excessive daytime sleepiness may warrant referral to a sleep specialist.
athleteDev: This review is about concussion recovery and brain health, not training or performance. It does not show how sleep after concussion affects performance, so it cannot guide performance or workload decisions.
rtp: The review can inform return-to-sport screening by showing that sleep disturbance is often reported after concussion and that current tools may miss some of it. It cannot set a sleep-based criterion for return to play, because no studies tested whether treating sleep changes recovery.

citation: Riegler KE, Guty ET, Thomas GA, Arnett PA. Sleep deprived or concussed? The acute impact of self-reported insufficient sleep in college athletes. J Int Neuropsychol Soc. 2021;27:35-46.
abstract: Objective: to examine the relationship between sleep difficulties and self-reported symptoms and neuropsychological performance at baseline and post-concussion in collegiate athletes. Method: 772 collegiate athletes completed a neuropsychological battery, grouped by hours slept the night before testing using cut-offs from the sample mean and SD. Results: insufficient sleep at baseline was associated with more overall and cluster symptoms but no objective performance differences; baseline insufficient sleepers differed from post-concussion sufficient sleepers only in sleep symptoms and headache. Conclusion: insufficient sleep at baseline can make athletes look similar to concussed athletes, so prior-night sleep may need to be considered when a baseline is used as a comparison.
tldr: College athletes who slept less the night before baseline testing reported more symptoms but did not score worse on cognitive tests. Ask about sleep before baseline and post-concussion testing before reading the results.
methods: Analysis of records from a university sports concussion programme (2002 to 2018). Tests were the ImPACT battery, the Post-Concussion Symptom Scale (PCSS), and paper-and-pencil and computerised neuropsychological measures, converted to z-scores from published norms. Aim 1 compared baseline athletes sleeping 5.78 hours or less (n=100) with those sleeping more than 7.07 hours (n=508). Aim 2 compared baseline athletes with short sleep (n=93) with post-concussion athletes with sufficient sleep (n=76). Sleep was a single self-report item.
findings: Aim 1: overall symptoms were higher in the short-sleep group (t(109.26)=4.07, P < .001, d=0.57), as were sleep, physical, cognitive and headache scores. The affective cluster did not differ (P=.08), and the memory and processing-speed composites did not differ (P=.50 and P=.91). Aim 2: overall symptoms and most clusters did not differ between short-sleep baseline athletes and sufficient-sleep post-concussion athletes. Sleep symptoms were higher in the baseline group, and headache was higher after concussion.
limitations: Sleep was one self-reported item for one night, which does not capture sleep quality, chronic patterns or disorders. Groups were defined by sample-based cut-offs, not a validated threshold, and the post-concussion group was older. Conflicts to note: the abstract says short sleepers reported more symptoms in each of the five clusters, but the affective cluster was not significant (P=.08, Table 5); and the Conclusions describe cognitive underperformance at baseline, but the objective composites did not differ, so the overlap with concussion is in symptom reports only. The null Aim 2 results do not show equivalence. Both aims are single-time comparisons.
practicalImplications: Record hours slept before baseline and post-concussion testing. An insufficiently rested baseline may inflate symptom scores and distort post-concussion comparisons. The authors also recommend screening for sleep problems as part of concussion care and referring athletes with sleep difficulties for treatment such as CBT-I, which this study did not test.
athleteDev: Ask athletes how much they slept before baseline testing, and where possible schedule baseline testing after a normal night's sleep. Screen sleep as a routine part of athlete health checks.
rtp: The study bears on return-to-play decisions because a baseline taken after short sleep may look like a concussed profile, which can skew symptom and cognitive comparisons. It gives no return-to-play criteria and does not show that sleep changes concussion outcomes.

citation: Grigg-Damberger MM. Sleep/Wake Disorders After Sports Concussion: Risks, Revelations, and Interventions. J Clin Neurophysiol. 2023;40(5):417-425.
abstract: Sleep-wake disturbances are among the most prevalent, persistent, and often disregarded sequelae of traumatic brain injury. They can accentuate other consequences of injury, negatively affect mood, exacerbate pain, and diminish cognitive abilities. Sleep-wake disturbances are an independent risk factor for prolonged recovery after sports-related concussion and can impede rehabilitation and return to preinjury activities.
tldr: Sleep problems after concussion are common and predict slower recovery, so athletes with persistent sleep complaints should be screened and referred. The review offers no trial evidence that treating sleep speeds return to play.
methods: Invited narrative review by a single author. No search strategy is described; the review summarises clinical, polysomnography, actigraphy, quantitative EEG, animal and athlete studies.
findings: Poor sleep quality in the acute phase of sports-related concussion predicted lingering symptoms, mood disturbance and cognitive disability a year later, and insomnia after concussion was linked to more persistent postconcussion syndrome in two athlete cohorts. Polysomnography in mild TBI usually shows no gross sleep architecture change, and actigraphy can reveal circadian disorders that look like insomnia. Small studies reported that morning blue light in 62 adults with mild TBI increased gray matter volume compared with placebo light, and that melatonin lengthened sleep compared with placebo in a secondary analysis of 72 children.
limitations: Narrative review with no described search method, mostly observational or small-sample studies, and many sleep findings drawn from mild TBI rather than sport-related concussion. The author declares no funding or conflicts of interest.
practicalImplications: Screen athletes after concussion for sleep complaints and for medical, psychiatric and medication causes. If sleep problems persist, refer to a sleep specialist; treat insomnia first with stimulus control, sleep restriction and cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia, and avoid sleep medications where possible.
athleteDev: Short sleep matters beyond recovery: under 8 hours a night was linked to 1.7 times the odds of sports injury in 160 adolescent athletes. The review does not test any performance intervention.
rtp: Relevant to recovery after concussion because it supports screening for and treating sleep disorders, which slow recovery. It does not set return-to-play criteria or test a return protocol; its activity guidance (24 to 48 hours of symptom-limited rest, then gradual activity) comes from the consensus guidelines it cites.

citation: Mendoza Barrios M, Deconinck E, Vanhee C, Lamme EK, 't Hart-Bakker I, Syversen PV, et al. SARMs, Metabolic Modulators and Growth Hormone Secretagogues in Suspected Illegal Medicines, Bought as Sport Performance Enhancers: A Retro- and Prospective Study Within the GEON. Drug Testing and Analysis. 2025.
abstract: Market-surveillance study by European and partner OMCL laboratories of suspected illegal products containing SARMs, metabolic modulators or growth hormone secretagogues, sold as sport performance enhancers.
tldr: Illegal products containing SARMs and related drugs are sold for sport performance, often labelled as medicines or sold as supplements. Products from unregulated sources can contain unapproved drugs, sometimes unlabelled or at very high doses.
methods: OMCL laboratories collected retrospective and prospective data from January 2018 to September 2023 using a harmonised reporting template, with mainly LC-MS screening. Results were summarised as counts by origin, product type, dosage form, molecule and quantity.
findings: Of 336 reported samples, 12 had no in-scope active compound, leaving 324 samples; samples with more than one target compound gave 354 valid results. About 86% of samples came from the illegal supply chain, 65% of results were presented as medicines and 24% as dietary supplements. Eighteen molecules were detected, led by ibutamoren (62 reports), ligandrol (48), ostarine (46), cardarine (45) and andarine (34).
limitations: Only OMCL results were counted, so the number of circulating products is higher. Quantitative data were limited and reported in mixed units. Health outcomes in consumers were not measured.
practicalImplications: Products labelled as medicines or supplements can contain unapproved SARMs or other drugs, and dosing varied widely, including very high-dose liquids and high-purity powders for self-dosing. The authors advise against buying these products from suspected websites that hide a physical address.
athleteDev: Performance Application: Unregulated products marketed for muscle gain or performance often lack ingredient labels and vary widely in dose. The study did not assess any performance effect.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: The study cannot inform return to sport, because it describes product contents and does not assess injury, recovery or clinical outcomes in athletes.

citation: Vasireddi N, Hahamyan HA, Kumar Y, Ng MK, Voos JE, Calcei JG. Social Media May Cause Emergent SARMs Abuse by Athletes: A Content Quality Analysis of the Most Popular YouTube Videos. The Physician and Sportsmedicine. 2022.
abstract: Objectives: To analyse the quality, educational content and reliability of the most relevant YouTube videos on SARMs. Methods: On 28 November 2021 the top 100 videos for 'SARMs' were coded for source, content category, JAMA reliability score, Global Quality Score (GQS), attitude toward SARMs and cycle advice. Results: Mean JAMA score was 1.6 ± 0.7 of 4 and mean GQS was 2.5 ± 1.1 of 5; patient videos had lower GQS than athletic trainer videos. Conclusion: Quality and reliability were low, and the authors argue that social media likely contributes to SARMs abuse.
tldr: The most viewed YouTube videos on SARMs were of low quality and reliability, and nearly half gave cycle advice. Staff should expect athletes to meet this content and be ready to correct it, but the study does not show that it causes drug use.
methods: Cross-sectional analysis of the first 100 YouTube videos for 'SARMs' in relevance order. Two authors independently scored each video for uploader type, content category, JAMA reliability (0 to 4), Global Quality Score (1 to 5), attitude toward SARMs and specific cycle or dosing support, and descriptive and regression statistics were used.
findings: Mean JAMA score was 1.6 ± 0.7 and mean GQS was 2.5 ± 1.1, with patient videos scoring lower than athletic trainer videos (2.11 vs 2.95, p < 0.01). Forty-seven percent of videos gave cycle help, and 40% took a positive attitude toward SARMs use. Videos averaged 147,994 views each.
limitations: Only 100 videos from a single search on one date, on one platform. Intraobserver variability was not measured, no video was linked to measured SARMs use, and the 'athletic trainer' source group included anyone with athletic training or coaching credentials. The authors' statement that social media likely causes abuse is not tested by the data.
practicalImplications: When athletes raise SARMs content, expect low-quality material, and note that nearly half of it gives cycle advice without clinical support. Point athletes to reliable sources and discuss the harms; the study does not show that any video changes behaviour.
athleteDev: Much of the online SARMs information athletes see is low quality, and some of it is positive about use. The study does not measure performance effects, dosing outcomes or use rates among athletes.
rtp: Cannot inform return to sport. It analyses YouTube videos rather than injured athletes or rehabilitation outcomes.

citation: Pillay L, Thompson C, Tabane C, Kirby J, Hendricks S, Swart J, et al. South African Institute of Drug-Free Sport Position Statement on CBD (Cannabidiol) and THC (Tetrahydrocannabinol). S Afr J Sports Med. 2023;35(1):1-4.
abstract: Unlabelled opening paragraph: CBD and THC have become easily available to athletes. Using them may expose an athlete to an adverse analytical finding (a positive test) and sanction, especially without a therapeutic use exemption. The statement aims to clarify the use of CBD and THC and their anti-doping risks, and the South African Sports Medicine Association supports it.
tldr: CBD is not prohibited, but THC is, and a CBD product can contain enough THC to cause a positive test. Athletes should check every product against the Prohibited List and obtain a therapeutic use exemption before any medical use of a THC-containing product.
methods: Position statement by a national anti-doping body, supported by the national sports medicine association. It reviews WADA rules, South African law, product types and the evidence base, with no original data and no described search method.
findings: CBD is not on the Prohibited List, while cannabis (THC) is prohibited in competition. WADA's 2022 expert group concluded that THC meets the criteria for the List because it is a health risk, mainly neurological, and its in-competition use violates the spirit of sport; it found no objective evidence of physiological performance enhancement but could not exclude neuropsychological enhancement. The urine threshold for an adverse analytical finding is 150 ng/ml, and 180 ng/ml triggers sanction. The statement adds that evidence for CBD and THC in anxiety, pain, sleep disorders and chemotherapy side effects is low in quality.
limitations: Position statement with no described search method or evidence grading, and the cited studies are mostly small or uncontrolled. It presents an anti-doping viewpoint, and the statement itself says South African cannabis legislation is still being approved in stages. The authors declare no conflicts of interest or funding.
practicalImplications: Athletes who use CBD should check each product, since some contain THC and a single positive test can bring sanctions. Medical use of a THC-containing product for a diagnosed condition needs a therapeutic use exemption before treatment starts, and evidence-based first-line options should be tried first.
athleteDev: THC is banned in competition, and WADA's 2022 group found no objective evidence that it enhances physical performance, although neuropsychological effects cannot be excluded. Staff should not treat THC as a performance aid, and should ask about CBD use because its THC content is a doping risk.
rtp: Limited return-to-sport value because it sets no return-to-play rules. It is relevant only where cannabinoids are used for pain, sleep or nausea during rehabilitation, where a THC-containing product needs a therapeutic use exemption.

citation: Tanisawa K, Wang G, Seto J, Verdouka I, Twycross-Lewis R, Karanikolou A, et al. Sport and exercise genomics: the FIMS 2019 consensus statement update. Br J Sports Med. 2020 (epub ahead of print).
abstract: Updates a previous consensus on sport and exercise genomics using a SWOT analysis and develops a guiding reference covering the strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats of the field, with emphasis on ethics, data protection and athlete privacy.
tldr: Genetic information from athletes has real potential, but most sport genetic findings are unreplicated. The guidance calls for replication studies, privacy safeguards and genetic counselling before genetic information is used for athletes.
methods: Consensus update built on a SWOT analysis. No sample, search protocol or formal voting method is reported.
findings: The authors state that most sport and exercise gene associations have not been replicated, that polygenic traits need very large samples (about 5,500 cases and as many controls to detect an odds ratio of 1.2 in a case-control GWAS), and that genetic testing may help evaluate athletes with abnormal cardiac screening or a family history of inherited cardiac disease. They list threats including re-identification of anonymised genotype data, inaccurate testing based on thin evidence, discrimination and gene doping.
limitations: The statement is an expert guidance document rather than an evidence synthesis, and the consensus process is not described. The authors acknowledge small samples and limited replication in the field, and say the guidance will be updated as evidence emerges.
practicalImplications: Before collecting athlete genetic data, plan consent, data protection and genetic counselling for results that could be misread. Treat sport genetic findings as research hypotheses until they are replicated.
athleteDev: Performance Application: The guidance does not support using genetic markers to select sports or set training. It says that selecting sports from a few variants is unlikely to be possible because athletic performance is polygenic.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: The statement does not address return to play. Its genetic-testing remarks concern evaluating athletes with abnormal cardiac screening or a family history of inherited cardiac disease.

citation: McNaughton M, Hunt D, Parmeter B, O'Brien M, Cook D, Meehan W, et al. Sport-Related Injury and Performance Enhancing Substance Use by Young Athletes. Sports Health. 2024.
abstract: Compares legal performance enhancing substance (PES) use and consideration of banned PES use in young athletes aged 6 to 25 with a season-ending injury, concussion, non-season-ending injury or no injury, using a cross-sectional dataset from 2013 to 2020. The authors found no association between injury group and PES use after adjustment, and identify male sex, depression history, weight training and belief that weight affects ability as factors linked to PES use.
tldr: Among young athletes at an injury prevention clinic, 14% reported legal PES use and 3% considered banned PES. Injury status was not associated with either after adjustment; male sex, depression history, weight training and belief that weight affects ability were.
methods: Cross-sectional analysis of an existing dataset from an injury prevention evaluation (April 2013 to March 2020). Athletes completed an electronic questionnaire covering PES use, injury history, sport contact level and other factors. Multivariable logistic regression used injury group as the exposure, with unadjusted and adjusted models.
findings: Of 952 athletes, 133 had a season-ending injury, 441 a non-season-ending injury, 85 a concussion and 293 no injury. Legal PES use was reported by 136 (14%) and consideration of banned PES use by 28 (3%). Unadjusted, season-ending injury versus no injury gave OR 2.74 for legal PES use and OR 4.01 (95% CI 1.15 to 13.96) for banned PES consideration. In the adjusted models, injury groups were not associated with legal PES use (season-ending injury OR 1.00, 95% CI 0.51 to 1.95). Male sex (OR 1.38), depression history (OR 3.01), weight training (OR 1.66) and belief that weight affects athletic ability (OR 1.75) were associated with legal PES use. Older age (OR 1.18) and male sex (OR 1.57) were associated with banned PES consideration.
limitations: Self-report may under-report PES use, and the authors could not determine whether PES use began before or after injury. The sample is one clinic's population with a wide age range and regional limits. The abstract's statement of no association refers to adjusted models; the unadjusted injury associations were significant. The text gives 954 athletes after exclusions while the tables use 952. The questionnaire offered only male or female sex options when it was designed.
practicalImplications: When seeing young athletes for injury prevention, ask about legal supplement use and weight-related beliefs, and give extra attention to the male, depression and weight-training flags reported here. Do not assume that an injured young athlete is more likely to use PES, because the adjusted analysis did not show this.
athleteDev: Performance Application: For young athletes who weight train or believe weight affects performance, coaches and clinicians can review supplement use and education needs. The study does not show that these practices improve performance or safety.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: The study does not support a PES-based change to return-to-play care, because injury status was not associated with PES use after adjustment. It cannot show whether PES use affects recovery.

citation: Lindsey B, Shaul Y, Martin J. Salivary biomarkers of tactical athlete readiness: A systematic review. PLoS One. 2025;20(4):e0321223.
abstract: PRISMA systematic review of 49 studies of salivary biomarkers measured before and after sleep loss, dehydration, environmental and muscular-fatigue stressors in tactical athletes and healthy adults.
tldr: Saliva can capture stress responses in the field, but cortisol and testosterone are inconsistent readiness markers. Proteomic and non-hormonal markers look more promising but are not yet practical for field use.
methods: PRISMA-guided review of PubMed, CINAHL, SPORTDiscus and Google Scholar, searched in early 2024, with duplicate screening, independent data extraction and Downs and Black quality ratings. Studies were grouped by stressor and biomarker and synthesised qualitatively without a pooled analysis.
findings: Of 49 studies, 27 were rated good and 22 fair. Hormonal markers were most studied, and cortisol changes were mixed across stressors. In the five dehydration studies, osmolality and total protein rose and flow rate fell, while proteomic and metabolomic panels discriminated fatigue at 83% and 96% accuracy in single small studies.
limitations: The authors report heterogeneity in methods, populations and assays, few power analyses, underrepresentation of women, and mostly quasi-experimental designs with a single post-stressor measure.
practicalImplications: Saliva osmolality, total protein and flow rate were the most consistent hydration signals, though from only five dehydration studies, so they are the best-supported field candidates for now. Cortisol and testosterone need baseline and diurnal control before they can support readiness decisions.
athleteDev: Performance Application: Salivary hydration markers may help monitor hydration around training. The review found no consistent link between cortisol or testosterone and performance outcomes.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: The review covers stress and readiness rather than injury recovery, so it cannot inform return to sport. Muscle-damage markers such as creatine kinase were studied after exercise, but sampling timelines varied and no study tested them for return decisions.

citation: Badby AJ, Ripley NJ, McMahon JJ, Mundy PD, Comfort P. Scoping review of methods of monitoring acute changes in lower body neuromuscular function via force plates. PLoS One. 2025;20(5):e0322820.
abstract: A scoping review of 30 within-group repeated-measures studies that used force plates to monitor acute changes in lower-body neuromuscular function. The studies differed widely in participants, test selection, data collection, metric definitions and phase terminology. The authors conclude that generalized conclusions about specific tests and metrics are premature until standardized methods are used and reported.
tldr: Force-plate monitoring studies differ widely in tests, metric definitions and protocols, so their results cannot yet be compared or combined. Jump height was the most used metric, and the authors call for the reliability and sensitivity of common metrics to be established before practical conclusions are drawn.
methods: Scoping review following PRISMA-ScR, with searches of PubMed, EBSCO, Web of Science and Ovid to 24 June 2024. Inclusion covered English-language peer-reviewed studies of athletes, physically demanding occupations, students and recreational athletes that used force plates to assess acute (under one week) changes in lower-body neuromuscular function. Reference lists of eligible studies were screened, and 30 studies were included. Data on demographics, protocols, hardware, tests, metrics and time points were charted qualitatively.
findings: Of the 30 studies, 466 participants were included. Countermovement jump was used in 23 studies, and 90 CMJ metrics were reported, with jump height the most common (14 studies). Peak force was calculated in different ways across studies, and braking, eccentric, propulsive and concentric phases were used inconsistently. Only 2 studies tracked body mass change, plate zeroing and body-weighing were each reported in only 6 studies, and 1000 Hz was the most common sampling rate (17 studies). After immediately post-activity testing, the most common time points were 24 h, 48 h and 72 h.
limitations: The review is qualitative and descriptive with no quality appraisal, and no protocol was pre-registered. Six studies lacked enough results to be tabulated. The sample was predominantly male, with only 5 studies including females; the Discussion gives different sex counts (19 male and 3 female studies, 319 participants) than the Results (26 and 5 studies, 466 participants), apparently from the 24 tabulated studies. The review did not evaluate the reliability or sensitivity of the metrics it describes.
practicalImplications: Practitioners using force plates to monitor acute change should fix and report the test protocol, including verbal cues, familiarization, surface, plate zeroing and body-weighing. They should also use several metric types (outcome, strategy, kinetic and ratio) rather than jump height alone, and check how their software defines peak force and phases before comparing with published values.
athleteDev: For performance staff, the review supports a standard countermovement jump protocol with consistent cues, zeroing and body-weighing, and tracking several metrics such as jump height, phase timing and force, with body mass alongside. Metric definitions differ across published work, so local software definitions should be checked before comparing with external benchmarks.
rtp: The review does not inform return-to-sport decisions. It excluded studies focused on rehabilitation progression and concussion recovery, so it cannot support using these metrics to judge readiness after injury.

citation: Toresdahl BG, Conway J, Miller TT, Goolsby MA, Geannette CS, Quijano B, et al. Serial Ultrasonography for the Assessment of Healing of Lower Extremity Bone Stress Injury and Correlation With Return to Sport/Exercise. Sports Health. 2024.
abstract: Prospective observational cohort of adults aged 18 to 50 with an MRI-confirmed exercise-related bone stress injury of the distal tibia, fibula or metatarsals. Serial ultrasound every two weeks for 12 weeks was correlated with pain (NRS) and return-to-sport ratings. Soft tissue edema and hyperemia decreased over time; hyperemia correlated with pain at weeks 4 and 6 and with return to sport at week 6.
tldr: Ultrasound of lower-leg and foot stress injuries showed edema and hyperemia fading over 12 weeks, and hyperemia tracked pain and return-to-sport ratings around weeks 4 to 6. The correlations are weak and the study is small, so ultrasound looks promising for monitoring but is not a return-to-sport test yet.
methods: Adults aged 18 to 50 with a recent exercise-related distal tibia, fibula or metatarsal bone stress injury confirmed by MRI were enrolled within four weeks of MRI and scanned every two weeks for 12 weeks. Two blinded musculoskeletal radiologists scored soft tissue edema, periosteal reaction, hyperemia (0 to 3) and callus. Patients completed pain (NRS) and return-to-sport surveys biweekly, and MRI was repeated at 12 weeks. Repeated-measures ANOVA, paired t tests and Spearman correlations were used.
findings: Of 31 enrolled, 30 were analysed. Soft tissue edema, periosteal reaction and hyperemia were seen on ultrasound at some point in 66.7%, 63.3% and 43.3% of patients. Soft tissue edema fell from 0.95 at week 2 to 0.34 at week 12 and hyperemia from 0.63 to 0.07 (both P < .01); periosteal reaction did not change significantly in Table 3 (P = .23). Hyperemia correlated with average pain at week 4 (rho 0.45, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.69) and week 6 (rho 0.42, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.67), and with return to sport at week 6 (rho -0.45, 95% CI -0.68 to -0.09); patients with hyperemia at week 6 had higher pain in later weeks (P = .04) but not clearly lower return-to-sport ratings (P = .06). Soft tissue edema correlated with pain at week 6 (rho 0.38). MRI marrow edema fell from 1.3 to 0.79 (P < .01), but it persisted in 53.3% at 12 weeks and did not correlate with pain or return to sport.
limitations: Single centre, no comparison group, small sample, and a 4-point subjective ultrasound scale with inter-observer variability. The return-to-sport scale was not validated, most patients had not fully returned by week 12, and no ultrasound correlations with clinical outcomes were significant after week 6. The Results text says periosteal reaction decreased significantly (all P < .01), but Table 3 gives P = .23; the abstract says 30 patients were enrolled, but the Results say 31 were enrolled and one was excluded after week 2; and Table 1 gives metatarsal 49.7% while the text gives 46.7%.
practicalImplications: Ultrasound every two weeks could track hyperemia and soft tissue edema alongside symptoms, which may help where repeat MRI is less useful. The authors note athletic training rooms may be able to use it, but the findings support clinical judgment rather than replacing it.
athleteDev: Not a performance application. Staff who manage progression after a bone stress injury could look at the trend in hyperemia and symptoms, but the study does not test load or training decisions.
rtp: Hyperemia at week 6 was associated with lower return-to-sport ratings, so it may be a useful added signal. The paper cannot set a clearance threshold: correlations were weak, the return-to-sport scale was not validated, and no prognostic cut-off was derived.

citation: Donati F, Biasini GM, de la Torre X, Botrè F. Serum myokines as potential biomarkers of myostatin inhibition in sport doping: a preliminary study on their baseline levels in elite athletes. Biology of Sport. 2024;41(2):175-183.
abstract: The authors measured serum myostatin and nine related myokines in elite athletes whose doping control samples were negative, to assess whether these markers could indicate myostatin inhibition. Concentrations varied by several orders of magnitude, females had higher FSTL-1 and musclin, and power athletes had higher IGF-1 and BDNF than endurance athletes. Musclin, FSTL-1 and oncostatin clustered most closely with myostatin.
tldr: Baseline serum levels of myostatin and related myokines were measured in 53 negative-testing elite athletes. The panel is a starting point for reference ranges, not a validated doping test.
methods: Serum from routine doping control samples from elite athletes (myostatin n=53; 41 males, 12 females; mean age 26.6 years) was assayed by ELISA, radioimmunoassay and multiplex bead array. Groups were compared with Mann-Whitney U tests, correlations were Kendall's tau-beta, and a principal component analysis was run on a paired subset (N=41).
findings: Myokine concentrations ranged from under 1 ng/mL (musclin, osteonectin) to above 10 ng/mL (BDNF, FSTL-1, IGF-1). FSTL-1 and musclin were higher in females (p<0.05), and IGF-1 and BDNF were higher in power than endurance athletes (p=0.006 and p=0.001). Myostatin correlated with oncostatin (tau 0.23, p<0.05); the text also describes a significant correlation with FSTL-1, but Table 3 gives 0.17 for that pair without a significance mark. The FOL/MYO ratio was below 1 and varied widely (mean 0.34, CV 64%).
limitations: The female subgroups are small (n=6 to 13 depending on the analyte), so sex differences may be unreliable, and the authors note this as a likely confounder. The samples come from athletes with negative routine doping control results, and the paper does not test any myostatin inhibitor or report intra-individual change over time. The text and Table 3 disagree on whether the myostatin-FSTL-1 correlation is significant. Abstract and results agree on the sex and sport comparisons.
practicalImplications: Anti-doping and research staff can use these values as a first reference for clean elite athletes, but a single sample cannot identify myostatin inhibition. The authors suggest that any future use would need repeated sampling within each athlete.
athleteDev: This study does not give training or performance recommendations. Its value to performance staff is limited to knowing that IGF-1 and BDNF differed between power and endurance athletes in this sample.
rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It measured baseline serum markers in athletes with negative doping control results and says nothing about injury, healing or recovery after injury.

citation: Halson SL. Sleep Monitoring in Athletes: Motivation, Methods, Miscalculations and Why it Matters. Sports Med. 2019.
abstract: This review outlines reasons for sleep disturbance in athletes, the advantages and disadvantages of methods to assess sleep (polysomnography, activity monitoring, consumer sleep technology, sleep diaries and questionnaires), considerations for feedback, and intervention and behaviour change strategies. It is written to give practitioners current evidence in an area where monitoring is growing faster than standards.
tldr: Athlete sleep monitoring needs validated tools, careful interpretation and supportive feedback. Research-grade actigraphy with a sleep diary is the most defensible option in this review, while consumer wearables and apps are better used to start conversations than to make decisions.
methods: Narrative review of the literature on sleep assessment in athletes. It describes each monitoring tool with its advantages and disadvantages, a suggested monitoring process, and a worked case of one Olympic athlete monitored with a 14-day actigraphy and diary period.
findings: Research-grade activity monitors agreed with polysomnography in athletes (81 to 90% agreement, 81 to 92% sensitivity), but their accuracy depends on the scoring threshold. In one study of 12 semi-professional soccer players, a consumer wearable's mean total sleep time difference from polysomnography was 51.5 min (SD 152.4) with very wide limits, and a popular sleep app showed no correlation with polysomnography for sleep efficiency. In one rugby league study, education and monitoring improved sleep only during the education period.
limitations: The review has no described systematic search, and its conclusions rest partly on small validation studies. The author notes that there are currently no published validation studies of some popular wearables, and that there are no standard monitoring procedures or guidelines for athletes.
practicalImplications: A practical approach is a 1 to 2 week actigraphy period with a sleep diary during a training cycle, with referral to a sleep physician if a sleep disorder is suspected. Consumer device and app data should be used as a starting point for discussion, and feedback should focus on what can be improved rather than on poor scores.
athleteDev: Performance staff could use a 14-day actigraphy and diary period during a training block to find routine problems such as inconsistent bed and wake times, as the case study does. Feedback should focus on the aspects that can be changed, and wearable sleep scores should not drive training decisions until they are validated.
rtp: The review does not address return-to-sport timing or injured athletes. Its only point relevant to rehabilitation staff is that a suspected sleep disorder should be investigated and referred to a sleep physician as a priority.

citation: Reilly T, Waterhouse J. Sports performance: is there evidence that the body clock plays a role? Eur J Appl Physiol. 2009;106:321-332.
abstract: Athletic performance shows a time-of-day effect with possible causes in environmental factors, the sleep-wake cycle and the internal body clock. The authors conclude that the body clock probably plays some role in sports performance rhythms, but the evidence does not separate it from time awake. They outline protocols to separate these roles and note that muscle fatigue is a serious barrier to experimental work.
tldr: Sports performance follows a time-of-day pattern that peaks in the late afternoon, and the body clock probably contributes to it. Current evidence cannot yet say how much of the pattern is the body clock rather than time awake or the environment.
methods: Narrative review of the time-of-day performance literature and chronobiological evidence, with suggested experimental protocols. No systematic search method is described.
findings: Many performance measures are higher in the late afternoon and early evening than in the morning. Reported rhythm peaks fall between about 15:30 and 20:30 hours, with amplitudes of 2 to 11 percent of the daily mean. The authors judge that the body clock probably plays some role, but the evidence is inconclusive.
limitations: The authors describe much of the data as poor quality, and many studies compared only two times of day, so sampling was too infrequent to describe a circadian rhythm. Muscle fatigue makes rigorous protocols long or unacceptable, and the body clock and time awake cannot yet be separated.
practicalImplications: When comparing athlete performance across the day, standardise and record test times, because the time of day alone can shift results. Where possible, test protocols should separate time awake from the body clock.
athleteDev: Performance measures tend to peak in the late afternoon and early evening, so training and testing schedules could take time of day into account. This review cannot say how much of that rhythm is the body clock.
rtp: This review cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It does not address injured athletes or rehabilitation outcomes.

citation: Haugen T, McGhie D, Ettema G. Sprint running: from fundamental mechanics to practice - a review. Eur J Appl Physiol. 2019.
abstract: The authors examine sprint running literature using the mechanical principles that govern accelerated running. They discuss spring-mass models and their limits, the link between sprint mechanics and metabolic demand, and the emphasis on total and horizontal force. They argue that power analysis based on isolated end-goal force is flawed and discuss some practical concepts in sprint coaching.
tldr: Sprint mechanics research can be misread when models or horizontal-force power figures are taken at face value. Coaches and analysts should check how a measure was derived before using it to explain sprint performance.
methods: Invited narrative review of sprint running mechanics literature, interpreted through fundamental mechanical principles. No systematic search method is described.
findings: Spring-mass models describe gross sprint kinematics such as step length, step rate and contact time, but the authors argue they have flaws when applied to accelerated running. Analyses based on total and horizontal force, and power derived from isolated end-goal force, are argued to be limited or flawed. Metabolic models of sprinting are described as promising but still model based.
limitations: The review is an argument rather than a systematic synthesis, and no search method is described. Its illustrative calculations use a few published data sets, and its views on practical sprint concepts are discussed rather than tested.
practicalImplications: Check how a sprint model or force measure was derived before treating it as a mechanism. Interpret horizontal-force power figures obtained from isolated force data with caution.
athleteDev: The authors suggest that sprint conditioning in most well-trained senior sprinters should target step rate, which they describe as the main within-athlete speed modulator, while longer step length, which requires strength, separates fast from intermediate sprinters. Model-based power figures should not be read as direct measures of an athlete's capacity.
rtp: This review does not address return to sport or rehabilitation and cannot be used to set return-to-sport criteria.
