citation: Mendiguchia J, Conceição F, Edouard P, Fonseca M, Pereira R, Lopes H, et al. Sprint versus isolated eccentric training: Comparative effects on hamstring architecture and performance in soccer players. PLoS ONE. 2020;15(2):e0228283.
abstract: The study compared Nordic hamstring exercise with sprint training, both added to regular soccer practice, on sprint performance, sprint mechanics and biceps femoris long head architecture. Six preseason weeks were compared across a soccer-only group, a Nordic group and a sprint group. The authors conclude that sprint training increased fascicle length more than Nordic training and also improved sprint performance and mechanics, while Nordic training did not improve sprint performance.
tldr: Adding sprint training to a soccer preseason improved short sprint times and acceleration mechanics and increased hamstring fascicle length in this small sample. Injury protection was not measured, so the fascicle result should not be read as injury prevention.
methods: Prospective randomised controlled study over six preseason weeks in 32 recruited soccer players who were allocated to three groups, with matching by position, playing status and previous hamstring injury. Nine players dropped out, leaving 23 analysed. Outcomes were 5 m and 20 m times and force-velocity mechanical outputs (F0, v0, Pmax, RFmax) from radar-measured 50 m sprints, and biceps femoris long head fascicle length, pennation angle and thickness by two-dimensional ultrasound, analysed with magnitude-based inference.
findings: In the sprint group, sprint performance and mechanics showed small to large pre-post improvements, with only a small, possibly real gain in maximal velocity (v0). The sprint group showed a moderate increase in fascicle length (about 16 percent), compared with a smaller increase in the Nordic group (about 7 percent) and a trivial change in the soccer-only group. The soccer-only and Nordic groups showed trivial to small negative sprint changes, and only the Nordic group showed a small increase in pennation angle.
limitations: Only 23 of 32 players were analysed, and the abstract reports the group sizes at recruitment (10, 12 and 10). Training and match load were not recorded, two-dimensional ultrasound has known limits for fascicle estimates, and injury outcomes were not measured. Between-group sprint comparisons with the soccer-only group were mostly trivial or unclear, and results rely on magnitude-based inference rather than hypothesis tests.
practicalImplications: Sprint work within preseason soccer practice may improve short sprint times and acceleration mechanics over six weeks. Staff should not replace Nordic hamstring exercise with sprint work on the basis of this study, because injury protection was not tested.
athleteDev: In this sample, sprint training within routine soccer practice improved 5 m and 20 m times and acceleration mechanics over six preseason weeks. Its effect on biceps femoris long head fascicle length was larger than that of the Nordic group.
rtp: The study excluded players with recent hip, knee or lumbo-pelvic joint injury, used previous hamstring injury only as a matching variable, and did not measure return to play. It cannot show how sprint or Nordic training should guide return-to-sport decisions after a hamstring injury.

citation: de Castro FMP, Alves GF, Oliveira LP, Tourinho Filho H, Puggina EF. Strength training with intermittent blood flow restriction improved strength without changes in neural aspects on quadriceps muscle. Science & Sports. 2018 (article in press; volume and pages not printed).
abstract: Low-intensity strength training with intermittent vascular occlusion increased muscle strength within the occlusion group in healthy resistance-trained men, while surface EMG measures of neural drive did not change over the training period.
tldr: Six weeks of low-load knee extension training with cuff occlusion raised predicted 1RM within the occlusion group in trained men, but strength did not differ significantly from the non-occluded group and EMG neural measures did not change. Use it as weak evidence of a strength gain, not of a neural adaptation.
methods: Twenty healthy resistance-trained men were randomized to low-load (20% predicted 1RM) unilateral knee extension with intermittent vascular occlusion (LIVO, n = 11) or without occlusion (LI, n = 9) for 6 weeks, 2 sessions per week, with the LI group matched to the LIVO group's repetition counts. Predicted 1RM and surface EMG (RMS and median frequency) of the vastus medialis and vastus lateralis were measured at weeks 1, 5 and 9, and EMG was also recorded in training sessions 1, 7 and 12.
findings: The LIVO group's predicted 1RM increased in both legs (right 36.5 to 47.9 kg; left 35.9 to 47.4 kg), while the LI group's increase (right 29.9 to 37.9 kg; left 29.8 to 36.9 kg) was not significant; there were no between-group differences in predicted 1RM. RMS was higher in the LIVO group than the LI group in several sets during training sessions, but RMS and median frequency did not change between time points within either group.
limitations: Small samples and a single unilateral exercise limit generalization. Predicted 1RM came from a repetitions-to-failure equation, not a measured maximum, and the LI group started with lower predicted 1RM. Hypertrophy was not measured, so the authors' suggestion that hypertrophy drove the gain is untested. The cuff pressure (mean 140 mmHg) may have altered motor unit recruitment and the EMG results.
practicalImplications: For healthy resistance-trained men, low-load training with cuff occlusion was followed by a significant knee extension strength gain over 6 weeks, but it was not shown to outperform the same work without occlusion. The gain did not come with a measurable change in EMG neural measures, so this study does not support using occlusion to improve neural drive.
athleteDev: Performance Application: Low-load training with intermittent occlusion improved knee extension strength within the occlusion group in trained men over 6 weeks, and the authors argue, without measuring it, that hypertrophy is the more likely cause. Where strength without added muscle mass is the goal, the authors consider high-intensity training the more appropriate choice.
rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport loading. It tested healthy, resistance-trained men and included no injured or rehabilitating participants.

citation: Kreider RB. Strength, conditioning, and nutritional considerations for high-level performers. Kinesiology Review. 2020;9(1):31-40.
abstract: Describes the history, professional preparation, program components and general principles of strength and conditioning and sport nutrition, their impact on high-level performance, and future trends in these fields.
tldr: A practitioner overview of how strength and conditioning and sport nutrition support high-level athletes, with general energy and macronutrient ranges by sport type. It is a narrative summary, not a systematic review of the evidence.
methods: Narrative overview by one author. No search strategy, inclusion criteria or evidence-grading method for the reviewed literature is described.
findings: The paper describes training principles (specificity, overload, progression and variation) and periodization phases, and cites studies in which multi-component programs improved strength, power and speed in male and female athletes. It gives recommended energy intakes (for example 45 to 60 kcal/kg/day for strength and power athletes) and carbohydrate and protein ranges by sport type (Table 2). It reports the ISSN classification in which creatine monohydrate, essential amino acids and protein (plus calcium HMB in untrained people) have strong evidence for muscle-mass gains during training, and beta-alanine, caffeine, carbohydrate, creatine, sodium bicarbonate, sodium phosphate, water and glucose electrolyte drinks, and energy drinks have strong evidence for performance (Tables 3 and 4).
limitations: The review does not describe how sources were selected, so it cannot be used to judge how complete the evidence is. Several figures, such as energy ranges, are general guidance and are not derived from the studies in the paper. The author discloses grants, consulting and expert witness roles.
practicalImplications: Strength and power athletes often need high energy intakes (45 to 60 kcal/kg/day) with carbohydrate and protein set by sport and training load, according to the author's ranges. Supplements should be chosen by evidence grade, legality in the sport, and third-party banned-substance testing.
athleteDev: Performance Application: Periodized training that varies exercise type and volume, combined with the energy and macronutrient ranges in Table 2, provides a framework for planning high-level athlete programs. The ISSN evidence tiers can help screen supplements before use.
rtp: This review does not address return to sport. It contains no rehabilitation or injury-specific evidence, so it cannot be used to set return-to-play loading or nutrition.

citation: Hendricks S, Till K, Scantlebury S, et al. Tackle Height and Tackle Success - An Analysis of 52,204 Tackle Events. European Journal of Sport Science. 2025; 25:e70003.
abstract: The authors compared the probability of tackle success when the tackler first contacted the ball-carrier at the shoulder, mid-torso or legs, for active, passive, smother and arm tackles, across seven male playing groups. Video of 271 matches was analysed with multilevel logistic regression that adjusted for tackle direction, sequence, number of tacklers and attacking intention. Active shoulder tackles had the highest success probability across levels, and arm tackles the lowest.
tldr: Active shoulder and smother tackles were the most successful tackle types at every level from U16 upward, and arm tackles were the least successful. Shoulder contact beat mid-torso contact in the junior groups, but the senior difference was only a few percentage points.
methods: Cross-sectional video analysis of competitive male rugby matches coded with a consensus video framework. Tackle success was modelled with multilevel logistic regression (random effects for country and match), with tackle type and first contact point as the main terms and situational covariates held at observed values. Separate models were fitted for each playing group, and adjusted probabilities were reported with 95% CIs.
findings: At Senior Elite, the adjusted success probability for active shoulder tackles was 86% at the shoulder, 82% at mid-torso and 78% at the legs; arm tackles were 75%, 69% and 65%. From U16 upward, active shoulder and smother tackles had the highest and similar success probabilities, although Table 4 shows a small significant gap at U18 Amateur (3 to 4 points, p = 0.043). In Table 3, shoulder contact beat mid-torso contact at every level (4 to 9 points), and at U12, U14 and U16 leg contact also beat mid-torso contact.
limitations: The abstract and text describe no difference between shoulder and mid-torso contact at senior levels, but Table 3 reports significant differences of about 4 percentage points at Senior Elite and Senior Amateur (p less than 0.001 for most tackle types); this report follows the table values. The text also says active shoulder and smother tackles did not differ from U16 upward (p greater than 0.05), while Table 4 gives p = 0.043 at U18 Amateur. The title gives 52,204 tackles, the abstract and methods give 51,106, and the stated 271 matches does not match the group counts, which sum to 266. Only male players were studied, ball-carrier body position was not coded, and tackle success was dichotomised.
practicalImplications: Coaches can use the tackle-type ranking in training, with smother tackles treated as equal in importance to active shoulder tackles from U16. Contact-height advice should weigh the small senior performance gap against the safety rationale the authors give for mid-torso contact.
athleteDev: Success rates differ by age group, so tackle training can target the contact point and tackle type that are most successful for each age group. The authors suggest greater emphasis on teaching the smother tackle, which has fewer standardised technical criteria than the active shoulder tackle.
rtp: Not applicable. The study measures tackle success in match video and does not assess injury, recovery or return-to-play criteria.

citation: Dennis MC, Goods PSR, Binnie MJ, Girard O, Wallman KE, Dawson BT, et al. Taking the plunge: When is best for hot water immersion to complement exercise in heat and hypoxia. Journal of Sports Sciences. 2022.
abstract: Ten recreationally active men completed three repeated-sprint sessions in hypoxia at 40 C and about 3000 m simulated altitude, with hot water immersion (HWI) before the session (PRE), after it (POST), or with no immersion (CON). PRE lowered power output in every sprint set and raised core temperature, while POST matched CON for power output and core temperature during exercise and gave a higher core temperature at the end of the post-exercise period.
tldr: Hot water immersion after a repeated-sprint session in the heat kept power output at control levels while adding heat load. Immersion before the session cut sprint power by about 15 to 17 percent.
methods: Ten recreationally active men completed a familiarisation and three randomised trials, each with 3 x 10 x 5-s all-out sprints in a heat and hypoxia chamber (40 C, 50% RH, FIO2 0.144). Each trial had 30 min of either hot water immersion at 40 C or seated rest at 21 C before and after exercise. Core temperature, power output, heart rate, thermal sensation and RPE were recorded and analysed with linear mixed models.
findings: PRE reduced mean power, peak power and total work by 14.8 to 16.8 percent versus POST and CON (all p < 0.001), with PRE core temperature higher during the pre-exercise period and exercise (p < 0.001 and p = 0.025). Time at 38.5 C or above was 48.1 +/- 22.5 min in PRE, 31.0 +/- 11.3 min in POST and 15.8 +/- 16.3 min in CON. POST power output and core temperature during exercise were similar to CON, and thermal sensation during exercise did not differ between conditions.
limitations: The effects were acute, so chronic heat acclimation and training effects could not be assessed. Core temperature could not be measured after the post-exercise immersion ended, so the full heat dose of POST is an estimate. Participants were recreationally active rather than trained athletes, and fitness was not measured.
practicalImplications: In a heat and hypoxia repeated-sprint session, placing hot water immersion after the session preserved sprint output while adding heat strain. Placing it before the session reduced sprint output, so it should not be used before high-intensity sprint work.
athleteDev: Post-session hot water immersion (30 min at 40 C) can add heat stress to a repeated-sprint session in hypoxia without reducing sprint power output in this sample. Its effect over repeated weeks is not known.
rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It tested healthy, recreationally active men in one acute session and included no injured athletes or return-to-play outcomes.

citation: Fox JL, Stanton R, Sargent C, Wintour SA, Scanlan AT. The Association Between Training Load and Performance in Team Sports: A Systematic Review. Sports Medicine. 2018.
abstract: The authors systematically searched PubMed, SPORTDiscus and PsycINFO for original research in team sports on training load and performance. Of 26 included studies, the authors found that heart rate-based high-intensity training load and the individualized training impulse model were associated with aerobic performance, while other load measures showed weak or no clear associations with aerobic, neuromuscular or game-related outcomes.
tldr: In team sports, the heart rate-based high-intensity training load is the training measure most consistently linked to aerobic gains. Other external load measures and session RPE show weak or no consistent links to performance.
methods: Systematic review of original research in PubMed, SPORTDiscus and PsycINFO to July 2018. Two authors assessed quality with the Downs and Black checklist, and the lead author extracted the data. The review did not pool effect sizes or run a meta-analysis.
findings: Twenty-six studies met the inclusion criteria, with quality scores from 6 to 10 out of 11. Training exposure was more strongly associated with aerobic performance than other external load measures, and high-intensity activity (90% of maximum heart rate or above) and the individualized training impulse model were strongly associated with aerobic performance. Other training impulse models and perceptual load measures showed weak associations, and there were no clear associations with neuromuscular variables or game-related statistics.
limitations: Many studies were small, most used soccer players, and the statistical analyses varied widely, so direct comparison between studies was difficult and effect sizes could not be pooled. Several studies reported only effect sizes or only significance, and all studies linking high-intensity activity to aerobic performance were in field-based sports, so the authors say application to court-based sports needs more work.
practicalImplications: Coaches should use heart rate-based high-intensity training load when aiming to improve aerobic capacity, and should be cautious about using session RPE, external load or common training impulse models to predict performance changes in team sports.
athleteDev: For team sport athletes, the review supports monitoring time spent at or above 90% of maximum heart rate to track aerobic development. It gives weak support for using session RPE or external load alone to predict changes in performance.
rtp: This review does not study injured athletes or return to sport and cannot be used to set return-to-play training loads.

citation: Harper DJ, Cervantes C, Van Dyke M, Evans M, McBurnie AJ, Dos Santos T, et al. The Braking Performance Framework: Practical Recommendations and Guidelines to Enhance Horizontal Deceleration Ability in Multi-Directional Sports. International Journal of Strength and Conditioning. 2024.
abstract: The article proposes a Braking Performance Framework to guide the choice of training methods for horizontal deceleration. It sets out exercises built on the known neuromuscular and biomechanical determinants of braking, with practical programming guidelines for practitioners.
tldr: Horizontal deceleration can be trained with eccentric, isometric, flywheel and change-of-direction exercises, sequenced by the athlete's needs. The authors offer practical programming guidelines drawn from existing evidence, which is limited for several methods.
methods: Narrative review and practical framework, with no described literature search. The authors draw on the known determinants of horizontal deceleration and on published studies of eccentric, isometric, flywheel, plyometric and change-of-direction training to propose exercise categories and programming tables.
findings: The authors propose a framework with three exercise categories: braking elementary exercises that build eccentric and tissue capacity, braking development exercises that target fast eccentric and concentric force and rate of force development, and braking performance exercises that train deceleration under game-like perceptual demands. They give programming guidance, such as in-season flywheel scheduling, and note limited research on heavy assisted braking steps and an unknown minimum effective dose for supplementary deceleration training.
limitations: No search method is described, so the selection of evidence cannot be checked. The authors acknowledge that the dose-response relationships and the effects of several exercise types are not well established, so many recommendations are expert judgement.
practicalImplications: Practitioners can use the framework to choose and progress braking exercises, moving from elementary eccentric and isometric work through development exercises toward unanticipated and game-specific decelerations. Progressions should be checked against the athlete's response, since dose-response evidence is limited.
athleteDev: Use the framework to target the eccentric and isometric determinants of deceleration, then progress toward braking in change-of-direction and game-like tasks. Adjust volume and intensity using the athlete's response, because the dose-response evidence is limited.
rtp: The framework is written for healthy athletes preparing for multi-directional sport, and the authors do not present it as a return-to-sport protocol. Use it for return-to-sport planning only with clinical judgement, because it has not been tested in injured athletes.

citation: Clemente FM, Scanlan AT, Ramirez-Campillo R, Martinho D, Thapa RK, Chamari K, et al. The Correlations Between Training Load Parameters and Physical Performance Adaptations in Team Sports: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Sports Medicine - Open. 2025;11:156.
abstract: The authors searched four databases for team sport studies with at least two weeks of training load and pre and post performance tests. Of 40 studies with 726 players, heart rate-based training impulse correlated with endurance adaptations (r = 0.43 to 0.63), and session RPE and external load showed limited associations with performance adaptations.
tldr: In team sport players, heart rate-based training impulse is the training load measure most closely linked to endurance gains. Session RPE and external load show weak links to performance adaptations, and the evidence is of very low certainty.
methods: Systematic review and meta-analysis following PRISMA 2020, searching PubMed, Scopus, SPORTDiscus and Web of Science, with an updated search in September 2025. Eligible studies included men or women in team sports at trained or developmental level with at least two weeks of training load and pre and post physical testing. Pooled correlations used random effects, study quality used the Downs and Black scale, and certainty used GRADE.
findings: Forty studies with 726 players were included, 27 of them in soccer and 4 in women only. Heart rate-based training impulse correlated with changes in maximal oxygen uptake (r = 0.63), velocity at 2 mmol/L lactate (r = 0.47) and velocity at onset of blood lactate accumulation (r = 0.43), while session RPE correlated with changes in velocity at 2 mmol/L lactate (r = 0.29) and showed a small correlation with sprint changes over more than 10 m (r = -0.23). Strength and jump power changes were not associated with training load, and all analyses were rated very low certainty under GRADE.
limitations: The authors note uneven coverage of the literature, with most external load studies in outdoor sports such as soccer and rugby, few indoor sport studies, and only four studies in women. All analyses were downgraded for risk of bias and imprecision, falling well below the optimal sample size of 800 participants, and some also for heterogeneity.
practicalImplications: Use heart rate-based training impulse when tracking endurance adaptations in team sport players. Do not rely on session RPE or external load alone to predict strength, power or speed gains, and treat the pooled correlations as a guide rather than a prescription.
athleteDev: For team sport players, heart rate-based training impulse is the most consistent training load signal for endurance development, such as VO2max and lactate thresholds. Strength, power and speed should be tracked with direct testing, since external and session load show weak links to them.
rtp: The review covers healthy team sport players and does not address injury or return to sport. It cannot be used to set return-to-play loads.

citation: Behan FP, Vermeulen R, Whiteley R, Timmins RG, Ruddy JD, Opar DA. The Dose-Response of the Nordic Hamstring Exercise on Biceps Femoris Architecture and Eccentric Knee Flexor Strength: A Randomized Interventional Trial. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2022 (ahead of print).
abstract: In 40 recreationally active men, six weeks of Nordic hamstring exercise at four volume patterns was compared for biceps femoris fascicle length and eccentric knee flexor strength. Initial high volume followed by low volume, and progressively increasing volume, raised both outcomes; low volume raised strength but not fascicle length.
tldr: In recreationally active men, a high-volume start followed by low volume, or steadily rising volume, increased hamstring fascicle length and eccentric strength over 6 weeks. Weekly low volume (48 total reps) increased strength but not fascicle length, and 8 reps every second week (24 total) changed neither.
methods: Forty recreationally active males were randomised to four 6-week NHE protocols with supervised sessions on 0 to 3 days per week, followed by 4 weeks of detraining. Weekly B-mode ultrasound measured biceps femoris long head fascicle length and pennation angle, and eccentric knee flexor strength was measured on a Nordbord device at baseline, posttest and during detraining; linear mixed models were used.
findings: After 6 weeks, fascicle length increased in group 3 (+0.83 cm, +7%, P = .027) and group 4 (+1.48 cm, +14%, P = .004), and pennation angle fell in groups 3 and 4. Eccentric strength increased in groups 2 (+53.6 N, +14%), 3 (+63.4 N, +17%) and 4 (+74.7 N, +19%), with no significant change reported for group 1. Group 4 was stronger than group 1 at posttest (+94.2 N). After 4 weeks of detraining, fascicle length had returned to baseline in groups 3 and 4, and group 3 strength fell significantly (-33.9 N) while group 4 kept its gains.
limitations: Groups of 10 recreationally active men; no untrained control group; fascicle length is an estimate. The abstract says strength returned to baseline in group 2 after detraining, but the results report no post hoc test for group 2 at that stage.
practicalImplications: Include at least one NHE session each week to keep eccentric strength rising. In this study, fascicle-length gains came only from the higher-volume protocols (176 or 358 total reps over 6 weeks), while 24 or 48 total reps did not change fascicle length.
athleteDev: Keep the NHE at least once weekly to maintain eccentric strength, and use an early higher-volume block if fascicle length is the goal. A 4-week break can erase fascicle-length gains, so plan maintenance exposure through the season.
rtp: Healthy recreationally active men only; no injured participants and no return-to-sport or re-injury outcome. It cannot set return-to-play loads or show that any protocol lowers hamstring injury risk, although the strength and architecture changes are relevant to later preventive planning.

citation: Cuthbert M, Ripley N, McMahon JJ, Evans M, Haff GG, Comfort P. The Effect of Nordic Hamstring Exercise Intervention Volume on Eccentric Strength and Muscle Architecture Adaptations: A Systematic Review and Meta-analyses. Sports Medicine. 2019.
abstract: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 studies on how Nordic hamstring exercise (NHE) training volume relates to eccentric hamstring strength and biceps femoris architecture. Pre-post effects were large across high and low volumes after 6 or more weeks, and volume alone did not show a clear trend.
tldr: Across studies, NHE protocols of 6 or more weeks produced large strength and fascicle gains at both high and low volumes. Lower, consistent volumes may suit squads where soreness limits compliance.
methods: PRISMA-guided search of three databases (293 records) to 1 December 2018; 13 studies with at least 4 weeks of NHE, pre-post means and SDs, and biceps femoris architecture data were included. Study quality was rated with TESTEX, risk of bias with the Cochrane tool for the RCTs and publication bias with a Rosenthal fail-safe N; Hedges' g values were calculated within studies and a random-effects model estimated between-study effects.
findings: After 6 or more weeks, both high and low volume protocols produced large to very large within-study gains in eccentric strength, and three fascicle length measures showed very large gains (g of 2.58 or more). Weekly volumes ranged from about 21 to 73 repetitions with no clear volume trend. Studies of 4 weeks showed trivial to small change, and control groups showed trivial or negative change (g of 0.14 or less).
limitations: Only 13 studies, two without a control group; several studies had low TESTEX scores and did not report compliance or blinded assessment; the review was not pre-registered; the volume conclusion rests on uncontrolled pre-post effects. The abstract gives g = 2.12 (high volume) and g = 2.28 (low volume) for strength, but the results attribute g = 2.12 to a single study of eccentric peak torque and do not report g = 2.28.
practicalImplications: Protocols of 6 or more weeks produced large gains in the included studies, and volume did not clearly change the result. Where soreness drives poor adherence, a lower and consistent weekly volume may be a reasonable option, with intensity progressed over time.
athleteDev: Run NHE blocks for at least 6 weeks, progress the exercise's intensity rather than adding volume, and track compliance. A lower consistent volume may suit squads where soreness limits adherence.
rtp: The review contains no injured athletes and does not measure return to sport or injury outcomes. Strength and fascicle changes are surrogate outcomes for injury risk, so it cannot show that any NHE volume reduces re-injury or sets return-to-sport loads.

citation: Alcaraz PE, Carlos-Vivas J, Oponjuru BO, Martinez-Rodriguez A. The Effectiveness of Resisted Sled Training (RST) for Sprint Performance: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Sports Medicine. 2018.
abstract: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 studies on resisted sled training and sprint time. Sled training improved early acceleration and full-sprint times pre-post, did not improve maximum-velocity sprint time, and was not better than sprinting without a sled.
tldr: Sled sprint training improved early acceleration in recreationally active and trained athletes, but it was no better than the same sprinting without a sled, and maximum-velocity sprint time did not improve significantly. The authors recommend 6 or more weeks at 2 to 3 sessions a week.
methods: Systematic search of PubMed, SPORTDiscus and Web of Science to January 2018 with PRISMA reporting; 13 studies (32 RST groups, 15 control groups) with sprint time data at 10 m (acceleration), 15 m or more (maximum velocity) and 20 m or more (full sprint). Quality was rated with PEDro (mean 8 of 10), and random-effects pooled effect sizes with subgroup analyses were calculated.
findings: Pre-post sprint time improved in the acceleration phase (ES 0.61, P = .0001; heterogeneity I2 = 28%) and full sprint (ES 0.36, P = .009), but not in the maximum-velocity phase (ES 0.27, P = .25). Studies with control groups showed no significant RST-versus-control difference in any phase (acceleration ES 0.09, P = .64). Acceleration effects were moderate in recreationally active (ES 0.75) and trained (ES 0.84) participants but small and non-significant in highly trained ones (ES 0.30) and in female samples (ES 0.14); loads below and above 20% of body mass gave similar effects (0.61 vs 0.63), though the higher-load effect was not significant.
limitations: Subgroup comparisons rest on few studies and are not controlled comparisons; the frequency result comes from one study; the pooled sample for maximum velocity is small (81 participants); the bias check was visual.
practicalImplications: For early acceleration in team sports, use a block of at least 6 weeks at 2 to 3 sessions a week, with about 160 m or more per session in the studies that showed the largest effects. Do not expect a top-speed gain from sled work, and keep sled loads near or below about 20% of body mass for sprint-replication work.
athleteDev: For early acceleration in soccer or rugby, a 6-week sled block at 2 to 3 sessions a week improved sprint times in the pooled studies, though unresisted sprinting did about as well. For top speed the review found no significant effect, and the authors suggest that vertical-force methods such as plyometrics may be needed.
rtp: Only healthy, at least recreationally active participants; no injured athletes and no injury or return-to-sport outcome. Sprint-time gains cannot be used to judge readiness to sprint after injury or to set graded return loads.

citation: O Brien J, Browne D, Earls D, Lodge C. The Effect of A Flywheel Hip Extension Vs A Traditional Hip Extension Exercise on Hamstring Strength. International Journal of Strength and Conditioning. 2024.
abstract: Twenty U-20 male soccer players did six weeks of either flywheel or traditional Romanian deadlift twice weekly. Both improved 3RM deadlift strength; only the flywheel group showed a significant gain in eccentric hamstring strength, and the authors describe its gain as superior.
tldr: In U-20 soccer players, six weeks of flywheel or traditional Romanian deadlift both raised 3RM strength. Only the flywheel version showed a significant eccentric hamstring gain, but the groups did not differ significantly on that outcome, so a flywheel advantage is not established.
methods: Random allocation to flywheel RDL (inertial load set by a power test; 4 sets of 6 with two extra submaximal pre-repetitions) or traditional RDL (80% of predicted 1RM), twice weekly for 6 weeks with matched set-RPE 8. Outcomes were 3RM RDL and peak eccentric force during the NHE on a Hamstring Solo device before and after training, analysed with a 2 x 2 group x time repeated-measures ANOVA.
findings: Eccentric strength rose 13% (37 N, P = .03, g = 0.51) in the flywheel group but 5% (14 N, P = .282) in the traditional group; the time x group interaction for eccentric strength was not significant (P = .18). 3RM rose 18% (19 kg, g = 1.07) in the flywheel group and 28% (26 kg, g = 0.99) in the traditional group, with a significant time x group interaction (P = .02) favouring the traditional group's larger gain.
limitations: No control group, six weeks only, small groups, and usual training was not controlled. The abstract and discussion describe superior eccentric gains for flywheel, but the interaction test was not significant (P = .18). The text effect sizes (g = 0.18, 0.51, 0.99 and 1.07) also differ slightly from Table 2 (0.2, 0.53, 1.0 and 1.11).
practicalImplications: Either flywheel or traditional RDL can build 3RM Romanian deadlift strength in youth soccer players over 6 weeks. The flywheel version may add an eccentric hamstring gain, but this trial does not show that it is better than a traditional RDL for that outcome.
athleteDev: Either flywheel or traditional RDL can build hip extension strength in youth players. Use the flywheel version if an eccentric gain is the goal, with the caveat that the group difference was not significant, and match intensity with set-RPE.
rtp: Players were healthy and uninjured; no injured athletes and no return-to-play outcome were studied. It is a strength-block study, so it cannot set return-to-sport loads or show reduced re-injury.

citation: Singh G, Bennett KJM, McGuigan H, Goddard SG, Stevens CJ. The Effect of a Synthetic-Grass Sport Surface on Physiology and Perception During Intermittent Exercise in Hot Conditions. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2024. Ahead of print.
abstract: Randomized crossover study of 13 team-sport athletes running intermittently for 50 minutes on synthetic and natural grass in hot conditions. Skin temperature, sweat rate and thermal sensation were higher on synthetic grass, while the change in core temperature, heart rate and effort did not differ.
tldr: Synthetic turf in hot conditions raised skin temperature, sweat rate and perceived heat in this group of athletes, but the rise in core temperature, heart rate and effort matched natural grass. Expect athletes to feel hotter on turf without assuming a larger core-temperature rise.
methods: Thirteen athletes (9 male, 4 female) completed two 50-minute standardized intermittent running protocols on synthetic and natural grass, a week apart, in a counterbalanced crossover design. Core temperature was measured with an ingestible telemetric capsule, and skin temperature, heart rate, sweat rate, RPE, thermal sensation and thermal comfort were recorded.
findings: Final skin temperature was higher on synthetic grass at the calf (40.1 vs 33.4 C), shoulder (36.6 vs 33.7 C) and chest (33.2 vs 31.8 C), and sweat rate was higher (1.5 vs 1.2 L per hour). Final core temperature was slightly higher on natural grass (38.4 vs 38.2 C, P=0.042), but the change in core temperature (1.3 vs 1.4 C) and heart rate, thermal comfort and RPE did not differ between surfaces.
limitations: Only 13 athletes were tested, and the authors note they were likely partly acclimatized from the Australian summer. Air and surface temperatures were measured higher over synthetic grass (Table 1), so the two surfaces were not identical environments. Results may not transfer to unacclimatized athletes, other sports or longer sessions, and performance was not measured.
practicalImplications: The study supports treating synthetic grass in heat as a thermal-comfort and skin-temperature issue, since athletes felt hotter and sweated more on it. It does not show a larger core-temperature rise, heart rate increase or effort increase, so this study alone does not justify changing session plans on turf.
athleteDev: For performance staff, the surface alone did not change core temperature, heart rate or effort in a 50-minute session, so it is not a reason on its own to cut training intensity. Sweat rate and thermal sensation were higher on synthetic grass, and the effect on performance remains unknown.
rtp: The study used one session per surface in trained or developmental athletes and did not measure injury, rehabilitation or return to play, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.

citation: Tan B, Hu A, Zheng Y. The Impact of Weekly Acceleration and Deceleration Loads on Neuromuscular Performance in Soccer: A Session-to-Session Analysis. Journal of Sports Science and Medicine. 2025;24:851-860.
abstract: This study examined weekly variations in accelerations, decelerations and neuromuscular performance in male under-19 soccer players, and whether accumulated acceleration and deceleration loads relate to neuromuscular changes across a weekly microcycle. Thirty-nine outfield players were monitored by GNSS over two consecutive weeks, with countermovement jump (CMJ), hamstring strength (HS) and delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS) measured before and after training. CMJ and HS fell significantly after training on all five days, most on MD-4 and MD-5, and DOMS peaked on MD-3. No significant correlations were found between daily acceleration or deceleration counts and changes in CMJ or HS.
tldr: In 39 under-19 players, CMJ and hamstring strength fell after training on every day and were lowest on MD-4 and MD-5, but single-day acceleration and deceleration counts did not predict those drops. Plan late-week loads using the cumulative pattern rather than one session's counts.
methods: Descriptive, repeated-measures observational study over two consecutive weeks with two under-19 teams in provincial competition. Accelerations and decelerations were counted by a 10 Hz GNSS vest for each training session. CMJ height and isometric hamstring strength were measured 30 minutes before and 15 minutes after each session, and a 0 to 6 DOMS scale was completed each morning before training. Values were averaged by day relative to match day, then analysed with repeated-measures ANOVA, Bonferroni post hoc tests and Pearson correlations.
findings: Post-training CMJ and hamstring strength were significantly below pre-training on every day (p < 0.001). The largest drops were on MD-4 (CMJ -7.9%, hamstring -7.9%) and MD-5 (CMJ -7.8%, hamstring -7.9%). Pre-training CMJ and hamstring strength declined from MD-1 to MD-4. DOMS peaked on MD-3 (mean 1.04). Acceleration and deceleration counts were highest on MD-4 (means 44.00 and 43.65). No daily count was significantly correlated with the post-pre change in CMJ or HS; MD-5 showed non-significant trends of r = -0.27 to -0.32 (p = 0.050 to 0.092).
limitations: Observational design with no control group, so the findings describe association only. The sample is modest, restricted to two youth male teams, and chosen by convenience; daily values were averaged across the two weeks, only two trials per test were used, and only acceleration and deceleration counts were analysed. The text has internal inconsistencies: it says MD-5 sessions produced relatively few accelerations and that pre-training MD-5 CMJ and HS were lower than MD-1 to MD-4, but Tables 1 and 3 show MD-5 pre-training values close to MD-1 and the second-highest acceleration counts; table values are reported here. Planned next-day DOMS correlations are not reported, and the MD-5 correlation trends did not reach significance.
practicalImplications: Track CMJ and hamstring strength before and after sessions across the week, and plan MD-4 and MD-5 loads with recovery in mind, since those were the lowest-performing days in this group. Do not use a single session's acceleration or deceleration count to predict same-day decline, because this study found no link. Combine GNSS counts with other load and wellness measures.
athleteDev: Use pre- and post-session CMJ and hamstring tests as a weekly fatigue check, and watch midweek soreness, which peaked on MD-3 here. Do not use session acceleration or deceleration counts alone to judge an individual player's same-day readiness, since the study found no relationship.
rtp: Not applicable to return to sport. Players recovering from injury were excluded, so the results cannot set return-to-play criteria or load limits for injured players.

citation: Courty P, Cisyk J. Sports injuries and game stakes: Concussions in the National Football League. Economic Inquiry. 2023.
abstract: NFL regular-season games differ in importance for playoff qualification. The authors build an incentive-based measure of how a win changes a team's qualification probability and relate it to concussions. Teams were 24 percentage points more likely to suffer a concussion in games where a win secures a playoff berth.
tldr: Concussion risk in NFL games appears higher when a win would secure playoff qualification. This is an observational finding from one league, so it should prompt readiness for high-stakes games rather than a firm risk estimate.
methods: Team-game panel of NFL regular-season games from 2012 to 2015, excluding neutral-site games and each team's final game (1896 observations; 1282 in a restricted sample meeting the approximation conditions). A swing measure of playoff odds was computed for each game, concussion events were taken from injury reports, and linear probability models included team, season and game fixed effects and game-condition controls, with standard errors clustered by team.
findings: The swing variable had a positive association with concussion incidence that reached the 5 or 10 percent significance level once team or season fixed effects were included (coefficients about 0.24 to 0.31 with controls). In-sample, a 40 percentage point swing was linked to about a 10 percentage point higher chance of at least one concussion, from a base of about 25 percent, and the authors extrapolate to 24 percentage points for a swing of one. Artificial turf was linked to 6 to 7 points higher risk, and some alternative swing definitions gave weaker or non-significant results.
limitations: Observational design with no direct measure of game intensity or exposure. The stakes measure depends on a model of playoff odds, and the 24 point figure lies outside the observed swing range. Injury data come from public reports, and the findings are limited to NFL regular-season games from 2012 to 2015.
practicalImplications: Concussion risk may rise in games where the stakes are high, so staff could plan extra sideline and concussion-protocol readiness for those games. The paper does not test any prevention measure.
athleteDev: This paper does not address athlete development or performance. It covers injury risk linked to game stakes only.
rtp: This study does not inform return to sport. It measures how often concussions occur in high-stakes games and says nothing about recovery time or clearance decisions.

citation: Freeman BW, Talpey SW, James LP, Young WB. Sprinting and hamstring strain injury: Beliefs and practices of professional physical performance coaches in Australian football. Physical Therapy in Sport. 2021;48:12-19.
abstract: This survey asked high-performance managers at Australian Football League clubs about their beliefs and practices for sprinting and hamstring strain injury. Nine of 18 invited managers responded. Sprinting, eccentric strength training and periodisation were seen as effective, and all coaches reported regular sprint exposure, but the speed thresholds they used for sprinting varied widely.
tldr: Nine AFL high-performance managers said sprinting and eccentric hamstring training help prevent hamstring injury, and all reported regular sprint exposure. Their definitions of sprinting speed varied widely, and GPS was the main tool for tracking maximum speed.
methods: An online, Delphi-validated questionnaire was sent to 18 AFL high-performance managers between November 2019 and February 2020. It used closed and open questions about beliefs, training practices and speed thresholds. Two researchers coded the open responses into themes.
findings: Nine of 18 managers responded, and all nine rated acceleration and maximum-speed sprinting as common or very common HSI activities. All used weekly eccentric hamstring strength testing and reported sprint training, while sprinting was defined as anything from above 85% to above 95% of maximum velocity. No respondent reported measuring sprinting faster than 85% of maximum velocity, and GPS was the main way maximum speed was tested (nine in the results, eight of nine in the discussion).
limitations: Small sample from one league (9 of 18 invited, all male), with anonymous self-report that may reflect response bias. Respondents were asked only about AFL experience, and the study did not compare coach beliefs with injury data. The count of coaches testing maximum speed with GPS differs between the results (n = 9) and the discussion (8 of 9).
practicalImplications: Staff can check whether the speed thresholds they use match how they define sprinting, since the most common definition of sprinting was above 90% of maximum velocity (5 of 9) but none reported measuring it above 85%. The survey does not show which sprint dose prevents HSI, so it supports reviewing thresholds and monitoring exposure rather than adopting a set dose.
athleteDev: Define sprint exposure with relative speed bands, such as a percentage of each athlete's maximum velocity, and make sure the bands used to prescribe and monitor sprinting match the definition the staff uses. Six of nine respondents said the sprint dose should be individualised to each athlete.
rtp: This survey cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It describes coach beliefs about prevention and training, not rehabilitation progression or readiness criteria for athletes returning from HSI.

citation: Generoso TO, Pelegrinelli ARM, Gonzalez FF, Pallone LV, Locks R, Guadagnin EC, et al. Squatting Biomechanics After Femoroacetabular Impingement Surgery: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Clin J Sport Med. 2025.
abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis pooled 3D squat biomechanics studies of patients who had hip impingement surgery, comparing each patient before and after surgery. Most studies found no significant change in kinematics or kinetics, while a few individual studies reported changes in squat depth, pelvic motion and hip or knee flexion.
tldr: Across six before-and-after studies of hip impingement surgery, squat mechanics changed little on average. Bone deformity alone may not explain the squat limits seen in these patients.
methods: PRISMA-guided search of six databases (last searched 12 December 2024) for 3D motion-analysis studies that compared the same FAI patients before and after surgery during squatting. Study quality was rated with MINORS, and five studies were pooled with random-effects models for seven kinematic outcomes. Where study populations overlapped, the study with the higher MINORS score was used.
findings: Six studies were reviewed, with 74 presurgical and 73 postsurgical patients tested 6 to 32 months after surgery, and the pooled analysis showed no significant pre- to post-surgery differences in the kinematic measures. Individual studies reported greater squat depth in one study, greater pelvic sagittal range of motion in another, and opposite changes in anterior pelvic tilt between two studies. Kinetic findings were inconsistent across the four studies that reported them.
limitations: Few studies and patients, with three studies drawing on one cohort, which limits the pooled estimates. Kinematic processing and data reporting differed between studies, most were case-control or cross-sectional with moderate quality, and participants came from orthopaedic clinics. Table 2 gives squat depth as a percentage of leg length without stating which direction means deeper, so Lamontagne 2011's lower postoperative value is hard to reconcile with the reported greater depth.
practicalImplications: Surgery alone did not reliably change squat mechanics on average, so staff should not assume that a squat pattern normalises after bone correction. The authors suggest that muscle-balance and rehabilitation work may influence outcomes, but the review did not test rehabilitation effects directly.
athleteDev: Do not assume that squat depth, pelvic motion or squat speed improve after hip impingement surgery. Assess squat mechanics after surgery rather than relying on the procedure to restore them. The evidence comes from clinical patients, so it does not set athlete loading or performance targets.
rtp: The review gives only a general picture: squat depth and motion patterns changed little on average 6 to 32 months after surgery. It cannot set return-to-sport or squat clearance criteria, because it did not study athletes or sport-specific tasks.

citation: Gebeyehu TF, Harrop JS, Dian JA, Matsoukas S, Vaccaro AR. Stingers - A Review of Current Understanding and Management. Applied Sciences. 2025;15:3510.
abstract: A narrative review of stingers, the brief loss of function in one arm after a stretch or compression injury to the brachial plexus or cervical nerve roots. It covers pathology, clinical features, imaging, electrodiagnostics, treatment, rehabilitation and return to play, and the authors rate all the literature reviewed as level IV and V evidence.
tldr: Most stingers are mild and clear within minutes, and conservative care usually works. Return to play rests largely on expert opinion, with symptom duration, repeat episodes and imaging guiding decisions. Surgery is rare and reserved for severe nerve root or nerve injury.
methods: Narrative review. PubMed and Google Scholar were searched for 'stingers' and 'burners' without Boolean operators, with title screening and a focus on English-language literature from the past five years, supplemented by reference lists and older foundational work. Sources included case reports, reviews, retrospective and prospective studies, expert opinion (including a modified Delphi consensus) and book chapters.
findings: Stingers accounted for 62.2% of NFL neck injuries in one study, and 50.3% of football players reported a lifetime stinger in a survey. In the Delphi consensus cited, 69.9% of spine surgeons agreed that first-time stingers under 5 minutes need no imaging, and 84.5% agreed imaging is indicated if symptoms last over 5 minutes or recur. Surgery is reserved for grade IIIA and IIIB injuries, and the review states that its timing and type remain unsettled.
limitations: The authors state the review is not systematic and does not cover all the literature. All the evidence reviewed is level IV and V, and incidence data are missing for sports such as MMA, judo and weightlifting. The 84.5% Delphi figure is used for two different statements (imaging after 5 minutes in section 8; same-day return without MRI in section 10), so check the source before citing it.
practicalImplications: For a first stinger that clears within five minutes, with full pain-free neck and shoulder motion and no weakness or sensory change, the review cites expert agreement for same-day return without imaging. Repeat episodes or symptoms lasting longer than five minutes call for imaging and serial examination. Staff should test the brachial plexus muscles in detail, not only grip strength, and rule out spinal cord or vascular injury before anything else.
athleteDev: Use the review's prevention points: avoid clothesline and spear tackling, use protective equipment such as a cowboy collar, restore neck motion, and strengthen the neck and shoulder girdle. Shoulder pad fit may matter, since one cited study linked pads to compression at Erb's point during tackling. The review gives no training dose or load guidance.
rtp: Return to play follows expert consensus. A first stinger with symptoms clearing within five minutes and no strength, sensory or range-of-motion loss is cited as a same-day return, while repeat or prolonged episodes need imaging and serial examination. Grade IIIA or IIIB injury is an absolute contraindication to return, and the authors lean toward MRI for every episode regardless of symptom duration.

citation: Kay AD, Rubley B, Talbot C, Mina M, Baross AW, Blazevich AJ. Stretch imposed on active muscle elicits positive adaptations in strain risk factors and exercise-induced muscle damage. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2018.
abstract: Six weeks of twice-weekly stretches imposed on maximally contracted knee extensors (isokinetic eccentric contractions) in 26 recreationally active adults increased eccentric strength, range of motion, stretch tolerance, elastic energy storage, muscle thickness, pennation angle and tendon stiffness, and reduced the CK response and soreness after a downhill run.
tldr: Six weeks of maximal eccentric stretches on the knee extensors improved range, stretch tolerance, strength and some damage markers in recreationally active adults. The study measured risk factors in healthy people, not injury rates.
methods: Randomized controlled trial with 13 participants in each group, matched by sex. The experimental group did five sets of 12 three-second maximal isokinetic eccentric knee extensor contractions (0 to 90 degrees, 30 degrees per second), twice weekly for 6 weeks, on both legs. Before and after training, range of motion, passive and active moments, ultrasound measures of vastus lateralis architecture and tendon stiffness, serum CK and DOMS were measured, with a 20-minute downhill run used to provoke muscle damage.
findings: In the experimental group, knee flexion range of motion increased by 5.2 degrees, peak passive moment by 55.4% and elastic energy storage by 73.0%. Isometric and eccentric knee extensor moments rose 17.4% and 29.5%. Vastus lateralis thickness rose 7.8%, pennation angle 9.0% and tendon stiffness 8.7%, while passive muscle-tendon stiffness fell 9.4% (not significant). The CK increase after the downhill run was smaller after training (46.0%) than before (107.6%), and knee extensor DOMS was absent or minimal after training. The control group showed no significant change in the mechanical, strength or architecture measures, and its CK rise after the downhill run was similar before (115.4%) and after (120.5%) the 6 weeks.
limitations: The number of participants was small, and the outcome measures were single laboratory tests. DOMS was only ranked for presence and severity across muscle groups, not scored on a scale. Fascicle strain during stretch was not measured, and tendon stiffness may be underestimated because knee movement was not corrected for. The abstract reports a CK change of -70.0%, but the results section reports -70.4%. Injury incidence was not measured.
practicalImplications: In recreationally active adults, a 6-week program of maximal eccentric knee extensor stretches improved range, strength and muscle-damage responses in the trained muscle. Staff could consider this approach for knee extensors in similar groups, but not as proof of injury prevention.
athleteDev: Performance Application: The program increased eccentric strength and tendon stiffness in the trained muscle, which the authors consider functionally important for athletic tasks. The paper does not test athletes or sport performance, so the link to sport performance is an inference.
rtp: This study cannot be used to set return-to-sport loading. It tested healthy recreationally active adults with no recent injury and measured no injured participants or return-to-play outcomes.

citation: Wasserman EB, Chretien A, Harmon KG, Putukian M, Okonkwo D, Solomon GS, et al. Subsequent musculoskeletal injury after concussion in National Football League players. Br J Sports Med. 2024.
abstract: In a retrospective cohort of NFL players from 2015 to 2021, the authors compared the hazard of subsequent time-loss lower extremity or any musculoskeletal injury after concussion with non-concussed players in the same game and with players returning from an upper extremity injury. Neither comparison showed a statistically significant difference, and the authors suggest that deconditioning or other factors linked to lost participation time may explain the higher injury risk seen after concussion in some settings.
tldr: Among NFL players, a concussion did not significantly raise the risk of later musculoskeletal injury over the season after adjustment for prior injuries. The authors suggest time away from sport, rather than the concussion itself, may be what matters, but they did not measure deconditioning.
methods: Retrospective cohort from the NFL electronic health record (2015 to 2021 preseason and regular season). Concussed players were compared with two groups: all non-concussed players from the same game, and players with a time-loss upper extremity injury. Cox proportional hazards models were adjusted for prior injuries, prior concussions, tenure and roster position, with follow-up measured in player-plays and sensitivity analyses at 30 and 60 days.
findings: Compared with non-concussed players in the same game, the adjusted hazard of time-loss lower extremity injury was 1.09 (95% CI 0.88 to 1.35) over the season and 1.12 (0.90 to 1.41) when days missed were included; for any time-loss musculoskeletal injury it was 1.06 (0.88 to 1.27) and 1.08 (0.89 to 1.31). At 30 days without days-missed adjustment, hazards were significantly higher (lower extremity 1.39, 1.07 to 1.82; any injury 1.36, 1.08 to 1.70) but not once days missed were included. Compared with upper extremity injury, season hazards were 0.78 (0.60 to 1.02) for lower extremity and 0.82 (0.65 to 1.04) for any musculoskeletal injury, with a significantly lower lower extremity hazard at 60 days (0.74, 0.56 to 0.98).
limitations: Men in one elite league, so findings may not transfer to women, other sports, or non-elite players. Follow-up was censored at the end of the season or roster removal, prior injury history before the NFL was not available, and rookies were excluded. The authors could not measure deconditioning, and the comparison groups differ in the time they spend at risk after an injury.
practicalImplications: Treat the time lost after a concussion as a reason for a structured, progressive conditioning plan before full return. The same plan is worth considering after any upper extremity injury that keeps an athlete out of sport. The study did not find extra musculoskeletal risk after concussion compared with other injured players, but it cannot rule out a modest increase.
athleteDev: Performance Application: Keep a player's physical conditioning up during any time away from sport, and plan the return with a graded build-up, since the authors suggest time lost, rather than the concussion itself, may drive later injury risk.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: The study supports a rigorous, staged return to sport after concussion and after an upper extremity injury, and it suggests that time lost is a key risk factor. It does not establish that a particular return protocol reduces injury, and the authors call for further research on that question.

citation: Finocchiaro G, Westaby J, Sheppard MN, Papadakis M, Sharma S. Sudden Cardiac Death in Young Athletes: JACC State-of-the-Art Review. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2024;83(2):350-370.
abstract: This state-of-the-art review covers the epidemiology and causes of sudden cardiac death in young athletes, including cardiomyopathies, channelopathies and coronary anomalies. It also addresses the difficulty of separating the athlete's heart from disease, preparticipation screening, resuscitation, and shared decision making about exercise when a cardiac condition is found.
tldr: Sudden cardiac death in young athletes is rare but usually linked to an inherited heart condition or coronary anomaly that was not detected beforehand. A cardiac diagnosis does not automatically end sport, and decisions should follow expert assessment and shared decision making.
methods: Narrative state-of-the-art review. No systematic search method is described. The authors draw on incidence studies, national registries, autopsy series and guideline statements from the United States, Europe and elsewhere, and summarise Table 2 comparing AHA/ACC and ESC recommendations for sports participation.
findings: Reported incidence of sudden cardiac death in young athletes varies widely, from 0.24 per 100,000 athlete-years in Minnesota high school athletes to 6.8 per 100,000 athlete-years in a screened UK adolescent football cohort. Inherited cardiac conditions (cardiomyopathies and channelopathies) and congenital coronary artery anomalies are the most common causes, and a structurally normal heart at autopsy is an increasingly common finding. Athlete's heart changes can overlap with cardiomyopathy and channelopathy findings, and the review describes ECG and imaging features that help separate them. Compulsory screening in Veneto, Italy, was linked to an 89% fall in incidence in one account, while a study in Israel, based on newspaper reports, found no reduction. The review also notes that recent guidelines take a more liberal, shared decision making approach to exercise in several cardiac conditions.
limitations: No search method is described, and the review relies on heterogeneous definitions and case ascertainment. The authors note that autopsy rates are declining and that some cohorts underestimate events. Evidence on the effects of intense exercise in people with cardiac disease is mainly from retrospective or observational studies, and the authors call for randomised trials.
practicalImplications: Use a holistic assessment combining personal and family history, ECG and imaging before clearing an athlete, and recognise that many cardiac findings are physiological. Keep resuscitation readiness high, with trained staff, a plan and access to an automated external defibrillator, and discuss exercise limits with the athlete and team physician when a condition is found.
athleteDev: Performance Application: Expect endurance and explosive-sport athletes to show heart changes that can overlap with cardiomyopathy, and route equivocal ECG or imaging findings for second-line cardiac investigation rather than assuming disease or normality. Keep emergency action plans and defibrillator access in place through the season.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: The review summarises guideline recommendations on sports participation after a cardiac diagnosis, such as cardiomyopathy or channelopathy, and recommends shared decision making; it notes athletes with myocarditis should refrain from intense exercise for at least 3 months. It does not provide a return-to-play protocol after cardiac arrest, and the authors note the evidence on high-intensity exercise is limited.

citation: Chambers CC, Lynch TS, Gibbs DB, Ghodasra JH, Sahota S, Franke K, et al. Superior Labrum Anterior-Posterior Tears in the National Football League. Am J Sports Med. 2017;45(1):167.
abstract: The authors analysed SLAP tears in NFL players using league injury surveillance data from 2000 to 2014 and Scouting Combine records from 2003 to 2011. SLAP tears were a small share of shoulder injuries, surgically treated tears caused much more time lost, and Combine athletes with prior repair who were drafted had fewer games played and started.
tldr: SLAP tears are uncommon in NFL players but cost substantial time when they need surgery. Players with a prior SLAP repair who were drafted played noticeably fewer games than matched peers.
methods: Two-part descriptive study. NFL Injury Surveillance System records of SLAP tears from 2000 to 2014 were analysed by position, play type, days and games lost and surgery. Scouting Combine athletes from 2003 to 2011 with a prior SLAP repair were identified from medical evaluations and compared with matched drafted controls on career length and performance score. Groups were compared with t tests and chi-square tests.
findings: SLAP tears were 3.1% of NFL shoulder injuries (65 cases), most often in offensive linemen (27.7%), and about two-thirds occurred in games. Surgical treatment (41.5% of cases) was associated with more days missed (140.2 vs 21.5, P < .001) and games missed (8.4 vs 2.6, P = .003) than nonoperative care. Of 2,965 Combine athletes, 25 reported a prior SLAP repair; 18 of them were drafted, and compared with 18 matched controls they had similar performance scores (3.63 for both) and years played (3.4 vs 4.0, P = .063), but fewer games played (33.7 vs 48.3, P = .049) and games started (19.6 vs 35.4, P = .036).
limitations: Small sample sizes and possible underreporting of less severe injuries, particularly in Combine self-reported history. The surveillance system did not record SLAP subtype, injury severity or surgical detail, so the time-loss comparison may reflect severity. Estimated return dates were included in days missed, and career statistics came from unofficial public sources. The authors call for confirmation in larger populations.
practicalImplications: Treat a SLAP tear in a contact athlete as a potentially career-affecting injury and plan for substantial time lost if surgery is needed. Three quarters of in-game SLAP tears occurred during contact with another player, most commonly while tackling or blocking, so the mechanism and play type are worth recording when a contact athlete presents with shoulder symptoms. The study did not test any prevention or treatment strategy.
athleteDev: Performance Application: Track shoulder surgical history at the Combine and in medical screening, since drafted players with a prior SLAP repair played and started fewer games than matched controls despite similar draft rates and performance scores. Expect linemen to be the most often affected, as offensive linemen had the most SLAP tears in both the NFL and Combine groups.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: Surgically treated SLAP tears in NFL players were followed by a mean of 140 days missed compared with about three weeks for nonoperative management, which gives a rough time-loss benchmark. The study does not measure return to prior performance level after surgery, so it cannot guide return-to-play criteria.

citation: Terry DP, Büttner F, Huebschmann NA, Gardner AJ, Cook NE, Iverson GL. Systematic Review of Pre-injury Migraines as a Vulnerability Factor for Worse Outcome Following Sport-Related Concussion. Frontiers in Neurology. 2022;13:915357.
abstract: This PRISMA systematic review of 27 studies asked whether pre-injury migraine is associated with slower recovery after sport-related concussion. Most studies found no association, and the authors judge the evidence to suggest, but not prove, that pre-injury migraine may be a vulnerability factor.
tldr: Most studies found no link between a pre-injury migraine history and slower concussion recovery, but the largest and best-designed studies hint at a higher risk in a subgroup of athletes. Staff should treat a migraine history as a possible risk marker to monitor, not a confirmed predictor.
methods: Systematic review following PRISMA and a PROSPERO-registered protocol. Searches of nine databases covered English-language studies to 15 May 2021, and studies of pre-injury migraine as a predictor of sport-related concussion recovery were included. Risk of bias was rated with QUIPS, levels of evidence with OCEBM, and a likelihood-ratio heuristic was used to summarize the mixed results without meta-analysis.
findings: Across 25 unique samples, 8,692 athletes had sport-related concussion and at least 1,015 had pre-injury migraine history (11.8%). Nineteen studies found no significant association with recovery, two had mixed findings, and four reported only positive findings, with six of 25 studies showing at least one significant result. In a prospective high school and college cohort (117 athletes with migraine), a lower share of migraine athletes had returned to school at 7, 14 and 21 days, with no difference in return to play. In a large emergency department cohort, 42.6% of youth with migraine versus 28.1% without had symptoms at 28 days (multivariable OR 1.73). The likelihood ratio at 80% power and alpha 0.05 favored the null for all studies (429,001) but favored the alternative for studies with 50 or more migraine participants (8.05, weak to moderate).
limitations: Pre-injury migraine was assessed by single self-report items in most studies, with little information on age of onset, frequency or treatment. Most studies were rated moderate risk of bias, many had fewer than 20 migraine participants, outcomes and time points varied, and confounding by sex and prior concussion was rarely handled. The authors also note that only published studies were included, so publication bias is possible.
practicalImplications: Staff can ask every athlete about pre-injury migraine history at baseline and after concussion, and consider it alongside other risk markers. The review does not support a specific monitoring threshold or a change in management for athletes with migraines.
athleteDev: Performance Application: the review does not study training, performance or load. Its relevance is to baseline screening, because athletes with migraines have been reported to show more symptoms and vestibular or ocular-motor provocation at preseason baseline testing, which can affect how baselines are interpreted.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: the review suggests a subgroup of athletes with pre-injury migraine may take longer to recover, with one large cohort showing more symptoms at 28 days, but most studies found no difference in return to play. It cannot set return-to-play criteria, and it should not be used to delay or accelerate clearance for an individual athlete.

citation: Stokes KA, Locke D, Roberts S, et al. Tackle characteristics associated with concussion in elite men's rugby union: unpicking the differences between tacklers and ball-carriers. BMJ Open Sport & Exercise Medicine. 2025;11:e002612.
abstract: The authors identified tackle characteristics associated with concussion for tacklers and ball-carriers in five seasons of English Premiership rugby union, using a case-control design. Of 231 video-identified concussions, 178 occurred to tacklers and 53 to ball-carriers, and these were compared with 9,963 control tackles. Lower tackles reduced the odds of concussion to ball-carriers, while the odds for tacklers were more nuanced but relatively low when contact was made with the ball-carrier's torso.
tldr: In elite rugby union, contacting the ball-carrier's torso carried relatively low concussion odds for both players, while head or neck contact with the ball-carrier was linked to high odds. Lower tackle height appears to reduce concussion risk for ball-carriers, but the tackler results are more mixed.
methods: Case-control study of male professional players in The English Premiership (2016/2017 to 2020/2021). Concussion cases were video-coded from club-reported events, and each was compared with control tackles from the same fixtures (25 tackles before and after the event). A random forest selected key variables, and generalised linear mixed models with player as a random effect estimated odds ratios with 90% CIs.
findings: For tacklers, every head-contact location raised odds versus no head contact; head-to-torso raised them about 6.5-fold (OR 6.5, 90% CI 4.0 to 10.7) and was among the lowest of the head-contact categories, and head-to-knee had the highest odds (OR 155.8, 90% CI 75.3 to 322.4). Head-to-hip occurred most often and had the highest number of concussions per 1,000 tackles (3.1). For ball-carriers, head-to-head contact had the highest odds (OR 104.3, 90% CI 56.7 to 192.0), and first contact to the head or neck had higher odds than torso contact (OR 27.2, 90% CI 15.2 to 48.7). The authors report that the random forest models had AUROC values of 0.73 to 0.84.
limitations: Only 54% of reported concussions could be identified on video, and ball-carrier events were harder to identify, which may bias the tackler-versus-ball-carrier comparison. The sample was small once several characteristics were combined, so interaction estimates are imprecise. Results come from one league over five seasons, and the 90% CIs are wide for several contact categories. The ball-carrier head and neck versus torso OR is printed with two different CIs (15.2 to 48.7 and 13.6 to 54.5).
practicalImplications: Coaches and policy makers can use the finding that torso contact carries lower concussion odds for both players, supporting tackle-height strategies that target the torso. Tackle coaching could also address head contact with a ball-carrier's hip or knee and with a teammate's head, which had higher odds for tacklers.
athleteDev: Tackle training can focus on initial contact with the ball-carrier's torso and on keeping the tackler's head away from the ball-carrier's hip, knee and a teammate's head. Very low tackles that brought the tackler's head onto the ball-carrier's knee had high odds, and an upright tackler making first contact with the ball-carrier's head or neck had higher tackler odds than upright contact to the torso, so body position and contact height are both training targets.
rtp: Not applicable. The study describes tackle characteristics associated with concussion occurrence and does not assess recovery, return-to-play timing or post-concussion management.

citation: Sherwood CP, Grogan F, McMurry TL, et al. Tackle techniques and characteristics associated with a concussion in tackling players in the National Football League. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2025.
abstract: The authors reviewed video of 51 NFL tackler concussions from the 2015 to 2019 seasons and 96 matched control tackles, coding 20 technique variables. Closing speed was significantly associated with concussion in every model, and the tackler leading with the helmet, helmet as primary contact or loading, and head placement across the ball carrier's path had the largest associations. Torso as the ball carrier's primary loading area had the lowest risk.
tldr: Tacklers who led with the helmet, took the main load on the helmet, or placed their head across the ball carrier's path had higher concussion odds in matched NFL tackles. Coaching players to target the torso and keep their head on the correct side may lower risk, although closing speed was the strongest factor.
methods: Matched case-control study using a qualitative video review of 1-on-1 pass and rush tackles. Each concussion case was matched to 1 to 3 control tackles using Next Gen Stats trajectory and closing speed, and 20 technique variables were coded for both groups. Conditional logistic regression adjusted for closing velocity, with false discovery rate correction across models.
findings: Tacklers who led with the helmet had an OR of 5.18 (95% CI 1.87 to 14.33), and helmet as primary loading had an OR of 4.61 (95% CI 1.41 to 15.05). Head placed across the ball carrier's path had an OR of 4.17 (95% CI 1.58 to 11.01) relative to head on the correct side, and a shoulder initial contact had an OR of 0.17 (95% CI 0.04 to 0.78) relative to helmet. Each 1 m/s increase in closing speed was associated with a roughly tenfold increase in risk, and ball-carrier torso loading had the lowest risk of the body parts coded.
limitations: The sample was small, with 51 cases and 96 controls, and several variables produced undefined or very wide odds ratios. Controls were matched on tracking data and closing speed, not on full kinematics, and the authors note that some variables were correlated with each other. The study was funded by the NFL, and the author list includes an NFL employee and authors with consulting ties to the NFL.
practicalImplications: Coaches can teach tacklers to keep the helmet out of the tackle, to place the head on the correct side of the ball carrier, and to target the torso, all of which were linked to lower concussion odds in this sample. Closing speed had the most consistent association, but the authors' recommendations focus on helmet involvement, head placement and torso targeting rather than on speed.
athleteDev: Technique training can focus on minimising helmet involvement, placing the head outside the ball carrier's path, and aiming for the torso. Shortening steps, bending at the waist and use of the arms were not significantly associated with tackler concussion in this NFL sample, unlike earlier rugby findings.
rtp: Not applicable. The study examines tackle technique and concussion occurrence in NFL games and does not assess recovery, return-to-play decisions or post-concussion management.

citation: Meintjes V, Forshaw P, den Hollander S, et al. Tackler and ball-carrier technique during moderate and severe injuries (≥8 days lost) compared with player-matched and team-matched injury-free controls in Elite Rugby Union. Br J Sports Med. 2021.
abstract: The authors scored tackler and ball-carrier technique in 74 moderate and severe (8 or more days lost) tackle injuries in the Currie Cup from 2014 to 2018. Each injury was compared with injury-free tackles by the same player and by teammates. Overall technical proficiency was significantly lower for the injury-causing event than for both control groups, for tacklers and ball-carriers, in front-on and side-on or behind tackles.
tldr: Tacklers and ball-carriers who were injured in moderate or severe tackle injuries in the Currie Cup scored lower on technique checklists than their own uninjured tackles and their teammates' uninjured tackles. The study identifies specific technique gaps that coaches can target in training.
methods: Case-control study using video from South African Rugby Union injury surveillance. For each injury, matched injury-free tackles by the same player (own controls) and by teammates (team controls) were identified within the same or most recent match, matched on tackle type, direction and role, with a target ratio of 1:5:5.
