A single analyst scored technical criteria on a 16-point or 11-point scale for tacklers and 14-point or 12-point scale for ball-carriers, and groups were compared with one-way ANOVA, Tukey post hoc tests and effect sizes.
findings: For front-on tackles, injured tacklers scored 6.19 of 16 (95% CI 4.89 to 7.48), compared with 8.90 for own controls and 9.93 for team controls. For side-on or behind tackles, injured tacklers scored 4.80 of 11, compared with 6.44 and 7.23. For ball-carriers, injured players scored 5.60 of 14 (front-on) and 5.17 of 12 (side-on or behind), compared with 8.08 and 8.16, and 7.39 and 7.75, respectively. For upright-to-bent body position and shoulder-first contact, injured front-on tacklers scored lower than team controls in both their injury and own-control tackles, which the authors read as an existing deficit in these players rather than a lapse during the injury event.
limitations: The analysis was univariate and did not adjust for player physical attributes, playing position, match context or the opponent's actions, and the authors note that technique scoring includes subjectivity. Only shoulder and arm tackles in front-on and side-on or behind direction were analysed, and of 288 moderate and severe contact injuries only 108 were identified on video and 74 met the criteria for analysis. The sample comes from one domestic competition over five seasons, so the results may not generalise to other competitions.
practicalImplications: Coaches and trainers can use the listed technique gaps to design tackle training, for example upright-to-bent body position and shoulder-first contact for tacklers, and shifting the ball and protecting it in the correct arm for ball-carriers. The authors suggest building team databases of technique scores to find individual deficits.
athleteDev: The study points to specific tackler techniques (keeping the back straight with the centre of gravity ahead, head on the correct side, head up and forward, using the arms after contact, and releasing the ball carrier) and ball-carrier techniques (awareness of the tackler, shifting the ball to the correct arm, explosiveness, and going to ground to present the ball) that scored lower in injury-causing tackles.
rtp: The authors suggest that knowing which techniques a player lacks could help the return-to-contact process and reduce re-injury risk, but the study did not test this. The technique scores therefore cannot be used as a return-to-play criterion on the basis of this paper.

citation: Edwards S, Gardner A, Tahu T, et al. Tacklers' Head Inertial Accelerations Can Be Decreased by Altering the Way They Engage in Contact with Ball Carriers' Torsos. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2022 (published ahead of print).
abstract: The authors used 3D motion capture to examine how four legal front-on, one-on-one torso tackles affected the head kinematics of tacklers and ball carriers, using 455 successful trials from 15 rugby players. Tackles differed in the height of contact on the ball carrier's torso and in the tackler's technique. The tackler had the highest peak head accelerations when contacting the lower torso, and a modified smother tackle reduced tackler linear head acceleration compared with the traditional upper-torso smother.
tldr: In a lab study of slow front-on tackles, contacting the hip area produced the highest tackler head accelerations, while a modified smother tackle with a pop-and-lock action produced lower tackler linear head acceleration. Mid-torso contact may lower tackler head loads, but it shifts more load to the ball carrier.
methods: Laboratory experimental study with a within-player design. Fifteen healthy male rugby players, paired in sessions, each completed 10 trials of each of four tackle instructions (dominant NRL, dominant torso and stick, smother NRL, and smother ball pop and lock) at 80% game intensity, with roles reversed. Full-body 3D motion capture (300 Hz) was used, and mixed general linear models compared peak resultant linear and angular head accelerations across instructions.
findings: For tacklers, the dominant NRL (hip-area) tackle produced significantly higher peak linear and angular head accelerations than the other three instructions (linear p less than 0.001 against each; angular p of 0.013 or lower against each). The smother ball, pop and lock tackle had lower tackler linear head acceleration than the smother NRL and dominant torso and stick tackles (p = 0.001 each); in the Table 2 post hoc tests, tackler angular acceleration differed only between the hip-area tackle and the others. For ball carriers, the dominant NRL tackle produced the smallest peak linear and angular head accelerations, and the pop-and-lock tackle produced higher ball-carrier accelerations than the smother NRL and dominant torso and stick tackles.
limitations: The abstract says mid and upper torso tackles produced the lowest ball-carrier head kinematics, but the results and discussion say the hip-area tackle did, so this report follows the results. The results text also says the pop-and-lock tackle lowered tackler angular acceleration versus two other tackles, but Table 2 and the discussion show angular differences only for the hip-area tackle. The study had 15 players, slow tackles, no ground contact, one expert coach, and 145 of 600 trials removed as unsuccessful, which may bias the findings. Injury history was not recorded, and the authors note that the behaviour change was tested only in one session.
practicalImplications: Coaches can consider mid-torso contact as a target for dominant tackles, since the hip-area tackle gave the highest tackler head accelerations in this lab setting. The authors note a trade-off, because the ball carrier's head loads rise with higher contact, so the change needs testing in match conditions before it is adopted.
athleteDev: The lower-acceleration modified tackles were performed with less head flexion and a straighter back than the standard NRL tackles, and in the pop-and-lock variant the head was placed outside the ball carrier's shoulder. These features were not tested on their own, and the results come from slow, expert-coached trials that did not go to ground.
rtp: Not applicable. The study measures head kinematics in healthy players during slow simulated tackles and does not assess concussion, recovery or return-to-play decisions.

citation: Brazier J, Antrobus M, Stebbings GK, Day SH, Heffernan SM, Cross MJ, et al. Tendon and ligament injuries in elite rugby: The potential genetic influence. Sports. 2019;7:138.
abstract: This narrative review summarises tendon and ligament injury incidence and severity in elite rugby union and rugby league and discusses tendon and ligament biology and possible genetic influences on injury. It proposes nine candidate genes for study in elite rugby and other invasion sports.
tldr: Tendon and ligament injuries are among the most frequent and severe in elite rugby, and genetic variation may partly explain why some players are more susceptible. The genetic link is not yet proven and the candidate genes need testing in large elite cohorts.
methods: Narrative review. A structured literature search used terms on elite rugby injury, injury mechanisms, tendon and ligament epidemiology, pathophysiology and genetics, and reference lists of the articles found were checked. Databases, dates and inclusion criteria are not reported.
findings: The authors report that rugby union has one of the highest reported injury incidences of professional sport and that tendon and ligament injuries are among the most severe. They describe the biology of tendons and ligaments and summarise evidence that genetic variation may influence injury susceptibility, but they state that much stronger evidence is needed. They propose nine candidate genes (COL1A1, COL3A1, COL5A1, MIR608, MMP3, TIMP2, VEGFA, NID1, COLGALT1) for study in elite rugby.
limitations: The review is narrative, with no reported search databases, dates or quality appraisal. The genetic evidence is limited and largely from candidate-gene studies. The authors note that very large samples, probably hundreds or thousands of players, would be needed for genetic studies in elite sport.
practicalImplications: Genetic markers are not ready for use in selecting or managing players. The authors suggest that genetic analysis of players already in large rugby injury databases could show whether the proposed genes relate to injury risk.
athleteDev: This paper does not provide a training or performance method. It identifies tendon and ligament injury as a major concern in rugby and proposes genetic research that may later inform individual load and injury-risk management.
rtp: This review cannot inform return-to-play decisions. It contains no return-to-play outcomes, rehabilitation data or clinical criteria, and its genetic markers are not validated for prognosis.

citation: Yeargin SW, Scarneo-Miller SE, Jardine J, Troyanos C, Lopez R. The Association Between Central Nervous System Function and Core Body Temperature in Patients With Exertional Heat Stroke. Clin J Sport Med. 2025.
abstract: The study describes central nervous system function using the Glasgow Coma Scale in patients with exertional heat stroke treated at a road race medical tent, and tests whether GCS relates to rectal temperature. The authors find only a weak overall correlation and none above 40 C, and conclude that GCS may not capture CNS dysfunction in this condition.
tldr: In 25 runners treated for exertional heat stroke, Glasgow Coma Scale scores tracked rectal temperature only weakly and not at the dangerous high temperatures. Rectal temperature should still guide cooling, and mental status alone should not be used to stop it.
methods: Retrospective cross-sectional review of deidentified medical charts from an 11 km race medical tent. Scribes recorded GCS subscales and cumulative scores at each rectal temperature reading, roughly every 3 minutes, and Spearman correlations tested the link between rectal temperature and GCS in the 22 patients with at least one documented GCS score.
findings: Of 25 patients (14 men, 11 women, aged 29 plus or minus 13 years), the mean initial rectal temperature was 41.0 plus or minus 0.6 C and the mean cumulative GCS was 14 plus or minus 3 (range 4 to 15). Confusion was the most frequently recorded CNS sign (19.8%). Overall, rectal temperature and GCS had a significant but weak negative correlation (rs = -0.255, p = 0.004, R2 = 0.06). At time points above 40 C, the correlation was not significant (rs = -0.209, p = 0.108), and the Eye, Verbal and Motor subscales were also not significant.
limitations: Charts were completed during busy care, so some variables were not recorded at every time point, and persistent signs were not always documented. Only patients who reached a station with their own chart were included. The study is from one race with 25 patients, and the authors say a universal GCS guideline cannot be drawn from it.
practicalImplications: Clinicians should keep using rectal temperature to guide cold water immersion and to decide when to stop cooling, and should not use GCS or mental status to decide when cooling is complete. Where rectal temperature cannot be measured, the authors suggest estimating cooling time from the likely core temperature, the body area in water and the water temperature, while noting this does not represent best practice.
athleteDev: Performance Application: The study concerns acute heat illness rather than performance. For staff at endurance events, it reinforces that rectal temperature measurement should be available at the medical tent.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: The paper covers acute treatment of exertional heat stroke in race patients and does not address return to sport. It cannot inform return timing or criteria after heat stroke.

citation: Chundi G, Dawar A, Fuller Z, Jones T, Lingam S, Galdi B. The Association Between Early Sport Specialization and Injury and Career Outcomes Among National Football League Athletes. European Journal of Sport Science. 2026;26:e70120.
abstract: The study tested whether playing only football in high school is associated with higher injury rates and shorter NFL careers than multisport participation. Among NFL draftees from 2011 to 2023, multisport athletes had fewer total and major injuries per 1000 snaps and longer careers.
tldr: Among NFL draftees, those who played several sports in high school had fewer injuries per snap and longer careers than those who played only football. The result is an association from observational data, so it does not show that early specialization causes harm.
methods: Retrospective cohort of NFL players drafted 2011 to 2023 who played at least 16 career games, excluding kickers and punters. High school sport history came from public records and injury data from online databases. Injury rates per 1000 snaps were compared using position-stratified incidence rate ratios, with false discovery rate correction for position analyses. Concussions, illnesses, upper extremity fractures and jaw or facial fractures were excluded from the injury counts, and multisport status meant at least one other varsity sport in grades 9 to 12.
findings: Of 2,556 players, about 64% were multisport athletes. Multisport athletes had lower total injury incidence (IRR 0.80, 95% CI 0.76 to 0.85) and major injury incidence (IRR 0.77, 95% CI 0.71 to 0.82), both p less than 0.001. They played 12.2 more NFL games (95% CI 9.2 to 15.1) and had 0.7 more career years (95% CI 0.5 to 0.9). By position, lower injury rates in multisport athletes remained significant after false discovery rate correction for defensive backs, defensive linemen, linebackers, running backs and wide receivers, but not for offensive linemen, quarterbacks or tight ends.
limitations: The retrospective design cannot establish causation, and the authors note that athleticism or coaching quality could explain both specialization and durability. Classification and injury reporting may be incomplete, minor in-play injuries were not captured, and models were not adjusted for age or other player characteristics. The cohort is male, elite and drafted only, and the authors note that definitions of early specialization vary across the literature. Classification used high school participation only, so specialization before age 14 could not be identified, and the authors note their definition aligns with what other studies call later specialization.
practicalImplications: Youth football programmes and families can use these results to support multisport participation in high school, since the study links it with fewer injuries and longer careers. Staff should not use the result to claim that early football specialization directly causes injury, because the study cannot separate it from athlete and coaching differences.
athleteDev: Performance Application: The findings support encouraging young football players to take part in other sports, since multisport history was linked with longer professional careers and more games played. The study does not measure performance itself.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: The study covers injury incidence and career length in professional players, not rehabilitation or return from a specific injury. It cannot inform return-to-play decisions.

citation: Sejersen C, Volianitis S, Secher NH. The athlete's heart: allometric considerations on published papers and relation to cardiovascular variables. European Journal of Applied Physiology. 2024.
abstract: The authors pooled left ventricular dimensions from published studies of male endurance athletes, weightlifters and untrained controls, scaled to body weight. Left ventricular internal diameter tracked stroke volume, cardiac output and blood volume, while wall thickness did not track these variables.
tldr: Among male athletes, the enlarged chamber size of the heart is linked to stroke volume and blood volume, while wall thickness is not. Heart size comparisons between sports should be scaled to body weight.
methods: The authors searched PubMed to April 2022 and added references from prior papers, and included male athletes aged 18 to 40 in endurance sports and weightlifting, with untrained controls. Left ventricular and atrial dimensions and cardiovascular variables were allometrically scaled to body weight and compared with one-way Welch ANOVA, and correlations were tested with Pearson's r. The authors describe the paper as a narrative review, though a search and pooled analysis were carried out.
findings: The search yielded 150 included studies, with 927 athletes and 173 controls. With scaling to body weight, left ventricular internal diameter was similar in weightlifters and controls and 7% to 15% larger in the other athletic groups, while wall thickness was 9% to 24% larger in all athletes. Internal diameter correlated with stroke volume, oxygen pulse, maximal oxygen uptake, cardiac output and blood volume (r about 0.9), and wall thickness did not correlate with these variables.
limitations: The heart and exercise data often come from different populations, and the cross-sectional measures at rest may not reflect sport-specific values. Posture and movement artefacts limit exercise measurements, disciplines within a sport were not separated, and scaling used group means rather than individual values. The authors describe the paper as a narrative review, but it also pooled data from a described PubMed search.
practicalImplications: When comparing heart dimensions across athletes of different body sizes, scale the values to body weight. The pooled data link a larger chamber diameter to blood volume and stroke volume, while the authors propose, without direct evidence here, that a thicker wall reflects the pressure needed to drive the enlarged chamber.
athleteDev: The paper gives context for the typical group-level heart size pattern across endurance sports and weightlifting in male athletes. The pooled group means are not individual reference norms and should not be used to judge a single athlete's heart.
rtp: The paper studies healthy male athletes and does not address injury, cardiac pathology or return to sport. It cannot be used to clear an athlete for return to sport or to judge cardiac risk.

citation: Iatropoulos S, Dandrieux PE, Navarro L, Blanco D, Edouard P. The Dose-Response Relationship of Exercise-Based Injury Prevention Programmes: Implications for Research and Practice. Sports Medicine. 2025.
abstract: Exercise-based injury prevention programmes need a period of consistent practice before they reduce injury risk. The authors explain the dose-response concept from pharmacology, show that most RCTs analyse injuries from the first day of the programme, and illustrate two statistical approaches that remove early injuries from the analysis.
tldr: Injury prevention programmes take weeks to work, so analysing injuries from day one can hide their effect. Plan start dates well before the period when protection is needed.
methods: Narrative Current Opinion. The authors outline dose-response concepts, screen the sport RCTs in six recent systematic reviews without a systematic search protocol, and re-analyse one earlier athletics RCT using two approaches.
findings: Of 36 screened RCTs, 33 (92%) did not account for dilution, re-injury or interaction effects, and three accounted for dilution only. In the athletics example, the odds ratio for weekly injury prevalence was 0.85 (0.67-1.09) in the primary analysis, 0.75 (0.56-1.01) after excluding the early period, 0.37 (0.25-0.55) with the inclusion approach and 0.28 (0.16-0.48) with the exclusion approach. The authors estimate that about 6 weeks were needed before this programme reached full effect. In the van der Horst Nordic hamstring trial, cited by the authors, the prevalence reduction was 67% for weeks 14-52 but 56% over the full 52 weeks.
limitations: The authors call the approaches promising but untested in other RCTs, and the screen was not systematic. Most worked examples come from a single trial.
practicalImplications: Start a prevention block several weeks before the period it should protect. Do not judge a programme by injuries that occur in its first weeks, and keep athletes on the programme after an early injury.
athleteDev: Start the injury prevention block several weeks before the competition period it is meant to protect, and keep training through an early injury, because the programme is still building its effect. This is a planning point, not a training-adaptation finding.
rtp: Not a return-to-sport study. It does not test rehabilitation, return criteria or re-injury after return, so it cannot set return-to-play timelines; the timing point applies only to prevention programmes.

citation: Lee C, Batomen B, Naidu D, Hoeber S, McCormack R, Steele R, et al. The Effect of Bye Weeks on Injury Event Rates in the Canadian Football League. Clin J Sport Med. 2024.
abstract: Retrospective cohort of CFL regular-season games from 2011 to 2018 testing whether a bye week changes the game injury event rate in the following week. The rate after a bye week did not differ meaningfully from non-bye weeks, and adding more bye weeks did not change that.
tldr: Bye weeks did not lower the CFL game injury rate in the following week or in the two or three weeks after. Recorded injuries rose once practice injuries were included, which the authors suggest reflects players being cleared to return rather than new injury.
methods: Historical cohort using the CFL injury surveillance database and official schedules for the 2011 to 2018 regular seasons, with preseason and playoff games excluded. Game injury incidence rate ratios were estimated with conditional quasi-Poisson regression, adjusted for game number, opponent, home or away, and team-year, with a lagged deviance residual term for autocorrelation.
findings: The primary IRR was 0.96 (0.87 to 1.05), and sensitivity analyses that used only the three pre-bye weeks as controls showed no reduction. Cumulative IRRs were 1.02 for two weeks and 1.00 for three weeks, and results were similar with one, two or three bye weeks. Adding practice injuries, the week-after-bye IRR was 1.14 (1.05 to 1.23), which the authors attribute to medical clearance for pre-existing injuries being recorded as new injuries.
limitations: Injury data were collected for clinical documentation rather than research, and the authors could not evaluate coaching or injury-reporting decisions. Practice exposure was not counted, and the residual time-trend confounding the authors note in their sensitivity analyses means the primary estimate should be read with caution.
practicalImplications: On this evidence, a bye week is not a tool for reducing game injuries in the CFL. Injury charting rules for new versus recurring injuries should be consistent, because the authors say the combined result depends on that distinction.
athleteDev: Bye weeks did not change game injury incidence in this sample, so any performance case for them rests on other effects such as rest and preparation time, which the authors discuss but did not measure. The authors suggest the first practices after a bye could be eased in case of deconditioning, but this was not tested.
rtp: The study does not measure return-to-play timing, re-injury or rehabilitation, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions after a bye week.

citation: Lutsic JJ, Lutsic SE, Ibrahim DS, Augusta MC, Robinson JD, Tong KM, et al. The Effect of Sport Specialization on Injury Risk in NCAA Athletes: Results From the SAFE Consortium. Clin J Sport Med. 2024.
abstract: Retrospective cohort of 211 NCAA athletes who completed a questionnaire on sport specialization and injury history. Highly specialized athletes reported more injuries, more upper and lower extremity injuries and more surgery than low specialized athletes.
tldr: In this NCAA sample, athletes classed as highly specialized reported more injuries, more upper and lower limb injuries and more surgery than low specialized athletes. The data are self-reported and retrospective, so use this as a reason to review training variety, not as proof of cause.
methods: An anonymous questionnaire was completed by collegiate athletes from Division I, II and III schools in the SAFE Consortium during the 2022 to 2023 school year. Specialization was classed low, moderate or high on a 3-point scale (single-sport focus, quitting other sports, year-round training), and injuries were grouped as upper or lower extremity, analyzed with chi-square tests and ANOVA.
findings: Of 211 completers, 157 (74.4%) reported an injury, and highly specialized athletes were more likely than low specialized athletes to report any injury (chi-square 19.81, P<0.0001). High specialization was associated with more upper extremity injuries (chi-square 7.17, P=0.007), lower extremity injuries (chi-square 4.11, P=0.04) and surgery (chi-square 6.76, P=0.009). Moderate specialization was associated with more lower extremity injuries (P=0.03) but not upper extremity injuries (P=0.052), and average days away from sport were 85 for low, 110 for moderate and 112 for high specialization, with no statistical test reported for the days.
limitations: Injuries were self-reported with recall bias, the questionnaire is not fully validated, and athletes reported injuries from both before and after NCAA registration, so the injury history spans youth sport. The abstract reports P<0.0001 for upper and lower extremity injuries, but the Results give P=0.007 and P=0.04; the Results values are reported here. Days away from sport were compared without a reported test, and the design is retrospective and cross-sectional in effect.
practicalImplications: The authors recommend educating athletes, parents and coaches about the link between high specialization and upper and lower extremity injuries, periodizing training and competition, monitoring for overuse signs and encouraging cross-training. These recommendations follow from the association, but this study did not test them.
athleteDev: Highly specialized athletes in this sample reported more injuries and more days away from practice and competition, so training variety and planned rest are reasonable topics for athlete development plans. The study does not show how much specialization is safe, or whether cross-training reduces risk.
rtp: Days away from sport were longer for highly specialized athletes (112 versus 85 days), but these are self-reported durations with no reported statistical test, and the study does not follow injured athletes through rehabilitation, so it cannot set return-to-play timelines.

citation: Kraeutler MJ, Belk JW, McCarty EC. The Effect of the Number of Carries on Injury Risk and Subsequent Season's Performance Among Running Backs in the National Football League. Orthop J Sports Med. 2017;5(2):2325967117691941.
abstract: Retrospective cohort of 275 NFL running back player-seasons from 2004 to 2014, comparing players with 150 to 250 carries and players with 300 or more carries. Players with fewer carries missed more games to injury the following season, and yards per carry did not differ significantly between groups.
tldr: High-carry running backs in this NFL sample did not show more injury or lower yards per carry the following season, and they missed fewer games than moderate-carry backs. Carry totals alone should not be used to predict next-season injury risk for running backs.
methods: ESPN NFL statistics and team injury reports were used for running backs with 150 to 250 carries (group A) or 300 or more carries (group B) in each regular season from 2004 to 2014; players with 251 to 299 carries were excluded. Changes between seasons within each group were tested with matched-pair t tests, between-group differences with t tests, and missed-game categories with chi-square tests.
findings: Group A missed more games in the season of interest (1.86 vs 0.19) and in the following season (3.27 vs 1.89), and a higher share of group A missed at least one game the next season (66% vs 49%, P=0.016). Yards per carry did not differ between groups in the preceding season (P=0.073) or the next season (P=0.24), and carries fell in both groups the next season. Overall, 62% of the running backs missed at least one game the next season, with concussion the most common cause of missed time.
limitations: The study is retrospective and depends on the accuracy of NFL game summaries and injury reports, and some players appear in more than one season, so the 275 player-seasons come from about 128 different players. Play-call distribution, offensive philosophy, line performance, opponent quality and weather were not controlled, and short receptions that count as running plays were not captured. The authors also note that yards per carry may be a weak measure of running back performance.
practicalImplications: Carry totals alone did not predict next-season injury or yards per carry in this sample, so workload decisions for running backs should use more than carry counts. According to the authors, running backs as a group had high missed-time rates regardless of carry totals.
athleteDev: For performance planning, carry volume did not explain next-season missed games or yards per carry in this sample, so carry counts should not be the sole basis for a running back's load plan. Carry totals fell for both groups the next season, partly because of rookies and multi-back offenses, the authors suggest, which limits what carry data can say about workload.
rtp: The study counts games missed in a season, not rehabilitation time or return to play after a specific injury, so it cannot set return-to-play timing for running backs.

citation: Mulcahey MK, Bernhardson AS, Murphy CP, Chang A, Zajac T, Sanchez G, et al. The Epidemiology of Ankle Injuries Identified at the National Football League Combine, 2009-2015. Orthop J Sports Med. 2018;6(7):2325967118786227.
abstract: Retrospective chart review of ankle injuries in 2,285 players at the 2009 to 2015 NFL Combine. Over half had a history of ankle injury, sprains were the most common type, and the proportion with injury varied by position, highest in running backs, offensive linemen and tight ends.
tldr: Over half of invited NFL Combine players had a past ankle injury, mostly sprains, and running backs, linemen and tight ends had the highest proportions. Use these as prevalence figures for history-taking and clinical awareness, not as injury rates.
methods: Charts of all 2,285 combine participants were reviewed for history, examination findings, radiographs and MRI, with ankle imaging performed in players who reported an ankle injury or had consistent findings. Injury types, locations, osteoarthritis and surgery were tabulated as simple percentages, and position-level injury percentages used all combine players at each position as the denominator (the column totals sum to 2,285, although the table labels them 'with imaging').
findings: Of 1,216 players (53.2%) with an ankle injury, 229 had injuries to both ankles, giving 1,445 injured ankles; sprains were 86.0% of these, and 137 ankle fractures were identified. Among players with radiographs, 611 (50.6%) had ankle osteoarthritis, and cartilage lesions were found on MRI in 69 of the 257 ankles imaged. Running backs (61.9%), offensive linemen (60.3%) and tight ends (59.4%) had the highest proportions with any ankle injury, while kickers (23.3%) and long snappers (37.5%) had the lowest.
limitations: The study is retrospective, and imaging was done only for players with a history or findings, so MRI findings come from about 10% of players. Injury timing was unclear, so acute and remote injuries are mixed, and exposure was not recorded, so injury rates cannot be compared directly with other sports. Physical examination data were incompletely reported, and surgical indications were not recorded.
practicalImplications: Clinicians evaluating football players should check ankle history, sprain type and early osteoarthritis, because these were common in this group. The authors call for prospective work on how prior injuries affect career length, so this paper alone does not justify a position-specific ankle program.
athleteDev: Prior ankle injury was common in this draft-eligible group and varied by position, so position-aware ankle history is a reasonable starting point for performance and medical planning. The study cannot say whether these injuries affect playing career or performance.
rtp: The study describes injury types and surgery use at the combine, not time to return to play or outcomes, so it cannot set return-to-play timelines for ankle injuries.

citation: Carver TJ, Schrock JB, Kraeutler MJ, McCarty EC. The Evolving Treatment Patterns of NCAA Division I Football Players by Orthopaedic Team Physicians Over the Past Decade, 2008-2016. Sports Health. 2018.
abstract: Survey of NCAA Division I head orthopaedic team physicians in 2008 and 2016 to 2017 on how they treat common football injuries. Preferences changed for ACL graft choice, shoulder stabilization, PCL reconstruction and pregame Toradol use, and physicians became more conservative about ACL return to play.
tldr: Team physicians in NCAA Division I football moved toward patellar tendon grafts, arthroscopic shoulder stabilization and arthroscopic single-bundle PCL reconstruction, and away from pregame Toradol. Use these results as a picture of current practice, since they are opinions rather than outcomes.
methods: The head orthopaedic team physician for each NCAA Division I football team was asked to complete a survey on experience, team coverage and treatment preference for common injuries, sent in 2008 and again between April 2016 and April 2017. Responses were compared with chi-square tests, with P less than 0.05 treated as significant.
findings: Patellar tendon autograft was preferred for ACL reconstruction by 83% in 2016 (67% in 2008), and arthroscopic anterior shoulder stabilization rose from 69% to 93%. Arthroscopic single-bundle PCL reconstruction was preferred by 83% (49% in 2008), and pregame Toradol use fell from 62% to 26%. Physicians also became more conservative on ACL return to play: 51% required 7 months or longer in 2016, compared with 70% who allowed return by 6 months in 2008.
limitations: The results reflect expert opinion rather than clinical outcomes, which the authors name as the main limitation. Response rates were 93% and 90%, and the two surveys were compared across different periods with chi-square tests, so changes in the respondent group could contribute to the differences.
practicalImplications: The authors note that treatment patterns shift over time, so older protocols may need checking against current practice. They attribute the decline in pregame Toradol use partly to NFL Physician Society task force recommendations, though they did not test that link.
athleteDev: The paper has little direct training content. Its relevance for performance staff is that more physicians now clear players after ACL reconstruction at 7 months or longer, which affects how training and competition loads are planned for those players.
rtp: The study reports physicians' preferred return-to-play timelines after ACL reconstruction, shoulder stabilization and fifth metatarsal fixation, but these are opinions and do not show that the timelines are safe or effective. Use it to describe current practice, not to set an individual athlete's clearance criteria.

citation: Anthis M, Gourd S, Kim B, Ruddy JD, Whiteley R, Timmins R, et al. The Fragility Index of Risk Factors for Hamstring Injuries. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther. 2024;54(10):672-678.
abstract: Objective: to determine the Fragility Index of hamstring injury risk factors, defined as the minimum number of participants who would need to change classification to make a risk factor statistically non-significant. Design: retrospective secondary data analysis. Methods: studies with 2x2 contingency data for hamstring injury risk factors were recalculated, moving one injured high-risk athlete at a time to the non-injured high-risk group until relative risk was no longer significant. Results: the median Fragility Index was 3 (Q1-Q3 2-6) for all significant risk factors, 3 (2-5) for modifiable and 3 (2-6) for nonmodifiable factors. Conclusion: most statistically significant hamstring injury risk factors are fragile associations.
tldr: Most statistically significant hamstring injury risk factors are fragile: moving about 3 injured high-risk athletes would often remove significance. Treat a single significant factor as preliminary and check the number of injuries behind it before acting.
methods: Systematic searches of eight databases (January 2019 to October 2022) and the 78 articles of a prior hamstring risk-factor review were screened. Forty-one studies with extractable 2x2 data were included, and relative risk with 95% CI was recalculated. Each significant factor was shifted one athlete at a time from the true-positive to the false-positive count until the lower CI reached 1. Risk of bias was rated with QUIPS.
findings: The median Fragility Index across 63 significant factors (of 262 variables reported) was 3 (Q1-Q3 2-6). Modifiable and nonmodifiable factors had medians of 3 (2-5) and 3 (2-6). Prior hamstring injury had a median of 4 (2-7.5) across 12 significant reports, and eccentric strength a median of 3.5 (2.75-4.25) across 8. These are counts of reclassified athletes, not effect sizes.
limitations: Only significant factors were analysed, which may overstate fragility for factors chosen for significance. The Fragility Index was designed for balanced trials and was applied to imbalanced observational data, and continuous variables were split at study-specific cut points. The abstract states that over 35% of all included risk factors had a Fragility Index of 2 or less, whereas the Discussion gives one third of significant risk factors; the Discussion figure is reported here. The corresponding author has financial ties to NordBord (VALD), and studies using that device were included.
practicalImplications: Before acting on a significant hamstring risk factor, check how many athletes would need to change status to remove the result. Where acting is cheap, a fragile finding can still justify a cautious response; where costs are high, wait for replication. Research reports should give the Fragility Index alongside sample size and injury counts.
athleteDev: A single significant hamstring risk factor, such as low eccentric strength or prior hamstring injury, is often fragile, so use it as a prompt to screen rather than a firm training target. Apply the same caution to any factor drawn from a small sample with few injuries.
rtp: It does not address return to sport. The studies concern who gets hamstring injuries, so the results cannot guide return-to-play timing, clearance or decisions after a current injury.

citation: Baar K. Stress relaxation and targeted nutrition to treat patellar tendinopathy. International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism. 2018 (accepted manuscript; volume and pages not printed).
abstract: Describes the rehabilitation of a professional basketball player with MRI-confirmed central core patellar tendinopathy, treated with gelatin ingestion and heavy isometric loading over 18 months. MRI improved, pain decreased, and performance improved; the author concludes the combined program can improve clinical outcomes in elite athletes.
tldr: In one elite basketball player, an 18-month program of isometric stress-relaxation loading with pre-load gelatin was followed by normalized MRI, less pain and large strength gains. This is a single uncontrolled case that supports trying the approach, not proving it works.
methods: Single-case study of one professional male basketball player (21 years old at first MRI). Twice-weekly mid-range isometric holds of 10 to 30 seconds at more than 80% 1RM (leg extension, leg press, Spanish squat), with 15 g gelatin and about 225 mg vitamin C taken one hour before loading. Follow-up MRIs were taken 15 months after the initial scan (about 12 months into the program) and 6 months later (about 18 months into the program), with the final images judged by a blinded orthopedic surgeon; the initial MRI was done on a different machine, and isometric strength was measured on an isokinetic dynamometer. Compliance was reported above 95% in season.
findings: MRI reactivity at the inferior pole of the patella decreased progressively and the surgeon declared the tendon normal at the final scan. The proximal tendon diameter fell from 10.8 mm to 8.16 mm (about 25%) and the mid-tendon diameter rose from 5.74 mm to 6.29 mm. Self-reported pain and tenderness decreased, and single-leg isometric strength increased by 196% (hamstring), 156% (leg extension) and 187.5% (leg press) across the program. Body mass fell 2.5 kg and lean mass fell slightly (75.6 kg to 74.7 kg) while body fat fell from 8.4% to 5.9%.
limitations: With one athlete and no control group, the cause of the change cannot be isolated from the gelatin, the loading, or natural healing. The abstract states that performance improved, but apart from isometric strength the results report no performance measure, so on-court performance claims are not supported by data in the text. Pain was self-reported, and the baseline MRI was taken on a different scanner from the follow-ups. Collagen synthesis was not measured, and the team-wide injury reduction was not quantified.
practicalImplications: For an elite athlete with chronic central core patellar tendinopathy, the author's program (progressive heavy isometric holds twice weekly plus 15 g gelatin with vitamin C an hour before loading) was followed by normal-appearing MRI and less pain in one case. Staff can consider it as one part of a supervised rehab plan, with MRI and pain tracked over time.
athleteDev: Performance Application: The paper gives a loading and nutrition template for keeping a tendon-affected athlete in strength work. It shows strength gains in one player across the program, but it does not show that the approach improves performance on court.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: The player kept competing during the program (more than 50 games per season, averaging more than 20 minutes) and was pain free at the final scan while playing more than 25 minutes a game, but the paper does not report when he returned to play or compare recovery time with other treatment. It cannot be used to set a return-to-play timeline or to guarantee tendon recovery in other athletes.

citation: Farooq H, Garbis NG, Moossighi R, Lam R, Cho E, Salazar DH. Surgically Treated Pectoralis Major Tears Impact the Play and Performance of National Football League Athletes. Arthroscopy, Sports Medicine, and Rehabilitation. 2022:e1-e6.
abstract: This descriptive epidemiologic study reviewed NFL players with surgically treated pectoralis major tears to assess return-to-play rate and changes in performance. Of 24 players, 20 (83%) returned to play, and performance scores fell significantly across the cohort, but not after stratifying by position or draft round.
tldr: Most NFL players (20 of 24) with surgically repaired pectoralis major tears returned to play, after a mean of about 302 days. Average performance scores fell after return, but the drop was not significant within position or draft-round groups.
methods: A descriptive epidemiologic study of NFL players from 1933 to 2013, using a public transactions archive to find pectoralis major tears that were treated surgically. Two blinded investigators confirmed the cases, and performance scores based on a previously published calculation were compared before and after injury using paired-samples t tests.
findings: Twenty-four players with surgically repaired tears were included, and 20 (83%) returned to play, with a mean return-to-play period of 302 days (SD 128). Across the 20 players, the mean performance score fell from 299.26 to 127.94 (difference 171.33, 95% CI 15.74 to 326.91, P = .033). The decrease was not significant in the defensive (P = .064), offensive (P = .366), round 1 or 2 (P = .075) or round 3 or later (P = .264) subgroups. No player returned in the same season as injury, and all four players who did not return played defensive positions.
limitations: The authors note low incidence and small numbers, which limit statistical power, and that the public database gives little information on tear severity, mechanism, concomitant injuries or operative technique. Findings may not apply to collegiate, high school or recreational athletes, and some tears may have been missed. The study has no control group and no adjustment for confounders.
practicalImplications: Staff can use these figures to set realistic expectations for NFL players after surgical repair of a pectoralis major tear, with about 83% returning and a mean of about 10 months away. The study does not identify factors that predict an individual's outcome.
athleteDev: Performance Application: the study shows a group-level drop in performance score after return, but the drop was not significant within position or draft-round groups. It does not provide training or load guidance for rebuilding performance.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: the study supports expecting most NFL players to return after surgical repair, with a mean of 302 days to play. It cannot be used for an individual clearance decision, because it has no measure of injury severity, operative technique or functional testing criteria.

citation: Mitchell A, Holding C. The management of a professional footballer recovering from a surgical repair of the proximal adductor longus tendon through a return-to-performance pathway. A case report. Research in Sports Medicine. 2024.
abstract: A 23-year-old professional footballer had a rupture of the proximal adductor longus tendon, was treated with surgical reattachment, and completed an eleven-phase return-to-performance pathway that combined clinical, performance and sport-specific criteria. The player returned to competitive play 12 weeks after surgery. The authors describe the shared decision-making process used by the interdisciplinary team.
tldr: A single professional footballer returned to competitive play at 12 weeks after surgical adductor longus reattachment using a phase-gated, criteria-based pathway. The case shows how the criteria were sequenced, but it cannot show what typical recovery looks like.
methods: Single-case clinical report. The player was managed through three gym phases and six grass phases, with progression gated by pain (2/10 or less), a confidence rating (80% or more), and objective measures such as adductor squeeze, hip range of motion, hop tests, force plate jumps, and GPS-monitored running loads.
findings: At weeks 6.5 to 7, adductor squeeze and hip range of motion were within 10% of pre-injury values, while plyometric and hop measures needed only 80% of pre-injury values, and running began at week 7. In grass phase 3 he reached 94% of peak speed, 96% of peak acceleration intensity and 84% of peak deceleration intensity. He completed a 45-minute U23 match at 12 weeks and joined the regular match schedule from week 14.
limitations: One player with no comparison group, so the pathway's effect cannot be separated from the player's own recovery. The abstract states return to competitive play at 12 weeks, while the body describes a U23 match at 12 weeks and full match play from week 14. Figure 2 and Table 1 values are not reproduced in the extracted text, and the adductor strength thresholds were taken from earlier published studies rather than tested here.
practicalImplications: Staff managing a surgical adductor longus repair can use this phase structure as a worked example of gating progression on pain, confidence and objective profiling. The case does not justify fixed return dates; the timeline came from one player's responses at each gate.
athleteDev: The pathway sequenced gym-based profiling (hop battery, force plate jumps, adductor and abductor strength) alongside GPS-limited running, acceleration and kicking progressions. Kicking distance rose from 2 m to 10 m in grass phase 1 and to 40 m in grass phase 2, alongside high-speed running and agility work.
rtp: This case describes one professional footballer's return after surgical adductor longus reattachment, with a U23 match at 12 weeks and full match play from week 14. It cannot establish expected return times for other players, other repair types, or other clubs, and it cannot show that the pathway caused the outcome.

citation: Tears C, Rae G, Hide G, Sinha R, Franklin J, Brand P, et al. The British Athletics Muscle Injury Classification grading system as a predictor of return to play following hamstrings injury in professional football players. Physical Therapy in Sport. 2022.
abstract: The authors compared the British Athletics Muscle Injury Classification (BAMIC) grade, oedema length and cross-sectional area on MRI with return to play after primary hamstring strain in 39 professional footballers. BAMIC grade had a weak but significant correlation with return to play, and BAMIC and Peetron's grading agreed only slightly.
tldr: The BAMIC grade on MRI is weakly linked to how long a professional footballer takes to return to play after a hamstring strain. It agrees only slightly with Peetron's grading, so it should be one input among several.
methods: Retrospective cohort at one professional English club, 2010 to 2019, with male players who had an MRI within 7 days of a primary hamstring strain. Two musculoskeletal radiologists graded the scans, and Pearson correlations and multiple regression were used to relate the grades and MRI measures to return to play, with kappa for agreement between the two grading systems.
findings: Among 39 injuries, BAMIC grade correlated weakly with return to play (r = 0.32, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.58, p = 0.05). Oedema length was weakly correlated (r = 0.3, p = 0.06) and cross-sectional area was not (r = 0.02, p = 0.91). The multiple regression explained 16% of the variance in return to play, and kappa for BAMIC against Peetron's was 0.21 (95% CI 0 to 0.42).
limitations: Only one club was studied, so the sample is small and the regression results are unstable. The authors acknowledge that the lack of significance for cross-sectional area and oedema length may reflect sample size, and call for larger replication. The retrospective design relies on historical MRI and medical records. The multiple regression model was not statistically significant (F p = 0.1), and the single-predictor BAMIC model explained only 10% of the variance, so the 16% figure is the multivariable model and it is not a significant fit.
practicalImplications: Grade hamstring strains with BAMIC alongside clinical findings and use the grade as a rough guide to return to play timing. Do not rely on oedema length or cross-sectional area as predictors, and expect weak prediction for individual players.
athleteDev: Not applicable. The paper studies injured players' return to play after a hamstring strain and does not address performance training.
rtp: Use BAMIC grading from the first MRI, within 7 days of onset, as one input to return-to-play planning for hamstring strains in professional football. The grade has only weak predictive value, so it should not be used alone to set a return date.

citation: Niering M, Seifert J. The Impact of Daylight Exposure on Injured Athletes: Implications for Rehabilitation. International Journal of Strength and Conditioning. 2024.
abstract: During injury rehabilitation and return to competition, factors such as psychological parameters, sleep quality and vitamin D levels affect outcomes. The authors review existing research and theory on daylight effects on athletes in rehabilitation, organised into sun-induced vitamin D synthesis, cognitive-behavioural processes, the circadian mechanism and visual processing of light. They propose a low-cost artificial daylight intervention that could accompany injury therapy in clinics and clubs.
tldr: Daylight may be a cheap add-on to injury rehabilitation, but no study has tested it in injured athletes. The supporting evidence comes from healthy or non-athlete samples, small studies and animal work, so treat the proposed light timing as a hypothesis to trial.
methods: Narrative review. PubMed, PsycINFO and Google Scholar were searched for records from 1 January 1960 to 20 October 2023, in German or English, using combined terms for daylight, sunlight or light with sports injury and injury rehabilitation terms. No criteria on study design, population or quality were applied. Reference lists of included studies were searched manually.
findings: No study has examined daylight exposure directly on the prevalence or rehabilitation of sports injuries. Related findings include: in high-performance athletes, 10 days of winter sunlight nearly matched a 6-week regimen of 6000 IU/day vitamin D for raising serum 25(OH)D and testosterone (Michalczyk et al. 2020); in two groups of ten male athletes, light exposure timed to the circadian rhythm had large effects on sleep duration after long-haul travel compared with no intervention, with small to moderate effects on jump and sprint measures (Fowler et al. 2021); and in non-athletes, artificial sunlight and vitamin D supplementation both raised 25(OH)D without a change in athletic performance (Carswell et al. 2018).
limitations: Not a systematic search, and no quality appraisal of included studies. Most evidence comes from non-athletes, animal models or very small samples (the cited studies of daylight and sleep in clinical populations had one to 20 participants). The authors note that most vitamin D and testosterone work has been done in males, so no conclusions can be drawn for females. The Table 1 effects come from studies that were not of injured athletes in rehabilitation, and the proposed protocol has not been evaluated.
practicalImplications: Daylight could be a low-cost adjunct, but the evidence is indirect. If it is tried, the authors propose timing sessions by chronotype (morning types 2 to 4 hours after waking, evening types after sunset, with sessions finished about three hours before bed), a dawn simulation device for 30 minutes before waking, a daylight LED for 30 minutes after waking, and group sessions. These are proposals and should be tracked for sleep, mood and rehabilitation progress.
athleteDev: Light timing is worth a small pilot rather than adoption as a performance tool. Evidence for better sleep and jump or sprint measures after circadian-timed light comes from one small study of male athletes, and vitamin D findings differed between athletes and non-athletes, so keep it alongside routine sleep and nutrition care and record sleep and performance if it is trialled.
rtp: It cannot show that daylight or light therapy shortens rehabilitation or speeds return to competition. The authors' suggestion that the approach could reduce injury duration is a hypothesis, not a finding of the review.

citation: Fisher SR, Rigby JH, Mettler JA, McCurdy KW. The Effectiveness of Photobiomodulation Therapy Versus Cryotherapy for Skeletal Muscle Recovery: A Critically Appraised Topic. J Sport Rehabil. 2019;28(5):526-531.
abstract: Critically appraised topic of five studies comparing photobiomodulation therapy (PBMT) with cryotherapy for muscle recovery after strenuous exercise. All five favoured PBMT, and the authors rate the evidence as grade B.
tldr: After hard exercise, photobiomodulation looked better than cryotherapy for muscle damage markers, soreness and muscle performance in this appraisal. The human evidence is three small trials, so treat PBMT as a promising option rather than a settled replacement for cryotherapy.
methods: The authors searched MEDLINE and SPORTDiscus and hand-searched reference lists for studies of level 2 evidence or higher that directly compared PBMT with cryotherapy after exercise. Five studies met the criteria, and the three human trials were scored on the PEDro scale (scores of 7 to 9).
findings: In the human trials, PBMT improved strength (maximal voluntary contraction) recovery and reduced soreness and creatine kinase relative to placebo over roughly 24 to 96 hours, while cryotherapy alone was not different from placebo, which the authors read as PBMT outperforming cryotherapy. In the futsal trial, LED therapy lowered creatine kinase and blood lactate from post-exercise values but peak and mean Wingate power did not differ between groups. In the rat studies, LED therapy produced less muscle damage and inflammation than cold-water immersion or passive recovery.
limitations: Two of the five studies are rat studies, so their results do not transfer directly to humans, and the authors call for more unbiased in vivo human research. Most human comparisons were each treatment against placebo rather than direct PBMT versus cryotherapy tests. All studies used low-powered PBMT devices, and treatment parameters varied, which the authors say may affect outcomes.
practicalImplications: The authors suggest PBMT can be considered in place of cryotherapy after exercise for muscle recovery, with the main gains in soreness and performance recovery. They also note that cryotherapy showed little benefit over placebo in these studies, and that more human research is needed before firm clinical recommendations.
athleteDev: The evidence concerns recovery between training or competition bouts, where PBMT was linked to faster return of muscle torque and lower soreness than placebo, while cryotherapy was not. It does not show that PBMT improves performance during a session, and the human samples were untrained men, men of unstated training status, or six professional futsal players.
rtp: The studies measured muscle damage, soreness and torque after exercise bouts rather than after injury, so this appraisal cannot inform rehabilitation or return to sport.

citation: Broatch JR, Petersen A, Bishop DJ. The Influence of Post-Exercise Cold-Water Immersion on Adaptive Responses to Exercise: A Review of the Literature. Sports Med. 2018.
abstract: Post-exercise cold-water immersion (CWI) is widely used to reduce fatigue and speed recovery between sessions, but reports suggest it may attenuate long-term adaptations. This review examines the molecular mechanisms by which CWI may alter signalling and adaptation in human skeletal muscle, focusing on mitochondrial biogenesis and muscle protein turnover. Single sessions of CWI may increase markers of mitochondrial biogenesis in the short term, but regular CWI has little to no effect on endurance adaptations, and evidence for resistance training suggests either no effect or a negative effect on strength and muscle mass.
tldr: Cold-water immersion after exercise can raise short-term markers of mitochondrial biogenesis, but regular use has little effect on endurance adaptations and may blunt strength and muscle gains after resistance training. There is no adaptation-based reason to add routine CWI, and some reason for caution in strength or hypertrophy blocks.
methods: Narrative review. A Scopus search using the keywords cold, skeletal muscle and exercise covered abstracts from 1963 to December 2017, and reference lists of included articles were searched. Articles were included if they addressed molecular mechanisms by which cold given during or after exercise alters skeletal muscle responses, including intracellular signalling, gene transcription and protein translation related to mitochondrial biogenesis and protein turnover.
findings: After a single endurance session, CWI increased PGC-1a mRNA in the cooled limb (up to about 9-fold), but two studies found no change in PGC-1a protein content up to 3 hours after exercise. Regular CWI during endurance training (3 to 6 weeks) had negligible or slightly beneficial effects on cycling performance in several studies, while one study using colder immersion (5 degrees C) found attenuated endurance and maximal oxygen uptake. Regular CWI during resistance training attenuated strength and muscle mass gains in some studies (including Roberts et al., 21 men, 12 weeks), but had no detrimental effect in others.
limitations: Many included studies immersed only one limb, used a single exercise or lower-body training only, and trained at 2 to 3 sessions per week, below the load of many athletes. Results differ between studies with similar protocols, and the authors note that some proposed mechanisms are speculative and unverified. Some cited molecular work is limited to small human samples and animal models, and the review was not systematic.
practicalImplications: Where the goal is endurance mitochondrial adaptation, the review gives no reason to add CWI to training. Where the goal is strength or muscle mass after resistance training, it gives no reason to add CWI and some reason for caution. Whether CWI changes adaptation when recovery between closely spaced sessions is limited has not been tested, so the review cannot settle that case.
athleteDev: Avoid making cold immersion a routine after every strength session, since some studies show blunted strength or muscle gains. The review found no study showing that regular CWI improves strength or muscle mass, and no conclusive evidence that it increases mitochondrial content or function.
rtp: It does not address return to sport or rehabilitation. The studies concern healthy exercisers' training adaptations; the review's background statement that CWI may reduce soft-tissue injury effects is not tested by the included evidence, so it cannot guide rehabilitation or return-to-play decisions.

citation: Greif DN, Emerson CP, Allegra P, Arizpe A, Mansour KL, Cade WH II, et al. Supplement Use in Patients Undergoing Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction: A Systematic Review. Arthroscopy: The Journal of Arthroscopic and Related Surgery. 2020.
abstract: This PRISMA systematic review asked whether a standardized dietary supplement can reduce post-operative muscle atrophy or improve rehabilitation after ACL reconstruction. Ten randomized trials were included, and protein or amino acid supplementation was the only type with potentially beneficial results.
tldr: Protein or amino acid supplements showed the most promising results for muscle recovery after ACL reconstruction, but the trials are small and of low quality. No specific protein protocol can be recommended, and creatine, vitamin C and E, and testosterone did not show benefit.
methods: Two reviewers searched MEDLINE, Scopus and the Cochrane Library in July 2019 following PRISMA. Only English-language randomized controlled trials of protein, amino acid, vitamin, hormone or other supplements in ACL reconstruction were included, and risk of bias was rated with the Cochrane tool.
findings: Among four protein or amino acid trials (177 patients), two reported significant advantages over placebo in isokinetic strength or in the number of rehabilitation sessions needed to reach benchmarks, two reported greater thigh hypertrophy, and one (Vidriero et al.) reported improved IKDC scores and less analgesic use; Holm et al.'s muscle biopsies showed no difference and the glucosamine trial found no benefit. One creatine trial (60 patients) found no between-group differences. Vitamin C and E trials found no benefit on serum cytokines or strength, peak isometric force was greater with placebo at three months, and biopsies showed more inflammatory cell infiltration in the vitamin group. One testosterone trial in six men found greater total lean mass at six weeks only, with no difference in injured-leg strength or clinical scores at any time point.
limitations: The review is limited by the small number of eligible trials, heterogeneity in supplements, doses, timing and outcomes, and a low overall quality of evidence. The population is ACL reconstruction patients rather than athletes in general, and the authors state the findings cannot be generalized to other knee sports procedures. Only one group's cohort was used across three vitamin trials, and the protein trial by Eraslan and Ulkar started supplements six weeks after surgery.
practicalImplications: Protein or amino acid supplementation may be considered as an adjunct to ACL rehabilitation, but this review does not identify a dose, timing or product. Creatine, vitamin C and E, and testosterone should not be expected to reduce post-operative atrophy on current evidence.
athleteDev: Performance Application: the trials enrolled ACL reconstruction patients rather than healthy athletes, so they cannot set a performance supplement protocol. The protein findings concern regaining quadriceps size and strength after surgery.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: the protein trials report faster rehabilitation benchmark achievement and some strength gains, which may inform rehab planning. The review does not show that any supplement shortens time to return to sport or lowers re-injury risk, so it cannot support a return-to-play decision.

citation: Miller KC, McDermott BP, Yeargin SW. Sweat Characteristics of Cramp-Prone and Cramp-Resistant Athletes. International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism. 2020 (ahead of print).
abstract: This multicenter cross-sectional study compared sweat rates and sweat electrolyte concentrations and content in 350 collegiate athletes with and without a history of exercise-associated muscle cramps. Within each sex, the groups did not differ, and sweat variables predicted cramp history only in American football.
tldr: Sweat rate and sweat electrolyte losses did not differ between college athletes with and without a cramp history in most sports, so fluid and electrolyte losses alone do not appear to explain cramps for most athletes. Heavy sweaters in American football may warrant individual hydration and electrolyte monitoring.
methods: Division I athletes from 11 sports completed one habitual practice or conditioning session. Sweat rate was calculated from pre- and post-exercise body mass corrected for fluid intake, and posterior forearm sweat patches were analysed for sodium, potassium and chloride. Crampers and non-crampers were compared by sex with two-way ANOVA, and ROC analysis with cut points tested which sweat variables predicted cramp history, with P < .01 as the significance threshold.
findings: Within each sex, no differences in sweat rate or sweat sodium, potassium or chloride concentration or content were found between crampers and non-crampers; female potassium content showed P = .03, which did not meet the study's P < .01 threshold. In American football, sweat rate and sodium, potassium and chloride content predicted cramp history (AUC 0.65-0.72, P <= .005); the authors also report that a sweat rate per body surface area above 0.75 L per hour per m2 carried about six times the odds of being cramp-prone, although that variable's AUC (0.62, P = .02) did not reach significance. With American football removed, no sweat variable predicted cramp history, and males lost more sweat and electrolytes than females.
limitations: Cramp history was self-reported, and the authors did not separate local from whole-body cramps. Field conditions could not control hydration status, fluid type or duration, and sweat patches collected primary sweat that may overstate concentrations. No athlete cramped during testing, about 71% of football data came from off-season conditioning, and the authors note possible type II errors; the sixfold odds figure for sweat rate per body surface area comes from a variable whose AUC was not significant (Table 5).
practicalImplications: Heavy-sweating American football players may benefit from individual sweat-rate monitoring, with electrolyte or fluid replacement considered for them. For most athletes, the study does not support routine fluid or electrolyte loading to prevent cramps, because over-drinking carries a risk of hyponatremia.
athleteDev: Performance Application: the study suggests sweat rate and sweat electrolyte losses vary widely by sex and sport, so hydration plans should be individualized rather than one size fits all. It does not test whether fluid or electrolyte interventions improve performance.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: the study does not address return to sport after injury, because athletes were excluded if they had injuries and none cramped during testing. It cannot be used to guide cramp management during return to play.

citation: Burke LM, Hawley JA. Swifter, higher, stronger: What's on the menu? Science. 2018;362(6416):781-787.
abstract: This review examines the nutritional approaches used to support elite athletic performance, including fuel use, periodized training nutrition, competition fueling and supplements. The authors argue that sports nutrition should reflect the specific demands of each sport and the periodization of training rather than a single athletic diet.
tldr: Sports nutrition should be matched to the demands of each sport and each training session, not a single athletic diet. Carbohydrate availability, periodized train-low sessions and a small set of supplements with good evidence form the core of the approach.
methods: A narrative review in Science, with no described systematic search or inclusion criteria. The authors discuss published research and examples from elite athletes, including their own work, and frame the evidence with a hierarchy of study designs.
findings: Carbohydrate is the main fuel for most sports, and daily carbohydrate intake typically varies from about 2 to 12 g per kg body mass across training cycles. Train-low sessions augment cellular responses, but translation to performance has been less clear: early studies failed to detect superior performance, while better integration of train-low and train-high sessions has been linked to superior performance in subelite populations. Competition guidance cites carbohydrate intakes of 30-60 g per hour for events up to 2-3 hours and 60-90 g per hour for ultra-endurance events. The review notes that few supplements have robust evidence, citing caffeine, creatine, bicarbonate, beta-alanine and nitrate, and that some interventions, such as beetroot juice, appear less effective in elite competitors.
limitations: As a narrative review, the article does not use a systematic search, so evidence selection cannot be verified. The authors state that most research participants are sub-elite, often male, and that studies with elite athletes are underpowered or rare. The authors receive funding and honoraria from sports nutrition and food industry partners, which they disclose.
practicalImplications: Staff can match carbohydrate, protein and fluid plans to the demands of each session and event rather than applying one diet. Train-low sessions are best treated as a targeted tool within a periodized plan, because their translation to performance has been less clear than their effect on cellular responses.
athleteDev: Performance Application: the review supports periodizing carbohydrate and protein around training sessions and planning event fueling, including gut training and mouth rinsing. It also notes that many supplements lack robust evidence and that the performance benefit of train-low strategies is less clear than their cellular effects.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: the review does not address injury rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot be used to guide return-to-play decisions.

citation: Bonilla DA, Pérez-Idárraga A, Odriozola-Martínez A, Kreider RB. The 4R's Framework of Nutritional Strategies for Post-Exercise Recovery: A Review with Emphasis on New Generation of Carbohydrates. Int. J. Environ. Res. Public Health. 2021;18:103.
abstract: The review summarises nutritional strategies for post-exercise recovery and proposes a 4R framework (Rehydrate, Refuel, Repair, Rest). It discusses new carbohydrate formulations, which the authors say need further research.
tldr: Nutrition after training can be organised as four steps: rehydrate, refuel, repair and rest. The authors favour carbohydrate plus protein for refuelling and cite creatine and pre-sleep casein as helpful, but they also note that adding protein does not raise glycogen synthesis when carbohydrate intake is sufficient, and newer bioengineered carbohydrates still need more research.
methods: Review using a database search of ScienceDirect, PubMed/MEDLINE and Google Scholar with the string 'nutrition AND (exercise recovery OR sports recovery)', plus hand-searching, which returned 1816 records screened by article type, text availability and suitability. English papers from 2010 onward were prioritised, and papers not analysing recovery, abstracts without full text, and studies of performance- and image-enhancing drugs were excluded.
findings: The authors recommend at least 150% of body weight lost to be replaced after exercise, with sodium if faster replacement is needed. For refuelling, they describe carbohydrate and protein together as a good strategy to replenish glycogen while supporting repair, at multiple intervals after exercise. For repair, they cite high-quality protein and creatine monohydrate, with tart cherry, beetroot juice and possibly ashwagandha as possible aids. For rest, they cite pre-sleep casein as effective for muscle adaptation during resistance training, with more research needed in endurance athletes. No pooled effect sizes are reported.
limitations: Screening criteria are loose (article type, text availability, suitability), and no risk-of-bias appraisal or sample-level results are reported. Several recommendations are drawn from studies the authors describe as heterogeneous, and the evidence for newer carbohydrates and for endurance athletes is limited. Two authors declare ties to supplement companies, including the Creapure creatine advisory board.
practicalImplications: Use the 4R framework as a structure for post-training nutrition planning, adjusting fluid, carbohydrate, protein and sleep choices to the sport, the time to the next session and the athlete. Do not apply the specific rehydration volume or supplement suggestions as fixed prescriptions, since the authors present them as a strategic framework.
athleteDev: Performance Application: Use the framework to plan recovery nutrition between sessions, with carbohydrate and protein at multiple intervals and fluid and sodium replacement matched to sweat losses. The paper gives no evidence on performance outcomes from these strategies.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: The paper is not designed for return to sport. It can inform general nutrition for recovery after training load increases, but it gives no criteria for returning from injury and does not address injured athletes.

citation: Bonilla DA, Stout JR, Gleeson M, Campbell BI, Escalante G, Rojas-Valverde D, et al. The 4Rs Framework of Sports Nutrition: An Update with Recommendations to Evaluate Allostatic Load in Athletes. Life. 2025;15:867.
abstract: The paper updates the 4Rs sports nutrition framework for post-exercise recovery within the allostasis model. It offers practical recommendations for assessing allostatic load in athletes and proposes a cautious allostatic load index for physique competitors and elite athletes.
tldr: The 4Rs (Rehydrate, Refuel, Repair, Recuperate) remain a practical recovery framework, and the paper adds a proposed biomarker index to track cumulative physiological stress in elite and physique athletes. The index is a starting point that still needs validation before use in decisions.
methods: Review incorporating PRISMA-ScR elements, with searches of PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science and Google Scholar using free-text terms on sports nutrition, allostasis and allostatic load, plus a biomarker database and manual reference-list searching. Results are presented in narrative form.
findings: The authors recommend replacing at least 150% of body mass lost, with sodium if faster replacement is needed. They cite about 1.2 g/kg per hour of carbohydrate for up to 4 hours after exercise for refuelling, and state that a ketogenic diet generally has neutral or negative effects on athletic performance compared with carbohydrate-rich diets. Creatine monohydrate may help recovery, while tart cherry, omega-3 fatty acids and dietary nitrate need further clinical research. The proposed ALindex sums 10 equally weighted biomarkers, each scored 0 or 1 against a cut-off, giving a 0 to 10 index; it is proposed but not tested in this paper.
limitations: The information is primarily associative, with little multilevel, causal or complexity-based analysis. The proposed biomarker set needs validation, and the authors note that sex-specific cut-offs and individual monitoring may be warranted for elite athletes. Blood draws must be standardised (rested, fasted, not after high-intensity work) for the index to be reliable. Several authors declare supplement-industry ties, including membership of a Creapure-sponsored creatine advisory board.
practicalImplications: Use the 4Rs as a structure for post-training nutrition, with carbohydrate and protein refuelling matched to the time to the next session. Treat the ALindex as an exploratory way to organise biomarker data for physique and elite athletes, and validate its cut-offs locally before using it to change training or nutrition.
athleteDev: Performance Application: The framework supports post-exercise nutrition planning, and the ALindex may help organise biomarker and load data to spot cumulative stress in elite and physique athletes. The paper does not show that using the index improves performance.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: The paper addresses recovery nutrition and allostatic load in athletes, and the authors mention injury recovery as part of the Recuperate step. It provides no return-to-sport criteria and no evidence on returning from injury.

citation: Dunn RA, Tinsley GM, Palmer TB, Benjamin CL, Sekiguchi Y. The Efficacy of Nutritional Strategies and Ergogenic Aids on Acute Responses and Chronic Adaptations to Exertional-Heat Exposure: A Narrative Review. Nutrients. 2024;16:3792.
abstract: Review of nutritional strategies and ergogenic aids (hydration, sodium, carbohydrate, protein, caffeine, nitrate, tyrosine and creatine) for acute exertional heat exposure and heat acclimation. The authors find robust evidence for some aids and equivocal findings for others, which depend on test type, duration, outcome and sex.
tldr: In this review, sodium before exercise in the heat, carbohydrate during prolonged sessions and creatine have the most support, while caffeine and carbohydrate-plus-protein results are mixed and nitrate and tyrosine showed no consistent benefit in heat. Treat the doses as starting points, since the underlying trials vary widely.
methods: Narrative review with a predetermined search of PubMed, SPORTDiscus, Scopus and Google Scholar through April 2024, for studies in human participants with ambient temperature above 28 C and, where relevant, heat acclimation of at least 5 days. Trial results are summarized in tables, but no formal risk-of-bias tool or pooled analysis is used.
findings: Sodium loading of 20 to 40 mg/kg 1 to 2 hours before exercise improved plasma volume and thermoregulation in some trials, and creatine did not impair thermoregulation and improved performance in some. Caffeine often raised core temperature, nitrate did not improve performance or thermoregulation in heat, and tyrosine results were mixed.
