Carbohydrate of 30 to 90 g per hour was recommended for prolonged exercise, and added protein showed no performance advantage when carbohydrate delivery was 60 g per hour or more.
limitations: There is no formal quality assessment, and the authors acknowledge selection bias, so the recommendations rest partly on judgment. Many trials are small, and the authors say sex-specific and modality-specific responses are unclear, which limits prescription for particular groups. The review concerns exercise in the heat in general, not injured athletes.
practicalImplications: The authors suggest sodium before exercise in the heat, carbohydrate at about 30 to 90 g per hour in prolonged sessions (toward the upper end for males), and added protein for recovery, which may help. They advise caution with caffeine because it can raise core temperature, and they note that nitrate and tyrosine have weak support in heat.
athleteDev: For performance in the heat, the review points to sodium before exercise and enough carbohydrate during long sessions as the most practical starting points. Caffeine can raise core temperature, and nitrate and tyrosine are not supported as reliable heat-performance aids in this review.
rtp: The review covers acute and chronic heat exposure in general exercise rather than injured athletes or recovery from injury, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.

citation: Lee JM, Pardoe HR, Parker DM, Pedersen M, Makdissi M, Abbott DF, et al. Structural brain differences in professional Australian rules footballers following mild traumatic brain injury: When head size matters. Front Neurol. 2026;17:1701097.
abstract: Quantified subcortical and cortical structural MRI differences between 31 recently concussed professional Australian rules footballers and 37 healthy non-athlete controls. Footballers had lower proportional hippocampal and amygdala volumes and reduced cortical thickness, but the volumetric findings depended on the intracranial volume estimation method used for normalization.
tldr: Recently concussed professional footballers had smaller hippocampal volumes than non-athlete controls, but the result depends on how head size is estimated. It is a useful cross-sectional signal, not a diagnostic or return-to-play marker.
methods: Retrospective case-control study of 31 professional male footballers scanned within 3 months of a suspected concussion (acute group 17, sub-acute group 14) and 37 healthy male controls. T1-weighted 3 T MRI was processed with FreeSurfer recon-all, and hippocampal and amygdala volumes were normalized to estimated total intracranial volume (eTIV). Vertex-wise cortical thickness and a subset of 12 players with follow-up scans were also analyzed, and two other intracranial volume estimates were compared as an exploratory step.
findings: Players had lower proportional bilateral hippocampal and amygdala volumes than controls at uncorrected p < 0.05, with the bilateral hippocampal differences remaining significant after Bonferroni correction. Players had a cluster of lower right lateral orbitofrontal cortical thickness (peak p = 0.013, exploratory). Players had larger eTIV than controls (p < 0.001). When normalized to segmentation-based total intracranial volume or supratentorial volume, only the right hippocampus differed. In 12 players with follow-up scans, no subcortical volume changed after correction, and a right hippocampal reduction (p = 0.042) did not survive correction. In an exploratory analysis of 25 players, smaller left hippocampal volume correlated with poorer CogSport learning scores (r = 0.44, p = 0.030).
limitations: The cohort is male and all players were professionals, and controls were non-athletes, so sport exposure, head size and injury history are confounded. Prior concussion history was not known. Most ROI results are uncorrected, and the choice of intracranial volume method changed which findings held. The longitudinal sample was small, the cognitive correlations were exploratory, and two scanner models were used.
practicalImplications: Staff interpreting hippocampal or amygdala volume results after concussion should check how intracranial volume was normalized, and should not treat a single MRI volume as evidence of injury or of a future problem. Clinical use needs a larger study with athlete controls and pre-injury baselines.
athleteDev: Performance Application: The study does not measure sport performance. Its only performance-adjacent finding is an exploratory link between smaller left hippocampal volume and poorer learning scores in a subset of players, which is not a basis for selection or training decisions.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: The study does not link MRI volumes to return-to-play timing, and it cannot be used to clear or hold a player. Most scans were taken within weeks of injury, and no recovery outcome was tied to the volume measures.

citation: Langdon S, Königs M, Adang EAM, Goedhart E, Oosterlaan J. Subtypes of Sport-Related Concussion: a Systematic Review and Meta-cluster Analysis. Sports Med. 2020.
abstract: The authors systematically reviewed 22 studies of sport-related concussion symptom clusters and their links to clinical outcome, aggregating the cluster findings with multiple correspondence analysis. They identified five symptom clusters, with the migraine cluster most often reported and most strongly linked to outcome.
tldr: Concussion symptoms appear to group into about five clusters, and the migraine-type cluster is the one most closely tied to longer recovery. Clinicians may use these groupings to think about symptom profiles, but treatment decisions based on them still need testing.
methods: Systematic review following MOOSE guidance, searching four databases from 1946 to December 2018 for studies that identified symptom clusters or linked clusters to outcomes after sport-related concussion. Two reviewers screened and extracted data, and risk of bias was assessed with an adapted Cochrane tool. Reported clusters were pooled with multiple correspondence analysis, and cluster-outcome links were summarised with effect sizes where available.
findings: Of 22 included studies (5,592 athletes), six found symptom clusters and 19 linked clusters to outcomes. The meta-analysis identified a migraine cluster (headache, light and noise sensitivity, nausea), a cognitive-emotional cluster, a sleep-emotional cluster, a neurological cluster (blurred vision, vomiting, neck pain) and an undefined feelings cluster. Migraine-type clusters were most frequently reported (24%) and linked to prolonged symptom duration and cognitive, balance and oculomotor deficits, with the largest effect sizes. The undefined feelings cluster was not linked to any outcome.
limitations: Most included studies had methodological limitations, and only 13.6% used exploratory data-driven clustering. Clusters were pooled from published reports rather than individual data, and the athletes were mostly adolescents. The authors note that only five included studies adjusted for covariates such as age, sex and time since injury, and all studies assessed symptoms within about the first month after injury. Whether particular clusters relate to specific functional impairments remains unclear.
practicalImplications: Record each athlete's symptom profile after concussion, paying particular attention to headache, light and noise sensitivity, cognitive, sleep and emotional symptoms, since clusters built from these were most often linked to prolonged recovery. Use the profile to guide assessment of headache, neurocognitive, emotional, neurological and sleep function, as the authors recommend, rather than assuming one pathway fits all athletes.
athleteDev: Performance Application: This review does not address training or performance directly. Its relevance is to recognising concussion profiles and to communicating with athletes about symptom patterns that predict a slower return to training.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: Symptom clusters, especially the migraine-type cluster, were linked to prolonged recovery and symptom duration, so they may help flag athletes who need a longer, more cautious return. The review does not show that cluster-based management shortens return to sport, and it cannot set return-to-play timelines.

citation: McDuff DR, Garvin M, Chang J, Thompson D. Substance Misuse in Elite Athletes: Early Detection, Brief Intervention and Referral to Treatment. Clin Sports Med. 2023.
abstract: This clinical review describes early detection, brief intervention and referral to treatment for alcohol, cannabis and tobacco/nicotine misuse in elite athletes. It highlights screening instruments, urine testing and brief motivational interventions, and the role of sports medicine staff in identifying misuse.
tldr: Sports medicine staff and athletic trainers are well placed to spot alcohol, cannabis and nicotine misuse early through pre-season screening and brief motivational conversations. Referral to addiction treatment is appropriate when brief steps do not work.
methods: Narrative clinical review. No systematic search method is described. The review draws on prevalence surveys, screening instruments and intervention studies in collegiate, professional and non-athlete samples.
findings: Binge drinking, cannabis use and nicotine use are common in collegiate and professional athletes, and use is higher in some sports. Screening tools such as AUDIT, CAGE-AID, CUDIT-R or CUDIT-SF, and the Brief Young Adult Alcohol Consequences and Brief Marijuana Consequences Questionnaires, can help identify misuse. Brief motivational interventions with personalized feedback have shown benefit in some athlete and student samples, and in baseball players, brief tobacco interventions were followed by higher quit rates (23% vs 13% at 2 years in one trial of high school players).
limitations: No search methods are described, so the evidence base cannot be reproduced. Many data sources are US collegiate surveys or non-athlete samples. The authors note that there are few recent brief-intervention studies for tobacco and limited data on current professional athletes.
practicalImplications: Add alcohol, cannabis and tobacco/nicotine questions to the pre-season physical and repeat screens after injury, trade or other transitions. Where screens are positive, use brief motivational feedback and refer on to an addiction specialist if it does not work.
athleteDev: Performance Application: Build screening into pre-season and transition routines, and train athletic trainers and coaches in brief motivational conversations. Keep counselling and referral pathways in place, since misuse can affect sleep, recovery, performance and injury risk.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: This review does not address return to sport. It covers substance misuse screening and referral, and it does not evaluate whether misuse affects return-to-play decisions.

citation: Campbell TR, Zamponi M, Leathers D, Cavallario J, Martinez JC, Mollica PA. Stability of salivary microRNA measures across an NCAA Division I football season: Implications for microRNA as a biomarker of concussion. PLoS One. 2026;21(1):e0339614.
abstract: This prospective study measured six pre-selected salivary microRNAs in 50 male NCAA Division I football players before and after one season. No microRNA changed significantly, but reliability across the season was low to moderate, so the markers may vary for reasons other than concussion.
tldr: Six salivary microRNAs did not change on average over a football season, but most were unreliable between pre-season and post-season samples. The authors advise against using this panel for concussion decisions in its current form.
methods: Prospective, observational study of 50 medically cleared male NCAA Division I football players. Saliva was collected before the first pre-season practice and within 72 hours of the final game, and quantitative PCR measured six target microRNAs with miR-361-5p as the endogenous control. Pre- and post-season values were compared with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, and reliability was assessed with intraclass correlation coefficients.
findings: Forty-nine players completed both samples, and no target microRNA differed significantly (p = .07 to .46, small effect sizes), while fatigue scores were unchanged (18.94 to 18.67, p = .684). ICCs were low for four targets and moderate for miR-29c-3p (0.52) and miR-27a-5p (0.65).
limitations: Single team, all male, with no adjustment for sub-concussive impacts, demographics, concussion history or playing position. The authors note that opposing individual changes cancelled out in group means, and Table 1 shows the number of players reporting previous concussions rising from 17 to 20 between collections without saying whether any occurred in-season. Reporting inconsistencies: the methods name miR-30e-5p but the results use miR-30c-5p; the abstract gives an ICC range of -.04 to .65, while Table 2 includes -0.16 for miR-7-1-3p; and the sign of the post-season miR-29c-3p median differs between Table 2 and the text.
practicalImplications: Staff should not treat a change in these salivary microRNAs as a sign of concussion, because the markers varied between pre-season and post-season samples in a cohort the authors describe as without a diagnosed concussive event. The results do not support using this panel in concussion decisions, as the authors conclude.
athleteDev: This study does not inform training or performance decisions. It did not test salivary microRNA as a load or fatigue marker, so it gives no basis for using it that way.
rtp: Not usable for return-to-sport or concussion clearance decisions. The study did not sample athletes at the time of or after a concussion, and its low reliability means these markers cannot establish recovery or readiness.

citation: Rabello LM, Dams OC, van den Akker-Scheek I, Zwerver J, O'Neill S. Substantiating the Use of Ultrasound Tissue Characterization in the Analysis of Tendon Structure: A Systematic Review. Clin J Sport Med. 2021;31(3):e161-e175.
abstract: The authors reviewed 27 studies to determine how ultrasound tissue characterization (UTC) can predict, diagnose and monitor tendon structure and tendinopathy, and to propose a standard scanning and analysis method. UTC was a possible adjunct for diagnosing Achilles tendinopathy and showed promise for monitoring load and treatment, but its predictive value was inconclusive.
tldr: Ultrasound tissue characterization may help show tendon changes in response to load or treatment and can add diagnostic information in Achilles tendinopathy. It has not been shown to predict who will develop tendinopathy, and scanning methods still need to be standardised before results can be compared.
methods: Systematic review following PRISMA guidance, with two reviewers screening in three rounds (titles, abstracts, then full text) and a third reviewer resolving disagreements. Data were extracted on design, participants, scanning method (position, scan direction, window size, area analysed) and whether UTC was used to predict, diagnose or monitor tendons. The review was narrative and descriptive, with no quality assessment or pooled analysis.
findings: Of 27 included studies, 18 examined the Achilles tendon, 5 the patellar tendon and 4 both. Predictive studies gave inconsistent results for Achilles tendinopathy, while a higher percentage of disorganised tissue (echo types III and IV) was linked to patellar tendinopathy in one study. For diagnosis, UTC separated symptomatic from asymptomatic Achilles tendons in some studies (one reported 83% accuracy). For monitoring, several studies showed changes in echo types after loading or treatment, although results varied across studies. Scanning methods differed widely across studies.
limitations: No formal quality assessment and no pooled analysis because the studies were heterogeneous in design, population and method. Most studies focused on mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy, and patellar tendon evidence is limited. Few diagnostic studies exist and there is no gold-standard reference for echo types. The search closed in September 2018 and several authors contributed multiple studies. The abstract reports 1972 search hits while the results report 1351.
practicalImplications: Use UTC as an adjunct to clinical assessment and conventional imaging, not as the sole basis for predicting tendinopathy. If UTC is used to track tendon response to load, use the same standardised method each time (position, scan direction, window size 9 or 17, contours no more than 5 mm apart) and compare repeat scans in the same way.
athleteDev: Performance Application: Consider UTC scans to track how Achilles or patellar tendons adapt to a loading block, using the same protocol each time. Do not use echo-type changes alone to decide how much load an athlete can take, since the link to symptoms is unclear.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: UTC may help monitor tendon structure during rehabilitation, but the review found no clear link between echo-type changes and clinical outcome, so it cannot be used alone to decide when an athlete is ready to return to sport.

citation: Gómez-Guerrero NA, González-López NM, Zapata-Velásquez JD, Martínez-Ramírez JA, Rivera-Monroy ZJ, García-Castañeda JE. Synthetic Peptides in Doping Control: A Powerful Tool for an Analytical Challenge. ACS Omega. 2022;7:38193-38206.
abstract: This review summarizes the role of peptides in doping, with emphasis on reference materials, sample pretreatment, instrumentation and method validation for detecting them in biological samples. The authors propose solid-phase peptide synthesis for in-house reference standards and high-resolution LC-MS for detection.
tldr: Peptide doping agents are hard to detect because they are short-lived and resemble natural molecules. Better reference materials, sample preparation and high-resolution LC-MS methods are the main tools the review identifies for detecting them.
methods: A narrative review of the peptides on the WADA prohibited list, the synthesis and characterization of reference materials, sample pretreatment methods (SPE, liquid-liquid extraction, protein precipitation, immunoaffinity and enzymatic digestion), LC and MS platforms, and the validation guidelines used. No systematic search or inclusion criteria are described.
findings: Peptide hormones, growth factors, insulins and vasopressin analogues are listed in WADA sections S2, S4 and S5, and insulins and similar peptides are hard to detect because of short half-lives and similarity to endogenous molecules. LC or reverse-phase SPE purification can yield synthetic peptides above 95% purity, and the authors propose solid-phase peptide synthesis as a route to in-house reference standards. Reversed-phase LC coupled to high-resolution MS (TOF or Orbitrap) is described as the preferred platform, and cited validation studies report limits of detection from about 0.02 to 20 ng/mL depending on peptide and matrix. The authors note that no specific validation guide has been established for peptides and that, unlike other doping agents, peptides lack adequate reference materials.
limitations: The review is narrative and does not state how studies were selected. Its validation examples draw mainly on spiked samples, clinical trials or pharmacokinetic studies; athlete samples were used less often (one cited study used 209 athlete serum samples for IGF-1). The article reports no clinical outcomes or effects on athletes.
practicalImplications: Staff can note that many WADA-listed peptides are short-lived and difficult to detect, so detection capability varies by compound and matrix. The review gives no clinical, training or nutrition protocol, and its findings should not be applied to athlete management.
athleteDev: Performance Application: the review explains why peptide agents such as growth hormone releasing peptides, insulin and erythropoietin appear on the WADA list, but it does not test their performance effects and gives no training guidance.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: the review does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to play, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions.

citation: Nobre TL, Rocha LY, Carbone PO, Grassi MCF, de Oliveira Júnior R, Caperuto EC. The Relationship of Infrared Thermography With the Identification of Changes in Biological Markers After Exercise: A Systematic Review. Journal of Bodywork & Movement Therapies. 2025 (in press).
abstract: This PRISMA systematic review asked whether changes in skin temperature measured by infrared thermography match the inflammatory and muscle-damage changes seen after exercise in trained people. Five studies were included, and the authors found few studies linking the method to biomarkers, with weak or inconsistent associations.
tldr: Infrared thermography is used widely in sport, but it has been tested against blood muscle-damage markers in only five small studies, and most found no clear link. Use it as a screening aid alongside clinical examination, not as a substitute for CK or lactate.
methods: A PRISMA systematic review registered in PROSPERO (CRD42022385463), with searches of PubMed, MEDLINE, LILACS, SciELO, SPORTDiscus and Embase in January 2023 and no language or date restriction. Two reviewers screened full texts, and the included studies were experimental trials of trained athletes of both sexes over 18 that measured infrared skin temperature alongside CK or lactate. Risk of bias was assessed with QUADAS-2.
findings: Five studies were included, with 81 athletes in total (10 to 21 per study) from rugby, soccer, sprint and distance running. Bandeira et al. (2014, rugby) found no correlation between skin temperature variation and serum CK. Fernandes et al. (2017, soccer) found skin temperature and CK moderately related in all regions after two consecutive matches, with CK higher 48 h after the second match. Korman et al. (2021, sprinters) found no correlation between leg skin temperature and CK over a 10-day camp. Perez-Guarner et al. (2019, half-marathon) reported that a regression model could not predict physiological stress from skin temperature, and Table 2 reports no skin temperature increase after the race. Rojas-Valverde et al. (2021, marathon) found higher skin temperature the day after the race but no correlation with muscle damage markers.
limitations: The authors note the small number of studies, differing protocols and sports, and few time points, which made correlation hard to establish. Most studies were rated uncertain on the reference standard domain of QUADAS-2. The text reports 55 men and 26 women, but Table 1 gives 60 men and 21 women, and the discussion says skin temperature rose 24 h before and 48 h after the half-marathon while Table 2 reports no post-race rise, so the table values are used here. Bandeira et al. measured only 48 h after training or a match, so no pre-session baseline existed.
practicalImplications: Staff can use infrared thermography to flag skin-temperature asymmetry for clinical follow-up, as the authors suggest, together with clinical examination. On current evidence it should not be used as a stand-in for CK or lactate to judge muscle damage after training or matches. Future protocols should measure skin temperature and biomarkers before and after sessions.
athleteDev: Performance Application: skin temperature changes were seen after matches, marathons and camps, but they did not consistently track muscle-damage markers. Using it to periodize training load would need baseline measures and a validated link to load, which these studies do not provide.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: no included study examined injury recovery, rehabilitation or return to play, so the review cannot inform return-to-play decisions. Its use for injury screening is discussed by the authors but not tested in these studies.

citation: Ellens S, Middleton K, Gastin PB, Varley MC. Techniques to derive and clean acceleration and deceleration data of athlete tracking technologies in team sports: A scoping review. Journal of Sports Sciences. 2022.
abstract: This scoping review mapped how acceleration and deceleration data from athlete tracking technologies in team sports are derived, cleaned and applied. A systematic search of four databases identified 276 eligible studies. Most studies (60%) did not report how the data were derived and cleaned, and the data were most often used as effort-based metrics to describe movement demands.
tldr: Acceleration and deceleration metrics from GPS and tracking systems depend heavily on how the raw data were derived, filtered and thresholded. Most published studies do not say what processing they used, so their numbers are hard to compare.
methods: Scoping review following PRISMA-ScR and JBI methodology, with PubMed, SPORTDiscus, Scopus and Web of Science searched from inception to August 2020 using sport, acceleration and tracking-technology terms. After screening 5015 records and assessing 354 full texts, 276 studies were included. Derivation, cleaning and metric criteria were extracted with a custom template.
findings: Most included studies used acceleration measures (n = 270) and 148 used deceleration measures. The derivation technique was not specified in 66% of studies and 88% did not mention any data cleaning; of studies that cleaned data, 48% used a low-pass Butterworth filter with cut-off frequencies from 0.02 to 15 Hz, rarely with a rationale. Number of efforts was the most used metric, and 59% of those studies defined an effort only by a set threshold.
limitations: The review did not assess study quality and included only English-language publications up to August 2020. One author ran the search and title screening, and two authors screened abstracts and full texts. The headline percentages are inconsistent across sections (abstract 60% with no derivation or cleaning information; results 66% derivation unspecified and 88% no cleaning; discussion 92% no cleaning), and the findings apply to team sports only.
practicalImplications: Practitioners should record which device, software version, derivation method, filter and cut-off, and effort criteria were used before comparing acceleration or deceleration counts across studies or systems. Metric thresholds and minimum effort durations should be stated alongside any reported effort counts.
athleteDev: Acceleration and deceleration effort counts depend on the tracking system, derivation method and cleaning filter used. Compare athletes or periods only within the same system and settings, and report those settings with the data.
rtp: This review cannot inform return to sport. It maps data processing methods across team-sport studies and contains no injured-athlete outcomes or return-to-play criteria.

citation: Hutchison MG, Di Battista AP, Pyndiura KL, Corallo DN, Lawrence DW, Richards D. Ten-word list performance in healthy athletes and athletes at 3-to-5 days following concussion. Clin J Sport Med. 2021.
abstract: Cross-sectional study of 363 healthy university athletes measured at preseason and 49 university athletes tested a median of 4 days after sport-related concussion, using the 10-word recall task from the SCAT-5. Recall did not differ between groups, and healthy females outperformed healthy males on both immediate and delayed recall.
tldr: The SCAT-5 10-word recall did not separate university athletes about 4 days after concussion from healthy athletes tested at preseason. Females recalled slightly more words than males at baseline, so sex should be considered when interpreting scores.
methods: Healthy university athletes completed preseason baseline testing (n = 363) and athletes with sport-related concussion were tested at a median of 4.0 days after injury (n = 49). Immediate recall (three trials, maximum 30) and delayed recall (one trial, maximum 10) of the 10-word list were compared between groups with separate analyses for males and females. Symptoms were recorded with an expanded 27-item Post-Concussion Symptom Scale.
findings: No significant difference in immediate recall (P = 0.228, Cohen's d = 0.18) or delayed recall (P = 0.908, Cohen's d = 0.02) between concussed and healthy athletes, and the null result held in male and female subsets. In healthy athletes, females scored higher than males on immediate recall (mean difference 1.0, P = 0.002) and delayed recall (mean difference 0.5, P = 0.006).
limitations: The concussed group was small (n = 49) and was compared with healthy athletes measured at a different time, not with its own preinjury baseline. The authors state that a larger concussed sample would have allowed subgroup analyses by sport type and concussion history, and controlling for the number of tests. The concussed athletes were older and more often had a concussion history than the healthy group (results held after adjustment), and the abstract conflicts with the results on the male count (220 vs 210) and the sex-difference P value for immediate recall (P < 0.001 vs P = 0.002); results values are reported here.
practicalImplications: In the 3 to 5 day window, the SCAT-5 10-word recall test did not separate concussed university athletes from healthy peers in this study. Staff should interpret scores with sex in mind and should not use this test alone to rule concussion in or out.
athleteDev: Use this as a baseline measure of the SCAT-5 10-word recall, noting that females scored higher than males at baseline in this sample. Do not use the 10-word list as a standalone marker of cognitive change.
rtp: This study cannot be used to clear an athlete to return to sport. It compared groups at one subacute time point and measured no return-to-play decisions or outcomes, and a normal recall score does not show that concussion has resolved.

citation: Hagen J, Himmler A, Clark J, Ramadan J, Stone J, Divine J, et al. Test and evaluation of heart rate derived core temperature algorithms for use in NCAA Division I football athletes. J Funct Morphol Kinesiol. 2020;5:46.
abstract: Validation study comparing heart-rate-derived core temperature estimates from Zephyr BioHarness devices with an ingestible core temperature pill in 13 male Division I football athletes during summer training camp. Overall concordance was 0.643, and concordance was 0.834 in the upper body fat group (above 6.0%).
tldr: Heart-rate-derived core temperature agreed only moderately with an ingestible pill in college football players during camp (concordance 0.643, which the authors call poor, with 78% of readings within 1 F). Agreement was much better in athletes above 6% body fat, and readings above about 102.5 F were rarely tested.
methods: Thirteen male Division I football athletes who were full participants in practice wore Zephyr BioHarness devices, which give an estimated core temperature (ECT) from heart rate, and swallowed an ingestible radio-frequency core temperature pill during summer training camp. Athletes were split into upper (above 6.0% body fat, n = 6) and lower (6.0% or below, n = 7) groups. Agreement was assessed with Lin's concordance correlation, Bland-Altman analysis and difference histograms.
findings: Overall concordance was 0.643 and 78% of paired values fell within +/-1.0 F of the pill. Overall bias was -0.192 F (95% CI -0.333 to -0.05), with limits of agreement of -1.803 to 1.42 F. In the upper body fat group, concordance was 0.834, 93% of values were within +/-1.0 F, and the authors report better accuracy than in the lower body fat group.
limitations: The sample was 13 male athletes from one team and one camp, so results may not generalise to other teams, sexes or conditions. The body-fat subgroups were small (6 and 7), so subgroup estimates are imprecise. Only 134 paired measurements were collected, and the post hoc power analysis showed 402 pairs would be needed for the full group, while most pill temperatures stayed below 102.5 F, so accuracy in the clinically important range above 105 F is untested. The 3-h pill ingestion window may not fully remove cold-water interference.
practicalImplications: Heart-rate-derived core temperature may help flag heat strain during football camp, but single readings can underestimate the pill by up to about 2 F. It was not validated at temperatures that signal exertional heat stroke, so it should not replace direct core temperature measurement when heat illness is suspected, and accuracy is lower in leaner athletes.
athleteDev: Use heart-rate-derived core temperature to track relative heat strain across camp sessions for football players, not as an exact core temperature for each athlete. Interpret values with the wide limits of agreement in mind.
rtp: This validation study cannot inform return-to-play decisions. It tested no injured athletes and no return-to-play or recovery outcomes, and it does not establish that the device can guide re-entry after exertional heat illness.

citation: Shitrit E, Valentin E, Baudrier N, Bohu Y, Rauline G, Lopes R, et al. The ALR-RSI score can be used to evaluate psychological readiness to return to sport after acute Achilles tendon tear. Knee Surgery, Sports Traumatology, Arthroscopy. 2023;31:4961-4968.
abstract: The study validated the ALR-RSI, a psychological readiness to return to sport score, after Achilles tendon repair in 50 patients using COSMIN methods. The score correlated strongly with EFAS, FAAM and VISA-A, discriminated patients who returned to sport from those who did not, and showed excellent reproducibility and internal consistency.
tldr: The French ALR-RSI psychological readiness score appears valid and reproducible after Achilles tendon repair in a small series of 50 patients. It may help flag patients who need psychological support, but it has not been tested for prediction in a new group.
methods: Validation following COSMIN methodology in patients who played sport at least monthly and had open Achilles repair at three centres. Patients completed the ALR-RSI, VISA-A, EFAS and FAAM 6 to 9 months after surgery, and 10 patients repeated the ALR-RSI after 15 days.
findings: 11 of 50 patients (22%) had returned to sport at a mean follow-up of 6.8 months, 4 at their pre-injury level and 7 at a lower level. ALR-RSI correlated strongly with EFAS (r = 0.68), FAAM Sport (r = 0.70), FAAM AVQ (r = 0.60) and VISA-A (r = 0.54). Scores were lower in non-returners (60.7 vs 83.2, p = 0.001), with an AUC of 0.83; a cut-off of 77.5 gave 82% sensitivity and 79% specificity, and none of the AUCs differed significantly between scores. Test-retest ICC was 0.99 in 10 patients and Cronbach alpha was 0.95. Sport type and level were not associated with return to sport.
limitations: The sample is small, with only 11 returners, and the authors note that a 12-month follow-up could have improved discrimination. The study only covered open repairs, and the null association of sport type and level with return to sport may reflect low power, as the authors note. The reproducibility sample is 10 patients.
practicalImplications: Clinicians could use the ALR-RSI alongside physical scores during Achilles repair rehabilitation to track psychological readiness and identify patients who may need psychological support. The 77.5 cut-off needs confirmation in an independent group before it is used to make return decisions.
athleteDev: Performance Application: The study measures no performance outcomes after return. Its use for performance staff is limited to a psychological readiness check during rehabilitation.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: The score can track psychological readiness to return to sport 6 to 9 months after Achilles repair. It cannot show when an athlete is physically ready, cannot predict who will return, and was validated against questionnaires rather than objective return criteria.

citation: Fox JL, O'Grady CJ, Scanlan AT. The Concurrent Validity of Session-Rating of Perceived Exertion Workload Obtained Face-to-Face Versus Via an Online Application: A Team Case Study. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2020.
abstract: The authors compared session RPE collected face-to-face in one season with session RPE collected by a phone-based online app in another season, in 16 semiprofessional male basketball players. Face-to-face ratings correlated more strongly with PlayerLoad and summated heart rate zone workload than the app ratings did.
tldr: In this one team, session RPE collected face-to-face tracked objective workload more closely than session RPE collected through a phone app. Basketball staff should check any app-based RPE against objective load before relying on it.
methods: Observational team case study across the 2018 and 2019 seasons. Players rated session RPE after each session, either face-to-face (2018) or through a phone-based app (2019), and workload was measured by microsensor PlayerLoad and summated heart rate zones. Repeated-measures correlations with 95% confidence intervals were used to compare the two reporting methods.
findings: All correlations were significant. Face-to-face session RPE correlated large with PlayerLoad (r = .69) and very large with summated heart rate zone workload (r = .74). The online app correlated small with PlayerLoad (r = .29) and moderate with summated heart rate zone workload (r = .34).
limitations: The two methods were compared in different seasons with partly different players, so season and method cannot be separated. Ratings were collected within 30 minutes (face-to-face) and within 60 minutes (online), heart rate was measured with different devices each season, and lower compliance with the app left 57 samples against 163 face-to-face.
practicalImplications: Collect session RPE face-to-face or within a short, consistent window, and do not assume app-based RPE has the same validity. Check any app-based RPE against objective workload before using it to guide training.
athleteDev: For basketball training load monitoring, the results favour collecting session RPE individually and soon after training. App-based RPE should be checked against PlayerLoad or heart rate zone workload before it guides load decisions.
rtp: The study is about training load monitoring in healthy players and does not address injury or return to sport. It cannot be used to set return-to-play loads.

citation: Minthorn LM, Fayson SD, Stobierski LM, Welch CE, Anderson BE. The Functional Movement Screen’s Ability to Detect Changes in Movement Patterns After a Training Intervention. Journal of Sport Rehabilitation. 2015;24(3):322-326.
abstract: Clinical question: does an individualised training programme improve movement patterns in adults who participate in high-intensity activities? The authors searched for level 3 or higher studies that used the Functional Movement Screen (FMS) before and after a training programme. Three studies met the criteria. One study found no significant change after a 12-week programme, and two reported significant changes in movement patterns. The clinical bottom line is inconsistent evidence (grade C).
tldr: Evidence that individualised training improves Functional Movement Screen patterns is inconsistent: two of three studies found gains and one found none. Use the FMS alongside other outcome measures, and do not read a higher FMS score as proof of better performance or lower injury risk.
methods: Critically appraised topic. Searches of the Cochrane Library, Medline, CINAHL and SPORTDiscus, plus reference lists and hand search, covered 2004 to 2013 and English-language studies. Eligible studies were level 3 or higher, used the FMS before and after an individualised training programme in physically active individuals or athletes, and excluded people under 18, those with current musculoskeletal injury, and those with restricted training. The three studies were graded by Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine levels.
findings: Bodden et al (cluster randomised trial, level 1b, mixed martial arts athletes) and Kiesel et al (cohort, level 2b, professional football players) reported significant changes in movement patterns after training. Frost et al (single-blinded randomised trial, level 1b) reported no significant change after a 12-week programme. Baseline FMS scores were similar across groups (12.8 to 13.3), except football linemen (11.8). The Frost programme targeted whole-body coordination and fitness rather than specific movement limitations.
limitations: Only three studies were appraised, and their designs and programmes differ. Kiesel et al had no control group, so gains could not be separated from repeated testing. The authors note that FMS gains may reflect participants' knowledge of the grading criteria, and that little evidence links higher FMS scores to better athletic performance. The Implications section attributes the non-significant result to study 3 (Kiesel), while the Results and Discussion attribute it to study 2 (Frost); the Results and Discussion are followed here.
practicalImplications: Exercises that directly address the movement patterns the FMS identifies may improve scores, whereas whole-body coordination or general fitness programmes may not. Use the FMS as one component of a wider assessment, and add other outcome measures when judging whether a training programme is working.
athleteDev: When an athlete's FMS shows a specific movement limitation, a corrective programme aimed at that pattern may improve the score, while a general fitness block is less likely to. Judge the programme by more than the FMS score, because score gains have not been shown to carry over to athletic performance.
rtp: It cannot guide return to sport or clearance. The included studies tested participants without current injury, and the authors state that it is unknown whether resolving movement limitations reduces injury risk.

citation: Hales ME, Johnson JD II. The Influence of Sport-Field Properties on Muscle-Recruitment Patterns and Metabolic Response. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2018 (ahead of print).
abstract: Eleven male athletes completed four agility circuits on two outdoor fields with different mechanical properties. Surface EMG, gas exchange, and 30-m sprint times were recorded before and after the circuits. The authors report that muscle activity differed between fields and that the field with greater energy return gave faster agility and sprint times, with largely similar metabolic responses.
tldr: The surface a player trains on changed how 11 male athletes recruited their leg muscles during agility work. The lower energy-return field produced more muscle activity and slower agility times, so surface mechanics are worth considering in conditioning.
methods: Eleven male athletes completed four consecutive agility circuits with 60 s rests on two outdoor fields, tested 7 days apart at the same time of day. Surface EMG was recorded from the vastus medialis, biceps femoris, gastrocnemius medial head and tibialis anterior, with a portable gas analyser for VO2, HR and energy expenditure. Field properties were measured with the ASTM F-1936 protocol, and 30-m sprints were run before and after the circuits.
findings: Energy restitution was lower on Field A (28.2%) than Field B (41.6%), and force reduction and vertical deformation also differed. Summed muscle activity differed between fields (F(1,20) = 5.78, P = .026) and was higher on Field A in every trial (Table 2, for example T1 740.8 vs 566.6), and agility circuits took longer there (P = .02). Pretest 30-m sprints were slower on Field A (4.67 vs 4.31 s), and metabolic variables changed across trials but did not differ significantly between fields overall.
limitations: Only 11 men and two fields were tested, with no injury outcomes, and the fatigue correlations were weak to moderate (r = .28 to .42). The EMG difference is reported as '<13%' in the abstract and 13% greater in the discussion, but the Table 2 means are about 30% higher on Field A. The field effect was analysed with field as a between-subject factor (F(1,20)) even though the same athletes ran on both fields.
practicalImplications: The authors recommend that player development staff consider a field's energy return and shock absorption when planning conditioning and training volume. They suggest preparing athletes on a surface with mechanical properties similar to the competition surface.
athleteDev: Where possible, prepare athletes on surfaces that resemble the competition surface, and plan drills and volume knowing that energy return changes muscle activity and agility times. The study does not show that any specific footwear or training change improves performance.
rtp: This study tested healthy athletes only and does not inform return-to-sport decisions or the timing of return after injury.

citation: Furrer R, Hawley JA, Handschin C. The Molecular Athlete: Exercise Physiology from Mechanisms to Medals. Physiol Rev 2023;103:1693-1787.
abstract: A review of skeletal muscle morphological, functional and molecular adaptations to endurance- and resistance-based training. It places these adaptations in the context of innate genetic and interindividual differences in exercise capacity, with particular attention to ageing athletes, and asks how adaptations translate from molecules to medals.
tldr: Adaptation to elite training involves a broad set of molecular and tissue changes, and the upper limits of adaptation remain poorly understood. Training methods still rely heavily on trial and error, so the mechanistic research should be read as context rather than a ready prescription.
methods: Narrative review covering skeletal muscle plasticity, oxygen transport, neuromuscular control, acute and chronic molecular mechanisms, muscle repair, genetics, ageing and the evolution of human movement, with a section on whether everyone can become an elite athlete. No systematic search method is described.
findings: The authors summarise the morphological, functional and signalling changes behind endurance and resistance adaptation, noting that insight into endurance-training regulation far exceeds that for resistance training and that the mechanisms of detraining and muscle memory remain rudimentary. Individual responses form a continuum, apparent non-responders may respond when training volume or intensity is increased, and evidence linking specific genetic variants to elite performance is weak. Exercise-mimetic compounds show no evidence of performance enhancement in humans, may reduce training adaptation, and may carry serious risks.
limitations: The review is narrative, with no described search or grading of evidence, and many mechanistic findings come from rodent and cell models. The authors acknowledge major gaps in understanding how training signals are integrated, how cross-talk between muscle and other tissues works, and where adaptive limits lie.
practicalImplications: The authors argue for closer links between basic science, sport science and coaches, and for personalised, evidence-based training. They suggest physical performance testing is likely more useful than commercial genetic testing for stratifying athletes, and caution against unvalidated compounds and quick fixes.
athleteDev: Use the mechanistic picture as background for training design rather than as a fixed prescription, since endurance adaptation is better characterised than resistance adaptation and individual response varies. Avoid compounds marketed as exercise mimetics, because human performance evidence for them is absent.
rtp: The review covers training adaptation in healthy and elite athletes and does not study injured athletes or return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions. Rehabilitation is mentioned only in passing.

citation: Loturco I, Dello Iacono A, Nakamura FY, Freitas TT, Boullosa D, Valenzuela PL, et al. The Optimum Power Load: A Simple and Powerful Tool for Testing and Training. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2022;17(2):151-159.
abstract: The optimum power load (OPL) is the load that maximizes power output in an exercise. It is derived from the load-velocity relationship using only bar force and bar velocity, and is assessed with a simple incremental test based on percentages of body mass. This brief review summarizes the evidence on OPL-based testing and training, including its links with sport performance, its use in post-activation potentiation protocols, and its effects on strength, speed, power, body composition and endurance. The authors conclude that OPL-based schemes are valid and simple, and can be used by coaches and sport scientists across sports and populations.
tldr: The optimum power load is a quick test that finds the load giving peak bar power, using set percentages of body mass. This review argues it is a simple, practical tool for testing athletes, setting training loads and choosing warm-up loads before power work.
methods: Brief narrative review of published OPL studies. No systematic search or quality appraisal method is described.
findings: Bar power at the OPL correlated moderately to very largely with sprint and vertical jump performance in several sports (for example r = .43 to .86 in young soccer players). It discriminated between sports, performance levels and sexes. OPL-based training produced similar or slightly greater strength, speed and power changes than traditional strength-power methods, with less total weight lifted and less neuromuscular fatigue. The authors also report that OPL-based potentiation protocols likely produce larger potentiation than heavy-load (above 85% 1RM) protocols, based on a limited number of studies.
limitations: The review does not explain how studies were chosen or how their quality was judged. Most of the evidence is short term, and the authors acknowledge a lack of long-term OPL trials. The endurance findings come from a few cyclist studies without a control group that kept endurance training alone, and the body-composition evidence is scarce and mainly from cyclists, with one 6-week study finding no change. Correlations are not evidence of causation, as the authors note.
practicalImplications: Coaches can find each athlete's OPL with an incremental bar-velocity test at set percentages of body mass and re-check it regularly, for example weekly. The authors suggest loads 20% above the OPL may suit change-of-direction and jump work and loads 20% below may suit short-sprint work, but this rests on a single cited study and is worded as 'possibly' more effective.
athleteDev: The OPL test can be used to profile an athlete's bar power and set training loads. Training at the OPL produced similar or slightly greater strength, speed and power gains than traditional methods in the cited studies, with less total load and fatigue.
rtp: The review does not cover injury, rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot be used to judge readiness after injury. Its load recommendations apply to healthy athletes in training.

citation: Hung CH, Su CH, Wang D. The Role of High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT) in Neuromuscular Adaptations: Implications for Strength and Power Development - A Review. Life. 2025;15:657.
abstract: The review examines peer-reviewed studies from 2000 to 2025 on how HIIT affects motor unit recruitment, fiber composition, neuromuscular efficiency, maximal strength, rate of force development, hypertrophy and power. It concludes that HIIT improves neural activation and explosive power, is less effective than resistance training for absolute strength and hypertrophy, and works best combined with resistance or plyometric training.
tldr: Sprint-based and plyometric HIIT improve explosive power and rate of force development, but HIIT is not a replacement for heavy resistance training for maximal strength. The authors favour combining the two with periodization.
methods: Narrative synthesis of literature found through PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and EBSCO using HIIT and neuromuscular keywords, covering 2000 to 2025, organized by theme. The text refers to 86 studies from its search, with no formal inclusion framework or meta-analysis.
findings: The authors report that HIIT increases motor unit recruitment and synchronization, with greater fast-twitch activation, shifts toward Type II and hybrid IIa fibers, and improved rate of force development and explosive power. They report HIIT is less effective than traditional resistance training for maximal strength and hypertrophy because it lacks progressive heavy overload.
limitations: No inclusion criteria, study counts by outcome, or quality grading are reported. The authors note long-term effects are understudied and data for youth and rehabilitation populations are sparse. Mechanistic claims are narrative and not graded for strength of evidence.
practicalImplications: Use sprint-based or plyometric HIIT to support explosive power and rate of force development, and keep heavy resistance training in the program for maximal strength and muscle size. Schedule HIIT so it does not reduce force output in lifting sessions, and individualize intensity and work-to-rest ratios.
athleteDev: Use HIIT, especially sprint and plyometric formats, as a time-efficient complement to strength training for explosive power, not as a replacement for heavy lifting. Sequence and periodize it to limit fatigue interference with strength work.
rtp: Return to play is mentioned only briefly, as early-phase neuromuscular rehabilitation, and injured athletes were not studied. The review cannot be used to set return-to-sport timelines or clearance criteria.

citation: Fullagar HHK, McCall A, Impellizzeri FM, Favero T, Coutts AJ. The Translation of Sport Science Research to the Field: A Current Opinion and Overview on the Perceptions of Practitioners, Researchers and Coaches. Sports Medicine. 2019.
abstract: A current opinion that reviews published survey and interview evidence on how practitioners, researchers and coaches acquire, value and apply sport science research. It also reviews the barriers that limit use of research in elite sport.
tldr: Coaches mostly learn through personal conversation and value research on tactics, technique and mental training, while practitioners and researchers prioritise fitness and recovery. Aligned goals, embedded research staff and coach-focused research may help close the gap between research and practice.
methods: Opinion piece reviewing published survey and interview studies of practitioners, researchers and coaches on how they source information, which research areas they value, and what barriers limit application. No search strategy is described, and the authors summarise the evidence in two tables and offer recommendations.
findings: Coaches prefer personal contact and experience, such as conversations with players and other coaches, over courses or journals, and they rate their knowledge highest in tactical and technical areas. Coaches value research on mental training, tactics and technical efficiency most, while practitioners and researchers value fitness and recovery research and rate research embedded in clubs as most applicable. Reported barriers include funding and time for practitioners, staff and manager buy-in for researchers, and research questions that do not match coaches' needs.
limitations: The paper describes itself as an opinion piece and reports no search method, so the evidence base cannot be audited. The cited data come from surveys of specific groups, such as 75 professional football coaches, 321 Turkish coaches and 205 Canadian coaches, and the authors note that peer-reviewed evidence on coaches' perceptions is limited. The recommendations were not tested.
practicalImplications: Practitioners should tailor research to coaches' priorities, such as tactical or mental training questions, and present it through conversation, case studies or simple graphs rather than journal articles alone. Organisations could agree shared goals, define each role, and fund embedded or applied research that answers the questions coaches actually ask.
athleteDev: Performance Application: Introduce new monitoring or analysis only after agreeing a shared performance goal and each person's role with the coach. Present the findings in the format the coach prefers, since the paper reports that coaches favour conversation, case studies and simplified graphs.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: The paper concerns how coaches and practitioners use sport science research in general, not return-to-play decisions. It cannot be used to judge which return-to-play tests or criteria are valid.

citation: Thurlow F, Weakley J, Townshend AD, Timmins RG, Morrison M, McLaren SJ. The Acute Demands of Repeated-Sprint Training on Physiological, Neuromuscular, Perceptual and Performance Outcomes in Team Sport Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Sports Med. 2023.
abstract: Systematic review and multilevel meta-analysis of 176 studies (908 samples) of overground repeated-sprint training in team sport athletes aged 16 or over. Pooled reference estimates were 163 bpm average heart rate, 10.7 mmol/L end-set blood lactate and 5.0% sprint decrement. Shuttle-based sprints, longer sprint distances and shorter inter-repetition rest increased or altered physiological and performance demands, while two fewer repetitions per set had a trivial effect on most outcomes.
tldr: Repeated-sprint training is physically demanding for team sport athletes, with pooled blood lactate of about 10.7 mmol/L. Longer sprints and shorter rest raise the demand, while dropping from six to four repetitions per set changed most outcomes very little.
methods: PRISMA-guided systematic search of PubMed, SPORTDiscus, MEDLINE and Scopus (to January 2022) for original studies of overground running repeated-sprint training in team sport athletes aged 16 or over. Data were pooled with multilevel mixed-effects meta-analysis, and programming moderators (sprint modality, repetitions per set, sprint distance, rest modality and rest duration) were tested by meta-regression against a reference of 6 x 30 m straight sprints with 20 s passive rest. Effects were judged against practical thresholds as trivial, substantial or inconclusive.
findings: Pooled estimates across protocols were average heart rate 163 bpm (90% CI 154 to 171), peak heart rate 182 bpm, end-set blood lactate 10.7 mmol/L, session RPE 6.5 deciMax, best sprint time 5.52 s and sprint decrement 5.0% (90% CI 4.7 to 5.3). Compared with the 6 x 30 m, 20 s passive rest reference, shuttle-based sprints increased average and best sprint times (1.42 s and 1.55 s slower) with a trivial effect on session RPE. Two more repetitions per set had trivial effects on most outcomes. A 10 m longer sprint increased blood lactate by 2.7 mmol/L and sprint decrement by 1.7%. A 10 s longer rest lowered blood lactate by 1.1 mmol/L and sprint decrement by 1.4%, with trivial effects on peak heart rate and session RPE. Active rest and rest modality effects were largely inconclusive.
limitations: CMJ height, creatine kinase and peak heart rate as a percentage of maximum had too few comparable samples to be meta-analysed, and moderators could not be tested for average heart rate or VO2. Many moderator effects had confidence intervals spanning trivial and substantial effects, and part of the variation reflected factors not modelled, such as age, fitness, sex, number of sets and data collection methods. Some values were digitised from figures or estimated rest times, samples were removed when authors could not clarify protocols, and the review excluded injured athletes and sprints at 30 C or above.
practicalImplications: To raise physiological demand and sprint decrement, longer sprint distances (over 30 m) and shorter rest (20 s or less) are the most consistent levers. To limit fatigue and protect sprint times, shorter sprints (15 to 25 m) with 30 s or more passive rest are suggested. Reducing from six to four repetitions per set changed most measured demands only trivially, so it may cut sprint volume without much loss of stimulus on average.
athleteDev: Sprint distance and rest duration can be set to target either higher metabolic and fatigue stress (longer sprints, shorter rest) or better sprint quality (shorter sprints, longer rest). Four rather than six repetitions per set kept most demands similar on average, so it may be used to lower sprint volume, though the effect for an individual athlete may differ.
rtp: The review included only healthy, non-injured athletes and excluded injured or returning athletes, so its demand estimates cannot set return-to-sport loading. The authors suggest gradually increasing sprint distance as a late-stage return-to-play progression, but this was not studied in injured athletes and should be treated as an untested extrapolation.

citation: Carstensen JB, Gaemelke T, Overgaard K, Andersen TB. The effect of fatiguing muscle contractions on kicking performance in experienced soccer players. Sports Biomechanics. 2024.
abstract: Sixteen male soccer players (5 professional, 11 amateur) completed kicking tests after a fatiguing quadriceps protocol or rest, on separate days in a randomised crossover design. Maximal voluntary isometric contraction force, stimulation force ratio and kicking speed and accuracy were measured before and after each condition.
tldr: Fatiguing the quadriceps lowered maximal kicking ball speed in experienced soccer players. Shooting accuracy did not change significantly, although the study was too small to rule out an effect.
methods: Randomised crossover with 16 analysed male players (17 recruited, one dropout) from amateur to professional level, aged 18 to 30 years with at least 10 years of organised play. On separate days, participants completed a fatiguing protocol (5 sets of 10 maximal voluntary concentric and eccentric knee extensions with the kicking leg) or a rest control. Maximal isometric force, the 15 Hz/50 Hz stimulation force ratio, maximum ball speed, foot speed and shooting accuracy were measured before and after. Paired t-tests and repeated-measures ANOVA with Bonferroni correction were used.
findings: The fatiguing protocol reduced maximal isometric force by 14.0 +/- 2.7% and the force ratio by 14.0 +/- 3.7%, with no reduction in control. Maximum ball speed fell 1.9% after fatigue (0.57 m/s), with no change on the control day, and the change differed significantly between conditions (2.1%). Maximum foot speed fell 5.87% after fatigue, but the between-day difference was not significant (p = 0.054). Shooting accuracy improved 13.3% on the control day (p = 0.02) but did not change on the fatigue day, and the between-condition difference was not significant (p = 0.18). The short axis of the kick dispersion ellipse widened by 53.9% after fatigue, significantly more than on the control day.
limitations: Only 16 players were analysed, and the authors state there was insufficient power for the accuracy outcome. The control-day accuracy improvement was unexpected by the authors and shows why a control condition matters when judging fatigue effects. Ball and foot speed were taken from each player's hardest kick, and accuracy kicks below 80% of maximum speed were discarded without being counted. Fatigue was induced in one muscle group with knee extensions, not match conditions. The ball-speed effect was small, at about 2%.
practicalImplications: Heavy quadriceps work can reduce maximum kicking speed in trained players for at least the 30 minutes or so of testing that followed. The study found no clear effect on accuracy, so it does not show that fatigue harms shot placement. Practitioners should not assume a shooting-accuracy loss from this evidence.
athleteDev: Fatiguing quadriceps work lowered maximum kick speed by about 2% in this group, but accuracy was not clearly affected. The study did not test how to sequence strength work and shooting practice.
rtp: This study cannot be used for return-to-play decisions. It tested healthy players with an induced quadriceps fatigue protocol and included no injury or rehabilitation outcomes.

citation: van den Bogaard T, Klous L, Cottle RM, Van Erp J, Daanen HAM. The effect of heat acclimation on critical environmental limits and rate of rectal temperature change. J Appl Physiol. 2025;138:1150-1160.
abstract: The study quantified how heat acclimation changes the critical environmental limit (WBGTcrit, the point where heat balance can no longer be maintained) and the rate of rectal temperature rise during exercise in the heat. Twenty-eight unacclimatized adults were split into a heat acclimation group, which completed 5 to 9 days of controlled-hyperthermia cycling in 35 C and 65% humidity, and a control group. WBGTcrit increased after 9 but not 5 days, and rectal temperature rise was only reduced 4 to 8 days after the protocol ended.
tldr: In active adults, 9 days of controlled-hyperthermia heat acclimation raised the heat level they could tolerate before core temperature kept climbing, but 5 days did not. The gain was still present 4 to 8 days after heat exposure stopped.
methods: Participants (heat acclimation 6 men and 9 women; control 6 men and 7 women; VO2max about 46 mL/kg/min) were matched on body mass, VO2max, sex, age and body surface area and allocated by available time. The acclimation group completed progressive heat stress tests (cycling at fixed heat production in 38 C with stepwise rising humidity) before, after 5 and 9 days of acclimation, and after 4 or 8 days without heat; controls completed two tests about 13 days apart. WBGTcrit was set by visual inspection of the rectal temperature curve, and analyses used mixed-model and repeated-measures ANOVA.
findings: WBGTcrit showed a group by time interaction (P = 0.016), rising from 28.5 to 30.5 C WBGT after 9 days in the acclimation group with no change after 5 days. The rate of rectal temperature rise showed no group by time interaction (P = 0.537); within the acclimation group it was lower 4 to 8 days after cessation than at baseline (0.6 versus 0.9 C/h). After 9 days, sweat loss rose by 165 mL/h and starting rectal temperature fell by 0.44 C relative to controls, and only starting rectal temperature showed decay after cessation.
limitations: Visual identification of WBGTcrit left many missing values, so only 6 to 7 acclimation participants contributed to the key analyses, and an objective segmented-regression method did not reproduce the visual result (r = 0.33). Groups were not randomized, rectal temperature responds slowly, and 9 days may not be the minimum effective dose. Controls also showed unexplained drops in skin temperature and heart rate between tests.
practicalImplications: With a controlled-hyperthermia protocol in warm-humid conditions, 5 days of heat acclimation did not raise the critical heat limit, while 9 days did. A short gap of 4 to 8 days without heat exposure after acclimation did not erase the WBGTcrit gain in this sample.
athleteDev: For athletes preparing for hot competition or preseason, the data suggest planning more than 5 days of controlled-hyperthermia heat sessions if the goal is a higher heat tolerance limit. The sample was active adults rather than athletes, so magnitudes may differ in trained athletes.
rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions after injury or heat illness. It measured heat tolerance in healthy adults and did not study recovery from exertional heat illness.

citation: Fashioni E, Langley B, Page RM. The effectiveness of a practical half-time re-warm-up strategy on performance and the physical response to soccer-specific activity. J Sports Sci. 2020;38(2):140-149.
abstract: The authors compared a half-time re-warm-up with a passive half-time break in 10 male soccer players completing a 60-minute soccer-specific protocol. The re-warm-up improved 20 m sprint time, squat jump and countermovement jump after the re-warm-up and early in the second half, with no significant change in 5 m or 10 m sprint, muscle soreness or PlayerLoad. Ratings of perceived exertion were higher after the re-warm-up.
tldr: A 3-minute bodyweight and plyometric re-warm-up at the end of a 15-minute half-time raised jump height right after half-time and gave a faster 20 m sprint 10 minutes into the second half in amateur players. It also raised perceived exertion, and the effects were short-term.
methods: Randomised, counterbalanced crossover trial with 10 male amateur soccer players. Each completed 4 x 15-minute periods of the SAFT90 soccer-specific protocol with a 15-minute half-time, either passive (control) or passive 12 minutes plus a 3-minute re-warm-up of jogging, skipping, dynamic stretches, tuck jumps and sprints. Sprint, squat jump, countermovement jump, heart rate, perceived exertion, muscle soreness and PlayerLoad were compared with two-way repeated-measures models and minimal detectable differences.
findings: Squat jump (30.17 vs 26.96 cm; d = 0.6) and countermovement jump height (31.53 vs 28.15 cm; d = 0.7) were higher immediately after half-time with the re-warm-up, and 20 m sprint time was faster at 55 minutes (3.32 vs 3.42 s; d = 0.6). Heart rate was higher straight after the re-warm-up, and perceived exertion was 1 to 2 units higher at 50, 55 and 60 minutes. No significant trial by time interactions were found for 5 m or 10 m sprint, muscle soreness or PlayerLoad.
limitations: Only 10 amateur male players were studied, in a simulated protocol rather than match play, and the authors note the response may be specific to their methods and participant level. The 20 m sprint and squat jump differences fell within the range of the minimal detectable difference, squat jump height was not maintained and was lower than control at 55 minutes (moderate effect, not significant), and mechanisms were not measured.
practicalImplications: A short, equipment-free re-warm-up at the end of half time produced acute jump and 20 m sprint gains early in the second half without changing soreness or PlayerLoad. It also raised perceived exertion in the second half, which the authors suggest may reflect the unfamiliar routine.
athleteDev: For performance staff, the study supports a 3-minute bodyweight and plyometric re-warm-up as a feasible half-time option, with small acute gains in jump and 20 m sprint performance in the first minutes of the second half. The jump benefit faded within the first post-half-time testing block.
rtp: Not applicable to return to sport. The participants were healthy amateur players and the outcomes were acute performance measures only.

citation: Feser EH, Macadam P, Cronin JB. The effects of lower limb wearable resistance on sprint running performance: a systematic review. European Journal of Sport Science. 2020;20(3):394-406.
abstract: Systematic review of ten studies (116 participants) on lower-limb wearable resistance during sprint running. Micro-loads of 0.6 to 5% body mass increased contact time and reduced step frequency, sprinting with 5% body-mass loads slowed total sprint time, unloaded sprints straight after WR use showed no significant change in total sprint time, and one longitudinal study in untrained participants found no significant change in maximal sprinting speed.
tldr: Lower-limb wearable resistance of up to 5% body mass mainly changes sprint mechanics, increasing contact time and reducing step frequency, with stride length largely unchanged. Its effect on sprint performance is small and has been little studied in training.
methods: Systematic review following PRISMA guidance. PubMed, SPORTDiscus and Web of Science were searched from inception to November 2018 with Boolean terms for limb, sprint and resistance. Eligible studies measured acute kinematic, kinetic or performance effects, or longitudinal effects, of lower-limb wearable resistance in injury-free participants. Of 692 records, ten were included and effect sizes were calculated as Cohen's d.
findings: Eight studies measured acute kinematics. Loads of 0.6 to 5% body mass on the thigh, shank or whole leg increased contact time (2.9 to 8.9%) and reduced step frequency (1.4 to 3.7%), while stride length was largely unchanged. While sprinting with the loads, only 5% body-mass WR significantly slowed total sprint time (by 2.0% and 3.3% in two studies), and in the three acute performance studies unloaded sprints after WR use showed no significant change in total sprint time. The one six-week study of 5% ankle loading in untrained participants increased stride length and reduced stride frequency without a significant change in maximal speed.
limitations: The included studies were small and mostly single-session, and the training study had a single post-test, so the effects of off-loading are unknown. Force production was not measured directly in most studies, and no information on the start and acceleration phases was given for the training study. The abstract reports total sprint time slowing of 0.6 to 7.4%, while the results text says only 5% body-mass loads produced a significant change in total sprint time.
practicalImplications: Coaches can use lower-limb loads of up to about 5% body mass to target step frequency and contact time in short sprint work. Loads should be progressed gradually because added rotational inertia may raise injury risk, and the review does not show that this improves sprint times.
athleteDev: Lower-limb wearable resistance can overload stride frequency and may encourage more horizontal force in acceleration work, with stride length unchanged. Its effect on sprint speed is not established.
rtp: The review includes only injury-free participants and does not study rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-play loading decisions.

citation: Yuan R, Sun H, Soh KG, Mohammadi A, Toumi Z, Zhang Z. The effects of mental fatigue on sport-specific motor performance among team sport athletes: a systematic scoping review. Frontiers in Psychology. 2023;14:1143618.
abstract: Scoping review of studies on how mental fatigue affects physical and technical sport-specific performance in team sport athletes. Mental fatigue impaired physical performance, measured as intermittent endurance and total distance, and technical performance in most studies, with small-sided game results more mixed.
tldr: Mental fatigue from prolonged cognitive tasks tends to reduce endurance and technical skill in team sport athletes, especially in laboratory tests. Effects on small-sided game distance are less consistent.
methods: Scoping review using the Arksey and O'Malley framework, with a search run between March and May 2022 (no date restrictions) of Web of Science, Scopus, PubMed, EBSCOhost databases, Google Scholar and grey literature. Eligible studies were randomised controlled trials in healthy team-sport athletes that compared a mentally fatiguing task with control and measured sport-specific physical or technical performance. Of 431 records, 18 met criteria at full-text stage, and 16 were retained after QualSyst quality appraisal.
findings: Eleven studies examined physical performance. Intermittent endurance fell after mental fatigue in several soccer, cricket and Australian football studies (for example, Yo-Yo IR1 distance of 1,203 m vs 1,410 m in one soccer study), while small-sided game distance was unchanged in some studies. Eleven studies examined technical performance, with impairments in ball losses, passing and shooting errors, and tackling in most soccer, basketball and Australian football studies. Perceived exertion rose in most studies that measured it.
limitations: Only English-language studies were included, and the review covers physical and technical skill but not perceptual-cognitive performance. Study counts are internally inconsistent (12 in the abstract, 16 in the methods and results, 19 in the psychophysiological section), and the number of studies per sport and format is small.
practicalImplications: Prolonged cognitively demanding work before training or matches may reduce endurance and skill execution, so coaches could plan the timing of cognitive workload around skill and conditioning sessions. The studies used induced fatigue in experiments, so the size of the effect in real competition is unknown.
athleteDev: Mental fatigue from prolonged cognitive tasks reduced endurance and technical outputs in most team-sport studies, so the timing of cognitive workload before skill or conditioning sessions is worth considering.
rtp: The review includes only healthy athletes without injury and does not address return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions.

citation: Thurlow F, Huynh M, Townshend A, McLaren SJ, James LP, Taylor JM, et al. The Effects of Repeated-Sprint Training on Physical Fitness and Physiological Adaptation in Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Sports Medicine. 2023.
abstract: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 40 studies of running-based repeated-sprint training (RST) in trained athletes aged 14 to 35. RST produced moderate gains in VO2max, Yo-Yo intermittent recovery distance and repeated-sprint decrement, and small gains in sprint, repeated-sprint average time, jump and change-of-direction measures. Changes to programming compared with a reference program gave little clear benefit.
tldr: Running repeated-sprint training improves aerobic fitness, intermittent running, sprint speed and jump height in trained athletes. Three sets of six 30 m sprints, twice weekly for 6 weeks, was effective and is a reasonable starting prescription.
methods: PRISMA systematic review of PubMed, SPORTDiscus and Scopus searched to 4 July 2023, registered on the Open Science Framework. Included trained or higher-calibre athletes aged 14 to 35 in running RST of 10 s or less with 60 s or less rest for 2 to 12 weeks; quality was rated with a modified Downs and Black index, and multilevel meta-analysis and meta-regression were run against a reference program of three sets of 6 x 30 m, twice weekly for 6 weeks.
findings: Pooled effects (Table 2, 90% CI) were VO2max 0.63 (0.36 to 0.91), YYIR1 0.60 (0.43 to 0.77), RSA decrement -0.63 (-0.86 to -0.40), 10 m sprint -0.34 (-0.47 to -0.21), 20 m sprint -0.45 (-0.69 to -0.21), CMJ height 0.27 (0.14 to 0.39) and change of direction -0.32 (-0.53 to -0.12). Compared with the reference program, one more session per week, one more week, 200 m more volume, two more reps, one more set or 10 m more distance was either non-substantial or came with compatibility with impairment in at least one outcome.
limitations: The abstract's effect sizes differ from Table 2 (VO2max 0.56 vs 0.63, 20 m sprint -0.48 vs -0.45, RSA decrement -0.61 vs -0.63, YYIR1 0.61 vs 0.60, CMJ 0.26 vs 0.27). Table 3 lists VO2max as 2.6 ml/kg/min while the text gives 2.2, and the YYIR1 raw-unit CI reads '1534 to 296', which is a typo. About a third of studies (13 of 40) had no control group, all RST was done alongside usual training, and the review could not model sprint modality or rest duration.
practicalImplications: Three sets of six 30 m straight-line sprints with 20 s passive rest, twice weekly for 6 weeks, is an effective default block. Four sets per session added to intermittent running gains, and a third weekly session impaired change-of-direction ability, so the authors advise against three weekly sessions outside short 2-week blocks.
athleteDev: Use 3 sets of 6 x 30 m, twice weekly for 6 weeks, as a time-efficient block, with 4 to 6 reps per set. A third weekly session did not add benefit and impaired change of direction in the reference comparison, so reserve it for short shock blocks.
