rtp: Limited return-to-sport use: the authors mention late-stage return-to-play as a possible use, but all included athletes were healthy and uninjured, so the data cannot set return-to-play sprint loads.

citation: Chen BY, Chen WH, Liu Y, Fiolo NJ, Fuchs PX, Huang CF, et al. The effects of velocity loss thresholds during resistance training on lower-limb performance enhancement: A systematic review with meta-analysis. International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching. 2024:1-15.
abstract: Meta-analysis of 13 studies (308 participants) of back-squat training with low (0 to 20%) or high (30 to 45%) velocity loss thresholds. Low thresholds gave larger heavy-load squat velocity, light-load squat velocity and sprint gains, while maximal strength gains were similar between thresholds.
tldr: Squat sets stopped at about 20% velocity loss gave better speed and power gains than sets allowed to lose 30 to 45%, while maximal strength changed similarly. Coaches may prefer low thresholds when speed or power is the goal.
methods: PRISMA systematic review (PROSPERO CRD42021247929) of five databases searched in May 2023. Included peer-reviewed randomised trials of back-squat training of at least 4 weeks that used velocity monitoring and ended sets at a set velocity loss threshold; effects were pooled as Hedges g with random-effects models, and meta-regression was run on linear-progression studies only.
findings: Between-group differences favoured low thresholds for heavy-load squat velocity (ES -0.40, p = 0.005), light-load squat velocity (ES -0.39, p = 0.025) and sprint time (ES -0.47, p = 0.022). The CMJ difference (ES -0.24, p = 0.088) and 1RM difference (ES -0.65, p = 0.630) were not significant, and 0-10% vs 20% thresholds did not differ significantly on any outcome.
limitations: The abstract and discussion describe the CMJ advantage of low thresholds as superior although p = 0.088, which is not significant. The sprint meta-regression p value is 0.010 in the abstract and discussion but 0.002 in the results. High-threshold group labels also vary between 30 to 40% and 30 to 45% across the text and figures, and the studies were short, squat-only programs.
practicalImplications: For speed or jump goals, stopping squat sets at about 20% velocity loss or less is the best-supported option. The authors' 10% or less recommendation for sprint rests on the meta-regression, since direct 0-10% vs 20% comparisons showed no significant difference; for maximal strength alone, a 0 to 40% range gave similar gains.
athleteDev: Use a velocity loss of 20% or less on squat sets when the goal is speed, power or jump height; the authors suggest 10% or less when sprint time is the priority, but this is less certain. Strength-only blocks can tolerate wider thresholds, but the review did not test these over a full training season.
rtp: Cannot inform return to sport: all included trials used healthy, non-injured, resistance-trained people, and no rehabilitation or return-to-play outcomes were assessed.

citation: Silva H, Nakamura FY, Bajanca C, Pinho G, Loturco I, Marcelino R. The impact of different warm-up strategies on acceleration and deceleration demands in highly trained soccer players. Eur J Sport Sci. 2024;24:88-96.
abstract: Nineteen highly trained U23 soccer players were tracked with 10 Hz GPS over four weeks across Reaction Speed, Run and Speed warm-up strategies. Speed warm-ups produced the highest acceleration and deceleration demands, and all strategies produced fewer than one high-intensity effort per minute.
tldr: Warm-up type changes how much acceleration and deceleration a soccer player performs, so warm-ups should be monitored as their own load rather than folded into the session total. Speed-based warm-ups were the most demanding and should be planned with the next match or session in mind.
methods: A cross-sectional GPS study (10 Hz) of 19 outfield players across 19 training sessions, in which coaches assigned Reaction Speed (8 to 15 min), Run (9 to 14 min) or Speed (14 to 20 min) warm-ups. Acceleration and deceleration efforts were classified by relative intensity against each player's mesocycle maximum and by starting speed, and compared with paired effect sizes.
findings: Speed warm-ups produced more high-intensity accelerations than Reaction Speed (ES 0.74, 90% CI 0.21 to 1.33) and more efforts starting above 20 km/h, and Reaction Speed produced more moderate-intensity accelerations than Run (ES 1.29). Run was the least demanding, with no high-intensity accelerations and no efforts above 25 km/h. Position differences emerged only within the Run warm-up.
limitations: One team, one coaching staff and four weeks of sessions limit generalization, and warm-up assignment was not randomized. The intensity bands depend on each player's maximum within the mesocycle, and the warm-ups were not standardized protocols such as FIFA 11+, which limits replication.
practicalImplications: The authors suggest matching the warm-up to the work that follows: Reaction Speed before technical-tactical sessions, Speed before high-intensity sessions and Run before longer or moderate sessions, and avoiding Speed warm-ups close to competition. These are untested recommendations, but monitoring the starting speed of repeated efforts follows from its strong effect on acceleration and deceleration counts.
athleteDev: Log warm-up type and count acceleration and deceleration efforts by starting speed, so warm-up load is tracked alongside the rest of the session.
rtp: This study does not inform return to sport, because it measured healthy training players and included no injured or rehabilitating athletes.

citation: Robbins SM, Bodnar C, Donatien P, Mirza R, Zhao ZY, Hoeber S, et al. The Influence of Time of Season on Injury Rates and the Epidemiology of Canadian Football Injuries. Clin J Sport Med. 2020.
abstract: Prospective cohort study using eight seasons of Canadian Football League injury surveillance data. Medical-attention and time-loss injury rates were analysed by week of season, player position, injury type and anatomical location, and the burden of ongoing time-loss injuries was tracked across the season.
tldr: In the CFL, injury rates fell slightly through the season (about 1% per week) and dropped further in the playoffs. Ongoing time-loss injuries built up during the regular season, so medical workload may rise late in the year.
methods: Routinely collected CFL surveillance data from 2011 to 2018 were analysed with Poisson regression, with athletes at risk as the offset. Game injury rates are expressed per 100 athletes at risk; practice injuries are reported as counts only because the number of players at practice was not recorded. Injury burden was the number of players with an uncleared time-loss injury in a given week.
findings: The game medical-attention rate was 45.2 per 100 athletes at risk and the time-loss game rate was 30.7 per 100. Weekly rates declined about 1% per week across the season (rate ratio 0.99), and time-loss rates in the playoffs were lower than in preseason (rate ratio 0.70). Quarterbacks, offensive backs and linebackers had the highest game injury rates, and joint/ligament injuries were the most common game injury type.
limitations: Injury data depended on information from players and medical staff, so underreporting is possible. Practice injury rates could not be calculated, and every injury was counted separately, so repeat injuries to one athlete count the same as injuries to different athletes.
practicalImplications: Medical staff can plan for a rise in ongoing time-loss injuries as the regular season progresses, and for lower new-injury rates in the playoffs. Quarterbacks, offensive backs and linebackers had the highest game injury rates in this dataset and may warrant closer monitoring.
athleteDev: Position-specific game injury rates can help set priorities for monitoring in a professional football setting, with the highest-rate positions first. The rates describe injuries in one league, so they should not be used to set training loads.
rtp: The study describes injury rates and ongoing time-loss burden across a season. It does not measure recovery times for specific injuries or return-to-play decisions, so it cannot inform when an individual player should return.

citation: Saito H, Kutsuna T, Akiyoshi N, Kobayashi Y, Ito S, Ikuno S, et al. The Protective Effect of Preseason Running Workload Against In-Season Hamstring Strain Injuries in Elite Soccer Players. Sports Health. 2025.
abstract: Preseason training may reduce hamstring strain injury (HSI) risk. This retrospective cohort study used GPS and injury data from 67 elite Japanese soccer athlete-seasons (2021 to 2023) to test whether preseason running workload was linked to in-season HSI. Higher preseason sprint distance and sprint count were each associated with lower odds of in-season HSI after adjustment for age, prior HSI, prior ACL injury and prior calf injury. The authors conclude that preseason sprint-focused running may help reduce HSI risk and support season readiness.
tldr: In this group of elite soccer players, more sprinting in the four weeks before the season was linked to fewer in-season hamstring strains. The link is observational and based on few injuries, so it supports planning sprint exposure rather than setting firm targets.
methods: Retrospective cohort study (STROBE reporting). GPS (10 Hz) and session RPE data from the final four weeks of preseason were used to calculate internal workload, total distance, high-speed distance (above 18 km/h), sprint distance and sprint count (above 24 km/h), and acceleration/deceleration count. Noncontact HSI diagnosed by club doctors within 12 months were the outcome. Univariable logistic regression and two multivariable models (direct adjustment for age, prior HSI, prior ACL and prior calf injury, and a propensity score built from the same factors) were used, with ROC analysis and Youden cutoffs.
findings: Seventeen HSI occurred among 67 athlete-seasons. Sprint distance per 100 m was associated with lower HSI odds (OR 0.896, 95% CI 0.822 to 0.976, P = 0.01; adjusted OR 0.892 to 0.899, P = 0.02). Sprint count per 10 sprints was associated with lower odds (OR 0.761, 95% CI 0.633 to 0.916, P = 0.004; adjusted OR 0.755 to 0.763, P = 0.004 to 0.005). AUCs were 0.721 for sprint distance and 0.739 for sprint count. Youden cutoffs were 842 m (sensitivity 0.59, specificity 0.88) and 33.5 sprints (sensitivity 0.59, specificity 0.94). Internal workload, total distance, high-speed distance and acceleration/deceleration count were not significantly associated after adjustment.
limitations: Retrospective, observational design, so the findings cannot show causation. Only 17 injuries, from elite players in one country, and cutoffs were derived and tested in the same data without external validation. 95 of 162 eligible athlete-seasons were excluded for missing GPS or injury data, and each remaining athlete-season was treated as independent although 67 seasons came from 42 athletes; the abstract describes the sample as 67 players. Unmonitored training and environmental conditions were not captured, intrinsic factors such as hamstring strength were not assessed, and injury severity was not analysed in depth.
practicalImplications: Track sprint distance above 24 km/h and sprint count across the final four weeks of preseason, and build sprint exposure progressively rather than leaving it to chance. Treat the cutoffs of about 840 m and about 34 sprints as reference points for flagging athletes with low sprint exposure, not as proven targets. The authors suggest combining GPS monitoring with strength and coordination assessment.
athleteDev: In this group, more preseason sprint distance and more sprint efforts were associated with fewer in-season hamstring strains. Use these measures as part of a planned preseason progression, and check how each athlete is tolerating sprint work.
rtp: The study examines injury risk, not recovery or return to play after an HSI, so it cannot be used to set return-to-play criteria or readiness standards after a strain.

citation: Bouchard MD, Dagher D, Keogh C, Alqahtani M, Khan M. The Role of Vitamin D in Postoperative Tendon Healing: A Scoping Review. Orthop J Sports Med. 2025;13(10):23259671251371300.
abstract: This scoping review of studies on vitamin D status and tendon healing after surgery found 10 non-randomized studies, most on rotator cuff repair. Vitamin D deficiency was generally associated with delayed healing, higher retear rates and poorer functional recovery, but the evidence was low quality and largely retrospective.
tldr: Low vitamin D status is associated with poorer healing after rotator cuff repair, but the studies are weak and cannot show that correcting it helps. Vitamin D should not be used as a healing intervention on this evidence alone.
methods: Systematic search of Embase, Ovid Medline and Emcare to November 2024, following PRISMA-ScR, with two independent screeners and a third to resolve disagreements. Observational studies and RCTs of adults undergoing tendon repair were included, and quality was rated with MINORS. Results were synthesized narratively.
findings: Ten studies were included: seven retrospective cohorts, one prospective cohort, one matched case-control and one case series. Most studies (8 of 10) examined rotator cuff repair, and five of the rotator cuff studies associated vitamin D deficiency with increased risk of tears, revision surgery, retears or poorer function. Half the studies used the same PearlDiver database.
limitations: No randomized trials and no prospective data collection in most studies, with low MINORS scores. Vitamin D deficiency was defined by ICD codes in three studies, and patient overlap limits independent conclusions. The included cohorts were surgical patients, none described as athletes, and the authors found no research on Achilles, patellar or flexor tendons.
practicalImplications: The authors suggest clinicians consider individualized vitamin D assessment as part of perioperative care for tendon repair. The evidence does not yet support supplementation to improve healing, and prospective studies and RCTs are needed.
athleteDev: This review does not show that vitamin D improves performance. Its finding concerns tendon healing after surgery in mostly non-athlete rotator cuff patients, so it should not drive performance supplementation decisions.
rtp: Not a return-to-sport study. It cannot be used to set rehabilitation timelines or return criteria, or to recommend vitamin D supplementation as part of return-to-play planning.

citation: Akavian I, Epstein Y, Rabotin A, Peretz S, Charkoudian N, Ketko I. The Significance of Body Surface Area to Mass Ratio for Thermal Responses to a Standardized Exercise-Heat Stress Test. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2025;57(1):88-93.
abstract: A retrospective review of 517 soldiers' heat tolerance test results after exertional heat illness examined whether body surface area to mass ratio relates to heat intolerance. Heat-intolerant men had a lower ratio than heat-tolerant men, and a higher ratio was associated with lower odds of intolerance. The authors suggest the ratio may inform return-to-duty and return-to-play decisions.
tldr: In men recovering from exertional heat illness, a lower body surface area to mass ratio was linked to failing the heat tolerance test. It is one factor to weigh in return decisions, not a stand-alone screen.
methods: Retrospective reanalysis of Israel Defense Forces heat tolerance test registry data (2007 to 2021) for 517 soldiers with exertional heat illness. Heat tolerance was defined by a rectal temperature plateau in the second hour of a 2-hour treadmill test at 40 degrees C and 40% relative humidity. Groups were compared with t tests, and logistic regression adjusted for age and modelled with splines.
findings: In men, heat-intolerant soldiers had lower body surface area to mass ratio than heat-tolerant soldiers (248 vs 262 cm2/kg, p < 0.01, d = 0.76). The odds ratio for intolerance was 0.97 per unit increase (95% CI 0.95 to 0.99), with the spline plateauing above about 270 cm2/kg. In women, a similar trend was not statistically significant.
limitations: Retrospective registry data from a young male military cohort, with no adjustment for fitness or acclimatization. Only 22 women were included, 3 of them heat-intolerant. Heat-intolerant men also weighed more and had higher body fat, and the authors could not rule out other causes such as reduced cardiovascular reserve.
practicalImplications: When managing return to play after exertional heat illness, a low body surface area to mass ratio may signal a higher chance of failing a heat tolerance test, most clearly in men. The authors recommend deciding return on the test result together with the athlete's history and planned activity, not on the ratio alone.
athleteDev: A low body surface area to mass ratio is one thing to note when an athlete shows poor heat tolerance on a standard test. It does not show which athletes will perform better in the heat, and the cohort was soldiers rather than athletes.
rtp: Directly relevant to return to play after exertional heat illness, but the study is observational and does not test whether the ratio predicts safe return. It should not be used alone to clear or hold an athlete, and the authors note that athletic settings with uniforms and different environments may behave differently.

citation: Hulm S, Timmins RG, Hickey JT, Maniar N, Lin Y-C, Knaus KR, et al. The Structure, Function, and Adaptation of Lower-Limb Aponeuroses: Implications for Myo-Aponeurotic Injury. Sports Med Open. 2024;10:133.
abstract: The aponeurosis is a fibrous connective tissue within and around muscle that is often conflated with the free tendon. This review describes the structure, mechanical behaviour and adaptation of lower-limb aponeuroses, and links aponeurotic injury to longer return-to-play times and higher re-injury rates. It highlights muscle-specific differences and gaps in adaptation research.
tldr: Aponeuroses differ widely between lower-limb muscles and should not be treated as one structure or as part of the free tendon. Aponeurotic involvement in a muscle strain has been linked to longer return to play and higher re-injury, but how aponeuroses adapt to training is poorly understood.
methods: Review using a retrospective, citation-based PubMed search from inception to August 2022 on the structure, mechanics and adaptation of human lower-limb aponeuroses, with studies that did not separate the aponeurosis from the free tendon excluded. One author screened the literature, and weighted means were used to aggregate dimension and strain data where studies were homogeneous.
findings: Longitudinal strain of the medial gastrocnemius anterior aponeurosis typically ranged from 4 to 7% at 90 to 100% MVIC, compared with 1 to 4% at 10 to 30% MVIC. In athletes, aponeurotic disruption was associated with longer return to play (88 days vs 14 to 21 days in one elite Australian football study) and re-injury rates of 31 to 63% for moderate and 33 to 57% for severe aponeurotic injuries across cited studies. Two 12-week overload studies showed small increases in vastus lateralis aponeurosis width (2%) or area (7%), and one 4-week unloading study showed reduced aponeurosis stress (44.5%) and elastic modulus (29%) with increased cross-sectional area.
limitations: Single-screener, citation-based search with no quality grading. Many structural and mechanical values come from cadaver and small in vivo imaging samples, and adaptation evidence is limited to a few studies. Re-injury figures come from observational work that differs in injury classification and follow-up length, and two studies found no significant increase in re-injury within 12 months.
practicalImplications: When a hamstring or calf strain involves the aponeurosis, plan for a longer return to play, and note the injury's location and orientation (central or peripheral, transverse or longitudinal) when estimating prognosis. The authors do not yet support aponeurosis measures as independent risk factors, so the findings should inform rehabilitation planning rather than screening.
athleteDev: Aponeurosis involvement signals a more complex injury, so build longer rehabilitation into planning and check the injury type and location before progressing load. The review does not show that changing aponeurosis properties improves performance.
rtp: Directly relevant: aponeurotic injuries were associated with longer return-to-play times and higher re-injury rates in athletes, and the authors call for rehabilitation tailored to these injuries. The review cannot give a specific return-to-sport timeline, because the reported figures come from different injury classifications and observation periods.

citation: Baker HP, Satinsky A, Lee CS, Seidel H, Dwyer E, Athiviraham A. The Targeting Rule Does Not Increase the Rate of Lower Extremity Injuries in NFL Players Over Two Seasons. The Physician and Sportsmedicine. 2021.
abstract: A retrospective review of NFL regular-season lower extremity injuries from 2016-2017 to 2019-2020 compared the periods before and after playing rule article 8 (the expanded helmet-hit rule). The lower extremity injury rate did not change significantly, total games lost rose, and the sport-related concussion rate fell.
tldr: The NFL's 2018 helmet-hit rule did not significantly change how often players were hurt in the lower extremities. Total games lost to those injuries rose, which may reflect more severe injuries or a few early season-ending injuries.
methods: Retrospective review of NFL players on publicly available weekly injury reports for lower extremity injuries in the 2016-2017 to 2019-2020 regular seasons. Injuries were cross-checked against at least two sources, assigned to pre- or post-rule cohorts by injury date, and compared as rates per 1000 athlete-exposures using incidence rate ratios.
findings: Of 3685 lower extremity injuries, the rate was 34.3 per 1000 athlete-exposures pre-rule and 33.6 post-rule (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.92-1.04). Games lost rose from 4011 to 5352 (P=0.01), and the IR placement difference was not significant (RR 1.15, 95% CI 0.99-1.33, P=0.06). The sport-related concussion rate fell from 5.5 to 3.3 per 1000 athlete-exposures (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.50-0.73).
limitations: Public injury reports lack detail on diagnosis, severity and clearance, and reporting or selection bias is possible. Only four seasons were studied, and the games-lost result was not adjusted for early season-ending injuries. The post-rule concussion rate here (3.3) is lower than the league-published rate for the same period (5.1), and the discussion says games missed due to concussion significantly decreased while Table 3 reports no significant difference (P=0.61).
practicalImplications: Staff should not assume the rule increased lower extremity injury rates in NFL players. Total games lost to lower extremity injury still rose, so injury rates alone may miss changes in time loss, and public injury reports under-count concussions compared with league data.
athleteDev: Not applicable to training or performance. The study measures injury rates and games lost, not athletic performance.
rtp: The paper reports games missed after lower extremity injuries, which is relevant to time-loss planning. It cannot be used to set return-to-play criteria because it has no clinical clearance, return decision or re-injury data.

citation: Bullock GS, Ward P, Impellizzeri FM, Kluzek S, Hughes T, Dhiman P, et al. The Trade Secret Taboo: Open Science Methods are Required to Improve Prediction Models in Sports Medicine and Performance. Sports Medicine. 2023.
abstract: Argues that sports prediction models are poorly developed and reported, partly because teams guard their data as trade secrets. Using open-science data from a prior systematic review of 30 sports injury prediction studies, the authors show that sharing practices were almost absent and call for shared data, code and protocols.
tldr: Sports prediction models are rarely built or validated in ways others can check, and team data is often kept private. Sharing de-identified data, code and protocols would allow larger and more reliable models.
methods: Current Opinion with a secondary extraction of open-science practices from the 30 studies in an earlier systematic review of sports injury prediction models. Practices assessed were protocol availability, study registration, TRIPOD reporting, data sharing, and availability of the model equation or code. The paper also describes options such as gatekeeper data warehouses and synthetic data sets.
findings: Only one of the 30 studies (3%) made its protocol publicly available, and that same study was the only one registered. Three (10%) reported following TRIPOD, four (13%) reported the full model equation, and no machine learning study provided model code. No study deposited data in an open-access database or shared it, although four used open-access datasets available online.
limitations: The extraction covers one earlier set of 30 studies, so it does not measure the wider sports literature. The paper is an opinion piece with recommendations that were not tested, and the authors acknowledge that journal incentives and limited open-science training also contribute to poor practice.
practicalImplications: Before using an injury-risk or load model, staff should ask whether it was validated on other squads and whether its method, code and data are available to check. Clubs could share de-identified data through gatekeeper warehouses or synthetic data sets to build larger samples without revealing athlete identity.
athleteDev: Performance Application: A training-load or readiness model is only as trustworthy as its validation, so staff should check that any model was tested on data outside the squad that built it before relying on it. The paper gives no training prescription or evidence of performance effects.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: The paper concerns injury prediction models in general, not return-to-play decisions. It supports caution about using an unvalidated model to judge an injured athlete's readiness, but it does not evaluate any return-to-play test or criterion.

citation: Matava MJ, Görtz S. The University of the National Football League: How Technology, Injury Surveillance, and Health Care Have Improved the Safety of America's Game. Journal of Knee Surgery. 2016;29(5):370-378.
abstract: A special-focus review of how the NFL has used medical technology, injury surveillance and an integrated health-care network, which the authors call the University of the NFL, to improve player safety. It covers concussion assessment, equipment and rule changes, electronic records, and the league's injury data.
tldr: The NFL's integrated medical network, sideline concussion monitoring and injury surveillance are described as having improved player safety. The review gives no comparison group, so the link between these measures and the injury trends is not tested.
methods: Narrative special-focus review by two orthopaedic surgeons describing the NFL's physician and athletic-trainer network, subcommittees, Combine medical evaluations, the ATC spotter program, centralised imaging and electronic medical records, and the league's injury surveillance. The article includes tables of concussion, ACL and MCL counts from 2011 to 2014. No search strategy is described.
findings: Concussions, counted across preseason and regular season, were 252 in 2011 and 202 in 2014, and the authors describe this as a 33% decline. ACL and MCL sprain totals were lower in 2014 than in 2011 (49 vs 55 for ACL and 138 vs 143 for MCL). The number of injuries in Thursday night games did not differ significantly from Sunday and Monday games over four years. The authors report 39 player-safety rule changes since 2005.
limitations: No search method is described, and much of the data come from league presentations and reports that the paper does not verify. The article has no comparison group, so the effect of the listed measures cannot be separated from other changes. The text gives a 33% concussion decline, but its own Table 1 totals (252 to 202) give about 20%; this summary uses the table values.
practicalImplications: Staff in other settings can use the model of shared team medicine: sideline spotters, shared imaging and electronic records, and periodic injury reports broken down by position, mechanism and game situation. The authors urge other leagues to consider it, but the paper does not test whether it reduces injuries.
athleteDev: Performance Application: The paper concerns medical care and injury surveillance rather than performance training. Its approach of coding injuries by position, mechanism and game situation could help a performance department link injury exposure to training and match load.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: The paper describes systems that support return-to-play care, such as shared imaging, electronic records and second opinions, but gives no return-to-play criteria or outcome data. It can inform planning for records access and care coordination. It cannot be used to set return-to-play decisions for concussion or orthopaedic injury.

citation: Myers NL, Mexicano G, Aguilar KV. The Association Between Noncontact Injuries and the Acute-Chronic Workload Ratio in Elite-Level Athletes: A Critically Appraised Topic. Journal of Sport Rehabilitation. 2020;29(1):127-130.
abstract: This critically appraised topic asks whether the session RPE acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR) is associated with noncontact injury in elite athletes. Three prospective cohort studies were included. The authors report that high ACWR was associated with 2.0 to 4.5 times greater injury risk in two of them, and that low chronic load with a low ACWR was associated with injury in the third.
tldr: Across three elite-level cohorts, a training spike, where the last week's load exceeds the 4-week average, was linked to more noncontact injuries the following week. The evidence is observational and limited to a few squads, so use it to flag load spikes, not as a precise injury threshold.
methods: Critically appraised topic. The authors searched SPORTDiscus, MEDLINE, EBSCOhost, PubMed and CINAHL Complete, plus reference lists, for 2014-2018 English-language studies of sRPE-based 1:4-week ACWR with noncontact injury as the primary outcome. Nine articles were screened and three prospective cohort studies were included: Colby et al (70 Australian footballers), Hulin et al (28 cricket fast bowlers) and McCall et al (171 football players).
findings: Colby et al recorded 97 noncontact lower body injuries over four seasons (9.8 per 1000 h), and a low chronic load with a low ACWR was associated with injury in the following week (adjusted incidence risk ratio 2.52; 95% CI 1.01-6.29). Hulin et al found acute workload above chronic workload was associated with next-week injury (RR 2.2; 95% CI 1.91-2.53), and fast bowlers with an ACWR above 200% had 4.5 times the risk of those at 50-99%. McCall et al recorded 123 noncontact time-loss injuries, and players with an ACWR above 1.38 had 2.13 times the risk (95% CI 1.20-3.77) of those between 0.60 and 0.97.
limitations: None of the three studies calculated statistical power before analysis, and the sample is limited to two football codes and cricket. Session RPE was collected only for practice and matches, so resistance and cross-training load were not captured. The authors' level A grading rests on three observational studies, and the CAT does not test whether ACWR changes injury outcomes.
practicalImplications: Track each athlete's session RPE load and compare the most recent week with the 4-week rolling average, paying attention to weeks where acute load exceeds chronic load. Also flag low chronic loads with low ACWR, which the authors link to injury, and read the ratio alongside injury history, strength and aerobic capacity.
athleteDev: Use sRPE-based ACWR (1-week acute to 4-week chronic) as a monitoring flag for training spikes and for long periods of low chronic load. Do not treat the 0.8 to 1.3 band as a safe zone.
rtp: This paper measured injury incidence in squads during the season and did not study return to sport. It cannot be used to set return-to-play loading or clearance for an injured athlete.

citation: Travis E, Scott-Bell A, Thornton C. The current state of concussion knowledge and attitudes in British American Football. The Physician and Sportsmedicine. 2022.
abstract: Surveyed 236 players, coaches and support staff in British American Football about concussion knowledge (Rosenbaum Concussion Knowledge and Attitudes Survey, RoCKAS), attitudes, reporting likelihood, education and risk perceptions. Knowledge was good (mean 21.0 of 25) and attitudes were generally safe (mean 55.6 of 65), but 45.3% would continue playing with a concussion-related headache and 48.3% had no education in the past 12 months.
tldr: Concussion knowledge in UK American football was generally good, but many participants said they would keep playing with a concussion-related headache. Safer attitudes were linked to a higher likelihood of reporting.
methods: An online survey was sent through BAFA email and social media in autumn 2021, and analysed with descriptive statistics, Pearson correlations and an independent t-test comparing offensive and defensive players' attitude scores. The survey included the RoCKAS knowledge and attitude indices, perceived risk items and education and policy questions.
findings: The mean knowledge score was 21.0 of 25 and the mean attitude score was 55.6 of 65. 45.3% would continue playing with a headache from a minor concussion, and 48.3% reported no concussion education in the past 12 months. Attitude scores correlated positively with likelihood of reporting to a coach or medic (r = .440, p < .001) and negatively with prior diagnosed concussion (r = -.231, p < .001); knowledge also correlated weakly with reporting likelihood (r = .172, p = .008). 63.6% had not accessed or read the BAFA concussion policy.
limitations: The design is cross-sectional and relies on self-report and recall, with likely selection bias from opt-in recruitment. Players, coaches and staff were analysed as one group, and the reported associations do not show causation. The abstract says there was no relationship between attitude and prior concussion history, but Table 5 reports a significant negative correlation (r = -.231, p < .001); this summary follows the table. Table 3 is headed 'percentage of safer responses', yet the 45.3% who would continue playing with a headache are described as the riskiest behaviour in the text; this summary follows the text's reading.
practicalImplications: Concussion education for BAF players, coaches and staff should cover under-reporting and the belief that playing benefits outweigh the risks. The authors recommend regular, BAF-specific education written into the governing body's concussion policy, but this survey did not test whether education changes reporting.
athleteDev: Performance Application: Staff in amateur American football should treat a player's stated willingness to play on with symptoms as a warning sign of under-reporting, and build clear reporting routines into training and match days. The study measured attitudes and self-report, not performance outcomes, so it cannot show how these attitudes affect training or match performance.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: The findings support asking athletes directly about symptoms and not relying on self-diagnosis, since many participants had self-diagnosed concussions without medical diagnosis. The survey cannot be used to set return-to-play criteria or to judge whether a return decision was safe, because it did not measure clinical recovery.

citation: Henning RJ. The differentiation of the competitive athlete with physiologic cardiac remodeling from the athlete with cardiomyopathy. Current Problems in Cardiology. 2024.
abstract: Reviews how to tell the normal 'athlete's heart' from hypertrophic, dilated and arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy in competitive athletes. It covers the evaluation of athletes with symptoms, normal ECG and echocardiographic values by sport type, diagnostic algorithms and criteria, and treatment, including exercise restriction, medication and implantable defibrillator decisions.
tldr: Athletes with persistent cardiac symptoms need a full evaluation, because an athlete's heart can look like cardiomyopathy and both missed and false diagnoses carry real risk. Sport-specific reference values and the diagnostic criteria in the review help separate normal remodeling from disease.
methods: Narrative clinical review of the literature with no described search method. The text covers history and examination, 12-lead ECG patterns classed as normal, borderline or abnormal, echocardiographic reference values for endurance, power, combined and mixed sports, and diagnostic and treatment guidance for hypertrophic, dilated and arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy.
findings: The review states that athletes with persistent symptoms need history, examination, ECG and transthoracic echocardiography, with exercise testing or continuous ECG when the diagnosis is uncertain. It gives sport-specific echo reference ranges (for example, LV diameter 55 mm, 95% CI 50.2 to 59.8, in endurance sports) and says systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve with an LVOT gradient points to hypertrophic cardiomyopathy rather than athlete's heart. For arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy it advises restricting athletes to low-level activity and cites a threshold of 650 MET-hours per year.
limitations: The paper is a narrative review without a described search, and it does not grade the strength of its sources. Some printed reference values contain typographical errors, and several treatment recommendations rely on self-reported ICD shock data from cited studies. The author reports a grant from the Cardiomyopathy Foundation.
practicalImplications: When an athlete has persistent cardiac symptoms or an abnormal ECG, staff should refer for a full cardiology evaluation rather than assume athlete's heart. Interpretation should use reference values for the athlete's sport type, and findings such as systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve should prompt a hypertrophic cardiomyopathy workup. Staff should avoid unnecessary restriction of training when the evaluation shows physiologic remodeling.
athleteDev: Performance Application: For athletes in endurance, power, combined or mixed sports, normal heart size and function differ by sport, so staff should compare cardiac findings with sport-matched norms before changing training load. The review does not measure performance outcomes, so it cannot show how cardiac remodeling affects training adaptation or competitive output.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: The review sets out return-to-play considerations for athletes with cardiomyopathy and implantable defibrillators, including shared decision-making, maximal exercise testing before participation when return is considered, and exercise restriction in arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy. It is a clinical summary for physician decision-making, so it cannot be used by staff to clear an individual athlete to return.

citation: Sharma A, Fletcher AN, Shah JK, Akoh CC, Parekh SG. The Effect of Thursday Night Football on Injuries in the National Football League. Journal of Orthopedics and Sports Medicine. 2023;5(3):304-310.
abstract: Analysed NFL gamebook records of in-game injuries in regular-season games from 2011 to 2015, comparing injury counts by weekday, season week and position. Thursday games had about the same number of injuries as Sunday games, Monday games had fewer, and a team's injuries did not change in the weeks before or after its Thursday game.
tldr: In NFL regular-season games from 2011 to 2015, Thursday games did not have significantly more in-game injuries than Sunday games, and Monday games had fewer. Injury counts rose later in the season.
methods: Descriptive epidemiological study of official NFL gamebook data for regular-season games from 2011 to 2015. Injury counts per game were compared by weekday, season quarter and position with one-way ANOVA and Tukey's HSD tests, and each team's injuries were compared across the Thursday game and the weeks before and after it.
findings: Mean in-game injuries per game were 21.4 on Sundays (1,115 games), 18.2 on Mondays (85 games) and 21.7 on Thursdays (80 games). Thursday versus Sunday gave p = 0.9264, and Monday had fewer injuries than Sunday (p = 0.0028) and Thursday (p = 0.0214). Injuries per team were 10.8 in the week before and 10.8 in the Thursday game, and 10.7 in the week after (p = 0.4971 and p = 0.7315). Week 17 had about twice the injury rate of Week 1 (31.1 vs 15.7 per game).
limitations: The authors list five seasons of data, possible human error or over-recording in official gamebooks, and a regular-season-only scope; the analysis also does not adjust for exposure or opponent, and only 80 Thursday games were available. The text gives the 2011 total as 4,467 while Table 2 gives 4,496, and it gives mean injuries per game for 2014 as 23.5 (13.3) while Table 2 gives 18.8 (4.7). Weekday totals in Table 4 (24,538 Sunday, 1,491 Monday, 1,683 Thursday) differ from Table 3 (24,435, 1,541, 1,736); this summary follows Table 3.
practicalImplications: Staff planning short-week schedules should note that these data show no clear added injury count for Thursday games, but a small increase cannot be ruled out. The authors suggest education on tackling technique and strength and conditioning for defensive players, and they suggest alternating Thursday and Sunday games with Monday games.
athleteDev: Performance Application: Staff can use these findings to think about how game spacing relates to in-game injury counts across a season, and to plan injury-prevention work for defensive positions. The study counted injuries only and did not measure performance, fatigue or recovery in individual players.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: The study does not address individual return-to-play decisions, re-injury after return, or the timing of return. The finding of no residual effect on the following week's injury count applies to team-level counts and cannot guide when an injured player should return.

citation: Perez JR, Burke J, Zalikha AK, Damodar D, Geller JS, Buskard ANL, et al. The Effect of Thursday Night Games on In-Game Injury Rates in the National Football League. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2020;48(8):1999-2003.
abstract: Used official NFL game book records of in-game injuries for regular-season games from 2013 to 2016 to compare injury rates across short, regular and long rest between games. Injuries were lower after short rest than after regular rest, and not different from long rest. Quarterbacks had a non-significant rise in injuries on Thursday games.
tldr: In NFL game-book data from 2013 to 2016, short rest before a game was not linked to more in-game injuries than regular rest, and it was linked to fewer. Quarterbacks showed a non-significant rise on short rest that needs more study.
methods: Descriptive epidemiologic study of in-game injuries from official NFL game books for all 32 teams in the 2013 to 2016 regular seasons. Rest periods were classed as short (4 days), regular (6 to 8 days) and long (10 or more days). Injuries per team-game were analysed with negative binomial regression, Wald chi-square pairwise tests, and exploratory analyses by position and injury location.
findings: There were 2,846 injuries in total. Injuries per team-game were 1.26 after short rest (95% CI 1.06 to 1.49), 1.53 after regular rest (95% CI 1.46 to 1.60) and 1.34 after long rest (95% CI 1.19 to 1.50). Short rest differed from regular rest (P = .03) but not from long rest (P = .56), and the overall test was significant (P = .01). Only the high-impact position group (tight end, fullback, linebacker) differed across rest categories (overall P = .005), and quarterbacks had 0.08 injuries per game on Thursdays against 0.05 on regular rest (non-significant).
limitations: The authors note that game books are kept for media coverage, so injuries that stop play are more likely to be recorded than minor injuries, and players who rotate in and out often, such as special teams players, may be under-reported. The analyses are unadjusted, so causal claims about rest are limited, and the quarterback analysis was underpowered (power 0.50). The quarterback P value is given as .08 in the abstract and results but .16 in the discussion.
practicalImplications: These data do not support assuming that short weeks increase in-game injury counts in the NFL. The higher quarterback rate on short rest was non-significant and underpowered, so the authors treat it as a question for larger studies rather than a finding to act on, and they call for work linking rest to injury mechanisms.
athleteDev: Performance Application: These data suggest that short rest did not raise in-game injury counts in this sample, but the authors note that short rest may still reduce preparedness, recovery and performance. The study did not measure those outcomes, so staff should track them directly rather than infer them from injury counts.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: The study counts in-game injuries at the team level and does not examine return-to-play timing, re-injury or individual clearance. It cannot be used to decide when an injured player should return after a short week, although its finding of no association between rest and injury type, including concussion, is a team-level result only.

citation: Dinç E, Arslan S, Akıkol M. The effect of cam and pincer morphology on hamstring injury rates and return to play in elite young male football players. Acta Orthop Traumatol Turc. 2023;57(1):36-39.
abstract: Seventy-five elite young male football academy players were screened radiologically for femoroacetabular impingement and followed for six seasons. Players with cam and/or pincer morphology (n = 23) were compared with those without (n = 52) for hamstring injury count, recurrence and treatment duration.
tldr: In one elite academy, young male football players with cam or pincer hip morphology had a higher rate of hamstring injury than players without it. Recurrence and time to return were higher too, but these differences were not statistically significant.
methods: Prospective data collection with retrospective analysis over six seasons in 75 elite young male academy players from one club. Hip morphology was assessed on pelvic radiographs at pre-season or pre-transfer examinations using alpha angle, lateral centre-edge angle and Tonnis angle criteria. Non-contact hamstring injuries, their treatment durations and recurrences were recorded. Chi-square and independent-samples t-tests were used, with P < 0.05 as significant.
findings: The hamstring injury rate was higher in players with cam and/or pincer morphology (14 of 23, 60.9%) than without (18 of 52, 34.6%; p = 0.034). Recurrence was 35.7% (5 of 14) vs 27.8% (5 of 18), p = 0.631. Treatment duration was 18.4 +/- 10.1 days vs 12.1 +/- 6.2 days, which was not significant. Morphology players were older (20.35 vs 18.92 years) and heavier (71.5 vs 67.7 kg), and these differences were significant.
limitations: The morphology group was small (n = 23) and the two groups differed in age and body weight, which were not adjusted for. Cam, pincer and mixed morphologies were grouped together, and the sample was one male academy in one country. Range of motion and muscle-length data were not collected. The Results text gives 60.09% and the Highlights 60.1% for injury in the morphology group, but 14 of 23 is 60.9%, which matches Table 2. No p-value is reported for the treatment duration comparison, and the printed inclusion criteria (including a hamstring injury diagnosis within 1 year of the radiograph) are hard to reconcile with the uninjured players in the sample.
practicalImplications: Screening for cam and pincer morphology could help identify young football players who may have a higher hamstring injury rate, so staff may want to monitor them more closely. The study does not show that morphology causes injury or that it changes recovery time. Hip morphology alone should not be used to decide training load or playing availability.
athleteDev: Young players with cam or pincer morphology may warrant closer hamstring monitoring and prevention work. This is an association from one academy, so it should guide monitoring rather than set training prescriptions.
rtp: The study reports time to return after hamstring injury, but the difference was not significant and the sample was small. It cannot set return-to-play criteria or show that morphology should change clearance timing.

citation: Hannah T, Dreher N, Shankar DS, Li AY, Dai J, Lovell MR, et al. The Effect of Game Importance on Concussion Incidence in the National Football League: An Observational Study. Cureus. 2019;11(11):e6252.
abstract: Concussion incidence in the NFL generally rises across the season but stagnates or falls in the final quarter. The authors compared concussion incidence in games where at least one team was still in the playoff hunt with games where both teams were eliminated or had clinched, using 166 concussions from weeks 13-16 of the 2012-2015 seasons. Incidence did not differ between the two game types, and plays per game was the main predictor. Running backs showed a higher incidence in hunt games.
tldr: In NFL weeks 13-16, games with playoff stakes did not have more concussions than games without stakes overall. Running backs were the one position with a higher rate in playoff-hunt games, but the counts are small.
methods: Concussions from weeks 13-16 of the 2012-2015 NFL regular seasons were taken from PBS Frontline Concussion Watch and matched to 256 games. Each game was classed by playoff status of the teams (in the hunt, clinched or eliminated) and compared using Welch-corrected ANOVA and t-tests. A multivariate regression tested the hunt effect alongside plays per game, altitude, temperature and dew point.
findings: Concussion incidence was 0.651 per game in hunt games and 0.623 per game in non-hunt games (p = 0.890). Running backs had higher incidence in hunt games (0.049 versus 0.00, p = 0.004), and tight ends showed a similar but non-significant trend. In the regression, game importance was not significant (p = 0.794), while total plays was (beta = 0.01605, p = 0.025).
limitations: Sample sizes are low in many game-type groups, which produced unequal variances. Week 17 was excluded because teams did not have to report concussions that week, so the data cover less than 50% of non-hunt games. The authors state that their assumptions about player behaviour may not hold. One author is employed by ImPACT Applications, the company behind the ImPACT test.
practicalImplications: Playoff stakes alone did not change overall concussion rates in this sample, so staff should not assume that high-stakes games carry more concussion risk for all players. Workload measured as plays per game was the stronger signal. Running backs in playoff-hunt games are worth watching, but the finding needs confirmation in a larger dataset.
athleteDev: For professional football staff, total plays per game (both teams' offensive plays combined) was associated with concussion incidence across games, while game importance was not. This is a game-level association, not evidence that changing play volume would lower concussion risk.
rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-play decisions for an individual player. It describes incidence across games and says nothing about recovery time or clearance after a concussion.

citation: Walker CR, Belisario J, Abramoff B. The Effect of Probable COVID-19 Infection on the National Football League Players' Performance and Endurance During the 2020 Season. Cureus. 2023;15(3):e35821.
abstract: The authors asked whether NFL players with probable COVID-19 in the 2020 season showed a drop in performance or endurance. Players who spent at least 10 days on the league's COVID-19 Injury Reserve list and had played in two or more games before and after were compared using snaps per game and PFF score per game. Across all players, neither measure changed significantly, but defensive backs and defensive linemen showed declines.
tldr: Among 78 NFL players with probable COVID-19 in 2020, overall performance grades and snap counts did not change significantly after infection. Declines in two small position groups need confirmation in larger samples.
methods: Retrospective single-arm cohort. Players were drawn from the NFL COVID-19 Injury Reserve list (at least 10 days, two or more games either side of listing, offensive or defensive position). Snaps per game and PFF score per game were compared before and after infection with within-group t-tests, overall and by position.
findings: PFF score fell from 62.15 to 61.73 (decrease 0.42, p = 0.33) and snaps per game fell from 38.99 to 38.10 (decrease 0.89, p = 0.30) across 78 players. Defensive backs (n = 6) lost 18.30 snaps per game (p = 0.03) and defensive linemen (n = 21) lost 3.77 PFF points (p = 0.03); no other position changed significantly, and changes were not correlated with age, BMI or days on the list. The authors judge the evidence inconclusive for other positions and for all players combined.
limitations: Confounders such as injuries to the player or teammates, trades, weekly game strategy, opponent difficulty and officiating were not analysed. Position groups were small, 16 position-level tests were run with no correction for multiple comparisons described, and infection status was inferred from injury-reserve listing rather than medical records, so symptomatic and asymptomatic cases could not be separated. The study also could not distinguish infection effects from extra rest before return.
practicalImplications: Across the group, performance grades and snap counts did not change clearly after probable COVID-19. The two significant position-level declines rest on small groups and uncorrected tests, so they are hypotheses rather than a basis for position-specific post-infection plans.
athleteDev: For performance staff, the main finding is that NFL players as a group returned from probable COVID-19 without a clear drop in snaps or PFF grade. The study does not show that defensive backs or linemen reliably lose output.
rtp: The study does not address medical clearance, cardiac screening or safe timing for return to play after COVID-19. It measured in-season output only and cannot set return criteria.

citation: Keerasomboon T, Soga T, Hirose N. The Effect of Variations in Knee and Hip Angles on Electromyographic Activity of the Hamstrings and Related Muscles During the Nordic Hamstring Exercise. Int J Sports Phys Ther. 2024;19(3):275-283.
abstract: The Nordic hamstring exercise is often performed on an inclined board, but isometric hamstring activation across different knee and hip angles has not been well described. The authors measured surface EMG of the hamstrings and related muscles during 5-second isometric Nordic contractions in 13 male volunteers, with knee angles of 30, 50 and 60 degrees and hip angles of 0, 30 and 45 degrees, on a platform inclined at 30 degrees. A knee angle of 30 degrees with hip 0 produced higher activity in three hamstring muscles than knee 50 or 60 degrees.
tldr: In 13 recreationally active men, isometric Nordic holds with the knee at 30 degrees and the hip at 0 degrees gave higher EMG in three hamstring muscles than knee angles of 50 or 60 degrees. This is an activation result, not a strength or injury result.
methods: Crossover study. Thirteen male volunteers performed isometric Nordic hamstring contractions on a 30-degree inclined platform at three knee angles (30, 50, 60 degrees) and three hip angles (0, 30, 45 degrees). Knee and hip angles were monitored with an electrical goniometer, and EMG normalised to maximal isometric contractions was compared with repeated-measures MANOVA and Tukey post hoc tests.
findings: Knee angle had a significant main effect on biceps femoris, semitendinosus and semimembranosus EMG, while hip angle did not. At a hip angle of 0 degrees, all three hamstring muscles showed significantly higher EMG at a knee angle of 30 degrees than at 50 or 60 degrees (p < 0.05), and erector spinae activity followed the same pattern. Semimembranosus EMG at knee 60 and hip 45 was higher than at knee 60 and hip 0 (p < 0.05).
limitations: The study had 13 male participants, which the authors call relatively small, and results may not apply to females. The board was inclined only at 30 degrees, and surface electrodes may have shifted between angles, with possible cross-talk between hamstring muscles. The study measured isometric EMG only and did not test strength or injury outcomes.
practicalImplications: When coaches use isometric Nordic holds on a 30-degree inclined board, a 30-degree knee angle with the hip at 0 degrees produced more hamstring EMG than 50 or 60 degrees in this group of recreational men. EMG is not a direct measure of strength gain or injury protection.
athleteDev: For strength staff, the study supports treating knee angle as a variable in isometric Nordic work, with 30 degrees and hip 0 giving higher hamstring activation in this sample. Whether this builds strength or reduces injury risk has not been tested.
rtp: Not directly applicable to return to sport. The participants were uninjured recreational men and the study measured activation only, so it cannot set loads or angles for a rehabilitation or return-to-play plan.

citation: Kung SM, Suksreephaisan TK, Perry BG, Palmer BR, Page RA. The effects of anticipation and visual and sensory performance on concussion risk in sport: a review. Sports Medicine - Open. 2020;6:54.
abstract: Reviews anticipation of head impacts and visual and sensorimotor performance as factors in sport-related concussion risk, and whether vision training may reduce concussion rates. Anticipation reduced head accelerations for mild-to-moderate impacts but less so for severe ones, and the evidence on visual performance is conflicting.
tldr: Anticipating a head impact may lower head acceleration for mild-to-moderate hits, but the benefit is inconsistent and does not clearly extend to severe impacts. Vision training looks promising for reducing concussion risk, but controlled evidence is lacking.
methods: Literature review of journal articles identified up to December 2019 through PubMed, SPORTDiscus, MEDLINE, Web of Science and CINAHL Complete using search terms on head acceleration, vision training, anticipation and concussion, plus reference-list checks. Only studies of healthy participants were included, and direct-impact studies were the focus for anticipation.
findings: Seven studies examined anticipation of direct impacts: five in vivo (samples of 9 to 32) and two computational. In youth ice hockey, anticipation reduced rotational acceleration for medium-intensity impacts but not severe ones, and linear acceleration was not clearly changed in most studies. Better visual performance was linked to lower head-impact severity or frequency in two of three studies.
limitations: Most included studies were small, single-team or laboratory studies, and the computational models were not checked against live impacts. The authors note the research area is in its infancy and that helmeted sports dominate the evidence.
practicalImplications: Anticipation and visual-motor training could be included as one part of a wider approach that also covers neck strength and protective positioning. Controlled trials are still needed before vision training is used to reduce concussion risk.
athleteDev: Vision and anticipation training may help athletes prepare for collisions, but the evidence is preliminary and the review does not show that such training reduces concussion in sport.
rtp: The review does not address return to sport after concussion and cannot inform return-to-play decisions.

citation: Kim S, Han S, Kim S, Moon J. The effects of knee ligament load using simulated hip abductor and hamstring muscle strengthening during cutting maneuver. Medicine. 2023;102(46):e35742.
abstract: Used musculoskeletal modelling of 40 healthy men performing a cutting task to simulate 30% strength increases in the hip abductors and hamstrings, comparing knee ligament forces and joint moments across models. Hamstring strengthening lowered ACL and MCL bundle forces and knee adduction and internal rotation moments.
tldr: In simulation, strengthening the hamstrings reduced the load on the ACL and MCL during a cutting movement, while strengthening the hip abductors did not. The result is model-based and needs confirmation in real training studies.
methods: Forty healthy young men ran at about 4.5 m/s and performed a left-side cutting maneuver onto a force plate, recorded with 16 infrared cameras at 150 Hz. OpenSim (gait2392 model with ACL and MCL bundles), using computed muscle control and forward dynamics, simulated four models: abductors 30% stronger, hamstrings 30% stronger, both, and control. Ligament forces and knee moments were compared with repeated-measures ANOVA.
findings: The hamstring model had lower anterior ACL bundle force (F = 5.858, P = .001) and inferior superficial MCL force (P = .016) than the abductor/hamstring and abductor models, and lower posterior superficial MCL force (P = .022) than the abductor and control models. Knee adduction and internal rotation moments differed across models (P = .028 and P = .014), with the authors reporting both lowest in the hamstring model. The abductor-only and combined models did not reduce ligament load.
limitations: The strength increase was simulated and not trained, the muscle force parameters come from cadaver data, only a 30% increase was modelled, and only one cutting speed was tested without fatigue or unanticipated conditions. The text says the hamstring model was lower than all other models for the knee moments, but the Table 3 footnotes mark significant pairs only for hamstring versus abductor and hamstring versus control, and the Table 2 post hoc markers do not fully match the text.
practicalImplications: Hamstring strength work may be worth prioritising for athletes who cut frequently, as one way to reduce the simulated load on the ACL and MCL. The study does not show that this reduces injury, and abductor strengthening alone did not reduce the simulated load.
athleteDev: Hamstring capacity may be a useful target in training for cutting sports, since hamstring strengthening lowered simulated ACL and MCL loads while abductor strengthening did not. The study did not measure real training effects on performance.
rtp: The study used healthy participants and simulated loads only, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions after ACL or MCL injury.

citation: Trofa DP, Obana KK, Herndon CL, Noticewala MS, Parisien RL, Popkin CA, et al. The Evidence for Common Nonsurgical Modalities in Sports Medicine, Part 1: Kinesio Tape, Sports Massage Therapy, and Acupuncture. JAAOS Glob Res Rev. 2020;4(1):e19.00104.
abstract: Narrative review of Kinesio taping, sports massage therapy and acupuncture in athletes and patients with musculoskeletal conditions, drawn from publications from 2006 to 2019. The evidence is low-level, with small, short-term effects for some uses and little evidence for sports performance.
tldr: Kinesio tape may be reasonable for athletes with shoulder symptoms before activity, but the benefit is small and short-term. Acupuncture has some support for carpal tunnel syndrome and as a low back pain adjunct, and evidence for sports massage and performance is weak.
methods: Narrative review of publications from 2006 to 2019 found through PubMed and Google Scholar, covering three modalities: Kinesio taping, sports massage therapy and acupuncture. No search terms, eligibility criteria or risk-of-bias method are reported.
findings: Kinesio tape trials showed short-term pain or range-of-motion changes, with no sustained benefit and conflicting strength results. For sports massage, a meta-analysis cited by the authors found immediate benefit for shoulder and neck pain but short-term benefit for shoulder pain only, and performance results were mixed (one study found higher jump height and less soreness, another no change in sprint speed). Acupuncture gave short-term carpal tunnel and adjunct low back pain benefit, while its performance evidence was conflicting.
limitations: The method is described only as a PubMed and Google Scholar search, so coverage is unknown and selection cannot be checked. The authors repeatedly note low-quality trials with short follow-up and limited blinding, and two authors disclose financial relationships with Arthrex, Smith and Nephew, and Stryker.
practicalImplications: The review supports trying Kinesio tape before activity for athletes with acute shoulder symptoms, with the expectation of a small, short-lived effect. Acupuncture can be considered as an adjunct for low back pain or carpal tunnel symptoms, and the authors say massage needs higher quality research before firm recommendations.
athleteDev: Kinesio tape is a low-cost option for athletes with shoulder symptoms before activity, but do not expect it to change strength or sprint performance. The review found no firm support for massage or acupuncture as performance aids.
rtp: Partly relevant: the review covers shoulder symptoms and low back pain, but it gives no return-to-play criteria or return-to-sport outcomes, so it cannot set return-to-sport timing.

citation: Trofa DP, Obana KK, Herndon CL, Noticewala MS, Parisien RL, Popkin CA, et al. The Evidence for Common Nonsurgical Modalities in Sports Medicine, Part 2: Cupping and Blood Flow Restriction. JAAOS Glob Res Rev. 2020;4(1):e19.00105.
abstract: Narrative review of cupping and blood flow restriction (BFR) training in athletes and patients. The authors report possible benefit for nonspecific neck, back and shoulder pain from cupping, and possible strength and endurance benefit from low-load BFR, with limited high-quality data.
tldr: Dry cupping may be reasonable for nonspecific neck, back or shoulder pain, and low-load BFR may build strength and endurance when cuff pressure is controlled. Evidence is limited, and a performance benefit for athletes is not established.
methods: Narrative review of publications from 2006 to 2019 found through PubMed and Google Scholar, covering the history, mechanisms, evidence and adverse events of cupping, and the background, evidence and adverse events of BFR training. No search terms or quality appraisal method are reported.
findings: For cupping, trials and meta-analyses suggest reduced chronic neck, back and shoulder pain, with some benefit in knee osteoarthritis and carpal tunnel syndrome, but the trials are small and of variable quality. For BFR, low-load training increased strength, endurance and cross-sectional area in several studies, and in a meta-analysis cited by the authors heavy-load training gave larger strength gains. A Japanese survey of 105 facilities reported rhabdomyolysis in 0.008% of BFR trainees.
limitations: The review is not systematic, and the authors note sparse recent research and mostly low-quality cupping trials. BFR studies vary in cuff type and pressure, in outcome measures (girth as a proxy for hypertrophy) and in follow-up length, and the athlete evidence is small.
practicalImplications: Dry cupping can be considered as an adjunct for interested athletes with neck, back or shoulder pain, since the authors judge the risk low when it is done properly. Low-load BFR can be added to rehabilitation and strength work with controlled cuff pressure, but heavy-load training remains the stronger option when maximal strength is the goal.
athleteDev: Low-load BFR can be used alongside sport training to build strength and endurance with controlled cuff pressure, but heavy-load work should remain the main strength stimulus. Cupping has no proven performance effect, so it should not be presented as a performance or recovery aid.
rtp: Partly relevant: BFR is described for rehabilitation after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction and distal radius fracture, with reduced pain and less atrophy in the cited trials, but the review gives no return-to-sport criteria or timing.

citation: Morrissey MC, Wu Y, Zuk EF, Livingston J, Casa DJ, Pescatello LS. The Impact of Body Fat on Thermoregulation During Exercise in the Heat: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. J Sci Med Sport. 2021.
abstract: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 10 studies (211 participants, mostly male) comparing high and low body fat groups during aerobic exercise in the heat. Pooled estimates found no between-group differences in core temperature, skin temperature or sweat loss.
tldr: Body fat did not show a clear independent effect on core temperature, skin temperature or sweat loss during exercise in the heat across these studies. Most studies did not control body mass, metabolic heat production or surface area, which limits what the pooled estimates can show.
methods: A PRISMA-guided search of multiple databases for healthy participants doing aerobic exercise in the heat with high versus low body fat groups. Random-effects robust variance estimation pooled core temperature, mean skin temperature and whole-body sweat loss for interventions with unbiased between-group comparisons, and study quality was rated with a modified Downs and Black checklist.
findings: Of 1,222 records, 10 studies with 211 participants qualified (high body fat group 36.7% versus low 17.7%), providing 18 interventions. Pooled estimates showed no differences in core temperature (ES 0.21, 95% CI -0.53 to 0.96), skin temperature or whole-body sweat loss (ES 0.28), and only 7 of 18 interventions normalized heat production to body mass.
limitations: Participants were mostly physically inactive (70%) children and adults under 30, and post-exercise core temperature stayed below 38°C, so the results do not cover hyperthermic conditions. Eight studies were of moderate and two of low methodological quality, and the authors call the unbiased-comparison analyses substantially underpowered. The abstract gives the low body fat group as 17.8% while the results give 17.69%.
practicalImplications: This review cannot show whether body fat on its own raises heat strain, because the pooled comparisons were null, underpowered and limited to core temperatures below 38°C. The one study that matched groups for body mass and surface area found higher core temperature in the high body fat group, so higher body fat should not be treated as harmless in the heat.
athleteDev: The pooled data cannot guide heat-training adjustments by body fat percentage. One included study found that obese boys acclimatized to heat more slowly than lean boys, but this was not tested in athletes.
rtp: This review does not inform return to sport or return to heat exposure after illness, because it studied healthy participants and gave no guidance on timing.

citation: Timmins RG, Filopoulos D, Giannakis J, Nguyen V, Ruddy JD, Hickey JT, et al. The Impact of Eccentric or Isometric Training on Strength, Architecture, and Sprinting across an Australian Football Season. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2023 (published ahead of print).
abstract: Twenty-five male semi-professional footballers completed 38 weeks of either Nordic hamstring or isometric knee flexor training alongside periodised sprinting. Both groups increased biceps femoris fascicle length and eccentric strength, isometric strength fell, and the Nordic group gained more sprint speed.
tldr: Nordic or isometric hamstring training combined with sprint training lengthened the biceps femoris and raised eccentric strength in footballers, while isometric strength fell in both groups. Sprint differences favouring the Nordic group were small and limited to the end of pre-season.
methods: An interventional cohort trial across pre-season and in-season with two allocated groups. Measures were ultrasound biceps femoris long head architecture, NordBord eccentric strength, force-plate isometric strength at 90/90, and a 40 m sprint with split times and force-velocity profiling. Training was matched for volume and time under tension (two sets of four 4-second repetitions), and linear mixed models assessed time and group effects.
findings: Both groups increased fascicle length from baseline (NHE 1.15 cm, ISO 0.81 cm, p<0.001 for each) and muscle thickness, and eccentric strength rose by 83 N in both groups from end of pre-season to end of the intervention. Isometric strength fell in both groups from baseline (NHE -45 N, ISO -80 N). The Nordic group improved its 5 m split within the group (-0.037 s), and at end of pre-season it had faster 40 m times (0.110 s) and higher maximal horizontal velocity (0.26 m/s) than the isometric group.
limitations: There was no control group, and the isometric group was older with a longer baseline fascicle length. The abstract reports the isometric fascicle gain as d=1.70 and the Nordic gain as 1.16 cm, while the results report d=0.81 and 1.15 cm, so the results values are used here. Injury incidence was not measured.
practicalImplications: Either hamstring exercise, paired with periodised sprinting, was followed by fascicle length and eccentric strength gains in this squad, so the isometric hold is a workable alternative where the Nordic is not used. The fall in 90/90 isometric strength may reflect joint angle or contraction mode specificity, so interpret that test cautiously during such programs.
athleteDev: Pair hamstring strength work with periodised sprinting. The Nordic group's sprint advantage was a between-group difference at end of pre-season with no within-group 40 m change, so it is not strong evidence that the Nordic improves sprint speed more than the isometric hold.
rtp: This study does not inform return to sport, because it followed healthy in-season athletes and measured no injury or return-to-play outcomes.

citation: Mai HT, Alvarez AP, Freshman RD, Chun DS, Minhas SV, Patel AA, et al. The NFL Orthopaedic Surgery Outcomes Database (NO-SOD): The Effect of Common Orthopaedic Procedures on Football Careers. Am J Sports Med. 2016 (published online June 16, 2016).
abstract: A case series of NFL athletes who had one of ten common orthopaedic procedures between 2003 and 2013, identified from team injury reports, press releases and other public records. Return to play, games played, career length and a standardised performance score were compared before and after surgery.
tldr: Most NFL players (79%) returned to play after common orthopaedic surgery, but patellar tendon repair had the lowest return rate (50%). ACL reconstruction and patellar tendon repair were followed by shorter careers and lasting drops in performance.
methods: Retrospective case series of 559 NFL athletes who were on an active roster or injured reserve at the time of surgery, confirmed by two sources. Return to play was defined as at least one regular-season game after surgery, and a position-specific performance score was compared with the season before injury. Offensive linemen and special teams players were excluded from the performance analysis, and procedures with fewer than 25 cases were excluded.
findings: Overall return to play was 79.4% (range 50.0% to 96.3%). Return was highest after forearm ORIF (96.3%), tibia IMN (90.9%) and sports hernia repair (90.2%), and lowest after patellar tendon repair (50.0%). Post-surgery career length was 1.6 years after ACL reconstruction and 1.5 years after patellar tendon repair. Performance fell in the first season after ACL reconstruction, Achilles repair, patellar tendon repair and tibia IMN, and stayed down after ACL reconstruction and patellar tendon repair; players who stayed in the league for seasons 2 and 3 returned to baseline games played.
limitations: Public-source data may miss some injuries, and players who left the league for non-medical reasons may be counted as not returning. Retirement confounds the post-surgery figures, the performance score excludes offensive linemen and special teams players, and the study does not compare rehabilitation protocols.
practicalImplications: Staff can use procedure-specific return rates and career outcomes to set realistic expectations and counsel players, especially after patellar tendon repair or ACL reconstruction. A first-season dip in games and performance is expected after several procedures, and performance did not recover after ACL reconstruction or patellar tendon repair.
athleteDev: Performance staff can use the first-season performance drop after ACL reconstruction, Achilles repair, patellar tendon repair and tibia IMN to plan a graded return and monitor output after surgery. The study has no data on specific training or load, so it does not set training prescriptions.
rtp: This study is directly about return to play in professional players: 79% returned overall, 50% after patellar tendon repair, and ACL reconstruction and patellar tendon repair were followed by shorter careers and sustained performance losses. It does not compare rehabilitation protocols, so it cannot show which rehabilitation approach improves return.

citation: DiCesare R, Tahir U, Noori A, Matthies NF, Chahal J, Paul RA, et al. The Use of Dual-Energy X-ray Absorptiometry (DEXA) in Evaluating Recovery After Musculoskeletal Injuries in Athletes: A Scoping Review. The Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2025;13(11):23259671251387342.
abstract: A scoping review of 12 studies (319 athletes, 34% female) on how DEXA has been used to track bone mineral density and body composition during recovery from musculoskeletal injury. Bone density fell after injury, mostly in the injured limb, and some rehabilitation approaches preserved bone and lean mass better than others.
tldr: DEXA can track bone and lean-mass loss after musculoskeletal injury in athletes. Bone density often fell 4-10% in the first 6 months and showed partial to near-complete recovery over 12-25 months after ACL injury, but the evidence is small and mostly observational, so DEXA is a monitoring tool rather than a return-to-play test.
methods: PRISMA-ScR scoping review of Ovid MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane CENTRAL and SportDISCUS (2000-2024) with two reviewers screening independently. Included studies had athletes with musculoskeletal injury, a baseline DEXA scan near the injury site and at least one follow-up scan. Because designs were heterogeneous, the results were synthesised narratively.
findings: Of 1132 unique records, 12 studies were included, seven of them on ACL reconstruction. Bone mineral density typically fell about 4-10% in the first 6 months after injury or surgery and was near baseline by 24 months in several ACL studies, and injured limbs lost about 7-14% lean mass during immobilisation before partial to full recovery. In the one randomised trial (17 athletes with blood flow restriction, 15 controls), time to return to sport was shorter with blood flow restriction (6.42 vs 8.30 months), and that group kept lean mass and lost less bone.
limitations: Most studies were observational or single-case reports with small samples, and the authors did not run a formal risk-of-bias assessment.
