The abstract says that running plus isometric exercise better preserved bone density than conventional programs, but the body reports no conventional comparison for that protocol, so that claim is not supported in the text. The authors also note that DEXA can overestimate trunk lean mass compared with MRI.
practicalImplications: Serial DEXA scans can show whether an injured limb is losing or regaining bone and lean mass, which can guide loading and rehabilitation intensity. Blood flow restriction is worth discussing when faster return and better lean-mass retention matter, but that rests on one small trial.
athleteDev: Performance Application: Baseline and serial DEXA scans can track limb asymmetry in lean mass during rehabilitation. A cited soccer study found no significant correlation between body composition asymmetry and injury, only marginal associations, and the review measures no performance outcomes, so it does not show that DEXA-guided programming improves performance.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: DEXA-measured bone and lean-mass recovery can be read alongside strength and functional tests when planning return to sport after ACL reconstruction or stress injury. The review cannot set return-to-play thresholds, because the authors state that validated thresholds are still needed and most evidence is observational.

citation: Angileri HS, Geier JA, Hadley SM Jr, McLoughlin DE, Owen MM, May JM, et al. The Use of Fantasy Points to Evaluate Return-to-Play Performance After Time-Loss Injuries in the National Football League. Cureus. 2025;17(12):e99333.
abstract: Retrospective descriptive epidemiology study of time-loss injuries in NFL offensive skill players over five seasons (2017 to 2022), comparing fantasy points per game in the injury year with the following season. Reported injuries were associated with a decline of -0.50 PPG (CI -0.67 to -0.33), with the largest declines for quarterbacks and for players with more than three years in the league.
tldr: Fantasy points per game fell by about 0.5 on average in the season after a time-loss injury, with the largest drop for quarterbacks. Fantasy points may be a low-cost, publicly available trend to watch, but they do not replace clinical return-to-play assessment.
methods: Retrospective descriptive study of injuries to quarterbacks, running backs, wide receivers, tight ends and fullbacks that caused at least one missed game over five NFL seasons, using public injury and statistics sources. Return to performance was the change in fantasy PPG between the injury year and the following season, with injured players' totals normalized to games played.
findings: The overall change was -0.50 PPG (CI -0.67 to -0.33). Quarterbacks declined by -1.95 PPG (CI -3.47 to -0.44) and wide receivers by -0.33 PPG; running backs declined by -0.7 PPG and fullbacks by -0.09 PPG. Shin (-3.24 PPG) and arm (-2.65 PPG) injuries had the largest declines, but their CIs cross zero. Games missed were not associated with PPG change (R2 = 0.0047). Injuries after a bye week were associated with a -1.22 PPG change, while injuries before a bye week were associated with a +0.25 PPG change.
limitations: Public, retrospective data with no severity detail (for example, sprain versus fracture), and games missed was not a usable severity proxy. Coaching, scheme, opposition and weather changes were not adjusted for. Injuries were counted separately when a player had more than one, and some values are inconsistent: the abstract says bye-week timing did not alter PPG, but Table 3 reports a CI (0.018 to 0.474) that excludes zero, and some CI bounds in Table 3 contain typographical errors. The tenure effect (-17.10 PPG, CI -21.61 to -12.59) is implausibly large and should be read with caution.
practicalImplications: Fantasy point trends may be added as a low-cost, objective supplement when following an offensive skill player's output after a time-loss injury, alongside clinical assessment. Position and injury location are useful context for expectations, with the caveat that the shin and arm estimates are imprecise.
athleteDev: Fantasy points per game may give a rough, publicly available performance trend to compare with a player's pre-injury level. The study reports group averages, not individual readiness, so it cannot set training loads or prescribe a progression.
rtp: The study can inform expectations that offensive skill players, especially quarterbacks, often produce fewer fantasy points in the season after a time-loss injury. It cannot show when an athlete is ready to return or whether recovery is complete, because fantasy points do not reflect injury severity and clinical evaluation is still needed.

citation: Nara G, Samukawa M, Oba K, Koshino Y, Ishida T, Kasahara S, et al. The deficits of isometric knee flexor strength in lengthened hamstring position after hamstring strain injury. Physical Therapy in Sport. 2022;53:91-96.
abstract: Compared isometric knee flexor peak torque and rate of torque development at 30, 60 and 90 degrees of knee flexion, and hamstring flexibility, between the limbs of 14 male athletes with a history of hamstring strain injury and 14 controls. Peak torque was lower in the previously injured limb at 30 degrees only, and rate of torque development and flexibility did not differ between limbs.
tldr: Athletes with a past hamstring strain still had lower isometric knee flexor strength in the injured leg, but only when the hamstring was stretched at 30 degrees of knee flexion. Rate of torque development did not differ between legs.
methods: Cross-sectional laboratory study. Participants with a history of HSI (self-reported, all returned to full training) and controls had isometric knee flexor peak torque and rate of torque development measured on an isokinetic dynamometer at 30, 60 and 90 degrees of knee flexion, seated with the hip at 85 degrees. Hamstring flexibility was measured with the active knee extension test. Analysis used two-way repeated-measures ANOVA with Bonferroni post-hoc tests.
findings: In the HSI group, peak torque in the injured limb was lower than in the uninjured limb at 30 degrees (P = 0.037, d = 0.55), with no difference at 60 or 90 degrees. Peak rate of torque development showed no limb differences at any angle, and active knee extension did not differ between limbs. The control group showed no between-limb differences in peak torque.
limitations: Injury was self-reported and mostly not diagnosed by a physician, so injury location and severity are unknown, and 64% of participants had no rehabilitation. Only male athletes were studied, time since injury varied from 1 month to 7 years, and four participants' injured side was non-dominant. The design is cross-sectional, and hip extensor activity and muscle architecture were not measured.
practicalImplications: Isometric knee flexor testing with the hip flexed and the knee at 30 degrees may show strength deficits that a standard hip-neutral or 0-degree test could miss. Isometric training at a lengthened hamstring range can be started early in rehabilitation, with pain monitored, as the authors suggest. Rate of torque development did not differ between legs, so it did not add information in this sample.
athleteDev: Performance Application: Strength staff can use a 30-degree isometric knee flexor test with the hip flexed to check between-leg strength in athletes with prior hamstring strain, and include lengthened-position isometric work in their hamstring programme. The study measured strength only, with no sprint or match performance outcomes, so it does not show that these changes improve on-field performance.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: The study shows that some athletes who have returned to full training still have lower isometric knee flexor strength at a lengthened hamstring position, so testing at that angle could be added to return-to-sport review. It cannot set a return-to-sport cut-off, because the design is cross-sectional and does not show that the deficit predicts reinjury.

citation: Pernigoni M, Alfieri AO, Kniubaitė A, Kamandulis S, Conte D, Lukonaitienė I. The Power of Belief: Investigating the Placebo Effect in Post-Exercise Recovery Strategies for Football Players. Healthcare. 2026;14:4.
abstract: The study asked whether a placebo intervention changes the time course of recovery after a football match. Eighteen youth male players completed two friendly matches in a randomized crossover design, followed by sham vagus nerve stimulation (placebo) or passive rest. Match play caused significant fatigue in jump, sprint, heart rate variability, soreness and perceived fatigue. No significant between-intervention differences were found at any time point, but effect sizes showed moderately lower perceived fatigue and dynamic soreness after the placebo at post-recovery. The authors conclude that placebo stimulation did not affect performance or heart rate variability but may support perceptual recovery.
tldr: In youth soccer players, a sham vagus nerve stimulation device did not change jump, sprint or heart rate variability recovery after a match compared with passive rest. Soreness and fatigue scores looked somewhat better after the sham session, but these differences were not statistically significant.
methods: Randomized crossover design with two friendly 11-a-side matches separated by 72 h. After each match, players sat for 20 min with either an inactive (sham) stimulation device (placebo) or in a quiet room (passive rest). Countermovement jump, 10 and 20 m sprint, Ln-rMSSD, static and dynamic soreness and perceived fatigue were measured pre-match, post-match, post-recovery and at 24 h. Linear mixed models and Friedman and Wilcoxon tests were used, with effect sizes reported.
findings: Match play significantly worsened countermovement jump, 10 m and 20 m sprint and Ln-rMSSD, and increased soreness and perceived fatigue, compared with pre-match. No significant time by intervention interaction was found for countermovement jump (p = 0.850), 10 m (p = 0.171), 20 m (p = 0.402) or Ln-rMSSD (p = 0.370), and no intervention main effect was significant. Effect sizes favored the placebo for dynamic soreness at post-recovery (r = 0.32) and perceived fatigue at post-recovery (r = 0.40) and pre-match (r = 0.34). Analysed sample was 18 players for performance and heart rate variability and 16 for perceptual measures.
limitations: Small single-team sample of youth males. Belief in the placebo was not measured. The placebo was compared with passive rest, not with a real recovery method. Perceived fatigue was already moderately lower in the placebo condition before the match, a baseline imbalance the authors acknowledge. Perceptual analyses include only 16 players, because nonparametric tests could not handle the missing 24 h data, and the study was powered on a single earlier study's effect size.
practicalImplications: Athletes' expectations about a recovery tool may matter for how they feel, so staff could consider how recovery options are explained. This study does not show a physical benefit from a sham device, so it should not replace evidence-based recovery or guide training load decisions. Future trials could include a placebo arm and a real recovery arm alongside passive rest, as the authors suggest.
athleteDev: After a match, a sham stimulation device did not improve jump, sprint or heart rate variability recovery in youth players. Soreness and fatigue scores were somewhat lower after the sham session, but not significantly, so they should not be used to set training loads.
rtp: Players were injury-free and the study measured short-term recovery after a friendly match, not return to play after injury, so it cannot be used to judge readiness after injury.

citation: Skorski S, Mujika I, Bosquet L, Meeusen R, Coutts AJ, Meyer T. The Temporal Relationship Between Exercise, Recovery Processes and Changes in Performance. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2019.
abstract: A brief review of the time courses of recovery across physiological systems after training and competition, and how they relate to changes in performance. The authors argue that recovery should be tailored to the individual athlete and periodized across the season.
tldr: Different physiological systems recover on different timelines, and those timelines rarely match the return of performance. Recovery strategies should be individualized and periodized, because too much recovery can blunt training adaptation.
methods: Narrative review of studies on recovery time courses in metabolic, neuromuscular, central and cardiocirculatory systems, with examples from team-sport and endurance studies. No search strategy is described. Two schematic figures show hypothetical time courses for carbohydrate resynthesis, inflammation, muscle damage, soreness and voluntary activation.
findings: In team-sport athletes, maximal strength, vertical jump and sprint performance are significantly impaired immediately after exercise, with full recovery taking 12 to more than 72 h. Inflammation markers peak 24 to 48 h after a soccer match and return to baseline by 48 to 120 h, while neuromuscular function returns to baseline between 5 and 96 h. Muscle glycogen can take 2 to 3 days to resynthesize after high-intensity training, and cardiac autonomic control returns to baseline in about 48 h on average. The authors conclude that no single parameter has yet shown a direct, causal link with performance recovery.
limitations: No systematic search is described, and the authors do not state how studies were selected. The authors note that results on the long-term effects of recovery interventions such as cold water immersion are still controversial. The time-course figures are hypothetical and schematic, not measured data.
practicalImplications: Staff should plan recovery around the training stimulus, since different systems recover on different timelines, rather than applying one fixed recovery window. Because physiological markers rarely track performance, staff should monitor several measures alongside performance tests. Recovery interventions should be periodized, since too much recovery can blunt adaptation in some training phases.
athleteDev: Use the different recovery timelines to space hard sessions, and track neuromuscular and performance measures across days rather than relying on one marker. Match recovery interventions to the training phase, since the authors note that some studies found regular cold water immersion blunted hypertrophy adaptations during strength training periods.
rtp: The review reports that neuromuscular function after team-sport matches returns to baseline over roughly 5 to 96 h, which can inform expectations for match fatigue. It cannot be used to set return-to-play criteria after injury, because it addresses training and match fatigue, not injury rehabilitation or clearance.

citation: Penggalih MHST, Sofro ZM, Oktarini KS, Ningrum RK. The correlation between sleep quality and performance in football athlete. Sleep and Biological Rhythms. 2021.
abstract: This cross-sectional study of 100 male football athletes examined whether sleep quality, measured with the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, is related to resting heart rate, blood pressure and VO2max measured by bleep test. The authors report significant correlations between sleep quality and all four indicators (p < 0.001), and conclude that sleep quality is related to the performance of football athletes.
tldr: In 100 male youth football academy students, poorer self-reported sleep went with higher resting heart rate and blood pressure and lower VO2max. The design shows association at one point in time, so it supports tracking sleep alongside fitness markers, not a claim that sleep changes performance.
methods: Cross-sectional study of 100 male students aged 13 to 18 at a football academy in Indonesia. Sleep quality was assessed with the PSQI (good if 5 or below), and resting heart rate and blood pressure were measured on waking with a digital sphygmomanometer. VO2max was measured with a bleep test, and Pearson and gamma correlation tests were used.
findings: Eighty-two percent of players had poor sleep quality, and 25% had a resting heart rate of 60 bpm or below. Pearson correlations with PSQI score were 0.384 for resting heart rate (r2 = 0.14), 0.421 for systolic pressure (r2 = 0.17), 0.469 for diastolic pressure (r2 = 0.21) and -0.412 for VO2max (r2 = 0.16), all p < 0.001. Gamma correlations were 0.768 for resting heart rate, 0.773 for systolic pressure, 1.00 for diastolic pressure and 0.68 for VO2max, and the authors describe 18% of players with good sleep as also having good resting heart rate, blood pressure and VO2max scores.
limitations: The design is cross-sectional, so no causal direction can be drawn, and only 18 players had good sleep quality. Sleep apnea, body mass index, diet, lifestyle and training adaptation were not examined, and the study does not measure sport performance. The abstract gives the diastolic coefficient as 4.69, while Table 4 gives 0.469, and the text states that 75% had high resting heart rate where Table 2 labels the same 75% as normal.
practicalImplications: Ask young players to track sleep with a questionnaire such as the PSQI, and read sleep alongside resting heart rate, blood pressure and fitness testing when judging recovery. Because 82% of these players had poor sleep, sleep is a practical area to review, although the study cannot show that improving sleep will change performance.
athleteDev: Include a sleep questionnaire with resting heart rate, blood pressure and bleep-test VO2max when monitoring young players' readiness. Treat the link as an association: the study shows poorer sleep alongside weaker cardiovascular and fitness markers, not that sleep changes performance.
rtp: The study used academy players and excluded anyone who dropped out because of injury or illness, so it does not address return to sport. It cannot be used to judge recovery from injury or readiness to return to training or competition.

citation: Leduc C, Weaving D, Owen C, Ramirez-Lopez C, Chantler S, Aloulou A, et al. The effect of acute sleep extension vs active recovery on post exercise recovery kinetics in rugby union players. PLoS ONE. 2022;17(8):e0273026.
abstract: Ten male university rugby union players completed a randomised single-blind crossover study comparing one night of sleep extension (time in bed up to 10 hours) with an early morning active recovery session after a late standardised training session. Physical, perceptual and cognitive recovery were measured before, immediately after, 14 h and 36 h after training.
tldr: A single night of sleep extension after late training improved cognitive recovery at 14 h in university rugby players, but did not improve lower-body neuromuscular recovery, and made sleep more fragmented. Recovery status at 36 h did not differ between sleep extension and an early morning recovery session.
methods: Randomised single-blind crossover over three weeks with 10 male university rugby players. Each week, players completed a standardised 19:30 full-contact session, then either extended sleep or attended a 07:30 active recovery session (15 min bike and 15 min mobility). Wristwatch actigraphy, a wellness questionnaire, a computerised Stroop test, heart rate recovery, running load index, countermovement jump and plyometric push-up were measured. Linear mixed models with effect sizes and magnitude-based decisions were used.
findings: Sleep extension increased time in bed (very large vs control, first night) and total sleep time (most likely, first night; 07:00 vs 04:35, about 2 h 25 min more than control), but also produced greater sleep fragmentation than control (between-group effect 2.85 [2.00 to 3.70]). At 14 h, Stroop completion time was most likely shorter with sleep extension (between-group effect -1.53 [-2.33 to -0.74]), heart rate recovery was likely better with active recovery (-1.00 [-1.85 to -0.16]), and plyometric push-up flight time was likely longer with active recovery (-0.78 [-1.65 to 0.08], p > 0.05). Countermovement jump mean power was most likely to likely lower than baseline from 0 h to 36 h in both conditions. No between-group difference in recovery status was observed at 36 h.
limitations: Twelve players were recruited but only 10 were analysed, and the study was in one squad. Actigraphy cannot measure sleep stages. Baseline sleep was below the recommended 7-9 hours, so a sleep debt may have masked effects. Chronotype was mid-range for all players and could not be analysed. There was no no-intervention control, so sleep extension was only compared with active recovery. The Discussion says HR recovery showed no substantial between-group difference, while the Results report a likely (p < 0.05) advantage for active recovery; the Results are used here.
practicalImplications: When a late session is followed by a short turnaround, extending sleep may help cognitive recovery at 14 h, but it did not improve lower-body neuromuscular recovery. Staff should not expect a single night of sleep extension to speed overall recovery. The study also suggests an early morning active recovery session may not be needed for recovery status by 36 h.
athleteDev: Sleep extension after late training may support cognitive readiness the next day, but it did not improve neuromuscular function and gave more fragmented sleep. Schedules that keep sleep timing consistent may be a safer option for performance staff to consider.
rtp: This study cannot be used to set return-to-play timing or clearance, since it measured healthy players after a standardised training session, not injury recovery.

citation: Romdhani M, Souissi N, Dergaa I, Moussa-Chamari I, Chaabouni Y, Mahdouani K, et al. The effect of caffeine, nap opportunity and their combination on biomarkers of muscle damage and antioxidant defence during repeated sprint exercise. Biology of Sport. 2022;39(4):1033-1042.
abstract: Fourteen highly trained male judo athletes completed four randomised, double-blind sessions: placebo with no nap, a 20-minute nap with placebo, 5 mg/kg caffeine, and caffeine plus a 20-minute nap. Repeated sprint power, plasma energy and muscle-damage markers, and antioxidant enzymes were measured around a running-based anaerobic sprint test.
tldr: A moderate caffeine dose (5 mg/kg) improved minimum sprint power and repeated sprint performance after a normal night's sleep, more than a 20-minute nap did. Caffeine also raised muscle-damage markers, while napping raised superoxide dismutase activity.
methods: Randomised, double-blind, counterbalanced crossover with 14 male international-level judo athletes, with sessions at least one week apart. Sessions were placebo, placebo with a 20-minute nap, caffeine (5 mg/kg), and caffeine with a nap, followed by the running-based anaerobic sprint test. Blood was sampled before and after exercise for lactate, glucose, creatine kinase, urea, AST, glutathione peroxidase and superoxide dismutase. Repeated-measures ANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc tests and Cohen's d were used.
findings: Compared with placebo, all treatments increased maximum and mean power on the sprint test (mean power rose by about 58 W with the nap, 90 W with caffeine and 128 W with caffeine plus nap, Table 2a). Minimum power was higher after caffeine and after caffeine plus nap than after placebo and than after the nap alone (versus nap: mean difference 58.6 W and 102 W). Post-exercise creatine kinase and urea were higher with caffeine, and AST was higher after caffeine plus nap than after the nap alone or caffeine alone. Superoxide dismutase rose versus placebo after the nap (p < 0.001) and after caffeine plus nap (p < 0.001), but not after caffeine alone. Glutathione peroxidase was not significant in the omnibus ANOVA or in any pairwise comparison against placebo in Table 2b. Plasma lactate rose only after the nap with placebo.
limitations: The sample was 14 male judo athletes, all caffeine-naive, which limits generalisation. The sprint test is a laboratory protocol and not sport-specific. Sleep during the nap opportunity was only rated subjectively. No female athletes were tested. The authors say a sleep-deprived study with the same caffeine dose found no benefit, so the result may depend on prior sleep. The Results text says glutathione peroxidase and superoxide dismutase rose only after napping, but Table 2b shows no significant glutathione peroxidase effect versus placebo; the table values were used here. The Discussion's explanations for the findings, such as aerobic glycolysis and sleep inertia, are not directly measured.
practicalImplications: In rested, caffeine-naive athletes, a 5 mg/kg caffeine dose improved repeated sprint performance more than a 20-minute nap. A nap alone improved maximum and mean sprint power but not minimum power. Eleven of 14 participants had their highest minimum power in the caffeine-plus-nap session. Caffeine also raised post-exercise muscle-damage markers, so staff should weigh that cost.
athleteDev: A 5 mg/kg caffeine dose before a repeated-sprint session can improve sprint power in rested, caffeine-naive athletes, and a short nap may add to this. Muscle-damage markers rose with caffeine, so the trade-off should be weighed. Results may not apply to habitual caffeine users.
rtp: This study cannot be used for return-to-play decisions. It tested healthy athletes in a laboratory sprint protocol and measured no injury or rehabilitation outcomes.

citation: Arc-Chagnaud C, Dugué B, Bouzigon R, Pla R, Bosquet L, D-day Consortium, et al. The effectiveness of cryostimulation exposure on sleep and recovery in male athletes: Timing considerations. Eur J Sport Sci. 2024.
abstract: The study aimed to test whether whole-body cryostimulation after training improves sleep and recovery, and which timing is best: immediately after training or one hour before bed. Twenty-two well-trained male athletes or triathletes completed three randomised crossover sessions. WBC did not change subjective or objective sleep, but it increased cardiac parasympathetic activity during deep sleep, most clearly after the exposure one hour before bed, where core body temperature was also lowest.
tldr: In trained male endurance athletes, cryostimulation after evening training did not change any sleep measure, whether given straight after training or one hour before bed. The before-bed timing gave the clearest deep-sleep heart rate variability and core temperature changes.
methods: Randomised controlled crossover protocol in 22 well-trained male athletes or triathletes, run in winter with outdoor training at 5 to 10 C. Each completed a 70-minute interval running session at 18:00 and one night of home sleep analysis under WBC after training, WBC one hour before their own bedtime, or control, with sessions seven days apart; WBC was 30 s at -25 C then 3 min at -70 C. Sleep was measured with an EEG headband, wrist actigraphy, overnight heart rate variability, an ingested temperature pill and perceptual scales, analysed with two-way repeated-measures ANOVA.
findings: No sleep parameter differed between the three nights, including total sleep time, slow-wave sleep, sleep efficiency, movements and perceived sleep quality. Heart rate variability showed a condition effect only in the 10-minute slow-wave sleep window, with RMSSD, PNS index, SD1 and LF/HF favouring the 22:00 condition over control; whole-night and first-4-hour values did not differ. Core body temperature fell more after bedtime in the 22:00 condition, and muscle soreness and perceived recovery did not differ significantly between conditions.
limitations: Only male participants were included, and the authors note that responses in women may differ and that the menstrual cycle was not considered. Each condition was measured over a single night in good sleepers during winter, which the authors say may not favour detecting sleep effects. The sample was small and well-trained, which limits extrapolation to other populations.
practicalImplications: Cryostimulation after evening training did not change sleep in this group at either timing, so the data do not support using it as a sleep aid. If it is used for recovery, exposure about one hour before bed produced larger deep-sleep parasympathetic and core temperature changes than exposure straight after training.
athleteDev: For performance staff using whole-body cryostimulation with trained male endurance athletes, the study suggests a session about one hour before bed gives stronger overnight autonomic and temperature responses than one straight after an evening session. Whether these responses improve next-day performance was not tested.
rtp: Not applicable to return to sport. The participants were healthy, well-trained athletes, and the study cannot show whether cryostimulation helps recovery after injury or during rehabilitation.

citation: Altarriba-Bartes A, Vicens-Bordas J, Peña J, Alarcón-Palacios F, Sixtos-Meliton LA, Matabosch-Pijuan M, et al. The effectiveness of two comprehensive recovery protocols on performance and physiological measures in elite soccer players: A parallel group-randomized trial. Int J Sports Sci Coach. 2023.
abstract: The authors compared two comprehensive post-game recovery protocols in 18 players from the Mexican U-21 national team, randomised to a foam roller and tart cherry protocol or a stretching protocol, both with a carbohydrate-protein shake and cold-water immersion. Creatine kinase, jump, hamstring strength, perceived recovery and soreness were measured up to 68 h after a game. Both protocols showed time effects, and no significant differences were found between them.
tldr: Two broad post-game recovery combinations gave similar creatine kinase, neuromuscular and soreness time courses in elite young players. Neither was shown to beat no intervention, because the trial had no control group.
methods: Parallel-group randomised trial (registered NCT04716049) with block randomisation stratified by playing position. Players were allocated to protocol (a), a carbohydrate-protein shake, foam roller, 10 min cold-water immersion and tart cherry juice concentrate (n = 9), or protocol (b), a shake, static stretching and intermittent cold-water immersion (n = 9), after an unofficial game and the day after. Creatine kinase (CK-MM), countermovement jump, hamstring maximal voluntary contraction, perceived recovery and soreness were measured before, immediately after, and at 20, 44 and 68 h post-game and analysed with mixed models.
findings: All outcomes showed large time effects, with no group main effect for any outcome. Creatine kinase peaked at 20 h and normalised by 68 h, while neuromuscular and perceptual outcomes returned to similar baseline levels by 44 h. Group by time interactions for countermovement jump, non-dominant hamstring strength and perceived recovery reflected changes only in protocol (a) at post-game and 20 h, including a 3.2 cm jump drop at 20 h versus 1.1 cm in protocol (b). The rise in creatine kinase from pre- to post-game correlated with accelerations, decelerations, high-speed running and sprint distance, but not total distance.
limitations: Only male players were studied, the convenience sample was small, and there was no control group because the authors judged one unsuitable in this professional context. The abstract describes the interaction changes as being in 'neuromuscular and muscle soreness', but the results table shows the muscle soreness interaction was not significant (p = .34) and the significant perceptual interaction was for perceived recovery.
practicalImplications: After a game, both recovery combinations in this trial produced similar time courses for creatine kinase, neuromuscular function and soreness, so the choice between them can rest on player preference and facilities. The trial cannot say whether either combination is better than standard care or rest.
athleteDev: For performance staff, the study suggests the two recovery combinations are interchangeable for elite young male players over a 68 h post-game window. The link between creatine kinase rise and acceleration, deceleration and sprint loads is a single-game correlation in 18 players, not a validated tool for judging recovery.
rtp: Not applicable to return to sport. The players were uninjured national-team members, and the study measured post-game recovery markers only, so it cannot guide rehabilitation or return-to-play decisions.

citation: Cochrane-Snyman KC, Cruz C, Morales J, Coles M. The effects of cannabidiol oil on noninvasive measures of muscle damage in men. Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise. 2021;53(7):1460-1472.
abstract: Investigated whether 150 mg CBD oil, compared with placebo, affects perceived soreness, arm circumference, joint angle, peak torque and RPE after eccentric elbow-flexor exercise in 13 untrained men. No condition effects or interactions were found, only time effects from the exercise-induced damage.
tldr: A 150 mg daily CBD dose taken after eccentric arm exercise did not change soreness, arm swelling, joint angle or strength compared with placebo in untrained men. Soreness and joint angle changed over time in both conditions, showing the exercise caused some muscle damage.
methods: Double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover design in which 13 untrained men took 150 mg CBD (two 75 mg doses 8 h apart) or placebo on the exercise day and at 24 and 48 h, after 6 sets of 10 maximal eccentric elbow-flexor actions on an isokinetic dynamometer. Soreness, arm circumference, hanging joint angle, peak torque and RPE were measured before, after and at 24, 48 and 72 h.
findings: No condition-by-time interaction or condition main effect was significant for perceived soreness, arm circumference, joint angle or peak torque (all P > 0.05). Time effects were significant for soreness (P < 0.001, partial eta squared 0.71), joint angle (P = 0.006) and RPE (P = 0.004). Peak torque fell about 12% from pre- to post-exercise across conditions, but this was not statistically significant across all visits.
limitations: Only 13 untrained men were studied, with a single dose and schedule (about 2 mg/kg per day) and no blood markers of inflammation or muscle damage. The abstract describes four ANOVAs while the methods describe five (RPE included), and the age is given as 21 years in one place and 21.85 years in another.
practicalImplications: For untrained adults, this dose and schedule of CBD oil would not be expected to reduce soreness or range-of-motion loss after heavy eccentric work, so the evidence does not support using it as a recovery aid at this dose.
athleteDev: The study tested untrained men, so it does not apply directly to trained athletes. It gives no support for CBD as a performance-recovery aid at this dose.
rtp: The study does not address injury rehabilitation or return to sport and cannot inform return-to-play decisions.

citation: Malta ES, Dutra YM, Broatch JR, Bishop DJ, Zagatto AM. The Effects of Regular Cold-Water Immersion Use on Training-Induced Changes in Strength and Endurance Performance: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis. Sports Medicine. 2020.
abstract: Meta-analysis of 8 controlled studies of regular post-training cold-water immersion (CWI) during resistance or endurance training. CWI was associated with smaller strength gains, but did not change endurance performance gains.
tldr: Regular cold-water immersion after resistance training appears to blunt strength gains. After endurance training it did not change aerobic performance gains in these studies.
methods: PRISMA systematic review of MEDLINE, CENTRAL and SPORTDiscus searched to 25 November 2019, registered on PROSPERO (CRD42018098898). Included controlled trials with CWI at 15 C or below after training of at least 3 weeks, with baseline and post-training strength or aerobic performance measures; quality was rated with the PEDro scale and risk of bias with the Cochrane tool, and effects were pooled as standardised mean differences.
findings: In resistance training, CWI reduced gains in 1RM, maximal isometric strength and strength endurance (overall SMD -0.60, 95% CI -0.87 to -0.33; p < 0.0001) and in ballistic efforts (overall SMD -0.61, 95% CI -1.11 to -0.11; p = 0.02). In endurance training, CWI had no effect on time-trial mean power or maximal aerobic power (overall SMD -0.07, 95% CI -0.54 to 0.53; p = 0.71) or on time-trial duration (overall SMD 0.00; p = 1.00).
limitations: Eight studies with 470 volunteers, mean PEDro quality 5.3 (moderate), no studies blinded, and most with unclear or high risk of bias for randomisation. Water temperature and duration varied widely across studies, and the endurance and resistance subgroups were small (4 to 5 studies each). Participants were trained, physically active, recreationally active or sedentary men rather than competitive athletes.
practicalImplications: The authors suggest avoiding regular cold-water immersion during training blocks focused on strength, hypertrophy or power, and say it may be most useful around competition when heavy resistance training is not typical. They note the optimal temperature and duration for training adaptation is unknown.
athleteDev: For strength, hypertrophy or power blocks, avoid scheduling regular post-session cold-water immersion. For endurance blocks, regular immersion did not change aerobic gains in these studies, so the decision should rest on recovery needs rather than expected adaptation.
rtp: Cannot inform return-to-sport decisions: all participants were healthy and the outcomes were training adaptations, not injury recovery, rehabilitation or readiness after injury.

citation: Renaghan E, Wishon MJ, Wittels HL, Feigenbaum LA, Bellamy K, Hatfield M, et al. The effects of relaxation techniques following acute, high intensity football training on parasympathetic reactivation. Front Sports Act Living. 2023;5:1267631.
abstract: Thirty-eight Division-I male football players were measured under three post-training conditions: 15 minutes of guided mindfulness, 15 minutes of rest, or no intervention. Both relaxation conditions produced larger drops in heart rate and respiration rate and larger HRV increases than no intervention.
tldr: A 15-minute guided mindfulness session or a seated rest period after high-intensity football training lowered heart rate and breathing rate and raised HRV more than usual post-training activity. Staff could use either as a low-equipment step, but the effect was measured in one squad over single sessions.
methods: Repeated-measures, non-randomised design with each athlete tested in all three conditions, one Monday per condition, after routine preseason training. Heart rate, respiration rate, SDNN and rMSSD were recorded with an armband monitor (Warfighter Monitor) before, during and after the 15-minute intervention and analysed by repeated-measures ANOVA with Tukey correction.
findings: Heart rate fell by 81.6 bpm after mindfulness, 66.4 bpm after rest and 40.9 bpm after no intervention, and both relaxation conditions produced larger falls than no intervention (p < 0.0000), with mindfulness larger than rest (p < 0.05). Post-intervention SDNN was 46.9 ms after mindfulness, 42.9 ms after rest and 33.1 ms after no intervention, and rMSSD was 17.9, 16.7 and 13.8 ms respectively.
limitations: Condition order was fixed by week, so condition and time cannot be separated, and the design is not randomised. Group sizes (35, 36, 33) do not match the stated sample of 38, no a priori power analysis was run, and four authors are employees of Tiger Tech Solutions, which owns the Warfighter Monitor. SDNN and rMSSD labels are inconsistent between the results text, Table 1 and Table 2, so the HRV values should be read with caution.
practicalImplications: A 15-minute guided mindfulness session or seated rest straight after a high-intensity session is a low-equipment way to lower heart rate and raise HRV in the short term. Mindfulness produced larger falls in heart rate and breathing rate than rest, but that comparison is also confounded by the fixed week order.
athleteDev: A 15-minute block of guided breathing or seated rest in the minutes after hard training can bring heart rate down faster than usual post-training activity. The study did not measure performance or next-day readiness, so it does not show that this improves either.
rtp: Cannot inform return-to-sport decisions: it tested starters after single training sessions, with no injured or returning players and no readiness or performance outcomes.

citation: Read DB, Williams S, Fullagar HHK, Weakley JJS. The effects of travel on performance: a 13-year analysis of the National Rugby League (NRL) competition. Science and Medicine in Football. 2022;6(1):60-65.
abstract: Analysis of 2,352 NRL matches (2007 to 2019) found that longer away travel was associated with a lower chance of winning and a smaller points difference. The effect of travel shrank over the 13 seasons, with no clear differences between states.
tldr: In the NRL, each 1,000 km of away travel was linked to a small drop in winning chances and in points margin. The effect has shrunk over time, but the win-probability estimate is imprecise.
methods: Exploratory retrospective analysis of official NRL match results from 2007 to 2019, excluding draws, play-offs and matches where a team played a home fixture outside its home city. Win or loss was modelled with a generalised linear mixed model and points difference with a linear mixed model, with team nested within season as a random effect and covariates for away disadvantage, turnaround time and opposition final ranking; travel was the straight-line distance from the away team's home stadium to the venue.
findings: Each 1,000 km of travel was associated with a 2.7% lower win probability (95% CI -5.7 to 0.3%) and a 1.1-point lower points difference (95% CI -2.0 to -0.2). Playing away had an odds ratio of 0.56 (0.48 to 0.66) for winning, and the travel effect was largest in 2007 to 2009 (-2.7%, 95% CI -4.7 to -0.6%) and close to zero in 2018 to 2019 (1.1%, 95% CI -1.2 to 3.3%).
limitations: Not all travel-related factors could be measured, travel outside matches was unknown, and no individual athlete measures were collected. The team's own ability was not modelled, and the single Victorian team (six titles in 13 seasons) showed no travel penalty, so the authors say a team-by-team analysis is needed.
practicalImplications: Coaches can estimate the likely effect of an away trip on match outcome and use it when planning travel logistics, sleeping arrangements and nutrition. The authors note that teams travelling more than 2,000 km for away matches could expect about 2.2 fewer points and a 5.4% lower winning likelihood on average.
athleteDev: Use the travel distance of an away fixture as a planning input for sleep, meals and logistics, because longer trips were linked to small average performance losses in this league. The study does not show that any specific travel strategy reduces those losses.
rtp: Does not inform return to sport: it analyses team match results for players in the competition, with no injury, rehabilitation or return-to-play data.

citation: Boukhris O, Trabelsi K, Suppiah H, Ammar A, Clark CCT, Jahrami H, et al. The Impact of Daytime Napping Following Normal Night-Time Sleep on Physical Performance: A Systematic Review, Meta-analysis and Meta-regression. Sports Med. 2023.
abstract: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 18 studies (269 physically active or athletic participants) comparing daytime naps with no nap after normal night sleep. Naps improved 5-m shuttle run highest distance, total distance and fatigue index, with no clear effect on muscle force.
tldr: A nap after a normal night's sleep improved 5-m shuttle run distance and reduced fatigue in these studies. The evidence for sprint, jump, Wingate, repeated sprint and endurance outcomes is too thin to recommend napping for those measures.
methods: A PRISMA-guided search of seven databases, supplemented by reference lists and expert contact, with QualSyst quality ratings. Random-effects meta-analysis, heterogeneity statistics, sensitivity and cumulative analyses, publication bias tests and meta-regression were used, and only physically active or athletic participants with normal night sleep were included.
findings: Compared with no nap, napping increased 5-m shuttle run highest distance (ES 1.026, 95% CI 0.718 to 1.334) and total distance (ES 0.737, 95% CI 0.488 to 0.985), and reduced fatigue index (ES 0.839, 95% CI 0.211 to 1.458). Muscle force did not change (ES 0.175, p=0.267). Meta-regression suggested a longer gap between the end of the nap and exercise was associated with a larger fatigue index reduction (p=0.04).
limitations: Most studies estimated nap duration or used actigraphy, so sleep stages and sleep inertia were not measured. Participants were almost all male, and studies after sleep restriction or deprivation were excluded, so the findings do not cover those conditions.
practicalImplications: After a normal night's sleep, a daytime nap before an afternoon session may help repeated shuttle-sprint performance like the 5-m shuttle run test. A longer gap between the end of the nap and exercise was linked to a larger fatigue index benefit, so allow time to clear sleep inertia; nap duration itself did not moderate the effect.
athleteDev: For repeated shuttle-sprint work after a normal night's sleep, a nap with enough time to wake fully before training may help. Benefits for sprint, jump, strength and endurance performance are not established.
rtp: This review does not inform return to sport, because it included physically active people and athletes after normal sleep and no injured or recovering athletes.

citation: Grgic J, Mikulic P, Schoenfeld BJ, Bishop DJ, Pedisic Z. The Influence of Caffeine Supplementation on Resistance Exercise: A Review. Sports Med. 2018.
abstract: A review that critically evaluates the evidence on caffeine supplementation before resistance exercise and gives practical guidelines on dosing. It covers maximal strength, muscular endurance, power, perceived exertion, pain, muscle damage, hormones, blood pressure, caffeine form, habitual intake, timing, genetics and placebo effects.
tldr: Caffeine appears to acutely raise maximal strength, muscular endurance and power in resistance exercise, and doses of 3 to 9 mg per kg about 60 minutes before exercise look adequate. It can raise blood pressure, so people with high blood pressure need caution.
methods: Narrative review of the caffeine and resistance exercise literature, covering 1RM, isometric and isokinetic strength, muscular endurance, power, delayed-onset muscle soreness, muscle damage, hormonal and cardiovascular responses, dose, timing, caffeine form and genetics. The authors draw on earlier meta-analyses, and no systematic search method is described.
findings: The authors report that caffeine increases 1RM and MVC strength and muscular endurance, and enhances power, with effects that may depend on dose and external load. Effects on perceived exertion and pain perception are inconsistent, and there is preliminary evidence that caffeine can reduce soreness. Caffeine acutely increases systolic blood pressure in several studies, while the hormone increases are of questionable practical significance.
limitations: The review is narrative, and most of the underlying studies have small samples, are mostly in men, and often include untrained or recreationally trained participants. Placebo effects and blinding are a concern, and the authors call for research in women, competitive powerlifters and weightlifters, and long-term adaptation.
practicalImplications: The authors suggest starting with a lower dose such as 3 mg per kg taken about 60 minutes before exercise, then adjusting to the individual. Athletes in power-dominated events may consider caffeine before training, and caution is advised for people with high blood pressure.
athleteDev: For strength and power sessions, a pre-session caffeine dose of about 3 to 9 mg per kg taken about 60 minutes before training may help, starting low and adjusting to the athlete's response. Evidence in trained athletes is thin because most studies used untrained or recreationally trained men.
rtp: This review does not study injured athletes or return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions. Its blood pressure findings are relevant to health screening rather than rehabilitation.

citation: Trommelen J, Betz MW, van Loon LJC. The Muscle Protein Synthetic Response to Meal Ingestion Following Resistance-Type Exercise. Sports Med. 2019.
abstract: A review of dietary and non-dietary factors that modify the muscle protein synthetic response to feeding after resistance-type exercise. It covers protein amount, protein type, digestion and absorption rate, mixed-meal composition, micronutrients, alcohol, habitual energy and protein intake, exercise, ageing, sex, body size and whole-body protein balance.
tldr: About 20 g of rapidly digestible protein gives a near-maximal muscle protein synthesis response after resistance exercise, and 40 g or more may suit slower proteins or long gaps between meals. Alcohol and prolonged energy restriction can blunt the response.
methods: Narrative review by the authors of studies on protein dose, protein type, digestion kinetics, mixed meals, micronutrients, alcohol, habitual intake, exercise, ageing, sex, body size and whole-body protein balance. No search method is described.
findings: Around 20 g of isolated, rapidly digestible protein gives a near-maximal response at rest and after exercise, and doubling to 40 g adds about 10 to 20%. Animal proteins generally produce more synthesis than plant proteins, and slower proteins may need 40 g or more for a prolonged response. Alcohol and prolonged energy restriction reduce the response, and a higher protein intake can offset some of the reduction during energy restriction; findings on excess body fat are inconsistent and likely confounded by activity level.
limitations: Most evidence comes from isolated protein drinks given over 4 to 5 hours, mostly in healthy young adults, so transfer to mixed meals, longer periods and older athletes is uncertain. Only one study has measured muscle protein synthesis after a mixed meal, and synthesis is a short-term marker that does not always match changes in muscle mass.
practicalImplications: A practical per-meal target after resistance exercise is about 20 g of high-quality, fast-digesting protein. Slower proteins or long gaps before the next meal may call for 40 g or more, and the authors suggest older athletes aim for about 30 g per meal. Binge drinking and high-dose antioxidant supplements should be avoided around training.
athleteDev: After resistance sessions, about 20 g of high-quality protein gives a near-maximal response, and slower proteins such as casein may need 40 g or more if the next meal is six or more hours away. Limit binge drinking around training, because alcohol blunts the response to protein.
rtp: This review concerns healthy, mainly young adults after resistance exercise and does not study injured athletes or return to sport. The authors note that disuse and lower intake can reduce the protein response, but this was not tested in injured athletes.

citation: Trommelen J, van Lieshout GAA, Nyakayiru J, Holwerda AM, Smeets JSJ, Hendriks FK, et al. The anabolic response to protein ingestion during recovery from exercise has no upper limit in magnitude and duration in vivo in humans. Cell Rep Med. 2023;4:101324.
abstract: Randomized, placebo-controlled tracer study in 36 healthy, recreationally active young men who ingested 0, 25 or 100 g of intrinsically labelled milk protein after a single bout of resistance exercise. The authors report that the magnitude and duration of the postprandial anabolic response, including plasma amino acid availability, muscle protein synthesis and whole-body protein balance, increased with the larger dose, while protein oxidation was barely affected.
tldr: A single 100 g protein dose after resistance exercise produced a larger and longer-lasting muscle protein synthesis response than 25 g in healthy young men. The study does not show that larger doses improve training outcomes, and it did not test athletes.
methods: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in healthy, recreationally active men aged 18 to 40, with 12 per group ingesting 0, 25 or 100 g of intrinsically labelled milk protein after a whole-body resistance exercise session. A quadruple isotope tracer feeding-infusion approach with plasma and muscle biopsies was sampled over 12 hours to measure amino acid kinetics, whole-body protein synthesis and oxidation, and muscle protein synthesis.
findings: Plasma amino acid availability and tracer incorporation into muscle were higher after 100 g than 25 g over the 12-hour period. Myofibrillar protein synthesis (the primary outcome, based on the plasma leucine precursor) differed between all three doses, and was about 20% higher with 100 g than 25 g in the first 4 hours and about 40% higher from 4 to 12 hours. Whole-body protein synthesis increased with both protein doses, while the rise in amino acid oxidation was negligible in comparison.
limitations: The sample was 12 healthy, recreationally active men per group, tested after a single session, so the findings may not extend to trained athletes, women, older adults or clinical groups. Several responses had not returned to baseline by 12 hours, and tracer recycling means the rates are likely underestimates, so the authors describe their 100 g estimates as minimal. The title's claim of no upper limit rests on testing only three doses within one 12-hour window.
practicalImplications: A single 100 g protein dose gave a greater and longer muscle protein synthesis response than 25 g after resistance exercise in healthy young men, so the 20 to 25 g per meal guidance may not cap the acute response. The study does not show that such doses are needed, practical or better for athletes, or that meal size changes training gains.
athleteDev: The study measured acute protein synthesis after one session, not strength, muscle mass or performance gains, so it cannot show that larger post-training protein doses improve adaptation. It is best used to inform recovery nutrition discussions about meal protein size, pending evidence from trained athletes.
rtp: Participants were healthy, recreationally active men with no injury, so the study cannot inform nutrition for recovery from injury or return to sport. The authors note that clinically compromised or less active people may respond differently, which would also apply to injured athletes.

citation: Grant WB, Lahore H, Rockwell MS. The Benefits of Vitamin D Supplementation for Athletes: Better Performance and Reduced Risk of COVID-19. Nutrients. 2020;12:3741.
abstract: This narrative review proposes that vitamin D supplementation could improve athletic performance and reduce the risk and severity of COVID-19 in athletes. It summarises observational COVID-19 studies, early vitamin D treatment trials, proposed mechanisms, and studies of vitamin D in athletes. The authors conclude that athletes should consider supplementation as an additional means of reducing COVID-19 risk, alongside official guidelines.
tldr: A narrative review argues that vitamin D could help athletes perform better and lower their COVID-19 risk, but most of the evidence is observational or from very small trials. Treat it as a hypothesis to check with a blood test and medical advice, not as proof that supplements protect athletes.
methods: Narrative review. The text gives no search strategy, selection criteria or quality appraisal. The authors draw on observational COVID-19 studies, two small treatment trials, mechanistic studies, and small studies in athletes and other adults, which are summarised in Tables 1 and 2.
findings: The review cites more than 15 observational studies in which lower 25(OH)D went with greater COVID-19 risk or severity, although three reported no benefit; one Chicago cohort of 489 patients gave a relative risk of 1.77 (95% CI 1.12 to 2.81) for vitamin D deficiency. Two small treatment trials are described: a calcifediol trial (50 treated, 26 controls) with one ICU admission among treated patients and 13 among controls, and a vitamin D3 trial (16 treated, 24 controls) in which 63% and 22% respectively became SARS-CoV-2 RNA negative. In athletes, the review tabulates a 12-week trial of 19 college swimmers given 5000 IU/day, whose 25(OH)D rose from 47 to 61 ng/mL and who did better on deadlift and vertical jump than controls, and a winter supplementation study of 118 NCAA Division I athletes in which the stress fracture rate fell from 7.5% to 1.7%. The review's own table also lists a meta-analysis of 163 healthy athletes given 5000 IU/day that found no significant effect on muscle strength, and the muscle-recovery trials it cites were in recreationally or modestly active adults, not athletes.
limitations: The review states no search or quality appraisal, so its choice of studies cannot be checked. The COVID-19 treatment trials are very small, and most athlete studies are small and short, with several observational. Two of three authors declare funding from Bio-Tech Pharmacal, Inc., and the 40 ng/mL target and 4000 to 10,000 IU/day dose are the authors' own advice, not outcomes tested in these studies. The abstract cites about 30 observational COVID-19 studies while the body text describes more than 15, and the COVID-19 trials were in hospitalised patients rather than athletes.
practicalImplications: Measure 25(OH)D in athletes at higher risk of low status, such as athletes with darker skin, who had lower 25(OH)D in the review's data, and discuss any supplementation with a physician or dietitian. The review's dosing advice rests on the authors' extrapolation, so it should not be applied as a standard protocol, and athletes should keep following official COVID-19 guidance on masks, distancing and testing.
athleteDev: Use 25(OH)D testing to identify athletes with low status. The performance evidence is mixed: one meta-analysis of 163 athletes found no significant strength effect, and the recovery benefits come from small trials in non-athlete adults, so gains for athletes with adequate levels are unclear.
rtp: The review addresses vitamin D, COVID-19 and general athletic performance, and it does not study return to sport after injury or illness. It recommends physician monitoring before athletes return after COVID-19 but gives no return-to-play protocol, so it cannot be used to clear an athlete.

citation: Stout JR, Kreider RB, Candow DG, Forbes SC, Rawson ES, Antonio B, et al. The birth of modern sports nutrition: tracing the path from muscle biopsies to creatine supplementation-A narrative review. Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition. 2025;22(sup1):2463373.
abstract: This narrative review traces sports nutrition research from the 1960s to the early 1990s at the Metabolic Research Laboratory in Stockholm. It covers muscle biopsy techniques, the links between muscle glycogen, diet and exercise, and the 1992 demonstration that oral creatine monohydrate raises muscle creatine. The authors conclude that these laboratory discoveries shaped current performance and clinical applications of sports nutrition.
tldr: A historical review traces how 1960s muscle biopsy work led to the rediscovery of creatine monohydrate in 1992. It explains where sports nutrition ideas came from, but it is not a systematic evidence review and several authors have industry ties.
methods: Narrative review that combines personal accounts, including first-hand perspectives from Roger Harris (the acknowledgments also credit Kent Sahlin for input), with seminal studies from the Metabolic Research Laboratory. The text describes no search strategy, selection criteria or quality appraisal, and the review states that it is not a comprehensive examination of sports nutrition research.
findings: Bergstrom and Hultman's 1966 biopsy study found that muscle glycogen fell in the exercised leg and rose to 50-60% above the rested leg after three days of high-carbohydrate diet. The 1967 study showed that starting glycogen level was closely related to endurance exercise duration. In the 1992 human study of 17 people aged 20-62 years, repeated 5 g creatine monohydrate doses over 4.5 to 21 days raised mean total creatine from 126.8 to 148.6 mmol/kg dry muscle, with the largest rises in people with the lowest starting levels, and no adverse effects were reported.
limitations: The text does not describe a placebo group for the 1992 study, and the review does not report sport performance outcomes from it, although the abstract says creatine significantly improved exercise performance. The review also notes that a 50 g per day trial in horses showed no change in muscle creatine, and that the early 1975 pilot in two swimmers was wrongly judged negative. The authors' disclosure lists industry grants, consulting, sponsored research and advisory roles, and the review was unfunded.
practicalImplications: The review supports the view that oral creatine monohydrate raises muscle creatine, and that high-carbohydrate intake raises muscle glycogen, which are the mechanisms behind two common practices. Because the review is historical and industry-linked, check current trials for the specific sport, dose and athlete group before recommending either practice.
athleteDev: Use the review as background for why carbohydrate loading (glycogen) and creatine loading (muscle creatine) are used. Confirm current evidence for any performance claim before building it into a programme, since the 1992 result reported in the text is a muscle measure, not a sport outcome.
rtp: This review is a historical account of muscle metabolism and supplement research in people and horses. It does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot guide return-to-play decisions or supplement use during rehabilitation.

citation: Jardine WT, Aisbett B, Kelly MK, Burke LM, Ross ML, Condo D, et al. The Effect of Pre-Exercise Hyperhydration on Exercise Performance, Physiological Outcomes and Gastrointestinal Symptoms: A Systematic Review. Sports Med. 2023.
abstract: Pre-exercise hyperhydration with osmotic aids is proposed to offset dehydration and heat stress during prolonged exercise in the heat. The authors searched three databases for English full-text studies comparing hyperhydration with a baseline or placebo condition, and rated study quality with the American Dietetic Association checklist. Thirty-eight studies were included. Hyperhydration may improve capacity during constant work rate exercise, which the authors attribute to lower heart rate and core temperature alongside higher plasma volume, and gastrointestinal symptoms varied across studies.
tldr: Pre-exercise hyperhydration may help capacity in constant-pace exercise in the heat, possibly by lowering heart rate and core temperature. The evidence is mostly from male participants, and gut symptoms vary widely.
methods: Systematic review of Medline Complete, SPORTDiscus and Embase (final search 11 October 2022) for English full-text studies comparing a hyperhydration intervention with baseline or placebo. Exercise studies had to involve at least recreational athletes (training at least three times and 5 h per week). Study quality was assessed with the American Dietetic Association Quality Criteria Checklist, with two authors screening and rating quality.
findings: Of 38 studies (403 participants, 361 male), 22 assessed performance or capacity. Two studies reported time-trial improvements (5.7-11.4%), three reported more work completed (4-5%), and five of seven time-to-exhaustion studies reported higher exercise capacity (14.3-26.2%). Nine studies reported lower mean heart rate during constant work rate exercise, eight reported lower mean core temperature, and ten reported higher plasma volume. Gastrointestinal symptoms were reported in 26 studies.
limitations: Most participants were male, and only one study included females only, with none adequately accounting for menstrual cycle phase. Few studies examined endurance running or field settings, and the capacity gains come from time-to-exhaustion tests, which the authors note are less reliable than time-trials. Gastrointestinal symptoms were not assessed with validated, reliable tools.
practicalImplications: In hot conditions, a hyperhydration protocol may help steady-pace endurance work, with lower heart rate and core temperature reported in several studies, but performance gains are reported in only a few studies. The review notes that splitting the dose into smaller aliquots did not increase gut symptoms, and symptoms may vary with product, dose and ingestion rate.
athleteDev: For endurance performance staff, the review supports testing pre-exercise hyperhydration as a heat strategy for constant-pace efforts, with attention to fluid retention and gut comfort. Expect the clearest effects on heart rate and core temperature rather than guaranteed time-trial gains.
rtp: Not applicable to return to sport. The review covers healthy athletes in performance trials in the heat and does not address injury, rehabilitation or clearance decisions.

citation: Barnard J, Roberts S, Lastella M, Aisbett B, Condo D. The Impact of Dietary Factors on the Sleep of Athletically Trained Populations: A Systematic Review. Nutrients. 2022;14:3271.
abstract: A systematic review of 35 studies that examined dietary factors and sleep or sleepiness in athletically trained people, 21 of them rated positive quality. Evening caffeine above about 2 mg/kg was associated with poorer sleep, while the protein and carbohydrate findings were mixed.
tldr: Late-day caffeine, especially above about 2 mg/kg, was the clearest dietary factor linked to poorer sleep in trained athletes. Carbohydrate and protein timing findings are mixed, and the probiotic and beetroot evidence rests on few small trials.
methods: A PRISMA systematic review (PROSPERO CRD42021264200) of four databases from inception to May 2022, with title and abstract screening by one reviewer, full-text review by two, and quality rating with the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics checklist. Included studies had trained or athletic adults, a dietary factor and a sleep or sleepiness outcome.
findings: Evening caffeine above about 2 mg/kg reduced sleep duration and sleep efficiency and increased sleep latency and wake after sleep onset in several studies. A high-GI meal after evening exercise improved polysomnography sleep in one study of recreationally trained men, but a basketball study showed no effect, and most tryptophan-rich protein trials showed no change. Probiotic and beetroot findings came from few small studies.
limitations: Only 61% of studies were randomized trials, and females made up 26% (82 of 314) of randomized trial participants in the results, which the limitations section rounds to 20%, so causality and generalization are limited. The abstract's claim about tryptophan-rich protein is stronger than the body-text results, where three of four studies found no sleep change.
practicalImplications: Screen athletes who report poor sleep for late-day caffeine and trial earlier or lower-dose intake, since evening caffeine above about 2 mg/kg was consistently linked to worse sleep. A high-GI carbohydrate meal after evening exercise is a reasonable individual test, since one study found better sleep after it.
athleteDev: The most actionable point for performance staff is timing: evening caffeine above about 2 mg/kg before training or competition was linked to shorter, less efficient sleep, so screen and adjust caffeine use around evening sessions.
rtp: This review does not inform return to sport, because it included only healthy, non-injured athletes and studied sleep outcomes, not recovery from injury.

citation: Bowman JK, Krywaruczenko D, De Flon BG, Boone RT. The Relationships Between Reaction Time Scores and False Start Penalties of Offensive Linemen in the National Football League (NFL). Perceptual and Motor Skills. 2024.
abstract: The study examined whether the Athletic Intelligence Quotient (AIQ) reaction time measures relate to false start penalties per game in NFL offensive linemen. Archival data from 85 linemen tested before the draft in 2014 to 2021 were analysed with ANOVA, correlations and hierarchical regression, controlling for draft pick and position. Higher accuracy on the choice reaction time task accounted for a statistically significant share of the variance in false starts per game beyond draft pick and position. The authors discuss the practical value of such cognitive assessments for player development.
tldr: In NFL offensive linemen, lower accuracy on a choice reaction time test was linked to more false start penalties per game, even after accounting for draft position and position played. The link is modest and based on one penalty type, so it is a reason for targeted development work rather than a selection rule.
methods: Archival analysis of 85 NFL offensive linemen (centers excluded) who completed the AIQ before the draft between 2014 and 2021 and played at least 17 games by the end of 2021. The outcome was false starts per game. Predictors were simple reaction time commission errors and choice reaction time d-prime. Analyses were a one-way ANOVA by position, zero-order correlations and hierarchical regression, entering draft pick, position, then the two reaction time measures. Only anonymised archival data were used.
findings: Tackles averaged 0.16 false starts per game, guards 0.10 and players who played both positions 0.12 (F(2,84) = 3.96, p = .02). Simple reaction time commission errors (r = .22) and choice reaction time d-prime (r = .29) were correlated with false starts per game (p < .05). Draft pick round was the first significant predictor (beta = .31). After draft pick and position were entered, the two reaction time measures added about 6% explained variance (delta F(2,76) = 3.00, p = .05). Choice reaction time d-prime was the only unique predictor (beta = .23), and the full model explained 21% of the variance (F(5,76) = 3.91, p = .003).
limitations: Small sample from one test battery, and the power analysis gave 80% power only for large effects, while the observed correlations were small (r = .22 to .29) and the added variance step sat at p = .05. Table 1 uses N = 82 while the text reports 85 linemen, Table 2 omits several coefficients, and Table 1 shows the choice reaction time correlation without a minus sign although the text describes a negative association. Centers were excluded, false starts are a narrow measure of line play, and scheme, coaching and opponent factors were not measured. The lead author is listed as Chief Science Officer of Athletic Intelligence Measures, LLC, although the article declares no conflicts of interest.
practicalImplications: For linemen who score low on choice reaction accuracy, coaches could consider extra practice on counts and cadences and drills with noise or simulated distraction, as the authors suggest. These ideas were not tested in this study, so they should be treated as hypotheses. Staff can track false starts as a simple game indicator alongside the test score.
athleteDev: In this sample, lower choice reaction time accuracy was linked to more false start penalties beyond draft position. It can inform planning of vigilance and count-based work, but the study does not show that such training reduces false starts.
rtp: The study looks at penalties in healthy players during games and does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to play, so it cannot be used for return-to-play decisions.

citation: Donnan KJ, Williams EL, Stanger N. The effect of exercise-induced fatigue and heat exposure on soccer-specific decision-making during high-intensity intermittent exercise. PLoS ONE. 2022;17(12):e0279109.
abstract: Nine well-trained male soccer players completed a 92-minute cycling intermittent sprint protocol at 32 C (hot) and 18 C (temperate), responding to soccer-specific decision-making trials throughout. Physical output, decision-making, appraisal, affect and plasma metanephrines were measured.
tldr: In nine trained soccer players, heat lowered soccer-specific decision-making during a prolonged intermittent sprint protocol. Power output also fell in the second half only in the heat, with a more threatening appraisal and higher stress hormone levels.
methods: Laboratory study with nine well-trained male soccer players, planned as a counterbalanced design for 10 players but stopped early because of the pandemic (five players began in 32 C, four in 18 C). Participants completed a 92-minute cycling intermittent sprint protocol (5-s sprints against 8% body mass with active recovery at 35% of the VO2peak from an incremental test) at 32 C and 50% relative humidity or 18 C and 50% relative humidity. Soccer-specific decision-making was scored against expert panel responses and verbal think-aloud reports were coded. Analysis used two-way repeated-measures ANOVA and content analysis.
findings: Decision-making scores were lower in 32 C than 18 C (86.87 +/- 7.95% vs 92.49 +/- 3.13%, main effect p = 0.030), but there was no condition by time interaction. Peak power fell in the second half of the protocol only in the heat (about 7%), with no significant between-condition difference in either half. Plasma normetanephrine was higher in the heat at half-time (p = 0.012) and post-exercise (p < 0.001), and metanephrine was higher post-exercise (p = 0.006 to 0.009). Players verbalised less future planning in the heat (p = 0.030, d = 0.20), and threat appraisal and unpleasant affect were higher in the heat (p = 0.007 and p = 0.008).
limitations: Only nine players were analysed, and the planned 10 were not reached. Trial order was only partly counterbalanced. A cycling protocol was used, which the authors say may produce less physiological strain than running. The decision-making task was visual only and did not reproduce dual-task demands of match play. Decision-making was lower in the heat at all time points, including pre-exercise in the chamber, so passive heat exposure may explain part of the effect. Laboratory motivation may differ from matches. The think-aloud findings need caution given the number of analyses run. Core temperature averaged about 38.4 C in the heat, with no main condition effect, and the authors say this is lower than typical team-sport values.
practicalImplications: In hot conditions, soccer players may make poorer decisions and lose work output, even when core temperature stays below common cut-offs. Staff planning training or matches in heat should consider decision-making as well as physical output. Players also reported more threat and unpleasant feelings in the heat, and the authors suggest strategies such as acclimatisation or re-appraisal could be considered.
athleteDev: Heat can lower decision-making and second-half work output during intermittent exercise, even when core temperature stays around 38.4 C. Staff should consider cognitive as well as physical demands when preparing players for hot conditions.
rtp: This study cannot be used for return-to-play decisions. It tested healthy trained players in a laboratory cycling protocol and includes no injury or rehabilitation outcomes.

citation: Mei Z, Zhang Y, Fan Q, Luo S, Luo S. The effects of mobile phone dependence on athletic performance and its mechanisms. Frontiers in Psychology. 2024;15:1391258.
abstract: Reviews how mobile phone dependence affects athletes' performance through individual and environmental factors, proposes neurobiological mechanisms centred on the brain reward system, and discusses the social cognitive model of self-regulation and the integrative model of self-control as explanatory frameworks.
tldr: Mobile phone dependence in athletes is linked to disrupted sleep, mental fatigue, poorer decision-making and weaker coach relationships. Coaches could monitor phone use and build self-regulation and self-control skills, but the mechanisms still need testing.
methods: Narrative review of previous studies on individual factors, environmental factors, neurobiological mechanisms and theoretical models of MPD and athletic performance. No search strategy is reported.
findings: Stress and weak self-control may drive heavy phone use, and phone use can impair attention and decision-making. In a volleyball trial, social-media use before training blocked the decision-making improvement seen in controls, and in an eight-week swimming trial, 30 minutes of smartphone use before training increased mental fatigue and internal training load and inhibited 100-m and 400-m performance gains. The review proposes that phone reward cues act on the brain reward system and that microwave radiation may affect dopaminergic circuits, but it cites no athlete studies that test these links.
limitations: No search method is reported. The authors note that causal links between MPD and performance are hard to establish because longitudinal studies are rare, and that the influence pathways and mechanisms need further investigation.
practicalImplications: Coaches could limit phone and social-media use before training, and support athletes in building self-regulation and attention-control skills such as mindfulness. Athletes under stress may need extra attention for signs of problematic phone use.
athleteDev: Phone use before training may reduce focus, decision-making and training gains. The authors suggest athletes avoid social media for at least two hours before sessions, but the review proposes this and does not test it.
rtp: The review does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions.

citation: Caceres-Ayala C, Pautassi RM, Acuña MJ, Cerpa W, Rebolledo DL. The functional and molecular effects of problematic alcohol consumption on skeletal muscle: a focus on athletic performance. Am J Drug Alcohol Abuse. 2022.
abstract: Narrative review of alcohol effects on skeletal muscle in humans, animal models and cell studies, with a focus on sportspeople. Acute and chronic alcohol impair recovery and muscle function through mechanisms that may reduce athletic performance, but binge drinking is understudied.
tldr: Alcohol after hard training can slow muscle recovery and reduce strength and power, especially in men. Most mechanisms come from animal and clinical studies, so staff should treat the performance link as plausible rather than measured in athletes.
methods: Narrative review of PubMed and Google Scholar literature on alcohol and skeletal muscle in humans and animal models, covering acute and chronic exposure, sex differences and molecular mechanisms. The authors summarise human exercise-recovery findings by dose and sex in a single figure.
findings: Acute alcohol after eccentric exercise increased muscle damage and impaired strength recovery in young men at about 1.0 g/kg, but not at 0.5 g/kg or when the exercise was a task participants were trained for; the doses tested in women (0.8 g/kg body mass, 0.88 and 1.09 g/kg lean mass) did not change recovery. Chronic alcohol reduces anabolic signalling and regeneration, and raises inflammation, fibrosis, oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction in animal and clinical studies.
